title: 1.01  What Assembly Is
body: A processor runs machine code - numbers that each mean one small instruction. Assembly gives every instruction a name, and an assembler turns the names back into the numbers. This course writes x86-64 assembly in Intel syntax with NASM, for Linux. A program has sections for data and code, labels that name addresses, and starts at _start. The processor's own language A processor does not understand C or Python. It runs machine code : bytes in memory, each group of them one small instruction such as "add these two registers" or "jump to that address". The bytes 48 01 d8 , for example, tell an x86-64 processor to add rbx to rax . Nobody wants to write bytes by hand, so each instruction has a short name, a mnemonic , and a program called an assembler translates the names into bytes: Assembly Machine code Means --- --- --- mov eax, 1 b8 01 00 00 00 put 1 in the register eax add rax, rbx 48 01 d8 rax = rax + rbx ret c3 return from a function One line of assembly is one instruction. There is no if , no for , no variables with types: only what the hardware does. Every language you have used is turned into these instructions in the end, by a compiler (C, Rust), or by an interpreter that is itself made of them (Python). Which assembly? Every processor family has its own instruction set, so there are many assembly languages: Family Found in --- --- x86-64 (also called x64, AMD64) most PCs, laptops and servers ARM64 (AArch64) phones, tablets, Apple-chip Macs, many servers RISC-V a newer open design, in microcontrollers and growing This course teaches x86-64 , written in Intel syntax ( mov eax, 1 : destination first), with the NASM assembler, for Linux . Lesson 6.05 compares ARM64. The ideas carry over to all of them. !note Why learn assembly? Few programs are written in assembly today, but reading it is a superpower: you see what your C, C++ or Rust really does, how fast it can be, why a crash happened, and how operating systems, debuggers, compilers and security exploits work. It also makes pointers, the stack and memory obvious forever. A whole program Here is a complete program. Press Run : nasm global _start section .data message: db "Hello from assembly!", 10 length equ $ - message section .text _start: mov eax, 1 ; system call 1: write mov edi, 1 ; to file 1: standard output lea rsi, rel message ; the address of the bytes mov edx, length ; how many bytes syscall ; ask Linux to do it mov eax, 60 ; system call 60: exit xor edi, edi ; with exit code 0 syscall Every part is explained in the next lessons, but you can read the shape already: - ; starts a comment , to the end of the line. - section .data holds data; section .text holds the instructions (the "text" of the program). - A name followed by a colon, like message: or _start: , is a label : a name for the address where the next byte goes. - db ("define bytes") puts bytes into the program: the letters of the message, then 10, the new line character. - _start is where the program begins, and global _start makes that name visible to the linker , which builds the final program file and needs to know where it starts. - The instructions are indented by convention; labels are not. No safety net A C program that reaches the end of main returns to the C library, which exits for you. An assembly program has no one to return to. If you leave out the exit system call at the end, the processor keeps running whatever bytes come next in memory, and the program crashes with a segmentation fault. Try it: delete the last three lines and run. How the website runs it The website sends your program to Compiler Explorer, which assembles it with NASM into an object file, links it with ld , and runs it on a 64-bit Linux machine, exactly like these commands: nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o ld hello.o -o hello ./hello elf64 is the format Linux uses for programs: ELF, the Executable and Linkable Format. quiz ? What does an assembler do? + Turns assembly mnemonics into machine code bytes - Runs assembly one line at a time - Turns C into assembly A compiler goes from C to assembly; the assembler goes from assembly to bytes. ? Which syntax does mov eax, 1 use, and what does it do? + Intel syntax: puts 1 into eax (the destination comes first) - AT&T syntax: copies eax into 1 - It is not valid assembly AT&T syntax, used by GNU tools by default, writes movl $1, %eax. ? What is _start? + The label where the program begins - A system call - A C function global _start tells the linker about it. ? What happens if an assembly program has no exit system call at the end? + The processor runs whatever bytes follow, and the program crashes - It exits normally - The assembler adds one There is nothing to return to.

title: Your own message
body: Change the program so it prints exactly these three lines, then exits with code 0: x86-64 assembly runs on the metal. No safety net! Put all three lines in one db (a new line is the number 10), let equ $ - label work out the length, and print them with one write system call.

title: 1.02  Registers
body: Registers are the processor's own tiny, fast storage - sixteen 64-bit general-purpose ones on x86-64, plus rip (the next instruction) and rflags. The low 32, 16 and 8 bits of each have their own names, such as eax, ax and al. Writing a 32-bit register clears the top half of the 64-bit one; writing 8 or 16 bits does not. Storage inside the processor Memory is big but, by the processor's standards, slow: reading it can take a hundred cycles. Registers are a handful of storage slots inside the processor itself, read and written in a fraction of a cycle. Almost every instruction works on registers, so programs constantly move values from memory into registers, work on them, and store the results back. x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers , each 64 bits: Register Traditional use --- --- rax accumulator: results, return values, system call numbers rbx base: a general register that functions keep safe rcx counter: loop counts, shift counts, 4th argument rdx data: the high half in multiply and divide, 3rd argument rsi , rdi source and destination index: the 2nd and 1st arguments rbp base pointer: the stack frame (lesson 5.03) rsp stack pointer : the top of the stack. Leave it alone for now r8 to r15 eight more, added when x86 went 64-bit The "traditional uses" come from the 1970s Intel 8086. Today most instructions work on any register, but some conventions (which registers hold arguments, which ones functions must keep) matter a lot, as module 5 shows. Two special registers cannot be used directly: rip , the instruction pointer, holds the address of the next instruction, and rflags holds the flags that comparisons set (lesson 2.04). Smaller views of the same register Each register has names for its lower parts, a history of how x86 grew from 16 to 32 to 64 bits: 64 bits low 32 low 16 low 8 --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al rbx ebx bx bl rcx ecx cx cl rdx edx dx dl rsi esi si sil rdi edi di dil rbp ebp bp bpl rsp esp sp spl r8 r8d r8w r8b ... r15 r15d r15w r15b eax is not a separate register: it is the bottom 32 bits of rax . (There are also ah , bh , ch , dh for bits 8 to 15 of the first four, a leftover you will rarely need.) demo-asm title: One register, four names init: rax=0x1122334455667788 mov al, 0xAA mov ax, 0xBBBB mov eax, 0xCC mov rax, -1 ret Step through it and watch rax : 1. mov al, 0xAA changes only the lowest byte. 2. mov ax, 0xBBBB changes only the lowest 16 bits. 3. mov eax, 0xCC sets the low 32 bits and clears the upper 32 . 4. mov rax, -1 sets all 64 bits to 1. !tip The 32-bit rule Writing a 32-bit register ( eax , r9d ) always zeroes the top 32 bits of the 64-bit register. Writing an 8- or 16-bit one leaves the rest alone. That is why compilers so often write mov eax, 5 instead of mov rax, 5 : it does the same thing with a shorter instruction. Values have no types A register holds 64 bits, nothing more. Whether those bits are a number, a character, an address or a negative number is up to the instructions you use on them. -1 and 18446744073709551615 are the same 64 bits (all 1s, in two's complement, from the Fundamentals course): add does not care, but comparisons and divisions come in signed and unsigned versions (lesson 3.03). quiz ? How many general-purpose registers does x86-64 have? + 16 - 8 - 64 rax to rsp, and r8 to r15. ? What is eax? + The low 32 bits of rax - A separate 32-bit register - An older name for rax that no longer works Changing eax changes rax. ? rax holds 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF. After mov eax, 1, what is rax? + 1 - 0xFFFFFFFF00000001 - 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF Writing a 32-bit register clears the upper half. ? Which register holds the address of the next instruction? + rip - rsp - rax rsp is the stack pointer.

title: Parts of a register
body: These tasks are checked by calling functions you write. A function here is a label, some instructions, and ret at the end. Its first argument arrives in rdi , the second in rsi , and it leaves its result in rax . (Module 5 explains why.) For example: nasm-norun same: ; same(x) gives back x mov rax, rdi ret Write these four, using only mov (and xor to clear a register), and the register names from the lesson: Function Result in rax --- --- keep32(x) the low 32 bits of x, the rest 0 keep16(x) the low 16 bits of x, the rest 0 keep8(x) the low 8 bits of x, the rest 0 with_low_byte(x, y) x, but with its lowest byte replaced by the lowest byte of y For example keep16(0x1122334455667788) is 0x7788 , and with_low_byte(0x1234, 0xAB) is 0x12AB .

title: 1.03  mov and Exit Codes
body: mov copies a value into a register - a constant, another register, or (later) memory. Both sides must be the same size. A program's exit code is the number it hands to the exit system call, and it is the simplest way to see a result. xor of a register with itself is the usual way to set it to 0. mov copies mov destination, source copies the source into the destination. The source is unchanged. nasm-norun mov eax, 42 ; a constant (an "immediate") into a register mov ebx, eax ; one register into another mov rcx, -7 ; negative numbers are fine mov edx, 0x2A ; hex: also 42 mov esi, 0b101010 ; binary: also 42 mov edi, 'A' ; a character: its code, 65 Rules: - The destination comes first: think eax = 42 . - Both sides must be the same size: mov eax, rbx is an error ("invalid combination of opcode and operands"). Use mov eax, ebx or mov rax, rbx . - A constant cannot be the destination ( mov 5, eax makes no sense). The exit code: your first result When a program ends, it hands a number to the operating system: its exit code . 0 means success; anything else usually means something went wrong. Exit is system call 60, and the code goes in rdi : nasm global _start section .text _start: mov ebx, 20 mov ecx, 22 mov edi, ebx ; the exit code will be 20... add edi, ecx ; ...plus 22 mov eax, 60 ; system call 60: exit syscall Run it: the website shows exit code 42 . Before you can print text, the exit code is a handy way to see a number. On Linux you would see it with echo $? after the program ends. Exit codes are a single byte: 0 to 255. Exit with 300 and you get 44 (300 − 256), the lowest 8 bits. Setting a register to zero You will see this everywhere: nasm-norun xor eax, eax ; eax = eax XOR eax, which is always 0 It means the same as mov eax, 0 , but the instruction is 2 bytes instead of 5, and processors recognise it and do it for free. Compilers always use it, and so does this course. Swapping and order Instructions run strictly in order, one after another. To swap two registers you need a third, or the special xchg instruction: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov eax, 3 mov ebx, 9 mov ecx, eax ; ecx = 3 mov eax, ebx ; eax = 9 mov ebx, ecx ; ebx = 3 xchg eax, ebx ; and swap them back with one instruction mov edi, eax ; exit code: 3 mov eax, 60 syscall quiz ? What does mov ecx, eax do? + Copies eax into ecx - Copies ecx into eax - Swaps them The destination comes first. ? Why is mov eax, rbx an error? + The two sides are different sizes - rbx cannot be read - mov only takes constants Use mov rax, rbx or mov eax, ebx. ? Which register holds the exit code for system call 60? + rdi - rax - rsi rax holds the system call number. ? What does xor eax, eax do? + Sets eax to 0 - Flips the bits of eax - Nothing Anything XOR itself is 0.

title: 1.04  System Calls write and exit
body: A program cannot touch the screen, files or the keyboard itself - it asks the operating system with the syscall instruction. On Linux the call's number goes in rax and its arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9, and the result comes back in rax. write (1) prints bytes, read (0) reads them, exit (60) ends the program. Asking the operating system Programs run in user mode , where the processor refuses to touch hardware directly. Printing, reading the keyboard, opening files, and even ending the program are done by the operating system's kernel , and a program asks for them with a system call . The syscall instruction switches the processor into the kernel, which does the work and comes back. On 64-bit Linux: Register Holds --- --- rax the system call's number; afterwards, its result rdi , rsi , rdx , r10 , r8 , r9 its arguments, in that order syscall itself changes rcx and r11 (it uses them to remember where to come back to), so don't keep anything there across a system call. The three you need Number Name Arguments Returns --- --- --- --- 0 read file, buffer address, maximum bytes bytes read (0 at the end) 1 write file, bytes' address, how many bytes written 60 exit exit code does not return Files are numbered: 0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. These are the same streams as stdin , stdout and stderr in C, whose printf ends up making exactly this write call. Printing nasm global _start section .data greeting: db "Hello, ", 0 name: db "Ada", 10 name_length equ $ - name section .text _start: mov eax, 1 ; write mov edi, 1 ; standard output lea rsi, rel greeting mov edx, 7 ; "Hello, " is 7 bytes syscall mov eax, 1 ; write again (rax now holds the last result, so set it again) mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel name mov edx, name_length syscall mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall - lea rsi, rel greeting puts the address of the label into rsi (lesson 4.01 explains lea and rel ). write needs to know where the bytes are, not what they are. - write prints exactly the number of bytes you ask for. Ask for 3 and you get Hel ; ask for too many and you print whatever follows in memory. - A system call puts its result in rax , so set eax again before the next call. Errors When a system call fails, it returns a negative number: minus an error code. write to file 9, which is not open, returns −9 ( -EBADF , "bad file descriptor"). C's library turns those into errno (from the C course). Here you can see it as an exit code: nasm global _start section .data text: db "lost", 10 section .text _start: mov eax, 1 mov edi, 9 ; a file that is not open lea rsi, rel text mov edx, 5 syscall ; rax = -9 neg rax ; make it positive mov rdi, rax ; exit code 9 mov eax, 60 syscall Standard error Write to file 2 instead of 1 and the text goes to standard error. On the website it still appears in the console, but it is a separate stream: running ./program out.txt in a terminal saves only standard output. !note Hundreds of system calls Linux has over 350 system calls: open (2), close (3), mmap (9) for memory, fork (57) and execve (59) for new programs, and more. Every program, in any language, does its work through them. The command strace ./program lists each one a program makes. quiz ? Where does the system call number go? + rax - rdi - rcx The arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9. ? write(1, address, 5) prints... + 5 bytes from the address, to standard output - The number 5 - The first line at the address write knows nothing about lines or terminators. ? What does a failing system call return in rax? + A negative error code - 0 - It crashes the program For example -9 for a bad file number. ? Which registers does syscall itself overwrite? + rcx and r11 - rax only - None Plus rax, which gets the result.

title: Three writes
body: Print this with three separate write system calls, one per line, each with its own label and its own length worked out by equ $ - label : Name: Grace Hopper Born: 1906 Known for: the first compiler Then exit with code 0. Remember that rax holds the result of each system call, so set it to 1 again before the next write .

title: 1.05  Data db, dw, dd, dq and equ
match: 1.05 Data db, dw, dd, dq and equ
body: db, dw, dd and dq put 1, 2, 4 and 8-byte values into the program, stored little-endian. A label is just the address of the next byte, $ is the current address, and equ names a constant such as a length. times repeats, .bss reserves zeroed space with resb and resq, and .rodata holds data that must not change. Defining bytes Directive Size Example --- --- --- db 1 byte db 65, "text", 10, 0 dw 2 bytes (a "word") dw 1000 dd 4 bytes (a "double word") dd 100000, -1 dq 8 bytes (a "quad word") dq 0x1122334455667788 These are not instructions: they tell the assembler to place bytes in the program file. In db , a string in quotes stands for its characters' codes, one byte each; there is no terminator unless you add 0 yourself. The names come from the 16-bit 8086, where a "word" was 16 bits; that is why a 32-bit value is a "double word". Instructions use the same names: byte , word , dword , qword . Little-endian x86 stores multi-byte values lowest byte first . dd 0x11223344 becomes the bytes 44 33 22 11 . The Fundamentals course has a demo of it. demo-bytes value: 287454020 order: little Labels are addresses A label means "the address where the next byte goes". It is not a variable and has no type or size: count: dd 5 only names the first of the four bytes. The instruction that uses it decides how many bytes to read. $ and equ $ is the address of the current position. $ - message , written right after the message, is "here minus where the message started": its length, worked out by the assembler. equ gives a name to a number. It takes no space in the program; it is like define in C: nasm global _start section .data banner: db " Xenon ", 10 banner_len equ $ - banner STDOUT equ 1 SYS_WRITE equ 1 SYS_EXIT equ 60 section .text _start: mov eax, SYS_WRITE mov edi, STDOUT lea rsi, rel banner mov edx, banner_len syscall mov eax, SYS_EXIT mov edi, banner_len ; exit code: the length, 14 syscall times times count thing repeats something: nasm global _start section .data line: times 20 db "=" db 10 line_len equ $ - line section .text _start: mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel line mov edx, line_len syscall mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The sections Section Holds Can change --- --- --- .text instructions no .data data with starting values yes .rodata read-only data: constant text and tables no (writing crashes) .bss space reserved and set to zero when the program starts yes .bss takes no room in the program file, only a note of how much to reserve. Reserve with resb (bytes), resw , resd , resq : nasm-norun section .bss buffer: resb 256 ; 256 bytes, all 0 counts: resq 10 ; ten 8-byte numbers, all 0 The operating system loads each section into memory with the right permissions: .text can run but not be written, .data can be written but not run. A program that writes to its own code crashes, which is a protection against attacks. quiz ? How many bytes does dd 7 take? + 4 - 1 - 8 d for double word: 4 bytes. ? db "Hi" - is there a zero byte at the end? + No, only the two letters - Yes, always - Only in .data Add , 0 yourself for a zero-terminated string. ? msg: db "hello" then len equ $ - msg. What is len? + 5 - The address of msg - 6 $ is the address after the five bytes. ? What is special about .bss? + It reserves zeroed space without storing it in the program file - It cannot be written - It holds instructions resb and friends reserve it.

title: 1.06  Xenon's Print and Read Routines
body: Turning a number into printed digits takes a loop and a division, which come later in the course. Until then, Xenon adds ready-made routines to any program that calls them - print_str, print_int, print_hex, print_bin, print_newline, read_int, read_char and read_line. Put the argument in rdi (and rsi), call, and expect rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi and r8 to r11 to change. Why routines? write prints bytes . To print the number 42 you need the bytes '4' and '2' , which means dividing by 10 and turning remainders into characters: a loop (module 3) with division (module 2). Lesson 2.05 builds it. Until then, the website gives you a small library. When your program calls one of these names and does not define it itself, the website adds the routine's code to the end of your program before assembling it. That is all: no magic in the processor. You can read their source in the Cheat Sheet - Routines reference page. The routines Routine Give it Does --- --- --- print_str rdi = address of a zero-terminated string prints it print_char dil (low byte of rdi ) = a character prints one character print_newline nothing prints a new line print_int rdi = a signed number prints it in decimal: -42 print_uint rdi = an unsigned number prints it in decimal print_hex rdi = a number prints 0x2a print_bin rdi = a number, rsi = how many bits prints 00101010 read_int nothing reads a whole number: rax = the number, rdx = 1, or 0 in both at the end of the input read_char nothing rax = the next character, or −1 at the end read_line rdi = a buffer, rsi = its size reads a line without its new line; rax = its length, or −1 at the end call call name jumps to a routine, which runs and then comes back to the instruction after the call (lesson 5.01 shows how). Arguments go in rdi , then rsi : the same registers C uses on Linux, so these routines are exactly like calling C functions. nasm global _start section .data label: db "The answer is ", 0 ; print_str needs the 0 at the end section .text _start: lea rdi, rel label call print_str mov edi, 42 call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, -1 call print_int ; -1 call print_newline mov rdi, -1 call print_uint ; the same bits, unsigned: 18446744073709551615 call print_newline mov edi, 255 call print_hex ; 0xff call print_newline mov edi, 5 mov esi, 8 call print_bin ; 00000101 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Registers that change A routine is allowed to use some registers for its own work, so after any call : May have changed Are kept as they were --- --- rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 , r9 , r10 , r11 rbx , rbp , rsp , r12 , r13 , r14 , r15 So keep values you still need in rbx or r12 to r15 while calling routines. This rule is the calling convention that every function on Linux follows (lesson 5.02). Reading numbers nasm global _start section .data ask: db "Two numbers: ", 0 said: db "Their sum is ", 0 section .text _start: lea rdi, rel ask call print_str call read_int ; rax = the first number mov rbx, rax ; keep it safe in rbx call read_int ; rax = the second add rbx, rax lea rdi, rel said call print_str mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall On the website an assembly program gets all of its input when it starts. When you run one that reads, the console asks for the input first: type each line, then press Enter on an empty line (or Ctrl+D) to start the program. In checked tasks the test's input is used. !warning Don't mix with your own read calls read_int , read_char and read_line read the input in big pieces and keep what they have not used yet. A program that also makes its own read system calls would miss those bytes. Use one or the other. quiz ? Which register holds the number for print_int? + rdi - rax - rsi The first argument always goes in rdi. ? After call read_int, where is the number? + rax, with rdx = 1 (or 0 in both at the end of the input) - rdi - On the stack Results come back in rax. ? You need a value to survive a call to print_int. Where should you keep it? + In rbx or r12 to r15 - In rcx - In rdi Routines keep rbx, rbp and r12 to r15 as they were. ? Does print_str need a zero byte at the end of the text? + Yes, it prints up to the 0 - No, it knows the length - Only for long strings Unlike write, which takes a length.

title: Sum and difference
body: Read two whole numbers with read_int , then print their sum and difference with the print routines, like this for the input 30 12 : 30 + 12 = 42 30 - 12 = 18 sum in hex: 0x2a Keep the numbers in registers the routines leave alone ( rbx , r12 to r15 ). sub rax, rsi subtracts rsi from rax. For the text pieces, define zero-terminated strings such as plus: db " + ", 0 and print them with print_str .

title: A number card
body: Read three whole numbers a, b and c, and print a card about them. For the input 7 -3 10 : +------------------------+ Xenon number card +------------------------+ a = 7 b = -3 c = 10 a + b + c = 14 a - b - c = 0 in hex: 0xe in binary: 00001110 the last one again: 10 - The three lines of the frame are one block of data, printed with a single write system call, with the dashes made by times . - in hex: and in binary: show the sum a + b + c; the binary has 8 bits ( print_bin with rsi = 8). - the last one again: is c, printed through a value you kept safe across all the calls before it. - The program ends with the exit system call and code 0.

title: 2.01  add, sub, inc, dec and neg
match: 2.01 add, sub, inc, dec and neg
body: add and sub combine two operands into the first, inc and dec add or take away one, and neg flips the sign. Results wrap around at the register's size, so 32-bit arithmetic wraps at 2 to the 32 and also clears the upper half. The same add instruction serves signed and unsigned numbers, because two's complement makes them the same bits. Two operands, one result x86 arithmetic overwrites its first operand: Instruction Does --- --- add rax, rbx rax = rax + rbx sub rax, 5 rax = rax − 5 inc rcx rcx = rcx + 1 dec rcx rcx = rcx − 1 neg rax rax = −rax There is no "c = a + b" in one instruction (except with lea , lesson 4.01): copy first, then add. nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rbx, 1000 mov rax, rbx add rax, 337 ; rax = 1337 sub rax, 1300 ; rax = 37 inc rax ; 38 dec rbx ; rbx = 999 neg rbx ; -999 add rax, rbx ; 38 - 999 = -961 mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Wrapping around A register has a fixed number of bits, so results wrap around like a car's odometer. With 8 bits, 255 + 1 is 0; with 64 bits, the biggest unsigned number plus one is 0 too. demo-asm title: Wrapping at 8, 32 and 64 bits init: rax=0 mov al, 255 add al, 1 mov eax, 0xFFFFFFFF add eax, 1 mov rax, -1 add rax, 1 ret Watch the CF (carry) flag in the demo: it is set each time a result wrapped past the top. Lesson 2.04 is about the flags. !tip 32-bit arithmetic clears the top too Like mov , any instruction writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper half. add eax, 1 with rax = 0x1_FFFFFFFF gives rax = 0 , not 0x2_00000000 . Use 64-bit registers when numbers can grow beyond about 4 billion. One add for signed and unsigned In two's complement (from the Fundamentals course), −1 is all 1 bits. Adding 1 to it gives all 0 bits: 0, which is right whether you read the bits as signed (−1 + 1) or unsigned (the largest value + 1, wrapping). That is the beauty of two's complement: the same add and sub work for both . Only comparisons, division and widening need to know which you mean. Instructions with memory Arithmetic can read or update memory directly (lesson 4.01 shows addressing): nasm-norun add rax, rel total ; rax += the 8 bytes at total add qword rel total , 5 ; the 8 bytes at total += 5 inc dword rel count ; the 4 bytes at count += 1 When neither operand is a register, NASM cannot tell the size, so you write it: byte , word , dword or qword . Only one operand may be in memory: add a , b does not exist. quiz ? What does sub rax, rbx do? + rax = rax - rbx - rbx = rbx - rax - rax = rbx - rax The first operand is the destination. ? al is 250. After add al, 10, what is al? + 4 - 260 - 255 260 wraps around at 256. ? Why can the same add instruction handle signed and unsigned numbers? + In two's complement both give the same bits - add checks the sign first - It cannot: there is a separate signed add Comparisons and division are where the difference matters. ? What is wrong with inc rel count ? + The size is unknown: write inc dword rel count (or another size) - inc cannot use memory - Nothing With no register in the instruction, NASM needs the size.

title: Adding and subtracting
where: 2.01 add, sub, inc, dec and neg
body: Write these functions (arguments in rdi , rsi , rdx ; result in rax ): Function Result --- --- add_sub(a, b, c) a + b − c negate(x) −x plus_two(x) x + 2, with two inc distance(a, b) b − a (it may be negative) add32(a, b) a + b done in 32-bit registers, so it wraps at 2³²: add32(0xFFFFFFFF, 1) is 0

title: 2.02  Multiplying and Dividing
body: imul multiplies with two or three operands and keeps the low bits of the answer. div and idiv divide the 128-bit number in rdx:rax by an operand, leaving the quotient in rax and the remainder in rdx - so rdx must be prepared first, with xor for unsigned and cqo for signed. Dividing by zero stops the program. imul Form Does --- --- imul rax, rbx rax = rax × rbx imul rax, rbx, 10 rax = rbx × 10 imul rcx, rel price rcx = rcx × the 8 bytes at price The answer of a 64 × 64-bit multiplication can need 128 bits; these forms keep the low 64 and drop the rest. For signed and unsigned numbers the low bits are the same, so imul serves both. nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rax, 12 imul rax, rax ; 144 imul rbx, rax, 3 ; rbx = 432 mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The old one-operand forms, mul rbx (unsigned) and imul rbx (signed), multiply rax by the operand and put the full 128-bit answer in rdx:rax : the high 64 bits in rdx , the low 64 in rax . You need them when the high half matters. Division: rdx:rax Division is the awkward one. div rbx divides the 128-bit number made of rdx (high half) and rax (low half) by rbx : - the quotient goes in rax , - the remainder in rdx . So before dividing, rdx must hold the right high half: Numbers Before Divide --- --- --- unsigned xor edx, edx (high half 0) div rbx signed cqo (copies rax's sign bit into all of rdx) idiv rbx nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rax, 17 xor edx, edx ; unsigned: rdx:rax = 17 mov ecx, 5 div rcx ; rax = 3, rdx = 2 mov rbx, rdx ; keep the remainder mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov rax, -17 cqo ; signed: rdx = all 1s, because -17 is negative mov ecx, 5 idiv rcx ; rax = -3, rdx = -2 (rounds towards zero, like C) mov rbx, rdx mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall !danger Forgetting rdx If rdx still holds something from earlier, div divides a huge 128-bit number, and when the quotient does not fit in 64 bits the processor raises a divide error : the program stops with exit code 136, "Floating point exception" (an old name: it is an integer problem). Always set rdx right before div , and remember that div also overwrites rdx . Dividing by zero does the same. The divisor cannot be a constant ( div 10 does not exist): put it in a register first. Dividing by constants without div div is slow (around 20 to 40 cycles, against 3 for imul ), so compilers avoid it: - Dividing an unsigned number by a power of two is a right shift: shr rax, 3 divides by 8 (lesson 2.03). - Dividing by other constants becomes a multiplication by a "magic" reciprocal, then a shift. You will see code like imul rax, rax, 1431655766 in compiler output and now know why (lesson 6.01). quiz ? Where does div put the quotient and remainder? + Quotient in rax, remainder in rdx - Quotient in rdx, remainder in rax - Both in rax It divides rdx:rax by the operand. ? What must you do before idiv rcx? + cqo, to fill rdx with the sign of rax - xor edx, edx - Nothing xor edx, edx is for unsigned div. ? What does imul rax, rbx, 10 do? + rax = rbx 10 - rax = rax rbx 10 - rbx = rax 10 The three-operand form. ? A program stops with exit code 136 at a div. What are the likely causes? + Dividing by zero, or a quotient too big because rdx was not prepared - A missing exit system call - Too many registers in use The processor raises a divide error.

title: Multiplying and dividing
body: Write these functions: Function Result --- --- square(x) x × x mul_add(a, b, c) a × b + c quotient(a, b) a ÷ b for signed numbers, rounded towards zero like C: quotient(-7, 2) is −3 remainder(a, b) the signed remainder: remainder(-7, 2) is −1 minutes(seconds) the whole minutes in an unsigned number of seconds: minutes(125) is 2 last_digit(n) the last decimal digit of an unsigned n The tests never divide by zero. Remember: div and idiv need rdx prepared, take their divisor in a register, and overwrite rdx . Note that the second argument arrives in rsi while rdx is about to be used for the division.

title: 2.03  Bit Instructions and Shifts
body: and, or, xor and not work on every bit at once and make masks for testing, setting and clearing bits. shl and shr shift bits left and right - multiplying and dividing unsigned numbers by powers of two - while sar keeps the sign for signed numbers. rol and ror rotate, a variable shift count goes in cl, and lea multiplies by 3, 5 and 9 in one step. and, or, xor, not Instruction Each result bit is 1 when Typical use --- --- --- and rax, rbx both bits are 1 keep some bits, clear the rest: and eax, 0xFF or rax, rbx either bit is 1 set bits: or eax, 0x20 xor rax, rbx the bits differ flip bits; xor eax, eax is 0 not rax the bit was 0 flip every bit test rax, rbx is an and that only sets the flags and throws the result away: the usual way to ask "is this bit set?" or "is this register zero?" ( test rax, rax ). nasm global _start section .text _start: mov ebx, 'a' ; 0110 0001 and ebx, 0xDF ; clear bit 5: 'A' (0100 0001) mov edi, ebx call print_char or ebx, 0x20 ; set bit 5 again: 'a' mov edi, ebx ; (print_char may change edi, so copy again) call print_char call print_newline mov edi, 0xF0 not edi ; ...FFFFFF0F and edi, 0xFF ; keep the low byte: 0x0F call print_hex call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The Fundamentals course shows why one bit separates upper and lower case in ASCII. Shifts Instruction Does Same as --- --- --- shl rax, n bits move left n places, 0s come in × 2ⁿ shr rax, n bits move right, 0s come in unsigned ÷ 2ⁿ sar rax, n bits move right, copies of the sign bit come in signed ÷ 2ⁿ (rounding down) rol rax, n / ror rax, n rotate: bits leaving one end come back at the other The count is a constant, or the register cl for a count worked out at run time ( shl rax, cl ). Only 6 bits of the count are used, so shifting a 64-bit register by 64 shifts by 0. demo-asm title: shr and sar on a negative number init: rax=-16 mov rbx, rax shr rax, 2 sar rbx, 2 ret shr treats −16 as a huge unsigned number; sar keeps it negative and gives −4. Masks with shifts Combine a shift and and to pull a field out of a number, like the C course's bit lessons: nasm-norun mov eax, edi shr eax, 8 ; move bits 8..15 to the bottom and eax, 0xFF ; keep just them and build a one-bit mask from a run-time position: nasm-norun mov ecx, esi ; the bit number, which must be in cl mov eax, 1 shl rax, cl ; rax = 1 << n or rdi, rax ; set bit n of rdi x86 also has single instructions for one bit: bt (test), bts (set), btr (clear), btc (flip). Multiplying with lea and shifts lea computes an address expression without touching memory, and the expression can be base + index × 1, 2, 4 or 8 . That makes it a quick multiplier: nasm-norun lea rax, rdi + rdi 2 ; rax = rdi 3 lea rax, rdi + rdi 4 ; rax = rdi 5 lea rax, rdi 8 + rdi ; rax = rdi 9 lea rax, rax + rax 4 add rax, rax ; with the line above: 10 Compilers turn x 10 into exactly that pair. quiz ? What does and eax, 0xFF do? + Keeps the low 8 bits of eax and clears the rest - Sets the low 8 bits to 1 - Adds 255 and with a mask keeps only the mask's bits. ? Which shift divides a negative number by 4 correctly? + sar rax, 2 - shr rax, 2 - shl rax, 2 sar copies the sign bit in. ? Where does a variable shift count go? + cl - rdx - Any register shl rax, cl. ? What does lea rax, rdi + rdi 4 compute? + rdi 5 - The value in memory at rdi 5 - rdi + 4 lea computes the address but never reads memory.

title: Bits and shifts
body: Write these functions, without imul , mul or div : Function Result --- --- is_odd(x) 1 if x is odd, else 0 ( and with 1) set_bit(x, n) x with bit n set; n from 0 to 63 (the count must be in cl ) times10(x) x × 10, with lea and/or shifts div8(x) a signed x ÷ 8 rounded down , with one shift: div8(-9) is −2 byte_of(x, k) byte k of x, k from 0 to 7: byte_of(0x1122334455667788, 1) is 0x77 swap_nibbles(x) the low byte of x with its two hex digits swapped: swap_nibbles(0xAB) is 0xBA

title: 2.04  The Flags
body: Arithmetic and logic instructions record facts about their result in rflags - ZF when it is zero, SF when it is negative, CF when an unsigned result wrapped, OF when a signed result overflowed. cmp and test set flags without keeping a result. adc and sbb use the carry to work on numbers bigger than a register. Notes about the last result Most arithmetic and logic instructions leave notes about their result in the rflags register. Four of the single-bit flags matter most: Flag Name Set when the result... --- --- --- ZF zero is 0 SF sign has its top bit set: negative, read as signed CF carry wrapped past the top or below 0, read as unsigned OF overflow is wrong, read as signed : two positives gave a negative, or two negatives a positive mov , lea , push and pop do not change the flags; add , sub , and , or , xor , neg , cmp , test and shifts do. ( inc and dec change all but CF.) demo-asm title: Watch the flags init: rax=0 mov eax, 5 sub eax, 5 sub eax, 1 mov eax, 0x7FFFFFFF add eax, 1 mov eax, 0xFFFFFFFF add eax, 1 ret Step through and read the flags after each line: 1. 5 - 5 is 0: ZF . 2. 0 - 1 is −1 (all 1s): SF , and CF , because as unsigned numbers 0 − 1 went below zero. 3. 0x7FFFFFFF + 1 : the biggest signed 32-bit number plus one becomes the most negative one: OF and SF. As unsigned it is fine (2,147,483,648), so no CF. 4. 0xFFFFFFFF + 1 wraps to 0: CF and ZF. As signed it is −1 + 1 = 0, perfectly fine, so no OF. The processor doesn't know whether you meant signed or unsigned, so it records both: CF for unsigned, OF for signed. cmp and test The next module's jumps read the flags. To set them without changing anything: - cmp a, b subtracts b from a, sets the flags, and throws the answer away. After cmp rax, rbx , ZF means they were equal, and CF means rax < rbx as unsigned numbers. - test a, b does an and , sets the flags and throws the answer away. test rax, rax sets ZF if rax is 0 and SF if it is negative. Bigger than 64 bits: adc and sbb The carry flag is the "carry the one" of long addition. adc (add with carry) adds the operand and CF, so you can add numbers of any size, 64 bits at a time: nasm-norun ; a 128-bit number in rdx:rax plus another in rcx:rbx add rax, rbx ; the low halves; CF = the carry out adc rdx, rcx ; the high halves, plus that carry sbb (subtract with borrow) does the same for subtraction. A neat trick: after cmp a, b , sbb eax, eax gives −1 if a < b as unsigned numbers and 0 otherwise, without any jump. Keeping a flag as a number adc with zero turns the carry into a number: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rax, -1 ; the largest unsigned 64-bit number xor ebx, ebx add rax, 1 ; wraps: CF = 1 adc rbx, 0 ; rbx = 0 + 0 + CF = 1 mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Lesson 3.05 shows setc , setz and friends, which do this for any flag. quiz ? Which flag says an unsigned result wrapped around? + CF, carry - OF, overflow - ZF, zero OF is the signed version. ? 0x7FFFFFFF + 1 in a 32-bit register sets which flag that 0xFFFFFFFF + 1 does not? + OF - CF - ZF As signed numbers, the first overflowed and the second did not. ? What does cmp rax, rbx change? + Only the flags - rax - rbx It subtracts and throws the result away. ? What is adc for? + Adding with the carry from the previous addition, for numbers bigger than a register - Adding two characters - Adding to the address Long addition, 64 bits at a time.

title: Carries and borrows
body: Use the carry flag, through adc and sbb , with no jumps : Function Result --- --- carry_out(a, b) 1 if the unsigned 64-bit sum a + b wraps around, else 0 add128_high(a_low, a_high, b_low, b_high) the high 64 bits of the 128-bit sum (a_high:a_low) + (b_high:b_low) below(a, b) 1 if a < b as unsigned numbers, else 0 sum_with_carry(a, b) a + b, plus 1 more if a + b wrapped: sum_with_carry(-1, 1) is 1 The four arguments of add128_high arrive in rdi , rsi , rdx and rcx .

title: 2.05  Printing Digits Yourself
body: To print a number, split it into decimal digits with div - by 100 for the hundreds, by 10 for the tens, the remainder for the units - and turn each digit into a character by adding '0'. Store the characters in a buffer and write them. print_int does the same with a loop, building the digits from the right. Digits are remainders The number 427 is 4 hundreds, 2 tens and 7 units. Division pulls them apart: quotient remainder --- --- --- 427 ÷ 100 4 27 27 ÷ 10 2 7 Each digit 0 to 9 becomes its character by adding '0' (48): the characters '0' to '9' have the codes 48 to 57, in order. So 4 becomes '4' (52). A three-digit printer nasm global _start section .bss digits: resb 4 ; three digits and a new line section .text _start: mov eax, 427 ; the number, 0 to 999 xor edx, edx mov ecx, 100 div ecx ; eax = hundreds, edx = the rest add al, '0' mov rel digits , al mov eax, edx ; the rest, 0 to 99 xor edx, edx mov ecx, 10 div ecx ; eax = tens, edx = units add al, '0' mov rel digits + 1 , al add dl, '0' mov rel digits + 2 , dl mov byte rel digits + 3 , 10 mov eax, 1 ; write the 4 bytes mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel digits mov edx, 4 syscall mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall - div ecx is the 32-bit form: it divides edx:eax by ecx . That is enough for small numbers and faster than the 64-bit form. - mov rel digits + 1 , al stores one byte at the address digits + 1 . Lesson 4.01 covers addresses. - This version always prints three digits: 7 comes out as 007 . Any number of digits A number can have up to 20 decimal digits (2⁶⁴ is about 1.8 × 10¹⁹). Instead of a fixed set of divisions, print_uint repeats one step: divide by 10, and the remainder is the last digit. Then the quotient's last digit is the one before, and so on, until the quotient is 0. Because the digits come out from right to left, it fills its buffer backwards: nasm-norun print_uint: sub rsp, 40 ; room on the stack for the digits (lesson 4.04) lea rsi, rsp + 32 ; start at the right-hand end mov rax, rdi mov ecx, 10 .digit: xor edx, edx div rcx ; rax = rax / 10, rdx = the last digit add dl, '0' dec rsi ; move one place left mov rsi , dl ; store the character test rax, rax jnz .digit ; more digits while the quotient is not 0 ... ; then write from rsi to the end jnz means "jump if not zero", back to .digit : a loop. That is the subject of module 3. After it, you will write your own version, and lesson 6.02 handles signed numbers and reading digits back in. Printing in other bases The same method works for any base: divide by 2 for binary, by 16 for hexadecimal (where digits 10 to 15 become 'a' to 'f' ). Since 2 and 16 are powers of two, shifts and masks replace the divisions: the last hex digit is n & 15 , and n 4 drops it. That is how print_hex works. quiz ? What is the character for the digit 7? + 7 + '0', which is 55 - 7 - '0' - 7 The digit characters are in order from 48. ? 427 divided by 10 leaves remainder 7. What does that give? + The last digit - The first digit - The number of digits Division by 10 peels digits off the right. ? Why does print_uint fill its buffer from the end? + Division by 10 produces the digits from right to left - Because the stack grows down - To print the number backwards The last digit comes out first. ? Before div ecx, why xor edx, edx? + div ecx divides edx:eax, so edx must be 0 for a 32-bit number - To clear the flags - To make the remainder 0 The 32-bit form uses edx as the high half.

title: A digital clock
body: Read a number of seconds from 0 to 86399 (one day) with read_int , and print it as a 24-hour clock time with two digits for each part, followed by a new line: Input Output --- --- 3725 01:02:05 0 00:00:00 86399 23:59:59 Do not use print_int or print_uint : work out each digit with div , add '0' , store the eight characters and the new line into a buffer in .bss , and print them with one write system call. Hours are seconds ÷ 3600; what is left, ÷ 60, gives the minutes; the remainder is the seconds. Each two-digit part is (part ÷ 10) and (part remainder 10).

title: 3.01  Compare and Jump
body: jmp always jumps to a label. A conditional jump such as je, jne, jl or jg jumps only when the flags say so, which usually means right after cmp or test. An if statement becomes a compare, a jump over the code that should not run, and a label. Labels starting with a dot are local to the label above them. jmp jmp label makes the processor continue at the label instead of the next line: it just puts a new address in rip . nasm-norun jmp done ; skip everything up to done mov eax, 99 ; never runs done: Conditional jumps A conditional jump looks at the flags and jumps only if its condition holds; otherwise it carries on with the next line. After cmp a, b : Jump Jumps if Meaning --- --- --- je / jz ZF = 1 a == b (or: the result was zero) jne / jnz ZF = 0 a != b jl SF ≠ OF a < b, signed jle ZF = 1 or SF ≠ OF a <= b, signed jg ZF = 0 and SF = OF a b, signed jge SF = OF a = b, signed jb CF = 1 a < b, unsigned ("below") jbe CF = 1 or ZF = 1 a <= b, unsigned ja CF = 0 and ZF = 0 a b, unsigned ("above") jae CF = 0 a = b, unsigned js / jns SF = 1 / 0 negative / not negative You never need to remember the flag formulas: read cmp rax, rbx followed by jl as "jump if rax < rbx". Lesson 3.03 explains the signed and unsigned pairs. if C's c-norun if (temperature < 0) { puts("Freezing"); } puts("Done"); becomes a compare and a jump over the body, using the opposite condition: nasm global _start section .data freezing: db "Freezing", 10, 0 done_msg: db "Done", 10, 0 section .text _start: call read_int ; the temperature cmp rax, 0 jge .after ; NOT below zero: skip the body lea rdi, rel freezing call print_str .after: lea rdi, rel done_msg call print_str mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Try it with -5 and with 12 as the input. if and else With an else , the "then" part must jump over the "else" part when it is done: nasm-norun cmp rax, rbx jle .else ; not (rax rbx) ; ... rax is bigger ... jmp .end .else: ; ... rbx is bigger or equal ... .end: demo-asm title: The larger of two numbers init: rdi=12, rsi=30 mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi jge done mov rax, rsi done: ret This shorter pattern is common: put one answer in place, and jump past the line that would replace it. Local labels Every label in a file must be unique, which gets tedious: .after , .loop , .done would be needed many times. In NASM a label starting with a dot is local : it belongs to the most recent ordinary label above it, so each function can have its own .done . nasm-norun max: mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi jge .done ; this is really max.done mov rax, rsi .done: ret min: mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi jle .done ; min.done: no clash mov rax, rsi .done: ret quiz ? After cmp rax, 10, which jump goes when rax is 10 or more (signed)? + jge - jg - jl jg would skip 10 itself. ? To skip the body of if (x == 0) { ... }, which jump do you use? + jne, the opposite condition - je - jmp Jump over the body when the condition does not hold. ? What does jmp do? + Always continues at the label - Jumps only if the last result was zero - Calls a function It sets rip to the label's address. ? What is special about a label like .done? + It is local to the ordinary label above it, so it can be reused elsewhere - It is the end of the program - It cannot be jumped to NASM joins it to the previous label's name.

title: Choices with jumps
body: Write these with cmp and conditional jumps (the numbers are signed): Function Result --- --- max(a, b) the larger abs_value(x) x without its sign ( abs and absolute are reserved words in NASM) sign(x) −1, 0 or 1 clamp(x, low, high) low if x < low, high if x high, otherwise x grade(score) the character 'A' for 90 and up, 'B' for 75 and up, 'C' for 50 and up, otherwise 'F' Use local labels ( .done ) so each function can reuse the same names.

title: 3.02  Loops
body: A loop is a jump backwards. Counting loops often count down to zero with dec and jnz, since dec sets the zero flag for free. A while loop tests at the top and a do-while at the bottom; compilers prefer the bottom test with one check in front. Reading until read_int reports the end of the input makes a loop over all the input. A jump backwards nasm global _start section .text _start: mov ebx, 1 ; i = 1 .loop: mov edi, ebx call print_int call print_newline inc ebx ; i++ cmp ebx, 5 jle .loop ; while i <= 5, go round again mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The counter lives in rbx because print_int may change rcx , rdx , rsi and rdi . Counting down to zero dec sets ZF when it reaches zero, so a loop that counts down needs no cmp : demo-asm title: Add up 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 init: ecx=5 xor eax, eax top: add eax, ecx dec ecx jnz top ret That is the classic assembly loop. (x86 even has a loop instruction that decrements rcx and jumps, but on modern processors it is slower than dec + jnz , so compilers never use it.) while and do-while A do-while tests at the bottom, so the body always runs at least once: nasm-norun .body: ; ... cmp ... jcc .body A while loop must test first, in case it should run zero times. The straightforward version tests at the top and jumps back from the bottom: nasm-norun .test: cmp ... jcc .end ; the opposite condition: leave the loop ; ... body ... jmp .test .end: That is two jumps per round. Compilers turn it into a single test in front plus a do-while, called a rotated loop, which takes one jump per round: nasm-norun cmp ... jcc .end ; skip the loop entirely if it should not run .body: ; ... body ... cmp ... jcc .body ; one jump per round .end: Reading until the end of the input read_int returns rdx = 0 when there are no more numbers. Testing it after each call makes a loop over the whole input: nasm global _start section .data s_count: db " numbers, total ", 0 section .text _start: xor ebx, ebx ; total xor r12d, r12d ; count .next: call read_int test rdx, rdx jz .done ; no more numbers add rbx, rax inc r12 jmp .next .done: mov rdi, r12 call print_int lea rdi, rel s_count call print_str mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Try it with several numbers on several lines. Loops inside loops Keep each counter in its own register that survives the calls inside (here r12 and r13 ): nasm global _start section .text _start: mov r12d, 1 ; row .row: mov r13d, 1 ; column .col: mov edi, ' ' call print_char inc r13d cmp r13d, r12d jle .col ; columns 1..row call print_newline inc r12d cmp r12d, 4 jle .row mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall quiz ? Why does dec ecx followed by jnz top work without a cmp? + dec sets the zero flag when ecx reaches 0 - jnz compares ecx with 0 itself - dec jumps automatically Arithmetic sets the flags as a side effect. ? Which loop always runs its body at least once? + One that tests at the bottom (do-while) - One that tests at the top (while) - Neither A while loop may run zero times. ? Why keep a loop counter in rbx or r12 to r15 when the loop calls print_int? + The routines may change rcx, rdx, rsi and rdi, but keep rbx and r12 to r15 - Only those registers can count - It is faster The calling convention again. ? How does a loop over all the input know when to stop? + read_int returns rdx = 0 at the end of the input - read_int returns -1 - The program crashes Test rdx after each call.

title: Loops
body: Write these with loops: Function Result --- --- sum_to(n) 1 + 2 + ... + n, or 0 when n < 1 factorial(n) n! for n from 0 to 20 (0! is 1) power(b, e) b to the power e, for e = 0 count_digits(n) the decimal digits of an unsigned n (0 has 1 digit) gcd(a, b) the greatest common divisor of two positive numbers: while b is not 0, (a, b) becomes (b, a mod b)

title: 3.03  Signed and Unsigned Conditions
body: The same bits compare differently as signed and unsigned numbers - all 1s is -1 or the largest number. cmp sets flags for both readings, and you choose with the jump - jl, jg for signed, jb, ja for unsigned. Using the wrong one is a classic bug, and one unsigned compare can check a whole range. Same bits, two orders Take rax = -1 and rbx = 1 . Which is bigger? - As signed numbers: −1 < 1. - As unsigned numbers: 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (18,446,744,073,709,551,615) 1. The bits do not say which reading you mean, so cmp sets flags for both, and the jump decides : signed unsigned --- --- --- < jl (less) jb (below) <= jle jbe jg (greater) ja (above) = jge jae Equality ( je , jne ) is the same for both. nasm global _start section .data s_less: db "signed: -1 is less than 1", 10, 0 s_above: db "unsigned: -1 is above 1", 10, 0 section .text _start: mov rbx, -1 cmp rbx, 1 jge .unsigned lea rdi, rel s_less call print_str .unsigned: cmp rbx, 1 jbe .done lea rdi, rel s_above call print_str .done: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Both messages print: the same comparison, read two ways. How the flags tell them apart cmp a, b works out a − b: - For unsigned numbers, a < b exactly when the subtraction had to borrow: CF = 1 . So jb is jc (jump if carry). - For signed numbers the sign of the result would tell you, except that the subtraction may overflow and flip it. So the rule is "less when SF ≠ OF": the sign is wrong exactly when overflow happened. Which one to use The values are Use --- --- sizes, counts, addresses, array indexes unsigned: jb , ja , ... characters (bytes 0 to 255) unsigned values that can be negative signed: jl , jg , ... C compilers choose from the declared types: int gives jl , unsigned and size_t give jb . In assembly there are no types: you must remember which you meant. !warning The negative index bug Checking an index with cmp rax, rcx / jge .out_of_range (signed) lets a negative index through, because −5 is less than the length. jae (unsigned) rejects it, since −5 as unsigned is huge. One unsigned compare checks both ends. A range in one compare The same trick checks whether a value is between low and high : subtract low , then compare unsigned against high - low . Anything below low wraps to a huge number: nasm-norun ; is the character in al a digit, '0' to '9'? sub al, '0' cmp al, 9 jbe .is_digit ; 0..9 after the subtraction: a digit Compilers do this all the time for if (c = '0' && c <= '9') . quiz ? rax = -1, rbx = 1. After cmp rax, rbx, does jb jump? + No: as unsigned, rax is the largest possible number, so it is above rbx - Yes, because -1 < 1 - It depends on the instruction before the cmp jl would jump, because as signed numbers -1 < 1. ? Which jump treats the numbers as signed? + jg - ja - jae Greater and less are signed; above and below are unsigned. ? Why is jae better than jge for checking an index against a length? + A negative index looks huge as unsigned, so it is caught too - jae is faster - jge does not work with lengths One unsigned compare checks both ends. ? What does sub al, '0' followed by cmp al, 9 and jbe test? + Whether al held a digit character - Whether al is negative - Whether al is 9 Values below '0' wrap to large numbers.

title: Signed or unsigned?
body: Choose the right jumps: Function Result --- --- max_signed(a, b) the larger as signed numbers: max_signed(-1, 1) is 1 max_unsigned(a, b) the larger as unsigned numbers: max_unsigned(-1, 1) is −1 (the largest unsigned value) is_digit(c) 1 if c is '0' to '9' , else 0, using one unsigned comparison in_range(x, low, high) 1 if low <= x <= high (signed, low <= high), else 0, with one subtraction and one unsigned comparison valid_index(i, length) 1 if 0 <= i < length (both signed numbers), else 0, with one comparison

title: 3.04  if, else and switch from C
match: 3.04 if, else and switch from C
body: Chains of if and else become a series of compares, each jumping to the next test. && jumps out at the first false part and at the first true part. A switch over close-together values becomes a jump table - an array of addresses indexed by the value - after one unsigned compare that sends everything out of range to default. else if chains c-norun if (score = 90) grade = 'A'; else if (score = 75) grade = 'B'; else if (score = 50) grade = 'C'; else grade = 'F'; Each test jumps to the next test when it fails, and each body jumps to the end: nasm-norun cmp rdi, 90 jl .not_a mov eax, 'A' jmp .end .not_a: cmp rdi, 75 jl .not_b mov eax, 'B' jmp .end .not_b: cmp rdi, 50 jl .not_c mov eax, 'C' jmp .end .not_c: mov eax, 'F' .end: && and C's && and stop as soon as the answer is known, and in assembly that is just where the jumps go: c-norun if (x = 1 && x <= 10) { ... } // both must hold if (c == ' ' c == '\n') { ... } // either is enough nasm-norun ; x = 1 && x <= 10: leave at the first part that fails cmp rdi, 1 jl .skip cmp rdi, 10 jg .skip ; ... body ... .skip: ; c == ' ' c == '\n': enter at the first part that holds cmp dil, ' ' je .body cmp dil, 10 jne .skip2 .body: ; ... body ... .skip2: switch and jump tables A switch over a few values could be a chain of compares. Over many close-together values, compilers build a jump table : an array of label addresses, and one indirect jump that picks an entry with the value as the index. nasm global _start section .data s_zero: db "zero", 10, 0 s_one: db "one", 10, 0 s_two: db "two", 10, 0 s_three: db "three", 10, 0 s_many: db "lots", 10, 0 section .rodata table: dq _start.case0, _start.case1, _start.case2, _start.case3 ; each case's address section .text _start: .next: call read_int test rdx, rdx jz .exit cmp rax, 3 ja .default ; unsigned: catches negative numbers too lea rcx, rel table jmp rcx + rax 8 ; jump to the address stored in table rax .case0: lea rdi, rel s_zero jmp .print .case1: lea rdi, rel s_one jmp .print .case2: lea rdi, rel s_two jmp .print .case3: lea rdi, rel s_three jmp .print .default: lea rdi, rel s_many .print: call print_str jmp .next .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Run it with the input 2 0 7 -1 3 . - dq _start.case0, ... stores the 8-byte addresses of the labels. The cases are local labels inside _start , and their full names are _start.case0 and so on. The table must spell them out, because inside the table a plain .case0 would belong to the label table . - jmp rcx + rax 8 reads 8 bytes from the table and jumps there: an indirect jump . - The one ja check sends both too-big and negative values to the default, the unsigned trick from lesson 3.03. Without it, a bad value would jump to whatever address happened to be in memory past the table. The table costs the same however many cases there are: one compare and one jump. Interpreters for languages like Python dispatch their instructions this way. quiz ? How does if (a && b) skip its body when a is false? + It jumps past the body right after testing a, without testing b - It tests both, then jumps - It cannot: && needs a special instruction Short-circuiting is just where the jumps go. ? What is in a jump table? + The addresses of the code for each case - The case values - A copy of each case's code jmp table + index 8 picks one. ? Why does the switch code check cmp rax, 3 / ja .default first? + So values outside 0 to 3, negative ones included, never index past the table - To make it faster - Because jmp cannot take a register One unsigned compare covers both ends. ? Each entry of the table is 8 bytes. Why? + Each is a 64-bit address - Each case has 8 instructions - The table is aligned So the index is multiplied by 8.

title: 3.05  Branch-Free Code cmov and setcc
body: Processors guess which way each jump will go and work ahead; a wrong guess wastes many cycles. cmovcc copies a value only if a condition holds, and setcc turns a condition into a 0 or 1 byte, so simple choices need no jump at all. Compilers use them for min, max, abs and boolean results. Why avoid jumps? A modern processor works on many instructions at once, in a long pipeline . When it meets a conditional jump it does not wait to find out the answer: it predicts which way the jump will go and carries on working down that path. If the guess was right, nothing is lost. If wrong, all that work is thrown away, which costs around 15 to 20 cycles. Predictors are very good at patterns (a loop that runs 1000 times is predicted right 999 times), but a jump that depends on random data is wrong about half the time. For small choices, it is better not to jump at all. cmov: copy only if cmovcc destination, source copies the source only when the condition holds. The conditions are the same letters as the jumps: cmove , cmovne , cmovl , cmovg , cmovb , cmova , ... demo-asm title: max(a, b) with no jump init: rdi=12, rsi=30 mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi cmovl rax, rsi ret The processor always runs all three instructions; there is nothing to guess. Some useful ones: nasm-norun ; abs(x) mov rax, rdi neg rax ; rax = -x, and the flags say whether -x is negative cmovs rax, rdi ; if -x is negative, x was positive: use x ; clamp x to at most 100 mov rax, rdi mov ecx, 100 cmp rax, rcx cmovg rax, rcx cmov cannot take a constant as its source, so put the constant in a register first, as above. setcc: a condition as a number setcc writes 1 or 0 into a byte register depending on the condition: nasm-norun ; return (a == b) xor eax, eax ; clear all of rax first... cmp rdi, rsi sete al ; ...because sete only writes al ret Clear the register before the cmp : xor changes the flags, so doing it after would wreck the comparison. Then sete al writes 1 or 0 into the low byte, and the rest is already 0. (The other way is movzx eax, al after the setcc .) Tricks with no compare at all Some answers fall straight out of arithmetic: nasm-norun ; sign(x): -1, 0 or 1 mov rax, rdi sar rax, 63 ; -1 if negative, else 0 xor ecx, ecx test rdi, rdi setg cl ; 1 if positive, else 0 or rax, rcx ; -1, 0 or 1 ; abs(x) with a mask mov rax, rdi sar rax, 63 ; all 1s if negative, else 0 xor rdi, rax ; flip the bits if negative sub rdi, rax ; and add 1 if negative: two's complement negation mov rax, rdi When to use them A jump is still better when the choice skips a lot of work (computing both sides costs more than a misprediction), or when the pattern is predictable. For a quick choice between two ready values, cmov or setcc wins. Compilers decide this for you at -O2 , which is why you see cmov in their output so often. quiz ? What does cmovl rax, rsi do after cmp rdi, rsi? + Copies rsi into rax only if rdi < rsi - Always copies rsi into rax - Jumps if rdi < rsi Conditional move: no jump. ? Why is a branch on random data slow? + The processor's guess is wrong about half the time, and each wrong guess throws away work - Jumps are always slow - Random data is slow to read Predictable branches are almost free. ? After sete al, what is in the rest of rax? + Whatever was there before, so clear eax before the compare - 0 - 1 setcc writes only one byte. ? Why must xor eax, eax come before cmp, not between cmp and sete? + xor changes the flags, which would destroy the comparison's result - xor is slow - sete needs eax to be 0 first to work Order matters with the flags.

title: 4.01  Addressing Modes
body: Square brackets mean memory. An address can be built from a base register, an index register times 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant, or relative to rip for labels. The size comes from the register or is written as byte, word, dword or qword. movzx and movsx widen small values, and lea computes an address without reading it. Brackets mean memory Without brackets an operand is a register or a number; with brackets it is the memory at that address : nasm-norun mov rax, rbx ; rax = rbx mov rax, rbx ; rax = the 8 bytes at the address in rbx mov rbx , rax ; store rax's 8 bytes at that address Only one operand of an instruction may be in memory: to copy memory to memory, go through a register. Building an address An x86 address can combine up to four parts: base + index scale + displacement Part Is --- --- base any register index any register except rsp scale 1, 2, 4 or 8 displacement a constant, or a label That covers almost everything a program needs in one instruction: C Assembly (rdi = the array, rsi = i) --- --- p- field at offset 16 rdi + 16 a i for 8-byte elements rdi + rsi 8 a i for 4-byte int s rdi + rsi 4 a i + 1 rdi + rsi 8 + 8 bytes i rdi + rsi Labels: rel A label is an address fixed when the program is built. Programs today are often loaded at a random address (a protection called ASLR), so code refers to its data relative to rip , the address of the current instruction: rel label . The assembler works out the distance. nasm-norun mov rax, rel total ; read the 8 bytes at total lea rsi, rel message ; the address of message itself ( default rel at the top of a file makes every label rip-relative, so you can leave out rel .) Sizes The register says how many bytes move: mov eax, rdi reads 4, mov al, rdi reads 1. When no register is involved, write the size: nasm-norun mov byte rdi , 'A' ; store one byte mov dword rdi + 4 , 100 ; store 4 bytes add qword rel count , 1 ; add to 8 bytes Widening: movzx and movsx To read a small value into a big register, say how to fill the rest: Instruction Fills the upper bits with For --- --- --- movzx eax, byte rdi 0s unsigned bytes, characters movsx rax, byte rdi copies of the sign bit signed bytes movsx rax, word rdi signed 16-bit numbers movsxd rax, dword rdi signed 32-bit numbers to 64 (32-bit unsigned needs nothing special: mov eax, rdi already clears the top half.) demo-asm title: The same byte, zero- and sign-extended init: rdi=0x2000, mem@0x2000=-3 movzx eax, byte rdi movsx rbx, byte rdi ret The byte is 0xFD : movzx gives 253, movsx gives −3. lea: the address, not the contents lea (load effective address) works out the address in brackets and puts the number in the register, without reading memory: nasm-norun lea rax, rdi + rsi 8 ; rax = the address of a i mov rax, rdi + rsi 8 ; rax = a i itself That is how C's &a i compiles, and it is also why lea doubles as an adder (lesson 2.03). nasm global _start section .data values: dq 10, 20, 30, 40 section .text _start: lea rbx, rel values ; the array's address mov rdi, rbx + 2 8 ; values 2 = 30 add rdi, rbx + 3 8 ; + values 3 = 70 call print_int call print_newline mov qword rbx , 99 ; values 0 = 99 mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall quiz ? What is the difference between mov rax, rbx and mov rax, rbx ? + The first copies rbx; the second reads the memory at the address in rbx - None - The second copies rax into rbx Brackets mean memory. ? rdi points at an array of 4-byte ints and rsi is i. Which is a i ? + dword rdi + rsi 4 - rdi + rsi - rdi 4 + rsi The index is multiplied by the element size. ? Why write mov byte rdi , 5 rather than mov rdi , 5? + Without a register, NASM does not know how many bytes to store - byte makes it faster - rdi is not allowed alone Write byte, word, dword or qword. ? What does lea rax, rdi + 8 do? + Puts the number rdi + 8 in rax, without touching memory - Reads the 8 bytes at rdi + 8 - Adds 8 to the memory at rdi Load effective address.

title: 4.02  Arrays
body: An array in assembly is an address and a count - nothing marks its end or its type. Loop with an index and a scaled address, or move a pointer along by the element size until it reaches the end. Arrays come from the data section, .bss, or the caller, and the code must know whether each element is 1, 4 or 8 bytes. An address and a count In memory an array is just elements side by side. Nothing records how many there are or what they are, so functions take the address of the first element and the count , exactly like C functions taking (const long values, size_t count) . Looping with an index nasm global _start section .data scores: dq 72, 95, 61, 88, 100, 54 count equ ($ - scores) / 8 ; 6: the bytes divided by the element size section .text _start: lea rsi, rel scores xor ecx, ecx ; i = 0 xor eax, eax ; total = 0 .loop: add rax, rsi + rcx 8 ; total += scores i inc rcx cmp rcx, count jb .loop ; while i < count (unsigned: it is an index) mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 470 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Looping with a pointer Instead of an index, move a pointer along by the element size and stop at the end address, the begin/end style from the C course: nasm-norun ; rdi = the array, rsi = the count. Returns the largest element (count = 1). max_of: lea rdx, rdi + rsi 8 ; end = one past the last element mov rax, rdi ; best = the first add rdi, 8 .loop: cmp rdi, rdx jae .done mov rcx, rdi cmp rcx, rax cmovg rax, rcx add rdi, 8 ; the next element jmp .loop .done: ret Both styles are common in compiler output; the pointer style saves the multiplication in the address (which is free anyway on x86) and frees a register. Element sizes C type Size Read with --- --- --- char , unsigned char , int8_t 1 movzx eax, byte rdi + rcx / movsx short , int16_t 2 movsx eax, word rdi + rcx 2 int , int32_t 4 mov eax, rdi + rcx 4 ( movsxd to 64 bits) long , pointers, int64_t 8 mov rax, rdi + rcx 8 Get the size wrong and you read pieces of two elements at once, with no error. Assembly will not stop you. Changing an array Storing works the same way in reverse. This doubles every element in place: nasm global _start section .data values: dq 1, -2, 3, 40 section .text _start: lea rbx, rel values xor ecx, ecx .double: shl qword rbx + rcx 8 , 1 ; values i = 2, right in memory inc rcx cmp rcx, 4 jb .double xor r12d, r12d ; print them .print: mov rdi, rbx + r12 8 call print_int mov edi, ' ' call print_char inc r12 cmp r12, 4 jb .print call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The print loop uses r12 , not rcx , because the routines may change rcx . !danger No bounds Reading values 10 of a 4-element array reads whatever follows it: other data, or memory that does not belong to the program (a segmentation fault). Every check is yours to write, usually one unsigned compare (lesson 3.03). quiz ? What does a function need to work on an array? + Its address and how many elements it has - Only its address - Only its name Nothing in memory marks the end. ? count equ ($ - scores) / 8 gives... + The number of 8-byte elements in scores - The size in bytes - The address of the last element $ - scores is the size in bytes. ? An array of 4-byte ints is at rdi. Which reads element rcx? + mov eax, rdi + rcx 4 - mov rax, rdi + rcx 8 - mov eax, rdi + rcx Scale by the element size, and read 4 bytes. ? Why does the pointer-style loop stop at jae rather than jge? + Addresses are unsigned numbers - jae is faster - jge does not work with registers Compare addresses and indexes unsigned.

title: 4.03  Strings
body: A string is bytes in memory, ending with a 0 byte by C's convention. Loops over strings read one byte at a time with movzx and stop at the 0. Length, copy, compare and case changes are all short loops. The string instructions rep movsb and rep stosb copy and fill whole blocks in one instruction. Bytes with a zero at the end Text is bytes: one per ASCII character (or several per character in UTF-8). Assembly has no string type, so programs follow a convention. The C convention, used by print_str and by every C library function, is a zero byte at the end. demo-text title: "Hi!" in memory text: Hi! Length nasm-norun ; rdi = a zero-terminated string. Returns its length. length: xor eax, eax .loop: cmp byte rdi + rax , 0 je .done inc rax jmp .loop .done: ret cmp byte rdi + rax , 0 compares one byte of memory with 0 directly: no register needed. Reading characters To work on a character, read it with movzx so the rest of the register is clean, then compare and change the low byte: nasm global _start section .data text: db "Hello, assembly world!", 0 section .text _start: lea rbx, rel text mov rsi, rbx .loop: movzx eax, byte rsi test al, al jz .done ; the 0 at the end cmp al, 'a' jb .next cmp al, 'z' ja .next sub al, 32 ; 'a' to 'z' become 'A' to 'Z' mov rsi , al ; write it back .next: inc rsi jmp .loop .done: mov rdi, rbx call print_str call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall This changes the string where it is, which works because it is in .data . Text in .rodata would crash when written. Copying and comparing nasm-norun ; rdi = destination, rsi = source. Copies the string with its 0. copy: .loop: movzx eax, byte rsi mov rdi , al inc rsi inc rdi test al, al jnz .loop ; the 0 was copied too: stop ret ; rdi, rsi = two strings. Returns 1 if they are equal. equal: .loop: movzx eax, byte rdi cmp al, rsi jne .no ; a difference test al, al jz .yes ; both ended together inc rdi inc rsi jmp .loop .yes: mov eax, 1 ret .no: xor eax, eax ret The destination must have room: copying a long string into a short buffer overwrites whatever follows, the buffer overflow of C, with no warning at all here. The string instructions x86 has instructions made for blocks of memory. With a rep prefix they repeat rcx times: Instruction Does, each time --- --- rep movsb copy the byte at rsi to rdi , then move both on rep stosb store al at rdi , then move it on repne scasb compare al with rdi , move on, stop at a match nasm-norun ; fill 64 bytes at buffer with '-' lea rdi, rel buffer mov al, '-' mov ecx, 64 rep stosb ; copy rcx bytes from rsi to rdi rep movsb They move forwards as long as the direction flag is clear, which the calling convention guarantees. Modern processors run rep movsb very fast for large blocks, and C's memcpy and memset often use it. quiz ? How does a C-style string mark its end? + With a zero byte - With its length stored first - With a new line print_str and the C library both rely on it. ? Why read characters with movzx eax, byte rsi ? + It reads one byte and clears the rest of the register - It reads the whole string - mov cannot read bytes mov al, rsi would leave the old upper bits. ? Which instruction copies rcx bytes from rsi to rdi ? + rep movsb - rep stosb - mov rdi , rsi Memory-to-memory mov does not exist. ? What happens when copy is given a destination that is too small? + It writes past the end, over whatever follows - It stops at the end of the buffer - It crashes at once, every time The function cannot know the buffer's size.
