title: 4.04  The Stack push and pop
body: The stack is memory that grows downwards from a high address, and rsp always points at its top. push moves rsp down 8 bytes and stores a value; pop loads it and moves rsp back up. It saves registers that must be kept, holds temporary space reserved with sub rsp, and must end exactly where it started. A stack of plates The stack is a region of memory the operating system gives every program, a few megabytes in size. rsp points at the item on top. It grows downwards : pushing makes rsp smaller. Instruction Same as --- --- push rax sub rsp, 8 then mov rsp , rax pop rbx mov rbx, rsp then add rsp, 8 The last thing pushed is the first popped: a "last in, first out" stack. demo-asm title: push and pop init: rax=11, rbx=22, rcx=33 push rax push rbx push rcx pop rax pop rbx pop rcx ret Step through and watch rsp and the values on the stack. Popping in the same order as pushing reverses them: afterwards rax = 33 and rcx = 11. Saving registers The most common use: keeping a register's value safe while you need the register for something else. A function that wants to use rbx (which it must give back unchanged) saves it first: nasm-norun sum_squares: ; rdi = a, rsi = b; returns a a + b b push rbx ; save the caller's rbx mov rbx, rdi imul rbx, rdi ; rbx = a a mov rax, rsi imul rax, rsi ; rax = b b add rax, rbx pop rbx ; give rbx back ret Pops must match pushes, in reverse order : push rbx , push r12 ... pop r12 , pop rbx . Temporary space Subtracting from rsp reserves bytes on the stack; adding gives them back. This is how functions get local arrays and buffers without .bss : nasm global _start section .text _start: sub rsp, 16 ; 16 bytes of space at rsp to rsp + 15 mov byte rsp , 'O' mov byte rsp + 1 , 'K' mov byte rsp + 2 , '!' mov byte rsp + 3 , 10 mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 mov rsi, rsp ; the address of the bytes on the stack mov edx, 4 syscall add rsp, 16 ; give the space back mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Reversing with the stack Since the stack reverses order, it can turn a string around: push every character, then pop them back in: nasm global _start section .data text: db "stressed", 0 section .text _start: lea rsi, rel text xor ecx, ecx ; how many pushed .push: movzx eax, byte rsi + rcx test al, al jz .popping push rax inc rcx jmp .push .popping: xor edx, edx .pop: cmp rdx, rcx jae .done pop rax mov rsi + rdx , al inc rdx jmp .pop .done: lea rdi, rel text call print_str ; desserts call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Rules !warning Leave the stack as you found it - Every push needs a pop (or an add rsp ) before the function returns, or ret will jump to a wrong address (lesson 5.01 shows why) and the program crashes. - Never read below rsp after the space is given back: the next push or system call overwrites it. - Before calling a function, rsp must be a multiple of 16 (lesson 5.02). The routines in this course do not mind, but C functions can crash otherwise. quiz ? What does push rax do? + Moves rsp down by 8 and stores rax at the new rsp - Stores rax at rsp and moves rsp up - Copies rax into rsp The stack grows downwards. ? After push rax, push rbx, pop rax, pop rbx - what happened? + rax and rbx were swapped - Nothing changed - Both hold the old rbx Last in, first out. ? How does a function make room for 32 bytes of local space? + sub rsp, 32, and add rsp, 32 before returning - push 32 - mov rsp, 32 Subtracting from rsp reserves space. ? A function pushes rbx and r12 at the start. In which order should it pop them? + pop r12, then pop rbx - pop rbx, then pop r12 - Either Reverse order.

title: Using the stack
body: The tests check that every function leaves rbx , rbp and r12 to r15 as it found them. These functions must use rbx and r12 (or other callee-saved registers) for their work, so save them with push and restore them with pop : Function Result --- --- sum_of_squares(a, b, c) a² + b² + c², keeping a running total in rbx reverse_string(s) reverses the string in place by pushing every character and popping them back largest_gap(array, n) the largest difference between two neighbours, array i+1 - array i , for n = 2; keep the best so far in r12

title: 4.05  Buffers and Input
body: Input arrives as bytes in a buffer, from the read system call or the read_line routine. Turning typed digits into a number is the reverse of printing - multiply what you have by 10 and add the next digit. Always pass the buffer's size, check what came back, and handle the end of the input. The read system call read (system call 0) copies up to a given number of bytes from a file into a buffer and returns how many it got: fewer than asked if that is all there is, 0 at the end of the input, negative on an error. nasm global _start section .bss buffer: resb 64 section .text _start: xor eax, eax ; read xor edi, edi ; standard input lea rsi, rel buffer mov edx, 64 ; at most 64 bytes syscall test rax, rax jle .exit ; nothing read, or an error mov rdx, rax ; echo exactly the bytes that came in mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel buffer syscall .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall A single read may return part of a line, or several lines at once: it returns whatever bytes are ready. Real programs loop until they have what they need. That bookkeeping is what read_line and read_int do for you. read_line read_line (from lesson 1.06) fills a buffer with exactly one line, without the new line, ends it with a 0, and returns its length, or −1 at the end of the input. The buffer and its size are yours: nasm global _start section .bss line: resb 100 section .data s_len: db " characters: ", 0 section .text _start: .next: lea rdi, rel line mov esi, 100 call read_line cmp rax, -1 je .exit mov rdi, rax call print_int lea rdi, rel s_len call print_str lea rdi, rel line call print_str call print_newline jmp .next .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Digits into a number Typed text "427" is the bytes 52, 50, 55. Converting it is printing in reverse: start at 0, and for each digit multiply by 10 and add the digit's value: Character number × 10 + digit --- --- 0 '4' 0 × 10 + 4 = 4 '2' 4 × 10 + 2 = 42 '7' 42 × 10 + 7 = 427 nasm-norun ; rdi = a string of digits. Returns its value (stops at the first non-digit). parse: xor eax, eax .loop: movzx ecx, byte rdi sub ecx, '0' cmp ecx, 9 ja .done ; not a digit (the 0 at the end included) imul rax, rax, 10 add rax, rcx inc rdi jmp .loop .done: ret The one unsigned compare checks for a digit (lesson 3.03). read_int is this loop, plus skipping spaces and handling a minus sign. Lesson 6.02 writes the whole thing. Buffer rules - Pass the real size, and never write past it. read_line is told the size and cuts long lines short; your own loops must count too. - Remember what the buffer holds after a call: read does not add a 0, while read_line does. - Check the result before using the buffer: 0 bytes or −1 means there is nothing there. quiz ? What does the read system call return at the end of the input? + 0 - -1 - The buffer's size A negative number means an error. ? Does one read call always return exactly one line? + No: it returns whatever bytes are ready, part of a line or several lines - Yes - Only on Linux That is why read_line exists. ? The text "35" is being parsed. After '3', the number is 3. What is it after '5'? + 35: 3 10 + 5 - 8: 3 + 5 - 53 Multiply by 10, then add the digit. ? Does the read system call put a 0 after the bytes it read? + No, it only returns how many it read - Yes - Only for text read_line adds one; read does not.

title: Numbers from text
body: Read lines with read_line until the input ends. Each line holds one whole number, possibly with a minus sign in front. Convert the text to a number yourself (no read_int ): multiply by 10 and add each digit. Then print the number, its double and its square: For the input 12 -7 300 print 12 doubled is 24, squared is 144 -7 doubled is -14, squared is 49 300 doubled is 600, squared is 90000 A line that is not a number (empty, a letter, a lone - , digits followed by something else) prints not a number: and the line.

title: A line report
body: Read text line by line and report on each line, then on the whole input. For Hello world assembly is fun x print 1: 11 chars, 2 words, reversed: dlrow olleH 2: 19 chars, 3 words, reversed: nuf si ylbmessa 3: 1 chars, 1 words, reversed: x lines: 3 longest: " assembly is fun" vowels: 7 - A word is a run of characters that are not spaces (only the space character counts here). - reversed: is the whole line backwards, spaces included (the second line's reversed text ends with the two spaces that started it). - longest: is the longest line in quotes (the first one if tied); with no lines at all print lines: 0 and nothing else. - vowels: counts a, e, i, o, u in either case, in all the lines. - Lines are at most 200 characters.

title: 5.01  call and ret
body: call pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack and jumps to the function; ret pops that address back into rip. That is all a function call is. Because the return address lives on the stack, a function must pop exactly what it pushed before ret, and functions can call other functions as deep as the stack allows. Two instructions You have used call print_int since module 1. Here is what it does: Instruction Same as --- --- call label push the address of the next instruction, then jmp label ret pop an address into rip : jump back to it The pushed address is the return address : where to carry on afterwards. Nothing else happens. There are no parameters, no local variables and no return values in the hardware: those are all conventions built from registers and the stack. demo-asm title: A call and a return init: rdi=7 call double add rax, 1 ret double: lea rax, rdi+rdi ret Step through and watch rsp and the stack: call pushes the return address (rsp goes down 8), ret pops it (rsp goes back up) and execution continues at add rax, 1 . (The last ret ends the demo.) Writing your own functions nasm global _start section .text ; square: rdi = x. Returns x x in rax. square: mov rax, rdi imul rax, rdi ret ; sum_of_squares: rdi = a, rsi = b. Returns a a + b b. sum_of_squares: push rbx push r12 mov r12, rsi ; keep b: square may change rsi call square ; a a (a is already in rdi) mov rbx, rax mov rdi, r12 call square ; b b add rax, rbx pop r12 pop rbx ret _start: mov edi, 3 mov esi, 4 call sum_of_squares ; 25 mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall - A function is a label, instructions, and ret . Write a comment saying what goes in and what comes out: nothing else will tell the reader. - Functions can be anywhere in .text ; the program still starts at _start . Make sure execution cannot "fall into" a function by accident. - sum_of_squares calls square , so it keeps what it needs in rbx and r12 , and saves the caller's values of those first. The return address must be on top When ret runs, whatever is on top of the stack is taken as the return address. If a function pushed something and forgot to pop it, ret jumps to that value instead, which is almost always a crash: nasm-norun broken: push rbx ; ... forgot pop rbx ... ret ; "returns" to the address that rbx held This is also how a classic stack buffer overflow attack works: a program writes past a local buffer on the stack, over the return address, and ret jumps wherever the attacker chose. Modern systems defend with stack canaries, non-executable stacks and address randomisation. Calls inside calls Each call pushes another return address, so calls nest naturally: _start calls sum_of_squares , which calls square , and each ret goes back exactly one level. The stack holds the chain of "where to go back to", which is what a debugger shows as the backtrace . quiz ? What does call square push on the stack? + The address of the instruction after the call - The address of square - The arguments That is the return address. ? What does ret do? + Pops the top of the stack into rip - Returns rax to the caller - Ends the program The value in rax is only a convention. ? A function does push rbx and returns without popping. What happens at ret? + It jumps to the address that was in rbx, and probably crashes - It returns normally - The assembler refuses it The return address must be on top. ? Why does sum_of_squares keep b in r12 before calling square? + square may change rsi, but must keep r12 - r12 is faster - square reads its argument from r12 Callee-saved registers survive calls.

title: Functions calling functions
body: Write square first, then build the others on it with call (each must call square , not multiply on its own): Function Result --- --- square(x) x × x cube(x) x × square(x) sum_of_squares(a, b) square(a) + square(b) distance2(x1, y1, x2, y2) the squared distance (x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)² Remember: square may change any scratch register ( rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 to r11 ), so keep what you need across a call in rbx or r12 to r15 , and save those with push and pop .

title: 5.02  The System V Calling Convention
body: Linux and macOS follow the System V AMD64 convention. Integer and pointer arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9, the rest on the stack, and the result comes back in rax. rbx, rbp, rsp and r12 to r15 must survive a call; everything else may be changed. rsp must be a multiple of 16 at every call. Why a convention? The hardware does not say where arguments go. If every function chose for itself, no code could call code written by someone else. A calling convention is the agreement that lets C, Rust, Go and your assembly call each other. Linux, macOS and the BSDs use the System V AMD64 convention; Windows uses its own (lesson 5.05). Arguments and results Registers --- --- integer and pointer arguments, in order rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 more than six pushed on the stack, the 7th at the lowest address floating-point arguments xmm0 to xmm7 integer or pointer result rax (and rdx for a 128-bit result) floating-point result xmm0 So the C function long clamp(long x, long low, long high) gets x in rdi , low in rsi , high in rdx , and returns in rax . Smaller types use the low part: an int argument is in edi , an int result in eax , and the upper bits are not guaranteed to be anything in particular. Who saves what Kind Registers Rule --- --- --- callee-saved ("non-volatile") rbx , rbp , r12 , r13 , r14 , r15 (and rsp ) a function must give them back unchanged: save with push , restore with pop caller-saved ("volatile", "scratch") rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 to r11 any call may change them: if you need one after a call, keep it somewhere safe Choose by how long a value must live: - Needed only until the next call? Use a scratch register: no saving needed. - Needed after a call? Put it in a callee-saved register (saving the caller's value first), or on the stack. The tests on this website check this rule after every call: change rbx without restoring it and the test reports it. Stack alignment At the moment of a call instruction, rsp must be a multiple of 16 . The call then pushes 8 bytes, so inside a function rsp is 8 more than a multiple of 16, until the function pushes or subtracts something. Why? Instructions that move 16 bytes at a time (SSE, used by C library functions like printf and memcpy ) can require 16-byte-aligned addresses, and compilers assume the rule holds. Break it and calls into C may crash on an instruction like movaps for no visible reason. nasm-norun my_function: ; on entry: rsp = 16n + 8 (the return address was pushed) push rbx ; rsp = 16n: aligned again call other ; fine pop rbx ret two_saves: push rbx ; 16n push r12 ; 16n - 8: not aligned! sub rsp, 8 ; 16n - 16: aligned call other add rsp, 8 pop r12 pop rbx ret At _start the stack is aligned, which is why _start can call functions directly. The red zone A function that calls nothing (a leaf function) may use the 128 bytes below rsp without moving rsp at all: the convention promises nothing else will touch them. Compilers use this "red zone" for small leaf functions. (The Linux kernel cannot rely on it, and Windows has no red zone.) Reading a C prototype C Arrives in Returns in --- --- --- size_t strlen(const char s) s in rdi rax void memset(void p, int c, size_t n) rdi , esi , rdx rax (p) int max3(int a, int b, int c) edi , esi , edx eax long sum8(long a, ..., long h) 6 registers, then g and h on the stack rax quiz ? Where does the third integer argument go? + rdx - rcx - r8 rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9. ? Which registers must a function give back unchanged? + rbx, rbp, rsp and r12 to r15 - rax, rcx and rdx - All of them The rest may be changed by any call. ? What must be true of rsp when a call instruction runs? + It is a multiple of 16 - It is a multiple of 8 - It is 0 Inside the function it is then 16n + 8. ? A value is needed after a call. Where can it be kept? + In a callee-saved register such as r12 (saved first), or on the stack - In rcx - In rdi Scratch registers may be changed by the call.

title: Following the convention
body: Function Result --- --- sum6(a, b, c, d, e, f) the total of all six arguments (they arrive in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9) pick(n, a, b, c, d) a if n is 0, b if 1, c if 2, d if 3, otherwise 0 scale_all(array, count, factor) multiplies every element of an 8-byte array in place by factor, by calling multiply(x, factor) for each one multiply(x, y) x × y min_max(array, count) returns the smallest element in rax and the largest in rdx (count = 1), like a C function returning a struct of two longs The tests also check that rbx , rbp and r12 to r15 are the same after each call as before.

title: 5.03  Stack Frames and Locals
body: A function's stack frame holds its return address, saved registers and local variables. The classic prologue pushes rbp and copies rsp into it, so locals sit at fixed offsets like rbp - 8 however the stack moves; the epilogue undoes it with leave and ret. Optimised code often skips rbp and addresses locals from rsp. A frame per call Each call gets its own region of the stack, its frame : the return address call pushed, the callee-saved registers the function saved, and room for local variables that do not fit in registers (arrays, buffers, values kept across calls). demo-stack title: Frames for main calling area, which calls square call main The program starts. main's frame holds its own locals. local w = 6 local h = 7 call area width=6 height=7 call pushes a return address; area's prologue saves rbp and makes room for its locals. local result = 42 A local kept at a fixed offset from rbp. call square x=6 square gets a frame too. Its locals are separate from area's. return 36 square's epilogue removes its frame; ret pops the return address. return 42 area returns, and its frame disappears in turn. set total = 42 return 0 The prologue and epilogue The traditional frame uses rbp as a fixed anchor: nasm-norun my_function: push rbp ; save the caller's rbp mov rbp, rsp ; rbp = the frame's base, fixed from now on sub rsp, 32 ; room for 32 bytes of locals: rbp - 32 to rbp - 1 mov qword rbp - 8 , 0 ; a local variable lea rdi, rbp - 32 ; the address of a local buffer ; ... the body: pushes and calls can move rsp, rbp stays put ... leave ; mov rsp, rbp then pop rbp ret Offset from rbp Holds --- --- rbp + 16 , rbp + 24 ... the 7th, 8th... arguments, if any, pushed by the caller rbp + 8 the return address rbp the caller's saved rbp rbp - 8 and below this function's locals Each frame's saved rbp points at the frame before it, so the frames form a linked list up the stack. Debuggers and profilers follow that chain to print a backtrace. Keep sub rsp a multiple of 16 (after push rbp the stack is aligned again), and call stays aligned. A local buffer A function can build text in a buffer on its own stack, as print_uint does. This one writes a number's digits into the caller's buffer, building them backwards in a local one first: nasm global _start section .bss out: resb 32 section .text ; to_text: rdi = destination buffer, rsi = an unsigned number. Writes its digits and a 0; returns the length. to_text: push rbp mov rbp, rsp sub rsp, 32 ; a local buffer at rbp - 32 .. rbp - 1 lea r8, rbp - 1 ; write digits backwards from the end mov rax, rsi mov ecx, 10 .digit: xor edx, edx div rcx add dl, '0' mov r8 , dl dec r8 test rax, rax jnz .digit inc r8 ; the first digit lea rcx, rbp sub rcx, r8 ; how many digits mov rax, rcx ; the result: the length mov rsi, r8 rep movsb ; copy them to the destination mov byte rdi , 0 leave ret _start: lea rdi, rel out mov esi, 90210 call to_text mov rbx, rax lea rdi, rel out call print_str mov edi, ' ' call print_char mov rdi, rbx call print_int ; 5 digits call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Without a frame pointer At -O2 , GCC and Clang usually leave rbp out ( -fomit-frame-pointer ), freeing it as a general register and addressing locals from rsp : rsp + 8 . It is faster, but the offsets change whenever rsp moves, so the code is harder to read. Debuggers then use separate unwind tables instead of the rbp chain. Small leaf functions often need no frame at all. quiz ? What does the prologue push rbp / mov rbp, rsp set up? + A fixed anchor for this frame, with the caller's rbp saved - Space for the arguments - The return address Locals are then at fixed offsets from rbp. ? Where is the return address, relative to rbp, after the classic prologue? + rbp + 8 - rbp - 8 - rbp rbp holds the saved rbp. ? What does leave do? + mov rsp, rbp then pop rbp - Returns from the function - Frees the heap ret follows it. ? Why do optimised builds often skip rbp? + It frees one more register; locals are addressed from rsp - rbp is slow - The stack is not used Debuggers use unwind tables instead.

title: A frame with a buffer
body: Write to_decimal(buffer, n) : it writes the signed number n into the buffer as text with a 0 at the end (a minus sign for negative numbers), and returns the number of characters, not counting the 0. Use a classic stack frame: push rbp , mov rbp, rsp , sub rsp, 32 for a local buffer where you build the digits backwards, then copy them to the caller's buffer, and finish with leave and ret . The most negative number, −9223372036854775808, has no positive twin: negating it gives itself. Divide it as an unsigned number after negating and it works.

title: 5.04  Recursion
body: A recursive function calls itself, and each call has its own frame, so it works like any other call - as long as values needed after the inner call are saved first. Every level costs stack space, a base case stops the descent, and recursion too deep runs off the end of the stack and crashes. Nothing special To the processor, a function calling itself is just another call : a new return address on the stack, and the same code running again with new register values. The only thing to get right is the usual rule: anything needed after the call must survive it . nasm global _start section .text ; factorial: rdi = n (0 to 20). Returns n!. factorial: cmp rdi, 1 jg .recurse mov eax, 1 ; the base case: 0! = 1! = 1 ret .recurse: push rbx mov rbx, rdi ; keep n: the inner call changes rdi lea rdi, rdi - 1 call factorial ; rax = (n - 1)! imul rax, rbx ; n (n - 1)! pop rbx ret _start: mov edi, 10 call factorial mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 3628800 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Each level saves the caller's rbx , then uses rbx for its own n . When the inner call returns, that level's n is still in rbx , because the inner call saved and restored it. Ten levels deep, there are ten saved rbx values and ten return addresses on the stack. Two calls: Fibonacci nasm-norun ; fib: rdi = n. Returns the nth Fibonacci number: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1. fib: cmp rdi, 1 jg .recurse mov rax, rdi ; fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1 ret .recurse: push rbx push r12 sub rsp, 8 ; keep rsp aligned for the calls mov rbx, rdi ; n lea rdi, rbx - 1 call fib ; fib(n - 1) mov r12, rax ; keep it across the second call lea rdi, rbx - 2 call fib ; fib(n - 2) add rax, r12 add rsp, 8 pop r12 pop rbx ret The first result must survive the second call, so it goes in r12 . This version makes about 2ⁿ calls; a loop does it in n steps, which is why recursion is not always the right tool. How deep can it go? The main stack on Linux is usually 8 MB. A frame of 32 bytes allows about 250,000 levels; past that, the next push writes below the stack's end, the processor faults, and the program dies with a segmentation fault : a stack overflow . Some languages turn tail calls (a call that is the last thing a function does) into jumps so they need no extra stack; C and assembly do so only when the optimiser chooses to, or when you write jmp yourself. quiz ? Why does factorial save n in rbx before calling itself? + The inner call overwrites rdi, and rbx is kept by every call - rbx is the only register imul can use - To make the call faster The usual rule for values needed after a call. ? What stops the recursion? + The base case returns without calling again - The stack running out - ret Without a base case it would recurse until it crashed. ? In fib, why is fib(n - 1) moved to r12 before the second call? + The second call would overwrite rax - r12 holds the result - To align the stack And r12 was saved, so it is the function's to use. ? What happens when recursion goes far too deep? + The stack runs out and the program crashes with a segmentation fault - The program slows down but finishes - The assembler warns A stack overflow.

title: Recursion
body: Write each of these as a recursive function (it calls itself): Function Result --- --- fact(n) n! for n from 0 to 20 fib(n) the nth Fibonacci number: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n−1) + fib(n−2); n up to 25 power(b, e) b to the power e by squaring: if e is 0, 1; if e is even, power(b, e/2) squared; if odd, b × power(b, e−1) digit_sum(n) the sum of the decimal digits of n = 0: digit_sum(n / 10) + n mod 10, and 0 for 0

title: 5.05  Working with C
body: Assembly functions that follow the calling convention can be called from C, and C functions from assembly, using global and extern and a linker. int values live in the low 32 bits with undefined upper bits. Windows x64 uses rcx, rdx, r8 and r9 with 32 bytes of shadow space and different saved registers. GCC's inline asm puts single instructions inside C. Assembly called from C Because your functions follow the System V convention, a C program can call them. The assembly side makes the name visible to the linker with global ; the C side declares the prototype: nasm-norun ; mathlib.asm global add_scaled section .text ; long add_scaled(long a, long b, long scale): a + b scale add_scaled: mov rax, rsi imul rax, rdx add rax, rdi ret c-norun // main.c include <stdio.h long add_scaled(long a, long b, long scale); // written in assembly int main(void) { printf("%ld\n", add_scaled(1, 2, 10)); // 21 return 0; } nasm -f elf64 mathlib.asm -o mathlib.o gcc main.c mathlib.o -o app That is how the hot loops of codecs, crypto libraries and game engines are written: most of the program in C, a few functions in hand-tuned assembly. C called from assembly The other way round, extern declares a name that another file defines, and the program is linked with the C library (so it starts at C's main rather than _start ): nasm-norun extern printf global main section .data format: db "%d squared is %d", 10, 0 section .text main: push rbx ; also aligns the stack to 16 mov ebx, 12 lea rdi, rel format mov esi, ebx imul ebx, ebx mov edx, ebx xor eax, eax ; variadic functions: al = how many vector registers are used call printf xor eax, eax ; return 0 from main pop rbx ret Built with gcc program.o -o program . The website links assembly without the C library, which is why the course uses system calls and Xenon's routines instead. int is 32 bits C's int is 32 bits, so an int argument is in edi and an int result in eax . The convention says nothing about the upper 32 bits of the register: they may hold anything. So: - Read int arguments through the 32-bit names ( edi , esi ), never the full register, unless you extend them first: movsxd rax, edi for a signed int , mov eax, edi for an unsigned . - char and short arguments are in dil , di and so on. C compilers rely on this, which is why their output is full of movsxd and 32-bit instructions. You can see C do it This C function contains one assembly instruction, written with GCC's inline assembly . Run it (it is C, compiled with GCC): c include <stdio.h long times_three(long x) { long result; __asm__("lea (%1,%1,2), %0" : "=r"(result) : "r"(x)); // GCC's own (AT&T) syntax return result; } int main(void) { printf("%ld\n", times_three(14)); return 0; } Inline assembly uses GCC's AT&T syntax by default (source first, % before registers), and the : "=r"(result) : "r"(x) parts tell the compiler which registers to use. It is handy for a single special instruction; for anything longer, a separate .asm file is clearer. Windows does it differently The Microsoft x64 convention, used by Windows, differs in the details: System V (Linux, macOS) Microsoft x64 (Windows) --- --- --- integer arguments rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 callee-saved rbx , rbp , r12 to r15 the same plus rdi , rsi and xmm6 to xmm15 before a call 32 bytes of shadow space reserved on the stack for the callee red zone 128 bytes none long 64 bits 32 bits Same instructions, different agreement: code written for one convention cannot simply be called with the other. (The website's C++ course compiles with MSVC by default, which follows the Windows convention.) quiz ? What does global add_scaled do? + Makes the label visible to the linker, so other files can call it - Makes the function run faster - Declares a C function extern is the opposite: a name defined elsewhere. ? A C function takes an int. Where is it, and what about the rest of the register? + In edi; the upper 32 bits of rdi may be anything - In rdi, sign-extended - On the stack Extend it yourself with movsxd if you need 64 bits. ? Where does the first integer argument go on Windows x64? + rcx - rdi - rax Then rdx, r8, r9. ? What is shadow space? + 32 bytes the caller reserves on the stack for the callee, in the Windows convention - The red zone - Memory the debugger uses System V has no shadow space.

title: Like a C compiler
body: Implement these C functions the way a C compiler would on Linux. Remember: an int argument is only in the low 32 bits ( edi , esi ), and the upper half of the register may hold anything. The tests deliberately put garbage there. c int add_ints(int a, int b); / a + b, wrapping at 32 bits / long widen(int x); / x as a 64-bit number: widen(-1) is -1 / unsigned widen_unsigned(unsigned x); / the 32-bit pattern of x with the upper half 0 / int is_negative(int x); / 1 if x < 0 / long dot3(const int a, const int b); / a 0 b 0 + a 1 b 1 + a 2 b 2 , each product done in 64 bits / The tests compare all 64 bits of rax . A 32-bit result written to eax has its upper half cleared, so add_ints(-2, -3) shows as 0xFFFFFFFB (−5 in 32 bits), and that is what the test expects.

title: A small maths library
body: Write a library of functions that call each other, all following the System V convention. The tests call every function and check that rbx , rbp and r12 to r15 come back unchanged. Function Result --- --- gcd(a, b) the greatest common divisor of two numbers = 0, recursively : gcd(a, 0) = a, otherwise gcd(b, a mod b) lcm(a, b) the least common multiple, a / gcd(a, b) × b, calling gcd ; lcm with a 0 is 0 is_prime(n) 1 if n is prime, else 0 (try divisors d while d × d <= n) nth_prime(k) the kth prime, k = 1: nth_prime(1) is 2; calls is_prime insertion_sort(array, n) sorts an array of signed 8-byte numbers in place, smallest first median(array, n) sorts the array (calling insertion_sort ) and returns the middle element, or for an even n the lower of the two middle ones binary_search(array, n, value) in a sorted array, the index of value, or −1; recursive on the half that can hold it, through a helper that takes the low and high bounds

title: 6.01  Reading Compiler Output
body: Compiler output follows recognisable patterns. Leaf functions have no frame, xor zeroes, lea does arithmetic, and test, setcc and cmov replace branches. Division by a constant becomes a multiplication by a magic reciprocal, loops are rotated with one test in front, and simple loops over arrays are vectorised to work on 16 bytes at a time. Where to look gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel file.c writes the assembly to file.s ; objdump -d -M intel program disassembles a finished program; Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) shows both live, colour-coded line by line. Its Intel syntax is the GNU assembler's, slightly different from NASM's: QWORD PTR rdi where NASM writes qword rdi , and movabs for a mov of a 64-bit constant. Everything below is real GCC 15 output at -O2 . Small functions c-norun long times9(long x) { return x 9; } int is_even(int x) { return x % 2 == 0; } nasm-norun times9: lea rax, rdi+rdi 8 ; x + x 8: no multiply at all ret is_even: mov eax, edi not eax ; flip the bits: the lowest is now 1 for even x and eax, 1 ret No push rbp , no frame: a leaf function that keeps everything in registers needs none. Arguments arrive in rdi ( edi for an int ), the answer leaves in rax ( eax ). Division by a constant c-norun unsigned long div10(unsigned long x) { return x / 10; } nasm-norun div10: movabs rax, -3689348814741910323 ; 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD mul rdi ; rdx:rax = x that mov rax, rdx ; keep the high 64 bits shr rax, 3 ret No div anywhere. The constant is about 2⁶⁷ ÷ 10, so taking the high 64 bits of the product (that is, dividing by 2⁶⁴) and shifting right by 3 more divides by 2⁶⁷ × 10 ÷ 2⁶⁷: by 10. The constant is chosen so the result is exact for every 64-bit x. mul takes about 3 cycles; div takes 20 to 40. Signed division adds a correction for negative numbers: nasm-norun sdiv3: ; long sdiv3(long x) { return x / 3; } movabs rax, 6148914691236517206 ; 0x5555555555555556, about 2^64 / 3 imul rdi sar rdi, 63 ; -1 if x was negative, else 0 mov rax, rdx sub rax, rdi ; add 1 for negative x, to round towards zero ret When you see a huge strange constant followed by mul or imul and a shift, think "division". Loops c-norun long sum(const long v, long n) { long t = 0; for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) t += v i ; return t; } nasm-norun sum: test rsi, rsi jle .L9 ; n <= 0: skip the loop entirely lea rdx, rdi+rsi 8 ; end = v + n xor eax, eax .L8: add rax, QWORD PTR rdi ; t += v add rdi, 8 ; v++ cmp rdi, rdx jne .L8 ret .L9: xor eax, eax ret The index i has disappeared: GCC turned v i into a moving pointer and compares it with an end pointer. The loop is rotated (one test before it, one jump per round), exactly as lesson 3.02 described. Vectorised loops At -O3 a simple loop over arrays becomes SIMD code that handles four int s per instruction (lesson 6.04): c-norun void add(int restrict d, const int restrict a, const int restrict b) { for (int i = 0; i < 1024; i++) d i = a i + b i ; } nasm-norun add: xor eax, eax .L2: movdqu xmm0, XMMWORD PTR rdx+rax ; 16 bytes of b: four ints movdqu xmm1, XMMWORD PTR rsi+rax ; four ints of a paddd xmm0, xmm1 ; four additions at once movups XMMWORD PTR rdi+rax , xmm0 ; store four results add rax, 16 cmp rax, 4096 jne .L2 ret 256 rounds instead of 1024. ( restrict promises the arrays do not overlap; without it GCC would add a check.) A reading checklist 1. Find the arguments: rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 (32-bit names for int s). 2. Find the result: whatever ends up in rax before ret . 3. Find the loops: backward jumps to a label. 4. Name each register by what it holds (a pointer, a count, a total) and write it as a comment. 5. Look for the patterns: xor reg, reg is 0, lea is arithmetic, a magic constant is a division, cmov and set are small if s. quiz ? A function multiplies by 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD, keeps rdx and shifts right by 3. What does it compute? + An unsigned division by 10 - A multiplication by 10 - A random number Magic reciprocal division. ? Why do optimised leaf functions often have no push rbp? + They keep everything in registers and need no frame - push rbp is not allowed at -O2 - The caller saves rbp for them Frames are only built when needed. ? In GCC's sum loop, what happened to the index i? + It became a pointer moving through the array, compared with an end pointer - It is in rcx - It is on the stack Compilers do this "strength reduction" all the time. ? What does paddd xmm0, xmm1 do? + Four 32-bit additions in one instruction - One 128-bit addition - Adds two doubles Lesson 6.04 is about SIMD.

title: Dividing without div
body: Do what GCC does: divide unsigned numbers by constants with mul and a magic number, never div . mul rdi multiplies rax by rdi into rdx:rax ; the high half, rdx , is the product divided by 2⁶⁴. Function Result GCC's recipe --- --- --- udiv10(x) x ÷ 10 high half of x × 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD , then shr by 3 udiv3(x) x ÷ 3 high half of x × 0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAB , then shr by 1 urem10(x) x mod 10 x − 10 × udiv10(x), with lea for the × 10 digit_sum(x) the sum of x's decimal digits a loop using the udiv10 recipe All the numbers are unsigned 64-bit, including the largest, 18446744073709551615.

title: 6.02  Parsing and Printing Numbers
body: Now you can write the routines you have been borrowing. Parsing skips spaces, reads an optional sign, and multiplies and adds digit by digit, with any base and an overflow check. Printing divides by the base to produce digits from the right, handles the sign and the most negative number, and maps digits above 9 to letters. Parsing in any base The rule from lesson 4.05 works for every base: value = value × base + digit . Hex digits a to f (or A to F ) are worth 10 to 15. nasm-norun ; parse: rdi = a string, rsi = the base (2 to 16). ; Returns the value in rax, and in rdx a pointer to the first character it did not use. parse: xor eax, eax .next: movzx ecx, byte rdi lea edx, rcx - '0' cmp edx, 9 jbe .have ; '0'..'9' or ecx, 0x20 ; lower case lea edx, rcx - 'a' cmp edx, 5 ja .stop ; not 'a'..'f' either add edx, 10 .have: cmp rdx, rsi jae .stop ; a digit too big for this base imul rax, rsi add rax, rdx inc rdi jmp .next .stop: mov rdx, rdi ret Returning "where it stopped" lets the caller check that the whole text was a number (it should stop at the 0), just like C's strtol . Overflow imul and add silently wrap if the number is too big. A careful parser checks the overflow flag after each step: jo .too_big right after the imul , and again after the add . For unsigned numbers, check the carry flag ( jc ) after add , and use mul (which sets CF and OF when the high half is not zero). Printing in any base Printing divides by the base: each remainder is the next digit from the right. nasm global _start section .data digits: db "0123456789abcdef" section .bss out: resb 72 section .text ; print_base: rdi = an unsigned number, rsi = the base (2 to 16). Prints it. print_base: lea r8, rel out + 71 ; the end of the buffer lea r9, rel digits mov rax, rdi .digit: xor edx, edx div rsi ; rdx = the next digit, from the right movzx ecx, byte r9 + rdx ; its character, from the table mov r8 , cl dec r8 test rax, rax jnz .digit inc r8 ; the first digit lea rdx, rel out + 72 sub rdx, r8 ; the length mov rsi, r8 mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 syscall ret _start: mov edi, 3054 mov esi, 10 call print_base call print_newline mov edi, 3054 mov esi, 16 call print_base ; bee call print_newline mov edi, 3054 mov esi, 2 call print_base call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Looking digits up in a table, r9 + rdx , avoids an if for digits above 9. Signed numbers To print a signed number: if it is negative, print - and print its negation as unsigned. That even works for the most negative number, −2⁶³: neg leaves it unchanged (it has no positive twin), but read as unsigned it is 2⁶³, exactly the right digits. To parse one: remember whether there was a - , parse the digits, then neg at the end. Skipping and checking A friendly parser also skips leading spaces and tabs, and the caller decides what to do with leftovers: "12abc" stops at a , so it is not a clean number. That is all read_int does: skip spaces, check for - , parse digits, and put back the character that stopped it, for the next read. quiz ? What is the value of "1f" in base 16? + 31 - 115 - 16 1 16 + 15. ? Why does parse return where it stopped? + So the caller can tell whether all the text was a number - So it can be called again for the next digit - It must, by the calling convention Like strtol's end pointer. ? How is the most negative number printed correctly? + Negate it and print the result as unsigned - It cannot be printed - Add 1 first neg leaves it unchanged, and as unsigned it is 2 to the 63. ? Which flag shows that imul overflowed? + OF (and CF) - ZF - SF only Check it with jo.

title: A base converter
body: Read lines with read_line . Each holds one unsigned number written in decimal ( 255 ), hexadecimal ( 0xff or 0XFF ) or binary ( 0b11111111 ). Parse it yourself and print it in all three bases: 255 = 0xff = 0b11111111 For the input 255 0x1F 0b101 0 banana 0x 12z print 255 = 0xff = 0b11111111 31 = 0x1f = 0b11111 5 = 0x5 = 0b101 0 = 0x0 = 0b0 not a number: banana not a number: 0x not a number: 12z The numbers fit in 64 bits. Write your own printing too: you may use print_str and print_char for text, but not read_int , print_int , print_uint , print_hex or print_bin . One function that prints in any base (dividing by the base, with a table of digit characters) does all three.

title: 6.03  Optimisation Basics
body: Speed depends less on how many instructions run than on what they wait for. Memory is far slower than registers and caches hide it only for data used together. Chains of dependent instructions cannot overlap, wrong branch guesses cost many cycles, and division is slow. Measure with rdtsc before and after every change. What is slow A modern x86 core can start several instructions per cycle, if they do not wait for each other. Rough costs: Operation Cycles (about) --- --- add , and , mov between registers under 1 (several per cycle) imul 3 reading memory that is in the L1 cache 4 to 5 a mispredicted branch 15 to 20 div (64-bit) 20 to 40 reading memory from the L3 cache about 40 reading memory from RAM 100 to 300 The Fundamentals course explains caches: memory moves in 64-byte lines , so reading one byte brings its neighbours too. Code that walks memory in order is fast; code that jumps around a big area waits for RAM over and over. Dependency chains nasm-norun ; one running total: every add waits for the one before .loop: add rax, rdi add rdi, 8 cmp rdi, rdx jne .loop Each add rax, ... needs the previous rax , so the additions happen one after another, however many the processor could do at once. Splitting the work into independent chains lets them overlap: nasm-norun ; four running totals, combined at the end .loop: add rax, rdi add rcx, rdi + 8 add r8, rdi + 16 add r9, rdi + 24 add rdi, 32 cmp rdi, rdx jne .loop add rax, rcx add r8, r9 add rax, r8 This is loop unrolling with several accumulators: fewer loop instructions per element, and four additions in flight at once. (The count must then be a multiple of four, or the leftovers handled separately.) Measuring: rdtsc Guessing about speed is usually wrong; measure. rdtsc reads the processor's time-stamp counter, which counts up at a steady rate, into edx:eax : nasm global _start section .bss array: resq 4096 section .data s_one: db "one total: ", 0 s_four: db "four totals: ", 0 section .text _start: lea rdi, rel array ; touch the array once first, so the timings mov ecx, 4096 ; do not include the operating system .warm: mov rdi , rcx ; handing out its memory on first use add rdi, 8 dec ecx jnz .warm lea rdi, rel s_one call print_str rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx mov rbx, rax ; the start time mov r12d, 1000 ; repeat to get a measurable time .rep1: lea rdi, rel array lea rdx, rdi + 4096 8 xor eax, eax .one: add rax, rdi add rdi, 8 cmp rdi, rdx jne .one dec r12d jnz .rep1 rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx sub rax, rbx mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline lea rdi, rel s_four call print_str rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx mov rbx, rax mov r12d, 1000 .rep4: lea rdi, rel array lea rdx, rdi + 4096 8 xor eax, eax xor ecx, ecx xor r8d, r8d xor r9d, r9d .four: add rax, rdi add rcx, rdi + 8 add r8, rdi + 16 add r9, rdi + 24 add rdi, 32 cmp rdi, rdx jne .four dec r12d jnz .rep4 rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx sub rax, rbx mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The numbers are "ticks", and they change from run to run (the machine is shared, and its clock speed varies), but the second loop is usually clearly faster. Real measurements repeat many times and take the minimum. On Linux, perf stat counts cycles, cache misses and mispredicted branches for a whole program. Rules of thumb 1. Measure first. Find where the time goes before changing anything. 2. Better algorithms beat better instructions. An O(n log n) sort in C beats a hand-tuned O(n²) one in assembly. 3. Keep data together and in order. Arrays beat linked lists; walk memory forwards. 4. Avoid unpredictable branches in hot loops: cmov , setcc and arithmetic (lesson 3.05). 5. Avoid div when a shift, a mask or a multiplication will do. 6. Break dependency chains with several accumulators. 7. Use SIMD for doing the same thing to many values (next lesson). Compilers already do most of this. Hand-written assembly wins mostly where you know something the compiler cannot: that arrays never overlap, that a value is always in range, or that a special instruction exists for the job. quiz ? Why can one running total limit a loop's speed? + Each addition must wait for the previous one - Registers can only be added once per loop - Additions are slow Independent accumulators can overlap. ? About how long does reading from RAM take, compared with a register add? + Hundreds of times longer - About the same - Twice as long Caches hide it only for data used together. ? What does rdtsc give? + A time-stamp counter in edx:eax, for measuring time - The time of day - The number of instructions run Subtract two readings. ? What is usually the biggest speed-up? + A better algorithm or data layout - Replacing mov with xchg - Writing everything in assembly Measure, then fix what matters.

title: Faster code
body: Function Result How --- --- --- popcount(x) how many 1 bits x has the popcnt instruction parity(x) 1 if x has an odd number of 1 bits, else 0 popcnt , then a mask sum_fast(array, n) the total of n signed 8-byte numbers, for any n = 0 four accumulators, four elements per round, then a loop for the 0 to 3 left over count_below(array, n, limit) how many elements are less than limit (signed) no branch inside the loop: setl or cmovl and an add

title: 6.04  SIMD Many Numbers at Once
body: SIMD instructions do the same operation on several values at once. Every x86-64 processor has sixteen 128-bit xmm registers that hold 16 bytes, 8 words, 4 dwords or 2 qwords, with instructions like paddb, paddd and paddq. movdqu loads and stores 16 bytes, and a horizontal sum combines the lanes at the end. AVX widens this to 256 and 512 bits. One instruction, many values SIMD means "single instruction, multiple data". An x86-64 processor has 16 registers xmm0 to xmm15 , each 128 bits wide, and instructions that treat them as several lanes : Lanes Add Example --- --- --- 16 × 8-bit bytes paddb pixels, text 8 × 16-bit words paddw audio samples 4 × 32-bit dwords paddd int arrays 2 × 64-bit qwords paddq long arrays 4 floats / 2 doubles addps / addpd graphics, physics Every x86-64 processor has SSE2, so these always work. Each lane is separate: a carry never crosses into the next lane. Moving data in and out Instruction Does --- --- movdqu xmm0, rsi load 16 bytes from any address ("u" for unaligned) movdqu rdi , xmm0 store 16 bytes movdqa the same, but the address must be a multiple of 16 movq xmm0, rax / movq rax, xmm0 move 64 bits between a general register and the low lane pxor xmm0, xmm0 zero a vector register Adding arrays nasm global _start section .data a: dq 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 b: dq 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 section .bss c: resq 6 section .text _start: lea rsi, rel a lea rdx, rel b lea rdi, rel c xor ecx, ecx ; byte offset .loop: movdqu xmm0, rsi + rcx ; two numbers of a movdqu xmm1, rdx + rcx ; two numbers of b paddq xmm0, xmm1 ; two additions at once movdqu rdi + rcx , xmm0 add rcx, 16 cmp rcx, 6 8 jb .loop xor ebx, ebx ; print c .print: lea rax, rel c mov rdi, rax + rbx 8 call print_int mov edi, ' ' call print_char inc rbx cmp rbx, 6 jb .print call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Horizontal sum Adding up all the elements of an array uses lanes as separate running totals (like the four accumulators of lesson 6.03), then combines them at the end, a horizontal step: nasm-norun pxor xmm0, xmm0 ; two totals: 0, 0 .loop: movdqu xmm1, rdi paddq xmm0, xmm1 ; add two elements, one into each total add rdi, 16 cmp rdi, rdx jb .loop pshufd xmm1, xmm0, 0x4E ; swap the two 64-bit halves paddq xmm0, xmm1 ; now both lanes hold the sum movq rax, xmm0 pshufd rearranges the four 32-bit pieces of a register; the constant 0x4E (binary 01 00 11 10 ) picks pieces 2, 3, 0, 1, which swaps the halves. Saturation and comparisons Some SIMD instructions have no ordinary equivalent: - paddusb adds bytes with saturation : 200 + 100 gives 255 instead of wrapping to 44. Perfect for brightening pixels. - pcmpeqb compares 16 bytes at once, giving 0xFF where they are equal and 0 elsewhere, and pmovmskb turns those 16 results into 16 bits of a general register. That is how fast strlen and memchr implementations scan 16 bytes per step. - pminub , pmaxub , pavgb : lane-wise minimum, maximum, average. Wider: AVX Newer processors add AVX2 (256-bit ymm registers: 8 ints at once) and AVX-512 (512-bit zmm : 16 ints). Code must check the processor supports them first (with the cpuid instruction), which is why compilers use only SSE2 unless told -mavx2 or -march=native . ARM's version is called NEON . quiz ? How many 32-bit ints does one xmm register hold? + 4 - 2 - 8 128 bits / 32. ? What does paddq xmm0, xmm1 do? + Two separate 64-bit additions, one per lane - One 128-bit addition - Four 32-bit additions q for quad word. ? Why is movdqu used instead of movdqa for arrays from anywhere? + movdqa requires a 16-byte-aligned address - movdqu is faster - movdqa only loads u for unaligned. ? 200 + 100 with paddusb gives... + 255 - 44 - 300 Unsigned saturation stops at the maximum.

title: SIMD
body: Use the xmm registers to handle several values per instruction: Function Result --- --- add_arrays(dest, a, b, n) dest i = a i + b i for n 8-byte numbers, n even: two at a time with paddq sum_pairs(array, n) the total of n 8-byte numbers, n even: two running totals in one xmm register, then a horizontal add brighten(pixels, n) adds 50 to each of n bytes with saturation (200 becomes 250, 230 becomes 255), n a multiple of 16: paddusb brighten needs 16 bytes of 50 to add: put them in your own data, fifty: times 16 db 50 , and load them with movdqu .

title: 6.05  Beyond x86 ARM64 and Debuggers
body: ARM64, in phones and Apple-chip Macs, is a load-store design with 31 registers and fixed 4-byte instructions, so arithmetic never touches memory directly. RISC-V is a small open design built on the same ideas. A debugger such as gdb steps through instructions and shows registers and memory, and objdump shows any program's machine code. The same ideas, another instruction set You now know how a processor works: registers, memory, flags, jumps, a stack, a calling convention. Every other instruction set is a variation on these themes. The big one is ARM64 (AArch64): almost every phone, Apple-chip Macs, and a growing share of servers. ARM64 at a glance x86-64 ARM64 --- --- --- registers 16 general 31 general ( x0 to x30 , 32-bit halves w0 to w30 ) plus a zero register instruction size 1 to 15 bytes always 4 bytes memory in arithmetic yes: add rax, rdi no: only ldr (load) and str (store) touch memory operands two: add rax, rbx overwrites rax three: add x0, x1, x2 return address pushed by call kept in register x30 by bl arguments rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 x0 to x7 result rax x0 The same C function, compiled by GCC for each: c-norun long sum(const long v, long n) { long t = 0; for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) t += v i ; return t; } nasm-norun ; x86-64 sum: test rsi, rsi jle .L9 lea rdx, rdi+rsi 8 xor eax, eax .L8: add rax, QWORD PTR rdi add rdi, 8 cmp rdi, rdx jne .L8 ret .L9: xor eax, eax ret // ARM64 (GCC 15, -O2) sum: cmp x1, 0 ble .L4 mov x2, x0 // the pointer add x1, x0, x1, lsl 3 // end = v + n 8 (lsl 3: shifted left by 3) mov x0, 0 // the total, in the result register .L3: ldr x3, x2 , 8 // load v, then v += 8 add x0, x0, x3 cmp x2, x1 bne .L3 ret .L4: mov x0, 0 ret The shape is identical: a test in front, a rotated loop, a moving pointer. ARM64 loads into a register first ( ldr with "post-increment", moving the pointer in the same instruction), then adds. Fixed-size instructions and load-store design make the processor's job of decoding easier, which is part of why ARM chips are so power-efficient. x86 chips do the same internally: they translate x86 instructions into simpler micro-operations. RISC-V is a newer open instruction set in the same style, free for anyone to build: 32 registers, lw / sw to load and store, add a0, a0, a1 . It appears in microcontrollers, storage drives and research chips, and anyone can design a RISC-V processor without a licence. Debuggers A debugger runs a program under control: stop at an instruction, step one at a time, look at registers and memory. On Linux, gdb : nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf program.asm -o program.o -g: debugging information ld program.o -o program gdb ./program (gdb) layout asm show the instructions (gdb) break _start stop at _start (gdb) run (gdb) stepi one instruction (nexti steps over calls) (gdb) info registers rax rbx rsp (gdb) x/16xb $rsp 16 bytes at rsp, in hex (gdb) x/s &message a string in memory (gdb) backtrace the chain of return addresses (gdb) continue The demos in this course do what stepi and info registers do. On Windows, Visual Studio and WinDbg have the same features; on macOS, lldb . Looking inside any program objdump -d -M intel /bin/ls less disassembles a real program: every instruction with its address and machine-code bytes. You can now read it. That is the starting point of reverse engineering, malware analysis and security research, and of understanding exactly what your own compiler produced. Where next - Read compiler output for code you write in C, C++ or Rust: Compiler Explorer with -O2 . - The Intel and AMD manuals (free) describe every instruction; Agner Fog's optimisation guides and instruction tables give real timings. - Write an operating system : the OSDev wiki starts from a boot sector in assembly. - Try ARM64 or RISC-V with QEMU, an emulator that runs other instruction sets on your computer. quiz ? Which ARM64 instructions are the only ones that touch memory? + Loads and stores, such as ldr and str - All of them - add and sub It is a load-store design. ? Where does ARM64's bl keep the return address? + In register x30 (the link register) - On the stack - In x0 A function that calls others saves x30 itself. ? What does gdb's stepi do? + Runs exactly one machine instruction - Runs to the end of the function - Steps one line of C nexti steps over calls. ? What does objdump -d show? + The machine code of a program, disassembled into instructions - The program's source code - The program's output Every program is readable at this level.

title: From ARM64 to x86-64
body: GCC compiled four C functions for ARM64 . Read them, work out what they do, and write the same functions for x86-64. ARM64 reminders: arguments arrive in x0 , x1 , x2 , and the result goes back in x0 . Instructions have three operands: sub x0, x0, x2 means x0 = x0 − x2. ldr x3, x2 , 8 loads the 8 bytes at x2 into x3, then adds 8 to x2. lsl 3 and lsr 63 shift an operand left by 3 or right by 63 on the way in. csel x0, x1, x0, ge picks x1 if the last comparison said "greater or equal", otherwise x0; csneg x0, x0, x0, ge picks x0 if "greater or equal", otherwise its negation. mystery1: mul x0, x0, x1 sub x0, x0, x2 ret mystery2: cmp x0, 0 csneg x0, x0, x0, ge ret mystery3: cmp x1, 0 ble .L8 mov x2, x0 add x1, x0, x1, lsl 3 mov x0, 0 .L7: ldr x3, x2 , 8 add x0, x0, x3, lsr 63 cmp x1, x2 bne .L7 ret .L8: mov x0, 0 ret mystery5: cmp x1, x0 csel x0, x1, x0, ge ret

title: An RPN calculator
body: Build a calculator for Reverse Polish Notation , where the operator comes after its numbers: 3 4 + is 7, and 3 4 + 2 is (3 + 4) × 2. No brackets are needed, and it is exactly how a stack works: numbers are pushed, and an operator pops two, works them out, and pushes the answer. Old HP calculators and the Forth and PostScript languages work this way, and so does the Java virtual machine. Read lines until the input ends. Each line is one calculation of tokens separated by spaces; print its result, or an error: 3 4 + 3 4 + 2 10 3 - -7 2 / -7 2 % 2 3 4 + 5 0 / 1 + 1 2 4 x prints 7 14 7 -3 -1 14 error: division by zero error: not enough numbers error: 2 numbers left error: unknown token x Token Does --- --- a whole number, perhaps with a - in front pushes it + - / pops b, then a, and pushes a + b, a − b, a × b, a ÷ b (rounded towards zero) % the remainder, with the sign of a, as in C dup pushes a copy of the top number swap swaps the top two - A line ends with exactly one number on the stack: print it. More than one: error: N numbers left . None (an empty line): print nothing. - An operator with fewer than two numbers (one for dup ): error: not enough numbers . Dividing by zero: error: division by zero . Anything else: error: unknown token and the token. After an error, skip the rest of the line. - A lone - is subtraction; - followed by digits is a negative number. - At most 100 numbers on the stack, and lines of at most 200 characters.

title: Cheat Sheet - Instructions
body: Intel syntax, NASM: the destination comes first. r is a register, m memory, imm a constant. Registers 64 32 16 8 System V role --- --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al result; system call number rbx ebx bx bl kept by calls rcx ecx cx cl 4th argument; shift count rdx edx dx dl 3rd argument; high half of mul and div rsi esi si sil 2nd argument rdi edi di dil 1st argument rbp ebp bp bpl kept by calls; frame base rsp esp sp spl stack pointer r8 , r9 r8d r8w r8b 5th, 6th arguments r10 , r11 scratch ( syscall changes r11 and rcx ) r12 to r15 r12d r12w r12b kept by calls Writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper 32 bits; writing 8 or 16 bits leaves the rest. Moving data Instruction Does --- --- mov r, r/m/imm · mov m, r/imm copy movzx r, byte/word m widen with 0s movsx r, byte/word m · movsxd r64, dword m widen with the sign lea r, address compute an address (or arithmetic) without reading memory xchg a, b swap push r/imm · pop r the stack: rsp −8 then store · load then rsp +8 cmovcc r, r/m copy if the condition holds setcc r8 1 or 0 by the condition Arithmetic and logic Instruction Does Flags --- --- --- add · sub a ± b all adc · sbb with the carry all inc · dec ± 1 all but CF neg −a all imul r, r/m · imul r, r/m, imm low 64 bits of a product CF, OF mul r/m · imul r/m rdx:rax = rax × operand CF, OF div r/m · idiv r/m rdx:rax ÷ operand: quotient rax , remainder rdx (prepare rdx with xor edx, edx or cqo ) and · or · xor · not bitwise (not: none) shl · shr · sar · rol · ror shifts and rotates, by imm or cl cmp a, b a − b, flags only all test a, b a AND b, flags only all popcnt r, r/m count the 1 bits bt · bts · btr · btc test, set, clear, flip one bit CF Jumps and calls Instruction Does --- --- jmp label · jmp m always (directly or through a table) je / jz · jne / jnz equal / not equal jl · jle · jg · jge signed comparisons jb · jbe · ja · jae unsigned comparisons js · jns · jo · jc sign, overflow, carry call label push the return address, jump ret pop the return address into rip syscall ask the kernel: number in rax , arguments rdi , rsi , rdx , r10 , r8 , r9 Memory base + index scale + displacement scale = 1, 2, 4 or 8 rel label relative to rip byte / word / dword / qword ... 1, 2, 4, 8 bytes String instructions, repeated rcx times with rep : movsb (copy rsi to rdi ), stosb (store al at rdi ). SIMD (SSE2, 128-bit xmm0 to xmm15) movdqu xmm, m · movdqu m, xmm · pxor · paddb / paddw / paddd / paddq · psubd · paddusb (saturating) · pcmpeqb · pminub · pmaxub · pshufd xmm, xmm, imm · movq r64, xmm Data and sections nasm-norun section .data ; data with starting values x: dq 42 ; db 1 byte, dw 2, dd 4, dq 8 s: db "text", 10, 0 n equ $ - s ; a constant: the bytes since s times 8 db 0 ; repeat section .rodata ; read-only data section .bss ; zeroed space buf: resb 256 ; resw, resd, resq section .text ; code global _start _start: System calls (Linux x86-64) rax Call Arguments --- --- --- 0 read rdi = file, rsi = buffer, rdx = most bytes 1 write rdi = file, rsi = bytes, rdx = how many 60 exit rdi = exit code Files: 0 standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. A failing call returns −error in rax .

title: Cheat Sheet - Routines
body: When a program calls one of these and does not define it itself, the website adds its code to the end of the program before assembling. They follow the System V calling convention: arguments in rdi , rsi ; result in rax ; rbx , rbp , rsp and r12 to r15 are kept, everything else may change. Routine Arguments Does --- --- --- print_str rdi = address of a zero-terminated string prints it print_char dil = a character prints it print_newline prints a new line print_int rdi = a signed number prints it in decimal print_uint rdi = an unsigned number prints it in decimal print_hex rdi = a number prints 0x and lower-case hex digits print_bin rdi = a number, rsi = bits (1 to 64) prints that many of its lowest bits read_int skips spaces and new lines, reads a whole number: rax = it, rdx = 1; at the end of the input both are 0 read_char rax = the next character, or −1 at the end read_line rdi = buffer, rsi = its size reads one line without its new line and adds a 0; rax = its length, or −1 at the end Don't mix read_int , read_char and read_line with your own read system calls: the routines read ahead and keep bytes for later. How they are written The output routines all end in one helper that makes the write system call: nasm-norun ;; xenon_write: rsi = bytes, rdx = how many. Writes them all to standard output. xenon_write: push rbx push r12 mov rbx, rsi mov r12, rdx .more: test r12, r12 jle .done mov eax, 1 ; system call 1: write mov edi, rel xenon_fd ; normally 1 mov rsi, rbx mov rdx, r12 syscall test rax, rax jle .done ; an error: give up quietly add rbx, rax ; write may do only part: carry on from there sub r12, rax jmp .more .done: pop r12 pop rbx ret ;; print_str: rdi = the address of a zero-terminated string. print_str: mov rsi, rdi xor edx, edx .len: cmp byte rsi + rdx , 0 je .go inc rdx jmp .len .go: jmp xenon_write ; a tail call: xenon_write's ret returns for us ;; print_uint: rdi = an unsigned number, printed in decimal. print_uint: sub rsp, 40 lea rsi, rsp + 32 ; digits are written backwards from here mov rax, rdi mov ecx, 10 .digit: xor edx, edx div rcx ; rax = rax / 10, rdx = the last digit add dl, '0' dec rsi mov rsi , dl test rax, rax jnz .digit lea rdx, rsp + 32 sub rdx, rsi call xenon_write add rsp, 40 ret ;; print_int: rdi = a signed number. print_int: test rdi, rdi jns print_uint ; not negative: print it as it is push rdi mov edi, '-' call print_char pop rdi neg rdi ; the most negative number stays itself, and prints right as unsigned jmp print_uint read_int reads its input in 4096-byte pieces with the read system call, keeps a position in that buffer, and puts back the character after a number so the next read sees it. Lesson 6.02 builds the same pieces yourself.

title: Common Errors
body: From the assembler (NASM) Message Usual cause --- --- invalid combination of opcode and operands the operands do not fit the instruction: different sizes ( mov eax, rbx ), two memory operands, a constant as the destination, or div 10 (the divisor must be a register or memory) operation size not specified neither operand is a register, so write the size: mov qword rdi , 0 symbol 'x' not defined a misspelt label, a local .label used from another function, or a routine name typed wrong label 'x' inconsistently redefined / symbol 'x' redefined the same label twice; use local labels ( .done ) inside functions expression syntax error , or label, instruction or prefix expected at start of line often a label or function named after a NASM keyword (see below) impossible combination of address sizes mixing 32- and 64-bit registers in one address: rdi + ecx 4 invalid effective address a scale other than 1, 2, 4 or 8, or rsp as the index parser: instruction expected a typo in an instruction, or a label without its colon Names NASM keeps for itself Some words cannot be used as labels or function names, because NASM reads them as keywords. Ones that catch people out: abs , absolute , times , byte , word , dword , qword , rel , seg , wrt , section , global , extern , align , struc , and the register names. Choose another name: abs_value , multiply , text . From the linker (ld) Message Means --- --- cannot find entry symbol _start no _start label, or it is not global (the website adds global _start for you) undefined reference to 'x' called but never defined, such as a misspelt routine relocation truncated to fit a 32-bit address form used for a label that is too far away: use rel label and lea When it runs What you see Usual cause --- --- Segmentation fault (exit code 139) reading or writing an address that is not yours: a register used as a pointer that holds a number, a missing rel ... , a store into .text or .rodata , or running off the end of the program because the exit system call is missing Floating point exception (exit code 136) div or idiv by zero, or a quotient too big because rdx was not cleared ( xor edx, edx ) or sign-filled ( cqo ) first a crash right after ret the stack was not left as it was: a push without its pop , or rsp changed and not restored a test says "changed rbx" (or rbp, r12 to r15) the function used a callee-saved register without saving it with push and restoring it with pop a value disappears after call print_int it was in a scratch register ( rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 to r11 ); keep it in rbx or r12 to r15 a loop never ends the counter is changed by a call inside the loop, or the jump goes to the wrong label a comparison seems backwards a signed jump ( jl , jg ) used for unsigned values, or the other way round; or the flags were changed between the cmp and the jump garbage in the upper half of a result an 8- or 16-bit write ( mov al, ... ) left the rest of the register as it was: clear it first or use movzx

title: Glossary
body: The terms from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Accumulator A register that collects a running total; several independent ones let additions overlap. (6.03) Address The number of a byte in memory. A label is one. (1.05, 4.01) Addressing mode A way to form an address: base + index × scale + displacement, or relative to rip. (4.01) Alignment Being at an address that is a multiple of some size; the stack must be 16-aligned at a call. (5.02) ARM64 The instruction set of phones and Apple-chip Macs: 31 registers, fixed 4-byte instructions, load-store. (6.05) Assembler The program that turns assembly into machine code: NASM here. (1.01) AT&T syntax The other way of writing x86 assembly, source first: movl $1, %eax . GCC's default. (1.01, 5.05) AVX Wider SIMD with 256-bit ymm and 512-bit zmm registers. (6.04) Backtrace The chain of return addresses on the stack, as a debugger shows it. (5.01) Branch prediction The processor guessing which way a jump will go and working ahead. (3.05) .bss The section of zeroed space reserved with resb and friends. (1.05) Callee-saved Registers a function must give back unchanged: rbx, rbp, rsp, r12 to r15. (5.02) Caller-saved Registers any call may change: rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, r8 to r11. (5.02) Calling convention The agreement on where arguments and results go and which registers survive a call. (5.02) Carry flag (CF) Set when an unsigned result wrapped around. (2.04) cmov A conditional move: copies only if a condition holds, with no jump. (3.05) cqo Fills rdx with the sign of rax, before idiv. (2.02) Debugger A program that runs another one step by step: gdb, lldb, WinDbg. (6.05) Dependency chain Instructions that each need the previous result, so they cannot overlap. (6.03) Directive An instruction to the assembler, not the processor: db, section, global, equ. (1.05) Displacement The constant part of an address. (4.01) ELF The file format of Linux programs. (1.01) Epilogue The end of a function that undoes its prologue: leave, ret. (5.03) equ Names a constant number. (1.05) Exit code The number a program hands to the exit system call; 0 means success. (1.03) Flags Single bits in rflags recording facts about the last result: ZF, SF, CF, OF. (2.04) Frame A function call's part of the stack: return address, saved registers, locals. (5.03) Horizontal sum Adding up the lanes of a SIMD register. (6.04) Immediate A constant written in an instruction: mov eax, 42 . (1.03) Intel syntax Destination first, no prefixes: mov eax, 1 . Used by NASM and this course. (1.01) Jump table An array of addresses for an indirect jump: a fast switch. (3.04) Kernel The core of the operating system, reached by system calls. (1.04) Label A name for an address. (1.01) Lane One of the values side by side in a SIMD register. (6.04) lea Load effective address: computes an address without reading memory. (4.01) Leaf function A function that calls no other functions. (5.02) Linker Joins object files into a program: ld here. (1.01) Little-endian Storing the lowest byte of a number first, as x86 does. (1.05) Local label A label starting with a dot, belonging to the label above it. (3.01) Machine code The bytes a processor runs. (1.01) Magic number division Dividing by a constant by multiplying with its reciprocal and shifting. (6.01) Mnemonic An instruction's name, such as mov or add. (1.01) NASM The Netwide Assembler, used in this course. (1.01) Overflow flag (OF) Set when a signed result is wrong because it did not fit. (2.04) Prologue The start of a function that builds its frame: push rbp, mov rbp, rsp. (5.03) Red zone 128 bytes below rsp that a leaf function may use on Linux. (5.02) Register A small storage slot inside the processor. (1.02) Return address The address call pushes and ret jumps back to. (5.01) rip The instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction. (1.02) RISC-V An open instruction set in the load-store style. (6.05) rsp The stack pointer: the address of the top of the stack. (4.04) Saturation Arithmetic that stops at the largest or smallest value instead of wrapping. (6.04) Section A part of the program: .text, .data, .rodata, .bss. (1.05) setcc Sets a byte to 1 or 0 by a condition. (3.05) Shadow space 32 bytes a caller reserves on the stack in the Windows convention. (5.05) Sign flag (SF) Set when a result's top bit is 1. (2.04) SIMD Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction working on several lanes. (6.04) Stack Memory that grows downwards, used for return addresses, saved registers and locals. (4.04) Stack overflow Running past the end of the stack, usually by recursing too deep. (5.04) System call A request to the operating system with the syscall instruction. (1.04) System V AMD64 The calling convention of Linux and macOS. (5.02) Two's complement The way negative numbers are stored, which lets one add serve signed and unsigned. (2.01) Unrolling Doing several rounds of a loop's work per jump. (6.03) x86-64 The 64-bit instruction set of most PCs and servers, also called x64 and AMD64. (1.01) xmm registers The 16 SIMD registers of 128 bits. (6.04) Zero flag (ZF) Set when a result is 0. (2.04)

title: 1.01  C and How It Builds
body:
C is a small, fast language close to the machine, created in 1972 to write Unix. A C program is text that a compiler turns into machine code in steps - preprocess, compile, assemble, link - and every program starts in a function called main. Why C C was created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1972 to write the Unix operating system (the Computer Fundamentals course tells the story in lesson 5.04). Fifty years later it is still everywhere: - operating system kernels: Linux, and the cores of Windows and macOS; - small chips in cars, washing machines, routers and medical devices; - databases (SQLite, PostgreSQL), and the interpreters of other languages: Python's main interpreter is written in C . C is small - the whole language fits in a short book - and it is close to the machine: you decide exactly how much memory each value takes and where it lives. That makes it fast and powerful, and also unforgiving: C trusts you, and does not stop you from making a mistake. This course teaches the power and the care together. The first program c include <stdio.h int main(void) { printf("Hello, world!
"); return 0; } Press Run . Line by line: Line Meaning --- --- include <stdio.h Bring in the declarations of the standard input/output functions, such as printf int main(void) Every C program starts in the function main . It takes nothing ( void ) and gives back an int { ... } The body of the function printf("Hello, world!
"); Print the text. 
 is a new line. Every statement ends with ; return 0; Finish, telling the operating system "all went well" (0). Any other number means something went wrong How C becomes a program C is a compiled language: before it runs, a compiler turns the text into machine code. It happens in four steps: 1. Preprocess : lines starting with are handled first. include <stdio.h is replaced by the contents of that header file. 2. Compile : the C code is translated into assembly for your CPU. 3. Assemble : the assembly becomes machine code, in an object file . 4. Link : your object file is joined with the libraries it uses (the machine code of printf lives in the C standard library) into one program. On your own computer you would run one command, which does all four: bash gcc hello.c -o hello or: clang hello.c -o hello ./hello On Windows with Visual Studio the command is cl hello.c . On this site, pressing Run does it for you with GCC. Compiler errors and warnings When the compiler cannot understand the code, it stops with an error and the line number. When the code is valid but suspicious, it gives a warning and builds anyway. Treat warnings as errors you have not met yet: most of them point at a real bug. c-norun include <stdio.h int main(void) { printf("Hello, world!
") // error: expected ';' before 'return' return 0; } The error is reported on the line after the missing semicolon, because that is where the compiler noticed. When an error makes no sense, look at the line above. Comments c include <stdio.h / A comment can span several lines like this. / int main(void) { // and this kind runs to the end of the line printf("Comments are ignored by the compiler.
"); return 0; } quiz ? Where does every C program start running? - At the first line of the file + In the function main - In stdio.h The operating system calls main. ? What does include <stdio.h do? + Before compiling, it inserts the declarations of the standard input/output functions, such as printf - It downloads a library from the internet - It starts the program The preprocessor replaces the line with the header's contents. ? What does return 0; at the end of main tell the operating system? + The program finished successfully - The program printed nothing - To run the program again 0 means success; other values mean an error. ? Which step joins your code with the code of printf? - Preprocessing - Assembling + Linking printf's machine code lives in the C standard library; the linker joins them.
