title: 6.05  Building a Hash Table
body: A hash table finds a value by its key in about constant time. A hash function turns the key into a number, which picks a bucket in an array; keys that land in the same bucket are chained in a short linked list. When the table gets too full it grows and every entry moves to its new bucket. It is the structure behind Python's dict. Looking things up fast Finding a word in an unsorted array means checking every element: with a million words, a million comparisons. A sorted array with binary search needs about 20. A hash table needs about one . The idea: turn the key into a number with a hash function , and use that number (modulo the table size) as an index into an array of buckets . A hash function A good hash function spreads keys evenly, so similar keys land far apart. FNV-1a is short and decent: c include <stdint.h include <stdio.h uint32_t hash_fnv1a(const char key) { uint32_t h = 2166136261u; // the FNV offset basis for (const unsigned char p = (const unsigned char )key; p; p++) { h ^= p; h = 16777619u; // the FNV prime; unsigned, so overflow wraps safely } return h; } int main(void) { const char words = {"cat", "cats", "act", "dog"}; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { uint32_t h = hash_fnv1a(words i ); printf("%-5s %10u bucket %u of 8\n", words i , h, h % 8); } return 0; } cat and cats differ by one letter but get completely different hashes. That is what a good hash function does. Collisions: chaining Two keys can land in the same bucket: a collision . The simplest fix is separate chaining : each bucket holds a linked list (lesson 4.05) of the entries that landed there. c-norun struct entry { char key; // our own copy of the text int value; struct entry next; // the next entry in the same bucket }; struct table { struct entry buckets; // an array of list heads size_t bucket_count; size_t size; // entries stored }; - Find : hash the key, walk that bucket's list comparing keys with strcmp . - Insert : find first; if the key exists, update its value; otherwise push a new entry on the front of the bucket's list. - Remove : unlink from the bucket's list, with the pointer-to-link trick from lesson 4.05, and free the key and the entry. Keeping it fast: the load factor The load factor is entries ÷ buckets. While it stays below about 1, each list is short and every operation is about one step. When it passes a limit (often 0.75 or 1), the table grows : allocate twice as many buckets and move every entry to hash % new_count . Each entry moves only now and then, so on average insertion stays constant time, the same argument as the doubling array in lesson 4.02. Ownership The table should copy the keys it stores, because the caller's text may be a buffer that gets reused for the next line of input. That means the table also frees them: one table_free walks every bucket, frees each key and entry, then frees the bucket array. Where they are Python's dict and set , JavaScript objects and Map , C++'s unordered_map , Rust's HashMap , database indexes, compiler symbol tables, caches: hash tables everywhere. Many use open addressing instead of chaining (a collision tries the next free slot in the array itself), which keeps everything in one block of memory and suits caches better. The project at the end of this module is a word counter built on your own table. !note Attacks on hash tables If an attacker can choose keys that all hash to the same bucket, every lookup becomes a long list walk and a server slows to a crawl. Languages defend against this with seeded hash functions (SipHash in Python and Rust) whose results depend on a random secret chosen at startup. quiz ? What is a collision in a hash table? + Two different keys landing in the same bucket - Two equal keys being inserted - The table running out of memory Chaining keeps both in that bucket's list. ? What is the load factor? + Entries divided by buckets - Buckets divided by entries - The size of the hash Keep it low by growing the table. ? Why must a hash table store its own copy of each key string? + The caller's buffer may be changed or reused after inserting - strcmp needs a copy - To make hashing faster And then the table must free those copies. ? Why use unsigned arithmetic inside a hash function? + Unsigned overflow wraps around and is well defined - It is faster than signed - Hash values must be positive Signed overflow would be undefined behaviour.

title: A hash table
body: Build a hash table from strings to ints with separate chaining. The types and the hash function are given; write the rest in solution.c : c struct entry { char key; int value; struct entry next; }; struct table { struct entry buckets; size_t bucket_count; size_t size; }; bool table_init(struct table t, size_t bucket_count); / all buckets empty (calloc) / bool table_put(struct table t, const char key, int value); / updates the value if the key exists, otherwise adds an entry with its OWN copy of the key. After adding, if size bucket_count, grow to twice as many buckets. / bool table_get(const struct table t, const char key, int value); / false if absent / bool table_remove(struct table t, const char key); void table_free(struct table t); / frees everything; the table becomes empty / A key goes in bucket hash(key) % bucket_count . Growing means allocating the new bucket array and moving every existing entry (no copying of keys) into its new bucket.

title: A word counter
where: C Close to the Machine projects
body: Count how often every word appears in a text, using a hash table you write yourself, and print the most common ones. For The cat sat on the mat. The dog sat on the cat! "Cats?" said the dog. print 16 words, 8 different the 5 cat 2 dog 2 on 2 sat 2 cats 1 mat 1 said 1 The rules: - A word is a run of letters ( isalpha ), turned into lower case. Everything else separates words, so don't is the two words don and t . Words longer than 63 letters are cut to their first 63. - The first line is N words, M different . With no words at all, print 0 words, 0 different and nothing else. - Then the top 10 words (or fewer), most common first, ties in alphabetical order, as "%-10s %d " followed by one per occurrence, but never more than 40 . - The input can be any size: the table must grow.

title: Cheat Sheet - C Syntax
body:
A program c-norun include <stdio.h int main(void) { printf("Hello, C!
"); return 0; } Types Type Usual size printf scanf --- --- --- --- char 1 byte %c " %c" int 4 bytes %d %d unsigned 4 bytes %u ( %x hex) %u long long 8 bytes %lld %lld double 8 bytes %f , %.2f , %g %lf size_t 8 bytes %zu %zu char (string) 8 bytes %s %63s (with a width!) any pointer 8 bytes %p with (void ) uint32_t etc. exact "%" PRIu32 "%" SCNu32 printf widths: %5d (right-aligned in 5), %-10s (left-aligned in 10), %05d (zero-padded), %.3f (3 decimals), %08x . Operators, highest precedence first --- --- () - . x++ x-- call, index, member ! ~ -x p &x ++x sizeof (type) one operand / % multiply, divide, remainder + - << shifts < <= = == != & then ^ then \ bitwise && then \ \ logical, short-circuit ?: conditional = += -= = /= %= &= \ = ^= <<= = assignment When in doubt, add parentheses: (flags & MASK) == 0 . Control flow c-norun if (a b) { ... } else if (a == b) { ... } else { ... } switch (c) { case 'a': ...; break; case 'b': case 'c': ...; break; default: ...; break; } while (condition) { ... } do { ... } while (condition); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... } break; // leave the loop continue; // next round Functions c-norun int add(int a, int b); // prototype (declaration) int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } void swap(int a, int b); // change the caller's variables static int helper(void); // private to this file int ( op)(int, int) = add; // function pointer Arrays and strings c-norun int a 5 = {1, 2, 3}; // rest are 0 size_t n = sizeof a / sizeof a 0 ; // only where a is declared char name 32 = "Ada"; // 4 bytes used: 'A' 'd' 'a' '\0' const char literal = "read-only"; fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin); // read a line, keeps the '
' line strcspn(line, "
") = '\0'; // remove it snprintf(out, sizeof out, "%s-%d", s, n); strcmp(a, b) == 0 // equal strings Pointers c-norun int x = 5; int p = &x; // p holds x's address p = 6; // x is now 6 p i // the same as (p + i) const int r; // cannot change r int const q = &x; // cannot change q int pp = &p; // pointer to a pointer Heap memory c-norun int v = malloc(n sizeof v); if (v == NULL) { / out of memory / } int bigger = realloc(v, 2 n sizeof v); if (bigger != NULL) v = bigger; free(v); v = NULL; Structures c-norun struct point { double x, y; }; typedef struct node { int value; struct node next; } Node; struct point p = {.x = 1, .y = 2}; p.x = 3; struct point pp = &p; pp- y = 4; // ( pp).y enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; Files c-norun FILE f = fopen("data.txt", "r"); // "w" "a" "rb" "wb" if (f == NULL) { perror("data.txt"); return 1; } fgets(line, sizeof line, f); fprintf(f, "%d
", n); fread(buffer, sizeof buffer 0 , count, f); fwrite(buffer, sizeof buffer 0 , count, f); fclose(f); Preprocessor c-norun include <stdio.h // system header include "mine.h" // your header define MAX 100 define SQUARE(x) ((x) (x)) ifndef MINE_H define MINE_H ... endif Building by hand gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -g main.c other.c -o program -lm gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g main.c -o program memory checks gcc -O2 main.c -o program optimised gcc -S -masm=intel main.c see the assembly

title: Common Errors
body: GCC's messages name the file, line and column: main.c:7:12: error: ... . Fix the first error first: later ones are often caused by it. Compiler errors Message Usual cause --- --- expected ';' before ... a missing semicolon at the end of the line before 'x' undeclared a misspelt name, a variable used outside its scope, or a missing include implicit declaration of function 'foo' no prototype before the call: include the header, or declare it higher up conflicting types for 'foo' the prototype and the definition disagree incompatible types when assigning assigning, say, a struct to an int, or an array to an array lvalue required as left operand of assignment assigning to something that is not a variable: 5 = x , a + b = c subscripted value is neither array nor pointer using on a plain number invalid type argument of unary ' ' dereferencing something that is not a pointer request for member 'x' in something not a structure . on a pointer (use - ), or a typo too few arguments to function the call does not match the declaration expected declaration or statement at end of input a missing closing } missing terminating " character a string not closed on the same line Warnings worth fixing Warning Means --- --- 'x' is used uninitialized reading a local before giving it a value: garbage format '%d' expects argument of type 'int', but argument 2 has type 'double' the printf letter does not match the value suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value if (x = 5) : you meant == comparison of integer expressions of different signedness int compared with size_t ; negative numbers break it control reaches end of non-void function a path that returns no value function returns address of local variable a dangling pointer passing argument 1 of 'f' discards 'const' qualifier handing read-only data to a function that may change it unused variable 'x' leftover code, or a typo using another name this statement may fall through a case without break array subscript N is above array bounds an index past the end that the compiler could see Linker errors Message Means --- --- undefined reference to 'foo' declared but never defined, or the file defining it was not built in undefined reference to 'sqrt' the maths library is missing: add -lm multiple definition of 'x' a variable or function defined in a header included by two files: declare it extern there undefined reference to 'main' no main function, or it is misspelt When it runs What you see Usual cause --- --- Segmentation fault (exit code 139) following NULL or a garbage pointer, an index far out of range, or a stack overflow from endless recursion Floating point exception (exit code 136) integer division or remainder by zero Aborted (exit code 134) a failed assert , a double free, or heap corruption detected by free strange characters after a string a missing '\0' terminator a loop that never ends the condition never becomes false, or scanf keeps failing on the same bad input numbers suddenly negative or tiny integer overflow: use a bigger type or check first heap-buffer-overflow , heap-use-after-free (Memory checks on) exactly what they say; the report gives the line runtime error: signed integer overflow (Memory checks on) undefined behaviour caught by the sanitizer

title: Glossary
body: The terms from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- AddressSanitizer A compiler option ( -fsanitize=address ) that checks every memory access and reports the first bad one. On the website: Memory checks. (4.06) Address The number of a byte in memory. &x gives the address of x . (3.01) Alignment Placing a value at an address that is a multiple of its size, which the processor reads fastest. (4.03) Amortised Averaged over many operations: a growing array's push is constant time on average even though it sometimes copies. (4.02) argc / argv The number of command-line words and the array of them, passed to main . (3.05) Array A fixed number of values of one type, side by side in memory. (2.04) assert A check that stops the program with a message if a condition is false. (5.04) Big-endian Storing the most significant byte of a number first. (5.02) Bitwise operator & \ ^ ~ << : operators that work on each bit separately. (5.01) Buffer overflow Writing past the end of an array into whatever memory follows. (2.04) Bucket One slot of a hash table, holding the entries whose hash leads there. (6.05) Callback A function passed to another function to be called by it. (6.01) calloc Allocates heap memory set to zero. (4.01) Capacity How many elements a growing array has room for, as opposed to its length. (4.02) Cast Converting a value to another type explicitly: (double)n . (1.04) Collision Two keys landing in the same bucket of a hash table. (6.05) Compiler The program that turns C source into machine code. (1.01) const Marks something read-only; const T p cannot change what it points at. (3.04) Dangling pointer A pointer to memory that has been freed or to a local that no longer exists. (3.03) Declaration Tells the compiler a name and its type: a prototype or an extern variable. (2.02) Definition Creates the thing itself: a function's body or a variable's storage. Exactly one per program. (5.05) Dereference Following a pointer to the value it points at: p . (3.01) Double free Freeing the same heap block twice. (4.01) enum A type whose values are named integer constants. (4.04) EOF The value input functions return at the end of the input. (2.01) errno A variable library functions set to an error code when they fail. (5.03) Exit code The number main returns: 0 for success. (1.01) extern Declares a variable defined in another file. (5.05) FILE The type of an open stream: a file, or stdin , stdout , stderr . (5.03) Function pointer A variable holding the address of a function, which can be called through it. (6.01) Hash function Turns a key into a number used to pick a bucket. (6.05) Hash table A structure that finds values by key in about constant time. (6.05) Header file A .h file of declarations that other files include . (5.05) Heap Memory allocated with malloc that lasts until free . (4.01) Include guard ifndef / define / endif around a header so it only counts once. (5.04) Inlining The optimiser pasting a function's body where it is called. (6.03) Linked list A chain of nodes, each pointing to the next. (4.05) Linker Joins object files and libraries into a program, matching calls to definitions. (1.01, 5.05) Little-endian Storing the least significant byte first, as x86 and ARM do. (5.02) Load factor Entries divided by buckets in a hash table. (6.05) Macro A define name the preprocessor replaces with text, possibly with parameters. (5.04) malloc / free Allocate and release heap memory. (4.01) Mask A number with 1 bits where you want to test, set or clear. (5.01) Memory leak Heap memory that is never freed. (4.01) NULL The pointer that points at nothing. (3.01) Object file A .o file: one compiled source file, not yet linked. (5.05) Off-by-one A loop or index that goes one too far or stops one short. (2.01) Optimiser The part of the compiler that makes code faster at -O2 . (6.03) Padding Unused bytes the compiler puts in a struct to keep fields aligned. (4.03) Pointer A variable holding an address. (3.01) Pointer arithmetic Adding to a pointer moves it by whole elements: p + 1 is the next one. (3.02) Preprocessor The first build stage, which handles lines starting with . (5.04) Prototype A function's first line ending in a semicolon, declaring it. (2.02) qsort The standard library's sort, given a comparison function. (6.01) realloc Resizes a heap block, moving it if needed. (4.02) Recursion A function calling itself. (2.02) Scope Where in the code a name can be used. (2.03) Segmentation fault The crash when a program touches memory it does not own. (3.01) Shadowing A local hiding an outer variable of the same name. (2.03) Short-circuit && and \ \ stopping as soon as the answer is known. (1.05) size_t The unsigned type for sizes and counts, printed with %zu . (2.04) sizeof Gives the size of a type or object in bytes. (1.02) Stack frame The memory a function call gets for its parameters and locals. (2.02) static On a local: keeps its value between calls. On a global or function: private to its file. (2.03) stdint.h The header with exact-width types like uint8_t and int64_t . (5.02) String An array of char ending in '\0' . (2.05) struct A type grouping named fields. (4.03) Tagged union A union with an enum saying which member is in use. (4.04) Terminator The zero byte '\0' that ends a string. (2.05) typedef Gives a type another name. (4.04) Undefined behaviour Code the C standard sets no rules for, such as signed overflow; anything may happen. (6.02) union A type whose members share the same memory. (4.04) Use after free Using heap memory after it was freed. (4.01) Valgrind A Linux tool that checks an unchanged program's memory use. (4.06) void \ A pointer to anything, which must be converted before use. (3.01) Warning A compiler message about legal but suspicious code. Treat them as errors. (1.01)

title: 1.01  How C++ Works
body: You write text (source code). A compiler translates it into machine code . A linker joins the pieces into one program that your computer runs directly. The big picture A computer's processor (the CPU) understands only numbers. Nobody wants to write programs as long lists of numbers, so we write them in a language people can read, and a tool translates that into the numbers the processor needs. C++ is one of those languages. The translating happens before the program runs. Step What it does Think of it as --- --- --- You write Type instructions into a text file ending in .cpp Writing a recipe Compiler Checks the file follows the rules of C++ and translates it Translating the recipe into the cook's language Linker Joins your translated code with ready-made library code Binding the chapters into one book Run The finished program starts Cooking You will hear three words constantly. They are worth learning now: - Source code : the text you write. - Build (or compile ): turn source code into a program. This is both steps above, compiler then linker. - Run : start the program that was built. Why translate ahead of time? Some languages, such as Python, are translated a line at a time while the program runs. C++ does all of that work once, in advance. !info The trade You get speed. Nothing stands between your program and the processor. That is why games, web browsers, operating systems and trading systems are written in C++. You pay with strictness. The compiler refuses to build anything it cannot make sense of. That feels harsh in week one. Later you will be glad of it, because every mistake it catches is one that never reaches your running program. Three kinds of mistakes Every programmer makes all three, every day. Knowing which kind you are looking at tells you where to look. When it shows up Name Example Who notices --- --- --- --- While building Compile error You forgot a ; The compiler. Nothing is built. While building Linker error You promised a function existed but never wrote it The linker. Nothing is built. While running Logic error (a bug ) It builds and runs, but prints the wrong total Only you !tip Errors are not a judgement A compile error is the compiler saying "I got stuck here". It gives you the line number. Read it, fix it, build again. Professionals do this hundreds of times a day. Where C++ came from C++ gets a new version every three years, named after the year. This course teaches modern C++ (C++20, with the useful parts of C++23). You do not need to know the history yet; the full story is in 13.10 C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next .

title: 1.02  Setup and Your First Program
body: There is nothing to install. Type the program, press Run , read what comes back. Then break it on purpose to see what errors look like. You are already set up Xenon has an editor and a real C++ compiler built in. Anywhere you see code with a Run button, you can change it and run it. You want to Do this --- --- Run the code in the editor Run , or Ctrl + Enter Have your answer to a task checked Check Try something of your own Open the Playground in the sidebar See what the compiler complained about The Problems tab under the editor Hello, World! This is the traditional first program. It puts one line of text on the screen. Press Run . cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "Hello, World!\n"; return 0; } Output: Hello, World! Do not worry about what each line means yet. That is the next lesson. For now, notice two things: - The text between the double quotes is what appears on the screen. - The \n at the end did not appear. It means "start a new line". The loop you will repeat for the rest of your life Nobody writes a program correctly in one go. Programming is this loop: write a little, run it, fix it, repeat. Small steps make it fast, because when something breaks you know it was the last thing you changed. Break it on purpose The quickest way to stop fearing error messages is to cause a few. In the program above: 1. Delete the ; at the end of the std::cout line and press Run . 2. Open the Problems tab. It names the line and explains the error in plain English. 3. Put the ; back and run again. Now try misspelling cout as cuot , and deleting the last } . !warning Always read the first error first One mistake can confuse the compiler so badly that it reports twenty errors below it. Fix the top one, build again, and most of the rest usually vanish. !tip Type the code, do not paste it Typing is slower, and that is the point. Your fingers learn where the brackets and semicolons go, and you make the small mistakes now, while they are cheap. Later: on your own computer Xenon is all you need for this course. When you start building bigger projects of your own, you will want a full development environment. On Windows the usual choice is Visual Studio Community (free) with the "Desktop development with C++" option. There is no hurry.

title: 1.03  Anatomy of a Program
body:
A program is a list of statements inside a function called main . They run from top to bottom. Each statement ends with ; . Comments are notes for humans. Hello World, line by line cpp include <iostream // 1. bring in the tools for printing int main() // 2. the program starts here { // 3. main's instructions begin std::cout << "Hi!
"; // 4. one instruction: print Hi! return 0; // 5. finish, and report "all went well" } // 6. main's instructions end Piece What it means --- --- include <iostream "I want to use the input/output tools." Without it, std::cout does not exist. int main() The starting point. Every program has exactly one main . { and } Braces mark where a group of instructions begins and ends. std::cout << "Hi!
"; Send the text Hi! to the screen. std:: "From the standard library", the toolbox that comes with C++. ; The end of an instruction, like a full stop ends a sentence. return 0; End main . 0 tells the operating system that nothing went wrong. Two words for what you just read: - A statement is one complete instruction. It ends with ; . - A function is a named group of statements. main is the one that runs first. Statements run top to bottom cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "One
"; std::cout << "Two
"; std::cout << "Three
"; return 0; } One Two Three The computer does one statement, then the next, and never skips ahead. When a program does something unexpected, walking through it one line at a time, in order, is how you find out why. Comments A comment is a note for whoever reads the code. The compiler ignores it completely. cpp // Everything after two slashes, to the end of the line, is a comment. / A comment between these markers can run over several lines. / !tip Say why, not what Weak: lives = lives + 1; // add one to lives . The code already says that. Useful: lives = lives + 1; // bonus life every 10,000 points . That is something the code cannot tell you. Putting // in front of a line switches it off without deleting it. This is called commenting out , and it is handy when you are hunting for a problem. Spacing is for people The compiler does not care about extra spaces or blank lines. To the compiler, these are identical: cpp std::cout<<"Hi"; std::cout << "Hi" ; People care a great deal. Indent the statements inside braces by four spaces, as every example here does, and your code will show its own structure. Four mistakes everybody makes Mistake What the compiler says --- --- Forgetting a ; expected ';' (often reported on the next line) Writing Main or MAIN No starting point found. C++ is case-sensitive : capitals matter. Leaving out include <iostream 'cout' is not a member of 'std' A { without its } An error at the very end of the file

title: 1.04  Variables and Initialization
body: A variable is a named box in memory that holds one value of one type . Always give it a starting value: int age{ 25 }; A variable is a labelled box Programs need to remember things: a score, a name, a price. A variable is a piece of the computer's memory with a name on it, so you can put a value in and look at it later. int age{ 25 }; double price{ 9.99 }; char grade{ 'A' }; ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ 25 │ │ 9.99 │ │ 'A' │ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ age price grade (an int) (a double) (a char) Creating one takes three parts: cpp int age{ 25 }; Part Here Meaning --- --- --- Type int What kind of value the box can hold Name age What you call it in the rest of the program Starting value { 25 } What is in the box to begin with Five types to start with Type Holds Examples --- --- --- int whole numbers 42 , -7 , 0 double numbers with a decimal point 3.14 , -0.5 char one single character, in single quotes 'x' , '7' bool a yes/no answer true , false std::string text, in double quotes (needs include <string ) "Hello" The type is fixed for the life of the variable. An int box can never hold text. Always give a starting value cpp int a{ 5 }; // a holds 5 int b{}; // empty braces: b holds 0 int c; // DANGER: c holds whatever happened to be in that memory !danger Never leave a variable uninitialized int c; reserves a box but puts nothing in it. The box contains leftover junk from whatever used that memory before. Your program might print 0, or 32767, or behave differently every time you run it. Always write the braces. You will see two other ways to give a starting value in other people's code. They work, but braces are safer: cpp int x = 4.7; // builds, and quietly throws away the .7 (x is 4) int y{ 4.7 }; // refuses to build: "narrowing conversion". The mistake is caught. Giving a variable its first value is called initialization . Changing the value later cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 10 }; // create the box, holding 10 score = 25; // replace the contents with 25 score = score + 5; // read 25, add 5, store 30 std::cout << score << '\n'; return 0; } Putting a new value into an existing variable is called assignment . The old value is gone. !note = does not mean "equals" In C++, = means "work out the right-hand side, then store it in the variable on the left" . That is why score = score + 5 makes sense: read the old score, add 5, store the result back. Choosing names Allowed Not allowed --- --- playerHealth , max_speed , count2 2count (starts with a digit) letters, digits and _ my-var , my var (hyphen, space) words C++ already uses: int , return , class A good name says what is in the box. secondsElapsed tells the reader something; s does not. This course uses camelCase : lower-case first word, a capital at the start of each later word.

title: 1.05  Input and Output
body:
std::cout << sends values out to the screen. std::cin brings values in from the keyboard. The arrows point the way the data moves. Follow the arrows A program that cannot show anything or ask anything is not much use. C++ gives you two tools for talking to the person at the keyboard. You write Read it as Data moves --- --- --- std::cout << x; "send x to the screen" from x to the screen std::cin x; "read from the keyboard into x" from the keyboard to x If you ever forget which arrows go with which, look at where they point. Printing with std::cout cpp include <iostream int main() { int apples{ 5 }; std::cout << "I have " << apples << " apples
"; std::cout << "Line 1
" << "Line 2
"; return 0; } I have 5 apples Line 1 Line 2 Three things to notice: - You can chain several << in one statement. Each piece is printed in order. - Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. A variable name without quotes prints the value inside the variable. - std::cout adds nothing for you. No spaces, no new lines. If you want a space between two things, put it inside the quotes. Special characters A backslash inside quotes starts a code for a character you cannot simply type. Code What it prints --- --- 
 the start of a new line 	 a tab (a jump to the next column) " a double quote \ one backslash !note You will also see std::endl std::cout << "Hi" << std::endl; also ends the line. It does a little extra work each time, so this course uses 
 , which is the normal choice. Reading with std::cin cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "Enter your age: "; int age{}; std::cin age; std::cout << "In 10 years you will be " << age + 10 << '
'; return 0; } Enter your age: 21 In 10 years you will be 31 The steps are always the same: The program stops at std::cin and waits until the person types something and presses Enter. Reading two values cpp int width{}; int height{}; std::cin width height; The person can type 3 7 on one line, or 3 , Enter, 7 , Enter. std::cin skips spaces and new lines to find the next value. Reading a whole line of text std::cin stops at the first space. That is fine for a number, but wrong for a full name. cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::cout << "Your full name: "; std::string name{}; std::getline(std::cin std::ws, name); std::cout << "Hello, " << name << "!
"; return 0; } Typed std::cin name stores std::getline(std::cin std::ws, name) stores --- --- --- Ada Lovelace Ada Ada Lovelace For now, treat std::getline(std::cin std::ws, name) as the recipe for "read the rest of the line". The std::ws part skips any leftover Enter from an earlier answer. Two mistakes to expect Mistake What happens --- --- Arrows the wrong way: std::cin << x A long, confusing compile error. Check the arrows first. Typing letters when the program wants a number The read fails and the variable is left at 0. You will learn to handle this in 3.07 Input Validation and assert .

title: 1.06  Operators and Expressions Basics
body: An expression is anything that works out to a value, such as 2 + 3 or price count . Operators are the symbols that do the work. One surprise: with whole numbers, 7 / 2 is 3 . Doing arithmetic The symbols + , - , , / and % are called operators . Something that works out to a value, like 7 + 2 , is called an expression . Operator Meaning Example Result --- --- --- --- + add 7 + 2 9 - subtract 7 - 2 5 multiply 7 2 14 / divide 7 / 2 3 (see below) % remainder 7 % 2 1 You can use an expression anywhere a value is expected: cpp include <iostream int main() { int price{ 4 }; int count{ 3 }; int total{ price count }; // store the result std::cout << total << '\n'; // 12 std::cout << total + 10 << '\n'; // 22, worked out and printed directly return 0; } Dividing whole numbers throws away the decimals This is the one that catches everybody. 7 / 2 is 3.5 in maths but C++ gives 3 9 / 10 is 0.9 in maths but C++ gives 0 When both numbers are whole numbers ( int ), the answer is a whole number too. The part after the decimal point is cut off. It is not rounded. If at least one side is a decimal number, you get a decimal answer: Expression Result Why --- --- --- 7 / 2 3 both whole 7.0 / 2 3.5 one side is a decimal 7 / 2.0 3.5 one side is a decimal !warning An average that comes out wrong int total{ 7 }; int count{ 2 }; then total / count is 3 , not 3.5 . To get the real answer from two int variables you convert one first. That is covered in 2.05 Type Conversion and static_cast . The remainder operator % % gives what is left over after dividing. Share 7 biscuits between 2 people: 7 biscuits, 2 people each person gets 7 / 2 = 3 left on the plate 7 % 2 = 1 It looks minor, and it turns up everywhere: Question Expression --- --- Is n even? n % 2 is 0 What is the last digit of 1234? 1234 % 10 is 4 What is 1234 without its last digit? 1234 / 10 is 123 90 seconds is how many minutes and seconds? 90 / 60 is 1 , 90 % 60 is 30 Which part is worked out first? The same order as in school maths: , / and % first, then + and - . Operators of equal rank go left to right. Brackets change the order: (2 + 3) 4 is 20 . !tip If you have to stop and think, add brackets Brackets cost nothing, and the next reader (often you, next week) will not have to stop and think either. Shortcuts for changing a variable Changing a variable based on its own value is so common that there are shorter ways to write it. Long form Short form Meaning --- --- --- x = x + 5; x += 5; add 5 to x x = x - 5; x -= 5; take 5 from x x = x 5; x = 5; multiply x by 5 x = x / 5; x /= 5; divide x by 5 x = x + 1; ++x; add 1 to x x = x - 1; --x; take 1 from x You will also see x++ . For now it does the same job as ++x . The small difference is explained in 2.08 Operators Deep Dive .

title: 1.07  Functions Basics
body:
A function is a named set of instructions you can use again and again. You hand it values ( arguments ), it does its work, and it can hand one value back (the return value ). A function is a machine Put values in, get a result out. You have already written one function, main . Now you will write your own. cpp include <iostream int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } int main() { int sum{ add(3, 4) }; std::cout << sum << '
'; // 7 return 0; } The parts of a function what it its what it needs hands back name to be given │ │ │ int add (int x, int y) { return x + y; the body: what it does } Word Meaning In the example --- --- --- Return type The type of value the function hands back int Parameter A variable that receives a value when the function is used x and y Call Using the function add(3, 4) Argument A value you give in the call 3 and 4 Return value What comes back 7 What happens when you call it 1. main pauses at the call. 2. The arguments are copied into the parameters. 3. The function's body runs. 4. return sends a value back, and main carries on where it stopped. !info The function gets copies Because the arguments are copied, changing x inside add changes nothing in main . The two functions have separate boxes. (When you do want a function to change the caller's variable, you use a reference: 4.03 References .) Functions that hand nothing back Some functions just do something. Their return type is void , which means "nothing". cpp include <iostream void printBanner() { std::cout << "==========
"; std::cout << " MY APP 
"; std::cout << "==========
"; } int main() { printBanner(); printBanner(); // written once, used twice return 0; } Empty brackets mean the function needs no values. You still have to write the brackets when you call it. The compiler reads from the top A function has to be known before the line that calls it. The simplest way is to write your functions above main . The other way is to announce the function first and write it later. The announcement is called a declaration : cpp include <iostream int add(int x, int y); // declaration: "this function exists" int main() { std::cout << add(3, 4) << '
'; return 0; } int add(int x, int y) // definition: the actual instructions { return x + y; } Variables inside a function stay inside cpp void countCoins() { int coins{ 5 }; // created here } // gone here int main() { countCoins(); // coins does not exist in main. Using it here is a compile error. return 0; } A variable created inside a function is called a local variable . It belongs to that function alone. Two functions can each have a variable called total without affecting each other. Why bother? Reason What it means --- --- Reuse Write the instructions once, call them as often as you like Readability calculateTax(price) says what is happening without showing how Easier fixing A mistake lives in one place, so you fix it in one place Smaller problems A big task becomes several small ones you can solve one at a time !tip One function, one job If you cannot give a function a short, clear name, it is probably doing two jobs. Split it. Three mistakes to expect Mistake What happens --- --- No return in a function that promised a value The compiler warns you, and the program misbehaves Calling without brackets: printBanner; Nothing happens. The brackets are what make it a call. Writing one function inside another Not allowed. Each function sits on its own, outside the others.

title: 1.08  Multiple Files and Headers
body: Real programs are split across files. A header ( .h ) says what exists . A source file ( .cpp ) says how it works . include the header wherever you need those functions. Why split a program up? A program in one file is fine at fifty lines. At five thousand it is a nightmare to find anything in. So programmers group related functions into their own files. That raises a problem you met in the last lesson: a function must be known before it is called. If add lives in another file, how does main.cpp know about it? The answer is a header file . Menu and kitchen Think of a restaurant. The menu lists what you can order. The kitchen is where the food is made. You only need the menu to order. File Contains Example --- --- --- mathx.h Declarations : the name of each function, what it needs and what it returns int add(int x, int y); mathx.cpp Definitions : the actual instructions int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } main.cpp Code that uses the functions add(2, 3) mathx.h cpp pragma once int add(int x, int y); int multiply(int x, int y); mathx.cpp cpp include "mathx.h" int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } int multiply(int x, int y) { return x y; } main.cpp cpp include <iostream include "mathx.h" int main() { std::cout << add(2, 3) << ' ' << multiply(2, 3) << '\n'; return 0; } In Xenon, tasks with several files show each file as a tab above the editor, and all of them are built together when you press Run . What include really does Nothing clever. It pastes the contents of the named file in at that spot, before the compiler starts. main.cpp as you wrote it main.cpp as the compiler sees it ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ include "mathx.h" │ ───▶ │ int add(int x, int y); │ │ │ │ int multiply(int x, int y);│ │ int main() { ... } │ │ int main() { ... } │ └──────────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────┘ Written as Used for --- --- include <iostream Headers that come with C++ include "mathx.h" Headers you wrote yourself How the pieces are joined Remember the compiler and the linker from the first lesson? This is where the linker earns its place. Each .cpp file is compiled separately . While compiling main.cpp , the compiler only has the declaration of add . It trusts that the real thing exists somewhere. The linker then checks that it does. !warning "Unresolved external symbol" This is the linker saying: "something calls add , but no file provides it." Either you declared a function and never wrote it, or its definition does not match the declaration exactly (a different name or different parameters). pragma once Put this as the first line of every header you write. It stops the header being pasted twice into the same file, which can cause "already defined" errors as programs grow. One rule to remember How many times? Where it goes --- --- --- Declaration ( int add(int x, int y); ) As often as you like The header Definition (the version with a body) Exactly once in the whole program A .cpp file If you put a function's body in a header, every file that includes it gets its own copy, and the linker complains that it has too many.

title: 1.09  Debugging Basics
body: A bug is a place where what the program does differs from what you expected . Debugging is finding that place. Do it with a method: read the message, look at the values, narrow it down. Bugs are normal Every programmer writes bugs all day. What separates a beginner from an expert is not how few bugs they write. It is how quickly they find them. That is a skill, and it has a method. The step people skip is the fourth. If you change things until it seems to work without knowing why, the bug is usually still there. First, which kind of problem is it? What you see Kind Where to look --- --- --- It will not build Compile or linker error The Problems tab. Start with the first message. It builds, then stops with an error Crash The message in the console, and the last thing printed before it It runs and gives the wrong answer Logic error The values of your variables, step by step Reading a compiler message main.cpp(8,5): error C2146: missing ';' before identifier 'std' │ │ │ └── what the compiler got stuck on │ │ └── column │ └── line └── file Go to that line. If it looks fine, look at the line above it. A missing ; is only noticed when the compiler reaches the next thing. Technique 1: print the values When the answer is wrong, some variable holds a value you did not expect. So look. cpp include <iostream int main() { int price{ 4 }; int quantity{ 3 }; int total{ price + quantity }; std::cerr << "DEBUG total=" << total << '\n'; std::cout << "You owe " << total << '\n'; return 0; } std::cerr works like std::cout . It is meant for messages to the programmer, not for the program's real output. The DEBUG label makes these lines easy to spot and delete when you have finished. Here the debug line shows total=7 . You expected 12, so the mistake is on the line that calculates total . Technique 2: be the computer Go through the program one line at a time and write down what every variable holds. This is called tracing , and it is the most reliable debugging tool there is. cpp int a{ 4 }; int b{ 5 }; int c{ 6 }; int average{ a + b + c / 3 }; After the line a b c average --- --- --- --- --- int a{ 4 }; 4 int b{ 5 }; 4 5 int c{ 6 }; 4 5 6 int average{ ... }; 4 5 6 4 + 5 + (6 / 3) = 11 The trace shows the problem. Division happens before addition, so only c is divided. The fix is brackets: (a + b + c) / 3 . !tip Do what the code says, not what you meant The difficult part of tracing is being honest. Your eyes see what you intended to write. Follow each symbol exactly as it is written. Technique 3: cut the problem in half When you have no idea where the mistake is, print a value in the middle of the program. Each check halves the search. Even in a thousand lines you find the spot in about ten checks. Technique 4: explain it out loud Describe your code line by line to someone else, or to an object on your desk. Programmers call this rubber duck debugging . You will often stop mid-sentence because you have just heard yourself say something that is not true. Writing fewer bugs Habit Why it helps --- --- Run after every few lines A new problem must be in the lines you just wrote Read every warning A warning usually means "this is legal, and probably not what you meant" Give every variable a starting value Removes a whole family of unpredictable behaviour Keep functions small A small piece is easy to check on its own Later: a debugger Professional tools such as Visual Studio include a debugger . It pauses a running program on any line you choose, shows every variable, and lets you move forward one line at a time. It automates the tracing you just did by hand. Once you know how to trace, a debugger takes minutes to learn.

title: 1.10  Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior
match: 1.10 Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior
body: Turn compiler warnings up and read them. Build in Debug while you work and Release when you finish. And meet the most important phrase in C++: undefined behaviour . The compiler has settings So far you have pressed Run and let the compiler get on with it. It has a few settings that matter, and Xenon has already chosen sensible ones. This lesson explains what they are, so they are not a mystery when you set up your own tools one day. Warnings: the compiler's advice An error means "I cannot build this". A warning means "I can build this, but it looks like a mistake". cpp include <iostream int main() { int total{ 10 }; int count{ 3 }; int unused{ 5 }; std::cout << total / count << '\n'; return 0; } This builds and runs. With warnings turned up, the compiler also tells you that unused is never used. Perhaps you meant to use it and forgot. Error Warning --- --- --- Does the program build? No Yes Should you fix it? You have to Yes, nearly always !tip Treat warnings as errors Xenon compiles at a high warning level and shows warnings in the Problems tab. Some tasks are marked strict : they only pass when there are no warnings at all. That is how professional teams work, and it is a good habit to start now. Debug and Release The same source code can be built in two ways. Debug Release --- --- --- Speed Slower Often many times faster Extra checks for mistakes Yes No Use it when You are still working You are finished, or measuring speed In an optimised build the compiler rearranges your code to run faster while producing the same results. Xenon uses Debug unless you change it, because the extra checks catch mistakes. You can switch in Settings . Which version of C++? C++ is revised every three years, and a compiler has to be told which version to follow. Xenon uses the newest. If you copy code from an old tutorial and it looks different from what you learn here, a different version is usually the reason. Undefined behaviour This is the single most important idea in the lesson. Most languages stop you when you do something senseless. C++ often does not. For certain mistakes, the rules of the language simply do not say what happens. That is called undefined behaviour , usually shortened to UB . You have already met one example: cpp int score; // never given a value std::cout << score << '\n'; // undefined behaviour This might print 0. It might print 32767. It might print something different on another computer or after an unrelated change. All of those are "allowed", because the rules promise nothing. !danger "It works on my machine" proves nothing Code with undefined behaviour can pass every test you run and still be wrong. The only safe approach is to know the rules and not break them. The Debug build's extra checks catch some cases for you, which is one more reason to use it. The ones you will meet in this course Mistake Covered in --- --- Reading a variable that was never given a value 1.04 Variables and Initialization A whole number growing too large for its type 2.02 Integers Dividing a whole number by zero 2.03 Floating Point Numbers Reading past the end of a list 5.01 std::vector Basics Following a pointer that points at nothing 4.04 Pointers Using something after it has been destroyed 7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory You do not need to understand these yet. Just notice the pattern: each is something a careful programmer checks for. The complete picture comes much later, in 13.01 Undefined Behavior and Object Lifetime . Words you cannot use as names C++ reserves about ninety words for itself, called keywords . You have used several already: int , double , return , void , true , false . You cannot name a variable or a function with one of them. The editor shows keywords in their own colour, so if a name you chose changes colour, pick another.

title: 2.01  Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types
body:
Memory is a long row of numbered bytes . A byte is 8 bits . A variable's type decides how many bytes it gets and what the bits in them mean. What the boxes are made of In Milestone 1 a variable was "a labelled box". Now look inside the box. Knowing what is in there explains why whole numbers have limits, why decimals are slightly inexact and why types matter at all. Bits and bytes A bit is a switch that is either 0 or 1 . Eight of them make a byte . Each bit is worth double the one to its right, and you add up the ones that are switched on: worth: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 bits: 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 64 + 1 = 65 Every extra bit doubles how many different values you can store. Bits Different values --- --- 1 2 8 (one byte) 256 16 65,536 32 about 4.3 billion 64 about 18 billion billion Memory is a street of numbered houses Your computer's memory is a very long row of bytes. Each one has a number, called its address . address: 1000 1001 1002 1003 1004 1005 1006 1007 ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐ │ int score (4 bytes) │ char │ bool │ free ... │ └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘ A variable is a run of neighbouring bytes with a name on it. The type gives the bits a meaning Bits on their own mean nothing. The pattern 01000001 is the number 65 if you treat it as a whole number, and the letter A if you treat it as a character. That is the job of a type. It tells the compiler two things: how many bytes to reserve, and how to interpret what is in them. The fundamental types These are built into the language. Everything else in C++ is made from them. Kind Type Usual size Holds --- --- --- --- True or false bool 1 byte true , false Character char 1 byte one character Whole number short 2 bytes about ±32 thousand int 4 bytes about ±2.1 billion long long 8 bytes about ±9.2 billion billion Decimal number float 4 bytes about 7 significant digits double 8 bytes about 15 significant digits Nothing void none "no value" !tip Your defaults Use int for whole numbers and double for decimals unless you have a reason not to. The others exist for special cases, which the next lessons cover. Asking how big something is sizeof reports the size of a type, or of a variable, in bytes. cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "bool: " << sizeof(bool) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "char: " << sizeof(char) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "int: " << sizeof(int) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "long long: " << sizeof(long long) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "double: " << sizeof(double) << " bytes
"; return 0; } !note Sizes are not identical everywhere The language only promises minimum sizes. An int is 4 bytes on every ordinary computer today, but long is 4 bytes on Windows and 8 on Linux and macOS. When the exact size matters, there are types with the size in their name, such as std::int32_t . They are in 2.02 Integers . Asking for the limits Fewer bytes means a smaller range. The header <limits tells you the exact ends of it. cpp include <iostream include <limits int main() { std::cout << std::numeric_limits<int ::max() << '
'; // 2147483647 std::cout << std::numeric_limits<int ::min() << '
'; // -2147483648 return 0; } Do not worry about the angle brackets yet. Read std::numeric_limits<int ::max() as "the largest int ".

title: How big is it?
