Print the total in megabytes, the same total in gigabytes (1 GB = 1024 MB), and how many gigabytes would be left on a 64 GB card: Total: 3000 MB That is 2.92969 GB Left on a 64 GB card: 61.0703 GB (That example is for 1200 2.5 .)

title: 2.02  Integers
body: Integers hold whole numbers. Signed ones can be negative; unsigned ones cannot. Going past the limit is overflow : unsigned wraps round to the other end, and signed is undefined behaviour. Signed and unsigned An integer is a whole number. Every integer type comes in two versions. 8 bits, signed : -128 ────────── 0 ────────── 127 8 bits, unsigned : 0 ─────────────────────────── 255 Both have 256 values to spend. The signed version spends half of them below zero. The unsigned version starts at zero and reaches twice as high. cpp int temperature{ -5 }; // signed: this is the default unsigned int population{ 8000 }; // unsigned: never negative Overflow What happens when a number goes past the end of its range? Think of a car's mileage counter rolling from 99999 back to 00000. cpp include <iostream int main() { unsigned int u{ 0 }; u = u - 1; std::cout << u << '\n'; // 4294967295 return 0; } The two versions behave very differently here. What overflow does --- --- Unsigned Wraps round to the other end. Guaranteed, on every computer. Signed Undefined behaviour. Anything may happen. !danger Signed overflow is undefined behaviour int big{ 2147483647 }; ++big; has no defined result. In practice you often see a large negative number, but nothing promises that. If a value might pass two billion, use a bigger type. Why not use unsigned for anything that cannot be negative? It sounds sensible: a count is never negative, so make it unsigned. In practice this causes more bugs than it prevents. cpp include <iostream int main() { unsigned int items{ 3 }; int change{ -1 }; std::cout << (change < items) << '\n'; // prints 0, meaning false return 0; } When signed and unsigned meet, the signed value is converted to unsigned. So -1 becomes 4294967295, which is not less than 3. !tip The rule this course follows Use plain int for counts and arithmetic. Keep unsigned for working with individual bits ( 2.09 Bit Manipulation ). Integers with an exact size When you need a guaranteed size, include <cstdint gives you types with the number of bits in the name. Type Bits Range --- --- --- std::int8_t / std::uint8_t 8 -128 to 127 / 0 to 255 std::int16_t / std::uint16_t 16 about ±32 thousand / 0 to 65,535 std::int32_t / std::uint32_t 32 about ±2.1 billion / 0 to 4.2 billion std::int64_t / std::uint64_t 64 about ±9.2 billion billion One more turns up constantly: std::size_t . It is the unsigned type C++ uses for sizes, including the result of sizeof . !warning The 8-bit types print as characters std::cout << std::int8_t{ 65 }; prints A , not 65 . On most systems these types are really char underneath. Writing whole numbers in code A value written directly in your code is called a literal . There are several ways to write an integer literal. cpp int decimal{ 255 }; int hex{ 0xFF }; // base 16, also 255 int binary{ 0b1111'1111 }; // base 2, also 255 int million{ 1'000'000 }; // ' is only there to help you read it long long big{ 9'000'000'000LL }; // LL marks the literal as long long Prefix or suffix Meaning --- --- 0x hexadecimal (base 16) 0b binary (base 2) ' between digits a separator the compiler ignores LL at the end this literal is a long long u at the end this literal is unsigned !warning A leading zero means octal 017 is not seventeen. A literal starting with 0 is read in base 8, so it is 15. Never pad a number with zeros. Two reminders from Milestone 1 - Dividing integers cuts off the decimals: 7 / 2 is 3 . - With % , the sign of the result follows the left-hand side: -7 % 3 is -1 .

title: Number bases
body: The same number can be written in different bases. Define four int variables using the literal style named in each comment, then print them. Printed normally they all come out in decimal: 255 10 8 1000000

title: Too big for an int
body: Read a number of years and print how many seconds that is (use 365 days per year). An int can only hold about 2.1 billion, and 100 years is already more than 3 billion seconds. Use a 64-bit integer type so large inputs work. For 1 print 31536000 . For 1000 print 31536000000 .

title: How far does light go?
body: Light travels about 299,792 kilometres every second. Read a number of days and print how many kilometres light covers in that time: In 1 days light travels 25902028800 km The answer overflows a 32-bit int straight away, so choose your types with care. Use named constants for the speed of light and the seconds in a day rather than bare numbers.

title: 2.03  Floating Point Numbers
body:
float and double store decimals approximately . 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 . Use double by default, never compare with == , and never use them where every cent must be exact. Decimals are approximate Write one third as a decimal and you get 0.3333... for ever. You have to stop somewhere, so what you write down is slightly off. Computers have the same problem in binary, with different numbers. In binary, 0.1 goes on for ever . The computer stores the closest value that fits. cpp include <iomanip include <iostream int main() { double x{ 0.1 + 0.2 }; std::cout << std::setprecision(17) << x << '
'; // 0.30000000000000004 std::cout << (x == 0.3) << '
'; // 0, meaning false return 0; } Types that work this way are called floating point types. How much precision do you get? A floating point number is stored like scientific notation: some significant digits, and a power that says where the point goes. 6.02 × 10^23 ──── ──── digits where the point goes ┌──────┬───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ sign │ exponent │ the digits │ │ 1 bit│ 11 bits │ 52 bits │ └──────┴───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ a double: 64 bits in total Only so many digits fit. Anything beyond that is rounded away. Type Size Reliable significant digits --- --- --- float 4 bytes about 7 double 8 bytes about 15 float holding 123456789 prints 123456792 (ran out of digits) double holding 123456789 prints 123456789 !tip Use double The extra precision is nearly always worth four more bytes. float is for cases where you hold millions of values and memory is tight, such as graphics. Writing decimal literals cpp double d{ 3.14 }; // a literal with a point is a double float f{ 3.14f }; // the f suffix makes it a float double big{ 6.02e23 }; // 6.02 × 10^23 double tiny{ 1.5e-9 }; // 0.0000000015 Controlling how they print By default std::cout shows about six significant digits. The header <iomanip lets you choose. cpp include <iomanip include <iostream int main() { double pi{ 3.14159265 }; std::cout << pi << '
'; // 3.14159 std::cout << std::setprecision(3) << pi << '
'; // 3.14 (3 significant digits) std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << pi << '
'; // 3.14 (2 digits after the point) return 0; } Setting Meaning --- --- std::setprecision(n) alone n significant digits in total std::fixed then std::setprecision(n) exactly n digits after the point Comparing safely Because of the tiny errors, asking "are these exactly equal?" is the wrong question. Ask "are these close enough?" cpp include <cmath bool approxEqual(double a, double b) { return std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9; } std::abs gives the size of the difference without its sign. If that is smaller than a tiny tolerance, treat the two as equal. Special values Floating point has three values that are not ordinary numbers. Expression Result Meaning --- --- --- 1.0 / 0.0 inf infinity -1.0 / 0.0 -inf negative infinity 0.0 / 0.0 nan "not a number" !danger Integers are different Dividing a floating point number by zero gives inf . Dividing an integer by zero ( 5 / 0 ) is undefined behaviour and usually crashes the program. Money Do not store money in a double . Errors of a fraction of a cent add up, and they anger accountants. Store the amount in the smallest unit as an integer: cpp std::int64_t priceInCents{ 1999 }; // 19.99

title: Close enough
body: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false in C++, because none of those values can be stored exactly in binary. The fix is to ask whether two numbers are nearly equal. Write bool approxEqual(double a, double b) that returns true when a and b differ by less than 0.000000001 (that is 1e-9 ). std::abs from <cmath gives the size of a number without its sign.

title: Two decimal places
body: Read a decimal number and print it with exactly two digits after the point. Input Output --- --- 3.14159 3.14 2 2.00 0.005 0.01 Use std::fixed and std::setprecision from <iomanip .

title: Fuel economy
body: Read the distance driven in kilometres and the fuel used in litres (both decimals). Print the fuel economy two ways: 7.5 L/100km 13.33 km/L (for 400 30 ). Litres per 100 km has one decimal; kilometres per litre has two .

title: 2.04  bool and char
body:
bool holds true or false , stored as 1 or 0. char holds one character, stored as a small number: 'A' is 65. bool : yes or no A bool holds the answer to a yes/no question. It is the type every decision in a program is built on. cpp include <iostream int main() { bool isAlive{ true }; bool hasKey{ false }; std::cout << isAlive << '
'; // 1 std::cout << std::boolalpha << isAlive << '
'; // true std::cout << !hasKey << '
'; // true return 0; } Two things to notice: - A bool prints as 1 or 0 unless you send std::boolalpha to std::cout first. - ! means not . It flips true to false and back. Where bools come from You rarely type true or false yourself. Usually a bool is the result of a comparison. Expression Value when age is 20 --- --- age = 18 true age == 21 false age % 2 == 0 true A function that returns bool reads like a question. Name it that way: isEven , hasKey , canJump . cpp bool isEven(int n) { return n % 2 == 0; } Numbers and bools convert to each other Converting Rule --- --- A number to bool 0 becomes false . Anything else becomes true . A bool to a number true becomes 1 , false becomes 0 . char : a number wearing a costume A char stores a small number. A standard table, called ASCII , says which character each number stands for. 'A' = 65 'B' = 66 ... 'Z' = 90 'a' = 97 'b' = 98 ... 'z' = 122 '0' = 48 '1' = 49 ... '9' = 57 ' ' = 32 '
' = 10 cpp include <iostream int main() { char c{ 'A' }; std::cout << c << '
'; // A std::cout << static_cast<int (c) << '
'; // 65 return 0; } static_cast<int (c) means "treat this value as an int ". It gets a full lesson next: 2.05 Type Conversion and static_cast . Why the table's order is useful The letters are in order and so are the digits. That makes some common jobs a single subtraction. Goal Expression Why it works --- --- --- Turn the character '7' into the number 7 '7' - '0' 55 − 48 = 7 Find a letter's position in the alphabet 'c' - 'a' 99 − 97 = 2 The next letter after c static_cast<char (c + 1) one further along the table !warning '7' is not 7 The character '7' is stored as 55. If you read a digit as a char and do arithmetic with it directly, the answers come out wrong by 48. For everyday checks, include <cctype has ready-made functions: Function Question or action --- --- std::isdigit(c) Is it a digit? std::isalpha(c) Is it a letter? std::isspace(c) Is it a space, tab or new line? std::toupper(c) / std::tolower(c) Convert the case Single quotes and double quotes Written Type What it is --- --- --- 'A' char exactly one character "A" text a string that happens to be one character long They are different types and cannot be swapped. char c{ "A" }; does not compile. Reading one character cpp char answer{}; std::cin answer; // skips spaces and new lines, then reads one character

title: isEven
body: Write bool isEven(int n) that returns true when n is even and false when it is odd. A comparison such as n % 2 == 0 already is a bool , so the whole function can be a single return .

title: The next letter
body: A char is really a small number (its ASCII code). Read one character and print the character that comes after it, followed by that character's code: Input Output --- --- a b 98 Y Z 90 4 5 53

title: Digit to number
body: The character '7' is not the number 7: its code is 55. Write int digitValue(char digit) that turns a digit character into the number it shows. cpp digitValue('7') // 7 digitValue('0') // 0 The digit characters '0' to '9' sit next to each other in the code table, in order.

title: Character report
body: Read one character and print a short report about it: Character: g Code: 103 Uppercase: G Is a letter: true Is a digit: false Use std::toupper , std::isalpha and std::isdigit from <cctype , and std::boolalpha so that bool values print as true and false . Those three functions return an int . Convert std::toupper 's result to char , and compare the other two with != 0 to get a real bool .

title: 2.05  Type Conversion and static_cast
body: C++ converts between types automatically when it has to. Some conversions lose information . When you want a conversion, say so with static_cast<Type (value) . Conversions happen without being asked Whenever a value of one type is used where another is expected, C++ converts it. This is called an implicit conversion : the compiler does it without you writing anything. cpp double d{ 5 }; // the int 5 becomes the double 5.0 int i = 3.9; // the double 3.9 becomes the int 3: the .9 is gone The first is harmless. The second lost information, and nothing warned you. Widening and narrowing Direction Safe? --- --- --- Widening To a type that can hold every value of the original Yes Narrowing To a type that cannot Only if you know the value fits This is why the course uses braces. Brace initialization refuses to narrow: cpp int a = 3.5; // compiles; a is 3 int b{ 3.5 }; // error: narrowing conversion Mixed arithmetic When an operator has two different types to work with, the compiler converts one side first so both match. Roughly, the "smaller" type is converted to the "larger" one. Expression Result type Note --- --- --- int + double double int + long long long long char + char int types smaller than int are widened to int first int + unsigned unsigned the trap from 2.02 Integers The important detail: the conversion happens one operator at a time , not for the statement as a whole. cpp include <iostream int main() { int total{ 7 }; int count{ 2 }; double wrong{ static_cast<double (total / count) }; // 3 double right{ static_cast<double (total) / count }; // 3.5 std::cout << wrong << ' ' << right << '\n'; return 0; } In the first line the division is finished, as integer division, before any double is involved. Converting on purpose static_cast is how you tell the compiler, and the next reader, "I mean this conversion". cpp static_cast<new type (value) cpp double price{ 9.99 }; int whole{ static_cast<int (price) }; // 9 char letter{ static_cast<char (72) }; // 'H' int code{ static_cast<int ('H') }; // 72 It also satisfies brace initialization, because you have stated your intent: cpp int b{ static_cast<int (3.5) }; // fine: 3 !tip Why not the shorter (int)price ? That older form comes from C and still compiles. It will attempt almost any conversion, including dangerous ones, and it is hard to search for. static_cast only performs sensible conversions and stands out in the code. Converting is not rounding static_cast<int cuts off the decimals. It does not round. For rounding, use <cmath . Call Result Rule --- --- --- static_cast<int (2.9) 2 cut off std::round(2.5) 3.0 to the nearest whole number std::floor(2.9) 2.0 always down std::ceil(2.1) 3.0 always up The <cmath functions return a double . To store a rounded value in an int , combine the two: cpp int rounded{ static_cast<int (std::round(2.7)) }; // 3 Other casts exist C++ has three more named casts for specialised jobs. You will not need them for a long time. The one you will meet is dynamic_cast , in 8.06 Object Slicing, Casting and Composition .

title: An honest average
body: Write double average(int total, int count) that returns total divided by count with decimals . cpp average(7, 2) // 3.5, not 3 Both parameters are int , so a plain total / count throws the decimals away before the result is ever returned. Convert one of them first.

title: Round properly
body: static_cast<int (2.7) gives 2 : it chops, it does not round. Write int roundToInt(double x) that rounds to the nearest whole number. cpp roundToInt(2.7) // 3 roundToInt(2.2) // 2 roundToInt(-2.7) // -3 std::round in <cmath rounds, but hands back a double .

title: Test score
body: Read how many questions a student got right and how many there were in total (two whole numbers). Print the score as a percentage with one decimal place: 7 of 9 correct: 77.8%

title: 2.06  const and constexpr
body: const means "this value never changes after it is set". constexpr means "this value is known while compiling ". Use them wherever you can: they prevent mistakes and cost nothing. const : a locked box Most values in a program never need to change after they are set. Marking them const lets the compiler enforce that. cpp const double gravity{ 9.81 }; gravity = 10.0; // error: you cannot assign to a const variable ┌──────────────┐ │ 9.81 │ gravity (locked: read only) └──────────────┘ Two rules: - A const variable must be given its value when it is created. - That value may come from anywhere, including the keyboard. It simply cannot change afterwards. cpp int age{}; std::cin age; const int ageNextYear{ age + 1 }; // set once while running, then locked !tip Make things const by default When you read const on a variable, you know its value at every later line without checking. In a long function that is a real help. Leave const off only when the value has to change. constexpr : worked out by the compiler Some values are known before the program ever runs: the number of seconds in a day, the size of a chess board. constexpr asks the compiler to calculate them during the build. cpp constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; constexpr int secondsPerDay{ 24 60 60 }; // the compiler stores 86400 int x{}; std::cin x; constexpr int bad{ x 2 }; // error: x is not known while compiling You will hear these two phases called compile time and run time . The distinction comes up again and again in C++. const constexpr --- --- --- Can change after it is set No No Value may come from input while running Yes No Calculated during the build Sometimes Always Use it for Any value you will not modify True constants: pi , maxPlayers , gridSize constexpr functions A function can be constexpr too. That means the compiler may run it during the build when its arguments are known. cpp include <iostream constexpr int square(int n) { return n n; } int main() { constexpr int a{ square(5) }; // worked out while compiling: 25 int side{}; std::cin side; int b{ square(side) }; // the same function, used while running std::cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n'; return 0; } One function serves both purposes. Replace magic numbers with names A magic number is a bare number in the code with no explanation. cpp total = price 1.08; // what is 1.08? cpp constexpr double salesTaxRate{ 0.08 }; total = price (1.0 + salesTaxRate); The second version explains itself. And when the rate changes, you change one line instead of hunting for every 1.08 . Sharing constants between files Constants that several files need go in a header, grouped under a name: cpp // constants.h pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } Any file that includes the header writes constants::pi . Take the namespace and inline parts on trust for now. Both are explained in Milestone 3: 3.05 Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces and 3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage . const parameters A parameter can be const as well: the function promises not to change it. cpp void printPrice(const double price) For a simple value that is copied anyway, this is optional. It becomes important with references, where it means "I will look at your data but not alter it": 4.03 References .

title: Name the magic number
body: This program works, but 3.14159 appears from nowhere in the middle of a formula. A reader has to guess what it is. Give it a name: define constexpr double pi{ 3.14159 }; and use pi in the formula. The output must not change. For a radius of 2 it prints 12.5664 .

title: Computed by the compiler
body: A constexpr function can be run by the compiler itself, before the program ever starts. Write constexpr int cube(int n) returning n n n . The tests include a static_assert , which only compiles if cube(3) can be worked out at compile time.

title: How long is that?
body: Read a number of days and print how many hours, minutes and seconds that is: 3 days is 72 hours 4320 minutes 259200 seconds No bare 24 or 60 may appear in your calculations. Define three named constants with constexpr and build on them: - hoursPerDay - minutesPerHour - secondsPerMinute

title: 2.07  Strings — std::string and std::string_view
body:
std::string owns its text and can change it. std::string_view is a cheap, read-only window onto text that lives somewhere else. Functions that only read text should take a std::string_view . A string is a row of characters std::string name{ "Hello" }; index: 0 1 2 3 4 ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ │ H │ e │ l │ l │ o │ name.length() is 5 └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ name 0 is 'H' name 4 is 'o' Each character has a position, called its index . Counting starts at 0 , so the last index is always the length minus one. !danger Stay inside the string name 5 on a five-character string reads past the end. That is undefined behaviour. The compiler will not stop you. Calling a string's own functions A std::string comes with functions attached. You call them with a dot after the variable: name.length() . Functions attached to a value like this are called member functions . cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string first{ "Ada" }; std::string last{ "Lovelace" }; std::string full{ first + ' ' + last }; std::cout << full << " has " << full.length() << " characters
"; // 12 std::cout << "Initials: " << first 0 << last 0 << '
'; // AL std::cout << "Surname starts at index " << full.find(last) << '
'; // 4 return 0; } The toolbox Assume std::string s{ "Hi" }; for each row. To Write Result --- --- --- Get the length s.length() 2 Get one character s 0 'H' Join two strings s + " there" "Hi there" Add to the end s += "!"; s is now "Hi!" Compare s == "Hi" true Check for empty s.empty() false Find text s.find("i") 1 Take a piece s.substr(0, 1) "H" (start index, how many) Insert s.insert(0, " ") " Hi" Remove s.erase(0, 1) "i" (start index, how many) Replace a piece s.replace(0, 1, "Oh") "Ohi" Converting between text and numbers: To Write Result --- --- --- Number to text std::to_string(42) "42" Text to int std::stoi("42") 42 Text to double std::stod("3.5") 3.5 !note When find finds nothing It returns a special value, std::string::npos . Always compare the result against it before using it as an index: cpp if (s.find("x") == std::string::npos) { / not there / } !warning "Hello" + " World" does not compile Text in quotes is a string literal , which is a more primitive thing than a std::string . The + only joins when at least one side is a real std::string : write std::string{ "Hello" } + " World" . std::string_view : look, do not copy Passing a std::string to a function copies the whole text, as with any other argument. For long text that is wasted work when the function only wants to read it. A std::string_view holds no text of its own. It records where some existing text is and how long it is. cpp include <iostream include <string include <string_view void greet(std::string_view name) { std::cout << "Hello, " << name << '
'; } int main() { greet("Ada"); // works with a literal std::string s{ "Grace" }; greet(s); // works with a std::string, without copying it return 0; } std::string std::string_view --- --- --- Owns the text Yes No Can change the text Yes No Cost of passing it to a function Copies every character Tiny: a location and a length Use it for Text you store or modify Parameters that only read !danger A view must not outlive what it looks at cpp std::string_view broken() { std::string temp{ "oops" }; return temp; // temp is destroyed here; the view now points at nothing } A view is only valid while the text it refers to still exists. This idea, something referring to data that has gone, returns in Milestone 4 under the name dangling .

title: Count the characters
body: Read a full name (it may contain spaces) and report how long it is, counting the spaces: Ada Lovelace has 12 characters

title: Initials
body: Write std::string initials(std::string_view first, std::string_view last) that builds a person's initials with full stops: cpp initials("Ada", "Lovelace") // "A.L." first 0 is the first character of a string. A std::string grows when you add characters or text to it with += .

title: Last name first
body: Write std::string lastNameFirst(std::string_view fullName) that turns "Ada Lovelace" into "Lovelace, Ada" . The name always has exactly one space. Find it with find(' ') , then cut the name into two pieces with substr . Call Meaning --- --- s.find(' ') index of the first space s.substr(0, n) the first n characters s.substr(n) everything from index n to the end

title: Username maker
body: A school gives every student a username made from the first letter of their first name, their whole last name, and the number of letters in the two names together. Read a first name and a last name (two words) and print the username: Grace Hopper - GHopper11 Print only the username.

title: 2.08  Operators Deep Dive
body: Comparisons ( == , < ...) produce a bool . Logical operators ( && , , ! ) combine bools and stop early when the answer is settled. ++x and x++ differ in the value they give back. ?: chooses between two values. Comparison operators Each of these compares two values and produces a bool . Operator Meaning 5 ? 3 --- --- --- == equal to false != not equal to true < less than false greater than true <= less than or equal to false = greater than or equal to true !danger = stores, == compares x = 5 puts 5 into x . x == 5 asks whether x is 5. Writing one where you meant the other is among the most common mistakes in C++, and it compiles. The compiler warns about it, which is one more reason to read warnings. Logical operators These combine yes/no answers. Operator Name True when --- --- --- a && b AND both are true a \ \ b OR at least one is true !a NOT a is false a b a && b a \ \ b !a --- --- --- --- --- true true true true false true false false true false false true false true true false false false false true cpp bool canVote{ age = 18 && isCitizen }; bool isWeekend{ day == 6 day == 7 }; bool isTeen{ age = 13 && age <= 19 }; !warning Ranges need two comparisons Maths lets you write 13 ≤ age ≤ 19. In C++, 13 <= age <= 19 compiles and is always true . It works out 13 <= age first, giving true or false , which is 1 or 0, and then compares that with 19. Short-circuit evaluation && and look at the left side first. If that already settles the answer, the right side is never run . This is a tool you can rely on, not just a speed-up: cpp if (count != 0 && total / count 10) When count is 0 the division never happens, so there is no divide-by-zero. Prefix and postfix ++ Both add one to the variable. They differ in the value the expression gives back. int x{ 5 }; int a{ ++x }; prefix: add first, then give the new value a is 6, x is 6 int b{ x++ }; postfix: give the old value, then add b is 6, x is 7 On a line of its own, ++x; and x++; do the same thing. !tip Two habits Use prefix ++x unless you specifically need the old value. And never change a variable with ++ and also use it elsewhere in the same expression: x++ + x++ has no dependable answer. The conditional operator ?: It chooses between two values according to a condition. cpp condition ? value if true : value if false cpp int larger{ (a b) ? a : b }; std::cout << (score = 50 ? "Pass" : "Fail") << '\n'; Use it to pick a value . To choose between actions , use if : 3.01 if and else . Precedence: what binds tightest Higher rows are worked out first. Level Operators --- --- 1 x++ x-- and function calls 2 ++x --x ! -x (negative) static_cast 3 / % 4 + - 5 << 6 < <= = 7 == != 8 && 9 \ \ 10 ?: = += and the other assignments You do not have to memorise this. Remember three facts: arithmetic comes before comparison, comparison before && , and && before . For anything else, add brackets. !warning Printing a comparison needs brackets std::cout << a < b; fails, because << is above < in the table. Write std::cout << (a < b); . Maths functions Call Result Header --- --- --- std::pow(2, 10) 1024 (as a double ) <cmath std::sqrt(16) 4 <cmath std::abs(-3) 3 <cmath std::max(a, b) , std::min(a, b) the larger, the smaller <algorithm

title: Leap year
body: Write bool isLeapYear(int year) . A year is a leap year when it divides by 4, except that century years (those that divide by 100) only count when they also divide by 400. Year Leap? Why --- --- --- 2024 yes divides by 4 2023 no does not divide by 4 1900 no century, not divisible by 400 2000 yes century, divisible by 400 Combine the three tests with && , and != . No if is needed.

title: In range
body: Write bool inRange(int value, int low, int high) that returns true when value is at least low and at most high . In maths you can write low <= value <= high . In C++ that compiles but means something else. Write two comparisons joined with && .

title: The larger one
body: Write int larger(int a, int b) that returns whichever of the two is bigger, using the conditional operator ? : . cpp condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

title: Ticket price
body: A cinema charges by age: Age Price --- --- under 5 0 5 to 17 8 18 to 64 12 65 and over 6 Read an age and print the price (just the number). You have not met if yet, and you do not need it: chain the conditional operator. cpp int price{ age < 5 ? 0 : (age < 18 ? 8 : ...) };

title: 2.09  Bit Manipulation
body:
Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of a number: & AND, OR, ^ XOR, ~ NOT, << and shift. They let you pack many on/off settings into one number and pull packed values apart. Why work with single bits? A bool takes a whole byte to store one yes/no answer. One byte has eight bits, so it could hold eight. When memory is tight, or a file format or a piece of hardware dictates the layout, programmers pack several small values into one number and operate on its bits directly. This lesson is the most technical in the milestone. It builds on 2.01 Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types and 2.02 Integers . Binary and hexadecimal position: 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 worth: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 bits: 0 0 0 0 1 1 0 1 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 13 Bits are numbered from the right, starting at 0. Hexadecimal (base 16) is the usual shorthand, because one hex digit is exactly four bits: Hex Binary Hex Binary --- --- --- --- 0 0000 8 1000 1 0001 A 1010 4 0100 D 1101 7 0111 F 1111 So 0xFF is 1111 1111 , a full byte of ones. The six operators Each works on every bit position separately. a = 1100 a = 1100 a = 1100 b = 1010 b = 1010 b = 1010 a & b = 1000 a b = 1110 a ^ b = 0110 both are 1 either is 1 they differ ~a = 0011 every bit flipped a << 1 = 1000 moved left one place: the top bit falls off, a 0 comes in a 2 = 0011 moved right two places Operator Name A result bit is 1 when --- --- --- & AND both bits are 1 \ OR either bit is 1 ^ XOR the bits are different ~ NOT the bit was 0 << left shift (moves bits left; each place doubles the value) right shift (moves bits right; each place halves the value) !warning Do not confuse these with the logical operators && and combine two bool values into one. & and combine two numbers bit by bit. And here << shifts bits; it only means "print" when the left side is std::cout . Seeing the bits std::bitset prints a number in binary and has functions for individual bits. cpp include <bitset include <iostream int main() { std::bitset<8 bits{ 0b0000'1101 }; std::cout << bits << '
'; // 00001101 bits.set(7); // switch bit 7 on bits.flip(0); // toggle bit 0 std::cout << bits << '
'; // 10001100 std::cout << bits.test(2) << '
'; // 1: bit 2 is on std::cout << bits.count() << '
'; // 3 bits are on return 0; } Bit flags A flag is a single yes/no setting. Give each flag its own bit by shifting a 1 into place. A value with one chosen bit set, used to pick that bit out, is called a mask . cpp include <cstdint constexpr std::uint8_t flagRead{ 1 << 0 }; // 0000 0001 constexpr std::uint8_t flagWrite{ 1 << 1 }; // 0000 0010 constexpr std::uint8_t flagExecute{ 1 << 2 }; // 0000 0100 There are exactly four things you ever do with a flag: To Write Why it works --- --- --- Switch on flags \ = mask; OR with 1 forces the bit to 1 Switch off flags &= ~mask; AND with 0 forces the bit to 0; all other bits are ANDed with 1 and survive Toggle flags ^= mask; XOR with 1 flips the bit Test (flags & mask) != 0 AND leaves only that bit; non-zero means it was on cpp std::uint8_t perms{ 0 }; perms = flagRead; // 0000 0001 perms = flagWrite; // 0000 0011 perms &= ~flagWrite; // 0000 0001 perms ^= flagExecute; // 0000 0101 bool canRead{ (perms & flagRead) != 0 }; // true Packing and unpacking with masks A colour on screen is three values from 0 to 255: red, green and blue. They are commonly packed into one 32-bit number written 0xRRGGBB . color = 0000 0000 1111 1111 1000 1000 0000 0000 0xFF8800 color 8 = 0000 0000 1111 1111 1000 1000 green is now at the bottom & 0xFF = 1000 1000 keep only the lowest 8 bits The pattern for extracting a field is always shift it to the bottom, then mask off the rest : cpp std::uint32_t color{ 0xFF8800 }; std::uint32_t red{ (color 16) & 0xFF }; // 0xFF std::uint32_t green{ (color 8) & 0xFF }; // 0x88 std::uint32_t blue{ color & 0xFF }; // 0x00 Packing is the reverse, shift each part into position, then OR them together : cpp std::uint32_t packed{ (red << 16) (green << 8) blue }; !warning Use unsigned types for bit work Shifting a negative signed number gives results that depend on details you do not want to rely on. This is the main job unsigned types exist for.

title: Power of two
body: A power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 ...) has exactly one bit switched on. Subtracting 1 from it flips that bit off and every lower bit on, so the two numbers share no bits: 8 = 1000 8 - 1 = 0111 8 & 7 = 0000 Write bool isPowerOfTwo(unsigned int n) using that trick. Zero is not a power of two.

title: Four bit tricks
body: Flags pack several on/off switches into one number. Write the four standard operations. bit is the position, counting from 0 at the right-hand end. Function Does Recipe --- --- --- setBit(flags, bit) switches the bit on OR with the mask clearBit(flags, bit) switches it off AND with the inverted mask toggleBit(flags, bit) flips it XOR with the mask testBit(flags, bit) is it on? AND with the mask, compare with 0 The mask for a bit is 1u << bit . The first three return unsigned int ; testBit returns bool .

To read one back, shift right with and keep the low 8 bits with & 0xFF .

title: 3.01  if and else
body:
if (condition) { ... } runs a block only when the condition is true. else if adds further choices and else catches everything left. Only the first branch that matches runs. Programs that decide Until now every statement ran, top to bottom, every time. Control flow is how a program chooses which statements to run. if is the foundation of it. cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 73 }; if (score = 90) { std::cout << "A
"; } else if (score = 80) { std::cout << "B
"; } else if (score = 70) { std::cout << "C
"; } else { std::cout << "F
"; } return 0; } Part Meaning --- --- if (condition) Run the block when the condition is true else if (condition) Otherwise, try this condition else Otherwise, when nothing above matched Each path through the statement is called a branch . The conditions are tested in order, and only the first true branch runs . The rest are skipped, even if their conditions would also be true. !tip Order does the work for you Because of that rule, else if (score = 80) does not need to say && score < 90 . If execution reaches it, the first test has already failed. Always use braces Without braces, an if controls exactly one statement. cpp if (lives == 0) std::cout << "Game over
"; resetGame(); // NOT part of the if. This runs every time. The indentation suggests one thing and the compiler does another. Write the braces every time, even for one line. Combining conditions Two nested tests can usually be flattened with && : cpp if (hasTicket) { if (age = 18) { std::cout << "Enjoy the film
"; } } cpp if (hasTicket && age = 18) { std::cout << "Enjoy the film
"; } The second says the same thing with less to read. Early return Deeply nested code is hard to follow. A common remedy is to deal with the unusual cases first and leave. cpp double safeDivide(double a, double b) { if (b == 0.0) { std::cout << "Cannot divide by zero
"; return 0.0; } return a / b; } A check at the top that rejects bad input is called a guard clause . With the problem cases out of the way, the main logic sits at the outer level with no indentation. A variable that belongs to the if You can create a variable inside the if itself. It exists only for that statement. cpp if (int remainder{ n % 3 }; remainder == 0) { std::cout << "divisible by three
"; } // remainder no longer exists here The part before the ; creates the variable and the part after is the condition. This keeps a helper variable from lingering where it is not needed. Four classic traps Written Problem --- --- if (x = 5) Assigns 5 to x , then treats 5 as true . You meant == . if (x 0); The ; ends the if . The block after it always runs. if (0 < x < 10) Always true. Write x 0 && x < 10 . if (a == b) with two double values Rounding makes this unreliable: 2.03 Floating Point Numbers The compiler warns about the first two.

title: 3.02  switch
body:
switch compares one value against a list of fixed options and jumps to the matching case . End each case with break , or execution carries on into the next one. One value, many options A long if / else if chain that keeps testing the same variable against fixed values is clearer as a switch . cpp include <iostream int main() { int choice{}; std::cin choice; switch (choice) { case 1: std::cout << "Starting a new game
"; break; case 2: std::cout << "Loading
"; break; case 3: std::cout << "Goodbye
"; break; default: std::cout << "Not an option
"; break; } return 0; } Part Meaning --- --- switch (value) The value to examine case 1: Where to jump to when the value is 1 break; Leave the switch default: Where to jump to when no case matches Fall-through A case is only a label : a place to jump to. It is not a block with an end. Without break , execution simply continues into whatever comes next. switch (2) case 1: print "one" case 2: print "two" jumps in here case 3: print "three" no break above, so this runs too default: print "other" and so does this Output: two three other Forgetting a break is the classic switch bug. Fall-through is useful in one situation: several values that share the same code. cpp switch (letter) { case 'a': case 'e': case 'i': case 'o': case 'u': std::cout << "vowel
"; break; default: std::cout << "consonant
"; break; } !tip Marking it as deliberate If a case does some work and you want it to continue into the next, write fallthrough ; at that point. It tells the compiler and the reader that the missing break is intended. return also leaves Inside a function, a return ends the function, and therefore the switch . No break is needed after it. cpp std::string_view dayName(int day) { switch (day) { case 1: return "Monday"; case 2: return "Tuesday"; case 3: return "Wednesday"; default: return "unknown"; } } The rules Rule Detail --- --- The value must be integer-like int , char , bool or an enum. Not std::string , not double . Each case must be a constant A literal, or a constexpr value. Not an ordinary variable. No ranges There is no case 1 to 5 . Use if for ranges. Variables inside a case need braces case 1: { int x{ 5 }; ... break; } switch or if ? Use switch when Use if when --- --- Comparing one value against several fixed values Testing ranges, such as score = 90 Menus, commands, single characters, enums Text, decimals or conditions that combine several variables switch becomes much more valuable once you meet enums in 4.05 Enums , where the compiler can warn you if you forget one of the options.

title: 3.03  Loops — while, do-while, for
body: Loops repeat code. while repeats as long as a condition holds. do-while runs the body at least once. for is built for counting. break leaves a loop and continue skips to the next round. Three loops, one idea All three repeat a block while a condition is true. They differ in when the condition is tested and where the counting lives. One pass through the body is called an iteration . while cpp int count{ 1 }; while (count <= 5) { std::cout << count << ' '; ++count; } // 1 2 3 4 5 The condition is tested before each iteration. If it is false at the start, the body never runs. If nothing in the body ever makes it false, the loop never ends: an infinite loop . do-while cpp int choice{}; do { std::cout << "Enter 1 to 3: "; std::cin choice; } while (choice < 1 choice 3); The condition is tested after each iteration, so the body always runs at least once. That suits "ask, then check the answer". Note the ; after the closing bracket. for A counting loop needs three things: a starting value, a condition and a step. for puts all three on one line. cpp // start condition step for (int i{ 0 }; i < 5; ++i) { std::cout << i << ' '; } // 0 1 2 3 4 Trace it: i i < 5 ? Action --- --- --- 0 true print 0, then ++i 1 true print 1, then ++i ... 4 true print 4, then ++i 5 false the loop ends The patterns you will write most: To loop over Write --- --- 0 up to n − 1 (n iterations) for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) 1 up to n for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i) 10 down to 1 for (int i{ 10 }; i 0; --i) Every second value for (int i{ 0 }; i < 20; i += 2) !tip Start at 0, test with < Programmers count from zero because indexes start at zero. for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) runs exactly n times and visits exactly the valid indexes of something with n elements. Make it your default shape. Which loop? Situation Loop --- --- You know how many iterations, or you are counting for You repeat until something happens, and it may already have happened while The body must run once before you can test do-while break and continue cpp for (int i{ 1 }; i <= 10; ++i) { if (i == 3) { continue; // skip the rest of this iteration } if (i == 7) { break; // leave the loop altogether } std::cout << i << ' '; } // 1 2 4 5 6 Statement Effect --- --- break Ends the loop immediately continue Ends this iteration; in a for loop the step still runs A loop written as while (true) relies on a break inside it to end. That is a normal pattern when the exit test belongs in the middle of the body. Nested loops A loop inside a loop. The inner loop runs in full for every single iteration of the outer one. cpp for (int row{ 1 }; row <= 3; ++row) { for (int col{ 1 }; col <= 4; ++col) { std::cout << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; } outer loop: 3 iterations inner loop: 4 iterations each time 12 stars in all The inner loop's limit can depend on the outer variable. Changing col <= 4 to col <= row gives a triangle: Building up a result A very common shape: create a variable before the loop and update it on each iteration. That variable is called an accumulator . cpp int sum{ 0 }; for (int i{ 1 }; i <= 100; ++i) { sum += i; } std::cout << sum << '\n'; // 5050 The same shape counts things, finds a maximum, builds a string, and much more. Three classic bugs Bug Cause Check --- --- --- Off by one <= where you needed < , or the wrong start Trace the first and the last iteration by hand Infinite loop Nothing in the body moves towards the exit Ask what changes on each iteration Unsigned countdown for (unsigned i{ 5 }; i = 0; --i) An unsigned value is always = 0 , so the test never fails

title: 3.04  Random Numbers
body: Create one random engine, seed it once, and use a distribution to turn its output into numbers in the range you want. Never create a new engine each time you need a number. Computers cannot be random A computer follows instructions exactly, so it cannot roll a real die. What it can do is run a formula whose output looks random: each number is calculated from the one before. These are called pseudo-random numbers. Because every number depends on the previous one, the starting value decides the whole sequence. That starting value is the seed . Three parts Part Job Like --- --- --- Seed The starting point of the sequence Shuffling a deck Engine Produces a long stream of raw, random-looking numbers The shuffled deck Distribution Converts raw numbers into what you asked for, such as 1 to 6 The rules for reading a card The code cpp include <iostream include <random int main() { std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; // one engine, seeded once std::uniform_int_distribution die{ 1, 6 }; // 1 to 6, both included for (int i{ 0 }; i < 10; ++i) { std::cout << die(rng) << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } Piece What it is --- --- std::mt19937 A well-tested engine (the "Mersenne Twister") std::random_device{}() Asks the operating system for an unpredictable seed std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 } Whole numbers from 1 to 6, each equally likely die(rng) Draw one number: the distribution takes what it needs from the engine Other distributions Distribution Produces --- --- std::uniform_real_distribution{ 0.0, 1.0 } Decimals from 0 up to, but not including, 1 std::bernoulli_distribution{ 0.5 } true or false , here with a 50% chance std::normal_distribution{ 170.0, 10.0 } A bell curve centred on 170 The same seed gives the same sequence seed 42 gives 17, 3, 88, 41, ... seed 42 gives 17, 3, 88, 41, ... identical seed 99 gives 62, 9, 14, 77, ... This is a feature. A fixed seed makes a "random" program repeatable, which is exactly what you need when testing or chasing a bug. cpp std::mt19937 testRng{ 42 }; // same numbers on every run You want Seed with --- --- Different results on every run (a game) std::random_device{}() Identical results on every run (a test) a fixed number One engine for the whole program !danger Do not create an engine inside the function that uses it cpp int roll() { std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; // a new engine on every call return std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 }(rng); } This throws away the engine after one number. It is slow, and you lose the quality the engine is designed to give over a long sequence. The usual solution is a small header that every file shares: cpp // random.h pragma once include <random namespace Random { inline std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; inline int get(int min, int max) { return std::uniform_int_distribution{ min, max }(rng); } } cpp int roll{ Random::get(1, 6) }; The engine is created once, when the program starts, and every call to Random::get draws from it. The namespace and inline keywords are explained in the next two lessons. !warning You will see rand() in old code std::rand() % 6 + 1 is the method inherited from C. Its numbers are of poor quality and slightly favour some results. Recognise it; do not write it.

title: Roll a die

The random engine is handed in (the & means the function uses the caller's engine rather than a copy, which you will learn about in milestone 4). Your job is the distribution: cpp std::uniform_int_distribution<int die{ 1, 6 }; return die(rng); The tests roll it thousands of times and check that every result is between 1 and 6 and that all six numbers turn up.

title: Random in a range
body: Write int randomBetween(std::mt19937& rng, int low, int high) returning a random whole number from low to high , both included.

title: Same seed, same game
body: A random engine started from the same seed always produces the same sequence. Games use this for replays, and tests use it to get repeatable results. Read a seed and a number of rolls. Seed a std::mt19937 with that seed, roll a six-sided die that many times, and print the rolls on one line separated by spaces, then how many sixes there were: Rolls: 1 5 2 6 4 Sixes: 1 (The exact numbers depend on the seed.) To match the expected output, create one engine, one std::uniform_int_distribution<int { 1, 6 } , and call it exactly once per roll.

title: 3.05  Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces
body:
Scope is where in the code a name can be used. Lifetime is when during the run the variable exists. Namespaces group names so that two things called the same do not clash. Two questions about every variable Question Called Decided --- --- --- On which lines may I use this name? Scope By where it is declared in the source For how long does the value exist in memory? Lifetime While the program runs For the local variables you have used so far the two coincide, which is why they are easy to mix up. They come apart in the next lesson. Every pair of braces is a scope A name declared inside a block can be used from its declaration to the block's closing brace. ┌─ main ───────────────────────────────────┐ │ int x{ 1 }; │ │ │ │ ┌─ if block ─────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ int y{ 2 }; │ │ │ │ can use: x, y │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌─ for block ──────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ int z{ 3 }; │ │ │ │ │ │ can use: x, y, z │ │ │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ z is out of scope │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ y and z are out of scope │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ Code can see outwards, never inwards. An inner block can use names from the blocks around it. An outer block cannot reach into an inner one. Lifetime of a local variable A local variable is created when execution reaches its definition and destroyed at the closing brace of its block. That is automatic, and it explains the name for this kind of lifetime: automatic storage duration . !tip Keep scopes small Declare each variable in the smallest block that needs it, as close to its first use as you can. Fewer lines can touch it, so fewer lines can break it. Shadowing An inner block may declare a name that already exists in an outer block. The inner one hides the outer one until its block ends. cpp include <iostream int main() { int apples{ 5 }; { int apples{ 10 }; // a second, separate variable std::cout << apples << '
'; // 10 } std::cout << apples << '
'; // 5 return 0; } This is legal and almost always a mistake. You think you are changing one variable and you are changing another. Give the inner variable a different name. Namespaces As programs grow, names collide. Two libraries may each have a function called add . A namespace is a named group that keeps them apart, in the way a surname separates two people called Sam. cpp include <iostream namespace Math { constexpr double pi{ 3.14159 }; int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } } namespace Game::Utils { int clamp(int value, int low, int high) { return value < low ? low : (value high ? high : value); } } int main() { std::cout << Math::add(2, 3) << ' ' << Math::pi << '
'; std::cout << Game::Utils::clamp(15, 0, 10) << '
'; // 10 return 0; } :: is the scope resolution operator . Read Math::add as "the add that lives in Math ". You have used it since your first program: std::cout is "the cout in std ". A name declared outside every function and every namespace belongs to the global namespace . using : shorter names, with a cost Form Effect Verdict --- --- --- using std::cout; Lets you write cout for this one name Fine inside a function or a .cpp file using namespace std; Brings in every name from std Avoid namespace GU = Game::Utils; A short alias for a long namespace Fine !danger Why this course never writes using namespace std; std contains thousands of names, including common words such as count , max , distance and swap . Importing all of them invites clashes with your own names, and the errors that result are baffling. In a header it is worse still, because it leaks into every file that includes that header.

title: Out of scope
body: This program should add the numbers 1 to 5 and print 15 . It does not compile, because total is defined inside the loop's braces and so does not exist on the line that prints it. (It would also be reset to zero every time round.) Move the definition to the right place.

title: Two functions, one name
body: Two teams both wrote a function called toMetres . One converts kilometres, the other miles. Put each in its own namespace so both can exist: - Metric::toMetres(double km) returns kilometres × 1000 - Imperial::toMetres(double miles) returns miles × 1609.344

title: The shadow
body: This program reads scores until it sees -1 , and should print the highest score. It always prints 0 . The bug is shadowing : a second variable with the same name hides the first one. Find it and fix it. (In the Problems tab the compiler even warns about it.) For the input 40 95 70 -1 the output should be: Highest: 95

title: 3.06  Global Variables, static and Linkage
body: Globals exist for the whole run of the program. Linkage decides whether other .cpp files can see a name. A static local keeps its value between calls. Avoid globals that can change. Global variables A variable defined outside every function is global . Any function below it in the file can use it. cpp include <iostream int g_score{ 0 }; void addPoints() { g_score += 10; } int main() { addPoints(); std::cout << g_score << '\n'; // 10 return 0; } Local variable Global variable --- --- --- Scope Its block The rest of the file Lifetime Until its block ends The whole run: created before main , destroyed after it If you give no value Unpredictable Zero Here scope and lifetime separate. This lifetime is called static storage duration . The g_ prefix is a common convention that marks a name as global. !danger Avoid globals that can change When any function anywhere can modify g_score , a wrong value makes every function a suspect. A function that only uses its parameters can be understood and tested on its own. Pass values in as arguments and hand results back with return . Global constants are fine. Nothing can change them, so nothing can break them. Linkage: can other files see it? Scope is about one file. In a program with several .cpp files there is a further question: can a name defined in one file be used from another? That property is linkage . Linkage Meaning --- --- External One shared thing that every file can refer to Internal Private to this file. Another file may use the same name for something else. What you write at file level decides which you get: Written outside any function Linkage Typical use --- --- --- void helper(); or a function definition external Functions other files call int counter{ 0 }; external (A changeable global: avoid) static void helper() internal A helper that only this file needs namespace { void helper() {} } internal The modern way to say the same constexpr int limit{ 5 }; internal A constant used in one file inline constexpr int limit{ 5 }; in a header external A constant shared by many files To use another file's external variable you declare it with extern : "this exists, and it is defined somewhere else". The usual place for such declarations is a header. inline : defined in a header, without breaking the rule You met the One Definition Rule in 1.08 Multiple Files and Headers : a definition may appear only once in the program. A header is pasted into every file that includes it, so anything defined in a header would break that rule. inline is the exception. It tells the linker: "this definition will turn up in several files; they are all the same one." cpp // constants.h pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double gravity{ 9.81 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } This is the standard way to share constants. It is also why the Random helper in 3.04 Random Numbers used inline . static locals: a function with a memory Put static on a local variable and it gets the long lifetime of a global while keeping the small scope of a local. cpp include <iostream int nextId() { static int s_id{ 0 }; // initialized once, the first time through return ++s_id; } int main() { std::cout << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << '\n'; // 1 2 3 return 0; } Call s_id before s_id after --- --- --- first 0 1 second 1 2 third 2 3 An ordinary local would be created afresh at 0 on every call. Only nextId can touch s_id , which makes this far safer than a global counter. One word, several meanings static is the most overloaded keyword in C++. Its meaning depends on where it appears. Where Meaning --- --- On a local variable Lives for the whole run and keeps its value between calls On a global variable or function Internal linkage: private to this file On a class member Shared by all objects of the class: 6.05 Static Members and Friends

title: A function with a memory
body: Write int nextId() that returns 1 the first time it is called, 2 the second time, 3 the third, and so on. A normal local variable starts afresh on every call. A static local is created once and keeps its value between calls.

title: Get rid of the global
body: applyDiscount reads and changes a global variable. That makes it hard to test and easy to break: any other function could change g_price behind its back. Rewrite it as a function that takes what it needs as parameters and returns its answer: double applyDiscount(double price, double percent) For a price of 200 and 15 percent it returns 170. There must be no global variable left.

title: Running average
body: A sensor produces one reading at a time. Write double runningAverage(double reading) that returns the average of every reading it has been given so far . cpp runningAverage(10.0) // 10 (just the one) runningAverage(20.0) // 15 (10 and 20) runningAverage(30.0) // 20 (10, 20 and 30) The function needs to remember two things between calls. Use static local variables: this is exactly what they are for.

title: 3.07  Input Validation and assert
body:
People type things you did not expect. When std::cin number receives letters it enters a fail state : you must clear() it and discard the bad input. Use assert to catch mistakes in your own code while developing. Two kinds of things go wrong Kind Example Whose fault Response --- --- --- --- Bad input The user types abc for their age Nobody's. It will happen. Detect it and ask again. Never crash. A bug Your function is called with a count of 0 The programmer's Stop loudly so it gets fixed A robust program treats these differently. This lesson covers both. What std::cin does with bad input int age{}; std::cin age; the user types: abc then Enter waiting input: a b c 
 ▲ cannot make a number from 'a' 1. age is set to 0 2. std::cin enters a FAIL STATE: every later is silently skipped 3. "abc" is STILL waiting to be read Point 2 is the dangerous one. After a single bad entry, every later read in the program does nothing, and a loop that asks again will spin for ever. The repair: clear, then discard Step Code Why --- --- --- Detect if (!std::cin) A stream used as a condition is false when it has failed Reset std::cin.clear(); Leaves the fail state so reading works again Discard std::cin.ignore(...) Throws away the bad characters still waiting A reusable getInt cpp include <cstdlib include <iostream include <limits include <string_view void ignoreLine() { std::cin.ignore(std::numeric_limits<std::streamsize ::max(), '
'); } int getInt(std::string_view prompt, int min, int max) { while (true) { std::cout << prompt; int x{}; std::cin x; if (!std::cin) { if (std::cin.eof()) { std::exit(0); // the input was closed: nothing more can arrive } std::cin.clear(); ignoreLine(); std::cout << "That is not a number. Try again.
"; continue; } ignoreLine(); if (x < min x max) { std::cout << "It must be between " << min << " and " << max << ".
"; continue; } return x; } } int main() { int age{ getInt("Enter your age (0-120): ", 0, 120) }; std::cout << "You are " << age << '
'; return 0; } Enter your age (0-120): abc That is not a number. Try again. Enter your age (0-120): 500 It must be between 0 and 120. Enter your age (0-120): 25 You are 25 ignoreLine reads as "skip characters, however many there are, up to and including the next new line". The long expression is simply the largest count the function accepts. Notice the shape: while (true) with continue for every rejection and a single return for success. It is the standard pattern for "keep asking until the answer is acceptable". !tip Keep this function Put getInt and ignoreLine in a header of your own. Almost every interactive program you write from here on needs them. assert : catching your own mistakes An assertion states something that must be true at that point if the program is correct. If it is false, the program stops at once and reports the file and line. cpp include <cassert double average(int total, int count) { assert(count 0 && "count must be positive"); return static_cast<double (total) / count; } Assertion failed: count 0 && "count must be positive", file main.cpp, line 5 The && "text" is a trick for attaching a message: a string literal counts as true, so it does not change the test, and it appears in the report. Property Detail --- --- Checked when While the program runs, in Debug builds In Release builds Removed entirely: no check, no cost Use it for Conditions that can only be false if the code has a bug !danger Never validate input with assert Assertions vanish in Release builds, so the check would disappear from the finished program. And bad input is not a bug: it deserves a polite message, not a crash. static_assert : checked by the compiler cpp static_assert(sizeof(int) = 4, "this program needs an int of at least 32 bits"); The condition must be something the compiler can work out. If it is false, the program does not build. There is no cost at run time at all. Choosing the right tool Situation Tool --- --- The user typed something unusable Validate and ask again Something outside your control failed (a missing file) Report and recover, later with exceptions: 9.05 Exceptions "This cannot happen" in your own logic assert An assumption about types or the platform static_assert

title: Ask until it is a number
match: Ask until it is a number
body: Write int readInt() that reads a whole number from std::cin and returns it. If the user types something that is not a number, it must recover and try again, as many times as it takes. When std::cin value fails, two things are wrong and both need fixing: 1. std::cin is in a failed state: std::cin.clear(); 2. the bad text is still waiting in the input: throw the rest of the line away with std::cin.ignore(...) . The tests feed it lines such as abc , x9 and then 12 , and expect 12 back.

title: A number in range
body: Write int readIntInRange(int low, int high) . It keeps reading until it gets a whole number between low and high (both allowed). Text that is not a number, and numbers outside the range, are both rejected.

title: Add up what you can
body: A file of measurements has been damaged: some entries are numbers and some are junk. Read entries separated by spaces or new lines until the input ends. Add up the whole numbers, count the entries you had to skip, and print: Sum: 20 Skipped: 2 (for the input 4 x 10 abc 6 ). Reading stops when there is nothing left. A read can fail for two reasons, and you must tell them apart: - the input ran out: std::cin.eof() is true, so stop; - the next entry is not a number: clear the error, read the junk into a std::string to remove it, count it, carry on.

title: 3.08  Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code
match: 3.08 Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code
body:
std::exit ends the program from anywhere; std::abort ends it at once with no clean-up. goto exists and you almost never want it. Testing each function with known inputs as you write it is the cheapest way to catch bugs. Ways a program ends How Clean-up Use it when --- --- --- return from main Complete Always, if you can std::exit(code) Partial A fatal problem deep in the program with no sensible way back std::abort() None Something is so wrong that continuing would do harm cpp include <cstdlib include <iostream include <string_view void fatal(std::string_view message) { std::cerr << "Fatal: " << message << '
'; std::exit(EXIT_FAILURE); } The number handed to std::exit , like the one returned from main , is the program's exit code . EXIT_SUCCESS (0) means it worked. Anything else means it did not, and other programs can check that. "Clean-up" will mean more in Milestones 6 and 7, when objects start releasing files and memory as they are destroyed. That is why returning from main is preferred: it is the only route on which everything is released properly. goto goto jumps to a labelled statement elsewhere in the same function. cpp int attempts{ 0 }; retry: ++attempts; if (attempts < 3) { goto retry; } It works, and a loop says the same thing more clearly. Code that jumps around freely becomes impossible to follow, which programmers call spaghetti code . Loops, break , continue and functions cover everything goto did, with structure a reader can see. The one case people defend is leaving several nested loops at once. A function with return does that better: cpp bool containsPair(int limit, int target) { for (int a{ 1 }; a <= limit; ++a) { for (int b{ 1 }; b <= limit; ++b) { if (a b == target) { return true; // leaves both loops } } } return false; } Testing your code This is the part of the lesson that will change how you work. A test is code that calls your function with inputs whose correct answer you already know, and checks the result. Every Check button you have pressed in Xenon has run tests like that against your code. Testing each function as you finish it means a failure can only be in the few lines you just wrote. Testing a whole program at the end means it could be anywhere. A small test function cpp include <iostream bool isLeapYear(int year) { return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) year % 400 == 0; } int testIsLeapYear() { if (isLeapYear(2024) != true) { return 1; } if (isLeapYear(2023) != false) { return 2; } if (isLeapYear(1900) != false) { return 3; } // divisible by 100 if (isLeapYear(2000) != true) { return 4; } // divisible by 400 return 0; } int main() { const int failed{ testIsLeapYear() }; if (failed != 0) { std::cout << "Test case " << failed << " FAILED
"; } else { std::cout << "All tests passed
"; } return 0; } Tests stay useful after they pass. Run them again whenever you change the function, and they tell you immediately if you broke something that used to work. Choosing test cases Typical values are the least likely to reveal a bug. Bugs gather at the edges. For clamp(value, 0, 10) : Kind of case Examples Why --- --- --- Ordinary 5 gives 5 Does it work at all? On the boundary 0 gives 0 , 10 gives 10 Catches < written for <= Just outside -1 gives 0 , 11 gives 10 Catches off-by-one errors Extremes The largest and smallest int Catches overflow Odd input Low limit above high limit Did you decide what should happen? Coverage A test can only find a bug in code it actually runs. Coverage measures how much of your code the tests execute. Level Meaning --- --- Statement coverage Every line ran at least once Branch coverage Every if went both ways at least once If no test ever makes a condition false, the else branch is untested, however many tests you have. !info Real projects use a testing framework Libraries such as Catch2 and GoogleTest remove the repetitive parts and report failures clearly. The idea is exactly the one above. See 13.09 Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling . The usual suspects When a test fails, check these first. They account for most logic errors in the first three milestones. Error Example --- --- Wrong comparison age 18 where = was meant Off by one i <= size Loop that never ends The step is missing Precedence a + b / 2 Integer division 1 / 2 x is always 0 Stray semicolon if (x); or for (...); = for == if (x = 0)

title: Write the tests yourself
where: 3.08 Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code
