title: 11.01  Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding
body: Every expression has a type and a value category : lvalue, xvalue or prvalue. In a template, T&& is a forwarding reference : it binds to anything and records whether the argument was an lvalue or an rvalue. std::forward<T (x) passes it on with that category intact, which is perfect forwarding . Value categories, precisely 7.05 Move Semantics used a two-way split into lvalues and rvalues. The standard uses three primary categories, defined by two independent properties: does the expression have identity (does it refer to a particular object), and may its resources be moved from ? Category Identity Movable Examples --- --- --- --- lvalue Yes No x , p , v 0 , a string literal xvalue ("expiring") Yes Yes std::move(x) , static_cast<T&& (x) prvalue ("pure rvalue") No Yes 42 , x + 1 , T{} , make() A value category is a property of an expression , not of an object or a type. The same object can be named by an lvalue expression ( x ) and by an xvalue expression ( std::move(x) ). !important A named rvalue reference is an lvalue cpp void f(std::string&& s) { g(s); // s is a name, so this expression is an lvalue: g copies g(std::move(s)); // an xvalue: g may move } The type of s is std::string&& . The value category of the expression s is lvalue, because it has a name and could be used again. This is what makes forwarding necessary. Forwarding references T&& has a special meaning when, and only when, T is a template parameter deduced from that very parameter. cpp template <typename T void wrapper(T&& arg); // forwarding reference: binds to anything void f(std::string&& s); // rvalue reference: binds to rvalues only auto&& x{ expression }; // also a forwarding reference Declaration Kind --- --- template <typename T void f(T&&) Forwarding reference auto&& Forwarding reference void f(Widget&&) Rvalue reference: no deduction template <typename T void f(const T&&) Rvalue reference: const disqualifies it template <typename T void f(std::vector<T &&) Rvalue reference: not of the form T&& Reference collapsing Two rules produce the behaviour. A special deduction rule. When an lvalue of type A is passed to T&& , T is deduced as A& . When an rvalue is passed, T is deduced as A . Reference collapsing. A reference to a reference, which can only arise through templates and aliases, collapses: & & becomes & & && becomes & && & becomes & && && becomes && an lvalue reference anywhere wins Argument T deduced as T&& becomes --- --- --- An lvalue std::string std::string& std::string& && , which collapses to std::string& An rvalue std::string std::string std::string&& So T itself encodes the argument's original value category. std::forward Inside wrapper , arg is a name and therefore an lvalue, whatever was passed. std::forward<T (arg) restores the original category by reading it back out of T . cpp include <iostream include <string include <utility void process(const std::string&) { std::cout << "copy\n"; } void process(std::string&&) { std::cout << "move\n"; } template <typename T void relay(T&& arg) { process(std::forward<T (arg)); } int main() { std::string name{ "Ann" }; relay(name); // copy relay(std::string{ "Bo" }); // move relay(std::move(name)); // move return 0; } std::forward<T (arg) is static_cast<T&& (arg) . With T as std::string& it collapses to an lvalue reference; with T as std::string it is an rvalue reference. std::move(x) std::forward<T (x) --- --- --- Produces Always an rvalue An lvalue or an rvalue, as recorded in T Use with An rvalue reference or object you are finished with A forwarding reference Template argument Deduced Must be written explicitly The standard use: wrapping construction cpp template <typename T, typename... Args std::unique_ptr<T make(Args&&... args) { return std::unique_ptr<T { new T(std::forward<Args (args)...) }; } Each argument reaches T 's constructor exactly as the caller supplied it: lvalues are copied from, rvalues moved from, and nothing is copied in between. std::make_unique , emplace_back and the constructor of std::thread all work this way. decltype and decltype(auto) Expression Yields --- --- decltype(x) where x is a name The declared type of x decltype((x)) , or any other lvalue expression of type T T& decltype( an xvalue ) T&& decltype( a prvalue ) T cpp int x{}; decltype(x) a{}; // int decltype((x)) b{ x }; // int&: the parentheses make it an expression, not a name auto strips references and top-level const . decltype(auto) deduces with the decltype rules, preserving them. That is what a forwarding wrapper needs for its return type: cpp template <typename F, typename... Args decltype(auto) call(F&& f, Args&&... args) { return std::forward<F (f)(std::forward<Args (args)...); } If f returns a reference, so does call . std::invoke(f, args...) generalises the call itself to member function pointers and member data pointers. Pitfalls Pitfall Why --- --- Forwarding the same argument twice The first use may move from it Overloading on a forwarding reference template <typename T void f(T&&) is an exact match for almost anything and beats f(const Widget&) for a non-const lvalue. Constrain it with a concept. A forwarding constructor It can hijack copy construction from a non-const lvalue. Constrain it. return (x); under decltype(auto) The parentheses make it T& : a reference to a local

title: Forward it untouched
body: receive has two overloads: one for objects that must be copied (lvalues) and one for temporaries that may be moved from (rvalues). Write template <typename T std::string relay(T&& widget) that passes its argument on to receive exactly as it arrived : an lvalue stays an lvalue, an rvalue stays an rvalue. Inside relay , widget has a name, so on its own it is always an lvalue. std::forward<T (widget) restores the original category.

title: A factory that wastes nothing
body: Write two helpers that construct objects in place, forwarding every argument perfectly so that nothing is copied on the way. - make<T (args...) : returns a std::unique_ptr<T built from the arguments. This is essentially std::make_unique . - emplaceBack(vector, args...) : constructs a new element at the end of a std::vector<T from the arguments and returns a reference to it. Both take a parameter pack of forwarding references ( Args&&... args ) and expand it with std::forward<Args (args)... . The tests use a type that counts how often it is copied. Passing a temporary through your helpers must cause zero copies.

title: 11.02  Type Traits
body: Type traits , in <type_traits , are compile-time questions about types and transformations of them: "is T an integer?", "T without its const". Each is a template yielding a value or a type . With if constexpr and static_assert , they let code adapt to the types it is given. Computing with types A type trait is a class template whose result is a member: a value for a question, or a type for a transformation. They are functions from types to values or to other types, evaluated entirely by the compiler. Using them to shape code is metaprogramming . Query traits cpp include <type_traits static_assert(std::is_integral_v<int ); static_assert(std::is_floating_point_v<float ); static_assert(std::is_pointer_v<int ); static_assert(std::is_same_v<int, signed int ); Trait Asks --- --- is_integral_v<T , is_floating_point_v<T , is_arithmetic_v<T What kind of number? is_pointer_v<T , is_reference_v<T , is_array_v<T , is_enum_v<T , is_class_v<T What category of type? is_const_v<T Is it const -qualified? is_same_v<T, U Are they exactly the same type? is_base_of_v<Base, Derived , is_convertible_v<From, To How are two types related? is_trivially_copyable_v<T Can it be copied as raw bytes? is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T Is its move constructor noexcept ? is_invocable_v<F, Args... Can F be called with these arguments? trait_v<T is a variable template, short for trait<T ::value . Transformation traits Trait Result --- --- remove_const_t<const int int remove_reference_t<int& int remove_cvref_t<const int& int add_pointer_t<int int decay_t<const int 5 const int : what passing by value does make_unsigned_t<int unsigned int conditional_t<condition, A, B A if true, otherwise B common_type_t<int, double double underlying_type_t<Enum The enum's integer type trait_t<T is an alias template, short for typename trait<T ::type . std::remove_cvref_t is the one you will reach for most. Inside a template with a forwarding reference, T may be Widget& or const Widget& , and most questions should be asked about plain Widget . Using traits static_assert : state a requirement cpp template <typename T void writeBytes(std::ostream& out, const T& value) { static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T , "writeBytes needs a trivially copyable type"); out.write(reinterpret_cast<const char (&value), sizeof(T)); } A violated requirement becomes a compile error with your message, in place of undefined behaviour at run time. if constexpr : one function, a branch per type cpp include <iostream include <string include <type_traits template <typename T std::string toString(const T& value) { if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, std::string ) { return value; } else if constexpr (std::is_arithmetic_v<T ) { return std::to_string(value); } else if constexpr (std::is_pointer_v<T ) { return value ? toString( value) : "null"; } else { static_assert(false, "toString: unsupported type"); } } int main() { const int n{ 42 }; std::cout << toString(n) << ' ' << toString(std::string{ "hi" }) << ' ' << toString(&n) << '\n'; return 0; } The condition of if constexpr is evaluated at compile time, and the branches not taken are discarded : they are not instantiated for that T . That is the whole point. std::to_string(value) would not compile for a std::string , and here it is never asked to. How traits are built There is no compiler magic in most of them. A trait is a primary template giving the general answer and specializations giving the exceptions ( 9.02 Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization ). cpp template <typename T struct IsPointer : std::false_type {}; // in general: no template <typename T struct IsPointer<T : std::true_type {}; // for anything of the form T : yes template <typename T inline constexpr bool isPointer_v{ IsPointer<T ::value }; static_assert(isPointer_v<int ); static_assert(!isPointer_v<int ); std::true_type and std::false_type are tiny classes with a static value of true or false . Inheriting from one is the conventional way to give a trait its result. A transformation works the same way, with a nested type as the result: cpp template <typename T struct RemoveConst { using type = T; }; template <typename T struct RemoveConst<const T { using type = T; }; template <typename T using RemoveConst_t = typename RemoveConst<T ::type; The typename keyword is required before RemoveConst<T ::type because it is a dependent name : until T is known, the compiler cannot tell whether ::type names a type or a value, and assumes a value unless told otherwise. A few traits cannot be written in the language at all and are supplied by the compiler: is_trivially_copyable , is_class , is_enum and underlying_type among them. Detecting capabilities Asking "does T have a size() member?" used to need the machinery of the next lesson. With C++20 it is one requires-expression ( 9.04 Concepts (C++20) ): cpp template <typename T inline constexpr bool hasSize{ requires(const T& t) { t.size(); } }; static_assert(hasSize<std::vector<int ); static_assert(!hasSize<int ); Traits or concepts? Type traits Concepts --- --- --- Produce A boolean or a type A named constraint Constrain a template Through enable_if : awkward Directly Take part in overload ordering No Yes, by subsumption Transform types Yes No Use concepts to constrain . Use traits to compute types, and inside if constexpr . Most standard concepts are defined in terms of traits.

Also the shortcut my::isSame<T, U as a variable template. - my::RemoveConst<T with a nested type : T with a top-level const stripped off. Also the alias my::RemoveConst_t<T .

title: 11.03  SFINAE, enable_if and Tag Dispatch
body: SFINAE , "Substitution Failure Is Not An Error": if substituting a type into a template's declaration produces invalid code, that overload is silently removed instead of causing an error. Code before C++20 used it, through std::enable_if , void_t and tag dispatch, to constrain templates. Concepts do the job better now, but you must be able to read it. The rule When the compiler considers a function template for a call, it deduces the template arguments and substitutes them into the declaration. If that substitution produces an invalid type or expression, the template is dropped from the set of candidates. The program is not ill-formed. The rule exists so that an overload set may contain templates that are only meaningful for some types. Library authors turned it into a way of deliberately making a template vanish unless a condition holds. !warning Only the immediate context counts SFINAE applies to failures in the function's declaration : its return type, its parameter types and its template parameter list. An error inside the function body is a hard error. This is why a constraint has to be expressed in the signature. std::enable_if enable_if is a trait built to fail on purpose. cpp template <bool Condition, typename T = void struct enable_if {}; // no member named type template <typename T struct enable_if<true, T { using type = T; // present only when the condition is true }; std::enable_if_t<false names a member that does not exist. That is a substitution failure, so the overload disappears. cpp include <iostream include <type_traits template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T , int = 0 T half(T x) { return x / 2; } template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_floating_point_v<T , int = 0 T half(T x) { return x T{ 0.5 }; } int main() { std::cout << half(10) << ' ' << half(3.0) << '\n'; // 5 1.5 // half("x"); error: no matching function, both overloads were removed return 0; } Read std::enable_if_t<condition, int = 0 as "an unused template parameter of type int , defaulted to 0, which only exists when the condition is true". The same device appears in three places: Position Looks like --- --- A defaulted template parameter template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<C, int = 0 The return type std::enable_if_t<C, T half(T x); An extra function parameter T half(T x, std::enable_if_t<C = nullptr); The same thing with concepts cpp auto half(std::integral auto x) { return x / 2; } auto half(std::floating_point auto x) { return x 0.5; } The requirement is stated, not encoded. That is why 9.04 Concepts (C++20) exist. Detecting members Two more tools make it possible to ask whether an expression is valid. Tool Does --- --- std::declval<T () Yields a T&& without constructing anything. Usable only where nothing is evaluated, such as inside decltype . std::void_t<Ts... Is void if every Ts is a valid type; otherwise substitution fails cpp template <typename, typename = void struct HasSize : std::false_type {}; template <typename T struct HasSize<T, std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<T ().size()) : std::true_type {}; static_assert(HasSize<std::string ::value); static_assert(!HasSize<int ::value); How it works, for HasSize<X : 1. The primary template gives the second argument its default, void , so the lookup is for HasSize<X, void . 2. The partial specialization is tried. If X has .size() , the decltype is a valid type, void_t is void , and the specialization matches HasSize<X, void and is preferred. 3. If not, substitution fails, the specialization is discarded, and the primary template's false_type remains. This is called the detection idiom . A trailing return type achieves a similar effect for functions: cpp template <typename C auto printSize(const C& container) - decltype(container.size(), void()) { std::cout << container.size() << '\n'; } The comma expression requires container.size() to be valid and then yields void as the return type. Tag dispatch A different technique with the same purpose: choose an implementation by overloading on an empty tag type. cpp template <typename It void advanceImpl(It& it, int n, std::random_access_iterator_tag) { it += n; // O(1) } template <typename It void advanceImpl(It& it, int n, std::input_iterator_tag) { while (n-- 0) { ++it; // O(n) } } template <typename It void myAdvance(It& it, int n) { advanceImpl(it, n, typename std::iterator_traits<It ::iterator_category{}); } Each iterator type declares its category as a tag type. The tags form an inheritance hierarchy, so a random-access iterator's tag also converts to input_iterator_tag , and overload resolution picks the most specific implementation available. Nothing is removed; ordinary overloading does the selection. The modern form needs no helper functions: cpp template <typename It void myAdvance(It& it, int n) { if constexpr (std::random_access_iterator<It ) { it += n; } else { while (n-- 0) { ++it; } } } How the techniques evolved Standard Tools for constraining and selecting --- --- C++98 Tag dispatch, specialization of traits C++11 enable_if , decltype , declval , SFINAE on expressions C++17 void_t , if constexpr C++20 Concepts and requires Write concepts in new code. Read SFINAE in everything written before 2020, including most of the libraries you will use.

title: Does it have this member?
body: Before concepts, the way to ask "does type T have a member function toString() ?" was the detection idiom , built on SFINAE and std::void_t . You will meet it in older code, so write it once by hand. Complete HasToString<T so that it derives from std::true_type when std::declval<T ().toString() is a valid expression, and from std::false_type otherwise. The primary template (already written) is the "no" answer. Add a partial specialization that is only viable when the expression compiles.

title: Overloads that switch themselves off
body: Write two overloads of twice : - for integral types it returns value 2 ; - for floating-point types it returns value 2.0 rounded to the nearest whole number ( std::round ), as the same floating type. Any other type must have no matching overload at all (not a compile error deep inside the function: the call itself must be rejected). Do it the pre-C++20 way with std::enable_if_t in the template parameter list, to see how it reads: cpp template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T , int = 0 (When you are done, try rewriting it with std::integral and std::floating_point . The tests accept either.)

title: 11.04  Compile-Time Programming — constexpr, consteval, constinit
body: Modern C++ can run real code inside the compiler : loops, std::vector , std::string , even new and delete , provided nothing allocated escapes to run time. constexpr may run at compile time, consteval must , and constinit guarantees a static variable is initialized at compile time while leaving it mutable. The keywords 2.06 const and constexpr introduced constexpr . Here is the full set. Keyword Applies to Meaning --- --- --- constexpr A variable Its value is a compile-time constant; implies const constexpr A function May be evaluated at compile time when its arguments are constant; otherwise runs normally consteval A function Must be evaluated at compile time. An immediate function . constinit A static or thread-local variable Initialized at compile time, but not const if constexpr A branch Selected at compile time; the other branch is discarded if consteval (C++23) A branch Taken when the function is being evaluated at compile time An evaluation done by the compiler is a constant evaluation . It is forced wherever the language needs a constant: the initializer of a constexpr variable, a template argument, an array bound, a case label, a static_assert . !note constexpr on a function is a permission, not a guarantee int x{ sq(5) }; with a non- constexpr x may or may not be folded by the optimiser. To be certain, initialize a constexpr variable, or make the function consteval . Real algorithms at compile time cpp include <array include <cstddef include <iostream constexpr bool isPrime(int n) { if (n < 2) { return false; } for (int i{ 2 }; i i <= n; ++i) { if (n % i == 0) { return false; } } return true; } template <std::size_t N constexpr std::array<int, N firstPrimes() { std::array<int, N result{}; std::size_t found{ 0 }; for (int n{ 2 }; found < N; ++n) { if (isPrime(n)) { result found++ = n; } } return result; } constexpr auto primes{ firstPrimes<10 () }; static_assert(primes 9 == 29); int main() { for (int p : primes) { std::cout << p << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } The loop runs in the compiler. The executable contains the finished table and no code to compute it. This is the modern way to build lookup tables. Containers at compile time Since C++20, dynamic allocation is permitted during constant evaluation, on one condition: everything allocated must be released before the evaluation ends. This is a transient allocation . cpp constexpr int sumOfSquares(int n) { std::vector<int values{}; for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i) { values.push_back(i i); } return std::accumulate(values.begin(), values.end(), 0); } // the vector is destroyed here, inside the evaluation static_assert(sumOfSquares(3) == 14); std::vector and std::string are usable inside a constexpr function. What you cannot do is make a constexpr variable of those types that holds heap memory, because that memory would have to survive into the running program. Return a std::array or a plain value instead. Hashing strings for a switch A switch needs integer constants ( 3.02 switch ). A constexpr hash function supplies them from strings and also runs normally on run-time input. cpp constexpr std::uint32_t hashName(std::string_view text) { std::uint32_t hash{ 2166136261u }; for (char c : text) { hash ^= static_cast<std::uint8_t (c); hash = 16777619u; } return hash; } switch (hashName(command)) // run time: hashes what the user typed { case hashName("jump"): jump(); break; // compile time: a case label must be a constant case hashName("run"): run(); break; } One function, used in both worlds. Two different strings can hash to the same value, so real code confirms the match afterwards. consteval cpp consteval int square(int n) { return n n; } constexpr int a{ square(8) }; // 64, computed by the compiler int x{ 3 }; int b{ square(x) }; // error: x is not a constant expression Use consteval when a run-time call would be a mistake. Its best-known use is validation : std::format checks its format string through a consteval constructor, which is how a wrong format string becomes a compile error ( 10.07 Formatting with stdformat and stdprint ). You can do the same: cpp consteval int checkedPercent(int value) { if (value < 0 value 100) { throw "percentage out of range"; // reaching a throw makes the evaluation fail } return value; } constexpr int volume{ checkedPercent(80) }; // fine // constexpr int bad{ checkedPercent(140) }; // compile error constinit A global with a dynamic initializer is initialized at program start, before main . Across different source files the order is unspecified, so one global's initializer may use another that has not been initialized yet. That is the static initialization order fiasco . cpp constinit int g_counter{ 0 }; // initialized at compile time; still modifiable constinit thread_local int t_calls{ 0 }; constinit makes the compiler verify that the initializer is a constant expression. A variable initialized at compile time exists before any code runs, so it cannot be caught in that ordering problem. Unlike constexpr , it does not make the variable const . Values with constexpr , types with templates The original way to compute at compile time was recursion through template instantiation ( 9.02 Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization ): cpp template <unsigned N struct Factorial { static constexpr unsigned value{ N Factorial<N - 1 ::value }; }; template < struct Factorial<0 { static constexpr unsigned value{ 1 }; }; Today: cpp constexpr unsigned factorial(unsigned n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n factorial(n - 1); } !tip The division of labour Compute values with constexpr functions: they are ordinary code, testable at run time too. Use templates and traits to compute types : 11.07 Template Metaprogramming Techniques . What is not allowed Restriction Detail --- --- Undefined behaviour The compiler rejects it during constant evaluation Input and output No streams, no files reinterpret_cast Not permitted Non-transient allocation Memory must be released before the evaluation ends Unbounded work Compilers limit the number of steps and the recursion depth The first row is a benefit. An overflow, an out-of-bounds index or a read of an uninitialized variable inside a constant evaluation is a compile error. Testing a constexpr function with static_assert therefore proves those cases are free of undefined behaviour.

title: Work done by the compiler
body: Write two constexpr functions so that a table of primes is computed during compilation and stored in the program ready-made. - constexpr bool isPrime(int n) - template <std::size_t N constexpr std::array<int, N firstPrimes() : the first N primes, in order. Ordinary loops and local variables are allowed in constexpr functions. The tests use static_assert , so if anything cannot be evaluated at compile time the build fails.

title: Checked at compile time
body: A consteval function must run during compilation. That makes it a validator: bad input is a compile error instead of a bug found later. Write consteval std::uint32_t rgb(std::string_view hex) . It takes a colour written as " RRGGBB" (upper or lower case hex digits) and returns it as the number 0xRRGGBB . If the text is not exactly followed by six hex digits, throw something. A throw that is actually reached during constant evaluation is not allowed, so the compiler stops with an error that points at the offending call. Write a small constexpr helper to convert one hex digit to its value.

title: 11.05  CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism
body: The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern : class Derived : public Base<Derived . The base knows the derived type at compile time, so it can call derived functions without virtual . That is static polymorphism. It suits mixins and interfaces with no run-time overhead. C++23's deducing this simplifies it. The shape of the pattern A class derives from a template and passes itself as the argument. cpp include <iostream template <typename Derived class Shape { public: double area() const { return static_cast<const Derived& ( this).areaImpl(); } }; class Square : public Shape<Square { public: double areaImpl() const { return m_side m_side; } private: double m_side{ 2.0 }; }; template <typename T void printArea(const Shape<T & shape) { std::cout << shape.area() << '\n'; } int main() { const Square square{}; printArea(square); // 4 return 0; } This is the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP). Inside Shape<Derived , the object is known to be a Derived , so the static_cast down to it is valid, and the call to areaImpl is an ordinary direct call that the compiler can inline. It is legal for Square to name itself as a template argument before it is complete, because the bodies of Shape<Square 's member functions are not instantiated until they are used, and by then Square is complete. Dynamic and static polymorphism virtual (dynamic) CRTP and templates (static) --- --- --- The call is resolved At run time, through the vtable At compile time Inlining Usually not possible Yes Per-object overhead A vptr None Different types in one container Yes: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape No: Shape<Square and Shape<Circle are unrelated types New types without recompiling users Yes No Code size One function body One instantiation per type Use CRTP when the set of types is known at compile time and the call sits on a hot path. Use virtual when types must be chosen or mixed at run time. The mechanics of the virtual side are in 8.04 How Virtual Works — vtables . Mixins The more common use of CRTP is not polymorphism. It is to inject functionality into a class. A base class used this way is a mixin . An object counter per class cpp template <typename T class Counted { public: static int alive() { return s_alive; } protected: Counted() { ++s_alive; } Counted(const Counted&) { ++s_alive; } ~Counted() { --s_alive; } private: static inline int s_alive{ 0 }; }; class Enemy : public Counted<Enemy { }; class Bullet : public Counted<Bullet { }; Counted<Enemy and Counted<Bullet are different classes, so each has its own static counter. A non-template base would give one counter shared by everything. The protected destructor prevents deletion through a Counted<T , so no virtual destructor is needed. Generating operators cpp template <typename D struct EqualityComparable { friend bool operator!=(const D& a, const D& b) { return !(a == b); } }; struct Point : EqualityComparable<Point { int x{}; int y{}; friend bool operator==(const Point& a, const Point& b) { return a.x == b.x && a.y == b.y; } }; The derived class supplies one operation and the mixin derives the rest. C++20's defaulted comparisons ( 6.07 Operator Overloading Basics ) have made this particular example unnecessary, but the technique is everywhere in older libraries. Removing clone boilerplate cpp template <typename Base, typename Derived class Cloneable : public Base { public: std::unique_ptr<Base clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Derived (static_cast<const Derived& ( this)); } }; class Circle : public Cloneable<Shape, Circle { // clone() is supplied }; Here CRTP and virtual functions work together: the hierarchy is dynamic, and the repetitive override is generated statically. Deducing this C++23 lets a member function declare its object parameter explicitly, and deduce its type. cpp struct Shape { double area(this const auto& self) { return self.areaImpl(); } }; struct Square : Shape { double side{ 2.0 }; double areaImpl() const { return side side; } }; self is deduced as the actual type of the object the function is called on, so no template base and no cast are required. The feature is called an explicit object parameter . It also removes the duplication between const and non-const overloads ( 6.04 this, const Member Functions and Chaining ): cpp class Text { public: template <typename Self auto&& at(this Self&& self, std::size_t i) { return std::forward<Self (self).m_text i ; } private: std::string m_text{}; }; One function serves const objects, non-const objects and temporaries, with the right return type for each. Pitfalls Pitfall Consequence Defence --- --- --- Naming the wrong type: class Circle : public Shape<Square Compiles; the static_cast is undefined behaviour Make the base constructor private and declare friend Derived; so only the named class can construct it The derived class omits areaImpl A confusing error, or endless recursion if base and derived use the same name Use distinct names, or constrain with a concept Expecting a common base type Shape<A and Shape<B share nothing Add a non-template base if run-time polymorphism is also needed

title: A mixin that writes operators for you

body: The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern: a class inherits from a template instantiated with itself . The base then knows the derived type at compile time and can call into it with no virtual functions. Write template <typename Derived struct Comparable . Any class that inherits from Comparable<Itself and provides == and < gets the other four comparisons for free: Operator Defined as --- --- a != b !(a == b) a b b < a a <= b !(b < a) a = b !(a < b) Write them as friend functions inside Comparable , taking const Derived& parameters.

title: Counting instances per class
body: Write template <typename T class Counted , a CRTP mixin that keeps track of how many objects of the inheriting class are alive. - Constructors (default, copy and move) add one; the destructor subtracts one. - static int alive() returns the count. - Because Counted<Enemy and Counted<Bullet are different classes , each gets its own separate counter. That is the whole trick. - Make the constructors and destructor protected : a Counted<T should only exist as part of a T .

title: 11.06  Type Erasure
body: Type erasure hides many unrelated concrete types behind one non-template interface, without requiring them to share a base class. std::function , std::any and the deleter of std::shared_ptr all use it. The recipe: an internal abstract Concept , a templated Model that wraps any type, and an outer wrapper with value semantics. The problem You want a single container of "anything that can be drawn": your Circle , your Sprite and a Text class from a library you cannot modify. They share no base class. Approach Limitation --- --- A common base class with virtual functions Every type must inherit from it, which is impossible for types you do not own, and intrusive for those you do A template std::vector<T holds one type only std::variant The set of types must be listed in advance Type erasure gives run-time polymorphism over types that know nothing about each other or about the interface. Concept and Model cpp include <iostream include <memory include <string include <utility include <vector struct Circle { double radius{}; }; struct Text { std::string content{}; }; void drawIt(const Circle& c) { std::cout << "Circle " << c.radius << '\n'; } void drawIt(const Text& t) { std::cout << "Text '" << t.content << "'\n"; } class Drawable { public: template <typename T Drawable(T value) : m_self{ std::make_unique<Model<T (std::move(value)) } {} Drawable(const Drawable& other) : m_self{ other.m_self- clone() } {} Drawable(Drawable&&) noexcept = default; Drawable& operator=(Drawable other) noexcept { std::swap(m_self, other.m_self); return this; } void draw() const { m_self- draw(); } private: struct Concept { virtual ~Concept() = default; virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual std::unique_ptr<Concept clone() const = 0; }; template <typename T struct Model final : Concept { explicit Model(T value) : data{ std::move(value) } {} void draw() const override { drawIt(data); } std::unique_ptr<Concept clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Model ( this); } T data; }; std::unique_ptr<Concept m_self{}; }; int main() { const std::vector<Drawable scene{ Circle{ 2.0 }, Text{ "hi" }, Circle{ 5.0 } }; for (const Drawable& item : scene) { item.draw(); } return 0; } Piece Role --- --- Concept A private abstract base listing the operations the wrapper needs Model<T A template that holds a T and implements Concept by forwarding to operations on T Drawable The public, non-template class. Its constructor template builds the right Model<T . Drawable (a value, copyable) heap ┌──────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ m_self ──────────┼──────▶ │ Model<Circle │ └──────────────────┘ │ vptr to Model<Circle 's │ │ Circle{ 2.0 } │ └────────────────────────────┘ Outside the constructor, the type Circle no longer appears anywhere: it has been erased. The inheritance and virtual dispatch are still there. They have moved inside the wrapper, where the compiler generates them per type. Circle and Text stay plain structs, and the requirement on them is purely structural: a drawIt overload must exist. Because Drawable deep-copies through clone() , it has value semantics : it can be copied, assigned, returned and stored in containers like an int . This is polymorphism without pointers or ownership in the user's code. In the standard library Type Erases Requires of the wrapped type --- --- --- std::function<R(Args...) Any callable Callable with Args... , result convertible to R , copyable std::move_only_function (C++23) Callables that cannot be copied The same, without copyability std::any Any type Copy-constructible The deleter of std::shared_ptr<T The deleter's type Callable with a T std::pmr::memory_resource An allocation strategy 13.03 Custom Memory Placement new, Allocators and PMR This explains a detail from 7.06 Smart Pointers : a shared_ptr 's deleter is not part of its type, while a unique_ptr 's is. The shared_ptr erases it in the control block, at the cost of an indirect call. Small buffer optimization Allocating every wrapped object on the heap is the main cost. Real implementations reserve a small buffer inside the wrapper, typically 16 to 32 bytes, and construct small objects directly in it, falling back to the heap for large ones. small object: wrapper: the object lives here no allocation large object: wrapper: pointer ───────────────┼──▶ heap std::function and std::any normally do this, which is why a std::function holding a lambda with one or two captures allocates nothing. The same idea applied to std::string is the small string optimization. Trade-offs Advantages Costs --- --- Works with unrelated types, including ones you cannot change Boilerplate for each erased interface Value semantics An indirect call, and possibly an allocation A non-template interface: faster builds and a stable binary interface The concrete type is hidden from the debugger and from the optimiser Mechanism Types Chosen --- --- --- Templates and CRTP Any, known at compile time Compile time std::variant A fixed list Run time Virtual functions Anything derived from the base Run time Type erasure Anything meeting the requirements Run time

title: Polymorphism without a base class
body: Circle , Square and (in the tests) other types have nothing in common except that each has area() and name() . They share no base class, and you are not allowed to give them one. Write class AnyShape : a single ordinary type that can hold any such object and forward the two calls to it. Then std::vector<AnyShape can mix them freely, and AnyShape copies like a value. This is type erasure . The standard recipe has three pieces, all private inside AnyShape : 1. struct Concept : an abstract interface with virtual area() , name() , and clone() . 2. template <typename T struct Model : Concept : holds one T and implements the interface by calling the T 's own functions. 3. A std::unique_ptr<Concept member. Public interface: - a constructor template taking any T (stores a Model<T ), - copy constructor and copy assignment (deep copy through clone() ), move operations, - double area() const and std::string name() const .

title: 11.07  Template Metaprogramming Techniques
body: Template metaprogramming treats types as data and templates as functions that run in the compiler. The core tools are type lists, std::index_sequence , recursive instantiation, fold expressions and if constexpr . They are what std::tuple , std::variant , serialization libraries and expression templates are built from. Templates as functions on types an ordinary function: values → f(...) → a value a metafunction: types → Template<... ::type or ::value → a type or a value cpp template <typename T struct AddPointer { using type = T ; }; AddPointer<int ::type p{}; // int A class template used this way is a metafunction : its template parameters are the inputs and a nested type or value is the output. The type traits of 11.02 Type Traits are metafunctions. The language they form is purely functional: there is no mutation, so iteration is expressed as recursion or as pack expansion. Type lists A type list is a template whose only purpose is to carry a pack of types. cpp include <cstddef include <type_traits template <typename... Ts struct TypeList {}; template <typename List struct Length; template <typename... Ts struct Length<TypeList<Ts... : std::integral_constant<std::size_t, sizeof...(Ts) {}; template <typename T, typename List struct Contains; template <typename T, typename... Ts struct Contains<T, TypeList<Ts... : std::bool_constant<(std::is_same_v<T, Ts ...) {}; template <typename List struct Front; template <typename Head, typename... Tail struct Front<TypeList<Head, Tail... { using type = Head; }; template <typename T, typename List struct PushFront; template <typename T, typename... Ts struct PushFront<T, TypeList<Ts... { using type = TypeList<T, Ts... ; }; struct Position {}; struct Velocity {}; struct Health {}; using Components = TypeList<Position, Velocity, Health ; static_assert(Length<Components ::value == 3); static_assert(Contains<Health, Components ::value); static_assert(std::is_same_v<Front<Components ::type, Position ); Every operation follows one shape. The primary template is declared and left undefined. A partial specialization on TypeList<Ts... pattern-matches the list and exposes its contents as a pack. From there a fold expression or a pack expansion does the work. Operation Technique --- --- Length sizeof...(Ts) Contains A fold over \ \ Front Match TypeList<Head, Tail... PushFront Re-expand into a new TypeList Recursion: the index of a type When each step depends on the last, recurse with one specialization for the base case and one for the general case. cpp template <typename T, typename List struct IndexOf; template <typename T, typename... Ts struct IndexOf<T, TypeList<T, Ts... : std::integral_constant<std::size_t, 0 {}; template <typename T, typename Head, typename... Ts struct IndexOf<T, TypeList<Head, Ts... : std::integral_constant<std::size_t, 1 + IndexOf<T, TypeList<Ts... ::value {}; static_assert(IndexOf<Health, Components ::value == 2); The first specialization matches when the head is T , and it is more specialized than the second, so it is preferred ( 9.02 Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization ). If T is absent, the recursion reaches TypeList< , which matches neither, and compilation fails on the undefined primary template. std::index_sequence : iterating by position std::get<I (tuple) needs I as a compile-time constant, so a run-time loop cannot visit a tuple. An index_sequence supplies the indices as a pack. cpp include <cstddef include <iostream include <tuple include <utility template <typename Tuple, std::size_t... Is void printTupleImpl(const Tuple& t, std::index_sequence<Is... ) { ((std::cout << (Is == 0 ? "" : ", ") << std::get<Is (t)), ...); } template <typename... Ts void printTuple(const std::tuple<Ts... & t) { printTupleImpl(t, std::index_sequence_for<Ts... {}); std::cout << '\n'; } int main() { printTuple(std::tuple{ 1, "two", 3.0 }); // 1, two, 3 return 0; } Tool Produces --- --- std::index_sequence<0, 1, 2 A type carrying a pack of indices std::make_index_sequence<N index_sequence<0, 1, ..., N-1 std::index_sequence_for<Ts... The same, with N as sizeof...(Ts) The pattern always has two layers: a public function creates the sequence, and an implementation function deduces Is... from it and expands a pattern over the indices. std::apply(f, tuple) , which calls f with the tuple's elements as separate arguments, is implemented exactly this way. For each type cpp template <typename... Ts, typename F void forEachType(F&& f) { (f.template operator()<Ts (), ...); } forEachType<int, double, char ( <typename T () { std::cout << sizeof(T) << ' '; }); // 4 8 1 <typename T () is a lambda with an explicit template parameter (C++20). The .template tells the compiler that the < after operator() begins a template argument list, which it cannot know for a dependent name. Expression templates A numeric library that returned a new vector from every + would allocate a temporary for each operator. Expression templates make the operators return a lightweight object whose type records the expression, and evaluate nothing until assignment. a + b + c has the type AddExpr<AddExpr<Vec, Vec , Vec and is evaluated as result i = a i + b i + c i in a single pass cpp template <typename L, typename R struct AddExpr { const L& left; const R& right; double operator (std::size_t i) const { return left i + right i ; } std::size_t size() const { return left.size(); } }; operator+ returns an AddExpr holding references to its operands. Assigning the final expression to a vector runs one loop calling operator , which the compiler inlines into the arithmetic on the elements. No temporaries are created. Eigen and other linear-algebra libraries are built on this. !danger Expression templates and auto auto sum{ a + b }; captures the expression object , with its references to a and b , not a vector. If either operand is a temporary, the references dangle. Libraries of this kind ask you to name the result type explicitly. Reflection Most metaprogramming exists to answer questions the language could not answer directly: what members does this struct have, what are this enum's enumerators? C++26 adds static reflection , which lets code inspect and generate declarations at compile time and should replace much of what this lesson describes. Compiler support is still arriving: 13.10 C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next . Guidelines Guideline Reason --- --- Prefer constexpr functions, concepts and if constexpr They are ordinary, readable code: 11.04 Compile-Time Programming — constexpr, consteval, constinit Keep metaprogramming inside libraries Expose a simple interface; contain the complexity Watch compile times Each instantiation costs time and memory in the compiler. Folds and pack expansions are far cheaper than recursion. Give good errors Constrain the entry points with concepts or static_assert so users see a message, not an instantiation trace

title: A list of types
body: Template metaprogramming treats types as data . The basic data structure is a list of types: an empty struct whose only content is its parameter pack. Using TypeList (provided), write three metafunctions. Each takes a list apart with a partial specialization that names the pack. - Length<List ::value : how many types. - Contains<T, List ::value : is T one of them? (a fold over with std::is_same_v ) - Front<List ::type : the first type.

title: Walk a tuple
body: A std::tuple holds values of different types, so an ordinary loop cannot visit them: the loop variable would need a different type each time round. The answer is to expand a pack of indices at compile time. Write: - template <typename... Ts std::string tupleText(const std::tuple<Ts... & t) : the elements written out, separated by ", " and wrapped in brackets, for example "(1, two, 3.5)" . An empty tuple gives "()" . - template <typename... Ts, typename F void forEach(const std::tuple<Ts... & t, F function) : calls function on every element in order. std::apply(callable, tuple) calls callable with the tuple's elements as separate arguments, which hands you a pack to fold over. (The lower-level tool is std::index_sequence ; either is fine.)
