For bindings to notice changes, the view model implements INotifyPropertyChanged , lists use ObservableCollection<T , and actions are ICommand s: csharp using System.Collections.ObjectModel; using System.ComponentModel; using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; using System.Windows.Input; var vm = new TodoViewModel(); vm.PropertyChanged += (_, e) = Console.WriteLine($"changed: {e.PropertyName}"); Console.WriteLine(vm.AddCommand.CanExecute(null)); vm.NewTitle = "Buy tea"; Console.WriteLine(vm.AddCommand.CanExecute(null)); vm.AddCommand.Execute(null); Console.WriteLine($"{vm.Items.Count} item, title now '{vm.NewTitle}', {vm.Summary}"); public abstract class ViewModelBase : INotifyPropertyChanged { public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged; protected bool Set<T (ref T field, T value, CallerMemberName string? name = null) { if (EqualityComparer<T .Default.Equals(field, value)) return false; field = value; PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name)); return true; } protected void Raise(string name) = PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name)); } public sealed class RelayCommand(Action execute, Func<bool canExecute) : ICommand { public event EventHandler? CanExecuteChanged; public bool CanExecute(object? parameter) = canExecute(); public void Execute(object? parameter) { if (CanExecute(parameter)) execute(); } public void NotifyCanExecuteChanged() = CanExecuteChanged?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty); } public sealed class TodoViewModel : ViewModelBase { private string _newTitle = ""; public ObservableCollection<string Items { get; } = new(); public RelayCommand AddCommand { get; } public TodoViewModel() { AddCommand = new RelayCommand(Add, () = !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(NewTitle)); Items.CollectionChanged += (_, _) = Raise(nameof(Summary)); } public string NewTitle { get = _newTitle; set { if (Set(ref _newTitle, value)) AddCommand.NotifyCanExecuteChanged(); } } public string Summary = Items.Count == 1 ? "1 item" : $"{Items.Count} items"; private void Add() { Items.Add(NewTitle.Trim()); NewTitle = ""; } } CallerMemberName fills in the property's name automatically. The CommunityToolkit.Mvvm package generates this plumbing from attributes ( ObservableProperty , RelayCommand ), but it is worth knowing what it writes. Why MVVM pays off The whole behaviour of the screen (when Add is enabled, what the summary says, what happens after adding) is in TodoViewModel , an ordinary class. It is tested like any other code, without opening a window, which is exactly what practice 6.04 does. The view can be redesigned without touching the logic, and the same view model can serve a WPF and an Avalonia view.

title: A view model
body: Write the view model behind a tip calculator window. It never touches a window, so it can be tested like any class: csharp public abstract class ViewModelBase : INotifyPropertyChanged public sealed class RelayCommand(Action execute, Func<bool canExecute) : ICommand // with NotifyCanExecuteChanged() public sealed class TipViewModel : ViewModelBase { public string BillText { get; set; } // what the user typed, "" at the start public int TipPercent { get; set; } // 15 at the start, kept between 0 and 30 public int People { get; set; } // 1 at the start, kept at 1 or more public string Total { get; } // e.g. "57.50", or "" when the bill is not valid public string PerPerson { get; } // the total divided between people, or "" public string Error { get; } // "Enter the bill amount" when BillText is not a positive number, else "" public RelayCommand AddPersonCommand { get; } public RelayCommand RemovePersonCommand { get; } // can execute only while People 1 public RelayCommand ResetCommand { get; } // back to "", 15, 1 } - The bill is parsed with the invariant culture. Total = bill × (1 + tip / 100) and per person = total / people, both rounded to cents (halves away from zero) and shown with 2 decimals. - Setting a property to the value it already has raises nothing . Otherwise PropertyChanged is raised for the property itself and then for every computed property that depends on it ( Total , PerPerson , Error ), in that order. Values outside the allowed range are clamped first. - When People changes, RemovePersonCommand raises CanExecuteChanged .

title: 6.05  Project: A Complete Application
body: Designing and building a whole application from the course's parts - a budget tracker with a domain library, commands parsed from input, services behind interfaces, JSON persistence with versions, reports with LINQ, error handling at the edges, tests, and where to go next with C . The application The final project is a budget tracker : record income and expenses, set monthly budgets per category, see a monthly report, undo mistakes, and save everything to a file. It is small enough to finish and has every part a real application has. The layers Domain (a class library in a real solution): records and the rules, no input or output. csharp-norun public record Transaction(int Id, DateOnly Date, decimal Amount, string Category, string Description) { public bool IsExpense = Amount < 0; } public class Ledger { private readonly List<Transaction _transactions = new(); private readonly Dictionary<string, decimal _budgets = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase); private int _nextId = 1; public IReadOnlyList<Transaction Transactions = _transactions; public Transaction Add(DateOnly date, decimal amount, string category, string description) { ... } public Transaction? UndoLast() { ... } public void SetBudget(string category, decimal monthly) { ... } public decimal? BudgetFor(string category) = _budgets.TryGetValue(category, out var b) ? b : null; } Reports : pure functions from a ledger and a month to a report record, written with LINQ, easy to test: csharp-norun public record CategoryLine(string Category, decimal Spent, decimal? Budget) { public bool Over = Budget is decimal b && Spent b; } public static MonthReport ForMonth(Ledger ledger, int year, int month) { var inMonth = ledger.Transactions.Where(t = t.Date.Year == year && t.Date.Month == month).ToList(); var byCategory = inMonth.Where(t = t.IsExpense) .GroupBy(t = t.Category) .Select(g = new CategoryLine(g.Key, -g.Sum(t = t.Amount), ledger.BudgetFor(g.Key))) .OrderByDescending(l = l.Spent).ThenBy(l = l.Category, StringComparer.Ordinal) .ToList(); ... } Storage behind an interface, with a version number in the file so later versions of the app can still read old files (lesson 5.04): csharp-norun public interface ILedgerStore { Task SaveAsync(Ledger ledger, string path); Task<Ledger? LoadAsync(string path); } Commands : the input is parsed into a command and its arguments, and each command has a small handler that validates the arguments, calls the domain, and returns the text to show. Errors that the user can fix (a bad date, an unknown command) become messages; bugs still throw. Building it step by step 1. Write the domain records and Ledger with their rules. Test them. 2. Write the report function. Test it with a ledger built in the test. 3. Write the command loop with add , list and quit ; run it by hand. 4. Add budget , report and undo , one at a time, each with its error messages. 5. Add save and load with JSON. 6. Read through the code: are names clear, is each method short, is every rule in the domain rather than in the input code? This order keeps a working program at every step: each feature is small, finished and checked before the next one starts. Where to go next - Web : ASP.NET Core minimal APIs and Blazor use everything in this course (DI, configuration, async, records, JSON). dotnet new webapi is a good start. - Data : Entity Framework Core maps classes to database tables; Dapper runs SQL with less ceremony. - Desktop and mobile : WPF or Avalonia with MVVM (lesson 6.04), or .NET MAUI. - Games : Unity and Godot are scripted in C . - Deeper C : Span<T and performance, source generators, System.Threading.Channels , and the Roslyn compiler APIs.

title: Parsing commands
body: The final project reads commands like add 2026-03-01 -12.50 food "Lunch with Ada" --tag=work --split . Write the parser: csharp public record ParsedCommand( string Name, IReadOnlyList<string Args, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string Options, IReadOnlySet<string Flags); public static class CommandParser { public static List<string Tokenize(string line) public static ParsedCommand? Parse(string line) } Tokenize splits on spaces (runs of spaces count as one). A token can be quoted with " ; inside quotes spaces are kept and \" is a quote and \\ a backslash. Quotes may start in the middle of a token: a"b c"d is one token ab cd . An unclosed quote throws FormatException("unclosed quote") . "" is an empty token. Parse tokenizes, then: - returns null for a blank line; - the first token, in lower case, is the Name ; - --key=value sets an option (keys in lower case; the value keeps its case and may be empty); a later one with the same key wins; - --flag (no = ) adds a flag in lower case; - a token -- on its own ends the options: every token after it is an argument, even if it starts with -- ; - everything else is an argument, in order. Only unquoted tokens can be options or flags: "--x" in quotes is an argument.

title: A budget tracker
body: Build the application from lesson 6.05: a budget tracker that reads commands, one per line, until quit or the end of the input. Split it into files: Program.cs (the command loop), Ledger.cs (the domain), Reports.cs and Storage.cs . add 2026-03-01 2500 salary March pay add 2026-03-02 -100 rent Storage unit add 2026-03-03 -12.50 food Lunch with Ada add 2026-03-09 -199.90 food Groceries budget food 200 report 2026-03 quit prints Added 1: 2026-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay Added 2: 2026-03-02 rent -100.00 Storage unit Added 3: 2026-03-03 food -12.50 Lunch with Ada Added 4: 2026-03-09 food -199.90 Groceries Budget for food: 200.00 Report for 2026-03 Income: 2500.00 Expenses: 312.40 Net: 2187.60 By category: food 212.40 of 200.00 OVER rent 100.00 Bye. Commands (the command word ignores case; blank lines are ignored; amounts use . and are printed with 2 decimals): Command Does Errors --- --- --- add <date <amount <category <description Adds a transaction; positive amounts are income, negative are expenses. The category is stored in lower case; the description is the rest of the line, words joined by single spaces. Prints Added <id : <date <category <amount <description . Ids count from 1. Fewer than 4 arguments: Usage: add <date <amount <category <description . A date not in yyyy-MM-dd form or not a real date: Bad date: <text . An amount that is not a number, is 0, or has more than 2 decimals: Bad amount: <text . budget <category <amount Sets a monthly budget: Budget for <category : <amount Not exactly 2 arguments: Usage: budget <category <amount . Amount not above 0: Bad amount: <text list or list <yyyy-MM Every transaction (or those in that month), by date then id, as <id <date <category padded to 10 <amount right-aligned in 9 <description ; or No transactions. Bad month: <text report <yyyy-MM Report for <month , then Income: , Expenses: and Net: lines (label left in 9 characters, amount right in 10; expenses shown positive), then, if there are expenses, By category: and a line per category: two spaces, the category in 10, the amount spent right in 8, then of <budget if it has one and OVER if the spending is above it. Categories by spending (most first), then name. A month with no transactions prints No transactions. after the title. Usage: report <month , Bad month: <text undo Removes the most recently added transaction still present: Removed <id , or Nothing to undo. save <file Writes everything as JSON: Saved <n transactions to <file Usage: save <file load <file Replaces everything with the file's contents: Loaded <n transactions from <file . New ids continue after the highest loaded id; undo starts empty. Usage: load <file ; a missing or invalid file: Could not load <file (nothing changes) quit Stops. Bye. is printed when the program ends, whether by quit or the end of the input. Anything else: Unknown command: <word

title: Cheat Sheet - C#
body: Basics csharp-norun Console.Write("Name? "); string name = Console.ReadLine() ?? title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Abstract class A class that cannot be created with new ; it shares code and declares members that derived classes must implement. (3.03) Access modifier public , private , protected or internal : who may use a member or type. (3.01) Assembly The .dll or executable a project compiles into. (6.01) async / await Marks a method that can pause at await until a task finishes, without blocking a thread. (5.01) Attribute Information attached to code in square brackets, such as Fact , read with reflection. (6.02) Auto-property A property whose hidden field the compiler creates: public string Name { get; set; } . (3.01) Base class The class another class derives from. (3.03) Binding A link in XAML between a control and a view-model property. (6.04) Boxing Wrapping a value type in an object, which happens when it is stored as object . (4.01) CancellationToken A token passed to long operations so the caller can ask them to stop. (5.02) Class A reference type describing objects: their data and behaviour. (3.01) Class library A project that builds a .dll for other projects to use. (6.01) Closure A lambda together with the outer variables it captures. (4.02) Collection expression 1, 2, 3 : one syntax to create arrays, lists and spans. (2.02) Composition root The one place where an application's objects are created and connected. (6.03) Constraint where T : ... : a requirement on a generic type parameter. (4.01) Constructor The method that runs when an object is created with new . (3.01) Deferred execution A LINQ query or iterator doing its work only when enumerated. (2.04) Delegate A type for references to methods; Func and Action are the common ones. (4.02) Dependency injection Giving a class the services it needs through its constructor. (6.03) Dictionary A collection of key-value pairs with fast lookup by key. (2.03) Dispose The method of IDisposable that releases a resource such as a file. (4.04) Encapsulation Keeping data private and exposing only safe operations on it. (3.01) Event A member that notifies subscribers that something happened; += subscribes. (4.02) Exception An object thrown to signal an error, caught with try / catch . (4.03) Exception filter catch (E e) when (condition) : catch only some exceptions of a type. (4.03) Extension method A static method usable as if it were a method of another type, marked with this on its first parameter. (3.05) Garbage collector The part of .NET that frees memory no longer referenced. (4.04) Generic A type or method with type parameters, such as List<T . (4.01) HashSet A collection of unique values with fast Contains . (2.03) HttpClient The class that sends HTTP requests; created once and reused. (5.05) IEnumerable<T The interface of everything that can be looped over with foreach . (4.05) Immutable Cannot be changed after creation, like strings and records. (1.04) Inheritance A class taking the members of a base class and extending them. (3.03) init A property accessor that allows setting only while the object is created. (3.01) Interface A contract of members that implementing types must provide. (3.04) Interpolated string $"Hello {name}" : a string with values inserted, optionally formatted. (1.04) Iterator A method using yield return to produce a sequence lazily. (4.05) JSON A text format for data, read and written with System.Text.Json . (5.04) Lambda An inline anonymous function: x = x 2 . (2.04) LINQ Query methods such as Where , Select and GroupBy on any sequence. (2.04) List<T A growable array. (2.02) Local function A method declared inside another method or in top-level statements. (2.01) lock A statement that lets only one thread at a time run a block. (5.02) MVVM Model-View-ViewModel: the UI pattern that keeps screen logic in a testable view model. (6.04) Namespace A named group of types: System.Collections.Generic . (3.05) NuGet .NET's package manager. (6.01) Nullable reference types The feature that makes string? mean "may be null" and warns about unchecked uses. (2.05) Nullable value type int? : a value type that can also be null. (2.05) Object initializer new Product { Name = "Tea" } : setting properties when creating an object. (3.01) out parameter A parameter the method must assign, used for extra results. (2.01) Overloading Several methods with the same name and different parameters. (2.01) override Replacing a base class's virtual or abstract member in a derived class. (3.03) Pattern matching Testing a value's type, shape or range with is and switch . (2.05) Polymorphism Calls on a base type running the version of the actual object's class. (3.03) Primary constructor Constructor parameters written after the type name: class Temperature(double c) . (3.01) Property A member that looks like a field but runs get and set code. (3.01) Record A type with value equality, with copies and generated members, made for data. (3.02) ref parameter A parameter that passes the caller's variable itself. (2.01) Reference type A type whose variables hold references to objects: classes, strings, arrays. (1.02) Reflection Inspecting types, methods and attributes at run time, and calling them. (6.02) Solution A file grouping several projects. (6.01) static Belonging to the type itself rather than to an instance. (3.05) StringBuilder A mutable buffer for building strings efficiently. (1.04) Struct A value type, copied on assignment. (3.02) Switch expression x switch { pattern = value, ... } : a switch that produces a value. (1.05) Task An operation in progress; Task<T produces a T . (5.01) Top-level statements Code written directly in Program.cs , wrapped in Main by the compiler. (1.01) Tuple A light group of values: (string Name, int Age) . (2.05) Type inference The compiler working out a type, as with var and generic arguments. (1.02) Unit test Code that checks a small part of a program automatically. (6.02) using Disposes an object at the end of a block (also: imports a namespace). (4.04) Value equality Two objects being equal when their data is equal, as for records. (3.02) XAML The markup language that describes WPF, WinUI, Avalonia and MAUI windows. (6.04) yield return Hands out the next value of an iterator and pauses. (4.05)

title: 1.01  What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
match: 1.01 What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
body: A dynamic-link library is compiled code that is not part of your .exe but is joined to it when the program starts or while it runs. This lesson explains what a DLL contains, how it differs from a static library, and the real reasons programs are split into them, along with the costs. Code that lives in another file Every Windows program you have built so far ends up as one .exe . The compiler turns each .cpp file into an object file, and the linker copies the code from every object file, and from every static library you use, into that one executable. A DLL (dynamic-link library) is the other choice. It is a file with the same format as an .exe (both are PE files, "Portable Executable") that holds compiled functions and data but has no main . It cannot run by itself. Instead, a running program asks Windows to map the DLL into its memory , and from then on it can call the DLL's functions as if they were its own. Look at almost any program on your computer and you find DLLs next to it, and many more in C:\Windows\System32 : kernel32.dll , user32.dll , d3d11.dll . Your own Hello, world already uses several. std::cout ends up calling WriteFile in kernel32.dll , and unless you link the C runtime statically, the C and C++ runtime themselves live in DLLs ( vcruntime140.dll , msvcp140.dll , ucrtbase.dll ). Static library or DLL Static library ( .lib ) DLL ( .dll plus its import .lib ) --- --- --- When the code joins your program At link time, copied into the .exe At load time or run time, mapped from the DLL file Files you ship Just the .exe The .exe and every DLL it needs Update a bug fix in the library Rebuild and reship every program that uses it Replace the DLL; programs pick it up next time they start Two programs using it Each has its own copy on disk and in memory One copy on disk; Windows can share its code pages between processes Calling a function A direct call Usually an indirect call through a table (lesson 1.05) Can go missing No Yes: "The code execution cannot proceed because X.dll was not found" Neither is "better". Lesson 4.05 comes back to choosing between them once you know all the costs. Why programs use DLLs 1. Sharing one copy. user32.dll is used by nearly every program. Windows loads its code once and maps the same physical memory pages into every process that uses it. Only pages a process writes to get private copies. With hundreds of processes, that saves a great deal of memory. 2. Updating parts separately. A graphics driver, a font engine or a game's audio library can be replaced without rebuilding the programs that use it, as long as the replacement keeps the same interface (milestone 3 is about keeping that promise). 3. Loading code you did not have at build time. A program can look in a folder, find DLLs it has never seen, load them and call into them. That is how plugin systems, mods and many editors work (lesson 5.01). 4. Reloading code while running. Game developers put gameplay code in a DLL, change it, rebuild it and swap it into the running game without restarting (lesson 5.03). 5. Language boundaries. A DLL with a plain C interface can be called from C , Python, Rust or a scripting language. The C ABI is the common language they all speak. The costs - Distribution. Every DLL is a file that can be missing, the wrong version, or the wrong architecture (a 32-bit DLL cannot load into a 64-bit process). - A boundary. Memory, exceptions and C++ library types do not cross safely between modules built with different settings (lesson 2.05 and 2.06). - Start-up time. Each DLL must be found, mapped and connected when the program starts. - Security. If Windows looks for a DLL in the wrong place, it can load the wrong file. Lesson 4.02 shows how to load only the files you meant. What is inside a DLL Because it is a PE file, a DLL has the same parts as an .exe : my_library.dll ├── headers which machine (x64), where each section goes, the entry point ├── .text machine code of the functions ├── .rdata read-only data, plus the EXPORT table: the names and addresses it offers ├── .data global variables ├── import table the DLLs and functions it needs in turn └── .reloc how to fix addresses if it is loaded somewhere unexpected (lesson 1.02) The export table is what makes a DLL a library: a list of names (and numbers, called ordinals) with the address of each function inside the file. A program that wants AddNumbers from my_library.dll looks that name up in the export table. !note Build along in Visual Studio The lessons in this course describe Visual Studio projects you build on your own Windows machine: a DLL project and a program that uses it. The website's compiler builds single programs, so the practice tasks here check the logic behind each idea rather than building real DLLs. Common mistakes !warning Thinking a DLL makes code faster Calls into a DLL go through an extra jump. Sharing memory helps the whole system, not one program's speed. !warning Shipping a program without its DLLs Run your program on a clean machine, or a fresh virtual machine, before you share it. Missing runtime DLLs are the most common cause of "it works on my machine". Knowledge check quiz ? What can a DLL not do on its own? + Run: it has no main and must be loaded into a process - Contain machine code - Contain global variables A DLL is loaded into another program's process and called from there. ? Two programs use the same DLL. What does Windows share between them? + The DLL's code pages in physical memory, until a process writes to a page - Their global variables - Their stacks Code is read-only and shared; data written by a process becomes that process's own copy. ? Which table lists the functions a DLL offers to other modules? + The export table - The import table - The relocation table Imports are what a module needs; exports are what it offers.

title: What sharing saves
where: 1.01 What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
body: When several processes use the same DLL, Windows keeps one copy of its code in memory and maps it into all of them. Write two functions: - long long sharedSavings(long long codeBytes, int processes) : how many bytes of memory sharing saves compared with every process having its own copy. With one process (or none) nothing is saved. - long long pagesFor(long long bytes) : how many 4096-byte pages are needed to hold bytes bytes. A part page still takes a whole page; 0 bytes take 0 pages. sharedSavings(1'000'000, 4) == 3'000'000 // four copies would cost 4 MB; sharing costs 1 MB pagesFor(4097) == 2

title: What to ship
where: 1.01 What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
body: A program uses several libraries. Some are static (their code is already inside the .exe ) and some are DLLs (files that must be shipped next to it). Write cpp std::vector<std::string shipList(const std::string& exe, const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string & libraries); Each library is a pair of a file name and its kind, "static" or "dll" . Return the files to put in the folder you give to users: - the .exe first; - then every DLL, sorted alphabetically; - each DLL only once, even if it is listed several times. Windows file names ignore case, so Audio.dll and audio.DLL are the same file: keep the spelling that came first; - no static libraries. shipList("game.exe", { {"physics.lib","static"}, {"audio.dll","dll"}, {"Audio.DLL","dll"}, {"fonts.dll","dll"} }) == { "game.exe", "audio.dll", "fonts.dll" }

title: 1.02  How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
match: 1.02 How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
body: Before main runs, the Windows loader finds every DLL the program needs, maps each one into memory once, loads their own dependencies, fixes up addresses and fills in the program's tables of function addresses. Knowing these steps explains most "DLL not found" and "entry point not found" errors. The loader When you start a program, Windows creates a process and then runs code in ntdll.dll called the loader . Its job is to turn files on disk into a ready-to-run address space. For each module (the .exe and every DLL) it: 1. Finds the file using the DLL search order (lesson 4.01). 2. Maps it into memory : it reserves a range of the process's address space and makes the file's sections appear there, with the right protection (code readable and executable, data readable and writable). 3. Relocates it if it could not be placed at its preferred address. 4. Loads its dependencies : every DLL listed in its import table, recursively. 5. Binds its imports : looks up each imported function in the other DLL's export table and writes the real address into this module's import address table (IAT). 6. Runs its initialisation : for a DLL, its DllMain with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH (lesson 2.04), which also constructs its global C++ objects. Only when all of that has worked does the program's own start-up code run, construct its globals and call main . Each DLL is loaded once The loader keeps a list of modules already in the process. If game.exe needs audio.dll and physics.dll , and both of those need math.dll , math.dll is still loaded only once . The second request just finds it in the list and increases its reference count . Dependencies are initialised before the modules that need them, so math.dll is ready by the time audio.dll 's initialisation runs. In the graph above one valid order is kernel32.dll , math.dll , audio.dll , physics.dll , then game.exe itself. That is a depth-first, dependencies-first walk, the order you will compute in the practice. Preferred addresses and relocation Every module is built for a preferred base address . Code that refers to a global variable often contains that variable's absolute address, worked out as base + offset . If the module really lands at its preferred base, all those addresses are already right. If something else already occupies that range, the loader puts the module elsewhere and has to relocate it: for every place listed in the .reloc section, it adds the difference between the actual base and the preferred base. Offsets inside a module are called RVAs (relative virtual addresses): address = base + RVA actual address after relocation = actual base + RVA fix-up applied to each stored address = actual base - preferred base With ASLR (address space layout randomisation), Windows deliberately picks a random base for most modules each time, to make attacks harder, so relocation is normal rather than rare. 64-bit code also uses addresses relative to the instruction pointer for most data, which needs no fix-ups at all. Two ways to connect Load-time linking Run-time linking --- --- --- How Link against the DLL's import library (lesson 1.05) Call LoadLibraryW and GetProcAddress yourself (lesson 2.03) When the DLL is loaded Before main Whenever your code asks If the DLL is missing The program will not start at all LoadLibraryW returns NULL and your code decides what to do Typical use Libraries the program always needs Optional features, plugins, hot reload When it goes wrong The loader's failures have recognisable messages: Message Meaning --- --- "The code execution cannot proceed because X.dll was not found." Step 1 failed for X.dll "The procedure entry point Foo could not be located in the dynamic link library X.dll." Step 5: X.dll was found but does not export Foo , usually because it is a different version "The application was unable to start correctly (0xc000007b)." Usually a 32-bit DLL in a 64-bit process, or the reverse A DllMain returned FALSE Step 6: initialisation of that DLL failed, so loading fails Common mistakes !warning Assuming dependencies are loaded in the order you list them The loader walks the dependency graph. Never rely on one DLL's initialisation having run before another's unless one depends on the other. !warning Mixing 32-bit and 64-bit A process is one or the other, and every DLL it loads must match. Knowledge check quiz ? Two DLLs in a program both depend on math.dll. How many times is math.dll mapped? + Once; the second request increases its reference count - Twice, once for each DLL - It depends on the order of the imports The loader keeps a list of loaded modules and reuses them. ? A module's preferred base is 0x180000000 but it lands at 0x7FF600000000. A stored address was 0x180001234. What is it after relocation? + 0x7FF600001234 - 0x180001234 - 0x7FF600000000 The fix-up adds (actual base - preferred base) to every listed address, so the RVA 0x1234 is kept. ? Which step of loading produces "The procedure entry point could not be located"? + Binding imports against the other DLL's export table - Mapping the file - Running DllMain The DLL was found, but it does not export that name.

title: Relocate an address
where: 1.02 How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
body: A module was built for a preferred base , but the loader put it at a different actual base . Write: - unsigned long long rvaOf(unsigned long long address, unsigned long long base) : the address as an offset from the module's base. - unsigned long long relocate(unsigned long long stored, unsigned long long preferredBase, unsigned long long actualBase) : the value a stored absolute address must become after the module moves. The offset from the base stays the same. rvaOf(0x180001234, 0x180000000) == 0x1234 relocate(0x180001234, 0x180000000, 0x7FF600000000) == 0x7FF600001234

title: The loader's order
where: 1.02 How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
body: The loader initialises a module only after every module it imports from. Write cpp std::vector<std::string loadOrder(const std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string & imports, const std::string& root); imports says which DLLs each module imports, in the order they are listed in its import table. A module that is not a key in the map imports nothing. Return the order the modules are initialised, root included, following these rules: - visit a module's imports in the order listed, depth first, and put the module itself after all of them; - every module appears once , the first time it is reached; - a module that has already been started (even if not finished) is not visited again, so a loop between two DLLs does not run forever. imports = { "game.exe": { "audio.dll", "physics.dll" }, "audio.dll": { "math.dll", "kernel32.dll" }, "physics.dll":{ "math.dll" }, "math.dll": { "kernel32.dll" } } loadOrder(imports, "game.exe") == { "kernel32.dll", "math.dll", "audio.dll", "physics.dll", "game.exe" }

title: 1.03  Your First DLL in Visual Studio
match: 1.03 Your First DLL in Visual Studio
body: Build a DLL and a program that uses it, in one Visual Studio solution. You meet the export macro pattern that lets one header serve both the library and the programs using it, and see where the .dll and its import .lib end up. The plan You will make one solution with two projects: Stones.sln ├── StoneMath/ a DLL project │ ├── stone_math.h the public header: what users of the DLL see │ └── stone_math.cpp the implementation └── StoneDemo/ a console program that calls the DLL └── main.cpp 1. The DLL project In Visual Studio: File, New, Project , choose Dynamic-Link Library (DLL) for C++, name it StoneMath . The template adds pch.h , framework.h and a dllmain.cpp . You can leave dllmain.cpp as it is for now (lesson 2.04 explains it), or turn off precompiled headers in Properties, C/C++, Precompiled Headers to keep things small. Note one setting the template made for you, in Properties, C/C++, Preprocessor, Preprocessor Definitions : STONEMATH_EXPORTS . Only the DLL project defines it. That is what the header uses to tell "building the library" from "using the library". 2. The export macro A function must be marked to appear in the DLL's export table. When building the DLL, the marker is __declspec(dllexport) . When a program uses the DLL, the same declaration should say __declspec(dllimport) , which lets the compiler call it through the import table directly. One header serves both by switching on STONEMATH_EXPORTS : cpp-norun // stone_math.h pragma once ifdef STONEMATH_EXPORTS define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllexport) else define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllimport) endif STONEMATH_API int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer); STONEMATH_API double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach); cpp-norun // stone_math.cpp include "stone_math.h" int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer) { if (stonesPerLayer <= 0) return 0; return (stones + stonesPerLayer - 1) / stonesPerLayer; // round up: a part layer is still a layer } double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach) { return stones kilosEach; } Build the project. In the output folder ( x64\Debug under the solution) you find: File What it is --- --- StoneMath.dll The library itself, needed at run time StoneMath.lib The import library : small, says "these names live in StoneMath.dll". Needed at link time StoneMath.pdb Debug symbols StoneMath.exp Export file the linker made along the way; you can ignore it !note Only marked functions are exported A function without STONEMATH_API is still in the DLL's code, but no other module can find it. That is how a DLL keeps helpers private. 3. The program that uses it Add a project to the same solution: Console App , named StoneDemo . cpp-norun // main.cpp include <iostream include "stone_math.h" int main() { std::cout << "Layers: " << stackHeight(10, 4) << '\n'; // 3 std::cout << "Weight: " << stackWeight(10, 2.5) << " kg\n"; // 25 } Three settings connect them: 1. Find the header. StoneDemo, Properties, C/C++, General, Additional Include Directories : $(SolutionDir)StoneMath . 2. Link the import library. Right-click StoneDemo, Add, Reference , tick StoneMath. Visual Studio then links StoneMath.lib and builds StoneMath first. 3. Run from the right place. Both projects already write to $(SolutionDir)x64\Debug , so StoneMath.dll sits next to StoneDemo.exe , which is the first place Windows looks. Set StoneDemo as the startup project and run it. 4. Break it on purpose - Delete StoneMath.dll from the output folder and run StoneDemo.exe from Explorer: the loader says it cannot find the DLL. The program never reaches main . - Remove STONEMATH_API from stackWeight , rebuild both: now the linker fails with LNK2019: unresolved external symbol , because the import library no longer lists it. Exporting a class You can put the macro on a class to export all its members: cpp-norun class STONEMATH_API Xenon { public: explicit Xenon(int stones); int height() const; private: int m_stones; }; It works, but it ties every program to the exact compiler, settings and class layout the DLL was built with. Milestone 3 shows why most long-lived DLLs export plain C functions instead. Common mistakes !warning Defining STONEMATH_EXPORTS in the program too Then the program's copy of the header says dllexport , and you get confusing link errors. Only the DLL project defines it. !warning Copying the DLL by hand into the wrong folder Debug and Release, and x64 and x86, each have their own output folder. Keep both projects writing to the same one. Knowledge check quiz ? Which file does the program's linker need? + StoneMath.lib, the import library - StoneMath.dll - StoneMath.pdb The import library tells the linker which DLL each function lives in. The DLL itself is needed when the program runs. ? Why does the header switch between dllexport and dllimport? + The same declaration must export the function when building the DLL and import it when building the program - Because dllexport only works in Release builds - To make the DLL smaller The project that defines STONEMATH_EXPORTS is the DLL; every other user of the header imports. ? A helper function in stone_math.cpp has no STONEMATH_API. Can StoneDemo call it? + No; it is in the DLL's code but not in its export table - Yes, any function in a DLL can be called - Only in Debug builds Only exported names can be found from outside the module.

title: The library's functions
where: 1.03 Your First DLL in Visual Studio
body: Write the two functions the StoneMath DLL in the lesson exports. On the website they are ordinary functions; in Visual Studio the same code goes into the DLL project. - int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer) : how many layers a stack of stones makes. A part layer still counts as a layer. If stonesPerLayer is 0 or less, or there are no stones, the answer is 0. - double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach) : the total weight. stackHeight(10, 4) == 3 stackWeight(10, 2.5) == 25.0

title: dllexport or dllimport
where: 1.03 Your First DLL in Visual Studio
body: The export macro in a DLL's public header expands to one thing while the DLL itself is being built and another everywhere else. Write cpp std::string apiMacroFor(bool buildingTheDll); that returns the text the macro should expand to: "__declspec(dllexport)" while building the DLL, "__declspec(dllimport)" for any program that uses it. Then write std::string exportsSymbol(const std::string& projectName) : the preprocessor symbol Visual Studio's DLL template defines for a project, which is the project name in upper case followed by _EXPORTS . Only letters and digits are kept; anything else becomes _ . exportsSymbol("StoneMath") == "STONEMATH_EXPORTS" exportsSymbol("my-lib 2") == "MY_LIB_2_EXPORTS"

title: 1.04  Exporting Functions and Data
body: There are two ways to say what a DLL exports, __declspec(dllexport) and a module-definition file ( .def ). This lesson covers both, plus ordinals , exporting variables, and what goes into the export table. The export table, up close Each entry in a DLL's export table has: - a name (optional), such as stackHeight ; - an ordinal , a number unique within the DLL; - an RVA : where the function or variable starts, relative to the DLL's base. Other modules find an export either by name or by ordinal. Names are the normal way. Ordinals are small numbers that are faster to look up and hide the name, but they are fragile: if ordinal 3 means a different function in the next version, every program built against the old one silently calls the wrong code. Way 1: __declspec(dllexport) You met this in lesson 1.03. The compiler writes an instruction for the linker into the object file, and the linker adds the name to the export table. It is easy and keeps the "this is public" information next to the declaration. The catch is the name . For a C++ function the exported name is the compiler's decorated (mangled) name, which also encodes the parameter types: int stackHeight(int, int) is exported as ?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z Lesson 2.01 explains decoration and how extern "C" gives you the plain name stackHeight instead, which is what you want for anything called from another language or loaded with GetProcAddress . Way 2: a module-definition file A .def file lists exports by hand. Add one to the DLL project ( Add, New Item, Module-Definition File ); Visual Studio sets Linker, Input, Module Definition File to it. LIBRARY StoneMath EXPORTS stackHeight @1 stackWeight @2 internalCounter @3 DATA debugDump @4 NONAME StackHeight = stackHeight Line Meaning --- --- LIBRARY StoneMath The DLL's name stackHeight @1 Export stackHeight with ordinal 1 internalCounter @3 DATA Export a variable , not a function debugDump @4 NONAME Export by ordinal only: no name in the table StackHeight = stackHeight Export the internal function stackHeight under a different public name Lines starting with ; are comments. The names in a .def file must match the symbols the compiler produced, so a .def file works most comfortably with extern "C" functions. Why use a .def file at all? - To give fixed ordinals that never change between versions. - To export a function under a different name than the one in the code. - To export plain names from code you cannot or do not want to change. Exporting variables A DLL can export a global variable: cpp-norun // in the DLL STONEMATH_API int g_stonesCreated = 0; // in the header, for users extern STONEMATH_API int g_stonesCreated; The program then reads and writes the DLL's variable directly. It works, but every program now depends on that variable's type and meaning. A function such as int stonesCreated() can change how it works without breaking anyone, so prefer functions. Lesson 3.01 turns that into a rule. Seeing what you exported Open a Developer Command Prompt and run: dumpbin /exports StoneMath.dll varies ordinal hint RVA name 1 0 00011023 stackHeight = @ILT+30(stackHeight) 2 1 000110A5 stackWeight = @ILT+160(stackWeight) 3 2 0001C000 internalCounter 4 000111D6 NONAME The hint is an index into the name table that lets the loader skip a search when it is right. Lesson 1.06 covers dumpbin and other tools. Common mistakes !warning Reusing an ordinal for a different function Programs that import by ordinal will call the wrong function. Once published, an ordinal belongs to its function forever. !warning Putting a C++ name with no extern "C" in a .def file The linker looks for a symbol called exactly that and does not find the decorated one. Use extern "C" for exported functions listed in a .def file. Knowledge check quiz ? What does NONAME mean in a .def file? + The function is exported by ordinal only, with no name in the export table - The function is not exported - The function has no parameters Other modules can only find it by its number. ? Why are ordinals risky across versions? + If an ordinal later refers to a different function, old programs silently call the wrong code - Ordinals are slower than names - Windows does not support them anymore Names describe what you call; numbers only describe a position. ? Which .def line exports the function stack_impl under the public name Stack ? + Stack = stack_impl - stack_impl = Stack - Stack @stack_impl The public name comes first, then the internal one.

title: Read a .def file
body: Write a reader for the EXPORTS lines of a module-definition file. cpp struct DefExport { std::string name; // the public name std::string internal; // the function in the code; the same as name when there is no "= ..." int ordinal{ -1 }; // -1 when no @number is given bool noName{ false }; // NONAME bool data{ false }; // DATA }; std::vector<DefExport readDef(const std::string& text); Rules: - Lines are separated by \n . Leading and trailing spaces do not matter. - Skip blank lines, comment lines starting with ; , the LIBRARY line and the EXPORTS line itself. - Every other line is one export: name , optionally = internal , optionally @number , then optionally the words NONAME and DATA in any order. Words are separated by spaces; = and @ may have spaces around them or not. LIBRARY StoneMath EXPORTS stackHeight @1 internalCounter @3 DATA debugDump @4 NONAME StackHeight = stackHeight gives four exports: {stackHeight, stackHeight, 1} , {internalCounter, internalCounter, 3, data} , {debugDump, debugDump, 4, noName} , {StackHeight, stackHeight, -1} .

title: Did the ordinals stay put?
body: A DLL exports by ordinal, so a new version must keep every published ordinal. Write cpp std::vector<std::string ordinalProblems(const std::map<std::string, int & oldVersion, const std::map<std::string, int & newVersion); Each map is export name to ordinal. Report, in this order: 1. for each name in the old version (in alphabetical order, as the map stores them): - missing from the new version: "<name was removed" ; - present with a different ordinal: "<name moved from @<old to @<new " ; 2. then, for each name that is new (alphabetical): if its ordinal was used by a different name in the old version, "@<n now means <newName , was <oldName " . An empty list means old programs keep working. old: { stackHeight: 1, stackWeight: 2, debugDump: 3 } new: { stackHeight: 1, stackWeight: 5, layers: 3 } problems: "debugDump was removed", "stackWeight moved from @2 to @5", "@3 now means layers, was debugDump"

title: 1.05  Import Libraries and Load-Time Linking
body: When a program links against a DLL's import library , the linker writes an import table into the program and calls go through the import address table , which the loader fills in. This lesson follows one call from your source code to the DLL. What an import library contains StoneMath.lib from lesson 1.03 is small. It contains no machine code for stackHeight . It contains, for each export: - the symbol the linker is looking for ( __imp_stackHeight , and a stub called stackHeight ), and - a record saying "this comes from StoneMath.dll , under the name stackHeight ". When StoneDemo's linker sees a call to stackHeight , it finds the symbol in the import library and records the dependency. The result in StoneDemo.exe is an import table : StoneDemo.exe imports StoneMath.dll stackHeight stackWeight KERNEL32.dll WriteFile GetStdHandle ... The import address table Alongside the names, the program has an import address table (IAT): one pointer-sized slot for every imported function. In the file the slots hold placeholders. At load time, the loader looks up each name in the DLL's export table and writes the real address into the slot (lesson 1.02, step 5). Your call compiles into an indirect call through that slot: asm ; with __declspec(dllimport) on the declaration call qword ptr __imp_stackHeight ; jump to whatever address the loader wrote into the slot Without dllimport , the compiler does not know the function is in a DLL. It emits a normal call stackHeight , and the linker makes stackHeight a tiny stub that jumps through the slot. It works, just with one extra jump. That is why the header from lesson 1.03 says dllimport for users. Following one call The cost is one memory read to fetch the address. The benefit is that the program does not need to know where StoneMath.dll will be loaded. When a name cannot be resolved At load time, every import must be found. If StoneDemo.exe was built against a StoneMath.dll that exported stackHeight and stackWeight , but the DLL on disk is an older one with only stackHeight , the loader stops with: varies The procedure entry point stackWeight could not be located in the dynamic link library StoneMath.dll. The program does not start. This is the strongest argument for never removing an export from a published DLL (milestone 3). Linking against a DLL without a project reference The project reference from lesson 1.03 is the easiest way in one solution. For a DLL from somewhere else you set two linker properties yourself: - Linker, General, Additional Library Directories : the folder with StoneMath.lib . - Linker, Input, Additional Dependencies : add StoneMath.lib . Or, in code, a comment that tells the linker: cpp-norun pragma comment(lib, "StoneMath.lib") You still need the DLL next to the program when it runs. Making an import library from a DLL Sometimes you have only a DLL (and its documentation). You can rebuild an import library from a .def file listing its exports: lib /def:StoneMath.def /out:StoneMath.lib /machine:x64 Common mistakes !warning Shipping only the .lib The import library is for building. Users of your program need the .dll . !warning Using an import library from a different version of the DLL The program then imports names the DLL on disk may not have. Keep the .lib and .dll from the same build together. Knowledge check quiz ? What does an import library contain? + The names of the DLL's exports and which DLL each comes from, but not their code - The full machine code of the DLL - Debug symbols It lets the linker connect calls to the DLL without including its code. ? Who fills in the import address table? + The loader, when the program starts - The linker, when the program is built - The DLL's DllMain The real addresses are not known until the DLL is mapped. ? A program imports stackWeight but the DLL on disk does not export it. What happens? + The program fails to start with "procedure entry point could not be located" - stackWeight returns 0 - The program starts and crashes when stackWeight is called Load-time linking resolves every import before main.

title: Resolve the imports
body: At load time, every import must be found or the program does not start. Write the check the loader makes: cpp std::string resolveImports(const std::map<std::string, std::set<std::string & exportsByDll, const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string & imports); - exportsByDll maps each DLL that exists to the names it exports. - imports is the program's import table: pairs of (DLL name, function name), in order. - DLL names ignore upper and lower case ( KERNEL32.dll is kernel32.dll ); function names do not. Return the message for the first import that fails, or an empty string if all of them resolve: - DLL not found: The code execution cannot proceed because <dll was not found. - Function not exported: The procedure entry point <function could not be located in the dynamic link library <dll . Use the DLL name as the import table spells it.

title: Fill the import address table
body: The loader writes the real address of each imported function into the import address table. Write cpp std::vector<unsigned long long fillIat(const std::vector<std::string & imports, const std::map<std::string, unsigned long long & exportRvas, unsigned long long dllBase); For each imported name, in order, the slot holds dllBase + rva of that export, or 0 if the DLL does not export it. fillIat({ "stackHeight", "stackWeight" }, { {"stackHeight", 0x1023}, {"stackWeight", 0x10A5} }, 0x7FFA10000000) == { 0x7FFA10001023, 0x7FFA100010A5 }

title: 1.06  Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
match: 1.06 Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
body: When a program will not start or calls the wrong thing, you need to see what a module exports, what it imports, and where each DLL really came from. This lesson covers dumpbin , the Dependencies tool, the debugger's Modules window and Process Monitor. dumpbin dumpbin comes with Visual Studio. Run it from a Developer Command Prompt (Start menu: "Developer Command Prompt for VS"). Command Shows --- --- dumpbin /exports X.dll The export table: ordinal, hint, RVA, name dumpbin /imports X.exe Every DLL the module imports from, and every function dumpbin /dependents X.exe Just the list of DLLs it needs directly dumpbin /headers X.dll Machine type (x64 or x86), preferred base, subsystem, characteristics A typical check when a program refuses to start: dumpbin /dependents on the .exe , then make sure every listed DLL exists, then dumpbin /exports on the suspicious one and compare against dumpbin /imports . varies Dump of file StoneDemo.exe Image has the following dependencies: StoneMath.dll MSVCP140D.dll VCRUNTIME140D.dll VCRUNTIME140_1D.dll ucrtbased.dll KERNEL32.dll The D at the end of the runtime names means debug runtime. Those DLLs exist only on machines with Visual Studio installed, which is why a Debug build will not run on a friend's computer (lesson 4.04). dumpbin /headers answers "is this 32-bit or 64-bit?": look for machine (x64) or machine (x86) . Dependencies Dependencies (https://github.com/lucasg/Dependencies) is a free, open-source tool that shows the whole dependency tree of a module, recursively, and marks in red anything it cannot find. It understands Windows' API sets (names like api-ms-win-core-file-l1-1-0.dll , which are redirected to real system DLLs), which confuses older tools. Open StoneDemo.exe in it, expand StoneMath.dll , and you see what StoneMath itself needs. The debugger's Modules window While debugging, Debug, Windows, Modules lists every module actually loaded, with: - Path : exactly which file was loaded. This answers "which copy of the DLL did it pick?" - Address : where it was mapped (lesson 1.02). - Symbol Status : whether its .pdb was found, so you can step into it. - Version : from its version resource (lesson 4.04). A DLL loaded with LoadLibraryW appears in the list the moment the call returns. Process Monitor When Windows looks for a DLL, it tries a sequence of folders (lesson 4.01). Process Monitor (https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/procmon) from Sysinternals records every file access. Filter on your process name and on paths ending in .dll , start the program, and you see each place the loader tried, with NAME NOT FOUND until it finds the file. That tells you exactly why the wrong copy was loaded, or why none was. Reading a loader failure, step by step 1. Note the exact message (lesson 1.02's table). 2. dumpbin /dependents the .exe : which DLLs does it need? 3. For each one, is it next to the program, or in a folder Windows searches? 4. Is it the right architecture? ( dumpbin /headers ) 5. If the message names a missing entry point , dumpbin /exports the DLL that was loaded (find its path in Process Monitor or the Modules window) and compare with what the program imports. Common mistakes !warning Inspecting the wrong copy There are often several copies of a DLL on a machine. Check the path Windows actually loaded, not the one you expected. !warning Running dumpbin from an ordinary prompt It is only on the PATH in a Developer Command Prompt. Knowledge check quiz ? Which command answers "which DLLs does this program need directly?" + dumpbin /dependents - dumpbin /exports - dumpbin /headers /imports gives the same list plus every function; /dependents is the short version. ? How can you see every folder Windows tried while looking for a DLL? + Record the program's start with Process Monitor and filter on .dll paths - dumpbin /imports - The Output window in Visual Studio Process Monitor shows every attempt, including the ones that failed. ? What does a name ending in D, such as MSVCP140D.dll, tell you? + The program was built in Debug and needs the debug C++ runtime - The DLL is damaged - The DLL is 32-bit Debug runtimes are only installed with Visual Studio.

title: Read dumpbin's export list
where: 1.06 Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
body: Write a reader for the table dumpbin /exports prints, so a tool can compare two versions of a DLL. cpp std::vector<std::string exportedNames(const std::string& dumpbinOutput); The table starts after the heading line that contains the words ordinal , hint , RVA and name . Each following line that starts (after spaces) with a number is one export: 1 0 00011023 stackHeight = @ILT+30(stackHeight) 2 1 000110A5 stackWeight = @ILT+160(stackWeight) 4 000111D6 NONAME - The columns are the ordinal, the hint (missing for an export without a name), the 8-digit hexadecimal RVA, then the name. - The name is the word right after the RVA. Anything after it ( = @ILT+... ) is ignored. - For NONAME , use followed by the ordinal, such as 4 . - Stop at the first blank line after the table has started, or at a line starting with Summary . Return the names in the order they appear.

title: Debug runtime or API set
where: 1.06 Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
body: Two small checks for a list of DLL names from dumpbin /dependents : - bool needsDebugRuntime(const std::vector<std::string & dlls) : true if any of them is a debug build of the Visual C++ runtime: msvcp140d.dll , vcruntime140d.dll , vcruntime140_1d.dll or ucrtbased.dll (any upper/lower case). - bool isApiSet(const std::string& dll) : true if the name is an API set, which starts with api-ms- or ext-ms- (any case). Windows redirects those to real DLLs, so a tool should not report them as missing.

title: A loader report
body: Put the milestone together: simulate what the Windows loader does when a program starts, and explain the result the way a good tool would. A module is described by what it imports and what it exports: cpp struct Module { std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string imports; // (dll, function), in import-table order std::set<std::string exports; // names this module offers }; std::vector<std::string loaderReport(const std::map<std::string, Module & onDisk, const std::string& program); onDisk holds every module that exists, keyed by file name. DLL names ignore case when you look them up; function names do not. The report is a list of lines: 1. Work out the load order exactly like lesson 1.02's practice: depth first, a module's dependencies (the DLLs in its imports, each counted once, in the order they first appear) before the module itself, every module once. Only modules that exist are visited. 2. Before printing anything, check every module you would load, in load order, including the program : - for each of its imports, in order: the DLL must exist, and must export the function; - stop at the first problem and return a single line, the loader's message from lesson 1.05's practice. 3. If everything resolves, return one line load <name per module in load order, then a final line start <program . If the program itself is not on disk, the report is the single line <program was not found. onDisk: game.exe imports (audio.dll, play) (KERNEL32.dll, WriteFile) audio.dll imports (kernel32.dll, CreateFileW) exports play, stop kernel32.dll exports WriteFile, CreateFileW loaderReport(onDisk, "game.exe") == { "load kernel32.dll", "load audio.dll", "load game.exe", "start game.exe" } Use the name of each module the way it is spelled as a key in onDisk .

title: 2.01  Name Mangling and extern "C"
body: C++ lets two functions share a name if their parameters differ, so the compiler gives every function a decorated name that encodes its parameter types. Those names are what a DLL exports by default. extern "C" turns decoration off, giving the plain names that GetProcAddress , .def files and other languages need. Why names are decorated In C++ these are three different functions: cpp-norun int area(int side); int area(int width, int height); double area(double radius); The linker, though, only knows symbol names: strings. To keep the three apart, the compiler gives each a decorated name (also called a mangled name) that includes the parameter types, the return type, the namespace and class, and more. With MSVC: Declaration Decorated name --- --- int area(int) ?area@@YAHH@Z int area(int, int) ?area@@YAHHH@Z double area(double) ?area@@YANN@Z int stackHeight(int, int) ?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z void reset() ?reset@@YAXXZ GCC and Clang use a completely different scheme ( _Z4areai ). That alone is a good reason not to export C++ names from a DLL meant for anyone else. Reading an MSVC name For a plain function outside any class or namespace, the pattern is: ? name @@ YA <return type <parameter types @Z (no parameters: XZ) - ? marks a decorated C++ name. - @@ ends the name and its (empty) scope. - Y means "a function outside a class", A means the default calling convention ( __cdecl ). - The type codes: Type Code Type Code --- --- --- --- void X int H char D unsigned int I bool _N long long _J float M double N - After the parameters comes @Z . A function with no parameters has X (void) as its parameter list and ends XZ with no @ . So ?add@@YAHHH@Z is "a free function add , returning int ( H ), taking int, int ( HH )". You will build exactly this decorator in the practice. To decode a name you do not recognise, Visual Studio ships undname : undname ?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z varies Undecoration of :- "?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z" is :- "int __cdecl stackHeight(int,int)" extern "C" Wrapping a declaration in extern "C" tells the compiler to use C linkage : no overloading, no decoration, the plain name. cpp-norun // stone_math.h ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { endif STONEMATH_API int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer); STONEMATH_API double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach); ifdef __cplusplus } endif Now dumpbin /exports lists stackHeight and stackWeight . The ifdef __cplusplus lets the same header be used from C, which does not know the words extern "C" . What you give up: - No overloading. Two extern "C" functions cannot share a name. Use distinct names: area_square , area_rect . - No C++ types in the signature that C cannot express , if you want other languages to call it. The compiler allows std::string in an extern "C" function, but no other language can construct one (lesson 2.06). The body of an extern "C" function is still C++. You can use classes, templates and the standard library inside it; only the name and signature are C. Which names to export A good rule for any DLL that outlives one build of one program: Export extern "C" functions with plain C types in their signatures. Keep C++ on the inside. Milestone 3 builds whole interfaces this way, including ones that give users objects and methods. Common mistakes !warning GetProcAddress(dll, "stackHeight") returns NULL The function was exported with its decorated name. Add extern "C" , or ask for the decorated name (fragile). !warning extern "C" in the .cpp file but not the header Callers then look for the decorated name and the linker cannot find it. Put extern "C" on the declaration everyone sees. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does C++ decorate function names? + So that overloaded functions with the same name get different linker symbols - To make the program faster - To hide the code from debuggers The linker only compares names, so the types have to be part of the name. ? What is the MSVC decorated name of int twice(int) ? + ?twice@@YAHH@Z - _twice - ?twice@@YAXXZ H for the int return, H for the one int parameter, then @Z. ? What does extern "C" change about a function? + Its linkage: the exported name is plain, and it cannot be overloaded - It must be written in C - It can no longer use C++ inside its body Only the name and signature follow C rules; the body is ordinary C++.

title: Decorate a name like MSVC
body: Write the decorator from the lesson for free functions with simple types: cpp std::string decorate(const std::string& name, const std::string& returnType, const std::vector<std::string & parameters); The result is ? + name + @@YA + the return type's code + the parameter codes + an ending: - with at least one parameter, the ending is @Z ; - with no parameters, the parameter list is X (void) and the ending is Z , so the name ends in XZ . Type Code Type Code --- --- --- --- void X int H char D unsigned int I bool _N long long _J float M double N If any type is not in the table, return an empty string. decorate("add", "int", { "int", "int" }) == "?add@@YAHHH@Z" decorate("reset", "void", {}) == "?reset@@YAXXZ" decorate("ratio", "double", { "float", "bool" }) == "?ratio@@YANM_N@Z"

title: Mangled or not
body: Write bool isDecorated(const std::string& symbol) that says whether an exported name is an MSVC-decorated C++ name. Those start with ? . Plain extern "C" names, and 32-bit names such as _name@8 , do not.

title: 2.02  Calling Conventions at the Boundary
body: A calling convention is the agreement about where a function's arguments go and who cleans up afterwards. On 64-bit Windows there is essentially one; on 32-bit Windows there are several, and they change the exported name. Getting the convention wrong across a DLL boundary corrupts the stack. The agreement every call relies on When main calls stackHeight(10, 4) , both sides must agree on: - where the arguments go: registers or the stack, and in which order; - where the return value comes back; - which registers the called function may change; - who removes the arguments from the stack afterwards. That agreement is the calling convention . Inside one program the compiler uses the same one everywhere, so you never think about it. Across a DLL boundary, the caller and the DLL were compiled separately, possibly by different compilers or languages, so the convention is part of the interface. 64-bit Windows: one convention On x64 Windows every function uses the Microsoft x64 calling convention : - the first four integer or pointer arguments go in RCX , RDX , R8 , R9 ; the first four floating-point ones in XMM0 to XMM3 ; - further arguments go on the stack; - the caller reserves 32 bytes of "shadow space" on the stack and cleans up; - the return value comes back in RAX (or XMM0 ). Keywords like __stdcall and __cdecl are accepted on x64 but ignored . Names are not decorated for them either: an extern "C" function is exported exactly as stackHeight . 32-bit Windows: several conventions 32-bit code is still around (older plugins, some game engines), and there the keyword matters: Convention Arguments Who cleans the stack extern "C" name --- --- --- --- __cdecl (default for C/C++) stack, right to left the caller _name __stdcall (the Win32 API, WINAPI ) stack, right to left the callee _name@N , N = bytes of arguments __fastcall first two in ECX , EDX , rest on stack the callee @name@N N is the total size of the arguments, each rounded up to 4 bytes: int stackHeight(int, int) as __stdcall is exported as _stackHeight@8 . That decoration is why so many old DLLs use a .def file: to export the plain name stackHeight from a __stdcall function. When the two sides disagree Suppose a DLL defines __stdcall but the program declares the function __cdecl and calls it through a function pointer (lesson 2.03). On 32-bit Windows: 1. The program pushes 8 bytes of arguments. 2. The DLL's function returns and, being __stdcall , removes 8 bytes. 3. The program, believing it is __cdecl , removes 8 more. The stack pointer is now 8 bytes wrong. Local variables and return addresses are read from the wrong places, and the program crashes somewhere unrelated, often much later. In a Debug build MSVC catches it with: varies Run-Time Check Failure 0 - The value of ESP was not properly saved across a function call. A portable habit Pick a convention for your public API and spell it out with a macro, so the header says it once: cpp-norun ifdef _WIN32 define STONEMATH_CALL __cdecl else define STONEMATH_CALL endif STONEMATH_API int STONEMATH_CALL stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer); typedef int (STONEMATH_CALL StackHeightFn)(int, int); // for GetProcAddress users On x64 the macro does nothing. On x86 it makes both sides agree, including people writing their own declarations from your documentation. Common mistakes !warning Declaring a function pointer without the convention A GetProcAddress result cast to the wrong function pointer type is the most common way to get a convention mismatch. Put the convention in the typedef. !warning Assuming 32-bit rules on x64 On x64 _name@8 decoration never happens. If you see it, you are looking at a 32-bit DLL. Knowledge check quiz ? How many calling conventions does ordinary x64 Windows code use? + One: the Microsoft x64 convention; __stdcall and __cdecl are ignored - Three, like 32-bit Windows - Two: one for C and one for C++ The keywords compile but have no effect on x64. ? What is the 32-bit exported name of extern "C" int __stdcall area(int, int)? + _area@8 - area - @area@8 __stdcall adds a leading underscore and @ plus the bytes of arguments. ? On 32-bit Windows, a __stdcall function is called as if it were __cdecl. What goes wrong? + The arguments are removed from the stack twice, so the stack pointer ends up wrong - Nothing; they are the same - The function returns the wrong type __stdcall's callee and __cdecl's caller both clean up.

title: 32-bit export names
body: On 32-bit Windows an extern "C" function's exported name depends on its calling convention. Write cpp std::string exportName32(const std::string& name, const std::string& convention, const std::vector<int & argumentSizes); - argumentSizes holds the size in bytes of each argument. Each one counts as at least 4 bytes and is rounded up to a multiple of 4 (a char takes 4 bytes on the stack, a double 8). Their total is N . - "cdecl" : _name - "stdcall" : _name@N - "fastcall" : @name@N - any other convention: the name unchanged. Then write int stackBytes(const std::vector<int & argumentSizes) returning N on its own. exportName32("area", "stdcall", { 4, 4 }) == "_area@8" exportName32("f", "stdcall", { 4, 8 }) == "_f@12" exportName32("g", "stdcall", { 1, 2 }) == "_g@8"

title: 2.03  Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
match: 2.03 Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
body:
Instead of linking against an import library, a program can load a DLL whenever it likes with LoadLibraryW , look up functions by name with GetProcAddress , call them through function pointers, and unload the DLL with FreeLibrary . This is the foundation of plugins and hot reload. Three functions cpp-norun HMODULE LoadLibraryW(LPCWSTR fileName); // map the DLL (and its dependencies); NULL on failure FARPROC GetProcAddress(HMODULE module, LPCSTR name); // address of an export; NULL if not found BOOL FreeLibrary(HMODULE module); // drop one reference; unmap at zero HMODULE is a handle to a loaded module. Its value is in fact the module's base address. Note that GetProcAddress takes an ANSI string (there is no W version), because export names are plain bytes. A complete example StoneMath from lesson 1.03, now with extern "C" exports (lesson 2.01). The program does not link StoneMath.lib and does not include its header: cpp-norun include <windows.h include <iostream using StackHeightFn = int ( )(int, int); // must match the DLL's declaration exactly int main() { HMODULE dll{ LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") }; if (!dll) { std::cerr << "Could not load StoneMath.dll, error " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } auto stackHeight{ reinterpret_cast<StackHeightFn (GetProcAddress(dll, "stackHeight")) }; if (!stackHeight) { std::cerr << "StoneMath.dll has no stackHeight
"; FreeLibrary(dll); return 1; } std::cout << stackHeight(10, 4) << '
'; // 3 FreeLibrary(dll); } The reinterpret_cast is needed because GetProcAddress returns a generic FARPROC . The compiler cannot check that the type you cast to is right: if the DLL's function takes (double, int) and you cast to int( )(int, int) , the call compiles and silently passes garbage. Keep function pointer types in a header shared with the DLL. !note Why not just link? Run-time loading lets the program start even when the DLL is missing, choose which DLL to load (say, renderer_d3d11.dll or renderer_vulkan.dll ), load DLLs it has never heard of (plugins), and unload and reload a DLL (hot reload). Errors When LoadLibraryW returns NULL , GetLastError() says why: Code Name Usual cause --- --- --- 126 ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND The DLL, or one of its dependencies , was not found 127 ERROR_PROC_NOT_FOUND A dependency is missing an export the DLL imports 193 ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT 32-bit DLL in a 64-bit process, or not a DLL at all 1114 ERROR_DLL_INIT_FAILED The DLL's DllMain returned FALSE Error 126 is confusing: the DLL you named may be right there, but something it needs is not. Lesson 1.06's tools find out which. Reference counting Each successful LoadLibraryW of the same DLL increases its reference count and returns the same HMODULE . Each FreeLibrary decreases it. The DLL is unmapped only when the count reaches zero. cpp-norun HMODULE a{ LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") }; // count 1, maps the DLL HMODULE b{ LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") }; // count 2, a == b FreeLibrary(a); // count 1, still mapped FreeLibrary(b); // count 0, unmapped After the last FreeLibrary , every function pointer you got from that DLL points at memory that no longer belongs to it. Calling one crashes. So does using any object, string or vtable the DLL created. Lesson 5.03 deals with this carefully. A small RAII wrapper Forgetting FreeLibrary on an error path is easy. Wrap the handle: cpp-norun class Library { public: explicit Library(const wchar_t file) : m_module{ LoadLibraryW(file) } {} ~Library() { if (m_module) FreeLibrary(m_module); } Library(const Library&) = delete; Library& operator=(const Library&) = delete; explicit operator bool() const { return m_module != nullptr; } template <typename Fn Fn get(const char name) const { return reinterpret_cast<Fn (GetProcAddress(m_module, name)); } private: HMODULE m_module; }; Common mistakes !warning Casting to the wrong function type The compiler cannot catch it. Share the typedef with the DLL. !warning Calling a function after FreeLibrary Pointers into an unloaded DLL are dangling. Drop them before you free the library. !warning Passing a relative name and getting the wrong file LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") searches several folders. Lesson 4.02 shows how to load exactly the file you mean. Knowledge check quiz ? LoadLibraryW fails with error 126, but StoneMath.dll is next to the program. What is the most likely cause? + One of StoneMath.dll's own dependencies is missing - The file is too large - GetProcAddress was called first 126 means "module not found", and it covers every module the loader needs. ? A DLL is loaded twice and freed once. Is it still mapped? + Yes; its reference count is still 1 - No; one FreeLibrary always unmaps it - Only in Debug builds Each LoadLibrary is matched by one FreeLibrary. ? Why must the function pointer type match the DLL's function exactly? + GetProcAddress returns an untyped address, so a wrong cast passes arguments the wrong way with no compiler error - Otherwise GetProcAddress returns NULL - Because the DLL checks the type The type is only in your cast; nothing checks it.

title: LoadLibrary's reference counts
where: 2.03 Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
body: Simulate how LoadLibraryW and FreeLibrary count references. Write a class cpp class ModuleTable { public: explicit ModuleTable(std::set<std::string filesOnDisk); int load(const std::string& name); // like LoadLibraryW bool free(int handle); // like FreeLibrary int count(const std::string& name) const; bool isLoaded(const std::string& name) const; }; - load returns 0 if the file is not on disk. Otherwise, if the module is not loaded yet, it is mapped and gets a new handle: 1 for the first module ever mapped, 2 for the next, and so on (never reused). If it is already loaded, its count goes up and the same handle is returned. - free with a handle of a loaded module decreases its count; at 0 the module is unmapped. It returns false for a handle that is not loaded (including one already freed completely). - count is the current reference count, 0 if not loaded. - Names ignore case: StoneMath.dll and stonemath.DLL are the same module. A module that is unmapped and loaded again gets a new handle, just as a real DLL may land at a new address.

title: Look it up or say why
match: Look it up or say why
where: 2.03 Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
body: A program loads a DLL at run time and looks up several functions with GetProcAddress . If any is missing it should say which. Write cpp std::string missingFunctions(const std::set<std::string & exports, const std::vector<std::string & wanted); Return an empty string if every wanted name is exported. Otherwise return "missing: " followed by the missing names in the order they were wanted, separated by ", " . Names are case-sensitive, as GetProcAddress is. missingFunctions({ "stackHeight", "stackWeight" }, { "stackHeight", "layers", "Stackweight" }) == "missing: layers, Stackweight"

title: 2.04  DllMain and the Loader Lock
body: A DLL can have an entry point, DllMain , that Windows calls when the DLL is loaded and unloaded and when threads start and end. It runs while the loader holds a lock, which makes most interesting work inside it dangerous. This lesson shows what DllMain is for, what it must never do, and what to do instead. The entry point cpp-norun include <windows.h BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE module, DWORD reason, LPVOID reserved) { switch (reason) { case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH: // the DLL was just mapped into a process DisableThreadLibraryCalls(module); // we do not need the two thread notifications break; case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH: // a new thread started in the process break; case DLL_THREAD_DETACH: // a thread is ending cleanly break; case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH: // the DLL is about to be unmapped // reserved != nullptr: the whole process is exiting; reserved == nullptr: FreeLibrary break; } return TRUE; // FALSE from PROCESS_ATTACH makes the load fail (error 1114) } The template in lesson 1.03 created exactly this in dllmain.cpp . You do not have to write a DllMain ; if you do not, the C runtime supplies one. What really runs at load time Before your DllMain is called with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH , the C runtime's own entry point ( _DllMainCRTStartup ) runs. It initialises the CRT for this DLL and then runs the constructors of the DLL's global C++ objects . At DLL_PROCESS_DETACH , after your DllMain returns, it runs their destructors . So a global like cpp-norun std::vector<std::string g_names{ "basalt", "granite" }; Logger g_log{ "stonemath.log" }; // opens a file in its constructor runs its constructor under the same conditions as DllMain , with the same rules. The loader lock While the loader maps DLLs, runs their entry points and updates its module list, it holds a process-wide lock: the loader lock . DllMain and global constructors run while it is held. Any other thread that wants to load a DLL, unload one, or even look up certain module information, waits for the lock.
