That makes these things dangerous inside DllMain (and in global constructors and destructors of a DLL): Do not Why --- --- Call LoadLibrary or FreeLibrary Changes the module list while it is being changed; can deadlock or load in the wrong order Create a thread and wait for it The new thread's start needs the loader lock (it sends DLL_THREAD_ATTACH ), which you hold: deadlock Wait on any lock another thread might hold while it needs the loader lock Deadlock Call into other DLLs that may not be initialised yet Only kernel32.dll is guaranteed ready Use COM, sockets, the registry, or user interface functions Each may load DLLs or wait on locks internally Microsoft's guidance is blunt: do as little as possible in DllMain . Setting variables, DisableThreadLibraryCalls , InitializeCriticalSection , TlsAlloc : fine. Anything that loads, waits or talks to other components: not fine. !warning Deadlocks here are intermittent Code that waits inside DllMain often works on your machine and hangs on someone else's, depending on timing and on which DLLs happen to be loaded already. What to do instead: explicit initialisation Give the DLL functions for setting up and tearing down, and have the program call them at a normal time: cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_init(const char logPath); // after LoadLibrary returns extern "C" STONEMATH_API void stonemath_shutdown(); // before FreeLibrary Inside stonemath_init , the loader lock is not held. You can open files, start worker threads and wait for them, load other DLLs, read settings. That is the pattern every plugin system in milestone 5 uses. Another useful pattern is lazy initialisation: set things up the first time a function needs them, guarded by std::call_once or a function-local static (which C++ makes thread-safe). Thread notifications DLL_THREAD_ATTACH arrives for threads started after the DLL was loaded, not for threads that already existed. DLL_THREAD_DETACH arrives when a thread ends cleanly, but not for every thread if the process is ending. Code that tries to track every thread through these notifications always has gaps; use thread-local storage ( thread_local ) instead, which the CRT manages for you. DisableThreadLibraryCalls turns the two notifications off, which saves work in programs with many threads. Process exit When the whole process exits, Windows ends every other thread first, abruptly, and then sends DLL_PROCESS_DETACH with reserved non-null. At that point other threads may have died holding locks, and memory your DLL depends on may already be gone. In that case the safest thing is to do nothing: the operating system reclaims all memory and handles anyway. Only clean up when reserved is null (an explicit FreeLibrary ). Common mistakes !warning Starting a worker thread in DllMain and joining it The join waits for a thread that is waiting for the loader lock you hold. Start and stop threads from an explicit init and shutdown function. !warning Global objects with heavy constructors in a DLL They run inside the loader lock too. Prefer creating them in an init function or on first use. Knowledge check quiz ? Which of these is safe inside DllMain? + Calling DisableThreadLibraryCalls - Calling LoadLibraryW - Starting a thread and waiting for it to finish Anything that loads modules or waits for another thread can deadlock on the loader lock. ? When do the constructors of a DLL's global objects run? + At DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, under the loader lock, before your DllMain - When the first exported function is called - When the program calls main The CRT's entry point constructs globals as part of attaching the DLL. ? What should a DLL that needs worker threads do instead of starting them in DllMain? + Offer an init function the program calls after LoadLibrary returns - Start them in DLL_THREAD_ATTACH - Use a global object whose constructor starts them Outside DllMain the loader lock is not held, so waiting and loading are safe.

title: Which notifications arrive?
body: Simulate the calls a DLL's DllMain receives. Write cpp std::vector<std::string dllMainCalls(const std::vector<std::string & events, bool disableThreadCalls); events describes what happens in the process, in order: Event Meaning --- --- "thread start" a thread starts "thread end" a thread ends cleanly "load" the program calls LoadLibraryW on the DLL "free" the program calls FreeLibrary on the DLL "exit" the process exits Return the DllMain calls in order, as strings: "PROCESS_ATTACH" , "THREAD_ATTACH" , "THREAD_DETACH" , "PROCESS_DETACH" and, for process exit, "PROCESS_DETACH (exit)" . The rules: - The DLL starts unloaded. load counts references (lesson 2.03): only the first load sends PROCESS_ATTACH , and only the free that brings the count to zero sends PROCESS_DETACH . A free while unloaded does nothing. - Thread events only reach DllMain while the DLL is loaded, and only if thread calls are not disabled. - disableThreadCalls means DisableThreadLibraryCalls is called in PROCESS_ATTACH : no THREAD_ notifications at all. - exit while loaded sends PROCESS_DETACH (exit) and nothing after it is processed. exit while unloaded sends nothing, and also ends the list. dllMainCalls({ "thread start", "load", "thread start", "thread end", "free" }, false) == { "PROCESS_ATTACH", "THREAD_ATTACH", "THREAD_DETACH", "PROCESS_DETACH" } The first thread started before the DLL was loaded, so it never produces a notification.

title: Safe in DllMain?
body: Write bool safeInDllMain(const std::string& action) for a list of things a programmer might want to do in DllMain . Return true only for these, which are safe: "DisableThreadLibraryCalls" , "InitializeCriticalSection" , "TlsAlloc" , "set a variable" , "OutputDebugString" . Everything else, such as "LoadLibrary" , "CreateThread and wait" , "open a socket" or "CoInitialize" , returns false : when in doubt, do it later in an init function.

title: 2.05  Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
match: 2.05 Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
body: Memory allocated in one module and freed in another can crash, because each module may have its own copy of the C runtime and its own heap . The fix is a simple rule: whoever allocates, frees. This lesson shows why it breaks and the standard patterns that keep it safe. The crash A DLL function returns a string the caller should free: cpp-norun // in StoneMath.dll extern "C" STONEMATH_API char describeStack(int stones) { char text{ new char 64 }; snprintf(text, 64, "%d stones", stones); return text; } // in the program char s{ describeStack(12) }; std::cout << s << '\n'; delete s; // may crash, may corrupt memory, may seem fine Whether it works depends on how both modules were built. Why: one CRT per module, sometimes new , delete , malloc and free belong to the C runtime library (CRT). Each module chooses how it gets its CRT: Setting What the module gets --- --- /MD (Multi-threaded DLL, the default) The shared runtime DLLs ( ucrtbase.dll , vcruntime140.dll ). Modules using the same version share one heap /MT (Multi-threaded, static) Its own private copy of the CRT linked inside, with its own heap /MDd , /MTd The same, but debug versions, with a different heap layout again If the DLL is built with /MT , its new takes memory from the DLL's private heap, and the program's delete gives it back to the program's heap, which has never seen that block. If the DLL is Debug and the program is Release, the heaps disagree about the block's layout. Either way the heap is corrupted, and the crash can come much later. Even when both use /MD today, a future version of the DLL might be built with a different compiler or setting. You cannot rely on it. The rule Memory is freed by the module that allocated it. Three patterns follow from it. 1. The library frees what it allocates cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API char stonemath_describe(int stones); // caller must call stonemath_free extern "C" STONEMATH_API void stonemath_free(char text); // frees with the DLL's own delete 2. The caller provides the buffer The Win32 API's favourite: the caller owns the memory, the DLL only writes into it. cpp-norun // Returns the number of characters needed, not counting the terminating zero. // Writes at most capacity characters including the zero. extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_describe_into(int stones, char buffer, int capacity); // Asking twice: once for the size, once for the text int needed{ stonemath_describe_into(12, nullptr, 0) }; std::string text(static_cast<std::size_t (needed), '\0'); stonemath_describe_into(12, text.data(), needed + 1); The practice has you write a function with exactly this contract. 3. Objects with a create/destroy pair For anything bigger than a string, the DLL hands out an opaque handle and offers a function to release it (lesson 3.01 builds a whole API this way): cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API Xenon xenon_create(int stones); extern "C" STONEMATH_API void xenon_destroy(Xenon xenon); What about std::string and std::vector? Passing a std::string by value or reference across the boundary means one module may grow or free a buffer the other allocated. And the layout of std::string differs between Debug and Release, and has changed between compiler versions. That is lesson 2.06's topic. For now: inside a DLL, use whatever you like; at its C interface, use pointers, sizes and plain structs. Finding leaks across a boundary Because ownership is now explicit, you can track it. Keep a count of live objects in the DLL: increase it in every create function, decrease it in every destroy function, and report anything left over in stonemath_shutdown . The practice builds such a tracker. Common mistakes !warning Freeing a DLL's memory with your own free or delete Use the DLL's free function. Even if it works today, it will break when either side's build settings change. !warning Off-by-one in buffer sizes Document whether a size includes the terminating zero, and test the boundary: a buffer exactly one character too small. Knowledge check quiz ? A DLL built with /MT allocates with new. The program frees with delete. What is wrong? + The DLL has its own private heap, so the program frees memory its heap never allocated - Nothing; new and delete are always shared - delete is slower across a DLL boundary Each statically linked CRT has its own heap. ? Which interface follows the "whoever allocates, frees" rule? + A create function paired with a destroy function in the same DLL - A function returning new char that the caller deletes - A function returning std::string by value The DLL's destroy function frees with the same heap that allocated. ? In the "caller provides the buffer" pattern, why call the function first with a null buffer? + To find out how large a buffer is needed - To initialise the DLL - Because the first call always fails The caller then allocates exactly enough and calls again.

title: The caller provides the buffer
where: 2.05 Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
body: Write a function with the Win32-style buffer contract from the lesson: cpp extern "C" int describe_into(int stones, char buffer, int capacity); The text it produces is "<stones stones" , or "1 stone" for exactly one. - It returns the length of the full text, not counting the terminating zero, whatever the buffer size. - If buffer is not null and capacity is at least 1, it writes as much of the text as fits plus a terminating zero within capacity bytes. A buffer that is too small gets a cut-off but still zero-terminated text. - If buffer is null or capacity is 0 or less, it writes nothing. describe_into(12, nullptr, 0) == 9 // "12 stones" needs 9 characters char b 4 ; describe_into(12, b, 4) == 9 // b holds "12 " and a zero

title: Track who owns what
where: 2.05 Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
body: A DLL can catch leaks across its boundary by counting what it hands out. Write a class cpp class OwnershipTracker { public: int create(const std::string& kind); // returns a new id: 1, 2, 3... bool destroy(int id); // false if the id is not live (never made, or destroyed already) int live() const; // how many objects are live std::vector<std::string leakReport() const; // one line per live object, oldest first }; The leak report lines look like "leaked xenon 3" : the kind and the id. OwnershipTracker t; int a = t.create("xenon"); // 1 int b = t.create("text"); // 2 t.destroy(a); t.leakReport() == { "leaked text 2" }

title: 2.06  Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
match: 2.06 Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
body: Besides memory, two other things must not cross a stable DLL boundary - exceptions and C++ library types such as std::string . This lesson shows what goes wrong, the "exception barrier" that turns exceptions into error codes at the edge of a DLL, and the rare case where exporting C++ types is fine. Exceptions escaping a DLL Inside a DLL, use exceptions as you normally would. The problem is an exception that leaves an exported function: - A program written in C, C , Rust or Python has no idea what a C++ exception is. Its stack is unwound by machinery it never set up, and it usually crashes. - Two C++ modules built with different compilers, or different exception settings ( /EHsc versus /EHa ), may not agree on how exceptions are represented. - An exception object such as std::runtime_error contains a std::string allocated by one module's CRT and destroyed by the other's (lesson 2.05). An extern "C" function is promising C behaviour, and C has no exceptions. So the rule is: No exception crosses a DLL's C interface. Catch everything at the edge and turn it into an error code. The exception barrier Every exported function gets the same wrapper. Writing it once as a helper keeps it consistent: cpp-norun enum StonemathResult : int { STONEMATH_OK = 0, STONEMATH_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, STONEMATH_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 2, STONEMATH_FAILED = 3, STONEMATH_UNKNOWN_ERROR = 4, }; template <typename Fn int barrier(Fn&& body) noexcept { try { body(); return STONEMATH_OK; } catch (const std::invalid_argument&) { return STONEMATH_INVALID_ARGUMENT; } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { return STONEMATH_OUT_OF_MEMORY; } catch (const std::exception&) { return STONEMATH_FAILED; } catch (...) { return STONEMATH_UNKNOWN_ERROR; } } extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_load(const char path, int stonesOut) { return barrier( & { if (!path !stonesOut) throw std::invalid_argument("null argument"); stonesOut = loadStonesFromFile(path); // ordinary C++ inside, may throw }); } The order of the catch clauses matters: the most specific types first, std::exception after them, and catch (...) last for anything else. noexcept on the barrier documents, and enforces, that nothing gets out. Lesson 3.02 adds a way to fetch the error's message as well. C++ types in the interface What about a DLL that exports functions like this? cpp-norun STONEMATH_API std::string describeStack(const std::vector<int & weights); It compiles, and it works as long as the DLL and every program using it are built with: - the same compiler and the same major version of its standard library; - the same configuration: std::string and std::vector have a different layout in Debug ( _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL=2 ) than in Release; - the same CRT setting ( /MD everywhere), so that one heap is shared. MSVC even helps: if you link modules with different _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL values, the linker stops with error LNK2038: mismatch detected . But that only catches modules linked together, not a DLL loaded at run time. So there are two kinds of DLL: Internal DLL Public, stable DLL --- --- --- Built Together with the program, same solution, same settings Separately, perhaps years apart, perhaps by others Interface C++: classes, std::string , exceptions are acceptable C: plain types, handles, error codes Example Splitting your own game into engine.dll and game.exe built together A plugin API, a library you sell, anything other languages call Most games' internal DLLs, and the hot-reload DLL in lesson 5.03, are the first kind. Plugin interfaces are always the second. Passing text and lists through a C interface Instead of std::string , pass a pointer and a length (or a zero-terminated string); instead of std::vector<int , a pointer and a count: cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_total_weight(const int weights, int count, long long totalOut); Inside, wrap them in std::string_view and std::span and you are back in comfortable C++. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting catch (...) Code you call can throw types that do not derive from std::exception . Without the last clause they escape. !warning Mixing Debug and Release modules with C++ types in the interface The layout of standard library types differs. Keep internal C++ interfaces to modules built together. Knowledge check quiz ? Why must exceptions not leave an extern "C" function? + Callers written in other languages, or built differently, cannot handle C++ exceptions, and the exception object crosses heaps - Exceptions are slower in DLLs - extern "C" functions cannot contain try blocks Catch at the edge and return an error code. ? In an exception barrier, why does catch (const std::exception&) come after catch (const std::invalid_argument&)? + Catch clauses are tried in order, so the general one would otherwise catch everything first - It does not matter - Because invalid_argument is not an exception Specific types first, then the base class, then catch (...). ? When is exporting std::string from a DLL acceptable? + When the DLL and its users are always built together with the same compiler and settings - Never, it does not compile - Always, std::string is standard That is an internal DLL; a public one uses C types.

title: An exception barrier
where: 2.06 Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
body: Write the barrier every exported function wraps its body in: cpp enum Result : int { RESULT_OK = 0, RESULT_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, RESULT_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 2, RESULT_FAILED = 3, RESULT_UNKNOWN = 4 }; int barrier(const std::function<void() & body) noexcept; It runs body and returns: - RESULT_OK if it returns normally; - RESULT_INVALID_ARGUMENT for std::invalid_argument and std::out_of_range (both mean the caller passed something bad); - RESULT_OUT_OF_MEMORY for std::bad_alloc ; - RESULT_FAILED for any other std::exception ; - RESULT_UNKNOWN for anything else that is thrown, such as an int . Then use it in an exported function: cpp extern "C" int parse_stones(const char text, int out) noexcept; It stores std::stoi(text) in out . A null text or out is an invalid argument (throw std::invalid_argument inside the barrier). std::stoi itself throws std::invalid_argument for text that is not a number and std::out_of_range for a number too large. A negative number of stones is also invalid. out is only written on success.

title: A C interface for a C++ class
match: A C interface for a C++ class
body: You have a C++ class, StoneBag , that you want to put in a DLL so that programs in any language, built with any compiler, can use it. Write its C interface , following every rule of this milestone: - plain extern "C" functions with C types only; - an opaque handle, created and destroyed by the library (whoever allocates, frees); - no exception escapes: every function returns a result code; - text is returned through a caller-provided buffer; - the library counts live bags so leaks can be reported. The class (keep it as it is, it is the "C++ on the inside"): cpp class StoneBag { public: void add(const std::string& name, int weight); // throws std::invalid_argument for an empty name or weight <= 0 int count() const; int totalWeight() const; std::string heaviest() const; // throws std::logic_error if the bag is empty }; The C interface to write: cpp enum BagResult : int { BAG_OK = 0, BAG_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, BAG_EMPTY = 2, BAG_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 3, BAG_FAILED = 4 }; struct BagHandle; // opaque: callers only ever see pointers to it extern "C" int bag_create(BagHandle out); extern "C" int bag_destroy(BagHandle bag); // null is allowed and does nothing (BAG_OK) extern "C" int bag_add(BagHandle bag, const char name, int weight); extern "C" int bag_count(const BagHandle bag, int out); extern "C" int bag_total_weight(const BagHandle bag, int out); extern "C" int bag_heaviest(const BagHandle bag, char buffer, int capacity, int lengthOut); extern "C" int bag_live_count(); // how many bags exist now - Any null handle or null output pointer is BAG_INVALID_ARGUMENT . - bag_add maps std::invalid_argument from the class to BAG_INVALID_ARGUMENT . - bag_heaviest on an empty bag returns BAG_EMPTY . Otherwise it stores the name's length in lengthOut and copies the name into buffer like lesson 2.05's practice (cut off and zero-terminated if too small; nothing written if buffer is null or capacity is 0). lengthOut may not be null. - Output values are only written when the result is BAG_OK .

title: 3.01  Designing a Stable C Interface
body: A library that other programs depend on for years needs an interface that can grow without breaking them. The standard shape is a set of extern "C" functions around opaque handles , with a consistent naming scheme and clear ownership. This lesson designs one from scratch and lists the rules that keep it stable. What "stable" means A DLL interface has two kinds of compatibility: - Source compatibility : code written against version 1's header still compiles with version 2's. - Binary compatibility (the ABI ): a program already built against version 1 still works when you replace the DLL with version 2, without recompiling. Binary compatibility is the one DLLs are about, and it is much stricter. Changing a function's parameter from int to long long is fine for source code (it still compiles) and fatal for binaries (the old program passes 4 bytes; the new DLL reads 8). The opaque handle The core idea: the library's types are never visible to callers. They get a pointer to a type they cannot see inside. cpp-norun // xenon.h, the public header pragma once include <stdint.h ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { endif typedef struct xenon_world xenon_world; // opaque: declared, never defined here XENON_API int xenon_world_create(xenon_world out); XENON_API void xenon_world_destroy(xenon_world world); XENON_API int xenon_world_add_stone(xenon_world world, int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t weight); XENON_API int xenon_world_stone_count(const xenon_world world, int32_t out); XENON_API int xenon_world_tallest(const xenon_world world, int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t height); ifdef __cplusplus } endif Inside the DLL: cpp-norun // xenon.cpp struct xenon_world // the real definition, only here { std::unordered_map<Point, std::vector<int , PointHash stacks; int stoneCount{ 0 }; }; Because callers never see the definition, you can change it in every version: add members, reorder them, swap the unordered_map for a grid. Their compiled code only stores a pointer. Naming Exported names share one flat namespace in the process. Prefix everything with the library's name, and name functions <library _<type _<verb : - xenon_world_create , xenon_world_destroy - xenon_world_add_stone , xenon_world_stone_count Callers can guess names, and nothing collides with another library's create . Fixed-size types int is 32 bits on Windows today, but long is 32 bits on Windows and 64 bits on Linux. For anything that crosses the boundary, use the <stdint.h types whose size is part of their name: int32_t , uint64_t , uint8_t . Use size_t only when you mean "a size in this process". Avoid bool in C interfaces (its size has varied between compilers); use int32_t with 0 and 1. Results and outputs Every function that can fail returns a result code, and returns values through out-parameters . That keeps one shape everywhere: cpp-norun int32_t count{ 0 }; if (xenon_world_stone_count(world, &count) != XENON_OK) { / handle it / } Lesson 3.02 designs the result codes and adds error messages. The stability rules Once version 1 is published: You may You may not --- --- Add new functions Remove or rename a function Add new result codes (callers must treat unknown codes as failure) Change a function's parameters or return type Change anything behind an opaque handle Change the layout of a struct callers can see (lesson 3.03 shows the safe way to grow one) Add a new enum value at the end Change the meaning or number of an existing enum value Fix bugs Change documented behaviour callers rely on If you truly must break one of these, it is a new major version (lesson 3.05), often with a new DLL name ( xenon2.dll ) so both can be installed side by side. Common mistakes !warning Putting a struct definition in the public header "just for convenience" Callers' code now knows its size and layout, so it can never change. Keep it opaque, or version it (lesson 3.03). !warning Using long or bool in the interface Their sizes are not the same everywhere. Use int32_t , int64_t , and int32_t for true/false. Knowledge check quiz ? What is binary compatibility? + Programs already compiled against the old DLL keep working with the new one, without recompiling - The new header still compiles with old code - Both DLLs have the same file size It is the promise a DLL interface makes. ? Why can a library change everything behind an opaque handle? + Callers only hold a pointer and never see the type's size or members - Because handles are integers - Because the compiler checks the layout at run time Their compiled code does not depend on the definition. ? Which change breaks binary compatibility? + Changing a parameter from int32_t to int64_t - Adding a new function - Adding members to an opaque struct Old programs still pass 4 bytes where the new DLL reads 8.

title: An opaque counter library
body: Write a small C interface around a C++ class, with an opaque handle: cpp typedef struct tally tally; // opaque extern "C" int32_t tally_create(const char name, tally out); // name must not be null or empty extern "C" void tally_destroy(tally t); // null is allowed extern "C" int32_t tally_add(tally t, int32_t amount); // amount may be negative extern "C" int32_t tally_value(const tally t, int64_t out); extern "C" int32_t tally_name_length(const tally t, int32_t out); Result codes: 0 success, 1 invalid argument (a null pointer, or an empty name). Inside, keep the running total as a 64-bit number and the name as a std::string : those details are yours to change later because callers never see them. tally_add adds to the total; the total starts at 0.

title: Is this change compatible?
body: Write bool breaksBinaryCompatibility(const std::string& change) for a published C interface. These changes break programs already compiled against it: "remove a function" , "rename a function" , "change a parameter type" , "change a return type" , "reorder struct members" , "renumber an enum value" , "change a visible struct's size" . These do not, and return false : "add a function" , "add a result code" , "change an opaque type's members" , "add an enum value at the end" , "fix a bug" . Anything not in either list: return true (assume it breaks until you have checked).

title: 3.02  Error Reporting Across a C API
match: 3.02 Error Reporting Across a C API
body: A C interface reports failure with result codes , but a code alone rarely tells a developer what went wrong. This lesson designs a result enum that can grow, adds a thread-local last error message like GetLastError , and shows how callers should handle codes they have never seen. Result codes Every function returns an int32_t result. Zero means success, which makes checks cheap and readable: cpp-norun typedef enum xenon_result { XENON_OK = 0, XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, XENON_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 2, XENON_NOT_FOUND = 3, XENON_IO_ERROR = 4, XENON_UNSUPPORTED = 5, XENON_INTERNAL_ERROR = 99, } xenon_result; Rules for codes: - Give every value an explicit number and never change it. A program compiled against version 1 has the numbers baked in. - Only add at the end (or in gaps you reserved). - Callers must treat an unknown nonzero code as a failure. Version 3 might return XENON_RATE_LIMITED = 6 , which version 1's program has never heard of. A switch over the codes needs a default: that says "failed". The return type is int32_t , not xenon_result , because the size of a C enum is not guaranteed to be the same everywhere. Messages: a thread-local last error A code says what kind of failure. A message says what exactly : "file 'world.xenon' line 12: weight must be positive". Windows itself solves this with GetLastError ; the same pattern works for any library: cpp-norun // in the DLL namespace { thread_local std::string t_lastError; } static int32_t fail(int32_t code, std::string message) { t_lastError = std::move(message); return code; } extern "C" XENON_API int32_t xenon_world_load(xenon_world world, const char path) { if (!world !path) return fail(XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT, "world and path must not be null"); ... } // returns the length; copies into buffer with the usual caller-buffer contract (lesson 2.05) extern "C" XENON_API int32_t xenon_last_error(char buffer, int32_t capacity); Why thread-local ? Two threads can call the library at once. With one global string, thread A's message could be overwritten by thread B's before A reads it. thread_local gives each thread its own. Should success clear the message? Windows does not (a successful call may leave the previous error), and callers should only read the message right after a failure. Either way, document it. A message for every code It also helps to have a fixed description for each code, which never changes and needs no buffer: cpp-norun extern "C" XENON_API const char xenon_result_name(int32_t code); // "XENON_OK", "XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT", ... and "XENON_UNKNOWN_RESULT" for anything else Returning a const char to a string literal is safe across the boundary: it lives in the DLL's read-only data and is never freed. Callers must not keep it after unloading the DLL. Checking results without drowning in ifs In C++ callers, a small helper turns codes back into exceptions on their side of the boundary, where both sides of the throw are in the same module: cpp-norun inline void check(int32_t result) { if (result == XENON_OK) return; std::string message(static_cast<std::size_t (xenon_last_error(nullptr, 0)), '\0'); xenon_last_error(message.data(), static_cast<int32_t (message.size()) + 1); throw std::runtime_error(std::string(xenon_result_name(result)) + ": " + message); } check(xenon_world_load(world, "world.xenon")); Lesson 3.06 builds a full C++ wrapper this way. Common mistakes !warning A switch with no default New versions add codes. Without a default, an unknown failure is silently treated as... whatever the code after the switch does. !warning A global last-error string Threads overwrite each other's messages. Use thread_local . !warning Returning a pointer to a std::string's buffer It dangles as soon as the string changes. Return string literals, or copy into a caller buffer. Knowledge check quiz ? Version 3 of a DLL returns code 6, which version 1's program does not know. What should the program do? + Treat it as a failure, because every nonzero code means failure - Treat it as success - Crash Unknown nonzero codes must count as failures; that is what lets the set of codes grow. ? Why is the last error message stored thread-locally? + So threads calling the library at the same time cannot overwrite each other's message - To save memory - Because global variables cannot hold strings in a DLL Each thread reads the message of its own last failure. ? Why does the function return int32_t rather than the enum type? + The size of a C enum is not guaranteed to be the same for every compiler - Enums cannot be returned from DLLs - int32_t is faster A fixed-size integer keeps the ABI exact.

title: A last-error message per thread
where: 3.02 Error Reporting Across a C API
body: Write the error-reporting half of a C library: cpp extern "C" const char lib_result_name(int32_t code); extern "C" int32_t lib_last_error(char buffer, int32_t capacity); int32_t lib_fail(int32_t code, const std::string& message); // used inside the library extern "C" int32_t lib_divide(int32_t a, int32_t b, int32_t out); // an example function that uses it - lib_result_name returns "LIB_OK" for 0, "LIB_INVALID_ARGUMENT" for 1, "LIB_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO" for 2, and "LIB_UNKNOWN_RESULT" for anything else. These are string literals, safe to return. - lib_fail stores message as the current thread's last error and returns code . - lib_last_error copies the current thread's last error into a caller buffer with the contract from lesson 2.05: returns the message length, writes a cut-off zero-terminated copy if the buffer is too small, writes nothing for a null buffer or capacity below 1. Before any failure on a thread, the message is empty. - lib_divide stores a / b in out . A null out fails with code 1 and the message "out must not be null" ; b == 0 fails with code 2 and "cannot divide <a by zero" . Success does not clear the last error.

title: 3.03  Versioned Structs and Function Tables
body: Sometimes callers need to see a struct, such as an options block. Windows' trick is to start every such struct with its own size , so the library can tell which version the caller was built with. The same idea, applied to a struct full of function pointers, gives a function table that can grow across versions. The problem with visible structs A creation function with many options is clumsy with a long parameter list. A struct is nicer: cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_world_options { int32_t width; int32_t height; int32_t gravity; } xenon_world_options; XENON_API int32_t xenon_world_create_ex(const xenon_world_options options, xenon_world out); Then version 2 needs a seed . Add it to the struct, and a program compiled against version 1 passes a 12-byte struct where version 2 reads 16. The seed comes from whatever memory follows: garbage. Size first The Win32 API's answer, used by hundreds of its structs ( cbSize in WNDCLASSEXW , dwSize in many others): the first member is the size of the struct, filled in by the caller . cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_world_options { uint32_t size; // the caller sets this to sizeof(xenon_world_options) int32_t width; // version 1 int32_t height; // version 1 int32_t gravity; // version 1 uint32_t seed; // version 2: added at the END } xenon_world_options; The caller always writes: cpp-norun xenon_world_options options{}; options.size = sizeof(options); options.width = 64; A program compiled against version 1 sets size to 16; one compiled against version 2 sets 20. The library reads only the fields that fit: cpp-norun int32_t xenon_world_create_ex(const xenon_world_options options, xenon_world out) { if (!options options- size < offsetof(xenon_world_options, seed)) return fail(XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT, "options too small"); WorldSettings s; s.width = options- width; s.height = options- height; s.gravity = options- gravity; // a field is present if the struct reaches past its end s.seed = options- size = offsetof(xenon_world_options, seed) + sizeof(options- seed) ? options- seed : 12345u; ... } offsetof(T, member) is the byte position of a member, from <stddef.h . A member is present when size = offsetof(T, member) + sizeof(member) . The rules that make this work: - New members only ever go at the end . - Never remove, reorder or resize a member. - Every new member has a sensible default for callers who did not send it. - A size bigger than the library knows (a newer program with an older DLL) is fine: read what you know, ignore the rest. Or reject it if you cannot honour fields you do not understand; decide and document. Function tables The same trick works for a whole interface. Instead of exporting thirty functions, export one that returns a table of function pointers: cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_api { uint32_t size; // of this table uint32_t version; // e.g. 2 int32_t ( world_create)(xenon_world out); void ( world_destroy)(xenon_world world); int32_t ( world_add_stone)(xenon_world , int32_t, int32_t, int32_t); // version 2: int32_t ( world_save)(const xenon_world , const char path); } xenon_api; XENON_API const xenon_api xenon_get_api(uint32_t wantedVersion); A program asks for the version it was built for. The library returns its table if it is at least that new, or NULL if it is too old. The program checks size before touching later members. This is how Vulkan, OpenXR and many game engines expose their APIs, and it suits plugins (milestone 5): one GetProcAddress gets everything. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to set size A zero size makes the library reject or misread the struct. Many APIs return an error for that; yours should too. !warning Inserting a new member in the middle Every member after it moves, so old programs' values land in the wrong fields. Always append. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does a versioned struct start with its size? + So the library can tell which members the caller's version of the struct contains - To align it in memory - Because C requires it Old callers send smaller sizes; the library only reads what is there. ? A struct member seed sits at offset 16 and is 4 bytes. The caller's size is 16. Is seed present? + No; it would need a size of at least 20 - Yes - Only if seed is nonzero Present means size = offset + sizeof(member). ? What does a function table export instead of many functions? + One function returning a versioned struct of function pointers - One DLL per function - A .def file The table can grow like any versioned struct.

title: Read a versioned options struct
body: A library's options struct has grown over three versions. Members were only ever added at the end: cpp struct WorldOptions { uint32_t size; // set by the caller to sizeof the struct it was compiled with int32_t width; // version 1 int32_t height; // version 1 int32_t gravity; // version 2 uint32_t seed; // version 3 }; Write cpp struct Settings { int32_t width; int32_t height; int32_t gravity; uint32_t seed; }; int32_t readOptions(const WorldOptions options, Settings out); - A member is present when options- size = offsetof(WorldOptions, member) + sizeof(member) . - width and height are required: a null options , a null out , or a size too small for height is an error, code 1 , and out is not written. - Missing later members get defaults: gravity 10, seed 12345. - A size larger than sizeof(WorldOptions) comes from a newer program: read what you know and ignore the rest. - Return 0 on success. Then write uint32_t versionOfSize(uint32_t size) : which version of the struct a size belongs to (1, 2 or 3; 3 for anything at least the version-3 size; 0 if smaller than version 1). Because each member's position is fixed, a version-1 caller's struct is just the first bytes of the full struct. The tests build smaller structs by setting size to what a version-1 or version-2 caller would send.

title: A versioned function table
body: A library exposes its interface as one function that returns a table of function pointers: cpp struct StoneApi { uint32_t size; uint32_t version; int32_t ( add)(int32_t, int32_t); // version 1 int32_t ( multiply)(int32_t, int32_t); // version 1 int32_t ( power)(int32_t, int32_t); // version 2 }; const StoneApi getStoneApi(uint32_t wantedVersion); Write getStoneApi for a library at version 2 : it returns a pointer to one static, fully filled table (with size set to sizeof(StoneApi) and version 2) when wantedVersion is 1 or 2, and nullptr for version 0 or anything above 2. power(b, e) raises b to the whole power e ; for e < 0 it returns 0. Then write the caller's side, which must not touch members its table lacks: cpp int32_t powerOrFallback(const StoneApi api, int32_t base, int32_t exponent); It uses api- power when the table is version 2 or newer and its size reaches past power ; otherwise it multiplies base by itself exponent times using api- multiply , starting from 1. A null api returns 0.

title: 3.04  COM-Style Interfaces with vtables
body: A C interface can still give callers objects with methods , if the object's layout is just a pointer to a table of functions. On Windows, an abstract C++ class with only virtual functions has exactly that layout, which is how COM, DirectX and many plugin systems work. This lesson builds a COM-style interface with reference counting and QueryInterface . An object is a pointer to a table Lesson 3.03's function table is close to an object already. Put the table pointer inside the object, and pass the object to each function: c typedef struct IStone IStone; typedef struct IStoneVtbl { uint32_t ( AddRef)(IStone self); uint32_t ( Release)(IStone self); int32_t ( Weight)(IStone self); } IStoneVtbl; struct IStone { const IStoneVtbl vtbl; }; // a C caller: int32_t w = stone- vtbl- Weight(stone); Now look at how MSVC lays out a C++ class that has only pure virtual functions and no data: cpp-norun struct IStone { virtual uint32_t AddRef() = 0; virtual uint32_t Release() = 0; virtual int32_t Weight() = 0; }; An IStone object is one hidden pointer, the vptr , to a table of three function pointers, in the order the functions are declared. A call stone- Weight() loads the vptr, loads entry 2, and calls it with the object pointer as the hidden first argument ( this ). That is the same layout as the C version. On Windows this layout is fixed by the platform's ABI, which is why a C++ interface like this can safely cross a DLL boundary between different compilers, and even be called from C, C , Rust or Python. What keeps it safe: - Only pure virtual functions , no data members, no constructors, and no virtual destructor : destructors' place in the vtable differs between compilers. The object deletes itself in Release . - Plain C types in every method's signature. - Never change an interface once published. Add a new interface instead ( IStone2 ), which is what QueryInterface is for. - Everything uses the __stdcall convention on 32-bit Windows (COM's STDMETHODCALLTYPE ); on x64 that does nothing. Reference counting Who deletes an object that several parts of a program hold? The object itself, when the last holder lets go. Each holder calls AddRef when it takes a reference and Release when it is done; Release deletes the object when the count reaches zero. cpp-norun class Basalt final : public IStone { public: uint32_t AddRef() override { return ++m_refs; } uint32_t Release() override { const uint32_t left{ --m_refs }; if (left == 0) delete this; // deleted by the module that created it return left; } int32_t Weight() override { return 7; } private: std::atomic<uint32_t m_refs{ 1 }; // the creator holds the first reference }; delete this inside the DLL means memory is freed by the module that allocated it (lesson 2.05) no matter who calls Release . The count is atomic so threads can share objects. QueryInterface: asking for more A later version adds a method. Changing IStone would break every compiled caller, so you define a new interface , and let callers ask an object whether it supports it: cpp-norun struct IStone2 : IStone { virtual int32_t Hardness() = 0; // appended after IStone's methods }; // Every interface identifies itself with a unique id (COM uses 128-bit GUIDs): constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone = 0x5354'0001; constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone2 = 0x5354'0002; // The base interface gains one more method, first in the table in real COM: virtual int32_t QueryInterface(uint32_t iid, void out) = 0; QueryInterface(IID_IStone2, &p) returns success and an AddRef -ed pointer if the object implements it, or "not supported" and nullptr if it does not. A caller built for version 2 asks for IStone2 ; if the DLL is older, it falls back to IStone . Old callers never ask, so nothing changes for them. Real COM's base interface is IUnknown with exactly three methods: QueryInterface , AddRef , Release . DirectX, the Windows shell and many audio APIs are built on it. You can use the pattern without any of COM's registration machinery. Smart pointers Calling AddRef and Release by hand is as error-prone as new and delete . Microsoft's Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr (and winrt::com_ptr ) call them automatically, like a std::shared_ptr whose count lives in the object. Lesson 3.06 writes a small one. Common mistakes !warning A virtual destructor in a cross-compiler interface Its vtable slot (or slots) are compiler-specific. Delete through Release instead. !warning QueryInterface that forgets to AddRef The caller will Release what it was given, which then frees the object too early. !warning Changing a published interface Add a new one. That is the whole point of QueryInterface. Knowledge check quiz ? Why can an abstract class with only pure virtual functions cross a DLL boundary between compilers on Windows? + Its layout is a single vptr to a table of function pointers in declaration order, fixed by the platform ABI - Because virtual functions are slower - Because the compiler checks it at run time That is the same layout as a C struct of function pointers. ? Who deletes a reference-counted object? + The object itself, in Release, when the count reaches zero - Whoever created it, always - The last caller, with delete delete this runs inside the module that allocated it. ? A caller asks QueryInterface for an interface the object does not implement. What should it get? + A "not supported" result and a null pointer - A pointer to the base interface - A crash The caller can then fall back to an older interface.

title: A COM-style stone
body: Implement a COM-style object with reference counting and QueryInterface : cpp constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone = 1; constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone2 = 2; constexpr int32_t OK = 0, NOT_SUPPORTED = 1, INVALID_ARGUMENT = 2; struct IStone { virtual int32_t QueryInterface(uint32_t iid, void out) = 0; virtual uint32_t AddRef() = 0; virtual uint32_t Release() = 0; virtual int32_t Weight() = 0; }; struct IStone2 : IStone { virtual int32_t Hardness() = 0; }; int32_t CreateStone(int32_t weight, int32_t hardness, IStone out); int liveStones(); - CreateStone makes a stone that implements both interfaces and hands back an IStone holding one reference. If hardness is 0 or less, make a plainer stone that implements only IStone (asking it for IStone2 must fail). A null out is INVALID_ARGUMENT . - AddRef and Release return the new count. Release deletes the object at 0. - QueryInterface(iid, &p) : for a supported interface, set p to the object as that interface, AddRef it , return OK . Otherwise set p to nullptr and return NOT_SUPPORTED . A null out is INVALID_ARGUMENT . - liveStones() returns how many stone objects exist right now (increase in the constructor, decrease in the destructor), so tests can check nothing leaks.

title: 3.05  Versioning and Compatibility
body: A version number is a promise about compatibility. Semantic versioning turns that promise into rules: major for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. This lesson applies it to DLLs, shows how a program checks the version it got at run time, and covers side-by-side installs for breaking changes. Semantic versioning A version is three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , such as 2.4.1 : Part Increase it when Example --- --- --- MAJOR You break compatibility: remove or change a function, change a visible struct 2.4.1 to 3.0.0 MINOR You add something without breaking anything: new functions, new codes, new struct fields at the end 2.4.1 to 2.5.0 PATCH You fix bugs without changing the interface 2.4.1 to 2.4.2 Increasing one part resets the parts after it to 0. A version can carry a pre-release label after a hyphen, 3.0.0-beta.2 , which sorts before 3.0.0 . For a DLL, this tells users exactly what is safe: A program built against version X.Y.Z works with any DLL version X.y.z where y.z ≥ Y.Z : the same major version, and at least as new. A newer minor version only adds things the old program does not use. An older minor version might lack a function the program needs. A different major version may have changed anything. Comparing versions Versions compare part by part, as numbers , not as text. As strings, "2.10.0" < "2.9.0" because '1' < '9' ; as versions, 2.10.0 is newer. The practice has you write this comparison properly. Checking at run time Load-time linking catches a missing function (the program will not start), but not a function whose behaviour changed in a breaking way. So well-behaved libraries let callers check: cpp-norun define XENON_VERSION_MAJOR 2 define XENON_VERSION_MINOR 4 define XENON_VERSION_PATCH 1 // The version of the DLL actually loaded, packed as major << 22 minor << 12 patch XENON_API uint32_t xenon_version(void); The header's macros say which version the program was compiled against; the function says which DLL it is running with: cpp-norun const uint32_t running{ xenon_version() }; const uint32_t major{ running 22 }, minor{ (running 12) & 0x3FF }; if (major != XENON_VERSION_MAJOR minor < XENON_VERSION_MINOR) { std::cerr << "This program needs xenon " << XENON_VERSION_MAJOR << '.' << XENON_VERSION_MINOR << " or newer\n"; return 1; } Packing the three parts into one integer, as Vulkan does, makes the version easy to pass around and compare: with 10 bits for minor and 12 for patch, a larger packed number is always a newer version. When you must break things Sometimes a major version is unavoidable. Then change the DLL's file name along with it: xenon2.dll . Programs built for version 1 keep loading xenon.dll ; programs built for version 2 load xenon2.dll ; both can be installed together. That is how the Visual C++ runtime does it ( msvcp140.dll versus the older msvcp120.dll ) and how Windows' own system DLLs stay compatible for decades. The alternative, replacing xenon.dll with an incompatible one, is what was once called DLL Hell : installing one program broke another that used the same file name with different expectations. The file version resource Windows also stores a version number inside the DLL file as a resource, shown in Explorer's Properties, Details tab. Lesson 4.04 adds one to your build. It is for people and installers; your code should check versions through its own function as above. Common mistakes !warning Comparing version strings as text "2.10" sorts before "2.9". Split them and compare numbers. !warning Shipping a breaking change as a minor version Every program built for the previous minor version may now fail. If you broke something, it is a major version. Knowledge check quiz ? A DLL adds two new functions and changes nothing else. Its version was 1.6.3. What is the next version? + 1.7.0 - 2.0.0 - 1.6.4 Additions without breaks are a minor increase, which resets the patch number. ? A program was built against version 2.3.0. Which DLL version works? + 2.5.1 - 2.2.9 - 3.0.0 Same major, and at least as new as 2.3.0. ? How do you ship a breaking version without breaking programs that use the old one? + Give the new major version a different DLL file name so both can be installed - Overwrite the old DLL - Increase the patch number Old programs keep loading the old file.

title: Semantic versions
body: Write the version tools a library and its callers need: cpp struct Version { int major{ 0 }; int minor{ 0 }; int patch{ 0 }; std::string pre; }; bool parseVersion(const std::string& text, Version& out); int compareVersions(const Version& a, const Version& b); // -1, 0 or 1 bool compatible(const Version& builtAgainst, const Version& running); std::string nextVersion(const Version& current, const std::string& change); - parseVersion accepts MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with non-negative whole numbers and no leading zeros (except 0 itself), optionally followed by - and a non-empty label: 2.4.1 , 3.0.0-beta.2 . Anything else returns false . - compareVersions compares major, minor, patch as numbers . With those equal, a version with a pre-release label is older than one without; two labels compare as plain strings. - compatible : the running version has the same major as the one the program was built against and is not older than it. - nextVersion(current, change) for change "break" , "add" or "fix" returns the next version as text, with no label: 1.6.3 + "add" is "1.7.0" . compareVersions(2.10.0, 2.9.0) == 1 compatible(2.3.0, 2.5.1) == true compatible(2.3.0, 3.0.0) == false

title: Pack a version into 32 bits
body: Like Vulkan, pack a version into one number: major << 22 minor << 12 patch , with 10 bits for minor and 12 for patch. Write cpp uint32_t packVersion(uint32_t major, uint32_t minor, uint32_t patch); void unpackVersion(uint32_t packed, uint32_t& major, uint32_t& minor, uint32_t& patch); Values that do not fit are cut to their field width: minor & 0x3FF , patch & 0xFFF .

title: 3.06  Wrapping a C API in Modern C++
match: 3.06 Wrapping a C API in Modern C++
body: A stable C interface is pleasant for the DLL and other languages, but tedious to use from C++. The answer is a thin header-only C++ wrapper on the caller's side - RAII classes that create and destroy handles, exceptions instead of result codes, std::string instead of buffers - while the DLL boundary stays pure C. Both worlds You now have a C interface that is safe across compilers and languages. Using it directly from C++ looks like this: cpp-norun xenon_world world{ nullptr }; if (xenon_world_create(&world) != XENON_OK) { / ... / } if (xenon_world_add_stone(world, 3, 4, 7) != XENON_OK) { xenon_world_destroy(world); / ... / } int32_t count{ 0 }; if (xenon_world_stone_count(world, &count) != XENON_OK) { xenon_world_destroy(world); / ... / } xenon_world_destroy(world); Every early return has to remember the destroy call. C++ programmers would rather write: cpp-norun xenon::World world; world.addStone(3, 4, 7); std::cout << world.stoneCount() << '\n'; A header-only wrapper Put a C++ wrapper in a second header, xenon.hpp , that includes xenon.h . Because it is header-only , its code compiles into the caller's module, with the caller's compiler and settings. Nothing C++ crosses the boundary: the wrapper only calls the C functions. cpp-norun // xenon.hpp pragma once include "xenon.h" include <stdexcept include <string include <utility namespace xenon { class Error : public std::runtime_error { public: Error(int32_t code, const std::string& what) : std::runtime_error(what), m_code{ code } {} int32_t code() const noexcept { return m_code; } private: int32_t m_code; }; inline void check(int32_t result) { if (result == XENON_OK) return; std::string message(static_cast<std::size_t (xenon_last_error(nullptr, 0)), '\0'); xenon_last_error(message.data(), static_cast<int32_t (message.size()) + 1); throw Error(result, std::string(xenon_result_name(result)) + ": " + message); } class World { public: World() { check(xenon_world_create(&m_handle)); } ~World() { xenon_world_destroy(m_handle); } World(World&& other) noexcept : m_handle{ std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr) } {} World& operator=(World&& other) noexcept { if (this != &other) { xenon_world_destroy(m_handle); m_handle = std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr); } return this; } World(const World&) = delete; World& operator=(const World&) = delete; void addStone(int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t weight) { check(xenon_world_add_stone(m_handle, x, y, weight)); } int32_t stoneCount() const { int32_t n{ 0 }; check(xenon_world_stone_count(m_handle, &n)); return n; } xenon_world get() const noexcept { return m_handle; } // for calling C functions the wrapper lacks private: xenon_world m_handle{ nullptr }; }; } The pieces: - RAII : the constructor creates, the destructor destroys. No path can forget. - Move-only : copying would mean two objects destroying the same handle. A move transfers the handle and leaves the source empty, so its destructor does nothing ( xenon_world_destroy(nullptr) must be allowed, which lesson 2.05's project required). - Exceptions on the caller's side : check turns a result code into an exception thrown and caught entirely in the caller's module, which is perfectly safe. - get() keeps the escape hatch open. A reference-counted handle For COM-style objects (lesson 3.04), the wrapper is a smart pointer that calls AddRef and Release : cpp-norun template <typename T class RefPtr { public: RefPtr() = default; explicit RefPtr(T adopt) noexcept : m_p{ adopt } {} // takes over an existing reference RefPtr(const RefPtr& o) noexcept : m_p{ o.m_p } { if (m_p) m_p- AddRef(); } RefPtr(RefPtr&& o) noexcept : m_p{ std::exchange(o.m_p, nullptr) } {} ~RefPtr() { if (m_p) m_p- Release(); } RefPtr& operator=(RefPtr o) noexcept { std::swap(m_p, o.m_p); return this; } T operator- () const noexcept { return m_p; } T get() const noexcept { return m_p; } private: T m_p{ nullptr }; }; Copying adds a reference, destroying releases one. The practice asks you to write the move-only kind for a C handle. Common mistakes !warning Putting the wrapper's code in the DLL Then C++ types cross the boundary again. Keep the wrapper header-only, compiled by the caller. !warning A copyable wrapper around a handle Two copies, two destroy calls, one crash. Delete the copy operations or count references. Knowledge check quiz ? Why is the C++ wrapper header-only? + Its code compiles into the caller's module, so only C crosses the DLL boundary - Headers are faster - DLLs cannot contain C++ code The wrapper uses the caller's compiler and settings. ? Why is the World wrapper move-only? + A copy would destroy the same handle twice - Moving is faster than copying - Because handles are integers Ownership of a handle must belong to exactly one object. ? Is it safe for the wrapper's check function to throw an exception? + Yes; it is thrown and caught in the caller's module, never across the DLL boundary - No; exceptions must never be used with DLLs - Only in Release builds The rule is about exceptions leaving the DLL, not about the caller's own code.

title: A move-only handle wrapper
where: 3.06 Wrapping a C API in Modern C++
body: Here is a C interface (already written, in the starter) that counts how many handles exist: cpp typedef struct counter counter; extern "C" int32_t counter_create(counter out); extern "C" void counter_destroy(counter c); // null is fine extern "C" int32_t counter_add(counter c, int32_t n); extern "C" int32_t counter_value(const counter c, int32_t out); int liveCounters(); Write a C++ wrapper class Counter on top of it: - The constructor creates a handle; if counter_create fails, it throws std::runtime_error . - The destructor destroys the handle. - It is move-only : copying is deleted; moving transfers the handle and leaves the moved-from object empty ( get() returns nullptr ), so it destroys nothing. - Move assignment destroys the handle it held before taking the new one, and is safe for self-assignment. - void add(int32_t n) and int32_t value() const call the C functions and throw std::runtime_error on a nonzero result (including use of an empty, moved-from object). - counter get() const noexcept . The tests use liveCounters() to check every handle is destroyed exactly once.

title: A library that can grow
body: Design and write version 2.1.0 of a small library, quarry , so that programs built against version 1.x of its interface and programs built against 2.x both work with it. Everything you need is in this milestone. The public interface (already declared in the starter) has: cpp // result codes: never renumbered enum : int32_t { QUARRY_OK = 0, QUARRY_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, QUARRY_NOT_FOUND = 2, QUARRY_UNSUPPORTED = 3 }; // a versioned options struct: version 1 had size, capacity; version 2 added depth at the end struct quarry_options { uint32_t size; int32_t capacity; int32_t depth; }; typedef struct quarry quarry; // opaque // a versioned function table struct quarry_api { uint32_t size; uint32_t version; // 1 or 2 int32_t ( create)(const quarry_options options, quarry out); // v1 void ( destroy)(quarry q); // v1 int32_t ( dig)(quarry q, const char stone); // v1 int32_t ( count)(const quarry q, const char stone, int32_t out); // v1 int32_t ( depth)(const quarry q, int32_t out); // v2 }; extern "C" uint32_t quarry_version(); // packed like lesson 3.05 extern "C" const quarry_api quarry_get_api(uint32_t major); // 1 or 2, else null extern "C" int32_t quarry_last_error(char buffer, int32_t capacity); // per thread, caller buffer What the functions do: - create : needs options and out ; options- size must cover capacity , and capacity must be at least 1, else QUARRY_INVALID_ARGUMENT . depth is read only if the caller's struct has it; the default is 3. A depth below 1 is invalid too. - dig(q, stone) records one stone of that kind (a non-empty name). It fails with QUARRY_UNSUPPORTED and the message "quarry is full" when the total number of stones would go above capacity . - count gives how many stones of that kind were dug; a kind never dug is QUARRY_NOT_FOUND . - depth (version 2 only) gives the depth the quarry was created with. - Every failure sets the thread's last-error message; use "<name must not be null" for null pointers (name being the parameter's name), and pick clear messages for the rest. Tests check the messages for null q in dig ( "q must not be null" ) and the full quarry. - quarry_version() is 2.1.0 packed as major << 22 minor << 12 patch . - quarry_get_api(1) must return a table a version-1 program can use safely: version 1 and a size that ends before depth . quarry_get_api(2) returns the full table with version 2.

title: 4.01  The DLL Search Order
body: When a program asks for a DLL by name rather than by full path, Windows tries a fixed list of places. Knowing that list explains why the wrong copy of a DLL sometimes loads, why "it works on my machine", and why putting your DLLs next to your .exe is the reliable choice. A name, not a path Most DLLs are requested by name only: the import table of your .exe says StoneMath.dll , and LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") gives no folder either. Windows then has to decide which file that means. Before any folder is searched Two checks come first: 1. Already loaded? If a module with that name is already in the process, it is reused. This is why loading StoneMath.dll from two places never gives you two copies: the second request finds the first. 2. Known DLLs. Windows keeps a list of core system DLLs ( kernel32.dll , user32.dll , ole32.dll and others, listed in the registry under KnownDLLs ). For those it always uses the copy in System32 , whatever folders come later. You cannot override kernel32.dll by putting a file next to your program. (There are also API sets , the api-ms-win-... names from lesson 1.06, which are redirected to real system DLLs without any search.) The standard search order If neither check settles it, a desktop application searches these places in order, and loads the first file with that name it finds: 1. The folder the application's .exe is in. 2. The system folder , C:\Windows\System32 . 3. The 16-bit system folder, C:\Windows\System . 4. The Windows folder , C:\Windows . 5. The current directory (the program's working directory). 6. Every folder on the PATH environment variable, in order. This is the order with safe DLL search mode , which has been on by default for many years. Without it, the current directory was searched second, which is why it was moved down: an attacker who could put a file in your working directory (a downloaded folder, a network share) could get it loaded before the system's copy. Lesson 4.02 goes further. What this means in practice - Put your DLLs next to your .exe . The application folder is searched first, so your copy wins, and the program works no matter what the user's PATH or working directory is. - Never rely on the current directory. It changes with shortcuts, command lines and file dialogs. - Never rely on PATH for your own DLLs. It is the last place searched and differs on every machine. Something earlier on PATH with the same name wins, which is the classic "works on my machine" story. - Avoid generic names. utils.dll or zlib.dll may already be loaded into the process by some other component, and Windows will happily give you that one instead (check 1 above). Seeing the search happen Process Monitor (lesson 1.06) shows every attempt. A program in C:\Games\Xenon asking for missing.dll produces a trail like: varies C:\Games\Xenon\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Windows\System32\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Windows\System\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Windows\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Users\you\Desktop\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND (the current directory) C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND (PATH...) A dependency's dependencies When StoneMath.dll itself imports zlib.dll , the same search runs, still based on the application's folder, not the folder StoneMath.dll came from. So if you load a DLL from a subfolder by full path, its own dependencies are not found in that subfolder unless you say so. Lesson 4.02 shows the flags that fix this, and lesson 5.01 uses them for plugins in their own folders. Common mistakes !warning Testing only on the development machine Your PATH contains Visual Studio, SDKs and tools with DLLs in them. A clean machine has none of that. Test there before shipping. !warning Assuming a DLL from a subfolder finds its friends in that subfolder Its dependencies are searched for from the application's folder. Use full paths and the search flags from lesson 4.02. Knowledge check quiz ? Where does Windows look first for a DLL requested by name (after checking what is already loaded and the known DLLs)? + The folder of the application's .exe - The current directory - The PATH That is why shipping DLLs next to the .exe is reliable. ? Why was the current directory moved later in the search order? + A file planted in the working directory could otherwise be loaded before the real system DLL - To make loading faster - Because the current directory is often empty That is safe DLL search mode. ? Can you replace kernel32.dll by putting your own copy next to your program? + No; it is a known DLL and always loaded from System32 - Yes, the application folder is searched first - Only for 32-bit programs Known DLLs bypass the folder search entirely.

title: Which file gets loaded?
body: Simulate the standard DLL search order for a request by name. Write cpp struct Machine { std::string appDir; // e.g. "C:\\Games\\Xenon" std::string currentDir; std::vector<std::string pathDirs; // PATH, in order std::set<std::string files; // every file that exists, as full paths std::set<std::string knownDlls; // names of known DLLs std::set<std::string alreadyLoaded; // full paths of modules already in the process }; std::string findDll(const Machine& m, const std::string& name); Return the full path that would be loaded, or an empty string if none is found. Folders are joined to the name with one backslash: appDir + "\\" + name . The order: 1. Already loaded : if any full path in alreadyLoaded ends with "\\" + name , return that path. 2. Known DLLs : if name is in knownDlls , return "C:\\Windows\\System32\\" + name (whether or not it is in files ). 3. Then the first folder, in this order, where the file exists: appDir , C:\Windows\System32 , C:\Windows\System , C:\Windows , currentDir , then each folder of pathDirs . Upper and lower case do matter in this simulation: compare names exactly.

title: 4.02  Loading Only the Files You Mean
match: 4.02 Loading Only the Files You Mean
body: Loading a DLL by bare name leaves the choice of file to the search order, which an attacker or an accident can influence. This lesson shows how to load exactly the file you intend - full paths, SetDefaultDllDirectories , AddDllDirectory and the LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_ flags - and how to check a plugin folder before loading anything from it. The risk If a program loads renderer.dll by name and that name is not found in the application folder, Windows keeps searching, eventually in the current directory and on PATH. Anyone who can put a file called renderer.dll in one of those places gets their code run inside your program. This is called DLL planting or DLL search-order hijacking , and it has been the cause of many real security problems. Accidents follow the same path: an old copy of a DLL in some folder on PATH gets loaded instead of yours. The defence is the same for both: never let Windows guess . 1. Use full paths for run-time loading Build the path from a folder you trust, normally the application's own: cpp-norun include <windows.h include <filesystem std::filesystem::path appFolder() { wchar_t buffer MAX_PATH {}; const DWORD length{ GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, buffer, MAX_PATH) }; // full path of our own .exe return std::filesystem::path(std::wstring(buffer, length)).parent_path(); } HMODULE renderer{ LoadLibraryW((appFolder() / L"renderer.dll").c_str()) }; GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, ...) returns the path of the .exe . With a full path, LoadLibraryW loads exactly that file (or fails). 2. Restrict the search for everything else Even with full paths for your own DLLs, those DLLs import others by name. Call this once, first thing in main : cpp-norun SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS); From then on, every name-only load in the process searches only: - the application folder ( LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR ), - System32 ( LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 ), - folders you add yourself with AddDllDirectory ( LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS ). The current directory and PATH are not searched any more. For a new program there is no reason not to do this. 3. LoadLibraryExW with search flags LoadLibraryExW takes flags that control the search for one call: cpp-norun HMODULE m{ LoadLibraryExW(path, nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) }; Flag Searches --- --- LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR The .exe 's folder LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 System32 LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS Folders added with AddDllDirectory LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR The folder of the DLL being loaded (only with a full path) LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS The first three together LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR solves lesson 4.01's subfolder problem: a plugin loaded from plugins\fog\fog.dll can now find plugins\fog\noise.dll , which it depends on. 4. Check what you are about to load A plugin folder is a place users (and installers) write files to. Before loading, check: - the path is absolute and really inside the folder you meant (no .. escaping out of it); - the file name ends in .dll ; - for software you distribute widely, that the file is signed with your certificate ( WinVerifyTrust ), so a replaced file is refused. Lesson 5.01's plugin loader does the first two; the practice for this lesson writes the path check. Data files that look like DLLs If you only want to read a DLL's resources (icons, strings, version info) without running any of its code, load it as data: cpp-norun HMODULE resources{ LoadLibraryExW(path, nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_IMAGE_RESOURCE) }; No DllMain runs and nothing is executable. Common mistakes !warning Calling SetDefaultDllDirectories after DLLs were already loaded by name It only affects loads that happen after it. Call it at the very start. !warning Building a plugin path from user input without checking it "..\\..\\Windows\\something.dll" escapes the plugin folder. Normalise the path and check its parent. Knowledge check quiz ? What does SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) remove from the search? + The current directory and the PATH folders - System32 - The application folder Only the application folder, System32 and added folders remain. ? A plugin loaded by full path from plugins\fog needs noise.dll from the same folder. Which flag helps? + LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR - LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE - LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 It adds the loaded DLL's own folder to the search for its dependencies. ? What is DLL planting? + Placing a file with a DLL's name where the search order finds it before the real one - Copying a DLL into System32 - Signing a DLL Full paths and restricted search directories prevent it.

title: Is this plugin path safe?
where: 4.02 Loading Only the Files You Mean
body: Before loading a DLL from a plugin folder, a program checks the path it is about to use. Write cpp std::string normalizePath(const std::string& path); bool safePluginPath(const std::string& pluginFolder, const std::string& candidate); normalizePath cleans up a Windows path: - / becomes \ ; repeated backslashes become one; a trailing backslash is removed (except right after a drive, C:\ ); - . parts are dropped and .. removes the part before it. A .. that would go above the drive (or above the start of a relative path) makes the whole result empty, "" . safePluginPath(folder, candidate) is true only if: - candidate is absolute : it starts with a drive letter, a colon and a backslash or slash ( C:\... ); - after normalising both, the candidate is inside the folder: it starts with the folder followed by \ (comparison ignores upper and lower case, as Windows does); - its file name ends with .dll (any case). normalizePath("C:\\Games//Xenon\\plugins\\.\\fog\\..\\fog.dll") == "C:\\Games\\Xenon\\plugins\\fog.dll" safePluginPath("C:\\Games\\Xenon\\plugins", "C:\\Games\\Xenon\\plugins\\..\\..\\Windows\\evil.dll") == false

title: Which flags search where?
where: 4.02 Loading Only the Files You Mean
body: Write std::vector<std::string searchedFolders(unsigned flags, const std::string& appDir, const std::string& dllDir, const std::vector<std::string & userDirs) returning the folders LoadLibraryExW searches for a DLL's dependencies, in this order: 1. dllDir if LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR (0x100) is set; 2. appDir if LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR (0x200) is set; 3. each of userDirs if LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS (0x400) is set; 4. "C:\\Windows\\System32" if LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 (0x800) is set. LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS (0x1000) means application folder, user folders and System32 together.

title: 4.03  Delay Loading
body: Delay loading gives you the convenience of linking against an import library with the timing of run-time loading. The DLL is loaded the first time one of its functions is called, not when the program starts. This lesson shows how to turn it on, what happens on the first call, and how to handle a DLL that turns out to be missing. Between the two Load time Delay load Run time --- --- --- --- Write code with Normal calls Normal calls LoadLibraryW and GetProcAddress DLL loaded Before main On the first call into it When you ask Missing DLL Program does not start An exception on the first call NULL , you decide Delay loading is ideal for a DLL that only some users need: an exporter for one file format, a voice-chat library, a crash reporter. The program starts faster and works without it, and your code still calls its functions normally. Turning it on Two linker settings on the program (nothing changes in the DLL): - Linker, Input, Delay Loaded Dlls : StoneMath.dll (this adds /DELAYLOAD:StoneMath.dll ). - Linker, Input, Additional Dependencies : add delayimp.lib , the helper library that does the loading. Keep linking StoneMath.lib as before. Your code does not change at all. What happens on the first call The linker writes each delay-loaded import with a placeholder that points at a small thunk instead of the real function. On the first call: 1. The thunk calls the delay-load helper, __delayLoadHelper2 . 2. The helper loads the DLL with LoadLibrary (if this is the first function from it) and finds the function with GetProcAddress . 3. It writes the real address into the delay-load import table, so the next call goes straight to the function. 4. It jumps to the function. So the first call is slower, every later call is as fast as a normal import. The practice simulates exactly this: a slot that resolves itself once. When the DLL is missing With load-time linking, a missing DLL stops the program before main . With delay loading, the problem appears on the first call, as a structured exception (not a C++ exception) with the code VcppException(ERROR_SEVERITY_ERROR, ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND) , or ERROR_PROC_NOT_FOUND for a missing function. Two ways to handle it: Check first. Before calling into the DLL, try to load it yourself: cpp-norun bool stoneMathAvailable() { // Loads the delay-loaded DLL now, or returns a failure instead of an exception. return SUCCEEDED(__HrLoadAllImportsForDll("StoneMath.dll")); } A failure hook. The helper calls a function you provide when loading fails, which can return a fallback: cpp-norun include <delayimp.h FARPROC WINAPI onDelayLoadFailure(unsigned notification, PDelayLoadInfo info) { if (notification == dliFailGetProc && std::strcmp(info- dlp.szProcName, "stackWeight") == 0) return reinterpret_cast<FARPROC (&fallbackStackWeight); // used instead of the missing function return nullptr; // nullptr: raise the exception as usual } ExternC const PfnDliHook __pfnDliFailureHook2 = onDelayLoadFailure; Unloading A delay-loaded DLL can also be unloaded with __FUnloadDelayLoadedDLL2("StoneMath.dll") if you link with /DELAY:UNLOAD . The thunks are reset so the next call loads it again. It is rarely needed; plugin systems and hot reload use LoadLibraryW directly instead. Limits - You cannot delay-load a DLL whose data (exported variables) you use directly; only function calls go through thunks. - kernel32.dll cannot be delay-loaded (the helper itself needs it). - Do not delay-load DLLs called from DllMain or global constructors (lesson 2.04): the first call would load a DLL under the loader lock. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting delayimp.lib The linker reports __delayLoadHelper2 as an unresolved external symbol. !warning Catching the failure with try/catch It is a structured exception, not a C++ exception. Check availability first, or use the failure hook. Knowledge check quiz ? When is a delay-loaded DLL loaded? + The first time the program calls one of its functions - Before main - Only when LoadLibraryW is called The thunk loads it on demand. ? What changes in the DLL to make it delay-loadable? + Nothing; delay loading is set up on the program's linker - It must export a special function - It must be rebuilt with /DELAYLOAD /DELAYLOAD and delayimp.lib go on the program. ? Why is only the first call slower? + The helper writes the real address into the import slot, so later calls skip it - Windows caches the DLL in memory - The first call is not slower The thunk replaces itself with the function's address.

title: A slot that loads itself
body: Delay loading replaces each import with a thunk that resolves the real function the first time it is called. Build the same mechanism with ordinary C++: cpp using Fn = int ( )(int); using Resolver = std::function<Fn(const std::string& name) ; // like LoadLibrary + GetProcAddress; nullptr if missing class DelaySlot { public: DelaySlot(std::string name, Resolver resolver, Fn fallback = nullptr); int call(int argument); // resolves on first use, then calls int resolveCount() const; // how many times the resolver has been asked bool resolved() const; // has a real function (not the fallback) been found? }; - The first call asks the resolver for the function. If it returns a function, the slot remembers it, and every later call goes straight to it without asking again. - If the resolver returns nullptr and there is a fallback , call the fallback this time. The slot does not remember failure: the next call asks the resolver again (the DLL might have been installed since). - If the resolver returns nullptr and there is no fallback, throw std::runtime_error with the message "cannot resolve <name " .

title: 4.04  Version Resources, Runtimes and Shipping
