body: Getting a program with DLLs onto someone else's computer means three things - giving each file a version resource so people and installers can tell versions apart, making sure the Visual C++ runtime is there (or not needed), and laying out the files so the search order finds the right ones. The version resource Right-click any DLL in Explorer, Properties, Details : file version, product version, description, copyright. That comes from a version resource compiled into the file. In Visual Studio, Add, Resource, Version creates one in a .rc file: VS_VERSION_INFO VERSIONINFO FILEVERSION 2,4,1,0 PRODUCTVERSION 2,4,1,0 BEGIN BLOCK "StringFileInfo" BEGIN BLOCK "040904b0" BEGIN VALUE "CompanyName", "Xenon" VALUE "FileDescription", "Stone maths for Xenon games" VALUE "FileVersion", "2.4.1.0" VALUE "OriginalFilename", "StoneMath.dll" VALUE "ProductVersion", "2.4.1" END END BLOCK "VarFileInfo" BEGIN VALUE "Translation", 0x409, 1200 END END The binary FILEVERSION is four 16-bit numbers , stored as two 32-bit values: dwFileVersionMS = major << 16 minor and dwFileVersionLS = build << 16 revision . Installers compare these numbers to decide whether a file on disk is older than the one they carry, so increase them with every release. The practice converts between the text and the two numbers. Reading it at run time takes GetFileVersionInfoSizeW , GetFileVersionInfoW and VerQueryValueW (from version.lib ), which return a VS_FIXEDFILEINFO with those two values. That is for display and diagnostics; your code's compatibility checks belong in the library's own version function (lesson 3.05). The Visual C++ runtime A program built with the default /MD setting needs the runtime DLLs: vcruntime140.dll , vcruntime140_1.dll , msvcp140.dll and the Universal CRT ( ucrtbase.dll , part of Windows 10 and later). On a fresh machine they may be missing. Three ways to deal with it: Approach How Notes --- --- --- Redistributable installer Run vc_redist.x64.exe from your installer The standard way; shared by all programs, updated by Windows Update App-local copy Copy the runtime DLLs next to your .exe Works without an installer; you must update them yourself Static runtime Build everything with /MT No runtime DLLs at all, but each DLL gets its own CRT and heap (lesson 2.05) The redistributable is the usual choice. The runtime DLLs from Visual Studio 2015 to 2022 are binary compatible : a program built with an older toolset works with the newer redistributable (never the other way round). !warning Never ship Debug builds Debug builds need the debug runtimes ( msvcp140d.dll , ucrtbased.dll ), which you are not allowed to redistribute and which only exist where Visual Studio is installed. Laying out the files XenonGame\ ├── XenonGame.exe ├── StoneMath.dll your DLLs: next to the .exe, found first (lesson 4.01) ├── engine.dll ├── vcruntime140.dll only if you ship the runtime app-locally ├── msvcp140.dll └── plugins\ └── fog\ ├── fog.dll loaded by full path (lesson 4.02) └── noise.dll found with LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR Before shipping, check the result on a clean machine (a fresh virtual machine is ideal): run dumpbin /dependents on every binary (lesson 1.06), confirm each listed DLL is either part of Windows, installed by the redistributable, or in your folder. Side-by-side assemblies, briefly Older Windows software uses manifests to bind a program to an exact version of a shared DLL in C:\Windows\WinSxS . You still meet them for one purpose: telling Windows to use version 6 of the common controls (modern-looking buttons) in a Win32 program. For your own DLLs, the app-local layout above is simpler and is what nearly every modern program does. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to increase the file version An installer that compares versions may then refuse to replace an older file with yours. !warning Copying only some runtime DLLs msvcp140.dll without vcruntime140_1.dll fails on machines without the redistributable. Use the installer, or copy the whole set from the Visual Studio redist folder. Knowledge check quiz ? A file version is 2.4.1.0. What is dwFileVersionMS? + 2 << 16 4 - 2.4 - 1 << 16 0 MS holds major and minor, LS holds build and revision. ? Why should a shipped program never be a Debug build? + It needs the debug runtime DLLs, which are not redistributable and are missing on normal machines - Debug builds cannot load DLLs - Debug builds are larger but otherwise fine Release builds use the redistributable runtime. ? What is the usual way to make sure the Visual C++ runtime is on a user's machine? + Run the vc_redist installer from your installer - Copy only msvcp140.dll - Ask the user to install Visual Studio The redistributable is shared and kept up to date.

title: File version numbers
body: A version resource stores the file version major.minor.build.revision as two 32-bit numbers. Write cpp struct FileVersion { uint32_t ms{ 0 }; uint32_t ls{ 0 }; }; bool parseFileVersion(const std::string& text, FileVersion& out); std::string formatFileVersion(const FileVersion& v); bool isNewer(const FileVersion& candidate, const FileVersion& installed); - parseFileVersion reads 1 to 4 parts separated by dots (missing parts are 0: "2.4" is 2.4.0.0 ). Each part is a whole number from 0 to 65535. Then ms = major << 16 minor and ls = build << 16 revision . Anything else returns false . - formatFileVersion gives back all four parts: "2.4.1.0" . - isNewer is how an installer decides to replace a file: compare ms first, then ls .

title: 4.05  Static Libraries, DLLs or Header-Only
body: You now know what DLLs cost and what they give. This lesson compares the three ways to package reusable C++ code - header-only, static library, DLL - and gives a short set of questions for choosing, with examples from real projects. The three packages Header-only. All the code is in headers, often templates or inline functions. Every program that includes them compiles its own copy. Examples: much of the standard library, {fmt} , nlohmann/json , Dear ImGui's helpers. Static library ( .lib ). Compiled once into object code; the linker copies what each program uses into its .exe . Examples: most libraries you get through a package manager by default. DLL. Compiled once into its own file; programs load it when they start or while they run. Examples: the Windows API, graphics drivers, the C runtime, plugin systems. Side by side Header-only Static library DLL --- --- --- --- Build cost for users Highest: recompiled in every file that includes it Low Low Optimisation across the boundary Full: the compiler sees everything Good (with link-time code generation) None: calls go through the import table Templates in the interface Yes Only already-used types Only through a C or COM-style interface Files to ship None None The DLL Update without rebuilding programs No No Yes Load or unload while running No No Yes Shared between processes No No Yes , code pages Usable from other languages No Only from C/C++ Yes , with a C interface ABI concerns None Same compiler and settings Must be designed for (milestone 3) Questions to choose with Ask them in order; the first "yes" usually decides. 1. Do other languages or other teams' programs need to call it? A DLL with a C interface. 2. Must it be loaded, swapped or unloaded while running (plugins, mods, hot reload)? A DLL. 3. Must it be updated without rebuilding the programs that use it (a driver, a shared component)? A DLL. 4. Is it mostly templates, or small? Header-only. 5. Otherwise: a static library. It is the simplest thing that works: one file to ship, no ABI to design, no search order, no loader lock. How real game projects use them - Engine as DLLs, during development only. Engines such as Unreal build each module ( Core , Renderer , Physics ...) as a DLL in development, so editing one module relinks one small DLL instead of the whole game, and enables hot reload. Shipping builds link the same code statically into one executable for speed and simplicity. Both use the same source; a build setting switches the export macro to nothing. - Gameplay code as a DLL while developing, reloaded on every rebuild (lesson 5.03). - Mods and plugins as DLLs with a stable C or COM-style interface (lessons 5.01 and 5.02). - Third-party SDKs (audio middleware, platform services) usually as DLLs, because they are updated separately from your game. One codebase, both ways The export macro from lesson 1.03 can do double duty: cpp-norun if defined(STONEMATH_STATIC) define STONEMATH_API // linked statically: no import or export elif defined(STONEMATH_EXPORTS) define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllexport) else define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllimport) endif Define STONEMATH_STATIC in both the library and the program when you build the library as a static .lib . Common mistakes !warning Making everything a DLL "for modularity" Modularity is about interfaces, not file formats. Every DLL adds a boundary with real rules. Use one when you need what only a DLL gives. !warning A header-only library that is huge Every file that includes it pays to compile it. Split heavy code into a compiled library and keep the header light. Knowledge check quiz ? A library must be callable from C and Python. What should it be? + A DLL with a C interface - A header-only library - A static library Other languages can only load DLLs and call C functions. ? Which package lets the compiler optimise across the boundary the most? + Header-only - DLL - They are all the same The compiler sees all of the code in each program. ? Why do engines often use DLLs in development but static linking for shipping? + DLLs make rebuilds faster and allow hot reload; static linking ships one fast, simple executable - Static linking is not allowed during development - DLLs are required by consoles The same source is built both ways with a switch in the export macro.

title: Choose the package
body: Turn the lesson's questions into a function: cpp struct Needs { bool otherLanguages{ false }; // other languages or teams' programs call it bool loadWhileRunning{ false }; // plugins, mods, hot reload bool updateSeparately{ false }; // replaced without rebuilding programs bool mostlyTemplates{ false }; bool small{ false }; }; std::string choosePackage(const Needs& needs); Return "DLL with a C interface" if other languages call it; otherwise "DLL" if it must load while running or update separately; otherwise "header-only" if it is mostly templates or small; otherwise "static library" .

title: LoadLibraryExW, simulated
body: Combine this milestone's rules into one simulation of LoadLibraryExW that loads a DLL and all of its dependencies , and reports where each one came from. cpp struct World { std::string appDir; std::string currentDir; std::vector<std::string pathDirs; std::vector<std::string userDirs; // added with AddDllDirectory bool defaultDirsSet{ false }; // SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) was called std::set<std::string knownDlls; std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string files; // full path - the DLL names it imports }; std::vector<std::string loadLibraryEx(const World& w, const std::string& file, unsigned flags); - file is either a full path (starts with a drive letter and :\ ) or a bare name. - The result lists every module loaded, dependencies first (as in lesson 1.02), each as name - full path , then ends with ok . If any module cannot be found, the result is instead the single line missing <name for the first one that fails, in load order. - Each module is loaded once; a dependency already loaded earlier in this call is reused (rule "already loaded"). Finding a file. A full path loads that exact file if it exists. For a bare name: 1. Already loaded in this call: reuse it. 2. A known DLL: C:\Windows\System32\<name , no search. 3. Otherwise search the folders, in order: - if the call's flags contain any LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_ value, or defaultDirsSet is true: the folders from lesson 4.02's drill (the flags of this call, plus LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS when defaultDirsSet and the call has none of its own), where the "DLL load dir" is the folder of the top DLL being loaded, and only applies if it was loaded by full path; - otherwise the standard order from lesson 4.01: application folder, C:\Windows\System32 , C:\Windows\System , C:\Windows , current directory, PATH folders. The flag values are those of lesson 4.02's drill. A folder and a name are joined with one backslash.

title: 5.01  A Plugin System
body: A plugin system lets your program load DLLs it was never built with - written later, by you or by players making mods. This lesson designs one for a game - a plugin folder, one required export, an API version check, an interface the host gives to the plugin, and clean loading and unloading - using everything from milestones 2 to 4. The contract A plugin system is a contract between the host (your game) and plugins (DLLs in a folder). Write it down as a header both sides compile against, xenon_plugin.h . It contains: 1. A version number for the contract itself. 2. What the host offers plugins: a table of functions they may call (lesson 3.03). 3. What a plugin offers the host: a table of callbacks the host calls. 4. The one exported function every plugin must have, with a fixed name. cpp-norun // xenon_plugin.h: shared by the game and every plugin pragma once include <stdint.h define XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION 1 // What the game offers a plugin. typedef struct xenon_host_api { uint32_t size; void ( log)(const char message); int32_t ( spawn_stone)(int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t weight); double ( time_seconds)(void); } xenon_host_api; // What a plugin offers the game. typedef struct xenon_plugin { uint32_t size; uint32_t api_version; // the XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION it was built with const char name; // string literal, lives as long as the DLL int32_t ( start)(const xenon_host_api host); // after loading void ( update)(double dt); // every frame void ( stop)(void); // before unloading } xenon_plugin; // Every plugin exports this, with exactly this name (extern "C"). typedef const xenon_plugin ( xenon_get_plugin_fn)(void); define XENON_GET_PLUGIN_NAME "xenon_get_plugin" Everything crosses as plain C: no std::string , no exceptions, no shared heap (milestone 2). Each side only calls through tables, so neither needs an import library for the other. A plugin cpp-norun // fog.cpp, built as fog.dll include "xenon_plugin.h" static const xenon_host_api g_host{ nullptr }; static int32_t start(const xenon_host_api host) { g_host = host; g_host- log("fog: hello"); return 0; } static void update(double) {} static void stop() { g_host- log("fog: goodbye"); g_host = nullptr; } static const xenon_plugin g_plugin{ sizeof(xenon_plugin), XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION, "Fog", start, update, stop }; extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) const xenon_plugin xenon_get_plugin(void) { return &g_plugin; } Note what it does not do: nothing in DllMain or global constructors (lesson 2.04). Real work starts in start , called by the host after LoadLibrary returns. The host's loader cpp-norun struct LoadedPlugin { HMODULE module; const xenon_plugin plugin; }; std::vector<LoadedPlugin loadPlugins(const std::filesystem::path& folder, const xenon_host_api& host) { std::vector<LoadedPlugin loaded; for (const auto& entry : std::filesystem::directory_iterator(folder)) { const auto& path{ entry.path() }; if (!entry.is_regular_file() path.extension() != L".dll") continue; HMODULE module{ LoadLibraryExW(path.c_str(), nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) }; if (!module) { logf("skipped %ls: could not load (error %lu)", path.c_str(), GetLastError()); continue; } auto get{ reinterpret_cast<xenon_get_plugin_fn (GetProcAddress(module, XENON_GET_PLUGIN_NAME)) }; const xenon_plugin plugin{ get ? get() : nullptr }; if (!plugin plugin- size < sizeof(xenon_plugin) plugin- api_version != XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION) { logf("skipped %ls: not a plugin for this version", path.c_str()); FreeLibrary(module); continue; } if (plugin- start(&host) != 0) { logf("skipped %s: start failed", plugin- name); FreeLibrary(module); continue; } loaded.push_back({ module, plugin }); } return loaded; } Every check matters: - Only .dll files , by full path , with the safe search flags (lesson 4.02). Plugins with their own dependencies keep them in their own folder. - The export must exist. A random DLL in the folder is skipped, not crashed on. - Size and version. A plugin built for another version of the contract is refused politely (lesson 3.05). - start can fail , and then the plugin is unloaded again. - A failing plugin never stops the others from loading. Unloading At shutdown, or when the player disables a plugin, the order is: call stop , forget every pointer the plugin gave you (its name , its tables, any objects), then FreeLibrary . Unload in the reverse order of loading, so a plugin that relied on another's services stops before them. Mods and trust A plugin runs inside your process with all of its permissions. For plugins you write yourself, that is fine. For mods made by players, treat the plugin folder as "code the player chose to run", like any program they download, and say so in your game's documentation. Many games that want untrusted mods use a scripting language with limited access (Lua, a WebAssembly runtime) instead of DLLs. Common mistakes !warning Keeping a plugin's name string after unloading it It points into the DLL's read-only data. Copy it into a std::string if you need it later. !warning Letting one bad plugin crash the whole load Check every step and skip what does not fit. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does the plugin contract use tables of function pointers in both directions? + Neither side needs an import library for the other, and the tables can be versioned - Function pointers are faster than exports - Because plugins cannot export functions One GetProcAddress gets the plugin's table; the host passes its own table in start. ? A DLL in the plugin folder has no xenon_get_plugin export. What should the host do? + Log it, FreeLibrary it and carry on with the other files - Crash - Call its DllMain Not every DLL in the folder is a plugin. ? What is the correct order for unloading a plugin? + Call stop, drop every pointer it gave you, then FreeLibrary - FreeLibrary, then call stop - Only FreeLibrary; stop is optional After FreeLibrary, none of its code or data exists any more.

title: Which files are plugins?
body: The host scans its plugin folder. For each file it gathers what it found, and must decide which plugins to keep. Write cpp struct Candidate { std::string file; // file name, e.g. "fog.dll" bool loads{ true }; // LoadLibraryExW succeeded bool hasExport{ true }; // GetProcAddress found xenon_get_plugin uint32_t tableSize{ 0 }; // plugin- size uint32_t apiVersion{ 0 }; // plugin- api_version std::string name; // plugin- name bool startOk{ true }; // plugin- start returned 0 }; struct ScanResult { std::vector<std::string kept; std::vector<std::string log; }; ScanResult scanPlugins(const std::vector<Candidate & files, uint32_t hostApiVersion, uint32_t requiredTableSize); Go through the files sorted by file name (case-insensitive) and apply the checks in this order. The first one that fails adds a line to log and skips the file: 1. The name must end in .dll (any case), otherwise: "<file : not a DLL" . 2. loads , otherwise: "<file : could not load" . 3. hasExport , otherwise: "<file : not a plugin" . 4. tableSize = requiredTableSize and apiVersion == hostApiVersion , otherwise: "<file : built for API version <apiVersion , need <hostApiVersion " . 5. A plugin name that has not been kept already (exact comparison), otherwise: "<file : duplicate plugin <name " . 6. startOk , otherwise: "<file : start failed" . A file that passes everything adds its plugin name to kept and the log line "<file : loaded <name " .

title: 5.02  A Plugin Registry and Capabilities
body: Once several plugins are loaded, the host needs to know what each one provides - new stone types, weather effects, console commands - and route requests to the right one. This lesson builds a registry that plugins register into during start , handles name clashes and dependencies between plugins, and cleans up everything a plugin registered when it unloads. Registering instead of exporting In lesson 5.01 a plugin offered fixed callbacks: start , update , stop . Real plugins add things to the game: three new stone types, a weather effect, two console commands. Rather than one export per thing, the host offers registration functions in its table, and the plugin calls them from start : cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_stone_type { uint32_t size; const char id; // "fog.ghost_stone" int32_t weight; int32_t ( on_place)(int32_t x, int32_t y); } xenon_stone_type; typedef struct xenon_host_api { uint32_t size; void ( log)(const char message); int32_t ( register_stone_type)(const void owner, const xenon_stone_type type); int32_t ( register_command)(const void owner, const char name, void ( run)(const char args)); } xenon_host_api; In the plugin: cpp-norun static const xenon_stone_type g_ghost{ sizeof(xenon_stone_type), "fog.ghost_stone", 2, onPlaceGhost }; static int32_t start(const xenon_host_api host) { if (host- register_stone_type(&g_plugin, &g_ghost) != 0) return 1; host- register_command(&g_plugin, "fog.thickness", setThickness); return 0; } The owner argument (the plugin's own table, a unique address) lets the host remember who registered each thing. The host's registry cpp-norun class Registry { public: int32_t addStoneType(const void owner, const xenon_stone_type& type); const xenon_stone_type stoneType(std::string_view id) const; void removeEverythingFrom(const void owner); // when a plugin unloads private: struct Entry { const void owner; xenon_stone_type type; std::string id; }; std::map<std::string, Entry, std::less< m_stones; }; Design decisions: - Copy what you keep. The registry stores its own copy of the struct and of the id text. Pointers into the plugin ( on_place ) are still pointers into its code, which is why... - Remove everything on unload. Before FreeLibrary , the host calls removeEverythingFrom(plugin) . Otherwise the registry holds function pointers into unmapped memory (lesson 2.03). - Names are namespaced by convention: pluginname.thing . Two plugins can both have a "ghost_stone" without clashing. - A clash is refused, not overwritten. If fog.ghost_stone is already registered by someone else, the second registration fails and the plugin can decide what to do. Silently replacing a registration makes bugs that depend on load order. Plugins that depend on plugins A "seasons" plugin might need the "weather" plugin's commands. Give each plugin a list of the plugins it requires , by name, and load them in dependency order: the same depth-first, dependencies-first walk as the loader itself (lesson 1.02). A plugin whose requirement is missing, or that is part of a cycle, is not started, and the host says why. Capabilities and versions per feature Instead of one version for the whole contract, a host can offer capabilities : named features with their own version, such as "stone_types": 2 , "commands": 1 . A plugin lists what it needs; the host starts it only if every need is met with at least that version. This lets the contract grow one feature at a time without every plugin being rebuilt. Common mistakes !warning Storing the plugin's pointers in the registry without an owner You then cannot find and remove them on unload, and the game crashes the first time it calls one. !warning Last registration wins The result depends on which DLL the directory listing returned first. Refuse duplicates and report them. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does the plugin pass an owner pointer when it registers something? + So the host can remove everything that plugin registered before unloading it - To prove it is a real plugin - Because function pointers need an owner to be called Removal by owner keeps the registry free of dangling pointers. ? Two plugins register the same id. What should the registry do? + Refuse the second registration and report the clash - Keep the second one - Keep whichever plugin loaded last Refusing makes the result independent of load order. ? In what order should plugins with dependencies be started? + Dependencies first, depth first, each once, like the Windows loader - Alphabetically - In the order the folder lists them A plugin's requirements must be running before it starts.

title: A registry that cleans up after plugins
match: A registry that cleans up after plugins
body: Write the host's registry for stone types: cpp class Registry { public: bool add(const std::string& owner, const std::string& id, int weight); // false if the id is taken int weightOf(const std::string& id) const; // -1 if unknown std::string ownerOf(const std::string& id) const; // "" if unknown int removeOwner(const std::string& owner); // removes all of its entries, returns how many std::vector<std::string ids() const; // all ids, sorted }; - An id may only be registered once. A second add with the same id fails and changes nothing, even if it comes from the same owner. - An id must be namespaced : it contains a . with at least one character before and after it, and the part before the first . must equal the owner. Otherwise add fails. - removeOwner is what the host calls before FreeLibrary .

title: Start plugins in dependency order
body: Each plugin lists the plugins it requires. Write cpp std::vector<std::string startOrder(const std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string & requires_, std::vector<std::string & problems); requires_ maps every available plugin to the names it requires. Return the order to start them in, and fill problems with one line per plugin that cannot start: - Visit plugins in alphabetical order; for each, start its requirements first (in the order listed, depth first), then the plugin itself, each only once. - A plugin whose requirement is not available cannot start: "<plugin needs <missing " . Any plugin that requires a plugin that cannot start also cannot start: "<plugin needs <requirement " . - A plugin that is part of a cycle (it requires itself directly or through others) cannot start: "<plugin is part of a cycle" . Plugins that require a plugin in a cycle cannot start either, with the needs message. - Each plugin gets at most one problem line: the first reason found. Problems are listed in the order they are discovered. requires_: { fog: , seasons: fog, weather , weather: , storms: weather, wind } order: fog, weather, seasons problems: "storms needs wind"

title: 5.03  Hot Reloading Code
body: Hot reloading means changing game code, rebuilding, and having the running game pick up the new code within a second, without restarting or losing your place. The trick is to put gameplay code in a DLL and swap it. This lesson covers the loop - watch, copy, unload, load - and the problems each step solves. The idea Split the game into two parts: - The host ( game.exe ): window, main loop, memory, input, loading assets. It rarely changes and keeps running. - The game code ( gameplay.dll ): the rules, movement, enemy behaviour. You change it all day. The host calls into the DLL through a small table, exactly like a plugin: cpp-norun typedef struct game_api { uint32_t size; void ( update)(game_state state, const game_input input, float dt); void ( render)(const game_state state, render_list out); } game_api; extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) const game_api get_game_api(void); All game state lives in memory the host owns and passes in (lesson 5.04 explains why). The DLL is just functions. The reload loop Every frame, before calling update , the host checks whether the DLL file has changed: cpp-norun FILETIME lastWrite(const wchar_t path); void Host::reloadIfChanged() { const FILETIME now{ lastWrite(L"gameplay.dll") }; if (CompareFileTime(&now, &m_loadedWriteTime) == 0) return; // unchanged // 1. Copy the new DLL to a fresh name and load the copy. const std::wstring copy{ L"gameplay_" + std::to_wstring(++m_generation) + L".dll" }; if (!CopyFileW(L"gameplay.dll", copy.c_str(), FALSE)) return; // the compiler may still be writing it: try next frame HMODULE fresh{ LoadLibraryW(copy.c_str()) }; auto get{ fresh ? reinterpret_cast<const game_api ( )() (GetProcAddress(fresh, "get_game_api")) : nullptr }; if (!get) { if (fresh) FreeLibrary(fresh); return; } // keep running the old code // 2. Swap: drop every pointer into the old DLL, then unload it. m_api = get(); if (m_module) FreeLibrary(m_module); m_module = fresh; m_loadedWriteTime = now; } Why copy before loading? A loaded DLL's file is locked : Windows maps it into memory and will not let anyone overwrite it. If the game loaded gameplay.dll itself, the next build would fail with "cannot open file for writing". Loading a copy leaves the original free for the compiler. Each reload uses a new name ( gameplay_7.dll ) because the previous copy may still be loaded at the moment you copy. Why only after the build has finished? The linker writes the DLL over several hundred milliseconds. If the host notices the new time stamp half-way through, it may copy a half-written file. Two common fixes: - Wait until the time stamp has been stable for a few checks (say 200 ms) before reloading. - Have the build write a small "lock" file first and delete it when done; reload only when the lock file is gone. The practice builds the "stable for several polls" watcher. The PDB problem The debugger also locks the DLL's PDB (debug symbols) while the DLL is loaded, so the next link fails to write gameplay.pdb . Give each build's PDB a unique name in Linker, Debugging, Generate Program Database File , for example $(OutDir)gameplay_$( System.DateTime ::Now.Ticks).pdb . Old PDB files pile up; delete them on start-up. What must not survive a reload After FreeLibrary on the old DLL, everything that pointed into it is invalid: - function pointers (the old game_api table, callbacks stored anywhere); - string literals from the old DLL; - vtables : any C++ object created by the old DLL's code has a vptr into the old DLL; - static and global variables inside the DLL, which are reset to their initial values in the new one. That is why state lives in host memory, and why the state is plain data without virtual functions. Lesson 5.04 handles state whose layout changes between builds. Common mistakes !warning Loading the DLL itself instead of a copy The next build cannot overwrite the locked file. !warning Keeping the old table after unloading Read the new table before freeing the old module, and never keep pointers to the old one. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does the host load a copy of the DLL instead of the DLL itself? + A loaded DLL's file is locked, so the compiler could not write the next build - Copies load faster - So the debugger can find the PDB The original must stay writable for the next build. ? The host sees a new time stamp on gameplay.dll. Why might reloading straight away fail? + The linker may still be writing the file - Time stamps are always wrong - FreeLibrary must be called first Wait until it has been stable, or until a lock file disappears. ? Which of these survives a hot reload? + Game state stored in memory the host owns - A static variable inside the DLL - A C++ object with virtual functions created by the old DLL Everything inside the old DLL's image is gone after FreeLibrary.

title: When to reload
body: The host checks the gameplay DLL's last-write time once per frame. It must reload only when the file has changed and the build has finished : the time has stayed the same for a few checks in a row. Write cpp class ReloadWatcher { public: ReloadWatcher(long long loadedTime, int stablePolls); bool poll(long long fileTime); // called once per frame with the file's current write time int generation() const; // how many reloads have happened std::string copyName() const; // the name of the copy to load for the current generation }; - loadedTime is the write time of the DLL that is loaded right now. - poll returns true exactly when the host should reload now : the file time differs from loadedTime , and this same time has now been seen on stablePolls consecutive polls (counting this one). After returning true , loadedTime becomes that time and generation() increases by one. - If the time changes again while waiting, the count starts over for the new time. - If the time goes back to loadedTime while waiting (the build was undone), stop waiting. - copyName() is "gameplay_<generation .dll" , starting at gameplay_0.dll before any reload. ReloadWatcher w{ 100, 3 }; w.poll(100) == false // unchanged w.poll(150) == false // changed, seen once w.poll(150) == false // twice w.poll(150) == true // three times: reload now, generation 1, copy gameplay_1.dll w.poll(150) == false // that is what is loaded now

title: 5.04  Keeping State Across a Reload
body: Hot reload is only useful if the game keeps its state - the player's position, the enemies, the score - while the code changes. This lesson shows the two strategies, host-owned memory and save and restore , and how to handle the hard case: a reload that changes the layout of the state itself. Strategy 1: the host owns the memory The simplest and fastest approach, popularised by Casey Muratori's Handmade Hero : the host allocates one big block of memory at start-up and hands it to the DLL every frame. The DLL keeps all of its state in that block, and none in its own globals: cpp-norun struct game_memory { uint64_t size; void storage; // allocated by the host once, never freed until exit bool initialised; // false the first time }; extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) void game_update(game_memory memory, const game_input input, float dt) { auto state{ static_cast<GameState (memory- storage) }; if (!memory- initialised) { new (state) GameState{}; memory- initialised = true; } state- player.x += input- moveX dt; } When the DLL is swapped, the block is untouched, so the new code finds the state exactly as the old code left it. The rules that make it work: - GameState is plain data : no virtual functions (their vptrs would point into the old DLL), no std::string or std::vector whose memory came from the old DLL's heap if it used its own CRT. Arrays with fixed sizes, plain structs, indices instead of pointers into code. - Memory that the game needs to grow comes from a simple arena inside the block, not from new . - No pointers to functions or string literals of the DLL are stored in the state. Strategy 2: save and restore If the state has to contain richer C++ objects, the DLL can instead write its state to bytes just before it is unloaded and read it back after the new one is loaded: cpp-norun // in the DLL's table uint64_t ( save_state)(void buffer, uint64_t capacity); // returns bytes needed int32_t ( load_state)(const void buffer, uint64_t size); The host calls save_state on the old DLL, unloads it, loads the new one and calls load_state . Slower, but it handles any state, and the same code doubles as your save-game system. When the layout changes Both strategies face the same hard case: you add a member to GameState , or change a type. The new code then reads the old bytes with the new layout, which is lesson 3.03's versioned-struct problem in another form. The same solution works: - Put a version number (and size) at the start of the saved state or the memory block. - When the new code sees an older version , it migrates : reads the old layout, fills new fields with defaults, writes the new layout. - When it sees a version it cannot read, it starts fresh rather than reading garbage, and logs why. cpp-norun struct StateHeader { uint32_t version; uint32_t size; }; // version 1: { int32_t x, y; } version 2: { int32_t x, y; int32_t health; } if (header.version == 1) { / copy x, y; health = 100; / } else if (header.version == 2) { / read as is / } else { / unknown: start a new game / } Many developers simply restart when the state layout changes, and reload freely for everything else. A version number makes that decision automatic instead of a crash. What hot reload is good for, and what not Excellent for: tuning movement and feel, fixing gameplay bugs while reproducing them, iterating on enemy behaviour, UI layout. Poor for: changes to data the host owns, changes to the host itself, and big structural changes, which still need a restart. Common mistakes !warning A static variable inside the gameplay DLL It resets on every reload. Move it into the state. !warning Reading old state with a new layout Values land in the wrong fields. Version the state and migrate or start fresh. Knowledge check quiz ? Why must game state kept in host memory have no virtual functions? + Each object's vptr would point into the old, unloaded DLL - Virtual functions are too slow for games - The host cannot allocate them Plain data survives the swap; code pointers do not. ? The state gained a new field and the new DLL finds version 1 data. What should it do? + Migrate: read the old layout, give the new field a default, write the new layout - Read it with the new layout - Crash, to make the developer restart A version number turns layout changes into a decision instead of garbage. ? Which strategy also works as a save-game system? + Save and restore through save_state and load_state - Host-owned memory - Neither The DLL serialises its state to bytes.

title: Migrate saved state
body: The gameplay DLL saves its state to bytes before a reload, and the new DLL reads it back. The state's layout has changed between versions: Version Fields after the header, in order --- --- 1 x (int32), y (int32) 2 x , y , health (int32) 3 x , y , health , stones (int32) Every saved state starts with a header of two uint32_t values: the version , then the size of everything that follows. All numbers are little-endian, 4 bytes each. Write the current (version 3) code's functions: cpp struct State { int32_t x{ 0 }; int32_t y{ 0 }; int32_t health{ 100 }; int32_t stones{ 0 }; }; std::vector<uint8_t saveState(const State& s); // always writes version 3 bool loadState(const std::vector<uint8_t & bytes, State& out); // reads version 1, 2 or 3 - loadState checks the header: at least 8 bytes, a version from 1 to 3, and a size that matches what that version needs (8, 12 or 16) and fits in the bytes after the header. If anything is wrong it returns false and leaves out untouched. - Missing fields get their defaults: health 100, stones 0. - A version above 3 comes from a newer DLL: return false (start fresh rather than guess).

title: 5.05  Capstone: A Moddable Game
body: Bring the whole course together in one Visual Studio solution - a small game whose gameplay hot-reloads while it runs, and which loads plugins that add new content through a versioned C interface. This lesson is the plan, the checklist and the order to build it in. What you build A small top-down game, "Xenon Builder": the player walks around a field and stacks stones into towers. It has three kinds of module: XenonBuilder.sln ├── Host/ XenonBuilder.exe: window, loop, input, memory, plugin loader, hot reload ├── Gameplay/ gameplay.dll: rules and movement, hot-reloaded ├── PluginApi/ xenon_plugin.h, xenon.hpp: shared headers only (no code) └── Plugins/ ├── Fog/ fog.dll: a new stone type and a console command └── Seasons/ seasons.dll: requires Fog; changes stone colours over time Milestone by milestone Part Lessons Done when --- --- --- A window and a loop in the host (Win32 or the console from earlier courses) The player moves with the arrow keys Gameplay in a DLL, loaded at run time 2.03, 3.03 get_game_api returns a versioned table the host checks Host-owned state 5.04 No globals in gameplay.dll ; the state has a version header Hot reload 5.03 Change the walking speed, rebuild: the running game changes speed without moving the player Safe loading 4.02 SetDefaultDllDirectories first thing; every DLL loaded by full path The plugin contract 5.01, 3.03 xenon_plugin.h with version, host table, plugin table The registry 5.02 Fog registers fog.ghost_stone and the fog.thickness command Plugin dependencies 5.02, 1.02 Seasons starts after Fog; without Fog, Seasons is skipped with a message Error handling at every boundary 2.06, 3.02 No exception crosses a DLL edge; failures are logged with messages Clean shutdown 2.04, 5.01 stop on each plugin in reverse order, registries emptied, then FreeLibrary Shipping 4.04 A Release build runs on a clean virtual machine Order to build in 1. Get the host working with the gameplay code statically linked first: the simplest version that runs. 2. Move gameplay into a DLL loaded with LoadLibraryW . Fix everything that breaks: globals, ownership, the interface. 3. Add hot reload. Edit, rebuild, watch it change. This is the part you will enjoy most. 4. Add the plugin loader with one plugin, then the registry, then the second plugin with its dependency. 5. Shut down cleanly and ship. Checklist before you call it finished - dumpbin /exports on each DLL shows only plain, intended names. - dumpbin /dependents on the Release build shows no debug runtime. - Removing fog.dll makes Seasons skip with a clear message, and the game still runs. - A DLL that is not a plugin in the plugin folder is skipped, not loaded into the game. - Ten hot reloads in a row leave no leaked plugin registrations and no growing memory. - Building while the game runs never fails with a locked file (DLL or PDB). - A plugin built against an older contract version is refused with a message, not a crash. Where to go next - The Tool Interfaces with Dear ImGui course adds an in-game editor to this project, which can reload with the gameplay DLL. - The Game Programming with raylib course gives the host a real renderer. - The Windows Programming with the Win32 API course goes deeper into the window and message loop the host is built on. Knowledge check quiz ? Why build the game with the gameplay code statically linked first? + To get the simplest working version before adding the rules a DLL boundary brings - DLLs cannot be used in the first version - Static linking is required for hot reload Then the move to a DLL shows exactly what has to change. ? What should happen when a plugin's dependency is missing? + Skip that plugin with a clear message and keep running - Refuse to start the game - Load the plugin anyway One missing mod must not stop the game.

title: A plugin host that reloads
body: Write the bookkeeping of a plugin host: which plugins run, in what order, what each one registered, and what happens when one is reloaded. Each plugin file is described by: cpp struct PluginFile { std::string name; // "fog" uint32_t apiVersion{ 1 }; std::vector<std::string requires_; // names of plugins that must be running first std::vector<std::string provides; // ids it registers when it starts, e.g. "fog.ghost_stone" }; class Host { public: explicit Host(uint32_t apiVersion); void addFile(const PluginFile& file); // a new file, or a new build replacing one with the same name std::vector<std::string startAll(); // start every plugin that is not running; returns log lines std::vector<std::string reload(const std::string& name); std::vector<std::string running() const; // names, in the order they were started std::string providerOf(const std::string& id) const; // "" if nobody provides it }; Starting. startAll visits the plugins that are not running in alphabetical order and starts each one's requirements first (in the order listed, depth first). A plugin starts if every check passes, in this order: 1. its apiVersion equals the host's, else log skip <name : API version <v , need <host ; 2. every requirement exists and is running (or can be started now), else skip <name : needs <requirement for the first one that fails; reaching a plugin that is already being started in this chain is a cycle: skip <name : cycle ; 3. it registers its provides ids in order. Each must start with <name . (else skip <name : <id is not <name . ) and must not be registered already (else skip <name : <id is taken ). If any registration fails, the ids it registered before the failure are removed again. A plugin that starts logs start <name and is added to the end of the running list. Each plugin is logged at most once per startAll (its first result). Reloading. reload(name) stops the plugin and every running plugin that requires it, directly or indirectly, in reverse start order , logging stop <x for each and removing everything each one registered. Then it calls startAll and appends its log. Reloading a plugin that is not running only runs startAll .

title: Cheat Sheet - DLL API
body: Building and exporting cpp-norun // One header for the DLL and its users (the DLL project defines MYLIB_EXPORTS) if defined(MYLIB_STATIC) define MYLIB_API elif defined(MYLIB_EXPORTS) define MYLIB_API __declspec(dllexport) else define MYLIB_API __declspec(dllimport) endif ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { endif MYLIB_API int32_t mylib_thing_create(mylib_thing out); MYLIB_API void mylib_thing_destroy(mylib_thing thing); ifdef __cplusplus } endif LIBRARY MyLib ; a .def file EXPORTS mylib_thing_create @1 mylib_thing_destroy @2 PublicName = internal_name hidden_entry @9 NONAME Loading at run time Function Use --- --- LoadLibraryW(path) Map a DLL; NULL on failure, see GetLastError() LoadLibraryExW(path, nullptr, flags) The same, with search flags or as a data file GetProcAddress(module, "name") An export's address ( FARPROC ); cast to the exact function type FreeLibrary(module) Drop one reference GetModuleHandleW(L"name.dll") Handle of an already-loaded module, no new reference GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, buf, n) Full path of your own .exe SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) First line of main : no current directory or PATH in searches AddDllDirectory(folder) Add a folder to LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS Flag Searches --- --- LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR The loaded DLL's own folder (full paths only) LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR The .exe 's folder LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS Folders from AddDllDirectory LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 System32 LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS Application, user folders, System32 LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE Map for resources only; no code runs Error codes from LoadLibrary Code Meaning --- --- 126 ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND The DLL or one of its dependencies was not found 127 ERROR_PROC_NOT_FOUND A dependency lacks an export that is imported 193 ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT Wrong architecture (32/64-bit) or not a PE file 1114 ERROR_DLL_INIT_FAILED DllMain returned FALSE The standard search order (name-only requests) Already loaded, then known DLLs, then: application folder, System32 , System , Windows , current directory, PATH. DllMain cpp-norun BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE module, DWORD reason, LPVOID reserved) { if (reason == DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) DisableThreadLibraryCalls(module); return TRUE; } Safe: set variables, DisableThreadLibraryCalls , InitializeCriticalSection , TlsAlloc . Not safe: LoadLibrary , FreeLibrary , waiting for threads or locks, COM, sockets, registry, UI. Do real work in an explicit init function. Rules at the boundary - Whoever allocates, frees: free functions, caller buffers, or create/destroy pairs. - No exceptions out of exported functions: catch everything, return codes. - No C++ library types in a public interface; pointer and length instead. - Fixed-size types ( int32_t , uint64_t ), no bool or long in C interfaces. - Result codes never renumbered; callers treat unknown nonzero codes as failure. - Visible structs start with their size and only grow at the end. Tools Command Shows --- --- dumpbin /exports X.dll Export table dumpbin /imports X.exe Imported DLLs and functions dumpbin /dependents X.exe Directly needed DLLs dumpbin /headers X.dll Machine type, base, characteristics undname ?name@@... Decodes a decorated C++ name Debug, Windows, Modules Every loaded module, its path and address Process Monitor Every place Windows looked for a file

title: Common Errors
body: Message or symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- "The code execution cannot proceed because X.dll was not found." The DLL, or one it depends on, is not next to the program or anywhere in the search order Ship it next to the .exe ; check dumpbin /dependents 1.02, 4.01 "The procedure entry point F could not be located in the dynamic link library X.dll." An older or different X.dll was loaded that lacks F Find which file was loaded (Modules window, Process Monitor); never remove exports 1.05 "The application was unable to start correctly (0xc000007b)." A 32-bit DLL in a 64-bit process, or the reverse Build every module for the same architecture 1.02 LoadLibraryW returns NULL, error 126 Module not found, often a dependency of the DLL you named Dependencies tool; LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR for plugin folders 2.03, 4.02 LoadLibraryW returns NULL, error 193 Wrong architecture, or not a DLL dumpbin /headers 2.03 LoadLibraryW returns NULL, error 1114 DllMain (or a global constructor) failed Move work out of DllMain into an init function 2.04 GetProcAddress returns NULL Name decorated because extern "C" is missing, or wrong case extern "C" ; check dumpbin /exports 2.01 LNK2019 unresolved external symbol for a DLL function Not exported, or the import library is not linked Add the export macro; link the .lib 1.03, 1.05 LNK2038 mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' Debug and Release code linked together Build all modules in the same configuration 2.06 LNK2019 __delayLoadHelper2 Delay loading without delayimp.lib Link delayimp.lib 4.03 "Run-Time Check Failure 0 - The value of ESP was not properly saved" Calling convention mismatch (32-bit) Put the convention in the function pointer typedef 2.02 Heap corruption or a crash when freeing a DLL's memory Freed by a module with a different CRT heap Let the DLL free what it allocates 2.05 The program hangs while loading a DLL Waiting on a thread or lock inside DllMain (loader lock) Explicit init and shutdown functions 2.04 Crash after FreeLibrary A function pointer, string, vtable or object from the DLL was used after unloading Drop every pointer before unloading 2.03, 5.03 The link fails with "cannot open file" during hot reload The loaded DLL or its PDB is locked Load a copy; give each PDB a unique name 5.03 State jumps or garbage after a hot reload State kept in DLL globals, or layout changed Host-owned memory; version and migrate state 5.04 A different copy of the DLL is loaded on another machine Search order found a copy on PATH or in the current directory Full paths, SetDefaultDllDirectories 4.01, 4.02 The program needs MSVCP140D.dll on a user's machine A Debug build was shipped Ship Release builds with the redistributable 4.04

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- ABI Application binary interface: the rules compiled code follows to work together, such as type sizes, struct layout, calling conventions and name decoration. A DLL's interface is a promise about its ABI. (3.01) AddRef / Release The two reference-counting methods of a COM-style interface. AddRef takes a reference; Release drops one and deletes the object at zero. (3.04) API set A name such as api-ms-win-core-file-l1-1-0.dll that Windows redirects to a real system DLL without any search. (1.06) ASLR Address space layout randomisation: Windows loads modules at random addresses to make attacks harder, so relocation is normal. (1.02) Binary compatibility Programs already compiled against one version of a DLL keep working with a newer one without being rebuilt. (3.01) Calling convention The agreement about where arguments go, where the result comes back and who cleans up the stack. x64 Windows has one; 32-bit Windows has several. (2.02) Capability A named feature of a plugin contract with its own version, which a plugin can require. (5.02) CRT The C runtime library: malloc , new , printf and friends. A module gets it shared ( /MD ) or private ( /MT ). (2.05) Decorated (mangled) name The symbol name a C++ compiler gives a function, encoding its scope and types so that overloads differ, such as ?add@@YAHHH@Z . (2.01) .def file A module-definition file that lists a DLL's exports by hand, with optional ordinals, NONAME and DATA . (1.04) Delay loading Linking against a DLL's import library but loading it only when one of its functions is first called. (4.03) DLL Dynamic-link library: compiled code and data in a separate PE file that a process maps and calls into. (1.01) DLL Hell Programs breaking because an installer replaced a shared DLL with an incompatible version of the same name. (3.05) DLL planting Placing a file with a DLL's name where the search order finds it before the real one. Also called search-order hijacking. (4.02) DllMain A DLL's optional entry point, called when the DLL is attached to or detached from a process and when threads start and end. (2.04) dllexport / dllimport __declspec attributes that put a symbol in a DLL's export table, and tell the compiler a symbol comes from a DLL. (1.03) Exception barrier A try/catch around the body of an exported function that turns every exception into an error code. (2.06) Export table The part of a PE file listing the names, ordinals and RVAs of what a module offers to others. (1.01) extern "C" C linkage: no name decoration and no overloading, so the exported name is plain. (2.01) FreeLibrary Drops one reference to a loaded DLL; at zero the DLL is unmapped. (2.03) Function table A versioned struct of function pointers returned by one exported function, used as an interface. (3.03) GetProcAddress Returns the address of a DLL's exported function by name or ordinal. (2.03) Header-only library Reusable code entirely in headers, compiled into every program that includes it. (4.05) Host The program that loads plugins or a hot-reloaded DLL and calls into them. (5.01) Hot reload Replacing a running program's code (a DLL) with a rebuilt version without restarting or losing state. (5.03) Import address table (IAT) A module's array of slots, one per imported function, filled by the loader with real addresses. (1.05) Import library A small .lib that tells the linker which DLL each function comes from, without containing their code. (1.05) Known DLLs Core system DLLs that Windows always loads from System32, whatever the search order says. (4.01) Loader The part of Windows (in ntdll.dll ) that maps modules into a process, resolves imports and runs initialisation. (1.02) Loader lock A process-wide lock held while modules are loaded and unloaded; DllMain and global constructors run under it. (2.04) LoadLibraryW / LoadLibraryExW Map a DLL into the process at run time, the second with flags that control the search. (2.03, 4.02) Opaque handle A pointer to a type that is declared but never defined for callers, so its contents can change between versions. (3.01) Ordinal A DLL export's number. Exports can be found by ordinal instead of name. (1.04) PE file Portable Executable: the file format of Windows executables and DLLs. (1.01) Plugin A DLL the host finds and loads at run time through a fixed contract, which it was not built with. (5.01) QueryInterface The COM-style method that asks an object for another interface it supports. (3.04) Reference count A count of holders. DLLs are counted by LoadLibrary and FreeLibrary; COM-style objects by AddRef and Release. (2.03, 3.04) Relocation Fixing stored absolute addresses when a module is loaded away from its preferred base. (1.02) RVA Relative virtual address: an offset from the start of a loaded module. (1.02) Safe DLL search mode The setting, on by default, that searches the current directory after the system folders. (4.01) Search order The list of places Windows tries when a DLL is requested by name only. (4.01) Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: major for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. (3.05) SetDefaultDllDirectories Restricts every later name-only load in the process to safe folders. (4.02) Static library A .lib whose code the linker copies into the executable. (1.01) Thunk A small piece of code that stands in for a function, such as the delay-load stub that loads the DLL on the first call. (4.03) Version resource Version information compiled into a PE file, shown in Explorer's Details tab. (4.04) Versioned struct A struct whose first member is its own size, so a library can tell which version the caller sent. (3.03) vtable / vptr The table of a class's virtual function pointers, and the hidden pointer to it at the start of each object. (3.04)

title: 1.01  Kinds of Documentation
body: Why reading documentation is a core programming skill, the four kinds of documentation (tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation) and what each is for, the other sources you will meet, and how to pick the right one for the question you have. The skill under every other skill Nobody remembers every function. Working programmers spend a large part of each day reading: a reference page to check what a function returns on failure, a guide to set up a library, a specification to see what a file format allows. The difference between a beginner and an experienced programmer is often not what they know, but how quickly and precisely they can find out . Reading documentation well means three things: 1. Knowing which kind of document answers your question. 2. Reading it precisely : every word on a reference page is there for a reason. 3. Turning what it says into code that handles every case it describes. This course trains all three, mostly with C++, then with Windows, Python, JavaScript and specifications. Four kinds of documentation Good documentation sets are usually split into four kinds, because each answers a different need. (This division is often called the Diátaxis framework.) Kind Answers Reads like Example --- --- --- --- Tutorial "I'm new, show me" a lesson: do this, then this "Your first window with raylib" How-to guide "How do I do X?" a recipe with steps "How to read a file asynchronously" Reference "What exactly does this do?" a dry, complete description the page for std::vector::insert Explanation "Why is it like this?" an essay or background article "About processes and threads" They mix badly. A tutorial that stops to list every parameter loses the learner; a reference page that tells a story hides the one fact you need. So when you search, decide first which one you want: - Learning something new: a tutorial , then explanation . - Trying to get a task done: a how-to , then the reference for each function it uses. - Debugging, or checking an edge case: the reference , always. Other sources you will meet Source Good for Watch out for --- --- --- Specifications and standards (the C++ standard, RFCs, file format specs) the final word on what is allowed dense, precise language (milestone 4) Header files and source code what really exists, in the version you have no explanations, easy to misread (lesson 4.03) Doc comments in code ( /// , docstrings) quick help in your editor may be short or out of date Release notes and changelogs what changed between versions easy to skip, costly when you do (lesson 5.03) Examples and samples seeing the pieces used together usually skip error handling (lesson 5.01) Q&A sites, forums, blog posts, AI answers quick pointers to the right function may be old, wrong, or for another version; confirm against the reference Treat the last row as leads, not facts : they tell you where to look, and the reference page tells you whether it is true. Where documentation lives For the languages and platforms in this course: - C++ standard library : cppreference.com (community reference), the standard itself for the final word. - Windows : Microsoft Learn (learn.microsoft.com), the Win32 and C runtime references. - Python : docs.python.org, the library reference and the language reference. - JavaScript : MDN Web Docs for the language and browser APIs, nodejs.org/docs for Node. - Unix-like systems : man pages ( man 2 open ). - Libraries : their own site, README, and headers. Bookmark the reference for each language you use. Searching the web for every question costs time and often lands on an old forum answer instead of the reference.

title: Implement it from the page
body: Two functions are documented below in the style of a reference page (lesson 1.02). Implement them so they behave exactly as described, edge cases included. slice cpp-norun std::string slice(const std::string& s, std::size_t pos, std::size_t count = std::string::npos); Returns the part of s that starts at pos and is count characters long, or as many as there are if fewer than count remain. - Return value : the characters in the range pos, pos + n) , where n is the smaller of count and s.size() - pos . When pos == s.size() the result is empty. - Exceptions : throws std::out_of_range if pos s.size() . lastChars cpp-norun std::string lastChars(const std::string& s, std::size_t count); Returns the last count characters of s . If count is at least s.size() , returns all of s . Never throws (except std::bad_alloc ).

title: 1.02  Anatomy of a Reference Page
body: The sections nearly every reference page has - synopsis, description, parameters, return value, errors, complexity, notes, requirements, examples and see also - what each one tells you, and the order to read them in when you have a question. The same shape everywhere Reference pages from cppreference, Microsoft, Python, MDN and man pages look different, but they share a structure. Once you know it, you can read any of them quickly. Here is a reference page for an imaginary function, written in the usual style. trim_left (sample page) Declared in header <textutil.h cpp-norun std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " \t\n"); // (1) std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, char c); // (2) Removes leading characters from s . 1. Removes every leading character that appears in chars . 2. Removes every leading character equal to c . Parameters - s : the text to trim - chars : the set of characters to remove; if empty, nothing is removed - c : the character to remove Return value A copy of s without the removed characters. If every character is removed, an empty string. Exceptions May throw std::bad_alloc if allocation fails. Complexity Linear in the size of s times the size of chars . Notes Characters are compared as bytes; multi-byte UTF-8 sequences in chars are treated as separate bytes. Example trim_left(" hello ") returns "hello " . See also trim_right , trim The sections Section Tells you Read it for --- --- --- Name and header / module what to include or import getting it to compile Synopsis / syntax every overload with exact types which version you are calling Description what it does, often per overload the main behaviour Parameters meaning and allowed values of each what you may pass Return value what comes back, in every case handling the result Errors / exceptions how failure is reported handling failure Complexity how cost grows choosing between options Notes / remarks surprises, edge cases, history the bugs you have not had yet Requirements / availability version, platform, library to link will it work where you ship Example the function in use a starting point (not production code) See also related functions finding a better fit Reading order Do not read a reference page top to bottom like a story. Go to the section that answers your question, then check the ones that could change the answer: 1. Synopsis : find the overload you are calling. With default arguments and overloads, trim_left(s, 'x') calls (2), not (1) with a one-character string. 2. Description and Parameters : what it does with your arguments, including the edge values (empty, zero, null, negative, too large). 3. Return value and Errors : every outcome you must handle. 4. Notes : always skim them. This is where pages hide "not thread-safe", "the result is not null-terminated", "deprecated", and "behaviour changed in version 3". 5. Requirements : once, before you rely on it. Words that matter Reference pages are written carefully, so small words carry meaning: - "must" , "shall" : a rule for you ; breaking it is an error, often undefined behaviour (lesson 1.04). - "may" : the function is allowed to do this. "May throw" means you must be ready for it even if you have never seen it happen. - "unspecified" : one of several results, with no promise which. "implementation-defined" : the compiler or library chooses and documents it. - "if ... otherwise" : two cases; check which applies. - "the behaviour is undefined" : anything can happen, including appearing to work.

title: The trim family
body:
Lesson 1.02 shows a reference page for trim_left . Implement it, and its "see also" functions trim_right and trim , exactly as documented: cpp-norun std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " 	
"); // (1) std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, char c); // (2) std::string trim_right(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " 	
"); // (3) std::string trim_right(std::string_view s, char c); // (4) std::string trim(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " 	
"); // (5) std::string trim(std::string_view s, char c); // (6) 1. Removes every leading character that appears in chars . If chars is empty, nothing is removed. 2. Removes every leading character equal to c . 3. and 4. are the same at the end of s . 5. and 6. remove from both ends. Return value : a copy of s without the removed characters; an empty string if every character is removed. Characters are compared as single bytes.

title: 1.03  Reading Signatures
body: Decoding the declarations at the top of C++ reference pages - parameter and return types, const, references and pointers, default arguments, overload sets, templates and their named requirements, noexcept and nodiscard - so a signature tells you how to call a function before you read a word of prose. A signature is a summary The declaration at the top of a reference page already answers most questions: what you pass, what you get back, what may be changed, and what may fail. Learn to read it first. cpp-norun nodiscard std::size_t count_words(const std::string& text, char separator = ' ') noexcept; Read it piece by piece: Piece Means --- --- nodiscard ignoring the result is almost certainly a bug; the compiler warns std::size_t returns a count, never negative const std::string& text reads your string without copying it and without changing it char separator = ' ' a default argument: you may leave it out noexcept never throws an exception Parameters: who owns what, who changes what Parameter type Meaning for the caller --- --- T (by value) the function gets its own copy; yours is untouched const T& read-only access to yours, no copy T& an output or in-out parameter : your object may be changed T&& the function may take over (move from) your object const T read-only access through a pointer; check the docs whether null is allowed T may be changed through the pointer; check whether null is allowed std::string_view , std::span<const T a read-only view; the function will not keep it after returning (unless it says so) std::unique_ptr<T by value the function takes ownership A non-const reference or pointer is the strongest signal on the page: something of yours changes. Find out what. Overload sets Many functions come as a numbered set of overloads. cppreference shows them as (1) , (2) ..., each with its own description: cpp-norun iterator insert(const_iterator pos, const T& value); // (1) iterator insert(const_iterator pos, size_type count, const T& value); // (3) template<class InputIt iterator insert(const_iterator pos, InputIt first, InputIt last); // (4) iterator insert(const_iterator pos, std::initializer_list<T list); // (5) The compiler picks one from your arguments, and the surprises come from conversions: v.insert(v.begin(), 3, 7) inserts three sevens (3), not 3 and 7. Identify the overload you are calling before reading the description. Templates and named requirements Generic functions are templates, and the names of their parameters are documentation: cpp-norun template<class InputIt, class T InputIt find(InputIt first, InputIt last, const T& value); template<class RandomIt, class Compare void sort(RandomIt first, RandomIt last, Compare comp); InputIt and RandomIt refer to named requirements : an input iterator can only be read once going forward; a random-access iterator can jump anywhere (like a vector's, unlike a list's). So std::sort on a std::list fails to compile, and the signature already told you. Compare must be a strict weak ordering : comp(a, a) must be false, which is why passing <= breaks std::sort in ways that are hard to see. Ranges and concepts (C++20) state requirements directly: cpp-norun template<std::random_access_iterator I, std::sentinel_for<I S, class Comp = std::ranges::less requires std::sortable<I, Comp constexpr I sort(I first, S last, Comp comp = {}); Long, but each line is a rule about what you may pass. Return types - bool : success or a yes/no answer; check which. - An iterator : often "end" means "not found". - std::pair<iterator, bool : std::map::insert tells you where the element is and whether it was inserted. - std::optional<T : may be empty. - void : nothing to check, but failure may still be reported by exception. - auto or a long template type: read the Return value section.

title: An overload set
body: Implement the four overloads of countOf documented below (lesson 1.03). Read each overload's description: they do not all count the same way. cpp-norun std::size_t countOf(std::string_view text, char c); // (1) std::size_t countOf(std::string_view text, std::string_view word); // (2) std::size_t countOf(const std::vector<int & values, int value); // (3) template<class Pred std::size_t countOf(const std::vector<int & values, Pred pred); // (4) 1. The number of characters in text equal to c . 2. The number of non-overlapping occurrences of word in text , searching from the left: after a match, the search continues after the end of that match. If word is empty, the result is text.size() + 1 (an empty word is found before every character and at the end). 3. The number of elements equal to value . 4. The number of elements x for which pred(x) returns true. pred is called exactly once per element, in order. Complexity : (1), (3) and (4) are linear in the size of the input; (2) is at most linear in text.size() times word.size() .

title: 1.04  Preconditions and Undefined Behaviour
body: The contract a reference page describes - preconditions you must meet, what the function guarantees in return, what happens on failure - half-open ranges, the difference between checked and unchecked functions, exception guarantees, and why "the behaviour is undefined" is the most important sentence on a page. A contract Every reference page describes a contract between you and the function: - Preconditions : what must be true when you call it. Your responsibility. - Postconditions : what will be true afterwards, if you met the preconditions. The function's responsibility. - Failure behaviour : what happens when it cannot do its job even though you called it correctly (out of memory, file missing). Preconditions are often written as "must", "shall", "requires", "expects", or as a list of allowed values: " count must not exceed size() ", " first and last must form a valid range", "the pointer must not be null". Undefined behaviour When a page says "the behaviour is undefined if ..." , it means breaking that precondition voids the contract completely. The program may crash, return garbage, corrupt something far away, or work perfectly on your machine and fail on another. The compiler is even allowed to assume it never happens and optimise accordingly. cpp-norun std::vector<int v; int x{ v 0 }; // operator : undefined if the index is not less than size() int y{ v.at(0) }; // at(): checks, and throws std::out_of_range v.front(); // undefined on an empty vector Many libraries offer such pairs: an unchecked fast version whose misuse is undefined, and a checked version that reports misuse. The reference page tells you which one you are calling. (Debug builds of the Microsoft library add checks to many unchecked functions, which helps while testing but is not a guarantee.) So, for every function you call, ask: what are its preconditions, and how do I know they hold? Either they are guaranteed by the code around the call (you just checked !v.empty() ), or you check them first. Half-open ranges Almost every C++ library function that takes a range uses the half-open convention first, last) : first is included, last is not. So: - the number of elements is last - first ; - an empty range has first == last ; - "not found" is usually returned as last . The same idea appears as "position and count" ( substr(pos, count) ) and in Python's slices s start:stop . When a page says "the range pos, pos + count) ", read it exactly that way. What happens on failure Reference pages describe failure in one of a few ways (lesson 2.02 goes deeper): Style You see You do --- --- --- exception "Throws std::out_of_range if ..." catch it where you can handle it, or let it propagate error value "Returns -1 / nullptr / end() / an error code" check the result every time error state "sets errno ", "call GetLastError " read it immediately after the call precondition only "the behaviour is undefined if ..." make sure it never happens Exception guarantees Pages for C++ functions that can throw often say what state things are left in: - No-throw guarantee ( noexcept ): it never throws. - Strong guarantee : if it throws, nothing changed, as if it was never called. std::vector::push_back gives this (for most element types). - Basic guarantee : if it throws, everything is still valid, but may have changed. - No guarantee : the page will say so, or say nothing; assume the worst.

title: Keeping the contract
body: Implement three functions whose pages state preconditions, half-open ranges and an exception guarantee (lesson 1.04). cpp-norun std::size_t findIndex(const std::vector<int & v, int value); Returns the index of the first element equal to value , or v.size() if there is none (the "one past the end" convention). Never throws. cpp-norun std::size_t removeRange(std::vector<int & v, std::size_t first, std::size_t last); Removes the elements with indices in the half-open range first, last) and returns how many were removed. The elements after the range keep their order. - Preconditions (checked): first <= last and last <= v.size() . - Exceptions : throws std::out_of_range if a precondition does not hold; v is then unchanged. cpp-norun void appendAll(std::vector<std::string & dest, const std::vector<std::string & src, std::size_t maxTotal); Appends copies of every element of src to the end of dest , in order. - Exceptions : throws std::length_error if dest.size() + src.size() would be greater than maxTotal . - Exception guarantee : strong. If the function throws, for this or any other reason, dest is exactly as it was. - Note : src and dest may be the same vector; then dest ends up with its contents twice.

title: A string library built from its reference
match: A string library built from its reference
body:
You are given the reference pages of a small string library, modelled on Python's string methods. Implement every function so that it matches its page exactly . The tests check each edge case the pages describe, and nothing they do not. cpp std::vector<std::string splitWhitespace(std::string_view s, int maxSplit = -1); std::vector<std::string split(std::string_view s, std::string_view sep, int maxSplit = -1); std::string join(const std::vector<std::string & parts, std::string_view sep); std::string replaceAll(std::string_view s, std::string_view from, std::string_view to, int maxCount = -1); bool startsWith(std::string_view s, std::string_view prefix, std::size_t start = 0); std::vector<std::string splitLines(std::string_view s, bool keepEnds = false); Whitespace in this library means the six characters space, 	 , 
 ,  ,   and \v . splitWhitespace splits s into words separated by runs of whitespace. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored, so an empty or all-whitespace string gives an empty list . If maxSplit is zero or more, at most maxSplit splits are made: after that many words, the rest of the string, with its leading whitespace removed but its trailing whitespace kept, is the last element. A negative maxSplit means no limit. split splits s at every occurrence of sep , from the left. Consecutive separators produce empty strings between them, and a separator at either end produces an empty string there; an empty s gives a list holding one empty string. At most maxSplit splits are made when it is zero or more; the rest of the string is the last element. Throws std::invalid_argument if sep is empty. join returns the parts with sep between each pair; no parts give an empty string. replaceAll returns a copy of s with occurrences of from replaced by to , found from the left without overlapping; if maxCount is zero or more, only the first maxCount are replaced. If from is empty , it matches at the start of s , between every two characters and at the end, so replaceAll("abc", "", "-") is "-a-b-c-" and with maxCount 2 it is "-a-bc" . startsWith returns whether the part of s beginning at index start begins with prefix . If start is greater than s.size() the result is false, even for an empty prefix; if it equals s.size() , only an empty prefix matches. splitLines splits s at line boundaries, which in this library are 
 ,  and the pair 
 (one boundary). A line ending at the very end of s does not create an extra empty line, so "a
" gives one line and the empty string gives none. If keepEnds is true, each line keeps its boundary characters.

title: 2.01  Finding Your Way Around cppreference
body: How cppreference.com is organised - by header and by topic - the layout of a class page with its member tables and version markers, what a function page adds (possible implementation, defect reports, examples), how it relates to the C++ standard, and fast ways to land on the right page. The reference for C++ cppreference.com is the reference most C++ programmers use every day. It is written by volunteers, closely follows the C++ standard, and covers the language and the whole standard library, version by version. The standard itself (the ISO document, with free drafts at eel.is/c++draft) is the final word; cppreference is its readable map. Two ways in - By header : the "Standard library headers" page lists every header ( <vector , <string , <charconv ...) and what it declares. Use it when you know where something lives or want to see what a header offers. - By topic : the main page groups the library: containers, algorithms, strings, numerics, input/output, filesystem, concurrency and so on. Use it when you know what you want to do but not the name. The fastest route in practice is a web search with the site name and the exact name: cppreference std::from_chars , cppreference vector insert .
