A class page The page for a class such as std::vector is mostly tables: Part What it gives you --- --- declaration template<class T, class Allocator = std::allocator<T class vector; , and the header description what it is, its guarantees (contiguous storage), its requirements on T member types value_type , size_type , iterator ... member functions every member, grouped: element access, iterators, capacity, modifiers non-member functions operator== , std::erase , std::swap ... deduction guides, notes, example, see also as on any page Each row links to a page of its own. Markers such as (C++11) , (C++20) , (deprecated in C++17) , (removed in C++20) tell you which version a member belongs to (lesson 2.04). A member listed as (constexpr since C++20) works in older versions too, just not at compile time. A function page Function pages follow the anatomy of lesson 1.02, with a few extras: - Overloads numbered (1) , (2) ..., each with version markers, and the description refers to them by number. - Template parameter requirements : " InputIt must meet the requirements of LegacyInputIterator ", with a link explaining exactly what that means. - Return value and Exceptions sections that cover every overload. - Complexity stated precisely: "Exactly last - first applications of the predicate". - Possible implementation : a short version of the code. Excellent for understanding; but the real library may differ, so rely on the stated behaviour, not on the sample code. - Defect reports : corrections to the standard after publication ("LWG 2192: behaviour changed for ..."). If your compiler behaves differently from the page, look here. - Example : a complete program with its output. You can usually run it on Compiler Explorer with one click. Reading a page for real Here is how you would answer "does std::stoi accept leading spaces, and what happens with "12abc" ?": 1. Open the page for std::stoi . The signature shows int stoi(const std::string& str, std::size_t pos = nullptr, int base = 10); . 2. The description says it discards leading whitespace and then reads as many characters as form a valid number, like std::strtol . So "12abc" gives 12. 3. The pos parameter: if not null, it receives the number of characters processed. So you can tell that "abc" was left over. 4. Exceptions: std::invalid_argument if no conversion could be performed, std::out_of_range if the value does not fit. And the neighbour in "see also", std::from_chars , works differently: it never skips whitespace, never throws, does not accept a leading + , and reports both where it stopped and an error code. Same job, different contract; the pages tell you which you need. cpp include <charconv include <iostream include <string int main() { std::size_t used{ 0 }; std::cout << std::stoi(" 12abc", &used) << " used " << used << '\n'; const std::string text{ "+12" }; int value{ 0 }; const auto ptr, ec { std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value) }; std::cout << "from_chars on +12: " << (ec == std::errc{} ? "ok" : "failed") << '\n'; }

title: Two ways to read a number
match: Two ways to read a number
body: Lesson 2.01 compared std::stoi and std::from_chars . Use their reference pages to implement two functions with very different contracts. cpp-norun std::optional<int parseStrict(std::string_view text); struct Leading { std::optional<int value; std::size_t used; std::string error; }; Leading readLeadingInt(const std::string& text); parseStrict accepts exactly: an optional single + or - , then one or more decimal digits, and nothing else : no spaces anywhere, no other characters, nothing after the digits. The value must fit in an int . Anything else gives an empty optional. (Note that std::from_chars itself does not accept a leading + .) readLeadingInt behaves like std::stoi in base 10, and reports what happened instead of throwing: - Leading whitespace is skipped, then an optional sign and as many digits as follow are read; reading stops at the first other character. - On success: value holds the number, used the count of characters processed (whitespace included), error is empty. - If there is no number at the start: value empty, used 0, error is "no number" . - If the number does not fit in an int : value empty, used 0, error is "out of range" .

title: 2.02  Return Values and Error Reporting
body: The many ways standard library functions report their results - end iterators, npos, pairs with a bool, optional, error codes, exceptions and the paired throwing and non-throwing overloads of std::filesystem - and how to read each from the reference page and handle it correctly. Read the Return value section every time Two functions that look alike can report results in completely different ways. The Return value and Exceptions sections are where you find out. The common patterns in the standard library: Pattern Example "Not found" or failure looks like --- --- --- end iterator std::find , map::find the last / end() you passed or own npos std::string::find std::string::npos , the largest size_t pair with a bool map::insert , set::insert .second == false : already there; .first points to the existing one std::optional your own APIs, many libraries empty optional result struct std::from_chars ec != std::errc{} ; ptr says where it stopped exception vector::at , std::stoi , std::filesystem std::out_of_range , std::invalid_argument , filesystem_error bool std::filesystem::remove false: there was nothing to remove (not an error!) Insert, and what "inserted" means Maps have several ways to add an element, and their pages differ in one crucial detail: what happens when the key already exists . Call Key missing Key present --- --- --- m key = value inserts overwrites m.insert({key, value}) inserts does nothing ; returns {it, false} m.try_emplace(key, args...) inserts does nothing, and does not even build the value m.insert_or_assign(key, value) inserts, returns {it, true} overwrites, returns {it, false} m.at(key) throws std::out_of_range returns a reference A common bug: using insert to update a value. It compiles, runs, and silently keeps the old value; the page said so. Two overloads: throwing and not throwing std::filesystem offers most functions twice: cpp-norun std::uintmax_t file_size(const std::filesystem::path& p); // (1) std::uintmax_t file_size(const std::filesystem::path& p, std::error_code& ec) noexcept; // (2) (1) throws std::filesystem::filesystem_error on failure. (2) never throws: it sets ec and returns a documented value, here static_cast<std::uintmax_t (-1) . Use (2) where failure is expected and normal (a file that may not exist), (1) where failure means something is really wrong. Results that need two answers std::from_chars reports where it stopped and whether it worked : cpp include <charconv include <iostream include <string_view void show(std::string_view text) { int value{ -1 }; const auto result{ std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value) }; std::cout << '"' << text << "\": "; if (result.ec == std::errc::invalid_argument) std::cout << "no number"; else if (result.ec == std::errc::result_out_of_range) std::cout << "too big"; else std::cout << value << ", stopped after " << (result.ptr - text.data()) << " chars"; std::cout << '\n'; } int main() { show("42"); show("42px"); show("px"); show("99999999999"); } To accept only a whole string, you must check both: no error, and ptr reached the end. The page tells you this indirectly ("on success, ptr points at the first character not matching the pattern"); turning such sentences into checks is the skill. Errors you can ignore and errors you cannot Some outcomes look like failures but are normal: std::filesystem::remove returning false for a missing file, map::insert finding the key. Others look harmless but are bugs: discarding the result of a nodiscard function, or an std::stoi that read "12abc" as 12 when you expected an error. The page decides which is which, not your intuition.

title: Choosing the right map call
body: Implement a small inventory on top of std::map<std::string, int . Every member's page states what happens when the item already exists or is missing; the map member functions in lesson 2.02 differ in exactly those cases, so pick each one to match. cpp-norun class Inventory { public: bool addNew(const std::string& item, int count); bool set(const std::string& item, int count); int countOf(const std::string& item) const; bool take(const std::string& item, int n); std::size_t removeEmpty(); std::size_t size() const; std::vector<std::string items() const; }; - addNew : adds the item with count only if it is not there yet. Returns true if it was added. An existing item's count is not changed. - set : sets the item's count, adding the item if it is missing. Returns true if the item was new . - countOf : the item's count, or 0 if it is missing. Never adds an item. - take : if the item exists and has at least n , subtracts n and returns true. Otherwise returns false and changes nothing. An item that reaches 0 stays in the inventory. - removeEmpty : removes every item whose count is 0 and returns how many were removed. - size : the number of items. items : their names in sorted order.

title: 2.03  Complexity and Invalidation
body: Two promises every container page makes - how cost grows (constant, amortised constant, logarithmic, linear) and which iterators, pointers and references stay valid after each operation - how to read the invalidation rules, and the bugs that come from ignoring them. Complexity is a guarantee Every function page on cppreference ends its description with Complexity . It is not a hint, it is a promise the library must keep, and it decides which container and which function you choose: Phrase Means Example --- --- --- constant the same cost whatever the size vector::operator , vector::size amortised constant usually constant, occasionally expensive, constant on average vector::push_back (sometimes reallocates) logarithmic grows slowly, like a binary search map::find , std::lower_bound linear in n proportional to the size std::find , vector::insert in the middle average constant, worst linear hash tables unordered_map::find O(n log n) comparisons sorting std::sort Read the exact wording: "linear in the distance between pos and the end" (inserting near the end of a vector is cheap), "exactly N applications of the predicate" (you can count on side effects happening exactly once each). Invalidation: when your iterators go bad Iterators, pointers and references into a container can become invalid when the container changes. Using an invalid one is undefined behaviour (lesson 1.04): it may read freed memory, read the wrong element, or crash. Each modifying function's page says what it invalidates, and the container pages have a summary table. For the containers you use most: Container Operation Invalidated --- --- --- vector , string push_back , insert , reserve if capacity changes all iterators, pointers, references vector , string insert / push_back without reallocation those at or after the insertion point (and end() ) vector erase those at or after the erased element deque insert at either end all iterators, but not references list , map , set insert nothing list , map , set erase only the erased element unordered_map insert causing a rehash all iterators, but not references The classic bugs cpp-norun // 1. Growing a vector while iterating over it for (int x : v) if (x % 2 == 0) v.push_back(x); // push_back may reallocate: the loop's iterators dangle // 2. Keeping a reference across a push_back int& first{ v 0 }; v.push_back(7); // may reallocate std::cout << first; // may read freed memory // 3. Erasing in a loop the wrong way for (auto it{ v.begin() }; it != v.end(); ++it) if ( it < 0) v.erase(it); // 'it' is invalid after erase; ++it is undefined The fixes come straight from the pages: - erase returns an iterator to the element after the erased one: it = v.erase(it); and only ++it when you did not erase. - Better still, std::erase_if(v, pred) (C++20) removes all matching elements in one linear pass. - For growing while reading, loop over indices up to the original size, or build the new elements in a separate vector and append them afterwards. - reserve before taking pointers, if the page's guarantee is what you need: "no reallocation takes place until the size exceeds the capacity". Microsoft's debug library checks many of these and stops the program with a debug assertion about an invalid or incompatible iterator. The release build does not check: the bug is still there, just silent.

title: Fixing invalidation bugs
body: Each function below was first written like this, and each version has undefined behaviour that the container's reference page warns about (lesson 2.03). Do not copy them; write correct versions with the documented results. cpp-norun // 1. Grows the vector while a range-for is walking it. void appendSquares(std::vector<int & v) { for (int x : v) v.push_back(x x); } // 2. Inserts through an iterator, then keeps using the old iterator. void duplicateEvens(std::vector<int & v) { for (auto it{ v.begin() }; it != v.end(); ++it) if ( it % 2 == 0) { v.insert(it + 1, it); ++it; } } // 3. Uses an iterator after erasing it. std::size_t removeNegatives(std::vector<int & v) { std::size_t n{ 0 }; for (auto it{ v.begin() }; it != v.end(); ++it) if ( it < 0) { v.erase(it); ++n; } return n; } // 4. The same, on a map. std::size_t removeShortKeys(std::map<std::string, int & m, std::size_t minLength) { std::size_t n{ 0 }; for (auto it{ m.begin() }; it != m.end(); ++it) if (it- first.size() < minLength) { m.erase(it); ++n; } return n; } What each must do: 1. appendSquares appends the square of every element that was in v when it was called, in order: {1, 2, 3} becomes {1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 9} . 2. duplicateEvens inserts a copy of each even element directly after it: {1, 2, 3, 4} becomes {1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4} . 3. removeNegatives removes every negative element, keeping the others in order, and returns how many it removed. 4. removeShortKeys removes every entry whose key is shorter than minLength and returns how many it removed.
