title: A vector built to its specification
match: A vector built to its specification
where: The C++ Standard Library Reference projects
body: Implement IntVector , a growable array of int , from the reference below. It follows std::vector closely, but its pages pin down details the standard leaves open, such as exactly how capacity grows, so the tests can check them. Manage the memory yourself ( std::unique_ptr<int or new / delete ); do not use std::vector inside it. cpp class IntVector { public: static constexpr std::size_t maxSize() { return std::size_t{ 1 } << 28; } IntVector(); explicit IntVector(std::size_t count, int value = 0); IntVector(std::initializer_list<int values); IntVector(const IntVector& other); IntVector(IntVector&& other) noexcept; IntVector& operator=(const IntVector& other); IntVector& operator=(IntVector&& other) noexcept; std::size_t size() const; std::size_t capacity() const; bool empty() const; int data(); int& operator (std::size_t i); int& at(std::size_t i); int& front(); int& back(); void push_back(int value); void pop_back(); std::size_t insert(std::size_t pos, int value); std::size_t insert(std::size_t pos, std::size_t count, int value); std::size_t erase(std::size_t pos); std::size_t erase(std::size_t first, std::size_t last); void resize(std::size_t n, int value = 0); void reserve(std::size_t n); void shrinkToFit(); void clear(); bool operator==(const IntVector& other) const; }; Construction. The default vector is empty with capacity 0. IntVector(count, value) holds count copies of value ; the initializer-list constructor holds the listed values (so IntVector{ 3 } holds one element, 3, while IntVector(3) holds three zeros). In all three, capacity equals size. A copy has the same elements and capacity equal to its size; copies are independent. After a move , the target has the source's elements and capacity, and the source is empty with capacity 0. Access. operator , front , back and pop_back do not check: calling them out of range or on an empty vector is undefined behaviour (never tested). at throws std::out_of_range if i = size() . data returns a pointer to the first element. Growth. A reallocation moves the elements to a new block of a given capacity. Reallocation happens only where stated below; otherwise pointers from data() stay valid. Member Behaviour Capacity --- --- --- push_back appends if full, becomes max(1, 2 × capacity) insert(pos, value) inserts before index pos ; returns pos if full, as push_back insert(pos, count, value) inserts count copies before pos ; returns pos ; count 0 changes nothing if size + count capacity , becomes max(2 × capacity, size + count) erase(pos) removes element pos ; returns pos unchanged erase(first, last) removes first, last) ; returns first unchanged resize(n, value) shrinks to n , or grows filling with value if n capacity , becomes n reserve(n) nothing else if n capacity , becomes n ; never shrinks shrinkToFit nothing else becomes size clear removes all elements unchanged Errors. Both insert s throw std::out_of_range if pos size() . erase(pos) throws std::out_of_range if pos = size() ; erase(first, last) if first last or last size() . reserve throws std::length_error if n maxSize() . In every case the vector is unchanged when they throw. Comparison. Two vectors are equal if they have the same size and the same elements in order; capacity does not matter.

title: 3.01  A Win32 Reference Page
body: Reading a Microsoft Learn page for a Windows API function from top to bottom - the syntax block and its types, parameter directions, the exact wording of the return value, the remarks where the surprises live, and the requirements table with header, library, DLL and minimum Windows version - using GetModuleFileNameW as the example. Where Windows documents itself Every Windows API function has a page on Microsoft Learn (learn.microsoft.com), under "Windows App Development Win32 API" or by searching the function name. The pages share one layout, and once you know it you can use functions you have never seen before. The Win32 course uses these functions; this milestone is about reading their pages precisely. We will read the page for GetModuleFileNameW , which gives the full path of an executable or DLL. What follows describes the page in our own words, section by section. Syntax cpp-norun DWORD GetModuleFileNameW( in, optional HMODULE hModule, out LPWSTR lpFilename, in DWORD nSize ); - Types are Windows typedefs: DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned integer, LPWSTR a pointer to a wide (UTF-16) string, HMODULE a handle to a loaded module. The "Windows Data Types" page lists them all. - Directions in brackets: in you provide, out the function fills, in, out both, and optional means you may pass null. (In headers these appear as SAL annotations; lesson 3.02.) - Names use the old Hungarian prefixes, which are worth decoding: lp long pointer, n or cch a count of characters, cb a count of bytes, h a handle, dw a DWORD , b a BOOL . Parameters The page describes each parameter. For this function: - hModule : the module whose path you want; null means the executable of the current process . - lpFilename : the buffer that receives the path. - nSize : the size of that buffer in characters ( WCHAR s), not bytes. "Characters, not bytes" is the kind of detail that causes buffer overruns when missed: a buffer of MAX_PATH wchar_t s is 520 bytes, and passing sizeof(buffer) would claim twice the real size. Return value This section must be read word by word. Paraphrased, it says: - On success , the return value is the length of the string copied, in characters, not including the terminating null. - If the buffer is too small , the path is truncated to nSize characters including the null, the function returns nSize , and the last error is set to ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER . - On failure , the return value is 0 ; call GetLastError for the reason. So a return value equal to nSize is not success; it is a truncated result. Code that only checks for 0 silently uses a cut-off path. The correct pattern, a loop that grows the buffer, is the first practice task. Remarks The remarks hold the surprises: which module handle to use for a DLL, what happens when the module was loaded from a long path, and an old Windows XP note that the result may not be null-terminated when truncated. Older pages often keep notes like this about past versions; check whether they apply to the systems you support. Requirements A table at the bottom: Requirement Value (summarised) --- --- Minimum supported client / server the first Windows version that has the function Header libloaderapi.h (include windows.h ) Library Kernel32.lib , to link against DLL Kernel32.dll , where it lives at run time There is also the line " Unicode and ANSI names : GetModuleFileNameW (Unicode) and GetModuleFileNameA (ANSI)". The plain name GetModuleFileName is a macro that picks one depending on whether UNICODE is defined. Call the W versions explicitly with wide strings: the A versions convert through the current code page and lose characters.

title: The grow-until-it-fits loop
body: Lesson 3.01 read the return value of GetModuleFileNameW : success returns the length without the null, a truncated result returns exactly the buffer size, and failure returns 0. The starter contains FakeGetModuleFileName , a stand-in with exactly that contract (and the tests change the path it reports). Do not change it. Write the caller: cpp-norun std::optional<std::wstring modulePath(); modulePath returns the full path, or an empty optional if the function fails or the path does not fit even in the largest buffer: 1. Start with a buffer of 260 characters ( MAX_PATH ). 2. Call FakeGetModuleFileName(buffer, size) . 3. A result of 0 is a failure: return an empty optional. 4. A result equal to size means the path was truncated : double the size, but to no more than 32 768 characters, and call again. If the call with 32 768 characters is still truncated, return an empty optional. 5. Any other result is the length of the path: return those characters.

title: 3.02  SAL Annotations and Buffer Sizes
body: The source annotation language in Windows headers - _In_, _Out_, _Inout_, _opt_, _Out_writes_ and friends - what each promises about a parameter, characters versus bytes, and the three patterns Windows uses for buffers whose size you do not know in advance. Annotations in the headers Open a Windows header and the declarations look like this: cpp-norun DWORD GetEnvironmentVariableW( _In_opt_ LPCWSTR lpName, _Out_writes_to_opt_(nSize, return + 1) LPWSTR lpBuffer, _In_ DWORD nSize); The _In_ , _Out_writes_... markers are SAL , the Source Annotation Language. They compile to nothing, but they document the contract precisely, and the compiler's code analysis ( /analyze ) checks calls against them. The documentation's in , out and optional come from the same information. Annotation Means --- --- _In_ read only; must not be null _In_opt_ read only; may be null _Out_ the function writes it; must not be null _Inout_ read and then written _In_reads_(n) reads n elements _In_reads_bytes_(n) reads n bytes _Out_writes_(n) writes up to n elements (the buffer must hold n ) _Out_writes_to_(n, count) buffer holds n , the function writes count _Outptr_ receives a pointer the function allocates or returns _Ret_maybenull_ the return value may be null _Success_(expr) the out parameters are valid only when expr is true _Out_writes_to_opt_(nSize, return + 1) above reads: the buffer may be null; it holds nSize characters; on success the function writes "return value + 1" characters (the string plus its null). Characters or bytes Windows counts in two units, and the names and annotations tell you which: - cch... , nSize "in characters", _Out_writes_(n) on a WCHAR : count wchar_t s . - cb... , "in bytes", _Out_writes_bytes_(n) : count bytes . A wide string of 10 characters plus its null is 22 bytes. Mixing them is one of the most common Windows bugs, either an overrun (bytes passed where characters were expected) or a truncation (the other way round). Three patterns for unknown sizes Often you cannot know how big the result will be. Windows functions use one of three patterns, and the Return value section tells you which: 1. Ask for the size first. Call with a null buffer (or too small a one); the function returns the size needed, then you allocate and call again. GetEnvironmentVariableW : if the buffer is too small, it returns the size required including the null; on success it returns the length excluding the null. Those two different meanings of the return value are how you tell the cases apart. 2. Grow until it fits. Some functions never tell you the size; they truncate. GetModuleFileNameW (lesson 3.01) returns nSize when truncated, so you double the buffer and try again. 3. Size in, size out. A pointer parameter holds the buffer size going in and receives the size needed or used coming out, often with the error ERROR_MORE_DATA (234) when the buffer was too small. The registry function RegQueryValueExW works this way with lpcbData , in bytes. Passing a null data pointer with a valid size pointer asks only for the size. In all three, the value can change between the calls : an environment variable or a registry value may be rewritten by another thread or process. Robust code loops: query, allocate, fetch, and if it is still too small, go round again.

title: Ask for the size, then fetch
match: Ask for the size, then fetch
body: FakeGetVariable in the starter imitates GetEnvironmentVariableW (lesson 3.02). Its page, in short: cpp-norun DWORD FakeGetVariable(const wchar_t name, wchar_t buffer, DWORD size); - If the variable does not exist: returns 0 , and g_lastError is ERROR_ENVVAR_NOT_FOUND (203). - If buffer is null or size is too small for the value and its terminating null: returns the size needed, including the null . The buffer is not written. - Otherwise: copies the value and a null, returns the length not including the null , and sets g_lastError to 0. An existing variable with an empty value therefore returns 0 here, with g_lastError 0. Other code may change the variable between your calls (the tests do, through g_beforeCall ). Write: cpp-norun std::optional<std::wstring readVariable(const std::wstring& name); It returns the value, an empty string for an existing empty variable, or an empty optional if the variable does not exist. Ask for the size with a null buffer first, then fetch; if the fetch reports that the buffer is too small (the value grew), go round again with the new size. If the variable disappears between the calls, the result is an empty optional.

title: 3.03  GetLastError, HRESULT and NTSTATUS
body: The three error systems you meet in Windows documentation - the per-thread last error, COM's HRESULT with its severity, facility and code bits, and the kernel's NTSTATUS - how a page tells you which one a function uses, how to decode each, and how to turn them into readable messages. Which system does this function use? The Return value section always names it. The common phrases: The page says System --- --- "If the function fails, the return value is zero (or NULL , INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE ). To get extended error information, call GetLastError ." last error "Returns ERROR_SUCCESS if successful, or a system error code." (registry functions) the error code is the return value; GetLastError is not used "If this function succeeds, it returns S_OK . Otherwise, it returns an HRESULT error code." HRESULT "Returns STATUS_SUCCESS or an error status" (native and driver APIs) NTSTATUS Note the second row: some functions return the error code directly, and calling GetLastError after them gives an unrelated value. The last error GetLastError returns a number kept per thread , set by the last function that chose to set it. Rules from the pages: - Read it immediately after the failed call; almost anything else may overwrite it. - Only read it when the page says the function failed. Many functions do not clear it on success, and some set it even on success (the page says so when it matters: CreateMutexW sets ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS while succeeding, which is how you detect an existing mutex). - The values are the system error codes : 2 ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND , 5 ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED , 87 ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER , 122 ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER , 234 ERROR_MORE_DATA ... listed on the "System Error Codes" pages. HRESULT COM and many newer APIs return an HRESULT , a 32-bit value with fields: text bit 31 severity: 0 success, 1 failure bits 16-26 facility: which area produced it (7 = Win32, 4 = ITF ...) bits 0-15 code So negative means failure : test with SUCCEEDED(hr) ( hr = 0 ) and FAILED(hr) ( hr < 0 ), never with hr == S_OK alone, because S_FALSE (1) is a success that means "it worked, but the answer is no". Values you will see constantly: Name Value Means --- --- --- S_OK 0x00000000 success S_FALSE 0x00000001 success, negative answer E_FAIL 0x80004005 unspecified failure E_INVALIDARG 0x80070057 an argument was invalid E_OUTOFMEMORY 0x8007000E allocation failed E_ACCESSDENIED 0x80070005 access denied Notice E_INVALIDARG is 0x8007 followed by 0x0057 : facility 7 (Win32) and code 87, ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER . The macro HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(x) builds such values: for a positive error code it ORs in the failure bit and facility 7; zero and values that are already HRESULT s (zero or negative) pass through unchanged. So when you see 0x8007xxxx , the low 16 bits are a plain Win32 error code you can look up. NTSTATUS The kernel and ntdll use NTSTATUS , also 32 bits, but with two severity bits at the top: Top two bits Severity Example --- --- --- 00 success STATUS_SUCCESS = 0 01 informational 0x40000000 and up 10 warning STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW = 0x80000005 11 error STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION = 0xC0000005 That last one is familiar: a crashing program's exit code 0xC0000005 (lesson 1.03 of the Processes and Communication course) is an NTSTATUS . Turning codes into messages FormatMessageW with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM turns a system error code (and many HRESULT s) into the text shown on the System Error Codes page. Log the number and the text: the number is searchable, the text is readable. Visual Studio's "Error Lookup" tool and the watch-window format @err,hr do the same while debugging.

title: Decoding Windows error values
body: Implement the decoding that lesson 3.03 describes, for HRESULT and NTSTATUS values. cpp-norun using HRESULT = std::int32_t; bool succeeded(HRESULT hr); bool failed(HRESULT hr); HRESULT hresultFromWin32(std::uint32_t error); struct HrParts { bool failure; unsigned facility; unsigned code; }; HrParts splitHresult(HRESULT hr); std::string describeHresult(HRESULT hr); std::string ntSeverity(std::uint32_t status); - succeeded is true for zero and positive values; failed for negative ones. - hresultFromWin32 : if the error code, read as an HRESULT , is zero or negative, it is returned unchanged; otherwise the result keeps its low 16 bits, with facility 7 and the failure bit set. - splitHresult : failure is bit 31, facility bits 16 to 26, code bits 0 to 15. - describeHresult returns, in this order of preference: the name for S_OK , S_FALSE , E_FAIL , E_INVALIDARG , E_OUTOFMEMORY or E_ACCESSDENIED (values in lesson 3.03); for any other failure with facility 7, Win32 error N with the code in decimal; otherwise HRESULT 0x and 8 upper-case hex digits. - ntSeverity returns success , information , warning or error from the top two bits.

title: 3.04  Structures, Flags and Versions
body: Reading the parts of Windows pages that describe data - structures whose first member gives their size, reserved fields, zero-initialisation, flag parameters that combine with OR versus parameters that take one value, mutually exclusive flags, and version requirements and _WIN32_WINNT. Structures that know their size Many Windows structures start with a member holding their own size: cb , cbSize , dwSize , dwOSVersionInfoSize . The page always says the same thing about it in some form: "The size of the structure, in bytes. You must set this member before calling the function." cpp-norun STARTUPINFOW si{}; // zero every member si.cb = sizeof(si); // then the size PROCESS_INFORMATION pi{}; CreateProcessW(..., &si, &pi); Why? Structures grow in new Windows versions. The size tells the function which version of the structure you compiled against , so it reads and writes only the members you have. A function that receives a size it does not know fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER rather than writing past the end of your memory. Forgetting to set it usually makes the call fail; setting it to the size of the wrong structure can make it write outside your object. Two more habits from the same pages: - Zero-initialise every structure ( {} ): members you do not set must usually be zero or null, and reserved members "must be zero" even though nothing uses them yet. Garbage in a reserved field is a bug waiting for the Windows version that starts using it. - Read each member's description for whether it is in (you fill it), out (the function fills it) or both. The same structure is often used both ways. Flags or a single value Parameters with named constants come in two kinds, and the wording says which: - "This parameter can be one or more of the following values": flags , combined with . Each value is a separate bit: FILE_SHARE_READ FILE_SHARE_WRITE . - "This parameter can be one of the following values": an enumeration . Combining values is wrong, and since they are often consecutive numbers ( CREATE_NEW 1, CREATE_ALWAYS 2, OPEN_EXISTING 3, OPEN_ALWAYS 4, TRUNCATE_EXISTING 5), OR-ing two gives a third, unintended one. CREATE_NEW CREATE_ALWAYS is 3, which is OPEN_EXISTING . Flag lists often come with rules: "cannot be combined with", "requires", "if this flag is specified, the x parameter must be ...". When a page has such rules, the function usually checks them and fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER ; some combinations are just documented as undefined. Versions The Requirements table gives the minimum Windows version. To use a function or structure member from a newer version, the headers must be told your target, through _WIN32_WINNT (or NTDDI_VERSION ), defined before including windows.h : cpp-norun define _WIN32_WINNT 0x0A00 // Windows 10 include <windows.h If you target an older version than a function needs, the declaration is hidden and the code does not compile; if you call a function your users' Windows does not have, the program fails to start, so for optional features look the function up at run time with GetProcAddress (the DLLs course covers this). Some members are documented "Windows 10, version 1703 and later": the structure is the same size, but older systems ignore the member.

title: Sized structures and flag rules
body: This time you are on the other side of the page: implement two functions of an imaginary system API so that they behave as their documentation (below) promises, the way lesson 3.04 describes. fillInfo cpp-norun struct InfoV1 { std::uint32_t cbSize; std::uint32_t processors; std::uint32_t pageSize; }; struct InfoV2 { std::uint32_t cbSize; std::uint32_t processors; std::uint32_t pageSize; std::uint32_t flags; std::uint64_t totalMemory; }; bool fillInfo(void info); info points to an InfoV1 or an InfoV2 whose cbSize the caller has set. The function fills in every member of that version except cbSize , using the constants kProcessors , kPageSize , kFlags and kTotalMemory , and returns true with g_lastError set to 0. It never writes beyond cbSize bytes. If info is null, or cbSize is not the size of one of the two structures, it returns false with g_lastError set to ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER and writes nothing. (The memory may not be aligned for the structure: copy bytes rather than casting the pointer.) checkOpenFlags and checkDisposition cpp-norun std::uint32_t checkOpenFlags(std::uint32_t flags); // "one or more of the following values" std::uint32_t checkDisposition(std::uint32_t value); // "one of the following values" flags combines FLAG_READ (0x1), FLAG_WRITE (0x2), FLAG_CREATE (0x4), FLAG_TRUNCATE (0x8), FLAG_APPEND (0x10) and FLAG_EXCLUSIVE (0x20). checkOpenFlags returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER if any other bit is set, if neither FLAG_READ nor FLAG_WRITE is set, if FLAG_TRUNCATE or FLAG_APPEND is set without FLAG_WRITE , if FLAG_TRUNCATE and FLAG_APPEND are both set, or if FLAG_EXCLUSIVE is set without FLAG_CREATE ; otherwise ERROR_SUCCESS (0). checkDisposition accepts exactly one of the values 1 to 5 ( CREATE_NEW to TRUNCATE_EXISTING ) and returns ERROR_SUCCESS ; anything else gives ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER .

title: A registry-style API built to its documentation
match: A registry-style API built to its documentation
body: Implement ValueStore , a small store of named values whose functions follow the conventions of the Windows registry API: error codes as return values, sizes in bytes passed through pointers, null meaning "I only want the size", and ERROR_MORE_DATA for buffers that are too small (lessons 3.01 to 3.04). The pages below are the whole contract; the tests check every sentence. cpp using DWORD = std::uint32_t; using LONG = std::int32_t; using BYTE = std::uint8_t; constexpr LONG ERROR_SUCCESS = 0, ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND = 2, ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER = 87, ERROR_MORE_DATA = 234, ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS = 259; constexpr DWORD REG_NONE = 0, REG_SZ = 1, REG_BINARY = 3, REG_DWORD = 4, REG_QWORD = 11; class ValueStore { public: LONG setValue(const wchar_t name, DWORD type, const BYTE data, DWORD cbData); LONG queryValue(const wchar_t name, DWORD type, BYTE data, DWORD cbData) const; LONG deleteValue(const wchar_t name); LONG enumValue(DWORD index, wchar_t name, DWORD cchName, DWORD type) const; DWORD count() const; }; Names. A null name and an empty name both mean the default value , whose name is the empty string. Names are compared ignoring the case of the letters A to Z , so Volume and VOLUME are the same value. A value keeps the spelling it was first created with. Names longer than 255 characters are rejected with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER . setValue creates the value or replaces an existing one's type and data (it keeps its place in the enumeration order; new values go at the end). It returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER , changing nothing, if data is null while cbData is not 0; if the type is REG_DWORD and cbData is not 4; if the type is REG_QWORD and cbData is not 8; or if the type is REG_SZ and cbData is odd. For REG_SZ , data that does not end with a null wchar_t (including empty data) is stored with one added. Any other type stores the bytes exactly. Returns ERROR_SUCCESS . queryValue : - If the value does not exist: ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND , nothing written. - If data is not null but cbData is null: ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER , nothing written. - If type is not null, it receives the value's type (also when the result is ERROR_MORE_DATA ). - If data is null: when cbData is not null it receives the size of the data in bytes; returns ERROR_SUCCESS . (Both null just checks that the value exists.) - If cbData is smaller than the data: cbData receives the size needed and the result is ERROR_MORE_DATA ; the buffer is not written. - Otherwise the data is copied, cbData receives its size, and the result is ERROR_SUCCESS . deleteValue removes the value, or returns ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND . Later values move up one place in the enumeration. enumValue gives the name (and, if type is not null, the type) of the value at index , in enumeration order. name and cchName must not be null ( ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER ). An index at or past the end gives ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS . cchName is the buffer size in characters, including the null ; if the name and its null do not fit, cchName receives the size needed including the null, and the result is ERROR_MORE_DATA . Otherwise the name and a null are copied, cchName receives the length without the null, and the result is ERROR_SUCCESS . count is the number of values.

title: 4.01  Python's Documentation
body: Finding and reading docs.python.org - the tutorial, library reference and language reference - Python signature notation with defaults, / and , the version notes that say when behaviour changed, how a page describes exceptions, and help(), docstrings and type stubs from inside Python. Three books in one site docs.python.org holds several documents, and knowing which to open saves time: Document For --- --- Tutorial learning the language from the start Library Reference built-in functions, types ( str , list , dict ) and every standard module: the one you will use most Language Reference the exact rules of the syntax and semantics, like the C++ standard HOWTOs how-to guides on single topics: sorting, logging, regular expressions What's New per version, what was added and changed Use the version selector at the top: pages differ between Python 3.9 and 3.13, and search engines often land on an old one. Reading a Python signature Python pages write signatures in Python syntax: python-norun str.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1) sorted(iterable, /, , key=None, reverse=False) int(x, /, base=10) - name=value : a default ; you may leave the argument out. - A / marks the end of positional-only parameters: sorted(iterable=x) is an error; you must write sorted(x) . - A marks the start of keyword-only parameters: sorted(x, None, True) is an error; you must write sorted(x, reverse=True) . - Older pages use brackets for optional arguments: range(start, stop , step ) . Defaults such as sep=None often stand for a different behaviour , not a value, and the description explains it. For str.split , sep=None means "split on runs of whitespace and drop empty strings", while any given separator means "split exactly at each occurrence, keeping empty strings". The project of milestone 1 implemented exactly this difference. What the description promises Python pages are prose more than tables, so read for these phrases: - "Raises ValueError if ..." , "If ... a TypeError is raised" : the exceptions to handle. - "Return a new list ..." versus "... in place" : sorted() returns a new list, list.sort() changes the list and returns None . Using x = x.sort() is a classic bug the page warns about. - "The result is guaranteed to be stable" , "CPython implementation detail: ..." : the first you may rely on; the second you may not, other Pythons can differ. - Exact edge rules: slicing s i:j:k documents what happens with negative and out-of-range indices and with a negative step (practice 4.01 implements them). Version notes Pages carry boxed notes that matter as much as the text: - Added in version 3.9. You cannot use it on 3.8. - Changed in version 3.7: for example, "dictionary order is guaranteed to be insertion order". Code relying on the new behaviour silently misbehaves on older versions. - Deprecated since version 3.12, will be removed in version 3.14. Plan to move away. From inside Python - help(str.split) prints the docstring, which usually summarises the page. - obj.__doc__ is the same text; your own functions get one when their first statement is a string literal. - Type hints and the typeshed stubs (what editors use for completion) show parameter and return types, which the prose sometimes leaves implicit. python-norun help(str.split) split(self, /, sep=None, maxsplit=-1) Return a list of the substrings in the string, using sep as the separator string. ...

title: Python's slice and division rules
body: Python's documentation defines slicing and integer division precisely, and both differ from C++. Implement them from these descriptions (summarised from the library and language references). Slices. s start:stop:step selects indices of a sequence of length len : cpp-norun std::vector<std::size_t sliceIndices(std::size_t length, std::optional<long start, std::optional<long stop, long step); 1. A step of 0 is an error: throw std::invalid_argument . 2. A missing start means the first index in the direction of travel: 0 for a positive step, len - 1 for a negative one. A missing stop means "past the end" in that direction: len for a positive step, and a position before index 0 for a negative step. 3. A given negative start or stop has len added to it. If it is still negative, it becomes 0 for a positive step, or the position before index 0 for a negative step. 4. A given start or stop at or beyond len becomes len for a positive step, or len - 1 for a negative step. 5. The result is start , start + step , start + 2 × step ... continuing while the index is before stop (less than it for a positive step, greater for a negative one). Floor division. Python's // rounds the quotient down (towards minus infinity), and % gives a result with the sign of the divisor , so that (a // b) b + a % b == a always holds. C++'s / and % truncate towards zero instead. cpp-norun long floorDiv(long a, long b); long floorMod(long a, long b); Both throw std::invalid_argument when b is 0 (Python raises ZeroDivisionError ).

title: 4.02  JavaScript, MDN and Node
body: Reading MDN Web Docs - syntax lines with optional parameters, return values and exceptions, the specification links and the browser compatibility tables - the ECMAScript specification behind them, and Node.js documentation with its stability index, callback and promise signatures and error codes. MDN Web Docs For JavaScript in the browser, the reference is MDN Web Docs (developer.mozilla.org), maintained by Mozilla with the other browser makers. Each page for a method follows a fixed layout: Section Contains --- --- Syntax every form of the call, one per line Parameters each parameter; optional ones marked Return value what comes back Exceptions TypeError , RangeError ... and when Description the behaviour in detail, including conversions Examples runnable snippets, often with live output Specifications a link to the exact section of the standard Browser compatibility a table of which browser version supports what The Syntax section lists each form separately instead of using brackets: js-norun parseInt(string) parseInt(string, radix) The traps are in the Description JavaScript converts types freely, and the Description section is where each method says how. Two famous examples, both clearly documented: - parseInt(string, radix) skips leading whitespace, reads an optional sign, and then as many valid digits as it can , ignoring the rest: parseInt("42px") is 42 and parseInt("1e3") is 1. Without a radix, a string starting with 0x is read as hexadecimal; with radix 10 it is not, so parseInt("0x1A", 10) is 0. A radix outside 2 to 36 gives NaN , and so does a string with no digits. Practice 4.02 implements these rules. - Array.prototype.sort() without a compare function converts the elements to strings and sorts them as text, so 10, 9, 1 .sort() gives 1, 10, 9 . The page says so in its first paragraph, and recommends passing (a, b) = a - b for numbers. Compatibility and Baseline The Browser compatibility table shows, per browser, the first version supporting each feature, with notes for partial support. Newer pages also show a Baseline badge: "widely available" means it has worked in all major browsers for a long time; "newly available" means only recent versions. Check it before using a new API in a site people visit with older browsers. The specification Behind MDN is the ECMAScript specification (tc39.es/ecma262) for the language and the WHATWG and W3C specifications for browser APIs. They are written as step-by-step algorithms ("1. Let S be ? ToString( string ). 2. Let R be ..."), which makes them precise and readable once you get used to them. MDN's Specifications section links straight to the right step list when you need the final word. Node.js documentation For JavaScript outside the browser, nodejs.org/docs has one page per module ( fs , http , path ...). Things to read for: - The Stability index next to each API: 0 Deprecated, 1 Experimental (may change or vanish), 2 Stable, 3 Legacy (kept, but there is a better way). Production code should stay on 2. - Signatures with types in a bulleted list: fs.readFile(path , options , callback) , where options can be a string or an object, and callback receives (err, data) . - Many modules come in three styles : callbacks ( fs.readFile ), promises ( fs/promises , await readFile(...) ), and synchronous ( fs.readFileSync , which blocks the whole program while it runs). - Errors carry a code such as ENOENT (no such file) or ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE , documented on the Errors page; check err.code , not the message text, which may change. - "Added in: v18.0.0" and History tables, like Python's version notes.

title: JavaScript's parseInt and default sort
body: Implement two JavaScript behaviours in C++, following the descriptions on their MDN pages (lesson 4.02) as summarised here. parseInt(string, radix) , with NaN represented by an empty optional: cpp-norun std::optional<double jsParseInt(std::string_view s, std::optional<int radix = std::nullopt); 1. Skip leading whitespace (here: space, \t , \n , \v , \f , \r ). 2. If the next character is - or + , remember the sign and skip it. 3. If radix is given and not 0: if it is below 2 or above 36 the result is NaN . If it is not 16, do not strip a 0x prefix in step 4. If radix is missing or 0, use 10. 4. Unless step 3 said not to, if the text now starts with 0x or 0X , skip those two characters and use radix 16. 5. Read the longest run of characters that are digits in the radix ( 0 - 9 , then a - z or A - Z for 10 to 35). Stop at the first character that is not; ignore the rest of the string. 6. If no digit was read, the result is NaN . Otherwise it is the sign times the value. Array.prototype.sort() without a compare function: cpp-norun std::vector<int jsDefaultSort(std::vector<int values); The elements are converted to strings ( -1 , 10 ...), compared as strings, character by character, and the sort is stable . The result is the elements in that order (still as numbers).

title: 4.03  Reading Headers and Source Code
body: What to do when the documentation is thin or missing - reading a library's header for its real declarations, defaults and doc comments, Doxygen tags, finding the implementation with Go to Definition, using a project's tests as examples, and reading the source of the standard library itself. When the docs are not enough Many libraries, especially small open-source ones, have a README and little else. Even good documentation has gaps. Then the code is the documentation, and it has one great advantage: it is exactly the version you are using. The usual order to look: 1. The header (or the module's public file): every declaration, with its exact types and defaults. 2. Doc comments in that header. 3. The project's tests : they show how the authors expect the API to be called, including edge cases. 4. The examples folder, if there is one. 5. The implementation , for what is still unclear. 6. The issue tracker : someone may have hit the same question; the answer may be "that is a bug". Reading a header A header is a contract summary. From this one you can learn a lot without seeing any code behind it: cpp-norun namespace tinyini { /// A parsed configuration file. class Config { public: /// Parses text . Returns std::nullopt on a malformed line and, if errorLine /// is not null, stores that line's number (1-based) there. static std::optional<Config parse(std::string_view text, int errorLine = nullptr); /// @return the value, or nullptr if the section or key does not exist. /// @note The pointer is valid until this Config is modified or destroyed. const std::string find(std::string_view section, std::string_view key) const; /// @return the value as an integer; std::nullopt if it is missing /// or is not a complete integer. std::optional<long long findInt(std::string_view section, std::string_view key) const; }; } // namespace tinyini - static + std::optional<Config : you create one by parsing, and parsing can fail. - int errorLine = nullptr : optional out-parameter; pass a pointer to get the line. - const std::string returned from a const function: you read it but do not own it, and the note tells you how long it lives. - findInt 's comment reveals a design decision: "missing" and "not a number" give the same result. If your program must tell them apart, use find first. Practice 4.03 depends on noticing exactly this. Doc comments and Doxygen Most C and C++ libraries write doc comments in the Doxygen style ( /// or / / ), which tools turn into web pages: Tag Means --- --- @brief one-line summary @param name a parameter; @param out name for outputs @return / @returns the return value @throws / @exception exceptions @pre , @post preconditions and postconditions @note , @warning remarks you should not skip @deprecated do not use in new code Editors show these comments when you hover over a call, so the habit of hovering often answers the question without opening a browser. Into the implementation In Visual Studio or VS Code, Go to Definition (F12) jumps from a call to its declaration, and again to the implementation if the source is available. Read with a question in mind ("what happens if the key is empty?") and follow only the code paths that answer it; reading a library front to back is rarely worth it. Two cautions: - Behaviour you find in the implementation but not in the documentation is not a promise . It may change in the next version. If you rely on it, write a test (lesson 5.02) so you notice. - Check you are reading the same version you build with: the main branch on GitHub may be ahead of your release. The standard library's own source Microsoft's C++ standard library is open source (github.com/microsoft/STL), as are libstdc++ (GCC) and libc++ (LLVM). It is dense code, with names like _Myfirst and _Mylast to avoid clashing with your macros, but stepping into std::vector::push_back in the debugger and seeing the growth and the debug checks for yourself is a good way to understand what the reference pages describe.

title: Using a library from its header
match: Using a library from its header
body: The starter contains tinyini , a small configuration library like the one in lesson 4.03. It has no web page: everything you need is in its doc comments . Do not change the library; read it, and use it to write loadSettings . cpp-norun struct ServerSettings { std::string host; int port; bool tls; int workers; }; std::optional<ServerSettings loadSettings(std::string_view text, std::string& error); loadSettings reads a configuration text and checks it in this order, stopping at the first problem. On a problem it returns an empty optional and sets error to the message shown; on success it sets error to an empty string. Setting Rule Message --- --- --- the text must parse line N , where N is the malformed line server host optional, default localhost ; if present it must not be empty bad server.host server port required missing server.port a whole number from 1 to 65535 bad server.port server tls optional, default false; if present it must be a boolean the library understands bad server.tls pool size optional, default 4; if present a whole number from 1 to 256 bad pool.size Notice that two messages for the port need you to tell "missing" from "not a number". Read what the library's functions return in each case.

title: 4.04  Man Pages, RFCs and Specifications
body: Reading the most precise documents you will meet - Unix man pages with their sections and ERRORS lists, RFCs with the MUST, SHOULD and MAY keywords of RFC 2119, ABNF grammars, errata, and turning one section of a specification into code and tests. Man pages On Linux and macOS, man shows the manual for commands and C functions. The manual is split into numbered sections, and the same name can exist in several: Section Contains Example --- --- --- 1 commands man 1 ls 2 system calls man 2 open 3 C library functions man 3 printf 5 file formats man 5 passwd 7 overviews and conventions man 7 signal A function's page has standard headings: NAME , SYNOPSIS (the include and prototype), DESCRIPTION , RETURN VALUE , ERRORS , NOTES , BUGS , SEE ALSO . The ERRORS section lists every errno value the call can set and why ( ENOENT : a component of the path does not exist; EACCES : permission denied), which is exactly the list your error handling has to consider. The same pages are online at man7.org, and many describe behaviour that Windows' C runtime copies. RFCs Internet protocols and formats are specified in RFCs (Requests for Comments) at rfc-editor.org: HTTP, TLS, JSON (RFC 8259), Base64 (RFC 4648), URIs (RFC 3986). An RFC never changes once published; corrections are listed as errata , and a newer RFC obsoletes or updates an older one (the header of each says which). Always check you are reading the current one. Requirement keywords Almost every RFC uses the keywords of RFC 2119 , in capitals, with exact meanings: Keyword Means --- --- MUST , REQUIRED , SHALL an absolute requirement MUST NOT , SHALL NOT an absolute prohibition SHOULD , RECOMMENDED do it unless you have a good, understood reason not to SHOULD NOT avoid unless you have a good reason MAY , OPTIONAL truly optional; others must cope either way A "MAY" for the sender becomes a "must handle" for the receiver: if a sender MAY add whitespace, every parser must accept it. Reading a spec well means sorting its sentences into these buckets. ABNF grammars Syntax in RFCs is written in ABNF (RFC 5234): text version = 1 DIGIT "." 1 DIGIT ; one or more digits, a dot, one or more digits DIGIT = %x30-39 ; the characters 0 to 9 hex-pair = 2HEXDIG ; exactly two hex digits header = name ":" WSP value ; WSP: zero or more spaces or tabs flag = "on" / "off" ; / is "or" option = "-" name ; is optional means "any number", 1 "at least one", n "exactly n", optional, / alternatives, "..." a literal (case-insensitive in ABNF), and %x41 a character by code. A grammar like this is a ready-made checklist for a parser and its tests. Turning a section into code The method that works for specifications of any size: 1. Read the section twice : once for the idea, once for the rules. 2. List every MUST and MUST NOT as a test case, including what to do with input that breaks them (reject? ignore?). 3. Collect the spec's own examples and test vectors ; many RFCs have an appendix of them (RFC 4648 section 10 lists Base64 test vectors). 4. Write the code, then run it against both lists. 5. Note every SHOULD and MAY you chose to follow or not, in a comment, so the next reader knows it was a decision. Practice 4.04 does this for Base64, and the milestone project for Semantic Versioning, a short specification with famously precise ordering rules.

title: Base64 from its specification
body: Implement Base64 encoding and decoding as RFC 4648 specifies it, following this summary of the relevant sections (lesson 4.04). Where the RFC lets a decoder choose ("MAY"), this summary makes the stricter choice, and your code MUST follow it. cpp-norun std::string base64Encode(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & data, bool url = false); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t base64Decode(std::string_view text, bool url = false); Encoding. Take the input 3 bytes (24 bits) at a time and write 4 characters, each standing for 6 bits, most significant first, using the alphabet A - Z (0 to 25), a - z (26 to 51), 0 - 9 (52 to 61), + (62) and / (63). A final group of 1 byte produces 2 characters, and of 2 bytes 3 characters, the missing low bits filled with zeros; the output is then padded with = to a multiple of 4 characters. The URL-safe variant ( url true) uses - instead of + and _ instead of / , and in this library is written without padding. Decoding MUST reject (return an empty optional) any input that encoding could not have produced: - standard variant: a length that is not a multiple of 4; = anywhere except as the last one or two characters; - URL-safe variant: any = ; a length that leaves 1 character over after the groups of 4 (one character cannot hold a byte); - both: any character outside the variant's alphabet (including spaces and line breaks); - both: a final character whose unused low bits are not zero (RFC 4648 calls such data non-canonical). Empty text decodes to no bytes.

title: Semantic Versioning from the specification
body: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (semver.org) is a short specification that almost every package manager relies on, and its rules for what counts as a valid version and which version is newer are exact. Below is a summary of the parts you need, plus a small range syntax defined for this project. Implement it so that every rule holds. cpp struct Version { std::uint64_t major, minor, patch; std::vector<std::string prerelease; std::vector<std::string build; }; std::optional<Version parseVersion(std::string_view text); int compareVersions(const Version& a, const Version& b); std::string toString(const Version& v); bool satisfies(const Version& v, std::string_view range); Valid versions (the specification's rules 2, 9 and 10): - The core is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH : exactly three non-negative whole numbers separated by dots. They must not have leading zeros ( 0 itself is fine). In this project they must also fit in 64 bits. - A pre-release may follow, after a hyphen: one or more identifiers separated by dots. Identifiers are non-empty and use only 0 - 9 , A - Z , a - z and - . An identifier made only of digits is numeric and must not have leading zeros. - Build metadata may follow, after a plus sign: one or more identifiers separated by dots, with the same characters, never empty, but leading zeros are allowed. - Nothing else is allowed: no spaces, no v prefix. parseVersion returns the parts, or an empty optional for anything invalid. toString writes a version back in the same form. Precedence (rule 11). compareVersions returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is lower than, equal to, or higher than b : 1. Compare major, minor and patch numerically, in that order. 2. If those are equal, a version without a pre-release is higher than one with a pre-release. 3. Otherwise compare the pre-release identifiers left to right: two numeric identifiers compare as numbers; two others compare as ASCII text; a numeric identifier is lower than a non-numeric one. If all compared identifiers are equal, the version with more identifiers is higher. 4. Build metadata is ignored : 1.0.0+a and 1.0.0+b are equal. Ranges (this project's own syntax). A range is one or more comparators separated by spaces, and a version satisfies it when it satisfies every comparator: Comparator Satisfied when the version is --- --- =V , V , =V , <V , <=V equal to, higher than ... V , by precedence ~X.Y.Z = X.Y.Z and < X.(Y+1).0 ^X.Y.Z = X.Y.Z and below the next version that changes the first non-zero part: < (X+1).0.0 if X 0; else < 0.(Y+1).0 if Y 0; else < 0.0.(Z+1) The versions in comparators may have pre-releases. Comparisons use plain precedence, so, for example, 2.0.0-alpha does satisfy ^1.2.3 (it is lower than 2.0.0 ). An empty range, a comparator with no operator, or an invalid version in a comparator throws std::invalid_argument .

title: 5.01  Turning an Example into Your Code
match: 5.01 Turning an Example into Your Code
body: Why documentation examples are not production code - what they leave out on purpose - and a dependable routine for adapting one - run it unchanged, understand every line against the reference, make it a function, add every error path the reference describes, release resources on every path, and test the edges. Examples are written to teach The example on a reference page exists to show one idea as clearly as possible. To stay short it usually leaves out exactly what your program needs: Left out Why it matters --- --- error handling the failure cases are on the page, just not in the example cleanup on error paths a handle or allocation leaks when something fails halfway loops for partial results a single read or send may do only part of the work buffer sizing fixed buffers like char buf 256 that are too small for real data real inputs hard-coded names, paths and values thread safety, encoding, limits outside the example's one idea Copying an example straight into a program is the most common way documentation causes bugs. The fix is a routine. The routine 1. Run it unchanged. In a scratch project, or Compiler Explorer. If it does not work as shown, you have learned something about your setup (version, platform, missing library) before mixing it with your own code. 2. Explain every line. For each call, open its reference page and check: what does each argument mean here? What can it return? This is where you find the cases the example ignores. 3. Make it a function with real parameters instead of hard-coded values, and a return type that can express failure ( std::optional , an error code, an exception, matching the rest of your program). 4. Add every error path the reference pages list. For each call: what happens if it fails, and what must already-acquired resources do then? 5. Release resources on every path. Wrap handles in RAII types (a small class whose destructor closes them, or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter), so early returns cannot leak. 6. Handle partial results. Anything that reads, writes, sends or receives in pieces needs a loop (the Networking course's sendAll is the classic case). 7. Test the edges the reference describes: empty input, the largest input, the failure of each call (practice 5.01 fakes them). An example, adapted A typical example for a file API looks like this: cpp-norun Handle h = fakeOpen("notes.txt"); char buffer 256 ; long n = fakeRead(h, buffer, sizeof buffer); std::cout << std::string(buffer, n); fakeClose(h); Reading the three reference pages shows five problems: fakeOpen can fail and return INVALID ; fakeRead may return fewer bytes than the file has, so one call does not read the whole file; it returns -1 on an error, which std::string(buffer, n) would turn into a huge length; a file longer than 256 bytes is cut off; and if anything throws between open and close, the handle leaks. The adapted version: cpp-norun class File { public: explicit File(Handle h) : h_{ h } {} ~File() { if (h_ != INVALID) fakeClose(h_); } File(const File&) = delete; File& operator=(const File&) = delete; Handle get() const { return h_; } private: Handle h_; }; std::optional<std::string readWholeFile(const std::string& name) { File file{ fakeOpen(name) }; if (file.get() == INVALID) return std::nullopt; std::string contents; char buffer 4096 ; for (;;) { const long n{ fakeRead(file.get(), buffer, sizeof buffer) }; if (n < 0) return std::nullopt; // error: the destructor still closes if (n == 0) return contents; // end of file contents.append(buffer, static_cast<std::size_t (n)); } } Longer than the example, and every added line traces back to a sentence on a reference page.

title: From example to robust code
where: 5.01 Turning an Example into Your Code
body: The starter contains a stand-in file API whose reference pages say: - Handle fakeOpen(const std::string& name) : opens a file; returns INVALID if it does not exist. - long fakeRead(Handle h, char buffer, std::size_t size) : reads up to size bytes (it may return fewer even before the end); returns the number read, 0 at the end of the file , or -1 on an error . - void fakeClose(Handle h) : closes the handle. Every handle that was opened must be closed exactly once. The documentation's example (lesson 5.01) is: cpp-norun Handle h = fakeOpen(name); char buffer 256 ; long n = fakeRead(h, buffer, sizeof buffer); return std::string(buffer, n); Write the robust version, and one function built on it: cpp-norun std::optional<std::string readWholeFile(const std::string& name); std::optional<std::size_t countLines(const std::string& name); - readWholeFile returns the whole contents, however many reads it takes and however long the file is; an empty optional if the file cannot be opened or any read fails. The handle is always closed. - countLines returns the number of lines: the number of \n characters, plus one if the file is not empty and does not end with \n . An empty file has 0 lines. An empty optional if reading fails.

title: 5.02  Checking Your Understanding with Experiments
body: Confirming what you think a page says with small, focused programs - one question per experiment, predicting the result first, trying the edge cases, using Compiler Explorer, turning experiments into learning tests that keep checking the behaviour - and the limits of experiments when behaviour is undefined or unspecified. Reading is not knowing After reading a reference page you have a belief about how a function behaves. A two-minute experiment turns it into knowledge, or shows you misread. Experienced programmers do this constantly, especially for anything with edge cases: rounding, string splitting, time zones, encodings, regular expressions. How to run an experiment 1. One question. "What does std::round(-2.5) return?" not "how does rounding work?". 2. Predict first. Write down what you expect before running it. A surprise is the whole point; without a prediction you will not notice one. 3. Smallest program. No framework, no project: a main with a few prints, or a test. 4. Cover the edges. Zero, negative, empty, the boundary value, one past it, the largest value. 5. Compare with the page. If the result disagrees with your reading, re-read. If it disagrees with the page itself, see lesson 5.03. cpp include <cmath include <iostream int main() { // Question: how do the rounding functions treat halves? // Prediction: round goes away from zero; nearbyint goes to even. for (double x : { 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -0.5, -2.5, 2.4999 }) std::cout << x << ": round " << std::round(x) << ", nearbyint " << std::nearbyint(x) << ", trunc " << std::trunc(x) << ", cast " << static_cast<int (x) << '\n'; } The pages explain the results: std::round rounds halves away from zero ; std::nearbyint uses the current rounding mode, which is round-half-to-even by default (so 0.5 and 2.5 both go to the even neighbour); std::trunc and the cast drop the fraction towards zero. Seeing all four side by side fixes it in memory better than reading four pages. Compiler Explorer godbolt.org compiles and runs small programs in the browser with many compilers and versions. It is ideal for experiments: you can check whether the behaviour differs between MSVC, GCC and Clang, or between C++17 and C++20, in seconds, and share a link to the result with a colleague. Learning tests An experiment you run once is forgotten; an experiment written as a test keeps checking: cpp-norun TEST("std::round rounds halves away from zero") { CHECK_EQ(std::round(2.5), 3.0); CHECK_EQ(std::round(-2.5), -3.0); } TEST("our JSON library keeps the order of object keys") { CHECK_EQ(json::parse(R"({"b":1,"a":2})").keys(), (std::vector<std::string { "b", "a" })); } Tests like the second one are called learning tests : they pin down behaviour of a library that your code relies on, especially behaviour the documentation is vague about. When you upgrade the library and one fails, you know immediately which assumption broke, instead of finding out from a bug report. What experiments cannot tell you An experiment shows what this compiler, library and machine did this time. That is the documented behaviour only when the page promises it: - Undefined behaviour can "work" in an experiment and fail elsewhere: reading past the end of an array may print plausible numbers. Never take a successful run as proof that something is allowed. - Unspecified and implementation-defined results (the order of iteration of an unordered_map , the size of long , the text of what() ) may differ between compilers or versions. - Timing and threads : a race condition may hide in a hundred runs and appear in the hundred-and-first. So the rule is: the page says what you may rely on; the experiment confirms you read it correctly.

title: Rounding, pinned down
body: Lesson 5.02 ran an experiment on the standard rounding functions. Use what it found, and their reference pages, to write four functions with exactly these behaviours. Run your own small experiment first if any row surprises you. cpp-norun double roundHalfAway(double x); double roundHalfEven(double x); double towardZero(double x); std::optional<int toIntChecked(double x); Function Rounds to the nearest whole number, and halves go ... Examples --- --- --- roundHalfAway away from zero 2.5 → 3, -2.5 → -3, 0.5 → 1 roundHalfEven to the even neighbour 2.5 → 2, 3.5 → 4, -2.5 → -2, 0.5 → 0 towardZero (no rounding: drops the fraction) 2.9 → 2, -2.9 → -2 toIntChecked drops the fraction like towardZero and returns the result as an int , or an empty optional if x is NaN, infinite, or the result does not fit in an int . (Converting such a value with static_cast<int is undefined behaviour, which is why this function exists.)

title: 5.03  When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
match: 5.03 When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
body: What to do when documentation and behaviour disagree - checking the version first, reading changelogs and migration guides, errata and known issues, weighing community answers and AI suggestions, reporting documentation bugs well, and protecting your code against behaviour that is not documented. First suspect: the version Most "the documentation is wrong" moments are really "I am reading the documentation for a different version". Check, in this order: 1. Which version of the library, language or OS are you actually using? ( --version , the package file, _MSC_VER , sys.version .) 2. Which version is the page about? Look for a version selector, "Added in", "(since C++20)", "Changed in version" notes. 3. Is there a changelog or release notes entry between the two? Changelogs and migration guides A changelog lists what changed in each release, usually grouped as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security. Many projects follow Semantic Versioning (the milestone 4 project), so the version number already warns you: a new major version may break your code, minor and patch versions should not. When you upgrade across several versions, read every entry in between, not only the latest: a key renamed in version 2 and a default changed in version 3 both affect you. Larger projects publish a migration guide ("Upgrading from 2.x to 3.0") that lists breaking changes with before-and-after code. Practice 5.03 is a migration written from a changelog. Things a changelog entry tells you that a reference page often does not: - what the old behaviour was, so you can recognise it in existing code; - whether a change is breaking or only a fix; - the deprecation timeline: a function marked deprecated in 2.3 may be removed in 3.0. When the page really is wrong Documentation is written by people and has mistakes, especially in corners: a wrong default, a missing error case, an example that no longer compiles. Signs you have found one: - your experiment (lesson 5.02) contradicts the page, on the version the page describes; - the implementation (lesson 4.03) clearly does something else; - the issue tracker or errata list mentions it. Then: 1. Trust the behaviour you can test , but write a learning test for it, since a fix might change it. 2. Check errata and issues : RFCs have errata pages; libraries have issue trackers; cppreference pages have discussion pages and are corrected quickly. 3. Report it , briefly and concretely: the page and section, what it says, what actually happens (with a minimal program), and the version. Most documentation is open to contributions: cppreference is a wiki, Microsoft Learn pages have an "Edit" link to GitHub, MDN is on GitHub too. Community answers and AI suggestions Answers from forums, Q&A sites, blog posts and AI assistants are often the fastest way to find which function to use. They are also often out of date, written for another platform or version, or simply wrong in a detail, and an AI suggestion can name a function or parameter that does not exist at all. Treat them as leads : - Look up every function they use on its reference page. - Check the date and version they were written for. - Prefer answers that link to documentation, and be suspicious of ones that only say "this works for me". - Run the experiment yourself. Building on undocumented behaviour Sometimes you must rely on something no page promises: an undocumented message format, the order of results, a timing. If you do: - Isolate it in one function, so there is one place to change. - Write a test that fails loudly if the behaviour changes. - Leave a comment saying it is undocumented and how you found out. - Prefer a documented alternative the moment one exists.

title: A migration written from a changelog
match: A migration written from a changelog
where: 5.03 When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
body: An application stores its settings as key-value pairs, and its file format has changed twice. Here is its changelog (lesson 5.03), newest first: text 3.0.0 Changed - The log_level value "warn" is now spelled "warning". Other values are unchanged. - host and port are replaced by a single key, address, written host:port. A missing host means localhost and a missing port means 80; if both are missing, no address is written. Added - retries, with the default "3" when it is absent. 2.0.0 Changed - timeout (whole seconds) is renamed timeout_ms and is now in milliseconds. Removed - legacy_mode is gone and must be dropped. - verbose ("true" or anything else) is replaced by log_level: "debug" when verbose was "true", otherwise "info". If verbose is absent, no log_level is added. Write the migration: cpp-norun std::map<std::string, std::string migrate(std::map<std::string, std::string config, int fromVersion); It takes settings written by version fromVersion (1, 2 or 3) and returns them as version 3 writes them: apply the 2.0.0 changes if fromVersion is 1, then the 3.0.0 changes if it is 1 or 2. Keys the changelog does not mention are kept unchanged. The result always has version set to "3" . Throw std::invalid_argument if fromVersion is not 1, 2 or 3, or if a timeout being migrated is not a whole number of seconds (digits only).

title: 5.04  Writing Documentation Others Can Use
body: Turning everything this course taught about reading documentation into writing it - doc comments that state the contract, what every function's documentation must answer, examples that are correct, READMEs that get someone started, changelogs, and keeping documentation true as the code changes. Write the page you wished you had Every frustration in this course came from documentation that left something out: the return value when the buffer is too small, the difference between missing and invalid, the version a feature arrived in. When you write code others use (including yourself in six months), write the documentation that would have saved you that time. Doc comments that state the contract For each public function, the comment should answer the questions of lesson 1.02, in a few lines: cpp-norun /// Reads a whole file into memory. /// /// @param path the file to read; may be relative to the current directory. /// @return the file's contents, or std::nullopt if the file cannot be opened /// or a read fails part way. An empty file gives an empty string. /// @throws std::bad_alloc if the file does not fit in memory. /// @note Not safe to call while another thread writes the same file. std::optional<std::string readWholeFile(const std::filesystem::path& path); A checklist for each function: - What it does, in one sentence starting with a verb. - Each parameter : meaning, units (bytes or characters, seconds or milliseconds), allowed values, whether null or empty is allowed. - The result in every case, including the empty, missing and failed ones. - Errors : exceptions, error codes, what state things are left in. - Preconditions the caller must meet, and what happens if they do not. - Ownership and lifetime of anything returned by pointer or reference. - Thread safety and complexity , when they are not obvious. Leave out what the signature already says (" count : the count"), and do not describe the implementation: say what , not how , so you can change the how. Examples that are correct An example in documentation is copied more than anything else you write (lesson 5.01), so: - make it compile and run , ideally by building it as part of your tests; - handle errors in it, or say plainly that it skips them for brevity; - show the most common use first, then the tricky ones. README and the four kinds A project's README is often the only page someone reads. It should say, in order: what the project does and for whom, how to install or build it, a minimal example that works, where the full documentation is, and the licence. Beyond that, keep the four kinds of documentation from lesson 1.01 apart: a tutorial for newcomers, how-to guides for tasks, the reference generated from your doc comments, and explanation for the design decisions. Changelogs Keep a CHANGELOG.md with one section per release and entries under Added , Changed , Deprecated , Removed , Fixed , Security . Write each entry for the person upgrading: what changed and what they must do about it. Mark breaking changes clearly, and match them to your version numbers (a breaking change means a new major version under Semantic Versioning). Keeping it true Documentation that is wrong is worse than none, because people trust it. Habits that keep it true: - Change the doc comment in the same commit as the behaviour. - Let tests check the claims you can test: every documented error case is a test case. - Compile the examples. - When someone asks a question the docs should have answered, fix the docs , not just the person's question.

title: Reading doc comments with a program
match: Reading doc comments with a program
body: Documentation tools such as Doxygen read /// comments out of source code (lessons 4.03 and 5.04). Write a small one. cpp-norun struct DocParam { std::string name; std::string text; }; struct DocComment { std::string summary; std::vector<DocParam params; std::string returns; std::vector<std::string throws; }; std::optional<DocComment docFor(std::string_view source, std::string_view functionName); std::vector<std::string missingParams(const DocComment& doc, const std::vector<std::string & parameterNames); Finding the function. Split source into lines (ignore a \r before each \n ). The declaration is the first line that is not itself a comment (after leading spaces it does not start with // ) and contains functionName followed, after optional spaces, by ( , where the character before the name is not a letter, digit or _ . If there is no such line, return an empty optional. The comment is the run of lines directly above the declaration that start (after leading spaces) with /// . Take each line's text after /// and trim the spaces at both ends. Then, in order: - A line starting with @param gives a new parameter: the next word is its name and the rest (trimmed) its text. - @return or @returns sets the return text; @throws adds an entry to throws . - Any other line starting with @ is an unknown tag: ignore it, and the lines after it, until the next known tag. - An empty line is skipped. - Any other line is a continuation : before the first tag it is part of the summary; after a known tag it continues that tag's text. Parts are joined with one space. If the declaration has no comment, the result is a DocComment with everything empty. missingParams returns the names in parameterNames that have no @param entry, in the order given.

title: Two libraries, one report
where: From Docs to Working Code projects
body: The starter contains two small libraries, each documented only by the comments in its code: minicsv , which reads CSV records, and minitpl , which fills in text templates. Without changing them, use them to build a report generator. Everything you need to know about how they behave, including how they report errors, is in their comments: read them as you would a reference page. cpp-norun std::optional<std::string report(std::string_view csv, std::string_view rowTemplate, std::string& error); report turns each data row of a CSV table into one line of text: 1. The first record of the CSV is the header: the column names. 2. For every following record (data rows numbered 1, 2, 3 ...), make a set of variables: each column name with that row's value, plus row , the row's number, unless a column is already called row . Render rowTemplate with them and add the result and a \n to the report. 3. Return the whole report and set error to an empty string. A table with a header and no data rows gives an empty report. On the first problem, stop, return an empty optional, and set error : Problem error --- --- the CSV has no records at all no header a record has a different number of fields from the header csv line N: expected K fields the CSV reader reports an error csv line N: followed by the reader's error text rendering a row fails row R: followed by the template's error text N is the line on which the problem record starts (the reader can tell you), K the number of header fields and R the data row number.

Synopsis : find the overload you are calling. 2. Description and Parameters : your arguments, including empty, zero, null, negative, too large. 3. Return value and Errors : every outcome. 4. Windows pages (milestone 3) Prefix / annotation Means --- --- cch , nSize "in characters" count of wchar_t cb count of bytes _In_ , _In_opt_ read; _opt_ : null allowed _Out_writes_(n) buffer holds n elements _Out_writes_bytes_(n) buffer holds n bytes Unknown size pattern Example --- --- ask for the size (null buffer) GetEnvironmentVariableW : too small returns size with null; success returns length without grow until it fits GetModuleFileNameW : returns nSize when truncated size in, size out RegQueryValueExW : ERROR_MORE_DATA (234) Error system Test --- --- last error GetLastError() immediately after a documented failure return code ERROR_SUCCESS (0) is success HRESULT SUCCEEDED(hr) is hr = 0 ; 0x8007xxxx = Win32 error xxxx NTSTATUS top bits: 00 success, 01 info, 10 warning, 11 error Structures: zero-initialise ( {} ), set cbSize = sizeof(...) , reserved members zero. title: Common Problems
body: Problem Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- The example from the docs does not compile docs for a different version, or a missing header check the version marker and the Requirements section 2.04, 5.03 The search result shows old behaviour an old page or forum answer open the official reference and pick your version 1.01 A call does something different from what you expected a different overload was chosen match your arguments to the numbered overloads 1.03 A program works in Debug and crashes in Release undefined behaviour the page warned about find the precondition you broke 1.04 A value was not updated in a map insert or try_emplace used to update use insert_or_assign or operator 2.02 "12abc" was accepted as a number std::stoi stops at the first bad character use std::from_chars and check ptr reached the end 2.01 A crash after push_back or erase an iterator or reference was invalidated follow the container's invalidation rules 2.03 A Windows path or string is cut off a truncated result was treated as success check for the documented truncation result and grow the buffer 3.01 A buffer overrun with a wide string bytes passed where characters were expected, or the reverse read whether the size is cch or cb 3.02 GetLastError returns a meaningless value read too late, or after a function that returns its own code read it at once, and only when the page says to 3.03 A COM call "failed" with S_FALSE tested hr == S_OK use SUCCEEDED(hr) and handle S_FALSE as documented 3.03 A Windows call fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER cbSize not set, or flags combined wrongly zero-initialise, set the size, check "one of" vs "one or more of" 3.04 Python x = x.sort() makes x None sort works in place and returns None use x.sort() or x = sorted(x) 4.01 JavaScript sorts numbers wrongly the default sort compares strings pass a compare function 4.02 A function returns nothing useful and has no docs undocumented library read the header, tests and source; write a learning test 4.03 Your parser rejects input another program accepts a MAY or SHOULD in the spec was treated as MUST sort the spec's sentences by RFC 2119 keyword 4.04 Code copied from an example leaks or crashes on errors examples skip error handling follow the adaptation routine 5.01 An upgrade broke something with no error a behaviour change listed in the changelog read every changelog entry between the versions 5.03 An AI or forum answer uses a function that does not exist an invented or outdated answer check every function on its reference page 5.03

title: Glossary
body: ABNF : Augmented Backus-Naur Form, the grammar notation used in RFCs. (4.04) Amortised constant : constant time on average over many calls, though a single call may be slow. (2.03) Basic guarantee : if a function throws, everything is still valid but may have changed. (1.04) Changelog : a list of what changed in each release: added, changed, deprecated, removed, fixed. (5.03) Compiler Explorer : godbolt.org, a website that compiles and runs small programs with many compilers. (5.02) Contract : the preconditions a caller must meet and the results a function promises in return. (1.04) cppreference : the community reference for C++ and its standard library. (2.01) Defect report : a correction to the C++ standard after publication. (2.01) Deprecated : still available but discouraged, and likely to be removed. (2.04) Doc comment : a comment in a special form ( /// , / / , a docstring) that tools turn into documentation. (4.03) Doxygen : the common tool and tag style ( @param , @return ) for C and C++ doc comments. (4.03) Errata : published corrections to a document such as an RFC. (4.04) Explanation : documentation that says why things are the way they are. (1.01) Feature-test macro : a macro such as __cpp_lib_format that says whether a feature is available. (2.04) Half-open range : first, last) , including first and excluding last . (1.04) How-to guide : documentation that walks through a task. (1.01) HRESULT : a 32-bit COM status code with severity, facility and code fields. (3.03) Implementation-defined : chosen by the compiler or library, which must document it. (1.02) Invalidation : an iterator, pointer or reference becoming unusable after a container changes. (2.03) Keyword-only parameter : a Python parameter after that must be passed by name. (4.01) Learning test : a test that pins down a library's behaviour your code relies on. (5.02) Man page : a Unix manual page, in numbered sections. (4.04) MDN : MDN Web Docs, the reference for JavaScript and web APIs. (4.02) Migration guide : instructions for upgrading across a breaking release. (5.03) Named requirement : a set of rules a template argument must meet, such as LegacyInputIterator. (1.03) NTSTATUS : the kernel's 32-bit status code, with two severity bits. (3.03) Overload set : several functions with the same name and different parameters. (1.03) Positional-only parameter : a Python parameter before / that cannot be passed by name. (4.01) Postcondition : what is true after a call that met its preconditions. (1.04) Precondition : what must be true before a call. (1.04) Reference : documentation that describes exactly what each part does. (1.01) RFC : a Request for Comments, the published specification of an internet standard. (4.04) RFC 2119 keywords : MUST, SHOULD, MAY and their negations, with exact meanings. (4.04) SAL : Microsoft's source annotation language, such as _In_ and _Out_writes_ . (3.02) Semantic Versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers that signal breaking changes. (4.04) Stability index : Node's label for how settled an API is. (4.02) Strong guarantee : if a function throws, nothing changed. (1.04) System error code : a Windows error number such as 2 ( ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND ). (3.03) Tutorial : documentation that teaches by leading a newcomer step by step. (1.01) Undefined behaviour : what happens when a precondition is broken: anything, with no guarantees. (1.04) Unspecified : one of several allowed results, with no promise which. (1.02)

title: 1.01  Complexity and Big O
body: How to describe an algorithm's speed independently of the computer - counting basic steps, Big O and its relatives Omega and Theta, the common growth classes, analysing sequential, nested and halving loops, best, worst and average cases, amortised cost, and space complexity. Why count instead of time? A stopwatch tells you how long one program took on one computer with one input. It cannot tell you what happens when the input is a thousand times bigger, and it changes with the compiler, the processor and whatever else is running. To compare algorithms we count how the number of basic steps grows with the size of the input, called n .
