Why does a rotation keep the tree a valid binary search tree? + It keeps the in-order sequence of keys the same - It sorts the subtrees - Rotations only move leaves - It does not; the tree must be checked afterwards A x B y C reads the same before and after a rotation at y. Summary - An AVL tree keeps every node's subtree heights within one of each other, which bounds the height by about 1.44 log₂ n. - Rotations restructure a node and its child in O(1) while keeping the in-order sequence. - Four cases (LL, RR, LR, RL) are fixed by one single or double rotation. - Insert and delete rebalance along the path back to the root: O(log n). - Red-black trees, treaps, skip lists and B-trees offer the same guarantees with different trade-offs.

title: An AVL tree
body: Build AvlSet , a self-balancing binary search tree of distinct int s: cpp class AvlSet { public: bool insert(int key); bool erase(int key); bool contains(int key) const; std::size_t size() const; int height() const; // -1 when empty std::vector<int toVector() const; // in order bool isValid() const; // checks the BST order, every stored height and every balance factor }; - Each node stores its height. After every insert or erase, update heights and rebalance the nodes on the path back to the root with the four rotation cases (lesson 4.03). - isValid recomputes everything from scratch: keys in order, stored heights correct, every balance factor in {−1, 0, +1}. The tests call it after many operations. - The tests insert 100,000 keys in sorted order (a plain BST would have height 99,999) and expect the height to stay within the AVL bound.

title: 4.04  Fenwick and Segment Trees
body:
Answering range questions on changing arrays - prefix sums and their weakness, the Fenwick (binary indexed) tree with its lowest-set-bit trick for O(log n) updates and prefix sums, segment trees for any associative operation such as minimum or maximum, building, point updates and range queries, and a first look at lazy propagation for range updates. Range queries Many problems ask questions about ranges of an array: the total sales between day 30 and day 90, the lowest temperature in a given hour, the number of active users between two IDs. If the array never changes, prefix sums answer range sums in O(1): prefix i = a 0 + a 1 + ... + a i-1 sum(l, r) = prefix r + 1 - prefix l Building them is O(n). But if the array changes , a single update to a i changes every prefix j with j i : O(n) per update. With many updates and many queries mixed, we need both to be fast. Structure Update a i Range sum Range min --- --- --- --- plain array O(1) O(n) O(n) prefix sums O(n) O(1) no Fenwick tree O(log n) O(log n) no (only for sums and similar) segment tree O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) The Fenwick tree A Fenwick tree (or binary indexed tree, Peter Fenwick, 1994) is an array t of the same size, using 1-based indexes, where t i stores the sum of a block of elements ending at i whose length is the lowest set bit of i: i (binary) lowest set bit t i holds --- --- --- 1 (0001) 1 a 1 2 (0010) 2 a 1..2 3 (0011) 1 a 3 4 (0100) 4 a 1..4 6 (0110) 2 a 5..6 8 (1000) 8 a 1..8 The lowest set bit of i is i & -i (two's complement makes this work). - prefix(i) : add t i , then remove the lowest set bit ( i -= i & -i ) and repeat until i is 0. For i = 7 (0111): t 7 + t 6 + t 4 = a 7 + a 5..6 + a 1..4 . - add(i, delta) : add delta to t i , then add the lowest set bit ( i += i & -i ) and repeat while i ≤ n : these are exactly the blocks that contain position i. Both loops run at most log₂ n times, since each step clears or carries a bit. cpp include <iostream include <vector class Fenwick { public: explicit Fenwick(int n) : t_(n + 1, 0) {} void add(int i, long long delta) // i is 1-based { for (; i < static_cast<int (t_.size()); i += i & -i) t_ i += delta; } long long prefix(int i) const // a 1 + ... + a i { long long s = 0; for (; i 0; i -= i & -i) s += t_ i ; return s; } long long sum(int l, int r) const { return prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1); } private: std::vector<long long t_; }; int main() { Fenwick f(10); int values = { 5, 3, 7, 9, 6, 4, 1, 2, 8, 10 }; for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i) f.add(i, values i - 1 ); std::cout << "sum 3..6 = " << f.sum(3, 6) << '
'; // 7 + 9 + 6 + 4 f.add(5, 100); // a 5 becomes 106 std::cout << "after the update, sum 3..6 = " << f.sum(3, 6) << ", total = " << f.prefix(10) << '
'; } The whole structure is one array and two four-line loops, and it is very fast in practice. It works for any operation that can be undone (sums, XOR, counts): the range trick prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1) needs subtraction. It cannot do range minimum. A classic use: counting inversions again. Walk the array from the right, and for each value ask the Fenwick tree how many smaller values have been seen (a prefix count), then add the value. O(n log n), the same as merge sort's method. Segment trees A segment tree is a binary tree over the array in which every node stores the answer for a segment : the root covers the whole array, its children cover the two halves, and so on down to single elements at the leaves. It works for any associative operation: sum, min, max, gcd, product, even "the two largest values". Like a heap (lesson 3.04), it lives in an array: node 1 is the root and the children of node i are 2i and 2i + 1 . An array of n elements needs at most 4n slots. - query(l, r) : starting at the root, if a node's segment is inside l, r , use its value; if it is outside, ignore it; otherwise ask both children and combine. At most about 4 log n nodes are visited. - update(i, value) : change the leaf and recompute every node on the path up to the root: O(log n). cpp include <algorithm include <climits include <iostream include <vector class MinTree { public: explicit MinTree(const std::vector<int & a) : n_(static_cast<int (a.size())), t_(4 a.size(), INT_MAX) { build(a, 1, 0, n_ - 1); } int min(int l, int r) const { return query(1, 0, n_ - 1, l, r); } void set(int i, int value) { update(1, 0, n_ - 1, i, value); } private: void build(const std::vector<int & a, int node, int lo, int hi) { if (lo == hi) { t_ node = a lo ; return; } int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; build(a, 2 node, lo, mid); build(a, 2 node + 1, mid + 1, hi); t_ node = std::min(t_ 2 node , t_ 2 node + 1 ); } int query(int node, int lo, int hi, int l, int r) const { if (r < lo hi < l) return INT_MAX; // no overlap if (l <= lo && hi <= r) return t_ node ; // fully inside int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; return std::min(query(2 node, lo, mid, l, r), query(2 node + 1, mid + 1, hi, l, r)); } void update(int node, int lo, int hi, int i, int value) { if (lo == hi) { t_ node = value; return; } int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (i <= mid) update(2 node, lo, mid, i, value); else update(2 node + 1, mid + 1, hi, i, value); t_ node = std::min(t_ 2 node , t_ 2 node + 1 ); } int n_; std::vector<int t_; }; int main() { MinTree temps({ 12, 9, 15, 7, 11, 14, 8, 10 }); std::cout << "coldest in hours 0..2: " << temps.min(0, 2) << ", 2..6: " << temps.min(2, 6) << '
'; temps.set(3, 13); std::cout << "after correcting hour 3, coldest in 2..6: " << temps.min(2, 6) << '
'; } The value for "no overlap" must be the operation's identity : INT_MAX for minimum, 0 for sums, 1 for products. Range updates and lazy propagation What if an update changes a whole range ("add 5 to every element from 100 to 900")? Updating each leaf costs O(n). Lazy propagation stores a pending update at the highest nodes that cover the range and pushes it down to the children only when a later operation needs to look inside. Both range updates and range queries become O(log n). It is the segment tree's most powerful extension, and the stretch goal of practice 4.04. quiz ? What is the lowest set bit of 12 (binary 1100)? - 1 - 2 + 4 - 8 12 & -12 = 4: the rightmost 1 is in the 4s place. ? Why can't a Fenwick tree answer range-minimum queries the way it answers range sums? + A range sum is prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1), but a minimum cannot be "subtracted" away - Fenwick trees cannot store negative numbers - Minimum is not associative - It can, in the same way The prefix trick needs an inverse operation, which min does not have. ? In a segment tree for range sums, what should a query return for a segment that does not overlap l, r ? - INT_MAX + 0 - 1 - the segment's own sum The identity of addition, so it does not change the combined result. Summary - Prefix sums answer static range sums in O(1) but updates cost O(n). - A Fenwick tree stores block sums sized by the lowest set bit: O(log n) update and prefix sum in a few lines. - A segment tree stores the answer for every segment of a recursive halving: O(log n) point updates and range queries for any associative operation. - Lazy propagation adds O(log n) range updates.

title: Range queries
body: Build a Fenwick tree and a segment tree, and use the Fenwick tree to count inversions: cpp class Fenwick { public: explicit Fenwick(std::size_t n); // n zeros; positions 0 .. n-1 void add(std::size_t i, long long delta); long long prefix(std::size_t count) const; // a 0 + ... + a count-1 ; prefix(0) is 0 long long sum(std::size_t l, std::size_t r) const; // a l + ... + a r , inclusive std::size_t lowerBound(long long target) const; // smallest count with prefix(count) = target (all values = 0) }; class MaxTree { public: explicit MaxTree(const std::vector<int & a); void set(std::size_t i, int value); int max(std::size_t l, std::size_t r) const; // inclusive; std::out_of_range if l r or r = size }; long long countInversionsFenwick(const std::vector<int & a); // O(n log n) using a Fenwick tree - Fenwick uses the lowest-set-bit trick internally (1-based inside, 0-based outside). lowerBound assumes no value is negative and returns n + 1 if even the whole sum is below target ; lowerBound(0) is 0. It must be O(log n): walk down the powers of two ("binary lifting") rather than binary searching over prefix . - MaxTree is a segment tree for range maximum. - countInversionsFenwick replaces each value by its rank among the sorted distinct values (coordinate compression), then walks from right to left asking how many smaller values were already seen.

title: 4.05  Union-Find
body:
Tracking groups that merge - the disjoint-set problem, a forest of parent pointers, find and union, union by size or rank, path compression, the nearly constant inverse-Ackermann bound, counting components and component sizes, and applications such as connectivity, image regions, percolation and (in lesson 5.04) Kruskal's algorithm. The problem Imagine a network of computers where cables are added one at a time, and at any moment you may be asked: "can computer 17 reach computer 42?". Or pixels in an image being merged into regions, or friends forming groups. Each case is a collection of disjoint sets that only ever merge : - union(a, b) : merge the set containing a with the set containing b, - find(a) : which set is a in? Two elements are connected if they have the same answer. Searching the graph for every question is O(n) or more. Union-find (also called a disjoint-set union, DSU) answers both operations in practically constant time . A forest of parent pointers Each set is a tree, and each element points to its parent ; a root points to itself and acts as the set's representative . find follows parent pointers up to the root. union finds both roots and makes one the parent of the other. Here {0, 1, 2, 3} and {4, 5, 6} are two sets, with roots 0 and 4. Elements are numbered 0 to n − 1, so the parents fit in a std::vector<int . Two improvements Done naively, the trees can become long chains, and find degrades to O(n). Two simple tricks fix that. Union by size : when merging, attach the root of the smaller tree under the root of the larger one. A node's depth then grows only when its tree at least doubles in size, so no tree is deeper than log₂ n. (Union by rank , an upper bound on the height, works the same way.) Path compression : during find , once the root is known, point every node on the way directly at the root . Later finds for any of them take one step. With both, any sequence of m operations on n elements takes O(m · α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function . It grows so slowly that α(n) ≤ 4 for any n that could ever fit in a computer: effectively constant. cpp include <iostream include <numeric include <utility include <vector class UnionFind { public: explicit UnionFind(int n) : parent_(n), size_(n, 1), components_(n) { std::iota(parent_.begin(), parent_.end(), 0); // everyone starts as their own root } int find(int x) { int root = x; while (parent_ root != root) root = parent_ root ; while (parent_ x != root) // path compression { int next = parent_ x ; parent_ x = root; x = next; } return root; } bool unite(int a, int b) { a = find(a); b = find(b); if (a == b) return false; // already in the same set if (size_ a < size_ b ) std::swap(a, b); // union by size: b is the smaller tree parent_ b = a; size_ a += size_ b ; --components_; return true; } bool connected(int a, int b) { return find(a) == find(b); } int sizeOf(int x) { return size_ find(x) ; } int components() const { return components_; } private: std::vector<int parent_, size_; int components_; }; int main() { UnionFind uf(10); std::vector<std::pair<int, int cables{ { 0, 1 }, { 2, 3 }, { 1, 3 }, { 5, 6 }, { 7, 8 }, { 8, 9 }, { 2, 0 } }; for (auto a, b : cables) std::cout << "unite(" << a << ", " << b << ") " << (uf.unite(a, b) ? "merged" : "already together") << '
'; std::cout << "connected(0, 3)? " << uf.connected(0, 3) << ", connected(4, 5)? " << uf.connected(4, 5) << '
'; std::cout << uf.components() << " groups; the group of 9 has " << uf.sizeOf(9) << " members
"; } unite returning false when the two are already connected is useful: in a graph, it means the new edge closes a cycle . What it can and cannot do Union-find answers "are these connected?" and "how big is this group?" but not " how are they connected?" (the path) and it cannot split sets: there is no efficient "un-union". For paths, use graph search (lesson 5.01). If edges are removed over time, a common trick is to process the operations backwards , so removals become unions. Applications - Dynamic connectivity : networks, friend groups, "are these two accounts linked?". - Image processing : labelling connected regions of pixels (unite each pixel with matching neighbours). - Percolation : in a grid of open and blocked cells, does water flow from the top to the bottom? Unite open neighbours, plus a virtual "top" and "bottom" node; it percolates when top and bottom are connected. Physicists use this to study phase transitions. - Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (lesson 5.04): add edges cheapest first, skipping any edge whose ends are already connected. - Grouping equivalences : merging accounts that share an email, or variables known to be equal in a compiler. quiz ? What does find(x) return? + The root of x's tree, which represents its whole set - x's parent - The size of x's set - Whether x has been united with anything Two elements are in the same set exactly when they have the same root. ? What does union by size do? - Attaches the larger tree under the smaller one + Attaches the smaller tree's root under the larger tree's root - Sorts the elements by size - Splits sets that grow too large A node only gets deeper when its tree at least doubles, so depths stay O(log n). ? unite(a, b) returns false because a and b are already connected. In a graph built edge by edge, what does that tell you? - The graph is disconnected + The edge (a, b) closes a cycle - a and b are the same node - The union-find is broken There was already a path between a and b; the new edge makes a second one. Summary - Union-find maintains disjoint sets under merging: find gives a set's root, unite links two roots. - Union by size (or rank) keeps trees shallow; path compression flattens them as they are used. - Together they make each operation O(α(n)), effectively constant. - It answers connectivity and group sizes, detects cycles, and powers Kruskal's algorithm, but cannot split sets or report paths.

title: Union-find and what it solves
body: cpp class UnionFind { public: explicit UnionFind(std::size_t n); std::size_t find(std::size_t x); // with path compression bool unite(std::size_t a, std::size_t b); // union by size; false if already together bool connected(std::size_t a, std::size_t b); std::size_t sizeOf(std::size_t x); std::size_t components() const; }; int countRegions(const std::vector<std::string & grid); // groups of ' ' cells joined up, down, left or right bool percolates(const std::vector<std::string & grid); // can water flow from the top row to the bottom row through '.' cells? int firstCycle(std::size_t n, const std::vector<std::pair<std::size_t, std::size_t & edges); // index of the first edge that closes a cycle, or -1 - find and unite must be nearly O(1): use union by size and path compression . The tests run a million operations. - percolates : water enters any open cell ( . ) of the top row and moves between open cells that share a side. Add two virtual nodes, "top" and "bottom", connected to every open cell of the first and last row. An empty grid does not percolate. - firstCycle : add the edges in order; the first one whose ends are already connected closes a cycle.

title: An ordered dictionary
body: Build a dictionary from words to whole numbers that keeps its keys sorted and answers order questions: the nearest keys, the rank of a key, the k-th key, and the count and sum of every key in a range, all in O(log n). Underneath is your own balanced binary search tree (an AVL tree is the natural choice) in which every node also stores the size and the sum of values of its subtree. set pear 40 set apple 10 set fig 25 set banana 20 range b g rank fig nth 1 floor grape ceil grape del apple min size prints added pear added apple added fig added banana 2 keys, sum 45: banana=20, fig=25 2 apple = 10 fig = 25 pear = 40 deleted apple banana = 20 3 Keys are single words, compared the way std::string compares them. Values are whole numbers from −1000000000000 to 1000000000000. Command Output --- --- set <key <value added <key or updated <key get <key the value, or not found del <key deleted <key , or not found min , max <key = <value , or empty floor <word the largest key <= the word as <key = <value , or none ceil <word the smallest key = the word, or none rank <word how many keys are smaller than the word nth <i the i-th smallest key, counting from 1, as <key = <value ; error: there is no key number <i if i is not from 1 to the size range <lo <hi <c keys, sum <s : <k1 =<v1 , <k2 =<v2 , ... for the keys in lo, hi in order; 1 key, ... for one; 0 keys for none (also when lo hi) count <lo <hi <c keys, sum <s for the same range, without listing them (this one must be O(log n)) size the number of keys bulk <prefix <n sets the keys <prefix 000001 to <prefix <n as 6 digits to the values 1 to n, in that (sorted) order; n is from 1 to 100000. Prints bulk: <a added, <u updated check balanced if the tree's height is at most 2·log₂(n + 1) (true for AVL and red-black trees; the empty tree counts as height −1), otherwise not balanced (height <h ) Mistakes print error: unknown command '<word ' , error: usage: <usage (written as in the first column, for example range <lo <hi ), error: the value must be a whole number from -1000000000000 to 1000000000000 , or error: n must be from 1 to 100000 . Blank lines are ignored.

title: 5.01  Graphs and Breadth-First Search
body:
Modelling connections - vertices and edges, directed, undirected and weighted graphs, adjacency matrices, adjacency lists and edge lists with their costs, breadth-first search and why it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, rebuilding the path from parent links, connected components, two-colouring (bipartite graphs), grids as implicit graphs, and multi-source BFS. Graphs A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges . It is the most general structure in this course: lists and trees are special graphs. Graphs model anything with connections: Domain Vertices Edges --- --- --- maps places roads (weighted by distance or time) social networks people friendships (undirected) or follows (directed) the web pages links (directed) build systems tasks "must happen before" (directed, no cycles) games board positions moves Vocabulary: an edge is directed (one way, u → v) or undirected (both ways). Edges may carry a weight . The degree of a vertex is its number of edges. A path is a sequence of vertices joined by edges; a cycle is a path that returns to its start. We write V for the number of vertices and E for the number of edges. Representing a graph Number the vertices 0 to V − 1. Then there are three common representations: Representation Memory Is u–v an edge? List u's neighbours --- --- --- --- adjacency matrix: bool m V V O(V²) O(1) O(V) adjacency list : vector<vector<int adj O(V + E) O(degree) O(degree) edge list: vector<pair<int,int O(E) O(E) O(E) Most real graphs are sparse (E is much smaller than V²: a road network has a few roads per junction), so the adjacency list is the default. A matrix suits small, dense graphs. An edge list suits algorithms that process edges in sorted order, like Kruskal's (lesson 5.04). cpp include <iostream include <vector int main() { int V = 5; std::vector<std::vector<int adj(V); auto addEdge = & (int u, int v) { adj u .push_back(v); adj v .push_back(u); }; // undirected: both directions addEdge(0, 1); addEdge(0, 2); addEdge(1, 3); addEdge(2, 3); addEdge(3, 4); for (int u = 0; u < V; ++u) { std::cout << u << ":"; for (int v : adj u ) std::cout << ' ' << v; std::cout << '
'; } } For a weighted graph, store pairs: std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, int adj with (neighbour, weight) . Breadth-first search Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph in layers, exactly like level-order traversal of a tree (lesson 4.01): first the start vertex, then all its neighbours, then all their unvisited neighbours, and so on. A queue holds the frontier, and a visited (or distance) array makes sure each vertex is processed once, since unlike a tree, a graph can reach a vertex by several routes. Because BFS reaches vertices in order of distance, the first time it reaches a vertex is along a shortest path (fewest edges). Recording each vertex's parent , the vertex it was discovered from, lets you rebuild that path backwards from the target. cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <queue include <vector int main() { int V = 8; std::vector<std::vector<int adj(V); for (auto u, v : std::vector<std::pair<int, int { { 0, 1 }, { 0, 2 }, { 1, 3 }, { 2, 3 }, { 3, 4 }, { 4, 5 }, { 2, 6 }, { 6, 5 } }) { adj u .push_back(v); adj v .push_back(u); } std::vector<int dist(V, -1), parent(V, -1); std::queue<int q; dist 0 = 0; q.push(0); while (!q.empty()) { int u = q.front(); q.pop(); for (int v : adj u ) if (dist v == -1) // first time we see v: that is the shortest way there { dist v = dist u + 1; parent v = u; q.push(v); } } for (int u = 0; u < V; ++u) std::cout << "dist " << u << " = " << dist u << '
'; std::vector<int path; for (int v = 5; v != -1; v = parent v ) path.push_back(v); std::reverse(path.begin(), path.end()); std::cout << "a shortest path from 0 to 5:"; for (int v : path) std::cout << ' ' << v; std::cout << '
'; } Vertex 7 has no edges, so its distance stays −1: unreachable. BFS visits each vertex once and looks at each edge once (twice for undirected), so it runs in O(V + E) . Mark a vertex as visited when it is pushed , not when it is popped. Otherwise the same vertex can enter the queue many times. Connected components In an undirected graph, a connected component is a maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other. Run BFS from every vertex not yet visited; each run discovers one whole component. The total is still O(V + E). (Union-find, lesson 4.05, also counts components, and handles edges arriving over time.) Two-colouring: bipartite graphs A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two groups with every edge going between the groups: students and courses, jobs and machines. BFS tests it: colour the start 0, its neighbours 1, their neighbours 0, and so on; the graph is bipartite exactly when no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. (Equivalently: it has no cycle of odd length.) cpp include <iostream include <queue include <vector bool bipartite(const std::vector<std::vector<int & adj) { std::vector<int colour(adj.size(), -1); for (std::size_t s = 0; s < adj.size(); ++s) { if (colour s != -1) continue; // a new component colour s = 0; std::queue<int q; q.push(static_cast<int (s)); while (!q.empty()) { int u = q.front(); q.pop(); for (int v : adj u ) { if (colour v == -1) { colour v = 1 - colour u ; q.push(v); } else if (colour v == colour u ) return false; } } } return true; } int main() { std::vector<std::vector<int square{ { 1, 3 }, { 0, 2 }, { 1, 3 }, { 2, 0 } }; // a 4-cycle std::vector<std::vector<int triangle{ { 1, 2 }, { 0, 2 }, { 0, 1 } }; // a 3-cycle std::cout << "square bipartite? " << bipartite(square) << ", triangle bipartite? " << bipartite(triangle) << '
'; } Grids are graphs A maze or a game map stored as a grid of characters is a graph in disguise: each open cell is a vertex, with edges to its open neighbours up, down, left and right. You never build an adjacency list; you compute the neighbours on the fly with direction offsets. cpp include <iostream include <queue include <string include <vector int main() { std::vector<std::string maze{ "S. .....", ". . .", ".... ...", " . . . .", ".. ... G" }; int rows = static_cast<int (maze.size()), cols = static_cast<int (maze 0 .size()); const int dr = { -1, 1, 0, 0 }, dc = { 0, 0, -1, 1 }; std::vector<std::vector<int dist(rows, std::vector<int (cols, -1)); std::queue<std::pair<int, int q; dist 0 0 = 0; q.push({ 0, 0 }); while (!q.empty()) { auto r, c = q.front(); q.pop(); for (int d = 0; d < 4; ++d) { int nr = r + dr d , nc = c + dc d ; if (nr < 0 nr = rows nc < 0 nc = cols maze nr nc == ' ' dist nr nc != -1) continue; dist nr nc = dist r c + 1; q.push({ nr, nc }); } } std::cout << "steps from S to G: " << dist 4 7 << '
'; } Multi-source BFS starts with several vertices in the queue at distance 0. It computes, for every cell, the distance to the nearest source in a single O(V + E) pass: the nearest exit for every room, how long fire takes to spread from several starting points, the distance from every pixel to the nearest edge. quiz ? Why does BFS find shortest paths in an unweighted graph? + It reaches vertices in order of their distance from the start, so the first visit is along a shortest path - It tries every possible path - It always moves towards the target - It uses a priority queue The queue processes all vertices at distance d before any at distance d + 1. ? A road network has 1,000,000 junctions and about 2,500,000 roads. Which representation? - an adjacency matrix + adjacency lists - an edge list only - a binary heap A matrix would need 10^12 entries; adjacency lists need memory proportional to V + E. ? When should BFS mark a vertex as visited? + When it is pushed onto the queue - When it is popped from the queue - After all its neighbours are processed - It does not need to Marking on push stops the same vertex being queued several times. Summary - Graphs are vertices and edges, directed or undirected, weighted or not; use adjacency lists for sparse graphs. - BFS explores in layers with a queue in O(V + E), giving shortest paths by number of edges; parent links rebuild the path. - Repeated BFS finds connected components; BFS two-colouring tests for bipartite graphs. - Grids are implicit graphs; multi-source BFS gives the distance to the nearest of several sources.

title: Breadth-first search
body: Graphs here are adjacency lists: adj u lists the neighbours of vertex u (for undirected graphs, each edge appears in both lists). cpp using Graph = std::vector<std::vector<int ; std::vector<int distances(const Graph& adj, int source); // -1 for unreachable vertices std::vector<int shortestPath(const Graph& adj, int from, int to); // the vertices on a shortest path, or {} if none int components(const Graph& adj); // for an undirected graph bool isBipartite(const Graph& adj); int nearestExitSteps(const std::vector<std::string & grid); // multi-source BFS on a grid - shortestPath : when several shortest paths exist, return the one BFS finds when it scans each adjacency list in order and records the first parent of each vertex. shortestPath(adj, v, v) is { v } . - nearestExitSteps : the grid has walls , open cells . , people P (open cells) and exits E . Return the largest number of steps any person needs to reach their nearest exit (moving up, down, left, right through non-wall cells), or -1 if some person cannot reach any exit. With no people, return 0. Start the BFS from all exits at once : one pass, O(rows × cols).

title: 5.02  Depth-First Search and Topological Order
body:
Going deep first - depth-first search recursively and with an explicit stack, discovery and finish order, finding cycles in directed graphs with three colours, directed acyclic graphs, topological sorting by DFS finish times and by Kahn's algorithm, using topological order for build systems, course prerequisites and longest paths, and a pointer to strongly connected components. Depth-first search Depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as far as it can, then backtracks to the most recent vertex that still has an unexplored edge. It is the natural way to explore a maze by hand: keep going until a dead end, then go back to the last junction. Recursively, DFS is a few lines: cpp include <iostream include <vector void dfs(int u, const std::vector<std::vector<int & adj, std::vector<bool & seen, std::vector<int & order) { seen u = true; order.push_back(u); for (int v : adj u ) if (!seen v ) dfs(v, adj, seen, order); } int main() { std::vector<std::vector<int adj{ { 1, 2 }, { 3 }, { 3, 4 }, { 5 }, { 5 }, {} }; // directed std::vector<bool seen(adj.size(), false); std::vector<int order; dfs(0, adj, seen, order); for (int u : order) std::cout << u << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } Like BFS it is O(V + E) . It does not find shortest paths, but the structure of its exploration answers many questions BFS cannot: cycles, topological order, bridges and articulation points, strongly connected components, and backtracking search (lesson 6.05). The recursion can go V levels deep, which overflows the stack on large graphs (a path of a million vertices). The iterative version uses an explicit stack. A simple form pushes a vertex's neighbours and marks vertices when popped; it visits in a slightly different order from the recursive one, but explores the same vertices. Discovery and finish Every vertex gets two moments in a DFS: when it is discovered (first entered) and when it finishes (all its descendants have been explored and the recursion returns). Finishing order is the key to the next two ideas. Cycles in directed graphs: three colours In an undirected graph, BFS or union-find detects cycles easily. In a directed graph, "I have seen this vertex before" is not enough: in 0 → 1, 0 → 2, 1 → 2 , vertex 2 is reached twice, but there is no cycle. A cycle exists exactly when DFS finds an edge to a vertex that is still on the current path (discovered but not finished). Track three states: - white : not discovered yet, - grey : discovered, still being explored (on the recursion stack), - black : finished. An edge to a grey vertex is a back edge : a cycle. cpp include <iostream include <vector enum Colour { White, Grey, Black }; bool hasCycle(int u, const std::vector<std::vector<int & adj, std::vector<Colour & colour) { colour u = Grey; for (int v : adj u ) { if (colour v == Grey) return true; // back edge if (colour v == White && hasCycle(v, adj, colour)) return true; } colour u = Black; return false; } bool hasCycle(const std::vector<std::vector<int & adj) { std::vector<Colour colour(adj.size(), White); for (std::size_t u = 0; u < adj.size(); ++u) if (colour u == White && hasCycle(static_cast<int (u), adj, colour)) return true; return false; } int main() { std::cout << "diamond: " << hasCycle({ { 1, 2 }, { 2 }, {} }) << '
'; std::cout << "loop: " << hasCycle({ { 1 }, { 2 }, { 0 } }) << '
'; } Topological order A directed graph with no cycles is a DAG (directed acyclic graph). DAGs describe dependencies: "compile util.cpp before linking", "take Algorithms before Compilers", "put on socks before shoes". A topological order lists the vertices so that every edge points forward : u comes before v for every edge u → v. Every DAG has at least one; a graph with a cycle has none. By DFS : a vertex finishes only after everything reachable from it has finished. So listing vertices in reverse finishing order puts every vertex before everything it points to. By Kahn's algorithm : count each vertex's in-degree (incoming edges). Vertices with in-degree 0 have no prerequisites, so they can go first. Output one, remove its outgoing edges (decrementing the in-degrees of its neighbours), and repeat with whatever reaches in-degree 0. If vertices remain that never reach 0, the graph has a cycle. cpp include <iostream include <queue include <string include <vector int main() { std::vector<std::string task{ "fetch", "configure", "compile", "test", "package", "docs" }; std::vector<std::vector<int adj(6); auto before = & (int a, int b) { adj a .push_back(b); }; before(0, 1); before(1, 2); before(2, 3); before(2, 4); before(3, 4); before(0, 5); before(5, 4); std::vector<int indegree(6, 0); for (const auto& out : adj) for (int v : out) ++indegree v ; std::queue<int ready; for (int u = 0; u < 6; ++u) if (indegree u == 0) ready.push(u); std::vector<int order; while (!ready.empty()) { int u = ready.front(); ready.pop(); order.push_back(u); for (int v : adj u ) if (--indegree v == 0) ready.push(v); } if (order.size() < adj.size()) std::cout << "there is a cycle
"; for (int u : order) std::cout << task u << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } Kahn's algorithm is O(V + E), easy to make iterative, and naturally reports cycles. Replacing the queue with a min-heap gives the lexicographically smallest topological order, useful when the output must be deterministic (practice 5.02). What topological order unlocks Processing vertices in topological order means every vertex is handled after all its predecessors. That turns several hard problems on general graphs into easy one-pass problems on DAGs: - Shortest and longest paths in O(V + E): relax each vertex's outgoing edges in topological order. Longest path is NP-hard in general graphs but linear in a DAG; it gives the critical path of a project plan (the minimum time to finish all tasks when independent tasks run in parallel). - Counting paths : the number of paths to v is the sum over its predecessors. - Dynamic programming (lesson 6.02) is, at heart, computing values over a DAG of subproblems in topological order. Strongly connected components In a directed graph, a strongly connected component is a maximal set of vertices that can all reach one another. Collapsing each one to a single vertex leaves a DAG. Kosaraju's algorithm finds them with two DFS passes (one on the graph to get finishing order, one on the reversed graph in reverse finishing order); Tarjan's does it in one. They are used to analyse web link structure, find circular dependencies, and solve 2-SAT problems. quiz ? In DFS cycle detection on a directed graph, which edge reveals a cycle? - An edge to a white (undiscovered) vertex + An edge to a grey vertex, one still on the current DFS path - An edge to a black (finished) vertex - Any edge to a vertex seen before An edge to a finished vertex can occur without a cycle, as in a diamond shape. ? Kahn's algorithm stops with some vertices never output. What does that mean? + The graph has a cycle among the remaining vertices - The graph is disconnected - The queue was too small - The order is not unique Vertices on a cycle wait for each other, so their in-degrees never reach 0. ? Why can longest paths be found quickly in a DAG but not in general graphs? - DAGs have fewer edges + Processing vertices in topological order means each vertex's best value is final before it is used - Longest paths are always shortest paths in a DAG - DAGs have no weights With no cycles, no later vertex can improve an earlier one. Summary - DFS goes deep and backtracks; it is O(V + E) and reveals the structure of a graph. - Three colours detect cycles in directed graphs: an edge to a grey vertex is a back edge. - A DAG has a topological order: reverse DFS finishing order, or Kahn's in-degree algorithm (which also detects cycles). - Topological order makes shortest and longest paths, path counting and dynamic programming on DAGs linear. - Strongly connected components collapse a directed graph into a DAG.

title: Depth-first search and dependencies
body: Directed graphs are given as a vertex count and a list of edges (u, v) meaning u → v. cpp using Edges = std::vector<std::pair<int, int ; std::vector<int topoOrder(int n, const Edges& edges); // the smallest topological order, or {} if there is a cycle std::vector<int findCycle(int n, const Edges& edges); // the vertices of some directed cycle in order, or {} long long countPaths(int n, const Edges& edges, int from, int to); // in a DAG std::vector<std::string buildOrder(const std::vector<std::string & lines); - topoOrder uses Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap instead of a queue, so that whenever several vertices are ready, the smallest number comes first. The result is the lexicographically smallest topological order. - findCycle uses DFS with three colours. When it finds an edge to a grey vertex v , the cycle is v , then the vertices on the current DFS path after it. Return them starting at v : for edges 0→1, 1→2, 2→0 from vertex 0, that is { 0, 1, 2 } . Any correct cycle is accepted by the tests. It must not recurse: the tests have a cycle of 100,000 vertices. - countPaths : the number of different paths from from to to in a DAG, by processing vertices in topological order. Duplicate edges count as different paths. Use long long . - buildOrder : each line is target: dep1 dep2 ... (a target with no dependencies is target: ). Return every name mentioned, in an order where each name comes after all its dependencies, choosing the alphabetically smallest available name at each step. If there is a cycle, return { "cycle" } .

title: 5.03  Shortest Paths with Dijkstra
body:
Shortest paths when edges have weights - why BFS no longer works, relaxation, Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue and lazy deletion, its O((V + E) log V) cost, rebuilding routes, why negative weights break it, Bellman-Ford and negative cycles, 0-1 BFS, and choosing the right shortest-path algorithm. Weighted edges On a map, roads have lengths or travel times. The route with the fewest roads is not necessarily the fastest: a motorway with three junctions can beat a single slow mountain road. BFS counts edges, so for weighted graphs we need something else. Formally: each edge u → v has a weight w(u, v) ≥ 0, the length of a path is the sum of its weights, and we want dist v , the length of the shortest path from a source s to every vertex v. Relaxation Every shortest-path algorithm is built on one operation. Keep a best-known distance dist v for every vertex (∞ at first, 0 for the source). Relaxing an edge u → v asks: is going through u better than what I know? if dist u + w(u, v) < dist v : dist v = dist u + w(u, v) parent v = u The algorithms differ only in which edges they relax, in what order . Dijkstra's algorithm Edsger Dijkstra's idea (1956): always process the unfinished vertex with the smallest known distance next. With non-negative weights, that distance can never improve later, since any other route would have to go through a vertex that is already at least as far. So the vertex is finished , and we relax its outgoing edges. A min-heap of (distance, vertex) pairs finds the smallest each time. When a distance improves, push the new pair; the old one stays in the heap and is skipped when popped because it is out of date ("lazy deletion"). This is simpler than updating entries inside the heap and just as fast in practice. cpp include <algorithm include <functional include <iostream include <limits include <queue include <string include <utility include <vector using Graph = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, long long ; // (neighbour, weight) const long long INF = std::numeric_limits<long long ::max(); std::pair<std::vector<long long , std::vector<int dijkstra(const Graph& g, int source) { std::vector<long long dist(g.size(), INF); std::vector<int parent(g.size(), -1); using Item = std::pair<long long, int ; // (distance, vertex) std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item , std::greater<Item pq; dist source = 0; pq.push({ 0, source }); while (!pq.empty()) { auto d, u = pq.top(); pq.pop(); if (d dist u ) continue; // an out-of-date entry for (auto v, w : g u ) if (dist u + w < dist v ) { dist v = dist u + w; parent v = u; pq.push({ dist v , v }); } } return { dist, parent }; } int main() { std::vector<std::string name{ "home", "bakery", "bridge", "park", "school" }; Graph g(5); auto road = & (int a, int b, long long minutes) { g a .push_back({ b, minutes }); g b .push_back({ a, minutes }); }; road(0, 1, 4); road(0, 2, 1); road(2, 1, 2); road(1, 3, 1); road(2, 3, 5); road(3, 4, 3); auto dist, parent = dijkstra(g, 0); for (int v = 0; v < 5; ++v) std::cout << name v << ": " << dist v << " min
"; std::vector<int route; for (int v = 4; v != -1; v = parent v ) route.push_back(v); std::reverse(route.begin(), route.end()); std::cout << "route to school:"; for (int v : route) std::cout << ' ' << name v ; std::cout << '
'; } The direct road from home to the bakery takes 4 minutes, but going via the bridge takes 1 + 2 = 3: Dijkstra finds it. Cost : each vertex is finished once, and each edge relaxed once, pushing at most one heap entry. With E heap operations of O(log E) = O(log V) each, Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V) . For a road network of millions of junctions, that is well under a second. (Production route planners add preprocessing such as contraction hierarchies to answer queries in microseconds.) To stop early when you only need one target, return as soon as the target is popped (not when it is first pushed: a shorter route may still turn up). Negative weights break it Dijkstra assumes a finished vertex can never get a shorter distance. A negative edge breaks that: with edges s → a (2), s → b (5) and b → a (−4), Dijkstra finishes a at distance 2, but s → b → a costs 1. Negative weights appear in real problems (costs and refunds, currency exchange as log-rates, energy gained and spent). For them use Bellman-Ford : relax every edge, V − 1 times over. After pass i, every shortest path using at most i edges is correct, and a shortest path has at most V − 1 edges. It is O(VE), much slower, but it also detects negative cycles : if a V-th pass still improves something, a cycle with negative total weight exists, and "shortest" is meaningless (you could loop forever, getting cheaper). cpp include <iostream include <limits include <optional include <tuple include <vector using Edge = std::tuple<int, int, long long ; // from, to, weight const long long INF = std::numeric_limits<long long ::max() / 4; std::optional<std::vector<long long bellmanFord(int V, const std::vector<Edge & edges, int source) { std::vector<long long dist(V, INF); dist source = 0; for (int pass = 0; pass < V; ++pass) { bool changed = false; for (auto u, v, w : edges) if (dist u != INF && dist u + w < dist v ) { dist v = dist u + w; changed = true; } if (!changed) return dist; // settled early if (pass == V - 1) return std::nullopt; // still improving after V - 1 passes: a negative cycle } return dist; } int main() { auto d = bellmanFord(3, { { 0, 1, 2 }, { 0, 2, 5 }, { 2, 1, -4 } }, 0); std::cout << "dist to 1: " << ( d) 1 << '
'; auto bad = bellmanFord(3, { { 0, 1, 1 }, { 1, 2, -2 }, { 2, 1, 1 } }, 0); std::cout << "negative cycle found? " << !bad.has_value() << '
'; } Special cases - Unweighted (all weights 1): plain BFS, O(V + E). - Weights 0 or 1 : 0-1 BFS uses a deque, pushing 0-weight neighbours to the front and 1-weight ones to the back. O(V + E). - A DAG : relax in topological order (lesson 5.02), O(V + E), and negative weights are fine. - All pairs on a small dense graph: Floyd-Warshall, three nested loops, O(V³). Situation Algorithm Time --- --- --- unweighted BFS O(V + E) weights 0/1 0-1 BFS O(V + E) non-negative weights Dijkstra O((V + E) log V) DAG, any weights topological order O(V + E) negative weights Bellman-Ford O(VE) all pairs, small V Floyd-Warshall O(V³) quiz ? Why can Dijkstra's algorithm finalise the vertex with the smallest tentative distance? + With non-negative weights, any other route to it passes through a vertex at least as far, so it cannot be shorter - Because it was discovered first - Because the heap is sorted - It cannot; it must check again later This is exactly the step that negative weights break. ? A popped heap entry (d, u) has d dist u . What should Dijkstra do? - Relax u's edges again with d + Skip it: a better distance for u was found after this entry was pushed - Stop: the algorithm has failed - Push it back That is lazy deletion: stale entries are simply ignored. ? Bellman-Ford still improves a distance on its V-th pass. What does that mean? - The graph is disconnected - The source is wrong + A negative-weight cycle is reachable from the source - More passes are needed Without negative cycles, all shortest paths are settled after V - 1 passes. Summary - Weighted shortest paths repeatedly relax edges: dist u + w < dist v . - Dijkstra finishes vertices in order of distance with a min-heap and lazy deletion: O((V + E) log V), non-negative weights only. - Parent links rebuild the route; stop early when the target is popped. - Bellman-Ford handles negative weights in O(VE) and detects negative cycles. - Choose by the weights: BFS, 0-1 BFS, Dijkstra, DAG relaxation, Bellman-Ford or Floyd-Warshall.

title: Weighted shortest paths
body: Weighted directed graphs are given as edge lists of (from, to, weight) : cpp using WEdges = std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, long long ; std::vector<long long dijkstra(int n, const WEdges& edges, int source); // -1 for unreachable; weights = 0 std::pair<long long, std::vector<int cheapest(int n, const WEdges& edges, int from, int to); // cost and path; (-1, {}) if none std::optional<std::vector<long long bellmanFord(int n, const WEdges& edges, int source); // nullopt if a negative cycle is reachable std::vector<long long zeroOneBfs(int n, const WEdges& edges, int source); // every weight is 0 or 1; -1 for unreachable - dijkstra uses a min-heap with lazy deletion and must handle 100,000 vertices and 300,000 edges quickly. - cheapest stops as soon as to is popped . If several cheapest paths exist, any one is accepted. - bellmanFord returns std::numeric_limits<long long ::max() for unreachable vertices (not -1, since distances can be negative here). It returns std::nullopt only if a negative cycle is reachable from the source. - zeroOneBfs uses a std::deque : 0-weight neighbours go to the front, 1-weight ones to the back. O(V + E).

title: 5.04  Minimum Spanning Trees
body:
Connecting everything as cheaply as possible - spanning trees, the cut property that makes greedy choices safe, Kruskal's algorithm with sorting and union-find, Prim's algorithm with a priority queue, the dense O(V^2) version of Prim for complete graphs, minimum spanning forests, and uses from network design to clustering. The problem A council wants to connect every village with roads, a company every office with fibre, an engineer every point of a circuit with wire. Each possible link has a cost. What is the cheapest set of links that connects everything ? The answer never contains a cycle (dropping any edge of a cycle keeps everything connected and saves money), so it is a tree that spans all vertices: a minimum spanning tree (MST). For V vertices it has exactly V − 1 edges. Note the difference from shortest paths: an MST minimises the total cost of the network, not the distance between any particular pair. The MST route between two villages can be long. The cut property Split the vertices into two groups in any way (a cut ). The cheapest edge crossing between the groups belongs to some minimum spanning tree. (If a spanning tree did not use it, adding it would create a cycle that crosses the cut a second time through a more expensive edge; swapping them gives a tree at least as cheap.) This makes greedy algorithms correct: repeatedly take the cheapest edge that is safe. Kruskal and Prim differ in which cut they look at. Kruskal's algorithm Sort all edges by cost. Go through them cheapest first, and add an edge unless it would close a cycle . Union-find (lesson 4.05) answers "would it close a cycle?" in effectively O(1): the ends are already connected exactly when find(u) == find(v) . cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <numeric include <string include <tuple include <vector struct UnionFind { std::vector<int parent, size; explicit UnionFind(int n) : parent(n), size(n, 1) { std::iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0); } int find(int x) { while (parent x != x) x = parent x = parent parent x ; return x; } // path halving bool unite(int a, int b) { a = find(a); b = find(b); if (a == b) return false; if (size a < size b ) std::swap(a, b); parent b = a; size a += size b ; return true; } }; int main() { std::vector<std::string town{ "Ash", "Birch", "Cedar", "Dale", "Elm" }; std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, int edges{ // (cost, a, b) { 7, 0, 1 }, { 5, 0, 3 }, { 8, 1, 2 }, { 9, 1, 3 }, { 7, 1, 4 }, { 5, 2, 4 }, { 15, 3, 4 }, { 6, 3, 2 } }; std::sort(edges.begin(), edges.end()); UnionFind uf(5); int total = 0; for (auto cost, a, b : edges) if (uf.unite(a, b)) { total += cost; std::cout << town a << " - " << town b << " (" << cost << ")
"; } std::cout << "total " << total << '
'; } Sorting dominates: O(E log E) . Kruskal is simple and works directly on an edge list. If the graph is not connected, it naturally produces a minimum spanning forest : one tree per component. Prim's algorithm Prim grows a single tree from a start vertex. At each step it adds the cheapest edge that connects the tree to a vertex outside it (the cut between "in the tree" and "not yet"). It looks just like Dijkstra, with one change: the priority of a vertex is the cost of the single edge that would attach it, not the length of a whole path. cpp include <functional include <iostream include <queue include <utility include <vector int main() { int V = 5; std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, int adj(V); // (neighbour, cost) auto link = & (int a, int b, int c) { adj a .push_back({ b, c }); adj b .push_back({ a, c }); }; link(0, 1, 7); link(0, 3, 5); link(1, 2, 8); link(1, 3, 9); link(1, 4, 7); link(2, 4, 5); link(3, 4, 15); link(3, 2, 6); std::vector<bool inTree(V, false); using Item = std::pair<int, int ; // (edge cost, vertex) std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item , std::greater<Item pq; pq.push({ 0, 0 }); int total = 0, added = 0; while (!pq.empty() && added < V) { auto cost, u = pq.top(); pq.pop(); if (inTree u ) continue; // already attached more cheaply inTree u = true; total += cost; ++added; for (auto v, c : adj u ) if (!inTree v ) pq.push({ c, v }); } std::cout << "total " << total << " with " << added << " vertices
"; } With a binary heap, Prim is O(E log V) . Both algorithms find a tree of the same total cost (the MST is unique when all edge costs differ). Dense graphs: O(V²) Prim When every pair of vertices can be linked, for example connecting points in the plane where any two can be wired together, E is about V²/2 and building the edge list alone is expensive. A version of Prim without a heap is then better: keep for every outside vertex the cheapest known cost to attach it, pick the minimum by scanning the array, and update the array from the new tree vertex. Each of the V steps scans V entries: O(V²) , with no edge list at all. Practice 5.04 uses it. Uses - Network design : roads, pipes, cables, circuit wiring. - Clustering : build the MST of points with distances as costs, then delete the k − 1 most expensive edges: what remains are k clusters whose closest members are as far apart as possible (single-linkage clustering). - Approximation : the MST gives a route at most twice the optimum for the travelling salesman problem with distances that obey the triangle inequality. - Image segmentation : pixels as vertices, colour differences as costs. quiz ? Why does a minimum spanning tree never contain a cycle? + Removing the most expensive edge of a cycle keeps everything connected and lowers the cost - Because trees cannot have weights - Because Kruskal sorts the edges - It can contain one cycle Any cycle has an edge that can be dropped without disconnecting anything. ? In Kruskal's algorithm, what does union-find decide? - Which edge is cheapest + Whether an edge's two ends are already connected, so adding it would close a cycle - The order of the vertices - The total cost unite(a, b) returning false means a and b are already in the same tree. ? How does Prim's priority differ from Dijkstra's? - It does not use a priority queue + A vertex's priority is the cost of the single edge attaching it, not the total path length from the start - It processes the largest edge first - There is no difference Prim minimises the tree's total weight, Dijkstra the distance from the source. Summary - A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices with V − 1 edges of least total cost. - The cut property makes greedy choices safe. - Kruskal: sort edges, add each unless union-find says it closes a cycle; O(E log E). - Prim: grow one tree with a min-heap of attaching edges; O(E log V), or O(V²) without a heap on dense graphs. - MSTs design networks, cluster data and approximate harder problems.

title: Minimum spanning trees
body: Undirected weighted graphs are edge lists of (a, b, cost) : cpp using CEdges = std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, long long ; long long kruskal(int n, CEdges edges, std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, long long & chosen); // -1 if not connected long long prim(int n, const CEdges& edges); // -1 if not connected long long connectPoints(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int & points); // Manhattan distances, O(n^2) std::vector<std::vector<int clusters(int n, CEdges edges, int k); - kruskal sorts the edges by cost (ties: keep the input order, so use a stable sort), adds each one unless union-find says it closes a cycle, fills chosen with the edges used in that order, and returns the total. If the graph is not connected, return -1 (and chosen holds the spanning forest). - prim grows one tree from vertex 0 with a min-heap; it must give the same total as kruskal . - connectPoints : every pair of points can be joined at a cost equal to their Manhattan distance x1 - x2 + y1 - y2 . Return the cheapest total that connects all points, using the heap-free O(n²) Prim from lesson 5.04 (the tests use 3,000 points: 4.5 million possible edges). - clusters : run Kruskal but stop when there are k components left. Return the components, each sorted, and the list sorted by first element.

title: 5.05  Grid Search and A*
body: Finding paths faster with a sense of direction - weighted grids, Dijkstra exploring in every direction, the A algorithm with f = g + h, admissible and consistent heuristics (Manhattan, Chebyshev, octile, Euclidean), tie-breaking, comparing how many cells each algorithm expands, and where A is used in games, robotics and puzzles. Searching with a goal in mind Dijkstra's algorithm expands vertices in order of their distance from the start, in every direction. If you only want the path to one goal, most of that work is wasted: searching for a route from Paris to Berlin, Dijkstra explores Spain just as eagerly as Germany. A\ (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, 1968) adds a sense of direction. For each vertex n it uses: - g(n) : the cost of the best known path from the start to n (Dijkstra's dist ), - h(n) : a heuristic , an estimate of the remaining cost from n to the goal, - f(n) = g(n) + h(n) : the estimated cost of the best path through n. A is Dijkstra with the priority queue ordered by f instead of g. Vertices that are close to the start and seem close to the goal come first. Admissible and consistent heuristics A finds the optimal path if h never overestimates the true remaining cost: h is admissible . If h also never drops by more than the edge cost along any edge (h(u) ≤ w(u, v) + h(v)), it is consistent , and then, as in Dijkstra, every vertex is final when popped and needs to be expanded only once. - h = 0 everywhere is admissible and consistent: A becomes Dijkstra. - The better h estimates the true distance (without overestimating), the fewer vertices A expands. - An overestimating h can make A faster but no longer guarantees the shortest path ("weighted A " does this deliberately). For grids, the right heuristic depends on the moves allowed, scaled by the cheapest cost of a step: Moves Heuristic Formula (dx, dy = distances to the goal) --- --- --- 4 directions Manhattan dx + dy 8 directions, diagonal costs 1 Chebyshev max(dx, dy) 8 directions, diagonal costs √2 octile max(dx, dy) + (√2 − 1)·min(dx, dy) any direction Euclidean √(dx² + dy²) A on a grid The grid below has walls ( ), open cells ( . , cost 1 to enter) and swamp ( ~ , cost 5 to enter). Moves go up, down, left and right, so Manhattan distance (times the cheapest step cost, 1) is admissible and consistent. cpp include <cstdlib include <functional include <iostream include <queue include <string include <tuple include <vector struct Result { int cost; int expanded; }; Result search(const std::vector<std::string & grid, int sr, int sc, int gr, int gc, bool useHeuristic) { int rows = static_cast<int (grid.size()), cols = static_cast<int (grid 0 .size()); auto h = & (int r, int c) { return useHeuristic ? std::abs(r - gr) + std::abs(c - gc) : 0; }; std::vector<int g(rows cols, 1 << 30); using Item = std::tuple<int, int, int ; // (f, -g, cell): ties prefer larger g, closer to the goal std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item , std::greater<Item open; g sr cols + sc = 0; open.push({ h(sr, sc), 0, sr cols + sc }); int expanded = 0; const int dr = { -1, 1, 0, 0 }, dc = { 0, 0, -1, 1 }; while (!open.empty()) { auto f, negG, cell = open.top(); open.pop(); if (-negG g cell ) continue; // stale entry ++expanded; int r = cell / cols, c = cell % cols; if (r == gr && c == gc) return { g cell , expanded }; for (int d = 0; d < 4; ++d) { int nr = r + dr d , nc = c + dc d ; if (nr < 0 nr = rows nc < 0 nc = cols grid nr nc == ' ') continue; int cost = g cell + (grid nr nc == '~' ? 5 : 1); int next = nr cols + nc; if (cost < g next ) { g next = cost; open.push({ cost + h(nr, nc), -cost, next }); } } } return { -1, expanded }; } int main() { std::vector<std::string grid(40, std::string(60, '.')); for (int r = 5; r < 35; ++r) grid r 30 = ' '; // a wall with gaps at the top and bottom for (int c = 10; c < 50; ++c) grid 20 c = '~'; // a band of swamp for (bool astar : { false, true }) { Result res = search(grid, 20, 2, 20, 57, astar); std::cout << (astar ? "A : " : "Dijkstra: ") << "cost " << res.cost << ", cells expanded " << res.expanded << '\n'; } } Both find the same cost, but A expands a fraction of the cells: Dijkstra floods the whole map before reaching the far side, while A heads for the goal and only spreads out where the wall forces it to. Tie-breaking matters on grids: many cells often share the same f. Preferring the one with the larger g (the one further along) makes A push towards the goal instead of widening the search front. The code orders by (f, −g) . Beyond grids - Games : units finding their way around maps; often with precomputed navigation meshes and hierarchical search for large maps. - Robotics : path planning in configuration spaces. - Puzzles : the 15-puzzle or Rubik's cube are graphs of states; the heuristic counts misplaced tiles or adds up each tile's Manhattan distance to its home. - Route planning : road networks use the straight-line distance divided by the top speed as an admissible time estimate, plus "landmark" heuristics precomputed from distances to a few reference points. When even A is too slow or memory-hungry, variants trade optimality or memory: IDA (iterative deepening, very little memory), jump point search (skips symmetric paths on uniform grids), and bidirectional search (searching from both ends at once). quiz ? What does A use as the priority of a vertex? - g(n), the cost so far - h(n), the estimated remaining cost + f(n) = g(n) + h(n) - the number of edges from the start The estimated cost of the cheapest path through n. ? Which heuristic is admissible for a grid with 4-direction moves costing at least 1? + Manhattan distance - twice the Manhattan distance - the number of walls on the map - Manhattan distance plus 10 It never overestimates: any 4-direction path needs at least dx + dy steps. ? What happens with h(n) = 0 for every vertex? - A fails to find a path + A behaves exactly like Dijkstra's algorithm - A becomes breadth-first search on weighted graphs - A becomes depth-first search With no estimate, the priority is just the cost so far. Summary - A orders the frontier by f = g + h, steering the search towards the goal. - With an admissible (never overestimating) heuristic it finds a shortest path; with a consistent one, each vertex is expanded once. - Match the heuristic to the moves: Manhattan, Chebyshev, octile or Euclidean, scaled by the cheapest step. - Break ties towards larger g; A then expands far fewer vertices than Dijkstra for a single goal.

title: A* on a weighted grid
body: The grid has walls , and open cells whose cost to enter is 1 for . or the digit itself for 1 to 9 . S is the start and G the goal (both cost 1 to enter). Moves go up, down, left and right. cpp struct SearchResult { long long cost; int expanded; std::vector<std::pair<int, int path; }; SearchResult dijkstraGrid(const std::vector<std::string & grid); SearchResult astarGrid(const std::vector<std::string & grid); - Both return the cheapest cost from S to G ( -1 and an empty path if unreachable), the number of cells expanded (popped from the priority queue and not skipped as stale), and the path as (row, column) pairs from S to G inclusive. - astarGrid orders the queue by f = g + h with the Manhattan distance to the goal as h , breaking ties in favour of the larger g . Stop when the goal is popped. - dijkstraGrid is the same search with h = 0 . - The tests check the costs, that paths are valid and cost what they claim, and that A expands far fewer cells than Dijkstra on open maps.
