title: 6.01  Greedy Algorithms
body:
Building a solution one locally best choice at a time - when greedy works and how to prove it with an exchange argument, interval scheduling by earliest finish time, counting meeting rooms with a sweep, why greedy coin change fails for some coin systems, Huffman coding with a priority queue, the fractional knapsack, and a checklist for spotting greedy problems. Choose the best-looking option, never look back A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, at each step taking the choice that looks best right now, and never reconsidering it. Dijkstra (always finish the closest vertex), Prim and Kruskal (always take the cheapest safe edge) are greedy. When greedy works, it is usually simple and fast. The hard part is knowing whether it works: for many problems the locally best choice leads to a globally bad answer. Interval scheduling You have one meeting room and a list of requested meetings, each with a start and end time. What is the largest number of meetings you can accept, with no two overlapping? Several greedy rules come to mind: the shortest meeting first, the one that starts first, the one with the fewest conflicts. Only one always works: always pick the meeting that finishes first among those that do not overlap what you have already accepted. cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <vector struct Meeting { int start, end; }; int maxMeetings(std::vector<Meeting m) { std::sort(m.begin(), m.end(), (const Meeting& a, const Meeting& b) { return a.end < b.end; }); int count = 0, freeAt = -1; // the room is free from this time on for (const auto& x : m) if (x.start = freeAt) // fits after the last accepted meeting { ++count; freeAt = x.end; } return count; } int main() { std::vector<Meeting requests{ { 1, 4 }, { 3, 5 }, { 0, 6 }, { 5, 7 }, { 3, 9 }, { 5, 9 }, { 6, 10 }, { 8, 11 }, { 8, 12 }, { 2, 14 }, { 12, 16 } }; std::cout << maxMeetings(requests) << " meetings
"; } Why it is right: the exchange argument. Take any optimal schedule. Its first meeting ends no earlier than the meeting greedy picked first (greedy chose the earliest finish of all). So you can swap the optimal schedule's first meeting for greedy's, and nothing else in it overlaps: it is still valid and just as large. Repeat for the second meeting, and so on. So greedy's schedule is as large as any optimal one. This is the standard way to prove a greedy algorithm correct: show that any optimal solution can be transformed step by step into the greedy one without getting worse. How many rooms? A related question: to hold all the meetings, how many rooms are needed? It is the largest number of meetings happening at the same moment. Sweep through time: turn each meeting into a +1 event at its start and a −1 event at its end, sort the events (ends before starts at the same time, since a room freed at 5 can be used by a meeting starting at 5), and track the running total. cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <utility include <vector int roomsNeeded(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int & meetings) { std::vector<std::pair<int, int events; // (time, +1 or -1); -1 sorts before +1 for (auto s, e : meetings) { events.push_back({ s, +1 }); events.push_back({ e, -1 }); } std::sort(events.begin(), events.end()); int now = 0, most = 0; for (auto t, change : events) most = std::max(most, now += change); return most; } int main() { std::cout << roomsNeeded({ { 0, 30 }, { 5, 10 }, { 15, 20 }, { 10, 15 }, { 25, 40 } }) << " rooms
"; } This sweep line idea (sort events, process them in order, keep a running state) solves many geometric and scheduling problems. When greedy fails: coin change To pay 63 cents with US coins (25, 10, 5, 1), take the largest coin that fits, repeatedly: 25 + 25 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1, six coins, which is optimal. That works for most real currencies, but not for every coin system. With coins 1, 3 and 4 , greedy pays 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), while 3 + 3 uses two. The greedy choice "take the biggest" closed off the better option. Lesson 6.02 solves coin change correctly for any coins with dynamic programming. Huffman coding Text files store each character in 8 bits. If some characters are far more common than others, giving them shorter codes saves space. Huffman coding builds the optimal prefix-free code (no code is the beginning of another, so the bit stream can be decoded unambiguously): 1. Put every character in a min-heap, weighted by its frequency. 2. Repeatedly remove the two lightest items and merge them into one with the combined weight. 3. The merges form a binary tree; a character's code is its path from the root (left = 0, right = 1). The greedy choice, merging the two rarest items, puts the rarest characters deepest. The total encoded size is the sum of all the merged weights: cpp include <functional include <iostream include <map include <queue include <string include <vector int main() { std::string text = "abracadabra alakazam"; std::map<char, long long freq; for (char c : text) ++freq c ; std::priority_queue<long long, std::vector<long long , std::greater<long long heap; for (auto c, f : freq) heap.push(f); long long bits = 0; while (heap.size() 1) { long long a = heap.top(); heap.pop(); long long b = heap.top(); heap.pop(); bits += a + b; // every character below this merge gets one more bit heap.push(a + b); } std::cout << text.size() << " characters: " << text.size() 8 << " bits plain, " << bits << " bits with Huffman coding
"; } Huffman coding is inside ZIP, gzip, PNG and JPEG, usually after another stage that finds repeated substrings. The fractional knapsack A thief can carry 50 kg and may take any fraction of each item (gold dust, not gold bars). Greedy works: sort by value per kilogram and take the best until the bag is full, taking part of the last item. If items cannot be split (the 0/1 knapsack ), greedy fails, and lesson 6.03 uses dynamic programming instead. Spotting greedy problems - There is a natural order (by end time, by cost, by ratio) and committing to the best item in that order never hurts. - You can sketch an exchange argument: "if an optimal solution did not take the greedy choice, swapping it in would not make it worse". - Try small counterexamples first. If greedy fails on a tiny case (like coins 1, 3, 4), switch to dynamic programming. quiz ? For interval scheduling with one room, which greedy rule always gives the most meetings? - shortest meeting first - earliest start first + earliest finish first - fewest overlaps first Finishing early leaves the most room for everything else; the exchange argument proves it. ? With coins 1, 3 and 4, what does "largest coin first" pay for 6? + 4 + 1 + 1, three coins, though 3 + 3 uses two - 3 + 3 - 4 + 2 - 1 × 6 A greedy choice can block a better combination; this coin system needs dynamic programming. ? In Huffman coding, which two items are merged at each step? - the two most frequent + the two least frequent - the first two in the alphabet - any two Merging the rarest items pushes them deepest, so they get the longest codes. Summary - A greedy algorithm commits to the locally best choice at every step. - Prove it with an exchange argument; disprove it with a small counterexample. - Interval scheduling: earliest finish first. Rooms needed: a sweep over start and end events. - Huffman coding and the fractional knapsack are greedy; coin change with arbitrary coins and the 0/1 knapsack are not.

title: Greedy choices
body: cpp int maxMeetings(std::vector<std::pair<int, int meetings); // (start, end); end start; one room int roomsNeeded(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int & meetings); // rooms to hold them all long long huffmanBits(const std::vector<long long & frequencies); // total bits of an optimal prefix code double fractionalKnapsack(std::vector<std::pair<double, double items, double capacity); // (weight, value) - A meeting (s, e) occupies the half-open time s, e) : one ending at 5 does not overlap one starting at 5. - huffmanBits repeatedly merges the two smallest weights with a min-heap and adds up the merged weights. With fewer than two symbols the answer is 0 (a single symbol needs no bits to tell it apart). Frequencies of 0 still take part. - fractionalKnapsack : take items by value per unit of weight, best first, taking a fraction of the last one. Items with weight 0 are always taken whole. - The tests use 100,000 meetings, so these must be O(n log n).

title: 6.02  Dynamic Programming
body:
Solving problems by combining answers to overlapping subproblems - why naive recursion explodes, memoisation (top-down), tabulation (bottom-up), the recipe of state, transition, base cases and order, counting paths in a grid, minimum coins for any coin system, counting the ways to make change, rebuilding the chosen solution, and saving memory by keeping only the rows you need. The problem with plain recursion The Fibonacci numbers are defined by F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2). Written directly as recursion: cpp include <iostream long long calls = 0; long long fib(int n) { ++calls; return n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); } int main() { for (int n : { 10, 20, 30 }) { calls = 0; long long f = fib(n); std::cout << "fib(" << n << ") = " << f << " took " << calls << " calls
"; } } The number of calls grows like 1.6ⁿ: fib(50) would take hours. The reason is that the same subproblems are solved again and again: fib(30) computes fib(28) twice, fib(27) three times, fib(26) five times... Dynamic programming (DP) applies when a problem has: 1. optimal substructure : the answer can be built from answers to smaller subproblems, and 2. overlapping subproblems : the same subproblems come up many times. It solves each subproblem once and stores the answer. Memoisation: top-down Keep the recursion, but remember every result in a table, and look it up before computing: cpp include <iostream include <vector long long fib(int n, std::vector<long long & memo) { if (n < 2) return n; if (memo n != -1) return memo n ; return memo n = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo); } int main() { std::vector<long long memo(91, -1); std::cout << "fib(90) = " << fib(90, memo) << '
'; } Each value from 2 to 90 is computed once: O(n). Memoisation is the easiest way to turn a correct but slow recursive solution into a fast one. Tabulation: bottom-up Or fill the table in an order where every subproblem's inputs are already known, with plain loops: cpp-norun std::vector<long long f(n + 1); f 0 = 0; f 1 = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) f i = f i - 1 + f i - 2 ; Tabulation avoids recursion (no stack overflow, less overhead) and often reveals that only the last few entries are needed, so the table can shrink: Fibonacci needs only two variables. The recipe Every DP solution answers four questions: 1. State : what does a table entry mean? (" ways r c = the number of paths from the top-left corner to cell (r, c)") 2. Transition : how is an entry computed from smaller ones? (" ways r c = ways r-1 c + ways r c-1 ") 3. Base cases : which entries are known directly? (" ways 0 0 = 1 ; blocked cells have 0") 4. Order : in what order can the table be filled so the inputs are always ready? ("row by row, left to right") The state is the creative part. If the transition needs information the state does not hold, add it to the state. Paths through a grid A robot moves only right or down through a grid with blocked cells. How many different paths lead from the top-left to the bottom-right corner? cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector int main() { std::vector<std::string grid{ "....", ". ..", "... ", " ..." }; int rows = 4, cols = 4; std::vector<std::vector<long long ways(rows, std::vector<long long (cols, 0)); for (int r = 0; r < rows; ++r) for (int c = 0; c < cols; ++c) { if (grid r c == ' ') continue; // no paths through a blocked cell if (r == 0 && c == 0) { ways r c = 1; continue; } if (r 0) ways r c += ways r - 1 c ; // arriving from above if (c 0) ways r c += ways r c - 1 ; // arriving from the left } std::cout << ways rows - 1 cols - 1 << " paths
"; } The table has rows × cols entries, each computed in O(1): O(rows × cols), compared with an exponential number of paths to enumerate. Coin change, done right Lesson 6.01 showed greedy coin change failing for coins 1, 3, 4. DP solves it for any coins: - State : best a = the fewest coins that make amount a (or "impossible"). - Transition : the last coin used is some c ; then best a = 1 + min over coins c ≤ a of best a − c . - Base case : best 0 = 0 . - Order : amounts from 0 up. Remembering which coin achieved each minimum lets you rebuild the actual coins afterwards, a technique that works for any DP: store the choice, then walk back from the final state. cpp include <climits include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int coins{ 1, 3, 4 }; int amount = 10; std::vector<int best(amount + 1, INT_MAX), lastCoin(amount + 1, -1); best 0 = 0; for (int a = 1; a <= amount; ++a) for (int c : coins) if (c <= a && best a - c != INT_MAX && best a - c + 1 < best a ) { best a = best a - c + 1; lastCoin a = c; } std::cout << "fewest coins for " << amount << ": " << best amount << " ("; for (int a = amount; a 0; a -= lastCoin a ) std::cout << lastCoin a << (a - lastCoin a 0 ? " + " : ""); std::cout << ")
"; } O(amount × number of coins). Note that this is pseudo-polynomial : polynomial in the value of the amount, not in the number of digits needed to write it. Counting, not optimising How many different ways are there to make 10 from coins 1, 3, 4, if the order of coins does not matter (1 + 3 and 3 + 1 are the same way)? Loop over the coins on the outside : then each combination is built in one fixed order of coins and counted once. cpp include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int coins{ 1, 3, 4 }; int amount = 10; std::vector<long long ways(amount + 1, 0); ways 0 = 1; for (int c : coins) for (int a = c; a <= amount; ++a) ways a += ways a - c ; std::cout << ways amount << " ways to make " << amount << '
'; } Swapping the two loops (amounts outside, coins inside) counts ordered sequences instead: 1 + 3 and 3 + 1 become different. A small change in loop order changes the meaning of the state. quiz ? What two properties make a problem suitable for dynamic programming? + optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems - sorted input and a greedy choice - a recursive definition and a base case - small input and integer values Recursion alone is not enough: DP pays off when the same subproblems repeat. ? What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation? - Memoisation is always faster + Memoisation keeps the recursion and caches results; tabulation fills a table iteratively in a dependency-respecting order - Tabulation only works for Fibonacci - They compute different answers Both solve each subproblem once; they differ in how the order of computation is chosen. ? In the "ways to make change" loop, why are the coins in the outer loop? - It is faster + So that each combination of coins is counted once, in a single fixed order - To find the fewest coins - Because the coins are sorted With amounts outside, 1 + 3 and 3 + 1 would be counted as different ways. Summary - DP solves overlapping subproblems once each and stores the results. - Memoisation adds a cache to recursion; tabulation fills a table with loops in a safe order. - Design with the recipe: state, transition, base cases, order. - Store the choice made at each state to rebuild the actual solution. - Coin change and grid paths show both optimising and counting DPs; loop order can change what is counted.

title: Dynamic programming basics
body: cpp long long stairWays(int n, const std::vector<int & steps); // ordered ways to climb n stairs, modulo 1000000007 std::vector<int fewestCoins(const std::vector<int & coins, int amount); // the coins used, sorted; {} if 0; {-1} if impossible long long changeWays(const std::vector<int & coins, int amount); // unordered combinations (no modulo; fits long long) long long gridPaths(const std::vector<std::string & grid); // right/down paths avoiding ' ' long long bestRobbery(const std::vector<int & houses); // max sum with no two adjacent houses - stairWays : you climb by any of the step sizes in steps at each move; different orders count as different ways (1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are two ways). stairWays(0, ...) is 1. Work modulo 1000000007; n can be 100,000. - fewestCoins returns the coins of one optimal answer in ascending order, rebuilt from the choices stored during the DP. If several optimal multisets exist, any one is accepted. - gridPaths : start at the top-left, finish at the bottom-right, moving only right or down; 0 if either corner is blocked. The result fits in long long for the test sizes. - bestRobbery : the classic "house robber": choose houses with the largest total value, never two neighbours.

title: 6.03  Classic Dynamic Programming Problems
body:
The problems every programmer meets - the 0/1 knapsack and why its one-row version loops backwards, the longest common subsequence (behind diff tools), edit distance (behind spelling correction and DNA alignment) with a one-row optimisation, and the longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n) with patience sorting. The 0/1 knapsack A hiker can carry W kilograms. Each item has a weight and a value, and must be taken whole or left. Which items maximise the total value? Greedy by value per kilogram fails here (a heavy valuable item can leave awkward unused space), but DP solves it: - State : best i w = the highest value using only the first i items within capacity w . - Transition : item i is either left ( best i−1 w ) or taken, if it fits ( best i−1 w − weight + value ): take the larger. - Base case : best 0 w = 0 . That is O(n × W) time. Since row i only needs row i − 1 , one row is enough, if you loop over capacities backwards : going downwards, best w − weight still holds the previous row's value, so each item is used at most once. Looping forwards would let an item be taken again and again (which is exactly the "unbounded knapsack"). cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int weight{ 1, 3, 4, 5 }, value{ 1, 4, 5, 7 }; int W = 7; std::vector<int best(W + 1, 0); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < weight.size(); ++i) for (int w = W; w = weight i ; --w) // backwards: each item at most once best w = std::max(best w , best w - weight i + value i ); std::cout << "best value with capacity " << W << ": " << best W << '
'; // Keeping the full table lets us rebuild which items were taken. std::size_t n = weight.size(); std::vector<std::vector<int t(n + 1, std::vector<int (W + 1, 0)); for (std::size_t i = 1; i <= n; ++i) for (int w = 0; w <= W; ++w) { t i w = t i - 1 w ; if (weight i - 1 <= w) t i w = std::max(t i w , t i - 1 w - weight i - 1 + value i - 1 ); } std::cout << "take items:"; for (std::size_t i = n, w = W; i 0; --i) if (t i w != t i - 1 w ) // the value changed, so item i - 1 was taken { std::cout << ' ' << i - 1; w -= weight i - 1 ; } std::cout << '
'; } Longest common subsequence A subsequence keeps some characters of a string in order, not necessarily adjacent: "ACE" is a subsequence of "ABCDE". The longest common subsequence (LCS) of two strings is the longest string that is a subsequence of both. diff and version control systems use LCS on lines to show what changed between two files; biologists use it on DNA. - State : L i j = the LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b . - Transition : if a i−1 == b j−1 , that character extends the LCS: L i−1 j−1 + 1 . Otherwise one of the two characters is not in it: max(L i−1 j , L i j−1 ) . cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <string include <vector std::string lcs(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) { std::vector<std::vector<int L(a.size() + 1, std::vector<int (b.size() + 1, 0)); for (std::size_t i = 1; i <= a.size(); ++i) for (std::size_t j = 1; j <= b.size(); ++j) L i j = a i - 1 == b j - 1 ? L i - 1 j - 1 + 1 : std::max(L i - 1 j , L i j - 1 ); std::string out; // walk back from the corner for (std::size_t i = a.size(), j = b.size(); i 0 && j 0;) { if (a i - 1 == b j - 1 ) { out += a i - 1 ; --i; --j; } else if (L i - 1 j = L i j - 1 ) --i; else --j; } std::reverse(out.begin(), out.end()); return out; } int main() { std::cout << lcs("AGGTAB", "GXTXAYB") << '
'; std::cout << lcs("dynamic programming", "dramatic programs") << '
'; } O( a × b ) time and space. Edit distance The edit distance (Levenshtein distance) between two words is the fewest single-character insertions , deletions and substitutions that turn one into the other. "kitten" → "sitting" takes 3: substitute k→s, substitute e→i, insert g. Spelling checkers suggest dictionary words at a small edit distance (the milestone project does), and DNA alignment uses weighted versions. - State : D i j = the edit distance between the first i characters of a and the first j of b . - Base cases : D i 0 = i (delete everything), D 0 j = j (insert everything). - Transition : D i j is the smallest of - D i−1 j + 1 (delete a i−1 ), - D i j−1 + 1 (insert b j−1 ), - D i−1 j−1 + (a i−1 == b j−1 ? 0 : 1) (keep or substitute). Each row only needs the previous one, so two rows (or one row plus a variable) are enough: O( a × b ) time, O( b ) space. cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <string include <vector int editDistance(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) { std::vector<int prev(b.size() + 1), cur(b.size() + 1); for (std::size_t j = 0; j <= b.size(); ++j) prev j = static_cast<int (j); for (std::size_t i = 1; i <= a.size(); ++i) { cur 0 = static_cast<int (i); for (std::size_t j = 1; j <= b.size(); ++j) cur j = std::min({ prev j + 1, cur j - 1 + 1, prev j - 1 + (a i - 1 == b j - 1 ? 0 : 1) }); std::swap(prev, cur); } return prev b.size() ; } int main() { for (auto a, b : { std::pair{ "kitten", "sitting" }, std::pair{ "flaw", "lawn" }, std::pair{ "", "abc" }, std::pair{ "same", "same" } }) std::cout << a << " - " << b << ": " << editDistance(a, b) << '
'; } Longest increasing subsequence Given a sequence of numbers, how long is the longest strictly increasing subsequence? For 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 5 , one answer is 1 4 5 6 ... or 1 2 3 5 : length 4. The direct DP, lis i = 1 + max(lis j ) over earlier j with a smaller value, is O(n²). A cleverer method, patience sorting , is O(n log n). Keep an array tails , where tails k is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far. The array is always sorted, so for each new value, binary search for the first tail that is ≥ it, and replace it (or append if there is none). The answer is the length of tails . cpp include <algorithm include <iostream include <vector int lisLength(const std::vector<int & values) { std::vector<int tails; for (int x : values) { auto it = std::lower_bound(tails.begin(), tails.end(), x); if (it == tails.end()) tails.push_back(x); // extends the longest run so far else it = x; // a smaller tail for runs of that length } return static_cast<int (tails.size()); } int main() { std::cout << lisLength({ 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5 }) << '
'; std::cout << lisLength({ 10, 9, 8, 7 }) << '
'; } tails is not itself an increasing subsequence of the input; it only tracks the best possible ends. Rebuilding an actual subsequence needs a parent index per element, as with coin change. Recognising these patterns Pattern Typical state Examples --- --- --- prefix of one sequence dp i Fibonacci, coin change, LIS, house robber prefixes of two sequences dp i j LCS, edit distance, sequence alignment items and capacity dp i w knapsack, subset sum, partition into equal halves interval dp l r matrix chain multiplication, palindromes, optimal BSTs subset of a small set dp mask travelling salesman on ~20 cities quiz ? Why does the one-row 0/1 knapsack loop over capacities from high to low? + So best w - weight still holds the previous item's row, and the item is counted at most once - It is faster - To sort the items - Because capacities must be processed in decreasing order in any DP Going upwards would reuse the current item: that is the unbounded knapsack. ? What is the edit distance between "flaw" and "lawn"? - 1 + 2 - 3 - 4 Delete the f and insert an n at the end. ? In the O(n log n) longest-increasing-subsequence method, what does tails k hold? - the k-th element of the input + the smallest last value of any increasing subsequence of length k + 1 found so far - the LIS itself - the number of subsequences of length k Keeping the smallest possible ends leaves the most room for later values to extend them. Summary - 0/1 knapsack: take or leave each item, O(n × W); one row looped backwards. - LCS and edit distance fill a table over prefixes of two strings, O( a × b ); edit distance needs only two rows. - Rebuild solutions by walking back through the table. - LIS takes O(n log n) with patience sorting and binary search. - Most DP problems follow a handful of state patterns.

title: Classic DP problems
body: cpp struct Item { int weight; int value; }; std::pair<int, std::vector<int knapsack(const std::vector<Item & items, int capacity); // best value and the chosen item indexes (ascending) std::string lcs(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); // one longest common subsequence int editDistance(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); int lisLength(const std::vector<int & values); // strictly increasing; O(n log n) std::vector<int lis(const std::vector<int & values); // one longest increasing subsequence - knapsack : 0/1 knapsack (each item at most once). Return the best total value and the indexes of one optimal choice. If several choices are optimal, any is accepted. - lcs may return any longest common subsequence; the tests check that it is common to both strings and has the right length. - editDistance uses insertions, deletions and substitutions, each costing 1, and only O( b ) memory: the tests compare strings of 5,000 characters. - lisLength must be O(n log n) (the tests use 200,000 values). lis returns an actual subsequence (any one of the longest), which needs a parent index for each element.

title: 6.04  Tries and String Matching
body:
Data structures and algorithms for text - tries for prefix lookups and autocompletion, the cost of naive substring search, the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm and its prefix function, Rabin-Karp with a rolling hash, what std::string::find and std::search do, and a glance at suffix arrays and Aho-Corasick for many patterns. Tries A trie (from re trie val, usually pronounced "try") is a tree that stores a set of strings by their characters. Each edge is a character, each path from the root spells a prefix, and a node is marked if the path to it is a complete word. The trie above holds "to", "tea", "ten", "i", "in" and "inn". Looking up a word of length L takes O(L) , however many words are stored. And unlike a hash table, a trie answers prefix questions directly: every word starting with "te" lies in the subtree below the node for "te". That makes tries the natural structure for autocompletion, spelling suggestions, IP routing tables (longest prefix match) and word games. cpp include <array include <iostream include <memory include <string include <vector class Trie { public: void insert(const std::string& word) { Node n = &root_; for (char ch : word) { auto& child = n- next ch - 'a' ; if (!child) child = std::make_unique<Node (); n = child.get(); ++n- passing; // how many words go through this node } n- word = true; } bool contains(const std::string& word) const { const Node n = walk(word); return n && n- word; } int countPrefix(const std::string& prefix) const { const Node n = walk(prefix); return n ? n- passing : 0; } std::vector<std::string complete(const std::string& prefix, std::size_t limit) const { std::vector<std::string out; std::string current = prefix; if (const Node n = walk(prefix)) collect(n, current, limit, out); return out; } private: struct Node { std::array<std::unique_ptr<Node , 26 next{}; bool word = false; int passing = 0; }; const Node walk(const std::string& s) const { const Node n = &root_; for (char ch : s) { n = n- next ch - 'a' .get(); if (!n) return nullptr; } return n; } static void collect(const Node n, std::string& current, std::size_t limit, std::vector<std::string & out) { if (out.size() = limit) return; if (n- word) out.push_back(current); for (int c = 0; c < 26; ++c) // children in alphabetical order if (n- next c ) { current.push_back(static_cast<char ('a' + c)); collect(n- next c .get(), current, limit, out); current.pop_back(); } } Node root_; }; int main() { Trie t; for (std::string w : { "tea", "ten", "to", "inn", "in", "i", "team", "tease", "tent" }) t.insert(w); std::cout << "contains te? " << t.contains("te") << ", contains tea? " << t.contains("tea") << '
'; std::cout << "words starting with te: " << t.countPrefix("te") << '
'; for (const auto& w : t.complete("te", 3)) std::cout << w << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } A depth-first walk visits children in alphabetical order, so completions come out sorted. The price of a trie is memory: an array of 26 pointers per node adds up. Compact variants store children in a small sorted vector or a hash map, or merge chains of single-child nodes (a radix tree ). Finding a pattern in a text How do you find every occurrence of a pattern P (length m) in a text T (length n)? The obvious way tries every starting position and compares character by character: O(n × m) in the worst case. Searching for aaaab in a text of a million a s compares almost five characters at every one of a million positions, and the work is thrown away each time. Knuth-Morris-Pratt The KMP algorithm (1977) never moves backwards in the text. When a mismatch happens after matching some characters, it already knows what those characters were (they are the start of the pattern), so it can tell how much of the pattern still matches without looking at the text again. That information is the prefix function : pi i is the length of the longest proper prefix of P 0..i that is also a suffix of it. For ababaca : 0 0 1 2 3 0 1 . After a mismatch with k characters matched, KMP continues as if pi k − 1 characters matched. cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector std::vector<int prefixFunction(const std::string& p) { std::vector<int pi(p.size(), 0); for (std::size_t i = 1, k = 0; i < p.size(); ++i) { while (k 0 && p i != p k ) k = pi k - 1 ; // fall back to a shorter border if (p i == p k ) ++k; pi i = static_cast<int (k); } return pi; } std::vector<std::size_t kmpSearch(const std::string& text, const std::string& p) { std::vector<std::size_t found; if (p.empty()) return found; std::vector<int pi = prefixFunction(p); for (std::size_t i = 0, k = 0; i < text.size(); ++i) { while (k 0 && text i != p k ) k = pi k - 1 ; if (text i == p k ) ++k; if (k == p.size()) { found.push_back(i + 1 - p.size()); k = pi k - 1 ; // keep going: matches may overlap } } return found; } int main() { for (int v : prefixFunction("ababaca")) std::cout << v << ' '; std::cout << '
'; for (auto pos : kmpSearch("abababcabababcab", "ababc")) std::cout << pos << ' '; std::cout << '
'; std::string big(1000000, 'a'); big += 'b'; std::cout << "found at " << kmpSearch(big, "aaaab") 0 << '
'; } The while loop inside the for loop looks quadratic, but k goes up by at most one per character and every step of the while lowers it, so the total work is O(n + m): the same amortised reasoning as the sliding-window deque in lesson 1.05. Rabin-Karp: matching with hashes Rabin-Karp compares hashes instead of characters. It computes the polynomial hash of the pattern and of each window of the text, sliding the window in O(1) per step with the rolling hash from practice 2.02. Only when the hashes are equal does it compare the actual characters, to rule out a collision. The expected time is O(n + m). Its strength is searching for many patterns of the same length at once (put their hashes in a hash set), and spotting repeated substrings, as plagiarism detectors do. In the standard library std::string::find is usually a simple, highly optimised search (often using memchr to jump to candidate first characters), fast in practice but O(n × m) in the worst case. C++17 added std::search with searcher objects, including std::boyer_moore_searcher and std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher . Boyer-Moore compares the pattern from its last character and uses mismatches to skip ahead by up to m characters, so on ordinary text it looks at only a fraction of the characters. cpp include <algorithm include <functional include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string text = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"; std::string pattern = "lazy"; auto it = std::search(text.begin(), text.end(), std::boyer_moore_searcher(pattern.begin(), pattern.end())); std::cout << "found at " << (it - text.begin()) << '
'; std::cout << "find: " << text.find("the", 1) << '
'; } More text structures - Aho-Corasick builds a trie of many patterns with KMP-like failure links and finds all of them in one pass over the text: antivirus scanners and grep -F with many words. - A suffix array is the sorted list of all suffixes of a text; with it, any pattern can be found by binary search in O(m log n), and it reveals repeated substrings. Suffix trees and the FM-index (behind DNA read aligners) push this further. quiz ? Why is looking up a word of length L in a trie O(L), regardless of how many words it holds? + The lookup follows one edge per character from the root - Tries are hash tables - The words are sorted - It is actually O(log n) The number of stored words does not affect the length of the path for one word. ? What is the prefix function of "aabaa"? - 0 1 2 3 4 + 0 1 0 1 2 - 0 0 0 1 2 - 1 2 0 1 2 For "aabaa" the longest border is "aa" (length 2); for "aab" there is none. ? What makes KMP linear even though it has a loop inside a loop? - The inner loop runs at most once + The matched length k rises by at most one per text character, and each inner step lowers it, so total inner steps are at most n - It skips characters like Boyer-Moore - It uses hashing This is amortised analysis: count the total work over the whole run. Summary - A trie stores strings character by character: O(L) lookups, prefix counts and sorted autocompletion. - Naive substring search is O(n × m) in the worst case. - KMP uses the prefix function to never re-read text: O(n + m). - Rabin-Karp matches rolling hashes and shines with many patterns of the same length. - The standard library offers find and Boyer-Moore searchers; Aho-Corasick and suffix arrays handle bigger text problems.

title: A trie and KMP
body: Build a trie of lowercase words, and the Knuth-Morris-Pratt search: cpp class Trie { public: bool insert(const std::string& word); // false if already present; words are lowercase a-z, possibly empty bool erase(const std::string& word); // false if absent bool contains(const std::string& word) const; int countPrefix(const std::string& prefix) const; // how many stored words start with it std::vector<std::string complete(const std::string& prefix, std::size_t limit) const; // alphabetical std::string longestCommonPrefix() const; // of all stored words; "" if none std::size_t size() const; }; std::vector<int prefixFunction(const std::string& p); std::vector<std::size_t findAll(const std::string& text, const std::string& pattern); // overlapping matches; {} for an empty pattern - Each node keeps how many words pass through it, so countPrefix is O(length of the prefix). erase decreases those counts and must leave the trie consistent (the tests insert again afterwards). - complete returns up to limit stored words that start with prefix , in alphabetical order (depth-first, children in letter order), including the prefix itself if it is a word. - findAll must be O(n + m): the tests search a million characters.

title: 6.05  Backtracking
body:
Searching through every possibility, cleverly - the choose, explore, unchoose pattern, generating subsets, permutations and combinations, the N-queens puzzle with constant-time safety checks, solving Sudoku, pruning dead ends early, branch and bound, and a first look at NP-complete problems, where exhaustive search is the best known exact method. When there is no shortcut Some problems have no known greedy rule or dynamic-programming structure: place eight queens on a chessboard so that none attacks another, fill in a Sudoku, find a subset of numbers that sums to a target. The fallback is to search : try the options one by one. Backtracking does that systematically and efficiently. It builds a solution one decision at a time, and as soon as a partial solution cannot possibly be completed, it abandons it ( backtracks ) and tries the next option. Every backtracking algorithm has the same shape: cpp-norun void search(State& state) { if (isComplete(state)) { record(state); return; } for (Choice c : choicesFor(state)) { if (!allowed(state, c)) continue; // prune: this choice cannot lead to a solution apply(state, c); // choose search(state); // explore undo(state, c); // unchoose } } It is a depth-first search (lesson 5.02) of a tree of partial solutions that is never built explicitly. Subsets and permutations Generating all subsets of n items makes one yes/no decision per item: 2ⁿ leaves. Generating all orderings (permutations) picks an unused item for each position: n! leaves. cpp include <iostream include <vector void subsets(const std::vector<int & items, std::size_t i, std::vector<int & chosen) { if (i == items.size()) { std::cout << '{'; for (std::size_t k = 0; k < chosen.size(); ++k) std::cout << (k ? "," : "") << chosen k ; std::cout << "} "; return; } subsets(items, i + 1, chosen); // leave items i out chosen.push_back(items i ); // choose it subsets(items, i + 1, chosen); // explore chosen.pop_back(); // unchoose } void permutations(std::vector<int & items, std::size_t pos) { if (pos == items.size()) { for (int x : items) std::cout << x; std::cout << ' '; return; } for (std::size_t i = pos; i < items.size(); ++i) { std::swap(items pos , items i ); // put items i in position pos permutations(items, pos + 1); std::swap(items pos , items i ); // undo } } int main() { std::vector<int chosen; subsets({ 1, 2, 3 }, 0, chosen); std::cout << '
'; std::vector<int items{ 1, 2, 3 }; permutations(items, 0); std::cout << '
'; } The standard library generates permutations in lexicographic order with std::next_permutation (start from a sorted range and loop while it returns true). N queens Place N queens on an N × N board so that no two share a row, a column or a diagonal. Place one queen per row; for each row, try every column that is not attacked. Tracking the used columns and the two kinds of diagonals in boolean arrays makes each safety check O(1): squares on the same "/" diagonal share row + col , and on the same "" diagonal share row − col . cpp include <iostream include <vector int n; std::vector<bool column, diag1, diag2; long long solutions = 0, nodes = 0; void place(int row) { ++nodes; if (row == n) { ++solutions; return; } for (int c = 0; c < n; ++c) { if (column c diag1 row + c diag2 row - c + n - 1 ) continue; // attacked: prune column c = diag1 row + c = diag2 row - c + n - 1 = true; place(row + 1); column c = diag1 row + c = diag2 row - c + n - 1 = false; } } int main() { for (n = 4; n <= 10; ++n) { column.assign(n, false); diag1.assign(2 n, false); diag2.assign(2 n, false); solutions = nodes = 0; place(0); std::cout << n << " queens: " << solutions << " solutions, " << nodes << " partial boards explored
"; } } There are 10¹⁰ ways to put one queen in each row of a 10 × 10 board, but pruning means only about 35,000 partial boards are ever explored. Sudoku A Sudoku solver is the same pattern: find an empty cell, try each digit that does not already appear in its row, column or 3 × 3 box, recurse, and undo if the recursion fails. A strong improvement is to choose the empty cell with the fewest possible digits first (the "most constrained variable" heuristic): it fails fastest when a branch is hopeless, and often has only one option. Practice 6.05 builds a solver. Pruning and branch and bound Backtracking is only as good as its pruning. Good pruning checks: - constraints as early as possible (the queen safety arrays), - feasibility : in subset sum with positive numbers, stop when the running total exceeds the target, or when even taking every remaining number cannot reach it, - symmetry : in N queens, the first queen only needs the left half of the first row (mirror the rest). For optimisation problems, branch and bound adds a bound: keep the best complete solution found so far, and abandon any partial solution whose optimistic estimate cannot beat it. This is how exact solvers for scheduling, routing and the knapsack with huge capacities work in practice. When search is the best we know For many important problems (the travelling salesman, Boolean satisfiability, graph colouring, subset sum, scheduling with constraints), no polynomial-time algorithm is known. They are NP-complete : a proposed solution is easy to check , and a fast algorithm for any one of them would give fast algorithms for all of them. Whether that is possible is the famous open question P vs NP . In practice, such problems are attacked with: - backtracking with strong pruning, and branch and bound, - dynamic programming when a parameter is small (subset sum with a small target, the travelling salesman on 20 cities with bitmask DP), - specialised solvers (SAT solvers, integer linear programming), - approximation algorithms with guarantees (the MST-based travelling-salesman tour from lesson 5.04), - heuristics such as local search and simulated annealing when "good enough" will do. quiz ? What are the three steps inside a backtracking loop? + choose, explore, unchoose - sort, search, return - divide, conquer, combine - push, pop, peek Apply a choice, recurse, then undo it so the next choice starts from the same state. ? How does the N-queens solver check diagonals in O(1)? - by scanning the board + squares on one diagonal share row + col, and on the other row - col; boolean arrays index by those - by sorting the queens - by hashing the board One array per diagonal direction records whether a queen already occupies it. ? What does branch and bound add to backtracking? - a heap of solutions + abandoning partial solutions whose best possible outcome cannot beat the best solution found so far - dynamic programming - random restarts A good bound prunes large parts of the search tree for optimisation problems. Summary - Backtracking searches the tree of partial solutions depth first: choose, explore, unchoose. - Subsets give 2ⁿ leaves and permutations n!; pruning is what makes search feasible. - Constant-time constraint checks (N queens) and choosing the most constrained variable first (Sudoku) cut the search dramatically. - Branch and bound prunes optimisation searches with bounds. - NP-complete problems have no known polynomial algorithm; search, DP on small parameters, solvers, approximations and heuristics are the tools.

title: Backtracking
body: cpp std::vector<std::vector<int combinationsSumming(std::vector<int numbers, int target); // each number at most once std::vector<std::vector<int uniquePermutations(std::vector<int numbers); // no duplicates, lexicographic order long long countQueens(int n); bool solveSudoku(std::vector<std::string & board); // 9 strings of 9 chars, '.' for empty - combinationsSumming : the numbers are positive and distinct. Return every subset that sums to target , each sorted ascending, and the list sorted lexicographically. Prune: stop extending a combination once its sum would pass the target (sort the numbers first). - uniquePermutations : the input may contain duplicates; return each distinct ordering once, in lexicographic order, without using a set to remove duplicates. (Sort first, and at each position skip a value equal to the previous one that is not in use.) - countQueens : the number of ways to place n non-attacking queens on an n × n board, with O(1) safety checks. The tests go up to n = 12. - solveSudoku fills the board in place and returns true, or returns false (leaving the board as it was) if there is no solution. Choose the empty cell with the fewest candidates first; the tests include a puzzle designed to be hard for plain backtracking.

title: A spelling checker
body: The capstone combines the last milestone's ideas: a trie stores the dictionary, and edit distance finds suggestions. Instead of computing the edit distance to every dictionary word separately, walk the trie depth first and carry one row of the edit-distance table down the tree: the row for a node is computed from its parent's row in O(length of the word being checked), words that share a prefix share the work, and a whole branch is skipped as soon as every entry of its row exceeds the allowed distance. add the quick brown fox jumps over lazy dog add quiet quilt quit quite check The quikc brown fox jumsp over teh lazy dgo. complete qui suggest quit 1 count prints added 12 words quikc: did you mean quick, quiet, quilt? jumsp: did you mean jumps? teh: did you mean the? dgo: did you mean dog? qui: quick, quiet, quilt, quit, quite quit: quit (0), quiet (1), quilt (1), quite (1) 12 words Words are runs of letters; they are compared in lower case, so The is the word the . title: Common Errors
body: Most bugs in this course are not compiler errors: the program runs, but gives a wrong answer, crashes on some inputs, or is far too slow. Test small cases by hand, the edge cases (empty input, one element, all equal, sorted, reversed) and large inputs. Wrong answers Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- Binary search loops forever or misses the first/last element Inconsistent range convention, or lo = mid with mid rounded down Use a half-open lo, hi) range and an invariant; when setting lo = mid , round mid up 2.01 Wrong result for large values (lo + hi) / 2 or a sum overflowing int lo + (hi - lo) / 2 ; accumulate in long long 2.01 A sort crashes or returns garbage A comparator using <= (not a strict weak ordering) Compare with < , and std::tie for several keys 3.01 Equal elements change order after sorting std::sort is not stable std::stable_sort 3.01 BFS gives wrong distances or is slow Marking vertices visited when popped, so they are queued many times Mark (set the distance) when pushing 5.01 Dijkstra gives a wrong distance A negative edge weight Bellman-Ford, or reformulate without negative weights 5.03 Dijkstra stops too early for a target Returning when the target is pushed, not popped Stop when it is popped 5.03 A directed graph is reported cyclic when it is not Treating an edge to any visited vertex as a cycle Only an edge to a grey (in-progress) vertex is a cycle 5.02 A hash set misses keys that are present The hash disagrees with == (equal keys hash differently) Hash exactly the fields == compares 2.02 Linear probing loses keys after erase Erasing by emptying the slot Use tombstones or backward-shift deletion 2.04 0/1 knapsack uses an item twice One-row DP looping capacities upwards Loop capacities from high to low 6.03 "Ways to make change" counts 1+3 and 3+1 separately Amounts in the outer loop Coins in the outer loop for combinations 6.02 Greedy gives a non-optimal answer No greedy-choice property (coins 1, 3, 4; 0/1 knapsack) Look for a counterexample; use DP 6.01 Union-find answers are wrong Uniting a and b instead of their roots parent find(b) = find(a) 4.05 AVL tree heights or sizes are wrong after rotations Updating the new root before the old one Update the lower node first, then the node that moved up 4.03 Crashes and undefined behaviour Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- Crash after push_back A pointer, reference or iterator into a vector that reallocated Keep indexes, or reserve first 1.03 Stack overflow on large inputs Deep recursion: DFS on a long path, destroying a long linked list, quicksort on sorted input Iterate with an explicit stack; destroy lists in a loop; recurse on the smaller side 1.04, 3.03, 5.02 Crash on an empty container front() , back() , top() or pop() on an empty container Check empty() first 1.05 Index out of range in a segment tree An array of 2n for the recursive version Allocate 4n for the recursive layout 4.04 Reading freed memory in a linked list Using a node after unique_ptr released it Read what you need (key, next) before moving the pointer 1.04 vector<bool surprises It is a packed bitset, not a real vector of bool Use std::vector<char when you need references or speed per element 4.05 Too slow Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- Fine for 1,000 items, hopeless for 100,000 An O(n²) algorithm hidden in a loop: find , erase(begin()) , insert at the front, copying a vector per call Choose an O(n log n) or O(n) method; pass by reference 1.01 A hash table is slow Many collisions from a poor hash (summing characters, XOR of fields, multiples of the bucket count) Use a mixing hash; combine fields with a mixing formula 2.02 Plain BST becomes slow Keys inserted in sorted order make a list Use a balanced tree (AVL, std::map ) 4.02 Recursion recomputes the same values No memoisation Cache results, or tabulate 6.02 Backtracking never finishes Pruning too late or not at all Check constraints as soon as a choice is made; choose the most constrained variable first 6.05 Debug build far slower than expected Debug iterators and no optimisation Measure in a Release build 1.02

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- A\ Shortest-path search ordered by f = g + h, where h estimates the remaining cost to the goal. (5.05) Adaptive Doing less work on easier inputs, as insertion sort does on nearly sorted data. (3.01) Adjacency list A graph stored as a list of neighbours for each vertex: O(V + E) memory. (5.01) Adjacency matrix A graph stored as a V × V table of edges: O(V²) memory, O(1) edge test. (5.01) Admissible heuristic An estimate that never overestimates the true remaining cost, so A stays optimal. (5.05) Amortised cost The average cost per operation over any sequence of operations, such as O(1) for push_back . (1.01) Augmenting a structure Storing extra data in each node (subtree size, sum) to answer new questions. (4.02) AVL tree A self-balancing BST in which every node's subtree heights differ by at most one. (4.03) Backtracking Building a solution choice by choice, abandoning partial solutions that cannot succeed. (6.05) Balance factor The height of a node's left subtree minus that of its right subtree. (4.03) BFS (breadth-first search) Exploring a graph in layers with a queue; finds fewest-edge paths. (5.01) Big O An upper bound on how a cost grows with the input size, ignoring constants. (1.01) Binary heap A complete binary tree in an array where every parent is at least (or at most) its children. (3.04) Binary search Finding a value in sorted data by halving the range: O(log n). (2.01) Binary search tree (BST) A binary tree with smaller keys to the left and larger keys to the right of every node. (4.02) Bipartite graph A graph whose vertices split into two groups with every edge between the groups. (5.01) Branch and bound Backtracking that prunes partial solutions whose best possible result cannot beat the best found. (6.05) Bucket One slot of a hash table, selected by hash % bucketCount . (2.02) Cache line The 64-byte block in which memory moves between RAM and the caches. (1.02) Chaining Handling hash collisions by keeping a list of entries in each bucket. (2.03) Collision Two different keys landing in the same bucket. (2.02) Comparator A function less(a, b) defining an order; it must be a strict weak ordering. (3.01) Complete binary tree A tree whose levels are all full except possibly the last, filled from the left. (3.04) Connected component A maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other. (5.01) Consistent heuristic A heuristic with h(u) ≤ w(u, v) + h(v) for every edge; each vertex is then expanded once. (5.05) Counting sort Sorting small integer keys by counting each value: O(n + k). (3.05) Cycle A path that returns to its starting vertex. (5.01) DAG A directed acyclic graph: directed edges and no cycles. (5.02) Deque A double-ended queue: O(1) push and pop at both ends. (1.05) DFS (depth-first search) Exploring a graph by going as deep as possible before backtracking. (5.02) Dijkstra's algorithm Shortest paths with non-negative weights, finishing vertices in order of distance with a heap. (5.03) Divide and conquer Splitting a problem into smaller copies, solving them, and combining the answers. (3.02) Dynamic array A contiguous array that grows by reallocating, like std::vector . (1.03) Dynamic programming Solving overlapping subproblems once each and storing the answers. (6.02) Edit distance The fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions turning one string into another. (6.03) Exchange argument Proving a greedy algorithm correct by transforming any optimal solution into the greedy one. (6.01) Fenwick tree An array of block sums sized by the lowest set bit: O(log n) updates and prefix sums. (4.04) Greedy algorithm Building a solution by always taking the locally best choice. (6.01) Hash function A function turning a key into a number; equal keys must give equal hashes. (2.02) Hash table A table that finds keys by hashing them to buckets: expected O(1) operations. (2.03) Heapsort Sorting by building a heap and repeatedly moving its root to the end: O(n log n), in place. (3.04) Height The number of edges on the longest path from a node down to a leaf. (4.01) In-order traversal Left subtree, node, right subtree; visits a BST's keys in sorted order. (4.01) In place Using only O(1) (or O(log n)) extra memory. (3.01) Insertion sort Inserting each element into the sorted prefix before it: O(n + inversions). (3.01) Introsort Quicksort that switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep, and insertion sort for small parts; std::sort . (3.03) Invariant A fact that holds before and after every step of a loop, used to reason about correctness. (2.01) Inversion A pair of positions whose elements are in the wrong order. (3.01) Kahn's algorithm Topological sorting by repeatedly removing vertices with in-degree zero. (5.02) KMP The Knuth-Morris-Pratt string search, using the prefix function to never re-read text: O(n + m). (6.04) Kruskal's algorithm A minimum spanning tree from edges taken cheapest first, skipping those that close a cycle. (5.04) Lazy deletion Leaving outdated heap entries in place and skipping them when popped. (5.03) Linear probing Open addressing that tries the following slots one by one. (2.04) Linked list A sequence of nodes, each pointing to the next (and, if doubly linked, the previous). (1.04) Load factor Entries divided by buckets (or slots) in a hash table. (2.03) Longest common subsequence The longest sequence appearing in order (not necessarily contiguously) in two strings. (6.03) Longest increasing subsequence The longest strictly increasing subsequence; O(n log n) by patience sorting. (6.03) Lower bound The first position whose value is at least the target. (2.01) Master theorem Solves recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(nᵈ) by comparing a with bᵈ. (3.02) Memoisation Caching the results of a recursive function so each input is computed once. (6.02) Merge sort Sort both halves, then merge them: O(n log n), stable, needs a buffer. (3.02) Minimum spanning tree The cheapest set of edges connecting all vertices, with no cycles. (5.04) Monotonic deque A deque kept in sorted order, giving sliding-window maxima in O(n). (1.05) NP-complete A problem whose solutions are easy to check but for which no fast algorithm is known. (6.05) Open addressing Storing hash entries in the array itself and probing for free slots. (2.04) Partition Rearranging elements around a pivot: smaller before, larger after. (3.03) Path compression Pointing every node on a union-find path directly at the root. (4.05) Pivot The element quicksort partitions around. (3.03) Prefix function For each position, the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix there. (6.04) Prefix sums Running totals that answer range sums in O(1) for unchanging data. (4.04) Prim's algorithm A minimum spanning tree grown from one vertex by always adding the cheapest attaching edge. (5.04) Priority queue A collection that always hands out its highest-priority element next. (3.04) Quickselect Finding the k-th smallest element by partitioning and recursing into one side: expected O(n). (3.03) Quicksort Partition around a pivot, then sort each side: O(n log n) on average. (3.03) Radix sort Sorting digit by digit with a stable counting sort: O(d(n + b)). (3.05) Rehashing Moving every entry into a bigger table when the load factor gets too high. (2.03) Relaxation Improving a vertex's distance via an edge: if dist u + w < dist v , update dist v . (5.03) Ring buffer A fixed array used as a queue with wrap-around indexes. (1.05) Rolling hash A hash of a sliding window updated in O(1) per step. (2.02) Rotation A local restructuring of a node and its child that keeps BST order. (4.03) Segment tree A tree storing the answer for every segment of a recursive halving: O(log n) range queries and updates. (4.04) Sentinel A dummy node that removes special cases, such as at the ends of a list. (1.04) Shunting-yard algorithm Evaluating expressions with an operator stack and a value stack. (1.05) Stable sort A sort that keeps equal elements in their original order. (3.01) Stack A last-in, first-out collection. (1.05) Strict weak ordering The rules a comparator must obey: irreflexive, transitive, with transitive equivalence. (3.01) Tabulation Filling a dynamic-programming table with loops in a safe order. (6.02) Tombstone A marker left by erasing from an open-addressing table so probes continue past it. (2.04) Topological order An order of a DAG's vertices in which every edge points forward. (5.02) Trie A tree that stores strings character by character; prefix queries in O(length). (6.04) Union-find A forest of parent pointers tracking disjoint sets under merging, in near O(1) per operation. (4.05) Union by size Attaching the smaller tree under the larger one in union-find. (4.05)

title: 1.01  What a Computer Is
body: A computer is a machine that follows a list of instructions, very fast and without getting bored. Every computer, from the first one to your phone, has the same four parts - input, processing, memory and output - and all of them are built from switches that are either on or off. A machine that follows instructions A calculator can add. A computer can add too, but that is not what makes it a computer. What makes it a computer is that it follows a list of instructions - a program - and the list can be changed. Give a computer a list that says "add up these marks and work out the average", and it is a school report tool. Give it a different list and the very same machine plays music, draws a game or sends a message. Nothing inside it changes except the list. !abstract In one sentence A computer is a machine that stores a list of instructions and carries them out one after another, very fast, and can store and change the information it is working on. Each instruction is tiny: "add these two numbers", "copy this number over there", "if this number is zero, jump to that instruction". A computer is not clever. It is fast - billions of tiny steps a second - and exact : it never skips a step and never gets bored. Everything impressive a computer does is built out of a huge number of simple steps. The four parts Every computer ever built has the same four jobs, done by different parts: Part Job Examples --- --- --- Input Gets information into the computer Keyboard, mouse, touch screen, camera, microphone, network Processing Carries out the instructions The CPU (central processing unit), the GPU for graphics Memory Holds the program and the data it is working on RAM while running, an SSD or hard drive to keep things when the power is off Output Gets results out Screen, speakers, printer, network Your phone has all four: the touch screen is both input and output, the chip inside does the processing, and it has memory for the apps that are running and storage for your photos. Hardware and software - Hardware is the part you can touch: chips, wires, the screen. - Software is the instructions: the programs. You cannot touch a program; it is information, like the words of a recipe are different from the paper they are printed on. The same hardware runs different software. That is the whole trick, and it is why a computer is so much more useful than a machine built for one job. Everything is switches Deep down, a computer is made of switches . Not light switches you flip by hand, but microscopic electronic ones called transistors , which can be turned on and off by electricity - billions of times a second. A modern chip has billions of them. A switch has only two states: on or off . Write on as 1 and off as 0 , and you have a bit (short for binary digit ). Every number, letter, photo and program inside a computer is stored as patterns of bits. This course spends a whole milestone on that, because it is the foundation everything else stands on. demo-bits title: Eight switches bits: 8 value: 77 Click the switches above. Eight of them together hold one number from 0 to 255. You will learn exactly why in milestone 2. Layers A computer is built in layers , each one hiding the details of the one below: Layer What it deals in Course milestone --- --- --- Apps you use Buttons, pictures, words Programming languages print("Hello") 5 Operating system Files, windows, running programs 6 Machine code Instructions as numbers 4 Logic gates and the CPU AND, OR, adding bits 4 Bits 0 and 1 2, 3 Transistors Switches made of silicon 1, 4 Programmers mostly work in the top layers, but knowing what is underneath explains why computers behave the way they do: why a number can "overflow", why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 , why a program can crash. By the end of this course you will be able to follow a single line of code all the way down to the switches. quiz ? What makes a computer different from a calculator? - It can work with bigger numbers + It follows a stored list of instructions that can be changed, so one machine can do many different jobs - It has a screen A calculator is built for one job. A computer runs whatever program it is given. ? Which part of a computer carries out the instructions? - The memory + The CPU - The keyboard The CPU (central processing unit) does the processing. Memory holds the program and data it works on. ? What is a bit? - A small program + A single 0 or 1: one switch that is off or on - Eight numbers "Bit" is short for binary digit. Everything inside a computer is stored as patterns of bits.

title: Input, processing, output
body: Every program has the shape from the lesson: input , processing , output . Write one in Python. Read a name and a year of birth, then print a greeting and how old the person turns in 2026: What is your name? Ada What year were you born? 1815 Hello, Ada! In 2026 you turn 211.
