title: 6.01  What an Operating System Does
body: The operating system is the program that runs the computer for every other program - it shares the CPU and memory between programs, gives them files and devices through one safe interface, keeps them from interfering with each other, and starts and stops them. Its core, the kernel, is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly. The program that runs the programs Turn on a computer with no operating system and you get a CPU fetching instructions from memory - and nothing to share it, no files, no windows, no way to start an app. The operating system (OS) is the software that turns bare hardware into something many programs and people can use at once. Operating system Runs on --- --- Windows most PCs macOS, iOS, iPadOS Apple computers, phones, tablets Linux most servers, supercomputers, many devices; Android is built on it Android most phones Many small "real-time" systems cars, routers, medical devices Its jobs Job What it means Lesson --- --- --- Run programs Load a program from disk into memory and start it; stop it when it ends or crashes 6.02 Share the CPU Switch between programs so quickly that they all seem to run at once 6.02 Share memory Give each program its own memory, and keep programs out of each other's 6.03 Files Turn a disk of numbered blocks into named files in folders 6.04 Devices Talk to keyboards, screens, disks, networks through drivers , so programs don't have to 6.04 Security Users, passwords, permissions: who may read which file Networking Send and receive data over Wi-Fi and cables 6.06 The kernel and user mode The core of the operating system is the kernel . It is the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly. The CPU itself enforces this with two modes: Mode Who runs in it May... --- --- --- Kernel mode (privileged) The kernel and drivers Do anything: any memory, any device, any instruction User mode (restricted) Every app: your browser, a game, Python Use only its own memory; cannot talk to devices; certain instructions cause an error When an app needs something only the kernel may do - read a file, print, open a network connection, get more memory - it makes a system call (5.06): a special instruction ( syscall on x86-64) that switches the CPU into kernel mode and jumps to a fixed entry point in the kernel. The kernel checks the request, does it, and switches back. This separation is why one crashing app does not crash the whole computer: it can only damage its own memory, and the kernel cleans up after it. A bug in the kernel or a driver, on the other hand, can bring everything down (the Windows "blue screen"). What you see vs. the kernel What people usually call "the operating system" includes much more than the kernel: the desktop and windows, the file browser, settings, the command line (a shell ), and many background services. Those are ordinary user-mode programs that come with the kernel. On Linux, the kernel is Linux itself; the rest (GNOME, KDE, the GNU tools) are separate projects packaged together into a distribution such as Ubuntu or Fedora. quiz ? What is the kernel? + The core of the operating system, the only code allowed to touch the hardware directly - The CPU's fastest core - The desktop and windows Everything else runs in user mode and asks the kernel through system calls. ? Why can an ordinary app not read the disk directly? + It runs in user mode, where the CPU does not allow direct access to devices; it must ask the kernel with a system call - Apps are too slow - The disk is locked when the computer is on The kernel checks every request, which keeps programs safe from each other. ? Why does one app crashing usually not crash the whole computer? + Each app only has its own memory, and the kernel stops it and cleans up - Apps cannot crash - The CPU restarts automatically User-mode isolation contains the damage.

title: 6.02  Processes, Threads and Scheduling
body: A running program is a process - its code, its memory, and its open files. Inside it, threads are the separate lines of execution. The scheduler shares the CPU cores by giving each thread a short time slice and switching between them hundreds of times a second, which is why many programs seem to run at once even on one core. Program vs. process A program is a file on disk: machine code and data (3.05). A process is a program while it runs : the operating system has loaded it into memory and keeps track of it. A process has Such as --- --- Its own memory its code, its variables, its stack (the Assembly course explains the stack) Its registers' values including the program counter: where it is up to Open files and connections file handles, network sockets An ID the PID , a number An owner the user who started it, which decides what it may access Run the same program twice (two browser windows from the same app, say) and you get two processes from one program. You can see the processes on your computer with Task Manager on Windows, Activity Monitor on macOS, or ps and top on Linux. Threads A process starts with one thread : one line of execution, with its own program counter, registers and stack, working through the code. A process can start more threads, which run at the same time and share the process's memory. A browser, for example, may use one thread to draw the page, another to download images, another to run a page's JavaScript. On a CPU with several cores (1.05), threads really do run simultaneously, one per core. !warning Shared memory is tricky Two threads changing the same variable at the same moment can lose updates, a bug called a race condition . If two threads each do count = count + 1 (read, add, write back) at the same time, both may read 5 and both write 6. Programs use locks to let only one thread at a time change shared data. Sharing the CPU: the scheduler A laptop has a handful of cores but hundreds of threads. How do they all run? The kernel's scheduler shares the cores out: 1. Pick a thread that is ready to run and give it a core. 2. Let it run for a time slice , a few milliseconds. 3. A timer interrupt (a signal from hardware that makes the CPU jump into the kernel) ends the slice. 4. Save that thread's registers, pick the next thread, load its registers, and let it run. This is a context switch . Because this happens hundreds of times a second, everything seems to run at once, even on a single core: that is multitasking . Each thread carries on exactly where it stopped, because its registers, including the program counter, were saved and restored. Waiting threads Most threads are not running at all, most of the time: they are waiting - for a key press, a network reply, a file read, a timer. The scheduler only gives cores to threads that are ready . That is why a computer with 300 threads can sit at 2% CPU: nearly all of them are waiting. Priorities Schedulers do not treat every thread the same. The thread drawing your mouse pointer or playing music gets priority over a background update, so the computer feels responsive. Modern schedulers also decide which core suits a thread best; phone and laptop chips mix fast "performance" cores and low-power "efficiency" cores. quiz ? What is the difference between a program and a process? + A program is a file; a process is a program running, with its own memory and state - They are the same thing - A process is a small program One program can be running as several processes at once. ? What does a context switch do? + Saves one thread's registers and loads another's, so the second carries on where it stopped - Switches the computer to another user - Changes which program is shown on screen It is how the scheduler shares a core between threads. ? Why might two threads adding 1 to the same counter lose updates? + Both may read the old value before either writes back, so one increment is lost - Threads cannot add - The scheduler adds numbers wrongly A race condition. Locks prevent it. ? Why is CPU usage often low even with hundreds of threads? + Most threads are waiting for something, and only ready threads use the CPU - The CPU is broken - Threads take turns sleeping on purpose Waiting for input, files or the network takes no CPU time.

title: A race condition
body: Two threads, A and B, each add 1 to a shared counter several times. Each addition is really three steps : read the counter into the thread's own register, add 1 to the register, write the register back. The scheduler (6.02) can switch threads between any two steps. Write run(schedule, start) : schedule is a string like "AAABBB" , where each letter means "that thread does its next step"; start is the counter's starting value. Each thread repeats read, add, write, read, add, write, ... Return the counter's final value. python run("AAABBB", 0) 2: A reads 0, adds, writes 1; then B reads 1, adds, writes 2 run("ABABAB", 0) 1: both read 0, both add, both write 1 - one update is lost Keep, for each thread, its register and which of the three steps comes next ( 0 read, 1 add, 2 write), for example in dictionaries: register = {"A": 0, "B": 0} , step = {"A": 0, "B": 0} .

title: How long does everyone wait?
body: When processes run one after another in the order they arrive (first come, first served, all arriving at time 0), each waits for everyone before it. Write: python def waiting_times(bursts) bursts i is how long process i needs; returns how long each one waits before starting def average_wait(bursts) waiting_times( 5, 3, 8 ) is 0, 5, 8 . Short jobs stuck behind a long one wait a long time, which is one reason schedulers share the CPU in small slices instead.

title: 6.03  Virtual Memory
body: Every process sees its own private, enormous row of addresses - virtual memory. The CPU translates each virtual address to a real place in RAM through page tables the kernel keeps, in pages of 4 KB. That keeps processes apart, lets programs use more memory than there is RAM, and makes a bad pointer crash only its own program. The problem Lesson 4.03 described memory as one long row of numbered bytes. But many processes run at once. If they all shared that one row: - one program could read another's passwords, or overwrite its data by accident; - two programs that both expect to start at address 0x400000 would collide; - a program could not use more memory than happened to be free in one piece. The trick: every process gets its own addresses With virtual memory , every process sees its own private row of addresses , starting near 0 and stretching far beyond the real RAM (on 64-bit systems, up to 128 TB or more). These are virtual addresses . When the program reads address 0x7ffe1234 , the CPU translates it to a physical address - a real place in RAM - using a table the kernel keeps for that process. The program never sees physical addresses at all. Both processes have a "page 0" at the same virtual address, but they land in different places in RAM. Neither can even name the other's memory. Pages Translating each byte separately would need an impossibly large table, so memory is translated in blocks called pages , usually 4 KiB (4,096 bytes). A virtual address splits in two: Part For a 4 KiB page Meaning --- --- --- Page number everything above the lowest 12 bits which page: looked up in the page table Offset the lowest 12 bits (2¹² = 4096) where in the page: copied as it is Example: virtual address 0x3A7C with 4 KiB pages has page number 0x3 and offset 0xA7C. If the page table says virtual page 3 lives in physical frame 0x51, the physical address is 0x51A7C. The CPU does the lookup in hardware on every memory access, with a small cache of recent translations (the TLB ) so it costs almost nothing. What it makes possible Feature How --- --- Isolation A process's page table only contains its own pages. Touching an address that is not mapped stops the program: a segmentation fault (Linux, macOS) or access violation (Windows) Protection Each page has permissions: read, write, execute. Code pages are read-only, so a bug cannot overwrite the program's own instructions More memory than RAM Pages not used lately can be written out to disk ( swap or the page file ) and the RAM reused. If the program touches that page again, the kernel brings it back. Slow, but it works Sharing Two processes running the same program can share the same physical pages of code, read-only Lazy loading When a program starts, its pages are only read from disk when first touched !info Why a crash says "segmentation fault" When a program follows a bad pointer - for example address 0, the null pointer - the CPU finds no mapping for that page and raises a fault. The kernel stops the program. Address 0 is deliberately left unmapped in every process so that this common bug is caught at once instead of silently corrupting memory. quiz ? What does virtual memory give each process? + Its own private range of addresses, translated by the CPU to real RAM - A second CPU - More disk space Two processes can use the same virtual address and land in different RAM. ? With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset part of virtual address 0x5123? - 0x5 + 0x123 - 0x5123 The lowest 12 bits (three hex digits) are the offset within the page. ? Why does following a null pointer crash the program? + Address 0 is left unmapped, so the CPU faults and the kernel stops the program - Zero cannot be stored in memory - The CPU cannot divide by zero The crash is deliberate: it catches the bug immediately. ? What happens when RAM runs out but a program needs more? + Pages not used lately are moved to disk, freeing RAM, and are brought back if needed - The program is stopped at once - The computer turns off Swapping. It is slow, which is why a computer with too little RAM feels sluggish.

title: Translate a virtual address
body: Do the CPU's job from lesson 6.03. Pages are 4 KiB (4,096 bytes). A page table is a dictionary from virtual page number to physical frame number; a page not in it is not mapped. python def split(address) (page number, offset) of a virtual address def translate(address, page_table) the physical address, or None for a page fault - split(0x3A7C) is (0x3, 0xA7C) . - With {3: 0x51} , translate(0x3A7C, ...) is 0x51A7C : the frame number followed by the same offset. - translate(0, {}) is None : address 0 is not mapped, which is how null pointers crash. address // 4096 and address % 4096 split an address; so do address 12 and address & 0xFFF , because 4,096 is 2¹².

title: 6.04  Files, Drivers and System Calls
body: A disk only stores numbered blocks; the file system turns them into named files in folders. Drivers let the kernel talk to each kind of device. Programs reach both through system calls - open, read, write, close - and running a program is itself a system call that loads an executable file into a new process. Disks store blocks, not files An SSD or hard drive only knows how to store and fetch blocks : fixed-size chunks (often 4 KiB) with numbers, 0, 1, 2, and so on. It has no idea what a file or a folder is. The file system is the kernel's way of organising blocks into files: It keeps track of So that --- --- Which blocks hold each file's bytes a file can be spread over many blocks, anywhere on the disk Each file's name, size, dates and permissions ls -l or Explorer can show them Folders (directories), which are lists of names paths like /home/ada/notes.txt or C:\Users\Ada\notes.txt can be followed Which blocks are free new files can be written Common file systems: NTFS (Windows), APFS (macOS), ext4 (Linux), FAT32 and exFAT (USB sticks and memory cards, readable everywhere). Deleting a file usually just marks its blocks as free; the bytes stay until something overwrites them, which is why deleted files can sometimes be recovered. Drivers Every model of disk, graphics card, Wi-Fi chip or printer is controlled differently. A driver is the piece of kernel-mode code that knows how to talk to one kind of device and presents it to the rest of the kernel in a standard way. Install a new graphics card and you install its driver; the kernel and every app then use it through the same interface as any other. System calls: the programmer's door Programs reach files, devices and everything else through system calls . On Linux, a few of the most used: Number (x86-64) Name Does --- --- --- 0 read read bytes from an open file or device 1 write write bytes 2 open open a file by name, get back a small number: a file descriptor 3 close close it 9 mmap map memory pages into the process 57 fork make a copy of this process 59 execve replace this process's program with another 60 exit end the process A file descriptor is just a number the kernel gives back to name an open file. Every process starts with three already open: 0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. That is why write(1, ...) prints (5.06): standard output is just file 1, and it might be a terminal, a file, or a pipe to another program - the program does not need to know which. Windows has the same ideas with different names ( CreateFile , ReadFile , WriteFile , handles instead of descriptors), and programs normally reach them through Windows' own libraries rather than raw system call numbers. In Python, open , read and write are thin wrappers around these calls: python with open("notes.txt", "w") as f: open(): a system call; the kernel gives back a descriptor f.write("first line\n") write(): copies bytes into the file system with open("notes.txt") as f: print(f.read(), end="") read() from the file, then write() to descriptor 1 Running a program Starting a program is a system call too. On Linux, a shell runs python3 main.py like this: 1. fork : copy the shell's process. Now there are two. 2. In the copy, execve("/usr/bin/python3", ...) : the kernel reads the executable file (an ELF file, 3.05), sets up fresh virtual memory (6.03), maps the code and data into it, sets the program counter to the program's entry point, and lets the scheduler (6.02) run it. 3. The original shell waits until the new process calls exit , then prints its prompt again. Windows does the equivalent in one call ( CreateProcess ). Either way, the operating system turns a file of bytes into a running process. quiz ? What does a disk itself know about files? + Nothing: it stores numbered blocks; the file system organises them into files and folders - It keeps a list of file names - It stores one file per block The file system is kernel software that tracks which blocks belong to which file. ? What is file descriptor 1? - The first file you opened + Standard output - Standard input 0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. ? What does a driver do? + Lets the kernel control one kind of device through a standard interface - Drives the computer's fan - Runs apps faster Every device model speaks differently; its driver translates.

title: A tiny file system
body: A disk is a list of blocks ; here each block is a string of exactly 4 characters. A file system's table maps each file name to (list of block numbers, size in characters) . The blocks of a file can be anywhere on the disk, in any order. python def read_file(disk, table, name) the file's text: its blocks joined in order, cut to its size; None if there is no such file def free_blocks(disk, table) the numbers of the blocks no file uses, smallest first python disk = "Hell", "xxxx", "o, w", "orld", "Bye!" table = {"hello.txt": ( 0, 2, 3 , 12), "bye.txt": ( 4 , 3)} read_file(disk, table, "hello.txt") "Hello, world" read_file(disk, table, "bye.txt") "Bye" (the size cuts off the !) free_blocks(disk, table) 1 "".join(parts) glues strings together; text :size keeps the first size characters.

title: 6.05  Booting: From Power Button to Desktop
match: 6.05 Booting: From Power Button to Desktop
body: When the power comes on, the CPU starts running firmware from a chip on the motherboard (UEFI, once BIOS), which checks the hardware and loads a boot loader from the disk. The boot loader loads the kernel, the kernel starts its drivers and the first process, and that process starts everything else, ending with the login screen. The chicken-and-egg problem The operating system lives on the disk. Reading the disk needs a program. But when the power comes on, RAM is empty: there is no program yet. How does a computer start? The answer is a chain of small programs, each loading a bigger one. This is called booting , from "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps". 1. Firmware The CPU is built to start fetching instructions from one fixed address when it powers on. That address is wired to a small flash memory chip on the motherboard that holds the firmware : on PCs since about 2010, UEFI ; before that, the BIOS (from the original IBM PC). The firmware: - tests the hardware (the POST , power-on self test: is there RAM? a keyboard?); - sets up the essentials: memory, the clock, the CPU's settings; - finds a disk to boot from, in the order set in its settings; - loads the boot loader from that disk into RAM and jumps to it. With Secure Boot , UEFI checks that the boot loader is digitally signed by a trusted maker before running it, so malware cannot slip in before the operating system starts. 2. The boot loader The boot loader is a small program whose job is to find the kernel and load it. Examples: Windows Boot Manager , GRUB (Linux), and Apple's iBoot . It may show a menu to choose between operating systems. It reads the kernel file from the file system into RAM, along with a small starter set of drivers, and jumps to the kernel's first instruction. 3. The kernel starts The kernel now takes over the machine: - switches the CPU into its full 64-bit mode and sets up virtual memory (6.03); - starts its drivers and detects devices; - mounts the main file system (makes the disk's files reachable); - starts the scheduler (6.02); - starts the first user-mode process . 4. The first process On Linux the first process has PID 1 : usually systemd (or the older init ). Every other process on the system descends from it, through fork and execve (6.04). It starts the background services - networking, sound, printing, logging - and finally the login screen. Windows does the same with its Session Manager and Winlogon. 5. Login and desktop You log in; the system starts your desktop (Explorer on Windows, Finder and the Dock on macOS, GNOME or KDE on Linux) and your startup apps. From power button to desktop, on a modern computer with an SSD, takes about 10 to 20 seconds. Sleep, hibernate, shut down What happens Starting again --- --- --- Sleep RAM stays powered and keeps everything; the rest switches off Instant: everything is still in RAM Hibernate RAM's contents are written to the disk, then the power goes off Slower: RAM is reloaded from the disk Shut down Programs are closed, files saved, power off A full boot !info Phones boot the same way A phone has its own firmware and boot loader (with signature checks at every step, so only the maker's software can run), then a Linux kernel (Android) or Apple's XNU kernel (iOS), then the first process and the home screen. quiz ? Where does the very first code run after power-on come from? - The hard drive + Firmware (UEFI or BIOS) in a chip on the motherboard - RAM RAM is empty at power-on; the CPU starts at an address wired to the firmware chip. ? What is the boot loader's job? + To find the kernel on the disk, load it into RAM and start it - To test the hardware - To show the desktop GRUB, Windows Boot Manager, iBoot. ? On Linux, what is process number 1? + The first user-mode process (usually systemd), which starts everything else - The kernel - The desktop Every other process descends from it. ? What is the difference between sleep and hibernate? + Sleep keeps RAM powered; hibernate saves RAM to disk and powers off completely - There is no difference - Hibernate is faster to wake from Sleep wakes instantly but uses a little power.

title: Which disk boots?
where: 6.05 Booting: From Power Button to Desktop
body: The firmware (6.05) tries the disks in its boot order and boots from the first one that is present and has a boot loader. Write: python def choose_boot(order, disks) order: list of disk names; disks: dict name - True if it has a boot loader Return the name of the disk to boot from, or "No bootable device" . A name in the order that is not in disks is not plugged in. python choose_boot( "USB", "SSD" , {"SSD": True}) "SSD": no USB stick is plugged in choose_boot( "USB", "SSD" , {"USB": False, "SSD": True}) "SSD": the stick has no boot loader choose_boot( "USB", "SSD" , {"USB": True, "SSD": True}) "USB" disks.get(name, False) gives False for a missing name.

title: 6.06  Networks and the Internet
body: Computers send data to each other in small packets, each with an address. IP addresses say where a packet goes, TCP makes delivery reliable and in order, and DNS turns names like example.com into addresses. The web is built on top - HTTP requests and responses carried by those packets - and every layer is still bits on wires and radio waves. Bits between computers A network sends bits from one computer to another: as voltages on copper wire, flashes of light in fibre-optic cable, or radio waves (Wi-Fi, 4G, 5G). Everything else is agreement about what those bits mean - protocols - in layers, like the rest of the computer. Packets Data is not sent as one long stream. It is cut into packets , usually up to about 1,500 bytes, and each packet travels on its own, with a header saying where it is going: Packets from one message may take different routes and arrive out of order; the receiving computer puts them back together. If one link fails, packets go around it. This design, from the US ARPANET of 1969, is why the internet keeps working when parts of it break. The layers Layer Protocol Job --- --- --- Link Ethernet, Wi-Fi Get bits to the next device on the same network Internet IP (Internet Protocol) Get a packet from one computer to another anywhere, using IP addresses Transport TCP , or UDP TCP: deliver everything, in order, resending what is lost. UDP: fast, no guarantees (games, video calls) Application HTTP , HTTPS, DNS, email... What the data means Each layer wraps the one above, like an envelope inside an envelope: an HTTP request goes inside TCP segments, inside IP packets, inside Wi-Fi frames. Addresses - An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number, written as four bytes in decimal: 93.184.215.14 . 32 bits is only about 4.3 billion addresses (2.06!) - not enough for every device on Earth, which is why home routers share one public address between all the devices behind them. - An IPv6 address is a 128-bit number, written in hex: 2606:2800:21f:cb07:6820:80da:af6b:8b2c . 2¹²⁸ is about 3.4 × 10³⁸, enough to never run out. - A port number (16 bits, 0 to 65,535) says which program on the computer the data is for: 443 for HTTPS, 80 for HTTP, 22 for SSH. DNS: names to numbers People remember names, computers need numbers. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet's phone book: your computer asks a DNS server "what is the address of example.com ?" and gets back an IP address. Then it connects to that address. The web When you open a web page: 1. DNS turns the name into an IP address. 2. Your browser opens a TCP connection to that address, port 443, and sets up TLS encryption (the S in HTTPS: nobody in between can read or change the data). 3. It sends an HTTP request : plain text like GET /index.html HTTP/1.1 plus some headers. 4. The server sends an HTTP response : a status ( 200 OK , or 404 Not Found ), headers, and the bytes of the page. 5. The browser reads the HTML, asks for each picture, style sheet and script the same way, and draws the page. The World Wide Web - pages, links and HTTP - was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989-91, on top of an internet that had existed for twenty years. How it all fits That web page is text (3.01) and pictures (3.04), in files (3.05), sent by a server's operating system (6.01) through system calls (6.04), cut into packets of bits (2.01), carried by electricity, light and radio, reassembled by your kernel, handed to your browser - a process (6.02) in its own virtual memory (6.03) - whose code, compiled from C++ (5.05) into machine code (4.05), runs fetch, decode, execute (4.04) on gates (4.01) made from transistors (1.04). That is the whole computer, from the first switch to the internet. Where next? The C course on this site writes programs close to the machine you now understand; the Assembly course writes the machine code itself. quiz ? Why is data sent as packets? + Small packets can travel separately, take different routes around failures, and be resent individually if lost - Wires can only carry 1,500 bytes at once - It makes the data encrypted The packet design makes the internet robust. ? What does DNS do? + Turns names like example.com into IP addresses - Encrypts web pages - Sends packets The internet's phone book. ? How many bits is an IPv4 address? - 8 + 32 - 128 Four bytes, which is why there are only about 4.3 billion. IPv6 uses 128 bits. ? What does TCP add on top of IP? + Reliable, in-order delivery, resending lost packets - Names for computers - Faster speed than UDP UDP skips those guarantees to be quicker.

title: IP addresses are numbers
body: An IPv4 address is one 32-bit number, written as four bytes. Write: python def to_number(address) "93.184.215.14" - 1572394766 def to_text(number) and back def same_network(a, b, prefix) True when the first prefix bits of the two addresses are equal same_network("192.168.1.20", "192.168.1.200", 24) is True : the first 24 bits ( 192.168.1 ) match. That is how your computer decides whether another device is on your home network or must be reached through the router. Shifting builds the number: (a << 24) (b << 16) (c << 8) d . To compare the top prefix bits, shift both numbers right by 32 - prefix .

title: A scheduler simulator
where: Operating Systems and Modern Computers projects
body: Simulate the round-robin scheduler of lesson 6.02 on one CPU core, and see how long everyone waits. The first input line is the time slice . Each following line is a process: a name, its arrival time and how long it needs to run (its burst ). Read until the end of the input. 3 A 0 5 B 1 3 C 2 1 The rules: - Time starts at 0. A process joins the back of the ready queue at its arrival time. (Processes that arrive at the same time join in the order they were listed.) - The CPU takes the process at the front of the queue and runs it for one time slice, or less if it finishes sooner. - If it still needs time, it goes to the back of the queue, after any processes that arrived up to the moment its slice ended. - When the queue is empty, the CPU is idle until the next arrival. Print every stretch of time, joining back-to-back stretches of the same process (or of idle) into one: t=START-END NAME . Then, in the order the processes were listed, when each finished and how long it waited (finish − arrival − burst), and finally the average wait with two decimals. For the example: t=0-3 A t=3-6 B t=6-7 C t=7-9 A A finished at 9, waited 4 B finished at 6, waited 2 C finished at 7, waited 4 Average wait: 3.33 There is always at least one process, and every burst is at least 1.

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Address The number of a byte in memory. (4.03) ALU Arithmetic logic unit: the part of the CPU that adds, subtracts and does logic on bits. (4.02) ARM64 The instruction set of phones, tablets and Apple-chip Macs. (1.05) ASCII The 1963 table giving English characters the numbers 0 to 127. (3.01) Assembler A program that translates assembly language into machine code. (5.01) Assembly language Machine instructions written as names ( mov , add ) and labels; one line per instruction. (5.01) Binary Base 2: counting with only 0 and 1, each place worth twice the one to its right. (2.02) Bit One binary digit: 0 or 1. (1.01) Boot loader The small program that loads the operating system's kernel. (6.05) Byte 8 bits; the unit memory is counted in. (2.03) Bytecode Instructions for a virtual machine rather than a real CPU (Java, C , Python). (5.03) Cache A small, fast memory holding copies of recently used data. (4.06) Carry The 1 passed to the next column when a column's sum is too big. (2.05) Code point The number Unicode gives a character, written U+ and hex. (3.01) Compiler A program that translates a high-level language into machine code before it runs. (5.02) Context switch Saving one thread's registers and loading another's. (6.02) Core One complete processor; a chip has several. (1.05) CPU Central processing unit: fetches and executes instructions. (1.01) DNS The system that turns names like example.com into IP addresses. (6.06) Driver Kernel code that controls one kind of device. (6.04) Encoding An agreed table turning characters into numbers (ASCII, UTF-8). (3.01) Endianness Which byte of a multi-byte number comes first in memory: little-endian (lowest first) or big-endian. (2.06) Executable A file of machine code the operating system can run. (3.05) Fetch, decode, execute The cycle every CPU repeats. (4.04) File descriptor The number a process uses for an open file: 0 input, 1 output, 2 errors. (6.04) File system The kernel's organisation of disk blocks into named files and folders. (6.04) Firmware Software stored in a chip on the motherboard (UEFI, BIOS) that starts the computer. (6.05) Flip-flop A circuit of gates that stores one bit. (4.03) Floating point Storing numbers like scientific notation in binary; approximate for most fractions. (3.03) Font A set of glyphs, one shape per character. (3.02) Framebuffer The memory holding the colour of every pixel on screen. (3.02) GPU A chip with thousands of simple cores, for graphics and AI. (1.05) Hexadecimal Base 16, digits 0 to 9 and A to F; one digit is four bits. (2.04) High-level language A language that lets you write what you mean, translated to machine code by a compiler or interpreter. (5.02) Instruction set The instructions a CPU family understands, and their encoding (x86-64, ARM64). (1.05) Integrated circuit Many transistors and their connections made on one chip of silicon. (1.04) Interpreter A program that carries out another program as it reads it. (5.03) Interrupt A hardware signal that makes the CPU jump into the kernel. (6.02) IP address The number that says where a packet goes: 32 bits (IPv4) or 128 bits (IPv6). (6.06) JIT Just-in-time compilation: compiling the busy parts of a program while it runs. (5.03) Kernel The core of the operating system; the only code allowed to touch hardware. (6.01) Kernel mode The CPU's privileged mode, for the kernel. (6.01) Linker Joins compiled pieces and libraries into one executable. (5.03) Logic gate A circuit giving one bit out from bits in: NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND. (4.01) Machine code A program as the bytes a CPU executes. (4.05) Magic number Fixed bytes at the start of a file saying what format it is. (3.05) Microprocessor A whole CPU on one chip. (1.04) Moore's law The observation that transistors per chip doubled about every two years. (1.04) Nibble 4 bits: one hexadecimal digit. (2.03) Operating system The software that runs the computer for every other program. (6.01) Overflow A result too big for the bits it is stored in, which then wraps around. (2.05) Packet A small piece of data sent across a network with its own address. (6.06) Page A block of memory (usually 4 KiB) mapped as a unit by virtual memory. (6.03) Pixel One dot of a picture or screen, stored as a colour. (3.04) Pointer A value that holds an address. (4.03) Process A program while it runs, with its own memory. (6.02) Program counter The register holding the address of the next instruction. (4.04) RAM Main memory: fast, and forgets everything without power. (4.03) Register A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. (4.03) RGB Red, green and blue light: three numbers that make a colour. (3.04) Scheduler The kernel part that shares CPU cores between threads. (6.02) Segmentation fault A crash from touching memory the process does not own. (6.03) Stored program Keeping the program in the same memory as its data. (1.03) System call A request from a program to the kernel, made with a special instruction. (5.06) TCP The protocol that makes delivery over the internet reliable and in order. (6.06) Thread One line of execution inside a process. (6.02) Transistor An electronic switch made of silicon; billions make a chip. (1.04) Truth table Every input of a logic circuit and its output. (4.01) Turing machine Turing's simple imaginary computer, able to compute anything computable. (1.03) Two's complement The way computers store negative numbers: flip the bits and add one. (2.05) Unicode One table giving every character of every language its own number. (3.01) User mode The CPU's restricted mode, for apps. (6.01) UTF-8 The usual way to store Unicode as bytes: 1 to 4 per character, ASCII unchanged. (3.01) Virtual machine A program that runs bytecode for an imaginary computer (the JVM). (5.03) Virtual memory Each process's private addresses, translated to real RAM by the CPU. (6.03) x86-64 The instruction set of most PCs and servers. (1.05)

title: 1.01  What Happens When a Program Runs
match: 1.01 What Happens When a Program Runs
body: A computer does one small thing at a time. It fetches an instruction from memory, works out what it means, and does it . Everything a game does, from drawing a frame to saving your progress, is billions of those small steps. Why this course starts here This course is about what is really going on inside a running game: where its numbers live, how the processor works through its code, what the operating system does around it, and how tools such as debuggers look inside. All of that rests on one picture of how a computer runs a program. If that picture is clear, later topics such as pointers, assembly language and debugging become ordinary consequences of it. If it is fuzzy, they stay mysterious however many times they are explained. So this lesson builds the picture, and it lets you operate a small computer yourself. Three parts that do all the work Part What it does Keeps its contents with the power off? --- --- --- CPU (processor) Carries out instructions, one after another It holds almost nothing Memory (RAM) Holds the program that is running and the numbers it is working with No Storage (SSD, hard disk) Keeps files, including program files, for the long term Yes A program on your disk is only a file. It does nothing until the operating system copies it into memory and tells the CPU where its first instruction is. From then on the CPU and memory do all the work, and storage is only touched when the program reads or writes a file. That is why this course spends so much time on memory. While a game is running, everything it knows is in memory: the player's health, the position of every monster, the level layout, and the game's own instructions. A program is a list of numbers Memory is a long row of numbered boxes, and each box holds a number. Nothing else. There are no words in there, no pictures and no C++. A program is stored in those boxes as numbers too. The people who design a CPU decide which number means which action. On the tiny machine you are about to use, the code works like this: Number Written as What the CPU does --- --- --- 1nn LOAD nn Copy the number in cell nn into register A 2nn ADD nn Add the number in cell nn to register A 3nn SUB nn Subtract the number in cell nn from register A 4nn STORE nn Copy register A into cell nn 5nn JUMP nn Carry on from cell nn instead of the next cell 6nn JUMPZ nn If register A is zero, carry on from cell nn 0 HALT Stop So the number 110 means "load cell 10", and 412 means "store into cell 12". The words LOAD and STORE are only there for people. The CPU sees 110 and 412 . !important The same number can be an instruction or a value Memory does not label its boxes. 110 is "load cell 10" when the CPU fetches it as an instruction, and it is just the quantity one hundred and ten when a program adds it to something. What a number means depends entirely on how it is used. This idea comes back throughout the course. A register is a storage slot inside the CPU itself. It is much faster to reach than memory, and there are very few of them. This machine has one for doing sums, called A. The cycle: fetch, decode, execute The CPU repeats three steps for as long as the power is on. 1. Fetch. A register called the program counter holds the number of the cell where the next instruction is. The CPU copies that cell's contents into its instruction register , then adds one to the program counter so it points at the following cell. 2. Decode. The CPU works out what the number in the instruction register means. 3. Execute. It does it: copies a number, adds, or changes the program counter. Then it goes back to step 1. That loop is the whole of how a computer runs a program. Here is a program that adds two numbers. Press Step and read the explanation each time. Watch three things: the program counter moving down the cells, register A changing, and cell 12 at the end. demo-cpu program: add Things to notice: - The program counter always names the cell that will be fetched next . It is the CPU's bookmark. - Nothing happened to memory until the STORE . Loading and adding only changed register A. - When the machine halted, the answer was sitting in cell 12. A program's results are simply whatever it left in memory. Now type different numbers into cells 10 and 11. The machine goes back to the start each time you change one. Then press Run . The program is the same four instructions; only the data changed. That separation between the instructions and the data they work on is what makes a program reusable. !info This machine is invented, but the idea is exact The processor in your computer has sixteen general registers instead of one, hundreds of instructions instead of seven, and its instructions are different lengths. Chapter 7 covers the real thing. The cycle of fetch, decode and execute is the same. Loops and decisions are jumps Left alone, the program counter just counts upward, so the CPU runs instructions in the order they sit in memory. JUMP and JUMPZ are the two instructions that put a different number in the program counter. That is all a loop or an if is at this level. This program counts down from 3 to 0. Step through it and watch the program counter go backwards when it reaches JUMP 1 . demo-cpu program: countdown The instructions in cells 1 to 4 run once for every count. Cell 1 is the question "has it reached zero yet?" and cell 4 is "go round again". Change the counter in cell 10 to 5 and run it again. It takes more instructions to finish, because the loop goes round more times, although the program itself did not get any longer. When you write a while loop or an if statement in C++, the compiler turns it into exactly this: a test that sets up a condition, and a jump that depends on it. A bigger program from the same seven instructions This machine has no multiply instruction. It can still multiply, by adding the same number again and again and counting how many times are left. demo-cpu program: multiply Run it and watch cell 12, the running total, grow by 4 on each trip round the loop. Then change cell 10 or cell 11 and run it again. Real processors do have a multiply instruction, but the lesson holds: complicated behaviour is built from a small set of simple instructions, repeated. From C++ to those numbers You do not write programs as numbers. You write something like this, and a compiler translates it into the CPU's instructions. cpp include <iostream int main() { int first{ 7 }; int second{ 5 }; int answer{ first + second }; std::cout << answer << '\n'; return 0; } 12 For the line int answer{ first + second }; a compiler for a real x64 processor produces instructions along these lines: asm mov eax, dword ptr first ; LOAD copy first into a register add eax, dword ptr second ; ADD add second to it mov dword ptr answer , eax ; STORE copy the register into answer It is the same three steps you watched in the first demonstration. The names first , second and answer are for you and the compiler. In the finished program they are gone, replaced by the numbers of the memory cells where those values live. Lesson 1.03 is about those cell numbers, which are called addresses. How fast this happens One core of a modern processor gets through billions of these steps every second. A game that draws 60 frames a second has about 16.7 milliseconds for each frame, and in that time one core can carry out tens of millions of instructions. That is why a game can move hundreds of objects, check their collisions, play sound and draw the screen, all between one frame and the next. Each of those jobs is still nothing more than loading numbers, doing arithmetic on them, storing them and jumping. Where the operating system comes in Three things happen when you start a program on Windows. 1. Windows finds the program file on disk and reads it. 2. It sets aside memory for the program and copies the program's instructions and starting data into it. A program that has been loaded and is running is called a process . 3. It sets the program counter to the program's first instruction and lets the CPU go. Windows also keeps many processes going at once by letting each use the CPU for a short slice of time, then switching to another. It keeps each process's memory separate from every other's. Chapter 6 covers processes and their memory in detail. Why this matters for games Take the picture you now have and look at a game with it. - Game state is numbers in memory. Health, gold, position, the current level: each is a number in some memory cell. - The game is a loop. Read the input, update the numbers, draw the picture, go round again. It is the countdown program with a much bigger body. - A debugger stops the cycle. Because the CPU does one instruction at a time, a tool can pause it between two instructions and show you every register and every memory cell. That is what Visual Studio's debugger does, and you will use it constantly in this course. Common misunderstandings !warning "The computer understands C++" It does not. The CPU only carries out its own numbered instructions. C++ exists for people, and a compiler has to translate it before anything can run. !warning "Instructions and data are kept in different kinds of memory" They sit in the same memory, as the same kind of numbers. Modern operating systems do mark regions as "may be run" or "may only be read", which is a safety measure you will meet later, but the bytes themselves are no different. !warning "Variables keep their names inside the machine" Names disappear when the program is compiled. Only cell numbers remain. This is why a debugger needs a separate file of symbols to show you names again. !warning "A computer does many things at the same moment" One core does one instruction at a time. It appears to do many things because it is fast and because the operating system switches between programs many times a second. A processor with several cores really does run several instruction streams at once, one per core. Knowledge check quiz ? What does the program counter hold? - The result of the most recent sum + The number of the memory cell that holds the next instruction - How many instructions have been run so far It is the CPU's bookmark. Fetch reads the cell it names, then moves it on by one. ? In the first demonstration, which instruction changed memory? - LOAD 10 - ADD 11 + STORE 12 LOAD and ADD only change register A, inside the CPU. STORE is the one that copies a value out into a memory cell. ? Cell 5 of a program's memory holds the number 110. What is it? - Always the instruction LOAD 10 - Always the value one hundred and ten + It depends on whether the CPU fetches it as an instruction or a program uses it as a value Memory does not label its contents. The same number is an instruction if the program counter reaches it, and plain data if an instruction reads it. ? How does this machine repeat a group of instructions? - It has a special LOOP instruction + A jump puts an earlier cell number into the program counter - The CPU remembers which instructions it has already run Loops and decisions are both made from jumps. JUMP always changes the program counter; JUMPZ changes it only when register A is zero. ? Where do the names of your C++ variables go when the program is compiled? - They are stored next to each value in memory - The CPU keeps a table of them + They are replaced by memory cell numbers and are not in the running program Names are for people and for the compiler. A debugger can show them again only because the compiler can write them to a separate symbol file.

title: Count the instructions
where: 1.01 What Happens When a Program Runs
body: The countdown program from the lesson looks like this, with the counter in cell 10 and the number one in cell 11: Cell Instruction --- --- 0 LOAD 10 1 JUMPZ 5 2 SUB 11 3 STORE 10 4 JUMP 1 5 HALT Write instructionsRun(start) . It returns how many instructions the machine executes, from the first LOAD up to and including the HALT , when cell 10 starts at start . Work it out on paper first: which instructions run once, and which run once per trip round the loop? Check your answer against the demonstration in the lesson, which counts instructions for you. start is never negative.

title: Build the machine
where: 1.01 What Happens When a Program Runs
body: Write the tiny computer from the lesson as a C++ function. run(memory) executes the program stored in memory , starting at cell 0 with register A at 0, and returns what register A holds when the machine stops. Each instruction is one number: the hundreds digit and above is the operation, and the last two digits are a cell number. Number Instruction Effect --- --- --- 1nn LOAD nn A becomes the number in cell nn 2nn ADD nn A goes up by the number in cell nn 3nn SUB nn A goes down by the number in cell nn 4nn STORE nn Cell nn becomes A 5nn JUMP nn The next instruction comes from cell nn 6nn JUMPZ nn If A is zero, the next instruction comes from cell nn anything else HALT The machine stops Follow the cycle: fetch the number the program counter points at and move the program counter on by one, decode it into an operation and a cell number, then execute it. The machine also stops if the program counter runs off the end of memory.

title: 1.02  Bits, Bytes and Hexadecimal
body:
Memory holds only bits , switches that are on or off. Eight bits make a byte , and hexadecimal is a shorthand that writes a byte as two digits. Once you can read hexadecimal, a screen full of memory stops looking like noise. Only two symbols The last lesson said that every memory cell holds a number. Electrically, a computer stores numbers using parts that have two steady states: charged or not, on or off. One such switch is a bit , and it can hold a 0 or a 1. One bit is not much use. A row of them is, in the same way that a single decimal digit only counts to 9 but a row of digits can write any number. Counting with place values In the decimal number 345, each position is worth ten times the one to its right: 3 hundreds, 4 tens, 5 ones. Binary works the same way, except each position is worth two times the one to its right. Position 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Worth 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 To read a binary number, add up the worth of every position that holds a 1. So 0100 1101 is 64 + 8 + 4 + 1, which is 77. Try it. Each button below is one bit. The small number on it is what that bit is worth. demo-bits bits: 8 value: 77 Things to try: - Switch every bit off, then make 200 . Start from the left: is 128 needed? Then 64? Keep going. - Switch every bit on. That is 255 , the largest value eight bits can hold. - Press << 1 a few times with only the rightmost bit on. Each shift left doubles the value, just as adding a zero to the end of a decimal number multiplies it by ten. - With 255 showing, press + 1 . There is no ninth bit to carry into, so the value wraps round to 0. Bytes, and how many values fit Eight bits make a byte . The byte is the unit that memory is measured and numbered in: when the last lesson talked about memory cells, each cell of a real computer is one byte. Every extra bit doubles the number of different values a group of bits can hold. Bits Bytes Different values Largest unsigned value --- --- --- --- 8 1 256 255 16 2 65,536 65,535 32 4 4,294,967,296 about 4.29 billion 64 8 about 18.4 quintillion about 1.8 × 10¹⁹ A value that needs more than one byte simply uses several bytes next to each other. This is where C++ types come from: a type says how many bytes a value takes and how to interpret them. cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "char: " << sizeof(char) << '
'; std::cout << "short: " << sizeof(short) << '
'; std::cout << "int: " << sizeof(int) << '
'; std::cout << "long long: " << sizeof(long long) << '
'; std::cout << "float: " << sizeof(float) << '
'; std::cout << "double: " << sizeof(double) << '
'; std::cout << "int : " << sizeof(int ) << '
'; return 0; } char: 1 short: 2 int: 4 long long: 8 float: 4 double: 8 int : 8 sizeof gives the size of a type in bytes. These are the sizes on 64-bit Windows, which is what this course targets. !tip When the exact size matters, say so C++ only promises minimum sizes for int and its relatives. The header <cstdint provides types with the size in the name: std::uint8_t is exactly one unsigned byte, std::int32_t exactly four signed bytes, std::uint64_t exactly eight unsigned bytes. Low-level code uses these whenever it is describing memory precisely. Hexadecimal: four bits per digit Binary is what the machine uses, but it is hard on the eyes. 1011 1110 1110 1111 is sixteen digits for one small number. Decimal is shorter, but there is no tidy relationship between decimal digits and bits. Hexadecimal (base 16, "hex" for short) fixes both problems. It has sixteen digits: 0 to 9, then A to F for the values ten to fifteen. Hex Binary Decimal Hex Binary Decimal --- --- --- --- --- --- --- 0 0000 0 8 1000 8 1 0001 1 9 1001 9 2 0010 2 A 1010 10 3 0011 3 B 1011 11 4 0100 4 C 1100 12 5 0101 5 D 1101 13 6 0110 6 E 1110 14 7 0111 7 F 1111 15 Sixteen is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, so one hex digit is exactly four bits . That is the whole reason hexadecimal is used. A byte is always two hex digits, a 32-bit value is always eight, and you can convert between hex and binary one digit at a time without doing any arithmetic. Below, the bits are grouped in fours and each group shows its hex digit underneath. Flip bits and watch only that group's digit change. demo-bits bits: 16 value: 48879 Hexadecimal numbers are written with 0x in front so they cannot be mistaken for decimal. 0x10 is sixteen, not ten. C++ accepts the same notation, and 0b for binary: cpp include <iostream int main() { int a{ 0xFF }; // hexadecimal: 255 int b{ 0b1111'1111 }; // binary: 255. The ' is only there to make it readable int c{ 255 }; // decimal std::cout << a << ' ' << b << ' ' << c << '
'; return 0; } 255 255 255 All three lines store exactly the same bits. Hexadecimal, binary and decimal are three ways of writing a number. The number in memory is the same whichever one you use. Reading hex without a calculator You will read a great deal of hexadecimal in this course, in debuggers, memory views and assembly listings. A few landmarks make it quick. Hex Decimal Worth remembering because --- --- --- 0x0A 10 A is ten 0x10 16 One "sixteen" 0x20 32 The space character 0x41 65 The letter A 0x7F 127 Largest positive value of a signed byte 0xFF 255 A byte with every bit on 0x100 256 One more than a byte can hold 0x1000 4,096 The size of a page of memory, as chapter 6 explains Adding in hex works like decimal, carrying at sixteen instead of ten. 0x1000 + 0x24 is 0x1024 . 0x0F + 0x01 is 0x10 . You will do sums like these whenever you work out where something sits in memory. Negative numbers: two's complement Bits have no minus sign, so negative numbers need a convention. Every modern computer uses two's complement . In a signed type, the leftmost bit is worth minus its usual amount. In a signed byte, the bits are worth: Position 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Worth −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 So 1111 1111 is −128 + 127, which is −1 , and a signed byte runs from −128 to 127. The explorer shows both readings of the same bits. Look at the Unsigned and Signed lines. demo-bits bits: 8 value: 255 title: The same bits, read two ways - With all bits on, the unsigned reading is 255 and the signed reading is −1. The bits did not change. The interpretation did. - To negate a number in two's complement: flip every bit, then add one. Set the value to 5, press Invert , then + 1 , and the signed reading is −5. - Press − 1 from 0. The unsigned reading jumps to 255 and the signed reading says −1. Both are correct descriptions of the same bits. This is why a type has to say whether it is signed. signed char and unsigned char hold identical bits and disagree about what half of them mean. Overflow A type has a fixed number of bits, so there is a largest value it can hold. Going past it does not produce an error. With unsigned types the value wraps round, exactly as you saw when 255 + 1 became 0. cpp include <cstdint include <iostream int main() { std::uint8_t health{ 250 }; health = static_cast<std::uint8_t (health + 10); // 260 does not fit in 8 bits std::cout << static_cast<int (health) << '
'; std::uint8_t lives{ 0 }; lives = static_cast<std::uint8_t (lives - 1); // below zero wraps to the top std::cout << static_cast<int (lives) << '
'; return 0; } 4 255 Healing a character from 250 health left it with 4. Taking a life from a player with none gave them 255. Both are real categories of game bug, and both come from forgetting that a type has edges. !warning Signed overflow is worse than wrapping For unsigned types, C++ guarantees the wrap-around. For signed types such as int , going past the largest value is undefined behaviour : the language makes no promise about what happens, and compilers are allowed to assume it never does. Do not rely on signed numbers wrapping. Byte order: which end comes first A 32-bit value takes four bytes, and those four bytes sit in four neighbouring memory cells. There are two sensible orders to store them in, and processors do not all agree. demo-bytes value: 0x12345678 The processors in PCs are little-endian : the lowest-value byte goes at the lowest address. So the number you would write as 0x12345678 sits in memory as the bytes 78 56 34 12 . This matters every time you look at raw memory. If a memory view shows E8 03 00 00 and you know an int lives there, you read the bytes back to front to get 0x000003E8 , which is 1000. It looks backwards at first and becomes automatic with practice. Switch the demonstration to Big-endian to see the other order. Network protocols and some file formats use it, so code that reads them has to swap the bytes. Printing numbers in other bases from C++ cpp include <bitset include <format include <iostream int main() { int value{ 200 }; std::cout << std::format("decimal {} hex 0x{:02X} binary {: 010b}
", value, value, value); std::cout << "bitset: " << std::bitset<8 (value) << '
'; std::cout << "literals: " << 0xC8 << ' ' << 0b1100'1000 << '
'; return 0; } decimal 200 hex 0xC8 binary 0b11001000 bitset: 11001000 literals: 200 200 In std::format , {:02X} means hexadecimal in capitals, at least two digits, padded with zeros. {: 010b} means binary with the 0b prefix, ten characters wide in all. std::bitset<8 prints exactly eight bits. Common mistakes !warning Reading a hex number as decimal 0x10 is sixteen. 0x64 is one hundred. If a number in a debugger looks odd, check which base the window is showing. Visual Studio can switch between them with a right-click. !warning Forgetting byte order when reading memory In a memory view, multi-byte values appear lowest byte first. 01 00 00 00 is the int 1, not sixteen million. !warning Assuming a type's size int is 4 bytes on the systems this course uses, but the language only promises "at least 2". Use sizeof to check, and the <cstdint types when the size is part of what you mean. !warning Mixing signed and unsigned Comparing a signed value with an unsigned one converts the signed value first, so −1 becomes a very large number. The compiler warns about this. Take the warning seriously. !warning Mixing up 1000 and 1024 A kilobyte in memory sizes is usually 1,024 bytes ( 0x400 ), because memory is counted in powers of two. Disk makers use 1,000. When exactness matters, write the number of bytes. Knowledge check quiz ? What is 0100 0001 as an unsigned number? - 41 + 65 - 129 The bits that are on are worth 64 and 1. In hexadecimal the same byte is 0x41 , which is where the wrong answer 41 comes from. ? Why is hexadecimal used instead of decimal when looking at memory? - It can store larger numbers - Computers calculate in hexadecimal internally + Each hex digit stands for exactly four bits, so a byte is always two digits Hexadecimal is only a way of writing numbers. Its advantage is the exact fit: four bits per digit, two digits per byte. ? A signed byte holds the bits 1111 1111 . What value is that? - 255 + -1 - -127 In two's complement the top bit is worth -128, and the other seven add up to 127. Read as unsigned, the same bits are 255. ? An int on a PC holds the value 0x0A0B0C0D . In what order do its bytes sit in memory, from the lowest address up? - 0A 0B 0C 0D + 0D 0C 0B 0A - D0 C0 B0 A0 PCs are little-endian: the lowest byte is stored first. The digits inside each byte are not reversed, only the order of the bytes. ? A std::uint8_t holds 200 and the program adds 100 to it. What does it hold now? - 300 - 255 + 44 300 does not fit in eight bits, so it wraps: 300 - 256 = 44. Unsigned arithmetic always wraps round like this.

title: Bits to a number
body: Write fromBinary(bits) . It is given a string of 0 and 1 characters, most significant bit first, and returns the number those bits stand for. fromBinary("1010") is 10. fromBinary("01001101") is 77. An empty string is 0. Do the conversion yourself, using place values. The standard library's conversion functions and std::bitset are not allowed here.

title: Number to hexadecimal
body: Write toHex(value) . It returns the hexadecimal digits of value as a string, in capitals, with no 0x in front and no leading zeros. toHex(255) is "FF" . toHex(256) is "100" . toHex(0) is "0" . Produce the digits yourself. std::hex , std::format and printf are not allowed here.

title: Bytes in memory order
body: A 32-bit number takes four bytes. On a PC they are stored little-endian : lowest byte first. Write two functions. - toBytes(value) returns the four bytes of value in the order they would sit in memory. toBytes(0x12345678) is { 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12 } . - fromBytes(bytes) does the reverse and returns the number those four bytes make. Use shifts and masks, the operations from the lesson, so that your code would give the same answer on any processor. memcpy and reinterpret_cast are not allowed here.

title: 1.03  Memory, Addresses and Pointers
body:
Memory is one long row of numbered bytes. A variable is a few of those bytes with a name, its address is the number of its first byte, and a pointer is a variable whose value is an address. One long row of bytes Put the last two lessons together. Memory is a row of cells, each cell is one byte, and every byte has a number. That number is the byte's address . Addresses are just counting: byte 0, byte 1, byte 2, and so on up to however much memory there is. On a 64-bit system an address is a 64-bit number, and it is always written in hexadecimal, for the reasons the last lesson gave. An address looks like 0x00B3F9A0 . There is nothing more to an address than that. It is the position of a byte in the row. Variables are named groups of bytes When you write int score{ 1200 }; the compiler picks four neighbouring bytes of memory, decides that those bytes are score , and puts the bits for 1200 in them. From then on, wherever your code says score , the compiled program uses those four bytes. The demonstration below shows five variables and the bytes they occupy. The table lists each variable; the grid underneath is the same memory in address order. demo-memory title: Five variables int score = 1200 char grade = 'A' double ratio = 0.75 bool alive = true short lives = 3 Work through these: - Click score in the table. Its four bytes light up in the grid. Its address is the address of the first of them. - Change score to 255, then 256, then 65536. Watch the bytes: 255 fills the first byte, and 256 needs the second. The first byte is the lowest one, which is the little-endian order from the last lesson. - Change score to -1. Every byte becomes FF . That is two's complement, also from the last lesson. - Change grade to B . One byte changes, from 41 to 42 . A char is a small number that happens to be displayed as a letter. - Look at the bytes of ratio . A double uses a different scheme, called floating point, so its bytes do not resemble the number at all. The type tells the program how to read them. Everything in a running program is stored this way. A game's health, gold and position are groups of bytes like these, at some address. Sizes, alignment and padding The grid has some cells marked ·· . Those are padding : bytes that belong to no variable. Processors read a 4-byte value fastest when its address is a multiple of 4, and an 8-byte value when its address is a multiple of 8. This is called alignment . To keep every variable aligned, the compiler leaves unused bytes in front of any variable that would otherwise start at an awkward address. Press Packed tight in the demonstration to see the same variables with no padding, then switch back. Packing saves a few bytes and makes every read of ratio and lives slower, which is why compilers do not do it unless told to. The clearest place to see padding from C++ is a struct , because the members of a struct are stored in the order you write them. cpp include <iostream struct Loose { char grade; // 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding so score is aligned int score; // 4 bytes char rank; // 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding at the end }; struct Tidy { int score; // 4 bytes char grade; // 1 byte char rank; // 1 byte, then 2 bytes of padding at the end }; int main() { std::cout << "Loose: " << sizeof(Loose) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "Tidy: " << sizeof(Tidy) << " bytes
"; return 0; } Loose: 12 bytes Tidy: 8 bytes Both structs hold the same three members, six bytes of real data. The order alone makes one of them half as big again as the other. A game with a hundred thousand objects notices that difference. !info Local variables are not promised an order The demonstration lays variables out in the order they are declared, the way a struct does. For ordinary local variables the compiler may choose any order it likes, and an optimising compiler may not store a variable in memory at all, keeping it in a register instead. The rules about size and alignment hold either way. Asking where a variable is The & operator, placed in front of a variable, gives its address. cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 1200 }; int lives{ 3 }; std::cout << "score is at " << &score << '
'; std::cout << "lives is at " << &lives << '
'; return 0; } score is at 000000A3D54FF9A4 lives is at 000000A3D54FF9A0 Run it and you will get different numbers from the ones shown here. Run it again and you will probably get different numbers again. That is expected, and the reason is at the end of this lesson. What stays the same is the distance between the two addresses. Pointers: variables that hold addresses An address is a number, so it can be stored in a variable. A variable that holds an address is called a pointer . cpp int score{ 1200 }; int p{ &score }; // p holds the address of score Read int as "address of an int". Two things about p matter, and beginners often blur them: You write It means --- --- p The address stored in p p The int that lives at that address &p The address of p itself, because p is a variable and lives somewhere too Putting in front of a pointer is called dereferencing it: go to the address and use what is there. p = 50; does not change p . It changes score . The demonstration has an array of four int values and a pointer p . Click a box to aim p at it. demo-pointers values: 10, 20, 30, 40 Try these, and read the line of C++ and the explanation after each one: - Click values 2 . The value of p changes to that box's address, and p becomes 30. - Press \ p += 1 . The number in the box goes up. The array was changed through the pointer, without its name being used. - Type a number next to p = and press Write . - Notice that &p never changes. p is a variable in its own right, with its own address, and only its contents change when you aim it somewhere else. Moving a pointer Press p++ in the demonstration and look at the address. It goes up by 4 , not by 1. Adding one to a pointer moves it forward by one element , not one byte. An int is four bytes, so p + 1 is the address four bytes further on, which is where the next int in an array lives. The compiler does the multiplication for you, using the type the pointer points at. This is called pointer arithmetic . An array is nothing more than its elements stored one after another with no gaps, so walking a pointer along it reaches each element in turn. cpp include <iostream int main() { int values 4 { 10, 20, 30, 40 }; int p{ values }; // an array's name turns into the address of its first element std::cout << p << '
'; // 10 ++p; // forward one int, which is 4 bytes std::cout << p << '
'; // 20 p = 99; // write through the pointer std::cout << values 1 << '
'; // the array changed std::cout << (p + 2) << '
'; // two ints further on: values 3 return 0; } 10 20 99 40 In fact values i is defined by the language to mean (values + i) . Square brackets are pointer arithmetic with a friendlier spelling. Addresses you must not use Keep pressing p++ until p goes past the last box. Nothing stops a pointer from holding an address that is outside the array. The pointer is only a number. What you must not do is dereference it there. The memory after the array belongs to something else, or to nothing, and reading or writing it is undefined behaviour : the program might crash, might quietly damage another variable, or might seem to work until the day it does not. Now press p = nullptr , then \ p += 1 . nullptr is the address 0, used by convention to mean "this pointer is not aimed at anything". The operating system makes sure nothing ever lives at address 0, so dereferencing a null pointer stops the program at once with an access violation . That is the most common crash in C and C++ programs, and it is the friendly one, because it happens immediately and at the line that is wrong. !tip Give every pointer a value when you create it A pointer that was never given a value holds whatever bytes happened to be there, which is an address to nowhere in particular. Start every pointer either at a real object or at nullptr , and check for nullptr before using a pointer that might be empty. Where memory comes from A running program's memory is divided into regions with different jobs. You will study each in chapter 2; for now it is enough to know that they exist. Region What lives there How long it lasts --- --- --- Code The program's instructions The whole run Static data Global variables and constants The whole run Stack Local variables of functions that are currently running Until the function returns Heap Memory the program asks for while it runs, with new or containers such as std::vector Until the program gives it back A pointer can hold an address in any of these regions. Much of the skill in low-level programming is knowing which region an address belongs to, and therefore how long it stays valid. Why addresses change between runs You saw that &score prints a different address each time the program runs. Two things cause that. First, the stack and the heap are handed out by the operating system while the program runs, and what a program gets depends on what happened before. Second, Windows deliberately loads programs at a different place in memory on each run. This is a security feature called address space layout randomisation , and chapter 6 explains it. What does not change is the layout . Inside a struct , score is always the same number of bytes from the start. Inside a program, a given global variable is always the same number of bytes from where the program was loaded. So low-level code and debugging tools describe locations as a base address plus an offset : find where the thing starts this time, then add a distance that never changes. You will use that idea constantly later in the course. Common mistakes !warning Confusing p with p p is an address. p is the value at that address. p = 5; tries to aim the pointer at address 5, which is almost never what was meant. p = 5; stores 5 in the thing it points at. !warning Using a pointer that was never set An uninitialised pointer holds leftover bytes. Dereferencing it reads or writes some unrelated part of memory. Always initialise pointers. !warning Keeping the address of a local variable after its function returns A local variable's bytes are reused as soon as the function ends. A pointer to them still holds the old address, but what is there now is something else. This is called a dangling pointer. !warning Going one step too far An array of four elements has indexes 0 to 3. values 4 and (p + 4) are outside it. Off-by-one mistakes with pointers do not produce an error message, only wrong behaviour. !warning Assuming a layout instead of checking it Padding means the size of a struct is often more than the sum of its members, and members are not always where you would guess. Use sizeof and, later in the course, offsetof rather than adding up sizes in your head. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the address of a variable? - The value stored in it + The position in memory of its first byte - The number of bytes it takes up Memory is a numbered row of bytes. A variable occupies one or more of them, and its address is the number of the first. ? An int is at address 0x1000 . int p points at it. What address is p + 1 ? - 0x1001 + 0x1004 - 0x1008 Adding one to a pointer moves it by one element. An int is four bytes, so the next int starts four bytes further on. ? After int score{ 7 }; int p{ &score }; p = 20; what is true? - p now holds 20 + score is now 20 - score is still 7, because only a copy changed p means "the int that p points at", which is score itself. Nothing was copied. p still holds the address of score . ? A struct has a char , then an int , then a char . Why is sizeof 12 and not 6? - Every member is rounded up to 4 bytes + Padding is added so the int starts at a multiple of 4, and so the whole struct is a multiple of 4 - The compiler reserves space for future members The int needs to be aligned, so three unused bytes follow the first char . Three more follow the last char so that the next struct in an array would also be aligned. ? What happens when a program dereferences a null pointer on Windows? - It reads the value 0 - Nothing, the statement is skipped + The operating system stops the program with an access violation Nothing is ever placed at address 0, precisely so that this mistake is caught the moment it happens. ? The same program prints a different address for the same variable each time it runs. Why? - The compiler is rebuilt each time + The operating system places the program and its stack at different addresses on each run - The variable's value is different each time Addresses are assigned at run time and Windows randomises them on purpose. The distances between things inside the program stay the same, which is why locations are described as a base plus an offset.

title: Swap through pointers
body: Write swapValues(a, b) . It is given the addresses of two int variables and exchanges their values. After swapValues(&x, &y) , x holds what y held and y holds what x held. The function receives addresses, so it has to work on the values at those addresses. std::swap is not allowed here: write the three steps yourself.

title: Sum with a moving pointer
body: Write sum(first, last) . first points at the first int of a run of ints, and last points one past the final one. It returns the total of all of them. For an array int values 4 { 10, 20, 30, 40 }; the call is sum(values, values + 4) and the answer is 100. When first and last are equal the run is empty and the total is 0. Walk a pointer along the memory. Square brackets are not allowed in this task.

title: Hex dump
body: A memory view shows bytes as pairs of hexadecimal digits. Write the function behind one. hexDump(data, size) is given the address of some memory and a number of bytes. It returns those bytes as text: two capital hex digits each, with a single space between bytes and none at the end. For int score{ 1000 }; the call hexDump(&score, sizeof(score)) returns "E8 03 00 00" . That is the little-endian layout from the last lesson, read straight out of memory. A size of 0 gives an empty string. data is a const void , an address with no type attached. To read bytes through it, convert it to a const unsigned char .

title: 1.04  How Source Code Becomes Machine Code
match: 1.04 How Source Code Becomes Machine Code
body:
The CPU only understands numbers, so C++ has to be translated before it can run. Four tools do it in turn: the preprocessor , the compiler , the assembler and the linker . Knowing what each one does explains most build errors and almost everything you will see in a debugger. From text to numbers In lesson 1.01 the tiny computer ran a program that was nothing but numbers in memory. A real CPU is the same. It has never heard of C++. A .cpp file is text for people, and something has to turn it into the numbers the processor executes. That job is split into stages. Each stage takes one kind of file and produces another. When you press Build in Visual Studio, all of these run one after another, so it feels like one step. It is worth knowing the stages apart, because each has its own kind of error. Stage 1: the preprocessor Every line that starts with is an instruction to the preprocessor , which works on plain text before any C++ is understood. Directive What the preprocessor does --- --- include <iostream Pastes the whole of that file in place of the line define MAX_PLAYERS 4 From here on, replaces the word MAX_PLAYERS with 4 ifdef _DEBUG ... endif Keeps or drops the lines in between, depending on whether _DEBUG is defined The result is one long file called a translation unit . Including <iostream alone adds tens of thousands of lines. You never see this file, but the compiler does. cpp include <iostream define GREETING "Hello from the preprocessor" define SQUARE(x) ((x) (x)) int main() { std::cout << GREETING << '
'; std::cout << SQUARE(7) << '
'; ifdef _DEBUG std::cout << "This is a debug build
"; endif return 0; } Hello from the preprocessor 49 This is a debug build The examples on this site are built as Debug builds, where _DEBUG is defined, so the last line appears. In a Release build the preprocessor removes that line before the compiler ever sees it. By the time the compiler sees main , the second line reads std::cout << ((7) (7)) << '
'; . The word SQUARE is gone.
