Macros are text substitution and nothing more, which is why modern C++ prefers constexpr variables and ordinary functions: those obey the language's rules for types and scope. !tip See the preprocessed file yourself In Visual Studio, open the project's properties, go to C/C++ → Preprocessor and set Preprocess to a File to Yes. Building then writes main.i , the text the compiler actually reads. Turn the option off again afterwards, because it stops the build from producing an executable. Stage 2: the compiler The compiler reads the translation unit, checks that it is valid C++, and translates every function into assembly language : a text form of machine instructions, one per line. This is the stage that reports most of the errors you meet, such as a missing semicolon, a type that does not match, or a name that does not exist. Here is a small function and what Microsoft's compiler turns it into, with optimisation switched on: cpp int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } asm addBonus PROC lea eax, DWORD PTR rcx+50 ret 0 addBonus ENDP Two instructions. The argument score arrived in a register called rcx , the result is left in a register called eax , and ret returns to whoever called the function. You do not need to read assembly yet: chapter 7 teaches it properly. For now, notice that each line is one small action, just like the tiny computer's instructions. Stage 3: the assembler The assembler turns each assembly line into its numeric encoding. ret becomes the single byte C3 . The lea line becomes three bytes, 8D 41 32 , and the 32 at the end is 50 in hexadecimal: the bonus itself, stored inside the instruction. addBonus: 8D 41 32 lea eax, rcx+32h C3 ret This is exactly what lesson 1.01 described: a program is numbers in memory. These four bytes are the function addBonus . When the game runs, they sit somewhere in memory, and calling addBonus means telling the CPU to fetch its next instruction from there. The assembler's output is an object file ( .obj on Windows). It holds the machine code for one .cpp file, plus a list of names it defines and names it uses but does not define. Stage 4: the linker A real program is many .cpp files, and each one is compiled on its own. If main.cpp calls addBonus but addBonus lives in score.cpp , then main.obj contains a call to a function whose address it does not know. It leaves a note: "fill in the address of addBonus here". The linker reads every object file and every library, matches each "I need" note with the "I define" entry that answers it, fills in the real addresses, and writes the final .exe . That explains the two classic linker errors: Error Meaning --- --- LNK2019: unresolved external symbol addBonus Something needs addBonus , and no object file or library defines it. Often a .cpp file is missing from the project, or a library was not added. LNK2005: addBonus already defined in main.obj Two object files both define it. Often a function body was written in a header that two .cpp files include. Neither is a mistake in the C++ syntax, which is why they only appear after compiling has succeeded. Why the stages matter later Everything in the rest of this course rests on this pipeline. - Debugging. The debugger shows you the running machine code and maps it back to your source lines using a separate file of debug symbols ( .pdb ) that the compiler and linker write alongside the program. - Assembly. Chapter 7 reads the compiler's output, the stage 2 text you saw above. - Libraries and DLLs. Chapter 4 shows how the linker can leave some addresses to be filled in when the program starts, which is how DLLs work. - Reverse engineering. Chapter 9 runs the pipeline backwards: from the numbers in an .exe back to something a person can understand. Common mistakes !warning Thinking include is like import in other languages It is a literal copy and paste of text. Including the same header twice pastes it twice, which is why headers start with pragma once . !warning Putting function bodies in headers without inline Each .cpp that includes the header gets its own copy of the function, and the linker reports already defined . Put the body in a .cpp file, or mark it inline . !warning Reading a linker error as a syntax error If the message starts with LNK , your code compiled. Look for a missing file, a missing library, or a declaration that does not match its definition exactly. !warning Macros with missing brackets define SQUARE(x) x x turns SQUARE(2 + 3) into 2 + 3 2 + 3 , which is 11. This is one reason to prefer constexpr functions. Knowledge check quiz ? Which stage turns include <vector into thousands of lines of code? + The preprocessor - The compiler - The linker The preprocessor handles every line, and include is a straight paste of the file's text. ? What does an object file ( .obj ) contain? - The finished program, ready to run + Machine code for one source file, plus lists of names it defines and names it still needs - The assembly language text for the whole program Each .cpp file becomes one object file. The linker later joins them and fills in the addresses that were missing. ? A build fails with LNK2019: unresolved external symbol . What is the most likely cause? - A missing semicolon - A spelling mistake inside a comment + A function is declared and called, but no compiled file or library defines it Linker errors appear after compiling has succeeded. Something is used but never defined in anything the linker was given. ? In the assembler output above, why does the byte 32 appear in the encoding of lea eax, rcx+50 ? - It is the size of the instruction + 50 in decimal is 0x32 in hexadecimal - It is the address of the function Numbers inside instructions are stored as bytes like everything else. Fifty is three sixteens and two, which is 0x32 .

title: Be the preprocessor
where: 1.04 How Source Code Becomes Machine Code
body: The preprocessor's define is plain text substitution. Write expand(line, defines) to do the same job for simple object-like macros. defines maps macro names to their replacement text. Replace every whole word in line that is a macro name with its replacement. A word is a run of letters, digits and underscores. Everything else in the line is copied unchanged. defines: MAX_HEALTH - 100, BONUS - 25 expand("hp = MAX_HEALTH + BONUS;") gives "hp = 100 + 25;" expand("MAX_HEALTH_BAR = 3;") gives "MAX_HEALTH_BAR = 3;" (a different word) One pass is enough: the replacement text is not itself expanded again.

title: 1.05  Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look
match: 1.05 Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look
body: When a function is called, the CPU has to remember where to come back to, and the function needs somewhere to keep its local variables. Both go on the stack , a region of memory that grows by one frame per call and shrinks again when the call returns. Two questions every call has to answer The tiny computer in lesson 1.01 had a JUMP instruction: carry on from a different cell. A function call needs more than that. When main calls heal , the CPU jumps into heal . When heal finishes, the CPU has to jump back , to the exact instruction after the call in main . So a call raises two questions: 1. Where do I return to? heal can be called from fifty different places. Each call must return to its own caller. 2. Where do my local variables live? heal may call itself, or be running in several threads at once. Each run needs its own copy of its locals. One idea answers both: a stack. A stack of frames A stack is a pile where you only ever add to the top or take from the top, like a pile of plates. The program reserves a region of memory for it when it starts, about one megabyte by default on Windows. Each time a function is called, a block of that region is set aside for the call. The block is called a stack frame , and it holds: - the return address : where in the caller to carry on afterwards, - the function's local variables , - some of its arguments , and some bookkeeping. When the function returns, its frame is released, and the caller's frame is on top again. Step through a small program. The arguments, locals and return addresses appear as each call happens. demo-stack title: main calls heal, which calls clamp call main The program starts. The operating system calls main, so main gets the first frame. local health = 40 local potion = 75 call heal current=40 amount=75 main calls heal. A new frame goes below main's, holding the return address and heal's arguments. local total = 115 heal works out 40 + 75 in a local variable. It lives in heal's frame, not main's. call clamp value=115 maxValue=100 heal calls clamp. A third frame. The return address says: carry on inside heal. return 100 clamp returns 100. Its frame is released, and execution goes back into heal, right after the call. return 100 heal returns 100 to main. heal's frame is released too. set health = 100 main stores the result. Only main's frame is left. return 0 main returns, and the program is over. Things to notice: - The newest frame always sits at the lowest address. On x64 Windows, as on most systems, the stack grows downwards in memory. - The stack pointer register, rsp , always holds the address of the top of the stack. Making a frame is just subtracting from rsp ; releasing it is adding back. That is why calls are fast. - total exists only while heal is running. Once heal returns, the memory it used is free to be reused by the next call. Seeing the stack grow from C++ You can watch the addresses yourself by printing the address of a local variable at different depths of recursion. cpp include <iostream void dive(int depth) { int marker{ depth }; // one local per call std::cout << "depth " << depth << ": marker is at " << &marker << '\n'; if (depth < 3) dive(depth + 1); } int main() { dive(1); return 0; } varies depth 1: marker is at 000000E1A3AFF6B4 depth 2: marker is at 000000E1A3AFF654 depth 3: marker is at 000000E1A3AFF5F4 Your addresses will differ, and they change between runs. What stays the same is the pattern: each deeper call's marker is at a lower address, here 0x60 (96) bytes lower each time. That gap is the size of one dive frame. Each call really does have its own marker , in its own place. Return values and the stack pointer How does clamp hand back 100? Small return values do not go through the stack at all. On x64 Windows they are left in the register rax , and the caller reads them from there straight after the call. The first four arguments travel in registers too ( rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 ), which is why addBonus in the last lesson found score in rcx . The exact rules are the calling convention , which chapter 7 covers in detail. The two instructions that make calls work are: Instruction What it does --- --- call heal Pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack ( rsp goes down by 8), then jumps to heal ret Pops that address off the stack ( rsp goes up by 8) and jumps to it That is the whole trick. call leaves a note of where to come back to, and ret reads it. When it goes wrong The stack is a fixed size. A recursive function that never stops calling itself keeps adding frames until the region is full. The next frame lands outside it, and Windows stops the program with a stack overflow (exception code 0xC00000FD ). cpp // Do not run this one: it never stops. int forever(int n) { return forever(n + 1) + 1; } Large local arrays use stack space too. int grid 1000000 ; inside a function asks for 4 MB of stack and will overflow on its own. Big data belongs on the heap , which chapter 2 covers. The other classic stack bug is returning the address of a local: cpp int makeScore() { int score{ 500 }; return &score; // score's frame is released as the function returns } The caller gets an address inside a frame that no longer exists. The next call reuses that memory, and the "score" changes underneath you. The compiler warns about this (warning C4172). It is one form of dangling pointer , a bug chapter 2 looks at closely. Common mistakes !warning Thinking locals keep their values between calls Each call gets a fresh frame. A local starts uninitialised (or with its initialiser) every time. Use a static local or a member variable for something that must survive. !warning Expecting the stack to grow upwards Newer frames are at lower addresses on x64. If you see addresses getting smaller as you go deeper, that is correct. !warning Huge arrays as local variables The default stack is about 1 MB. Use std::vector or another heap allocation for anything large. !warning Returning a pointer or reference to a local The frame is gone once the function returns. Return the value itself instead. Knowledge check quiz ? What two things does every function call need the stack for? - Storing the program's code and its global variables + Remembering where to return to, and holding the call's local variables - Holding the heap and the list of open files The return address lets the CPU come back to the right place in the caller; the frame gives each call its own locals. ? On x64 Windows, a function calls itself three levels deep. Where is the deepest call's frame? - At the highest address, above the others + At the lowest address, below the others - In the same place as the first frame, which it overwrites The stack grows downwards: each new frame is placed below the previous one. ? What does the ret instruction do? + Pops the return address off the stack and jumps to it - Pushes the return value onto the stack - Ends the program call pushed the return address; ret takes it back off and carries on from there. ? Why does int grid 1000000 ; inside a function usually crash? - int arrays cannot be that long + It needs about 4 MB of stack, more than the 1 MB the stack has by default - The compiler rejects it Locals live in the frame. A frame bigger than the whole stack overflows it immediately.

title: How deep does it go?
where: 1.05 Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look
body: A profiler has recorded what a program did as a list of events. Each event is either "call" (a new frame goes on the stack) or "return" (the top frame comes off). Write maxDepth(events) , which returns the largest number of frames that were on the stack at the same time. Before the first event the stack is empty. { "call", "call", "return", "call", "call", "return", "return", "return" } gives 3 If a "return" arrives when the stack is already empty, the recording is broken: return -1 .

title: 1.06  What the Operating System Does for a Program
match: 1.06 What the Operating System Does for a Program
body:
Between your program and the hardware sits the operating system . It loads the program into memory, gives it a private address space , shares the CPU between hundreds of programs, and is the only way to reach files, the screen or the network. Each of these ideas gets its own chapter later; this lesson is the map. The program is not alone On the tiny computer from lesson 1.01, one program owned the whole machine. A Windows PC runs hundreds of programs at once: the game, the browser, the music player, dozens of background services. None of them can be allowed to overwrite another's memory or hog the processor forever. The operating system (OS) is the program that makes sharing possible. Its core, the kernel , runs with full control of the hardware. Everything else, including your game, runs with restricted rights and has to ask the kernel for anything that touches the outside world. Chapter 15 looks inside the kernel. For now, five jobs matter. 1. Loading the program An .exe on disk is a file in the PE format (Portable Executable). When you start it, the Windows loader : 1. Creates a new process : the container for one running copy of a program. 2. Maps the .exe file's code and data into the process's memory. 3. Loads every DLL the program needs (such as kernel32.dll and the C++ runtime), and fills in the addresses of the functions the program calls in them. 4. Creates the first thread and starts it at the program's entry point, which eventually calls your main . Chapter 9 takes the PE format apart byte by byte. Chapter 4 builds DLLs of your own. 2. Giving each process its own memory Every process gets its own virtual address space . The addresses your program prints are not positions in the RAM chips. They are positions in a private, pretend memory that the OS and the processor translate to real memory behind the scenes. Two programs can both use the address 0x7FF61000 , and they reach different physical memory. That is how Windows keeps programs from reading or wrecking each other: there is simply no address in one process that leads to another process's memory. Memory is handed out in pages , which are 4,096 bytes ( 0x1000 ) each on x64. Chapter 6 explains the translation and how to explore your own address space. 3. Sharing the processor A CPU has a handful of cores, and there are thousands of threads that want to run. The OS scheduler gives each thread a short turn, a time slice of a few milliseconds, then saves its registers and lets another thread run. It switches so often that everything appears to run at once. This is why your game's frame time is never perfectly steady, and why one program stuck in an endless loop does not freeze the whole PC. Chapter 6 covers threads and scheduling. 4. Being the only door to the hardware User-mode programs cannot touch the disk, the graphics card or the network directly. They call system calls , functions that switch the CPU into kernel mode, do the work with full rights and switch back. On Windows you almost never make system calls yourself. You call documented functions in DLLs, the Windows API , and those make the system calls for you. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { SYSTEM_INFO info{}; GetSystemInfo(&info); // asks Windows about the machine and the address space std::cout << "Page size: " << info.dwPageSize << " bytes
"; std::cout << "Allocation granularity: " << info.dwAllocationGranularity << " bytes
"; std::cout << "Lowest usable address: " << info.lpMinimumApplicationAddress << '
'; return 0; } Page size: 4096 bytes Allocation granularity: 65536 bytes Lowest usable address: 0000000000010000 GetSystemInfo is part of the Windows API, declared in <windows.h and implemented in kernel32.dll . Chapter 5 is all about this API: how to read its documentation, handle its errors and use its strange string types. Even std::cout ends in a system call. The C++ library collects your text, then calls WriteFile in kernel32.dll , which asks the kernel to put the bytes on the console. 5. Keeping track of who owns what When your program opens a file, the kernel creates an object to represent the open file and hands your process a handle : a small number that means "that file I opened". Threads, processes, events and windows are all handled the same way. The kernel checks every handle against the process's rights, and closes everything a process left open when it exits. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "This process has id " << GetCurrentProcessId() << '
'; std::cout << "Its main thread has id " << GetCurrentThreadId() << '
'; return 0; } varies This process has id 18324 Its main thread has id 20916 Run it twice and the numbers change: every run is a new process with a new id. Open Task Manager → Details while a program is running and you can find it by this id. What this means for low-level work Every topic later in the course is about one of these jobs, seen up close. OS job Where the course goes deeper --- --- Loading programs and DLLs Chapter 4 (DLLs), chapter 9 (the PE format) Private virtual memory Chapter 6 (address spaces, pages, protection) Scheduling Chapter 6 (threads), chapter 8 (debugging threads) System calls and the Windows API Chapter 5, chapter 15 Handles and rights Chapter 5 (handles), chapter 6 (access rights) !note Rights are a feature, not an obstacle Much of what the OS does is say no: no, you cannot read that process; no, you cannot load that driver. These rules are what keep a PC stable and keep one bad program from compromising the others. The course works with them, using documented interfaces on programs you write yourself. Common mistakes !warning Thinking a pointer value is a place in RAM It is a virtual address, meaningful only inside its own process. The same number in another process leads somewhere else, or nowhere. !warning Assuming your thread runs without interruption The scheduler can pause it between any two instructions. Code that shares data between threads has to be written for that, as chapter 6 shows. !warning Forgetting that handles must be closed Windows closes them when the process exits, but a long-running game that opens files or threads in a loop and never closes them will run out. Knowledge check quiz ? Two processes print the same pointer value. What does that tell you? - They are sharing that piece of memory + Nothing in particular: each process has its own address space, so the same address can lead to different memory - One of them has crashed Virtual addresses are private to each process. The OS maps them to physical memory separately for each one. ? What is a process? + The container for one running copy of a program: its address space, its threads and its handles - Another name for an .exe file - A single function running on the CPU The .exe is the file on disk. Starting it creates a process. Starting it twice creates two processes. ? How big is one page of memory on x64 Windows? - 1,024 bytes + 4,096 bytes ( 0x1000 ) - 65,536 bytes 65,536 is the allocation granularity, which chapter 6 explains. A page is 4 KB. ? How does a normal Windows program read a file from disk? - It talks to the disk controller directly + It calls a Windows API function, which makes a system call into the kernel - It reads the disk's memory addresses with a pointer User-mode code cannot touch hardware. The kernel and its drivers do that on the program's behalf.

title: Pages for an allocation
where: 1.06 What the Operating System Does for a Program
body: The operating system hands out memory in whole pages. Asking for even one byte costs a full page. Write pagesNeeded(bytes, pageSize) , the number of pages needed to hold bytes bytes, and roundUpToPage(bytes, pageSize) , the number of bytes that is actually reserved. pagesNeeded(1, 4096) = 1 pagesNeeded(4096, 4096) = 1 pagesNeeded(4097, 4096) = 2 roundUpToPage(5000, 4096) = 8192 Zero bytes need zero pages. Use whole-number arithmetic only: no floating point and no ceil .

title: 1.07  Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course
match: 1.07 Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course
body: The examples on this site run in your browser, but from chapter 4 on you will build real Windows programs, step through them in a debugger and read their memory. That takes Visual Studio on your own PC. This lesson installs it with the right parts, creates a console project, and sets the options the course assumes. Why Visual Studio Visual Studio is Microsoft's development environment for Windows. It brings together the three tools this course leans on most: - the MSVC compiler and linker , which produce the same kind of code as the Windows programs you will study, - the Windows SDK , the headers and libraries for the Windows API, - the Visual Studio debugger , which can pause a program, show its memory and registers, and step through its machine code. The Community edition is free for individual learners. It runs on Windows 10 and 11. The examples on this site use the same compiler, so code that runs here behaves the same way there. !note Visual Studio, not Visual Studio Code Visual Studio Code is a separate, lighter editor. It can be set up for C++, but its debugger and project system are not what this course describes. Install Visual Studio (the purple icon). Installing 1. Download the Visual Studio Community installer from Microsoft's website: visualstudio.microsoft.com . 2. Run it. When it asks which workloads to install, tick Desktop development with C++ . 3. On the right, under Installation details , make sure these are ticked. Most are on by default: - MSVC v143 (or newer) x64/x86 build tools - Windows 11 SDK (the newest listed; it also builds programs for Windows 10) - C++ AddressSanitizer (used in chapter 2) - C++ CMake tools for Windows (optional) 4. Press Install . It needs several gigabytes and some time. Later chapters add more: chapter 16 installs the Windows Driver Kit , and says exactly which version to match. Nothing else is needed now. Creating a project 1. Start Visual Studio and choose Create a new project . 2. Pick Console App with the C++ tag. Not "Empty Project" and not a C one. 3. Name it, for example chapter01 , choose a folder, and tick Place solution and project in the same directory to keep the folders simple. 4. Press Create . Visual Studio opens chapter01.cpp with a "Hello World" program in it. Press Ctrl+F5 (Start Without Debugging). A console window opens and shows the output, and stays open until you press a key. A project builds one program or library. A solution groups projects that belong together; chapter 4 uses this to build a game and a DLL side by side. Settings the course assumes Open the project's properties: right-click the project in Solution Explorer and choose Properties . At the top, set Configuration to All Configurations and Platform to x64 , so the changes apply to both Debug and Release builds. Where Setting Value Why --- --- --- --- General C++ Language Standard ISO C++20 Standard ( /std:c++20 ) or newer The course uses std::format , std::span and other C++20 features C/C++ → General Warning Level Level 4 ( /W4 ) More warnings catch more mistakes C/C++ → General Treat Warnings As Errors Yes ( /WX ), optional Stops warnings from piling up unread Advanced Character Set Use Unicode Character Set The default; chapter 5 explains what it changes And in the toolbar at the top of the window, make sure the platform box says x64 , not x86. Everything in this course assumes 64-bit programs: 8-byte pointers, the x64 registers, the x64 calling convention. Debug and Release The toolbar's configuration box switches between two ways of building the same code. Debug Release --- --- --- Optimisation Off On ( /O2 ) Code matches the source line by line Yes Not closely: code is merged, reordered or removed Extra checks Uninitialised stack memory filled with 0xCC , heap checks, iterator checks None Speed Slow Fast Use it for Writing and debugging Measuring performance, and shipping Most of this course uses Debug . Chapter 4 compares the two in detail, and chapter 7 reads optimised Release code on purpose. !tip The 0xCC pattern In a Debug build, uninitialised local variables are filled with the byte 0xCC . If a variable shows up as -858993460 (which is 0xCCCCCCCC ) in the debugger, you have read it before giving it a value. You will meet this pattern in the next lesson. Where the output goes After a build, the program is in a folder named after the platform and configuration: chapter01\ chapter01.cpp chapter01.vcxproj x64\ Debug\ chapter01.exe the program chapter01.pdb its debug symbols Release\ chapter01.exe You can run the .exe from there by double-clicking it, but a console program closes its window as soon as it finishes. Run it from a terminal instead: open Tools → Command Line → Developer PowerShell , then: powershell cd x64\Debug .\chapter01.exe The Developer PowerShell also has the compiler on its path, so you can try the build stages from lesson 1.04 by hand: powershell cl /EHsc /std:c++20 /c main.cpp compile only: makes main.obj cl /EHsc /std:c++20 /FA main.cpp compile and link, and also write main.asm dumpbin /disasm main.obj show the machine code inside the object file Common mistakes !warning Building for x86 A 32-bit build has 4-byte pointers and a different calling convention, and nothing in chapters 6, 7 or 9 will match. Check the platform box says x64. !warning Changing settings for one configuration only If Debug builds work and Release builds fail with odd errors, a setting was probably changed with only Debug selected. Use All Configurations when setting project-wide options. !warning Picking the wrong project template "Console App" under C++ is the one. Templates for C , or a "Windows Desktop Application", start from different code. Knowledge check quiz ? Which workload do you need in the Visual Studio installer for this course? - .NET desktop development + Desktop development with C++ - Game development with Unity It brings the MSVC compiler, the Windows SDK and the C++ debugger. ? A variable shows as -858993460 in the debugger. What does that suggest? + It was read before being given a value, in a Debug build - It holds a very large negative score - The debugger is broken -858993460 is 0xCCCCCCCC , the pattern Debug builds use to fill uninitialised stack memory. ? Why should the platform be set to x64? - x86 programs cannot run on Windows 11 + The course's material on pointers, registers and calling conventions describes 64-bit programs - Visual Studio Community only supports x64 Both build fine, but a 32-bit program has different pointer sizes, registers and calling conventions from everything the course explains.

title: 1.08  Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change
match: 1.08 Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change
body: A debugger pauses a running program so you can look inside it. This lesson walks through a first session in Visual Studio: setting a breakpoint , stepping one line at a time, reading variables in the Locals and Watch windows, and opening the Memory window to watch the bytes of a variable change. Why use a debugger Printing values with std::cout works, but it shows you only what you thought to print, and only after the program has moved on. A debugger stops the program while it is running and lets you look at everything: every variable, every byte of memory, every register, and the chain of calls that led here. It is also the tool that ties together everything in this chapter. You will see the stack from lesson 1.05, the bytes from lesson 1.02 and the addresses from lesson 1.03, in a real program, live. The program to debug Create a console project (lesson 1.07) and replace the code with this: cpp include <iostream struct Player { int health; int gold; float speed; }; int addGold(Player& player, int amount) { player.gold += amount; return player.gold; } int main() { Player hero{ 100, 0, 1.5f }; int total{ 0 }; for (int round{ 1 }; round <= 3; ++round) { total = addGold(hero, round 10); hero.health -= 15; } std::cout << "health " << hero.health << ", gold " << total << '\n'; return 0; } health 55, gold 60 Make sure the configuration box says Debug and the platform x64 . Step 1: a breakpoint Click in the grey margin to the left of the line Player hero{ 100, 0, 1.5f }; . A red dot appears: a breakpoint . It tells the debugger "pause just before this line runs". Press F5 (Start Debugging). The program starts, reaches the breakpoint and stops. A yellow arrow in the margin marks the line that will run next . It has not run yet. Step 2: the Locals window At the bottom of the screen, find the Locals window (if it is not there: Debug → Windows → Locals ). It lists every local variable of the current function. Right now hero and total have not been initialised, so they hold whatever was in that stack memory. In a Debug build that is the 0xCC filler from the last lesson: total probably shows -858993460 . Key Command What it does --- --- --- F10 Step Over Run the current line, including any function it calls, and stop at the next line F11 Step Into If the line calls a function, go into it and stop at its first line Shift+F11 Step Out Run until the current function returns, then stop in the caller F5 Continue Run until the next breakpoint, or the end Press F10 once. hero now shows {health=100 gold=0 speed=1.50000000} . Values that just changed are shown in red. Expand hero with the little triangle to see each member. Step 3: stepping into a function Press F10 until the yellow arrow reaches total = addGold(hero, round 10); , then press F11 to step into addGold . Look at two windows now: - Locals shows player and amount , the locals of addGold . The locals of main are gone from view because this is a different frame. - Call Stack ( Debug → Windows → Call Stack ) lists the frames on the stack, newest at the top: addGold , then main , then the runtime code that called main . This is the stack from lesson 1.05, for real. Double-click the main line and the Locals window switches to main 's variables, then double-click addGold to go back. Press Shift+F11 to step out. You are back in main , and total holds the returned value. Step 4: the Watch window The Watch window shows any expression you type, kept up to date as you step. Open Debug → Windows → Watch → Watch 1 and add these lines: hero.gold &hero &hero.gold sizeof(Player) hero.health 2 &hero shows the address of hero on the stack, and &hero.gold shows an address 4 higher, because gold comes straight after the 4-byte health . sizeof(Player) is 12: three 4-byte members. Step 5: the Memory window Now the most important window for this course. Open Debug → Windows → Memory → Memory 1 . In its Address box, type &hero and press Enter. You see raw bytes, in hexadecimal, sixteen per row by default. The first twelve are hero : 0x000000A1B2CFF7A8 46 00 00 00 1e 00 00 00 00 00 c0 3f cc cc cc cc \_ health _/ \_ gold _/ \_ speed _/ (The address and the values will depend on where you paused.) Read them with lesson 1.02's rules: - 46 00 00 00 is little-endian for 0x00000046 , which is 70. - 1e 00 00 00 is 0x1E , which is 30. This is the second time round the loop: 10 + 20 gold so far, and 100 − 15 − 15 health. - 00 00 c0 3f is the float 1.5. Floating-point numbers have their own bit layout, which chapter 2 explains. - cc cc cc cc after it is Debug-build filler: memory nobody has written. Now press F10 to step through the loop. Each time a value changes, its bytes turn red in the Memory window. Watch gold go up by 10, 20, 30 and health go down by 15, byte by byte. !tip Changing values while paused Double-click a value in the Locals or Watch window to type a new one, or type over the hex digits in the Memory window. The program carries on with the changed value. Try setting hero.health to 1000 and pressing F5 to see the final line change. What you just did In one session you used the four ideas this chapter introduced: Idea Where you saw it --- --- Programs run one instruction at a time (1.01) Stepping line by line, with the yellow arrow showing what runs next Values are bytes, often written in hex (1.02) The Memory window, little-endian int s Variables live at addresses (1.03) &hero and &hero.gold in the Watch window Calls make stack frames (1.05) The Call Stack window, and Locals switching between frames Chapter 4 returns to the debugger for conditional breakpoints, data breakpoints (stop when a particular address changes) and the Registers and Disassembly windows. Common mistakes !warning Debugging a Release build Variables appear as "optimised away" and the yellow arrow jumps around. Switch to Debug for this kind of session. !warning Thinking the highlighted line has already run The yellow arrow marks the next line. Values change after you step over it. !warning Reading a multi-byte value front to back 14 00 00 00 is 20, not a huge number. Little-endian puts the lowest byte first. !warning Pressing F5 instead of F10 F5 runs on to the next breakpoint, or to the end. If the program finishes in a flash, you probably meant to step. Knowledge check quiz ? The yellow arrow is on the line total = addGold(hero, 10); . Which key runs that line and stops on the next line of main ? + F10 (Step Over) - F11 (Step Into) - Shift+F11 (Step Out) Step Over runs the whole line, including the call, and stops at the next line of the same function. ? While paused inside addGold , what does the Call Stack window show at the top? + addGold , with main below it - main , with addGold below it - Only addGold The newest frame is listed first. main is waiting underneath for addGold to return. ? The Memory window shows 1e 00 00 00 where an int lives. What is its value? - 30,000,000 + 30 - 1,966,080 Little-endian: the lowest byte comes first, so the value is 0x0000001E , which is 30. ? Why is &hero.gold exactly 4 more than &hero ? - Addresses always go up in fours + gold is stored straight after health , which takes 4 bytes - The debugger adds 4 to every member's address A struct's members are laid out in order. Chapter 2 shows when the compiler adds gaps between them.

title: Fix the average
where: 1.08 Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change
body: A game's results screen shows the average score of a round. The function below was written in a hurry and gives wrong answers. Step through it in your head the way a debugger would, find the bugs and fix them. averageScore(scores) must return the mean of the scores as a double . For an empty list it must return 0.0 instead of dividing by zero. averageScore({ 3, 4 }) = 3.5 averageScore({ 10, 20, 30 }) = 20.0 averageScore({}) = 0.0 There are three separate bugs. Keep the overall shape of the function.

title: 2.01  The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses
match: 2.01 The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses
body:
Lesson 1.05 introduced the stack. This lesson looks at a real x64 Windows frame: the return address , the 32-byte shadow space , saved registers, locals and the 16-byte alignment rule. It also covers how big the stack is, how recursion uses it, and how to replace deep recursion with a loop. What is really in a frame The demonstration in lesson 1.05 showed a frame as a return address plus some variables. A real frame on 64-bit Windows has a few more parts, always in the same order. Here is the frame of a function update that was called by tick , drawn with higher addresses at the top: higher addresses ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ ... tick's own locals ... │ tick's frame ├───────────────────────────────┤ │ shadow space for update │ 32 bytes that tick reserved for update's │ (4 slots × 8 bytes) │ first four register arguments ├───────────────────────────────┤ │ return address into tick │ pushed by the call instruction ├───────────────────────────────┤ ◀ update starts here │ saved registers │ registers update must give back unchanged │ update's local variables │ │ space for update's own calls │ shadow space for the functions it calls └───────────────────────────────┘ ◀ rsp while update runs lower addresses The parts, from the top: Part Who makes it Why it is there --- --- --- Shadow space (home space) The caller The first four arguments arrive in registers rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 . The caller always leaves 32 bytes where the called function may store them, for example so a debugger can show them. Return address The call instruction Where to continue in the caller. 8 bytes. Saved registers The called function Some registers ( rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 to r15 ) must have the same value after a call as before. A function that wants to use them saves the old values first and restores them before returning. Locals The called function Its local variables, and temporaries the compiler needs. Outgoing area The called function Room for the shadow space, and any arguments beyond the fourth, for the functions it calls. The rules come from the Microsoft x64 calling convention , which chapter 7 reads at the instruction level. The alignment rule At the moment of every call , rsp must be a multiple of 16. The call pushes an 8-byte return address, so inside the function rsp is 8 off, and the function's first job is to subtract enough to make it a multiple of 16 again. That is why frames are always sized in odd-looking amounts such as 40 or 56 bytes: shadow space and locals, plus 8 to fix the alignment. The rule exists because some instructions that work on 16-byte blocks of data, used heavily for floating point and in game maths, require 16-byte-aligned addresses. Locals live at fixed offsets The compiler decides where each local lives inside the frame when it compiles the function. At run time there is no searching: a local is always " rsp plus 40" or similar. That is why reading a local costs the same as reading any other memory. You can see the offsets by printing addresses. cpp include <cstdint include <iostream void frameTour() { int a{ 1 }; double b{ 2.0 }; char name 12 { "frame" }; const auto base{ reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t (&a) }; std::cout << "a at offset 0
"; std::cout << "b at offset " << static_cast<std::intptr_t (reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t (&b) - base) << '
'; std::cout << "name at offset " << static_cast<std::intptr_t (reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t (&name) - base) << '
'; } int main() { frameTour(); return 0; } varies a at offset 0 b at offset 36 name at offset 68 The exact offsets depend on the compiler, its version and the build settings. In a Debug build the compiler leaves gaps between locals on purpose and fills them with 0xCC , so that writing past the end of one local is more likely to be caught. In a Release build, locals are packed tightly, and some never reach memory at all because they live entirely in registers. How big is the stack? Each thread gets its own stack. On Windows the main thread's stack is 1 MB by default. That is plenty for normal code: a typical frame is tens or hundreds of bytes, so even a chain of a thousand calls uses only a fraction of it. Two things eat stack quickly: - Big locals. A local int grid 512 512 is a full megabyte. - Deep recursion. A recursive function that goes 100,000 calls deep, at 100 bytes a frame, needs 10 MB. The size is a linker setting ( Linker → System → Stack Reserve Size , or /STACK ), and threads created with CreateThread or std::thread can be given their own size. Raising it hides the problem rather than fixing it, though. The usual fix is to move big data to the heap (next lesson) and turn deep recursion into a loop. Recursion versus an explicit stack Recursion is natural for anything shaped like a tree or a flood: exploring a maze, filling a region of a tile map, walking a scene graph. Here is a flood fill written recursively, the way it is often first written: cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector void fill(std::vector<std::string & map, int x, int y) { if (y < 0 y = static_cast<int (map.size())) return; if (x < 0 x = static_cast<int (map y .size())) return; if (map y x != '.') return; map y x = '~'; // flooded fill(map, x + 1, y); fill(map, x - 1, y); fill(map, x, y + 1); fill(map, x, y - 1); } int main() { std::vector<std::string map{ " ", " .. .. ", " .. .. ", " .. ", " ", }; fill(map, 1, 1); for (const std::string& row : map) std::cout << row << '
'; return 0; } ~~ .. ~~ .. .. It works, and for this map it is fine. But every cell flooded is one more frame, and on a 1000 × 1000 open map the chain of calls can be hundreds of thousands deep. The program dies with a stack overflow. The fix is to keep the "cells still to visit" in a container you manage yourself, on the heap, and loop until it is empty. The program's call stack then stays one frame deep, however big the map. This is the practice task for this lesson. Seeing frames in the debugger In Visual Studio, pause anywhere and open Debug → Windows → Call Stack . Each line is a frame. Right-click and turn on Show Parameter Values to see the arguments of every call. Open Debug → Windows → Registers to see rsp , then type rsp into the Memory window's address box to look at the raw frame. The return address appears as an 8-byte value that looks like 00007FF6xxxxxxxx : an address inside your program's code. Common mistakes !warning Assuming locals are in declaration order The compiler is free to place them in any order, and to keep some only in registers. Never compute the address of one local from another. !warning Raising the stack size to fix a recursion crash It moves the limit; it does not remove it. A bigger level will crash again. Use an explicit stack or queue for anything whose depth depends on input data. !warning Forgetting that every thread has its own stack A local in one thread's function is invisible to other threads. Sharing data between threads goes through the heap or globals, with proper synchronisation (chapter 6). Knowledge check quiz ? What is the 32-byte shadow space for? + It is room the caller leaves where the called function may store its four register arguments - It holds the return address and saved registers - It is padding that is never used The first four arguments travel in rcx , rdx , r8 and r9 . The caller always reserves 32 bytes so the called function has a place to spill them. ? At the moment of a call instruction, rsp must be a multiple of what? - 8 + 16 - 32 The x64 Windows convention requires 16-byte alignment at every call. The pushed return address then leaves rsp 8 off inside the function, and the function fixes that when it sets up its frame. ? A flood fill on a huge open map crashes with a stack overflow. What is the best fix? - Increase the stack size in the linker settings + Keep the cells still to visit in a container on the heap and loop until it is empty - Make the function inline Any depth that depends on input data can outgrow any fixed stack. An explicit container grows on the heap instead. ? Which of these does the called function have to restore before it returns? - rax + rbx - rcx rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi and r12 to r15 are non-volatile: callers rely on them being unchanged. rax carries the return value and rcx the first argument; both may be overwritten.

title: Flood fill without recursion
where: 2.01 The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses
body: Write floodFill(map, x, y) . It floods the region of '.' cells connected to the cell at column x , row y , changing each one to '~' , and returns how many cells it changed. Cells connect up, down, left and right, not diagonally. Any other character is a wall. If the starting cell is outside the map or is not '.' , nothing changes and the result is 0. The function must not call itself. Keep the cells still to visit in a std::vector used as a stack, so the program's own stack stays small however big the map is. .. .. ~~ .. .. .. - ~~ .. floodFill(map, 1, 1) returns 4 .. ..

title: 2.02  The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time
match: 2.02 The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time
body:
The stack is fast but small, and everything on it disappears when its function returns. For data whose size or lifetime is only known at run time (a level loaded from disk, a list of bullets), programs ask the heap for memory. This lesson shows how new , delete , smart pointers and containers use it, what it costs, and what a Debug build does to help you catch heap mistakes. Why a second kind of memory Stack memory has two limits: 1. Its lifetime is tied to a function call. A local disappears when its function returns. A level loaded inside loadLevel must outlive loadLevel . 2. Its size is fixed when the program is compiled. The compiler must know how big a frame is. A level whose size is read from a file cannot be a local array. The heap answers both. It is a large area of the process's memory managed by an allocator : you ask for a number of bytes at run time, it finds a free block and gives you its address, and the block stays yours until you give it back. Stack Heap --- --- --- Size decided At compile time At run time Lifetime Until the function returns Until you free it Speed of getting memory One subtraction from rsp A search through the allocator's free blocks Typical capacity 1 MB per thread Gigabytes, limited by the system Freed by Returning delete , a smart pointer, or a container new and delete new asks the heap for room for an object, constructs it there and returns a pointer. delete destroys the object and gives the memory back. cpp include <iostream struct Monster { int health; int damage; }; int main() { Monster boss{ new Monster{ 500, 40 } }; // lives on the heap std::cout << "boss has " << boss- health << " health
"; boss- health -= 120; std::cout << "boss has " << boss- health << " health
"; delete boss; // gives the memory back boss = nullptr; // the old address is no longer valid int count{ 5 }; int scores{ new int count { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 } }; // an array sized at run time std::cout << "third score " << scores 2 << '
'; delete scores; // arrays need delete return 0; } boss has 500 health boss has 380 health third score 30 The pointer boss itself is a local on the stack. The Monster it points at is on the heap. When main returns, the pointer disappears, but the Monster would not: if nobody calls delete , its memory stays reserved until the process exits. That is a memory leak . Don't use raw new and delete in modern code Every new needs exactly one matching delete , on every path through the program, including early returns and exceptions. That is hard to get right by hand, so modern C++ gives the job to objects that free memory in their destructors. cpp include <iostream include <memory include <vector struct Monster { int health; int damage; }; int main() { // One object, one owner: freed automatically when boss goes out of scope. std::unique_ptr<Monster boss{ std::make_unique<Monster (Monster{ 500, 40 }) }; std::cout << "boss: " << boss- health << '
'; // Many objects: the vector owns a heap block and grows it as needed. std::vector<Monster wave; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 4; ++i) wave.push_back(Monster{ 50 + i 10, 5 }); std::cout << "wave of " << wave.size() << ", last has " << wave.back().health << '
'; return 0; } // wave and boss free their heap memory here boss: 500 wave of 4, last has 80 std::vector , std::string , std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr all use the heap underneath. Lesson 2.04 explains the rule that makes this safe ( RAII ), and lesson 3.07 opens up std::vector to show exactly how it manages its block. What an allocation costs Asking the heap for memory is not free. The allocator has to find a suitable free block, split it, record that it is in use, and later merge it back when it is freed. Each allocation also carries hidden bookkeeping bytes beside it. Games care about this because they run the same code sixty or more times a second. Allocating a few objects at start-up costs nothing noticeable. Allocating thousands of small objects every frame (every bullet, every particle, every temporary string) adds up to real time and scatters data across memory, which is slow to read. Common answers, which later lessons build: - Reserve up front. vector.reserve(1000) gets one block big enough for the whole wave. - Reuse. Keep dead objects in a pool and recycle them instead of freeing (lesson 3.10). - Arenas. Grab one large block per frame or per level and hand out pieces of it by moving a pointer along, then release the whole block at once. This is the practice task for this lesson. Where heap memory comes from On Windows, new calls the C runtime's malloc , which uses a heap managed by Windows itself (the functions HeapAlloc and HeapFree in kernel32.dll ). The heap in turn gets large regions of memory from the operating system a page at a time with VirtualAlloc , which chapter 6 covers. Most of the time only the top of that chain matters. The bottom of it matters when you look at memory in a debugger, because it explains why heap addresses look different from stack addresses. What a Debug build does to the heap In a Debug build, Microsoft's C runtime wraps every allocation with extra checks and fills memory with recognisable patterns. Learn them: you will see them constantly in the Memory window. Byte pattern Meaning --- --- CD CD CD CD Heap memory that was allocated but not yet written ("clean") DD DD DD DD Heap memory that has been freed ("dead"). Reading it means you used a pointer after delete . FD FD FD FD Guard bytes ("no man's land") placed just before and after each block. If they change, something wrote past the end. CC CC CC CC Uninitialised stack memory (lesson 1.07) When you delete a block, the Debug runtime checks its guard bytes. If you wrote one element past the end of a new int 5 , it notices and stops the program with a "HEAP CORRUPTION DETECTED" message naming the block. Release builds do none of this, which is why heap bugs often "only happen in Release": they were there all along, just not caught. Common mistakes !warning new with delete, or new with delete Arrays made with new must be freed with delete . Mixing them is undefined behaviour. The simplest fix is to use std::vector instead. !warning Using a pointer after delete The memory may be handed out again for something else. Set raw pointers to nullptr after deleting, or better, use std::unique_ptr . !warning Allocating in the hot loop Building a temporary std::string or std::vector inside per-frame code allocates every frame. Hoist it out of the loop and reuse it, or reserve once. !warning Thinking a leak is harmless because the program ends Games run for hours. A few bytes leaked per frame is megabytes per hour, and leaks inside long-running servers or tools eventually exhaust memory. Knowledge check quiz ? A level's size is read from a file when the game starts. Where should its tile data go? - In a local array inside loadLevel + On the heap, for example in a std::vector - In the shadow space Its size is only known at run time and it must outlive the function that loads it. Both point to the heap. ? In a Debug build, you look at a pointer's target and see DD DD DD DD . What has happened? + The memory was freed, and the program is still using a pointer to it - The memory was allocated but never written - Something wrote past the end of the block DD is the Debug heap's "dead memory" fill, written when a block is freed. ? Why do games avoid allocating many small objects every frame? - The heap only allows a fixed number of allocations + Each allocation takes time and scatters data, and doing it thousands of times per frame adds up - Small objects must go on the stack Allocation is a search plus bookkeeping. Reserving, pooling and arenas avoid repeating it every frame. ? What frees the memory owned by a std::vector local? - You must call delete on it - The operating system, when the program exits + The vector's destructor, when the vector goes out of scope Containers and smart pointers free their heap memory in their destructors. That is the RAII idea in lesson 2.04.

title: A frame arena
where: 2.02 The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time
body: Games often allocate scratch memory for one frame from an arena : a single block from which pieces are handed out by moving an offset forward, and which is reset all at once at the end of the frame. Complete the class Arena . Its constructor receives the size of the block in bytes. Instead of real pointers, it hands out offsets into the block, which keeps the task easy to test. - allocate(size, align) returns the offset of a new piece of size bytes, starting at the first offset at or after the current position that is a multiple of align . It moves the position to just after the piece. If the piece would not fit, it returns -1 and changes nothing. - used() returns the current position. - reset() moves the position back to 0. align is always a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. Arena a{ 64 }; a.allocate(3, 1) - 0 (bytes 0..2) a.allocate(4, 4) - 4 (skips 3 to reach a multiple of 4) a.allocate(8, 8) - 8 a.used() - 16 a.allocate(64, 1) - -1 (does not fit; nothing changes)

title: 2.03  Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory
match: 2.03 Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory
body:
Besides the stack and the heap, a running program has memory that exists for its whole life: its code , its constants and its global and static variables . These come straight from the .exe file, in named sections . Knowing the layout tells you at a glance what kind of thing an address points to. Three kinds of storage Every object in a C++ program has a storage duration : how long its memory exists. Storage duration Examples Lives Memory comes from --- --- --- --- Automatic Locals, function arguments Until the block or function ends The stack Dynamic Anything from new , containers' contents Until freed The heap Static Globals, static variables, string literals The whole run of the program The program's own image The last row is this lesson's subject. Static storage is not allocated while the program runs at all. It is laid out by the compiler and linker, written into the .exe file, and mapped into memory by the loader before main starts. Sections of an executable The linker groups everything with static storage into sections , each with its own purpose and its own memory protection. Section Holds Protection when loaded --- --- --- .text The machine code of every function Read and execute .rdata Read-only data: string literals, const globals, tables the compiler generates Read only .data Global and static variables that start with a value Read and write .bss part of .data Globals that start at zero. They take no room in the file, only in memory Read and write .pdata , .reloc , .idata ... Bookkeeping for exceptions, relocation and imports Read only The protections are enforced by the processor, page by page. Writing to .rdata or .text crashes the program with an access violation . Chapter 6 explains page protection, and chapter 9 reads these sections straight out of an .exe . cpp include <iostream int g_highScore{ 1200 }; // .data: starts with a value, can change int g_frameCount; // zero-initialised: takes no space in the .exe file const int g_maxLives{ 3 }; // .rdata (or folded straight into the code) const char g_title{ "Dungeon" }; // the pointer is in .data; the characters are in .rdata int nextId() { static int counter{ 0 }; // static local: lives in .data, initialised once return ++counter; } int main() { std::cout << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << '
'; std::cout << g_highScore << ' ' << g_frameCount << ' ' << g_maxLives << ' ' << g_title << '
'; return 0; } 1 2 3 1200 0 3 Dungeon The static local counter behaves like a global with a private name. It is initialised once, the first time nextId runs, and keeps its value between calls because it is not in any stack frame. The whole picture Put the three kinds of storage together and you have the outline of a process's memory. On 64-bit Windows the exact addresses are randomised (lesson 6.09), but the families are recognisable: You can see the families by printing one address of each kind: cpp include <iostream include <memory int g_global{ 7 }; void someFunction() {} int main() { int local{ 1 }; auto onHeap{ std::make_unique<int (2) }; static int staticLocal{ 3 }; std::cout << "code " << reinterpret_cast<void (&someFunction) << '
'; std::cout << "literal " << static_cast<const void ("hello") << '
'; std::cout << "global " << &g_global << '
'; std::cout << "static " << &staticLocal << '
'; std::cout << "heap " << onHeap.get() << '
'; std::cout << "stack " << &local << '
'; return 0; } varies code 00007FF7A3E413B6 literal 00007FF7A3E5AC28 global 00007FF7A3E61000 static 00007FF7A3E61004 heap 0000020E6C8F5E30 stack 000000E4F1CFF6A4 Look at the first four. They share most of their digits ( 00007FF7A3E... ), because code, literals and globals are all parts of the same image, loaded as one block. Within it, code comes first, then read-only data, then writable data. The heap and the stack are somewhere else entirely, and each looks different. With a little practice you can tell what a pointer points at from its value alone: a very useful skill in the Memory window. Initialisation order, and why globals are risky Globals with simple constant initial values are written straight into the .data section by the linker, so they are ready before any code runs. Globals that need code to initialise them (a std::string , a std::vector , anything with a constructor) run that code before main , in an order that is only defined within one .cpp file . Across files, the order is unspecified. A global in a.cpp that uses a global from b.cpp during its own initialisation may see it not yet constructed. This is called the static initialisation order fiasco . The usual fix is the pattern nextId used: a function holding a static local. The local is initialised the first time the function is called, whatever order things happen in, and C++ guarantees this is safe even with threads. cpp include <string const std::string& defaultPlayerName() { static const std::string name{ "Adventurer" }; // built on first use, then kept return name; } More generally, mutable globals make code hard to follow and hard to test, because any function might change them. Use them sparingly. Constants are fine. Common mistakes !warning Writing through a pointer to a string literal char s = (char )"hello"; s 0 = 'J'; crashes: the characters are in read-only .rdata . Copy the text into a std::string or a char array first. !warning Returning a pointer to a static buffer A function that fills a static char buffer 64 and returns it hands every caller the same buffer, so the second call overwrites what the first caller still holds. It is also unsafe with threads. !warning Assuming globals in different files are initialised in a particular order They are not. Use a function with a static local for anything that other globals depend on. Knowledge check quiz ? Which section holds the characters of the string literal "Game Over" ? - .text + .rdata - .data Literals are read-only data. Writing to them is an access violation. ? A static int counter{ 0 }; inside a function. How many times is counter initialised? + Once, the first time the function runs - Every time the function is called - Never: statics are always zero A static local lives in static storage for the whole program and is initialised the first time control reaches its declaration. ? Two addresses are 00007FF6C1A21000 and 00007FF6C1A3B0E0 . What is the most likely relationship? + They are both inside the same loaded image, such as the program's own code and data - One is on the stack and one is on the heap - They belong to two different processes They share their high digits and differ only in the low ones: about 100 KB apart, typical of sections within one module. ? Why does a zero-initialised global array of a million int s not make the .exe four megabytes bigger? - The compiler compresses it + Zero-initialised data takes no space in the file: the loader just provides zeroed memory for it - Globals are always allocated on the heap The file only records how much zeroed memory is needed, not the zeros themselves.

title: Ids that keep counting
where: 2.03 Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory
body: Every object the game creates needs a unique id. Write nextEntityId() , which returns 1 the first time it is called, then 2, then 3, and so on, for the whole run of the program. Do not use a global variable: keep the counter inside the function, in static storage. The starter is almost right, but it returns 1 every time.

title: 2.04  Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
match: 2.04 Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
body:
An object's lifetime runs from the end of its construction to the start of its destruction. Outside that window its memory may still be there, but using it is a bug. This lesson traces lifetimes for locals, temporaries, heap objects and members, and introduces RAII : tying every resource to an object's lifetime so it is released automatically. Memory and objects are not the same thing Memory is bytes at an address. An object is a value of some type that lives in those bytes for a while. The two have separate lives: - The memory can exist before the object is created in it (a stack frame is set up before its locals are constructed). - The memory can exist after the object is gone (a freed heap block is still mapped; a returned function's frame is still part of the stack). An object's lifetime starts when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts. C++ only promises anything about an object during its lifetime. Reading or writing it outside that window is undefined behaviour , even if the bytes are still there. Watching constructors and destructors The clearest way to see lifetimes is a type that announces itself. cpp include <iostream include <string struct Noisy { std::string name; explicit Noisy(std::string n) : name{ std::move(n) } { std::cout << " + " << name << '
'; } ~Noisy() { std::cout << " - " << name << '
'; } }; Noisy g_global{ "global" }; void level() { std::cout << "level starts
"; Noisy a{ "a" }; { Noisy b{ "b" }; std::cout << "inner block ends
"; } Noisy c{ "c" }; std::cout << "level ends
"; } int main() { std::cout << "main starts
"; level(); Noisy boss{ new Noisy{ "boss" } }; delete boss; std::cout << "main ends
"; return 0; } + global main starts level starts + a + b inner block ends - b + c level ends - c - a + boss - boss main ends - global Read it carefully. Every rule of object lifetime is in that output: Kind of object Lifetime starts Lifetime ends --- --- --- Global Before main After main returns Local At its declaration At the end of the enclosing block { } Several locals in one block In declaration order In reverse order: c before a Heap object At new At delete The reverse order matters: c was created after a and might depend on it, so it is destroyed first. Temporaries A temporary is an unnamed object created in the middle of an expression, such as the result of std::string("Lv") + "1" . It lives until the end of the full expression : roughly, until the next semicolon. cpp include <iostream include <string std::string levelName(int n) { return "Level " + std::to_string(n); } int main() { std::cout << levelName(3) << '
'; // fine: used within the same expression const char text{ levelName(4).c_str() }; // the string dies at the semicolon... // ...so text now points into freed memory. Using it here would be a bug. const std::string& kept{ levelName(5) }; // a const reference extends the temporary's life std::cout << kept << '
'; return 0; } Level 3 Level 5 The middle line is a classic: c_str() returns a pointer into the string's buffer, and the string is a temporary destroyed at the end of the line. The pointer survives; the characters do not. Binding the temporary to a const reference, as on the third line, keeps it alive as long as the reference, but only in that direct form. Lifetime bugs in real code These are the shapes lifetime bugs take. Each compiles. Each "works" sometimes. cpp include <string include <string_view include <vector struct Enemy { int health; }; int dangling() { int local{ 5 }; return &local; // 1. address of a local that is about to die } std::string_view nameView() { std::string name{ "Grim" }; return name; // 2. a view of a string that is about to die } void invalidated(std::vector<Enemy & enemies) { Enemy& first{ enemies 0 }; enemies.push_back(Enemy{ 10 }); // 3. may move every element to a new block... first.health = 0; // ...so first may refer to freed memory } The third one deserves attention because it involves no delete at all. When a std::vector runs out of capacity, it allocates a bigger block, moves the elements across and frees the old block. Every pointer, reference and iterator into the old block is now dangling . Lesson 3.07 shows exactly when this happens. RAII: let lifetimes do the cleaning up Destructors run automatically and reliably: at the end of a block, on return , and when an exception passes through. C++ uses this to manage every kind of resource, not just memory. The idea is called RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation), and it is simple: 1. Acquire the resource in a constructor. 2. Release it in the destructor. 3. Hold the object by value (as a local or a member), so its lifetime is the resource's lifetime. Resource RAII type --- --- Heap memory std::unique_ptr , std::vector , std::string A file std::ifstream , std::ofstream A lock std::lock_guard , std::scoped_lock A Windows handle A small class of your own that calls CloseHandle (chapter 5) "Undo this change when I'm done" A small class of your own, as in the practice task cpp include <iostream class ScopedTimerName { public: explicit ScopedTimerName(const char name) : m_name{ name } { std::cout << "begin " << m_name << '
'; } ~ScopedTimerName() { std::cout << "end " << m_name << '
'; } private: const char m_name; }; int loadLevel(bool fail) { ScopedTimerName scope{ "loadLevel" }; if (fail) return -1; // the destructor still runs return 1; } int main() { loadLevel(true); loadLevel(false); return 0; } begin loadLevel end loadLevel begin loadLevel end loadLevel Whichever way loadLevel leaves, "end" is printed. Code written in this style cannot forget to clean up, because there is no cleanup code to forget. Common mistakes !warning Keeping c_str() , data() or a string_view of a temporary The pointer outlives the string. Keep the std::string itself if you need the text later. !warning Holding a reference into a vector while adding to it push_back , insert , resize and reserve can move every element. Store indices instead, or re-read the reference after the change. !warning Manual cleanup at the end of a function An early return or an exception skips it. Put the cleanup in a destructor. !warning Capturing locals by reference in a lambda that outlives them A callback stored for later that captured & refers to locals of a function that has long since returned. Knowledge check quiz ? Three locals a , b , c are declared in that order in one block. In which order are they destroyed? - a , b , c + c , b , a - In no particular order Reverse order of construction, so later objects, which may depend on earlier ones, go first. ? How long does the temporary in std::cout << makeName() << '
'; live? - Until the end of the function + Until the end of the full expression, at the semicolon - Until the next delete Temporaries die at the end of the full expression they were created in. ? Why can Enemy& first = enemies 0 ; enemies.push_back(e); first.health = 0; be a bug? + push_back may move the elements to a new block, leaving first referring to freed memory - References to vector elements are never allowed - push_back destroys the first element When capacity runs out, the vector reallocates and frees the old block. ? What is RAII? - A way to allocate memory faster + Tying a resource to an object: acquired in the constructor, released in the destructor - A Windows API for handles Because destructors run automatically, the resource is released on every path out of the scope.

title: Undo it on the way out
match: Undo it on the way out
where: 2.04 Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
body: A debug tool sometimes changes a setting for a moment, for example making the game run at quarter speed while a single frame is examined, and must always put it back, however the function exits. Write the RAII class ScopedValue . Its constructor receives a reference to an int and a temporary value. It remembers the old value and sets the int to the temporary one. Its destructor puts the old value back. cpp int speed{ 100 }; { ScopedValue slow{ speed, 25 }; // speed is 25 here } // speed is 100 again Copying a ScopedValue would restore the value twice, so delete the copy constructor and copy assignment.

title: 2.05  Alignment and Padding in Detail
body:
Every type has an alignment : the addresses it may start at must be a multiple of it. To keep each member of a struct aligned, the compiler inserts unused padding bytes. This lesson gives the exact rules, shows how to predict a struct's size and members' offsets, and how to arrange members so less memory is wasted. Why alignment exists Memory is a row of bytes, but the processor does not read it one byte at a time. It fetches aligned chunks: 8, 16 or 64 bytes at once. A 4-byte int that starts at an address divisible by 4 always falls inside one chunk. One that starts at address 6 might straddle two chunks and need two fetches, and some instructions refuse misaligned data altogether. So compilers follow a simple rule: a value of a type with alignment N is placed at an address that is a multiple of N. On x64 Windows, a basic type's alignment is the same as its size: Type Size Alignment --- --- --- char , bool , std::uint8_t 1 1 short , std::int16_t 2 2 int , float , std::int32_t 4 4 long long , double , any pointer 8 8 alignof(T) gives a type's alignment, just as sizeof(T) gives its size. The three rules for a struct The compiler lays out a struct's members in the order they are declared and follows three rules: 1. Each member starts at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment. Any skipped bytes are padding . 2. The struct's own alignment is the largest alignment of any member. 3. The struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment, adding tail padding if needed. This keeps every element of an array of the struct aligned. Work through one by hand: cpp struct Pickup { char kind; // offset 0, size 1 // padding: offsets 1..3, so the int can start at a multiple of 4 int amount; // offset 4, size 4 bool active; // offset 8, size 1 // padding: offsets 9..15 double expires; // offset 16, size 8 }; // largest alignment is 8; 24 is already a multiple of 8, so sizeof is 24 Of 24 bytes, 14 hold data and 10 are padding. See it laid out, then try the packed view to compare: demo-memory title: struct Pickup, in declaration order char kind = 'H' int amount = 25 bool active = true double expires = 12.5 Reordering to save space The fix is to declare members from the largest alignment to the smallest. Then each member already lands on a suitable offset and padding only appears at the very end, if at all. cpp include <cstddef include <iostream struct PickupWasteful { char kind; int amount; bool active; double expires; }; struct PickupTidy { double expires; // 0 int amount; // 8 char kind; // 12 bool active; // 13, then 2 bytes of tail padding }; int main() { std::cout << "wasteful: " << sizeof(PickupWasteful) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "tidy: " << sizeof(PickupTidy) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "offsets: expires " << offsetof(PickupTidy, expires) << ", amount " << offsetof(PickupTidy, amount) << ", kind " << offsetof(PickupTidy, kind) << ", active " << offsetof(PickupTidy, active) << '
'; return 0; } wasteful: 24 bytes tidy: 16 bytes offsets: expires 0, amount 8, kind 12, active 13 A third smaller for the same information. For one object it does not matter. For a game holding 100,000 pickups, particles or tiles, it is the difference between 2.4 MB and 1.6 MB, and fewer bytes means fewer trips to memory when the game loops over them every frame. !tip offsetof and the Watch window offsetof(Type, member) from <cstddef gives a member's offset in bytes. In Visual Studio you can also type &obj.member and &obj into the Watch window and subtract. Controlling alignment Sometimes you need a different layout on purpose. More alignment with alignas . Data used with wide maths instructions often has to start on a 16-byte boundary, and data shared between threads is sometimes aligned to 64 bytes so two threads never write the same cache line. cpp include <iostream struct alignas(16) Vec4 { float x, y, z, w; }; struct alignas(64) PerThreadCounter { long long value; }; int main() { std::cout << alignof(Vec4) << ' ' << sizeof(Vec4) << '
'; std::cout << alignof(PerThreadCounter) << ' ' << sizeof(PerThreadCounter) << '
'; return 0; } 16 16 64 64 Less alignment with pragma pack . File formats and network packets have exact byte layouts with no padding. pragma pack(push, 1) tells the compiler to place members one after another with no gaps. cpp include <cstdint include <iostream pragma pack(push, 1) struct SaveHeader { char magic 4 ; // "SAVE" std::uint16_t version; std::uint32_t length; }; pragma pack(pop) int main() { std::cout << sizeof(SaveHeader) << '
'; // 4 + 2 + 4, no padding return 0; } 10 Use packing only for data that has to match an outside format byte for byte. Accessing misaligned members is slower, and taking a pointer to one is dangerous because code using that pointer assumes it is aligned. Chapter 9 uses packed structs to read the headers of .exe files. Padding is not zero Padding bytes are not set to anything in particular. In a Debug build a local struct's padding shows CC ; elsewhere it holds leftovers. Two consequences: - Comparing structs with memcmp can say two equal structs differ, because their padding differs. Compare member by member, or define operator== . - Writing a struct to a file or the network as raw bytes writes the padding too, which may leak leftover memory contents and wastes space. Write members individually, or use a packed struct you fully initialise. Common mistakes !warning Adding up member sizes to get sizeof The struct also contains padding. Use sizeof , or work through the three rules. !warning Packing everything to save memory Reordering members usually saves the same space without misaligned access. Keep pragma pack for outside formats. !warning Forgetting pragma pack(pop) Without it, every struct after it in the file, including ones in headers included later, is packed too. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the size of struct A { char c; double d; }; on x64 Windows? - 9 - 12 + 16 d needs an offset that is a multiple of 8, so 7 padding bytes follow c . 1 + 7 + 8 = 16. ? What is the alignment of struct B { char c; int i; short s; }; ? - 1 + 4 - 8 A struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members, here the int 's 4. ? Why is struct C { int i; char c; }; 8 bytes, not 5? + Tail padding rounds the size up to a multiple of the struct's alignment, so arrays of it stay aligned - char takes 4 bytes inside a struct - The compiler adds a hidden pointer In an array, the second element starts right after the first. Size 8 keeps its int at a multiple of 4. ? When is pragma pack(push, 1) the right tool? - Whenever memory is tight + When a struct must match an outside byte layout exactly, such as a file header - To make access faster Packing removes padding at the cost of misaligned access. Reordering members is the usual way to save space.

title: Be the compiler's layout engine
body: Write layout(members) , which works out the layout of a struct the way the compiler does. Each member is described by its size and its alignment, in declaration order. The function returns a Layout holding the offset of every member, the struct's total size and its alignment, following the three rules from the lesson: 1. Each member starts at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment. 2. The struct's alignment is the largest member alignment (1 for an empty struct). 3. The size is rounded up to a multiple of the struct's alignment. For an empty list, return no offsets, alignment 1 and size 0. { {1,1}, {4,4}, {1,1}, {8,8} } - offsets 0 4 8 16, size 24, align 8 { {8,8}, {4,4}, {1,1}, {1,1} } - offsets 0 8 12 13, size 16, align 8

title: 2.06  How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
match: 2.06 How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
body:
A class in memory is only its data members, laid out by the alignment rules. Member functions, static members and access specifiers take no space in the object. Inheritance puts the base class's members first, and a class with virtual functions gains a hidden pointer at the front. Knowing this lets you read any object's bytes in a debugger.
