What is, and is not, inside an object Here is a class that looks large: cpp include <iostream include <string class Character { public: static int s_count; // one shared copy, in static storage Character(int hp, float x, float y) : m_health{ hp }, m_x{ x }, m_y{ y } { ++s_count; } void move(float dx, float dy) { m_x += dx; m_y += dy; } int health() const { return m_health; } bool alive() const { return m_health 0; } private: int m_health; float m_x; float m_y; }; int Character::s_count{ 0 }; int main() { Character hero{ 100, 2.0f, 3.5f }; hero.move(1.0f, 0.0f); std::cout << "sizeof(Character) = " << sizeof(Character) << '
'; std::cout << "characters made = " << Character::s_count << '
'; return 0; } sizeof(Character) = 12 characters made = 1 Twelve bytes: just m_health , m_x and m_y . The rest is not stored in objects at all: Part of the class Where it lives --- --- Non-static data members In every object, laid out by the rules of lesson 2.05 Member functions Once, in the program's .text section, like any function static data members Once, in static storage (lesson 2.03) public , private , protected Nowhere. They are checked by the compiler and leave no trace in the program How does move know which object to change, then? It receives the object's address as a hidden first argument called this . hero.move(1.0f, 0.0f) compiles to roughly Character::move(&hero, 1.0f, 0.0f) , and inside, m_x means this- m_x : "the float 4 bytes after the address in this ". On x64 Windows, this arrives in rcx like any first argument. You will see this in chapter 7. struct and class are the same thing The only difference between struct and class is the default access: public for struct , private for class . Their layout rules are identical. This course uses struct for plain bundles of data and class for types that guard their data, but the memory looks the same. Inheritance: the base comes first A derived class contains a complete copy of its base class's members, called the base subobject , at the start, followed by its own members. cpp include <cstdint include <iostream struct Entity { int id; float x, y; }; struct Monster : Entity { int health; std::uint8_t level; }; template <typename T, typename M std::ptrdiff_t offsetIn(const T& object, const M& member) { return reinterpret_cast<const char (&member) - reinterpret_cast<const char (&object); } int main() { Monster m{}; std::cout << "id " << offsetIn(m, m.id) << '
'; std::cout << "x " << offsetIn(m, m.x) << '
'; std::cout << "y " << offsetIn(m, m.y) << '
'; std::cout << "health " << offsetIn(m, m.health) << '
'; std::cout << "level " << offsetIn(m, m.level) << '
'; std::cout << "size " << sizeof(Monster) << '
'; Entity asEntity{ &m }; // a Monster converts to an Entity with no adjustment std::cout << "same address: " << (static_cast<void (asEntity) == static_cast<void (&m)) << '
'; return 0; } id 0 x 4 y 8 health 12 level 16 size 20 same address: 1 Because the Entity part sits at offset 0, a Monster and the Entity made from it hold the same address. Code that only knows about Entity can work with a Monster without knowing anything else about it. That is what makes inheritance-based designs work at the machine level. With multiple inheritance , each base gets its own region, one after the other. Converting to the second base then changes the address: the compiler adds that base's offset. It is one reason game code tends to avoid deep or multiple inheritance. Virtual functions add a hidden pointer As soon as a class has a virtual function, every object of it carries one extra hidden member: a pointer, called the vptr , at offset 0. It points to a table of function addresses for that object's actual type, the vtable . Lesson 3.05 is about exactly this; for now, watch the size change: cpp include <iostream struct Plain { int health; void hurt(int n) { health -= n; } }; struct WithVirtual { int health; virtual void hurt(int n) { health -= n; } virtual ~WithVirtual() = default; }; int main() { std::cout << sizeof(Plain) << ' ' << sizeof(WithVirtual) << '
'; return 0; } 4 16 Eight bytes for the vptr, then the int , then 4 bytes of tail padding to keep the size a multiple of 8. If you look at an object of a class with virtual functions in the Memory window, its first 8 bytes always look like an address inside the program's image: that is the vptr. Empty classes A class with no data members still has sizeof 1, because every object must have a distinct address. But when an empty class is used as a base , the compiler may give it no space at all (the empty base optimisation ). Since C++20, the attribute no_unique_address (spelled msvc::no_unique_address for MSVC) lets an empty member take no space either. Reading an object in the debugger Put it together and you can decode objects by hand. Suppose a Monster from above shows this in the Memory window: 07 00 00 00 00 00 20 41 00 00 a0 c0 3c 00 00 00 05 cc cc cc Bytes Member Value --- --- --- 07 00 00 00 id 7 00 00 20 41 x 10.0 (the bit pattern of a float ; lesson 2.11) 00 00 a0 c0 y −5.0 3c 00 00 00 health 60 05 level 5 cc cc cc tail padding (Debug fill) This is the core skill behind using memory views, and later behind chapter 9's work of reconstructing the layout of a type from compiled code. Common mistakes !warning Thinking member functions make objects bigger They do not. Only data members (and a vptr, if there are virtual functions) take space. !warning Assuming private members are protected at run time Access control is a compile-time rule. In memory, private members are bytes like any others. !warning Writing an object with virtual functions to a file Its first 8 bytes are a pointer that will be wrong the next time the program runs. Save the data members, not the raw object. Knowledge check quiz ? A class has three int members, ten member functions and a static int . What is its sizeof ? + 12 - 16 - 56 Only the non-static data members are stored in each object. ? Where does a derived class's base subobject go? + At the start of the derived object, at offset 0 for a single base - At the end of the derived object - In a separate heap block The base's members come first, so a pointer to the derived object is also a valid pointer to its base. ? Why is sizeof(WithVirtual) 16 when its only data member is an int ? - virtual doubles the size of every member + A hidden 8-byte vptr is added at the front, and the size is padded to a multiple of 8 - Virtual functions are stored inside the object The vptr points to the class's table of virtual functions. The functions themselves are in the code section. ? How does a member function know which object it is working on? - Each object stores a copy of its functions + The object's address is passed as a hidden argument, this - It looks the object up in a global list obj.f(x) is compiled much like f(&obj, x) .

title: Save a player as bytes
where: 2.06 How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
body: Writing a struct to a file as raw memory would include its padding (leftover bytes) and depend on the compiler's layout. Save files are written member by member instead, in a fixed format. Write savePlayer(p) , which returns the bytes of a Player in this exact format, with no padding, all numbers little-endian: Bytes Field --- --- 0 to 3 id , a std::uint32_t 4 to 5 health , a std::int16_t 6 level , a std::uint8_t 7 to 10 gold , a std::uint32_t So every saved player is exactly 11 bytes, even though sizeof(Player) is 12. Then write loadPlayer(bytes) , which reads the same format back.

title: 2.07  Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
match: 2.07 Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
body:
An array is the simplest data structure there is: elements side by side, with no gaps and no bookkeeping. Element i is at the start address plus i times the element size. Two-dimensional data such as a tile map is stored the same way, one row after another. This lesson shows the arithmetic, why the order you loop in matters for speed, and how games store grids. Side by side, nothing else cpp include <iostream int main() { int scores 5 { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 }; std::cout << "sizeof(scores) = " << sizeof(scores) << '
'; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 5; ++i) std::cout << "scores " << i << " is " << (reinterpret_cast<char (&scores i ) - reinterpret_cast<char (&scores 0 )) << " bytes from the start
"; return 0; } sizeof(scores) = 20 scores 0 is 0 bytes from the start scores 1 is 4 bytes from the start scores 2 is 8 bytes from the start scores 3 is 12 bytes from the start scores 4 is 16 bytes from the start Twenty bytes for five 4-byte int s: an array holds nothing but its elements. It does not store its own length, and nothing at run time stops you reading scores 5 or scores -1 . The compiler turns scores i into exactly the arithmetic from lesson 1.03: address of scores i = address of scores 0 + i × sizeof(int) That is a multiplication and an addition, which is why indexing an array is as fast as memory access gets. Arrays of structs The same rule holds for any element type. An array of Pickup from lesson 2.05 places each struct right after the previous one, padding included, which is exactly why a struct's size is rounded up: so that pickups 1 starts properly aligned. pickups 0 pickups 1 pickups 2 ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬────────── │ 24 bytes │ 24 bytes │ ... └──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴────────── +0 +24 +48 std::array<T, N is a plain array wrapped in a struct: same bytes, but it knows its size, can be copied and returned, and checks bounds in Debug builds with .at() . std::vector<T keeps its elements in exactly the same side-by-side form, in a heap block (lesson 3.07). Everything in this lesson applies to all three. Two dimensions: rows one after another Memory is one-dimensional. A grid has to be flattened. C++ stores a two-dimensional array row by row (called row-major order ): all of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on. cpp include <iostream int main() { char map 3 4 { { ' ', ' ', ' ', ' ' }, { ' ', '.', '.', ' ' }, { ' ', ' ', ' ', ' ' }, }; const char flat{ &map 0 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 12; ++i) std::cout << flat i ; std::cout << '
'; std::cout << "map 1 2 is element " << (&map 1 2 - flat) << " of the flat run
"; return 0; } .. map 1 2 is element 6 of the flat run The formula, with width the number of columns: index of (row, column) = row × width + column Games almost always store maps this way on purpose, as one flat std::vector of size width × height , with a small function for the index. The size can then be chosen at run time, the whole map is one allocation, and saving it is one write. cpp include <iostream include <vector struct TileMap { int width{ 0 }; int height{ 0 }; std::vector<char tiles; TileMap(int w, int h, char fill) : width{ w }, height{ h }, tiles(static_cast<std::size_t (w h), fill) {} char& at(int x, int y) { return tiles static_cast<std::size_t (y width + x) ; } bool inside(int x, int y) const { return x = 0 && y = 0 && x < width && y < height; } }; int main() { TileMap map{ 6, 3, '.' }; map.at(0, 0) = '@'; map.at(5, 2) = ' '; for (int y{ 0 }; y < map.height; ++y) { for (int x{ 0 }; x < map.width; ++x) std::cout << map.at(x, y); std::cout << '
'; } return 0; } @..... ...... ..... Notice (x, y) in the interface and y width + x inside: x is the column, y the row. Mixing these up is the most common grid bug there is. Loop order and the cache The processor does not fetch single bytes from main memory. It fetches 64-byte blocks, called cache lines , and keeps recently used ones in small, very fast memories called caches . Reading the next byte along is almost free, because it arrived with the line. Jumping far away means waiting for a new line, which can take a hundred times longer than a cache hit. So the order in which you visit a grid matters: cpp // Fast: walks memory in order, using every byte of each cache line. for (int y{ 0 }; y < height; ++y) for (int x{ 0 }; x < width; ++x) total += map.at(x, y); // Slow for big maps: jumps a whole row ahead every step. for (int x{ 0 }; x < width; ++x) for (int y{ 0 }; y < height; ++y) total += map.at(x, y); Both visit every tile once and give the same answer. On a 4000 × 4000 map, the first is typically several times faster. The rule: make the innermost loop walk along the last index , so it moves through memory in order. Chapter 17 measures effects like this properly. Arrays decay to pointers Passing a plain array to a function passes only the address of its first element. The size is lost: cpp void printAll(int scores ) // really: int scores { // sizeof(scores) here is 8, the size of a pointer, not of the array. } That is the root of many overruns: the function has no idea where the array ends. Pass a std::span<int (C++20), which carries the pointer and the length together, or pass a std::vector or std::array by reference. Common mistakes !warning Swapping x and y With y width + x , x must be less than width and y less than height . Writing x width + y works only for square maps and scrambles everything else. !warning Off-by-one at the edges A map width wide has columns 0 to width - 1 . Looking at a neighbour at x + 1 from the last column reads into the next row, not off the map. Check with an inside function first. !warning Looping column by column over big grids Put the row loop outside and the column loop inside. !warning Expecting a function to know an array's size A plain array passed to a function becomes a pointer. Use std::span , std::array or std::vector . Knowledge check quiz ? An array of double starts at address 0x1000 . Where is element 3? - 0x1003 - 0x100C + 0x1018 3 × 8 bytes = 24 = 0x18 , so element 3 is at 0x1000 + 0x18 . ? A tile map is 10 wide and stored row-major. Which index holds the tile at x = 3, y = 2? + 23 - 32 - 5 2 × 10 + 3 = 23. ? Which loop order is faster for a large row-major grid? + Rows in the outer loop, columns in the inner loop - Columns in the outer loop, rows in the inner loop - Both are always the same speed The inner loop should walk through memory in order, so each cache line fetched is fully used. ? Inside void f(int a ) , what is sizeof(a) on x64? - The size of the whole array + 8, the size of a pointer - 4, the size of one int An array parameter is really a pointer. The length is not passed.

title: Count the neighbours
where: 2.07 Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
body: A tile map is stored as one flat string, row after row, width tiles per row. Write countAround(tiles, width, x, y, wanted) . It returns how many of the eight tiles around (x, y) equal wanted . Tiles outside the map do not count, and the tile at (x, y) itself does not count. tiles = " . " "..." " . " (stored as " . ... . ", width 3) countAround(tiles, 3, 1, 1, ' ') = 4 countAround(tiles, 3, 0, 0, '.') = 3 The number of rows is tiles.size() / width .

title: 2.08  Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
match: 2.08 Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
body:
Text in memory is a run of numbers, one or more per character. A C string is a char array ending in a zero byte. std::string keeps its own length and stores short text inside the object itself. And which numbers stand for which characters depends on the encoding : ASCII, UTF-8, or the UTF-16 that Windows uses internally. Characters are numbers A char is a one-byte number. When text is printed, each number is looked up in a table to find the character to draw. The original table is ASCII , which covers English letters, digits and punctuation in the values 0 to 127: Character Decimal Hex --- --- --- '0' to '9' 48 to 57 0x30 to 0x39 'A' to 'Z' 65 to 90 0x41 to 0x5A 'a' to 'z' 97 to 122 0x61 to 0x7A space 32 0x20 newline '
' 10 0x0A the terminator '\0' 0 0x00 A few patterns are worth knowing because they turn up in code all the time: '7' - '0' is 7, which converts a digit character to its value; and upper and lower case letters differ by exactly 32 ( 0x20 ), a single bit. cpp include <iostream int main() { const char digit{ '7' }; std::cout << digit - '0' << '
'; // 55 - 48 std::cout << static_cast<char ('g' - 32) << '
'; // lower to upper case std::cout << static_cast<int ('A') << ' ' << static_cast<int ('a') << '
'; return 0; } 7 G 65 97 C strings: up to the zero C, and the Windows API, represent text as a C string : a pointer to the first character of a char array, with the end marked by a byte holding 0. Nothing records the length; functions like strlen find it by walking along until they reach the zero. cpp include <cstring include <iostream int main() { const char name { "Rook" }; // 5 bytes: R o o k \0 std::cout << sizeof(name) << ' ' << std::strlen(name) << '
'; for (unsigned char c : name) std::cout << std::hex << static_cast<int (c) << ' '; std::cout << '
'; return 0; } 5 4 52 6f 6f 6b 0 sizeof counts the array, terminator included. strlen counts the characters before it. The difference of one is behind countless bugs: - Copying a 10-character name into a char 10 leaves no room for the terminator. The next function to read it walks off the end until it happens to find a zero. - Forgetting the terminator at all, for example after copying bytes with memcpy , has the same effect. - strcpy and strcat write until they hit the source's terminator, however small the destination. They are a classic source of buffer overruns, which is why MSVC warns about them and offers strcpy_s and friends, which take the destination size. std::string: length, capacity and a small buffer std::string fixes these problems by storing the length itself and managing its memory. On 64-bit MSVC a std::string object is 32 bytes in a Release build: std::string (Release x64, 32 bytes) ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 16 bytes: either the characters │ short text lives right here │ themselves (up to 15), or │ │ a pointer to a heap block │ long text lives on the heap ├──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 8 bytes: size (characters in use) │ ├──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 8 bytes: capacity (room available) │ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ (Debug builds add 8 more bytes for iterator checking, so sizeof differs between configurations.) The interesting part is the small string optimisation (SSO) . Strings of up to 15 characters are stored directly inside the object, with no heap allocation at all. Longer strings get a heap block, and the first 8 of those 16 bytes hold a pointer to it. cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string shortName{ "Rook" }; std::string longName{ "Rook the Unbreakable of the Northern Wastes" }; std::cout << shortName.size() << " chars, capacity " << shortName.capacity() << '
'; std::cout << longName.size() << " chars, capacity " << longName.capacity() << '
'; const auto object{ reinterpret_cast<const char (&shortName) }; const char text{ shortName.data() }; std::cout << "short text is inside the object: " << (text = object && text < object + sizeof(shortName)) << '
'; return 0; } 4 chars, capacity 15 43 chars, capacity 47 short text is inside the object: 1 For games this matters: short names, tags and keys cost no allocation, and long text does. A std::string still keeps a zero after its characters, so c_str() can hand it straight to C-style functions. std::string_view is a pointer and a length, 16 bytes, with no ownership. It is ideal for passing text to a function that only reads it, provided the text outlives the view (lesson 2.04). Encodings: beyond ASCII ASCII has no room for é , ß , Ж , 日 or emoji. Modern text uses Unicode , which gives every character a number called a code point ( é is U+00E9, 日 is U+65E5). An encoding decides how those numbers become bytes. Encoding Unit ASCII text Used by --- --- --- --- UTF-8 1 to 4 bytes per character Identical to ASCII Files, the web, most libraries, Linux UTF-16 2 or 4 bytes per character Every character takes 2 bytes Windows internally, wchar_t on Windows cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string utf8{ "caf\xC3\xA9" }; // "café" in UTF-8: é is two bytes std::wstring utf16{ L"café" }; // the same text in UTF-16 std::cout << "UTF-8 bytes: " << utf8.size() << '
'; std::cout << "UTF-16 units: " << utf16.size() << " (" << utf16.size() sizeof(wchar_t) << " bytes)
"; std::cout << "sizeof(wchar_t) = " << sizeof(wchar_t) << '
'; return 0; } UTF-8 bytes: 5 UTF-16 units: 4 (8 bytes) sizeof(wchar_t) = 2 Two consequences for low-level work: - size() is not the number of characters once text is not plain ASCII. "café" is 4 characters but 5 UTF-8 bytes. - In memory, UTF-16 text looks spaced out. L"Rook" is 52 00 6F 00 6F 00 6B 00 00 00 : every ASCII letter followed by a zero byte. When you search memory for text, search for both forms. Visual Studio's Memory window can show bytes as ANSI or Unicode text; right-click to switch. Chapter 5 deals with the Windows side: most Windows API functions come in an A version taking narrow strings and a W version taking UTF-16, and the course uses the W versions with conversions at the edges. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting room for the terminator A C string of n characters needs n + 1 bytes. !warning Using strcpy into a fixed buffer Use std::string , or strcpy_s / strncpy_s with the destination size, and make sure the result is terminated. !warning Treating size() as a character count It counts bytes (or UTF-16 units). For player-facing text, use a Unicode-aware library when the count matters. !warning Keeping c_str() after changing the string Appending can move the characters to a new heap block, or out of the small buffer. Get the pointer again after any change. Knowledge check quiz ? How many bytes does char word { "Lava" }; occupy? - 4 + 5 - 8 Four characters plus the terminating zero byte. ? On 64-bit MSVC, which of these strings is stored inside the std::string object with no heap allocation? + "Goblin" - "The Goblin King of the Eastern Mountains" - Neither: std::string always uses the heap Up to 15 characters fit in the small buffer. ? In memory you see 48 00 50 00 00 00 . What is most likely there? - Two large numbers + The UTF-16 string "HP" - The UTF-8 string "HP" 0x48 is H , 0x50 is P ; the zero byte after each is the high half of a 2-byte UTF-16 unit, and 00 00 ends it. ? What does '5' - '0' evaluate to? + 5 - 53 - '5' Digits are consecutive in ASCII, so subtracting '0' gives the digit's value.

title: A safe name copy
where: 2.08 Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
body: An old part of a game keeps player names in fixed char buffers. Write copyName(dest, destSize, src) , a safe version of strcpy : - It copies the C string src into the buffer dest , which has room for destSize bytes. - If src is too long, it copies as many characters as fit and still ends dest with a zero byte . - It never writes more than destSize bytes. - It returns the number of characters copied, not counting the terminator. - If destSize is 0 it writes nothing and returns 0. char buf 5 ; copyName(buf, 5, "Rook") - 4, buf holds "Rook" copyName(buf, 5, "Grimbold") - 4, buf holds "Grim" Write the loop yourself: library string functions are not allowed here.

title: 2.09  Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
match: 2.09 Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
body: Memory bugs are the hardest bugs in C++ because the symptom often appears far from the cause, or only sometimes. This lesson names the main kinds ( buffer overruns , use after free , double free , uninitialised reads and leaks ), shows what each one looks like when it strikes, and gives the habits that prevent them. Why these bugs are different Most bugs are wrong logic: the code does what it says, and what it says is wrong. Memory bugs are worse. The code breaks one of the language's rules, the behaviour becomes undefined , and anything can happen: - it works perfectly, every time you test it; - it works in Debug and crashes in Release; - it crashes, but somewhere else entirely, minutes later; - it quietly changes a different variable, and the game misbehaves in a way that seems impossible. That last one is the nastiest. A write past the end of one array changes whatever happens to sit next to it in memory, which might be a player's health, a pointer, or the allocator's own bookkeeping. You will see these effects in this course's tools, so it is worth knowing their shapes. 1. Buffer overrun Writing (or reading) past the end of an array or buffer. cpp struct Player { char name 8 ; int gold; }; void rename(Player& p, const char newName) { int i{ 0 }; while (newName i != '\0') { p.name i = newName i ; ++i; } // no limit! p.name i = '\0'; } // rename(p, "Maximilian") writes 11 bytes into an 8-byte array. // The extra bytes land in gold, which suddenly holds 28,257 if it was 0: the bytes 61 6E 00 are "an" and its terminator. The program does not crash. The player's gold changes to a nonsense number, and nobody looking at the gold code will ever find out why. Off-by-one loops ( <= instead of < ) are the most common cause; unchecked copies like this one are the most dangerous, because the length comes from outside. Prevention: use containers that know their size ( std::string , std::vector , std::array , std::span ), use .at() or Debug iterator checks while developing, and never copy data whose length you have not checked against the destination. 2. Use after free Using memory through a pointer after it has been freed. cpp Enemy target{ findNearestEnemy() }; removeDeadEnemies(); // deletes target's Enemy, among others target- health -= 10; // writes into freed memory If the freed block has been handed out again, the write corrupts whatever now lives there. If not, it may seem to work. In a Debug build the freed block is filled with DD , so reading it gives obviously wrong values like -572662307 ( 0xDDDDDDDD ). Prevention: be clear about who owns each object. Use std::unique_ptr for ownership; refer to objects that can disappear by id or handle and look them up each time, instead of keeping raw pointers to them. Lesson 3.10 builds exactly such a system for game entities. 3. Dangling pointers and references The general form of use after free: a pointer or reference that outlives what it refers to. Lesson 2.04 showed the common shapes: a pointer to a local that has returned, a view of a temporary string, a reference into a vector that has since grown. Prevention: return values, not pointers to locals; do not store views or pointers into containers that might change; prefer indices into a vector over pointers to its elements. 4. Double free Freeing the same block twice. cpp Texture t{ new Texture{} }; cache.add(t); // the cache will delete it when cleared... delete t; // ...and so does this code The allocator's bookkeeping is corrupted. The Debug runtime usually stops the program on the second delete ; a Release build may crash much later, inside an unrelated allocation. Prevention: one owner per object. Smart pointers make ownership visible in the type: a std::unique_ptr cannot be copied, so two owners cannot both think they should free it. 5. Uninitialised reads Reading a variable before giving it a value. cpp int damage; // no initialiser if (critical) damage = 50; health -= damage; // garbage when critical is false In Debug, the garbage is 0xCCCCCCCC (-858993460), which at least looks wrong. In Release it is whatever was on the stack, which is often a plausible-looking number, so the bug hides. Prevention: always initialise, with braces: int damage{ 0 }; . Turn on warning level 4: MSVC warns about many uninitialised uses (C4700, C4701). 6. Leaks Memory that is allocated and never freed. Leaks do not corrupt anything; they just make the process grow until it runs out of memory or slows the machine down. cpp void spawnWave() { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 20; ++i) { Monster m{ new Monster{} }; if (!placeOnMap(m)) continue; // leaked: nobody will ever delete m world.add(m); } } Prevention: never write new without immediately handing the result to an owner ( std::make_unique , a container). Then early return s, continue s and exceptions cannot leak. The Debug runtime can list leaks when the program exits: call _CrtSetDbgFlag(_CRTDBG_ALLOC_MEM_DF _CRTDBG_LEAK_CHECK_DF) at the start of main , and Visual Studio's Output window shows every block still allocated at the end, with its size and contents. A summary table Bug Typical symptom Debug-build clue --- --- --- Buffer overrun Neighbouring data changes; heap corruption message on delete FD guard bytes changed Use after free Strange values, or corruption elsewhere Values like 0xDDDDDDDD Double free Crash in delete or a later allocation Debug assertion in the heap Uninitialised read Random behaviour, different in Release Values like 0xCCCCCCCC or 0xCDCDCDCD Leak Memory use grows over time Leak report at exit Debugging a memory bug When something changes that should not: 1. Make it repeatable. Find inputs that trigger it every time. 2. Find what changed. Use a data breakpoint (lesson 4.09) on the variable that goes wrong: the debugger stops on the exact instruction that writes it, and the Call Stack shows who did it. 3. Run a sanitizer. AddressSanitizer, in the next lesson, catches overruns and use after free at the moment they happen, with the line numbers of the allocation, the free and the bad access. Common mistakes !warning "It works on my machine" Undefined behaviour may happen to work in one build and not another. Code that only works by luck is not working. !warning Fixing the symptom Adding a check where the corrupted value is used hides the problem. Find the write that caused it. !warning Raw new in game code Every raw new is a potential leak, double free or dangling pointer. Prefer containers and smart pointers. Knowledge check quiz ? A player's gold changes to a huge random number right after they rename their character. What kind of bug is most likely? + A buffer overrun from the name into the gold that follows it in memory - A memory leak - A double free The name copy wrote past the end of its array into the next member. ? In a Debug build a variable reads -572662307 ( 0xDDDDDDDD ). What does that point to? - An uninitialised local + Use of heap memory after it was freed - An integer overflow The Debug heap fills freed blocks with DD . ? Which habit prevents leaks from early returns and exceptions? - Calling delete at the end of every function + Handing every allocation to an owning object, such as a std::unique_ptr or a container - Using malloc instead of new Owners free memory in their destructors, which run on every path out of the scope. ? What is the best tool for finding which instruction changes a variable unexpectedly? - More std::cout lines + A data breakpoint on that variable's address - Rebuilding in Release A data breakpoint stops the program on the exact write, with the call stack showing who made it.

title: Plug the leak
where: 2.09 Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
body: spawnWave(count, blocked) creates count monsters and returns the ones that could be placed. A monster is placed unless its index appears in blocked . Monsters that cannot be placed are thrown away. It gives the right answers, but every monster that cannot be placed is leaked. The tests check for leaks. Fix it so that nothing leaks, and keep it returning a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Monster .

title: 2.10  Catching Memory Bugs with AddressSanitizer
body: AddressSanitizer (ASan) is a compiler feature that adds a check to every memory access. It stops the program at the exact moment of a buffer overrun or use after free, and prints where the memory was allocated, where it was freed and where it was misused. Visual Studio supports it with one switch. This lesson shows how it works and how to read its reports. The idea The previous lesson's bugs are hard because nothing happens at the moment of the mistake. A Debug build's patterns help after the fact; AddressSanitizer catches the mistake as it happens . When you compile with ASan, the compiler adds a small check before every load and store. The check asks: "is the address about to be touched part of a live object?" If not, the program stops immediately with a report. To answer that question quickly, ASan keeps shadow memory : for every 8 bytes of the program's memory, one byte of shadow says how many of those 8 are valid to use. Around every heap block, stack array and global it places red zones , bytes marked as forbidden. Freed heap blocks are marked forbidden too, and held back for a while before being reused, so a late use of one is still caught. heap block of 10 bytes, as ASan sees it ┌────────┬──────────┬──┬──────────────────┐ │ red │ 10 bytes │ │ red zone │ │ zone │ usable │6 │ (forbidden) │ └────────┴──────────┴──┴──────────────────┘ ▲ bytes 10..15: forbidden, though in the same 8-byte group The checks make a program about twice as slow and use more memory. That is fine for testing, and ASan builds are not meant for shipping. Turning it on in Visual Studio 1. Install the C++ AddressSanitizer component (lesson 1.07 ticked it). 2. Project Properties → C/C++ → General → Enable Address Sanitizer: Yes ( /fsanitize=address ). 3. In the same properties, under C/C++ → General , set Debug Information Format to Program Database (/Zi) if it is not already, and turn Edit and Continue off; ASan is not compatible with it. 4. Build and run under the debugger (F5). When ASan finds an error, the debugger stops on the bad line and the Output window shows the report. Reading a report: heap buffer overflow cpp-norun include <iostream int main() { int scores{ new int 4 { 10, 20, 30, 40 } }; int total{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i <= 4; ++i) // <= is one too many total += scores i ; std::cout << total << '\n'; delete scores; return 0; } Without ASan this usually prints a wrong total and carries on. With ASan it stops on the fifth read: ==14260==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x11b5c0420040 READ of size 4 at 0x11b5c0420040 thread T0 0 0x7ff6d4e81103 in main C:\code\scores\main.cpp:8 1 0x7ff6d4e8b4e8 in invoke_main exe_common.inl:78 ... 0x11b5c0420040 is located 0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region 0x11b5c0420030,0x11b5c0420040) allocated by thread T0 here: 0 0x7ffe4c0d8d5b in operator new ... 1 0x7ff6d4e81069 in main C:\code\scores\main.cpp:5 Read it from the top: Line What it tells you --- --- heap-buffer-overflow The kind of bug: past the end of a heap block READ of size 4 An int was read (a write would say WRITE) 0 ... main.cpp:8 The exact line that did it: total += scores i ; 0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region It touched the byte just after a 16-byte block, which is 4 int s allocated by ... main.cpp:5 Where that block came from: the new int 4 That is the whole investigation done for you: what went wrong, where, and with which block. Reading a report: use after free cpp-norun include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int health{ 100, 80 }; int& first{ health 0 }; health.push_back(60); // reallocates: first now refers to freed memory first -= 10; std::cout << health 0 << '\n'; return 0; } ASan reports heap-use-after-free , with three stacks: where the bad access happened ( first -= 10 ), where the memory was freed (inside push_back , called from your line), and where it was originally allocated (the vector's constructor). That third-party "freed inside push_back " line is exactly the clue that points at iterator and reference invalidation from lesson 2.04. What ASan catches, and what it does not Catches Does not catch --- --- Heap buffer overflow and underflow Reading uninitialised memory Stack buffer overflow Leaks, on Windows (use the CRT leak report) Global buffer overflow Overruns that stay inside the same object, such as from one struct member into the next Use after free Logic errors Use after return or scope (with extra options) Data races between threads Double free, mismatched new / delete The "same object" row deserves attention: the Player::name overrun in lesson 2.09 writes into gold , which is part of the same struct. Both are inside one live object, so ASan sees nothing wrong. Prevention there is still std::string and bounds checks. Using it well - Run your tests and a play session under ASan regularly , not only when something breaks. Bugs that have not caused a crash yet are the cheapest to fix. - Fix the first report first. One overrun can cause later, confusing reports. - Keep a separate configuration. In Configuration Manager, copy Debug to a new configuration called ASan with the option on, so normal debugging stays fast. - Third-party code may need to be rebuilt with ASan, or its errors may show up inside your program's reports. Common mistakes !warning Shipping an ASan build It is slower and depends on the ASan runtime DLL. ASan is for testing only. !warning Mixing ASan and Edit and Continue Visual Studio refuses to build with both. Switch Edit and Continue off for the ASan configuration. !warning Assuming no report means no memory bugs ASan only checks code paths that actually ran, and it misses overruns within one object. It finds a lot; it does not prove correctness. Knowledge check quiz ? When does AddressSanitizer report a buffer overrun? + At the moment the bad read or write happens - When the program exits - When the corrupted value is next used Every access is checked as it happens, which is what makes ASan so much more useful than finding the damage later. ? A report says "0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region". What happened? + The code touched the first byte after the end of a 16-byte block - The code read a 16-byte value - 16 bytes leaked "To the right" means past the end; "0 bytes" means immediately after it. ? Which of these does ASan not catch? - Use after free - Heap buffer overflow + An overrun from one struct member into the next member of the same struct Both members belong to one live object, so the access is to valid memory as far as ASan can tell. ? What is shadow memory? - A copy of the program kept for debugging + Extra memory where ASan records which bytes of the program's memory are valid to use - Memory used by the GPU One shadow byte describes eight bytes of real memory.

title: 2.11  Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio
match: 2.11 Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio
body: The Memory window shows raw bytes, and this chapter has given you everything you need to read them. This lesson puts it together: setting the window's display, recognising pointers, Debug patterns, text and floating-point numbers at a glance, and decoding a whole object by hand. Setting the window up Open it while paused: Debug → Windows → Memory → Memory 1 (Visual Studio has four, so you can keep several places open). The useful controls: Control What it does --- --- Address box Type any expression that gives an address: &hero , ptr , names.data() , 0x00000052A3CFF7A8 , rsp . Press Enter. Reevaluate automatically (the circular arrows) Keeps following the expression as you step: useful for a pointer that changes. Columns How many units per row. Set it to 16 bytes, or to 8 when looking at pointers. Right-click → 1-, 2-, 4- or 8-byte integer Groups bytes into numbers, already put back into the right order for little-endian. Right-click → 32-bit or 64-bit floating point Shows each group as a float or double . Right-click → Signed / Unsigned / Hexadecimal display How the numbers are written. Right-click → ANSI / Unicode text (the column on the right) Shows the bytes as one-byte or UTF-16 characters. You can also drag a variable from the code editor or Locals window into the Memory window to jump to its address. Recognising what you are looking at With practice you can tell what a group of bytes is from its shape alone. Here is the catalogue for a 64-bit Windows program: You see (bytes, as shown) It is probably --- --- xx xx xx xx f6 7f 00 00 A pointer into the program's own image (code or globals): high bytes 00 00 7f f6 or nearby xx xx xx xx fe 7f 00 00 A pointer into a system DLL xx xx xx xx 0X 0X 00 00 with small X A heap pointer: two high bytes zero, then smallish xx xx xx xx xx 00 00 00 , 8-byte aligned, near rsp A stack address cc cc cc cc Uninitialised stack memory (Debug) cd cd cd cd Allocated, never written heap memory (Debug) dd dd dd dd Freed heap memory (Debug) fd fd fd fd Heap guard bytes (Debug) 00 00 80 3f The float 1.0 00 00 00 00 00 00 f0 3f The double 1.0 xx 00 xx 00 xx 00 , letters in the right-hand column with dots between UTF-16 text Small numbers followed by 00 00 00 Small int s: counts, ids, health Pointers stand out most: eight bytes ending in 00 00 , with the high bytes repeating the same few values. Since x64 programs only use the lower 47 bits of an address, the top two bytes of a user-mode pointer are always zero. Reading floating-point numbers float and double are not stored like integers. A 32-bit float has three parts: bit 31 30 ......... 23 22 ...................... 0 ┌──────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐ │ sign │ exponent (8) │ fraction (23) │ └──────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘ value = (-1)^sign × 1.fraction × 2^(exponent − 127) You will rarely decode one by hand, because the Memory window can do it for you. But a few values are worth recognising, because they appear constantly in game data such as positions, speeds and scales: Value float bits Bytes in memory --- --- --- 0.0 0x00000000 00 00 00 00 0.5 0x3F000000 00 00 00 3f 1.0 0x3F800000 00 00 80 3f 2.0 0x40000000 00 00 00 40 10.0 0x41200000 00 00 20 41 100.0 0x42C80000 00 00 c8 42 −1.0 0xBF800000 00 00 80 bf A rule of thumb: a 4-byte group whose last byte is 3f , 40 , 41 , 42 , bf , c0 , c1 or c2 and whose first bytes are often 00 is very likely a float of modest size. You can see a value's bits from C++ by copying its bytes into an integer. std::bit_cast (C++20) does it in one step: cpp include <bit include <cstdint include <format include <iostream int main() { for (float f : { 1.0f, -1.0f, 0.5f, 100.0f, 0.1f }) std::cout << std::format("{: 6} - 0x{:08X}\n", f, std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t (f)); return 0; } 1 - 0x3F800000 -1 - 0xBF800000 0.5 - 0x3F000000 100 - 0x42C80000 0.1 - 0x3DCCCCCD 0.1 has no exact binary form, which is why its bits look busy. It is also why comparing floats with == after arithmetic often fails. Decoding a whole object Here is the routine for any object, using everything from this chapter. 1. Find its type's layout. Work through the members and the alignment rules (lesson 2.05), or let the Watch window tell you with &obj.member . 2. Point the window at the object. Type &obj in the Address box. Set 8 or 16 columns. 3. Split the bytes by offset. Mark where each member starts. 4. Read each member with the right rule: little-endian integers, float bits, a pointer (follow it by typing it into a second Memory window), padding to skip. 5. Check against the Locals window. Once your reading matches, you understand the layout. Try it on this object: cpp struct Item { const char name; // 0 float weight; // 8 std::int32_t count; // 12 bool stackable; // 16, then 7 bytes of tail padding }; 0x0000004F8C8FF8A0 e8 4c 2b a1 f6 7f 00 00 00 00 00 3f 0c 00 00 00 0x0000004F8C8FF8B0 01 cc cc cc cc cc cc cc - Bytes 0 to 7: e8 4c 2b a1 f6 7f 00 00 is the pointer 0x00007FF6A12B4CE8 : in the program's image, so name points at a string literal in .rdata . - Bytes 8 to 11: 00 00 00 3f is the float 0.5. - Bytes 12 to 15: 0c 00 00 00 is 12. - Byte 16: 01 is true . - Bytes 17 to 23: cc , tail padding in a Debug build. Common mistakes !warning Reading pointers byte by byte Switch the window to 8-byte integers in hexadecimal and the pointers read naturally, already reversed into the right order. !warning Forgetting the window keeps the old address When you step into a different function, the window still shows the same address, which may now belong to a different frame. Use Reevaluate automatically , or type the expression again. !warning Treating every 4-byte group as an int Positions and speeds are usually floats. If an "int" is a huge number like 1,065,353,216, try reading it as a float: that one is 1.0. Knowledge check quiz ? You see the eight bytes 30 12 4a 9c f6 7f 00 00 . What is it most likely to be? + A pointer into the program's own code or data - A double-precision number - UTF-16 text Eight bytes ending in f6 7f 00 00 is the typical shape of an address in the program's image. ? What float is stored as the bytes 00 00 80 3f ? - 128.0 + 1.0 - 0.0 Read little-endian, the bits are 0x3F800000 : sign 0, exponent 127, fraction 0, which is 1.0. ? An int that should be small reads 1,065,353,216 in the Watch window. What is a likely explanation? + The memory actually holds the float 1.0, and it is being read as an int - The int overflowed - The memory was freed 1,065,353,216 is 0x3F800000 , the bit pattern of 1.0f. ? Why do user-mode pointers on x64 Windows always end in 00 00 in memory? - Pointers are always multiples of 65,536 + Only the lower 47 bits of an address are used, so the top two bytes are zero, and little-endian puts them last - The Memory window adds them The highest bytes of the value come last in memory, and for user-mode addresses they are zero.

title: Read values out of raw bytes
match: Read values out of raw bytes
where: 2.11 Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio
body: A memory viewer receives a block of raw bytes and has to show the values in it. Write three readers. Each takes the bytes and an offset into them, and reads a little-endian value starting at that offset. - readU32(bytes, offset) reads a 4-byte unsigned integer. - readI16(bytes, offset) reads a 2-byte signed integer. - readF32(bytes, offset) reads a 4-byte float . If the value would run past the end of bytes , the reader returns std::nullopt instead. bytes: 0c 00 00 00 00 00 80 3f 9c ff readU32(bytes, 0) = 12 readF32(bytes, 4) = 1.0 readI16(bytes, 8) = -100 readU32(bytes, 8) = nullopt (only 2 bytes left) For the float, build the 32-bit pattern first, then turn the pattern into a float with std::bit_cast (from <bit ) or std::memcpy .

title: 3.01  Pointers to Pointers
body:
A pointer is a variable, so it has an address too, and a pointer can hold that address. A pointer to a pointer lets a function change which object another pointer points at, and it is how arrays of pointers, command-line arguments and many Windows API "out" parameters work. A pointer is just another variable Lesson 1.03 showed that a pointer is a variable holding an address. Like every variable, the pointer itself lives somewhere in memory and has an address of its own. Nothing stops you storing that address in another variable: cpp include <iostream int main() { int gold{ 250 }; int p{ &gold }; // p holds the address of gold int pp{ &p }; // pp holds the address of p std::cout << "gold = " << gold << '
'; std::cout << " p = " << p << '
'; std::cout << " pp = " << pp << '
'; pp = 300; // follow pp to p, follow p to gold, write there std::cout << "gold = " << gold << '
'; return 0; } gold = 250 p = 250 pp = 250 gold = 300 Read the types from the right: int is a pointer to (a pointer to an int). Each in an expression follows one arrow. Expression Type Means --- --- --- pp int The address of p pp int The value of p : the address of gold pp int The value of gold In memory, all three are just numbers in boxes: pp 's 8 bytes hold p 's address, p 's 8 bytes hold gold 's address, and gold 's 4 bytes hold 250. Why you would want one: changing someone else's pointer A function receives copies of its arguments. Pass it a pointer and it can change the thing pointed at, but not the caller's pointer itself. To change the caller's pointer, the function needs that pointer's address. cpp include <iostream struct Enemy { const char name; int health; }; // Makes target point at the weakest living enemy, or nullptr if none are alive. void pickWeakest(Enemy enemies, int count, Enemy target) { target = nullptr; for (int i{ 0 }; i < count; ++i) { Enemy e{ &enemies i }; if (e- health 0 && ( target == nullptr e- health < ( target)- health)) target = e; } } int main() { Enemy pack { { "wolf", 30 }, { "bat", 0 }, { "rat", 12 } }; Enemy aim{ nullptr }; pickWeakest(pack, 3, &aim); std::cout << "aiming at the " << aim- name << '
'; return 0; } aiming at the rat pickWeakest writes into target , which is the caller's aim . This "out parameter" style is everywhere in C and in the Windows API, where functions return an error code and hand back the object they created through a pointer to your pointer. Chapter 5 is full of calls like this: cpp // The function writes the new object's address into iface. IUnknown iface{ nullptr }; HRESULT hr{ CreateSomething(IID_PPV_ARGS(&iface)) }; In modern C++ code you would more often return the pointer, or pass Enemy & (a reference to a pointer, lesson 3.03). But you need to read the form fluently. Arrays of pointers The other common use is an array whose elements are pointers. main can receive the program's command-line arguments that way: cpp include <iostream int main(int argc, char argv) { // argv points at an array of argc pointers, each pointing at one argument's characters. std::cout << "argc = " << argc << '
'; for (int i{ 1 }; i < argc; ++i) std::cout << "argument " << i << ": " << argv i << '
'; return 0; } Run with game.exe --level 3 , argv 0 is the program's path, argv 1 points at "--level" and argv 2 at "3" . argv 1 2 is 'l' : index into the array of pointers, then into the characters. argv ──▶ ┌─────────┐ │ argv 0 │──▶ "C:\games\game.exe" ├─────────┤ │ argv 1 │──▶ "--level" ├─────────┤ │ argv 2 │──▶ "3" ├─────────┤ │ nullptr │ └─────────┘ Arrays of pointers also let you sort or reorder large objects cheaply: shuffle 8-byte pointers instead of copying the objects. Pointer arithmetic still works one level down argv + 1 moves along the array of pointers by one pointer (8 bytes). (argv + 1) + 2 moves along the characters of the second argument by two characters. Each level has its own element size, and pointer arithmetic always uses the size of the thing pointed at. Common mistakes !warning Passing the pointer when the function needs its address pickWeakest(pack, 3, aim) does not compile, which is good. With void parameters it might, and then the function writes over the wrong thing. Match the number of s. !warning Forgetting the parentheses in ( target)- health target- health means (target- health) , which is something else entirely. !warning Following a null pointer at either level Check pp before pp , and pp before pp . Knowledge check quiz ? int x{ 5 }; int p{ &x }; int pp{ &p }; What is the type of pp ? - int + int - int One removes one level: pp is p , an int . ? Why does a function need an Enemy parameter to change which enemy the caller's Enemy points at? + It needs the address of the caller's pointer in order to write a new value into it - Pointers cannot be passed to functions - Enemy parameters are read-only Arguments are copies. To change the caller's variable, a function needs its address, and here the variable is itself a pointer. ? In int main(int argc, char argv) , what is argv 2 0 ? + The first character of the third command-line argument - The third character of the first argument - The number of arguments argv 2 is the third pointer in the array; 0 takes the first character it points at.

title: Aim at the largest
body: Write aimAtLargest(values, count, target) . It makes the caller's pointer, whose address is target , point at the largest of the count ints starting at values . If several are equally large, aim at the first of them. If count is 0, set the caller's pointer to nullptr . The function returns nothing: its only result is the change to the caller's pointer. cpp int scores { 4, 9, 2, 9 }; int best{ nullptr }; aimAtLargest(scores, 4, &best); // best now points at scores 1

title: 3.02  Following Pointers Through Objects
body: Real programs are webs of objects joined by pointers: a world holds a player, a player holds an inventory, an inventory holds items. Getting from one object to another means following a chain of pointers, each step a read of an address and an offset. This lesson shows what that looks like in memory, how to follow it safely, and what it costs. A small web of objects cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector struct Item { std::string name; float weight; }; struct Inventory { std::vector<Item slots; // pointers to items stored elsewhere float maxWeight{ 30.0f }; }; struct Player { int health{ 100 }; Inventory inventory{ nullptr }; }; struct World { Player player{ nullptr }; }; int main() { Item sword{ "sword", 6.5f }; Item rope{ "rope", 2.0f }; Inventory bag{ { &sword, &rope } }; Player hero{ 100, &bag }; World world{ &hero }; // world - player - inventory - slots 0 - name std::cout << world.player- inventory- slots 0 - name << '\n'; return 0; } sword That one line follows four arrows. Each - means "read the pointer stored here, go to that address, then move to a member at a fixed offset". In memory it looks like this: (The offsets here are those of a Release build, where std::vector is 24 bytes and std::string 32.) What the CPU actually does Following one link is two simple steps: load 8 bytes from (object address + member offset), and use the result as the next address. Written as the arithmetic a debugger or a memory tool would do: player = read8(address of world + 0) inventory = read8(player + 8) slotArray = read8(inventory + 0) the vector's data pointer item = read8(slotArray + 0 8) name = item + 0 This is exactly what the debugger's Watch window does when you expand world.player- inventory , and it is the skill chapter 9 uses to rebuild an unknown program's data structures: find an object, see that offset 8 holds a pointer, follow it, and work out what kind of object is there. Every arrow can be null Each link in the chain can be missing: the player might not have an inventory yet, a slot might be empty. Following a null pointer is undefined behaviour, and on Windows it crashes with an access violation reading location 0x0000000000000008 or similar. The small number in that message is a clue: it is the offset of the member being read from a null object. So code that walks a chain checks each step, or guarantees in its design that the link cannot be null: cpp float carriedWeight(const World& world) { if (!world.player !world.player- inventory) return 0.0f; float total{ 0.0f }; for (const Item item : world.player- inventory- slots) if (item) total += item- weight; return total; } Two habits help: - Prefer references or values where a link is always present. If every player always has an inventory, make it a member Inventory inventory; rather than a pointer. Then there is nothing to check and one fewer arrow to follow. - Use a pointer when the link is genuinely optional, and check it. std::optional and nullptr checks say so in the code. The cost of chasing pointers Each arrow is a memory read whose address depends on the previous read. The processor cannot start fetching the item until it knows the item's address, which it only learns after fetching the inventory, and so on. If the objects are scattered around the heap, each step is likely to miss the cache and wait for main memory. This chain of dependent loads is called pointer chasing , and it is one of the main reasons data-heavy code is slow. Game engines therefore prefer: - objects stored by value inside the objects that own them, so they sit in the same cache lines; - arrays of objects rather than arrays of pointers to objects, so a loop walks memory in order (lesson 2.07); - indices or handles into such arrays instead of raw pointers (lesson 3.10). std::vector<Item above is the slow shape; std::vector<Item is the fast one, when the items do not need to be shared. Common mistakes !warning Long unchecked chains a- b- c- d- value crashes if any link is null, and the crash message only tells you the final offset. Check optional links, or restructure so they are not optional. !warning Storing pointers to elements of a vector The vector may move its elements (lesson 2.04). Store indices instead. !warning Assuming the debugger's offsets match your release build Debug builds of standard containers are bigger. Offsets you work out in one configuration can differ in the other. Knowledge check quiz ? A crash says "access violation reading location 0x0000000000000010". What is the most likely cause? + Code read a member at offset 16 of an object through a null pointer - The program ran out of memory - A function returned 16 Null plus a member offset gives a tiny address like 0x10. Look for an unchecked pointer whose member at offset 16 was being read. ? Why is following a long chain of pointers through scattered heap objects slow? - Pointers are slower to read than integers + Each read needs the previous one's result as its address, and each may miss the cache - The compiler cannot optimise - Dependent loads cannot overlap, so every cache miss along the chain is paid in full. ? When should a member be a pointer rather than a value? + When the link is genuinely optional or the object is shared or owned elsewhere - Always, because pointers are smaller - Never If an object always has exactly one of something, a value member is simpler, safer and faster.

title: Weigh the backpack safely
body: Write carriedWeight(world) . It follows the chain world.player , then inventory , then every item pointer in slots , and returns the total weight of the items. Any link may be missing: a null player, a null inventory or a null slot. A missing player or inventory means the weight is 0; a null slot is simply skipped. The function must never follow a null pointer.

title: 3.03  References Under the Hood
body:
A reference looks like a second name for an object, and in the language that is exactly what it is. In the machine, a reference that has to be stored or passed is an address, the same as a pointer. This lesson shows both views, the rules that make references safer than pointers, and the ways they can still dangle. Two views of the same thing In C++, a reference is an alias: another name for an existing object. cpp include <iostream void heal(int& health, int amount) { health += amount; // changes the caller's variable } int main() { int hp{ 40 }; int& alias{ hp }; // alias is another name for hp alias -= 10; heal(hp, 25); std::cout << hp << '
'; std::cout << (&alias == &hp) << '
'; // same object, same address return 0; } 55 1 Now look at what the compiler generates. These two functions compile to identical machine code: cpp void healRef(int& health, int amount) { health += amount; } void healPtr(int health, int amount) { health += amount; } asm healRef PROC ; healPtr is exactly the same add DWORD PTR rcx , edx ; add amount (edx) to the int at the address in rcx ret 0 healRef ENDP The caller passes the address of hp in rcx in both cases. At the machine level, a reference parameter is a pointer . The difference is entirely in the rules the compiler enforces at the source level. The rules that make references safer Pointer Reference --- --- --- Can be null Yes No: must be bound to an object when created Can be changed to refer to something else Yes No: bound once, for life Needs or - to reach the object Yes No: used like the object itself Can do arithmetic Yes No Can be stored in containers Yes No (use std::reference_wrapper ) Each rule removes a way to go wrong. A function taking Player& never needs to check for null, and its body reads like normal code. That is why modern C++ uses references for "must be there" parameters and pointers only where "might be absent" or "can be re-aimed" is part of the meaning. cpp void applyDamage(Player& target, int amount); // there is always a target Enemy findNearest(const Vec2& from); // there might be none: nullptr const references: reading without copying Passing a large object by value copies it. Passing it by const reference passes 8 bytes (an address) and promises not to change it: cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector struct Level { std::string name; std::vector<int tiles; }; int countWalls(const Level& level) // no copy of a possibly huge vector { int walls{ 0 }; for (int t : level.tiles) if (t == 1) ++walls; return walls; } int main() { Level cave{ "cave", { 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0 } }; std::cout << countWalls(cave) << '
'; return 0; } 3 The rule of thumb: pass small, cheap-to-copy types ( int , float , a small Vec2 ) by value, and everything else by const& , unless the function needs its own copy. A const& can also bind to a temporary, which it then keeps alive (lesson 2.04). That is why countWalls(Level{ "tmp", { 1 } }) works. When a reference takes no space at all When a reference is a local alias inside one function, the compiler usually does not store it anywhere. int& alias{ hp }; just tells the compiler that alias means hp , and it generates code using hp 's location directly. Only references that must cross a boundary (parameters, return values, members) become stored addresses. A reference member makes the object hold an 8-byte address: cpp include <iostream struct Camera { const float& targetX; // follows something else's x position float offset; }; int main() { float playerX{ 10.0f }; Camera cam{ playerX, -2.0f }; playerX = 15.0f; std::cout << cam.targetX + cam.offset << '
'; std::cout << sizeof(Camera) << '
'; return 0; } 13 16 Sixteen bytes: an 8-byte address, a 4-byte float, 4 bytes of padding. Reference members also make the class impossible to assign (a reference cannot be re-bound), which is usually more trouble than it is worth. Prefer a pointer member for "refers to something owned elsewhere". References can dangle too A reference is an address with no null check needed, but it is still an address, and the object can die before the reference does: cpp const std::string& badName() { std::string name{ "Ghost" }; return name; // the local dies; the caller gets a dangling reference } MSVC warns about this one (C4172). It cannot warn about the subtler cases: a reference into a std::vector that later grows, or a reference member to an object destroyed first. The rules from lesson 2.04 apply to references exactly as they do to pointers. Common mistakes !warning Returning a reference to a local Return by value. Copies of return values are usually optimised away completely. !warning Thinking references are free in every case Passing an int by const int& passes an address and makes the function read through it. For small types, pass by value. !warning Reference members in classes that need to be copied or assigned Use a pointer, or std::reference_wrapper , instead. Knowledge check quiz ? What does void f(int& x) receive in its first register when called? + The address of the caller's int - A copy of the int 's value - Nothing: references are compile-time only A reference parameter is passed exactly like a pointer. ? Which of these can a pointer do that a reference cannot? - Refer to an object on the heap + Be made to refer to a different object after it is created - Be passed to a function A reference is bound once, when it is created, and always refers to that object. ? Which is the best parameter type for a function that reads a large Level without changing it? - Level - Level + const Level& No copy, no null check, and the const documents that the function only reads it.

title: Clamp and swap in place
body: Write two small functions that change their caller's variables through references. - clampInPlace(value, low, high) changes value so it is no less than low and no more than high . Assume low <= high . - orderPair(a, b) swaps a and b if needed so that afterwards a <= b . Neither returns anything. Do not use pointers.

title: 3.04  Function Pointers and Callbacks
body:
Functions live in memory too, so they have addresses, and a variable can hold one. A function pointer lets code decide at run time which function to call: the basis of callbacks, command tables, state machines and plugin systems. This lesson covers raw function pointers, std::function and lambdas, and what each costs. A function has an address Lesson 1.04 showed that a function is a run of machine-code bytes in the .text section. Calling it means jumping to its first byte. That address can be stored in a variable, passed around and called later. cpp include <iostream int doubleIt(int x) { return x 2; } int squareIt(int x) { return x x; } int main() { int ( op)(int){ &doubleIt }; // op is a pointer to a function taking int and returning int std::cout << op(7) << '
'; op = &squareIt; // aim it at a different function std::cout << op(7) << '
'; std::cout << "doubleIt lives at " << reinterpret_cast<void (&doubleIt) << '
'; return 0; } varies 14 49 doubleIt lives at 00007FF6E1A21082 The declaration syntax is awkward. Read int ( op)(int) as " op is a pointer to a function that takes an int and returns an int ". A type alias makes it readable: cpp using UnaryOp = int ( )(int); UnaryOp op{ &doubleIt }; In assembly, a normal call is call doubleIt , with the address fixed when the program is linked. A call through a pointer is call rax (or call qword ptr ... ): the address is read from a register or memory at run time. That small difference is what makes everything in this lesson possible. Callbacks: letting the caller decide A callback is a function you pass to other code for it to call. The standard library's algorithms are built on them, and so are event systems. cpp include <iostream include <vector struct Enemy { const char name; int health; bool flying; }; // Calls visit for every enemy that matches. void forEachEnemy(const std::vector<Enemy & enemies, bool ( matches)(const Enemy&), void ( visit)(const Enemy&)) { for (const Enemy& e : enemies) if (matches(e)) visit(e); } bool isFlying(const Enemy& e) { return e.flying; } void printName(const Enemy& e) { std::cout << e.name << '
'; } int main() { std::vector<Enemy enemies{ { "bat", 8, true }, { "rat", 5, false }, { "wasp", 3, true } }; forEachEnemy(enemies, &isFlying, &printName); return 0; } bat wasp forEachEnemy knows nothing about flying or printing. The caller supplies both decisions. Command tables A table of function pointers maps names or numbers to actions. Debug consoles, input bindings, network message handlers and bytecode interpreters all work this way. cpp include <iostream include <map include <string include <utility include <vector struct Game { int gold{ 0 }; int health{ 100 }; }; void giveGold(Game& g, int n) { g.gold += n; } void heal(Game& g, int n) { g.health += n; } void hurt(Game& g, int n) { g.health -= n; } int main() { using Command = void ( )(Game&, int); const std::map<std::string, Command commands{ { "gold", &giveGold }, { "heal", &heal }, { "hurt", &hurt } }; Game game; const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int typed{ { "gold", 50 }, { "hurt", 30 }, { "heal", 5 } }; for (const auto& name, amount : typed) { const auto found{ commands.find(name) }; if (found != commands.end()) found- second(game, amount); } std::cout << "gold " << game.gold << ", health " << game.health << '
'; return 0; } gold 50, health 75 Adding a command means adding one line to the table. Chapter 11 builds the game's debug console exactly like this, and chapter 13 uses the same idea for plugins: a plugin is, at heart, a table of function pointers the game calls. Lambdas and std::function Raw function pointers can only point at plain functions. They cannot carry extra data, such as "only enemies within 10 metres of this position". C++ has two tools for that. A lambda is an unnamed function written in place. A lambda that captures nothing converts to a plain function pointer. One that captures variables is an object holding copies of (or references to) them, with an operator() . std::function<Signature holds any callable: a function pointer, a lambda with captures, or an object with operator() . cpp include <functional include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<std::function<void() onLevelEnd; int score{ 0 }; onLevelEnd.push_back( { std::cout << "save the game
"; }); onLevelEnd.push_back( &score { score += 100; std::cout << "bonus, score now " << score << '
'; }); for (const auto& callback : onLevelEnd) callback(); return 0; } save the game bonus, score now 100 Tool Can carry data Cost of a call Typical use --- --- --- --- Function pointer No One indirect call C APIs, Windows callbacks, plugin tables Template parameter taking a lambda Yes Often none: the compiler can inline it std::sort , algorithms std::function Yes An indirect call, and possibly a heap allocation when created Stored callbacks, event lists The Windows API uses plain function pointers for its callbacks, because it is a C interface. A window's message handler (chapter 5) is a function pointer you give to Windows, and Windows calls it for every message. Common mistakes !warning Capturing by reference in a callback that outlives the scope &score stores a reference to score . If the callback runs after the function holding score has returned, it writes into a dead frame (lesson 2.04). Capture by value, or make sure the data outlives the callback. !warning Calling a null function pointer It jumps to address 0 and crashes. Check optional callbacks before calling them. !warning Using std::function in the hottest loops Each call is indirect and cannot be inlined. For per-element work in a tight loop, pass the lambda as a template parameter instead. Knowledge check quiz ? What does int ( f)(float) declare? + A pointer to a function that takes a float and returns an int - A function that returns a pointer to an int - An array of floats Read from the name outwards: f is a pointer ( f ) to a function taking (float) returning int . ? Which kind of lambda can be converted to a plain function pointer? + One that captures nothing - One that captures by value - Any lambda A captureless lambda has no data to carry, so it is just a function. Capturing lambdas are objects. ? Why do Windows API callbacks use plain function pointers instead of std::function ? - std::function is slower to call + The Windows API is a C interface, and C only has plain function pointers - Function pointers can carry captured data C++ types like std::function cannot cross a C boundary.

title: A debug console's command table
body: Build the core of a debug console. A Console holds a table that maps command names to functions. Each command function receives the Game and one whole-number argument. - addCommand(name, fn) registers a command. Registering a name again replaces the old function. - run(line) takes a line such as "gold 50" : a name, one space, and a number. It calls the matching command and returns true . If there is no such command, or the line is not a name followed by a number, it changes nothing and returns false . Commands are plain function pointers of type void ( )(Game&, int) . cpp Console console; console.addCommand("gold", &giveGold); console.run("gold 50"); // true, gold is now 50 console.run("fly 1"); // false, nothing happens

title: 3.05  Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
match: 3.05 Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
body:
A virtual call picks the function to run from the object's real type, at run time. Compilers do it with a vtable : a table of function pointers, one per class, and a hidden vptr in every object pointing at its class's table. This lesson shows the layout, walks through a virtual call step by step, and explains what it costs. The problem virtual functions solve cpp include <iostream include <memory include <vector struct Entity { virtual ~Entity() = default; virtual void update() { std::cout << "entity idles
"; } virtual int damage() const { return 0; } }; struct Goblin : Entity { void update() override { std::cout << "goblin sneaks
"; } int damage() const override { return 4; } }; struct Dragon : Entity { void update() override { std::cout << "dragon breathes fire
"; } int damage() const override { return 40; } }; int main() { std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entity world; world.push_back(std::make_unique<Goblin ()); world.push_back(std::make_unique<Dragon ()); world.push_back(std::make_unique<Entity ()); int total{ 0 }; for (const auto& e : world) { e- update(); // which update? decided by the object, at run time total += e- damage(); } std::cout << "total damage " << total << '
'; return 0; } goblin sneaks dragon breathes fire entity idles total damage 44 The loop only knows it has an Entity . The compiler cannot know, when it compiles e- update() , which function to call: that depends on the object at run time. So it cannot emit call Goblin::update . It needs a way to look the function up. One table per class, one pointer per object For every class with virtual functions, the compiler builds a vtable : an array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function, stored in the read-only .rdata section. Every object of that class gets a hidden first member, the vptr , holding the address of its class's vtable. The constructor sets it. Every Goblin shares the one Goblin vtable. Slots are in the order the virtual functions were first declared in the base class, so update is in the same slot in every class's table. That is the key: the caller knows the slot number at compile time, even though it does not know the class. A virtual call, step by step e- update() compiles to roughly this (MSVC x64, with e in rcx ): asm mov rax, QWORD PTR rcx ; 1. read the vptr from offset 0 of the object call QWORD PTR rax+8 ; 2. read slot 1 of the vtable, and call that address 1. Load the vptr from the object. 2. Load the function pointer from the vtable at slot × 8 . Here slot 1, offset 8, because slot 0 holds the destructor. 3. Call it, with the object's address still in rcx as this . Two memory reads and an indirect call. That is all "dynamic dispatch" is. Seeing the vptr The vptr is ordinary memory. Implementation details like this should never be relied on in real code, but looking at them once makes the idea concrete: cpp include <cstdint include <cstring include <iostream struct Entity { virtual ~Entity() = default; virtual int damage() const { return 0; } }; struct Goblin : Entity { int damage() const override { return 4; } }; struct Dragon : Entity { int damage() const override { return 40; } }; std::uintptr_t vptrOf(const void object) { std::uintptr_t vptr{}; std::memcpy(&vptr, object, sizeof vptr); // the first 8 bytes of the object return vptr; } int main() { Goblin a, b; Dragon c; std::cout << "two goblins share a vtable: " << (vptrOf(&a) == vptrOf(&b)) << '
'; std::cout << "a dragon has a different one: " << (vptrOf(&a) != vptrOf(&c)) << '
'; std::cout << "sizeof(Goblin) = " << sizeof(Goblin) << '
'; return 0; } two goblins share a vtable: 1 a dragon has a different one: 1 sizeof(Goblin) = 8 Goblin has no data members, yet it is 8 bytes: just the vptr. In the Visual Studio debugger, expanding an object shows the vptr as __vfptr , and expanding that lists the vtable's entries with their function names. This is also why the first 8 bytes of many objects in a memory view look like an address inside the program's image: they are vptrs into .rdata . Chapter 9 uses vtables to discover the classes in a compiled program, because each vtable is a list of a class's virtual functions. Construction and destruction The vptr changes while an object is being built. During the Entity part of constructing a Goblin , the vptr points at Entity 's vtable; only when the Goblin constructor body runs does it point at Goblin 's. So a virtual call inside a constructor or destructor calls the version for the class currently being built , not the most derived one. This surprises people once, and then they remember it. It is also why a base class used through pointers needs a virtual destructor . delete e on an Entity calls the destructor through the vtable; without virtual , only ~Entity runs and the Dragon part is never destroyed. The cost Cost Size --- --- Memory 8 bytes per object for the vptr, one small table per class Each call Two dependent loads and an indirect call Optimisation The compiler usually cannot inline a virtual call For a few hundred calls per frame, none of this matters. For millions (every particle, every tile), it can. Engines often avoid virtual calls in the hottest loops by keeping objects of one type together in arrays and processing each array with ordinary calls. Chapter 10's entity-component designs are partly a response to this. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting the virtual destructor Deleting a derived object through a base pointer without one is undefined behaviour and usually leaks the derived part. !warning Calling virtual functions from constructors They do not dispatch to the derived class yet. Move such work to a separate init step if needed. !warning Misspelling an override Without override , a typo in the name or a missing const silently creates a new function instead of overriding. Always write override . !warning Copying objects with vptrs as raw bytes Saving them to a file or memcpy -ing into unrelated memory copies an address that means nothing elsewhere. Knowledge check quiz ? Where is the vptr stored? + In each object, normally at offset 0 - In each class's vtable - In a global list of objects Every object of a class with virtual functions carries its own vptr, set by its constructor. ? Two Goblin objects exist. How many Goblin vtables are there? + One, shared by both - Two, one per object - None until a virtual function is called The vtable belongs to the class and lives in .rdata . Objects only hold pointers to it. ? What does call QWORD PTR rax+8 do in a virtual call? - Calls the function at address 8 + Reads the function pointer in slot 1 of the vtable that rax points at, and calls it - Jumps forward 8 bytes rax holds the vptr; rax+8 is the second 8-byte entry of the table. ? A virtual function is called from inside the base class's constructor while a Dragon is being built. Which version runs? + The base class's version - Dragon 's version - Neither: it is a compile error During the base constructor the vptr still points at the base class's vtable.
