A circle uses a as its radius (use 3.14159265358979 for pi); a rectangle uses a and b as width and height. - circleName , rectName : return "circle" and "rectangle" . - the two tables kCircleTable and kRectTable , filled with the right functions; - makeCircle(r) and makeRect(w, h) , which return a Shape aimed at the right table; - totalArea(shapes) , which adds up the areas by calling through each shape's table .

title: 3.06  Linked Lists from Scratch
body: A linked list stores each element in its own node, and each node points to the next. Inserting and removing anywhere is cheap, but finding anything means following pointers one at a time. Building one by hand is the best practice there is for pointers, and it explains why games use them rarely and carefully. Nodes and links An array keeps its elements side by side. A linked list scatters them: each element sits in a separately allocated node , together with a pointer to the next node. The list itself only remembers the first node, the head . cpp struct Node { int value; Node next; // nullptr in the last node }; Walking the list means following next until it is null: cpp include <iostream struct Node { int value; Node next; }; int main() { Node c{ 9, nullptr }; Node b{ 3, &c }; Node a{ 7, &b }; Node head{ &a }; for (Node n{ head }; n != nullptr; n = n- next) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } 7 3 9 Inserting Adding at the front takes a constant amount of work, however long the list is: make a node, point it at the old head, make it the new head. cpp void pushFront(Node & head, int value) { head = new Node{ value, head }; } Inserting after a node you already have is just as cheap: two pointer writes, no elements moved. Compare an array, where inserting at the front means shifting every element along by one. Removing, and the pointer-to-pointer trick Removing a node means making whatever pointed at it point at its successor instead. The first node is pointed at by head ; every other node is pointed at by the previous node's next . Treating those two cases separately is clumsy: cpp // Clumsy: a special case for the head. void removeFirstClumsy(Node & head, int value) { if (head && head- value == value) { Node dead{ head }; head = head- next; delete dead; return; } for (Node n{ head }; n && n- next; n = n- next) if (n- next- value == value) { Node dead{ n- next }; n- next = dead- next; delete dead; return; } } The neat way is to walk with a pointer to the link itself, a Node (lesson 3.01). It starts at &head and moves to &node- next . Whichever link it holds, removing the node it points at is the same one line: cpp void removeFirst(Node & head, int value) { for (Node link{ &head }; link != nullptr; link = &( link)- next) { if (( link)- value == value) { Node dead{ link }; link = dead- next; // whoever pointed at dead now skips it delete dead; return; } } } This is one of the few places where makes code shorter and clearer, and it is a classic interview question. The practice task asks you to write it. The cost: walking is slow Operation Array / std::vector Linked list --- --- --- Get element number i One calculation Follow i pointers Insert or remove at the front Move every element Two pointer writes Insert or remove in the middle, given its position Move the elements after it Two pointer writes Loop over everything Walks memory in order Jumps around the heap: one cache miss per node, likely Extra memory None One pointer (8 bytes) per element, plus allocator overhead That last-but-one row usually decides it. Looping over a std::vector<int of a million elements reads contiguous memory the processor can stream in. Looping over a list of a million nodes follows a million dependent pointers into scattered heap blocks (lesson 3.02's pointer chasing). In practice the vector is often ten times faster or more, even for workloads with many inserts, because shifting contiguous memory is so cheap. So the standard advice is: default to std::vector . Use a list only when you have measured a reason. Where lists do appear in games - Intrusive lists : the next pointer lives inside an object that already exists for another reason, such as all the enemies in one grid cell of a spatial partition. No extra allocations, and an object can unlink itself in constant time. - Free lists in pools (lesson 3.10): unused slots point to the next unused slot, so allocating is "take the head". - Engines' own systems , such as lists of timers or render commands, often allocated from an arena so the nodes are close together anyway. The standard library has std::list (doubly linked) and std::forward_list (singly linked) if you need one. Common mistakes !warning Using a node after deleting it In n = n- next after delete n , the read is from freed memory. Save next first. !warning Losing the rest of the list Overwriting head before saving the old head leaks every node. Draw the arrows before writing the code. !warning Forgetting to free the nodes A list built with new needs a loop that deletes every node, or nodes owned by std::unique_ptr . Knowledge check quiz ? What is the cost of reading the 1000th element of a linked list? - One memory read + Following 999 next pointers from the head - Sorting the list first There is no index arithmetic: the only way to a node is through the ones before it. ? In removeFirst , why does link have type Node ? + It points at the link (either head or some node's next ) that may need to change - Because nodes are stored in a two-dimensional array - To make the function faster Changing a pointer requires its address. link = dead- next updates whichever pointer pointed at the dead node. ? Why is a std::vector usually faster to loop over than a linked list with the same elements? + Its elements are contiguous, so the processor reads them in order from cache; list nodes are scattered and each step depends on the last - Vectors use less memory per element because they compress values - Linked lists must be sorted Contiguous memory is streamed efficiently; pointer chasing waits on memory at every step.

title: A singly linked list

A list is represented by its head pointer, which is nullptr for an empty list. - pushFront(head, value) adds a node at the front. - size(head) counts the nodes. - removeAll(head, value) removes and deletes every node holding value , and returns how many it removed. - clear(head) deletes every node and sets head to nullptr . Use the pointer-to-pointer technique from the lesson for removeAll , so the head needs no special case. The tests check that nothing leaks.

title: 3.07  How std::vector Really Works
body:
std::vector is three pointers and a heap block. Its size is how many elements are in use, its capacity how many fit before it must grow. When it grows, it allocates a bigger block, moves everything across and frees the old one, which is why pointers into a vector can suddenly dangle. Knowing this lets you use the most important container in C++ efficiently. Three pointers A std::vector<T object is 24 bytes in a Release build, three pointers: std::vector<int (Release x64) heap block ┌───────────────┐ ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ │ first ────────┼──────────────────────▶│ 10 │ 20 │ 30 │ 40 │ ?? │ ?? │ │ last ────────┼───────┐ └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ │ end ────────┼───┐ │ ▲ ▲ └───────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ size() = last − first = 4 (last points just past the 40) capacity() = end − first = 6 (end points just past the block) - first points at element 0 ( data() returns it), - last points just past the last element in use, - end points just past the end of the block. size() and capacity() are subtractions. The elements in use are exactly an array, which is why everything from lesson 2.07 applies: indexing is one calculation, and looping walks memory in order. Growing When push_back finds size() == capacity() , there is no room. The vector then: 1. allocates a new, bigger block; 2. moves (or copies) every element into it; 3. destroys the old elements and frees the old block; 4. adds the new element. That is expensive, so the new block is not just one bigger. Microsoft's implementation grows by half again each time (a factor of 1.5); others use 2. Because the growth is a fixed factor, the total work averages out to a constant amount per push_back , but individual pushes are occasionally very slow. cpp include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int v; std::size_t lastCapacity{ v.capacity() }; std::cout << "capacity " << lastCapacity; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 100; ++i) { v.push_back(i); if (v.capacity() != lastCapacity) { lastCapacity = v.capacity(); std::cout << ' ' << lastCapacity; } } std::cout << '
'; return 0; } capacity 0 1 2 3 4 6 9 13 19 28 42 63 94 141 Thirteen reallocations to reach 100 elements, each copying everything so far. If you know roughly how many elements are coming, say so up front: cpp std::vector<Bullet bullets; bullets.reserve(512); // one allocation; no regrowth until 512 reserve changes capacity, not size: the vector is still empty, but the room is there. resize(n) changes size, creating or destroying elements. Growth invalidates pointers Step 3 above frees the old block. Every pointer, reference and iterator to an element pointed into that block, and now dangles: cpp-norun include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int v{ 1, 2, 3 }; int first{ &v 0 }; v.push_back(4); // capacity was 3: reallocates std::cout << first << '
'; // reads freed memory return 0; } The rules, briefly: Operation What it invalidates --- --- push_back , emplace_back , insert Everything, if it reallocates; otherwise elements at or after the insertion point reserve (to a bigger capacity) Everything erase Elements at or after the erased position pop_back Only the removed element Reading, writing existing elements Nothing The robust habit in game code is to refer to vector elements by index , not by pointer. An index stays meaningful when the block moves. Lesson 3.10 builds on this. Inserting and erasing in the middle The elements are contiguous, so inserting or erasing anywhere except the end has to shift every later element by one place. Erasing the first of a million elements moves 999,999 of them. When order does not matter, which in games it often does not, use swap and pop : move the last element into the hole and shrink by one. cpp include <iostream include <vector void removeAtUnordered(std::vector<int & v, std::size_t i) { v i = std::move(v.back()); // the last element fills the hole v.pop_back(); // and the end shrinks by one } int main() { std::vector<int enemies{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 }; removeAtUnordered(enemies, 1); for (int e : enemies) std::cout << e << ' '; std::cout << '
'; return 0; } 10 50 30 40 Constant time, however big the vector. And to remove every element that matches a condition, std::erase_if(v, predicate) (C++20) does it in one pass, moving each kept element at most once. emplace_back versus push_back push_back(obj) copies or moves an existing object into the vector. emplace_back(args...) constructs the element directly in the vector's memory from constructor arguments, skipping the temporary. For simple types the difference is nothing; for objects that are expensive to move, emplace_back can save work. A vector of objects or of pointers? std::vector<Enemy std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy --- --- Enemies stored side by side: fast to loop over Pointers side by side; enemies scattered on the heap Growing moves the enemies themselves Growing moves only the pointers; the enemies stay put Pointers to enemies dangle after growth Pointers to enemies stay valid All elements must be the same type Can hold derived classes (polymorphism) Games favour the left column for anything numerous and processed every frame, and use indices to refer to elements. Common mistakes !warning Keeping &v i or an iterator across a push_back Store the index instead, or re-take the pointer after the change. !warning Erasing inside a range-based for loop The loop's hidden iterators are invalidated. Use std::erase_if , or an index loop that does not advance when it erases. !warning Calling reserve inside a loop v.reserve(v.size() + 1) before each push defeats the growth factor and reallocates every time. Reserve once, before the loop. !warning Confusing reserve with resize After reserve(10) , v 0 is still out of range: the size is 0. Knowledge check quiz ? A vector has size 6 and capacity 6. What happens on push_back ? + A bigger block is allocated, the 6 elements are moved into it, the old block is freed, and the new element is added - The block is extended in place by one element - The program throws an exception A heap block cannot grow in place, so the vector moves to a new, larger one. ? Why does a vector grow by a factor (such as 1.5×) instead of by one element at a time? - To waste less memory + So that the total cost of many push_backs averages out to a constant per element - Because the heap only allocates in powers of two Growing by one would copy everything on every push: the cost would grow with the square of the size. ? What does v.reserve(100) do to an empty vector's size? + Nothing: the size stays 0, only the capacity changes - Sets it to 100 - Sets it to 100 default-constructed elements reserve makes room; resize changes the number of elements. ? What is the cost of swap-and-pop removal? + Constant, whatever the size of the vector - Proportional to the number of elements after the removed one - Proportional to the size of the vector One move and one pop_back . The order of the elements changes, which is the price.

title: 3.08  Hash Tables
body:
A hash table finds a value by its key in about the same time however many entries it holds. A hash function turns the key into a number that picks a bucket , and the table only has to look in that one place. This lesson explains hashing, collisions and load factor, compares std::unordered_map with std::map , and shows where games use them. The problem A game has 5,000 item definitions and looks them up by name: "iron_sword", "health_potion". Searching a vector of them means comparing names one by one, up to 5,000 comparisons per lookup. A sorted vector with binary search needs about 13. A hash table usually needs one or two. The idea: compute where it goes A hash function turns a key into a number, its hash . The table keeps an array of buckets and stores each entry in bucket number hash % bucketCount . To find a key, compute its hash, go straight to that bucket, and look only there. A good hash function has two properties: - Deterministic : the same key always gives the same hash. - Well spread : similar keys give very different hashes, so entries scatter evenly over the buckets. Here is a simple, widely used string hash, FNV-1a . It mixes each byte in with an XOR, then multiplies by a carefully chosen prime to spread the bits: cpp include <cstdint include <format include <iostream include <string_view std::uint32_t fnv1a(std::string_view text) { std::uint32_t hash{ 2166136261u }; // the FNV "offset basis" for (unsigned char c : text) { hash ^= c; hash = 16777619u; // the FNV prime } return hash; } int main() { for (const char key : { "iron_sword", "iron_swore", "health_potion", "" }) std::cout << std::format("{: 14} - 0x{:08X} bucket {}
", key, fnv1a(key), fnv1a(key) % 8); return 0; } iron_sword - 0xAB515E15 bucket 5 iron_swore - 0xAA515C82 bucket 2 health_potion - 0xA92D125F bucket 7 - 0x811C9DC5 bucket 5 A change in the last letter moves the key to a different bucket. Notice, though, that iron_sword and iron_swore share some hex digits: FNV-1a is simple and fast, and the last byte it sees is only mixed in lightly. Hash tables that need better spreading run a short final "mixing" step over the result, like the hash function in this lesson's practice task. Games often hash asset names once, at build time, and refer to assets by the 32-bit hash at run time: comparing two numbers is much cheaper than comparing two strings. Collisions Different keys can land in the same bucket: there are endlessly many possible keys and only so many buckets. This is a collision , and every hash table has a strategy for it. Strategy How it works Used by --- --- --- Separate chaining Each bucket holds a small linked list of the entries that landed there std::unordered_map Open addressing Entries live directly in the bucket array; on a collision, try the next bucket (or another probe sequence) until a free one is found Many fast game-engine and third-party hash maps A lookup computes the hash, goes to the bucket, then compares keys until it finds a match. With a good hash and enough buckets, that is one or two comparisons. Load factor and rehashing The load factor is entries divided by buckets. As it rises, collisions become common and lookups slow down. So when the load factor passes a limit (1.0 for std::unordered_map by default), the table rehashes : it allocates more buckets and reinserts every entry, because hash % bucketCount changes when bucketCount does. Like vector growth, this is expensive once and cheap on average, and reserve(n) avoids it if you know the size in advance. std::unordered_map and std::map cpp include <iostream include <map include <string include <unordered_map int main() { std::unordered_map<std::string, int prices{ { "rope", 5 }, { "lantern", 12 }, { "sword", 40 } }; prices "shield" = 30; // insert if (auto it{ prices.find("lantern") }; it != prices.end()) std::cout << "lantern costs " << it- second << '
'; std::cout << "contains torch: " << prices.contains("torch") << '
'; std::map<std::string, int sorted{ prices.begin(), prices.end() }; for (const auto& name, price : sorted) std::cout << name << ' '; // always in key order std::cout << '
'; return 0; } lantern costs 12 contains torch: 0 lantern rope shield sword std::unordered_map std::map --- --- --- Structure Hash table Balanced binary tree (lesson 3.09) Lookup About constant time on average Grows with the logarithm of the size Iteration order Unspecified, changes as it grows Sorted by key Key needs A hash and == < Pick unordered_map for fast lookup, map when you need the keys in order. Both allocate a node per entry, so neither is especially cache friendly; performance-sensitive engines often use open-addressing tables instead. Where games use hashing - Asset and string lookup by name or by precomputed hash. - Spatial hashing : hash a grid cell's (x, y) to find the objects near a point without a grid for the whole world. - Caches : remember the result of an expensive calculation keyed by its inputs. - Detecting change : hash a save file or a block of data and compare hashes. (Hashes for this need to be strong; FNV-1a is fine for spotting accidents, not for detecting deliberate tampering.) Common mistakes !warning Relying on unordered_map iteration order It can differ between runs, compilers and sizes. Sort the keys, or use std::map , when order matters, such as when writing a save file. !warning Using operator to check whether a key exists m key inserts a default value if the key is missing. Use find or contains . !warning Keeping pointers or iterators across a rehash Rehashing invalidates iterators (though unordered_map keeps pointers to elements valid, since each lives in its own node). Knowledge check quiz ? What does a hash table do with a key's hash? + Uses it to choose a bucket, so the lookup only searches that bucket - Stores the hash instead of the key - Sorts the entries by hash hash % bucketCount picks the bucket; only the entries there are compared. ? Two different keys land in the same bucket. What is that called? - A rehash + A collision - Undefined behaviour Collisions are normal; the table's strategy (chaining or probing) handles them. ? Why does a hash table rehash when its load factor gets high? + Too many entries per bucket means more collisions and slower lookups, so it adds buckets and redistributes the entries - To sort its entries - To free memory Keeping entries per bucket low keeps lookups near constant time. ? You need to print all items in alphabetical order. Which container fits best? - std::unordered_map<std::string, Item + std::map<std::string, Item - Either; they iterate the same way std::map keeps its keys sorted; unordered_map has no meaningful order.

title: A hash table with open addressing
match: A hash table with open addressing
body: Build IdTable , a hash table mapping std::uint32_t ids to int values, using open addressing with linear probing . The table has a fixed number of slots, given to the constructor. Each slot is either empty or holds one key and its value. - The home slot of a key is hash(key) % slotCount , where hash is the function given below. - insert(key, value) : start at the home slot and move one slot at a time (wrapping round to 0 after the last slot) until you find either the same key, whose value you then replace, or an empty slot, where you put the new entry. Return true . If every slot is full of other keys, return false . - find(key) : probe the same way. Return the value if you meet the key; return std::nullopt when you reach an empty slot or have looked at every slot. - size() : how many keys are stored. There is no removing in this task (removal in open addressing needs special "deleted" markers).

title: 3.09  Trees and Graphs
body: When data has branches rather than a single line, pointers or indices join it into trees and graphs . Games are full of them: the scene graph of objects attached to other objects, the binary search tree inside std::map , the graph of rooms in a dungeon, and the grid a monster searches to find the player. This lesson covers the shapes, the two ways to walk them, and a shortest-path search. Trees A tree is a set of nodes where each node has one parent (except the single root ) and any number of children . There are no loops. The most visible tree in a game is the scene graph : a sword is attached to a hand, the hand to an arm, the arm to a knight, the knight to a horse. Move the horse and everything attached moves with it. cpp include <iostream include <memory include <string include <vector struct SceneNode { std::string name; float x{ 0 }; // position relative to the parent std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SceneNode children; SceneNode add(std::string childName, float childX) { children.push_back(std::make_unique<SceneNode (SceneNode{ std::move(childName), childX, {} })); return children.back().get(); } }; // Depth-first: handle a node, then each child's whole subtree in turn. void printWorld(const SceneNode& node, float parentX, int depth) { const float worldX{ parentX + node.x }; std::cout << std::string(depth 2, ' ') << node.name << " at " << worldX << '\n'; for (const auto& child : node.children) printWorld( child, worldX, depth + 1); } int main() { SceneNode world{ "world", 0, {} }; SceneNode horse{ world.add("horse", 10) }; SceneNode knight{ horse- add("knight", 0.5f) }; knight- add("sword", 0.75f); world.add("tree", 3); printWorld(world, 0, 0); return 0; } world at 0 horse at 10 knight at 10.5 sword at 11.25 tree at 3 Each node owns its children through std::unique_ptr , so destroying a node destroys its whole subtree. Each position is relative to the parent, and the walk adds them up on the way down: that is how attaching works. Binary search trees A binary search tree gives each node at most two children with a rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, everything in the right is larger. Finding a key means comparing at each node and going left or right, so a balanced tree of a million entries needs about 20 comparisons. std::map and std::set are balanced binary search trees (red-black trees in the common implementations). That is why they keep keys in order and why lookups cost "about log n" comparisons, not constant time like a hash table (lesson 3.08). Graphs A graph drops the tree's rules: any node can connect to any other, and connections can form loops. The nodes are often called vertices and the connections edges . Game graph Vertices Edges --- --- --- Dungeon layout Rooms Doors Navigation mesh Walkable regions Shared borders Tile map Walkable tiles Steps to neighbouring tiles Dialogue Lines of dialogue Player choices Quest dependencies Quests "Must finish first" Graphs are usually stored as an adjacency list : for each vertex, a list of the vertices it connects to. A tile map is a graph that needs no stored edges at all, because a tile's neighbours can be calculated from its position. Two ways to walk Every tree and graph algorithm builds on one of two orders of visiting: Depth-first search (DFS) Breadth-first search (BFS) --- --- --- Order Go as deep as possible down one branch, then back up Visit everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away, ... Natural tool A stack (or recursion) A queue Good for Visiting everything, scene graphs, flood fills Shortest paths where every step costs the same On a graph with loops, both must remember which vertices they have already visited, or they go round forever. The flood fill in lesson 2.01 was a depth-first search on a tile map. Shortest path on a grid with BFS To find how many steps a monster needs to reach the player, run a breadth-first search from the monster. Because BFS visits tiles in order of distance, the first time it reaches a tile, it has found the shortest way there. cpp include <iostream include <queue include <string include <vector // Steps from (sx, sy) to (tx, ty) moving up, down, left or right through '.' tiles; -1 if unreachable. int shortestSteps(const std::vector<std::string & map, int sx, int sy, int tx, int ty) { const int h{ static_cast<int (map.size()) }, w{ static_cast<int (map 0 .size()) }; std::vector<int dist(static_cast<std::size_t (w h), -1); // -1 means not reached yet std::queue<std::pair<int, int frontier; dist static_cast<std::size_t (sy w + sx) = 0; frontier.push({ sx, sy }); const int dx { 1, -1, 0, 0 }, dy { 0, 0, 1, -1 }; while (!frontier.empty()) { const auto x, y = frontier.front(); frontier.pop(); if (x == tx && y == ty) return dist static_cast<std::size_t (y w + x) ; for (int d{ 0 }; d < 4; ++d) { const int nx{ x + dx d }, ny{ y + dy d }; if (nx < 0 ny < 0 nx = w ny = h map ny nx == ' ') continue; int& seen{ dist static_cast<std::size_t (ny w + nx) }; if (seen != -1) continue; seen = dist static_cast<std::size_t (y w + x) + 1; frontier.push({ nx, ny }); } } return -1; } int main() { const std::vector<std::string map{ " ", " M.. ... ", " . . . . ", " . ... P ", " ", }; std::cout << shortestSteps(map, 1, 1, 7, 3) << '\n'; return 0; } 12 The queue is the whole trick: tiles are taken out in the order they were discovered, so all tiles at distance 3 come out before any at distance 4. Storing which tile each one was reached from (a "came from" array) lets you walk back from the target to recover the actual path. When steps have different costs (mud is slower than road), BFS becomes Dijkstra's algorithm , and with a distance estimate to guide it, A\ , which most game pathfinding uses. Chapter 11's monsters use this. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting the visited set on a graph A search on a graph with loops never ends. Mark vertices when you first discover them. !warning Recursion on deep trees A very deep or degenerate tree (one long chain) can overflow the stack, as in lesson 2.01. Use an explicit stack for data that might be deep. !warning Marking visited when popping instead of when pushing In BFS, mark a tile when you add it to the queue. Otherwise the same tile can be queued many times. Knowledge check quiz ? What makes a tree different from a general graph? + Every node except the root has exactly one parent, and there are no loops - Trees cannot be stored with pointers - Trees always have exactly two children per node A binary tree has at most two children; a tree in general may have any number. ? Why does breadth-first search find the shortest path when every step costs the same? + It visits places in order of their distance from the start, so the first time it reaches the target is by a shortest route - It tries every possible path and keeps the shortest - It always moves towards the target The queue ensures all places at distance n are handled before any at distance n + 1. ? What data structure drives a breadth-first search? - A stack + A queue - A hash table First in, first out: places are explored in the order they were discovered. ? What kind of structure is std::map built on? - A hash table + A balanced binary search tree - A sorted vector That is why it keeps keys in order and looks them up in logarithmic time.

title: Find the path, not just its length
match: Find the path, not just its length
body: Write findPath(map, sx, sy, tx, ty) . It returns the tiles of a shortest path from (sx, sy) to (tx, ty) , including both ends , as (x, y) pairs in order from start to target. Moves are up, down, left and right; ' ' tiles are walls; every other character is walkable. If the target cannot be reached, return an empty vector. If the start is the target, return just that one tile. When several shortest paths exist, any of them is accepted: the tests check that your path is valid and as short as possible. Use a breadth-first search, recording for each tile the tile it was reached from.

title: 3.10  Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
match: 3.10 Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
body: A game creates and destroys objects constantly: bullets, particles, enemies, pickups. This lesson puts the chapter together into the structures engines use for them: dense arrays with swap-and-pop, object pools with free lists, and generational handles that let code refer to an object safely even after it has been destroyed and its slot reused. What games need A shooter might fire 50 bullets a second, each living for a second or two. A particle effect might spawn thousands of sparks. The container holding them must: 1. Loop fast , every frame, over everything alive. 2. Add and remove cheaply , many times per frame. 3. Let other code refer to an object (the missile's target, the player's selected unit) without that reference turning into a dangling pointer when the object dies. No single standard container does all three. These are the patterns engines combine. Pattern 1: a dense vector with swap-and-pop Keep live objects side by side in a std::vector , and remove with swap-and-pop (lesson 3.07): cpp include <iostream include <vector struct Bullet { float x; float speed; float life; }; void update(std::vector<Bullet & bullets, float dt) { for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i < bullets.size(); ) { Bullet& b{ bullets i }; b.x += b.speed dt; b.life -= dt; if (b.life <= 0) { bullets i = bullets.back(); // swap-and-pop: the last bullet takes this slot bullets.pop_back(); // don't advance i: the moved bullet needs updating too } else ++i; } } int main() { std::vector<Bullet bullets{ { 0, 10, 0.05f }, { 0, 20, 1 }, { 0, 30, 0.05f }, { 0, 40, 1 } }; update(bullets, 0.1f); for (const Bullet& b : bullets) std::cout << b.speed << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } 40 20 Fast to loop over, cheap to remove from. But it fails requirement 3: an object's position in the vector changes whenever another object is removed, so neither a pointer nor an index to it stays valid. Pattern 2: a pool with a free list A pool allocates a fixed array of slots once and never moves them. Each slot is either in use or free. The free slots form a linked list threaded through the slots themselves (an intrusive list, lesson 3.06), so finding a free slot is "take the head of the free list" and freeing one is "push it back on". slots: 0: bullet 1: free → 3 2: bullet 3: free → 4 4: free → end freeHead = 1 No heap allocations after start-up, objects never move, so a slot index stays valid while its object lives. Looping over the live objects means skipping free slots, which is slower than a dense vector when the pool is mostly empty. The remaining problem: stale references Suppose a missile stores "my target is slot 7". The target dies and slot 7 is freed. A moment later a new enemy is spawned into slot 7. The missile now chases the wrong enemy, and nothing tells it so. Index 7 is a dangling reference, just as a pointer would have been. Pattern 3: generational handles The fix is to give every slot a generation counter, incremented each time the slot is freed. A handle to an object is the pair (slot index, generation at the time). To use a handle, check that the slot's current generation still matches: The missile's handle says generation 3, the slot now says 4, so the lookup returns null: "your target no longer exists". The new bat in slot 7 gets handles with generation 4, which work normally. cpp struct Handle { std::uint32_t index; std::uint32_t generation; }; Eight bytes, trivially copyable, safe to store anywhere, safe to save to a file, and impossible to dangle. This is the approach used by most modern engines for entities, resources and anything else whose lifetime other systems cannot predict. The practice task is to build one. Choosing Need Use --- --- Many short-lived objects nobody else refers to (particles, bullets) Dense std::vector with swap-and-pop Objects referred to from elsewhere (enemies, units, items in the world) A pool with generational handles Both fast loops and stable handles A pool for identity plus a dense array of the data, with an index map between them (a "slot map" or "sparse set": the same idea, one step further) Few objects, created rarely Whatever is simplest: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T is fine Chapter 10 uses these in its entity-component system. Common mistakes !warning Advancing the index after swap-and-pop The element moved into slot i has not been processed yet. Only advance when nothing was removed. !warning Storing raw pointers to pooled objects for later They stay valid in memory, but may point at a different object after reuse. Store handles. !warning Letting the generation counter wrap round quickly With a 32-bit counter it would take billions of reuses of one slot, which is fine. An 8-bit counter wraps after 256 and can, rarely, let a stale handle match again. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does a dense vector with swap-and-pop not give objects stable references? + Removing one object moves another into its slot, so positions change - Vectors cannot be indexed - Swap-and-pop allocates memory The last element is moved to fill the gap, so its index changes. ? What does a pool's free list link together? + The unused slots, through a "next free" index stored in each free slot - The live objects, in creation order - Every slot, used or not Allocating takes the head of the free list; freeing pushes the slot back on. ? A handle says (slot 12, generation 5). The pool's slot 12 has generation 6. What does a lookup return? - The object in slot 12 + Nothing: the object the handle referred to has been destroyed - The object, after updating the handle A different generation means the slot has been freed since the handle was made.

title: A pool with generational handles
where: 3.10 Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
body: Build EnemyPool , a pool of Enemy objects with a fixed number of slots, handed out through generational handles. - The constructor receives the number of slots. All start free, with generation 0. - create(enemy) puts enemy in a free slot and returns a Handle holding that slot's index and current generation. If no slot is free, it returns std::nullopt . - get(handle) returns a pointer to the enemy if the handle is still valid (the index is in range, the slot is in use, and its generation matches), otherwise nullptr . - destroy(handle) frees the slot if the handle is valid, incrementing the slot's generation so old handles stop working, and returns true ; otherwise it returns false and changes nothing. - alive() returns how many slots are in use. When creating, any free slot may be used; a free list is the efficient way, but a simple search is accepted.

title: 4.01  Solutions, Projects and Build Configurations
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A real game is not one .cpp file. It is a solution holding several projects , such as the game, an engine library, a tools DLL and a test runner, each built in several configurations and for one or more platforms . This lesson shows how Visual Studio organises that, where the settings live, and how to set up a multi-project solution you will reuse for the rest of the course. Solutions and projects Lesson 1.07 created one console project. From now on the course builds several things that belong together: a game, a library it uses, a DLL it loads, tests that check them. Visual Studio's structure for this is: Thing File What it is --- --- --- Solution .sln A list of projects, plus which of them to build in which configuration Project .vcxproj One output (an .exe , .dll or .lib ), its source files, and all its compiler and linker settings Filters .vcxproj.filters Only the folders shown in Solution Explorer. They do not have to match folders on disk User settings .vcxproj.user Your personal debugging settings, such as command arguments. Not shared A .vcxproj file is XML that you can open in a text editor. Everything in the Properties dialog ends up in it, which is useful when comparing two projects' settings or reviewing a change in version control. A solution for the course Here is the layout the rest of the course assumes. Create it now so later lessons can add to it. course\ course.sln engine\ Static library (.lib): shared code, such as maths, the tile map, memory helpers game\ Console app (.exe): the game itself, uses engine plugin\ Dynamic library (.dll): built in lesson 4.05 tests\ Console app (.exe): unit tests for engine 1. File → New → Project → Blank Solution , name it course . 2. Right-click the solution → Add → New Project → Static Library , name it engine . 3. Add a Console App named game , and another named tests . 4. Right-click game → Add → Reference → tick engine . Do the same for tests . 5. Right-click game → Set as Startup Project : F5 now runs the game. The reference does two things: it makes engine build before game , and it links engine.lib into game.exe automatically. You still have to tell the compiler where engine 's headers are: in game 's properties, C/C++ → General → Additional Include Directories , add $(SolutionDir)engine . Configurations and platforms Every project is built in a configuration for a platform . Visual Studio starts you with two of each: x64 Win32 (x86) --- --- --- Debug Debug, 64-bit Debug, 32-bit Release Release, 64-bit Release, 32-bit Each of the four combinations has its own complete set of settings. That is powerful (Debug can have checks Release does not), and it is the cause of the most common project mistake: changing a setting in one combination and wondering why another behaves differently. When a setting should apply everywhere, select All Configurations and All Platforms at the top of the Properties dialog before changing it. You can add your own configurations in Build → Configuration Manager . Common additions: - ASan : Debug plus AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10). - Profile : Release with debug information and profiling hooks, for measuring (chapter 8). Macros in settings Paths in project settings use macros so they work on any machine. The ones you will use most: Macro Expands to --- --- $(SolutionDir) The folder holding the .sln , with a trailing backslash $(ProjectDir) The folder holding the .vcxproj $(Configuration) Debug or Release (or your own) $(Platform) x64 or Win32 $(OutDir) Where the project's output goes $(TargetPath) The full path of the .exe or .dll being built A tidy convention is to send every project's output to one folder per configuration, so the game, its DLLs and its tests end up side by side: set General → Output Directory to $(SolutionDir)bin\$(Platform)\$(Configuration)\ for all projects and all configurations. Property sheets When five projects need the same settings (C++20, warning level 4, the same output folder), setting them five times invites mistakes. A property sheet ( .props file) holds settings that several projects share. Open View → Other Windows → Property Manager , right-click a project → Add New Project Property Sheet , set things there, then add the same sheet to the other projects. Change it once and every project follows. Building from the command line Everything Visual Studio does can be done from the Developer PowerShell, which is how build servers do it: powershell msbuild course.sln /p:Configuration=Release /p:Platform=x64 /m /m builds projects in parallel. Being able to build without the IDE is useful for scripts, and for checking that a build does not secretly depend on something only your IDE session had set up. Common mistakes !warning Settings changed in one configuration only If Debug works and Release does not, compare the two configurations' settings. Use All Configurations for project-wide options. !warning Including another project's headers by relative path include "../engine/tilemap.h" breaks when files move. Add the folder to Additional Include Directories and write include "tilemap.h" . !warning Committing .vs , bin , obj and x64 folders They are build output and caches. A .gitignore for Visual Studio projects excludes them. Knowledge check quiz ? What does adding a project reference from game to engine do? + Builds engine first and links its output into game - Copies engine 's source files into game - Adds engine 's headers to the include path It sets the build order and the linking. Include directories are a separate setting. ? Where are a project's compiler and linker settings stored? - In the .sln file + In the .vcxproj file (and any property sheets it uses) - In the Windows registry The solution only lists projects; each project file holds its own settings. ? What does $(Configuration) expand to? + The name of the configuration being built, such as Debug - The full path of the output file - The project's folder Macros let one setting work for every configuration and machine.

title: 4.02  Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
match: 4.02 Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Lesson 1.04 introduced the four build stages. This lesson goes deeper into the rules that decide which file needs what: declarations versus definitions , headers and include guards, the one definition rule , inline and static , and how the linker matches symbols between object files. These rules explain almost every "already defined" and "unresolved" error you will meet. Declarations and definitions C++ separates saying something exists from saying what it is. Declaration: "this exists" Definition: "here it is" --- --- --- Function int addBonus(int score); int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } Global variable extern int g_highScore; int g_highScore{ 0 }; Class class Player; (a forward declaration) class Player { int health; }; A declaration is enough to use a function: the compiler only needs to know its name, parameters and return type to generate a call. The call's target address is left for the linker. A definition is what produces machine code or storage. Headers carry declarations Each .cpp file is compiled alone (it becomes one translation unit ). For main.cpp to call a function defined in score.cpp , main.cpp needs its declaration. A header file is simply a convenient way to paste the same declarations into every file that needs them: cpp // score.h pragma once int addBonus(int score); // declaration // score.cpp include "score.h" int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } // the one definition // main.cpp include "score.h" int main() { return addBonus(10); } // a call, resolved by the linker pragma once stops a header from being pasted twice into the same translation unit, which would otherwise repeat its class definitions and fail. The older, portable form is an include guard : cpp ifndef SCORE_H define SCORE_H int addBonus(int score); endif The one definition rule The one definition rule (ODR) says, roughly: - every function and global variable that is used must be defined exactly once in the whole program; - a class, an inline function or a template may be defined in every translation unit that uses it, but all those definitions must be identical. That second point is why class definitions and templates live in headers, and why ordinary function bodies do not. Break the first point and the linker complains: Situation Linker error --- --- A function is declared and called, but defined nowhere LNK2019: unresolved external symbol A function body written in a header included by two .cpp files LNK2005: already defined in main.obj A global int g_score{ 0 }; in a header LNK2005 as well Ways to make a definition safe in a header Keyword Effect Use for --- --- --- inline "Identical definitions may appear in many files; keep one" Small functions in headers; inline variables (C++17) for header constants static (at namespace scope) "Private to this translation unit": each file gets its own separate copy Helpers used only in one .cpp Unnamed namespace { ... } Same as static , for everything inside Several file-private helpers constexpr variable Implicitly inline (since C++17) for static data members; namespace-scope constexpr variables are internal to each file Compile-time constants Templates and functions defined inside a class body are implicitly inline , which is why they can live in headers. Symbols: what the linker actually matches Each object file contains a symbol table : names it defines and names it needs. C++ names are mangled into strings that encode the namespace, parameter types and more, so that overloads get different symbols: int addBonus(int) ?addBonus@@YAHH@Z int addBonus(float) ?addBonus@@YAHM@Z void Player::heal(int) ?heal@Player@@QEAAXH@Z The linker matches these strings exactly. So a declaration that differs from its definition in any detail (a const , a parameter type, a namespace) produces a different symbol, and the result is LNK2019 even though "the function is right there". The error message shows the mangled name and a readable version; compare it carefully with your definition. extern "C" turns mangling off, giving the plain name addBonus . That is how C++ code exposes functions to C, and how DLLs usually export functions so other languages and GetProcAddress (lesson 4.05) can find them by a simple name. You can see an object file's symbols with: powershell dumpbin /symbols score.obj dumpbin /exports plugin.dll undname "?addBonus@@YAHH@Z" Order of the stages, once more Changing a.cpp recompiles only a.obj , then re-links. Changing a header recompiles every .cpp that includes it, directly or indirectly. That is why large projects keep headers small, use forward declarations where they can, and avoid including heavy headers in other headers. Common mistakes !warning A declaration that does not quite match its definition void heal(int) declared, void heal(long) defined: two different symbols, and an unresolved external. Copy declarations from definitions exactly. !warning Globals defined in headers Declare extern int g_score; in the header and define it in one .cpp , or use inline int g_score{ 0 }; . !warning Including a header to get a type you only point to If a header only uses Player or Player& , a forward declaration class Player; is enough, and saves recompiling when player.h changes. Knowledge check quiz ? Which is a definition, not just a declaration? - int addBonus(int score); - extern int g_lives; + int g_lives{ 3 }; It creates the variable's storage. The others only announce that something exists elsewhere. ? Two .cpp files include a header containing int square(int x) { return x x; } . What happens? + The linker reports that square is already defined - It compiles and links fine - The compiler reports a syntax error Each file gets a definition, breaking the one definition rule. Marking it inline fixes it. ? Why does a declaration void heal(int) not link to a definition void heal(unsigned) ? + The parameter types are part of the mangled symbol, so they are two different symbols - The linker ignores parameters - unsigned cannot be used in definitions C++ symbols encode the parameter types so that overloads can coexist. ? What does extern "C" change? + It turns off name mangling, so the symbol is the plain function name - It makes the function run faster - It makes the function private to one file Plain names are what C code, other languages and GetProcAddress expect.

title: Be the linker

body: Write linkErrors(objects) , a tiny linker that only checks symbols. Each ObjectFile has a name, the symbols it defines and the symbols it needs . The function returns the list of errors, in this order: 1. For every symbol defined in more than one object file: "duplicate X" , once per symbol, with symbols in alphabetical order. 2. For every symbol needed by some object file but defined in none: "unresolved X" , once per symbol, with symbols in alphabetical order. A symbol that an object file both needs and defines itself is fine. No errors means an empty list. main.obj defines main needs addBonus, printf score.obj defines addBonus needs (nothing) crt.lib defines printf - no errors without score.obj - { "unresolved addBonus" }

title: 4.03  Reading Compiler and Linker Errors
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Build errors look intimidating because one mistake can produce a screen of messages. This lesson gives a method (find the first error, read its code, go to its line, ignore the cascade), and a field guide to the MSVC errors and warnings you will meet most often, with what each usually means. The method 1. Use the Output window, not just the Error List. The Error List sorts and groups messages; the Output window ( View → Output , "Show output from: Build") shows them in the order they happened, with the full text and the "see declaration of..." notes that follow each one. 2. Fix the first error first. One missing ; or } makes the compiler misread everything after it, producing dozens of follow-on errors that vanish once the first is fixed. Rebuild after each fix. 3. Read the code. C codes come from the compiler, LNK codes from the linker. Warnings are C4xxx . Searching for the code (for example "C2664") finds Microsoft's page explaining it. 4. Go to the line, then look just before it. The compiler reports where it noticed the problem, which is often the line after the real mistake. 5. Read the types in the message slowly. Most of a long message is the names of the types involved. The interesting part is usually "cannot convert from X to Y". A worked example cpp-norun include <string include <vector struct Item { std::string name; int weight; }; int totalWeight(const std::vector<Item & items) { int total{ 0 } for (const Item& item : items) total += item.weight; return total; } MSVC reports: main.cpp(8,19): error C2143: syntax error: missing ';' before 'for' main.cpp(10,9): error C2065: 'item': undeclared identifier main.cpp(10,9): error C2228: left of '.weight' must have class/struct/union Three errors, one mistake. The first one names the real problem: int total{ 0 } on line 7 is missing its ; , which the compiler only noticed on reaching for on line 8. Because it then misread the for , it never declared item , so lines 10's errors are just a cascade. Add the semicolon and all three disappear. Compiler errors you will see most Code Message (shortened) Usually means --- --- --- C2143 syntax error: missing ';' before ... A missing ; , ) or } just before the reported spot C2065 undeclared identifier A typo, a missing include , or a name used before its declaration C3861 identifier not found Same, for a function call C2039 is not a member of Typo in a member name, or the wrong type C2664 cannot convert argument N from X to Y The argument has the wrong type; read X and Y carefully (const? pointer vs reference?) C2440 cannot convert from X to Y An assignment or initialisation with the wrong type C2662 cannot convert 'this' pointer from const X to X& Calling a non- const member function on a const object: make the function const C2280 attempting to reference a deleted function Copying something that cannot be copied, such as a std::unique_ptr ; use std::move or a reference C2027 use of undefined type Only a forward declaration is visible where the full class is needed: include its header C2011 type redefinition A header included twice without pragma once C1083 cannot open include file Wrong file name, or the folder is missing from Additional Include Directories Linker errors Code Usually means --- --- LNK2019 Unresolved external symbol : declared and used, never defined in anything linked. Missing .cpp in the project, missing library in Linker → Input, or a declaration that does not match its definition exactly (lesson 4.02). LNK2001 Also unresolved, usually for a variable or a virtual function's vtable: a class with a virtual function declared but never defined LNK1120 "N unresolved externals": a summary; fix the LNK2019s above it LNK2005 Already defined : a function or global defined in a header included by several .cpp files LNK1104 Cannot open file: often the .exe is still running and locked, or a library path is wrong LNK1168 Cannot open X.exe for writing: the program is still running. Close it. A linker error message contains the symbol, mangled and readable. The readable form tells you exactly which function and which overload is missing. Warnings worth treating as errors Warnings point at code that compiles but is probably wrong. At warning level 4 these are the most valuable: Warning Meaning --- --- C4700 Uninitialised local variable used C4701 Potentially uninitialised local variable used C4172 Returning the address of a local variable C4244 Conversion that may lose data, such as double to int C4267 size_t to int conversion, possible loss of data C4018 / C4389 Signed and unsigned comparison C4715 Not all control paths return a value C4996 Using a function marked unsafe or deprecated, such as strcpy Turning on Treat Warnings As Errors ( /WX ) keeps the list at zero, which is the only way warnings stay useful: once there are fifty of them, nobody reads the fifty-first. Template errors Errors inside templates (including the standard library) can run to dozens of lines, because the compiler reports the whole chain of instantiations. Read them from the bottom of the "see reference to..." chain, where the template was first used from your code: that is the line to look at. The usual causes are passing a type that lacks something the template needs (no < for std::sort , not copyable for std::vector::push_back ). Common mistakes !warning Fixing errors from the bottom of the list Later errors are often caused by earlier ones. Fix the first and rebuild. !warning Trusting the reported line exactly Look at the line before, especially for missing semicolons and braces. !warning Ignoring warnings C4700, C4172 and C4715 are bugs the compiler has already found for you. Knowledge check quiz ? A build shows 40 errors. What should you do first? + Fix the first error in the Output window and rebuild - Fix the error that appears most often - Start from the last error Most of the rest are probably a cascade from the first. ? error C2280: attempting to reference a deleted function appears when pushing a std::unique_ptr into a vector. What is the fix? + Move it in: v.push_back(std::move(ptr)); - Make the pointer const - Use new instead unique_ptr cannot be copied; its copy constructor is deleted. It can be moved. ? LNK1168: cannot open game.exe for writing . What is the most likely cause? - A missing library + The program is still running from the last build - A syntax error in main Windows will not let the linker overwrite an executable that is running. ? Which warning tells you a function can end without returning a value? - C4244 + C4715 - C4996 Falling off the end of a non-void function is undefined behaviour.

title: 4.04  Static Libraries
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A static library ( .lib ) is a bundle of object files. Linking it into a program copies in the parts the program uses, so the result is one self-contained .exe . This lesson builds the course's engine library, shows how the linker pulls code out of it, and covers the settings that must match between a library and the program that uses it. A bundle of object files When a project's Configuration Type is Static library (.lib) , its build stops after compiling: instead of linking the object files into an executable, the librarian ( lib.exe ) packs them into one .lib file with an index of the symbols each defines. When a program links against engine.lib , the linker looks up each unresolved symbol in the index and copies in only the object files that define what is needed . If the game never calls anything in random.obj , none of it ends up in the .exe . Building the engine library In the course solution from lesson 4.01, engine is already a static library project. Give it some real code: cpp // engine/vec2.h pragma once struct Vec2 { float x{ 0 }; float y{ 0 }; }; Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b); Vec2 operator (Vec2 v, float s); float length(Vec2 v); cpp // engine/vec2.cpp include "vec2.h" include <cmath Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b) { return { a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y }; } Vec2 operator (Vec2 v, float s) { return { v.x s, v.y s }; } float length(Vec2 v) { return std::sqrt(v.x v.x + v.y v.y); } cpp // game/main.cpp include <iostream include "vec2.h" int main() { Vec2 position{ 1, 2 }; Vec2 velocity{ 3, 4 }; position = position + velocity 0.5f; std::cout << position.x << ", " << position.y << " speed " << length(velocity) << '\n'; return 0; } With the project reference and include directory from lesson 4.01 in place, building the solution builds engine.lib first, then compiles main.cpp and links it with engine.lib . The output prints 2.5, 4 speed 5 . Without a project reference (for example, a library someone else built), you tell the linker yourself: - Linker → General → Additional Library Directories : the folder containing the .lib ; - Linker → Input → Additional Dependencies : the file name, engine.lib ; - or, in code, pragma comment(lib, "engine.lib") . Settings that must match Object files compiled with different settings may not work together, and the linker catches some (not all) of these mismatches: Setting Must match because Mismatch error --- --- --- Platform (x64 / x86) 64-bit and 32-bit code cannot be mixed LNK1112: module machine type conflicts Runtime library ( /MD , /MDd , /MT , /MTd ) Each object file asks for a particular C runtime; they must agree LNK2038: mismatch detected for 'RuntimeLibrary' Debug / Release ( _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL ) Standard containers have different layouts in Debug and Release LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' C++ standard, struct packing, other defines that change layout A class laid out differently in two files is a silent ODR violation Usually none: just strange crashes The LNK2038 checks exist because these mismatches used to cause baffling crashes: a std::vector passed from a Release library to Debug code has a different layout on each side. So build every library in the same configuration as the program . A project reference does this automatically; a pre-built library usually ships in both Debug and Release forms for this reason. The runtime library choice deserves a note. /MD links the C and C++ runtime as DLLs (the user needs the Visual C++ Redistributable installed); /MT copies the runtime into your executable. Either is fine for this course; just be consistent across every project in the solution. Static libraries versus DLLs Static library DLL (next lesson) --- --- --- When code is joined At link time, copied into the .exe At run time, loaded from a separate file Files to ship Just the .exe The .exe and every .dll Updating the library Rebuild and relink the program Replace the .dll Loading code chosen at run time (plugins) Not possible Possible Sharing between programs Each program has its own copy One file can be shared The course uses a static library for the engine, which the game always needs, and a DLL for plugins, which the game chooses to load. Common mistakes !warning Linking a Debug library into a Release program LNK2038 warns you. Use project references, or link the matching build of the library. !warning Expecting a static library to work without its headers The .lib holds code; your program still needs the declarations from its headers to call it. !warning Global objects in a static library that nothing references The linker only pulls in object files that define something needed. A self-registering global in an otherwise unreferenced .obj is silently left out. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a static library contain? + Object files, plus an index of the symbols they define - A finished program - Only header files It is an archive of compiled code, ready to be linked. ? The game uses only length from engine.lib . What gets copied into game.exe ? + The object file that defines length (and anything it needs) - The whole library - Nothing; it is loaded at run time The linker pulls in object files on demand, by symbol. ? LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' . What does it mean? + A Debug-built library is being linked with Release-built code, or the other way round - The library is 32-bit - A function is missing Debug and Release standard containers have different layouts; mixing them is unsafe.

title: 4.05  Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL
match: 4.05 Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body:
A DLL is a library that stays a separate file and is joined to a program when it runs. This lesson builds a DLL, exports functions from it, uses it in the two ways Windows offers ( load-time linking through an import library, and run-time loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress ), and covers the rules about DllMain , memory and C++ types across the boundary. What a DLL is A dynamic-link library is built much like an .exe : compiled and linked into a PE file (chapter 9) with code, data and imports. The difference is that it has no main ; instead it exports functions and variables for programs to use. kernel32.dll , user32.dll and the C++ runtime are all DLLs, and every Windows program uses dozens of them. The Windows loader maps a DLL into the process's address space and fills in the addresses of its exports wherever the program needs them. One DLL file on disk can be loaded into many processes at once. Building one Add a project to the course solution: Dynamic-Link Library (DLL) , named plugin . Replace its code with: cpp // plugin/plugin.h: shared with the programs that use the DLL pragma once ifdef PLUGIN_EXPORTS define PLUGIN_API extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) else define PLUGIN_API extern "C" __declspec(dllimport) endif PLUGIN_API int pluginVersion(); PLUGIN_API int scaleDamage(int damage, int level); cpp // plugin/plugin.cpp include "plugin.h" int pluginVersion() { return 3; } int scaleDamage(int damage, int level) { return damage + damage level / 10; } In the plugin project's properties, add PLUGIN_EXPORTS to C/C++ → Preprocessor → Preprocessor Definitions (the DLL template usually adds a similar name already). The same header then means "export" inside the DLL and "import" everywhere else. - __declspec(dllexport) puts the function in the DLL's export table . - extern "C" gives it a plain, unmangled name (lesson 4.02), so it can be found as scaleDamage rather than ?scaleDamage@@YAHHH@Z . Building produces two files: plugin.dll , the code, and plugin.lib , a small import library that only says "these symbols live in plugin.dll". powershell dumpbin /exports plugin.dll ordinal hint RVA name 1 0 00011023 pluginVersion 2 1 00011028 scaleDamage Using it, way 1: load-time linking Add a project reference from game to plugin (or link plugin.lib ), include plugin.h , and call the functions normally: cpp include <iostream include "plugin.h" int main() { std::cout << "plugin version " << pluginVersion() << '
'; std::cout << "level 5 damage: " << scaleDamage(40, 5) << '
'; return 0; } The linker uses the import library to record, in game.exe 's import table , that it needs scaleDamage from plugin.dll . When the game starts, the loader finds plugin.dll (in the .exe 's folder first, then the system folders and PATH ), maps it, and fills in the addresses. If the DLL is missing, the game does not start at all: Windows shows "The code execution cannot proceed because plugin.dll was not found." Using it, way 2: run-time loading The program can instead load the DLL itself, when and if it chooses, and look functions up by name. No import library and no reference are needed, which is exactly what a plugin system wants: the game does not know at build time which plugins exist. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream using ScaleDamageFn = int ( )(int, int); int main() { HMODULE module{ LoadLibraryW(L"plugin.dll") }; if (!module) { std::cout << "no plugin found, error " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } auto scale{ reinterpret_cast<ScaleDamageFn (GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage")) }; if (scale) std::cout << "level 5 damage: " << scale(40, 5) << '
'; FreeLibrary(module); return 0; } - LoadLibraryW maps the DLL and returns an HMODULE , which is the address the DLL was loaded at. - GetProcAddress looks a name up in its export table and returns the function's address, or null. - The result is cast to the right function pointer type (lesson 3.04). The cast is a promise you make: if the signature is wrong, the call corrupts the stack or registers. - FreeLibrary unloads it. Any pointer into the DLL is invalid after that. Chapter 13 builds a full plugin system on this. DllMain: keep it tiny A DLL may define DllMain , which Windows calls when the DLL is loaded into a process, unloaded, and when threads start and stop: cpp include <windows.h BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE module, DWORD reason, LPVOID) { if (reason == DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) DisableThreadLibraryCalls(module); return TRUE; } DllMain runs while Windows holds the loader lock , a lock that serialises all DLL loading in the process. Doing almost anything interesting there (loading another DLL, waiting for a thread, calling into COM, even some C++ static initialisation that does those things) can deadlock the process. The rule: in DllMain , do nothing that could wait or load. Put real initialisation in an exported init function that the program calls after loading. Rules for the boundary A DLL and the program that loads it are built separately, possibly by different compilers or settings. So the interface between them should be simple: - Plain C types across the boundary : integers, floats, pointers to plain structs, function pointers. Passing std::string or std::vector across works only if both sides were built with the same compiler version and settings, and is a common source of crashes. - Free memory on the side that allocated it. If the DLL allocates with its own runtime, it should provide a function to free it too. Mixing heaps between modules is a classic crash. - Version your interface. An exported pluginVersion (like the one above) lets the program refuse a plugin built for an incompatible interface. Common mistakes !warning The DLL is not next to the .exe Set every project's output directory to the same folder (lesson 4.01), or the loader cannot find it. !warning Forgetting extern "C" GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage") returns null because the exported name is mangled. !warning Calling functions after FreeLibrary The code is gone from memory; the call jumps into nothing and crashes. !warning Real work inside DllMain Deadlocks under the loader lock are hard to diagnose. Export an init function instead. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the import library ( plugin.lib ) produced alongside plugin.dll for? + It tells the linker which symbols live in the DLL, so a program can link to them at build time - It contains a copy of the DLL's code - It is needed by LoadLibrary The import library holds no code. It lets the linker record the DLL dependency in the program's import table. ? Why is extern "C" usually used for DLL exports meant for GetProcAddress ? + It exports the plain function name instead of a mangled C++ name - It makes the function faster - GetProcAddress only works with C code GetProcAddress looks names up exactly as they appear in the export table. ? A program links to plugin.dll at load time, and the DLL is missing. What happens? + The program fails to start, with a message naming the missing DLL - The program starts and calls to the DLL return 0 - The program starts and crashes on the first call Load-time dependencies are resolved before main runs. Run-time loading lets a program cope with a missing DLL. ? Why should DllMain do as little as possible? + It runs under the loader lock, and waiting or loading other DLLs there can deadlock - It runs before memory is available - It is called only once per computer Do real setup in a separate exported function the program calls after loading.

title: 4.06  Managing Dependencies with vcpkg
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Real projects use other people's libraries: a window and input library, an image loader, a user interface toolkit. vcpkg is Microsoft's package manager for C and C++: you list the libraries a project needs in a vcpkg.json file, and it downloads, builds and links them with settings that match your project. This lesson sets it up for the course's later chapters. The problem vcpkg solves Using a third-party C++ library by hand means: find its source, build it with the right compiler, platform, runtime library and configuration (lesson 4.04's matching rules), copy its headers somewhere, add include and library paths to your project, and repeat for every library it depends on, and again for every machine that builds your project. vcpkg automates all of that. It knows how to build thousands of libraries, builds each one to match your project's triplet (for example x64-windows : 64-bit, DLL runtime), and plugs the results into MSBuild so your project finds headers and libraries automatically. Getting vcpkg Visual Studio 2022 includes a copy of vcpkg, available in the Developer PowerShell as vcpkg . To check: powershell vcpkg --version If the command is not found, install the vcpkg package manager component from the Visual Studio Installer (Individual components tab), or clone it yourself: powershell git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat C:\dev\vcpkg\vcpkg integrate install integrate install connects vcpkg to every MSBuild project for your user account. Manifest mode: dependencies in a file The modern way to use vcpkg is manifest mode : a vcpkg.json file next to your solution lists what the project needs, so anyone who builds it gets the same libraries. powershell cd course vcpkg new --application vcpkg add port fmt vcpkg add port sdl2 That creates and fills vcpkg.json : json { "dependencies": "fmt", "sdl2" } Then, in each project that should use vcpkg: Properties → vcpkg → Use Vcpkg Manifest: Yes . The next build reads the manifest, builds the listed libraries (the first time takes a while; later builds reuse the results) and adds their include folders, libraries and DLLs to the project. DLLs are copied next to your .exe automatically. cpp-norun include <fmt/core.h int main() { fmt::print("{} has {} health\n", "Rook", 87); return 0; } No include paths, no library paths, no copying: the manifest is the only thing you wrote. Triplets: matching the build A triplet names the platform and the linkage vcpkg should build for. Triplet Platform Libraries built as C runtime --- --- --- --- x64-windows 64-bit DLLs DLL ( /MD ) x64-windows-static 64-bit Static .lib Static ( /MT ) x64-windows-static-md 64-bit Static .lib DLL ( /MD ) vcpkg picks x64-windows for an x64 project by default and builds Debug and Release versions of every library, linking the right one for each configuration. If your projects use /MT (as the course's static builds might), set Properties → vcpkg → Use Static Libraries: Yes so the libraries match. Pinning versions By default, vcpkg uses whichever versions its own copy currently has. For a project you want to build the same way next year, add a baseline , which pins every library to the versions vcpkg had at a particular commit: powershell vcpkg x-update-baseline --add-initial-baseline The manifest gains a "builtin-baseline" line. Commit vcpkg.json to version control; do not commit the vcpkg_installed folder it creates, which is build output. Libraries this course uses later Library vcpkg port Used in --- --- --- SDL2: windows, input, simple 2D drawing sdl2 Chapter 11 (the small game) Dear ImGui: immediate-mode user interfaces imgui sdl2-binding,sdl2-renderer-binding Chapter 14 (tool interfaces) Catch2 or GoogleTest: unit testing catch2 , gtest Chapter 17 fmt: formatting (most of it is now std::format ) fmt Optional Common mistakes !warning Mixing manifest mode and manually copied libraries Two copies of a library's headers on the include path, from different versions, cause confusing errors. Let vcpkg own each library. !warning A triplet that does not match the runtime library A static-runtime project with DLL-runtime libraries gives LNK2038 . Match them with the vcpkg project settings. !warning Committing vcpkg_installed It is large and machine-specific build output. Add it to .gitignore . Knowledge check quiz ? What does vcpkg.json describe? + The libraries a project depends on - How to build vcpkg itself - The project's compiler settings Anyone building the project gets the same dependencies from the manifest. ? What is a vcpkg triplet? + The target platform and how libraries should be built and linked, such as x64-windows-static - Three versions of the same library - A group of three packages It ensures the libraries are built to match the project. ? Why add a baseline to the manifest? + To pin library versions so the project builds the same way later - To make the build faster - To enable static linking Without it, versions follow whatever vcpkg copy is installed.

title: 4.07  The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack
match: 4.07 The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Lesson 1.08 was a first session. This lesson covers the debugger as a daily tool: every way of controlling execution (run to cursor, step into a specific call, set the next statement), moving around the Call Stack, breaking when an exception is thrown, Just My Code, and attaching to a program that is already running. How a debugger stops a program It helps to know what a breakpoint is. When you set one on a line, the debugger finds the first machine instruction for that line and overwrites its first byte with 0xCC , the int 3 instruction. When the CPU reaches it, the processor raises a breakpoint exception ; Windows sees that a debugger is attached to the process and hands it the event. The debugger then puts the original byte back, shows you the line, and waits. Stepping works similarly: the debugger sets temporary breakpoints, or turns on the processor's trap flag , which raises an exception after every single instruction. Chapter 12 uses these same Windows debugging events to build a tiny debugger of your own. Controlling execution Command Key What it does --- --- --- Start Debugging / Continue F5 Run until a breakpoint, an exception, or the end Step Over F10 Run the current line, including calls, stop at the next line Step Into F11 Go into the function the line calls Step Out Shift+F11 Run until the current function returns Run To Cursor Ctrl+F10 Run until the line the cursor is on, as if it had a one-time breakpoint Run to Click The green arrow that appears when hovering at the left of a line Same, with the mouse Step Into Specific Right-click → Step Into Specific Choose which call to step into when a line makes several, such as update(getPlayer(), clamp(x)) Set Next Statement Ctrl+Shift+F10, or drag the yellow arrow Make a different line run next, skipping or repeating code Break All Ctrl+Alt+Break Pause the program wherever it is, for example when it seems stuck Stop Debugging Shift+F5 End the program Restart Ctrl+Shift+F5 End and start again Set Next Statement is powerful and dangerous: it changes where the CPU goes next without running the code in between. It is excellent for re-running a function after changing a variable, and can crash the program if you skip something important such as a constructor. Use it within one function. Break All is the answer to "my game froze": pause, open the Call Stack, and see what every thread is doing (chapter 8 covers threads). The Call Stack window, as a tool Debug → Windows → Call Stack (Ctrl+Alt+C) lists the frames from the current function down to the start of the thread (lesson 1.05). Using it well: - Double-click a frame to make it current: the editor shows that function's line, and Locals and Watch show that frame's variables. This is how you find out why a function was called with a bad argument: go up one frame and look at the caller's variables. - Right-click → Show External Code reveals frames from the standard library and Windows, hidden by default. - Right-click → Show Parameter Values / Parameter Types puts the arguments on each line. - Run To Cursor in an earlier frame (select it, then Ctrl+F10 on a line) runs until control comes back up to that point. Just My Code By default, Visual Studio's Just My Code setting hides and skips code that is not yours: the standard library, Windows, third-party libraries without debug information. Step Into then does not wander into std::vector 's internals. When you need to see inside them (for example, to watch a std::vector reallocate), turn it off in Tools → Options → Debugging → General → Enable Just My Code . Breaking on exceptions By default, the debugger stops only on exceptions nobody catches. That is often too late: by then the stack has unwound past the code that threw. Open Debug → Windows → Exception Settings (Ctrl+Alt+E) and tick the categories you want to stop on when thrown : - C++ Exceptions : stop at any throw , even if it will be caught. Good for "something throws and gets swallowed somewhere". - Win32 Exceptions → Access violation (0xC0000005) : usually already on. Stops at the exact instruction that read or wrote bad memory, with the full stack intact. When the debugger stops on an access violation, the message says "reading location 0x..." or "writing location 0x...". As lesson 3.02 explained, a small address there means a null pointer plus an offset. Attaching to a running program You do not have to start a program from Visual Studio to debug it. Debug → Attach to Process (Ctrl+Alt+P) lists running processes; pick yours and press Attach. Breakpoints, Break All and the windows all work, provided the debugger can find the program's .pdb symbols (lesson 8.02). This is how you debug a game that only misbehaves after an hour of play, a program started by another program, or a tool you want to inspect without restarting it. You can attach only to your own processes unless Visual Studio runs as administrator, and Windows refuses debugging of protected system processes entirely. Debug → Detach All lets the program carry on without the debugger.
