Common mistakes !warning A breakpoint that never hits A hollow red circle means the debugger could not place it: the code is not loaded yet, the build is out of date, or the line has no code (in Release, the compiler may have removed or merged it). Rebuild in Debug. !warning Set Next Statement across function boundaries Moving the yellow arrow into a different function leaves the stack in a state the code does not expect. Stay within one function. !warning Stopping too late on exceptions Turn on "break when thrown" for C++ exceptions to see where an exception starts, not just where it ends. Knowledge check quiz ? What does the debugger write into your program's code to make a breakpoint? + The byte 0xCC (the int 3 instruction) over the first byte of the line's first instruction - A call to a special debugging function - Nothing; the CPU checks a list of breakpoints itself The CPU raises an exception when it executes int 3 , and Windows passes it to the debugger. ? A line calls three functions. How do you step into only the second? - Press F11 twice + Right-click → Step Into Specific, and choose it - Set a breakpoint and press F10 Step Into Specific lists every call on the line. ? Your game freezes. What do you do in the debugger first? + Break All, then look at the Call Stack of each thread - Restart it - Add more breakpoints Break All pauses the program wherever it is, which shows what it is stuck doing. ? Where do you go to stop as soon as any C++ exception is thrown, even if it is caught later? + Exception Settings, ticking C++ Exceptions - The Call Stack window - The Breakpoints window By default the debugger only stops on unhandled exceptions.

title: 4.08  Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows
match: 4.08 Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: The debugger's windows show a paused program's state at every level, from C++ expressions down to CPU registers and machine instructions. This lesson covers the tricks that make them far more useful: format specifiers , pseudo-variables , viewing arrays through pointers, the Registers and Disassembly windows, and how they connect to everything in chapters 1 to 3. Locals, Autos and Watch Window Shows --- --- Locals Every local variable in the current frame Autos Variables used on the current and previous line, plus the return value of a function you just stepped over Watch 1-4 Any expressions you type, kept up to date as you step QuickWatch (Shift+F9) One expression, in a dialog, for a quick look DataTips Hover over a variable in the editor; pin it to keep it on screen The Watch window evaluates nearly any C++ expression: player.health 2 , enemies.size() , &grid 3 4 , target , levels current .name , even function calls (careful: a call runs real code and can change state). Format specifiers Add a comma and a specifier after an expression to change how it is shown: Expression Shows --- --- health,x In hexadecimal flags,b In binary ptr,10 or ptr, 10 The 10 elements starting at ptr , as an array name,s A char as a string; ,su for a UTF-16 wchar_t ; ,s8 for UTF-8 value,d In decimal obj,! The raw structure, ignoring any custom visualiser ptr,na A pointer without the "address and then the value" decoration hr,hr An HRESULT decoded into its name err,wm A Windows error code as its message, such as "The system cannot find the file specified." ,10 is the one you will use most: a raw int scores shows only the first element, and scores,10 shows ten. For a std::vector , the debugger already shows all elements, using a visualiser that understands the type. Pseudo-variables The Watch window understands some names that are not in your code: Name Value --- --- $err The thread's current GetLastError() value. Use $err,hr to see its meaning (chapter 5) $ReturnValue The value the function you just stepped out of returned $tid , $pid Current thread and process id @rsp , @rip , @rax , ... (or $rsp ) A CPU register's value (int )(@rsp + 0x28) reads an int at an offset from the stack pointer: useful when reading an optimised function whose locals have no names. The Memory window, revisited Lesson 2.11 covered reading bytes. Two more tricks: - Drag a variable from the editor or from Locals into the Memory window to jump to its address. - Edit in place : click a byte and type new hex digits. The program continues with the change. This is a quick way to test how code reacts to an unusual value without changing the source. The Registers window Debug → Windows → Registers (Ctrl+Alt+G) shows the CPU's registers for the current thread at the current instruction: RAX = 0000000000000041 RBX = 0000000000000000 RCX = 000000F3A1AFF6C8 RDX = 0000000000000032 RSI = 0000000000000000 RDI = 0000000000000000 R8 = 0000000000000000 R9 = 0000000000000000 R10 = 0000000000000000 RIP = 00007FF6E1A2185E RSP = 000000F3A1AFF6A0 RBP = 0000000000000000 EFL = 00000246 - RIP is the instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction (the program counter from lesson 1.01). - RSP is the stack pointer (lesson 1.05). - RCX, RDX, R8, R9 hold the first four arguments at the start of a function, and RAX holds a function's return value just after it returns (lesson 2.01). - EFL is the flags register; right-click to show individual flags such as ZF (zero) and CF (carry), which chapter 7 explains. Values that changed in the last step are shown in red, just as in Locals. The Disassembly window Debug → Windows → Disassembly (Ctrl+Alt+D), or right-click → Go To Disassembly , shows the machine instructions the compiler produced, interleaved with your source lines: player.health -= amount; 00007FF6E1A21859 mov rax,qword ptr player 00007FF6E1A2185E mov ecx,dword ptr rax 00007FF6E1A21860 sub ecx,dword ptr amount 00007FF6E1A21863 mov rax,qword ptr player 00007FF6E1A21868 mov dword ptr rax ,ecx In this window, F10 and F11 step one instruction at a time instead of one line, and the Registers window changes with every step. This is the bridge between C++ and the machine: one line of source became five instructions, each of them a simple step like the tiny computer's. Right-click options let you show code bytes (the actual numbers, as in lesson 1.04), hide source lines, and show symbol names. Chapter 7 teaches how to read all of this. For now, step through a simple function in the Disassembly window with the Registers window open and watch RIP move along by each instruction's size. Common mistakes !warning Watch expressions that call functions They run real code every time the window updates. A function with side effects changes your program while you look at it. !warning Reading a raw pointer to an array scores shows one element. Use scores,10 . !warning Trusting $err much later GetLastError is overwritten by later API calls. Check it straight after the call that failed. Knowledge check quiz ? How do you see 20 elements of an int data in the Watch window? + Type data,20 - Type data 20 - Type data 20 The ,N format specifier shows N elements starting at the pointer. ? Which register holds the address of the next instruction to run? - RSP + RIP - RAX RIP is the instruction pointer; RSP is the stack pointer. ? You just stepped out of a function. Where can you see what it returned? + In $ReturnValue , or the Autos window - In RIP - Only by adding a print statement The debugger records the return value as you step out or over a call. ? What does F10 do while the Disassembly window has focus? + Steps one machine instruction - Steps one source line - Continues to the next breakpoint In the Disassembly window, stepping is per instruction.

title: 4.09  Conditional and Data Breakpoints
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A plain breakpoint stops every time. In a game loop that runs 60 times a second, that is useless. Conditions , hit counts and filters make a breakpoint stop only when it matters; tracepoints log without stopping; and data breakpoints stop on the exact instruction that changes a piece of memory, which is the fastest way to find who corrupted a value. Making breakpoints selective Right-click a breakpoint's red dot → Conditions (or hover and press the gear icon) to add any of these: Setting Stops when Example --- --- --- Conditional expression, Is true The expression is true enemy.health < 0 Conditional expression, When changed The expression's value differs from last time player.state Hit count It has been reached a given number of times = 500 , = 100 , is a multiple of 60 Filter On a particular thread or process ThreadId = 12345 Conditions are evaluated by the debugger each time the line is reached, which makes the program slower while the breakpoint is set; that is usually fine. A typical use: an enemy occasionally gets negative health and you do not know which one or when. Put a breakpoint on the line that subtracts damage, with the condition health - amount < 0 && id == 17 . The game runs normally until exactly that moment. Tracepoints: printing without stopping Tick Actions in the same settings panel and the breakpoint becomes a tracepoint : instead of (or as well as) stopping, it writes a message to the Output window. Put expressions in braces: frame {frameCount}: {name} takes {amount} damage, health now {health} Leave Continue code execution ticked and the program does not pause at all. It is std::cout debugging without editing, rebuilding or remembering to remove the lines afterwards. Special keywords like $FUNCTION , $CALLER and $TID add context. Data breakpoints: who changed this? Lesson 2.09's hardest bug was "something overwrote this value, and I don't know what". A data breakpoint stops the program on the instruction that writes to a given address, whoever does it, wherever the code is. 1. Run to a point where the variable exists, for example a breakpoint just after hero is constructed. 2. In Locals or Watch, right-click the variable → Break When Value Changes . Or Debug → New Breakpoint → Data Breakpoint , and enter an address expression such as &hero.gold and a size of 4 bytes. 3. Continue (F5). When any instruction changes those bytes, the debugger stops just after it, showing the line and the Call Stack. If the culprit is an overrun from the neighbouring name array (lesson 2.09), the stack points straight at the copy loop. How it works, and its limits Data breakpoints use the processor's debug registers . x64 CPUs have four of them, DR0 to DR3 , each holding an address to watch for writes (or reads). The CPU itself checks every memory access against them, so the program runs at full speed. The hardware imposes limits: Limit Why --- --- At most 4 data breakpoints at a time 4 debug registers Each watches 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes The hardware's sizes The address must be aligned to that size Hardware requirement An address, not a variable A local's address is only valid while its frame exists; the breakpoint stays on the address after the frame is gone That last row matters. Set a data breakpoint on a local, return from the function, and the breakpoint now watches whatever reuses that stack memory. Visual Studio removes data breakpoints when the process ends, but not when a frame ends; delete them yourself when they are no longer meaningful. A worked hunt The Debug heap reported "HEAP CORRUPTION DETECTED after normal block 312". Steps: 1. Turn on _CrtSetDbgFlag leak checking and rerun to confirm block 312 is the same each run (allocation numbers are stable if the program does the same things). 2. Call _CrtSetBreakAlloc(312) at the start of main : the debugger stops when block 312 is allocated, and the Call Stack shows what it is. 3. Note its address and size. Set a data breakpoint on the 8 bytes just after its end, where the guard bytes are. 4. Continue. The program stops on the instruction that writes past the end. That is the whole bug, found in four steps without reading a single line of unrelated code. Common mistakes !warning Slow conditions on very hot lines A condition evaluated millions of times per second makes the game crawl. Put the breakpoint on a less frequent line, or add a cheap check in code temporarily. !warning Data breakpoints left on reused memory After the variable's lifetime ends, the address belongs to something else. Delete the breakpoint. !warning Watching more than 8 bytes Hardware only watches up to 8 bytes per breakpoint. For a larger region, watch the specific field that goes wrong, or the guard bytes at its edge. Knowledge check quiz ? How do you make a breakpoint stop only on the 500th time it is reached? + Give it a hit count condition of = 500 - Press F5 499 times - Use a data breakpoint Hit counts let the debugger count for you. ? What does a tracepoint do? + Writes a message, which can include variable values, to the Output window, optionally without stopping - Stops the program on every line - Records the program so it can be replayed It is logging added from the debugger, without changing the code. ? Why can there be at most four data breakpoints at once? + They use the CPU's four debug address registers - Visual Studio limits them to save memory - Windows only allows four per process The processor checks memory accesses against DR0 to DR3 in hardware. ? A data breakpoint is set on a local variable, and its function returns. What does the breakpoint watch now? + The same address, which now belongs to whatever reuses that stack memory - Nothing; it is removed automatically - The variable's new location Data breakpoints watch addresses, not variables.

title: Which write hits the watch?
body: A data breakpoint watches size bytes starting at address watch . The program performs a series of memory writes; each Write has a starting address and a length in bytes. Write firstHit(writes, watch, size) , which returns the index of the first write that touches any byte of the watched range, or -1 if none does. A write of length bytes at address touches the bytes address to address + length - 1 . The watched range is watch to watch + size - 1 . Two ranges touch if they overlap by at least one byte. watch 0x1008, size 4 (bytes 0x1008..0x100B) writes: { 0x1000, 8 } bytes 0x1000..0x1007: just misses { 0x100C, 4 } bytes 0x100C..0x100F: just misses { 0x1004, 8 } bytes 0x1004..0x100B: hits - answer 2

title: 4.10  Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes
match: 4.10 Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A Release build runs the same source code many times faster, because the optimiser rewrites it: it keeps values in registers, inlines functions, removes work whose result is unused, and assumes your code has no undefined behaviour. This lesson shows each transformation, explains why some bugs only appear in Release, and sets up a build that is both optimised and debuggable. The same code, two programs Compile this function in each configuration: cpp int sumTo(int n) { int total{ 0 }; for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i) total += i; return total; } Debug ( /Od , no optimisation) does exactly what the source says, keeping every variable in memory so the debugger can show it: asm sumTo PROC mov DWORD PTR rsp+8 , ecx ; store n to its stack slot sub rsp, 24 mov DWORD PTR total$ rsp , 0 mov DWORD PTR i$ rsp , 1 jmp SHORT $check $next: mov eax, DWORD PTR i$ rsp inc eax mov DWORD PTR i$ rsp , eax $check: mov eax, DWORD PTR n$ rsp cmp DWORD PTR i$ rsp , eax jg SHORT $done mov eax, DWORD PTR i$ rsp mov ecx, DWORD PTR total$ rsp add ecx, eax mov DWORD PTR total$ rsp , ecx jmp SHORT $next $done: mov eax, DWORD PTR total$ rsp add rsp, 24 ret 0 sumTo ENDP Release ( /O2 ) keeps everything in registers, and may restructure the loop, unroll it, or even recognise the pattern and compute the answer with arithmetic. Every loop iteration in the Debug version reads and writes memory several times; the Release version barely touches memory at all. For code like this, Release is commonly 5 to 50 times faster. What the optimiser does Transformation What it means What you see in the debugger --- --- --- Register allocation Variables live in registers instead of on the stack "Variable is optimised away and not available" Inlining A small function's body is pasted into its caller; there is no call The function never appears in the Call Stack; breakpoints in it may not hit Constant folding Expressions with known values are computed at compile time int x = 60 60; becomes 3600 ; no multiplication in the code Dead code elimination Work whose result is never used is removed Breakpoints on those lines have nowhere to go Loop transformations Unrolling, moving invariant work out of loops, vectorising with SIMD instructions Stepping jumps around unpredictably Reordering Instructions are moved to keep the processor busy The yellow arrow seems to go backwards None of this changes what a correct program does. The C++ standard lets the compiler make any change whose effect on the program's visible behaviour cannot be detected, the as-if rule . Why some bugs only appear in Release The as-if rule only applies to programs without undefined behaviour. The optimiser is allowed to assume there is none, and it uses that assumption aggressively: - Uninitialised variables hold 0xCC filler in Debug, which is at least consistent. In Release they hold whatever was in that register or stack slot, which changes with unrelated code. - Signed overflow : the compiler may assume i + 1 i is always true for an int , and remove a check that relied on wrap-around. - Out-of-bounds reads : in Debug, the read gets the neighbouring variable; in Release, the neighbour may be in a register and the read gets something else. - Timing and threads : a variable shared between threads without synchronisation may be kept in a register in Release, so one thread never sees the other's change (chapter 6). And Debug builds hide bugs with their extra help: 0xCC fill, guard bytes, iterator checks and assert all vanish in Release, because NDEBUG is defined there. So when something "only breaks in Release", the answer is almost never "the optimiser has a bug". It is almost always undefined behaviour in your code that Debug happened to tolerate. AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10) and warnings at level 4 find most of these. Debugging an optimised build You can debug Release builds, and you sometimes must, because the bug only happens there. Make it easier: 1. Generate debug information in Release : C/C++ → General → Debug Information Format: Program Database (/Zi) and Linker → Debugging → Generate Debug Info: Yes . This costs nothing at run time; the .pdb is a separate file. 2. Keep optimisation on, but optionally add /Zo (enhanced optimised debugging, on by default in recent versions), which records where variables live in registers so more of them can be shown. 3. To debug one function without optimisation inside an optimised build, wrap it: cpp pragma optimize("", off) void suspiciousFunction() { // compiled without optimisation, so every variable is visible } pragma optimize("", on) Many studios use a third configuration for day-to-day work: optimised enough to run at a playable speed, with full debug information and asserts still enabled. In Visual Studio you can create it by copying Release in Configuration Manager and removing NDEBUG from its preprocessor definitions. The settings that differ Setting Debug Release --- --- --- Optimisation /Od (off) /O2 (speed) Runtime library /MDd (debug runtime) /MD _DEBUG / NDEBUG _DEBUG defined NDEBUG defined: assert does nothing Basic runtime checks /RTC1 : stack frame checks, uninitialised use Off Iterator debugging On ( _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL=2 ) Off Whole-program optimisation Off /GL and /LTCG : the linker can inline across files Incremental linking On (fast rebuilds) Off Common mistakes !warning Measuring performance in Debug Debug can be ten times slower, unevenly. Always measure speed in Release (chapter 17). !warning Putting real work inside assert assert(loadLevel(name)); loads the level in Debug and does nothing at all in Release. Do the work first, then assert on the result. !warning Blaming the optimiser Look for undefined behaviour first: uninitialised values, overruns, signed overflow, data races. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does the debugger say "variable is optimised away" in Release? + The optimiser kept the variable in a register, or removed it, so it has no fixed memory location to show - Release builds have no variables - The .pdb file is missing With /Zi the debugger can sometimes still find it in a register, but not always. ? A program works in Debug and crashes in Release. What is the most likely cause? - A bug in the compiler's optimiser + Undefined behaviour in the program, which Debug happened to tolerate - Release builds use less memory Uninitialised values, overruns and data races behave differently once code is optimised. ? What happens to assert(x 0); in a Release build? + It is removed entirely, because NDEBUG is defined - It still checks, but does not stop the program - It becomes a compile error Asserts are a Debug-only safety net. ? What does inlining do? + Replaces a call with a copy of the called function's body - Moves a function to a DLL - Makes a function inline in the header No call happens, which is faster and lets the optimiser work across the two.

title: 5.01  Handles and Kernel Objects
body:
Files, threads, processes, events and many other resources are kernel objects : they live inside the Windows kernel, and your program refers to them only through handles . This lesson explains what a handle is, the rules for getting and closing one, the two different "invalid" values, and how to wrap handles in an RAII class so they can never leak. Objects you cannot touch When a program opens a file, Windows creates a file object inside the kernel: a structure recording which file, the current position, the access rights granted, and more. That structure lives in kernel memory, which user-mode code cannot read (lesson 1.06). So instead of a pointer, the program gets a handle , a small number that identifies the object within this process. Every process has its own handle table . A handle value means nothing outside its process, just like a virtual address. When you pass the handle back to Windows, for example to ReadFile , the kernel looks it up in your table, checks the rights recorded there, and acts on the object. Many kinds of object work this way: Object Created by Used for --- --- --- File CreateFileW Reading and writing files, pipes, devices Thread CreateThread Running code in parallel (chapter 6) Process CreateProcessW , OpenProcess Starting programs, waiting for them (chapter 6) Event, mutex, semaphore CreateEventW , CreateMutexW , ... Synchronising threads (chapter 6) File mapping CreateFileMappingW Shared memory between processes (chapter 12) Windows also has window handles ( HWND ), GDI handles ( HBRUSH , HDC ) and module handles ( HMODULE ). They look similar but are managed by different parts of Windows and closed with different functions. This lesson is about kernel object handles, closed with CloseHandle . Getting and closing a handle cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { HANDLE ready{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr) }; // a manual-reset event, not yet signalled if (ready == nullptr) { std::cout << "CreateEventW failed: " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } SetEvent(ready); // signal it const DWORD result{ WaitForSingleObject(ready, 0) }; // is it signalled? (don't wait) std::cout << (result == WAIT_OBJECT_0 ? "the event is signalled" : "not signalled") << '
'; CloseHandle(ready); // give the handle back return 0; } the event is signalled The rules: 1. Every handle you open, you must close , exactly once, with the matching function. Kernel objects are reference-counted: the object is destroyed when its last handle is closed. 2. After closing, the value is meaningless. Windows reuses handle values, so a stale handle can end up referring to a different object, just like a dangling pointer (lesson 2.09). 3. When the process ends, Windows closes everything it left open. That is a safety net, not a plan: a game that leaks a handle per frame runs out within hours. Task Manager can show leaks: on the Details tab, right-click the column headers → Select columns → Handles . A number that keeps growing while the game runs is a handle leak. Two kinds of "invalid" A historical wart: failing functions do not all return the same value. Function Returns on failure --- --- CreateFileW INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (which is -1 ) CreateEventW , CreateThread , OpenProcess , most others nullptr (0) The documentation for each function says which. Checking for the wrong one is a classic bug: if (h == nullptr) after CreateFileW never catches a failure. An RAII wrapper Lesson 2.04's RAII idea is a perfect fit. A small class owns the handle and closes it in its destructor: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <utility class UniqueHandle { public: UniqueHandle() = default; explicit UniqueHandle(HANDLE h) : m_handle{ h } {} ~UniqueHandle() { reset(); } UniqueHandle(const UniqueHandle&) = delete; // one owner only UniqueHandle& operator=(const UniqueHandle&) = delete; UniqueHandle(UniqueHandle&& other) noexcept : m_handle{ std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr) } {} UniqueHandle& operator=(UniqueHandle&& other) noexcept { if (this != &other) { reset(); m_handle = std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr); } return this; } HANDLE get() const { return m_handle; } explicit operator bool() const { return m_handle != nullptr && m_handle != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE; } void reset() { if ( this) CloseHandle(m_handle); m_handle = nullptr; } private: HANDLE m_handle{ nullptr }; }; int main() { UniqueHandle event{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, TRUE, nullptr) }; if (!event) return 1; std::cout << (WaitForSingleObject(event.get(), 0) == WAIT_OBJECT_0) << '
'; return 0; } // closed here, on every path out of main 1 Treating both nullptr and INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as "no handle" makes the class safe whichever function produced the value. The Windows Implementation Libraries (WIL, available through vcpkg as wil ) provide polished versions of this for every handle type: wil::unique_handle , wil::unique_hfile , wil::unique_event . Common mistakes !warning Checking CreateFileW 's result against nullptr It returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure. Read each function's documentation. !warning Closing a handle twice The second CloseHandle may close an unrelated object that reused the value. Under a debugger, Windows raises an "invalid handle" exception for it. !warning Closing a window, module or GDI handle with CloseHandle They have their own functions: DestroyWindow , FreeLibrary , DeleteObject , ReleaseDC . !warning Copying a raw handle into two owners Only one should close it. If two parts of the program genuinely need their own handle, use DuplicateHandle . Knowledge check quiz ? What is a handle? + A per-process number that identifies a kernel object in that process's handle table - A pointer to the kernel object's memory - A global id shared by every process The object lives in kernel memory; the handle is how your process names it. ? What does CreateFileW return when it fails? - nullptr + INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE - 0 or -1, at random Most other creation functions return nullptr ; CreateFileW is one of the exceptions. ? A kernel object has two open handles. One is closed. What happens to the object? + Nothing yet: it is destroyed when its last handle is closed - It is destroyed immediately - The other handle becomes invalid Kernel objects are reference-counted. ? Why wrap handles in an RAII class? + So they are closed exactly once, automatically, on every path out of the scope - Because raw handles cannot be passed to Windows functions - To make them faster The destructor guarantees CloseHandle runs, even on early returns and exceptions.

title: An owner for any kind of handle
match: An owner for any kind of handle
body: Windows has many handle types, each closed by a different function. Write ScopedResource , an RAII owner that works for all of them: it holds a raw value of type void and a pointer to the function that closes it. - The constructor takes the value and the close function. The value nullptr and the value kInvalid (which stands in for INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE ) both mean "nothing owned". - The destructor calls the close function on the value, if something is owned. - release() gives up ownership without closing, returning the value. - reset() closes whatever is owned now and becomes empty. - get() returns the value; owns() says whether something is owned. - It can be moved (ownership passes to the new object, the old one becomes empty) but not copied. The tests use a pretend close function that counts calls, so this runs anywhere.

title: 5.02  Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
match: 5.02 Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
body:
The Windows API reports failure in several ways: a BOOL that is FALSE , a null or invalid handle, an HRESULT , or a status code. The details usually come from GetLastError . This lesson shows each pattern, how to turn an error number into a readable message, how HRESULT s are built, and how to read a Microsoft documentation page so you know which pattern a function uses. Three patterns 1. BOOL plus GetLastError. Many functions return BOOL (an int ): non-zero for success, FALSE (0) for failure. On failure, the reason is a number kept per thread, fetched with GetLastError() . cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { if (!DeleteFileW(L"C:\this\file\does\not\exist.txt")) { const DWORD error{ GetLastError() }; // read it straight away std::cout << "DeleteFileW failed with error " << error << '
'; } return 0; } DeleteFileW failed with error 3 Error 3 is ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND . GetLastError must be called immediately : almost any later API call, including some done inside std::cout , may overwrite it. 2. Handles plus GetLastError. Creation functions return nullptr or INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (lesson 5.01), and again GetLastError says why. 3. HRESULT. COM-based APIs (DirectX, the Windows shell, audio) return an HRESULT directly: a 32-bit code where negative means failure. Test them with the SUCCEEDED(hr) and FAILED(hr) macros, never with == 0 or != 0 , since some success codes are not zero. Turning a number into a message FormatMessageW looks up the text Windows has for an error code, in the user's language: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string std::wstring describeError(DWORD error) { wchar_t buffer{ nullptr }; const DWORD length{ FormatMessageW( FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM FORMAT_MESSAGE_IGNORE_INSERTS, nullptr, error, 0, reinterpret_cast<wchar_t (&buffer), 0, nullptr) }; std::wstring text{ length ? std::wstring(buffer, length) : L"unknown error" }; LocalFree(buffer); // FormatMessage allocated it while (!text.empty() && (text.back() == L'
' text.back() == L'')) text.pop_back(); return text; } int main() { HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(L"no_such_save.dat", GENERIC_READ, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (file == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { const DWORD error{ GetLastError() }; std::wcout << L"error " << error << L": " << describeError(error) << L'
'; } else CloseHandle(file); return 0; } error 2: The system cannot find the file specified. The ones you will meet most: Code Name Meaning --- --- --- 2 ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND No such file 3 ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND A folder in the path does not exist 5 ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED You do not have the rights (lesson 6.08) 6 ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE A closed or wrong handle 32 ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION Another program has the file open without sharing 87 ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER An argument is wrong 122 ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER The buffer you passed is too small: call again with a bigger one 126 ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND LoadLibrary could not find the DLL or one it depends on In the debugger, $err,hr in the Watch window shows the current value with its name (lesson 4.08), and Tools → Error Lookup decodes any number. Inside an HRESULT An HRESULT packs three fields into 32 bits: 31 30..27 26..16 15..0 ┌───┬───────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ S │ flags │ facility (11) │ code (16) │ └───┴───────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ S = 1: failure (so failures are negative as signed ints) - Severity (bit 31): 1 is failure. - Facility : which subsystem the code comes from, such as FACILITY_WIN32 (7) or FACILITY_DXGI . - Code : the error number within that facility. A Win32 error code can be wrapped as an HRESULT with HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(error) : error 2 becomes 0x80070002 . You will recognise that shape everywhere: 0x8007xxxx is "a Win32 error, number xxxx". Reading a documentation page Every function's page on Microsoft's site (search "CreateFileW function") has the same sections, and each answers a question you must ask: Section Answers --- --- Syntax The exact declaration, parameter types and annotations such as in , out , in, optional Parameters What each one means, what values are allowed, and whether null is accepted Return value What success and failure look like, and whether to call GetLastError Remarks The important details: threading rules, ownership of buffers, what to free and with what, common traps Requirements Which header to include, which .lib to link, which DLL implements it, and the oldest Windows version The Return value and Remarks sections are where most bugs are prevented. For example, CreateFileW 's Return value section says it returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure; ReadFile 's Remarks explain when it can succeed but read fewer bytes than asked. Many functions also follow a two-call pattern for variable-sized results: call once with a null or small buffer to learn the size needed (often failing with ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER ), allocate, then call again. Common mistakes !warning Calling GetLastError too late Store it in a variable on the very next line after the failing call. !warning Calling GetLastError after success Its value is only meaningful when the function reported failure. Some functions leave an old value there on success. !warning Testing an HRESULT with if (hr) S_FALSE is 1 and means success. Use SUCCEEDED and FAILED . Knowledge check quiz ? A function returns FALSE . How do you find out why? + Call GetLastError() immediately afterwards - Check errno - Look at the return value's bits Many Windows functions record the reason per thread, for GetLastError to read. ? What does 0x80070005 mean? + A failure HRESULT wrapping Win32 error 5, access denied - Success with a warning - Memory address 0x80070005 Severity bit set, facility 7 (Win32), code 5. ? Which section of a documentation page says whether to call GetLastError ? - Syntax + Return value - Requirements It describes what success and failure look like for that particular function. ? Why use FAILED(hr) instead of hr != 0 ? + Some success codes, such as S_FALSE , are not zero - HRESULT values are always negative - The comparison does not compile Only the severity bit separates success from failure.

title: Take an HRESULT apart
where: 5.02 Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
body: Write decode(hr) , which splits a 32-bit HRESULT value into its parts and returns them in an HrParts : - failed : true if bit 31 is set; - facility : bits 16 to 26 (11 bits); - code : bits 0 to 15. Then write fromWin32(error) , which builds the HRESULT that wraps a Win32 error code the way HRESULT_FROM_WIN32 does: 0 stays 0 (success); anything else becomes failure, facility 7, and the low 16 bits of the error as the code. decode(0x80070005) - failed, facility 7, code 5 decode(0x00000001) - not failed, facility 0, code 1 fromWin32(2) - 0x80070002 Work with the bits yourself: the Windows macros are not available here.

title: 5.03  Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
match: 5.03 Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
body: Most Windows API functions that take text exist twice: an A version for 8-bit "ANSI" strings and a W version for UTF-16 "wide" strings. Windows works in UTF-16 internally; the rest of the world, and most libraries, use UTF-8. This lesson explains the A/W split, why the course always calls the W functions, and how to convert between UTF-8 and UTF-16 at the edges of your program. Two versions of everything Look up CreateFile in the documentation and you find CreateFileA and CreateFileW . The same goes for MessageBox , LoadLibrary , GetModuleFileName and hundreds of others. Version Strings are C++ type Literal --- --- --- --- A ("ANSI") 8-bit, in the system's current code page char , std::string "text" W ("wide") UTF-16 wchar_t , std::wstring L"text" The plain name CreateFile is a macro that becomes CreateFileW when the project defines UNICODE (Visual Studio's default, "Use Unicode Character Set") and CreateFileA otherwise. The TCHAR type and TEXT("...") macro follow the same switch. They exist for code that once had to build both ways; new code does not need them. The W versions are the real ones. Windows has stored and processed text as UTF-16 since Windows NT. An A function converts your string to UTF-16 using the current code page (a table, such as Windows-1252 for Western Europe), calls the W function, and converts any results back. Characters that do not exist in that code page are lost, typically turned into ? . A player named Zoë or Сергей , or a save folder under a user name with such letters, breaks A-function code on many machines. So the rule for this course: call the W functions explicitly ( CreateFileW , MessageBoxW ), with std::wstring or L"..." strings. But the rest of the program uses UTF-8 Files, network protocols, JSON, most cross-platform libraries and your own source code use UTF-8 (lesson 2.08). So programs keep text as UTF-8 internally and convert to UTF-16 only when calling Windows. The conversion functions are MultiByteToWideChar and WideCharToMultiByte , using the two-call pattern from lesson 5.02: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string std::wstring widen(const std::string& utf8) { if (utf8.empty()) return {}; const int needed{ MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), static_cast<int (utf8.size()), nullptr, 0) }; std::wstring out(static_cast<std::size_t (needed), L'\0'); MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), static_cast<int (utf8.size()), out.data(), needed); return out; } std::string narrow(const std::wstring& utf16) { if (utf16.empty()) return {}; const int needed{ WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, 0, utf16.data(), static_cast<int (utf16.size()), nullptr, 0, nullptr, nullptr) }; std::string out(static_cast<std::size_t (needed), '\0'); WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, 0, utf16.data(), static_cast<int (utf16.size()), out.data(), needed, nullptr, nullptr); return out; } int main() { const std::string name{ "Zo\xC3\xAB" }; // "Zoë" in UTF-8: 4 bytes const std::wstring wide{ widen(name) }; // 3 UTF-16 units std::cout << name.size() << " UTF-8 bytes, " << wide.size() << " UTF-16 units\n"; std::cout << "round trip ok: " << (narrow(wide) == name) << '\n'; return 0; } 4 UTF-8 bytes, 3 UTF-16 units round trip ok: 1 These two small functions are worth keeping in your engine library. With them, the pattern is: UTF-8 everywhere in your code, widen() right before a W call, narrow() on anything Windows gives back. How UTF-8 and UTF-16 encode a character Knowing the encodings lets you recognise text in memory and write conversions yourself, which is this lesson's practice task. UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point. The first byte's high bits say how many bytes follow: Code points Bytes Pattern --- --- --- U+0000 to U+007F 1 0xxxxxxx U+0080 to U+07FF 2 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800 to U+FFFF 3 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000 to U+10FFFF 4 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx ë is U+00EB, binary 000 1110 1011 . In the 2-byte pattern that is 110 00011 10 101011 = C3 AB , the two bytes in the example. UTF-16 uses one 16-bit unit for code points up to U+FFFF. Anything above (most emoji, some rare scripts) is split into two units called a surrogate pair : subtract 0x10000, put the top 10 bits in a unit 0xD800 + top , and the bottom 10 bits in 0xDC00 + bottom . So even in UTF-16, one character can take two units. Telling Windows to use UTF-8 Since Windows 10 version 1903, an application can declare in its manifest that its A functions should use UTF-8 as the code page ( <activeCodePage UTF-8</activeCodePage ). That makes A functions safe for any text. It is a reasonable option for new programs, but calling W functions works on every version and makes the intent obvious, so the course sticks with W. The console is a separate matter: to print UTF-8 correctly in a console window, call SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) at start-up (lesson 5.09). Common mistakes !warning Calling A functions with UTF-8 Without the UTF-8 manifest, A functions interpret bytes in the current code page, garbling everything that is not ASCII. !warning Casting between char and wchar_t (LPCWSTR)"file.txt" compiles, and passes bytes that Windows reads as nonsense UTF-16. Convert with widen , or use L"..." literals. !warning Counting characters with size() UTF-8 bytes and UTF-16 units are not characters. std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size() is 2. !warning Mixing std::cout and std::wcout Using both on the same stream in one program leads to missing output. Pick one, or convert and use std::cout throughout. Knowledge check quiz ? What does CreateFileA do with its file name? + Converts it from the current code page to UTF-16, then calls CreateFileW - Uses it directly; Windows works in 8-bit text - Converts it to UTF-8 Windows works in UTF-16 internally; the A functions are converting wrappers. ? How many bytes does UTF-8 use for the character é (U+00E9)? - 1 + 2 - 4 U+0080 to U+07FF take two bytes in UTF-8. ? A program keeps all its text as UTF-8. What should it do to open a file whose name the user typed? + Convert the name to UTF-16 with MultiByteToWideChar and call CreateFileW - Call CreateFileA with the UTF-8 bytes - Cast the char to wchar_t Convert at the boundary, then call the W function. ? Why can std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size() be 2? + The emoji is above U+FFFF, so UTF-16 needs a surrogate pair of two units - Wide strings always store two units per character - Because of the terminating zero Only code points up to U+FFFF fit in one UTF-16 unit.

title: UTF-8 to UTF-16 by hand
where: 5.03 Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
body: Write toUtf16(utf8) , which converts UTF-8 text into UTF-16 units, the job MultiByteToWideChar does. Use std::u16string so the code works on any platform. Decode each character from its UTF-8 bytes (1 to 4 of them, using the table in the lesson) into a code point, then encode the code point as UTF-16: - code points up to U+FFFF become one unit; - code points from U+10000 to U+10FFFF become a surrogate pair: subtract 0x10000, then the high unit is 0xD800 + (value 10) and the low unit 0xDC00 + (value & 0x3FF) . If the input is not valid UTF-8 (a byte that cannot start a character, a sequence cut short, or a continuation byte that does not start with the bits 10 ), return std::nullopt .

title: 5.04  Files and Directories
body:
Games read assets and configuration and write save files and logs. This lesson uses the Windows file API directly ( CreateFileW , ReadFile , WriteFile ), shows where a game should keep its files, how to list a directory, how to save without ever leaving a half-written file, and when the portable std::filesystem and std::fstream are the better choice. Opening a file Every file operation starts with CreateFileW , which both creates new files and opens existing ones despite its name: cpp HANDLE file{ CreateFileW( L"settings.ini", // path GENERIC_READ, // what you want to do: GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE or both FILE_SHARE_READ, // what others may do while you have it open nullptr, // security attributes: default OPEN_EXISTING, // what to do if it exists or not (see below) FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, // flags nullptr) }; // template file: unused The creation disposition decides what happens depending on whether the file exists: Value If it exists If it does not --- --- --- OPEN_EXISTING Open it Fail (error 2) CREATE_NEW Fail (error 80) Create it CREATE_ALWAYS Truncate it to empty Create it OPEN_ALWAYS Open it Create it TRUNCATE_EXISTING Truncate it Fail The share mode is often overlooked. It says what other handles may do to the file while yours is open. With 0 , no one else can even read it, and they get ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION (32). That is why a game that holds its log file open with share mode 0 stops you viewing the log while it runs. Reading and writing cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string include <vector int main() { wchar_t tempDir MAX_PATH {}; GetTempPathW(MAX_PATH, tempDir); const std::wstring path{ std::wstring{ tempDir } + L"xenon_demo_save.txt" }; // Write HANDLE out{ CreateFileW(path.c_str(), GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, CREATE_ALWAYS, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (out == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { std::cout << "create failed " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } const std::string text{ "level=4
gold=1250
" }; DWORD written{ 0 }; WriteFile(out, text.data(), static_cast<DWORD (text.size()), &written, nullptr); CloseHandle(out); // Read it back HANDLE in{ CreateFileW(path.c_str(), GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (in == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { std::cout << "open failed " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } LARGE_INTEGER size{}; GetFileSizeEx(in, &size); std::vector<char buffer(static_cast<std::size_t (size.QuadPart)); DWORD read{ 0 }; ReadFile(in, buffer.data(), static_cast<DWORD (buffer.size()), &read, nullptr); CloseHandle(in); DeleteFileW(path.c_str()); std::cout << "wrote " << written << " bytes, read " << read << ":
" << std::string(buffer.data(), read); return 0; } wrote 18 bytes, read 18: level=4 gold=1250 Note the DWORD out parameters: WriteFile and ReadFile report how many bytes they actually moved. A ReadFile that returns success with read == 0 means end of file. A read can also return fewer bytes than asked (for pipes and network files especially), so code that needs an exact amount loops until it has it. Where a game should put its files The folder the .exe is in ( C:\Program Files\... ) is read-only for normal users. Writing saves there fails with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED , or worse, gets silently redirected by compatibility shims. Windows provides per-user folders, found with SHGetKnownFolderPath : Folder Known folder id Typical path For --- --- --- --- Saved Games FOLDERID_SavedGames C:\Users
ame\Saved Games Save files Local AppData FOLDERID_LocalAppData C:\Users
ame\AppData\Local Settings, caches, logs Roaming AppData FOLDERID_RoamingAppData ...\AppData\Roaming Settings that follow the user between PCs on a domain Documents FOLDERID_Documents C:\Users
ame\Documents Things the user made and wants to find, such as screenshots cpp include <shlobj.h pragma comment(lib, "shell32.lib") std::wstring savedGamesFolder() { PWSTR path{ nullptr }; std::wstring result; if (SUCCEEDED(SHGetKnownFolderPath(FOLDERID_SavedGames, 0, nullptr, &path))) result = path; CoTaskMemFree(path); // the documentation says to free it this way return result + L"\MyGame"; } Saving safely If the game crashes, or the power goes, halfway through writing a save file, the player loses their save. The standard technique: write to a temporary file, then replace the real one in a single step . 1. Write the whole save to slot1.sav.tmp . 2. Call FlushFileBuffers and close it, so the data is on disk. 3. MoveFileExW(L"slot1.sav.tmp", L"slot1.sav", MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH) , or ReplaceFileW . At every moment, either the old complete save or the new complete save is on disk, never a broken mixture. Listing a directory cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { WIN32_FIND_DATAW entry{}; HANDLE find{ FindFirstFileW(L"C:\Windows\ .exe", &entry) }; if (find == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) return 1; int count{ 0 }; do { if (!(entry.dwFileAttributes & FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY)) ++count; } while (FindNextFileW(find, &entry)); FindClose(find); // not CloseHandle: find handles have their own close function std::cout << "found " << (count 0 ? "some" : "no") << " programs
"; return 0; } found some programs The portable alternative For ordinary game files, the C++ standard library is simpler and works on every platform: cpp include <filesystem include <fstream namespace fs = std::filesystem; for (const auto& entry : fs::directory_iterator{ "levels" }) if (entry.path().extension() == ".lvl") loadLevel(entry.path()); std::ofstream log{ fs::path{ "logs" } / "game.log", std::ios::app }; On Windows, std::filesystem::path stores UTF-16 internally and calls the W functions, so it handles any characters correctly. Use the Windows API directly when you need what the standard library does not expose: share modes, overlapped (asynchronous) I/O, memory-mapped files (chapter 12), file change notifications, or exact error codes. Common mistakes !warning Writing next to the .exe It works on your machine because you are an administrator or the game is in your own folder. On players' machines it fails. Use Saved Games or AppData. !warning Overwriting a save in place A crash mid-write destroys it. Write a temporary file and replace atomically. !warning Share mode 0 on files others need to read Logs and config files should usually allow FILE_SHARE_READ . !warning Assuming one ReadFile reads everything Check the bytes-read count, and loop when you need an exact amount. Knowledge check quiz ? Which creation disposition opens a file if it exists and creates it if not? - CREATE_ALWAYS + OPEN_ALWAYS - OPEN_EXISTING CREATE_ALWAYS also creates when missing, but truncates an existing file to empty. ? Another program cannot open your game's log while the game runs, getting error 32. Why? + The game opened the file with a share mode that does not allow reading - The log file is too large - Windows locks all files a game opens Error 32 is a sharing violation: the existing handle's share mode forbids it. ? Why should save files not be written to the game's installation folder? + Under Program Files it is read-only for normal users - Windows deletes files there on restart - It is slower Use the per-user Saved Games or AppData folders. ? How do you update a save file so a crash can never leave it half-written? + Write a temporary file completely, then replace the real file with it in one step - Write the new save in small pieces - Delete the old file first, then write the new one The move or replace is atomic: the file is always either the old version or the new one.

title: Split a Windows path
body: Write splitPath(path) , which splits a Windows file path into its folder, its file name without the extension, and its extension, the way a game might when deciding where to put a backup or which loader to use. - The folder is everything before the last \ or / (either separator may appear), without that separator. If there is no separator, the folder is empty. - The extension is everything from the last . in the file-name part onwards, including the dot. A dot at the very start of the file name (as in .gitignore ) does not start an extension. No dot means no extension. - The stem is the file-name part without the extension. C:\Games\Save\slot1.sav - "C:\Games\Save", "slot1", ".sav" levels/forest.v2.lvl - "levels", "forest.v2", ".lvl" README - "", "README", "" C:\Users\.config - "C:\Users", ".config", ""

title: 5.05  Windows and the Message Loop
body: A Windows program with a window does not ask "has a key been pressed?". Windows tells it, by putting messages in a queue that the program reads in a message loop and hands to a window procedure . This lesson explains window classes, messages, the loop, and the variant games use so they can keep rendering when no messages arrive. Event-driven programs A console program runs top to bottom and asks for input when it wants it. A windowed program is the other way round: it sits waiting, and the operating system sends it events : a key was pressed, the mouse moved, the window was resized, the window needs repainting, the user clicked Close. Windows delivers these as messages . Each message is a small structure: cpp struct MSG { HWND hwnd; // which window it is for UINT message; // what happened: WM_KEYDOWN, WM_MOUSEMOVE, WM_PAINT, ... WPARAM wParam; // extra information, meaning depends on the message LPARAM lParam; // more extra information DWORD time; POINT pt; }; Every thread that creates a window gets a message queue . Windows appends messages to it; the program takes them out one at a time. Window classes and the window procedure Before creating a window you register a window class : a template naming, among other things, the window procedure , the function Windows calls for every message to windows of that class. It is a callback (lesson 3.04): you give Windows a function pointer, and Windows calls it. cpp LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT message, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (message) { case WM_KEYDOWN: if (wParam == VK_ESCAPE) DestroyWindow(hwnd); // Esc closes the window return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); // ask the message loop to end return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, message, wParam, lParam); // default handling for everything else } The switch handles the messages the program cares about. Everything else must go to DefWindowProcW , which implements the standard behaviour: moving the window when its title bar is dragged, resizing, the system menu, closing on Alt+F4. A window procedure that returns 0 for everything produces a window that cannot be moved or closed. The message loop cpp MSG msg{}; while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { TranslateMessage(&msg); // turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages for typed text DispatchMessageW(&msg); // calls the window procedure of msg.hwnd } - GetMessageW takes the next message from the queue, waiting if it is empty. It returns 0 when it finds WM_QUIT , which PostQuitMessage puts in the queue, and -1 on error. - DispatchMessageW looks up the window's class and calls its window procedure. That is the whole skeleton of every classic Windows program: register a class, create a window, loop until WM_QUIT . The next lesson writes a complete one. Some messages skip the queue entirely: Windows calls the window procedure directly for them (they are "sent" rather than "posted"), for example WM_CREATE during CreateWindowExW and WM_SIZE during resizing. So a window procedure can be called from inside other API calls, not only from DispatchMessageW . Messages you will handle most Message Sent when Useful data --- --- --- WM_CREATE The window is being created WM_DESTROY The window is being destroyed Post WM_QUIT here WM_CLOSE The user asked to close (X button, Alt+F4) Ask "save first?" here, or call DestroyWindow WM_PAINT Part of the window needs redrawing Use BeginPaint / EndPaint WM_SIZE The client area changed size New width and height in lParam WM_KEYDOWN , WM_KEYUP A key went down or up Virtual-key code in wParam (lesson 5.07) WM_CHAR Text was typed (after TranslateMessage ) The UTF-16 character in wParam WM_MOUSEMOVE , WM_LBUTTONDOWN , ... Mouse movement and buttons Coordinates in lParam (lesson 5.07) WM_TIMER A timer set with SetTimer fired Timer id in wParam WM_ACTIVATE The window gained or lost focus Pause the game when it loses focus The game loop variant GetMessageW waits when there are no messages. A game cannot wait: it must update and draw 60 or more times a second whether or not the player touches anything. Games use PeekMessageW , which returns immediately, and run a frame whenever the queue is empty: cpp bool running{ true }; while (running) { MSG msg{}; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) // handle everything waiting... { if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } if (!running) break; updateGame(); // ...then run one frame renderGame(); } Draining all waiting messages each frame, not just one, keeps input responsive and the window behaving normally. Chapter 10 builds the full game loop with proper timing around this. Common mistakes !warning Not calling DefWindowProcW for unhandled messages The window cannot be moved, resized or closed normally. !warning Forgetting PostQuitMessage in WM_DESTROY The window disappears but the message loop keeps waiting, and the process keeps running invisibly. Check Task Manager. !warning Long work inside the window procedure While it runs, no other messages are handled, and after a few seconds Windows marks the window "Not Responding". Do slow work elsewhere, or in steps. !warning Using GetMessageW in a game The game only updates when a message arrives, such as when the mouse moves. Use PeekMessageW . Knowledge check quiz ? What does DispatchMessageW do? + Calls the window procedure of the window the message is for - Puts a message in the queue - Translates key presses into characters It finds the window's class and calls the function registered for it. ? A program's window closes but the process keeps running. What is the most likely cause? + WM_DESTROY does not call PostQuitMessage , so the message loop never ends - DefWindowProcW was called - The window class was not registered The loop keeps waiting for messages for a window that no longer exists. ? Why do games use PeekMessageW instead of GetMessageW ? + PeekMessageW returns immediately when the queue is empty, so the game can run a frame instead of waiting - PeekMessageW is faster at reading messages - GetMessageW does not work with games A game must update continuously, not only when messages arrive. ? What should a window procedure do with a message it does not handle? + Pass it to DefWindowProcW and return its result - Return 0 - Ignore it and return 1 The default procedure implements the standard window behaviour.

title: 5.06  A First Win32 Application
body: Put the last lesson together into a complete windowed program: wWinMain , registering a class, creating a window, a game-style loop, and drawing a moving square with GDI using a back buffer so it does not flicker. About 120 lines of plain Windows API, and every one explained. The project In Visual Studio, create a new Windows Desktop Application project (not Console App), or change an existing project's Linker → System → SubSystem to Windows (/SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS) . A Windows-subsystem program has no console, and starts at wWinMain instead of main . This program cannot run on the course website, which runs console programs only. Build it in Visual Studio. The whole program cpp include <windows.h // ---------- the game state ---------- struct Game { float x{ 100.0f }, y{ 100.0f }; // square position, in pixels float vx{ 180.0f }, vy{ 120.0f }; // velocity, in pixels per second int width{ 640 }, height{ 360 }; // client area size }; static Game g_game; // ---------- drawing ---------- static void render(HWND hwnd) { HDC screen{ GetDC(hwnd) }; // Draw into an off-screen bitmap first, then copy it to the window in one go: no flicker. HDC back{ CreateCompatibleDC(screen) }; HBITMAP bitmap{ CreateCompatibleBitmap(screen, g_game.width, g_game.height) }; HGDIOBJ oldBitmap{ SelectObject(back, bitmap) }; RECT all{ 0, 0, g_game.width, g_game.height }; HBRUSH background{ CreateSolidBrush(RGB(18, 20, 26)) }; FillRect(back, &all, background); DeleteObject(background); RECT square{ static_cast<LONG (g_game.x), static_cast<LONG (g_game.y), static_cast<LONG (g_game.x) + 40, static_cast<LONG (g_game.y) + 40 }; HBRUSH teal{ CreateSolidBrush(RGB(95, 211, 196)) }; FillRect(back, &square, teal); DeleteObject(teal); BitBlt(screen, 0, 0, g_game.width, g_game.height, back, 0, 0, SRCCOPY); SelectObject(back, oldBitmap); // put the original back before deleting DeleteObject(bitmap); DeleteDC(back); ReleaseDC(hwnd, screen); } // ---------- updating ---------- static void update(float dt) { g_game.x += g_game.vx dt; g_game.y += g_game.vy dt; if (g_game.x < 0 g_game.x + 40 g_game.width) g_game.vx = -g_game.vx; // bounce if (g_game.y < 0 g_game.y + 40 g_game.height) g_game.vy = -g_game.vy; } // ---------- messages ---------- static LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT message, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (message) { case WM_SIZE: g_game.width = LOWORD(lParam); g_game.height = HIWORD(lParam); return 0; case WM_KEYDOWN: if (wParam == VK_ESCAPE) DestroyWindow(hwnd); return 0; case WM_ERASEBKGND: return 1; // we paint everything ourselves: skip the default erase (less flicker) case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, message, wParam, lParam); } // ---------- start-up and the loop ---------- int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE instance, HINSTANCE, PWSTR, int showCommand) { WNDCLASSEXW wc{}; wc.cbSize = sizeof(wc); wc.lpfnWndProc = WindowProc; // the callback wc.hInstance = instance; // this program's module wc.hCursor = LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_ARROW); wc.lpszClassName = L"XenonWindow"; if (!RegisterClassExW(&wc)) return 1; RECT size{ 0, 0, 640, 360 }; // the client area we want... AdjustWindowRect(&size, WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, FALSE); // ...grown to include borders and title bar HWND hwnd{ CreateWindowExW(0, wc.lpszClassName, L"Bouncing square", WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, size.right - size.left, size.bottom - size.top, nullptr, nullptr, instance, nullptr) }; if (!hwnd) return 1; ShowWindow(hwnd, showCommand); LARGE_INTEGER frequency{}, previous{}, now{}; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&frequency); // ticks per second of the high-resolution clock QueryPerformanceCounter(&previous); bool running{ true }; while (running) { MSG msg{}; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) { if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } if (!running) break; QueryPerformanceCounter(&now); const float dt{ static_cast<float (now.QuadPart - previous.QuadPart) / static_cast<float (frequency.QuadPart) }; previous = now; update(dt); render(hwnd); Sleep(1); // be polite to the CPU; chapter 10 does timing properly } return 0; } Walking through it Start-up. wWinMain receives the program's HINSTANCE (the address its .exe was loaded at, lesson 4.05's HMODULE ) and how the window should first appear. It fills in a WNDCLASSEXW , registers it, and creates one window of that class. AdjustWindowRect matters: the size passed to CreateWindowExW includes the title bar and borders, so without it the drawable client area would be smaller than 640 by 360. Time. QueryPerformanceCounter reads a high-resolution clock, typically ticking 10 million times a second. The difference between two readings, divided by the frequency, is the elapsed time in seconds. Moving by velocity × dt makes the square move at the same speed on a fast PC and a slow one, a theme chapter 10 develops. Drawing. GDI (the Graphics Device Interface) is Windows' original 2D drawing API. It is slow by modern standards but simple and always available. Every GDI object you create ( CreateSolidBrush , CreateCompatibleBitmap , CreateCompatibleDC ) must be deleted, and an object selected into a device context must be deselected before it is deleted: that is the oldBitmap dance. Handle leaks here show up in Task Manager's GDI objects column and eventually stop the program drawing at all. Double buffering. Drawing the background and then the square directly onto the window would briefly show the empty background each frame: flicker. Drawing both into an off-screen bitmap and copying it to the window with one BitBlt means the window only ever shows complete frames. What a real game does differently This program is the skeleton every Windows game has underneath. Real games replace the GDI drawing with a GPU API (Direct3D, Vulkan or OpenGL) and usually use a library such as SDL to create the window and read input, which chapter 11 does. But the window class, the message loop and the timing are the same ideas, and when something goes wrong at that level (a window that will not close, input that stops, a frame-rate collapse when the window is dragged) this is the code you will be debugging. Common mistakes !warning Building as a console application The linker complains that main is missing. Set SubSystem to Windows, or create the project from the Windows Desktop Application template. !warning Creating GDI objects every frame without deleting them The program runs out of GDI handles (10,000 per process by default) and stops drawing. Delete each one, or create them once at start-up. !warning Sizing the window instead of the client area Use AdjustWindowRect so the drawable area is the size you intended. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does the program call AdjustWindowRect before CreateWindowExW ? + The size given to CreateWindowExW includes the borders and title bar, so it must be enlarged to leave a 640 by 360 client area - To centre the window on the screen - To make the window resizable The client area is the drawable part inside the frame. ? What does drawing into an off-screen bitmap and copying it with BitBlt prevent? + Flicker, because the window never shows a half-drawn frame - Memory leaks - The window becoming unresponsive This technique is called double buffering. ? Why does the square move by velocity dt ? + So it moves at the same speed in seconds whatever the frame rate - Because GDI requires it - To make it bounce A fixed step per frame would make it faster on faster computers.

title: 5.07  Keyboard, Mouse and Timers
body: Input arrives as messages whose details are packed into wParam and lParam . This lesson unpacks them: virtual-key codes, the bits of a key message, typed characters, mouse coordinates and buttons, and when to read the keyboard's current state instead. It ends with timers and the high-resolution clock that games use for timing. Keys: messages and virtual-key codes When a key goes down, the window with keyboard focus receives WM_KEYDOWN ; when it comes up, WM_KEYUP . (Alt combinations and F10 arrive as WM_SYSKEYDOWN and WM_SYSKEYUP instead.) wParam holds a virtual-key code : a number for the key, independent of keyboard layout. Key Code --- --- Letters 'A' to 'Z' (0x41 to 0x5A): the upper-case letter, whatever the shift state Digits (top row) '0' to '9' (0x30 to 0x39) Arrows VK_LEFT , VK_UP , VK_RIGHT , VK_DOWN Space, Enter, Escape, Tab VK_SPACE , VK_RETURN , VK_ESCAPE , VK_TAB Shift, Ctrl, Alt VK_SHIFT , VK_CONTROL , VK_MENU (or VK_LSHIFT , VK_RCONTROL ... for one side) F1 to F12 VK_F1 to VK_F12 The bits in lParam A key message's lParam packs several facts into 32 bits: 31 30 29 28..25 24 23..16 15..0 ┌────┬────┬────┬───────┬────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ up │was │alt │ │ext │ scan code (8) │ repeat count │ │ │down│ │ │ │ │ (16) │ └────┴────┴────┴───────┴────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ Bits Meaning --- --- 0 to 15 Repeat count : how many auto-repeats this message stands for 16 to 23 Scan code : the physical key's position, independent of layout 24 Extended key (right-hand Ctrl and Alt, the arrow block) 30 Previous state : 1 if the key was already down before this message 31 Transition: 0 for key down, 1 for key up Bit 30 is the useful one for games. Holding a key generates a stream of WM_KEYDOWN messages (auto-repeat). If "jump" should happen once per press, ignore messages where bit 30 is set: cpp case WM_KEYDOWN: { const bool repeat{ (lParam & (1 << 30)) != 0 }; if (wParam == VK_SPACE && !repeat) jump(); return 0; } Reading bit fields like this, with shifts and masks, is exactly lesson 1.02's material applied, and you will do it constantly in low-level code. The practice task is a set of these decoders. Typed text: WM_CHAR For text entry (a player name, a chat box, a debug console) do not use WM_KEYDOWN : it knows nothing about Shift, Caps Lock, dead keys or the user's keyboard layout. TranslateMessage in the message loop turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages whose wParam is the actual UTF-16 character typed, 'a' , 'A' , 'é' or 'Ж' as appropriate. Use Message --- --- Game controls (move, jump, fire) WM_KEYDOWN / WM_KEYUP , or the current state Typing text WM_CHAR Polling the current state Sometimes you want to ask "is W held down right now?" rather than track every message. GetAsyncKeyState(vk) answers: its top bit ( 0x8000 ) is set when the key is currently down. cpp if (GetAsyncKeyState('W') & 0x8000) player.y -= speed dt; Games often combine both: messages for discrete events (a press that toggles a menu), and either polling or a key-state array kept up to date from the messages for continuous movement. GetAsyncKeyState reports keys even when your window is not focused, so check focus ( WM_ACTIVATE ) before acting on it. The mouse Mouse messages put the cursor position, in client-area coordinates , in lParam : x in the low 16 bits, y in the high 16 bits, both signed (they can be negative when the mouse is captured and dragged outside the window). cpp include <windowsx.h // GET_X_LPARAM, GET_Y_LPARAM case WM_MOUSEMOVE: { const int x{ GET_X_LPARAM(lParam) }; const int y{ GET_Y_LPARAM(lParam) }; const bool leftHeld{ (wParam & MK_LBUTTON) != 0 }; aimAt(x, y, leftHeld); return 0; } Do not use LOWORD and HIWORD for coordinates: they are unsigned, so -1 becomes 65535. GET_X_LPARAM casts to short first. Message Meaning --- --- WM_MOUSEMOVE The cursor moved WM_LBUTTONDOWN / UP , WM_RBUTTON... , WM_MBUTTON... Buttons WM_MOUSEWHEEL Wheel turned: amount in the high word of wParam , in multiples of WHEEL_DELTA (120) wParam flags MK_LBUTTON , MK_RBUTTON , MK_SHIFT , MK_CONTROL : what is held during the message For first-person camera controls, cursor positions are the wrong tool: the cursor stops at the screen edge. Games use raw input ( RegisterRawInputDevices and WM_INPUT ), which reports the mouse's actual movement without acceleration or edge limits. Timers and clocks SetTimer(hwnd, id, milliseconds, nullptr) posts WM_TIMER every so often. It is fine for "autosave every five minutes" or blinking a cursor. It is not precise: messages only arrive when the queue is checked, and the default resolution is about 15.6 ms. For anything to do with frame timing, use the high-resolution performance counter , as lesson 5.06 did: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { LARGE_INTEGER frequency{}, start{}, end{}; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&frequency); QueryPerformanceCounter(&start); volatile double sink{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1'000'000; ++i) sink = sink + i 0.5; // something to time QueryPerformanceCounter(&end); const double ms{ 1000.0 static_cast<double (end.QuadPart - start.QuadPart) / static_cast<double (frequency.QuadPart) }; std::cout << "frequency is " << (frequency.QuadPart 0 ? "positive" : "zero") << ", took " << (ms = 0 ? "a measurable" : "a negative") << " time\n"; return 0; } frequency is positive, took a measurable time (The example prints words instead of numbers because the actual times differ on every machine.) std::chrono::steady_clock uses the same counter on Windows and is the portable choice. Common mistakes !warning Using WM_KEYDOWN for text input It ignores Shift, layout and accents. Use WM_CHAR . !warning Acting on every auto-repeat Check bit 30 of lParam for one-shot actions. !warning LOWORD(lParam) for mouse coordinates Negative coordinates become huge positive numbers. Use GET_X_LPARAM and GET_Y_LPARAM . !warning Timing frames with SetTimer or GetTickCount Both are too coarse. Use QueryPerformanceCounter or std::chrono::steady_clock . Knowledge check quiz ? A key held down produces many WM_KEYDOWN messages. How do you tell the first one from the repeats? + Bit 30 of lParam is 0 for the first and 1 for repeats - The repeat count is always 0 for the first - wParam changes for repeats Bit 30 records whether the key was already down. ? The player types é . Which message carries that character? - WM_KEYDOWN + WM_CHAR - WM_MOUSEMOVE TranslateMessage turns key presses into characters according to the keyboard layout. ? Why use GET_X_LPARAM instead of LOWORD for a mouse x coordinate? + It treats the 16 bits as signed, so negative coordinates come out correctly - It is faster - LOWORD gives the y coordinate Coordinates can be negative while the mouse is captured outside the window. ? Which is the right clock for measuring frame times? - SetTimer - GetTickCount + QueryPerformanceCounter (or std::chrono::steady_clock ) It has sub-microsecond resolution; the others are about 15 ms coarse.

title: Unpack the input messages
body: Window messages pack several values into wParam and lParam . Write the decoders a window procedure needs. Treat lParam as the 64-bit value it is on x64, but only its low 32 bits matter here. - mouseX(lParam) and mouseY(lParam) : the low 16 bits and the next 16 bits, each read as a signed 16-bit number. - repeatCount(lParam) : bits 0 to 15 of a key message. - scanCode(lParam) : bits 16 to 23. - isRepeat(lParam) : true if bit 30 is set. - isKeyUp(lParam) : true if bit 31 is set. - wheelSteps(wParam) : the high 16 bits of the low 32 bits of wParam as a signed number, divided by 120 (one notch of the wheel). mouseX(0x00C80064) = 100, mouseY(0x00C80064) = 200 mouseX(0x0000FFFF) = -1 repeatCount(0x40150001) = 1, scanCode(...) = 0x15, isRepeat(...) = true wheelSteps(0xFF880000) = -1

title: 5.08  Loading Libraries at Run Time
body:
Lesson 4.05 loaded a DLL of your own. This lesson looks at the loader's side: the search order Windows uses to find a DLL, why that order is a security risk and how to restrict it, finding modules that are already loaded, getting a module's file path, using functions that only exist on newer versions of Windows, and delay loading . Where Windows looks for a DLL When a program calls LoadLibraryW(L"plugin.dll") with a bare file name, or when its import table lists plugin.dll , the loader searches a sequence of places. For a normal desktop application the standard search order, simplified, is: 1. DLLs already loaded in the process with that name, and a list of known DLLs (core system DLLs that always come from the system folder). 2. The folder the application's .exe is in. 3. The system folder, C:\Windows\System32 . 4. The Windows folder. 5. The current working directory . 6. Each folder on the PATH environment variable. The first match wins. This is why putting your DLLs next to your .exe (lesson 4.01's shared output folder) works. The risk: loading the wrong DLL A search order is also an attack surface. If an attacker can put a file with the right name in a folder that is searched before the real one, your program loads their code with your program's rights. This is called DLL search-order hijacking (or "DLL planting"), and it has affected many real applications. The current directory (step 5) and PATH (step 6) are the classic weak points: a double-clicked document can make its own folder the current directory. Defend your programs: Defence How --- --- Remove the current directory and other unsafe locations from the search for the whole process Call SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) at the very start of main Search only the system folder for system DLLs LoadLibraryExW(L"bcrypt.dll", nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32) Load your own DLLs by full path Build the path from the .exe 's folder (below) and pass it to LoadLibraryExW Do not load DLLs from folders ordinary users can write to Especially for anything that runs with administrator rights This matters for the plugin system in chapter 13: a game that loads every .dll in a mods folder is, by design, running code from that folder, so the folder's location and permissions are part of the design. Finding the program's own folder cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string std::wstring exeFolder() { std::wstring path(MAX_PATH, L'\0'); for (;;) { const DWORD length{ GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, path.data(), static_cast<DWORD (path.size())) }; if (length == 0) return {}; if (length < path.size()) { path.resize(length); break; } path.resize(path.size() 2); // truncated: try a bigger buffer } return path.substr(0, path.find_last_of(L"\/")); } int main() { const std::wstring folder{ exeFolder() }; std::cout << "found the program's folder: " << (folder.empty() ? "no" : "yes") << '
'; return 0; } found the program's folder: yes GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, ...) gives the path of the .exe ; passing a DLL's HMODULE instead gives that DLL's path. It does not report how much space it needed; it truncates silently and returns the buffer size, hence the loop. Modules that are already loaded GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll") returns the HMODULE of a DLL that is already loaded, without loading it or changing its reference count. GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) returns the .exe 's own module, the same value as wWinMain 's HINSTANCE . An HMODULE is simply the address where the module's image starts in memory, which is why chapter 9 can read a loaded module's headers directly from it. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { HMODULE kernel{ GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll") }; HMODULE self{ GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) }; std::cout << "kernel32 is loaded: " << (kernel != nullptr) << '
'; std::cout << "the exe's first two bytes: " << static_cast<const char (static_cast<const void (self)) 0 << static_cast<const char (static_cast<const void (self)) 1 << '
'; return 0; } kernel32 is loaded: 1 the exe's first two bytes: MZ Every executable and DLL starts with the letters MZ , the signature of its header. Chapter 9 starts there. Using newer functions when they exist A game may want a function that only exists on newer versions of Windows, while still running on older ones. Linking to it normally would stop the game starting at all on an older system (the loader fails on the missing import). Look it up at run time instead: cpp using SetThreadDescriptionFn = HRESULT (WINAPI )(HANDLE, PCWSTR); void nameThisThread(const wchar_t name) { auto fn{ reinterpret_cast<SetThreadDescriptionFn ( GetProcAddress(GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll"), "SetThreadDescription")) }; if (fn) fn(GetCurrentThread(), name); // shown in the debugger's Threads window (chapter 8) } Delay loading Delay loading is a linker feature that gives you run-time loading with normal-looking calls. Add a DLL to Linker → Input → Delay Loaded Dlls and link its import library as usual. The linker replaces each import with a small stub; the first call to any function in that DLL loads it then. If the DLL never gets used (an optional feature the player never turns on), it is never loaded, and the program still starts when it is missing. Common mistakes !warning Loading DLLs by bare name from a program with high privileges Use full paths and SetDefaultDllDirectories . Search-order hijacking is a real attack. !warning Calling FreeLibrary on a handle from GetModuleHandleW GetModuleHandleW does not increase the reference count, so freeing it can unload a DLL that something else still uses. !warning Assuming GetModuleFileNameW fits in MAX_PATH Long paths are possible. Check the returned length and grow the buffer. Knowledge check quiz ? Why is the current working directory in the DLL search order a security risk? + An attacker who controls that folder can place a DLL with the right name there, and the program loads it - It makes loading slower - The current directory is always read-only This is DLL search-order hijacking. ? What does GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) return? + The module handle (load address) of the program's own .exe - A handle to the current thread - Null It is the same value as the HINSTANCE given to wWinMain . ? A game wants to use a function that only exists on Windows 11 but still start on Windows 10.
