What should it do? + Look the function up with GetProcAddress at run time and use it only if found - Link to it normally - Copy the function's code into the game A normal import of a missing function stops the program from starting at all. ? What does delay loading do? + Loads a DLL the first time one of its functions is called, instead of at start-up - Loads DLLs in the background - Delays the program's start until all DLLs are found Unused DLLs are never loaded, and a missing optional DLL does not stop the program starting.

title: 5.09  The Console API
body:
The console window is more than a place for std::cout . With the console API and virtual terminal sequences you can move the cursor, use colours, hide the cursor, read individual key presses and redraw a whole screen without flicker: enough for a text-mode game or a live tool display. This lesson covers both the classic API and the modern escape sequences. Handles to the console A console program has three standard handles, fetched with GetStdHandle : Handle For --- --- STD_INPUT_HANDLE Keyboard and mouse input STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE Text output STD_ERROR_HANDLE Error output They are like file handles (lesson 5.01): WriteFile works on the output handle. But the console also has its own functions that understand it as a grid of character cells with colours and a cursor. !note Run these in a real console The examples in this lesson need a real console window. The course website captures program output instead of showing a console, so build and run them in Visual Studio. Colours and positions, the classic way cpp-norun include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { HANDLE out{ GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE) }; SetConsoleTextAttribute(out, FOREGROUND_GREEN FOREGROUND_INTENSITY); std::cout << "HP 87/100
"; SetConsoleTextAttribute(out, FOREGROUND_RED FOREGROUND_INTENSITY); std::cout << "Poisoned
"; SetConsoleTextAttribute(out, FOREGROUND_RED FOREGROUND_GREEN FOREGROUND_BLUE); // back to grey SetConsoleCursorPosition(out, COORD{ 20, 0 }); // column 20, row 0 std::cout << "Gold 1250"; SetConsoleCursorPosition(out, COORD{ 0, 3 }); return 0; } Colours are 4 bits each for text and background (16 colours); positions are a COORD of column and row, counted from 0. Virtual terminal sequences Modern Windows consoles (and Windows Terminal) also understand the same escape sequences used by Linux and macOS terminals: special strings starting with the ESC character ( \x1b ) that the terminal interprets instead of printing. They are often simpler than the API, work across platforms, and support 24-bit colour. Turn them on once: cpp HANDLE out{ GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE) }; DWORD mode{ 0 }; GetConsoleMode(out, &mode); SetConsoleMode(out, mode ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING); SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8); // and print UTF-8 correctly (lesson 5.03) Sequence Effect --- --- \x1b H Cursor to the top-left \x1b row;colH Cursor to a position, counted from 1 \x1b 2J Clear the screen \x1b 31m ... \x1b 37m Text colour: red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white (30 is black) \x1b 1m Bold / bright \x1b 38;2;r;g;bm Any 24-bit text colour \x1b 0m Reset all colours and styles \x1b ?25l / \x1b ?25h Hide / show the cursor cpp-norun std::cout << "\x1b 2J\x1b ?25l"; // clear, hide cursor std::cout << "\x1b 1;1H\x1b 32mHP 87/100\x1b 0m"; // green, top-left std::cout << "\x1b 1;21H\x1b 38;2;255;200;60mGold 1250\x1b 0m"; // gold-coloured, column 21 Drawing a whole screen without flicker Clearing and reprinting the screen every frame flickers, for the same reason as lesson 5.06: the user sees the empty screen in between. The text-mode version of double buffering is to build the entire frame as one string and write it in a single call, starting with "cursor home" rather than "clear": cpp-norun std::string frame{ "\x1b H" }; // home, not clear: overwrite in place for (int y{ 0 }; y < height; ++y) { for (int x{ 0 }; x < width; ++x) frame += (x == px && y == py) ? '@' : map y x ; frame += '
'; } WriteConsoleA(out, frame.data(), static_cast<DWORD (frame.size()), nullptr, nullptr); One write per frame means the console updates all at once. Reading keys without Enter std::cin waits for a whole line. A game needs individual key presses as they happen. ReadConsoleInputW returns input records , one per event, and GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents says whether any are waiting, so a loop never blocks: cpp-norun HANDLE in{ GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT_HANDLE) }; DWORD waiting{ 0 }; GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents(in, &waiting); while (waiting-- 0) { INPUT_RECORD record{}; DWORD read{ 0 }; ReadConsoleInputW(in, &record, 1, &read); if (record.EventType == KEY_EVENT && record.Event.KeyEvent.bKeyDown) handleKey(record.Event.KeyEvent.wVirtualKeyCode); // the same virtual-key codes as lesson 5.07 } Put the three pieces together (an input loop, game state, a whole-frame string) and you have a complete text-mode game engine in under a hundred lines. Many classic roguelike games are exactly this. A console for a windowed game A game built for the Windows subsystem (lesson 5.06) has no console, which makes std::cout logging disappear. During development you can give it one: cpp AllocConsole(); // create a console window for this process FILE stream{ nullptr }; freopen_s(&stream, "CONOUT$", "w", stdout); // point stdout at it Chapter 11's debug console uses a different approach, drawing text inside the game itself, but AllocConsole is the quickest way to get logging into a windowed program. Common mistakes !warning Escape sequences printing as garbage Enable ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING first. Older consoles may not support it at all. !warning Counting rows and columns from 0 in escape sequences \x1b 1;1H is the top-left. The COORD API counts from 0; escape sequences count from 1. !warning Clearing the screen every frame Home the cursor and overwrite instead, writing the whole frame in one call. !warning Using std::cin for game input It waits for Enter. Read input records instead. Knowledge check quiz ? What does the sequence \x1b 5;10H do? + Moves the cursor to row 5, column 10, counting from 1 - Prints the numbers 5 and 10 - Sets the colour to 5;10 H positions the cursor; escape-sequence rows and columns start at 1. ? How do you avoid flicker when redrawing a text-mode game screen? + Build the whole frame as one string starting with "cursor home", then write it in one call - Clear the screen before each frame - Print one character at a time The console then shows complete frames only. ? Why use ReadConsoleInputW instead of std::cin for a text-mode game? + It delivers individual key events without waiting for Enter, and can be checked without blocking - std::cin cannot read letters - It is the only way to read numbers Games need each key press as it happens.

A text-mode game draws each frame by writing one string full of escape sequences. Write the pieces that build that string. - moveTo(row, col) returns the sequence that moves the cursor to a position. ' , with the character at the player's position replaced by @ . If the player's position is outside the map, draw the map without them. frame({ " ", " ... ", " " }, 1, 2) == "\x1b H 
 .@.

title: 6.01  Programs, Processes and Modules
body:
A program is a file; a process is a running instance of one, with its own address space, threads and handles; a module is an executable or DLL loaded into a process. This lesson makes the distinction concrete by starting a child process, waiting for it, reading its exit code, and passing it a command line. Three words, three things Is Example --- --- --- Program A file on disk C:\Games\Dungeon\dungeon.exe Process A running instance: an address space, one or more threads, a handle table, a security token Two copies of dungeon.exe running are two processes Module An .exe or .dll mapped into a process dungeon.exe , kernel32.dll , plugin.dll inside one process A process does not run code by itself. Threads run code; the process is the container that gives them memory and resources. Every process starts with one thread and may create more (lesson 6.05). When the last thread ends, or any thread calls ExitProcess , the process ends and Windows frees everything it held. Starting another program Games start other processes more often than you might think: a crash reporter, a launcher starting the game, an updater, a level editor launching the game to test a level. The function is CreateProcessW : cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string int main() { std::wstring commandLine{ L"cmd.exe /c exit 7" }; // must be writable: CreateProcessW may modify it STARTUPINFOW startup{}; startup.cb = sizeof(startup); PROCESS_INFORMATION info{}; if (!CreateProcessW(nullptr, commandLine.data(), nullptr, nullptr, FALSE, CREATE_NO_WINDOW, nullptr, nullptr, &startup, &info)) { std::cout << "CreateProcessW failed: " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } WaitForSingleObject(info.hProcess, INFINITE); // a process handle is signalled when it ends DWORD exitCode{ 0 }; GetExitCodeProcess(info.hProcess, &exitCode); std::cout << "the child exited with code " << exitCode << '
'; CloseHandle(info.hThread); // CreateProcessW gives you two handles: CloseHandle(info.hProcess); // close both return 0; } the child exited with code 7 The pieces: - The command line is one string, not an array: the program name followed by its arguments. The new process splits it into argv itself. Arguments containing spaces must be quoted: L""C:\My Games\editor.exe" --level "forest 2"" . - PROCESS_INFORMATION returns a handle to the new process, a handle to its first thread, and both ids. You own both handles and must close them, even if you do not need them. - Waiting. A process handle is a kernel object that becomes signalled when the process ends, so WaitForSingleObject waits for it. The exit code is whatever the child returned from main or passed to ExitProcess . Exit code 0 conventionally means success; anything else is an error number the program chose. Windows itself uses some large values: 0xC0000005 (3221225477) means the child crashed with an access violation. Process ids and handles A process has a process id (PID), a number unique among running processes, shown in Task Manager. A PID is not a handle: to do anything with a process you hold only the id of, you must open a handle to it with OpenProcess , asking for specific access rights, which Windows may refuse (lesson 6.08). cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { const DWORD myId{ GetCurrentProcessId() }; HANDLE me{ OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, FALSE, myId) }; wchar_t path MAX_PATH {}; DWORD size{ MAX_PATH }; const bool ok{ me && QueryFullProcessImageNameW(me, 0, path, &size) }; std::cout << "opened myself and read my image name: " << (ok ? "yes" : "no") << '
'; if (me) CloseHandle(me); return 0; } opened myself and read my image name: yes GetCurrentProcess() returns a pseudo-handle , the special value -1, meaning "the current process", which never needs closing. Modules inside a process Every process has at least one module, its .exe , and nearly always dozens of DLLs. Each module occupies its own range of the address space, starting at its HMODULE (lesson 5.08). Visual Studio's Modules window lists them while debugging; lesson 6.07 lists them from code. Common mistakes !warning Passing a string literal as the command line CreateProcessW may write into the buffer, so a literal crashes. Use a std::wstring or a wchar_t array. !warning Forgetting info.hThread Two handles come back, and both leak if not closed. !warning Unquoted paths with spaces C:\My Games\editor.exe is read as the program C:\My with arguments. Quote the program name and any argument containing spaces. !warning Confusing a PID with a handle A PID identifies a process; to act on it you need a handle from OpenProcess . Knowledge check quiz ? Two copies of the same game are running. How many processes and how many program files are there? + Two processes, one program file - One process, two program files - One process, one program file Each running instance is its own process with its own address space. ? How do you wait for a child process to finish? + WaitForSingleObject on its process handle, which becomes signalled when it ends - Call Sleep until it disappears from Task Manager - Read its exit code in a loop Process handles are waitable kernel objects. ? A child process's exit code is 3221225477 ( 0xC0000005 ). What happened? + It crashed with an access violation - It succeeded - It was closed by the user 0xC0000005 is the status code for an access violation. ? What is the difference between a process id and a process handle? + The id names the process system-wide; a handle is a per-process reference with specific rights, obtained from OpenProcess or CreateProcessW - They are the same number - Handles are only for threads Windows checks rights when the handle is opened.

title: Split a command line
body: A process receives its command line as one string and splits it into arguments. Write splitCommandLine(line) using these rules (a simplified version of what Windows programs do): - Arguments are separated by one or more spaces. - A double quote " starts or ends a quoted section. Spaces inside a quoted section are part of the argument. The quote characters themselves are not part of it. - Quoted and unquoted parts next to each other belong to the same argument: --name="Rook Smith" is the single argument --name=Rook Smith . - "" on its own is an empty argument. - Leading and trailing spaces produce no arguments. editor.exe --level "forest 2" - { "editor.exe", "--level", "forest 2" } "C:\My Games\a.exe" -x - { "C:\My Games\a.exe", "-x" } a "" b - { "a", "", "b" }

title: 6.02  Virtual Address Spaces
body: Every address a program uses is virtual : the processor translates it, page by page, into a physical location in RAM using page tables the operating system maintains for each process. This lesson explains the translation, the size and shape of a 64-bit address space, why some addresses are impossible, and what happens when a page is not in RAM at all. Every address is translated Lesson 1.06 said each process has a private address space. Here is how that works. Every time the CPU reads or writes memory, the address goes through the memory management unit (MMU), part of the processor, which translates it from a virtual address to a physical address : a real location in the RAM chips. Translation happens in units of pages , 4,096 bytes ( 0x1000 ) each. An address splits into two parts: virtual address 0x00007FF6A1234567 └────────┬───────┘└┬┘ page number offset within the page: 0x567 0x7FF6A1234 The page number is looked up and replaced with a physical frame number ; the offset stays the same. So within a page, bytes keep their order, but two neighbouring virtual pages can be anywhere in physical memory, in any order. Because each process has its own page tables, the same virtual page number leads to different frames in different processes. When the scheduler switches to another process, it switches the CPU to that process's tables (by loading the register CR3 ), and the whole address space changes in one step. Four levels of tables A 64-bit address space is enormous. A single flat table with one entry per page would be gigabytes per process. So the tables are a tree with four levels, and only the parts that are actually used exist. On x64, the 48 significant bits of an address split like this: 47 39 38 30 29 21 20 12 11 0 ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────────┐ │ level 4 │ level 3 │ level 2 │ level 1 │ offset │ │ 9 bits │ 9 bits │ 9 bits │ 9 bits │ 12 bits │ └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴────────────┘ Each 9-bit index picks one of 512 entries in a table; each entry points to the next level's table; the last level gives the physical frame. The practice task splits addresses this way. Walking four tables for every memory access would be slow, so the CPU caches recent translations in the TLB (translation lookaside buffer). Nearly all accesses hit the TLB and cost nothing extra. Code that jumps randomly across a very large amount of memory misses it, which is another reason (besides the cache, lesson 2.07) to keep data compact. The shape of a 64-bit address space x64 processors use 48 bits of address today, not 64. The top 16 bits must all copy bit 47, which splits the space into two halves with a huge gap between them: Range Size Used by --- --- --- 0x00000000'00000000 to 0x00007FFF'FFFFFFFF 128 TB User mode : your process (the gap) Not valid: using an address here is an immediate fault 0xFFFF8000'00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF'FFFFFFFF 128 TB Kernel mode : shared by all processes, inaccessible from user mode Addresses in the valid ranges are called canonical . That is why every user-mode pointer you print starts with 0000 , and why the top two bytes in the Memory window are always 00 00 (lesson 2.11). A pointer like 0x12345678'9ABCDEF0 is not just invalid, it is impossible, and is a sure sign of corrupted data. Within the user half, Windows places the program's modules near the top ( 0x00007FF... ), and stacks and heaps lower down, at addresses randomised each run (lesson 6.09). The first 64 KB ( 0x0 to 0xFFFF ) are never mapped, so that a null pointer plus a small offset always faults. Pages that are not in RAM A page table entry can also say "not present" . Touching such a page raises a page fault , an exception the kernel handles: Why it was not present What the kernel does --- --- The page was never committed (lesson 6.03), or is in the gap The access is invalid: the program gets an access violation It was committed but never touched yet Finds a free frame, fills it with zeros, maps it, and resumes the program: a demand-zero fault It was moved out to the page file on disk to free RAM Reads it back, maps it, resumes: a hard fault, which takes milliseconds It is part of a file mapping (the .exe 's code, a DLL) Reads it from the file, maps it, resumes The program never notices the middle three, except as a pause. This is how a 100 GB address space can exist on a PC with 16 GB of RAM, and why a game that uses more memory than the machine has starts to stutter: its pages are going to and from disk. Task Manager's Commit size and Working set columns show how much memory a process has committed and how much is currently in RAM. Common mistakes !warning Thinking a pointer value is a RAM location It is virtual. The physical location may change and is never visible to user-mode code. !warning Ignoring a non-canonical pointer in a crash A pointer with random high bits is corrupted data: look for whatever overwrote it, not for the code that used it. !warning Assuming memory use is the same as RAM use Committed memory may be in the page file; RAM in use is the working set. Knowledge check quiz ? What does the MMU replace when it translates an address? + The page number, with a physical frame number; the offset within the page stays the same - The whole address, with a random one - Only the offset Translation works page by page. ? Why does every user-mode pointer on x64 Windows start with 0000 ? + User addresses are in the lower 128 TB, so the top 16 bits are zero - Windows wastes the first two bytes - Pointers are padded for alignment Canonical user-mode addresses have bits 48 to 63 equal to bit 47, which is 0. ? What is a demand-zero page fault? + The first touch of committed memory, where the kernel provides a zero-filled page and the program continues - A crash caused by a null pointer - A page that was written to disk It is invisible to the program, apart from a tiny delay. ? Why are page tables a tree rather than one flat array? + So that only the parts of the huge address space actually in use need tables - Because the CPU cannot read arrays - To make translation faster than a flat table A flat table for 48-bit addresses would need billions of entries per process.

title: Split a virtual address
body: Write split(address) , which splits a 64-bit x64 virtual address into the parts the MMU uses: - offset : the low 12 bits; - level1 to level4 : four 9-bit table indices, level1 from bits 12 to 20, level2 from bits 21 to 29, level3 from bits 30 to 38, level4 from bits 39 to 47; - canonical : true if bits 48 to 63 are all equal to bit 47. Also write pageNumber(address) , the address shifted right by 12. split(0x00007FF6A1234567): offset 0x567, level1 0x34, level2 0x109, level3 0x1DA, level4 0xFF, canonical

title: 6.03  Pages, Protection and Committing Memory
body: Under the heap sits VirtualAlloc , which manages memory directly in pages. A region of the address space can be free , reserved (set aside, but with no memory behind it) or committed (backed by memory), and every committed page has a protection : readable, writable, executable, or none. This lesson uses these tools directly, and shows how games use them for huge growable arrays, guard pages and catching bugs. Three states for every page State Means Costs --- --- --- Free Not in use; any access faults Nothing Reserved Set aside: no other allocation will use these addresses. Still no memory behind it; any access faults Almost nothing (some bookkeeping) Committed Backed by memory (RAM or page file). Can be accessed according to its protection Counts against the system's commit limit; RAM used once touched VirtualAlloc moves pages between these states. Reserving is done in units of the allocation granularity , 64 KB; committing and protection work per 4 KB page. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { // Reserve 1 GB of address space: no memory is used yet. const SIZE_T reserveSize{ 1ull << 30 }; char base{ static_cast<char (VirtualAlloc(nullptr, reserveSize, MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_NOACCESS)) }; if (!base) { std::cout << "reserve failed\n"; return 1; } // Commit just the first two pages, readable and writable. VirtualAlloc(base, 2 4096, MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_READWRITE); base 0 = 42; // fine: committed base 8191 = 7; // fine: last byte of the second page std::cout << "first byte " << static_cast<int (base 0 ) << ", committed memory starts zeroed: " << static_cast<int (base 100 ) << '\n'; // base 8192 = 1; // would be an access violation: reserved, not committed VirtualFree(base, 0, MEM_RELEASE); // give back the whole reservation return 0; } first byte 42, committed memory starts zeroed: 0 Reserving a gigabyte took no memory at all, only addresses, which a 64-bit process has plenty of. Committed pages always start filled with zeros: Windows never hands one process another process's old data. Protection Every committed page carries a protection, enforced by the processor on each access: Constant Read Write Execute Typical use --- --- --- --- --- PAGE_NOACCESS Guard regions, reserved space PAGE_READONLY ✓ Constants ( .rdata ) PAGE_READWRITE ✓ ✓ Heap, stack, globals ( .data ) PAGE_EXECUTE_READ ✓ ✓ Code ( .text ) PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE ✓ ✓ ✓ Rarely legitimate: avoid Combined with the section table of lesson 2.03, this is why writing to a string literal or to your own code crashes: those pages are mapped read-only. VirtualProtect changes a page's protection. One legitimate use in games: make a big table read-only after loading it , so any accidental write anywhere in the program crashes immediately at the culprit, instead of silently corrupting the data. cpp VirtualProtect(itemTable, tableBytes, PAGE_READONLY, &oldProtection); !note Why writable and executable are kept apart A page that is both writable and executable lets any bug that writes memory also plant code to run. Windows' Data Execution Prevention (DEP) makes data pages non-executable, and modern compilers, the loader and security features all assume code pages are not writable. Programs that generate code at run time (JIT compilers, emulators) write into a read-write page, then switch it to execute-read before running it, never holding both at once. Guard pages and catching overruns A page marked PAGE_NOACCESS placed right after a buffer turns an overrun into an immediate crash at the exact instruction, much like AddressSanitizer's red zones (lesson 2.10) but enforced by the hardware for free. Debugging tools use this idea: Windows' page heap (enabled per program with the gflags tool) places every heap allocation at the end of its own page, followed by an inaccessible page, so a write one byte past the end faults instantly. Thread stacks use the related PAGE_GUARD flag: the page just below the stack's committed part is a guard page, and touching it commits more stack. That is how a thread's stack grows up to its reserved size, and why a stack overflow is detected: the guard page is finally hit with nothing reserved below it. Reserve big, commit as you go Reserving and committing separately gives a pattern games use for large, growable data: reserve the maximum size up front (say 4 GB of addresses for an asset buffer), then commit pages only as the buffer actually fills. Unlike std::vector (lesson 3.07): - the data never moves , so pointers into it stay valid forever; - growing never copies anything; - unused space costs no memory. Some engines build their entity arrays and frame allocators this way. Common mistakes !warning Using memory that is only reserved Reserved pages fault on any access. Commit them first. !warning Freeing with the wrong size VirtualFree(base, 0, MEM_RELEASE) releases an entire reservation; the size must be 0 and the address must be exactly what VirtualAlloc returned. !warning PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE "to be safe" It is the opposite of safe. Use the narrowest protection that works. !warning Using VirtualAlloc for small objects Each allocation is at least one 4 KB page and 64 KB of address space. Use the heap for small objects. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the difference between reserving and committing memory? + Reserving sets aside addresses only; committing backs them with memory so they can be used - Reserving is for the stack and committing for the heap - There is no difference Reserved pages still fault on access; committed pages are usable. ? A 1 GB region is reserved and two pages committed. Roughly how much memory does the program use for it? + About 8 KB, once those pages are touched - 1 GB - Nothing at all, ever Only committed pages are backed, and only touched pages take RAM. ? Why are code pages not writable? + So bugs or attacks that write memory cannot change or plant code - Because code is stored on disk - To make the program faster Keeping writable and executable apart is a basic defence. ? What happens when a program writes to a PAGE_NOACCESS page? + An access violation, at the exact instruction that tried - The write is ignored - The page is committed automatically That is what makes no-access guard pages useful for catching overruns.

title: Describe a page's protection
body: Tools that show memory regions describe each page's protection in a short form, the way Linux's /proc/maps and many debuggers do: three characters for read, write and execute, using a letter when allowed and - when not. Write describe(protection) for these Windows protection values: Constant Value Result --- --- --- PAGE_NOACCESS 0x01 "---" PAGE_READONLY 0x02 "r--" PAGE_READWRITE 0x04 "rw-" PAGE_WRITECOPY 0x08 "rw-" PAGE_EXECUTE 0x10 "--x" PAGE_EXECUTE_READ 0x20 "r-x" PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE 0x40 "rwx" PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY 0x80 "rwx" The value may also have modifier flags added in its higher bits, such as PAGE_GUARD ( 0x100 ) or PAGE_NOCACHE ( 0x200 ): ignore everything above the low 8 bits. If PAGE_GUARD is present, append " guard" . For any other low-byte value, return "???" .

title: 6.04  Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery
match: 6.04 Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery
body:
VirtualQuery answers "what is at this address?": the region's start and size, its state, protection and type. Walking it across the whole address space produces a map of your process: the modules, heaps, stacks and reserved areas. This lesson builds that map, the same view tools like VMMap show, and uses it to identify what any pointer points at. Asking about an address cpp MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; VirtualQuery(someAddress, &info, sizeof(info)); VirtualQuery fills a MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION describing the region containing the address: a run of consecutive pages that all share the same state, protection and type. Field Meaning --- --- BaseAddress Start of the region containing the address RegionSize Size of the region, in bytes AllocationBase Start of the original VirtualAlloc (or mapping) the region belongs to State MEM_FREE , MEM_RESERVE or MEM_COMMIT (lesson 6.03) Protect Current protection, such as PAGE_READWRITE Type MEM_IMAGE (an exe or DLL), MEM_MAPPED (a file mapping) or MEM_PRIVATE (heap, stack, VirtualAlloc ) What is this pointer? The Type and AllocationBase fields identify where any pointer leads. For an image, AllocationBase is the module's HMODULE , so GetModuleFileNameW gives its name: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <memory include <string const char kind(const void p) { MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; if (!VirtualQuery(p, &info, sizeof(info)) info.State != MEM_COMMIT) return "not committed memory"; if (info.Type == MEM_IMAGE) return (info.Protect & (PAGE_EXECUTE PAGE_EXECUTE_READ PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)) ? "code in a module" : "data in a module"; if (info.Type == MEM_MAPPED) return "a mapped file"; return "private memory (heap, stack or VirtualAlloc)"; } int g_global{ 1 }; int main() { int local{ 2 }; auto heap{ std::make_unique<int (3) }; std::cout << "main: " << kind(reinterpret_cast<const void (&main)) << '
'; std::cout << "g_global: " << kind(&g_global) << '
'; std::cout << "a literal: " << kind("text") << '
'; std::cout << "local: " << kind(&local) << '
'; std::cout << "heap: " << kind(heap.get()) << '
'; std::cout << "nullptr+16: " << kind(reinterpret_cast<const void (16)) << '
'; return 0; } main: code in a module g_global: data in a module a literal: data in a module local: private memory (heap, stack or VirtualAlloc) heap: private memory (heap, stack or VirtualAlloc) nullptr+16: not committed memory A crash reporter or a debugging tool does exactly this to say "the bad pointer pointed into freed space" or "the crash was in plugin.dll's code". Walking the whole address space Regions are consecutive, so you can walk them all: start at address 0, query, then jump to BaseAddress + RegionSize , until VirtualQuery fails at the end of user space. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { SIZE_T committed{ 0 }, reserved{ 0 }; int regions{ 0 }, imageRegions{ 0 }; MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; for (const char at{ nullptr }; VirtualQuery(at, &info, sizeof(info)) == sizeof(info); at = static_cast<const char (info.BaseAddress) + info.RegionSize) { ++regions; if (info.State == MEM_COMMIT) committed += info.RegionSize; if (info.State == MEM_RESERVE) reserved += info.RegionSize; if (info.State == MEM_COMMIT && info.Type == MEM_IMAGE) ++imageRegions; } std::cout << regions << " regions, " << imageRegions << " committed image regions
"; std::cout << committed / 1024 << " KB committed, " << reserved / (1024 1024) << " MB reserved
"; return 0; } varies 212 regions, 63 committed image regions 6044 KB committed, 2056 MB reserved Even a tiny program has a couple of hundred regions: every DLL contributes several (one per section with a different protection: code, read-only data, writable data), plus heaps, the stack and its guard page, and areas Windows reserves for itself. The reserved total is large because of reservations such as the stack's 1 MB and heap segments, which cost no memory. Reading the map A typical slice of the map, written out the way the practice task does: 00000097A1A00000 1004 KB reserved private thread stack (reserved part) 00000097A1AFB000 12 KB rw- guard private stack guard page 00000097A1AFE000 8 KB rw- private stack (committed part) 0000022F7B4A0000 1024 KB rw- private heap segment 00007FF6A1200000 4 KB r-- image game.exe headers 00007FF6A1201000 108 KB r-x image game.exe .text 00007FF6A121C000 40 KB r-- image game.exe .rdata 00007FF6A1226000 8 KB rw- image game.exe .data The sections of game.exe from lesson 2.03 are visible directly as regions with their protections. The thread stack shows reserve-then-commit-as-it-grows with its guard page from lesson 6.03. Microsoft's VMMap (part of the free Sysinternals tools) shows this map for any process with a friendly interface, and Visual Studio's diagnostic tools can too. Writing the walk yourself is the best way to understand what they show. Common mistakes !warning Not advancing past free regions Free regions are regions too. Always step by BaseAddress + RegionSize , whatever the state. !warning Treating Protect as meaningful for free or reserved regions It only describes committed pages; for reserved regions, AllocationProtect holds the protection the reservation was made with. !warning Reading memory just because VirtualQuery said it was committed Another thread can free it a moment later. Tools that read arbitrary memory must be prepared for the read to fail (chapter 12). Knowledge check quiz ? What does VirtualQuery describe? + The region of consecutive pages, sharing state, protection and type, that contains the given address - Only the single page containing the address - The whole process A region is a run of pages with identical attributes. ? A pointer's region has type MEM_IMAGE and protection PAGE_EXECUTE_READ . What does it point at? + Code inside a loaded exe or DLL - A heap block - A thread's stack Image regions are modules; execute permission means the code section. ? How do you get from one region to the next when walking the address space? + Query at BaseAddress + RegionSize of the current region - Add 4,096 to the address - Call VirtualQuery with a null pointer again Regions are consecutive and cover the whole space, free parts included.

title: Summarise a memory map
where: 6.04 Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery
body: A memory tool receives a list of regions from a VirtualQuery walk and has to present them compactly. Write two functions. merge(regions) combines neighbouring regions that have the same state, protection and type into one: a region is a neighbour of the previous one when it starts exactly where the previous one ends. The input is sorted by address. Regions that are not touching, or that differ in any attribute, stay separate. totals(regions) returns how many bytes are committed, how many reserved and how many free. { 0x1000, 0x1000, COMMIT, rw, PRIVATE } { 0x2000, 0x2000, COMMIT, rw, PRIVATE } - merged with the one before: { 0x1000, 0x3000, ... } { 0x4000, 0x1000, COMMIT, r, PRIVATE } - different protection: separate { 0x6000, 0x1000, COMMIT, r, PRIVATE } - not touching (gap at 0x5000): separate

title: 6.05  Threads and the Scheduler
body: A thread is a path of execution with its own registers and its own stack, running inside a process and sharing everything else. The scheduler decides which threads run on which cores and for how long. This lesson creates threads with std::thread and the Windows API, splits work between them, and explains what the scheduler does with them. What a thread has of its own All threads of a process share its address space, its heap, its globals and its handles. Each thread has only a few things of its own: Per thread Why --- --- Registers, including rip and rsp So it can be paused and resumed exactly where it was A stack (1 MB reserved by default) For its own calls and locals (lessons 1.05, 2.01) Thread-local storage Variables declared thread_local A thread id, a priority, a last-error value GetLastError is per thread Because memory is shared, threads can work on the same data with no copying. That is their great advantage and, as the next lesson shows, their great danger. Creating threads The portable way is std::thread (or std::jthread in C++20, which joins itself automatically): cpp include <iostream include <numeric include <thread include <vector int main() { std::vector<long long values(10'000'000); std::iota(values.begin(), values.end(), 1); // 1, 2, 3, ... 10,000,000 const unsigned parts{ 4 }; std::vector<long long partial(parts, 0); // one result slot per thread: no sharing std::vector<std::thread workers; const std::size_t chunk{ values.size() / parts }; for (unsigned t{ 0 }; t < parts; ++t) { const std::size_t begin{ t chunk }; const std::size_t end{ t == parts - 1 ? values.size() : begin + chunk }; workers.emplace_back( &values, &partial, t, begin, end { long long sum{ 0 }; for (std::size_t i{ begin }; i < end; ++i) sum += values i ; partial t = sum; }); } for (std::thread& w : workers) w.join(); // wait for every thread to finish std::cout << "total " << std::accumulate(partial.begin(), partial.end(), 0LL) << '\n'; return 0; } total 50000005000000 The pattern is the simplest safe one: each thread works on its own slice and writes its own result slot; the main thread waits with join and combines the results. Nothing is written by two threads, so nothing needs locking. A std::thread must be joined (waited for) or detached (left to run on its own) before it is destroyed; destroying a joinable thread calls std::terminate . std::jthread joins in its destructor, which is why it is usually the better choice. Underneath, on Windows, std::thread calls CreateThread (through the C runtime). The direct form: cpp DWORD WINAPI worker(void parameter) { auto job{ static_cast<Job (parameter) }; job- run(); return 0; // the thread's exit code } HANDLE thread{ CreateThread(nullptr, 0, &worker, &job, 0, nullptr) }; WaitForSingleObject(thread, INFINITE); // like join() CloseHandle(thread); The thread function is a callback (lesson 3.04) taking one void , through which you pass whatever the thread needs. How many threads? std::thread::hardware_concurrency() reports how many threads the processor can run truly at once: cores, doubled on processors with simultaneous multithreading (Hyper-Threading). Creating more threads than that for CPU-heavy work does not make it faster: the extra threads just take turns. Games usually create a fixed set of worker threads at start-up, about one per core minus one or two, and feed them small jobs through a queue (a job system ). Creating a thread costs tens of microseconds and a megabyte of address space, far too much to do per task. The scheduler Windows decides, many times a second, which ready thread runs on each core: - Each thread has a priority . The highest-priority ready threads run first. - Threads of equal priority take turns in time slices (quanta) of a few milliseconds. - A thread that waits (for input, a file, a lock, Sleep ) leaves the core straight away, and another thread runs. - Switching from one thread to another, a context switch , saves one thread's registers and loads another's. It costs a few microseconds. Things this explains in games: - Sleep(1) sleeps for at least a millisecond, often up to 15.6 ms with the default timer resolution. A frame limiter built on Sleep is imprecise (chapter 10). - A game whose main thread spins in a busy loop takes a core at 100% for nothing. - Raising a thread's priority rarely helps and can starve other threads, including Windows' own; leave priorities alone unless you have measured a reason. Common mistakes !warning Destroying a std::thread without joining it The program terminates. Join it, detach it, or use std::jthread . !warning Capturing locals by reference in a thread that outlives them The thread reads a dead stack frame. Join before the locals go out of scope, as the example does. !warning One thread per task Creating threads is expensive. Create a few workers once and give them jobs. !warning Expecting Sleep(1) to sleep for exactly one millisecond It sleeps for at least that, often much longer. Knowledge check quiz ? What does each thread have that is not shared with the other threads of its process? + Its registers and its stack - Its own heap - Its own copy of the global variables Heap, globals, code and handles are shared; registers and stack are per thread. ? Why does the summing example give each thread its own slot in partial ? + So no two threads write the same memory, and no locking is needed - Because threads cannot return values - To use less memory Separate outputs, combined after join , is the simplest safe pattern. ? A thread calls Sleep(5) . What happens on its core? + The thread leaves the core, and the scheduler runs another ready thread - The core stays idle for 5 ms - The whole process pauses A waiting thread gives up the core immediately. ? What does std::thread::hardware_concurrency() tell you? + How many threads the processor can run truly in parallel - How many threads the process may create - How many threads are currently running More CPU-bound threads than this only take turns.

title: Share out the work
body: Before starting worker threads, a program splits total items into parts contiguous ranges, one per thread. Write splitRanges(total, parts) , which returns parts pairs { begin, end } (end is one past the last item) that together cover 0 to total exactly once, in order. The ranges must be as even as possible: their sizes differ by at most one, with the larger ranges first. splitRanges(10, 3) - {0,4} {4,7} {7,10} sizes 4, 3, 3 splitRanges(2, 4) - {0,1} {1,2} {2,2} {2,2} If parts is 0, return an empty vector.

title: 6.06  Data Races, Mutexes and Events
body:
When two threads use the same memory and at least one writes, without coordination, the result is a data race : undefined behaviour that shows up as lost updates, torn values and bugs that vanish under the debugger. This lesson shows a race, then the tools that prevent them: mutexes , atomics , condition variables and Windows events , and the classic trap of deadlock . A race you can see cpp-norun include <iostream include <thread int main() { int score{ 0 }; auto addPoints = &score { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1'000'000; ++i) ++score; }; std::thread a{ addPoints }; std::thread b{ addPoints }; a.join(); b.join(); std::cout << score << '
'; // should be 2,000,000 return 0; } varies 1318772 Each run prints a different number, almost never 2,000,000. ++score looks like one step but is three: read score into a register, add one, write it back. If both threads read 41, both write 42, and one point is lost: The C++ rules go further than "points get lost": any unsynchronised access by two threads where one writes is undefined behaviour, so the optimiser may also keep score in a register for the whole loop. The symptoms are not limited to wrong totals. Atomics: indivisible operations For a single counter or flag, std::atomic makes each operation indivisible. The processor provides special instructions ( lock xadd , lock cmpxchg ) that do read-modify-write as one step: cpp include <atomic include <iostream include <thread int main() { std::atomic<int score{ 0 }; auto addPoints = &score { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1'000'000; ++i) ++score; }; std::thread a{ addPoints }; std::thread b{ addPoints }; a.join(); b.join(); std::cout << score << '
'; return 0; } 2000000 Atomics are right for counters, flags ("stop now") and simple statistics. They do not help when several values must change together, such as moving an item from one list to another. Mutexes: one thread at a time A mutex (mutual exclusion) guards a section of code: a thread that calls lock on a mutex another thread holds waits until it is released. Always lock with an RAII guard (lesson 2.04), so the mutex is released on every path: cpp include <iostream include <mutex include <string include <thread include <vector class EventLog { public: void add(std::string line) { std::lock_guard lock{ m_mutex }; // locked here... m_lines.push_back(std::move(line)); } // ...released here std::size_t size() { std::lock_guard lock{ m_mutex }; return m_lines.size(); } private: std::mutex m_mutex; std::vector<std::string m_lines; }; int main() { EventLog log; std::vector<std::thread threads; for (int t{ 0 }; t < 4; ++t) threads.emplace_back( &log, t { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1000; ++i) log.add("thread " + std::to_string(t)); }); for (auto& th : threads) th.join(); std::cout << log.size() << " lines
"; return 0; } 4000 lines Without the mutex, two push_back s at once can both decide to grow the vector, and the program corrupts its heap. The rule: every access to shared mutable data, reads included, happens while holding the same mutex. Keep the locked section short: do slow work (formatting, file writes) outside it. Waiting for something to happen Threads often need to wait until another thread has done something: a job is available, loading has finished. Spinning in a loop checking a flag wastes a whole core. Proper waiting puts the thread to sleep until it is woken: Tool Use --- --- std::condition_variable Wait until a condition on data guarded by a mutex becomes true (a queue is not empty) std::latch , std::barrier (C++20) Wait until N threads have reached a point std::future / std::promise Wait for one result from another thread Windows event ( CreateEventW ) A kernel object that is signalled or not; threads wait on it with WaitForSingleObject ; works across processes too A Windows event is like a flag that threads can sleep on. A manual-reset event stays signalled until reset (good for "loading finished": everyone may proceed); an auto-reset event wakes one waiter and resets itself (good for "one job available"). cpp HANDLE loaded{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr) }; // manual-reset, starts unsignalled // loader thread, when done: SetEvent(loaded); // main thread: WaitForSingleObject(loaded, INFINITE); // sleeps until then The practice task builds the most common combination: a thread-safe queue that consumers can wait on. Deadlock Two threads, two mutexes. Thread 1 locks A then waits for B. Thread 2 locks B then waits for A. Both wait forever: a deadlock . The game freezes with 0% CPU. Prevent it by: - always taking locks in the same order everywhere in the program; - locking several mutexes at once with std::scoped_lock lock{ a, b }; , which avoids deadlock internally; - never calling unknown code (callbacks, virtual functions) while holding a lock. When a game freezes, Break All in the debugger and look at each thread's call stack in the Threads window: two threads each waiting in a lock function, each holding what the other wants, is the signature of a deadlock (chapter 8). Common mistakes !warning Reading shared data without the lock "because it's only a read" A read concurrent with a write is still a data race. !warning Using volatile for thread communication In C++, volatile does not make anything atomic or ordered. Use std::atomic . !warning Holding a lock while doing slow work Every other thread that needs it waits. Copy what you need, unlock, then work. !warning Waiting with a busy loop Use a condition variable, an event, or a future, so the waiting thread sleeps. Knowledge check quiz ? Why can two threads doing ++score lose updates? + ++score is a read, an add and a write; both threads can read the same old value - Integers cannot be shared between threads - The scheduler skips some increments Without synchronisation, the steps of the two threads interleave. ? When is std::atomic enough on its own? + For a single value updated by indivisible operations, such as a counter or a flag - Whenever several values must change together - Never; a mutex is always needed Changes involving several values need a mutex around all of them. ? Thread 1 holds mutex A and waits for B; thread 2 holds B and waits for A. What is this? + A deadlock - A data race - A context switch Taking locks in a consistent order, or with std::scoped_lock , prevents it. ? What is the difference between a manual-reset and an auto-reset event? + A manual-reset event stays signalled until reset, releasing every waiter; an auto-reset event releases one waiter and resets itself - Manual-reset events are faster - Auto-reset events work only within one process Choose by whether one or all waiting threads should proceed.

title: A job queue for worker threads
match: A job queue for worker threads
body: Build JobQueue , a thread-safe queue of int jobs that worker threads can wait on. - push(job) adds a job and wakes one waiting worker. - pop() waits until a job is available and returns it. If the queue has been closed and is empty, it returns std::nullopt instead of waiting, so workers know to finish. - close() marks the queue closed and wakes every waiting worker. Jobs already queued are still handed out. - tryPop() returns a job if one is waiting, or std::nullopt immediately. Use a std::mutex and a std::condition_variable . The tests start several worker threads.

title: 6.07  Listing Processes and Modules
body: Task Manager, Process Explorer and every debugger start by asking Windows "what is running?". This lesson uses the Tool Help API to list running processes and the modules loaded in your own process, the building block of crash reporters, launchers that check whether the game is already open, and the tools in chapter 12. Snapshots The Tool Help API works in two steps: take a snapshot of some part of the system, then walk through it. A snapshot is a copy taken at one moment, so it does not change while you read it (processes that start or end afterwards are not reflected). Snapshot flag Lists --- --- TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS Every running process TH32CS_SNAPTHREAD Every thread in the system TH32CS_SNAPMODULE The modules (exe and DLLs) of one process Listing processes cpp include <windows.h include <tlhelp32.h include <iostream include <string int main() { HANDLE snapshot{ CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0) }; if (snapshot == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) return 1; PROCESSENTRY32W entry{}; entry.dwSize = sizeof(entry); // must be set before the first call int count{ 0 }; bool sawMyself{ false }; for (BOOL more{ Process32FirstW(snapshot, &entry) }; more; more = Process32NextW(snapshot, &entry)) { ++count; if (entry.th32ProcessID == GetCurrentProcessId()) sawMyself = true; // entry.szExeFile is the file name, entry.th32ParentProcessID the parent, entry.cntThreads the thread count } CloseHandle(snapshot); std::cout << "found " << (count 1 ? "several" : "too few") << " processes, including this one: " << (sawMyself ? "yes" : "no") << '\n'; return 0; } found several processes, including this one: yes Each PROCESSENTRY32W gives the process id, its parent's id, its thread count and its executable's file name (not the full path). To learn more (the full path, memory use, start time) you open the process by id with OpenProcess asking for PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION , which Windows grants for almost every process, and call functions such as QueryFullProcessImageNameW (lesson 6.01) or GetProcessTimes . A common real use: a game launcher or the game itself checking whether another copy is already running before starting a second one. (The more robust way to enforce "one copy only" is a named mutex : CreateMutexW(nullptr, FALSE, L"MyGame.SingleInstance") , then check whether GetLastError() returned ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS .) Listing your own modules cpp include <windows.h include <tlhelp32.h include <iostream include <string int main() { HANDLE snapshot{ CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPMODULE, GetCurrentProcessId()) }; if (snapshot == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) return 1; MODULEENTRY32W module{}; module.dwSize = sizeof(module); bool kernel32{ false }; int count{ 0 }; for (BOOL more{ Module32FirstW(snapshot, &module) }; more; more = Module32NextW(snapshot, &module)) { ++count; if (_wcsicmp(module.szModule, L"kernel32.dll") == 0) kernel32 = true; // module.modBaseAddr is where it is loaded, module.modBaseSize its size, module.szExePath its full path } CloseHandle(snapshot); std::cout << "modules loaded: " << (count 3 ? "many" : "few") << ", kernel32.dll among them: " << (kernel32 ? "yes" : "no") << '\n'; return 0; } modules loaded: many, kernel32.dll among them: yes Each MODULEENTRY32W gives a module's base address and size, exactly the ranges lesson 6.04's VirtualQuery walk found as MEM_IMAGE regions. Combining them turns any code address into "module + offset", the form crash reports use (lesson 6.09). A crash report's module list When a game crashes, a useful report says not just "crashed at 0x00007FF6A1235F10 " but "crashed in game.exe at offset 0x35F10 ", together with the list of loaded modules and their versions. With that, a developer can open the matching build's .pdb and find the exact source line, even though addresses differ on the player's machine. Chapter 8 builds this with crash dumps; the module list above is half of it. Rights and limits Listing names and ids of all processes needs no special rights. Opening other processes for more than limited information, or listing their modules, requires access rights that Windows grants only for processes running as the same user and at the same or lower integrity level, and never for protected processes (next lesson). Tools in this course look at processes you start yourself. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to set dwSize Process32FirstW fails if the structure's size field is not set first. !warning Treating a process name as unique Many processes can have the same file name. Use the process id, and check the full path if it matters. !warning Holding on to a PID for a long time When a process ends, its id can be reused by a new, unrelated process. Hold a process handle instead if you need to keep referring to it. Knowledge check quiz ? What does CreateToolhelp32Snapshot capture? + A copy of the chosen information (processes, threads or modules) at one moment - A live view that updates as processes start and stop - An image of a process's memory You walk the copy; later changes are not reflected. ? Two processes are both called game.exe . How do you tell them apart? + By their process ids, and if needed their full paths - You cannot - By the order they appear in the snapshot File names are not unique; ids are unique among running processes. ? Why is "module + offset" more useful in a crash report than a raw address? + Modules load at different addresses on different machines, but an offset within a module matches the build's symbols everywhere - It is shorter - Raw addresses are secret The offset can be looked up in the matching .pdb to find the source line.

title: 6.08  Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No
match: 6.08 Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No
body: "Access is denied" (error 5) is Windows checking rights. Every process carries a token saying who it runs as; every securable object has a security descriptor saying who may do what; and every handle is opened for specific access rights . This lesson explains the check, integrity levels and UAC, protected processes , and the principle of asking for no more than you need. The check behind every handle When a program opens an object (a file, a process, a registry key, an event), it asks for specific rights, and Windows decides there and then: - The token is attached to every process when it starts, inherited from the user who logged in. It lists the user, their groups (Administrators, Users...), their privileges, and an integrity level. - The security descriptor of an object holds an access control list (ACL): entries such as "Users: read", "Administrators: full control". - The access mask is the set of rights requested, as bits: for a file FILE_READ_DATA , FILE_WRITE_DATA , DELETE ...; for a process PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION , PROCESS_TERMINATE , PROCESS_VM_READ ... The check happens once, when the handle is opened . The handle then carries the granted rights, and every later use is checked against them only: a file handle opened for reading cannot be used to write, whatever the user's rights. Ask for what you need The most common cause of error 5 in a program's own code is asking for more than it needs: GENERIC_ALL , PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS , KEY_ALL_ACCESS . A normal user may be allowed to read a file but not change it, and a request for all access then fails, though a request for read access would have succeeded. The fix is also the security principle of least privilege : request exactly the rights the code uses. cpp // Fails for files the user may only read: HANDLE f{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE, ...) }; // Succeeds, and documents what the code does: HANDLE f{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, ...) }; Integrity levels and UAC Each token and each object also has an integrity level : Low, Medium, High or System. A process cannot write to objects at a higher integrity level than its own, whatever the ACL says. Level Typical processes --- --- Low Sandboxed browser tabs Medium Everything a user normally runs, including games High Programs run "as administrator" System Windows services With User Account Control (UAC), even an administrator's programs normally run at Medium, with the administrator group switched off in their token. "Run as administrator" (and the consent prompt) starts a process with the elevated High-integrity token. This is why a game should never need elevation: it runs at Medium, writes to the user's folders (lesson 5.04), and can be compromised without giving the attacker the whole machine. Protected processes Some processes are protected (Protected Process Light, PPL): Windows' own security components, antivirus engines, and some anti-cheat services. Even an administrator cannot open them for anything beyond limited query rights, cannot read their memory, inject code into them or debug them; only code signed with specific certificates may run inside them. This is a deliberate wall: it keeps malware from tampering with security software, and it is enforced by the kernel itself. The practical lesson for tool builders: when Windows refuses access to something, that is usually the system working as designed. The tools in this course work on processes you start yourself, at the same integrity level, where the rights are yours. Privileges Separate from object rights, a token holds privileges : system-wide abilities such as SeShutdownPrivilege (shut down the machine), SeLoadDriverPrivilege (load kernel drivers) and SeDebugPrivilege (open any non-protected process regardless of its security descriptor). Administrators' elevated tokens contain several privileges, disabled until a program explicitly enables them with AdjustTokenPrivileges . Normal programs never need them; development tools like debuggers do, which is why Visual Studio asks to restart elevated when you try to attach to a process running as administrator. Common mistakes !warning Asking for all access Request the specific rights the code uses. It succeeds more often and limits damage if the program is compromised. !warning "It works as administrator, so let's always run elevated" Find which right is missing instead. Games and tools should run as a normal user. !warning Assuming error 5 means a bug in the parameters It is a security decision. Check which rights you requested, the object's ACL, and the integrity levels. Knowledge check quiz ? When does Windows check whether you may write to a file? + When the handle is opened with write access requested; later writes are checked against the handle's granted rights - On every single write call, by looking at the user's groups again - Never: files are not secured The access check happens at open time. ? A program running as a normal user asks for GENERIC_ALL on a file it may only read. What happens? + The open fails with access denied, though asking for read access alone would have worked - It gets a handle with read access only - It gets full access anyway Windows grants all of the requested rights or none. ? What does UAC elevation change? + The process runs with the full administrator token at High integrity, instead of a filtered Medium token - It makes the program faster - It turns off the access check Without elevation, an administrator's programs run with the administrator group disabled. ? Why can even an administrator not read the memory of a protected process? + The kernel enforces the protection regardless of the caller's token - Its security descriptor is empty - Protected processes have no memory Protected Process Light shields security components from tampering.

title: 6.09  Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses
match: 6.09 Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses
body:
Run a program twice and its code, heap and stack land at different addresses. That is ASLR , a security feature. This lesson explains why it exists, how a module that can load anywhere still works ( relocations and RIP-relative code), how to turn any address into a stable module + offset (RVA) form, and why raw pointers must never be saved in files. Different every time cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int g_global{ 0 }; int main() { int local{ 0 }; std::cout << "exe loaded at " << static_cast<void (GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)) << '
'; std::cout << "a global at " << &g_global << '
'; std::cout << "a local at " << &local << '
'; std::cout << "kernel32 at " << static_cast<void (GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll")) << '
'; return 0; } varies exe loaded at 00007FF7C3E20000 a global at 00007FF7C3E3A030 a local at 0000009B4C2FF8D4 kernel32 at 00007FFE4C0A0000 Run it again and the first three lines change. (System DLLs like kernel32.dll are randomised once per boot, so they stay the same until you restart.) But look at the first two: the global is always the same distance after the exe's start, here 0x1A030 , whatever the start is. Why randomise Many attacks on programs depend on knowing where something is in memory: a function to jump to, a structure to overwrite. Address space layout randomisation (ASLR) makes those addresses different on every run and every machine, so an attacker who finds a memory bug still does not know where to aim. It is on by default for everything built with modern Visual Studio (the linker option /DYNAMICBASE , plus /HIGHENTROPYVA for 64-bit programs to use the full range). How code works at any address If a module can be loaded anywhere, how does its code find its own globals and functions? - RIP-relative addressing. Most x64 instructions that touch globals or call functions use an offset from the current instruction ( rip ): "the global 0x1A030 bytes ahead of this instruction". Since the code and the data move together, the offset is always right. This is why x64 code mostly needs no fixing up. - Relocations. A few values in a module are absolute addresses, such as a table of pointers, or a vtable pointing at functions. The linker records each of them in the module's relocation table ( .reloc section). When the loader puts the module somewhere other than its preferred image base , it adds the difference to every one of those values. The preferred image base for 64-bit executables built by Visual Studio is 0x140000000 , and for DLLs 0x180000000 . With ASLR, the loader nearly always picks a different address, so these numbers appear only in the file, in tools such as dumpbin /headers , and in disassemblers that show the program as if it were loaded at its preferred base. RVAs: addresses that do not move Because everything inside a module keeps its distance from the module's start, the stable way to name a location in a module is its offset from the start: its relative virtual address (RVA). RVA = address − module base address address = module base address + RVA Executable files use RVAs everywhere: the entry point, the start of each section, every import and export is an RVA (chapter 9). Debugging and crash tools use them too: "crashed at game.exe+0x35F10 " means the same instruction on every machine, and it can be found in the build's .pdb or in a disassembler by adding it to the image base the tool displays. crash at 0x00007FF7C3E55F10 game.exe loaded at 0x00007FF7C3E20000 RVA 0x35F10 in a disassembler showing image base 0x140000000: 0x140035F10 The practice task builds this conversion against a list of modules, as a crash reporter or a debugger does. Never save raw pointers ASLR is the clearest reason never to write pointers into save files, network messages or caches. The next run of the game has a different layout, so a saved address means nothing. Save ids, indices or handles (lesson 3.10), and rebuild pointers after loading. The same goes for a "pointer" written down from a debugger session: it is valid only for that one run. Common mistakes !warning Hard-coding addresses Any absolute address learned in one run is wrong in the next. Store module-relative offsets, or better, look things up by name or id. !warning Turning off ASLR "to make debugging easier" It weakens every user's security. Learn to read RVAs instead; the debugger and symbols do the arithmetic for you. !warning Confusing an RVA with a file offset An RVA is an offset in memory once loaded. Sections can sit at different offsets in the file on disk (chapter 9 shows how to convert). Knowledge check quiz ? What stays the same between two runs of a program with ASLR? + The distance (RVA) of each function and global from the start of its module - The address of the stack - The address the exe is loaded at Modules move as a whole; everything inside keeps its offset. ? Why does most x64 code not need relocating when it is loaded at a new address? + It reaches globals and functions with RIP-relative offsets, which do not change when code and data move together - x64 programs are always loaded at their preferred base - The CPU translates addresses automatically Only stored absolute addresses, listed in the relocation table, need fixing up. ? game.exe is loaded at 0x00007FF600000000 and a crash is at 0x00007FF600012345 . What is the RVA? + 0x12345 - 0x7FF600012345 - 0x140012345 RVA = address − module base. ? Why must save files not contain raw pointers? + Addresses change between runs, so a saved pointer is meaningless when loaded - Pointers are too large to save - Save files are read-only Save ids or indices and rebuild pointers after loading.

If it is in no module, return "?+0xADDRESS" with the full address in the same style. - toPreferred(rva, imageBase) : the address a disassembler would show for that RVA, given the module's preferred image base. modules: game.exe at 0x7FF600000000, size 0x50000 plugin.dll at 0x7FFE20000000, size 0x8000 locate(0x7FF600012345) = "game.exe+0x12345" locate(0x7FFE20000000) = "plugin.dll+0x0" locate(0x1234) = "?+0x1234" toPreferred(0x12345, 0x140000000) = 0x140012345

title: 7.01  Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
match: 7.01 Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
body: x64 assembly is the text form of the machine code your C++ becomes. This chapter teaches you to read it, and occasionally to write it. It starts with the registers , the processor's handful of built-in variables, their 64, 32, 16 and 8-bit names, and the shape every instruction follows: an operation and its operands. Why learn to read assembly You will rarely write assembly. You will read it often: - in the debugger's Disassembly window, when a crash happens in code without source, or in optimised code where the source view no longer matches what runs (lesson 4.10); - in compiler output , to see what your C++ really costs (lesson 7.11); - in reverse engineering , where it is all there is (chapter 9). The tiny computer of lesson 1.01 had one register and seven instructions. An x64 processor has the same ideas on a larger scale. The general-purpose registers x64 has sixteen 64-bit general-purpose registers. Each is a variable built into the processor: reading and writing them takes no memory access at all. Register Traditional role In the Windows calling convention (lesson 7.06) --- --- --- rax Accumulator Return value rbx Base Must be preserved by functions rcx Counter 1st integer argument rdx Data 2nd integer argument rsi Source index Must be preserved rdi Destination index Must be preserved rbp Base pointer Must be preserved; sometimes the frame pointer rsp Stack pointer The top of the stack (lesson 1.05) r8 , r9 3rd and 4th integer arguments r10 , r11 Scratch r12 to r15 Must be preserved There are also special registers: rip (the instruction pointer, the program counter of lesson 1.01), rflags (the flags, lesson 7.04), and sixteen 128-bit xmm registers for floating point (lesson 7.09). Smaller names for parts of a register Each register can be used at several widths, through different names for its lower parts: 63 31 15 7 0 ┌────────────────────────────────┬───────────────┬────────┬──────┐ │ rax │ │ │ eax │ │ │ │ ax │ │ │ │ ah │ al │ └────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┴────────┴──────┘ 64-bit 32-bit 16-bit 8-bit --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al rbx ebx bx bl rcx ecx cx cl rdx edx dx dl rsi , rdi , rbp , rsp esi , edi , ebp , esp si , di , bp , sp sil , dil , bpl , spl r8 ... r15 r8d ... r15d r8w ... r15w r8b ... r15b So an int (4 bytes) usually lives in an e register, a char or bool in an 8-bit one, a pointer or long long in a full r register. One rule surprises everyone once: writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit register. Writing 8 or 16 bits leaves the rest unchanged. Compilers rely on this constantly: mov eax, 1 is a shorter instruction than mov rax, 1 and has the same effect. The shape of an instruction Each line of assembly is one instruction: an operation (the mnemonic ) and up to two or three operands . In the syntax Microsoft's tools use (Intel syntax), the destination comes first : asm mov eax, 5 ; eax = 5 add eax, ecx ; eax = eax + ecx mov rsp+8 , eax ; the 4 bytes at address rsp+8 = eax An operand is one of three kinds: Kind Example Means --- --- --- Register ecx The value in a register Immediate 5 , 0FFh , -1 A constant stored inside the instruction itself (lesson 1.04 saw 0x32 inside an lea ) Memory rsp+8 , dword ptr rcx The value at an address, worked out from registers and constants Most instructions allow at most one memory operand: there is no "add memory to memory". Values are brought into registers, worked on, and written back, just like the tiny computer's LOAD, ADD, STORE. Watching registers change Step through this. Watch which register changes on each line, and especially what mov eax does to the upper half of rax : demo-asm title: Register widths init: rax=-1 mov al, 7 mov ax, 300 mov eax, 5 mov rcx, rax add rcx, 10 ret - After mov al, 7 and mov ax, 300 , only the low bits change: rax was all ones (-1), and its upper bytes stay ones. - mov eax, 5 clears the whole upper half: rax becomes exactly 5. - ret ends the function, and whoever called it finds its answer in rax . !note Two syntaxes Microsoft's tools and most Windows debuggers use Intel syntax (destination first, mov eax, 5 ). Linux tools default to AT&T syntax ( movl $5, %eax : source first, % before registers, $ before constants). They are the same instructions written differently. This course uses Intel syntax throughout. Common mistakes !warning Reading operands in the wrong order In Intel syntax, mov a, b copies b into a. The destination is first. !warning Forgetting that writing a 32-bit register zeroes the top half mov eax, -1 leaves rax as 0x00000000FFFFFFFF , not -1. !warning Expecting two memory operands add a , b does not exist. One side must be a register or a constant. Knowledge check quiz ? Which register holds a function's return value on x64 Windows? + rax - rcx - rsp rcx , rdx , r8 and r9 bring arguments in; rax carries the result out. ? rax holds -1 (all bits set). After mov eax, 2 , what is in rax ? + 2 - 0xFFFFFFFF00000002 - -2 Writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits. ? In sub ecx, 10 , which operand receives the result? + ecx , the first operand - 10 - Neither; the result goes to rax Intel syntax puts the destination first. ? Which of these is a memory operand? - r9d - 0x40 + qword ptr rdx+16 Square brackets mean "the value at this address".

title: A register with many names
where: 7.01 Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
body: Model one x64 general-purpose register and the rules for writing its smaller parts. Write the class Register : - get64() , get32() , get16() , get8() return the low 64, 32, 16 or 8 bits (as unsigned values). - set64(v) replaces all 64 bits. - set32(v) writes the low 32 bits and clears the upper 32 , as the processor does. - set16(v) writes the low 16 bits and leaves the other 48 unchanged. - set8(v) writes the low 8 bits and leaves the other 56 unchanged. Values passed to the smaller setters may have extra high bits: only the bits that fit are used. Register r; r.set64(0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF); r.set8(7); // get64() = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF07 r.set16(300); // get64() = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF012C r.set32(5); // get64() = 5

title: 7.02  Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
match: 7.02 Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
body: Most instructions in real code just move data: between registers, from memory into a register, from a register back to memory. This lesson covers mov and its widening relatives movzx and movsx , the addressing modes that let one instruction compute an address like base + index × scale + offset , and lea , which does that arithmetic without touching memory at all. mov mov destination, source copies a value. It never changes the source and never sets the flags. asm mov eax, 10 ; constant into a register mov ecx, eax ; register to register mov eax, dword ptr rcx ; 4 bytes from memory at the address in rcx, into eax mov qword ptr rsp+20h , rax ; 8 bytes from rax into memory at rsp+0x20 mov byte ptr rdx , 1 ; the constant 1 into one byte of memory The size comes from the register ( eax is 4 bytes, rax 8). When there is no register to tell it (a constant stored to memory), the size is written out: byte ptr , word ptr (2), dword ptr (4), qword ptr (8). Disassemblers show the ptr sizes on every memory operand, which is a gift when reading code: dword ptr rcx+8 tells you there is a 4-byte value 8 bytes into whatever rcx points at. Widening: movzx and movsx Loading a 1-byte char or 2-byte short into a 32-bit register needs to fill the extra bits, and how depends on whether the type is signed: Instruction Fills the new upper bits with For --- --- --- movzx eax, byte ptr rcx Zeros ( zero extension ) unsigned char , bool , std::uint16_t movsx eax, byte ptr rcx Copies of the sign bit ( sign extension ) signed char , short movsxd rax, ecx Sign extension from 32 to 64 bits int to long long or to an index The byte 0xFF becomes 255 with movzx and -1 with movsx . This is two's complement from lesson 1.02, done by hardware. Addressing modes A memory operand can compute its address from up to four parts: base + index × scale + displacement reg reg 1,2,4,8 constant Form Typical C++ --- --- rcx p rcx+8 p- member at offset 8 (lesson 2.06) rcx+rdx 4 array i for 4-byte elements: base address rcx , index rdx rcx+rdx 8+10h p- items i where items is an array of 8-byte values at offset 0x10 rip+1234h A global variable, relative to the instruction (lesson 6.09) The scale can only be 1, 2, 4 or 8: exactly the sizes of char , short , int / float and pointers/ double . Indexing arrays of those types costs no extra instructions at all. Step through a loop that sums an array. rdi holds the array's address; rdi+rcx 4 is values i : demo-asm title: Summing int values 4 through rdi+rcx 4 init: rdi=0x2000, mem@0x2000=10 20 30 40 xor eax, eax xor ecx, ecx next: add eax, dword ptr rdi+rcx 4 inc ecx cmp ecx, 4 jl next ret lea: the address calculator lea ("load effective address") computes the address of a memory operand and puts the address itself into the destination, without reading memory: asm lea rax, rcx+rdx 4 ; rax = rcx + rdx 4 (&array i ) lea rax, rcx+10h ; rax = rcx + 16 (&p- member) lea rcx, rip+1F2Ah ; rcx = the address of a global or string literal Because the address hardware can add two registers, scale one of them and add a constant in a single step, compilers also use lea for plain arithmetic that has nothing to do with addresses: C++ Compiled --- --- x + 50 (into a different register) lea eax, rcx+32h (lesson 1.04's example) a + b lea eax, rcx+rdx x 5 lea eax, rcx+rcx 4 x 9 + 3 lea eax, rcx+rcx 8+3 When you see lea in compiler output, ask whether it is computing a pointer or just doing quick arithmetic. Both are common. Common mistakes !warning Confusing mov rax, rcx with lea rax, rcx mov reads the 8 bytes at the address; lea puts the address itself in rax . One is p , the other is p . !warning Reading rcx+rdx 4 as "rcx plus rdx plus 4" The 4 scales the index: it is element rdx of an array of 4-byte values. !warning Assuming mov sets flags It does not. A comparison needs cmp or test . Knowledge check quiz ? What does mov eax, dword ptr rcx+8 do? + Copies the 4 bytes at address rcx+8 into eax - Sets eax to rcx+8 - Adds 8 to the value at rcx The brackets read memory; lea would compute the address instead. ? The byte at rdx is 0xFE . What does movsx eax, byte ptr rdx put in eax? + -2 - 254 - 0xFE000000 Sign extension copies the top bit, so 0xFE as a signed byte, -2, stays -2. ? Which C++ expression is rcx+rdx 8 most likely to come from? + p i where p points at 8-byte values such as pointers or doubles - p + i + 8 - p- member at offset 8 Base, index and a scale equal to the element size: array indexing. ? Why might a compiler emit lea eax, rcx+rcx 2 ? + To compute x 3 in one instruction - To read memory at x 3 - To compare x with 3 lea does arithmetic with the address hardware and never touches memory.

title: Work out the address
where: 7.02 Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
body: Write effectiveAddress(base, index, scale, displacement) , which computes the address a memory operand base + index scale + displacement refers to, exactly as the processor does: in 64-bit arithmetic that wraps round. displacement may be negative. Also write widen(byte, isSigned) , which returns the 32-bit value movsx (when isSigned is true) or movzx (when false) would produce from one byte, as an unsigned 32-bit number. If scale is not 1, 2, 4 or 8, the instruction cannot be encoded: effectiveAddress returns std::nullopt . effectiveAddress(0x2000, 3, 4, 0) = 0x200C effectiveAddress(0x1000, 0, 1, -8) = 0xFF8 widen(0xFE, true) = 0xFFFFFFFE widen(0xFE, false) = 0xFE

title: 7.03  Arithmetic and Bit Operations
body: The arithmetic instructions ( add , sub , imul , inc , dec , neg , div ) and the bit instructions ( and , or , xor , not , shl , shr , sar ) are the processor's whole calculator. This lesson covers each, the flags they set as a side effect, and the tricks compilers use, such as replacing division by a constant with multiplication. The two-operand pattern x64 arithmetic usually has two operands, and the result replaces the first: Instruction Effect C++ --- --- --- add a, b a = a + b a += b sub a, b a = a - b a -= b imul a, b a = a × b (signed, keeps the low bits) a = b imul a, b, 7 a = b × 7 (three-operand form) a = b 7 inc a / dec a a = a ± 1 ++a / --a neg a a = -a a = -a There is no separate instruction for unsigned multiplication of the kind C++ needs: since the low bits of a product are the same either way (two's complement again), imul serves both. The flags Most arithmetic and logic instructions also set bits in the flags register describing their result. Four matter most: Flag Set when the result... --- --- ZF (zero) is zero SF (sign) has its top bit set: negative, read as signed CF (carry) did not fit as an unsigned number (a carry out of, or borrow into, the top bit) OF (overflow) did not fit as a signed number Watch them change.
