The first add overflows as signed (127 + 1 in a byte), the second as unsigned: demo-asm title: Flags after arithmetic on bytes mov al, 127 add al, 1 mov al, 255 add al, 1 mov al, 5 sub al, 5 ret - 127 + 1 in a byte is 0x80 : SF set (negative as signed), OF set (signed overflow), CF clear (128 fits unsigned). - 255 + 1 is 0 with a carry out: ZF and CF set (unsigned overflow), OF clear. - 5 - 5 is 0: ZF set. The processor does not know whether your bytes are signed or unsigned. It computes the bits once and reports both kinds of overflow; the next instruction decides which flags it cares about. Lesson 7.04 uses this for comparisons. Division div (unsigned) and idiv (signed) are the odd ones out. They divide the double-width value in rdx:rax (or edx:eax ) by the operand, putting the quotient in rax and the remainder in rdx : asm mov eax, ecx ; the number to divide cdq ; sign-extend eax into edx:eax idiv r8d ; eax = quotient, edx = remainder Division is slow: tens of cycles, against one for an add. Dividing by zero, or INT_MIN / -1 , raises an exception (integer divide by zero, code 0xC0000094 ). So compilers avoid div whenever they can: C++ What the compiler emits --- --- x / 8 (unsigned) shr eax, 3 x % 8 (unsigned) and eax, 7 x / 10 (unsigned) A multiplication by a "magic" constant ( 0xCCCCCCCD ) and a shift x / 8 (signed) A shift plus a small correction so negative numbers round towards zero When you see a strange large constant multiplied and then shifted in compiler output, it is almost always division by a constant. Bit operations Instruction Effect Typical use --- --- --- and a, b Keep bits set in both Masking: x & 0xFF , testing flags or a, b Set bits set in either Combining flags xor a, b Flip bits set in b Toggling; xor eax, eax sets eax to zero not a Flip every bit ~x shl a, n Shift left by n: multiply by 2ⁿ x << n shr a, n Shift right, filling with zeros: unsigned divide by 2ⁿ x n for unsigned sar a, n Shift right, copying the sign bit x n for signed xor eax, eax deserves a mention because it is everywhere: XOR of anything with itself is zero, and the instruction is shorter than mov eax, 0 . Whenever you see it, read "eax = 0". Bit tricks are everywhere in game and systems code: packing flags into one integer, extracting fields (lesson 5.07's lParam ), hashing (lesson 3.08), rounding up to alignment (lesson 2.02's arena). Common mistakes !warning Reading CF as "the result was negative" CF is unsigned overflow. "Negative" is SF. !warning Assuming shr and sar are interchangeable For negative numbers they differ: sar keeps the sign, shr makes the number large and positive. !warning Forgetting that div uses rdx Code that divides must set up rdx first ( cdq , cqo , or xor edx, edx ), and the remainder overwrites it. Knowledge check quiz ? After mov al, 200 then add al, 100 , which flag tells you the unsigned result did not fit? + CF - OF - ZF 300 does not fit in a byte; the carry out of the top bit sets CF. ? What does xor ecx, ecx do? + Sets ecx to zero - Flips every bit of ecx - Leaves ecx unchanged Any value XOR itself is 0. It is the usual way to zero a register. ? A compiler turned n / 16 into shr eax, 4 . What does that tell you about n ? + It is unsigned (for a signed value, a correction for negative numbers would be needed) - It is a float - It is always zero A logical right shift divides an unsigned number by a power of two. ? Which instruction shifts right while keeping the sign of a negative number? - shr + sar - shl Arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit into the new top bits.

title: The flags after an add
body: Write add8(a, b) , which simulates the instruction add al, bl on two bytes and returns the 8-bit result together with the four flags it sets: - zf : the result is zero; - sf : bit 7 of the result is set; - cf : the true unsigned sum did not fit in 8 bits; - of : the true signed sum (treating a and b as std::int8_t ) did not fit in 8 bits. Then write sub8(a, b) for sub al, bl . For subtraction, cf is set when b is larger than a as unsigned numbers (a borrow), and of when the true signed difference does not fit. add8(127, 1) - result 0x80, sf, of add8(255, 1) - result 0, zf, cf sub8(3, 5) - result 0xFE, sf, cf

title: 7.04  Flags, Comparisons and Jumps
body: Every if , loop and switch in C++ becomes a comparison that sets the flags and a conditional jump that reads them. This lesson covers cmp and test , the family of j cc jumps and which ones mean signed or unsigned, and the branch-free alternatives setcc and cmov . cmp and test Lesson 7.03 showed that arithmetic sets the flags. Two instructions exist only to set them: Instruction Computes Keeps Used for --- --- --- --- cmp a, b a − b Only the flags; a is unchanged Comparing two values test a, b a AND b Only the flags Checking for zero ( test eax, eax ) or particular bits test eax, eax is the idiom for "is eax zero?": ANDing a value with itself gives the value, so ZF is set exactly when it is zero, and SF when it is negative. Conditional jumps A conditional jump goes to a label if a condition on the flags holds, and otherwise falls through to the next instruction. The condition names come in signed and unsigned versions, because "less than" means different things for signed and unsigned numbers (lesson 1.02): After cmp a, b , jump if... Signed Unsigned Flags tested --- --- --- --- a == b je / jz je / jz ZF = 1 a != b jne / jnz jne / jnz ZF = 0 a < b jl jb ("below") SF ≠ OF / CF = 1 a <= b jle jbe ZF = 1 or SF ≠ OF / CF = 1 or ZF = 1 a b jg ja ("above") ZF = 0 and SF = OF / CF = 0 and ZF = 0 a = b jge jae SF = OF / CF = 0 always jmp jmp none So the jump tells you the type : jl / jg after a cmp means the compiler treated the values as signed; jb / ja means unsigned (or pointers, or sizes). When reverse engineering, that is often your first clue to a variable's type. An if, compiled cpp int clampHealth(int h) { if (h 100) h = 100; return h; } asm clampHealth PROC cmp ecx, 100 ; compare h with 100 jle keep ; if h <= 100, skip the assignment mov ecx, 100 keep: mov eax, ecx ; return h ret clampHealth ENDP Notice the inverted condition : C++ says "if h 100, do this", and the compiler writes "if h <= 100, jump over this". That inversion is so common that reading compiled code, you learn to flip conditions automatically. demo-asm title: clampHealth with h = 140 init: ecx=140 cmp ecx, 100 jle keep mov ecx, 100 keep: mov eax, ecx ret With a value of 100 or less in ecx , the jle would be taken instead and mov ecx, 100 skipped. Branch-free versions: setcc and cmov A jump that the processor cannot predict is expensive: modern CPUs guess which way each branch goes and start working ahead, and a wrong guess throws that work away (10 to 20 cycles). For simple choices, compilers often avoid the jump entirely: Instruction Effect --- --- setl al (and sete , setg , setb ...) al = 1 if the condition holds, else 0: a bool result cmovg eax, edx (and every other condition) eax = edx if the condition holds; otherwise eax is unchanged asm ; return a b; ; return a b ? a : b; (std::max) cmp ecx, edx mov eax, edx setg al cmp ecx, edx ret cmovg eax, ecx ret demo-asm title: std::max(8, 3) without a jump init: ecx=8, edx=3 mov eax, edx cmp ecx, edx cmovg eax, ecx ret Common mistakes !warning Reading the jump as the C++ condition Compilers usually jump around the body, so the jump's condition is the opposite of the if . !warning Mixing up jl and jb jl is signed less-than, jb unsigned. For -1 against 1, jl jumps (−1 < 1) and jb does not (0xFFFFFFFF is above 1). !warning Forgetting what set the flags A conditional jump uses whatever instruction last set the flags, which is not always the line right above it. Knowledge check quiz ? What does test eax, eax followed by jz done do? + Jumps to done if eax is zero - Jumps if eax is not zero - Compares eax with zero and stores the result AND of a value with itself is zero only when the value is zero, setting ZF. ? After cmp ecx, edx , the compiler uses ja . What does that suggest about ecx and edx? + They are being compared as unsigned values - They are being compared as signed values - They are floats ja / jb are the unsigned conditions; jg / jl the signed ones. ? The C++ says if (x == 0) { ... } . Which jump is the compiler most likely to emit before the body? + jne , to skip the body when x is not zero - je - jmp The jump goes around the body, so its condition is inverted. ? Why do compilers sometimes use cmov instead of a jump? + To avoid the cost of a branch the processor might predict wrongly - Because cmov is shorter than mov - Because jumps cannot be conditional A mispredicted branch costs many cycles; a conditional move never mispredicts.

title: Will it jump?
body: Write taken(condition, flags) , which says whether a conditional jump with that condition is taken, given the four flags. condition is the part after the j : "e" , "z" , "ne" , "nz" , "l" , "le" , "g" , "ge" , "b" , "be" , "a" , "ae" , "s" , "ns" . Use the flag rules from the lesson's table. For an unknown condition, return std::nullopt . flags after cmp 3, 5: ZF 0, SF 1, CF 1, OF 0 taken("l", ...) = true (3 < 5 as signed) taken("b", ...) = true (3 < 5 as unsigned) taken("g", ...) = false

title: 7.05  The Stack, push, pop, call and ret
match: 7.05 The Stack, push, pop, call and ret
body: Four instructions manage the stack from lesson 1.05 at the machine level. push and pop add and remove 8-byte values; call pushes a return address and jumps; ret pops it and jumps back. This lesson steps through them, shows a function's prologue and epilogue , and explains what a corrupted stack does to ret . push and pop The stack grows downwards, and rsp always points at the value on top (lesson 1.05). Instruction Does Equivalent to --- --- --- push rbx rsp −= 8, then store rbx at rsp sub rsp, 8 / mov rsp , rbx pop rbx load rsp into rbx, then rsp += 8 mov rbx, rsp / add rsp, 8 On x64, push and pop always move 8 bytes. Their main use in compiled code is saving and restoring the non-volatile registers ( rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 to r15 ) that a function must give back unchanged (lesson 2.01). call and ret Instruction Does --- --- call target push the address of the next instruction (the return address ), then jump to target ret pop the return address into rip : continue there ret 0 the same (the number is how many extra bytes to pop; always 0 on x64) Step through a function that saves rbx , uses it, and returns. Watch the stack panel: call pushes the return address, push rbx saves the caller's rbx below it, and they come off again in reverse order. demo-asm title: call, push, pop and ret init: ecx=6, rbx=77 call square add eax, 1 ret square: push rbx mov ebx, ecx imul ebx, ecx mov eax, ebx pop rbx ret At the end, rax is 37 and rbx is back to 77: square used rbx but restored it, as the calling convention requires. Prologue and epilogue Most compiled functions start and end with a fixed pattern that builds and dismantles their stack frame: asm update PROC push rbx ; prologue: save non-volatile registers used below push rdi sub rsp, 40 ; reserve the frame: locals + 32 bytes of shadow space, aligned ... ; the body add rsp, 40 ; epilogue: release the frame pop rdi ; restore in reverse order pop rbx ret update ENDP The numbers follow the alignment rule from lesson 2.01: on entry rsp is 8 off a multiple of 16 (the return address), two pushes make it 8 off again (24 bytes), and sub rsp, 40 brings the total to 64, a multiple of 16, ready for this function's own calls. Older code, and code compiled for easier debugging, also sets up rbp as a frame pointer : asm push rbp mov rbp, rsp ; rbp marks the frame; locals are at rbp-8, rbp-16 ... sub rsp, 48 ... mov rsp, rbp pop rbp ret x64 Windows code usually omits it. The debugger and Windows find frames through unwind information that the compiler stores in the .pdata and .xdata sections, describing each function's prologue so the stack can be walked without a frame pointer (lesson 8.02). When the stack is corrupted ret trusts whatever 8 bytes are at rsp . If a buffer overrun on the stack (lesson 2.09) has overwritten the return address, ret jumps to that garbage, and the crash happens at a nonsense address with a nonsense call stack. This is also the classic way attackers hijack programs, which is why compilers add defences: - Stack cookies ( /GS , on by default): the prologue puts a secret value between the locals and the return address, and the epilogue checks it before ret . An overrun that reaches the return address changes the cookie first, and the program is stopped with a security check failure instead of jumping. - Control-flow guard and shadow stacks (on recent CPUs and Windows) check calls and returns against what is allowed. When you see a crash at a strange address with a broken call stack, suspect a stack overrun and turn on AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10). Common mistakes !warning Unbalanced push and pop Every push in a function must be matched by a pop (or an add rsp ) before ret , or ret pops the wrong value. !warning Popping in the wrong order Registers must be restored in the reverse order they were saved. !warning Reading ret 0 as "return 0" The 0 is a byte count for the stack, not the return value. The return value is in rax . Knowledge check quiz ? What does call square push onto the stack? + The address of the instruction after the call - The address of square - The value of rax ret later pops it to continue after the call. ? A function's prologue is push rbx then push rsi . In what order must its epilogue restore them? + pop rsi , then pop rbx - pop rbx , then pop rsi - Either order The stack is last in, first out. ? What does a stack cookie protect? + The return address, by detecting overruns from locals before ret uses it - The heap - The code section The epilogue checks the cookie and stops the program if it changed. ? In square above, why does the function push and pop rbx ? + rbx is non-volatile: the caller expects it unchanged after the call - rbx holds the return address - imul requires it Functions may use non-volatile registers only if they restore them.

title: 7.06  The Microsoft x64 Calling Convention
body: A calling convention is the agreement between a caller and the function it calls: where arguments go, where the result comes back, which registers survive the call and who cleans up the stack. On 64-bit Windows there is one convention for everything. Knowing it lets you read any function's arguments in the debugger, follow calls in disassembly, and write assembly that C++ can call. Why a convention is needed The compiler that builds a caller and the compiler that built the function might be different programs, years apart: your game calling CreateFileW in kernel32.dll , a plugin calling the engine, C++ calling assembly. They only work together if both follow the same rules. On x64 Windows those rules are the Microsoft x64 calling convention , and every compiler targeting Windows follows it. Arguments The first four arguments go in registers, the rest on the stack: Argument Integer or pointer Floating point --- --- --- 1st rcx xmm0 2nd rdx xmm1 3rd r8 xmm2 4th r9 xmm3 5th and later On the stack, at rsp+28h , rsp+30h , ... at the moment of the call The position decides the register, not the type: in f(int a, float b, int c) , a is in rcx , b in xmm1 (second position), and c in r8 . - A member function's hidden this is the first argument: it is in rcx , and the visible arguments shift along by one. - Structs of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes are passed in a register as if they were an integer. Any other size is copied by the caller to memory, and a pointer to the copy is passed. Return values - Integers, pointers, and structs of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes come back in rax . - float and double come back in xmm0 . - Larger structs: the caller passes a hidden pointer (in rcx , moving the other arguments along) to space it has reserved, the function fills it in, and returns that pointer in rax . Shadow space The caller always reserves 32 bytes of shadow space (home space) on the stack just above the return address, even if the function takes fewer than four arguments (lesson 2.01). The function may store its register arguments there. Debug builds do exactly that, which is why the debugger can show a function's arguments even after the registers have been reused. at the moment the function starts: rsp+28h 5th argument (if any) rsp+20h shadow space for r9 rsp+18h shadow space for r8 rsp+10h shadow space for rdx rsp+8 shadow space for rcx rsp return address Volatile and non-volatile registers Volatile: the function may destroy them Non-volatile: the function must preserve them --- --- rax , rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , r10 , r11 rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 , r13 , r14 , r15 , rsp xmm0 to xmm5 xmm6 to xmm15 A caller that needs a volatile register's value after a call must save it somewhere first. A function that wants to use a non-volatile register must save and restore it (lesson 7.05's push rbx / pop rbx ). Reading a call in disassembly cpp float applyDamage(Player& p, int amount, float armour, bool critical); ... applyDamage(hero, 40, 0.25f, true); asm mov r9b, 1 ; 4th: critical = true (in r9) movss xmm2, dword ptr __real@3e800000 ; 3rd: armour = 0.25f (3rd position: xmm2) mov edx, 40 ; 2nd: amount (rdx) lea rcx, hero ; 1st: &hero (a reference is a pointer, in rcx) call applyDamage movss dword ptr result , xmm0 ; the float result comes back in xmm0 Arguments are often loaded in an order unrelated to the C++ order; what matters is which register each ends up in. 0x3e800000 is the bit pattern of 0.25 (lesson 2.11). Variadic functions For printf and other functions with ... , floating-point values among the first four arguments are passed in both the integer register and the xmm register for their position, because the callee cannot know which one to look at. Common mistakes !warning Mapping the 2nd argument to xmm0 because it is the first float Registers follow the argument's position. The 2nd argument, float or not, uses the 2nd slot: rdx or xmm1 . !warning Forgetting this In a member function, rcx is this and the first visible argument is in rdx . !warning Calling a function with less than 32 bytes reserved Hand-written assembly must reserve shadow space before every call, even to functions with no arguments. Knowledge check quiz ? Where is the third argument of void f(int a, int b, int c, int d, int e) ? + r8 - rdx - On the stack rcx, rdx, r8, r9 for the first four; the fifth goes on the stack. ? Where is y in void g(int x, double y) ? + xmm1 , because it is the second argument - xmm0 , because it is the first floating-point argument - rdx The position decides the register. ? In player.heal(25) , which register holds 25? + rdx , because this takes rcx - rcx - r8 The hidden this is the first argument. ? A function changes rbx and r10 . Which must it restore before returning? + Only rbx - Only r10 - Both rbx is non-volatile; r10 is volatile and may be destroyed.

title: Where does each argument go?
body: Write argumentLocations(types, isMember) . types lists a function's parameter types in order, each 'i' (integer or pointer) or 'f' (float or double). If isMember is true, there is also a hidden this pointer before them, which takes the first slot but is not included in the result. Return where each listed parameter is passed under the Microsoft x64 calling convention: - slots 1 to 4: "rcx" , "rdx" , "r8" , "r9" for integers, "xmm0" to "xmm3" for floats, chosen by the slot number ; - slot 5 and later: " rsp+28h " , " rsp+30h " , " rsp+38h " and so on (8 bytes apart, as seen at the start of the function), whatever the type. argumentLocations("ifi", false) = { "rcx", "xmm1", "r8" } argumentLocations("ii", true) = { "rdx", "r8" } (this is in rcx) argumentLocations("iiiiif", false) = { "rcx", "rdx", "r8", "r9", " rsp+28h ", " rsp+30h " }

title: 7.07  Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch
match: 7.07 Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch
body: Control flow in C++ compiles into a small set of recognisable shapes built from comparisons and jumps. This lesson teaches you to recognise them: if and if / else , while and for loops (and how compilers rotate them), short-circuit && and , and the jump table a switch becomes. Recognising shapes is how you read disassembly quickly. The method When reading compiled code, do not try to understand each instruction in isolation. Look for the shape : 1. Find the jumps. Each conditional jump is a decision; each backward jump (to a lower address) is a loop. 2. Group the instructions between jumps into basic blocks : straight runs with one way in and one way out. 3. Draw the blocks and the arrows between them. The picture is the control flow, and it maps back to if , while and switch . Disassemblers such as Ghidra and IDA draw this graph for you (chapter 9). With practice you see it directly in the listing. if and if/else cpp int grade(int score) { if (score = 50) return 1; return 0; } asm cmp ecx, 50 jl fail ; inverted: skip the "then" part when score < 50 mov eax, 1 ret fail: xor eax, eax ret With an else , the "then" block ends with an unconditional jmp over the "else" block to the code after both: (Optimisers often replace small if/else assignments with cmov , lesson 7.04, so there may be no jump at all.) Loops A while loop literally compiled would test at the top and jump back to the test at the bottom: two jumps per iteration. Compilers rotate loops instead: test once before entering, then test again at the bottom with a single backward jump. cpp int sum(const int values, int count) { int total{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < count; ++i) total += values i ; return total; } asm xor eax, eax ; total = 0 test edx, edx ; count <= 0? then skip the loop entirely jle done xor r8d, r8d ; i = 0 top: add eax, rcx+r8 4 ; total += values i inc r8d ; ++i cmp r8d, edx ; i < count? jl top ; backward jump: the loop done: ret The backward jump to top is the signature of a loop. The block before it is the guard that skips the loop when it would run zero times. Step through it with three values: demo-asm title: The rotated loop, count = 3 init: rcx=0x2000, edx=3, mem@0x2000=5 7 9 xor eax, eax test edx, edx jle done xor r8d, r8d top: add eax, dword ptr rcx+r8 4 inc r8d cmp r8d, edx jl top done: ret In optimised builds, loops may also be unrolled (the body repeated several times per jump) or vectorised (processing four or eight elements per instruction, lesson 7.11), which changes the shape but not the backward jump. && and C++ guarantees short-circuit evaluation: in a && b , b is not evaluated if a is false. That becomes a chain of jumps, each able to skip straight to the outcome: cpp if (enemy != nullptr && enemy- health 0) attack(enemy); asm test rcx, rcx ; enemy == nullptr? je skip ; then the whole condition is false cmp dword ptr rcx+8 , 0 ; enemy- health 0? jle skip call attack skip: Two conditional jumps to the same label is the shape of && . For , the first test jumps to the "true" block instead. switch and jump tables A switch over a few cases compiles to a chain of comparisons. Over many dense cases (values close together), the compiler builds a jump table : an array of addresses, one per case, and jumps through it with a single indexed jump. cpp const char stateName(int state) { switch (state) { case 0: return "idle"; case 1: return "walking"; case 2: return "running"; case 3: return "jumping"; case 4: return "falling"; default: return "?"; } } asm cmp ecx, 4 ja default_case ; unsigned compare: also catches negative values! movsxd rax, ecx lea rdx, __ImageBase mov eax, rdx+rax 4+table_rva ; read the case's offset from the table add rax, rdx jmp rax ; jump to that case Three things to recognise: - One unsigned comparison ( ja ) checks the range: a negative value, seen as unsigned, is huge, so it also goes to default . One check covers both ends. - An indexed load from a table, scaled by 4 or 8. - An indirect jump ( jmp rax ). Sparse cases (1, 100, 5000) get a chain of comparisons or a binary search instead. Common mistakes !warning Reading every jump as an if Backward jumps are loops; a jmp at the end of a block is usually the "skip the else" jump. !warning Expecting the loop test at the top Rotated loops test at the bottom, with a guard before the loop. !warning Missing the range check before a jump table The cmp and ja before it tell you the number of cases. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the signature of a loop in disassembly? + A conditional jump backwards, to a lower address - Any cmp instruction - A call Looping means going back to code that already ran. ? Why does a rotated loop have a test before the loop as well as at the bottom? + To skip the loop entirely when it should run zero times - Because the CPU requires two tests - To count the iterations The bottom test decides whether to go round again; the guard handles the zero-iteration case. ? Two conditional jumps lead to the same label just before a call . What C++ is this likely to be? + if (a && b) call(); - if (a b) call(); - A switch Either condition failing skips the call. ? Why does a jump table's range check use ja instead of jg ? + An unsigned comparison also sends negative values to the default case with one check - jg does not exist - The cases are always unsigned Negative numbers read as unsigned are larger than any case.

title: 7.08  Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
match: 7.08 Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
body: In assembly there are no types, only addresses and sizes. A struct member is a fixed offset from a pointer; an array element is base plus index times size; a pointer chain is a series of loads. This lesson shows how each C++ data access compiles, and how to work backwards from the offsets and sizes in disassembly to the data structures behind them. Members are offsets cpp struct Monster { int id; // +0 float x, y; // +4, +8 int health; // +12 Monster target; // +16 }; void hurt(Monster m, int amount) { m- health -= amount; if (m- health <= 0) m- target = nullptr; } asm hurt PROC sub dword ptr rcx+0Ch , edx ; m- health -= amount (offset 12, 4 bytes) jg alive mov qword ptr rcx+10h , 0 ; m- target = nullptr (offset 16, 8 bytes) alive: ret hurt ENDP Every member access is pointer + offset with a size. Reading this cold, with no source, you could still say: the first argument points at a structure; at offset 0xC there is a 4-byte integer that is compared with zero; at offset 0x10 an 8-byte value that is set to zero, probably a pointer. That is how chapter 9 rebuilds unknown structs. sub also set the flags, so the compiler used them directly for the <= 0 test with jg : no separate cmp . Optimisers do this whenever they can. Arrays of structs An element of an array of structs is base + index × sizeof(struct) + member offset . When the size is 1, 2, 4 or 8 the scale does it; otherwise the index is multiplied first: cpp struct Particle { float x, y, vx, vy, life; }; // 20 bytes float lifeOf(const Particle particles, int i) { return particles i .life; } asm movsxd rax, edx ; i, widened to 64 bits lea rax, rax+rax 4 ; i 5 movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+rax 4+10h ; particles + i 20 + 16: the life member ret i 5 4 = i 20 (the struct size) plus 0x10 (the offset of life ). When you see an index multiplied by an odd constant, divide to get the element size. Pointer chains world- player- inventory- gold (lesson 3.02) is one load per arrow: asm mov rax, qword ptr rcx+18h ; world- player (player is at offset 0x18 in World) mov rax, qword ptr rax+40h ; - inventory (inventory at 0x40 in Player) mov eax, dword ptr rax+8 ; - gold (gold at 8 in Inventory) Each qword load produces the address for the next. A run of dependent 8-byte loads like this is a pointer chain, and its offsets are the layouts of each struct in turn. Objects with virtual functions A virtual call (lesson 3.05) has its own fingerprint: asm mov rax, qword ptr rcx ; load the vptr from offset 0 call qword ptr rax+18h ; call slot 3 of the vtable (0x18 / 8) A load from offset 0 of an object followed by an indirect call through that value plus an offset: a virtual call. The offset divided by 8 is the slot number. Working backwards: a reading table You see Probably --- --- dword ptr rcx+N A 4-byte member ( int , float , enum) at offset N of the struct rcx points to qword ptr rcx+N then used as an address A pointer member at offset N movss / movsd with a memory operand A float / double member movzx eax, byte ptr rcx+N , then test al, al A bool member rcx+rdx 4 , rcx+rdx 8 An array of 4- or 8-byte elements imul rdx, rdx, 38h then rcx+rdx An array of 56-byte structs mov rax, rcx then call rax+N A virtual call, slot N/8 lea rcx, rdi+20h then call Passing the address of a member (or base subobject) at offset 0x20 Common mistakes !warning Assuming the same register means the same object Registers are reused constantly. Track what each one holds at each point. !warning Forgetting padding when guessing a layout A 4-byte member at offset 0 followed by an 8-byte one at offset 8 means padding at 4 to 7, not a hidden member (lesson 2.05). !warning Reading lea as a load lea rcx, rdi+20h takes an address; it does not read the member. Knowledge check quiz ? mov eax, dword ptr rcx+0Ch with rcx holding a struct pointer. What is being read? + A 4-byte member at offset 12 - The 12th element of an array - A pointer at offset 12 dword ptr is 4 bytes; +0Ch is the member's offset. ? Code computes lea rax, rax+rax 2 and then reads rcx+rax 8 . What is the element size? + 24 bytes - 8 bytes - 3 bytes The index is multiplied by 3, then scaled by 8. ? What does mov rax, rcx followed by call qword ptr rax+10h indicate? + A virtual call to slot 2 of the object's vtable - A call to a function at address rcx + 16 - Reading an array The first load fetches the vptr; 0x10 / 8 = slot 2.

title: Rebuild a struct from its accesses
match: Rebuild a struct from its accesses
where: 7.08 Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
body: A reverse engineer has collected every memory access a function makes through one struct pointer: each one an offset and a size in bytes (1, 2, 4 or 8). Write guessLayout(accesses) , which turns them into a list of fields, the way a disassembler's "create structure" feature does: - Each distinct offset becomes one field. If an offset was accessed with different sizes, use the largest. - Fields are listed in order of offset. - Each field's type name comes from its size: 1 "uint8_t" , 2 "uint16_t" , 4 "uint32_t" , 8 "uint64_t" . - Gaps between fields (bytes not covered by any field) become padding fields named "pad" of type "uint8_t N " , where N is the gap size, so the offsets add up. There is no padding after the last field. accesses: {0x0,4} {0x10,8} {0xC,4} {0x0,4} fields: 0x0 uint32_t 0x4 uint8_t 8 (pad) 0xC uint32_t 0x10 uint64_t

title: 7.09  Floating Point with SSE
body: x64 code does floating-point maths in the 16 xmm registers with SSE instructions. Scalar instructions like addss work on one float ; packed ones like addps work on four at once, the start of SIMD . This lesson reads typical game maths in assembly: loading constants, arithmetic, comparisons, conversions between ints and floats, and a first look at vectorised code. The xmm registers Each xmm0 to xmm15 register is 128 bits wide: room for four float s or two double s. (Newer processors extend them to 256-bit ymm and 512-bit zmm registers with AVX; the ideas are the same.) For ordinary scalar maths the compiler uses only the lowest lane: xmm0: float 3 float 2 float 1 float 0 <- scalar code uses lane 0 only 127 31 0 Instruction names end in a suffix saying what they work on: Suffix Means Example --- --- --- ss S calar S ingle: one float addss xmm0, xmm1 sd S calar D ouble: one double mulsd xmm0, xmm2 ps P acked S ingle: four float s addps xmm0, xmm1 pd P acked D ouble: two double s subpd xmm3, xmm4 Everyday float code cpp float speedAfterFriction(float speed, float friction, float dt) { return speed (1.0f - friction dt); } asm speedAfterFriction PROC mulss xmm1, xmm2 ; friction dt movss xmm3, dword ptr __real@3f800000 ; load the constant 1.0f subss xmm3, xmm1 ; 1.0f - friction dt mulss xmm0, xmm3 ; speed (...) ret ; result in xmm0 speedAfterFriction ENDP - Arguments arrive in xmm0 , xmm1 , xmm2 by position (lesson 7.06); the result leaves in xmm0 . - There are no float immediates: constants live in read-only data and are loaded from memory. MSVC names them after their bits, so __real@3f800000 is 1.0f (lesson 2.11's table). Reading those names tells you the constants directly. - movss loads and stores one float; movaps / movups move all 128 bits (aligned or unaligned). Conversions and comparisons Instruction Does C++ --- --- --- cvtsi2ss xmm0, eax int to float static_cast<float (i) cvttss2si eax, xmm0 float to int, truncating towards zero static_cast<int (f) cvtss2sd xmm0, xmm0 float to double passing a float to printf comiss xmm0, xmm1 / ucomiss compare, setting ZF, CF (and PF) a < b sqrtss , minss , maxss square root, minimum, maximum std::sqrt , std::min xorps xmm0, xmm0 zero the register 0.0f Float comparisons set the flags like an unsigned integer compare, so they are followed by ja , jb , jae , jbe , not jg / jl . Comparisons involving NaN ("not a number") are "unordered" and set the parity flag, which is why you sometimes see an extra jp after them. SIMD: four at once The packed instructions do the same operation on every lane in one go. Adding two arrays of floats four elements per instruction is up to four times the work per instruction: asm top: movups xmm0, rcx+rax ; load 4 floats from a movups xmm1, rdx+rax ; load 4 floats from b addps xmm0, xmm1 ; 4 additions in one instruction movups r8+rax , xmm0 ; store 4 results add rax, 16 ; advance by 4 floats cmp rax, r9 jb top Optimising compilers produce loops like this automatically from plain C++ ( auto-vectorisation ) when the loop is simple enough: no dependencies between iterations, no function calls in the body, data laid out contiguously. That last condition is a big part of why engines store data as structures of arrays (all x values together, all y values together) rather than arrays of structures for the hottest loops. You can also write SIMD by hand with intrinsics ( _mm_add_ps and friends from <immintrin.h ), which map one-to-one onto these instructions. Precision and determinism float has about 7 significant decimal digits; double about 16. Results can differ with optimisation settings (the compiler may reorder a + b + c only under /fp:fast , which is not the default) and between processors for some library functions. For lockstep multiplayer games and replays, which need bit-identical results everywhere, programs keep the default /fp:precise , avoid /fp:fast , and sometimes use fixed-point integers for game logic instead. Common mistakes !warning Expecting float arguments in rcx/rdx Floating-point arguments use the xmm register of their position. !warning Reading a float comparison's ja as unsigned integers After comiss , ja / jb are simply "greater"/"less" for floats. !warning Converting with truncation when rounding was meant static_cast<int (2.9f) is 2. Use std::lround to round. Knowledge check quiz ? What does mulss xmm0, xmm1 do? + Multiplies the single float in the lowest lane of xmm0 by the one in xmm1 - Multiplies four floats in each register - Multiplies two doubles ss means scalar single precision. ? Why does compiled float code load constants from memory? + x64 instructions cannot hold floating-point immediates - Constants are faster from memory - The compiler cannot compute them They are stored in read-only data, often named after their bit pattern. ? What is the advantage of addps over addss ? + It adds four pairs of floats in one instruction - It is more precise - It works with integers Packed instructions operate on every lane at once: SIMD. ? After comiss xmm0, xmm1 , which jump means "xmm0 is greater"? + ja - jg - jl Float compares set the flags like an unsigned comparison.

title: 7.10  Writing Assembly Functions with MASM
body: Microsoft's assembler, MASM ( ml64.exe ), ships with Visual Studio. This lesson writes a few functions in assembly, adds them to a C++ project, and calls them from C++, following the calling convention by hand. Writing even a little assembly makes reading it much easier, and shows exactly what the compiler does for you. When to write assembly Almost never in game code. Compilers produce excellent code, and intrinsics (lesson 7.09) cover most hand-tuned SIMD. Hand-written assembly survives in a few places: the start-up code of operating systems and runtimes, a handful of instructions compilers cannot express, and teaching. 64-bit MSVC does not even support inline __asm blocks; assembly goes in separate .asm files. We write it here to learn: every rule in this chapter must be followed by hand, and the assembler will not save you. Setting up a project 1. In your course solution, right-click the project → Build Dependencies → Build Customizations → tick masm . 2. Add a new file named maths.asm (choose a C++ file and rename it). In its properties, Item Type should now be Microsoft Macro Assembler . 3. Build: ml64.exe assembles maths.asm into maths.obj , and the linker joins it with your C++ objects like any other (lesson 4.02). A first function masm ; maths.asm: int addThree(int a, int b, int c) .code addThree PROC lea eax, rcx+rdx ; a + b (a in ecx, b in edx) add eax, r8d ; + c (c in r8d) ret ; result in eax addThree ENDP END cpp-norun // main.cpp include <iostream extern "C" int addThree(int a, int b, int c); // declared in C++, defined in assembly int main() { std::cout << addThree(1, 2, 39) << '\n'; } extern "C" matters: the assembly defines the plain name addThree , and without extern "C" the C++ side would look for the mangled ?addThree@@YAHHHH@Z and fail with LNK2019 (lesson 4.02). A loop and a non-volatile register masm ; long long sumArray(const int values, long long count) .code sumArray PROC push rbx ; we use rbx below, and it is non-volatile: save it xor eax, eax ; total = 0 (64-bit: writing eax clears the top of rax) xor ebx, ebx ; i = 0 test rdx, rdx jle done ; count <= 0: nothing to add next: movsxd r9, dword ptr rcx+rbx 4 ; values i , sign-extended to 64 bits add rax, r9 inc rbx cmp rbx, rdx jl next done: pop rbx ; restore it before returning ret sumArray ENDP END Nothing here needed rbx : r10 (volatile) would have done without the push and pop. Using it shows the rule: touch a non-volatile register, and you must save and restore it. Calling C++ from assembly Calling out is where the convention bites. Before a call , rsp must be 16-byte aligned and 32 bytes of shadow space reserved: masm ; void logTwice(int value) calls the C++ function extern "C" void logValue(int) EXTERN logValue:PROC .code logTwice PROC push rbx ; entry: rsp was 8 off a multiple of 16; after this push it is aligned sub rsp, 32 ; shadow space for the calls: still aligned (8 + 8 + 32 = 48 bytes in all) mov ebx, ecx ; keep value in a non-volatile register across the calls call logValue ; ecx still holds value mov ecx, ebx ; ecx is volatile: logValue may have changed it call logValue add rsp, 32 pop rbx ret logTwice ENDP END The arithmetic: on entry rsp is a multiple of 16 minus 8 (the return address). push rbx subtracts 8 (now a multiple of 16), sub rsp, 32 keeps it a multiple of 16, and leaves the 32 bytes of shadow space the callee may use. Getting this wrong works most of the time and then crashes inside some library function that uses aligned SSE stores: one of the hardest bugs to trace back. !note Unwind information Functions that change rsp or save registers should, strictly, also describe their prologue to Windows with MASM's .PUSHREG , .ALLOCSTACK and .ENDPROLOG directives (using PROC FRAME ), so exceptions and the debugger can walk the stack through them. For learning exercises that never throw, it can be left out; production assembly must include it. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting extern "C" The linker cannot match the assembly's plain name with a mangled C++ declaration. !warning Misaligned stack at a call Count every push and sub rsp from entry: at the call , rsp must be a multiple of 16, with 32 bytes of shadow space reserved. !warning Keeping values in volatile registers across a call rcx , rdx , r8 to r11 and rax may all change. Keep anything you need afterwards in a non-volatile register or on the stack. Knowledge check quiz ? Why must the C++ declaration of an assembly function be extern "C" ? + So the C++ side looks for the plain, unmangled name the assembly defines - Because assembly is written in C - To make the call faster Otherwise the linker searches for a mangled symbol that does not exist. ? Inside logTwice , why is the value kept in ebx between the two calls? + rbx is non-volatile, so logValue must leave it unchanged; ecx might be overwritten - ebx is faster than ecx - call requires it Anything needed after a call must be in a non-volatile register or memory. ? What two conditions must hold at every call instruction in your assembly? + rsp is a multiple of 16, and 32 bytes of shadow space are reserved above it - rax is zero and rbx holds the return address - The flags are cleared Both come from the Microsoft x64 calling convention.

title: 7.11  What Optimised Code Looks Like
body: Release builds rarely look like their source. Functions disappear into their callers, loops are unrolled and vectorised, variables never touch memory, and branches become arithmetic. This lesson is a field guide to the transformations you will meet in optimised disassembly, so that you can map it back to the C++ (or, when reverse engineering, to something like it). The same function, three ways cpp int countAlive(const int health, int n) { int alive{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) if (health i 0) ++alive; return alive; } Debug ( /Od ): every variable in memory, every line separate, one element per iteration, a real branch for the if . Easy to follow, slow. Optimised ( /O2 ), roughly: asm xor eax, eax ; alive = 0 test edx, edx jle done ; ... (a vectorised loop handles 8 elements at a time here, see below) scalar: cmp dword ptr rcx , 0 setg r8b ; r8b = health i 0 ? 1 : 0 (no branch) add eax, r8d ; alive += that add rcx, 4 ; walk a pointer instead of indexing dec edx jnz scalar done: ret Notice what changed: - alive and i live only in registers. - The if became setg plus add : branchless code, because whether a monster is alive is unpredictable and a mispredicted branch is costly (lesson 7.04). - health i became a pointer that moves along ( add rcx, 4 ), and the loop counts down to zero, so dec sets ZF for the jump without a cmp . The vectorised part, for large n , compares 4 or 8 values at once with pcmpgtd (packed compare greater-than), uses the all-ones result lanes as -1, and subtracts them from a counter vector: eight comparisons and additions per instruction pair, then adds the lanes together at the end. Field guide You see It was probably --- --- A call is missing; the callee's body appears inline Inlining : small functions are copied into their callers A loop body repeated 4 or 8 times per jump Unrolling : fewer jumps, more work per iteration xmm / ymm packed instructions in integer or float loops Vectorisation (lesson 7.09) setcc , cmov , sbb , and with -1 masks instead of jumps Branch removal A constant where you expected arithmetic Constant folding A multiply by a large odd constant then a shift Division by a constant (lesson 7.03) lea doing sums and small multiplies Strength reduction (lesson 7.02) A loop that counts down, or a pointer that advances Induction variable rewriting jmp to another function at the end instead of call + ret Tail call : the callee returns straight to our caller Code you wrote is gone entirely Dead code elimination : its result was never used A function's code shared by several functions with identical bodies Identical COMDAT folding ( /OPT:ICF ) Inlining and the missing functions Inlining matters most for reading. A small getter like int health() const { return m_health; } usually vanishes: the caller simply reads rcx+0Ch . Calls to it no longer exist in the program, so a breakpoint in it may never hit, and a reverse engineer sees one large function where the source had ten small ones. With link-time code generation ( /GL + /LTCG ), functions from different .cpp files can be inlined into each other too. Tail calls cpp int damageFor(const Weapon& w, int level) { return scaleDamage(w.baseDamage, level); } asm damageFor PROC mov ecx, dword ptr rcx+8 jmp scaleDamage ; not call: scaleDamage's ret returns to our caller damageFor ENDP damageFor has nothing to do after the call, so it jumps instead of calling, and damageFor never appears in the call stack while scaleDamage runs. Debugger call stacks in optimised code can skip frames for this reason. Reading optimised code well 1. Find the structure first : loops (backward jumps), calls, returns. Ignore the clever arithmetic until you know what the function's shape is. 2. Track values, not variables : one C++ variable may live in different registers at different points, and one register may hold different variables. 3. Expect the vectorised and scalar versions of a loop side by side : a SIMD loop for most of the elements and a plain "remainder" loop for the last few. 4. Use the symbols : with a .pdb , the Disassembly window interleaves source lines; even when they are out of order, they tell you which C++ each instruction came from. Common mistakes !warning Concluding a function is never called It may be called everywhere, inlined into each caller. !warning Reading a vectorised loop instruction by instruction First find the scalar remainder loop, which does the same thing one element at a time and is much easier to read. !warning Assuming the source order of operations The optimiser reorders anything whose order does not change the result. Knowledge check quiz ? A small getter function has no call to it anywhere in an optimised build. Why? + It was inlined: its body was copied into each caller - It is never used - Getters cannot be called in Release Inlining removes the call entirely. ? Why might an if inside a loop compile to setg and add instead of a jump? + To avoid mispredicted branches when the condition is unpredictable - Because jumps are not allowed in loops - Because if is not supported in Release Branchless code costs the same every iteration. ? A function ends with jmp otherFunction instead of call and ret . What is this? + A tail call: otherFunction returns directly to our caller - An infinite loop - A crash The current function has no more work after the call, so it jumps instead. ? What usually accompanies a vectorised loop? + A scalar loop handling the leftover elements - A second vectorised loop doing the same work again - A call to a library function The number of elements is rarely a multiple of the vector width.

title: 8.01  Thinking Like a Debugger
body: Debugging is a method, not a talent. This lesson sets out the method experienced engineers use: make the bug happen reliably, form a hypothesis, test it with the smallest possible experiment, and narrow the search by halving it. It covers minimal reproductions , bisecting code and history, and the habits that make the tools in the rest of this chapter effective. The loop Every effective debugging session runs the same loop: The common failure is skipping steps: changing code at random ("maybe it's this"), or fixing the first suspicious thing without confirming it caused the symptom. A fix you cannot explain is a guess, and guesses usually move a bug rather than remove it. Step 1: reproduce A bug you can trigger on demand is half solved. A bug that happens "sometimes" is the hardest kind, so the first job is to make it reliable: - Write down the exact steps, inputs, save file, settings and build. - Remove randomness: fix the random seed, fix the time step, record the input. - For "sometimes" bugs, run it in a loop (a script that starts the game a hundred times) and look for what the failing runs have in common. - Check the obvious variables: Debug or Release? Your machine or another? Fresh install or old settings? Step 2: observe precisely "It crashes" is not an observation. "It crashes with an access violation reading 0x10 , in Inventory::weight , called from Hud::draw , only after picking up an item while the inventory screen is open" is. The debugger's job (chapter 4) is to turn vague symptoms into precise ones: the exact instruction, the exact values, the exact call stack. Read error messages and crash details completely, as lesson 4.03 said for compiler errors. The address, the exception code (lesson 8.04) and the module are each clues. Step 3: one hypothesis at a time A good hypothesis is specific and testable: "the item pointer is stale because the inventory vector grew" can be tested with a data breakpoint or a log line. "Something's wrong with memory" cannot. Test it with the cheapest experiment that could prove it wrong : a conditional breakpoint, a log line, an assert, changing one input. If the experiment shows the hypothesis is wrong, that is progress too: one possibility is gone. Narrowing the search: halve it When you do not know where a bug is, do not read code hoping to spot it. Bisect : split the search space in half, find out which half contains the bug, repeat. Each step halves the remaining space, so even a huge search is short: about 10 steps for a thousand possibilities, 20 for a million. What to bisect How --- --- History : which change introduced the bug? git bisect : mark a known good and a known bad commit; Git checks out the midpoint, you test and answer "good" or "bad", repeat Input : which part of a level or save file triggers it? Delete half the content; does the bug remain? Code path : where does a value go wrong? Check the value at the midpoint of the computation with a breakpoint or log Time : when does state become corrupt? Log or assert the invariant every frame; find the first frame it fails The practice task implements the search at the heart of this. Minimal reproductions Once a bug is reliable, shrink it: remove everything that is not needed for it to happen. A 30-line program that shows the bug is far easier to reason about than a whole game, and very often the act of shrinking it reveals the cause. It is also what you need to report a bug in someone else's library or compiler. Habits that pay off - Check your assumptions out loud. Explaining the code line by line to someone else, or to a rubber duck, forces you to notice the step you were skipping. - Change one thing at a time , and keep notes of what you tried. - Suspect your newest code first , and your oldest assumptions second. - When the impossible happens, an assumption is wrong. "This pointer can't be null here" is a hypothesis to test, not a fact. - After fixing, write a test that would have caught it (chapter 17), so it stays fixed. Common mistakes !warning Changing several things at once If the bug disappears, you do not know which change fixed it, or whether one of them just hid it. !warning Debugging a different build than the one that fails If it only fails in Release, debug the Release build (lesson 8.06). !warning Stopping at the first suspicious code Confirm it causes the symptom: does the bug go away when it is fixed, and come back when it is restored? Knowledge check quiz ? Why is reproducing a bug reliably the first step? + Without it, you cannot tell whether an experiment or fix made any difference - Because the debugger only works on reproducible bugs - It is not important; finding the code matters more Every later step depends on being able to trigger the bug on demand. ? A bug appeared somewhere in the last 512 commits. How many tests does bisecting need, at most? + About 9 - 256 - 512 Each test halves the range: 2⁹ = 512. ? What makes a good hypothesis? + It names a specific cause and can be proved wrong by a quick experiment - It explains every bug in the program - It is the first idea that comes to mind Specific and testable is what makes progress possible.

title: Find the first bad build
body: A bug appeared somewhere in a list of builds numbered 0 to count - 1 . Build 0 is known to be good and the last build is known to be bad; once a build is bad, every later build is bad too. Write firstBad(count, isBad) , which returns the number of the first bad build. isBad(n) tests build n , and testing is slow, so the function must use as few tests as possible: a binary search, like git bisect . The tests count your calls. You may assume count = 2 , isBad(0) is false and isBad(count - 1) is true; do not test those two. count 10, builds 0..5 good, 6..9 bad - 6

title: 8.02  Call Stacks and Symbols
body: A call stack turns a crash address into a story: which function, called from where, with what. Making that work needs symbols : the .pdb files that map machine code back to names and source lines. This lesson covers what is in a PDB, how debuggers find the right one, Microsoft's symbol server for Windows' own DLLs, how stacks are walked without frame pointers, and how to capture a stack trace from inside your own program. What symbols are The compiler and linker throw names away: in the .exe , a function is just bytes at an RVA. The program database ( .pdb ) file written alongside it keeps everything a debugger needs to get the names back: In the PDB Lets the debugger --- --- Function names and their RVA ranges Name the function containing any address Line number tables Map each instruction to a source file and line Types and struct layouts Show player.health instead of raw bytes Local variables and where they live Fill the Locals window Frame data Help walk the stack A PDB matches exactly one build . The exe records a unique signature (a GUID and an age) and the PDB's file name in its debug directory; the debugger only loads a PDB whose signature matches. Rebuild even without changing anything, and the old PDB no longer fits. That is why you keep the PDB of every build you ship : without it, a crash report from that build can only show raw addresses. How the debugger finds symbols For each loaded module, the debugger searches, in order: 1. The path recorded in the exe (where the PDB was written at build time). 2. The folder the module was loaded from. 3. The symbol path : folders and symbol servers you configure ( Tools → Options → Debugging → Symbols ). Visual Studio's Modules window shows, for every DLL and exe, whether symbols loaded and from where. "Cannot find or open the PDB file" there explains a call stack full of game.exe!00007ff6a1235f10() instead of names. The Microsoft symbol server Windows' own DLLs have public symbols too: Microsoft publishes them on a symbol server , a web service that hands out the PDB matching each DLL's signature. Turn it on in Visual Studio (tick Microsoft Symbol Servers ) or set the environment variable used by WinDbg and other tools: _NT_SYMBOL_PATH=srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols srv means "use a symbol server", C:\Symbols is a local cache, and the URL is Microsoft's server. With it, call stacks through Windows code show names like ntdll.dll!RtlUserThreadStart and kernel32.dll!BaseThreadInitThunk instead of raw addresses, which is often exactly where the interesting part of a crash is. Studios run their own symbol servers for their builds, so any crash from any shipped version can be symbolised. Walking the stack without frame pointers Lesson 7.05 said x64 Windows code usually does not keep a frame pointer in rbp . So how does a debugger find each caller? Every function's prologue is described in unwind information in the exe's .pdata and .xdata sections: "this function pushed rbx and rdi, then subtracted 40 from rsp". Given the current rip and rsp , the debugger finds the function containing rip , applies its unwind description in reverse to recover the caller's rsp and the return address, and repeats. Windows uses the same data to unwind the stack when an exception is thrown. This is also why corrupt stacks look so strange: if the return address on the stack has been overwritten (lesson 7.05), the unwinder follows garbage, and the call stack ends abruptly or shows nonsense. Capturing a stack in your own program A crash reporter or an assert (next lesson) wants the call stack as text. C++23's std::stacktrace does it portably: cpp include <iostream include <stacktrace void deepInside() { const auto trace{ std::stacktrace::current() }; std::cout << "captured " << (trace.size() = 2 ? "a stack with several frames" : "almost nothing") << '\n'; // std::cout << trace; // prints each frame: function, file and line, when symbols are available } void middle() { deepInside(); } int main() { middle(); return 0; } captured a stack with several frames Printing the whole trace (the commented line) gives function names and source lines when the PDB is next to the exe. On Windows the lower-level tools are CaptureStackBackTrace (just the return addresses) and the DbgHelp library ( SymFromAddr , SymGetLineFromAddr64 ) to turn them into names. Without symbols, store the addresses as module + RVA (lesson 6.09) and symbolise them later on a machine that has the PDB. Reading a call stack game.exe!Inventory::totalWeight() Line 42 game.exe!Hud::drawWeight(const Player & player) Line 118 game.exe!Hud::draw(const World & world) Line 87 game.exe!Game::render() Line 210 game.exe!wWinMain(...) Line 35 kernel32.dll!BaseThreadInitThunk() ntdll.dll!RtlUserThreadStart() Read from the top: the crash is in totalWeight at line 42; it was called by drawWeight , which was called by draw , and so on down to the thread's start in Windows. Double-click any frame to see its variables (lesson 4.07). The bug is often not in the top frame, but in a caller that passed it something bad. Common mistakes !warning Not keeping the PDBs of shipped builds A crash report from players is then just numbers. Archive every released build's PDB, or run a symbol server. !warning A PDB from a different build It will not load, even if the code looks the same. Rebuild and keep exe and PDB together. !warning Shipping PDBs to players Private PDBs contain your full source structure. Ship none, or stripped public ones ( /PDBSTRIPPED ), and keep the full ones yourself. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does a call stack show game.exe!00007ff6a1235f10() instead of a function name? + The debugger could not load a matching PDB for game.exe - The function has no name - The program was built in Release Without symbols, only addresses are known. Check the Modules window. ? How does the debugger know a PDB belongs to a particular exe? + The exe records a signature (GUID and age) that the PDB must match exactly - By the file name only - By the date Each build gets a new signature, so only that build's PDB fits. ? How can a debugger walk an x64 stack when functions do not use a frame pointer? + Using the unwind information in .pdata / .xdata that describes each function's prologue - It guesses from the stack contents - It cannot The same data drives exception unwinding. ? What does srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols in a symbol path do? + Downloads matching symbols for Windows DLLs from Microsoft's server and caches them in C:\Symbols - Uploads your symbols to Microsoft - Disables symbols Public symbols turn Windows frames into names.

title: Read a stack frame
body: Tools print stack frames in the form module!function+0xOFFSET , for example game.exe!Player::update+0x2a . When symbols are missing, the function part is absent: game.exe+0x35f10 . Write parseFrame(text) , returning the module, the function (empty if absent) and the offset as a number. The offset is hexadecimal, written with 0x , in either case. If the text does not fit the form (no +0x , nothing before it, no hex digits after it), return std::nullopt . "game.exe!Player::update+0x2a" - module "game.exe", function "Player::update", offset 0x2A "ntdll.dll+0x1F00" - module "ntdll.dll", function "", offset 0x1F00 "no offset here" - nullopt Function names can contain :: , < , and spaces, but never ! or + .

title: 8.03  Asserts and Logging That Help
body:
The best bugs to fix are the ones the program reports itself, at the moment things go wrong. Asserts check assumptions and stop immediately when one is false; logs record what happened so you can reconstruct it later. This lesson shows how to write both well: static_assert and assert , a better assert macro, log levels, and a ring buffer that keeps the last moments before a crash. Asserts: check your assumptions Every piece of code assumes things: this index is in range, this pointer is not null, this list is sorted. An assert turns an assumption into a check that stops the program, in a debugger-friendly way, the moment it is violated: cpp include <cassert int& Grid::at(int x, int y) { assert(x = 0 && x < width && "x out of range"); assert(y = 0 && y < height && "y out of range"); return cells static_cast<std::size_t (y width + x) ; } When an assert fails in a Debug build, the program stops with the condition, file and line; under the debugger it breaks right there, with the call stack showing who passed the bad coordinates. The string after && is a trick: a string literal is always true, so it does not change the condition, but it appears in the failure message. Two properties to remember: - assert does nothing in Release builds ( NDEBUG is defined, lesson 4.10). Never put work that must happen inside it. - Asserts are for programming errors ("this can never happen if the code is right"), not for things that can legitimately happen at run time, such as a missing file or bad player input. Those need real error handling. static_assert: checks at compile time Some assumptions can be checked by the compiler, costing nothing at run time: cpp include <cstdint struct SaveHeader { char magic 4 ; std::uint32_t version; std::uint32_t length; }; static_assert(sizeof(SaveHeader) == 12, "SaveHeader must match the file format"); static_assert(sizeof(void ) == 8, "This code assumes a 64-bit build"); static_assert(alignof(SaveHeader) == 4); int main() { return 0; } If someone adds a member to SaveHeader , the build fails with that message instead of saves silently breaking. Use static_assert for layouts, sizes, and template requirements. A better assert The standard assert is minimal. Most engines write their own, adding a formatted message, a log line, a break into the debugger, and the option to keep checks on in some release builds: cpp include <cstdio include <cstdlib include <intrin.h ifndef GAME_ASSERTS ifdef NDEBUG define GAME_ASSERTS 0 else define GAME_ASSERTS 1 endif endif if GAME_ASSERTS define GAME_ASSERT(condition, message) \ do { \ if (!(condition)) { \ std::fprintf(stderr, "Assertion failed: %s
 %s
 at %s:%d
", condition, message, \ __FILE__, __LINE__); \ std::fflush(stderr); \ __debugbreak(); / stops here under a debugger; crashes cleanly without one / \ std::abort(); \ } \ } while (false) else define GAME_ASSERT(condition, message) do { (void)sizeof(condition); } while (false) endif - condition turns the condition's source text into a string for the message. - __debugbreak() is the int 3 instruction from lesson 4.07: under a debugger it stops exactly at the failing line. - do { ... } while (false) makes the macro behave like one statement, so it is safe after an if without braces. - The disabled version uses sizeof(condition) so the condition is still compiled (and type-checked) but never evaluated. Logging Logs record what the program did, so you can understand a bug after the fact, on a player's machine, or in a situation you cannot reproduce. Useful logs have: Property Why --- --- Levels : trace, debug, info, warning, error So you can turn detail up or down without changing code A time stamp and frame number So you can line events up A category : "audio", "net", "save" So you can filter Facts, not feelings "loaded level 3 (forest) in 412 ms, 1,204 entities", not "level loaded!!" Cheap when disabled Messages below the current level should cost almost nothing What to log: start-up and configuration, level loads and saves, network connections, every error and warning with the values involved, and occasional performance summaries. What not to log: anything every frame at normal levels (the file becomes useless), passwords, tokens or personal data. The last moments before a crash Writing every debug message to a file is too slow, but the most useful messages are the ones just before a crash. A ring buffer solves this: keep the last N messages in memory, overwriting the oldest, and dump them in the crash handler (next lesson). The practice task builds one. Common mistakes !warning Side effects inside asserts assert(file.open(path)) opens the file only in Debug. Do the work, then assert on its result. !warning Asserting on things that can really happen A missing file, bad input or a lost connection must be handled in Release too. !warning Logging every frame Nobody can read it, and it slows the game. Log events and summaries. !warning Logging secrets or personal data Logs get attached to bug reports and shared. Keep them clean. Knowledge check quiz ? What happens to assert(x 0) in a Release build? + Nothing is checked: the line compiles to nothing - It still checks but only logs - It becomes a static_assert NDEBUG disables it. ? Which kind of check is right for "this struct must be exactly 16 bytes"? + static_assert(sizeof(T) == 16) - assert(sizeof(T) == 16) - A log line Sizes are known at compile time, so the compiler can check them. ? Why use __debugbreak() in a custom assert? + It stops the debugger exactly at the failing line, with the call stack intact - It makes the program faster - It writes a crash dump It is the int 3 breakpoint instruction. ? What is a ring buffer of log messages good for? + Keeping the most recent messages cheaply in memory so they can be written out when the program crashes - Sorting messages - Sending logs over the network The oldest messages are overwritten, so memory use stays fixed.

title: The last N log lines
body: Build RecentLog , which keeps only the most recent log lines in a fixed amount of memory, overwriting the oldest when full. - The constructor receives the capacity (at least 1). - add(line) stores a line. When the log is full, the oldest line is dropped. - lines() returns the stored lines, oldest first . - size() returns how many lines are stored; dropped() how many have been overwritten so far. Store the lines in a std::vector<std::string of exactly capacity slots, used as a ring: keep the index where the next line goes and wrap it round to 0 at the end. Do not erase from the front of a vector. RecentLog log{ 3 }; add "a", "b", "c", "d" - lines() = { "b", "c", "d" }, dropped() = 1

title: 8.04  Crash Dumps
body: When a game crashes on a player's machine, you cannot attach a debugger. A crash dump captures the crashed process's state (threads, stacks, registers, some or all memory) into a file you can open later in Visual Studio or WinDbg as if you had been there. This lesson explains exception codes, writing a minidump from your own crash handler, collecting dumps with Windows Error Reporting, and opening them. What happens when a program crashes A "crash" on Windows is an unhandled exception : the processor or the program raised an exception (an access violation, a divide by zero, a C++ throw nobody caught), and nothing handled it. Windows then calls the process's unhandled exception filter , which by default hands the crash to Windows Error Reporting and ends the process. Each exception has a code. The ones you will see most: Code Name Usual cause --- --- --- 0xC0000005 Access violation Null or dangling pointer, out-of-bounds access, writing to read-only memory 0xC00000FD Stack overflow Runaway recursion, huge locals (lesson 1.05) 0xC0000094 Integer divide by zero x / 0 or x % 0 with integers 0xC000001D Illegal instruction Jumping into data, or an instruction the CPU does not support 0xC0000409 Stack buffer overrun / fail fast A /GS cookie check failed (lesson 7.05), or abort() -style fast fail 0x80000003 Breakpoint An int 3 / __debugbreak() with no debugger attached 0xE06D7363 C++ exception A throw that was never caught (the hex spells "msc" in ASCII) For an access violation, the exception record also says whether it was a read, write or execute, and the address: the clues from lessons 3.02 and 6.02. Minidumps A minidump ( .dmp ) is a snapshot of a process: the list of modules with their versions and signatures, every thread's registers and stack, the exception record, and optionally some or all of the heap. Opened with the matching PDBs (lesson 8.02), it shows the call stack and variables at the moment of the crash. Dump type Contains Size --- --- --- Small ( MiniDumpNormal ) Modules, threads, stacks, exception Tens to hundreds of KB With data segments and indirectly referenced memory Also globals and memory pointed to from the stacks A few MB Full memory ( MiniDumpWithFullMemory ) Everything in the address space As big as the process's memory Small dumps are usually enough for a call stack and the locals on the stack. Full dumps let you inspect any object, at a cost. Writing one yourself A game installs its own filter at start-up, so it can write a dump (and its recent log lines, lesson 8.03) before exiting: cpp include <windows.h include <dbghelp.h pragma comment(lib, "dbghelp.lib") static LONG WINAPI writeCrashDump(EXCEPTION_POINTERS info) { HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(L"crash.dmp", GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, CREATE_ALWAYS, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (file != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { MINIDUMP_EXCEPTION_INFORMATION exception{}; exception.ThreadId = GetCurrentThreadId(); exception.ExceptionPointers = info; exception.ClientPointers = FALSE; MiniDumpWriteDump(GetCurrentProcess(), GetCurrentProcessId(), file, static_cast<MINIDUMP_TYPE (MiniDumpWithDataSegs MiniDumpWithIndirectlyReferencedMemory), &exception, nullptr, nullptr); CloseHandle(file); } return EXCEPTION_EXECUTE_HANDLER; // let the process end } int wmain() { SetUnhandledExceptionFilter(&writeCrashDump); // ... the game ... } Notes from experience: - Write dumps to a folder the user can write (lesson 5.04), with a time stamp in the name. - The crashed process may be badly damaged (a corrupt heap, an exhausted stack). The most robust crash reporters do as little as possible in the crashed process and let a separate small watchdog process write the dump, using MiniDumpWriteDump on the crashed process from outside. - Some failures ( 0xC0000409 fast fail, stack overflow on a thread with no stack left) bypass or break the filter; the system's own reporting is the fallback. Letting Windows collect dumps Windows Error Reporting can save a dump for every crash of a given program, with no code at all, using a registry key (for developers' and testers' machines): HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\game.exe DumpFolder (REG_EXPAND_SZ) %LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps DumpType (REG_DWORD) 1 = mini, 2 = full DumpCount (REG_DWORD) 10 You can also write a dump of any running process from Task Manager → Details → right-click → Create dump file , which is handy for a game that is hung rather than crashed. Opening a dump In Visual Studio, File → Open → File and choose the .dmp . The summary page shows the exception code, the faulting module and the module list; press Debug with Native Only . With matching symbols (and the source, if you have it), you land on the crashing line with the Call Stack, Locals and Threads windows working, though you cannot step: the process is a snapshot, not running. WinDbg (next lesson) opens the same files and has !analyze -v , which reads the exception, finds the faulting frame and summarises the likely cause. Common mistakes !warning Dumps without matching PDBs A dump is only as useful as the symbols you can load for it. Archive the PDBs of every build you give to anyone. !warning Doing heavy work inside the crash handler Allocating, loading DLLs or taking locks in a crashed process can hang. Keep the handler minimal. !warning Only collecting full dumps They can be gigabytes. Small dumps with a little extra memory are usually enough and far easier to collect from players. Knowledge check quiz ? A crash report shows exception code 0xC0000005 . What kind of error is it? + An access violation: reading, writing or executing memory that is not allowed - A stack overflow - An uncaught C++ exception Look at the access type and address in the exception record next. ? What does a small minidump contain? + The modules, every thread's registers and stack, and the exception record - The program's source code - Only the crash address Enough for call stacks and stack locals when symbols are available. ? Why might a crash reporter write the dump from a separate process? + The crashed process may be too damaged to run much code safely - MiniDumpWriteDump only works between processes - To make the file smaller A healthy watchdog process can capture the crashed one from outside. ? What does 0xE06D7363 mean? + A C++ exception was thrown and never caught - Divide by zero - A breakpoint The low bytes spell "msc", for Microsoft C++.

title: Describe a crash
body: A crash reporter receives an exception code and, for access violations, two more facts: the kind of access (0 read, 1 write, 8 execute) and the address. Write describe(code, access, address) , which returns a one-line summary: Code Summary --- --- 0xC0000005 "access violation reading 0x..." , "writing 0x..." or "executing 0x..." with the address in upper-case hex, followed by " (null pointer)" if the address is below 0x10000 0xC00000FD "stack overflow" 0xC0000094 "integer divide by zero" 0xC0000409 "stack buffer overrun" 0xE06D7363 "unhandled C++ exception" anything else "exception 0x..." with the code as 8 upper-case hex digits access and address are only used for access violations. describe(0xC0000005, 0, 0x10) = "access violation reading 0x10 (null pointer)" describe(0xC0000005, 1, 0x7FF6A1230000) = "access violation writing 0x7FF6A1230000" describe(0x80000003, 0, 0) = "exception 0x80000003"

title: 8.05  A First Look at WinDbg
body: WinDbg is Microsoft's command-line-driven debugger. It does everything Visual Studio's debugger does and much more, opens any crash dump, and is the only debugger for the Windows kernel (chapter 16). This lesson installs it and teaches the two dozen commands that cover nearly all everyday work, mapped to the Visual Studio windows you already know. Why another debugger Visual Studio's debugger is the most comfortable way to debug your own code. WinDbg is worth knowing because: - it opens crash dumps from anywhere, quickly, with !analyze summarising them; - it can debug programs and machines where Visual Studio is not installed; - it has powerful commands for heaps, handles, locks and Windows internals; - it is the kernel debugger: chapters 15 and 16 depend on it. Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store (search "WinDbg"; older guides call the new version "WinDbg Preview"). It has a modern window with source, locals and call stack panes, but its heart is the command window . Getting started - File → Launch executable to start a program under the debugger, Attach to process for a running one, or Open dump file for a .dmp . - First, set up symbols (lesson 8.02): .symfix C:\Symbols ; use Microsoft's symbol server, caching in C:\Symbols .sympath+ C:\code\game\x64\Debug ; add your own PDB folder .reload ; load symbols with the new path The everyday commands Task WinDbg Visual Studio equivalent --- --- --- Continue g F5 Step over / into p / t F10 / F11 Step out gu Shift+F11 Breakpoint on a function bp game!Player::update F9 Breakpoint on a source line bp main.cpp:42 (with backticks) F9 List / clear breakpoints bl / bc Breakpoints window Data breakpoint: break on write to 4 bytes ba w4 0x0000004f8c8ff8a0 Lesson 4.09 Call stack k ( kp with parameters, kn numbered) Call Stack Switch to frame n .frame n Double-click a frame Locals dv ( dv /t with types) Locals Show a typed object dt game!Player 0x... or dt player Watch Registers r ( r rax for one) Registers Memory as bytes / dwords / qwords db addr / dd addr / dq addr Memory window Memory as text da addr (ASCII), du addr (UTF-16) Memory window, text column Disassemble u addr ( uf function for the whole function) Disassembly Loaded modules lm ( lmvm game for details) Modules Threads ~ ( ~2s switches to thread 2; ~ k stacks of all threads) Threads Evaluate an expression ? rsp + 0x20 Watch Help .hh command Commands that start with . are debugger meta-commands; those starting with ! are extensions , larger commands supplied by DLLs loaded into the debugger. Analysing a crash dump Open a dump from lesson 8.04 and run: !analyze -v It reads the exception record, finds the faulting thread and frame, applies heuristics, and prints a summary: EXCEPTION_CODE: (NTSTATUS) 0xc0000005 - The instruction at 0x7ff6a1235f10 referenced memory at 0x10. The memory could not be read. FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE: C:\code\game\inventory.cpp FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE_NUMBER: 42 STACK_TEXT: game!Inventory::totalWeight+0x20 game!Hud::drawWeight+0x45 game!Hud::draw+0x9a ... Then dig in with k , .frame , dv and dt as in a live session. .ecxr switches the debugger's context to the moment of the exception (the registers when it happened), which matters for dumps where the current context is the crash handler. Useful extensions Command Shows --- --- !heap -s Summary of the process heaps !handle Open handles and their types (spotting handle leaks, lesson 5.01) !locks Critical sections that are held, and by which thread (deadlocks, lesson 8.07) !peb The process environment block: command line, environment, loaded modules !address addr What kind of memory an address is in (lesson 6.04's VirtualQuery , done for you) Common mistakes !warning Forgetting symbols Without .symfix and your PDB path, everything is addresses. Fix symbols before anything else. !warning Reading a dump's stack without .ecxr You may be looking at the crash handler's stack instead of the crash. !warning Typing g by habit in a dump A dump is not running: it cannot continue. Use the inspection commands. Knowledge check quiz ? Which WinDbg command shows the call stack? + k - g - lm kp adds parameters, kn frame numbers. ? What does !analyze -v do? + Reads the exception in a dump or broken-in process and summarises the likely cause, faulting frame and stack - Lists all modules - Steps one instruction It is the usual first command on a crash dump. ? How do you look at the 4-byte values at an address? + dd address - db address - du address db shows bytes, dd double words (4 bytes), dq quad words, du UTF-16 text. ? What does .symfix do? + Points the symbol path at Microsoft's public symbol server - Fixes corrupted PDB files - Removes all symbols Follow it with .reload .

title: 8.06  Debugging Optimised Code
body: Some bugs only appear in Release builds, and crash dumps from players are always from optimised code. Debugging it is harder (variables vanish, lines run out of order, functions disappear into their callers) but entirely possible. This lesson gives a practical toolkit: make Release builds debuggable, read values from registers and the disassembly, switch optimisation off selectively, and use logging where stepping fails.
