What goes wrong in the debugger Lesson 4.10 explained what the optimiser does; here is what that looks like when you debug: Symptom Cause --- --- "Variable is optimised away and not available" It lives only in a register, which has since been reused, or it was removed The yellow arrow jumps backwards and forwards Instructions from different lines were interleaved A breakpoint in a function never hits The function was inlined into its callers A function is missing from the call stack Inlined, or left by a tail call (lesson 7.11) Locals show wrong values The debugger reads a stack slot the optimised code no longer uses None of this means the debugger is broken. It means the source is only an approximation of what runs, and you sometimes have to look at what really runs. Make Release builds debuggable These settings cost nothing at run time and should be on for every Release build: Setting Effect --- --- C/C++ → General → Debug Information Format: /Zi Writes a full PDB for Release Linker → Debugging → Generate Debug Info: /DEBUG Links the PDB C/C++ → Command Line: /Zo (default in recent versions) Records which register each variable is in at each point, so more locals are visible Linker → Optimization → /OPT:REF, /OPT:ICF (keep them) Unaffected; note that ICF can merge identical functions, so a call stack may show a different name with the same body Reading values the debugger cannot show When a variable is "optimised away", the value usually still exists somewhere: 1. Open the Disassembly window (Ctrl+Alt+D) at the current instruction. 2. Find the instruction that last loaded or computed the value. mov ebx, dword ptr rcx+0Ch tells you ebx holds the member at offset 12 of whatever rcx pointed to. 3. Read the register in the Registers window, or in Watch as @ebx . 4. For objects, cast a register in Watch: (Player )@rdi . Function arguments are in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 only at the very start of a function (lesson 7.06); optimised code moves them into non-volatile registers or overwrites them soon after. Set the breakpoint on the function's first instruction (right-click → Go To Disassembly, F9 on the first line) to catch them in place. Turn optimisation off where you are looking When you need to step through one area of a Release build comfortably: cpp pragma optimize("", off) void Inventory::recalculate() { // compiled without optimisation in an otherwise optimised build } pragma optimize("", on) Or disable it for a whole .cpp file: right-click the file → Properties → C/C++ → Optimization: Disabled (/Od) . Remember to remove these: they are debugging aids, not fixes. If the bug disappears when optimisation is turned off in one place, that is itself a strong clue: undefined behaviour (uninitialised values, overruns, data races, lesson 4.10) in or near that code. Logging and asserts in Release Stepping is often impractical in timing-sensitive or rare bugs. Use the tools from lesson 8.03, kept enabled in a test configuration: - a ring-buffer log dumped on crash; - asserts enabled in an "optimised with checks" configuration; - tracepoints (lesson 4.09), which work in optimised code at instruction level. Bugs that only appear in Release A checklist, roughly in order of how often each is the cause: 1. Uninitialised variables : Debug's 0xCC fill was consistent; Release's garbage is not. Turn on warning level 4 (C4700, C4701). 2. Out-of-bounds access : Debug's padding and guard bytes absorbed it. Run AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10). 3. Data races : Release keeps values in registers and reorders memory accesses (lesson 6.06). 4. Code inside assert that no longer runs. 5. Timing : Release runs faster, changing the order of events between threads or frames. 6. Signed overflow or other undefined behaviour the optimiser exploited. 7. A compiler bug : possible, but almost always the last explanation, after everything above. Common mistakes !warning Giving up when a variable is optimised away Look at the disassembly: the value is usually in a register. !warning Fixing a Release-only bug by turning optimisation off That hides it. Find the undefined behaviour. !warning Trusting the source view's line in optimised code Check the Disassembly window to see which instruction actually faulted. Knowledge check quiz ? The debugger says a local is "optimised away". What should you try? + Look in the disassembly for the register that holds it, and read that register - Rebuild in Debug and hope it reproduces - Assume the value is zero Optimised code keeps most values in registers. ? A bug disappears when one file is compiled with /Od . What does that suggest? + Undefined behaviour in or near that code, which the optimiser exposed - The optimiser has a bug in that file - The file should always be built with /Od UB behaves differently under optimisation; find and fix it. ? Where are a function's first four arguments most reliably found in optimised code? + In rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 at the function's first instruction - In the shadow space, always - On the heap Optimised code soon moves or overwrites them.

title: 8.07  Debugging Threads
body: Multithreaded bugs are timing-dependent, so they hide when you look for them. This lesson covers the tools that make them visible: naming threads, the Threads and Parallel Stacks windows, freezing threads to force an ordering, diagnosing deadlocks from call stacks, and finding races with careful logging and data breakpoints. Name your threads The first step costs one line per thread. Give each thread a name, and every tool shows it instead of a bare id: cpp include <windows.h include <thread void startAudioThread() { std::jthread audio{ { SetThreadDescription(GetCurrentThread(), L"Audio mixer"); // ... } }; } SetThreadDescription (Windows 10 1607 and later; lesson 5.08 showed how to call it safely on older systems) names the thread for Visual Studio, WinDbg, crash dumps and profilers. The Threads window Debug → Windows → Threads lists every thread when the program is paused: its id, name, location (the function it is in) and priority. Double-click a thread to switch to it: the Call Stack, Locals and editor then show that thread's view. A yellow arrow marks the current thread. Right-click → Freeze suspends a thread so it will not run when you continue; Thaw releases it. Freezing is a powerful way to force an interleaving : freeze the main thread at a chosen line, let a worker run past a critical point, then thaw the main thread. A race that appears once in a thousand runs can be reproduced every time this way. Parallel Stacks Debug → Windows → Parallel Stacks draws every thread's call stack at once, merging the frames they share into a graph. With twenty worker threads, you see at a glance that eighteen are idle in the job queue's wait, one is in physics, and one is stuck somewhere unexpected. Diagnosing a deadlock The game freezes and the CPU usage is near zero: the signature of a deadlock (lesson 6.06), as opposed to an infinite loop, which shows 100% of a core. 1. Break All (Ctrl+Alt+Break). 2. Open Parallel Stacks or go through the threads in the Threads window. Look for threads waiting inside lock functions: std::mutex::lock , EnterCriticalSection , WaitForSingleObject , RtlpWaitOnCriticalSection . 3. For each, find which lock it waits for (the argument to the lock call, visible in its frame) and which locks it holds (locks taken in earlier frames of its own stack). 4. Draw the arrows: "thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1". A cycle is a deadlock. In WinDbg, !locks lists Windows critical sections that are held, with the owning thread, and ~ k prints every thread's stack, which does steps 2 and 3 quickly. The practice task automates step 4: finding a cycle in "who waits for whom". Finding races Data races are harder: there is no hang and no crash at the moment of the race, only a wrong value later. Approaches, cheapest first: - Think about ownership. For each piece of shared data, which threads touch it and which lock protects it? Data touched by two threads with no lock in common is the suspect. - Data breakpoints (lesson 4.09) on the corrupted value: the debugger stops on whichever thread writes it, and the Threads window shows what the others were doing. - Logging with thread ids and sequence numbers , written to a lock-free per-thread ring buffer (formatting and locks inside logging change the timing enough to hide the bug). - Stress : run the suspected code in a tight loop with many threads to make the race frequent. - Tools : Clang's ThreadSanitizer (on Linux builds, or Clang on Windows with limits) detects races automatically; on MSVC, the Concurrency Visualizer extension shows which threads ran when. Common mistakes !warning Stepping a single thread and expecting others to wait When you step, all threads run (unless frozen). Breakpoints in shared code can hit on any thread. !warning Adding a log line and the bug disappears Logging changes timing. That does not mean the bug is fixed; it confirms it is timing-dependent. !warning Fixing a deadlock by adding a timeout The cycle is still there. Fix the lock order. Knowledge check quiz ? The game freezes with almost no CPU use. What is most likely? + A deadlock: threads waiting on each other - An infinite loop - A memory leak An infinite loop would keep a core busy. ? What does freezing a thread in the Threads window let you do? + Stop it from running while others continue, to force a particular order of events - Make it run faster - Kill it permanently Forced interleavings make rare races reproducible. ? Why is SetThreadDescription worth calling? + Debuggers, dumps and profilers then show each thread's name - It makes threads safer - It sets the thread's priority Named threads make every multithreaded investigation faster.

title: Find the deadlock
body: From a paused program you have collected, for each thread, the locks it holds and the single lock it is waiting for (or none). Write findDeadlock(threads) , which returns the ids of the threads in a deadlock cycle, or an empty vector if there is none. Thread A "waits for" thread B when A is waiting for a lock that B holds. A deadlock is a cycle in that relation: A waits for B, B waits for C, ..., which waits for A. Return the cycle's thread ids starting from the smallest id in the cycle and following the waits-for direction. If several cycles exist, return the one containing the smallest thread id of any cycle. thread 1: holds {A}, waits for B thread 2: holds {B}, waits for A thread 3: holds {}, waits for A - { 1, 2 } (3 is blocked behind the deadlock but not part of the cycle)

title: 8.08  Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
match: 8.08 Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
body: When a game is slow, the cause is almost never where you would guess. A profiler measures where the time actually goes. This lesson covers the two kinds of profiler ( sampling and instrumenting ), Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool, frame-based instrumentation with scoped timers, and how to read the results to find the few places worth optimising. Measure, don't guess Programmers are famously bad at predicting which code is slow. A function that looks expensive runs once per level; an innocent-looking std::string built every frame runs a million times. So the rule is: measure first , in a Release build (lesson 4.10), on realistic content, and optimise only what the measurement points at. Typically a small fraction of the code accounts for most of the time; finding that fraction is the whole job. Two kinds of profiler Sampling profiler Instrumenting profiler --- --- --- How Interrupts the program thousands of times a second and records the call stack each time Code you add (or the compiler adds) records the start and end time of each marked section Shows Statistically, which functions are on the stack most often Exact times for each marked section, frame by frame Overhead Low; no code changes Small per marker; you choose what to mark Good for "Where does the time go overall?" "Why was this frame slow?", spikes, timelines across threads Examples Visual Studio CPU Usage, Windows Performance Analyzer, Superluminal, VTune Tracy, Optick, PIX markers, your own scoped timers Games use both: sampling to find hot spots, instrumentation to understand frame-to-frame behaviour. Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool 1. Switch to Release (with /Zi and /DEBUG for symbols, lesson 8.06). 2. Debug → Performance Profiler (Alt+F2), tick CPU Usage , press Start . 3. Play the slow part of the game, then stop. The report lists functions by: - Self CPU : time spent in the function's own code; - Total CPU : time in the function and everything it calls . Start from the hot path (the report highlights it): the chain of calls with the highest total time from main down. A function with high total but low self time is not itself slow; something it calls is. A function with high self time is where the actual work happens. Double-click to see the source with per-line costs. Instrumenting frames yourself A scoped timer measures the time from its construction to its destruction (RAII again, lesson 2.04): cpp include <chrono include <cstdio class ScopedTimer { public: explicit ScopedTimer(const char name) : m_name{ name }, m_start{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() } {} ~ScopedTimer() { const auto us{ std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds (std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - m_start).count() }; std::printf("%-12s %6lld us\n", m_name, static_cast<long long (us)); } private: const char m_name; std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point m_start; }; void updateFrame() { ScopedTimer frame{ "frame" }; { ScopedTimer t{ "physics" }; / ... / } { ScopedTimer t{ "ai" }; / ... / } { ScopedTimer t{ "render" }; / ... / } } Printing every frame is too noisy and too slow; real systems record the samples into a buffer and either show a live overlay (average and worst over the last second) or send them to a viewer such as Tracy, which draws a timeline of every frame across all threads. The practice task builds the aggregation step: totals, counts and worst cases per name. Reading frame times A game at 60 frames per second has 16.7 ms per frame for everything. A useful habit is to think in milliseconds per frame rather than frames per second, because milliseconds add up: physics 3 ms + AI 2 ms + rendering 9 ms = 14 ms, room to spare. Frames per second do not add. Look at the worst frames as well as the average. A game that averages 8 ms but has a 40 ms frame every few seconds stutters , and players notice stutter more than a lower steady frame rate. Spikes usually come from occasional work: an allocation-heavy event, loading, garbage collection in a script language, a file write on the main thread. What usually turns out to be slow Common culprit Usual fix --- --- Allocations every frame (strings, vectors, new ) Reuse, reserve, pools, arenas (lessons 2.02, 3.10) Pointer chasing over scattered objects Contiguous arrays, data-oriented layouts (lessons 2.07, 3.02) Searching linearly in large containers every frame Hash maps, spatial grids (lesson 3.08) Work done every frame that could be done once Cache the result, recompute only on change Waiting: locks, file I/O, synchronous GPU reads on the main thread Move it to another thread or make it asynchronous Chapter 17 returns to performance with careful benchmarking. Common mistakes !warning Profiling a Debug build Debug distorts everything: some functions are ten times slower, others hardly change. Profile Release. !warning Optimising what you guess is slow Measure first; you will usually be surprised. !warning Reading total time as self time A function at the top of the call tree always has a large total. Look for where the self time is. !warning Only watching the average frame time Spikes cause stutter. Track the worst frames too. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a sampling profiler do? + Interrupts the program regularly and records the call stack, building statistics of where time is spent - Records the exact start and end time of every function - Measures memory use It needs no code changes and has low overhead. ? A function shows 90% total CPU but 1% self CPU. What does that mean? + It is not slow itself; functions it calls account for the time - It is the slowest function in the program - The profiler is wrong Follow the hot path into its callees. ? Why think in milliseconds per frame rather than frames per second? + Milliseconds of different systems add up to the frame time; frame rates do not add - Milliseconds are more precise - Frames per second cannot be measured 60 fps means a budget of 16.7 ms shared by everything. ? A game averages 60 fps but stutters. What should you look at? + The worst frame times, and what happened in those frames - Only the average frame time - The size of the executable Occasional spikes cause stutter.

title: Summarise the timings
where: 8.08 Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
body: A frame profiler records samples: each one a section name and how many microseconds it took. Write summarise(samples) , which returns one Row per name with: - name ; - count : how many samples it had; - total : the sum of its times; - worst : its largest single time; - average : total / count , as a double . Rows are sorted by total , largest first; names with equal totals are sorted alphabetically. { "render", 9000 } { "physics", 3000 } { "render", 11000 } { "ai", 2000 } - render count 2 total 20000 worst 11000 average 10000 physics count 1 total 3000 worst 3000 average 3000 ai count 1 total 2000 worst 2000 average 2000

title: 9.01  What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules
match: 9.01 What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules
body: Reverse engineering means working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. It is how security researchers find vulnerabilities, how malware is analysed, how old software is kept running and how file formats are documented for interoperability. This lesson sets out what it involves, the tools, and the legal and ethical ground rules this course follows. Running the pipeline backwards Lesson 1.04's pipeline turned source into machine code. Reverse engineering goes the other way, recovering understanding, never the original source, from the compiled program: The earlier chapters were the preparation: the PE format of chapter 6's modules, the assembly of chapter 7, the debuggers of chapters 4 and 8, and the layouts of chapters 2 and 3. Who does it, and why Field What they reverse engineer --- --- Security research Software, to find and responsibly report vulnerabilities before attackers do Malware analysis Malicious programs, to understand them, detect them and remove them Interoperability File formats and protocols, so that other programs can read and write them (many open-source tools exist because of this) Preservation and compatibility Old software and games whose source is lost, to keep them running on new systems Debugging and support Third-party libraries and drivers without source, when they misbehave inside your program Learning How compilers, operating systems and well-written programs work Static and dynamic analysis - Static analysis examines the program without running it: reading the file's headers and the disassembly, following cross-references (lessons 9.02 to 9.06, 9.08). Tools: Ghidra, IDA, Binary Ninja, dumpbin . - Dynamic analysis runs it and watches: breakpoints, memory, calls into the operating system (lesson 9.07). Tools: x64dbg, WinDbg, Visual Studio, Process Monitor. Each answers what the other cannot. Static analysis sees every path, including ones that rarely run; dynamic analysis sees real values and resolves indirect calls. Real work alternates between them. The ground rules for this course Reverse engineering is a legitimate, widely practised skill. Like any capability, how it is used matters, and the law varies by country. The rules this course follows: 1. Practise on programs you have the right to analyse : programs you compiled yourself (lesson 9.10 builds a series of practice targets), open-source programs (where you can check your conclusions against the source), and challenges published specifically as practice ("crackmes" and capture-the-flag tasks). 2. Read the licence. Many licences restrict reverse engineering. Some laws allow limited reverse engineering for specific purposes such as interoperability (for example, Article 6 of the EU Software Directive) or good-faith security research, with conditions. When it matters, ask someone qualified rather than assuming. 3. Do not use it to cheat other people. Altering online games to gain an advantage over other players, or bypassing anti-cheat systems, harms those players, breaks the terms you agreed to and can break the law. This course does not teach that, and it does not teach defeating copy protection or licence checks. 4. Report vulnerabilities responsibly. If you find a security flaw, tell the vendor privately, through their security contact or bug bounty programme, and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly. 5. Handle malware with care. Real malicious samples belong in an isolated virtual machine with no access to your files or network, which lesson 15.08 sets up. The practice targets in this course are harmless programs you build yourself. What you can expect to recover Survives compilation Lost --- --- The machine code and its control flow Comments, formatting, local variable names String literals and constants Most type information (structs become offsets, lesson 7.08) Imported and exported function names Templates and inline functions as separate entities Class names (through RTTI, lesson 9.06), if not disabled Macros, constexpr values folded into code Everything, if a PDB is available The original structure of the source files Recovering a program's logic is slow, careful work, done function by function. Recovering its exact source is impossible. Good reverse engineers are patient, take notes, and name things as they understand them. Common mistakes !warning Starting with a large, unfamiliar program Practise on small programs you wrote, where you can check every conclusion against the source. !warning Trusting the decompiler blindly Decompiler output is a guess at C code. Check important conclusions against the assembly. !warning Assuming that being able to do it means being allowed to Check the licence and the law, and stay within the ground rules. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the difference between static and dynamic analysis? + Static analysis examines the program without running it; dynamic analysis runs it and observes its behaviour - Static analysis is for small programs, dynamic for large ones - They are the same thing Each reveals things the other cannot; real work uses both. ? Which of these is lost when a program is compiled without a PDB? - String literals - Imported function names + Local variable names Locals become registers and stack offsets. ? Which practice targets does this course use? + Programs you compile yourself, open-source programs, and challenges published for practice - Commercial online games - Anti-cheat software These are targets you clearly have the right to analyse.

title: 9.02  The PE File Format
body:
Every .exe and .dll on Windows is a Portable Executable (PE) file: a set of headers describing the program, followed by its sections of code and data. This lesson walks through the headers in order (the DOS header and MZ , the PE signature, the file header, the optional header and its data directories, and the section table) and reads them from C++. The overall shape ┌──────────────────────────┐ offset 0 │ DOS header ("MZ") │ 64 bytes; e_lfanew at offset 0x3C says where the PE header is ├──────────────────────────┤ │ DOS stub │ a tiny DOS program: "This program cannot be run in DOS mode." ├──────────────────────────┤ offset e_lfanew │ "PE\0\0" signature │ 4 bytes │ File header (COFF) │ 20 bytes: machine, number of sections, ... │ Optional header │ 240 bytes for 64-bit: entry point, image base, data directories ├──────────────────────────┤ │ Section table │ 40 bytes per section: name, RVA, size, file offset, flags ├──────────────────────────┤ │ .text │ code │ .rdata │ constants, import and export tables, RTTI │ .data │ writable globals │ .pdata │ unwind information (lesson 8.02) │ .rsrc │ resources: icons, version information │ .reloc │ relocations (lesson 6.09) └──────────────────────────┘ The same layout appears in memory once the loader maps the file: GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) points at the MZ (lesson 5.08), and every RVA in the headers is an offset from there. The DOS header For backward compatibility with 1980s DOS, every PE file starts with a DOS header. Only two fields matter now: Offset Field Value --- --- --- 0x00 e_magic 0x5A4D : the bytes 4D 5A , "MZ" 0x3C e_lfanew The file offset of the PE signature (often 0x80 to 0x100) The NT headers At e_lfanew come the NT headers : the signature, the file header and the optional header. Field Where Meaning --- --- --- Signature +0 0x00004550 : the bytes 50 45 00 00 , "PE\0\0" FileHeader.Machine +4 0x8664 for x64, 0x14C for 32-bit x86, 0xAA64 for ARM64 FileHeader.NumberOfSections +6 How many entries the section table has FileHeader.TimeDateStamp +8 When it was linked (or a hash, for reproducible builds) FileHeader.SizeOfOptionalHeader +20 Where the section table starts, relative to the optional header FileHeader.Characteristics +22 Flags: executable, DLL, large-address-aware ... OptionalHeader.Magic +24 0x20B for 64-bit (PE32+), 0x10B for 32-bit OptionalHeader.AddressOfEntryPoint +24+16 RVA where execution starts (the C runtime's start-up code, which calls main ) OptionalHeader.ImageBase +24+24 Preferred load address: 0x140000000 for exes (lesson 6.09) OptionalHeader.SizeOfImage Size of the whole image in memory OptionalHeader.DllCharacteristics Security flags: ASLR (dynamic base), DEP (NX compatible), CFG ... OptionalHeader.DataDirectory 16 the last 128 bytes RVA and size of the import table, export table, resources, relocations, debug data ... The data directories are the index of the file: each entry points (by RVA and size) at one important table. The ones you will use most: Index Directory --- --- 0 Export table (lesson 9.03) 1 Import table (lesson 9.03) 2 Resources 3 Exception (unwind) data, .pdata 5 Base relocations 6 Debug directory: the PDB's name and signature (lesson 8.02) 12 Import address table (IAT) The section table After the optional header, one 40-byte entry per section: Field Meaning --- --- Name 8 bytes, such as .text\0\0\0 VirtualSize Size in memory VirtualAddress RVA where the section starts in memory SizeOfRawData Size in the file (rounded up to the file alignment, often 512) PointerToRawData Offset where the section starts in the file Characteristics Flags: code, initialised data, readable, writable, executable Sections start on 4 KB page boundaries in memory, but only 512-byte boundaries in the file, so an RVA and a file offset differ: converting between them needs the section table (lesson 9.03's practice task). Reading the headers from C++ <windows.h defines all these structures ( IMAGE_DOS_HEADER , IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 , IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER ), so a loaded module's headers can be read directly: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string int main() { const auto base{ reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char (GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)) }; const auto dos{ reinterpret_cast<const IMAGE_DOS_HEADER (base) }; const auto nt{ reinterpret_cast<const IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 (base + dos- e_lfanew) }; std::cout << "MZ found: " << (dos- e_magic == IMAGE_DOS_SIGNATURE) << '
'; std::cout << "PE found: " << (nt- Signature == IMAGE_NT_SIGNATURE) << '
'; std::cout << "x64: " << (nt- FileHeader.Machine == IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_AMD64) << '
'; std::cout << "64-bit header: " << (nt- OptionalHeader.Magic == IMAGE_NT_OPTIONAL_HDR64_MAGIC) << '
'; std::cout << "ASLR enabled: " << ((nt- OptionalHeader.DllCharacteristics & IMAGE_DLLCHARACTERISTICS_DYNAMIC_BASE) != 0) << '
'; const IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER section{ IMAGE_FIRST_SECTION(nt) }; bool hasText{ false }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < nt- FileHeader.NumberOfSections; ++i) if (std::string(reinterpret_cast<const char (section i .Name), 5) == ".text") hasText = true; std::cout << "has .text: " << hasText << '
'; return 0; } MZ found: 1 PE found: 1 x64: 1 64-bit header: 1 ASLR enabled: 1 has .text: 1 dumpbin /headers game.exe prints all of this from the file on disk, and tools like PE-bear and CFF Explorer show it graphically. For an untrusted file, never cast raw file bytes to these structures without checking every offset against the file's size first: malformed files are a classic attack on parsers. The practice task parses from a byte buffer with those checks. Common mistakes !warning Mixing RVAs and file offsets Header fields are RVAs (memory offsets). In a file on disk, convert through the section table before reading. !warning Assuming a fixed offset for the PE header Always read e_lfanew . !warning Trusting the sizes in a file Check every offset and count against the actual file size before using it. Knowledge check quiz ? Which two bytes start every PE file? + 4D 5A ("MZ") - 50 45 ("PE") - 7F 45 ("\x7FE") "MZ" is the DOS header's signature; the PE signature comes later, at e_lfanew. ? What does e_lfanew hold? + The file offset of the PE signature and NT headers - The entry point - The number of sections It is at offset 0x3C of the DOS header. ? What is the value of FileHeader.Machine for a 64-bit x86 program? + 0x8664 - 0x14C - 0x20B 0x20B is the optional header's magic for PE32+. ? What are the data directories? + A table of RVAs and sizes pointing at the import table, export table, resources, relocations and other key structures - The folders the program was built in - The list of sections They are the index of the file's important tables.

title: Parse a PE header safely
body: Write parseHeaders(file) , which reads the main facts from the bytes of a PE file, checking every offset before reading. Return std::nullopt if anything is missing or wrong. Read these, all little-endian (lesson 1.02): 1. At offset 0: the two bytes 'M' 'Z' . 2. At offset 0x3C : a 4-byte e_lfanew . 3. At e_lfanew : the four bytes 'P' 'E' 0 0 . 4. At e_lfanew + 4 : Machine (2 bytes). At e_lfanew + 6 : NumberOfSections (2 bytes). At e_lfanew + 20 : SizeOfOptionalHeader (2 bytes). 5. At e_lfanew + 24 , the optional header: Magic (2 bytes) must be 0x20B (64-bit); AddressOfEntryPoint at optional + 16 (4 bytes); ImageBase at optional + 24 (8 bytes). 6. The section table starts at e_lfanew + 24 + SizeOfOptionalHeader . Each entry is 40 bytes: the name is the first 8 bytes (stop at the first zero byte), VirtualAddress at entry + 12 (4 bytes). Return the machine, the entry point, the image base, and the sections' names and virtual addresses.

title: 9.03  Imports, Exports and the Loader
body: A program's import table lists every function it uses from DLLs; a DLL's export table lists every function it offers. Together they are a map of what a program can do and how its modules connect. This lesson reads both, explains the import address table that the loader fills in at start-up, and shows how to convert RVAs to file offsets so tables can be read from a file on disk. Why imports matter so much For a reverse engineer, the import table is often the most informative part of a program. A program that imports CreateFileW , ReadFile and CryptDecrypt reads and decrypts files; one importing WSAStartup and send uses the network; one importing CreateWindowExW has a window. Before reading a single instruction, the imports outline what the program does. Tools list them first for this reason: powershell dumpbin /imports game.exe dumpbin /exports plugin.dll The import table Data directory 1 (lesson 9.02) points at an array of import descriptors , one per DLL, ending with an all-zero entry: Field Meaning --- --- Name RVA of the DLL's name, such as "KERNEL32.dll" OriginalFirstThunk RVA of the import lookup table : what to import FirstThunk RVA of the import address table (IAT): where the addresses go Each lookup table entry is 8 bytes. If the top bit is set, the function is imported by ordinal (a number); otherwise the entry is the RVA of a hint/name entry: a 2-byte hint followed by the function's name, "CreateFileW\0" . What the loader does When the program starts (lesson 1.06), the loader, for each import descriptor: 1. loads the DLL (finding it by the search order, lesson 5.08) if it is not already loaded; 2. for each function in the lookup table, finds its address in the DLL's export table; 3. writes that address into the corresponding slot of the IAT . The program's code never contains the address of CreateFileW itself. Every call to an imported function goes through the IAT: asm call qword ptr __imp_CreateFileW ; read the address from the IAT slot, then call it So in disassembly, calls to imported functions are indirect calls through a fixed set of memory slots, and disassemblers label them with the function names, which makes them easy landmarks. After loading, the IAT is made read-only, so it cannot be changed by accident. The export table A DLL's data directory 0 points at its export directory , which holds three parallel arrays: Array Holds --- --- AddressOfFunctions RVAs of the exported functions, indexed by ordinal minus the base AddressOfNames RVAs of the exported names, sorted alphabetically so they can be binary-searched AddressOfNameOrdinals For each name, the index into the functions array GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage") (lesson 4.05) binary-searches the names, takes the matching ordinal index, and returns module + AddressOfFunctions index . An export can also be forwarded : its "address" points at a string such as "NTDLL.RtlAllocateHeap" , meaning "this function really lives in another DLL". Many kernel32.dll exports are forwarders. RVA to file offset All these tables use RVAs, which are offsets in memory . To read them from the file on disk, convert each RVA through the section table (lesson 9.02): find the section whose range contains the RVA, then file offset = RVA − section.VirtualAddress + section.PointerToRawData because a section's bytes are at VirtualAddress in memory and at PointerToRawData in the file. An RVA that falls in no section's file data (for example in zero-filled .bss space) has no file offset. The practice task writes this function; every PE tool has it at its core. Reading your own imports at run time A loaded module's tables are already in memory at module + RVA , with no conversion needed: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string int main() { auto base{ reinterpret_cast<unsigned char (GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)) }; const auto nt{ reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 (base + reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_DOS_HEADER (base)- e_lfanew) }; const IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY dir{ nt- OptionalHeader.DataDirectory IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT }; bool importsKernel32{ false }; int dlls{ 0 }; for (auto d{ reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR (base + dir.VirtualAddress) }; d- Name != 0; ++d) { ++dlls; std::string name{ reinterpret_cast<const char (base + d- Name) }; if (_stricmp(name.c_str(), "KERNEL32.dll") == 0) importsKernel32 = true; } std::cout << "imports from several DLLs: " << (dlls = 1 ? "yes" : "no") << ", including KERNEL32.dll: " << (importsKernel32 ? "yes" : "no") << '\n'; return 0; } imports from several DLLs: yes, including KERNEL32.dll: yes Delay-load and dynamic imports Not every DLL a program uses appears in its import table. Delay-loaded DLLs (lesson 5.08) have their own table (data directory 13), and anything loaded with LoadLibraryW and GetProcAddress at run time appears only as strings in the program, which is why reverse engineers search for DLL and function names among a program's strings (lesson 9.06) as well as reading the import table. Common mistakes !warning Reading table RVAs as file offsets Convert through the section table first, or the tables will appear to contain garbage. !warning Assuming every import is by name Entries with the top bit set are imported by ordinal; there is no name to read. !warning Concluding a program never uses a function because it is not imported It may be loaded at run time with GetProcAddress . Knowledge check quiz ? What does the loader write into the import address table? + The real addresses of the imported functions, found in each DLL's export table - The names of the functions - The program's own functions Calls to imports go through these slots. ? How does a call to an imported function look in disassembly? + An indirect call through a memory slot, such as call qword ptr __imp_CreateFileW - A direct call to the DLL's address - A jump to the import descriptor The code reads the address from the IAT at run time. ? A section has VirtualAddress 0x5000 and PointerToRawData 0x3400. What is the file offset of RVA 0x5120? + 0x3520 - 0x5120 - 0x8520 0x5120 − 0x5000 + 0x3400. ? What is a forwarded export? + An export entry that refers to a function in another DLL, by name - A function exported twice - A function that has been removed Many kernel32 exports forward to ntdll.

title: RVA to file offset
body: Write rvaToOffset(sections, rva) , which converts a relative virtual address into a file offset using a PE file's section table. An RVA belongs to a section when it is at least the section's virtualAddress and less than virtualAddress + max(virtualSize, rawSize) . The file offset is rva - virtualAddress + pointerToRawData . But a section's file data only covers rawSize bytes: if the RVA is inside the section but at or beyond virtualAddress + rawSize , it is zero-filled memory with no file data, so return std::nullopt . Also return std::nullopt for an RVA in no section. The sections may be given in any order. .text VA 0x1000 vsize 0x3A10 raw 0x3C00 at 0x400 .data VA 0x5000 vsize 0x2000 raw 0x200 at 0x4000 rvaToOffset(0x1234) = 0x634 rvaToOffset(0x5100) = 0x4100 rvaToOffset(0x5300) = nullopt (beyond .data's file data)

title: 9.04  Static Analysis with a Disassembler
body:
A disassembler turns a program's machine code back into assembly and organises it into functions, cross-references and control-flow graphs; a decompiler goes one step further, to C-like pseudocode. This lesson sets up Ghidra , the free, open-source reverse engineering suite, and walks through analysing a small program you built yourself: finding main , reading the listing and the decompiler side by side, and annotating as you learn. The tools Tool Cost Notes --- --- --- Ghidra Free, open source (from the US National Security Agency) Disassembler and decompiler for many processors; the course uses it IDA Free / IDA Pro Free version is limited; Pro is expensive The long-time industry standard Binary Ninja Paid, affordable personal licence Modern interface and scripting dumpbin /disasm Comes with Visual Studio A raw listing with no analysis: useful for quick checks Ghidra needs a Java runtime (JDK 17 or later). Download it from its official GitHub releases page, unzip it, and start ghidraRun.bat . A target to analyse Build this in Visual Studio in Release , x64, and keep the source closed while you analyse it. (You will check your conclusions at the end.) cpp include <cstdio include <cstring struct Hero { char name 16 ; int level; int xp; }; int xpForLevel(int level) { return level level 100; } void gainXp(Hero& hero, int amount) { hero.xp += amount; while (hero.xp = xpForLevel(hero.level + 1)) { ++hero.level; std::printf("%s reached level %d!
", hero.name, hero.level); } } int main() { Hero hero{}; std::strcpy(hero.name, "Rook"); hero.level = 1; for (int quest{ 0 }; quest < 5; ++quest) gainXp(hero, 250); std::printf("Final: level %d, %d xp
", hero.level, hero.xp); return 0; } To make it a fair exercise, do not give Ghidra the PDB at first: move x64\Release\ .pdb somewhere else. Importing and analysing 1. File → New Project , non-shared, in a folder of your choice. 2. File → Import File , pick the .exe . Ghidra recognises it as "Portable Executable (PE)", x86:LE:64. Accept. 3. Double-click it to open the CodeBrowser , and say Yes to analyse it with the default analysers. Ghidra now disassembles everything reachable from the entry point and exports, finds functions, follows cross-references, identifies standard library code it recognises ( function signatures for the C runtime), and builds a decompilation for each function. The main windows Window Shows --- --- Program Trees The PE sections (lesson 9.02) Symbol Tree Imports, exports, functions, labels Listing The disassembly, with addresses, bytes, labels and cross-references Decompile C-like pseudocode for the function under the cursor Function Graph (Window menu) Basic blocks and arrows (lesson 7.07) Defined Strings (Window menu) Every string Ghidra found Finding main The entry point is the C runtime's start-up code, not main . Two quick ways to find main : - In Defined Strings , find "Final: level %d, %d xp
" , double-click it, and look at its cross-reference (the XREF annotation): the function that uses it is main . Strings are the fastest way into unfamiliar code (lesson 9.08). - Or follow the entry point's code until a call with three arguments set up from argc , argv , envp -like values just before the program exits: that is the start-up code calling main . Reading the decompiler with the listing Ghidra's decompiler for gainXp might show something like: c void FUN_140001070(longlong param_1, int param_2) { int iVar1; (int )(param_1 + 0x14) = (int )(param_1 + 0x14) + param_2; while (iVar1 = (int )(param_1 + 0x10), (iVar1 + 1) (iVar1 + 1) 100 <= (int )(param_1 + 0x14)) { (int )(param_1 + 0x10) = iVar1 + 1; printf("%s reached level %d!
", param_1, iVar1 + 1); } return; } Everything from earlier chapters is visible: param_1 is a pointer (it is used with offsets); offset 0x10 and 0x14 are 4-byte members (lesson 7.08); xpForLevel has been inlined (lesson 7.11), so its formula appears directly; and the printf format string tells us param_1 points at a name and offset 0x10 is a level. Now annotate , which is most of the work: - Rename the function ( L key): gainXp . - Rename the parameters: hero , amount . - Create a structure (Data Type Manager → New → Structure) Hero with a char 16 name, an int level at 0x10 and an int xp at 0x14, and retype param_1 as Hero ( Ctrl+L ). The decompiler now prints hero- level and hero- xp . - Add comments ( ; key) for anything you work out. Annotations propagate: every other function that uses a Hero now reads better too. That snowball effect is why careful naming early pays off. Checking your work Open the source and compare. Then give Ghidra the PDB ( File → Load PDB File ) and look at the same function: names, types and line numbers appear, and you can see exactly what the PDB contributes (lesson 8.02) and what you had to reconstruct. Common mistakes !warning Believing every detail of the decompiler output It is reconstructed C, sometimes with wrong types or awkward casts. For anything important, check the listing. !warning Reading top to bottom from the entry point Start from something meaningful: a string, an import, an exported function. !warning Not saving your annotations Ghidra saves them in the project; save often, and keep the project with your notes. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a decompiler produce? + C-like pseudocode reconstructed from the machine code - The original source code - The program's PDB file It is a readable approximation, not the original source. ? What is the quickest way to find the function that prints a particular message? + Find the string in the strings list and follow its cross-reference - Read every function from the entry point - Search the import table Strings and their cross-references are the usual way in. ? Why does creating a struct type and applying it to a parameter help so much? + The decompiler then shows member names instead of offsets, everywhere that type is used - It makes the program run faster - It recovers the original variable names automatically Annotations propagate across the program.

title: 9.05  Recognising Functions, Loops and Branches
body: Disassemblers find most functions automatically, but understanding a function means recognising its parts: where it starts and ends, what its arguments and result are, and how its control flow maps to if , loops and switch . This lesson turns chapter 7's patterns into a reading routine for unknown functions, and covers the cases where automatic analysis gets function boundaries wrong. Where functions start and end A disassembler finds functions by following calls from known starting points (the entry point, exports, the .pdata unwind table from lesson 8.02, which lists most functions' start and end RVAs on x64). Signs of a function start: - it is the target of call instructions; - it begins with a typical prologue : saving non-volatile registers ( push rbx , mov rsp+8 , rbx ), sub rsp, N ; - it is listed in .pdata ; - it follows padding bytes ( CC or 90 ) after the previous function's ret . Signs of an end: ret after an epilogue, or a jmp to another function (a tail call, lesson 7.11). Automatic analysis goes wrong when code is only reached through pointers (a vtable, a callback table, a jump table it did not decode), or when data sits in a code section. Ghidra then shows bytes that are not disassembled; pressing D (disassemble) and F (create function) at a likely start fixes it. A reading routine For each unknown function: 1. Signature first. Which of rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , xmm0 to xmm3 are read before being written? Those are the arguments (lesson 7.06). Is rax / eax / xmm0 set just before every ret ? That is a result. eax set but only al used by callers suggests a bool . 2. Calls next. Which functions does it call, and are any of them imports (named for you) or functions you already named? Calls often explain more than everything else together. 3. Constants and strings. Format strings, error messages, magic numbers ( 0x5A4D is "MZ"; 0x3F800000 is 1.0f). 4. Control flow. Draw or view the graph: loops are back edges, decisions are diamonds, switch is a jump table (lesson 7.07). 5. Memory accesses. Offsets from argument registers are struct members (lesson 7.08). 6. Name it , even provisionally ("probably_load_config"), and move on. Refine later. Loops in the graph A loop shows up in a function graph as an arrow going back up to a block that dominates it (one that every path into the loop passes through). Its parts: Recognising the induction variable (the register incremented each time round and compared against a limit) tells you what the loop iterates over; the memory accesses that use it tell you the array and its element size. The practice task finds loops from a list of jumps, the first step automatic tools perform. Branches that are not ifs Not every conditional jump is an if in the source: Pattern Source --- --- A compare and jump straight after a call, to an error path if (!ok) return error; or an exception-free error check test rax, rax / je after a call returning a pointer A null check A jump to a block that calls a function with a string like "Assertion failed" An assert cmp against a value, then a call to a function that never returns ( abort , a throw helper) A bounds check or failed precondition Several jumps to one block that sets the same return value Early returns merged by the compiler When there are no symbols for library code Functions from the C and C++ runtime are compiled into your program. Without a PDB, they look like any other unknown function. Ghidra's Function ID analyser recognises many by their bytes, and recognising the common ones by behaviour saves a lot of time: memcpy / memset (byte loops or rep movsb / rep stosb ), strlen (a loop looking for a zero byte), operator new (calls malloc , throws on failure), std::string constructors (lesson 2.08's small buffer: compares a length with 15). Common mistakes !warning Assuming the disassembler found every function Code reached only through pointers may be missing. Look for undisassembled bytes in code sections. !warning Reading every register as an argument Only registers read before being written in the function's first block are arguments. !warning Spending hours inside runtime library code Recognise it, name it, and move on to the program's own logic. Knowledge check quiz ? How can you tell which registers are a function's arguments? + They are argument registers (rcx, rdx, r8, r9, xmm0-xmm3) read before being written - They are the registers used most in the function - They are always all four Unused argument registers are simply never read. ? What marks a loop in a function graph? + A back edge: an arrow from a later block back up to an earlier one that dominates it - Any conditional jump - A call instruction The target of the back edge is the loop's head. ? test rax, rax / je error straight after a call. What is it probably? + A null check on the pointer the call returned - A loop - A switch Functions returning pointers use null to signal failure.

title: Find the loops
body: A disassembler has listed every jump in a function: each one has the address it is at and the address it jumps to. A jump whose target is at or before its own address is a back edge , and its target is the head of a loop. Write loopHeads(jumps) , which returns the distinct loop-head addresses, sorted ascending, together with, for each head, how many back edges lead to it (a loop with continue statements can have several). jumps: 0x1010 - 0x1040 (forward: an if) 0x1030 - 0x1018 (back edge) 0x1050 - 0x1018 (back edge to the same head) 0x1060 - 0x1060 (a jump to itself: an infinite loop of one instruction) result: { 0x1018, 2 }, { 0x1060, 1 }

title: 9.06  Recognising Classes, Vtables and Strings
body: C++ programs leave distinctive traces even without symbols: vtables in read-only data list each polymorphic class's virtual functions, RTTI records often hold class names outright, constructors write vptrs, and strings reveal messages, file names and formats. This lesson shows how to find and use each, and how a strings -style scan works. Vtables Lesson 3.05 showed that each class with virtual functions has a vtable, an array of function pointers, in .rdata , and each object stores a pointer to it at offset 0. In a stripped program, vtables are among the most useful structures you can find: - Each vtable is a list of one class's virtual functions , in declaration order. - Classes related by inheritance have vtables with the same layout : slot 3 is the same virtual function (overridden or not) in every one. - A vtable entry pointing at the same function as the base class's entry means that function was not overridden . How to find them: in Ghidra, look in .rdata for runs of 8-byte values that are all addresses of functions in .text . Ghidra's analysis usually labels them vftable when RTTI is present. Constructors and destructors A constructor can be recognised by what it does with the vptr: asm Goblin_ctor: mov rsp+8 , rcx sub rsp, 28h call Entity_ctor ; base class constructor first lea rax, Goblin_vftable ; then store this class's vtable... mov rcx, rsp+30h mov rcx , rax ; ...into offset 0 of the object mov dword ptr rcx+18h , 10 ; initialise members ... The pattern "call another constructor, then store a vtable address into this , then initialise members" identifies a constructor, its base class's constructor, and its vtable all at once. Destructors do the reverse: store their own vtable, destroy members, then call the base destructor. Every place a vtable's address is written is a constructor or destructor of that class. RTTI: class names for free Unless a program is compiled with /GR- , MSVC stores run-time type information for each polymorphic class, used by dynamic_cast and typeid . Just before each vtable sits a pointer to a "complete object locator", which leads to a type descriptor containing the class's decorated name as a string: .?AVGoblin@@ .?AVEntity@@ .?AV?$vector@HV?$allocator@H@std@@@std@@ .?AV means "a class", and the rest is the class name in MSVC's name-mangling format (lesson 4.02); undname or Ghidra demangles them. A class hierarchy descriptor also lists each class's base classes , so RTTI can recover the whole inheritance tree. Searching a stripped program's strings for .?AV often lists every polymorphic class it has. Strings Programs are full of text: messages, log lines, file names, registry keys, format strings, URLs, error descriptions, command names. They survive compilation unchanged (lesson 2.03's .rdata ), and each one is a label for the code that uses it: String found Suggests --- --- "Failed to open save file %s" The function using it loads saves; the %s argument is the path "config.ini" , "Settings" Configuration loading "Assertion failed: %s, file %s, line %d" The program's assert handler (lesson 8.03) "kernel32.dll" , "VirtualAlloc" A function loaded at run time with GetProcAddress (lesson 9.03) "%d/%d" , "HP" Interface drawing Remember both encodings (lesson 2.08): Windows programs often store UTF-16 strings, which look like H.P. with zero bytes between the letters in a byte view. Tools search for both. The classic tool is strings (in Microsoft's Sysinternals suite): it scans any file for runs of printable characters of at least some minimum length. The practice task writes one. Common mistakes !warning Assuming RTTI is always there Programs built with /GR- have none; vtables still exist but are unnamed. !warning Treating every run of addresses in .rdata as a vtable Jump tables and other pointer arrays look similar. A vtable is referenced by constructors that store it into objects. !warning Searching only for ASCII strings Windows programs use UTF-16 heavily. Search both forms. Knowledge check quiz ? Where is a class's vtable stored? + In read-only data ( .rdata ), once per class - In each object - On the heap Objects hold only a pointer to it. ? How can you recognise a constructor without symbols? + It calls the base constructor, then writes a vtable address into offset 0 of the object - It is the first function in the program - It always has the most arguments Every write of a vtable address into an object marks a constructor or destructor. ? What is .?AVGoblin@@ ? + The decorated name of the class Goblin , stored as RTTI - An error message - A file name .?AV introduces a class's decorated name. ? Why search for UTF-16 strings as well as ASCII? + Windows programs often store text as UTF-16, which an ASCII-only scan misses - UTF-16 strings are always longer - ASCII strings are not stored in programs Wide strings appear with a zero byte between ASCII letters.

title: Your own strings tool
body: Write findStrings(bytes, minLength) , which scans a block of bytes for text the way the strings tool does, in both encodings: - ASCII : a run of at least minLength printable bytes (0x20 to 0x7E inclusive). - UTF-16 : a run of at least minLength two-byte units, each a printable ASCII byte followed by a zero byte, starting at an even offset. Return every string found, as an offset and the text (UTF-16 strings converted to their ASCII letters), sorted by offset. A UTF-16 string's bytes are not also reported as ASCII (its letters are separated by zeros, so they are never minLength long as ASCII anyway, for minLength = 2 ). bytes: 00 'H' 'P' ':' ' ' '9' '9' 01 'S' 00 'a' 00 'v' 00 'e' 00 00 00 minLength 4 - { 1, "HP: 99" } { 8, "Save" }

title: 9.07  Dynamic Analysis with a Debugger
body: Static analysis shows every path a program could take; dynamic analysis shows what it actually does, with real values. This lesson uses a debugger on a program without its source ( x64dbg as well as the debuggers you know): breaking on API calls, watching arguments and return values, following indirect calls, and tracing the path through code to confirm what static analysis suggested. Why run it Some questions are slow to answer from the listing alone: - Which of five possible callbacks does this indirect call rax actually reach? - What does this decryption routine produce? - Which branch is taken with real input? - What values does this function receive? A debugger answers them in seconds. The usual rhythm is: form a hypothesis in the disassembler, confirm it in the debugger, write the conclusion back as a name or comment in the disassembler. x64dbg x64dbg is a free, open-source debugger designed for working without source. Its main window shows the disassembly, registers, the stack and a memory dump all at once, much like the Visual Studio windows of lesson 4.08 side by side. Download it from its official site, and use x64dbg.exe (not x32dbg ) for 64-bit programs. Visual Studio and WinDbg can do everything below too; x64dbg is simply convenient when there is no source or PDB. As always in this chapter, practise on the targets from lesson 9.10 or other programs you have the right to analyse. Breaking on API calls Imports are the landmarks (lesson 9.03). Breaking on them shows you exactly when the program does something significant, and with what: Want to know Break on --- --- Which files it opens CreateFileW What it writes WriteFile Which DLLs it loads at run time LoadLibraryW , LoadLibraryExW , GetProcAddress Which registry keys it reads RegOpenKeyExW , RegQueryValueExW When it allocates large blocks VirtualAlloc In x64dbg type bp CreateFileW in the command bar; in WinDbg bp kernelbase!CreateFileW . When it stops, the arguments are in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 (lesson 7.06): for CreateFileW , rcx points at the file name, so follow it in the dump as a UTF-16 string. Then run to return (Ctrl+F9 in x64dbg) to see the result in rax , and step out to land in the code that called it: that is the program's own function that opens the file, now found. Following indirect calls Virtual calls, callbacks and function tables (lessons 3.04, 3.05) appear as call rax or call qword ptr rax+18h , which static analysis cannot always resolve. Put a breakpoint on the indirect call, run, and step into it: you are now in the actual target, and can name it in your static notes ("slot 3 of this vtable is Goblin::update "). Tracing a path When you need to know which way a series of branches went for a given input: - Step over the region (F8), watching the jumps: x64dbg shows whether each conditional jump will be taken before you step it. - Use conditional breakpoints and logging breakpoints (lesson 4.09) to record values each time a location is hit without stopping. - Use trace features (x64dbg's "Trace over" with a condition, or WinDbg's wt ) to record every instruction executed until a condition holds, then inspect the record. Watching memory change Data breakpoints (hardware breakpoints, lesson 4.09) work the same without source: right-click an address in the dump → Breakpoint → Hardware, on write. Run, and the debugger stops on whatever instruction changes it, telling you which function owns that data. Combined with lesson 9.08's cross-references, this is how unknown data is tied to the code that uses it. Patching for experiments Debuggers can change instructions in memory. During analysis this is useful for experiments: force a branch the other way to see what the alternative path does, or skip a call. Changes are made only to the running copy in memory, are gone on restart, and are for understanding your practice targets. (Changing software to bypass licence checks or protections is outside this course's ground rules, lesson 9.01.) Common mistakes !warning Breaking on a high-traffic function without a condition CreateFileW or VirtualAlloc may be called thousands of times at start-up. Add a condition or enable the breakpoint only when you reach the interesting part. !warning Reading arguments after the function has started The argument registers are reliable only at the function's first instruction. !warning Forgetting that the program may behave differently under a debugger Timing changes, and some programs check for debuggers. If behaviour differs, note it as a finding. Knowledge check quiz ? You break on CreateFileW . Where is the file name? + Pointed to by rcx , as a UTF-16 string - In rax - At the top of the stack It is the first argument. ? How do you find the program's own function that opens a particular file? + Break on CreateFileW , check the name, then step out to the caller - Search the import table for the file name - Look at the entry point Stepping out lands in the code that made the call. ? What is the advantage of dynamic analysis for call qword ptr rax+18h ? + Stepping into it shows the actual target at run time - It removes the indirect call - It lists every possible target Static analysis may not know which object rax points to.

title: 9.08  Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
match: 9.08 Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
body: A cross-reference (xref) records that one place in a program refers to another: a call to a function, a read of a global, a use of a string. Following xrefs, backwards to "who uses this?" and forwards to "what does this use?", is how you navigate an unknown program. This lesson covers the kinds of xref, how disassemblers find them, and how to decode a call instruction's target yourself. What a cross-reference is When an instruction mentions an address (calls it, jumps to it, reads or writes it, or takes it with lea ), the disassembler records a reference from that instruction to that address. Seen from the target, those are its xrefs : every place that refers to it. Kind Example Meaning --- --- --- Call call 140001070 Code that calls this function Jump jmp 140001200 / jne ... Code that branches here Read mov eax, 140005010 Code that reads this data Write mov 140005010 , eax Code that writes this data Offset (address taken) lea rcx, 140004120 Code that takes this address: passing a string, a callback, a table Data an 8-byte pointer in a vtable or table Data that points here In Ghidra, the XREF n : annotation at each label lists them, and References → Show References to (Ctrl+Shift+F) opens the full list. Navigating with xrefs Most reverse engineering is moving along xrefs from something you understand to something you do not: Typical starting points: - Strings (lesson 9.06): follow the string's xref to the code that prints or uses it. - Imports : xrefs to CreateFileW list every place the program opens files. - A global you found in the debugger (lesson 9.07): its read and write xrefs list every function that uses it. - A vtable : its xrefs are constructors and destructors (lesson 9.06). How call targets are found Disassemblers find most code xrefs by decoding instructions. The most common, the near call , is easy to decode by hand: the byte E8 followed by a 4-byte signed displacement relative to the address of the next instruction: address 140001000: E8 6B 00 00 00 call 140001070 └┘ └──────────┘ op rel32 = 0x0000006B target = address of next instruction + rel32 = (140001000 + 5) + 0x6B = 140001070 The displacement is relative (lesson 6.09's RIP-relative idea), so the same bytes work wherever the module is loaded. Negative displacements call backwards. Scanning code for E8 bytes and computing targets finds call xrefs, with one caveat: E8 can also appear inside other instructions' operands, so real disassemblers decode instruction by instruction rather than scanning blindly. The practice task does the simple scan on a buffer known to contain only calls and padding. RIP-relative data references ( mov eax, rip+disp32 , lea rcx, rip+disp32 ) work the same way: target = next instruction's address + displacement. Xrefs the analysis misses Some references are invisible to static analysis: - Addresses computed at run time ( base + index 8 into a table it did not decode). - Functions found with GetProcAddress from a string. - Pointers stored in data structures built at run time. Dynamic analysis fills these gaps: a breakpoint or hardware watchpoint shows the real reference, and you add it manually (Ghidra lets you add references by hand). Common mistakes !warning Forgetting reads versus writes "Who writes this global?" usually narrows things far more than "who uses it?". Filter xrefs by kind. !warning Computing a relative target from the instruction's own address Relative displacements count from the address of the next instruction. !warning Trusting a lack of xrefs No xrefs found does not mean unused: the reference may be computed at run time. Knowledge check quiz ? A call at 0x140002000 is encoded E8 F0 FF FF FF . Where does it call? + 0x140001FF5 - 0x140002005 - 0x1400020F0 rel32 = 0xFFFFFFF0 = -16; next instruction at 0x140002005; 0x140002005 - 16 = 0x140001FF5. ? What do the xrefs to a vtable usually point to? + The constructors and destructors that store it into objects - Every virtual call - The class's data members Virtual calls read the vptr from the object, not the vtable's address directly. ? How can you find every place a program opens a file? + List the cross-references to the imported CreateFileW - Search for .txt in the strings - Read the entry point Every call to an import goes through its IAT slot, and each is an xref.

title: Who calls this function?
where: 9.08 Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
body: You are given a block of machine code that contains only near calls ( E8 followed by a 4-byte little-endian signed displacement) and single-byte padding ( CC or 90 ), and the address the block is loaded at. Write two functions. - callTargets(code, base) returns every call in the block as a pair: the call's own address and the address it calls, in order. - callersOf(code, base, target) returns the addresses of the calls whose target is target . A call's target is the address of the next instruction ( call address + 5 ) plus the displacement. A call cut off by the end of the block is ignored. base 0x140001000, code: E8 6B 00 00 00 CC E8 F0 FF FF FF callTargets - { 0x140001000, 0x140001070 }, { 0x140001006, 0x140000FFB }

title: 9.09  Reconstructing Structs from Compiled Code
body: Types disappear in compilation, but every struct leaves a trail of offsets and sizes in the code that uses it. This lesson is a step-by-step method for rebuilding a struct definition from those accesses, combining static evidence (offsets, sizes, instructions used) with dynamic evidence (values seen in the debugger), and recording the result as a type the disassembler can apply everywhere. The evidence an access gives Each instruction that touches a struct member tells you three things (lesson 7.08): Evidence Example Tells you --- --- --- Offset rcx+14h A member starts at 0x14 Size dword ptr , byte ptr , qword ptr It is 4, 1 or 8 bytes Instruction movss vs mov ; movsx vs movzx ; jl vs jb afterwards float or integer; signed or unsigned Use Passed to printf with %s ; followed as a pointer; compared with 0 and branched A string pointer or buffer; a pointer; a flag or count A method 1. Pick one struct pointer and find every function that receives it (from xrefs and from the calls in its creator). 2. Collect accesses : every reg+offset with that pointer, noting offset, size and instruction. The disassembler's structure editor helps: Ghidra's Auto Create Structure on a parameter does a first pass. 3. Lay them out by offset (this is lesson 7.08's practice task). Gaps are either padding (lesson 2.05) or members this code never touches. 4. Type the members using instructions and uses: movss means float; a value compared with jl / jg is signed; an 8-byte member that is dereferenced is a pointer, and what it points to is another struct to rebuild. 5. Name them from strings and context: a member printed with "HP: %d" is health. 6. Check alignment : a 4-byte member at an offset that is not a multiple of 4 suggests the struct is packed, or you mis-read an access. 7. Confirm dynamically : break where the struct is used and look at it in the debugger's memory view (lesson 2.11); the values should make sense with your types (floats look like floats, pointers like pointers, counts are small). 8. Apply the type to the parameter and globals, and iterate: the decompiler output improves, revealing more. A worked example A function in a stripped target contains: asm movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+8 ; float at 8 addss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+10h ; float at 0x10 movss dword ptr rcx+8 , xmm0 mov eax, dword ptr rcx+18h ; 4-byte integer at 0x18 test eax, eax jle dead ; signed compare with 0: health-like movzx edx, byte ptr rcx+1Ch ; 1-byte unsigned at 0x1C, then tested: a bool test dl, dl ... mov rax, qword ptr rcx+20h ; 8 bytes at 0x20, then used as an address: a pointer mov rcx, qword ptr rax ; reading through it: its first member Elsewhere, a constructor stores a vtable address at rcx , and a function prints rcx+0Ch as a float alongside rcx+8 with "pos %.1f,%.1f" . Reconstruction: cpp struct Entity // reconstructed { void vftable; // 0x00 written by the constructor (lesson 9.06) float x; // 0x08 printed with "pos %.1f,%.1f" float y; // 0x0C float vx; // 0x10 added to x each update: a velocity float vy; // 0x14 (by symmetry with x/vx; confirm in the debugger) int health; // 0x18 signed, compared with 0 bool alive; // 0x1C // 0x1D..0x1F padding before the pointer Entity target; // 0x20 dereferenced, and its first member looks like a vtable }; // size 0x28 if nothing follows (check the allocation size in the creator) The size can usually be confirmed where objects are created: operator new(0x28) or a HeapAlloc with that size right before the constructor call. Recording it In Ghidra, create the structure in the Data Type Manager , fill in the members, and Retype the parameter ( Ctrl+L ) in every function that receives it. Keep a notes file alongside: which evidence supports each member, and which are guesses. When new evidence contradicts a guess, you will know which to revisit. Common mistakes !warning Assuming you have seen every member Code you have not looked at may use offsets you have not seen. Mark uncertain regions as unknown rather than as padding. !warning Ignoring the creator The allocation size and the constructor's initial values are some of the best evidence for a struct's size and members. !warning Over-trusting names A member you called "health" is a hypothesis until behaviour confirms it. Knowledge check quiz ? A member is read with movss at offset 0x8. What type is it most likely? + float - int - A pointer movss moves a single-precision float. ? How can you find a struct's total size? + Look at the allocation size passed to operator new or the allocator just before its constructor is called - Add up the offsets - It cannot be found Creators reveal sizes directly. ? An 8-byte member is loaded and then used as an address. What is it? + A pointer to another object, whose type you reconstruct the same way - A double - A pair of ints Following it leads to the next struct.

title: 9.10  Practice Targets You Compile Yourself
body: The best way to learn reverse engineering is on programs whose source you can check afterwards. This lesson gives a graded series of practice targets to write, build without symbols, and analyse with the chapter's tools, from a single function to a small game with classes and a file format, along with how to set up the builds and how to check your answers. The routine For each target: 1. Write it, or have a friend write it so you do not know the answers. 2. Build it Release, x64 , and move the .pdb out of the folder. 3. Analyse it statically in Ghidra and dynamically in x64dbg or Visual Studio, writing down your conclusions: names, types, what each function does, the format of any file. 4. Check against the source. For each mistake, find which evidence misled you. 5. Load the PDB into Ghidra and compare the two views. Repeat a target with /Od (unoptimised) for an easier version, and with /O2 /GL (whole-program optimisation, more inlining) for a harder one. Level 1: single functions Write a program with half a dozen small functions and call them from main with values read from std::cin , so the optimiser cannot fold everything into constants: - int clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) - unsigned popcount(unsigned x) (count set bits with a loop) - int sumSquares(const int a, int n) - bool isPalindrome(const char s) - float lerp(float a, float b, float t) Goal : name each function and give its signature from the assembly alone. Watch for cmov in clamp , the loop in popcount (or the popcnt instruction, if the compiler uses it), vectorisation in sumSquares , and xmm registers in lerp . Level 2: control flow - A switch on a command letter with eight cases (find the jump table, lesson 7.07). - A state machine with an enum and a loop. - A function with early returns and && / conditions. Goal : reconstruct the control flow as C++ that behaves identically, and test it against the original with the same inputs. Level 3: data structures - A struct with mixed members ( int , float , bool , pointer, char 16 ) passed to several functions. - A singly linked list built from user input and walked. - A std::vector<Item with push_back and a loop. Goal : rebuild the structs (lesson 9.09), including size and padding, and recognise the standard library's inlined code (vector growth, lesson 3.07). Level 4: classes - A small hierarchy with virtual functions: Shape with area() and name() , three derived classes, a vector of std::unique_ptr<Shape . Goal : find every vtable and its RTTI name (lesson 9.06), match each slot to a function, identify constructors and destructors, and draw the hierarchy. Then rebuild with /GR- and do it again without the names. Level 5: a file format Write a program that saves and loads a simple binary file: a header with a magic number and version, a count, then records of mixed fields, little-endian (lesson 2.06's practice). Analyse the program and a file it wrote. Goal : write a specification of the format (offsets, sizes, meanings) good enough that someone could write a compatible reader, and then write that reader yourself. This is exactly what interoperability work looks like. Level 6: a small game Take the game you will build in chapter 11 (or any small game of your own), build it without symbols, and pick a feature: how damage is calculated, how a level file is loaded, how the save format works. Goal : document the feature completely from the binary, as if you had never seen the source. Other sources of practice - Open-source programs : build one in Release without symbols and analyse it; the source is there to check you. - Capture-the-flag competitions often include reverse engineering challenges, made and published for exactly this purpose. - Crackme collections : small programs published by their authors as reverse engineering exercises. Use ones explicitly offered for practice, run unfamiliar binaries only inside a virtual machine (lesson 15.08), and treat downloaded executables as untrusted. Common mistakes !warning Starting with something too big Each level should take an evening or two. If a target takes weeks, step back a level. !warning Not checking your answers The value of self-made targets is the answer key. Use it, and learn from each mistake. !warning Running downloaded practice binaries on your main machine Use a virtual machine for anything you did not build yourself. Knowledge check quiz ? Why read values from std::cin in a practice target? + So the optimiser cannot compute the results at compile time and remove the functions - Because std::cin is easier to reverse engineer - To make the program interactive With constant inputs, an optimising compiler may fold everything into a few printed constants. ? What does building with /GR- change for a reverse engineer? + RTTI is removed, so class names are no longer available from the binary - Optimisation is turned off - Symbols are added Vtables remain, but nameless. ? What is the most valuable part of a self-built target? + The source, which lets you check every conclusion - Its small size - That it is fast to compile Checking answers is how you calibrate your judgement.

title: 10.01  The Game Loop
body: Every real-time game is built around one loop that runs as long as the game does: read input , update the world, render a frame, repeat, dozens of times a second. This lesson builds that loop step by step, explains what belongs in each phase, and shows how an engine is organised around it. The heart of every game A word processor waits for the user to do something. A game does not wait: monsters move, timers tick and the screen redraws whether or not the player touches anything. So at the centre of every game engine is a loop: Each trip round the loop produces one frame . At 60 frames per second the whole loop has 16.7 ms (lesson 8.08). cpp include <chrono include <iostream struct World { float x{ 0 }; float speed{ 2.0f }; int frames{ 0 }; bool running{ true }; }; void processInput(World&) { / read keys; set flags such as world.running = false on Escape / } void update(World& w, float dt) { w.x += w.speed dt; // move 2 units per second, however long the frame was ++w.frames; if (w.x = 1.0f) w.running = false; } void render(const World& w) { std::cout << "frame " << w.frames << ": x = " << w.x << '\n'; } int main() { World world; const float dt{ 0.1f }; // pretend each frame takes 0.1 s, so the output is the same every run while (world.running) { processInput(world); update(world, dt); render(world); } return 0; } frame 1: x = 0.2 frame 2: x = 0.4 frame 3: x = 0.6 frame 4: x = 0.8 frame 5: x = 1 A real game measures dt with a clock (lesson 5.07) instead of pretending; the next lesson covers how to use it well. What goes in each phase Phase Does Must not --- --- --- Input Drain the window messages (lesson 5.05's PeekMessage loop), read devices, turn them into actions (lesson 10.05) Change the world directly Update Advance the simulation by dt : movement, physics, AI, timers, animation, game rules, spawning and removing entities Draw anything, or wait for anything Render Draw the world as it is now : sprites, models, effects, interface Change the world Keeping these separate is what lets engines run update at a fixed rate while rendering as fast as possible (lesson 10.02), run rendering on another thread, record and replay input, or run a server with no rendering at all. The engine around the loop An engine is mostly the systems that the loop calls each frame: A small game calls these in a fixed order on one thread. A large engine spreads their work across worker threads with a job system (lesson 6.05) while keeping the same overall order, because order matters: physics must run after movement is decided and before rendering, or the frame shows stale positions. Starting and stopping Around the loop sit initialisation (create the window, load the first level, start subsystems in dependency order) and shutdown (stop them in the reverse order, as RAII does for objects, lesson 2.04). Many engine bugs are ordering bugs here: audio shut down before the entities that still play sounds, a resource released before the renderer stops using it. Common mistakes !warning Updating in the render phase Rendering must only read the state, or the result depends on how often frames are drawn. !warning Waiting inside the loop Blocking on a file, the network or a lock stalls every frame. Move slow work to other threads (lesson 6.05) and check its result each frame. !warning Moving by a fixed amount per frame x += 2 moves twice as fast at 120 fps as at 60. Multiply by dt . Knowledge check quiz ? What are the three phases of the game loop? + Process input, update the world, render the frame - Load, play, save - Compile, link, run They repeat every frame for as long as the game runs. ?
