Why should rendering never change the game state? + The state would then depend on how many frames are drawn, which varies between machines - Rendering is too slow - The GPU cannot write to memory Updates belong in the update phase, driven by time. ? Why multiply speeds by dt ? + So movement is the same per second regardless of the frame rate - To make the game run faster - Because the compiler requires it A fixed step per frame makes speed depend on frame rate.

title: 10.02  Time Steps and Frame Rates
body: How much time does each update simulate? Using the real frame time (a variable time step ) is simple but makes physics behave differently on fast and slow machines. Most games run the simulation at a fixed time step , consuming real time from an accumulator , and smooth the picture with interpolation . This lesson builds that loop and covers frame limiting and vsync. Variable time step The simplest loop measures how long the last frame took and updates by that much: cpp while (running) { const double now{ clock() }; const double dt{ now - previous }; previous = now; update(dt); render(); } It works, and many small games use it. Its problems show up at the edges: - Physics depends on dt . Integrating motion in bigger steps gives different results: a jump reaches a different height at 30 fps than at 144 fps, collisions can be missed when a fast object moves past a wall in one big step ("tunnelling"). - One slow frame (a disk read, a hitch) produces a huge dt that throws objects across the level. - Nothing is reproducible : the same input gives different results on different machines, which breaks replays and networked games that must agree exactly. Fixed time step The standard solution: the simulation always advances in the same small step (for example 1/60 s), and the loop runs as many of those steps as real time requires. cpp include <iostream int main() { const double step{ 1.0 / 60.0 }; // the simulation always moves in 1/60 s steps double accumulator{ 0.0 }; int updates{ 0 }; // Real frame times, in seconds: a fast frame, normal frames, and one slow hitch. const double frames { 0.008, 0.016, 0.017, 0.050, 0.016 }; for (double frameTime : frames) { accumulator += frameTime; // real time owed to the simulation int thisFrame{ 0 }; while (accumulator = step) { // update(step); // always the same step accumulator -= step; ++thisFrame; } updates += thisFrame; const double alpha{ accumulator / step }; // how far we are into the next step, 0 to 1 std::cout << "frame of " << frameTime 1000 << " ms: " << thisFrame << " update(s), alpha " << static_cast<int (alpha 100) << "%\n"; } std::cout << "total updates " << updates << '\n'; return 0; } frame of 8 ms: 0 update(s), alpha 48% frame of 16 ms: 1 update(s), alpha 44% frame of 17 ms: 1 update(s), alpha 46% frame of 50 ms: 3 update(s), alpha 46% frame of 16 ms: 1 update(s), alpha 42% total updates 6 Real time flows into the accumulator ; the simulation takes it out in fixed bites. A fast frame may run no update at all; a slow frame runs several to catch up. The simulation always sees the same step , so it behaves identically on every machine, and with the same inputs, it produces the same results every time. The spiral of death If one update takes longer than step to compute, each frame owes more updates than the last, and the game grinds to a halt trying to catch up. Guard against it by capping how much time one frame may add: cpp accumulator += std::min(frameTime, 0.25); // never try to catch up more than a quarter of a second The game then runs in slow motion under extreme load instead of freezing. Interpolation: smooth pictures between steps With a 60 Hz simulation on a 144 Hz monitor, several frames are rendered between two updates. Drawing the latest state each time would make movement stutter. Instead, keep the previous and current state of each object and draw a blend, using alpha from the loop above: drawn position = previous + (current − previous) × alpha What is drawn lags the simulation by up to one step (about 16 ms), which players do not notice, in exchange for perfectly smooth motion. The practice task computes these numbers. Frame rate, vsync and limiting Technique Effect --- --- Vsync on The GPU waits for the monitor's refresh before showing a frame: no tearing, frame rate capped at the refresh rate, slightly more input latency Vsync off Frames shown as soon as ready: lowest latency, possible tearing (top and bottom of the screen from different frames) Variable refresh (G-Sync, FreeSync) The monitor refreshes when a frame is ready: no tearing, low latency A frame limiter The game waits until a target frame time has passed: saves power and heat; must wait precisely ( Sleep is coarse, lesson 6.05), typically sleeping most of the remaining time and spinning briefly at the end Common mistakes !warning Feeding a variable dt straight into physics Use a fixed step for anything that must be stable or reproducible. !warning No cap on the accumulator One long stall leads to a spiral of catch-up updates. !warning Interpolating game logic Interpolation is only for drawing. Game rules always use the simulated state. Knowledge check quiz ? With a fixed step of 1/60 s, how many updates does a 50 ms frame run (starting with an empty accumulator)? + 3, with about 0.0 to 16.7 ms left over in the accumulator - 1 - 50 50 ms holds three 16.7 ms steps, with a small remainder carried to the next frame. ? Why does a fixed time step make replays possible? + The same inputs always produce the same updates, since every update uses the same step - It records every frame - It makes the game run faster A variable step makes results depend on frame timings. ? What does alpha in the fixed-step loop represent? + How far real time has got into the next simulation step, used to blend previous and current states when drawing - The frame rate - The number of updates this frame It is the leftover accumulator divided by the step. ? What problem does capping the accumulator solve? + The spiral of death, where the game falls further behind trying to catch up - Tearing - Input lag Under extreme load the game slows down instead of freezing.

title: A fixed-step clock
body: Write the class FixedStepClock , the timing part of a fixed-time-step game loop. - The constructor receives the step length in seconds and the maximum frame time that will be counted (the cap against the spiral of death). - advance(frameTime) adds the frame's real time (capped at the maximum) to the accumulator, then removes whole steps while at least one step is held. It returns how many updates should run this frame. - alpha() returns the leftover fraction of a step, accumulator / step , from 0 up to (but not including) 1. Also write interpolate(previous, current, alpha) , which blends two positions for drawing. FixedStepClock clock{ 0.01, 0.25 }; clock.advance(0.025) - 2, alpha 0.5 clock.advance(0.005) - 1, alpha 0.0 (0.005 + 0.005 left over = one step) clock.advance(5.0) - 25 (capped at 0.25 s) To avoid floating-point surprises, the tests use steps and frame times that are exact in binary or compare with a small tolerance.

title: 10.03  Entities, Components and Systems
body: How should a game represent its thousands of objects? Deep inheritance trees ( Monster : Character : Entity ) become rigid and slow. Many engines use entity-component-system (ECS) design instead: an entity is just an id, components are plain data attached to it, and systems are loops over every entity with a given set of components. This lesson explains why, and builds a small ECS on the sparse set structure. The trouble with deep hierarchies The object-oriented first attempt at a game world looks like this: Then the designers ask for a barrel that can fly, a monster that can be picked up like a prop, and a player who can turn into a barrel. Each request fits awkwardly into the tree, and features drift up into the base class until Entity has a hundred members, most unused by most objects. Performance suffers too: each object is a separate heap allocation with a vptr, updating them means a virtual call each, and their data is scattered (lessons 3.02, 3.05). Composition: entities, components, systems ECS splits things differently: Part Is Example --- --- --- Entity An id. Nothing else. Entity{ 42 } Component A small, plain struct of data, attached to an entity Position{ x, y } , Velocity{ vx, vy } , Health{ hp } , Sprite{ textureId } System A function that loops over every entity having certain components Movement: every entity with Position and Velocity A flying barrel is just an entity with Position , Velocity , Sprite and Breakable . A monster you can pick up has Carryable added. No class hierarchy has to change: behaviour comes from which components an entity has, and which systems act on them. cpp void movementSystem(World& world, float dt) { for (Entity e : world.with<Position, Velocity ()) { Position& p{ world.get<Position (e) }; const Velocity& v{ world.get<Velocity (e) }; p.x += v.vx dt; p.y += v.vy dt; } } Why it is fast Each component type is stored in its own dense array : all Position s side by side, all Velocity s side by side. A system walks those arrays in order, which is exactly what caches and vectorisation want (lessons 2.07, 7.09): no pointer chasing, no virtual calls, every byte loaded is used. This layout is called data-oriented design , and it is the main reason large engines adopted ECS. The sparse set How do you store components so that you can (a) loop over all of them densely, (b) find an entity's component instantly, and (c) add and remove them cheaply? The usual answer is a sparse set per component type: sparse: indexed by entity id → position in the dense arrays (or "none") 0 : none 1 : 0 2 : none 3 : 2 4 : 1 dense: entity ids in order 1 4 3 components, same order {P1} {P4} {P3} Operation How Cost --- --- --- Does entity e have it? sparse e != none Constant Get e's component components sparse e Constant Add to e Append to the dense arrays; sparse e = new index Constant (amortised) Remove from e Swap-and-pop (lesson 3.07): move the last element into e's slot, fix the moved entity's sparse entry Constant Loop over all Walk the dense arrays Fast, contiguous It combines lesson 3.07's swap-and-pop with lesson 3.10's stable ids. The practice task builds one. Systems that need several components world.with<Position, Velocity () must find entities that have both . With sparse sets, loop over the smaller of the two sets and check the other with a constant-time lookup. Larger engines group entities by their exact set of components into archetypes , each stored as its own table, so every system's loop is a straight walk with no checks; that is how Unity's DOTS and the flecs library work. EnTT , a popular open-source C++ ECS, is built on sparse sets. When not to use ECS ECS shines with many similar objects and simple, repeated behaviour. For a game with a few dozen unique objects, or for one-off logic (a boss's scripted sequence, the user interface), plain classes are simpler and fine. Many shipped games mix both: an ECS for the crowd, ordinary objects for the rest. Common mistakes !warning Putting logic in components Components are data. Behaviour lives in systems. !warning Keeping pointers to components Removing another entity's component can move this one (swap-and-pop). Store the entity id and look the component up. !warning Adding or removing components while a system loops over them The arrays change under the loop. Queue structural changes and apply them after the system finishes. Knowledge check quiz ? In ECS, what is an entity? + Just an id that components are attached to - A class with virtual functions - A system All its data lives in components; all behaviour in systems. ? Why are ECS systems often faster than looping over objects with virtual update functions? + Each system walks contiguous arrays of plain data, with no virtual calls or pointer chasing - Systems run on the GPU - Components are smaller than objects Data-oriented layout suits caches and vectorisation. ? In a sparse set, how is a component removed in constant time? + The last component is moved into its slot (swap-and-pop), and the moved entity's sparse entry is updated - All later components are shifted down - The slot is marked empty and skipped The dense arrays stay dense.

title: A sparse set of components
body: Build ComponentStore<T , the sparse-set container behind an ECS, for entity ids from 0 up to a maximum given to the constructor. - add(entity, component) : attach the component (replace it if the entity already has one). - has(entity) , get(entity) (returns a pointer, or nullptr if the entity has none). - remove(entity) : detach it in constant time using swap-and-pop; returns true if there was one. - size() , entities() (the dense array of entity ids) and components() (the dense array of components, same order). Entity ids outside the range are treated as having no component, and add ignores them.

title: 10.04  A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
match: 10.04 A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
body: Rendering turns the game's state into pixels, mostly on the GPU . This lesson follows a frame from the CPU's side (what to draw, culling, sorting, draw calls ) through the GPU's pipeline ( vertex shaders , rasterisation , pixel shaders , depth testing) to the screen, with the coordinate transforms in between. It is a map for the graphics work in chapter 11 and beyond. The CPU and the GPU The GPU is a separate processor with thousands of simple cores, built to run the same small program on huge numbers of vertices and pixels in parallel. The CPU does not draw pixels; it prepares work for the GPU and submits it through a graphics API: Direct3D 11/12 on Windows, Vulkan , OpenGL , or Metal on Apple systems. Libraries like SDL and raylib (chapter 11) sit on top of these. The CPU's part Each frame the renderer: 1. Collects what might be visible: sprites, models, particles, interface. 2. Culls : skips everything outside the camera's view (a rectangle in 2D, a pyramid-shaped frustum in 3D). Cheap bounding-box tests remove most objects before any GPU work. The practice task does this for 2D. 3. Sorts : transparent objects back to front (so blending is correct); opaque objects by material or texture, to minimise state changes. 4. Submits draw calls : each tells the GPU "draw these triangles with this shader, these textures and these settings". Draw calls have a CPU cost of their own. Drawing ten thousand sprites as ten thousand separate calls is slow; batching them (many sprites sharing a texture atlas in one call) or instancing (one model drawn many times in one call) is how games draw large scenes. Coordinates and transforms Positions pass through several coordinate systems on the way to the screen: Space Meaning --- --- Model (local) space Relative to the object itself: a character model's feet at (0, 0, 0) World space Where it is in the level (the scene graph of lesson 3.09 combines these) View (camera) space Relative to the camera Clip space / NDC After projection: what lies inside the view becomes the range −1 to 1 Screen space Pixels on the render target Each step is a matrix multiplication, combined into one matrix per object and applied to every vertex by the vertex shader. In 2D the idea is the same with simpler maths: subtract the camera's position, multiply by the zoom, and add half the screen size to put the camera's centre in the middle. The GPU's part - Vertex shader : a small program run once per vertex, transforming its position into clip space and passing along data such as texture coordinates and colours. - Rasterisation : fixed hardware works out which pixels each triangle covers and interpolates the vertex data across them. - Pixel (fragment) shader : run once per covered pixel, computing its colour: sampling textures, applying lighting. - Output merging : the depth test discards pixels behind something already drawn (using the depth buffer); blending combines transparent pixels with what is behind them. Shaders are written in their own languages (HLSL for Direct3D, GLSL for OpenGL and Vulkan) and compiled for the GPU. Buffers and presenting The GPU draws into a back buffer while the monitor shows the front buffer ; at the end of the frame they are swapped ( present ), the same idea as lesson 5.06's double buffering. With vsync, the swap waits for the monitor's refresh (lesson 10.02). Where the time goes Bottleneck Symptom Typical fix --- --- --- CPU: too many draw calls GPU often idle; CPU busy in the renderer Batching, instancing, fewer state changes GPU: too many pixels (fill rate) Slower at higher resolutions; heavy effects Cheaper pixel shaders, lower resolution effects, less overdraw GPU: too many vertices Slower with detailed models regardless of resolution Level of detail (simpler models far away) Transfers Stalls when uploading textures mid-game Upload during loading, or asynchronously GPU profilers (PIX for Direct3D, RenderDoc for most APIs, vendor tools) show where a frame's GPU time goes, like lesson 8.08's CPU profiling. Common mistakes !warning One draw call per sprite Batch sprites that share a texture, or use an atlas. !warning Reading back from the GPU every frame The CPU waits for the GPU to finish. Avoid it, or read results a frame or two later. !warning Drawing everything without culling Off-screen objects still cost CPU and GPU time. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a vertex shader do? + Runs once per vertex, transforming its position (and passing data on) for rasterisation - Runs once per pixel to compute its colour - Sorts the objects in the scene Pixel shaders compute colours; vertex shaders place vertices. ? Why batch many sprites into one draw call? + Each draw call has a CPU cost; fewer, larger calls draw the same thing faster - The GPU can only draw one call per frame - Batching makes the sprites sharper Submission overhead adds up with thousands of calls. ? What does the depth test do? + Discards pixels that are behind something already drawn at that position - Measures how far the camera is from the scene - Sorts transparent objects It uses the depth buffer, one depth value per pixel. ? What is culling? + Skipping objects that cannot be visible, such as those outside the camera's view, before drawing - Removing objects from the game - Compressing textures Cheap tests save expensive drawing.

title: A 2D camera with culling
where: 10.04 A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
body: Write the core of a 2D renderer's camera. - toScreen(camera, worldX, worldY) converts a world position to screen pixels: subtract the camera's position (the world point at the centre of the screen), multiply by the zoom, then add half the screen's width and height. Screen y grows downwards and so does world y here, so no flip is needed. - visible(camera, box) says whether an axis-aligned world rectangle ( x , y of its top-left corner, w , h ) overlaps the area the camera shows. A box exactly touching the edge, with no overlap, is not visible. - cull(camera, boxes) returns the indices of the visible boxes, in order. camera at (100, 50), zoom 2, screen 800 x 600 toScreen(100, 50) = (400, 300) the camera's centre is the screen's centre toScreen(110, 50) = (420, 300) the camera shows world x 100 ± 200 and y 50 ± 150

title: 10.05  Input Handling
body: Raw input (keys, mouse buttons, gamepad sticks) is not what game code should depend on. Engines turn it into actions ("jump", "move left"), track for each one whether it was pressed , held or released this frame, and let players rebind the keys. This lesson builds that layer, and covers gamepads, dead zones and input buffering. From devices to actions Game code should never ask "is the space bar down?". It should ask "does the player want to jump?". The difference matters as soon as you support rebinding, a gamepad, or a second keyboard layout: Pressed, held and released Lesson 5.07 showed two ways to read keys: messages, and the current state. For game controls the cleanest model is: once per frame, take a snapshot of every action's state (down or up), and keep the previous frame's snapshot. Then for each action: Query Previous Now Use for --- --- --- --- held (any) down Continuous actions: walking, aiming, charging pressed up down One-shot actions: jump, fire one shot, open a menu released down up Releasing a charged attack, ending a drag Because the snapshot is taken once at the start of the frame (lesson 10.01's input phase), every system in that frame sees the same answer. Checking the live key state in the middle of an update lets two systems disagree about whether a key was pressed. There is one trap: a tap shorter than a frame can be missed by pure polling, because the key is already up again when the snapshot is taken. Recording "went down at least once this frame" from the key-down messages, as well as the current state, fixes it. Bindings and rebinding A binding maps a physical input to an action. Keep them in data, not code: cpp enum class Action { MoveLeft, MoveRight, Jump, Attack, Count }; struct Binding { int key; Action action; }; std::vector<Binding bindings{ { 'A', Action::MoveLeft }, { VK_LEFT, Action::MoveLeft }, { 'D', Action::MoveRight }, { VK_RIGHT, Action::MoveRight }, { VK_SPACE, Action::Jump }, { 'J', Action::Attack }, }; Several keys may map to one action (an action is down if any of its keys is down). Rebinding is then just editing the table and saving it with the settings (lesson 10.07). Use virtual-key codes or, for layout-independent positions such as WASD, scan codes (lesson 5.07). Gamepads and dead zones On Windows, Xbox-compatible controllers are read with XInput ( XInputGetState ) or the newer GameInput API; libraries like SDL (chapter 11) cover many controllers. Analogue sticks report numbers (for XInput, −32768 to 32767 per axis), and a stick at rest never reads exactly zero: it drifts by a few percent. A dead zone ignores small values: cpp float applyDeadZone(float value, float deadZone) // value from -1 to 1 { const float magnitude{ std::abs(value) }; if (magnitude < deadZone) return 0.0f; // Rescale so movement starts smoothly from 0 just outside the dead zone. return std::copysign((magnitude - deadZone) / (1.0f - deadZone), value); } For a 2D stick, apply the dead zone to the length of the (x, y) vector, not each axis separately, or diagonal movement feels wrong. Input buffering Players press buttons slightly early. If the jump button was pressed three frames before the character landed, a strict game ignores it and the player feels the game "ate" their input. Buffering remembers recent presses for a short window (often 100 to 150 ms) and acts on them as soon as the action becomes possible. Its cousin, coyote time , still allows a jump for a few frames after walking off a ledge. Small touches like these are a large part of why some games "feel" responsive. Common mistakes !warning Hard-coding keys in game logic Map keys to actions in one place, so rebinding and gamepads work everywhere. !warning Reading live key state during the update Snapshot once per frame so every system agrees. !warning No dead zone on analogue sticks Characters drift on their own. Apply a dead zone to the stick vector. !warning Acting on input while the window is unfocused GetAsyncKeyState sees keys typed in other programs. Ignore input when the game is not in front. Knowledge check quiz ? An action was up last frame and is down now. Which queries are true? + pressed and held - Only released - Only held Pressed is the transition; held is the current state. ? Why take one input snapshot per frame? + So every system in that frame sees the same input state - To save memory - Because keys can only be read once Mixing live reads makes systems disagree. ? What is a dead zone for? + Ignoring the small readings an analogue stick reports when it is at rest - Disabling input during loading screens - Making buttons harder to press Without it, characters creep around on their own. ? What does input buffering do? + Remembers a press for a short time so it can take effect as soon as the action becomes possible - Stores all input for replays - Delays input to make the game harder It forgives presses that come slightly early.

title: Actions from keys
body: Build the class InputMap , which turns key states into action states each frame. - bind(key, action) adds a binding. Several keys may share an action, and one key may drive several actions. - update(keysDown) takes the set of keys that are down this frame and computes each action's state. An action is down if any of its bound keys is down. The previous frame's state is kept. - held(action) , pressed(action) , released(action) as in the lesson. Before the first update , everything is up. Actions and keys are plain int s here. bind(32, JUMP); bind(87, JUMP) // Space and W both jump update({32}) pressed(JUMP), held(JUMP) update({32, 87}) held(JUMP) only (still down: no new press) update({}) released(JUMP)

title: 10.06  Loading and Managing Resources
body: Textures, sounds, models, levels and fonts are resources : large, loaded from disk, shared between many users, and expensive to load twice. A resource manager loads each one once, hands out handles to it, counts who is still using it, unloads it when nobody is, and ideally loads in the background. This lesson designs one, and covers asset pipelines and hot reloading. What a resource manager does Without one, every part of the game that needs goblin.png loads it itself: the same texture ends up in memory five times, loaded five times, and nobody knows when it is safe to free. A resource manager fixes that: Job How --- --- Load each resource once Keep a table from name (or a hash of the name, lesson 3.08) to the loaded resource Share it Hand out handles (or reference-counted pointers) instead of copies Know when it is unused Count references; or unload a whole level's resources together Keep the game responsive Load in the background, show a placeholder until ready Handles, not raw pointers As with entities (lesson 3.10), handing out raw pointers to resources is fragile: if the resource is unloaded or reloaded, the pointer dangles. Engines hand out handles (an index and generation), and the renderer looks the resource up each time it uses it. That also makes hot reloading possible: replace the texture behind the handle, and everything using it shows the new one next frame. Reference counting The simplest lifetime rule: each resource counts how many users hold it. acquire increments the count (loading the resource the first time); release decrements it, and at zero the resource can be unloaded. std::shared_ptr does exactly this automatically, which makes it a reasonable first design: cpp include <iostream include <map include <memory include <string struct Texture { std::string name; int width{ 0 }, height{ 0 }; }; class TextureCache { public: std::shared_ptr<Texture get(const std::string& name) { if (auto existing{ m_loaded name .lock() }) return existing; // still alive: share it auto fresh{ std::make_shared<Texture (Texture{ name, 64, 64 }) }; // "load" it ++m_loads; m_loaded name = fresh; // remember it without owning it return fresh; } int loads() const { return m_loads; } private: std::map<std::string, std::weak_ptr<Texture m_loaded; int m_loads{ 0 }; }; int main() { TextureCache cache; auto a{ cache.get("goblin.png") }; auto b{ cache.get("goblin.png") }; // the same texture, not loaded again std::cout << "shared: " << (a == b) << ", loads: " << cache.loads() << '\n'; a.reset(); b.reset(); // nobody uses it now: it is freed auto c{ cache.get("goblin.png") }; // so it is loaded again std::cout << "loads after release: " << cache.loads() << '\n'; return 0; } shared: 1, loads: 1 loads after release: 2 The cache holds weak_ptr s, which observe without keeping the resource alive. In practice, unloading the moment the count reaches zero causes churn (a texture unloaded and reloaded as an enemy dies and another spawns), so engines often keep unused resources for a while, or unload per level. The practice task builds an explicit reference-counted cache. Loading without freezing Loading a large file on the main thread stalls the game for its duration. Better: 1. The main thread requests the resource and immediately gets a handle whose state is "loading". 2. A worker thread (lesson 6.05) reads the file and decodes it. 3. GPU resources must be created through the graphics API, often on the main or render thread, so the worker passes the decoded data back through a queue (lesson 6.06's job queue). 4. Until the resource is ready, the game uses a placeholder (a grey texture, a silent sound), or the level waits behind a loading screen. Asset pipelines Source assets ( .psd , .blend , .wav ) are rarely what the game loads. An asset pipeline converts them at build time into formats that load fast: textures compressed into GPU formats with mipmaps, models flattened into vertex buffers, many small files packed into one archive with a table of contents. The game then reads exactly what it needs with almost no processing, and a level loads in a few large reads instead of thousands of small ones. Hot reloading During development, reloading a resource the moment its file changes (watching the folder with ReadDirectoryChangesW , then replacing the data behind the handle) lets artists and designers see changes without restarting the game. It is one of the biggest productivity features an engine can have, and handles make it straightforward. Common mistakes !warning Loading the same file in several places Go through the manager, so it is loaded once and shared. !warning Keeping raw pointers to resources They dangle on unload or reload. Use handles or reference-counted pointers. !warning Loading synchronously in the middle of gameplay The game freezes for the load. Preload, or load in the background with a placeholder. Knowledge check quiz ? What problem does a resource manager solve first? + Loading each resource only once and sharing it between all its users - Compressing files - Drawing textures Loading the same texture several times wastes time and memory. ? Why does the cache in the example hold weak_ptr s? + To find resources still in use without keeping them alive itself - Because shared_ptr cannot be stored in a map - To make lookups faster When the last user lets go, the texture is freed even though the cache remembers its name. ? What is an asset pipeline? + Build-time tools that convert source assets into formats the game loads quickly - The order resources are drawn in - A thread that loads files Games load preprocessed data, not artists' source files.

title: A reference-counted resource cache
body: Build ResourceCache , which loads resources by name, shares them, and unloads them when unused. - The constructor receives a loader function, int(const std::string&) , which "loads" a resource and returns its id (in a real engine, a texture). The cache must call it only when needed. - acquire(name) returns the resource's id, calling the loader only if the resource is not currently loaded, and increments its reference count. - release(name) decrements the count. When it reaches zero, the resource is unloaded (forgotten). Releasing a name that is not loaded does nothing. - refCount(name) returns the current count (0 if not loaded); loadedCount() how many resources are loaded.

title: 10.07  Game State and Save Files
body: Saving a game means deciding what state matters, writing it in a format that will still load after the game is updated, and never leaving a corrupted file behind. This lesson covers what to save and what to rebuild, binary and text formats, versioning and migrating old saves, checksums that detect damage, and writing files safely. What to save A running game holds far more state than needs saving. Divide it: Save Rebuild on load Do not save --- --- --- The player's position, stats, inventory, quest flags Anything derived: collision grids, pathfinding data, cached totals Pointers and handles (lesson 6.09): they mean nothing next time What has changed in the world: opened chests, killed bosses Static level content: it comes from the level file Rendering state, GPU resources Settings the player chose Temporary effects that do not matter A useful principle: save the minimum from which everything else can be rebuilt . Small saves are fast to write, and less saved state means fewer ways for a save to be inconsistent. References between saved objects (a quest that refers to an NPC) are saved as ids , and resolved back to objects after loading, never as pointers. Binary or text Binary Text (JSON, INI, your own) --- --- --- Size and speed Small and fast Larger and slower to parse Readable by people No Yes: easy to inspect and debug Robust to change Needs explicit versioning Easier to add fields (unknown keys can be ignored) Editable by players Hard Easy, which may or may not be wanted Many games use text during development and binary when shipping, or text for settings and binary for saves. Whichever you choose, write fields individually in a defined byte order (lesson 2.06), never by dumping structs from memory: padding, pointers and compiler differences would all leak into the file. A header with a version Every save file should start with a small fixed header: cpp // Written field by field, little-endian, 16 bytes: // magic 4 bytes 'S','A','V','E' what kind of file this is // version 4 bytes format version how to read the rest // length 4 bytes bytes after the header // checksum 4 bytes CRC-32 of those bytes - The magic number rejects files that are not saves at all. - The version lets the game read old formats after updates. - The checksum detects corruption: truncated writes, disk errors, a file damaged in transfer. Versioning and migration Games change after release, and players expect their saves to keep working. The usual approach: each format version gets a loader, and old versions are migrated step by step to the current one: Each migration is small and tested once, and a save from any old version passes through all of them. Never reuse a version number for a different layout, and keep test saves from every released version so you can check old saves still load. Checksums A checksum is a number computed from all the bytes, stored alongside them. On loading, recompute it; if it differs, the data is damaged. CRC-32 is the standard choice: it catches accidental corruption (bit flips, truncation, garbage) with very high probability, and it is cheap. The practice task implements it. A CRC detects accidents , not deliberate tampering: anyone who edits a save can recompute it. Preventing cheating in a single-player game is rarely worth it; in multiplayer, anything that matters must live on the server, not in a file on the player's machine. Writing safely Lesson 5.04's technique applies fully: write the whole save to a temporary file, flush it, then atomically replace the old save. Keeping the previous save as a backup ( slot1.sav.bak ) as well means even a save that was written correctly but contains a game bug can be recovered. Common mistakes !warning Dumping structs to disk with fwrite(&state, sizeof state, ...) Padding, pointers and layout differences make the file fragile and unportable. Write fields one by one. !warning No version number The first update that changes the format breaks every existing save. !warning Overwriting the save in place A crash mid-write destroys it. Write a temporary file and replace. !warning Trusting the file A save may be damaged or edited. Check the magic, the version, the checksum and every length before using the data. Knowledge check quiz ? Why are references between saved objects stored as ids rather than pointers? + Pointers are memory addresses that will be different when the game runs again - Ids are smaller - Pointers cannot be written to files ASLR and new allocations change every address between runs. ? What is a save file's version number for? + Telling the loader which format the rest of the file uses, so old saves can be migrated - Showing the player which save is newest - Detecting corruption Each format change gets a new version and a migration from the old one. ? What does a CRC-32 checksum detect? + Accidental damage to the data, such as truncation or flipped bits - Deliberate editing by the player - Which version of the game wrote the file Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is not tamper protection.

title: CRC-32
body: Implement crc32(data) , the standard CRC-32 used by ZIP, PNG and countless save formats, the bit-by-bit way: 1. Start with crc = 0xFFFFFFFF . 2. For each byte: crc ^= byte ; then 8 times: if the lowest bit of crc is 1, crc = (crc 1) ^ 0xEDB88320 , otherwise crc = 1 . 3. The result is crc ^ 0xFFFFFFFF . Then write verify(data, expected) , which says whether data 's CRC-32 equals expected . crc32("") = 0x00000000 crc32("123456789") = 0xCBF43926 (the standard check value)

title: 10.08  Scripting and Data-Driven Design
body: Engines get faster to work with when behaviour and content move out of C++ and into data : monster stats in a file, levels from an editor, dialogue in a table, and, for logic, scripts in an embedded language such as Lua. Designers can then change the game without recompiling it. This lesson covers data files, a small configuration parser, embedding a scripting language, and the trade-offs. Hard-coded versus data-driven cpp // Hard-coded: changing a goblin needs a programmer and a rebuild. Monster makeGoblin() { return Monster{ "Goblin", 30, 4, 1.2f }; } ini ; monsters.ini: a designer edits this, the game reloads it goblin health = 30 damage = 4 speed = 1.2 troll health = 120 damage = 15 speed = 0.6 When monster stats, weapon tables, level layouts, loot tables and dialogue live in data files: - Designers iterate without programmers : change a number, reload (lesson 10.06's hot reloading), play. - Modders can change the game too (chapter 13). - The code gets smaller and more general : one Monster loader instead of a function per monster. Formats Format Good for --- --- INI / key-value Settings, simple tables. Trivial to parse (the practice task) JSON Nested data: items with lists of effects. Many C++ libraries (nlohmann/json, simdjson, RapidJSON) CSV / spreadsheets Large tables edited by designers in a spreadsheet: balance numbers, localisation Custom binary Shipping builds, produced by the asset pipeline from the formats above (lesson 10.06) Whatever the format, validate on load : a misspelt key or a negative health should produce a clear message naming the file and line, not a crash three levels later. Scripting languages Data files describe what ; some things need logic : a boss's attack pattern, a quest's conditions, a cutscene's sequence. Writing all of that in C++ means a rebuild for every tweak. Many engines embed a scripting language : Language Notes --- --- Lua Tiny, fast, easy to embed in C++; used in a great many games Python Common in tools and editors, heavier to embed in a shipping game C Unity's language; managed runtime GDScript Godot's own Visual scripting Node graphs for non-programmers (Unreal's Blueprints) Your own small command language Enough for debug consoles and simple sequences (lesson 3.04's command table) Embedding Lua looks like this: the C++ side registers functions scripts may call, then runs script files: cpp-norun include <lua.hpp static int luaSpawn(lua_State L) // callable from Lua as spawn("goblin", x, y) { const char kind{ luaL_checkstring(L, 1) }; const double x{ luaL_checknumber(L, 2) }; const double y{ luaL_checknumber(L, 3) }; world.spawn(kind, static_cast<float (x), static_cast<float (y)); return 0; // no return values } int main() { lua_State L{ luaL_newstate() }; luaL_openlibs(L); lua_register(L, "spawn", &luaSpawn); if (luaL_dofile(L, "scripts/wave1.lua") != LUA_OK) std::fprintf(stderr, "script error: %s\n", lua_tostring(L, -1)); lua_close(L); } lua -- scripts/wave1.lua for i = 1, 5 do spawn("goblin", 100 + i 32, 200) end spawn("troll", 300, 240) The script can only do what the registered functions allow, which keeps it safe and the engine in charge. Trade-offs Benefit Cost --- --- Fast iteration, no recompiling Scripts run slower than C++; keep heavy loops in C++ Designers and modders can work independently Two languages to debug; errors appear at run time instead of compile time Behaviour can change after shipping (patches as data) The boundary between C++ and script needs careful design The rule most engines follow: systems in C++, content and one-off logic in data and scripts . Common mistakes !warning No validation of data files Report problems with the file name, line and key at load time. !warning Moving hot loops into scripts Scripts are for decisions, not for processing ten thousand particles per frame. !warning Exposing everything to scripts Register a deliberate, small set of functions; scripts and mods should not reach arbitrary engine internals. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the main advantage of data-driven design? + Content and balance can change without recompiling the game - The game runs faster - No validation is needed Designers iterate on data files directly. ? When is an embedded scripting language more appropriate than a data file? + When content needs logic, such as a boss's attack pattern or a quest's conditions - For a table of monster stats - For the physics engine Data describes what; scripts describe how and when. ? How does a Lua script call into the engine? + Through C++ functions the engine registered with the Lua state - By reading the engine's memory directly - It cannot The registered set defines what scripts are allowed to do.

title: Read an INI file
body: Write parseIni(text) , which reads INI-style data into a map from "section.key" to value, and reports errors with line numbers. Rules, line by line (lines are separated by \n ; ignore a \r at the end of a line): - Blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is ; or are ignored. - name starts a section. Keys before any section belong to the section "" , stored as ".key" . - key = value stores a value. Spaces around the key and the value are trimmed. The value may contain = . - Anything else is an error: record "line N: ..." (N counted from 1, the message after the colon is up to you) and carry on. - A key repeated in the same section keeps the last value. ; enemies goblin health = 30 name = Goblin = small - "goblin.health" = "30", "goblin.name" = "Goblin = small"

title: 10.09  Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game
match: 10.09 Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game
body: One of the best ways to learn engine architecture is to read a real one. Many shipped games and engines have released their source. This lesson is a method for approaching a large, unfamiliar codebase: building it, finding the main loop, tracing one feature end to end, and recognising the patterns from this chapter in someone else's code. Why read real code Everything in this chapter (the loop, time steps, entities, rendering, input, resources, saves, scripting) exists in every shipped game, solved under real constraints. Reading how experienced teams did it shows trade-offs no tutorial covers: what they simplified, what they optimised, which corners they cut to ship. Where to find source Project Notes --- --- id Software's games (Doom, Quake, Quake III Arena) Released under the GPL; small, clear C codebases, widely studied OpenTTD , Wesnoth , SuperTuxKart , Cataclysm: DDA Large open-source games in C++, actively developed Godot A complete open-source engine in C++ raylib A small, very readable C library for games (used in the planned raylib course) Dear ImGui The interface library of chapter 14, a famously readable single codebase Respect each project's licence: reading and learning is always fine; reusing code in your own project means following the licence's terms. A method 1. Build and run it Clone the repository, follow its build instructions, and get it running under your debugger. A codebase you can run and step through is ten times easier to understand than one you can only read. Note what you had to install: the dependencies are a first map of the architecture. 2. Map the top level Look at the folder structure and the largest directories. Typical names: engine , game , render / gfx , audio / snd , net , ui , script , tools , platform / sys . Write a one-line guess for each and correct it later. 3. Find the main loop Search for the entry point ( main , WinMain , wWinMain , or the platform layer's equivalent), then step into it with the debugger until you reach the loop that runs every frame. Note what it calls each frame and in which order: that is lesson 10.01's diagram for this engine. Quake III, for example, has Com_Frame doing exactly input, events, server frame, client frame and rendering. 4. Trace one feature end to end Pick something small and visible: what happens when the player presses fire, picks up an item or opens a door. Follow it from input to effect: Use the tools you have: search for the string on screen or in the console, set breakpoints, use the IDE's "find all references" (Shift+F12 in Visual Studio) and "go to definition" (F12), and the call stack at each breakpoint. 5. Look for the patterns As you go, match what you see with this chapter: Look for Lesson --- --- Fixed or variable time step, and how dt is computed 10.02 How game objects are stored: inheritance tree, components, arrays of structs 10.03 Handles versus pointers between objects 3.10 Where the renderer culls and batches 10.04 Binding tables and action layers 10.05 The resource cache and file formats 10.06 Save code, and how it handles versions 10.07 Data files and any scripting 10.08 6. Write it down Keep notes as you go: a diagram of the main systems, the frame's order of calls, the path of your traced feature. Explaining the architecture in a page of your own words is the test of whether you understood it. Common mistakes !warning Reading files top to bottom Large codebases are read by following execution, not alphabetically. !warning Trying to understand everything Pick one feature and follow it; the rest will become familiar along the way. !warning Not running it Reading without a debugger leaves you guessing which code actually runs. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the best first step with an unfamiliar game codebase? + Build it and run it under a debugger - Read every file in alphabetical order - Rewrite it in another language Being able to step through it makes everything else faster. ? How do you find the code behind a visible feature? + Search for strings it shows, set breakpoints, and follow references and call stacks from there - Guess the file name - Read the main loop only Follow execution from something you can see. ? Why trace one feature end to end? + It crosses most of the engine's major systems in a concrete, followable path - Because features are independent - To find bugs Input, logic, entities, rendering and audio all appear along the way.

title: 11.01  Project Setup and a Window
body: This chapter builds a complete small game, a top-down dungeon crawler called Delve , using the ideas from chapters 1 to 10. It starts here: a Visual Studio project with SDL2 from vcpkg, a window and renderer, and the fixed-time-step game loop from lesson 10.02. By the end of the chapter you will have a game with a map, a player, monsters, items, levels, saves and a debug console. What we are building Delve is a top-down, tile-based dungeon crawler: - a map made of tiles (walls, floor, doors, stairs) loaded from text files; - a player moved with the keyboard, one tile at a time; - monsters that hunt the player with breadth-first search (lesson 3.09); - health, items and an inventory; - several levels, saving and loading; - an in-game debug console; - and a packaged Release build you can give to a friend. It is small enough to finish and large enough to need everything from chapters 1 to 10. Later chapters use it as their test subject: chapter 12 builds tools that inspect it, chapter 13 adds mods to it, and chapter 14 gives those tools an interface. Why SDL2 SDL2 (Simple DirectMedia Layer) is a widely used, open-source C library that handles the platform-specific parts of a game: creating a window, a hardware-accelerated 2D renderer, keyboard, mouse and gamepad input, audio, and timing. It runs on Windows, Linux, macOS and consoles. Underneath, on Windows, it does exactly what chapter 5 did by hand (a window class, a message loop, Direct3D for drawing), so we can concentrate on the game. Setting up the project 1. Create an empty solution delve and a Console App project delve inside it (lesson 4.01). A console app is convenient while developing: std::cout output appears in the console window next to the game. 2. In the project's properties, for All Configurations: C++ standard C++20 , warning level 4 , platform x64 (lesson 1.07). 3. In a terminal in the solution folder, set up vcpkg in manifest mode (lesson 4.06): powershell vcpkg new --application vcpkg add port sdl2 4. In the project properties, vcpkg → Use Vcpkg Manifest: Yes . 5. Create the folder layout: delve\ vcpkg.json delve.sln delve\ main.cpp the loop game.h/.cpp the game state and rules tilemap.h/.cpp the map (lesson 11.02) render.h/.cpp drawing input.h/.cpp actions and bindings (lesson 10.05) data\ levels\ level files (lesson 11.02) A window and a loop cpp-norun // main.cpp define SDL_MAIN_HANDLED // we write our own main; SDL must not replace it include <SDL.h include <algorithm include <cstdio int main() { if (SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_VIDEO SDL_INIT_EVENTS) != 0) { std::fprintf(stderr, "SDL_Init failed: %s\n", SDL_GetError()); return 1; } SDL_Window window{ SDL_CreateWindow("Delve", SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, 960, 640, SDL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE) }; SDL_Renderer renderer{ SDL_CreateRenderer(window, -1, SDL_RENDERER_ACCELERATED SDL_RENDERER_PRESENTVSYNC) }; if (!window !renderer) { std::fprintf(stderr, "could not create the window: %s\n", SDL_GetError()); return 1; } const double step{ 1.0 / 60.0 }; // fixed simulation step (lesson 10.02) double accumulator{ 0.0 }; Uint64 previous{ SDL_GetPerformanceCounter() }; const double frequency{ static_cast<double (SDL_GetPerformanceFrequency()) }; float boxX{ 100.0f }; bool running{ true }; while (running) { // 1. Input: drain every waiting event (lesson 5.05's PeekMessage loop, done by SDL). SDL_Event event; while (SDL_PollEvent(&event)) { if (event.type == SDL_QUIT) running = false; if (event.type == SDL_KEYDOWN && event.key.keysym.sym == SDLK_ESCAPE) running = false; } // 2. Update in fixed steps. const Uint64 now{ SDL_GetPerformanceCounter() }; accumulator += std::min((now - previous) / frequency, 0.25); previous = now; while (accumulator = step) { boxX += 120.0f static_cast<float (step); // 120 pixels per second if (boxX 900.0f) boxX = 0.0f; accumulator -= step; } // 3. Render. SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(renderer, 18, 20, 26, 255); SDL_RenderClear(renderer); SDL_Rect box{ static_cast<int (boxX), 300, 40, 40 }; SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(renderer, 95, 211, 196, 255); SDL_RenderFillRect(renderer, &box); SDL_RenderPresent(renderer); // swap buffers (lesson 10.04); waits for vsync } SDL_DestroyRenderer(renderer); // shut down in reverse order of creation SDL_DestroyWindow(window); SDL_Quit(); return 0; } Build and run: a dark window with a teal box sliding across it. Every concept is from earlier lessons: the event loop is lesson 5.05's, the fixed step and accumulator lesson 10.02's, the clear-draw-present cycle lesson 10.04's double buffering. Structuring for growth Before adding features, split the game state from the platform code. main.cpp will only own the window, the loop and timing; a Game class owns everything else: cpp-norun // game.h pragma once include "input.h" struct SDL_Renderer; class Game { public: bool load(const char firstLevel); void update(const InputState& input, double dt); // fixed step: game rules only void render(SDL_Renderer renderer) const; // drawing only: never changes state bool wantsToQuit() const { return m_quit; } private: bool m_quit{ false }; // map, entities, inventory ... added in the next lessons }; The division follows lesson 10.01: update changes state, render only reads it. Keeping SDL out of Game::update also means the game's rules can be unit-tested without a window (chapter 17), which is how this chapter's practice tasks work: they test the game's logic pieces on their own. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting SDL_MAIN_HANDLED Without it, SDL renames main and expects its SDL2main library to provide the real entry point, and the link fails. !warning The DLL is missing at run time vcpkg copies SDL2.dll next to the exe. If you move the exe, move the DLL with it (lesson 11.08 packages both). !warning Drawing in the update loop Keep update and render separate, as lesson 10.01 explained. Knowledge check quiz ? Why use SDL2 instead of the raw Windows API from chapter 5? + It handles windows, input, rendering and audio portably, so the chapter can focus on the game - The Windows API cannot create windows - SDL2 is faster than Direct3D Underneath, it does on Windows what chapter 5 did by hand. ? What does SDL_PollEvent correspond to in chapter 5? + The PeekMessage loop that drains waiting window messages without blocking - GetMessage - CreateWindowEx It returns immediately when no events are waiting. ? Why keep SDL out of Game::update ? + So the game rules can run and be tested without a window - Because SDL is slow - Because SDL cannot be used in classes Logic separated from the platform is testable and portable.

title: 11.02  Drawing a Tile Map
body: Delve's world is a grid of tiles stored in a flat array (lesson 2.07) and loaded from a plain text file (lesson 10.08), where each character is a tile and special characters mark where the player and monsters start. This lesson writes the level format, the loader with validation, and the renderer that draws the visible part of the map around a camera. The level format Levels are text files that anyone can edit in Notepad: data/levels/01.txt: the first floor @... ..g .... ... ..k.+... .... .. Character Meaning --- --- Wall . Floor + Door (closed; opens when walked into) Stairs down to the next level @ Player start (floor underneath) g , k , t A goblin, kobold or troll start (floor underneath) Lines starting with followed by a space are comments. Every map row must be the same width. The tile map cpp-norun // tilemap.h pragma once include <string include <vector enum class Tile : unsigned char { Floor, Wall, Door, Stairs }; struct Spawn { char kind; int x; int y; }; class TileMap { public: int width() const { return m_width; } int height() const { return m_height; } bool inside(int x, int y) const { return x = 0 && y = 0 && x < m_width && y < m_height; } Tile at(int x, int y) const { return inside(x, y) ? m_tiles static_cast<size_t (y m_width + x) : Tile::Wall; } void set(int x, int y, Tile t) { if (inside(x, y)) m_tiles static_cast<size_t (y m_width + x) = t; } bool walkable(int x, int y) const { const Tile t{ at(x, y) }; return t == Tile::Floor t == Tile::Stairs; } int m_width{ 0 }, m_height{ 0 }; std::vector<Tile m_tiles; // row-major: index = y width + x }; Note at returns Wall outside the map: anything that asks about a tile beyond the edge gets a sensible answer instead of an out-of-bounds read, which removes a whole class of bugs (lesson 2.09) from the movement and AI code. Loading with validation Loading follows lesson 10.08's rules: read line by line, skip comments, and report problems with a line number. The practice task writes parseLevel , which turns the text into a TileMap , the player's start and a list of monster spawns, and rejects levels that are ragged, have no player or several players, or contain unknown characters. Drawing it Each tile is drawn as a 32-pixel square. Lesson 10.04's camera keeps the player in the middle of the screen, and culling skips tiles that are off screen: cpp-norun // render.cpp include <SDL.h include "tilemap.h" constexpr int kTile{ 32 }; void drawMap(SDL_Renderer r, const TileMap& map, float cameraX, float cameraY, int screenW, int screenH) { // Which tiles can be on screen? Only loop over those (culling, lesson 10.04). const int firstX{ std::max(0, static_cast<int ((cameraX - screenW / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; const int firstY{ std::max(0, static_cast<int ((cameraY - screenH / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; const int lastX{ std::min(map.width() - 1, static_cast<int ((cameraX + screenW / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; const int lastY{ std::min(map.height() - 1, static_cast<int ((cameraY + screenH / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; for (int y{ firstY }; y <= lastY; ++y) // rows outside, columns inside (lesson 2.07) { for (int x{ firstX }; x <= lastX; ++x) { switch (map.at(x, y)) { case Tile::Wall: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 58, 63, 72, 255); break; case Tile::Floor: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 26, 29, 35, 255); break; case Tile::Door: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 140, 98, 57, 255); break; case Tile::Stairs: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 240, 198, 116, 255); break; } const SDL_Rect cell{ static_cast<int (x kTile - cameraX + screenW / 2.0f), static_cast<int (y kTile - cameraY + screenH / 2.0f), kTile - 1, kTile - 1 }; SDL_RenderFillRect(r, &cell); } } } Coloured squares are enough to play with. To use artwork, load one tile sheet image with SDL_image ( vcpkg add port sdl2-image ) into an SDL_Texture , and draw each tile with SDL_RenderCopy from the right part of the sheet: one texture shared by every tile, which is lesson 10.04's batching in practice. Common mistakes !warning Indexing with x height + y Row-major storage is y width + x (lesson 2.07). !warning Trusting level files Validate shape and characters on load, with line numbers in the messages. !warning Drawing every tile of a huge map Loop only over the tiles that can be on screen. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does TileMap::at return Wall for positions outside the map? + So movement and AI code never read out of bounds and treat the edge as solid - Because the map is surrounded by walls in memory - To make drawing faster A safe default removes a class of out-of-bounds bugs. ? A level is 40 tiles wide. Which index holds the tile at x = 5, y = 3? + 125 - 83 - 205 3 × 40 + 5. ? How does the renderer avoid drawing off-screen tiles? + It computes the range of tile coordinates the camera can see and loops only over those - It draws everything and the GPU discards the rest - It never scrolls Culling by range is cheap and exact for a grid.

title: Load a level
body: Write parseLevel(text) for Delve's level format. The text has lines separated by \n (ignore a trailing \r ). Lines that start with " " (hash and space) are comments, and blank lines are ignored; every other line is a map row. Tiles: wall, . floor, + door, stairs. @ is the player start and g , k , t are monster starts; all four have floor underneath. Return a Level with the width, height, the tiles as a row-major string using only , . , + and , the player's start, and the monster spawns in reading order (top to bottom, left to right). If the level is invalid, return std::nullopt : - no map rows at all, - rows of different lengths, - an unknown character, - not exactly one @ . / @.g / - width 5, height 3, tiles " ... ", player (1,1), spawns { g at (3,1) }

title: 11.03  A Player That Moves
body: Delve is turn-based on a grid: each key press moves the player one tile, and the world (monsters, doors) responds. This lesson connects lesson 10.05's input actions to movement, handles walls, doors and stairs, adds key repeat for held keys, and makes moves look smooth by sliding between tiles in the renderer only. Turns on a grid Many roguelike games, Delve included, are turn-based : nothing in the world happens until the player acts, then every monster takes its turn. The game loop still runs at 60 frames per second (input, animation and drawing need it), but the game rules advance one turn per player action. Actions and moves Using lesson 10.05's input map, the movement actions become a direction: cpp-norun struct Dir { int dx; int dy; }; std::optional<Dir movementFrom(const InputMap& in) { if (in.pressed(Action::Up)) return Dir{ 0, -1 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Down)) return Dir{ 0, 1 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Left)) return Dir{ -1, 0 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Right)) return Dir{ 1, 0 }; return std::nullopt; } Bindings put both the arrow keys and WASD on these actions, and a gamepad's d-pad later just adds more bindings. Moving into a tile What happens depends on what is in the target tile. Keeping the decision in one function makes the rules easy to read and test: Target Result Takes a turn? --- --- --- Floor Move there Yes Stairs Move there; the level is complete (lesson 11.06) Yes Closed door The door opens and becomes floor; the player stays Yes Wall, or outside the map Nothing: a bump No A monster Attack it instead of moving (lesson 11.05) Yes A bump not costing a turn matters for feel: walking into a wall by mistake should not let monsters catch up. The practice task implements this table as tryMove . Holding a key Pressing an arrow for every step is tiring in long corridors. Holding the key should repeat the move, after a short delay, at a steady rate: cpp-norun // A held movement key repeats: the first move on press, then after 0.25 s, then every 0.08 s. if (auto dir{ movementFrom(input) }) { tryMove( dir); m_repeatTimer = 0.25; m_heldDir = dir; } else if (heldDirection(input) == m_heldDir) { m_repeatTimer -= dt; if (m_repeatTimer <= 0) { tryMove(m_heldDir); m_repeatTimer += 0.08; } } The update runs at a fixed step, so the repeat rate is the same on every machine (lesson 10.02). Smooth movement, without changing the rules The player's logical position is a whole tile: the rules (collision, monster AI, saving) only ever see whole tiles. To avoid the character teleporting a tile at a time on screen, the renderer draws it sliding from the previous tile to the current one over a short time: cpp-norun // In the player's state: int x, y; int fromX, fromY; float slide; (slide goes 0 → 1 after each move) const float t{ std::min(player.slide, 1.0f) }; const float drawX{ (player.fromX + (player.x - player.fromX) t) kTile }; const float drawY{ (player.fromY + (player.y - player.fromY) t) kTile }; This is lesson 10.02's interpolation applied to a turn-based game: the simulation is exact and simple, and only the picture is smooth. The camera follows the drawn position, not the logical one, so it glides too. Common mistakes !warning Letting a bump cost a turn Players feel cheated when walking into a wall lets monsters move. Only real actions take turns. !warning Mixing drawn and logical positions Collision and AI must use the whole-tile position; only rendering uses the sliding one. !warning Moving on held without a repeat timer The player rushes across the map at 60 tiles per second. Knowledge check quiz ? The player walks into a wall. What should happen? + Nothing, and no turn passes - The player moves into the wall - A turn passes but the player stays still Bumps should be free, so mistakes do not let monsters act. ? What does walking into a closed door do in Delve? + Opens it, using the turn, while the player stays where they are - Moves the player through it - Nothing Opening and passing are separate actions. ? Why is the sliding position used only for drawing? + The rules stay simple and exact on whole tiles, while the picture is smooth - Because floats cannot be compared - To save memory It is interpolation for presentation only.

title: The rules of a step
body: Write tryMove(map, width, x, y, dx, dy, monsterAt) for Delve. map is the level's row-major tile string ( wall, . floor, + door, stairs, as in the previous practice task) and width its width; (x, y) is the player; (dx, dy) the direction. monsterAt(tx, ty) returns true if a monster stands on that tile. Return a MoveResult : what happened, whether a turn was used, and the player's new position. Apply the lesson's table, in this order: 1. The target is outside the map, or a wall: Bump , no turn, position unchanged. 2. A monster is on the target: Attack , a turn, position unchanged. 3. A door: OpenDoor , a turn, position unchanged, and the door becomes floor in map . 4. Stairs: Descend , a turn, the player moves there. 5. Floor: Move , a turn, the player moves there.

title: 11.04  Monsters and Simple AI
body: Delve's monsters need to notice the player, chase them around walls, and attack when adjacent. This lesson gives each monster a small state machine , and replaces per-monster pathfinding with one distance map (a breadth-first search from the player, lesson 3.09) that every monster follows downhill. It is simple, fast, and the basis of AI in many roguelikes. A state machine per monster Each monster is in one of a few states, and simple rules move it between them: State Each turn --- --- Idle Wander randomly, or stand still; check whether the player is within sight range Chasing Step one tile towards the player Attacking Hit the player (lesson 11.05) States are just an enum in a component (lesson 10.03) and a switch in the AI system: small, readable and easy to debug, which matters more than sophistication for most game AI. Chasing: one search for all monsters Each chasing monster needs the next step towards the player around the walls. Running a separate BFS from every monster to the player works, but it repeats almost the same work for each one. Instead, run one BFS starting from the player , recording every reachable tile's distance (in steps) to the player: ....... 8765456 . ... → 9 345 . @.... A @1234 map distance map (A is 10; walls have none) Now every monster, wherever it is, finds its next step by looking at its four neighbours and moving to the one with the smallest distance : it walks "downhill" to the player. One search per turn serves any number of monsters, and each monster's decision is just four lookups. This structure is called a distance map (or "Dijkstra map", or flow field). The practice task builds it. Useful variations come almost for free: - Fleeing : a monster with low health moves to a neighbour with a larger distance, away from the player. - Several goals : start the search from every item and the monster heads to the nearest one. - Terrain costs : treat mud as costing 2 steps (Dijkstra's algorithm instead of BFS) and monsters route around it. Taking turns fairly After the player acts, every monster acts once, in a fixed order (for example by entity id). A few details make it robust: - Recompute the distance map once after the player moves, before any monster acts. - Two monsters may want the same tile. Process them in order and let the second one choose again (or wait) if the tile is now taken. - Monsters that are far away and idle can skip the expensive parts entirely. Seeing the player "Sees the player" can start simple: within 8 tiles by distance-map steps (which already accounts for walls, so monsters do not notice the player through a wall). A proper line-of-sight check traces a line across the grid (Bresenham's line algorithm) and stops at the first wall; it is a good extension once the basics work. Common mistakes !warning Running a pathfinding search per monster per turn One distance map from the player serves them all. !warning Letting monsters move onto each other Check occupancy as each monster moves, not only before the turn starts. !warning AI that is too clever Players enjoy monsters that are readable and predictable. Simple rules, clearly communicated, beat complex ones. Knowledge check quiz ? How does a monster use the distance map to chase the player? + It steps to whichever neighbouring tile has the smallest distance value - It runs its own search each turn - It moves in a straight line towards the player Walking downhill on the distance map follows a shortest path around walls. ? Why build the distance map from the player rather than from each monster? + One search then answers every monster's question, however many there are - Monsters cannot be searched from - It gives longer paths The work is shared instead of repeated. ? How can a frightened monster flee using the same map? + Move to a neighbour with a larger distance value - Delete the map - Move randomly Uphill on the map leads away from the player.

title: A distance map and a chasing step
match: A distance map and a chasing step
body: Write two functions for Delve's monster AI. The map is a row-major tile string with a width; is a wall and every other tile is walkable. distanceMap(map, width, goalX, goalY) returns a vector with one entry per tile: the number of steps (up, down, left, right) from that tile to the goal, or -1 for walls and tiles that cannot reach the goal. The goal itself is 0. nextStep(map, width, distances, x, y) returns the neighbouring tile a monster at (x, y) should step to: the walkable neighbour with the smallest distance, which must be smaller than the monster's own distance. Check neighbours in the order up, down, left, right, and on a tie keep the first. If no neighbour is closer (the monster is at the goal, or cannot reach it), return the monster's own position.

title: 11.05  Health, Items and Inventory
body: Combat and loot turn Delve into a game. This lesson adds health and attack components, a damage formula with a little randomness, death and drops, item definitions loaded from data, pickups, and an inventory where identical items stack . Every number lives in a data file, so balancing never needs a rebuild. Components for combat Following lesson 10.03, combat is a few components and one system: cpp-norun struct Health { int current; int maximum; }; struct Attack { int power; int accuracy; }; // accuracy: chance to hit, in percent struct Defence { int armour; }; struct Drops { std::string itemId; int chance; }; // percent The player and every monster have Health , Attack and Defence ; values come from monsters.ini (lesson 10.08), so a troll is just a different set of numbers. The damage formula When an attacker hits a defender: 1. Roll to hit : a random number from 1 to 100; it hits if the roll is at most the attacker's accuracy. 2. Damage : power − armour / 2 , plus a small random spread (−1 to +1), but at least 1 so every hit matters. 3. Subtract from the defender's health; at 0 or below, the defender dies. cpp-norun int rollDamage(const Attack& a, const Defence& d, Random& rng) { if (rng.range(1, 100) a.accuracy) return 0; // a miss const int base{ a.power - d.armour / 2 }; return std::max(1, base + rng.range(-1, 1)); } Two habits make combat code easy to balance and test: - One random number generator object , passed in, never rand() scattered around. Seed it from the time in normal play and from a fixed number for tests and replays (lesson 10.02's determinism). - Log every combat event to the message log (lesson 8.03's ring buffer, shown on screen): "The goblin hits you for 3. (HP 17/20)". Players need the feedback, and you need it to see whether the numbers feel right. Death and drops When a monster dies, the combat system removes its entity (lesson 3.10's handles mean nothing else is left pointing at it) and, according to its Drops component, may place an item on its tile. The player dying ends the run with a "you died" screen showing the last few log lines, so the player knows why. Items from data ini ; items.ini potion name = Healing potion heal = 10 stack = 5 dagger name = Rusty dagger power = 2 stack = 1 gold name = Gold coins stack = 999 An item definition (the data) is shared; an item in the world or inventory is just a definition id and a count. That keeps inventories small and makes "how many potions do I have?" a lookup. The inventory The inventory is a fixed number of slots (say 10). Each slot holds an item id and a count, up to that item's stack limit. Picking up items: 1. First top up existing slots of the same item, up to the stack limit. 2. Then put the rest into empty slots. 3. Whatever does not fit stays on the floor. picking up 7 potions (stack 5) with slots: potion 4 dagger 1 empty empty → potion 5 dagger 1 potion 5 potion 1 nothing left over Using an item removes one from its slot, and an empty slot becomes free. The practice task implements adding and removing with exactly these rules, which is the part most likely to hide off-by-one bugs. Common mistakes !warning Damage that can be zero or negative High armour should reduce damage, not heal the target. Clamp to at least 1 on a hit. !warning Calling rand() everywhere Use one seeded generator object so tests and replays are repeatable. !warning Copying item definitions into every slot Store an id and a count; look the definition up when needed. Knowledge check quiz ? Why clamp damage to at least 1 on a hit? + So a hit always matters, and armour can never turn an attack into healing - To make the game easier - Because health cannot be negative Without it, high armour makes damage zero or negative. ? Why pass a random generator object around instead of calling rand() ? + It can be seeded with a fixed number, making tests and replays repeatable - rand() does not exist in C++ - It is always faster Determinism needs control over the random numbers. ? An inventory has potion 4 and one empty slot; potions stack to 5. Seven potions are picked up. What happens? + The first slot becomes 5, the empty slot gets 5, and 1 potion stays on the floor - All seven fit in the first slot - The pickup fails Top up existing stacks first, then fill empty slots, and leave the rest.

title: A stacking inventory
body: Build Delve's Inventory : a fixed number of slots, each empty or holding an item id and a count. - The constructor receives the number of slots and a map from item id to its stack limit . - add(id, count) puts items in following the lesson's rules: first top up existing slots holding the same id (in slot order) to the stack limit, then fill empty slots (in slot order). It returns how many items did not fit. Unknown ids do not fit at all. - remove(id, count) takes items out, from the last slot holding that id backwards, emptying slots that reach 0. If there are fewer than count in total, it removes nothing and returns false . - count(id) returns the total held; slot(i) returns slot i as a pair of id and count (an empty slot is {"", 0} ).

title: 11.06  Levels and Saving
body: Delve gets several floors connected by stairs, and the ability to save and continue. This lesson handles level transitions (what persists between floors and what is rebuilt), designs Delve's save format using lesson 10.07's header, version and checksum, and writes it safely, so a crash or power cut never costs the player their run. Moving between floors When the player steps onto the stairs (lesson 11.03's Descend ), the game: 1. Keeps what belongs to the player : health, inventory, experience. 2. Discards everything belonging to the old floor : its map, monsters, items on the ground, its distance map. 3. Loads the next level file (lesson 11.02) and spawns its monsters. 4. Places the player at the new level's start and shows "Floor 2" in the message log. Making that split explicit (a PlayerState that survives levels, a FloorState that does not) keeps the transition simple and is exactly the line the save format follows. cpp-norun struct PlayerState { int health{ 20 }, maxHealth{ 20 }; int power{ 3 }, armour{ 1 }; Inventory inventory{ 10, itemStackLimits() }; }; struct FloorState { int floor{ 1 }; TileMap map; std::vector<MonsterInstance monsters; // kind, position, health, AI state std::vector<ItemOnFloor items; std::vector<bool openedDoors; }; What a Delve save contains Lesson 10.07's principle: save the minimum from which everything else can be rebuilt. Saved Rebuilt on load --- --- The floor number The map: reload data/levels/NN.txt Changes to the map: doors opened Distance maps, rendering state Each surviving monster: kind, position, health, state Monster stats: from monsters.ini by kind Items on the floor: id, count, position Item names and effects: from items.ini by id The player's position, health and inventory The random generator's state Saving the random generator's state means a reloaded game continues exactly as it would have, which makes bugs that happen after loading reproducible. The format A text body inside lesson 10.07's binary header is a practical choice: easy to read while developing, protected by the checksum. SAVE version 1 length 214 crc 0x9A3C11F0 (16-byte binary header) floor 2 player 7 4 hp 14 20 power 4 armour 1 inv potion 3 inv dagger 1 door 12 5 monster g 9 4 hp 6 chasing monster g 15 2 hp 9 idle item gold 40 3 7 rng 2463534242 Each line starts with a keyword, so loading is a loop over lines with a switch on the first word, and an old save missing a newer keyword still loads with defaults. The version in the header decides which keywords exist (lesson 10.07's migrations). Saving safely Following lesson 5.04: 1. Build the whole save in memory as a string. 2. Compute the CRC-32 (lesson 10.07) and write the header and body to slot1.sav.tmp in the Saved Games folder. 3. Flush and close it, then replace slot1.sav with it atomically, keeping the previous file as slot1.sav.bak . On loading, check the magic, the version and the checksum before reading a single line; if anything fails, offer the backup. Delve saves automatically on each new floor and when quitting, so a run can always be continued, and the practice task writes the save and load of the player's part. Common mistakes !warning Saving the level map wholesale The map comes from the level file; save only what changed (opened doors). !warning Forgetting the random generator's state A reloaded game then diverges from the original, and bugs after loading cannot be reproduced. !warning Saving during a monster's turn Save only between turns, when the state is consistent. Knowledge check quiz ? What survives a transition to the next floor? + The player's state: health, inventory, stats - The old floor's monsters - The old floor's map Everything belonging to the floor is discarded and rebuilt from the next level file. ? Why save the random generator's state? + So the game continues after loading exactly as it would have, keeping behaviour reproducible - To make saves smaller - To prevent cheating Without it, the reloaded game takes different random outcomes. ? Why start each line of the save body with a keyword? + Loading becomes a simple loop over lines, and older saves missing new keywords still load with defaults - To make the file larger - Because the checksum needs it Keyword lines are easy to extend across versions.

title: Save and load the player
body:
Write the player part of Delve's save format. savePlayer(p) returns the text, one line per fact, each ending in 
 : player X Y hp HEALTH MAXHEALTH power POWER armour ARMOUR inv ID COUNT (one line per inventory entry, in order) loadPlayer(text) reads it back. It must accept the lines in any order, ignore blank lines and lines whose keyword it does not know (a newer version may have added some), and return std::nullopt if the player line is missing or malformed (wrong number of fields, wrong labels, or non-numbers), or an inv line is malformed or has a count below 1. savePlayer({ 7, 4, 14, 20, 4, 1, { { "potion", 3 }, { "dagger", 1 } } }) == "player 7 4 hp 14 20 power 4 armour 1
inv potion 3
inv dagger 1
"

title: 11.07  A Debug Console
body: Every serious game has a hidden console for its developers: press a key, type god , give potion 5 or goto 3 , and test anything without playing up to it. This lesson builds Delve's console from lesson 3.04's command table: text input, a command registry with help text, argument parsing, history, output, and a rule that keeps it out of the shipped game.
