Why a console Testing the troll on floor 5 by playing through floors 1 to 4 every time wastes hours. A debug console lets developers and testers change the game's state directly: Command Effect --- --- help List every command with a one-line description god Toggle invulnerability give potion 5 Add items to the inventory heal Restore full health goto 3 Jump to floor 3 spawn troll Spawn a monster next to the player reveal Show the whole map seed 1234 Re-seed the random generator, to reproduce a bug save / load Save and load immediately Chapter 13 extends the same idea into an in-game debug menu, and chapter 14 gives tools a full interface; the console is the simplest and most flexible form. The registry Lesson 3.04's command table becomes a registry where each command has a name, a short help text and a function that receives the arguments: cpp-norun using Args = std::vector<std::string ; using Handler = std::function<std::string(Game&, const Args&) ; // returns a line to print struct Command { std::string help; Handler run; }; class Console { public: void add(std::string name, std::string help, Handler run) { m_commands std::move(name) = { std::move(help), std::move(run) }; } std::string execute(Game& game, const std::string& line) { const Args words{ splitCommandLine(line) }; // lesson 6.01's practice task: quotes allowed if (words.empty()) return ""; const auto found{ m_commands.find(words 0 ) }; if (found == m_commands.end()) return "unknown command: " + words 0 + " (try help)"; return found- second.run(game, Args(words.begin() + 1, words.end())); } private: std::map<std::string, Command m_commands; // sorted, so help lists them alphabetically }; Registering a command is one line wherever the feature lives: cpp-norun console.add("give", "give ITEM COUNT : add items to the inventory", (Game& g, const Args& a) { if (a.empty()) return std::string{ "usage: give ITEM COUNT " }; const int count{ a.size() 1 ? std::atoi(a 1 .c_str()) : 1 }; const int left{ g.player.inventory.add(a 0 , count) }; return "gave " + std::to_string(count - left) + " " + a 0 ; }); Each command validates its own arguments and returns a message, so mistakes produce a helpful line instead of a crash. Text input with SDL The console opens with the backquote key ( , below Escape). While it is open: - SDL's SDL_StartTextInput delivers typed characters as SDL_TEXTINPUT events, already in UTF-8 and respecting the keyboard layout (lesson 5.07's WM_CHAR , through SDL). - Backspace, Enter, Escape and the arrow keys come through as normal key events. - Game controls are ignored, so typing w does not move the player. The console draws a dark band over the top third of the screen with the last lines of output (from lesson 8.03's ring buffer) and the input line. History Pressing Up recalls the previous command, as in a terminal. The history is a list of past commands and a cursor; the practice task implements its exact behaviour, including the detail that typing a new line and pressing Up then Down restores what you were typing. Keeping it out of the shipped game The console is a cheat menu. In a single-player game that may be fine to leave reachable, but at least the game-changing commands should be compiled only into development builds: cpp-norun ifndef DELVE_SHIPPING registerDebugCommands(console); // god, give, goto, spawn ... endif with DELVE_SHIPPING defined in a separate Shipping configuration (lesson 4.01). In multiplayer games, anything that changes shared state must also be refused by the server: a client-side console can only ever be trusted for the client's own view. Common mistakes !warning Commands that crash on bad arguments Every handler checks its arguments and returns a usage message. !warning Typing in the console also moves the player While the console is open, route keys to it only. !warning Shipping cheat commands by accident Compile them out of shipping builds. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does each command carry a help text? + So help can list every command and what it does, keeping the console self-documenting - Because the compiler needs it - To make commands faster A console nobody remembers how to use is not much use. ? Why use SDL's text input events rather than key-down events for typing? + They deliver the actual characters typed, respecting Shift, the keyboard layout and accents - Key-down events do not exist in SDL - They are faster Like WM_CHAR in lesson 5.07. ? How do you keep cheat commands out of the released game? + Register them only in development builds, behind a preprocessor setting off in the shipping configuration - Hide the console key - Ask players not to use them Code that is not compiled cannot be used.

title: Console history
body: Build History , the command history behind Delve's console, with the behaviour of a typical terminal. - submit(line) records a submitted command (empty lines and a line identical to the most recent entry are not recorded), and resets browsing. - up(current) is called when Up is pressed, with the text currently in the input line. The first press saves current as the draft and returns the most recent command; each further press returns an older one, stopping at the oldest (pressing Up there returns the oldest again). With no history, it returns current unchanged. - down() moves to a newer entry. Moving past the newest returns the saved draft, and browsing ends. If not browsing, it returns the draft (initially empty). - The history keeps at most capacity entries (given to the constructor), dropping the oldest. submit "give potion 5", submit "heal" up("go") - "heal" up("...") - "give potion 5" up("...") - "give potion 5" (the oldest; stays) down() - "heal" down() - "go" (the draft is back)

title: 11.08  Polish and Packaging
body: The difference between a working prototype and a game people enjoy is polish : feedback for every action, a little motion, sound, and no rough edges. The difference between a game on your machine and one on a friend's is packaging : a Release build with everything it needs, version information, and a test on a clean system. This lesson finishes Delve. Feedback for every action Players should never wonder whether something happened. Each action gets a visible, and ideally audible, response: Event Feedback --- --- Hitting a monster A brief flash on the monster, a number floating up, a short sound Being hit A red flash at the screen's edges, a small screen shake Missing "miss" floating up, a different sound Picking up an item The item slides to the inventory bar; the slot pulses Low health The health bar pulses; a heartbeat sound Bumping a wall A tiny nudge of the player sprite towards the wall and back All of these are presentation only : they live in the renderer and never change game state (lesson 10.01), so they cannot introduce gameplay bugs. Screen shake, for example, is a random offset added to the camera that decays over a fraction of a second: cpp-norun // Called when the player is hit: strength in pixels. void addShake(float strength) { m_shake = std::min(m_shake + strength, 12.0f); } // Each frame, in the renderer: const float ox{ m_shake rng.unit() 2 - m_shake }; const float oy{ m_shake rng.unit() 2 - m_shake }; drawWorld(cameraX + ox, cameraY + oy); m_shake = std::max(0.0f, m_shake - 40.0f frameTime); // fades in about a quarter of a second Use a separate random generator for presentation, so effects do not consume numbers from the gameplay generator and change the game's outcomes (lesson 11.05). Sound SDL_mixer ( vcpkg add port sdl2-mixer ) plays sound effects and music in a few lines. Keep sounds short and quiet by default, give every sound a slight random pitch or choose between two or three variants so repetition does not grate, and give players volume settings for effects and music separately. Settings and accessibility A settings screen (saved like lesson 10.07's files, in AppData) should cover at least: key bindings (lesson 10.05), volume, window or full screen, screen shake on/off, and text size. Turning off screen shake and flashes matters to players sensitive to motion, and costs one boolean. The Release build Lesson 4.10's checklist, applied: 1. Build Release x64 with /Zi and linker /DEBUG , and archive the PDB with the version number (lesson 8.02): crash dumps from players are useless without it. 2. Define DELVE_SHIPPING to remove debug commands (lesson 11.07). 3. Install the crash handler that writes a minidump and the recent log (lesson 8.04). 4. Add version information : a VERSIONINFO resource (Add → Resource → Version) with the product name and version, shown in the file's Properties dialog and recorded in crash dumps. 5. Turn on all the security options that are on by default (ASLR, DEP, /GS , control-flow guard) and leave them on. Packaging A Delve release is a folder: Delve-1.0.0\ Delve.exe SDL2.dll from vcpkg_installed\x64-windows\bin SDL2_mixer.dll data\ levels\ .txt items.ini monsters.ini sounds\ .wav README.txt how to play, controls, where saves are kept LICENSES.txt SDL's licence (zlib) and any others you used Zip it, or build an installer (Inno Setup and WiX are free; MSIX for the Microsoft Store). Two details people forget: - Third-party licences. SDL's zlib licence is permissive, but you must keep its notice; check every library you ship. - The Visual C++ runtime. If you build with /MD (the default), players need the Visual C++ Redistributable. Either ship its installer, or build with /MT so the runtime is inside your exe (lesson 4.04). Test on a clean machine The game works on your PC because everything it needs is already installed there. Test the zip on a clean Windows installation, ideally a virtual machine (lesson 15.08 sets one up) restored to a fresh snapshot each time: missing DLLs, a missing runtime, paths that assume your folders, and writing next to the exe (lesson 5.04) all show up immediately. Common mistakes !warning Not keeping the PDB of the build you released Every crash report from that version becomes unreadable. !warning Testing only on the development machine Use a clean virtual machine. !warning Polish that changes the game Effects belong in the renderer, with their own random numbers. Knowledge check quiz ? Why should screen shake use a different random generator from the gameplay? + So turning effects on or off cannot change the game's random outcomes - Because shake needs better random numbers - To make it faster Presentation must never affect game state. ? Why test the packaged game on a clean virtual machine? + It reveals missing DLLs, runtimes and assumptions about your own machine's setup - Games run faster in virtual machines - To check the graphics card Your development PC hides missing dependencies. ? What must you keep for every build you release? + Its PDB files, to read crash dumps from that version - The obj files - The vcpkg cache Symbols match exactly one build.

title: 12.01  Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs
match: 12.01 Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs
body:
Development tools often need to see inside a running game from a separate program: a stats panel, a level editor that previews live, a profiler. Each process has its own private memory (lesson 6.02), so tools need a deliberate channel. This lesson surveys the documented ways (the game publishing data through shared memory , pipes or sockets; the debugging API for a process you start; dumps) and builds a shared-memory channel, the method the rest of this chapter uses. The problem The game and the tool are separate processes. A pointer in one means nothing in the other, and Windows' access checks (lesson 6.08) decide who may look at whom. So how does a tool show the game's frame time, the player's health or the number of live monsters? There are several documented ways, and they differ in who cooperates : Method The game cooperates? Good for --- --- --- Shared memory (file mapping) Yes: the game writes a block of data that the tool maps too Fast, continuous data: stats, graphs, live values Named pipes or sockets Yes: they exchange messages Commands and events: "spawn a troll", "level loaded" Log files and ETW events Yes Records over time, profiling (lesson 8.08) The debugging API on a process the tool starts No code in the game, but the tool must be its debugger Debuggers and crash catchers (lesson 12.03) Crash dumps No Inspecting state after the fact (lesson 8.04) The first rows are how professional engines connect their editors and tools: the game publishes what tools may see, through an interface designed for it. That is reliable (no guessing at memory layouts), fast, survives game updates when versioned properly (lesson 12.06), and needs no special rights. This chapter builds that kind of tooling for Delve, plus a small debugger for a program the tool launches itself. !note Ground rules The tools here inspect programs you build yourself, or programs started by your own tool. Reading or changing the memory of other people's software, particularly online games and anything protected by anti-cheat, is outside this course (lesson 9.01's ground rules): it harms other players, breaks the terms you agreed to, and is often illegal. Shared memory with a file mapping Windows can map the same block of physical memory into two processes' address spaces. Each sees it at its own virtual address, but writes by one are visible to the other. The block is a file mapping object, created by name: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream struct Telemetry // the agreed layout: plain data only, no pointers (lesson 6.09) { unsigned version; unsigned frame; float frameMs; int playerHp; }; int main() { // The game creates a named, page-file-backed mapping big enough for the struct... HANDLE game{ CreateFileMappingW(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, nullptr, PAGE_READWRITE, 0, sizeof(Telemetry), L"Local\XenonDemoTelemetry") }; auto written{ static_cast<Telemetry (MapViewOfFile(game, FILE_MAP_WRITE, 0, 0, sizeof(Telemetry))) }; // ...and a tool opens the same name. (Here in one process, to keep the example runnable.) HANDLE tool{ OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, L"Local\XenonDemoTelemetry") }; const auto read{ static_cast<const Telemetry (MapViewOfFile(tool, FILE_MAP_READ, 0, 0, sizeof(Telemetry))) }; written = Telemetry{ 1, 1234, 16.4f, 17 }; std::cout << "two different addresses: " << (static_cast<const void (written) != static_cast<const void (read)) << '
'; std::cout << "the tool sees frame " << read- frame << ", hp " << read- playerHp << '
'; UnmapViewOfFile(read); CloseHandle(tool); UnmapViewOfFile(written); CloseHandle(game); return 0; } two different addresses: 1 the tool sees frame 1234, hp 17 Two different virtual addresses, one block of physical memory. Points to note: - INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as the file means "backed by the page file": pure shared memory, no file on disk. - The name Local\... is visible to processes in the same login session. Choose names unique to your game. - The tool opens the mapping read-only ( FILE_MAP_READ ): least privilege (lesson 6.08). A stats panel has no business writing into the game. - The layout contains only plain values, never pointers: an address in the game is meaningless in the tool. - Reading while the game writes can produce a torn snapshot (half old, half new). Lesson 12.04 fixes this with a sequence counter. Pipes for commands Shared memory is ideal for "the current state". For messages ("load level 3", "screenshot taken") a named pipe ( CreateNamedPipeW in the game, CreateFileW on \.\pipe
ame in the tool) carries a stream of bytes both ways, like a local network connection. Many engines run a small command server this way so editors can control the game; it is the debug console of lesson 11.07, reachable from outside. Common mistakes !warning Putting pointers or std::string in shared memory Their contents are addresses in one process. Use fixed-size plain data. !warning Opening the mapping writable in the tool Read-only is all a viewer needs, and protects the game from tool bugs. !warning Treating the shared block as always consistent Without a protocol (lesson 12.04), the tool may read a half-updated state. Knowledge check quiz ? Why can a tool not simply follow a pointer it got from the game? + The pointer is a virtual address in the game's address space; in the tool's process it means nothing - Pointers are encrypted - Tools have no memory Each process has its own private address space (lesson 6.02). ? What makes shared memory work between two processes? + Both map the same named file-mapping object, so the same physical memory appears in each address space - Windows copies the data between them every frame - They use the same virtual addresses Each sees it at its own address, but it is the same memory. ? Which channel suits sending a command such as "load level 3" from an editor to the game? + A named pipe (or socket) carrying messages - A crash dump - A file mapping holding the current frame number Pipes carry streams of messages; shared memory holds current state.

title: 12.02  A Memory Viewer
body: A hex viewer that shows raw memory with addresses, bytes and text is one of the most useful debugging tools there is, and the Memory window of lesson 2.11 is one. This lesson builds one for your own process and for a process your tool launched: reading with ReadProcessMemory , coping with pages that cannot be read, and formatting the classic three-column view. The classic layout Address 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F Text 0000020E6C8F5E30 52 6F 6F 6B 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 Rook............ 0000020E6C8F5E40 0E 00 00 00 14 00 00 00 00 00 80 3F ?? ?? ?? ?? ...........?.... Three columns: the address of the row, sixteen bytes in hex, and the same bytes as text (printable characters as themselves, everything else as a dot). Bytes that could not be read are shown as ?? , which a good viewer must handle because memory can be freed, never committed, or protected (lesson 6.03). Reading your own process safely In your own process you can read memory directly through a pointer, but only if it is committed and readable; touching anything else crashes the viewer. Ask first with VirtualQuery (lesson 6.04): cpp bool readable(const void address, size_t size) { MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; if (!VirtualQuery(address, &info, sizeof(info))) return false; if (info.State != MEM_COMMIT) return false; if (info.Protect & (PAGE_NOACCESS PAGE_GUARD)) return false; const auto end{ static_cast<const char (info.BaseAddress) + info.RegionSize }; return static_cast<const char (address) + size <= end; // a longer read may cross into the next region } Even this has a gap: another thread could free the memory between the check and the read. In a viewer for your own process that is acceptable; in a tool that must never crash, read through ReadProcessMemory on the current process, which returns failure instead of faulting. Reading another process you started For a process the tool launched itself (and so has full rights to, lesson 6.08), ReadProcessMemory copies bytes from its address space: cpp SIZE_T got{ 0 }; std::vector<unsigned char buffer(256); const BOOL ok{ ReadProcessMemory(child, reinterpret_cast<LPCVOID (address), buffer.data(), buffer.size(), &got) }; - The handle needs PROCESS_VM_READ (and PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION for VirtualQueryEx ). A process you created with CreateProcessW comes with a full-access handle. - If any page in the range is unreadable, the call fails and got reports how much was copied, which may be less than asked. A robust viewer reads page by page (4,096 bytes, lesson 6.02), so one bad page only blanks its own part. - VirtualQueryEx(child, ...) is VirtualQuery for another process, and tells you in advance which pages are readable. Formatting The practice task writes the formatter: given a starting address, the bytes, and which of them were readable, produce the three-column lines. Separating reading (the platform part) from formatting (pure logic) means the formatter can be tested without any process at all, as every practice task in this course has done. Making it useful Features that turn a hex dump into a tool: - Follow a pointer : click 8 bytes that look like an address (lesson 2.11) and jump there. - Interpretations : show the selected bytes as int , float , double , and as a pointer, side by side. - Highlight changes : re-read every 100 ms and colour bytes that changed (Visual Studio's Memory window does this when stepping). - Bookmarks and type overlays : apply a struct layout (lesson 9.09) so offsets show member names. Chapter 14 gives the viewer a proper interface with Dear ImGui; chapter 18's first capstone completes it. Common mistakes !warning Reading a whole range in one call One unreadable page fails the whole read. Read page by page. !warning Showing stale data as current Mark the time of the last successful read, and show unreadable bytes as ?? , never as zeros. !warning Asking for more access than reading needs A viewer needs PROCESS_VM_READ and query rights only. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a viewer show for bytes it could not read? + A marker such as ?? , never a made-up value like 0 - Zeros - Nothing: the row is skipped Showing zeros would mislead whoever reads the dump. ? Why read another process's memory one page at a time? + An unreadable page then only blanks its own bytes instead of failing the whole read - Pages are the only size ReadProcessMemory accepts - It is faster Protection and commitment are per page. ? Why keep the formatting separate from the reading? + The formatting is pure logic that can be tested without a running process - Formatting must run on another thread - Windows requires it Testable logic, thin platform layer.

title: Format a hex view
body:
Write hexView(address, bytes, readable) . bytes and readable have the same length; readable i says whether bytes i was actually read. Produce one line per 16 bytes, starting at address (which you may assume is a multiple of 16): - the row's address as 16 upper-case hex digits, then two spaces; - 16 byte columns, each two upper-case hex digits (or ?? if unreadable) followed by one space, with one extra space after the eighth; for a short last row, pad the missing bytes with three spaces each (and the extra space if the gap includes the middle); - then two more spaces (in addition to the last column's trailing space) and the text: each readable byte from 0x20 to 0x7E as itself, anything else (including unreadable bytes) as . . Missing bytes on a short last row add nothing to the text. Lines end with

title: 12.03  A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
match: 12.03 A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
body:
Visual Studio, WinDbg and x64dbg are all built on the same Windows debugging API . This lesson uses it directly to write a tiny debugger: it launches a program of yours as its debuggee, receives debug events (process and thread creation, DLL loads, exceptions, debug output, exit), reports them, and continues. It demystifies every debugger you have used, and is the core of crash-catching tools. How debugging works on Windows A debugger is an ordinary program that has a special relationship with its debuggee : Windows suspends the debuggee whenever something interesting happens and sends the debugger a debug event describing it. The debuggee stays frozen until the debugger says to continue. Every debugger you have used is this loop with a large interface around it. The debug event loop cpp-norun include <windows.h include <cstdio include <string int wmain(int argc, wchar_t argv) { if (argc < 2) { std::wprintf(L"usage: tinydbg program.exe
"); return 1; } std::wstring command{ L""" + std::wstring(argv 1 ) + L""" }; STARTUPINFOW si{ sizeof(si) }; PROCESS_INFORMATION pi{}; if (!CreateProcessW(nullptr, command.data(), nullptr, nullptr, FALSE, DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS, nullptr, nullptr, &si, &pi)) { std::wprintf(L"could not start it: %lu
", GetLastError()); return 1; } bool running{ true }; while (running) { DEBUG_EVENT ev{}; if (!WaitForDebugEvent(&ev, INFINITE)) break; DWORD status{ DBG_CONTINUE }; switch (ev.dwDebugEventCode) { case CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"process started, image at %p
", ev.u.CreateProcessInfo.lpBaseOfImage); CloseHandle(ev.u.CreateProcessInfo.hFile); // the event hands us a file handle: close it break; case LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"DLL loaded at %p
", ev.u.LoadDll.lpBaseOfDll); CloseHandle(ev.u.LoadDll.hFile); break; case OUTPUT_DEBUG_STRING_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"debuggee says something (OutputDebugString)
"); break; case EXCEPTION_DEBUG_EVENT: { const EXCEPTION_RECORD& er{ ev.u.Exception.ExceptionRecord }; const bool firstChance{ ev.u.Exception.dwFirstChance != 0 }; std::wprintf(L"exception 0x%08lX at %p (%s chance)
", er.ExceptionCode, er.ExceptionAddress, firstChance ? L"first" : L"second"); if (er.ExceptionCode == EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT) status = DBG_CONTINUE; // the initial breakpoint, or ours else status = DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED; // let the program's own handlers see it break; } case EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"process exited with code %lu
", ev.u.ExitProcess.dwExitCode); running = false; break; } ContinueDebugEvent(ev.dwProcessId, ev.dwThreadId, status); } CloseHandle(pi.hThread); CloseHandle(pi.hProcess); return 0; } Run it on any small program of your own ( tinydbg.exe delve.exe ) and you will see the process start, every DLL load in order ( ntdll , kernel32 , KernelBase , the C++ runtime, SDL...), an initial breakpoint exception ( 0x80000003 , lesson 8.04) that Windows raises in every debugged process just before its own code runs, and finally the exit. First and second chance When the debuggee raises an exception, the debugger gets it twice if needed: 1. First chance : before the program's own exception handlers run. A debugger normally continues with DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED , letting the program handle it (a C++ throw that is caught arrives here and is harmless). 2. Second chance : only if nothing in the program handled it. The program is about to crash. This is the moment to write a crash dump (lesson 8.04) with the process frozen exactly at the fault, which is how out-of-process crash reporters work: they are tiny debuggers. Breakpoints, by hand A software breakpoint (lesson 4.07) is now easy to understand in code: 1. Read and remember the byte at the address ( ReadProcessMemory ). 2. Write 0xCC there ( WriteProcessMemory , then FlushInstructionCache ). 3. When the EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT arrives with that address, the instruction pointer has moved one byte past the CC . Restore the original byte, move rip back by one with GetThreadContext / SetThreadContext , and continue (setting the trap flag to single-step once, so the breakpoint can be re-armed after the instruction runs). Reading registers is GetThreadContext on the thread from the event (with CONTEXT_FULL ), and the call stack is StackWalk64 from the DbgHelp library with symbols loaded (lesson 8.02). Everything Visual Studio's debugger shows is built from these calls. Rights and limits A debugger needs full access to its debuggee. Launching the debuggee yourself grants that. Attaching to a running process ( DebugActiveProcess ) requires the same rights as Visual Studio's Attach (lesson 4.07): your own processes at your integrity level; protected processes refuse (lesson 6.08). Only one debugger can be attached to a process at a time. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to close the file handles in events CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT and LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT hand you file handles; not closing them leaks one per DLL. !warning Continuing every exception as handled DBG_CONTINUE on a real exception re-executes the faulting instruction forever. Pass the program's own exceptions on with DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED . !warning Exiting the debugger while the debuggee runs By default the debuggee is killed with it. Call DebugActiveProcessStop (or DebugSetProcessKillOnExit(FALSE) ) to detach first. Knowledge check quiz ? What happens to the debuggee while the debugger handles an event? + It is suspended until the debugger calls ContinueDebugEvent - It keeps running normally - It is restarted Every thread waits while the debugger inspects it. ? What is a second-chance exception? + An exception the program did not handle itself, so it is about to crash - A breakpoint hit twice - An exception in the debugger The debugger saw it first-chance, passed it on, and nothing handled it. ? How does a software breakpoint work? + The debugger writes 0xCC over an instruction's first byte; executing it raises a breakpoint exception that the debugger receives - The processor watches a list of addresses - Windows pauses the program every few instructions Hardware breakpoints use debug registers instead (lesson 4.09).

title: Follow the debug events
where: 12.03 A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
body: A debugger keeps a picture of its debuggee from the stream of debug events. Write Tracker , which processes simplified events and answers questions. Each Event has a kind and, depending on the kind, a base address, a name , a code and a firstChance flag: kind Meaning --- --- "load" A module name loaded at base "unload" The module at base unloaded "exception" An exception code at address base , first or second chance "exit" The process exited with code handle(event) returns what the debugger should tell Windows, as the lesson describes: "continue" for everything except exceptions that are not breakpoints ( 0x80000003 ), for which it returns "not-handled" . The tracker also answers: - modules() : the names of the currently loaded modules, ordered by base address; - crashed() : whether a second-chance exception was seen; - exitCode() : the exit code, or std::nullopt if the process has not exited.

title: 12.04  A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
match: 12.04 A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
body: Delve will publish its live state (frame time, floor, the player's health and position, monster count) in shared memory for tools to read. The hard part is consistency: the game writes while the tool reads, so the tool must never see half an update. This lesson designs the shared block with a header and version, and protects it with a sequence lock , a lock-free scheme where the writer never waits. What the game publishes cpp-norun // telemetry.h: shared by Delve and its tools. Plain data, fixed sizes, no pointers. pragma once include <atomic include <cstdint struct TelemetryV1 { std::uint32_t magic; // 'DLVT' std::uint32_t version; // 1 std::uint32_t size; // sizeof(TelemetryV1): lets old tools read newer games (lesson 12.06) std::atomic<std::uint32_t sequence; // the sequence lock, below std::uint64_t frame; float frameMs; std::int32_t floor; std::int32_t playerX, playerY; std::int32_t playerHp, playerMaxHp; std::int32_t monstersAlive; std::uint32_t turn; }; Every field is a fixed-size number at a fixed offset (lesson 2.05), the same in both programs because both include the same header. The header fields ( magic , version , size ) let a tool check, before trusting anything, that it is looking at the right kind of block and knows how to read it (lesson 10.07's save header, applied to memory). The consistency problem The game updates all these fields once per frame. A tool reading them at the same moment might copy playerX from the new frame and playerY from the old one, a position the player was never at. With a dozen fields, torn reads happen often enough to matter (lesson 6.06's data races, between processes). A mutex shared between processes would work (a named mutex), but then the game could be made to wait by a slow or stuck tool, which is unacceptable: a tool must never be able to make the game stutter. The sequence lock A sequence lock (seqlock) lets one writer update freely while readers detect and retry torn reads: Writer (the game, once per frame): 1. Increment sequence (it becomes odd : "update in progress"). 2. Write all the fields. 3. Increment sequence again (it becomes even : "consistent"). Reader (the tool): 1. Read sequence . If it is odd, the writer is mid-update: try again shortly. 2. Copy all the fields into a local struct. 3. Read sequence again. If it changed, the writer updated during the copy: discard and retry. If it is the same (and even), the copy is consistent. cpp-norun // Game side, each frame: t- sequence.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_acq_rel); // odd: writing t- frame = frame; t- frameMs = ms; t- playerX = x; / ... / t- sequence.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_release); // even: done // Tool side: bool readSnapshot(const TelemetryV1 t, TelemetryV1& out) { for (int attempt{ 0 }; attempt < 100; ++attempt) { const std::uint32_t before{ t- sequence.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; if (before & 1) continue; // being written: try again copyFields(out, t); // plain copy of the data fields std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire); if (t- sequence.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == before) return true; // nothing changed meanwhile } return false; // the game is writing constantly: report "busy" } The writer never waits for anyone: tools can be slow, stuck or crashed and the game does not notice. Readers occasionally retry, which costs nothing noticeable because the write takes well under a microsecond. Seqlocks are used in operating system kernels for exactly this pattern: frequently updated data with one writer and readers that can retry. The memory-order arguments make sure the processor and compiler do not reorder the field writes across the sequence updates (lesson 6.06's atomics); the practice task models the protocol's logic. Creating the channel in Delve At start-up, Delve creates the mapping Local\Delve.Telemetry.<process id (including the id lets several copies of the game run side by side), fills in magic , version and size , and publishes each frame. If creating it fails, the game simply runs without telemetry: tools are optional, the game is not. In shipping builds the channel can be left on (it is harmless) or compiled out like the console (lesson 11.07). Common mistakes !warning Locking between the game and a tool A stuck tool must never be able to stall the game. The writer must not wait. !warning Trusting the block without checking its header Check the magic, version and size before reading fields. !warning Forgetting that a reader can loop forever Bound the retries and report "busy" instead of hanging the tool. Knowledge check quiz ? What does an odd sequence number mean? + The writer is in the middle of an update; readers must not trust what they copy - The data is consistent - The game has crashed The writer increments once before and once after writing. ? A reader copies the fields and then finds the sequence number has changed. What should it do? + Discard its copy and try again - Use the copy anyway - Wait for the writer with a mutex The writer updated during the copy, so it may be torn. ? Why is a seqlock better than a shared mutex here? + The game never waits, so a slow or stuck tool cannot make it stutter - It uses less memory - It works without shared memory Only readers retry; the writer always proceeds.

title: The sequence-lock protocol
where: 12.04 A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
body: Model a sequence lock without threads, so its logic can be tested step by step. A SharedBlock holds a sequence number and two values that must always be read together. The writer is split into steps so tests can interleave it with readers: - beginWrite() increments the sequence; - writeA(v) and writeB(v) set the values; - endWrite() increments the sequence again. The reader is also split: - beginRead() returns the sequence number it saw (the reader's "ticket"), or std::nullopt if it is odd (a write is in progress); - copy() returns the two values as they are right now; - validate(ticket) returns true if the sequence still equals the ticket. Finally, readConsistent(block) is a complete reader using those steps: try up to 3 times; return the pair if a copy is validated, otherwise std::nullopt .

title: 12.05  A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
match: 12.05 A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
body: With Delve publishing its telemetry, a separate tool can show it live: frame times with a graph, the floor, the player's health and position, how many monsters are alive. This lesson builds that tool as a console program (chapter 14 gives it a graphical interface): finding running copies of the game, reading snapshots on a timer, keeping a history for graphs, and coping when the game starts, stops or restarts. What the panel shows Delve telemetry · pid 18324 · v1 connected ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── frame 48211 frame time 7.9 ms (min 6.8 · avg 8.2 · max 21.4) ▁▁▂▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▇▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁ last 60 samples floor 3 turn 412 player (17, 9) hp 14 / 20 ███████░░░ monsters alive 6 Every value comes from one consistent snapshot (lesson 12.04). The graph shows the last 60 frame times, scaled so the slowest is the tallest bar, and the spike in it is exactly the kind of stutter lesson 8.08 warned about, now visible while playing. Finding the game The telemetry block's name includes the game's process id (lesson 12.04), so the tool: 1. Lists processes named delve.exe (lesson 6.07's snapshot). 2. For each, tries OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, L"Local\\Delve.Telemetry.<pid ") . 3. Maps the first that opens and checks magic , version and size before reading anything else (lesson 12.06 covers what to do with versions it does not know). If several copies are running, it can show a list to choose from. The read loop cpp-norun while (running) { TelemetryV1 snap{}; if (!connected) tryConnect(); else if (!readSnapshot(block, snap)) showStatus("busy"); // retries exhausted (lesson 12.04) else if (snap.frame == lastFrame) staleFor += interval; // the game is paused, or frozen else { staleFor = 0; lastFrame = snap.frame; history.push(snap.frameMs); draw(snap, history); } if (connected && !processStillRunning(pid)) disconnect(); // the game exited: start looking again Sleep(100); // 10 updates a second is plenty for people } Three states matter and should be shown clearly: State Detect Show --- --- --- Connected and live The frame number advances The values Connected but stale The frame number has not changed for a second "paused or not responding", values greyed out Not connected No mapping found, or the process exited "waiting for Delve...", and keep looking Checking whether the process is still running uses a process handle opened with SYNCHRONIZE and WaitForSingleObject(handle, 0) (lesson 6.01: a process handle is signalled when it exits). The mapping itself stays valid while the tool has it open, even after the game exits, so the frame counter alone cannot tell "exited" from "frozen". Drawing in the console Lesson 5.09's techniques do the drawing: enable virtual terminal sequences, build the whole screen into one string starting with "cursor home", and write it in one call so it never flickers. The bars use the Unicode block characters ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█ , written in UTF-8 after SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) . The practice task computes the statistics and the bar characters from the history. Common mistakes !warning Treating an unchanged frame number as "the game exited" It also means paused or frozen. Check the process handle separately. !warning Reading as fast as possible People cannot read 1,000 updates a second, and it wastes a core. 10 to 30 per second is plenty. !warning Crashing when the game restarts Unmap, close and go back to searching; the new copy has a new process id and a new block. Knowledge check quiz ? How does the tool tell "the game is paused" from "the game has exited"? + The frame number stopping only means not updating; whether the process handle is signalled shows whether it exited - Both are shown by the frame number - The tool cannot tell The mapping outlives the game while the tool holds it open. ? Why does the tool include the process id when opening the mapping? + Each running copy of the game publishes its own block under a name containing its process id - Mapping names must be numbers - To make the name secret It lets several copies run side by side. ? How often should a stats panel read snapshots? + About 10 to 30 times a second: enough for people, cheap for the machine - As fast as possible - Once a minute Faster than people can read wastes CPU for nothing.

title: Frame-time history and a sparkline
where: 12.05 A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
body: Build FrameHistory , which keeps the last capacity frame times (milliseconds) for the stats panel. - push(ms) adds a sample, dropping the oldest when full. - min() , max() , average() over the stored samples (0 when empty). - sparkline() returns one character per sample, oldest first, chosen from the eight levels " ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█" without the space, that is the characters ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█ (as UTF-8 strings). The tallest bar ( █ ) is the maximum; a sample v gets level round(7 v / max) , from 0 ( ▁ ) to 7 ( █ ). If the maximum is 0, every sample is ▁ . Return the characters joined into one UTF-8 std::string . push 8, 8, 16, 8 - min 8, max 16, average 10 sparkline = "▅▅█▅" (7 8 / 16 = 3.5, rounds to 4: ▅)

title: 12.06  Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
match: 12.06 Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
body: The game will change: new fields in the telemetry, new commands on the pipe. Tools built for last month's game should keep working, and new tools should cope with old games. This lesson designs for that: append-only layouts with a size field, version and capability checks, feature flags, and the rules that let both sides evolve without breaking each other. Why interfaces need versions A tool and a game are built separately, often by different people, and updated at different times. Every shared structure and message format is an interface , and like lesson 4.05's DLL interfaces, changing it carelessly breaks whoever is on the other side: - Insert a field in the middle of the telemetry struct, and every older tool reads the wrong offsets: health shows the floor number. - Rename a pipe command, and old tools send commands the game no longer understands. The goal is compatibility in both directions : Situation Should --- --- New tool, old game Read what the old game provides; hide features it lacks Old tool, new game Keep working with the fields it knows; ignore new ones Truly incompatible change Be detected and reported clearly, never misread Rule 1: append, never insert or reorder Add new fields only at the end of a structure. Then every field keeps its offset forever, and an older tool reading the beginning of a newer block reads exactly what it expects. cpp-norun struct TelemetryV2 // version 2 = version 1 + new fields at the end { // ---- version 1: never change these ---- std::uint32_t magic, version, size; std::atomic<std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint64_t frame; float frameMs; std::int32_t floor, playerX, playerY, playerHp, playerMaxHp, monstersAlive; std::uint32_t turn; // ---- added in version 2 ---- std::uint32_t features; // capability flags, below float cpuMs; // time spent in update std::int32_t itemsOnFloor; }; Removing a field becomes "stop updating it" (leave it in place, write 0), never actually deleting it. Rule 2: the size field tells the reader what exists The header's size is the size of the struct the writer used. A reader then knows exactly which fields are present: - A field whose end offset is within size exists and is valid. - A field beyond size does not exist in this game: show "not available". cpp-norun bool has(const TelemetryHeader& h, std::size_t fieldOffset, std::size_t fieldSize) { return fieldOffset + fieldSize <= h.size; } // has(header, offsetof(TelemetryV2, cpuMs), sizeof(float)) - is CPU time published? The reader copies min(h.size, sizeof(its own struct)) bytes and zero-fills the rest, so an old tool reading a new game copies only what it knows, and a new tool reading an old game gets zeros it knows not to trust. Rule 3: major and minor versions Some changes cannot be made compatible (a field's meaning changes, units change from pixels to tiles). Split the version into major and minor : Change Version --- --- Fields added at the end Minor + 1: compatible, nothing breaks Meaning or layout of existing data changed Major + 1: incompatible; tools for the old major must refuse A tool accepts any minor version of the majors it supports, and clearly reports "this game uses telemetry format 3.x; this tool supports 2.x" otherwise. The practice task implements this decision. Rule 4: feature flags for optional things Not everything is "present or not" by version. A features bit field (lesson 1.02's bits) says which optional parts the game actually provides right now: 0x1 "AI debug data", 0x2 "physics counters". Tools show panels only for set flags. It also lets a shipping build publish less than a development build of the same version. Messages on pipes The same rules apply to messages (lesson 12.01's pipes): - Every message starts with a type and a length , so a reader can skip types it does not know. - New message types get new numbers; old numbers are never reused for different meanings. - On connecting, each side sends a hello with its version and features, and both use the common subset. Common mistakes !warning Inserting a field in the middle "where it belongs" Every later field moves, and every older tool misreads them. Append. !warning Reading fields beyond the writer's size They contain whatever is in memory there, or nothing. Check against size . !warning Silently accepting an unknown major version Refuse with a clear message; misread data is worse than none. Knowledge check quiz ? Where must new fields go in a shared structure? + At the end, so every existing field keeps its offset - Wherever they fit best - At the start Inserting moves later fields and breaks older readers. ? A tool's struct is 64 bytes; the game's header says size 48. What does that mean? + The game is older: fields past byte 48 do not exist there and must be treated as unavailable - The game is newer - The data is corrupt The size field tells the reader what the writer provided. ? When must the major version change? + When existing data changes meaning or layout, so older readers would misread it - Whenever a field is added - Every release Additions at the end only need a minor version.

title: Can this tool read that game?
match: Can this tool read that game?
where: 12.06 Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
body: A tool supports telemetry major version toolMajor and knows minor versions up to toolMinor . A game publishes a header with its major , minor and size (bytes). Write check(toolMajor, toolMinor, gameMajor, gameMinor) : - different major versions: Incompatible ; - same major, game minor higher than the tool's: NewerGame (works; the tool ignores fields it does not know); - same major, game minor lower than the tool's: OlderGame (works; some fields will be missing); - otherwise Exact . Then fieldAvailable(gameSize, offset, size) : true if a field at offset of size bytes lies entirely within the game's struct size. Guard against overflow in offset + size .

title: 12.07  Testing and Hardening a Tool
body: A tool that crashes, hangs or shows wrong numbers is worse than none: people stop trusting it. This lesson hardens the chapter's tools: treating everything read from another process as untrusted input, validating snapshots, timeouts and reconnection, running with least privilege, and testing the logic separately from the platform code, including deliberately feeding it garbage. Everything from outside is untrusted The telemetry block, pipe messages and memory read from another process all come from a different program, which may be an older or newer version, half-initialised, crashed in the middle of writing, or simply buggy. Treat it exactly like a file from the internet: Check Why --- --- Header: magic, version, size (lesson 12.06) Is this even the right kind of data? Sizes and counts against limits A count of 2 billion monsters means corruption, not a busy floor Ranges Health between 0 and its maximum; positions inside the map; frame time positive and below, say, 10 seconds Consistency Frame number never goes backwards (except after a restart, which the process id change reveals) Strings Fixed-size character arrays must contain a terminator within their size (lesson 2.08) A value that fails a check is shown as invalid, not used to index arrays or size allocations. The practice task writes a validator returning a list of problems. Never hang Every wait in a tool needs a limit: - Sequence-lock reads retry a bounded number of times (lesson 12.04). - Pipe reads use overlapped I/O or a timeout, so a game that stops responding does not freeze the tool. - Opening the game's mapping happens on a timer, not in a tight loop. If the game is frozen, the tool should say so (lesson 12.05's "stale" state) and stay responsive. Least privilege The chapter's tools need very little: - Read-only views of the shared memory ( FILE_MAP_READ ). - PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION SYNCHRONIZE on the game's process, to watch whether it runs. - No administrator rights, ever: if a tool seems to need elevation, something in its design is wrong (lesson 6.08). Asking for little keeps the tool working for ordinary users and limits the harm any bug in it can do. Testing the logic Every practice task in this course has followed one structure: the logic (formatting, validation, version checks, statistics, protocols) is plain C++ with no Windows calls, tested in isolation; a thin platform layer does the Windows calls. That pays off most in tools: - Unit tests feed the logic known inputs, including recorded real snapshots, and check the outputs. - Garbage tests feed it random bytes, truncated blocks, wrong versions, extreme values. The tool must report problems, never crash. Chapter 17 automates this as fuzzing . - End-to-end tests run the real game with a scripted input and check the tool shows what was expected. Failure modes to rehearse Before calling a tool done, try each of these on purpose: 1. Start the tool with no game running. 2. Start the game, then the tool; close the game; start it again. 3. Pause the game in the debugger while the tool watches. 4. Run two copies of the game. 5. Run an older and a newer build of the game against the same tool. 6. Corrupt the shared block from a test program (write random bytes into it). A tool that handles all six calmly can be trusted. Common mistakes !warning Using an untrusted count to size an allocation A corrupt count of billions turns into a crash or an out-of-memory. Validate against a sensible limit first. !warning Waiting without a timeout A frozen game must not freeze its tools. !warning Testing only the happy path Rehearse the failure modes; they are what users will hit. Knowledge check quiz ? A telemetry snapshot says 3 billion monsters are alive. What should the tool do? + Treat the snapshot as invalid and report it, rather than using the number - Display 3 billion - Allocate an array of 3 billion entries Implausible values mean corruption or a version mismatch. ? Why keep a tool's logic free of Windows calls? + So it can be unit-tested and fed garbage without a running game - Windows calls are slow - The compiler requires it A thin platform layer around pure logic is easy to test. ? What rights does a read-only stats tool need on the game's process? + Limited query information and synchronize, to see whether it is still running - Full access - Administrator rights Least privilege: nothing more than its job needs.

title: Validate a snapshot
body: Write problems(snapshot, previousFrame) , which checks a telemetry snapshot from Delve and returns a list of problem names, in this order, for each check that fails: Check Problem name --- --- magic is 0x54564C44 "magic" version is 1 "version" size is at least 48 "size" frame is not less than previousFrame "frame went backwards" frameMs is greater than 0 and less than 10000 "frame time" floor is between 1 and 99 "floor" playerMaxHp is between 1 and 10000, and playerHp between 0 and playerMaxHp "health" monstersAlive is between 0 and 10000 "monsters" If the magic number is wrong, return only { "magic" } : nothing else in the block can be trusted. An empty list means the snapshot is valid. Remember that frameMs could be NaN (not a number): it must fail the check.

title: 13.01  How Games Support Mods
body: Many of the most loved games owe much of their life to mods : changes and additions made by players. Games that support modding on purpose provide layers for it: replaceable data and assets, scripting, plugin APIs and official editors. This lesson surveys those layers, how mods are found and loaded in order, how conflicts arise, and the responsibilities that come with letting other people's code run inside your game. Layers of modding Layer What modders change Example Risk to the game --- --- --- --- Data Numbers and definitions: items, monsters, levels A monsters.ini with tougher trolls Low: data is validated on load Assets Textures, models, sounds, text A new tile set or translation Low Scripts Behaviour, through an embedded language (lesson 10.08) A new boss fight in Lua Medium: limited by the API the game exposes Plugins Native code (DLLs) through a plugin API A new rendering effect or game system High: native code can do anything the game can Official tools Whole levels and campaigns, in the developers' editor Map editors, mod kits Low to medium Delve will support the first four in this chapter: data and asset overrides (lesson 13.02), and a plugin API for DLLs (13.03, 13.04), with scripting as an extension of lesson 10.08. Mods as a folder with a manifest Each mod is a folder with a small description, its manifest : mods\ tougher-trolls\ mod.ini name, version, author, which game versions it supports data\monsters.ini overrides the base game's file lantern-light\ mod.ini plugin.dll native code (lesson 13.04) textures\light.png ini ; mod.ini name = Lantern light version = 1.2.0 author = Ada game = 1.0, 1.1 requires = tougher-trolls The game reads every manifest at start-up, shows a list where players enable mods and choose their order, and refuses mods for incompatible game versions with a clear message, rather than loading them and crashing. Load order and conflicts When two mods change the same thing, one has to win. Games resolve this with a load order : mods later in the list override earlier ones, and the base game is first. Whole-file replacement means the last mod's file wins completely and the earlier mod's changes vanish: a conflict . Smarter games merge at the level of individual entries, so tougher-trolls can change troll health and easy-mode change goblin damage without fighting (lesson 13.02's practice task). Dependencies ( requires ) add ordering constraints: a mod must load after the mods it builds on (lesson 13.04's practice task sorts them). Responsibilities Supporting mods means letting other people's work run inside your game, for your players. That brings duties: - Stability : a broken mod should fail clearly ("mod X failed to load: ..."), not crash the game or corrupt saves. Lesson 13.07 covers isolation. - Safety : native plugins can do anything, so players should only install them from sources they trust, and the game should make it obvious when native code is involved. Data and script mods are much safer, which is why many games restrict mods to them. - Saves : record which mods (and versions) a save was made with, and warn when loading it without them. - Online play : anything affecting other players must be controlled by the server, and mods that change gameplay usually belong only in single-player or in servers that opt in. Modding games you did not make is governed by their licence and community rules. Common mistakes !warning Loading every mod without checking versions Read the manifest and refuse incompatible mods with a clear message. !warning Silent conflicts Show which mods change the same files or entries, so players can fix their load order. !warning Letting mods corrupt saves Record the mod list in each save, and warn before loading it with different mods. Knowledge check quiz ? What decides which mod wins when two change the same entry? + The load order: later mods override earlier ones - The newest mod file - The largest mod The base game is first; each mod in the list overrides what came before. ? Why are data and script mods safer than plugin DLLs? + Data is validated and scripts can only use the functions the game exposes, while native code can do anything the game can - They are smaller - They load faster Many games limit mods to data and scripts for this reason. ? What does a mod's manifest typically contain? + Its name, version, author, the game versions it supports, and the mods it requires - Its source code - A copy of the game The game uses it to list, order and check mods.

title: 13.02  Data Mods and Scripting
body: The simplest and safest mods change data. This lesson gives Delve a layered file system that looks for each file in the enabled mods (last first) before the base game, then improves on whole-file replacement by merging data entries so several mods can change different things in the same file. It ends by opening the game's scripting to mods, with limits. A layered file system The game never opens data\monsters.ini directly. It asks the virtual file system for monsters.ini , which searches the layers from the top: layer 3: mods\easy-mode\data\ (last in the load order: searched first) layer 2: mods\tougher-trolls\data\ layer 1: data\ (the base game: searched last) cpp-norun class VirtualFileSystem { public: void addLayer(std::filesystem::path root) { m_layers.push_back(std::move(root)); } // base first, mods after // The path of the file that wins, or nothing if no layer has it. std::optional<std::filesystem::path find(const std::string& relative) const { for (auto it{ m_layers.rbegin() }; it != m_layers.rend(); ++it) // top layer first if (auto candidate{ it / relative }; std::filesystem::exists(candidate)) return candidate; return std::nullopt; } // Every layer's version, base first: for merging. std::vector<std::filesystem::path findAll(const std::string& relative) const; private: std::vector<std::filesystem::path m_layers; }; Every asset the game loads, textures, sounds, levels, goes through find . Replacing a texture is then just putting a file with the same name in a mod folder. This is the same idea games use for their own patches: a patch is a layer above the original data. Validate paths. A mod asks for files by relative name; reject names containing .. or absolute paths, so a mod cannot reach files outside its own and the game's folders (lesson 17.04). Merging instead of replacing Whole-file replacement makes mods fight: two mods both shipping monsters.ini means only the last one's file is used. Merging works entry by entry: 1. Load the base game's monsters.ini into a map of section.key → value (lesson 10.08's INI parser). 2. For each enabled mod in load order, load its monsters.ini (if any) and overwrite only the keys it contains . 3. The result is the base game plus every mod's changes, with later mods winning only where they touch the same key. base: troll.health = 120 goblin.damage = 4 tougher-trolls: troll.health = 200 easy-mode: goblin.damage = 2 merged: troll.health = 200 goblin.damage = 2 both mods apply The practice task implements the merge and reports which keys were changed by more than one mod, the true conflicts a mod manager should show. Mod scripts If the game embeds a scripting language (lesson 10.08), mods can add behaviour too: each mod's scripts\ folder is run at start-up, and scripts register for events the game publishes ("monster died", "level loaded"; lesson 13.05 builds the event system): lua -- mods/lantern-light/scripts/main.lua on("level_loaded", function(floor) if floor = 3 then message("It is getting dark. Your lantern flickers.") end end) The game decides exactly which functions scripts may call ( on , message , spawn ...), and each mod's scripts should run in their own environment so they cannot overwrite another mod's functions. A script error is caught, reported with the mod's name, and the mod is disabled for the session, without taking the game down (lesson 13.07). Common mistakes !warning Opening files directly in game code Go through the virtual file system so mods (and patches) can override them. !warning Accepting .. in paths from mods A mod could then read or overwrite files anywhere. Reject them. !warning Whole-file replacement for shared data Merge entries so independent mods can coexist. Knowledge check quiz ? In which order does the layered file system search? + From the last mod in the load order down to the base game - From the base game up - Alphabetically The topmost layer that has the file wins. ? Two mods change different keys of monsters.ini . With merging, what happens? + Both changes apply - Only the last mod's file is used - The game refuses to start Merging overwrites only the keys each mod contains. ? Why reject .. in file names requested by mods? + It could reach files outside the mod and game folders - Windows does not allow it - It is slower Mods must stay within their own layer.

title: Merge mod data
body: Write mergeData(base, mods) . base maps "section.key" to a value. mods is the list of enabled mods in load order; each has a name and its own map of entries. Return: - values : the merged data, starting from base and applying each mod's entries in order, later mods overwriting earlier ones; - source : for each key in values , the name of the mod that set it last, or "base" ; - conflicts : the keys set by two or more mods (whatever the base had), in alphabetical order. base: troll.health 120, goblin.damage 4 tougher-trolls: troll.health 200 easy-mode: goblin.damage 2, troll.health 90 - troll.health 90 (from easy-mode), goblin.damage 2 (from easy-mode) conflicts: { "troll.health" }

title: 13.03  Designing a Plugin Interface
body: A plugin is native code built separately from the game, possibly with a different compiler version, that the game loads at run time. The interface between them must therefore be a stable C interface : plain types, function pointers, explicit versions and sizes. This lesson designs Delve's plugin API in both directions (the host API the game offers plugins, and the plugin API plugins offer the game) using lessons 4.05, 3.04 and 12.06. Two directions - The host API is what the game lets plugins do. It defines the plugin's powers, so it is designed carefully and kept small. - The plugin API is what every plugin must provide, so the game can initialise it, call it each frame, and shut it down. Rule 1: a C interface, not C++ classes The game and a plugin may be built with different compilers, settings or standard library versions. Lesson 4.05 explained why std::string , std::vector and C++ classes with virtual functions must not cross that boundary. The interface uses only: - integers, floats, and fixed-size plain structs; - const char strings in UTF-8, valid only for the duration of the call (copy them if you need them later); - function pointers; - opaque handles ( typedef struct DelveEntity DelveEntityHandle; , or plain integer ids, lesson 3.10). Rule 2: tables of function pointers, with a version and a size Both directions are structs of function pointers , the hand-made vtables of lesson 3.05's practice task, each starting with lesson 12.06's version and size: cpp-norun // delve_plugin.h: the only header plugins include. C-compatible. pragma once include <stdint.h define DELVE_API_VERSION_MAJOR 1 define DELVE_API_VERSION_MINOR 0 typedef struct DelveHostApi { uint32_t size; // sizeof(DelveHostApi) as the game was built: fields past it do not exist uint16_t versionMajor, versionMinor; void ( log)(const char message); int ( spawnMonster)(const char kind, int x, int y); // returns an entity id, or -1 int ( giveItem)(const char itemId, int count); // returns how many did not fit int ( playerHealth)(void); void ( subscribe)(const char eventName, void ( handler)(const char eventName, int64_t value, void user), void user); // version 1.1 and later add fields here, at the end only } DelveHostApi; typedef struct DelvePluginApi { uint32_t size; uint16_t versionMajor, versionMinor; const char name; int ( init)(const DelveHostApi host); // return 0 for success void ( update)(double dt); // may be null if the plugin needs no per-frame work void ( shutdown)(void); } DelvePluginApi; // The one function every plugin DLL exports: // extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) int delvePluginEntry(DelvePluginApi out); // The game passes a zeroed struct whose size it sets; the plugin fills it in. Why this shape: - One exported function ( delvePluginEntry ) instead of many keeps GetProcAddress lookups to one and the export table simple (lesson 4.05). - Function pointers in a struct let the game add functions later (at the end, lesson 12.06) without breaking old plugins. - size and the version let each side check what the other supports: a plugin built for API 1.0 runs on a 1.3 game; a plugin needing 1.3 refuses politely on a 1.0 game. - void user in callbacks lets a plugin get back its own state when the game calls it, since C function pointers carry no data (lesson 3.04). Rule 3: ownership is explicit Every pointer crossing the boundary has a documented owner and lifetime: - Strings passed into a plugin call are valid only during the call. - The host API table stays valid until shutdown returns. - Memory a plugin allocates, the plugin frees; memory the game allocates, the game frees (lesson 4.05: different heaps). Write these rules in comments in the header: it is the plugin authors' only documentation. Rule 4: the host API decides what plugins can do Every function in DelveHostApi is a capability given to code you did not write. Expose gameplay-level operations (spawn, give, read health, subscribe to events), validated like console commands (lesson 11.07), not raw pointers into the game's internals. A plugin that can only call spawnMonster("goblin", x, y) cannot corrupt the entity storage; one handed a pointer to it can. Native code can still do anything in principle (it runs in your process), but a good API means well-behaved plugins never need to. Common mistakes !warning C++ types in the interface std::string , std::vector , exceptions and classes do not cross a DLL boundary safely. Use C types. !warning No version or size The first change to the API breaks every existing plugin silently. !warning Exposing internal pointers Give plugins operations, not access to your data structures. !warning Throwing exceptions across the boundary C++ exceptions must not escape a plugin into the game (or the reverse). Catch them at the boundary and return error codes. Knowledge check quiz ? Why is the plugin interface written in C rather than C++ classes? + The game and plugins may be built with different compilers or settings, and only plain C types and function pointers are reliably compatible - C is faster - DLLs cannot contain C++ Lesson 4.05's rules for DLL boundaries. ? Why does every API table start with a size and version? + So each side can tell which functions the other provides, and add new ones at the end without breaking old plugins - To make the struct aligned - Windows requires it Lesson 12.06's versioning, applied to function tables. ? What is the void user parameter in the event callback for? + It lets the plugin pass its own state pointer, which the game hands back when it calls the callback - It holds the event's value - It is reserved for the game C function pointers carry no data; this pointer does.

title: Check a plugin's table
body: Before the game calls a plugin, it checks the PluginTable the plugin filled in. Write validatePlugin(table, hostMajor, hostMinor) , which returns a list of problems (empty if the plugin can be used), checking in this order: 1. size must be at least kMinimumSize (the size of version 1.0 of the table): otherwise "table too small" , and stop. 2. versionMajor must equal hostMajor : otherwise "wrong major version" , and stop. 3. versionMinor must not be greater than hostMinor : otherwise "needs a newer game" . 4. name must not be null or empty: otherwise "no name" . 5. init and shutdown must not be null: otherwise "missing init" / "missing shutdown" . ( update is optional.) Then write callUpdate(table, dt) , which calls update only if it is not null and the table's size covers it, and returns whether it was called.

title: 13.04  Plugins as DLLs
body: With the interface designed, Delve can load plugins: find each enabled mod's DLL, load it safely, call its entry point, validate what it returns, order plugins by their dependencies, call them each frame, and unload them cleanly. This lesson writes the plugin manager, and adds hot reloading of your own plugins during development. Loading one plugin cpp-norun using EntryFn = int ( )(DelvePluginApi ); std::optional<LoadedPlugin loadPlugin(const std::filesystem::path& dll, const DelveHostApi& host) { // Load by full path, searching only the plugin's own folder and the system for its dependencies (lesson 5.08). HMODULE module{ LoadLibraryExW(dll.c_str(), nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) }; if (!module) { logError("could not load ", dll, ": error ", GetLastError()); return std::nullopt; } auto entry{ reinterpret_cast<EntryFn (GetProcAddress(module, "delvePluginEntry")) }; DelvePluginApi api{}; api.size = sizeof(api); // tell the plugin how big our table is if (!entry entry(&api) != 0 !validatePlugin(api, DELVE_API_VERSION_MAJOR, DELVE_API_VERSION_MINOR).empty()) { logError(dll, " is not a valid Delve plugin"); FreeLibrary(module); return std::nullopt; } if (api.init(&host) != 0) { logError(api.name, " failed to initialise"); FreeLibrary(module); return std::nullopt; } return LoadedPlugin{ module, api }; } Each step can fail, and each failure is logged with the plugin's path or name and leaves the game running without it. validatePlugin is lesson 13.03's practice task. Load order with dependencies Mods declare what they require (lesson 13.01's manifest). A plugin must be initialised after everything it requires, and shut down before them. Finding such an order is a topological sort : repeatedly take a mod whose requirements are all already placed. If at some point no mod can be placed, the requirements form a cycle (A requires B, B requires A), and those mods cannot be loaded. The practice task implements it, preferring the player's chosen order where the dependencies allow. Calling plugins cpp-norun void PluginManager::update(double dt) { for (LoadedPlugin& p : m_plugins) // in load order if (p.api.update) p.api.update(dt); } void PluginManager::shutdown() { for (auto it{ m_plugins.rbegin() }; it != m_plugins.rend(); ++it) // reverse order { it- api.shutdown(); FreeLibrary(it- module); // after this, no pointer into the DLL may be used } m_plugins.clear(); } Shutting down in reverse order mirrors lesson 2.04's destructor order: a plugin may depend on those loaded before it. Before FreeLibrary , the game must forget every callback the plugin registered (event handlers, console commands), or a later event would call into unloaded code (lesson 4.05). Hot reloading your own plugins During development, rebuilding a plugin and reloading it without restarting the game makes iteration fast: 1. Watch the plugin's DLL file for changes (lesson 10.06's ReadDirectoryChangesW ). 2. Copy the new DLL to a temporary name and load the copy, because Windows locks a loaded DLL file and the compiler could not overwrite it otherwise. (The PDB has the same problem; give each build a unique PDB name.) 3. Call the old plugin's shutdown , remove its callbacks, FreeLibrary it, then init the new one. 4. State that must survive the reload (a debug tool's settings) is saved by shutdown and restored by init , or kept on the game's side. Hot reloading is for your own development builds; players restart the game to update mods. Common mistakes !warning Loading plugins by bare name Use full paths and restricted search flags, so a plugin's dependencies cannot be hijacked (lesson 5.08). !warning Keeping callbacks after unloading Unregister everything a plugin registered before FreeLibrary . !warning Shutting down in load order Shut down in reverse, so dependents go before what they depend on. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a topological sort of mods produce? + An order in which every mod comes after all the mods it requires - Mods sorted by name - Mods sorted by size A cycle in the requirements makes such an order impossible. ? Why copy a plugin DLL before loading it for hot reloading? + Windows locks a loaded DLL's file, so the build could not overwrite it otherwise - Copies load faster - To make it read-only Loading the copy leaves the original free for the compiler. ? Why must a plugin's callbacks be removed before FreeLibrary ? + After unloading, calling them would jump into memory that no longer holds the plugin's code - To save memory - Windows requires it A dangling function pointer is as dangerous as a dangling data pointer.

title: Order mods by their requirements
body: Write loadOrder(mods) . Each mod has a name and the names it needs ( requires is a keyword in C++20, so it cannot be a member name). The list is in the player's preferred order. Return: - order : the names in an order where every mod comes after all the mods it requires. Among mods that are ready (all their requirements placed), always take the one that comes first in the player's list , so the player's order is kept wherever the requirements allow. - missing : mods that require a mod not in the list (they cannot load, and neither can anything requiring them), alphabetical. - cycle : mods left over because their requirements form a cycle, alphabetical. Mods in missing or cycle do not appear in order . player's order: ui (requires core), core, extra (requires ui, missing-mod), maps - order: core, ui, maps (ui must wait for core) missing: extra

title: 13.05  Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
match: 13.05 Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
body: Instrumentation means adding observation points to a program: measuring how long functions take, counting calls, recording events, letting plugins react to what happens. The cleanest way is to design the points in from the start: scoped timers, an event bus that plugins and tools subscribe to, and indirection through function pointers where behaviour should be replaceable. This lesson builds those, and looks at compiler-assisted instrumentation for your own builds. Observation points you design in Code becomes observable and extensible when it announces what it does at well-chosen places. Three patterns cover nearly everything: Pattern Use Example --- --- --- Scoped timers How long did this take? PROFILE_SCOPE("ai") at the top of the AI system Events Something happened; whoever cares can react "monster died", "level loaded", "item picked up" Replaceable functions Let a plugin or test change one behaviour A damage formula stored in a function pointer the plugin can replace Scoped timers Lesson 8.08's ScopedTimer , wrapped in a macro so it can be compiled out: cpp-norun ifdef DELVE_PROFILE define PROFILE_SCOPE(name) ProfileScope profileScope_ __LINE__{ name } else define PROFILE_SCOPE(name) ((void)0) endif void updateMonsters(World& w) { PROFILE_SCOPE("monsters"); // ... } Each ProfileScope records a start and end time into a per-thread buffer; once a frame the samples are summarised (lesson 8.08's practice task) and published through the telemetry channel (lesson 12.04), where the stats panel graphs them. That is a complete profiling pipeline built from this course's pieces. An event bus Hard-wiring "when a monster dies, update the quest, play a sound, drop loot, notify plugins" into the combat code makes it grow without end. An event bus decouples them: the combat code publishes "monster died", and any number of systems, plugins and tools subscribe to it. Design details that matter: - Subscriptions return a handle used to unsubscribe, which is essential for plugins being unloaded (lesson 13.04). - Priorities decide the order handlers run in, when it matters (the quest system before the "you win" check). - Unsubscribing during dispatch (a handler that removes itself) must be safe: mark the handler removed and clean up after the dispatch finishes, rather than erasing from the list being iterated (lesson 3.07). - A handler that throws must not stop the others, and must be reported (lesson 13.07). The practice task builds this bus. Replaceable functions Where you want behaviour to be swappable, put a function pointer at the decision point, with a default: cpp-norun using DamageFn = int ( )(const Attack&, const Defence&, Random&); DamageFn g_damageFormula{ &defaultDamage }; // plugins may set this through the host API int resolveHit(const Attack& a, const Defence& d, Random& rng) { return g_damageFormula(a, d, rng); } Tests use the same indirection to substitute a fixed formula. It costs one indirect call (lesson 3.04), which is nothing outside the hottest loops. Compiler-assisted instrumentation For deeper investigation of your own builds, MSVC can insert a call at the start and end of every function: compile with /Gh (calls a function named _penter on entry) and /GH ( _pexit on exit), which you write yourself, for example to record a call trace or count calls per function. It slows the program considerably, so it belongs in a special build configuration, but it instruments every function without touching the source. For instrumenting functions of your own program at run time in test builds, Microsoft's open-source Detours library intercepts calls to chosen functions (including Windows API functions your program calls) and redirects them to your own code, which can record the call and pass it on. It is useful for testing how your program behaves when, say, file writes fail. As with the rest of this chapter, it is for your own programs and your own test builds. Common mistakes !warning Hard-coding every reaction at the source of an event Publish events and let systems subscribe; the source stays small. !warning Erasing handlers while dispatching Mark them and remove them after the dispatch. !warning Leaving profiling in shipping builds by accident Compile it out with a macro. Knowledge check quiz ? What problem does an event bus solve? + The code where something happens does not need to know about every system that reacts to it - It makes events happen faster - It replaces function calls entirely Publishers and subscribers are decoupled. ? Why must subscribing return something that can unsubscribe? + Plugins and systems that go away must remove their handlers, or the bus will call into freed code - To count subscribers - Because events are expensive Lesson 13.04's unloading depends on it. ? What do MSVC's /Gh and /GH options do? + Insert calls to _penter and _pexit at the start and end of every function, for instrumentation builds - Turn on optimisation - Generate debug symbols You supply those functions, for example to trace calls.

title: An event bus
where: 13.05 Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
