body: Build EventBus for Delve. - subscribe(event, priority, handler) registers a std::function<void(long long value) for an event name and returns a subscription id (any number unique to this bus). - publish(event, value) calls every handler for that event, highest priority first ; handlers with equal priority run in the order they subscribed. It returns how many handlers ran. - unsubscribe(id) removes a subscription and returns whether it existed. It must be safe to call from inside a handler during publish , including for the handler itself or for one that has not run yet in this dispatch (which then must not run). - Handlers subscribed during a publish do not run in that same dispatch.

title: 13.06  A Debug Menu Inside the Game
match: 13.06 A Debug Menu Inside the Game
body: A console is fast for people who remember commands; a debug menu drawn over the game is faster for everyone else: checkboxes for god mode and map reveal, sliders for monster speed, buttons to spawn things, live graphs. This lesson registers tweakable variables in one place, draws them with Dear ImGui (previewing chapter 14), and lets plugins add their own sections. Tweakables Game feel comes from dozens of numbers: player move time, monster sight range, screen shake strength, drop chances. Changing them by editing code and rebuilding is slow. A tweakable is a variable registered once with a name, a range and a description, which the debug menu (and console, and save of settings) can then show and change while the game runs: cpp-norun float g_moveSlideSeconds{ 0.12f }; int g_sightRange{ 8 }; bool g_godMode{ false }; void registerTweakables(Tweakables& t) { t.addFloat("player.slide", &g_moveSlideSeconds, 0.0f, 0.5f, "Seconds to slide between tiles"); t.addInt ("monster.sight", &g_sightRange, 1, 30, "Tiles at which monsters notice the player"); t.addBool ("cheat.god", &g_godMode, "Player takes no damage"); } The registry stores, for each name, a pointer to the variable, its type and its limits. Everything else is built on that table: - the debug menu draws a slider or checkbox per entry, grouped by the part of the name before the dot; - the console gets set monster.sight 12 and get player.slide for free (lesson 11.07); - values can be saved to tweaks.ini and loaded at start-up (lesson 10.08), so a good setting found while playing survives. Setting from text must parse, range-check and clamp, which is exactly the part worth testing: the practice task builds the registry's core. Drawing it with Dear ImGui Dear ImGui draws interfaces in immediate mode : every frame, the code that draws the menu simply calls one function per widget, and the function returns whether the user changed it. There is no separate interface state to keep in sync. Chapter 14 covers it fully; here is enough for a menu: cpp-norun void drawDebugMenu(Tweakables& t, Game& game) { ImGui::Begin("Debug"); if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Cheats")) { ImGui::Checkbox("God mode", &g_godMode); if (ImGui::Button("Reveal map")) game.revealMap(); if (ImGui::Button("Full health")) game.player.health = game.player.maxHealth; } if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Tweakables")) for (Tweakable& tw : t.all()) tw.drawWidget(); // SliderFloat / SliderInt / Checkbox by type if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Performance")) ImGui::PlotLines("Frame ms", frameHistory.data(), frameHistory.size()); ImGui::End(); } ImGui is added with vcpkg ( imgui sdl2-binding,sdl2-renderer-binding , lesson 4.06), initialised once with the SDL window and renderer, and drawn last each frame, on top of the game. The menu opens with F1; while it has the mouse or keyboard focus, the game ignores that input ( ImGui::GetIO().WantCaptureMouse and WantCaptureKeyboard ). Plugin sections Plugins (lesson 13.04) can add their own sections: the host API gains addDebugSection(name, drawFunction, user) , the game calls each registered draw function inside the menu, and unregisters it when the plugin unloads. A plugin author then gets a place for their own debugging tools without touching the game. Keep it out of release builds Like the console's cheat commands (lesson 11.07), the menu and every tweakable that changes gameplay are compiled only into development builds. Tweakables that are really player settings (volume, shake) move to the real settings screen instead. Common mistakes !warning Tweaking values that are cached elsewhere If a system copied g_sightRange at start-up, changing it does nothing. Read tweakables where they are used. !warning No limits on tweakables A slider from 0 to a billion is useless and a typed value out of range can break the game. Give every tweakable a sensible range, and clamp. !warning The game reacting to clicks meant for the menu Check ImGui's capture flags before passing input to the game. Knowledge check quiz ? What does registering a tweakable give you? + One table from which the debug menu, console commands and saved settings are all built - A faster variable - A constant that cannot change Register once, use everywhere. ? What does "immediate mode" mean for Dear ImGui? + The interface is described anew each frame by function calls that return whether the user changed something - The interface appears instantly - The interface has no memory No separate widget objects to keep in sync with the data. ? Why check WantCaptureMouse before handling game input? + So clicks and keys used by the debug menu do not also act in the game - To find out where the mouse is - To enable the menu The menu and the game must not both react to the same input.

title: A tweakable registry
where: 13.06 A Debug Menu Inside the Game
body: Build Tweakables , the registry behind the debug menu. It holds integer, floating-point and boolean variables by name. - addInt(name, int value, min, max) , addFloat(name, float value, min, max) , addBool(name, bool value) register a variable. Registering a name again replaces the old entry. - set(name, text) parses text for that variable's type and stores it, clamped into its range: integers with std::stoi -like rules (the whole text must be a number), floats likewise, booleans from "true" / "false" / "1" / "0" / "on" / "off" . It returns a message: "name = value" on success (integers as digits, floats with std::to_string -like default formatting is not required: use std::format("{}", v) , booleans as true / false ), "unknown: name" for an unknown name, or "bad value: text" if the text cannot be parsed. On failure the variable is unchanged. - get(name) returns the current value as text in the same format, or std::nullopt for an unknown name. - names() returns all names, sorted. int sight = 8; addInt("monster.sight", &sight, 1, 30) set("monster.sight", "50") - "monster.sight = 30" (clamped) set("monster.sight", "lots") - "bad value: lots" (sight still 30)

title: 13.07  Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
match: 13.07 Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
body: A game with mods is a platform other people build on. This lesson covers the architecture that keeps it stable: isolating failures so one broken mod cannot take the game down, budgets for mod work, keeping saves safe, versioning everything mods touch, diagnosing problems from players' reports, and the honest limits of isolating native code. Failures must stay local With twenty mods installed, something will go wrong eventually. The architecture decides whether that means "mod X stopped working, the game told you why" or "the game crashes on start-up and nobody knows why". Kind of mod How to contain a failure --- --- Data Validate on load; report the mod, file, line and key; skip the bad entry (lessons 10.08, 13.02) Scripts Catch script errors at each call into the script; report the mod and line; disable that mod's scripts for the session Plugins Catch C++ exceptions at the boundary; validate tables (lesson 13.03); count failures and disable a plugin that keeps failing The practice task builds the plugin guard: every call into a plugin goes through it, exceptions are caught and recorded against the plugin, and after a few failures the plugin is switched off for the rest of the session with a message to the player. The limits of isolating native code A plugin DLL runs inside the game's process with the same memory and rights (lesson 13.04). Catching exceptions handles the polite failures. An impolite one (a plugin writing through a dangling pointer, corrupting the heap) cannot be contained in-process: it can corrupt anything, and the crash may appear somewhere else entirely (lesson 2.09). The honest options: - Accept it and diagnose well : crash dumps (lesson 8.04) that record which plugins were loaded and which module the crash was in, so players and authors can find the culprit. - Offer safer layers : data and scripts (sandboxed, with only the functions the game exposes) cover most mods; native plugins are for the few that need them. - Out-of-process plugins : run plugins in a separate process talking through pipes or shared memory (chapter 12's channels). A crash there kills only the helper process. It costs speed and complexity, so it is used where stability matters most, such as editors and browsers. Budgets A mod that spends 20 ms per frame turns a smooth game into a slideshow, and players blame the game. Measure each plugin's and script's time per frame with lesson 13.05's scoped timers, show it in the debug menu and a mod list, and warn when one exceeds its budget. Scripting languages can also limit instruction counts per call, stopping infinite loops. Saves and mods Lesson 11.06's save format records the enabled mods and their versions. On loading: - Missing mod: warn, and either refuse or load with its content removed (items from a missing mod become "unknown item" placeholders rather than crashing the loader). - Different version: warn; the mod may provide a migration (lesson 10.07) for its own saved data. - Mods store their own data in namespaced sections ( mod.lantern-light.fuel ) so they cannot collide with each other or with the game. Diagnosing players' problems Most mod problems arrive as "the game crashes, I have 40 mods". Make diagnosis possible: 1. The log (lesson 8.03) starts with the game version and the full, ordered mod list with versions. 2. Every warning and error names the mod responsible. 3. Crash dumps include the module list; the crash report says which module the crash happened in (lesson 8.02). 4. A safe mode start option disables all mods, so players can confirm whether mods are involved, and a "disable half" option lets them bisect (lesson 8.01) to the culprit. Common mistakes !warning One bad mod stops the game from starting Validate, report and skip; never let a single mod's failure become the game's failure. !warning Claiming plugins are "sandboxed" Native code in your process is not. Be honest with players and offer safer layers. !warning Logs that do not say which mod Every message about a problem should name its source. Knowledge check quiz ? A plugin's update throws a C++ exception every frame. What should the game do? + Catch it at the boundary, record it against the plugin, and disable the plugin after a few failures, telling the player - Let it crash the game so the author notices - Ignore it forever Failures stay local, and are reported. ? Why can a native plugin's memory corruption not be fully contained inside the game process? + It shares the game's memory, so it can damage anything, and the crash may happen far from the cause - Because exceptions are disabled - Because DLLs are read-only Isolation from memory corruption needs a separate process. ? What is safe mode for? + Starting with all mods disabled, to find out whether a problem is caused by mods - Running the game faster - Protecting saves from players Then bisect the mod list to find the culprit.

title: A plugin guard
where: 13.07 Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
body: Build PluginGuard , through which the game calls every plugin. - call(plugin, fn) calls fn (a std::function<void() ) for the named plugin, unless that plugin is disabled. If fn throws any exception, the guard catches it, records one failure for the plugin together with the exception's message ( what() for std::exception , "unknown error" otherwise), and returns false . A successful call returns true ; a call to a disabled plugin returns false without running fn . - After maxFailures failures (given to the constructor) a plugin is disabled for the rest of the session. - disabled(plugin) says whether it is disabled; failures(plugin) how many failures it has; lastError(plugin) the last recorded message (empty if none). - report() lists, alphabetically, a line for every plugin with at least one failure: "name: N failure(s), last: MESSAGE" , followed by " (disabled)" if it is disabled.

title: 13.08  Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools
match: 13.08 Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools
body: Many games ship official modding support: editors, mod kits, scripting APIs and workshop integration. Working with them is the most productive and least fragile way to mod other people's games. This lesson covers what official tools usually provide, how to learn an unfamiliar one, the licensing of mod content, and how the design ideas of this chapter look from the modder's side. What official support usually provides Provided What it means for you --- --- An editor or mod kit The developers' own tools (or a version of them) for building levels, items and quests Documented data formats Files you can change with confidence, often with a schema A scripting API The functions the game exposes to mods, with documentation (lesson 13.02) A plugin SDK Headers and libraries for native plugins (lesson 13.03), versioned with the game Distribution A workshop or mod portal: upload, update, dependencies, ratings Rules A licence or end-user agreement for mods: what you may do and distribute Games known for strong official support include those built on engines that ship their editors (Unreal Engine's mod kits for particular games, the Source SDK, Bethesda's Creation Kit) and games with scripting layers designed for mods (Factorio's Lua API, Minecraft's data packs and resource packs, many strategy games). Godot and Unity games sometimes expose their own systems in similar ways. Learning an unfamiliar mod kit The approach is the same as lesson 10.09's for reading source: 1. Read the official documentation and examples first. Mod kits encode the developers' intentions; working against them leads to fragile mods. 2. Start from an example mod that does something close to what you want, change one thing, and get it loading. 3. Learn the data model : what objects exist (items, actors, quests), how they reference each other (by id, lesson 10.07), and how load order and overrides work (lesson 13.02). 4. Use the official debugging aids : in-game consoles, log files, validation tools. The log is where most "why does my mod not load" questions are answered. 5. Join the community : modding communities keep wikis of undocumented behaviour, which save days. Making mods that last The game will be patched. Mods that survive updates: - use only documented interfaces, not internal details; - change entries , not whole files, where the game supports merging (lesson 13.02), so they coexist with other mods; - declare their dependencies and supported game versions in their manifest (lesson 13.01); - namespace their own ids ( yourname_lantern , not lantern ) so they cannot collide with other mods; - keep their own saved data separate and versioned (lesson 13.07). These are the same rules this chapter followed from the game's side, now applied as a mod author. Licensing and permissions - A game's mod licence or end-user agreement says what you may do: commonly, mods may be shared free of charge but not sold, and may not include the game's own assets beyond what the tools produce. - Content you include must be yours or properly licensed: music, textures and models from other sources carry their own licences. - Other modders' work belongs to them: ask before building on or redistributing it, and credit it. - Online games deserve particular care: mods that change shared gameplay are usually allowed only where the game explicitly supports them (official servers with mod support, or private servers), never as a way to gain an advantage over other players. Common mistakes !warning Ignoring the official tools and working around them Unsupported approaches break with every patch. !warning Shipping assets you do not own Use your own work or properly licensed material, and credit it. !warning Generic ids Namespace everything your mod adds. Knowledge check quiz ? What is usually the first step with an unfamiliar mod kit? + Read the official documentation and start from an example mod - Reverse engineer the game's executable - Rewrite the game's data files from scratch Mod kits encode how the developers intend mods to work. ? Why namespace the ids your mod adds? + So they cannot collide with the game's ids or other mods' ids - To make them shorter - Because the game requires capital letters Two mods adding a lantern item would otherwise conflict. ? What do mod licences commonly allow and forbid? + Sharing mods free of charge is commonly allowed; selling them or redistributing the game's own assets usually is not - Anything at all - Nothing at all Always read the specific game's terms.

title: 14.01  Immediate-Mode Interfaces
body: Most application toolkits are retained mode : you create widget objects once and keep them in sync with your data. Immediate mode turns that around: every frame, code describes the whole interface with function calls, and each call both draws its widget and reports what the user did. This lesson explains the model, why it suits tools and games so well, and how it works underneath, with ids , hot and active widgets. Two ways to build an interface Retained mode (Windows controls, Qt, web pages): you create a button object, give it a callback, and it lives until you destroy it. When your data changes, you must update every widget that shows it; when a widget changes, a callback updates your data. Keeping the two in sync is a large part of interface code. Immediate mode (Dear ImGui, Nuklear, many in-house game tools): there are no widget objects in your code. Every frame you call functions that describe the interface as it should look now , reading directly from your data: cpp-norun // Every frame: ImGui::Begin("Player"); ImGui::Text("Health: %d / %d", player.hp, player.maxHp); // always shows the current value ImGui::SliderInt("Speed", &player.speed, 1, 10); // writes straight into your variable if (ImGui::Button("Heal")) player.hp = player.maxHp; // true on the frame it was clicked ImGui::End(); There is nothing to keep in sync: the interface is a function of your data, recomputed each frame, like rendering the game itself (lesson 10.01). Retained Immediate --- --- --- Widget objects in your code Yes, created and destroyed No Keeping data and interface in sync Your job Automatic: redrawn from data each frame Showing or hiding parts Create, destroy, show, hide An if around the calls Lists of changing length Add and remove widgets A for loop Cost Only changes are redrawn The whole interface is re-described every frame (cheap for tools) Best for Polished applications, accessibility, text-heavy forms Tools, debug interfaces, editors inside games How a button knows it was clicked If no button object exists between frames, how does Button("Heal") know the mouse went down on it last frame and up on it now? The library keeps a little state itself, keyed by an id for each widget, computed from its label (and the window and any pushed ids): - The hot widget is the one the mouse is over this frame. - The active widget is the one the mouse button went down on, and it stays active until the button is released. - A button reports a click when the mouse is released over it while it is active : press on it, release on it. So the only state that survives between frames is "which id is active" (plus a few things like scroll positions and window placement), not a tree of objects. The practice task implements exactly this logic. Ids and why labels must be unique Because ids come from labels, two buttons both labelled "Delete" in one window would share an id and behave as one. ImGui's answers: - "Delete 3" : text after is part of the id but not shown; - ImGui::PushID(i) / PopID() around each item in a loop, so every row's widgets get distinct ids. Forgetting this is the most common immediate-mode bug: clicking one row's button activates another. Why tools and games use it Game engines are already redrawing everything every frame, already have the data in memory, and need interfaces that change constantly with the game (debug views, editors, profilers). Immediate mode fits that loop exactly, and a tool window is a few dozen lines, so engineers actually write them. That is why Dear ImGui is in so many engines and tools, and why the next lessons use it for the chapter 12 tools. Common mistakes !warning Duplicate labels in one window Widgets share an id and behave strangely. Use suffix or PushID . !warning Keeping your own copies of values just for the interface The point is to read and write your real data directly. !warning Doing expensive work while describing the interface The description runs every frame; cache anything slow. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the main difference between immediate and retained mode? + Immediate mode re-describes the whole interface from the data every frame; retained mode keeps widget objects that must be kept in sync - Immediate mode is drawn by the GPU, retained mode by the CPU - Retained mode cannot show buttons No widget objects means nothing to keep in sync. ? When does an immediate-mode button report a click? + When the mouse is released over it while it is the active widget, that is, it was also pressed on it - As soon as the mouse is pressed over it - Whenever the mouse is over it Press and release on the same widget. ? Two "Delete" buttons in one window both react when either is clicked. Why? + They have the same label, so the same id - ImGui cannot draw two buttons - The window is too small Use Delete 1 , or PushID per row.

title: An immediate-mode button
body: Implement the heart of an immediate-mode interface: the hot and active logic for buttons. A Ui object is used once per frame: - beginFrame(mouseX, mouseY, mouseDown) starts a frame with the current mouse state. - button(id, x, y, w, h) is called for each button this frame. It returns true when the button was clicked : the mouse button was released this frame, over this button, and this button was the active one. - endFrame() finishes the frame. Rules, as in the lesson: - A button is hot if the mouse is inside its rectangle ( x <= mouseX < x + w , likewise for y). - If the mouse button goes down this frame (it was up last frame) while a button is hot, that button becomes active (if several overlap, the last one drawn wins). - The active button stays active while the mouse is held, even if the mouse moves off it. - When the mouse button is released, the active id is cleared at the end of the frame (whether or not a click happened). - active() returns the active id, or 0 for none; hot() the hot id of the last frame (0 for none; the last one drawn wins).

title: 14.02  Setting Up Dear ImGui
body: Dear ImGui is a small, widely used C++ library for immediate-mode interfaces. It does not draw anything itself: back ends connect it to a platform (for windows and input) and a renderer (for drawing). This lesson sets it up with vcpkg and the SDL2 back ends used by Delve, explains the per-frame calls, fonts and DPI scaling, and builds a standalone tool application for chapter 12's tools. How ImGui is put together The core turns widget calls into draw lists (triangles, textures, clip rectangles); a renderer back end submits them with whatever graphics API the program uses (lesson 10.04). Back ends exist for SDL, Win32, GLFW, DirectX 9 to 12, OpenGL, Vulkan, Metal and more, so ImGui fits into almost any engine. Installing In the project's vcpkg.json (lesson 4.06): powershell vcpkg add port imgui sdl2-binding,sdl2-renderer-binding The features in brackets build the SDL2 platform back end and the SDL renderer back end along with the core. The setup and the frame cpp-norun define SDL_MAIN_HANDLED include <SDL.h include <imgui.h include <imgui_impl_sdl2.h include <imgui_impl_sdlrenderer2.h int main() { SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_VIDEO); SDL_Window window{ SDL_CreateWindow("Delve Tools", SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, 1280, 800, SDL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE SDL_WINDOW_ALLOW_HIGHDPI) }; SDL_Renderer renderer{ SDL_CreateRenderer(window, -1, SDL_RENDERER_ACCELERATED SDL_RENDERER_PRESENTVSYNC) }; IMGUI_CHECKVERSION(); ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGuiIO& io{ ImGui::GetIO() }; io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableKeyboard; // keyboard navigation ImGui::StyleColorsDark(); ImGui_ImplSDL2_InitForSDLRenderer(window, renderer); ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_Init(renderer); bool running{ true }; while (running) { SDL_Event e; while (SDL_PollEvent(&e)) { ImGui_ImplSDL2_ProcessEvent(&e); // ImGui sees every event first if (e.type == SDL_QUIT) running = false; } ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_NewFrame(); // 1. start the frame ImGui_ImplSDL2_NewFrame(); ImGui::NewFrame(); ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); // 2. describe the interface ImGui::Begin("Hello"); ImGui::Text("Frame time %.2f ms", 1000.0f / io.Framerate); ImGui::End(); ImGui::Render(); // 3. build the draw lists SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(renderer, 18, 20, 26, 255); SDL_RenderClear(renderer); ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData(), renderer); // 4. draw them SDL_RenderPresent(renderer); } ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_Shutdown(); // shut down in reverse order ImGui_ImplSDL2_Shutdown(); ImGui::DestroyContext(); SDL_DestroyRenderer(renderer); SDL_DestroyWindow(window); SDL_Quit(); } Every ImGui program has these four steps per frame: new frame, describe, render, draw. In a game (lesson 13.06) the same steps run after the game has drawn its own frame, so the interface sits on top. The demo window ImGui::ShowDemoWindow() shows every widget ImGui has, each with a short explanation. Its source, imgui_demo.cpp , is the best reference there is: when you want a widget, find it in the demo window, then find the code that drew it. Keep the demo one menu click away in every tool you write. Fonts and DPI ImGui's built-in font is small and sharp at 100% display scaling. On high-DPI screens (laptops at 150%, 4K monitors) load a proper font at a size scaled for the display: cpp-norun const float scale{ dpiScaleForWindow(window) }; // e.g. from SDL_GetDisplayDPI / 96 io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf", 16.0f scale); ImGui::GetStyle().ScaleAllSizes(scale); Include the font file with the tool, under its own licence (Inter, for example, uses the SIL Open Font License). Input sharing ImGui_ImplSDL2_ProcessEvent gives ImGui every event. In a game, check io.WantCaptureMouse and io.WantCaptureKeyboard before the game uses an event (lesson 13.06); in a standalone tool, ImGui is the whole interface and there is nothing to share. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting one of the four frame steps Missing NewFrame or Render produces assertion failures or nothing on screen. !warning Calling ImGui functions outside a frame Widget calls are only valid between NewFrame and Render . !warning Blurry or tiny text on high-DPI screens Load a real font at a scaled size and scale the style. Knowledge check quiz ? What do ImGui's back ends do? + Connect the core to a platform for input and windows, and to a graphics API for drawing - Store your data - Compile the interface ahead of time The core only produces draw lists. ? What are the four steps of every ImGui frame? + Start the frame, describe the interface, render to draw lists, draw them with the renderer back end - Load, parse, layout, save - Create widgets, show them, hide them, destroy them Describe happens between NewFrame and Render . ? Where is the best reference for how to use a particular widget? + The demo window and its source file, imgui_demo.cpp - The draw lists - The back end's source Every widget is shown there with the code that draws it.

title: 14.03  Windows, Widgets and Layout
body: This lesson covers the ImGui toolkit you will use in every tool: windows and child regions, the common widgets (text, buttons, checkboxes, sliders, inputs, combos), how ImGui lays widgets out (top to bottom by default, SameLine to go across, groups, columns of fixed width), ids in loops, and disabling widgets. Windows cpp-norun ImGui::SetNextWindowSize({ 420, 300 }, ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); // only the first time ever; afterwards the user's size is kept if (ImGui::Begin("Monsters", &m_showMonsters)) // the bool adds a close button { // ... widgets ... } ImGui::End(); // always call End, even if Begin returned false Begin returns false when the window is collapsed or hidden, so you can skip describing its contents, but End must still be called. Child windows ( BeginChild / EndChild ) create scrolling regions inside a window: a log view, a list that scrolls while buttons stay put. The everyday widgets Widget Call Changes --- --- --- Text Text("HP %d", hp) , TextColored , TextWrapped , TextDisabled Nothing Button if (Button("Heal")) ... Returns true on click Checkbox Checkbox("God mode", &god) Toggles a bool Slider SliderInt("Sight", &sight, 1, 30) , SliderFloat Drag to set a value in a range Drag DragFloat("Speed", &speed, 0.05f) Drag to change without fixed limits Input InputInt("Gold", &gold) , InputText("Name", buf, sizeof buf) Typed values Combo Combo("Kind", &index, kinds, count) Picks one from a list Colour ColorEdit3("Tint", rgb) Edits a colour Separator, spacing Separator() , Spacing() , SeparatorText("Combat") Visual grouping Every widget that edits a value returns true on the frame the value changed, which is when to apply side effects (save a setting, send a command to the game): cpp-norun if (ImGui::SliderInt("Sight range", &m_sight, 1, 30)) sendToGame("set monster.sight " + std::to_string(m_sight)); // only when it actually changed Layout ImGui places widgets top to bottom , each on its own line, at the window's full width minus padding. To change that: Need Call --- --- Next widget on the same line SameLine() A fixed width for the next widget SetNextItemWidth(120) , or PushItemWidth / PopItemWidth for several Fill the remaining width SetNextItemWidth(-FLT_MIN) Treat several widgets as one block BeginGroup() / EndGroup() Indent Indent() / Unindent() Align text with framed widgets on the same line AlignTextToFramePadding() Columns A table (lesson 14.04) with no borders cpp-norun ImGui::AlignTextToFramePadding(); ImGui::Text("Floor"); ImGui::SameLine(80); // continue at x = 80, so rows line up ImGui::SetNextItemWidth(120); ImGui::InputInt(" floor", &m_floor); // hides the label but keeps an id ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Go")) sendToGame("goto " + std::to_string(m_floor)); This layout model is simple: a cursor moves down (or right, after SameLine ), and each widget advances it by its size plus spacing. The practice task implements a version of it. Ids in loops As lesson 14.01 warned, widgets in a loop need distinct ids: cpp-norun for (const MonsterInfo& m : snapshot.monsters) { ImGui::PushID(m.id); // every widget inside gets an id including m.id ImGui::Text("%s (%d, %d) hp %d", m.kind, m.x, m.y, m.hp); ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::SmallButton("kill")) sendToGame("kill " + std::to_string(m.id)); ImGui::PopID(); } Disabling BeginDisabled(condition) / EndDisabled() greys out and blocks the widgets between them: for example, the commands that need a connection to the game, while the tool is not connected (lesson 12.05). Common mistakes !warning Skipping End when Begin returns false Begin and End must always be paired. !warning Applying side effects every frame Act on the frame a widget returns true, not every frame. !warning Labels used as both text and id in loops PushID per item, or suffixes. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a slider's return value mean? + The value was changed by the user this frame - The slider is visible - The value is within range Use it to apply side effects only when needed. ? How do you put a button to the right of a text label? + Call SameLine() between them - Put them in the same function call - Use two windows Widgets go top to bottom unless told otherwise. ? What does " floor" do as a label? + Shows no text but gives the widget the id "floor" - Shows " floor" - Disables the widget Text after is part of the id only.

title: A layout cursor
body: Implement the layout model behind ImGui-style windows. A Layout places widgets inside a content area that starts at (left, top) and is width wide. - Each item(w, h) places a widget of that size and returns its top-left position. - Normally an item goes at the start of a new line: x at left , y below the previous line. A line's height is the tallest item on it; the next line starts spacingY below that. - sameLine() makes the next item continue on the current line, spacingX to the right of the previous item. - sameLineAt(x) makes the next item continue on the current line at left + x . - indent(d) moves left (for new lines) by d ; negative values unindent. - An item with w of -1 fills the remaining width of the line: from its x to left + width (where left is the content area's original left edge plus any indent). Return its size too. Return Placed{ x, y, w, h } for each item. Layout l{ 10, 20, 300, 8, 4 }; // left, top, width, spacingX, spacingY item(100, 20) - (10, 20) item(50, 30) - (10, 44) // new line: 20 + 20 + 4 sameLine(); item(60, 10) - (68, 44) item(-1, 16) - (10, 78, 300, 16) // new line below the 30-high line; fills the width

title: 14.04  Tables, Trees and Plots
body: Tools mostly show data: lists of entities, hierarchies of objects, numbers over time. ImGui's tables give sortable, resizable, scrollable columns; trees show hierarchies such as a scene graph; plots show values over time. This lesson uses each for Delve's tools, including clipping long lists so a table of ten thousand rows stays fast. Tables cpp-norun const ImGuiTableFlags flags{ ImGuiTableFlags_Borders ImGuiTableFlags_RowBg ImGuiTableFlags_Resizable ImGuiTableFlags_Sortable ImGuiTableFlags_ScrollY }; if (ImGui::BeginTable("monsters", 4, flags, { 0, 300 })) { ImGui::TableSetupScrollFreeze(0, 1); // keep the header row visible when scrolling ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Id", ImGuiTableColumnFlags_DefaultSort); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Kind"); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Position"); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("HP"); ImGui::TableHeadersRow(); if (ImGuiTableSortSpecs sort{ ImGui::TableGetSortSpecs() }; sort && sort- SpecsDirty) { sortRows(m_rows, sort- Specs 0 .ColumnIndex, sort- Specs 0 .SortDirection == ImGuiSortDirection_Ascending); sort- SpecsDirty = false; // sort only when the user changed the order } for (const Row& r : m_rows) { ImGui::TableNextRow(); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d", r.id); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::TextUnformatted(r.kind.c_str()); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d, %d", r.x, r.y); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d", r.hp); } ImGui::EndTable(); } ImGui handles the header clicks, resizing and scrolling; your code sorts the data when SpecsDirty says the order changed. A filter box above the table ( InputText with a hint) completes it. The practice task writes the sorting and filtering logic, with stable sorting so rows with equal values keep their relative order. Long lists: clipping Describing ten thousand rows every frame is wasteful when only thirty are visible. ImGuiListClipper tells you which rows are on screen: cpp-norun ImGuiListClipper clipper; clipper.Begin(static_cast<int (m_rows.size())); while (clipper.Step()) for (int i{ clipper.DisplayStart }; i < clipper.DisplayEnd; ++i) drawRow(m_rows static_cast<size_t (i) ); It is lesson 10.04's culling, for interfaces: the cost depends on what is visible, not on the size of the data. Trees Hierarchies (a scene graph, lesson 3.09; folders; a struct's members, lesson 9.09) use tree nodes: cpp-norun void drawNode(const SceneNode& n) { const ImGuiTreeNodeFlags flags{ n.children.empty() ? ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_Leaf : ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_None }; if (ImGui::TreeNodeEx(&n, flags, "%s (%.1f, %.1f)", n.name.c_str(), n.x, n.y)) // the pointer is the id { for (const auto& child : n.children) drawNode( child); ImGui::TreePop(); } } TreeNodeEx returns true when the node is open, and you then draw its children and call TreePop . Selection, drag and drop and context menus ( BeginPopupContextItem ) build an editor's hierarchy panel from the same pieces. Plots ImGui::PlotLines and PlotHistogram draw simple graphs from an array, enough for lesson 12.05's frame times: cpp-norun ImGui::PlotLines(" frame", m_frameMs.data(), static_cast<int (m_frameMs.size()), 0, "frame ms", 0.0f, 33.0f, ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 80)); For real charting (several series, axes, zoom, markers) the separate ImPlot library (also in vcpkg) extends ImGui with full plotting. A frame-time plot with a line at 16.7 ms (lesson 8.08's budget) makes stutter obvious. Common mistakes !warning Sorting every frame Sort only when SpecsDirty is set, or when the data changes. !warning Describing every row of a huge list Use ImGuiListClipper . !warning Unstable sorting Rows with equal values jump around each time the list is re-sorted. Use a stable sort with a tie-breaker. Knowledge check quiz ? Who sorts a sortable ImGui table's data? + Your code, when ImGui reports the sort order changed - ImGui sorts its own copy of the rows - The renderer ImGui only tracks which column and direction the user chose. ? What does ImGuiListClipper do? + Tells you which rows are visible, so only those are described each frame - Removes rows from the data - Clips text that is too long Cost then depends on what is on screen. ? How does a tree node know whether to draw its children? + TreeNodeEx returns true when the node is open - It always draws them - A separate call checks Then draw the children and call TreePop .

title: Filter and sort table rows
body: Write visibleRows(rows, filter, column, ascending) for a monster table. Each Row has an id , a kind , an x , a y and hp . 1. Filter : keep rows whose kind contains filter as a substring, ignoring upper and lower case. An empty filter keeps everything. 2. Sort by column : 0 id, 1 kind, 2 position (by y , then x ), 3 hp; ascending or descending. 3. Rows that compare equal on the chosen column are ordered by id , ascending, whatever the direction, so the order never jumps around. Return the resulting rows.

title: 14.05  Settings That Persist
body: A tool that forgets its window positions, open panels and last connection every time it starts is tiring to use. ImGui saves window layout itself to an .ini file; your tool saves its own settings alongside. This lesson covers both, where to store them, versioning them, and the classic bug of windows restored onto a monitor that is no longer connected. What ImGui saves for you ImGui remembers each window's position, size, collapsed state and (with docking) its docked layout, keyed by window title, and writes them to imgui.ini in the current directory every few seconds and on exit. Two adjustments make that robust: cpp-norun static std::string g_iniPath; // must outlive the ImGui context: ImGui keeps the pointer g_iniPath = (settingsFolder() / "layout.ini").string(); io.IniFilename = g_iniPath.c_str(); - Store it in the user's settings folder (Local AppData, lesson 5.04), not the current directory, which may be read-only or change with how the tool was started. - Window titles are ids: renaming a window loses its saved layout. "Monsters monsters" shows "Monsters" but uses the stable id monsters , so the visible title can change (with a count, say) without forgetting the layout. Your own settings Everything else the tool needs to remember is yours to save: Setting Example --- --- Which panels are open show.monsters = true Preferences refresh.ms = 100 , theme = dark , font.size = 16 Recent things Last connected process name, recent files Table state Sorted column (ImGui can also save table column widths and order itself, with ImGuiTableFlags_Reorderable , _Hideable ) Lesson 10.08's INI format is ideal: readable, easy to edit by hand when something goes wrong, tolerant of new and missing keys. Save on exit and whenever a setting changes (debounced, for example at most once per second), so a crash does not lose them, using lesson 5.04's write-to-temporary-then-replace. Versioning settings As with saves (lesson 10.07), include a version, and handle: - Missing keys (an older settings file): use the default. - Unknown keys (a newer one): ignore them, and preserve them when writing back if you can, so switching between tool versions does not destroy settings. - Invalid values (hand-edited): validate and fall back to the default, with a log message, never crash on bad settings. Restoring windows safely The classic bug: a tool remembers that its main window was at x = 2600 on the second monitor. The user unplugs that monitor, starts the tool, and the window opens off-screen where it cannot be seen or dragged back. Before restoring a saved window rectangle: 1. Get the work areas of the monitors currently connected (on Windows, EnumDisplayMonitors / GetMonitorInfoW ; with SDL, SDL_GetDisplayUsableBounds ). 2. If the saved rectangle does not overlap any of them enough to grab its title bar, move it onto the primary monitor. 3. If it is larger than the monitor, shrink it to fit. The practice task implements this clamping, which applies equally to the main window of a game. Common mistakes !warning imgui.ini in the current directory Point io.IniFilename at the user's settings folder, with a string that outlives the context. !warning Renaming windows and losing their layout Use id for a stable id with a changing title. !warning Restoring a window off-screen Check the saved position against the monitors that exist now. Knowledge check quiz ? What does ImGui save automatically? + Window positions, sizes, collapsed state and docking layout, keyed by window id - All your tool's settings - The data shown in windows Everything else is up to your code. ? What does the title "Monsters (12) monsters" achieve? + It shows "Monsters (12)" but keeps the stable id "monsters", so the saved layout survives the changing count - It creates three windows - It hides the window Text before is shown; the id comes from after it. ? A saved window position is on a monitor that is no longer connected. What should the tool do? + Move (and if needed shrink) the window onto a monitor that exists - Restore it exactly where it was - Delete the settings file Otherwise the window opens where the user cannot see it.

title: Keep a restored window on screen
match: Keep a restored window on screen
body: Write restoreWindow(saved, monitors) . saved is the window rectangle from the settings file; monitors lists the work areas of the monitors connected now, the first being the primary one. Rectangles are { x, y, w, h } . Rules: 1. A window is reachable on a monitor if its title bar strip, the top 32 pixels of the window ( y to y + 32 , full width), overlaps that monitor by at least 64 pixels horizontally and some amount vertically. 2. If the window is reachable on some monitor, keep its position, but shrink its width and height so it is no larger than that monitor (use the first monitor on which it is reachable). 3. Otherwise, place it on the primary monitor: shrink it to fit, then centre it there. 4. If there are no monitors at all, return the saved rectangle unchanged. primary {0, 0, 1920, 1040}, second {1920, 0, 1920, 1040} saved {2600, 100, 800, 600}, both monitors - unchanged saved {2600, 100, 800, 600}, only the primary - {560, 220, 800, 600} (centred)

title: 14.06  A Complete Tool Window
body: This lesson assembles the chapter into one application: Delve Inspector , a tool with a docked layout that connects to a running copy of Delve and shows its live stats, monsters, a memory view of the telemetry block and a command panel, with a command palette, settings that persist, and the hardening from chapter 12. It is the template for the tools in chapter 18's capstones. The layout ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ File View Game Help ● connected · delve 18324 │ ├───────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Overview │ Frame time ▁▁▂▁▁▇▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▂ avg 8.2 ms · worst 21.4 ms │ │ floor 3 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ turn 412 │ Monsters filter: gob │ │ hp 14 / 20 │ Id │ Kind │ Position │ HP │ │ monsters 6 │ 3 │ goblin │ 17, 9 │ 6 │ │ │ 7 │ goblin │ 20, 4 │ 9 │ │ Heal God ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ Telemetry block (hex) │ │ │ 0000 44 4C 56 54 01 00 00 00 40 00 00 00 ... DLVT....@ │ └───────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ With ImGui's docking (enable ImGuiConfigFlags_DockingEnable ; the vcpkg port's docking-experimental feature on versions where docking lives on its own branch), each panel is an ordinary Begin / End window that the user can dock, undock, tab and rearrange, and the arrangement is saved with the layout (lesson 14.05). The structure Three layers, as chapter 12 recommended: a thin platform layer that talks to the game, a model of pure, tested logic, and views that only draw the model and send user actions back. Each view is a function a few dozen lines long. The frame cpp-norun void Inspector::frame() { m_connection.poll(); // reconnect if needed; read a snapshot at most every 100 ms if (auto snap{ m_connection.latest() }) m_model.update( snap); ImGui::DockSpaceOverViewport(); drawMenuBar(); drawOverview(); // reads m_model only drawFrameTimes(); drawMonsters(); drawHexView(); drawCommandPalette(); // Ctrl+P if (m_showDemo) ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(&m_showDemo); } Commands ("heal", "god", "goto 3") go to the game through its command pipe (lesson 12.01) as console lines (lesson 11.07), never by writing into the game's memory: the game stays in charge of its own state, and the tool works with any build that understands the commands. The command palette Tools grow many commands. A command palette (Ctrl+P, as in many editors) lists them all, filtered as you type by fuzzy matching : typing gt3 finds "Goto floor 3". Matching characters in order, with bonuses for matches at the start of words, ranks useful results first. The practice task implements the scoring. Finishing touches - Status bar : connection state, game version, telemetry version (lesson 12.06), last error. - Keyboard shortcuts for common actions, shown in menus. - Logging of the tool's own actions and errors to a file (lesson 8.03). - Hardening : the six failure modes of lesson 12.07, rehearsed. - Packaging : like lesson 11.08, a Release build with its DLLs, licences (ImGui's MIT licence, SDL's zlib) and a readme. Common mistakes !warning Views that compute Keep logic in the model, where it can be tested; views only draw and forward actions. !warning Tools that write into the game's memory Send commands through the game's interface and let it change its own state. !warning A tool with no status Always show whether it is connected, to what, and whether the data is current. Knowledge check quiz ? What are the three layers of the inspector? + A platform layer that talks to the game, a model of pure logic, and ImGui views that draw the model - Input, update and render - Debug, Release and Shipping Separating them keeps the logic testable and the views simple. ? How does the inspector change things in the game? + By sending commands through the game's command pipe, which the game executes itself - By writing into the game's memory - By editing the save file The game stays in charge of its own state. ? What does fuzzy matching in a command palette do? + Finds commands whose names contain the typed characters in order, ranking better matches first - Matches only exact names - Sorts commands alphabetically gt3 finds "Goto floor 3".

title: Fuzzy matching for a command palette
match: Fuzzy matching for a command palette
body: Write fuzzyScore(query, candidate) , which decides whether a command palette entry matches what was typed, and how well. - Matching ignores case. Every character of query must appear in candidate in order (not necessarily next to each other). If not, return std::nullopt . An empty query matches everything with score 0. - Score: start at 0. For each matched query character, add 1. Add 5 more if that candidate character is at the start of a word (the first character, or after a space, - , _ or . ). Add 3 more if it directly follows the previously matched character. - Match greedily: each query character matches the earliest possible candidate character after the previous match. Then write rank(query, candidates) , which returns the matching candidates sorted by score (highest first), ties in their original order. fuzzyScore("gt3", "Goto floor 3") - 1+5 (G, word start) + 1 (t) + 1+5 (3, word start) = 13 fuzzyScore("xyz", "Goto floor 3") - nullopt

title: 15.01  User Mode and Kernel Mode
body: Lesson 1.06 introduced the kernel as the part of Windows with full control of the hardware. This chapter looks inside. It starts with the boundary itself: the processor's privilege levels , what runs in kernel mode (the kernel, the HAL, drivers), how kernel memory is shared by all processes, and why code running there must be held to a far higher standard than anything in user mode. Two privilege levels x64 processors have hardware privilege levels , called rings . Windows uses two: Ring Mode What runs there What it can do --- --- --- --- 0 Kernel mode The Windows kernel, the hardware abstraction layer, device drivers Everything: any memory, any instruction, the hardware 3 User mode Every application, including games and most services Only its own address space; privileged instructions fault; hardware only through the kernel The processor itself enforces the difference. In ring 3, instructions that control the hardware (disabling interrupts, loading page tables, talking to devices directly) cause an exception, and pages marked "supervisor only" in the page tables (lesson 6.02) cannot be touched. The only way up is a controlled gate: the system call (lesson 15.02). What lives in kernel mode - ntoskrnl.exe holds the executive (the managers this chapter covers: objects, memory, I/O, processes, security) and the kernel proper (scheduling, interrupts, low-level synchronisation). - hal.dll , the hardware abstraction layer, hides differences between motherboards and interrupt controllers. - Drivers ( .sys files) are kernel modules: PE files like DLLs (lesson 9.02), loaded into kernel space, extending the kernel with support for devices and file systems. - win32k.sys is the kernel side of windows and graphics (lesson 5.05's messages are partly managed here). One kernel address space, shared by everything Lesson 6.02 showed each process's private lower half of the address space. The upper half is kernel space, and it is the same in every process: the kernel, every driver, and the kernel's data (the pools, lesson 15.04) are mapped at the same kernel addresses whichever process is running. Pages there are marked supervisor-only, so user code cannot touch them, but all kernel-mode code can touch all of it. That sharing is the key to the rest of this chapter: - A driver's global variable is one variable for the whole machine, not per process. - A driver writing through a bad pointer can corrupt the kernel, other drivers, or any process's data, because there is no boundary between kernel components. - There is no "this driver crashed, the rest carries on". An unhandled fault in kernel mode means the system cannot know what else is damaged, so Windows stops the machine with a bug check (the blue screen, lesson 15.07). The standard kernel code is held to In user mode, a crash ends one process and the operating system cleans up (lesson 1.06). In kernel mode: User mode Kernel mode --- --- A crash ends the process A crash stops the whole machine A leak is freed when the process exits A leak lasts until reboot Bad pointers fault in your own space Bad pointers can silently corrupt anything Many runtime libraries and C++ features available A restricted environment: no standard library, careful exceptions, limited stack (lesson 16.02) Debug with Visual Studio on the same machine Debug from a second machine or a VM's host (lesson 15.08) That is why the rest of this course treats kernel work as something done only in a virtual machine , only with drivers you write for learning, with testing tools turned on, and why production drivers go through extensive testing and Microsoft's signing requirements (lesson 16.09). Common mistakes !warning Thinking a driver is "like a DLL that runs as administrator" It runs in ring 0 with the whole kernel's memory reachable. The rules, and the consequences of mistakes, are different. !warning Assuming kernel globals are per process Kernel space is shared; a driver's globals are machine-wide. !warning Experimenting with kernel code on your main PC Use a virtual machine you can restore (lesson 15.08). Knowledge check quiz ? What enforces the separation between user mode and kernel mode? + The processor: privileged instructions and supervisor-only pages fault in ring 3 - Windows checks every instruction in software - Nothing; programs promise to behave Hardware privilege levels are the foundation. ? Why is the kernel half of the address space the same in every process? + The kernel and drivers are shared by the whole system and mapped at the same addresses for every process - Each process gets a copy of the kernel - Kernel memory is not virtual Supervisor-only pages keep user code out. ? Why does an unhandled fault in a driver stop the whole machine? + Kernel components share memory with no boundaries, so the system cannot know what has been damaged - Drivers are always critical - Windows cannot restart drivers Continuing could corrupt data, so Windows bug-checks.

title: 15.02  System Calls: Crossing the Boundary
body: Every time a program opens a file, allocates memory or waits on an event, it crosses from user mode into the kernel and back. This lesson follows one call, CreateFileW , through kernelbase.dll and ntdll.dll to the syscall instruction and into the kernel's system service dispatcher, and explains the rule that makes the boundary safe: the kernel never trusts anything that comes from user mode. Following CreateFileW down - The documented Windows API (lesson 5.x) lives in kernel32.dll and kernelbase.dll . It translates friendly parameters into the kernel's. - The native API is in ntdll.dll : functions named Nt... (and Zw... ). Each is a few instructions: put the system call number in eax , and execute syscall . - The syscall instruction switches the processor to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel's single entry point, which uses the number to find the right kernel function in its system service table . - The kernel's function does the work and returns an NTSTATUS code; sysret returns to user mode; kernelbase converts the status into a Win32 error for GetLastError (lesson 5.02). You can see a stub in the debugger: in any program, open the Disassembly window at ntdll!NtCreateFile (lesson 4.08): asm ntdll!NtCreateFile: mov r10, rcx ; the syscall instruction overwrites rcx, so the first argument moves to r10 mov eax, 55h ; the system call number (it differs between Windows versions) test byte ptr 7FFE0308h , 1 jne use_int2e ; an alternative path on some systems syscall ; into the kernel ret The numbers change between Windows builds, which is one reason programs use the documented API rather than calling syscall themselves. NTSTATUS Kernel functions return NTSTATUS values, 32-bit codes like HRESULT s (lesson 5.02): negative for errors. Common ones: STATUS_SUCCESS (0), STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED ( 0xC0000022 ), STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND ( 0xC0000034 ), STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ( 0xC000000D ). Lesson 8.04's exception codes are NTSTATUS values too: 0xC0000005 is STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION . Chapter 16's drivers return these from every function. The kernel never trusts user mode A system call hands the kernel values from user mode: numbers, and pointers into user memory . Any of them may be wrong by accident or by malice: a pointer into kernel space, a length that overflows, a buffer another thread changes while the kernel reads it. The kernel defends itself with three rules, and every driver that accepts requests from user mode must follow them too (lesson 16.07): 1. Probe : check that a user pointer and length describe memory entirely within the user part of the address space ( ProbeForRead , ProbeForWrite ), so a caller cannot trick the kernel into reading or writing kernel memory on its behalf. Watch for overflow: address + length must not wrap around. 2. Capture : copy the user's data into kernel memory once , and then use only the copy. Otherwise another user thread can change the data between the kernel checking it and using it: a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) bug. 3. Guard the access : user memory can be freed or protected at any moment by another thread, so kernel code touches it only inside a structured exception handler ( __try / __except ) that turns a fault into an error status instead of a bug check. The practice task implements the probing arithmetic. Previous mode The kernel records whether a call came from user mode or from kernel code (the previous mode ). Calls from kernel mode (drivers calling ZwCreateFile ) skip some checks because kernel callers are trusted. This is why drivers must be careful never to pass user-supplied pointers on to kernel functions as if they were their own: the checks that protected the kernel would be skipped. Common mistakes !warning Calling Nt functions or syscall directly in applications Undocumented, changing between versions, and unnecessary. Use the Windows API. !warning Checking a user buffer, then reading it again later Capture it once into kernel memory; the user can change it between the two reads. !warning Forgetting overflow in range checks address + length can wrap past the end of the address space and appear valid. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a function in ntdll like NtCreateFile do? + Puts the system call number in eax and executes syscall to enter the kernel - Opens the file itself in user mode - Calls kernelbase It is a tiny stub; the work happens in the kernel. ? Why must the kernel copy user data before checking and using it? + Another user thread could change the data between the check and the use - Copying makes it faster - User memory cannot be read from the kernel This is the time-of-check to time-of-use problem. ? What does probing a user buffer check? + That the whole range lies in user address space, without arithmetic overflow - That the buffer contains valid data - That the buffer is aligned to a page Otherwise a caller could make the kernel touch kernel memory for it.

title: Probe a user buffer
body: A kernel component receives a pointer and a length from user mode. Write probe(address, length, alignment) , which applies the kernel's rules: - A zero length is always accepted (nothing will be touched). - alignment (1, 2, 4 or 8) must divide address : otherwise "misaligned" . - The whole range address to address + length - 1 must lie in user space, that is below kUserLimit ( 0x00007FFFFFFF0000 ), and the addition must not wrap round: otherwise "out of range" . - Otherwise "ok" . Check alignment before the range. probe(0x1000, 16, 8) - "ok" probe(0x1004, 16, 8) - "misaligned" probe(0x00007FFFFFFEFFF0, 32, 1) - "out of range" (runs past the user limit) probe(0xFFFFF80000000000, 8, 8) - "out of range" (kernel address)

title: 15.03  Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
match: 15.03 Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
body: Lesson 5.01 showed handles from the user's side. Inside the kernel, the object manager creates every kernel object (files, processes, threads, events, devices, registry keys), gives each a header with its type, reference counts and security, keeps a namespace of named objects, and maintains each process's handle table. This lesson looks at all of that, and at the object names drivers use. Every object has a header Each kernel object is a block of kernel memory: an object header managed by the object manager, followed by the object's own body (an event's signalled state, a file's position): In the header Meaning --- --- Type Which kind of object: Process, Thread, File, Event, Device, Key, Section ... Each type has its own procedures (open, close, delete) and its own access rights Handle count How many handles, in all processes, refer to it Pointer (reference) count How many references in total, including the kernel's own pointers Security descriptor Who may do what (lesson 6.08) Name For named objects, its place in the namespace An object is deleted only when both counts reach zero. Kernel code that keeps a pointer to an object takes a reference ( ObReferenceObject ) and later releases it ( ObDereferenceObject ), the kernel's equivalent of lesson 10.06's reference counting. Forgetting to release keeps the object alive until reboot; releasing twice frees it while still in use, usually ending in a bug check. Handles, from the inside A handle (lesson 5.01) is an index into the process's handle table , maintained by the object manager. Each entry holds a pointer to the object and the access mask granted when it was opened. When a user calls, say, SetEvent(h) , the kernel: 1. looks up h in the calling process's table ( ObReferenceObjectByHandle ); 2. checks the object's type is right (an Event), and the granted access includes what the operation needs; 3. takes a reference while it works, and drops it afterwards. The access check against the security descriptor happened only once, when the handle was created (lesson 6.08). The object namespace Named objects live in a tree, like a file system for the kernel: \ ├── Device\ │ ├── HarddiskVolume3 the C: volume │ ├── Null │ └── XenonEcho a device created by chapter 16's driver ├── Driver\ loaded drivers ├── GLOBAL??\ "DOS device" names: symbolic links │ ├── C: → \Device\HarddiskVolume3 │ └── XenonEcho → \Device\XenonEcho ├── BaseNamedObjects\ named events, mutexes, sections from user mode │ └── (Local\ and Global\ names, lesson 12.01) └── Sessions\ ... per-session namespaces Symbolic links connect friendly names to devices. The user-mode path C:\save.dat becomes \??\C:\save.dat in the kernel; \?? looks in the caller's own and then the global DOS device directory, where C: is a symbolic link to \Device\HarddiskVolume3 ; the object manager follows it, and the rest of the path ( \save.dat ) is handed to the file system driver on that device. The practice task resolves paths through links like this, including stopping a link that points back at itself. Chapter 16's driver creates a device object ( \Device\XenonEcho ) and a symbolic link to it ( \??\XenonEcho ), so a user program can open it with CreateFileW(L"\\\\.\\XenonEcho", ...) : the \\.\ prefix is user mode's way of saying \??\ . Seeing it Sysinternals WinObj shows the whole namespace: devices, drivers, symbolic links and named objects. Sysinternals Handle and Process Explorer's lower pane list every handle a process holds, with types and names, which is how you find which program has a file locked (lesson 5.04's sharing violations). Common mistakes !warning Holding an object pointer without a reference The object can be deleted underneath you. Reference it for as long as you keep the pointer. !warning Unbalanced reference counts A missing dereference leaks the object until reboot; an extra one frees it while still in use. !warning Confusing user-mode and kernel-mode names \\.\Name from user mode corresponds to \??\Name (a link) in the kernel, which points at \Device\Name . Knowledge check quiz ? When is a kernel object deleted? + When both its handle count and its reference (pointer) count reach zero - When its creator exits - When its first handle is closed Kernel code's own references keep it alive too. ? What does a handle table entry store? + A pointer to the object and the access rights granted when the handle was opened - The object's whole contents - The object's name only Rights are checked once, at open time. ? What does \??\C: refer to? + A symbolic link in the DOS device directory that points to a device such as \Device\HarddiskVolume3 - The C: folder on disk - A registry key The object manager follows the link to the device.

title: Resolve a path through symbolic links
match: Resolve a path through symbolic links
where: 15.03 Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
body: Model how the object manager resolves names. links maps symbolic-link names to their targets, for example "\??\C:" to "\Device\HarddiskVolume3" . Write resolve(path, links) : - Repeatedly find the longest link name that is a prefix of the current path at a component boundary (the link name is the whole path, or is followed by \ ). Replace that prefix with the link's target. - Stop when no link matches, and return the final path. - If more than 16 replacements happen, the links form a loop: return std::nullopt . links: \??\C: - \Device\HarddiskVolume3 \??\Echo - \Device\XenonEcho resolve("\??\C:\Games\save.dat") = "\Device\HarddiskVolume3\Games\save.dat" resolve("\??\Echo") = "\Device\XenonEcho" resolve("\??\Cx\file") = "\??\Cx\file" (\??\C: is not a whole component of \??\Cx)

title: 15.04  The Memory Manager
body: The kernel's memory manager provides every process's virtual address space (chapter 6) and also manages kernel memory. This lesson covers the kernel side: paged and non-paged pool , why the difference matters so much in drivers, pool tags for tracking allocations, memory descriptor lists (MDLs) for describing buffers, and how the memory manager handles page faults. What the memory manager does Job Seen before --- --- Building and switching each process's page tables Lesson 6.02 Reserving, committing and protecting user memory ( VirtualAlloc ends here) Lesson 6.03 Handling page faults: demand-zero pages, paging in from disk Lesson 6.02 Working sets: deciding which pages stay in RAM Lesson 6.02 File mappings and shared memory Lesson 12.01 Kernel memory: the pools This lesson Paged and non-paged pool Kernel code allocates memory from pools , the kernel's heaps, shared by all drivers: Pool Can be paged out to disk? Usable at --- --- --- Paged pool Yes Only when page faults are allowed: IRQL below DISPATCH_LEVEL (lesson 15.06) Non-paged pool No: always in RAM Any IRQL, including interrupt handlers Why both? Non-paged memory is precious: it permanently consumes RAM. But some kernel code runs at times when a page fault cannot be handled (while holding a spin lock, in an interrupt or DPC, lesson 15.06), and touching paged memory then, if it has been paged out, crashes the machine with IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL or PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA . So drivers put in non-paged pool exactly the data that code at high IRQL touches, and everything else in paged pool. The same rule applies to code : a driver function that may run at DISPATCH_LEVEL must be in non-paged memory. Drivers mark functions that only run at PASSIVE_LEVEL as pageable with pragma alloc_text(PAGE, ...) and assert their IRQL with the PAGED_CODE() macro. Allocating with tags cpp-norun // A 4-character tag identifies who allocated it: here 'Echo', written backwards in memory as a little-endian integer. constexpr ULONG kTag{ 'ohcE' }; auto buffer{ static_cast<char (ExAllocatePool2(POOL_FLAG_NON_PAGED, size, kTag)) }; if (!buffer) return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES; // allocation can fail: always check // ... use it ... ExFreePoolWithTag(buffer, kTag); - ExAllocatePool2 (Windows 10 2004 and later) zero-initialises memory, unlike its predecessor ExAllocatePoolWithTag , which avoided a whole class of information-leak bugs. - Every allocation carries a pool tag , a four-character code chosen by the driver. Tools such as !poolused in WinDbg and Sysinternals PoolMon show how much memory each tag holds, which is how kernel memory leaks are found: a tag whose usage keeps growing points at the guilty driver. The practice task builds this kind of tracking. - Leaked pool memory is never reclaimed until reboot, because there is no process to clean up after (lesson 15.01). Memory descriptor lists When a driver needs to work with a buffer that belongs to a user process, for example to read data directly into it, it cannot simply keep the user's virtual address: that address is only valid in that process, and the pages could be paged out or freed. An MDL (memory descriptor list) describes the buffer by its physical pages : 1. Build an MDL for the user range ( IoAllocateMdl ). 2. Lock the pages in RAM ( MmProbeAndLockPages , inside __try , with the probing rules of lesson 15.02). 3. Map them into kernel space if needed ( MmGetSystemAddressForMdlSafe ), giving an address valid in any process context and at raised IRQL. 4. Unlock and free when done. Chapter 16's "direct I/O" (lesson 16.07) has the I/O manager do these steps for the driver. Page faults, from the kernel's side When a thread touches a page that is not present (lesson 6.02), the processor raises a page fault and the memory manager runs: - Is the address valid for this process (committed or a mapping)? If not: an access violation exception in user mode, a bug check in kernel mode if nothing handles it. - If valid: find a free physical page, fill it (zeros, or read from the page file or a mapped file, which means waiting for disk I/O), update the page table, and resume the thread. Waiting for disk is why a page fault can only be handled at low IRQL: at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above, the thread cannot wait. Common mistakes !warning Paged memory touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL or higher Works until the page happens to be paged out, then crashes the machine. Use non-paged pool for anything touched at raised IRQL. !warning Not checking pool allocations Pool allocation can fail; return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES . !warning Keeping a user virtual address in a driver It is meaningless in another process context. Use an MDL or copy the data. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the difference between paged and non-paged pool? + Paged pool may be written out to disk and can only be touched where page faults are allowed; non-paged pool always stays in RAM - Paged pool is faster - Non-paged pool is for user mode High-IRQL code must only touch non-paged memory. ? What is a pool tag for? + Identifying which driver (and which kind of allocation) each block of kernel memory belongs to, for tracking and finding leaks - Encrypting allocations - Aligning memory Tools like PoolMon show usage per tag. ? Why does a driver use an MDL rather than a user virtual address? + An MDL describes the physical pages, which can be locked in RAM and mapped so the buffer is usable from any process context - MDLs are faster to type - User addresses are always invalid The user address only means something in the original process.

title: Track pool usage by tag
body: Kernel memory leaks are found by tracking allocations per pool tag. Build PoolTracker , a model of what PoolMon shows. - allocate(tag, bytes) records an allocation and returns an id for it (unique, starting at 1). - free(id, tag) records that allocation's release. If the id is unknown or was already freed, or the tag does not match the one it was allocated with, return a description of the error ( "double free or bad id" , "tag mismatch" ) and change nothing; otherwise return "" . - usage() returns, for every tag that still holds memory, the tag, the number of live allocations and their total bytes, sorted by bytes, largest first (ties alphabetical by tag). - tagText(tag) turns a tag as stored in memory (four characters, little-endian in a 32-bit number, so 'ohcE' in code reads Echo ) into a 4-character string.

title: 15.05  The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
match: 15.05 The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
body: Every read, write and device request in Windows becomes an I/O request packet (IRP) handed to a stack of drivers by the I/O manager . This lesson explains IRPs, driver and device objects, how a request travels down a device stack and its completion travels back up, the kinds of drivers (filter, function, bus), and the frameworks (WDM and KMDF) drivers are written with. Requests as packets When a program calls ReadFile on a file or a device, the I/O manager in the kernel builds an IRP , a structure describing the request: Part of an IRP Meaning --- --- Major function What kind of request: IRP_MJ_CREATE (open), IRP_MJ_READ , IRP_MJ_WRITE , IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL (custom commands, lesson 16.05), IRP_MJ_CLOSE ... Parameters Length, offset, the control code ... in the current stack location Buffers Where the data is, described in one of three ways (lesson 16.07) I/O status When finished: an NTSTATUS and how many bytes were transferred The I/O manager then hands the IRP to the driver responsible for the target device. Drivers never call each other's functions directly; everything goes through IRPs. Driver objects and device objects Object One per Holds --- --- --- Driver object Loaded driver The table of dispatch routines : one function per major function the driver handles Device object Device the driver manages (a disk, a port, or a purely software device like chapter 16's) The device's state, and which driver handles it When DriverEntry (lesson 16.02) runs, the driver fills its driver object's dispatch table: driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_READ = EchoRead; . When an IRP for one of its devices arrives, the I/O manager calls the matching routine. Device stacks Most hardware is handled by several drivers layered on top of each other, each adding something: Each driver, given an IRP, does one of three things: 1. Complete it itself ( IoCompleteRequest ) with a status, if it can satisfy the request. 2. Pass it down to the next driver in the stack ( IoCallDriver ), possibly after changing it, optionally asking to be told when it completes (a completion routine). 3. Queue it (mark it pending) to finish later, for example when hardware responds. The practice task simulates a request going down a stack until one driver completes it, and the completion coming back up through the drivers that asked to see it. Kind of driver Role --- --- Bus driver Discovers devices on a bus (PCI, USB) and creates their lowest device objects Function driver The main driver for a device: knows how to operate it Filter driver Sits above or below and adds or changes behaviour: encryption, compression, monitoring Software-only driver No hardware; provides a service to user mode through a device object (chapter 16's driver is one) Asynchronous by design Device I/O takes time. Rather than making the caller's thread wait inside the driver, an IRP can be pending : the driver returns STATUS_PENDING at once, and completes the IRP later from an interrupt or a worker. User mode sees this as overlapped (asynchronous) I/O, or simply as ReadFile returning when the I/O manager finally completes the request. This design is why Windows I/O can keep thousands of requests in flight. WDM and KMDF Framework Notes --- --- WDM (Windows Driver Model) The original model: drivers handle IRPs directly, including all the plug-and-play and power management requests. Powerful and error-prone KMDF (Kernel-Mode Driver Framework) A library over WDM that handles the standard plug-and-play, power and queueing logic, and gives drivers objects with reference counting and cleanup. Microsoft's recommended choice for new drivers UMDF Drivers for some device classes that run in user mode , so a bug crashes only a host process, not the machine. Preferred whenever the device type allows it Chapter 16 starts with a minimal WDM-style driver to see the raw mechanism, and the same ideas carry over to KMDF. Common mistakes !warning Completing an IRP and then touching it After IoCompleteRequest , the IRP belongs to the I/O manager and may already be freed. !warning Both completing and passing down the same IRP Each IRP must be completed exactly once, by one driver. !warning Writing a kernel driver when a user-mode one would do UMDF, or an ordinary service, keeps bugs out of the kernel. Knowledge check quiz ? What is an IRP? + A structure describing one I/O request, passed by the I/O manager to drivers - A kind of interrupt - A driver's configuration file Major function, parameters, buffers and status. ? A filter driver receives an IRP it does not need to change. What does it do? + Passes it down to the next driver with IoCallDriver - Completes it with success - Deletes it Filters add behaviour only where they need to. ? Why is KMDF recommended over writing WDM drivers directly? + It handles the standard plug-and-play, power and queueing logic correctly, leaving less error-prone code for the driver writer - KMDF drivers run in user mode - WDM no longer works UMDF is the user-mode framework.

title: Send a request down a device stack
match: Send a request down a device stack
where: 15.05 The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
body: Simulate an IRP travelling through a device stack. The stack is a list of drivers from the top down. Each Driver has a name, a function decide(major) returning what it does with a request of that major function ( "complete" or "pass" ), the status it completes with, and whether it wants a completion callback . Write send(stack, major) , returning a Trace : - path : the names of the drivers the request visited going down, in order; - completedBy : the driver that completed it; - status : its status; - callbacks : the names of drivers above the completing one that asked for a completion callback, in the order the completion travels back up (nearest the completing driver first). If every driver passes the request, the bottom of the stack has no one left to pass to: the request completes with "STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST" , completedBy is "(none)" , and every driver that asked for a callback gets one.

title: 15.06  Interrupts, IRQLs and Scheduling
body: Hardware demands attention at any moment through interrupts , and the kernel must decide what can interrupt what. Windows does this with interrupt request levels (IRQLs). The IRQL a piece of code runs at decides what it may do: whether it can wait, touch paged memory, or be preempted. This lesson explains the levels, DPCs , spin locks , and the rules that cause the most famous blue screen of all. Interrupts When a device needs the processor (a network packet arrived, a disk read finished, a key was pressed) it raises an interrupt . The processor stops what it is doing, saves enough state to resume, and runs the driver's interrupt service routine (ISR). A clock also interrupts regularly, which is how the scheduler gets control to switch threads (lesson 6.05). But an interrupt can arrive while the kernel is in the middle of something delicate, even while handling another interrupt. Windows needs rules for what may interrupt what. IRQLs Each processor has a current IRQL (interrupt request level). Code at a given IRQL can only be interrupted by something at a higher level. The levels that matter for drivers: IRQL Runs May wait? May touch paged memory?
