Scheduler can switch thread? --- --- --- --- --- PASSIVE_LEVEL (0) Normal threads: all user code, most driver code, DriverEntry , most dispatch routines Yes Yes Yes APC_LEVEL (1) Asynchronous procedure calls, some file system code Limited Yes Yes DISPATCH_LEVEL (2) The scheduler itself, DPCs , code holding a spin lock No No No: the thread keeps the processor DIRQL (3 and up) Device interrupt service routines No No No The two crucial rules for DISPATCH_LEVEL and above: 1. No waiting. The scheduler runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL, so code at that level or above cannot be switched out. Waiting on an event or a mutex there would wait forever, so it is forbidden. 2. No paged memory. A page fault may need to wait for the disk (lesson 15.04), which is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL. Touching paged memory there crashes the machine with bug check IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL ( 0xA ) or DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL ( 0xD1 ), the most famous blue screens, usually caused by a driver. The practice task encodes these rules as a checker. DPCs: doing the work later An ISR runs at a high IRQL, blocking everything below, so it must be very short: acknowledge the device and note what happened. The rest of the work goes into a deferred procedure call (DPC), queued by the ISR and run soon after at DISPATCH_LEVEL, where other device interrupts can still get through. Work that needs to wait or touch paged memory goes one step further down, into a work item that runs in a system thread at PASSIVE_LEVEL. Spin locks Lesson 6.06's mutexes make a waiting thread sleep, which is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL. For data shared with DPCs or ISRs, drivers use spin locks : - Acquiring a spin lock raises the IRQL to DISPATCH_LEVEL (so the holder cannot be preempted on its processor), then spins (busy-waits) until the lock is free, in case another processor holds it. - Code holding a spin lock therefore follows every DISPATCH_LEVEL rule: no waiting, no paged memory, and should hold it for only a few microseconds, because other processors may be spinning. cpp-norun KIRQL old; KeAcquireSpinLock(&m_lock, &old); // IRQL is now DISPATCH_LEVEL m_queue.push(item); // short, non-paged work only KeReleaseSpinLock(&m_lock, old); // back to the previous IRQL For data used only at PASSIVE_LEVEL, drivers use waiting locks such as fast mutexes or executive resources instead. Finding out the current IRQL KeGetCurrentIrql() returns it. Well-written drivers assert their assumptions: PAGED_CODE() at the top of pageable functions checks the IRQL is below DISPATCH_LEVEL, and Driver Verifier (lesson 15.07) adds checks that catch IRQL mistakes immediately rather than in rare situations. Common mistakes !warning Waiting at DISPATCH_LEVEL Including while holding a spin lock. It hangs or bug-checks the machine. !warning Touching paged memory or calling pageable code at DISPATCH_LEVEL Works until the page is paged out; then IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL . !warning Long work in an ISR or under a spin lock Everything else on that processor, and processors spinning for the lock, waits. Defer to a DPC or a work item. Knowledge check quiz ? At which IRQL do normal threads, including DriverEntry , run? + PASSIVE_LEVEL - DISPATCH_LEVEL - DIRQL Everything that may wait and use paged memory runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ? Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not wait on an event? + The scheduler itself runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL, so the waiting thread could never be switched out for the event to be set - Events do not exist in the kernel - It would use too much memory Waiting there would hang that processor. ? What does acquiring a spin lock do to the IRQL? + Raises it to DISPATCH_LEVEL until the lock is released - Lowers it to PASSIVE_LEVEL - Nothing So all DISPATCH_LEVEL rules apply while holding it. ? What is a DPC for? + Doing an interrupt's follow-up work at DISPATCH_LEVEL, so the ISR itself can be very short - Waiting for a user-mode thread - Loading a driver Work that must wait goes further down, to a work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

title: An IRQL rule checker
body: Driver Verifier and static analysis tools catch IRQL mistakes. Write a simple checker for a sequence of operations a driver performs on one code path. The code path starts at a given IRQL (0 PASSIVE, 1 APC, 2 DISPATCH, 3 and up device levels). Each operation is a string: Operation Effect / rule --- --- "acquire_spinlock" Raises the IRQL to 2 (remember the old level). Not allowed above 2 "release_spinlock" Restores the IRQL from before the matching acquire. Not allowed without a matching acquire "wait" Only allowed below 2 "touch_paged" Only allowed below 2 "touch_nonpaged" Always allowed "call_pageable" Only allowed below 2 Write checkPath(startIrql, ops) , returning a list of problems, each "step N: OPERATION at IRQL L" (N from 1). When an operation is not allowed, report it and carry on as if it had happened (a release without an acquire leaves the IRQL unchanged). At the end, if spin locks are still held, add "end: N spin lock(s) still held" .

title: 15.07  Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
match: 15.07 Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
body: When kernel-mode code fails, Windows stops the machine with a bug check (the blue screen) rather than risk corrupting data. This lesson explains why, what the stop code and parameters mean, the most common driver bug checks, how kernel crash dumps are collected and read with !analyze , and how Driver Verifier turns rare driver bugs into immediate, diagnosable ones. Why stop everything? In user mode, an access violation ends one process; Windows still has an intact kernel to clean up after it (lesson 1.06). In kernel mode there is no such referee. If a driver writes through a bad pointer, the damage could be anywhere in the shared kernel address space (lesson 15.01): the file system's caches, another driver's data, the memory manager's tables. Continuing might write corrupted data to disk. So when the kernel detects a condition it cannot safely recover from, it calls KeBugCheckEx , which: 1. stops all processors, 2. writes a crash dump to the page file (copied to C:\Windows\MEMORY.DMP or C:\Windows\Minidump\ on the next boot), 3. shows the stop screen with a stop code , and restarts. Stopping is the safe choice. A blue screen loses unsaved work; silent corruption could lose everything. Reading a stop code A bug check has a code and four parameters whose meaning depends on the code. The ones caused most often by drivers: Code Name Usual meaning --- --- --- 0x0A IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL Paged or invalid memory touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above (lesson 15.06) 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL The same, in a driver; parameter 4 is the faulting address in the driver 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA Referenced invalid memory: a bad or freed pointer 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION An exception during a system call, often in a driver handling a user request 0x7E SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED An exception in a system thread that nothing handled 0xC4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION Driver Verifier caught a rule violation (below) 0x19 BAD_POOL_HEADER Pool corruption: an overrun into the next allocation 0xC2 BAD_POOL_CALLER Bad pool request: double free, wrong IRQL for the pool type 0xCE DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS A driver unloaded while timers, DPCs or IRPs still referred to its code 0xEF CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED A process Windows cannot run without ended Microsoft's Bug Check Code Reference documents every code and its parameters. The practice task decodes the common ones. Reading a kernel dump Open MEMORY.DMP or a minidump in WinDbg (lesson 8.05), fix the symbols ( .symfix , .reload ) and run: !analyze -v It reports the bug check and its parameters, the faulting module (very often the culprit driver's name, such as XenonEcho.sys ), the call stack at the crash, and the source line if the driver's PDB is available. lm lists loaded drivers; !irql shows the IRQL at the time of the crash; !pool and !poolused investigate pool problems (lesson 15.04). Kernel dumps are configured in System Properties → Advanced → Startup and Recovery : a small memory dump is enough for most driver bugs; a kernel memory dump contains all kernel memory for harder ones. Driver Verifier Many driver bugs only crash in rare situations: when memory happens to be paged out, when an allocation fails, when two processors race. Driver Verifier ( verifier.exe , built into Windows) makes them happen every time , by adding checks to chosen drivers: Option Catches --- --- Special pool Overruns and use-after-free in pool memory, at the faulting instruction (like page heap, lesson 6.03) Force IRQL checking Paged memory touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL even when it is currently in RAM (by paging it out) Pool tracking Leaks: unfreed pool when the driver unloads I/O verification IRPs completed twice, completed with bad status, leaked Deadlock detection Lock order violations Low resources simulation Code that does not handle allocation failure DDI compliance checking Calls made against the documented rules Turn it on for your own driver , in the virtual machine (lesson 15.08), from an administrator prompt ( verifier /standard /driver XenonEcho.sys , then reboot), and leave it on throughout development. A bug Verifier catches gives bug check 0xC4 with parameters describing exactly which rule was broken, instead of a mysterious crash weeks later. Microsoft requires drivers to pass Verifier testing before signing them for release. Common mistakes !warning Ignoring the faulting module !analyze names it; that is where to look first. !warning Developing a driver without Driver Verifier Its checks find in minutes what otherwise takes months of rare crashes. !warning Testing kernel code on your everyday PC A bug check there costs your work and possibly your data. Use a VM with snapshots. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does Windows stop the whole machine on a kernel-mode fault? + Kernel components share memory without boundaries, so the damage could be anywhere; continuing risks corrupting data - To force the user to restart - Because kernel code cannot handle exceptions at all Stopping with a dump is the safe choice. ? What usually causes bug check 0xD1 ? + A driver touching paged or invalid memory at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above - Running out of disk space - A user program crashing Parameter 4 is the faulting address in the driver. ? What does Driver Verifier do? + Adds checks to chosen drivers that make rare bugs (overruns, IRQL mistakes, leaks, bad IRP handling) fail immediately and clearly - Speeds up drivers - Signs drivers It turns occasional crashes into reproducible ones.

title: Decode a stop code
where: 15.07 Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
body: Write describeBugCheck(code, parameters) , which turns a bug check into a short summary for a crash report. parameters holds the four bug check parameters. Code Return --- --- 0x0A "IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL: address 0x{p1} at IRQL {p2}" 0xD1 "DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL: address 0x{p1} at IRQL {p2}, code at 0x{p4}" 0x50 "PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA: {read or write} 0x{p1}" , where parameter 2 is 0 for a read and anything else for a write 0xC4 "DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION: rule 0x{p1}" 0x19 "BAD_POOL_HEADER" anything else "BUGCHECK 0x{code}" Addresses and codes are written in upper-case hex without leading zeros; the IRQL in decimal. ( 0x0A and 0x19 as codes are written exactly as in the table's names, not formatted.) describeBugCheck(0xD1, { 0x10, 2, 0, 0xFFFFF80612345678 }) == "DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL: address 0x10 at IRQL 2, code at 0xFFFFF80612345678"

title: 15.08  Building a Virtual Machine Lab
body: Kernel experiments belong in a virtual machine : a whole Windows installation running as a program on your PC, which can crash, be debugged from outside, and be restored to a clean state in seconds. This lesson sets up the lab used by chapter 16: a Windows VM with snapshots , test signing enabled inside it, kernel debugging from the host with WinDbg over the network, and the habits that keep your real machine safe. Why a VM Without a VM With a VM --- --- A driver bug crashes your PC and loses your work It crashes the VM; your PC carries on A kernel debugger needs a second physical computer The host debugs the guest A broken system takes hours to repair Restore a snapshot in seconds Test-signing mode weakens your everyday system Only the lab VM is in test mode Every kernel lesson from here on assumes this lab. Never load a driver you are developing on your everyday machine. Choosing a hypervisor Hypervisor Notes --- --- Hyper-V Built into Windows 10/11 Pro, Enterprise and Education (enable "Hyper-V" in Windows Features). Good kernel debugging support VMware Workstation Pro Free for personal use; mature, good snapshots VirtualBox Free and open source Any works. Give the VM 2 or more processors, 4 GB or more of RAM, and 64 GB of disk. Install Windows 10 or 11 from Microsoft's official ISO; an unactivated installation is fine for a lab. Setting up the guest Inside the VM, from an administrator command prompt: cmd :: 1. Allow test-signed drivers (lesson 16.09). Only in the lab VM. bcdedit /set testsigning on :: 2. Turn on kernel debugging over the network to the host. :: Replace the IP with the host's address on the VM network; the command prints a key for the host. kdnet.exe 192.168.50.1 50000 :: 3. Write a kernel memory dump on bug checks. :: (Or System Properties Advanced Startup and Recovery.) kdnet.exe comes with the Windows Driver Kit's debugging tools (lesson 16.01); copy it and VerifiedNICList.xml from the host's C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64\ into the VM. Restart the VM; the desktop shows "Test Mode" in a corner, which is how you know it worked. Also: - Turn Secure Boot off in the VM's settings if test signing will not enable (Secure Boot prevents changing boot configuration this way). - Disable automatic restart on system failure so you can read stop codes. - Create a shared folder, or copy files over the network, to move built drivers from host to guest. Snapshots Take a snapshot as soon as the guest is set up and working: "clean, test mode, debugging on" . Before each experiment, take another or know which to return to. When a driver leaves the VM unbootable, revert in seconds instead of repairing it. Snapshots are the most valuable feature of the lab. Connecting the kernel debugger On the host, start WinDbg (lesson 8.05) → Attach to kernel → Net , enter the port (50000) and the key printed by kdnet in the guest, and start the session. Restart the guest; WinDbg connects as it boots. Now WinDbg controls the guest's whole kernel : Command Effect --- --- Break (Ctrl+Break) Freezes the entire VM, every processor, at once g Lets it run again lm Loaded kernel modules (drivers) bp XenonEcho!DriverEntry Breakpoint in your driver, even before it loads ( bu , "unresolved breakpoint", for drivers not yet loaded) !process 0 0 Every process in the guest !analyze -v After a bug check, analyse it live ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF Show DbgPrint / KdPrint output from drivers in the debugger Kernel debugging stops the entire guest operating system while you inspect it, which is exactly what is needed: nothing changes underneath you. Habits that keep you safe - Build on the host; copy to the guest; load only in the guest. - Keep the guest off your main network shares and without your personal accounts. - Revert to a clean snapshot after anything unusual. - Keep test signing only in the lab VM, never on your main machine (lesson 16.09 explains why). Common mistakes !warning Loading a development driver on your main PC One mistake costs a blue screen and possibly your work. Always the VM. !warning No snapshot before an experiment Take one; restoring takes seconds, repairing takes hours. !warning Enabling test signing on your everyday system It weakens its protection against unsigned drivers. Lab VM only. Knowledge check quiz ? Why develop drivers in a virtual machine? + Crashes stay inside the VM, the host can kernel-debug it, and snapshots restore a clean system in seconds - Drivers run faster in VMs - Drivers cannot run on real hardware And it keeps test signing off your everyday system. ? What does bcdedit /set testsigning on do? + Allows the guest to load drivers signed with a test certificate instead of a production signature - Turns off all driver checks - Enables Driver Verifier Lab VM only. ? What happens to the guest when you break into it with the kernel debugger? + The whole operating system, all processors, freezes until you continue - Only your driver pauses - Nothing; it keeps running So nothing changes while you inspect it.

title: 16.01  Installing the Windows Driver Kit
body: Drivers are built with the Windows Driver Kit (WDK), an extension to Visual Studio that adds kernel headers and libraries, driver project templates, signing, deployment and analysis tools. This lesson installs matching versions of Visual Studio, the SDK and the WDK on the host, creates the chapter's driver project, and explains what is different about building kernel code. What the WDK adds Part What it is for --- --- Kernel headers ( ntddk.h , wdm.h , wdf.h ) Declarations of kernel functions and structures Kernel libraries ntoskrnl.lib , hal.lib , the KMDF libraries Project templates Empty WDM driver, KMDF driver, UMDF driver, and more Build settings The kernel environment: no C runtime, /kernel mode, special linker options Signing Test-signs the driver automatically on build (lesson 16.09) Tools Debugging tools (WinDbg, kdnet ), Driver Verifier helpers, static analysis (Code Analysis for drivers), InfVerif for installation files Installing The WDK must match your Visual Studio and Windows SDK versions exactly. Microsoft's "Download the Windows Driver Kit" page lists the current combination; follow its steps in order: 1. Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload (lesson 1.07). In Individual components , add the MSVC Spectre-mitigated libraries for x64 (driver projects require them) and the Windows SDK version the WDK page names. 2. The Windows SDK of the matching version, if not installed by step 1. 3. The WDK installer of the same version. At its end, let it install the Windows Driver Kit Visual Studio extension . Everything is installed on the host . The VM (lesson 15.08) only runs the result. The chapter's project In Visual Studio: File → New → Project , search for Kernel Mode Driver, Empty (KMDF) or Empty WDM Driver , and name it XenonEcho . This chapter uses a minimal WDM-style software driver first (lessons 16.02 to 16.07), because seeing the IRPs directly makes the I/O model of lesson 15.05 concrete; lesson 16.10 notes what KMDF would take care of for you. Project settings to check (Configuration All , Platform x64 ): Setting Value Why --- --- --- Driver Settings → Target OS Version Windows 10 or later The oldest Windows the driver supports C/C++ → Warning level Level 4, warnings as errors Kernel code deserves every warning Driver Signing → Sign Mode Test Sign Signs the .sys with a test certificate on build (lesson 16.09) Inf2Cat / Stampinf Off for a software-only driver loaded with sc No installation package needed for this chapter's driver Add a second project to the solution, an ordinary Console App called EchoClient , for the user-mode program that talks to the driver (lesson 16.06). What is different about kernel builds - No C runtime and no C++ standard library. There is no printf , std::vector or new by default. Kernel code uses kernel functions: ExAllocatePool2 for memory (lesson 15.04), RtlCopyMemory , RtlStringCbPrintfA , KdPrint for debug output. - C++ is allowed, carefully. Classes, templates, RAII and constexpr work. Exceptions and RTTI are off; global objects with constructors are not supported without extra work; anything that allocates must use the pools. - Stack is small : 12 KB to 24 KB on x64 kernel threads, versus 1 MB in user mode (lesson 2.01). Large locals and deep recursion are not acceptable. - Every function's IRQL matters (lesson 15.06): document and assert it. - Static analysis is part of the build: run Analyze → Run Code Analysis with the driver rules; it understands IRQL annotations and catches real bugs. The output of a build is XenonEcho.sys (a PE file like a DLL, lesson 9.02), its .pdb , and with test signing a test certificate ( .cer ). Common mistakes !warning Mismatched Visual Studio, SDK and WDK versions Install the exact combination Microsoft's download page lists. !warning Missing Spectre-mitigated libraries Driver builds fail with an error naming them; add them in the Visual Studio installer. !warning Reaching for the standard library It is not available in the kernel. Use the kernel's functions. Knowledge check quiz ? Where are the Visual Studio, SDK and WDK installed? + On the host development machine; the VM only runs the built driver - In the virtual machine - On both, with different versions Build on the host, test in the VM. ? Why can a driver not call printf or use std::vector ? + The C runtime and C++ standard library are not available in kernel mode; kernel code uses kernel functions instead - They are too slow - Drivers cannot output text KdPrint and the pool allocation functions take their place. ? Roughly how big is a kernel thread's stack on x64? + 12 KB to 24 KB - 1 MB - Unlimited So large locals and deep recursion are out.

title: 16.02  A Driver That Says Hello
body: The smallest useful driver has two functions: DriverEntry , called when it loads, and an unload routine, called when it is removed. This lesson writes them, prints to the kernel debugger, loads the driver in the lab VM as a service, watches its messages in WinDbg, and unloads it, the complete cycle every later lesson builds on. The code cpp-norun // driver.cpp include <ntddk.h extern "C" DRIVER_INITIALIZE DriverEntry; // declarations with the WDK's annotation types DRIVER_UNLOAD EchoUnload; void EchoUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(driver); KdPrint(("XenonEcho: unloading\n")); } extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING registryPath) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(registryPath); driver- DriverUnload = EchoUnload; // without this, the driver can never be unloaded KdPrint(("XenonEcho: hello from the kernel, IRQL %u\n", KeGetCurrentIrql())); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } Line by line: - DriverEntry is the driver's main . The I/O manager calls it once, at PASSIVE_LEVEL (lesson 15.06), with the driver object (lesson 15.05) and the path of the driver's registry key. It must be extern "C" so its name is not mangled (lesson 4.02). - It returns an NTSTATUS (lesson 15.02). Returning a failure code makes the I/O manager unload the driver at once, without calling its unload routine, so a failing DriverEntry must clean up anything it already did (lesson 16.03). - DriverUnload must be set for the driver to be stoppable. It undoes everything DriverEntry set up. - KdPrint sends text to an attached kernel debugger. It compiles to nothing in Release builds. ( DbgPrintEx is the always-present version with component ids and levels.) - UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER silences warning C4100 for unused parameters, which matters because warnings are errors. Loading it in the VM Copy XenonEcho.sys (and its test certificate, lesson 16.09) to the lab VM, for example to C:\Drivers\ . A software-only driver like this one can be loaded as a kernel service with the built-in sc tool, from an administrator prompt in the VM: cmd sc create XenonEcho type= kernel binPath= C:\Drivers\XenonEcho.sys sc start XenonEcho sc stop XenonEcho sc delete XenonEcho (The space after each = is required by sc .) sc create writes the service's registry key under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\XenonEcho ; sc start asks the kernel to load the driver and call DriverEntry ; sc stop calls the unload routine and unloads it. Hardware drivers are installed differently, through an INF file that plug and play uses to match them with devices; software drivers like this one do not need one. Seeing the output With WinDbg connected to the VM's kernel (lesson 15.08), enable debug output once per session and start the driver: kd ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF kd g XenonEcho: hello from the kernel, IRQL 0 XenonEcho: unloading Without a debugger attached, Sysinternals DebugView run as administrator in the VM (with "Capture Kernel" enabled) shows the same messages. To stop in your code, set a breakpoint before starting the driver: kd bu XenonEcho!DriverEntry kd g bu sets an unresolved breakpoint that is placed when the module loads. When sc start runs, the whole VM freezes at DriverEntry , and you can step through it with p and inspect driver with dt nt!_DRIVER_OBJECT poi(driver) (lesson 8.05). When it goes wrong - sc start fails with error 577 ( ERROR_INVALID_IMAGE_HASH ): the driver is not signed in a way the VM accepts. Check test signing is on and the driver is test-signed (lesson 16.09). - Error 2: the path in binPath is wrong. - A bug check: the VM stops, WinDbg breaks in with the bug check, and !analyze -v names your driver (lesson 15.07). Revert to your snapshot if the VM cannot boot. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to set DriverUnload The driver can then never be stopped without a reboot. !warning Missing extern "C" on DriverEntry The linker cannot find the entry point. !warning Loading on the host Only in the lab VM. Knowledge check quiz ? When is DriverEntry called, and at which IRQL? + Once, when the driver is loaded, at PASSIVE_LEVEL - Every time a program opens the driver - At DISPATCH_LEVEL It is the driver's equivalent of main . ? What happens if DriverEntry returns a failure status? + The driver is unloaded immediately without its unload routine being called, so it must clean up first - Windows bug-checks - The driver keeps running Lesson 16.03 handles partial set-up. ? Where does KdPrint output go? + To an attached kernel debugger (or DebugView capturing kernel output) - To a console window - To a log file automatically It compiles away in Release builds.

title: Read an NTSTATUS
body: Every driver function returns an NTSTATUS . Its top two bits are the severity : 0 success, 1 informational, 2 warning, 3 error. The NT_SUCCESS macro treats success and informational codes (severity 0 or 1) as success. Write: - ntSuccess(status) : what NT_SUCCESS returns (true when the value, read as a signed 32-bit number, is not negative); - severity(status) : "success" , "informational" , "warning" or "error" ; - name(status) : the name for these well-known codes, or "" : Code Name --- --- 0x00000000 STATUS_SUCCESS 0x00000103 STATUS_PENDING 0x80000005 STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW 0xC0000001 STATUS_UNSUCCESSFUL 0xC000000D STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER 0xC0000010 STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST 0xC0000022 STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED 0xC0000023 STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL 0xC000009A STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES

title: 16.03  The Driver Lifecycle
body: A driver sets things up in DriverEntry (devices, links, memory, timers) and must tear every one of them down in its unload routine, in reverse order, leaving nothing behind. If set-up fails halfway, it must undo exactly the steps that succeeded. This lesson builds that discipline: the load and unload sequence, the service registry key, cleanup on partial failure, and why anything left behind after unload crashes the machine. Load to unload The service's registry key ( HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\XenonEcho ) records the type (kernel driver), the file, and the start type : on demand ( sc start ), at boot, or at system start. The lab always uses on-demand, so a broken driver never loads automatically. The unload rule After DriverUnload returns, the driver's code and global data are unmapped . Anything that still refers to them becomes a pointer into nothing: Left behind What happens later --- --- A timer or DPC still queued It fires and jumps into unmapped code: bug check 0xCE (DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS) A device object Requests can still be routed to a driver that is gone A symbolic link Programs can open a name pointing at a deleted device Pool memory Leaked until reboot (lesson 15.04); Driver Verifier reports it A registered callback The kernel calls it later: bug check An IRP still pending Completing it later touches freed state So unload undoes everything , in reverse order of creation, waiting where necessary (for example, KeCancelTimer and flushing queued DPCs with KeFlushQueuedDpcs ) until nothing can call into the driver any more. It is lesson 2.04's RAII and destructor-order rule, enforced by the hardware. Partial failure in DriverEntry DriverEntry does several steps that can each fail. If step 3 fails, steps 1 and 2 must be undone before returning the failure, because the unload routine will not be called. The clear way to write it is to record what succeeded and undo it in reverse: cpp-norun extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING) { NTSTATUS status{ STATUS_SUCCESS }; PDEVICE_OBJECT device{ nullptr }; bool linkCreated{ false }; do { status = IoCreateDevice(driver, sizeof(EchoState), &kDeviceName, FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, FALSE, &device); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) break; status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&kLinkName, &kDeviceName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) break; linkCreated = true; // ... more steps, each followed by a check and a "created" flag ... } while (false); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) // undo, in reverse, only what succeeded { if (linkCreated) IoDeleteSymbolicLink(&kLinkName); if (device) IoDeleteDevice(device); return status; } driver- DriverUnload = EchoUnload; return STATUS_SUCCESS; } The practice task simulates this: given which steps succeed, produce the cleanup calls in the right order. Reference counting and in-flight work Unload can arrive while requests are still being processed on other processors. The I/O manager will not unload a driver while it still has device objects with open handles (the device's reference count, lesson 15.03), so a program holding the device open keeps the driver loaded, and sc stop fails until it closes. Work the driver started itself (timers, work items, threads) is the driver's responsibility to stop and wait for in unload. Common mistakes !warning Unload that forgets one thing Every resource created in DriverEntry needs a matching release in unload. Write them as pairs. !warning Cleanup in the wrong order Reverse order of creation: links before devices, timers stopped before freeing what they use. !warning Partial failure that leaks Undo exactly the steps that succeeded before returning a failure from DriverEntry . Knowledge check quiz ? What happens to a timer the driver forgot to cancel when it unloads? + It fires later and jumps into the unloaded driver's code, causing a bug check - Windows cancels it automatically - Nothing; timers do not outlive drivers Bug check 0xCE is exactly this. ? In which order does unload release resources? + The reverse of the order DriverEntry created them - The same order - Any order Later resources may depend on earlier ones. ? DriverEntry created a device, then failed to create the link. What must it do? + Delete the device and return the failure status - Return the failure; unload will clean up - Ignore it and return success The unload routine is not called when DriverEntry fails.

title: Set up and roll back
body: Model a driver's set-up sequence. Each Step has a name, the name of the call that undoes it, and whether it succeeds. Write initialise(steps) , which runs the steps in order and returns a Result : - If every step succeeds: ok is true, calls lists the step names in order. - If a step fails: stop there. calls lists the names of the steps attempted (including the failing one), followed by the undo calls of the steps that succeeded , in reverse order. ok is false. Then write unload(steps) , the unload routine for a fully initialised driver: the undo calls of all steps in reverse order. steps: create device / delete device, create link / delete link (fails), allocate state / free state initialise - ok false, calls { "create device", "create link", "delete device" }

title: 16.04  Device Objects and Symbolic Links
body: For a user program to talk to a driver, the driver needs a device object to receive requests and a symbolic link that gives it a name user mode can open. This lesson creates both in DriverEntry , removes them in unload, controls who may open the device with a security descriptor , and adds the create and close dispatch routines that make opening and closing work. The device object cpp-norun UNICODE_STRING kDeviceName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING kLinkName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\??\\XenonEcho"); PDEVICE_OBJECT device{ nullptr }; NTSTATUS status{ IoCreateDevice( driver, // the owning driver sizeof(EchoState), // extra bytes for the driver's per-device state (the device extension) &kDeviceName, // its name in the object namespace FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, // device type: also used in the IOCTL codes (lesson 16.05) FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, // apply the device's security to every open, including of sub-paths FALSE, // not exclusive: several handles may be open at once &device) }; - The device appears as \Device\XenonEcho in the object namespace (lesson 15.03), visible in WinObj. - The device extension is a block of non-paged memory attached to the device, sized by the second argument, where the driver keeps its state ( static_cast<EchoState (device- DeviceExtension) ). Keeping state there instead of in globals keeps the driver ready for more than one device. - UNICODE_STRING is the kernel's string type: a length in bytes , a maximum length, and a pointer to UTF-16 characters that are not necessarily zero-terminated . Always use the length. The symbolic link Device names under \Device are not reachable from the Win32 API directly. A symbolic link in the \?? directory (lesson 15.03) gives the device a DOS device name: cpp-norun status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&kLinkName, &kDeviceName); From user mode, the device is then opened as \\.\XenonEcho (lesson 16.06). In unload, the link is deleted ( IoDeleteSymbolicLink ) before the device ( IoDeleteDevice ), the reverse of creation (lesson 16.03). Create and close Opening the device sends an IRP_MJ_CREATE to the driver, and closing the last handle sends IRP_MJ_CLOSE (after IRP_MJ_CLEANUP ). A driver that does not handle them gets the default, which fails the request, so even a minimal driver handles them: cpp-norun NTSTATUS EchoCreateClose(PDEVICE_OBJECT, PIRP irp) { irp- IoStatus.Status = STATUS_SUCCESS; irp- IoStatus.Information = 0; IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } // in DriverEntry: driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CREATE = EchoCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CLOSE = EchoCreateClose; Every dispatch routine follows this shape: fill in IoStatus (the status, and in Information how many bytes were transferred), complete the IRP exactly once (lesson 15.05), and return the same status. Who may open it By default a device created with IoCreateDevice gets the security of its device type, which for many types lets any user open it. That is rarely what a driver wants: every request a user can send is code the kernel will run on their behalf. Choose deliberately: - IoCreateDeviceSecure (from wdmsec.h ) takes an SDDL string describing the security descriptor. For example SDDL_DEVOBJ_SYS_ALL_ADM_ALL allows only SYSTEM and administrators; a custom string can add specific users or groups. - Each IOCTL can also require read or write access to the handle (lesson 16.05), so a user with read access cannot perform write operations. For the lab's echo driver, administrators only is the right default. Common mistakes !warning Treating UNICODE_STRING as zero-terminated Always use its Length (in bytes). !warning Deleting the device before the link Delete in reverse order of creation. !warning Leaving the device open to every user Use IoCreateDeviceSecure with an SDDL string that allows only who needs access. !warning Not handling create and close Opening the device then fails with "invalid device request". Knowledge check quiz ? How does a user-mode program open the device \Device\XenonEcho ? + Through the symbolic link \??\XenonEcho , which it opens as \\.\XenonEcho - Directly by \Device\XenonEcho - Through the registry The link gives the device a name in the DOS device directory. ? What is the device extension? + Memory attached to the device object where the driver keeps per-device state - A file name extension - An extra driver Its size is passed to IoCreateDevice . ? What must a dispatch routine always do with an IRP it handles itself? + Set its status and information, complete it exactly once, and return the same status - Pass it down - Free it Lesson 15.05's rules.

title: Names for a device
body: Write deviceNames(base) , which builds the three names a driver and its client use for a device called base : - the kernel device name \Device\<base ; - the symbolic link name \??\<base ; - the user-mode path \\.\<base . base must be 1 to 32 characters, each a letter, a digit or an underscore; otherwise return std::nullopt . (Driver authors keep names simple: no spaces, no backslashes that would create sub-paths.) Also write byteLength(text) : the Length a UNICODE_STRING holding text would have: the number of UTF-16 units times 2, without a terminator. text here is plain ASCII.

title: 16.05  IOCTLs: Talking to a Driver
body: Reads and writes move bytes; most driver interfaces need commands : "echo this", "give me your statistics", "reset". Those are I/O control codes (IOCTLs), sent with DeviceIoControl and received as IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL . This lesson explains how a control code packs device type, function, buffering method and required access into 32 bits, and writes the driver's dispatch routine for the echo driver's commands. Control codes An IOCTL is a 32-bit number built by the CTL_CODE macro from four fields: 31 16 15 14 13 2 1 0 ┌────────────┬──────┬────────────────────┬──────┐ │ DeviceType │Access│ Function │Method│ │ (16 bits) │ (2) │ (12 bits) │ (2) │ └────────────┴──────┴────────────────────┴──────┘ Field Meaning --- --- DeviceType The device's type, as passed to IoCreateDevice . Values below 0x8000 are reserved for Microsoft; your own drivers use 0x8000 and up Function Which command. Values 0x800 and up are for vendors Method How buffers are passed: METHOD_BUFFERED (0), METHOD_IN_DIRECT (1), METHOD_OUT_DIRECT (2), METHOD_NEITHER (3); lesson 16.07 Access The access the caller's handle must have: FILE_ANY_ACCESS (0), FILE_READ_ACCESS (1), FILE_WRITE_ACCESS (2), or both (3) cpp-norun // echo_ioctl.h: shared by the driver and the client, like lesson 13.03's plugin header. define ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE 0x8001 define IOCTL_ECHO_PING CTL_CODE(ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x800, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS) define IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO CTL_CODE(ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x801, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_ACCESS FILE_WRITE_ACCESS) define IOCTL_ECHO_STATS CTL_CODE(ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x802, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_ACCESS) struct EchoStats { unsigned long long requests; unsigned long long bytesEchoed; }; The access bits are enforced by the I/O manager before the driver ever sees the request: a handle opened without write access cannot send IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO . Choosing them carefully is part of the driver's security (lesson 16.04). The practice task encodes and decodes these codes. The dispatch routine cpp-norun NTSTATUS EchoDeviceControl(PDEVICE_OBJECT device, PIRP irp) { auto state{ static_cast<EchoState (device- DeviceExtension) }; const PIO_STACK_LOCATION stack{ IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp) }; const auto& p{ stack- Parameters.DeviceIoControl }; NTSTATUS status{ STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST }; ULONG_PTR information{ 0 }; switch (p.IoControlCode) { case IOCTL_ECHO_PING: status = STATUS_SUCCESS; break; case IOCTL_ECHO_STATS: if (p.OutputBufferLength < sizeof(EchoStats)) { status = STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL; break; } // METHOD_BUFFERED: the I/O manager gave us one system buffer for input and output (lesson 16.07). static_cast<EchoStats (irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer) = state- stats; information = sizeof(EchoStats); status = STATUS_SUCCESS; break; case IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO: status = EchoEcho(state, irp, p, information); // lesson 16.07 writes this, carefully break; } irp- IoStatus.Status = status; irp- IoStatus.Information = information; // how many bytes to copy back to the caller IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return status; } // in DriverEntry: driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = EchoDeviceControl; - Unknown codes fall through to STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST . Never assume a code is one you know. - Every length is checked before any buffer is touched (lesson 16.07 is entirely about this). - Information tells the I/O manager how many bytes of the output to copy back for METHOD_BUFFERED ; it must never exceed the output length. - Updating state- stats from several processors at once needs synchronisation: interlocked operations ( InterlockedIncrement64 ) or a lock (lesson 15.06). Common mistakes !warning Function numbers below 0x800 or device types below 0x8000 Those ranges are reserved for Microsoft. !warning FILE_ANY_ACCESS for commands that change state Require the access the operation needs, so read-only handles cannot perform it. !warning Trusting the control code Handle only codes you define; everything else returns STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST . Knowledge check quiz ? What four fields make up an IOCTL code? + Device type, required access, function number and buffering method - Driver name, version, size and checksum - Process id, thread id, address and length Packed by the CTL_CODE macro into 32 bits. ? Who enforces an IOCTL's access bits? + The I/O manager, against the caller's handle, before the driver sees the request - The driver, if it remembers to - Nobody A handle without the required access cannot send the code. ? What does IoStatus.Information hold when completing a buffered IOCTL? + How many bytes of output the I/O manager should copy back to the caller - The control code - The status It must never exceed the output buffer's length.

title: Build and read control codes
body: Implement ctlCode(deviceType, function, method, access) , which packs the four fields exactly as the CTL_CODE macro does: (deviceType << 16) (access << 14) (function << 2) method and decode(code) , which splits a control code back into its fields. Also write isVendorCode(code) : true when the device type is at least 0x8000 and the function is at least 0x800 , the ranges set aside for drivers other than Microsoft's. ctlCode(0x8001, 0x801, 0, 3) = 0x8001E004 decode(0x8001E004) = device 0x8001, function 0x801, method 0, access 3

title: 16.06  A User-Mode Client
body:
The other half of the driver is an ordinary program: it opens the device by its symbolic link with CreateFileW , sends commands with DeviceIoControl , and reports errors clearly. This lesson writes the echo driver's client using chapter 5's handles and errors, wraps the protocol in a small class, and covers the details that trip people up: buffer sizes, ERROR_MORE_DATA , and the driver not being loaded. Opening the device cpp-norun include <windows.h include <cstdio include "echo_ioctl.h" // shared with the driver (lesson 16.05) UniqueHandle openEcho() // lesson 5.01's RAII handle { HANDLE h{ CreateFileW(L"\\.\XenonEcho", // the symbolic link, as \.\XenonEcho GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE, // the access our IOCTLs require (lesson 16.05) 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr) }; return UniqueHandle{ h }; // treats INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as empty } If the driver is not loaded, CreateFileW fails with error 2 ( ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND : there is no such name); if the device's security does not allow this user, error 5 ( ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED , lesson 16.04). A good client reports these in plain words: "The XenonEcho driver is not loaded: run sc start XenonEcho in the lab VM." Sending a command cpp-norun bool ping(HANDLE device) { DWORD returned{ 0 }; return DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_ECHO_PING, nullptr, 0, nullptr, 0, &returned, nullptr) != FALSE; } std::optional<EchoStats stats(HANDLE device) { EchoStats s{}; DWORD returned{ 0 }; if (!DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_ECHO_STATS, nullptr, 0, &s, sizeof(s), &returned, nullptr)) return std::nullopt; if (returned != sizeof(s)) return std::nullopt; // never trust the length blindly, even from our own driver return s; } DeviceIoControl takes the control code, an input buffer and its size, an output buffer and its size, and returns how many bytes the driver put in the output (the IRP's Information , lesson 16.05). The driver's NTSTATUS becomes a Win32 error for GetLastError (lesson 5.02): STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL arrives as ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER , STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST as ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION . Echo, with a variable size cpp-norun std::optional<std::string echo(HANDLE device, const std::string& text) { std::string reply(text.size(), '\0'); DWORD returned{ 0 }; if (!DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO, const_cast<char (text.data()), static_cast<DWORD (text.size()), reply.data(), static_cast<DWORD (reply.size()), &returned, nullptr)) return std::nullopt; reply.resize(returned); return reply; } The protocol is the client and driver's shared contract, exactly like lesson 13.03's plugin API: a shared header, explicit sizes, versions if it will change (lesson 12.06), and validation on both sides. The practice task builds a versioned message format for requests and replies with careful parsing. A small client program cpp-norun int wmain() { UniqueHandle device{ openEcho() }; if (!device) { const DWORD error{ GetLastError() }; if (error == ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND) std::wprintf(L"XenonEcho is not loaded (sc start XenonEcho, in the lab VM)
"); else std::wprintf(L"could not open XenonEcho: error %lu
", error); return 1; } std::wprintf(L"ping: %s
", ping(device.get()) ? L"ok" : L"failed"); if (auto reply{ echo(device.get(), "hello, kernel") }) std::printf("echo: %s
", reply- c_str()); if (auto s{ stats(device.get()) }) std::printf("requests %llu, bytes echoed %llu
", s- requests, s- bytesEchoed); return 0; } Run it in the VM with the driver loaded, under the kernel debugger with a breakpoint in EchoDeviceControl , and you can follow one request from DeviceIoControl in user mode, through the system call (lesson 15.02), to your dispatch routine and back. Common mistakes !warning Opening the device with less access than the IOCTL requires The request fails with access denied before reaching the driver. !warning Ignoring the returned byte count Use it to size the result, and check it is what you expected. !warning Cryptic errors Translate the common cases (not loaded, access denied) into instructions the user can follow. Knowledge check quiz ? The client's CreateFileW(L"\\.\XenonEcho", ...) fails with error 2. What is the likely cause? + The driver is not loaded, so the symbolic link does not exist - The user is not an administrator - The IOCTL code is wrong Error 5 would suggest access denied. ? How does a driver's NTSTATUS reach the client? + DeviceIoControl fails and GetLastError returns the corresponding Win32 error - As the return value of DeviceIoControl - Through the output buffer For example STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL becomes ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER . ? What does the returned argument of DeviceIoControl receive? + The number of output bytes the driver reported in the IRP's Information field - The NTSTATUS - The size of the input buffer Size results by it, and check it.

title: A versioned request format
body: The echo protocol's next version sends structured requests. Each message is bytes laid out as: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 version , little-endian, currently 1 2 2 flags 4 4 length of the payload that follows, little-endian 8 length the payload Write encode(flags, payload) , which builds a version 1 message, and decode(bytes) , which parses one and returns the version, flags and payload, or std::nullopt if: - the message is shorter than the 8-byte header; - the version is not 1; - length is larger than the bytes actually present after the header, or larger than kMaxPayload (4096); - there are extra bytes after the payload. Use only explicit byte arithmetic, no memcpy of structs (lesson 2.06).

title: 16.07  Validating Buffers and Staying Safe
body: A driver that accepts requests from user mode is a doorway into the kernel, and many serious Windows vulnerabilities have been driver bugs in exactly this code. This lesson covers the three ways buffers reach a driver ( buffered , direct and neither I/O), and the rules that keep a driver safe: check every length, never return more than was written, never leak kernel memory, and handle every failure. Why this matters Lesson 15.02 explained that the kernel never trusts user mode. A driver's dispatch routines are kernel code run with user-supplied inputs: lengths, control codes and buffer contents chosen by whoever opened the device. A bug that lets a caller read or write memory it should not becomes a way to take over the machine. Vulnerable drivers are a well-known attack route, which is why Windows maintains a blocklist of known-vulnerable signed drivers and why Microsoft's signing process includes testing (lesson 16.09). Writing this code carefully is not optional. Three ways to pass buffers The method in the control code (lesson 16.05) decides how the I/O manager presents the caller's buffers: Method What the driver gets Safety --- --- --- METHOD_BUFFERED One system buffer in non-paged pool, max(input, output) bytes. The I/O manager copies the input in before the call and copies Information bytes out after Safest: the driver never touches user memory. Best for small requests METHOD_IN_DIRECT / METHOD_OUT_DIRECT Input in a system buffer; the output (or second) buffer described by an MDL whose pages the I/O manager has probed and locked (lesson 15.04) Safe, avoids copying large data METHOD_NEITHER The raw user pointers The driver must probe, capture and guard every access itself (lesson 15.02's three rules). Avoid unless there is a strong reason The echo driver uses METHOD_BUFFERED throughout, and so should yours unless measurements show copying is too slow. The rules for every request 1. Check every length before touching any buffer. Input at least as large as the structure you will read; output at least as large as what you will write. Return STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL (or STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ) otherwise. 2. Treat every field read from the input as hostile. Counts, sizes, offsets and indices inside the request get the same checks as the lengths, including overflow in arithmetic ( count sizeof(T) can wrap, lesson 15.02). 3. Set Information to exactly the number of bytes written, never more than the output length. With buffered I/O, the I/O manager copies Information bytes from the system buffer back to the caller; a larger number copies out whatever else is in that pool memory: an information leak . 4. Never leak kernel memory. Zero output structures before filling them (padding bytes too, lesson 2.05). ExAllocatePool2 zero-initialises, which is one reason it replaced the older function (lesson 15.04). 5. Handle every failure. Allocations can fail; return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES . Never assume. 6. Keep the state consistent across processors. Requests can arrive on several processors at once (lesson 15.06): protect shared state. The echo handler, carefully cpp-norun NTSTATUS EchoEcho(EchoState state, PIRP irp, const auto& p, ULONG_PTR& information) { const ULONG in{ p.InputBufferLength }; const ULONG out{ p.OutputBufferLength }; if (in == 0) return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER; if (in kMaxEchoBytes) return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER; // a limit protects the pool if (out < in) return STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL; // we will write exactly in bytes // Buffered I/O: input and output share the system buffer, and the input is already there. // Echoing means leaving it in place and reporting that many bytes as output. information = in; // never more than out InterlockedIncrement64(&state- stats.requests); InterlockedAdd64(&state- stats.bytesEchoed, in); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } Every number that comes from the caller ( in , out ) is checked before it is used; the output count is exactly what is valid; the shared statistics use interlocked operations. The practice task writes the general validator that checks a request against these rules. Tools that help - Driver Verifier (lesson 15.07) with I/O verification catches IRPs completed wrongly and leaks. - Code Analysis for drivers (lesson 16.01) and its annotations ( _In_reads_bytes_ , _IRQL_requires_max_ ) find length and IRQL mistakes at build time. - Fuzzing the IOCTL interface from user mode with random codes, lengths and contents (lesson 17.03) finds what review misses. Run it in the lab VM, with Verifier on. Common mistakes !warning Reading the input before checking its length Even one field read from a too-short buffer reads past it. !warning Information larger than what was written Leaks pool contents to user mode. !warning METHOD_NEITHER without probing, capturing and guarding A classic source of exploitable driver bugs. Prefer buffered I/O. !warning Trusting sizes inside the request A count field in the request is as untrusted as the buffer length. Knowledge check quiz ? With METHOD_BUFFERED , what does the driver work with? + A system buffer in non-paged pool, into which the I/O manager copied the input and from which it copies the output - The caller's user-mode pointers - An MDL The driver never touches user memory directly. ? Why must Information never exceed the bytes actually written? + The I/O manager copies that many bytes back to the caller, so extra bytes would leak whatever was in kernel memory - It would crash the client - It makes the request slower An information leak can reveal kernel addresses and data. ? A request contains a count of items. How should the driver treat it? + As untrusted input: check it, and the arithmetic based on it, against the buffer length and limits before using it - Trust it, since the length was already checked - Ignore it Fields inside requests are as hostile as the lengths.

title: Validate an IOCTL request
body: A driver's "read records" command takes a request header from the input buffer and writes records to the output buffer. Write validate(input, inputLength, outputLength) , the checks the dispatch routine performs before touching anything, returning a Decision : a status name and the exact number of bytes the driver will write. The input begins with a header, if the input is long enough: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 first : index of the first record wanted 4 4 count : how many records Each record is 24 bytes; the driver holds 100 records (indices 0 to 99). Check, in this order: 1. inputLength is at least 8 (the header): otherwise "STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL" . 2. count is at least 1: otherwise "STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER" . 3. first + count does not exceed 100, computed without overflow : otherwise "STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER" . 4. outputLength is at least count 24 : otherwise "STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL" . If all pass: "STATUS_SUCCESS" with bytes equal to count 24 . On any failure, bytes is 0. input holds inputLength bytes; read the fields little-endian from it only after check 1.

title: 16.08  Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
body: With WinDbg attached to the lab VM (lesson 15.08), you can break into your driver's code, step through it, and inspect every kernel structure involved in a request. This lesson is a working session: breakpoints on driver load and on dispatch routines, debug output with levels, examining driver and device objects and IRPs with !drvobj , !devobj and !irp , and analysing a bug check your driver caused. Before you start - WinDbg on the host is connected to the VM's kernel (lesson 15.08) and the VM is running. - Symbols: .symfix for Microsoft's, plus your build folder for the driver's PDB: .sympath+ C:\code\XenonEcho\x64\Debug , then .reload . - Debug output enabled: ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF (or for DbgPrintEx with your own component and level, ed nt!Kd_IHVDRIVER_Mask 0xF ). Breaking into your driver Goal Command --- --- Stop at DriverEntry before the driver is loaded bu XenonEcho!DriverEntry (an unresolved breakpoint, placed when the module loads) Stop in a dispatch routine bp XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl Stop only for one control code Set the breakpoint on a line inside that case (F9 in the source window), rather than on the function Step over / into / out p / t / gu Show locals and parameters dv /t Show the call stack k ( kP with parameters) Continue g Break in at any time Ctrl+Break Start the driver in the VM ( sc start XenonEcho ); WinDbg stops at DriverEntry , and the entire VM freezes while you step through it. Then run the client (lesson 16.06) and stop in EchoDeviceControl for each request. With the PDB loaded, WinDbg's source window follows along; the Locals and Call Stack panes behave like Visual Studio's (lesson 4.07). Looking at kernel structures The ! extensions understand the I/O manager's objects (lesson 15.05): kd !drvobj XenonEcho 7 Driver object (ffffa50c1a2b3e30) is for: \Driver\XenonEcho Device Object list: ffffa50c19f0c8a0 ... Dispatch routines: 00 IRP_MJ_CREATE fffff8063f5e1010 XenonEcho!EchoCreateClose 02 IRP_MJ_CLOSE fffff8063f5e1010 XenonEcho!EchoCreateClose 0e IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff8063f5e1080 XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl ... kd !devobj ffffa50c19f0c8a0 Device object (ffffa50c19f0c8a0) is for: XenonEcho \Driver\XenonEcho DriverObject ffffa50c1a2b3e30 Current Irp 00000000 RefCount 1 Type 00008001 Flags 00000040 DevExt ffffa50c19f0c9f0 ... - !drvobj shows the driver's devices and, with flag 7, its dispatch table: a quick check that DriverEntry filled it in correctly. - !devobj shows a device's reference count (open handles, lesson 16.03), type (your 0x8001 ) and extension. - Inside a dispatch routine, !irp @rdx (the IRP is the second argument, so it is in rdx at the routine's first instruction, lesson 7.06) shows the request: major function, control code, buffer lengths, and the system buffer's address, which db can then dump. - dt XenonEcho!EchoState <address shows your device extension with field names, from the PDB. A bug check, end to end Introduce a bug on purpose in the lab driver, for example reading the input header before checking its length in a copy of lesson 16.07's handler, and send it a 1-byte request. With Driver Verifier's special pool on (lesson 15.07), the read past the system buffer faults at once. WinDbg breaks in with the bug check; then: kd !analyze -v ... PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA (50) Invalid system memory was referenced. ... FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE: C:\code\XenonEcho\dispatch.cpp FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE_NUMBER: 48 ... STACK_TEXT: XenonEcho!EchoReadRecords+0x1a XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl+0x6c nt!IofCallDriver+0x55 nt!IopSynchronousServiceTail+0x1a8 nt!IopXxxControlFile+0x5e5 nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile+0x56 nt!KiSystemServiceCopyEnd+0x25 ntdll!NtDeviceIoControlFile+0x14 KERNELBASE!DeviceIoControl+0x6b EchoClient!wmain+0x84 That one stack is the whole of chapters 15 and 16: the client's DeviceIoControl , the system call (lesson 15.02), the I/O manager building and dispatching the IRP (lesson 15.05), and your dispatch routine at the line that read too far. Fix the check, rebuild, revert the VM to the snapshot if needed, and test again. Common mistakes !warning Breakpoints that never hit Check symbols with lm v m XenonEcho and that the loaded driver is the build whose PDB you gave WinDbg. !warning Forgetting the debug output mask KdPrint output is filtered until the mask is set. !warning Leaving the VM frozen While stopped in the debugger the whole guest is frozen: continue with g when done. Knowledge check quiz ? Why use bu rather than bp for DriverEntry ? + The driver is not loaded yet, so the breakpoint must be resolved when its module loads - bp does not work in the kernel - bu is faster Unresolved breakpoints wait for the module. ? What does !drvobj XenonEcho 7 show? + The driver object, its device objects and its dispatch routine table - The driver's source code - All IRPs in the system A quick check that DriverEntry set things up correctly. ? In the bug check stack, what does nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile represent? + The kernel side of the system call made by the client's DeviceIoControl - A function in the driver - The client program Lesson 15.02's path, seen in a real stack.

title: 16.09  Test Signing
body: 64-bit Windows loads only kernel drivers with a trusted digital signature: driver signature enforcement . During development, drivers are signed with a test certificate and loaded on machines in test mode , which is why the lab VM has it on. This lesson explains how signing works, sets up test signing, explains how real drivers are signed for release, and why test mode belongs only in a lab. Why Windows requires signatures A kernel driver can do anything (lesson 15.01). If any program could load any driver, malware would simply load its own and take full control of the machine. So 64-bit Windows enforces driver signature enforcement (DSE): a driver is loaded only if it carries a valid signature chaining to a certificate Windows trusts for kernel code, and for current Windows releases that means a signature from Microsoft itself, obtained through Microsoft's signing service after the driver's author has been verified. A signature does two things: it proves who published the driver (accountability), and that the file has not been changed since it was signed (integrity). Microsoft can also revoke signatures and block known-vulnerable drivers (lesson 16.07), and features such as Hypervisor-protected Code Integrity (memory integrity) enforce these rules even against kernel-level tampering. How a signature works, briefly 1. A hash of the driver file is computed. 2. The hash is signed with the publisher's private key ; the signature and the publisher's certificate are embedded in the file (or in a catalog .cat file for installed driver packages). 3. When loading, Windows recomputes the hash, checks the signature with the certificate's public key, and checks the certificate chains to a root it trusts for kernel drivers, and that it has not been revoked. Change one byte of a signed driver and the hash no longer matches: it will not load. Test signing for development Getting every development build signed by Microsoft would be impossible, so Windows has a test mode for development machines: - On the test machine (the lab VM): bcdedit /set testsigning on , then restart (lesson 15.08). The desktop shows "Test Mode". - The driver is signed with a test certificate that the developer creates. Visual Studio's driver projects do this automatically: with Driver Signing → Sign Mode: Test Sign , the build creates a test certificate ( XenonEcho.cer ) and signs XenonEcho.sys with it. - In test mode, Windows accepts drivers signed with test certificates, provided the certificate is trusted on that machine. For drivers loaded as services with sc , test mode with a test-signed driver is usually enough; installing the test certificate into the VM's Trusted Root and Trusted Publishers stores (with certmgr or the Certificates console) covers the remaining cases. You can check a signature with signtool verify /v /kp XenonEcho.sys (kernel-mode policy), or in the file's Properties → Digital Signatures tab. Why test mode stays in the lab Test mode weakens a fundamental protection: it lets the machine load drivers signed by anyone who can make a test certificate, which is anyone at all. That is fine in a disposable VM that holds nothing of value, and unacceptable on a computer you use for anything else. Never turn on test signing (or disable signature enforcement in any other way) on your everyday machine, and be suspicious of any software that asks you to. Signing for release Drivers distributed to other people go through Microsoft's Partner Center (Hardware Dev Center): Step Purpose --- --- An extended validation (EV) code-signing certificate for the company Proves the publisher's identity to Microsoft Attestation signing (for testing and limited release), or full Windows Hardware Compatibility Program certification with the HLK test suite Microsoft checks and tests the driver Microsoft signs the driver Windows then trusts it on every machine That process is deliberate: it is why Windows users can trust that a driver came from an accountable publisher, and it is far outside an individual learner's needs. For this course, test signing in the lab VM is all you need. Common mistakes !warning Disabling signature checks on your main PC "to make it work" Use the lab VM. Test mode on an everyday machine weakens its security for everything. !warning Changing the .sys after signing Any change breaks the signature. Sign as the last build step (Visual Studio does). !warning Assuming a signed driver is safe A signature proves who published it and that it is unchanged, not that it has no bugs; vulnerable signed drivers exist, which is why Windows blocks known ones. Knowledge check quiz ? What does driver signature enforcement do? + Loads only kernel drivers with a valid signature trusted for kernel code - Scans drivers for viruses - Makes drivers run faster Without it, any program could load code into the kernel. ? What does test mode ( bcdedit /set testsigning on ) allow? + Loading drivers signed with test certificates, for development - Loading any unsigned file - Running user programs as administrator Only ever in a lab machine. ? What does a valid signature prove? + Who published the driver and that the file has not changed since signing - That the driver has no bugs - That the driver is fast Signed drivers can still be vulnerable.

title: 16.10  Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine
match: 16.10 Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine
body: This project assembles chapter 16 into a complete, working pair: the XenonEcho driver with ping, echo and statistics commands, and its client. It gives the full driver source with every rule from the chapter applied, a build-load-test-unload checklist for the lab VM with Driver Verifier on, a test plan including hostile inputs, and a note on what KMDF would do for you. The driver cpp-norun // XenonEcho: an educational software driver. Build in Debug, test-signed; load only in the lab VM. include <ntddk.h include "echo_ioctl.h" namespace { UNICODE_STRING kDeviceName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING kLinkName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\??\\XenonEcho"); constexpr ULONG kMaxEchoBytes{ 4096 }; struct EchoState { EchoStats stats; // updated with interlocked operations }; } extern "C" DRIVER_INITIALIZE DriverEntry; DRIVER_UNLOAD EchoUnload; _Dispatch_type_(IRP_MJ_CREATE) _Dispatch_type_(IRP_MJ_CLOSE) DRIVER_DISPATCH EchoCreateClose; _Dispatch_type_(IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL) DRIVER_DISPATCH EchoDeviceControl; static NTSTATUS Complete(PIRP irp, NTSTATUS status, ULONG_PTR information) { irp- IoStatus.Status = status; irp- IoStatus.Information = information; IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); // exactly once; do not touch irp afterwards return status; } NTSTATUS EchoCreateClose(PDEVICE_OBJECT, PIRP irp) { return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, 0); } NTSTATUS EchoDeviceControl(PDEVICE_OBJECT device, PIRP irp) { auto state{ static_cast<EchoState (device- DeviceExtension) }; const auto& p{ IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp)- Parameters.DeviceIoControl }; void buffer{ irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer }; // METHOD_BUFFERED for every code below switch (p.IoControlCode) { case IOCTL_ECHO_PING: return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, 0); case IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO: { const ULONG in{ p.InputBufferLength }; if (in == 0 in kMaxEchoBytes) return Complete(irp, STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER, 0); if (p.OutputBufferLength < in) return Complete(irp, STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0); InterlockedIncrement64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.requests)); InterlockedAdd64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.bytesEchoed), in); return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, in); // the input is already in the system buffer } case IOCTL_ECHO_STATS: { if (p.OutputBufferLength < sizeof(EchoStats)) return Complete(irp, STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0); EchoStats copy{}; // zeroed: no stray bytes leave the kernel copy.requests = static_cast<unsigned long long (InterlockedCompareExchange64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.requests), 0, 0)); copy.bytesEchoed = static_cast<unsigned long long (InterlockedCompareExchange64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.bytesEchoed), 0, 0)); RtlCopyMemory(buffer, &copy, sizeof(copy)); return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, sizeof(copy)); } default: return Complete(irp, STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST, 0); } } void EchoUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver) { IoDeleteSymbolicLink(&kLinkName); // reverse order of creation if (driver- DeviceObject) IoDeleteDevice(driver- DeviceObject); KdPrint(("XenonEcho: unloaded\n")); } extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING) { PDEVICE_OBJECT device{ nullptr }; NTSTATUS status{ IoCreateDevice(driver, sizeof(EchoState), &kDeviceName, ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, FALSE, &device) }; if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) return status; RtlZeroMemory(device- DeviceExtension, sizeof(EchoState)); status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&kLinkName, &kDeviceName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) { IoDeleteDevice(device); // undo what succeeded (lesson 16.03) return status; } driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CREATE = EchoCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CLOSE = EchoCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = EchoDeviceControl; driver- DriverUnload = EchoUnload; KdPrint(("XenonEcho: loaded\n")); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } For production you would create the device with IoCreateDeviceSecure and an SDDL string limiting access (lesson 16.04); in the lab, testing from an administrator prompt, the plain call keeps the listing short. The client is lesson 16.06's program. Checklist 1. Build both projects (x64, Debug). The driver build test-signs XenonEcho.sys (lesson 16.09). Run Code Analysis and fix every warning. 2. Revert the VM to the clean snapshot (lesson 15.08). Connect WinDbg; set ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF . 3. Copy XenonEcho.sys and EchoClient.exe into the VM. 4. Enable Driver Verifier for the driver (administrator prompt in the VM), and restart: verifier /standard /driver XenonEcho.sys 5. Load : sc create XenonEcho type= kernel binPath= C:\Drivers\XenonEcho.sys then sc start XenonEcho . WinDbg shows "XenonEcho: loaded". 6. Test with the client, then the hostile tests below. 7. Unload : sc stop XenonEcho , check "unloaded" appears and !poolused shows nothing left for your tag. sc delete XenonEcho . 8. Revert the VM. Test plan Test Expect --- --- Ping Success Echo "hello, kernel" The same text back, returned = 13 Echo 0 bytes ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER Echo 4097 bytes ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER Echo 100 bytes into a 50-byte output ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER Stats into a 4-byte output ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER Stats after 3 echoes requests 3, bytes the sum An undefined code (function 0x900 ) ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION Echo from 8 threads at once, 10,000 times each Correct totals (interlocked statistics) sc stop while the client holds the device open Fails until the client closes it Random codes and lengths for a minute (lesson 17.03's fuzzing) No bug check, no Verifier violation All of this with Driver Verifier on. A pass means the driver behaves correctly on every path you can reach from user mode. What KMDF would do for you The same driver in KMDF (lesson 15.05) would replace the dispatch table with I/O queues ( WdfIoQueueCreate ), get request buffers with checked helpers ( WdfRequestRetrieveInputBuffer(request, minimumSize, ...) fails if the buffer is too small), tie the device's lifetime and cleanup to framework objects so unload ordering is automatic, and handle plug and play and power for hardware drivers. For any real driver, start with KMDF; you now know what it is doing underneath. Common mistakes !warning Testing without Driver Verifier Bugs that only appear under memory pressure or particular timing will otherwise reach users. !warning Skipping the hostile tests Correct requests passing proves little; the incorrect ones are where drivers fail. !warning Running any of this outside the lab VM Everything in this chapter is for the VM. Knowledge check quiz ? Why are the statistics updated with interlocked operations? + Requests can be handled on several processors at once, so plain increments could lose updates - Interlocked operations are required for all kernel code - To make the numbers larger Lesson 6.06's data races, in the kernel. ? What does the driver do with an undefined control code? + Completes it with STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST , which the client sees as ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION - Ignores it - Bug-checks Only defined codes are handled. ? What must be true after sc stop for the driver to have unloaded cleanly? + The device and link are gone, nothing remains queued, and no pool memory is left under its tag - The VM must restart - The client must still be running Lesson 16.03's rule: leave nothing behind.

title: 17.01  Unit Tests for Low-Level Code
body: Every practice task in this course has been checked by unit tests. This lesson turns that around: writing tests for your own low-level code with a framework such as Catch2 or GoogleTest, structuring code so it can be tested (pure logic, injected clocks, random numbers and platform calls), and deciding what is worth testing in games, tools and drivers. What a unit test is A unit test calls one piece of code with chosen inputs and checks its outputs, automatically, in milliseconds. A suite of them runs on every build: cpp-norun include <catch2/catch_test_macros.hpp include "inventory.h" TEST_CASE("potions stack up to their limit") { Inventory inv{ 4, { { "potion", 5 } } }; REQUIRE(inv.add("potion", 7) == 0); CHECK(inv.slot(0) == std::pair<std::string, int { "potion", 5 }); CHECK(inv.slot(1) == std::pair<std::string, int { "potion", 2 }); } The course's practice harness works the same way ( TEST , CHECK , CHECK_EQ ). Real projects use a framework: Framework Notes --- --- Catch2 Header-friendly, readable, TEST_CASE and sections; vcpkg port catch2 GoogleTest Widely used, fixtures and mocking (GoogleMock); vcpkg port gtest ; Visual Studio's Test Explorer runs it Microsoft Native Unit Test Framework Built into Visual Studio's C++ test project template doctest Very fast to compile, Catch2-like Put tests in a separate project (lesson 4.01's tests ), linked against the engine library, and run it after every build, locally and in continuous integration (lesson 17.08). Designing code to be testable Code is easy to test when its logic does not reach directly for things the test cannot control: Hard to test Make it testable by --- --- Calls QueryPerformanceCounter or std::chrono directly Passing a clock (an interface or function) in; tests use a fake clock they advance by hand Calls rand() Passing a seeded random generator in Opens files, windows, devices Separating the platform layer from pure logic (lesson 12.07): parse text, not files Uses global state Passing state in, or resetting it per test Big functions doing everything Small functions with inputs and outputs This is why the practice tasks always asked for a function taking data and returning data: parseLevel(text) rather than loadLevel(path) , tryMove(map, ...) rather than code buried in the game loop. The practice task for this lesson injects a clock into a cooldown timer. What to test Test Example --- --- Normal cases A potion heals 10 Edges Health exactly 0; an inventory exactly full; the first and last tile of a map Invalid input A ragged level file, a negative count, an unknown command Regression tests For every bug fixed, a test that would have caught it (lesson 8.01) Round trips Save then load gives the same state (lesson 11.06) Properties For any random input, sorting gives an ordered result of the same length Not everything needs a unit test: rendering and "does it feel right" are checked by people, and drivers' kernel code is tested in the VM (lesson 16.10). But every piece of pure logic, the majority of most programs, can and should be. Testing low-level code specifically - Bit and byte code (lessons 1.02, 2.06, 9.02): test against known byte sequences, written out in the test, including the edges (0, maximum values, negative numbers). - Parsers of untrusted data (save files, network messages, PE headers): test valid, truncated, oversized and nonsense inputs; then fuzz them (lesson 17.03). - Concurrency (lesson 6.06): tests that run many threads are useful but cannot prove absence of races; combine with careful design and tools. - Memory : run the test suite under AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10) in a separate configuration, so tests also catch overruns and use-after-free. Common mistakes !warning Tests that depend on time or randomness They pass and fail at random. Inject the clock and the generator. !warning Testing only the happy path Bugs live at edges and in invalid input. !warning Tests that are slow or need setup Unit tests should run in seconds with no outside dependencies, or nobody runs them. Knowledge check quiz ? Why pass a clock into a cooldown timer instead of reading the system time inside it? + So a test can control time exactly and check the behaviour deterministically - Reading the system time is slow - Timers cannot read the time A fake clock makes timing logic testable. ? What is a regression test? + A test added for a fixed bug, so it cannot come back unnoticed - A test that runs slowly - A test of old features only Every fixed bug deserves one. ? Which code benefits most from tests with truncated and nonsense inputs? + Parsers of untrusted data, such as save files and network messages - Rendering code - Constant definitions Then fuzz them too.

title: A cooldown you can test
body: Write Cooldown , an ability cooldown that reads time through an injected clock, so tests can control time. - The constructor takes a clock ( std::function<double() , returning seconds) and a duration in seconds. - ready() : true if the ability may be used now: it has never been used, or at least duration seconds have passed since the last use. - use() : if ready, records the current time as the last use and returns true ; otherwise returns false and changes nothing. - remaining() : seconds until ready (0 if ready now). Then write the test-side helper FakeClock : now() returns the current fake time (starting at 0), advance(seconds) moves it forward.

title: 17.02  Sanitizers and Static Analysis
body: Tools find bugs that tests and reviews miss. Sanitizers add checks while the program runs (AddressSanitizer for memory, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer for undefined behaviour); static analysis examines the code without running it (compiler warnings, MSVC's /analyze , clang-tidy, annotations). This lesson sets up each for a Visual Studio project and shows the classes of bug each one catches. Two kinds of tool Sanitizers (dynamic) Static analysis --- --- --- How Instrument the program; check while it runs Analyse the source without running it Finds Bugs on the paths actually executed Possible bugs on any path, including rare ones False alarms Almost none: it saw the bug happen Some: it may flag code that cannot actually go wrong Cost A slower test build Longer build time They complement each other, and both complement tests.
