Sanitizers Sanitizer Catches On Windows --- --- --- AddressSanitizer (ASan) Overruns, use-after-free, double free (lesson 2.10) MSVC /fsanitize=address ; clang-cl too UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) Signed overflow, invalid shifts, misaligned pointers, out-of-range enum values, null dereferences clang-cl ( -fsanitize=undefined ) ThreadSanitizer (TSan) Data races (lesson 6.06) Not on Windows; run tests on Linux builds with clang or gcc if your code is portable MemorySanitizer Reads of uninitialised memory Linux only A practical setup: an ASan configuration in Visual Studio for the test suite and play sessions (lesson 2.10), and, if the code builds with clang, a clang-cl configuration with ASan and UBSan together. Visual Studio installs clang-cl with the "C++ Clang tools for Windows" component. UBSan catches problems ASan cannot, such as int overflow (lesson 1.02), which can silently break checks like if (a + b < a) because the optimiser assumes signed overflow never happens. Compiler warnings The cheapest static analysis is already in your compiler: - Warning level 4 ( /W4 ) and warnings as errors ( /WX ): lesson 4.03's table of valuable warnings. - /permissive- for standard conformance (Visual Studio's default for new projects). - Selected extra warnings with /w14xxx (enable warning xxxx at level 1), for example /w14062 (an enumerator not handled in a switch ) and /w14265 (a class with virtual functions but no virtual destructor). MSVC Code Analysis Analyze → Run Code Analysis (or /analyze on every build) runs a deeper analysis: null dereferences on some paths, buffer overruns it can prove, uninitialised memory, resource leaks, misuse of Windows APIs, and the C++ Core Guidelines checks ( /analyze with the Core Check rule sets). It understands SAL annotations (source annotation language) that describe what functions expect: cpp-norun // "dest points to destSize bytes the function writes; src is a zero-terminated string it reads." size_t copyName(_Out_writes_z_(destSize) char dest, size_t destSize, _In_z_ const char src); With the annotation, the analyzer checks every caller passes a buffer at least destSize long, and checks the function itself never writes past it. The Windows headers are fully annotated, which is how /analyze catches misuse of Windows API calls. Driver projects use the same annotations for IRQL rules (lesson 16.01). clang-tidy clang-tidy (included with Visual Studio's clang tools; enable it in Properties → Code Analysis → Clang-Tidy ) checks style and bug patterns with hundreds of configurable checks: bugprone- (suspicious patterns such as sizeof mistakes, swapped arguments), performance- (unnecessary copies), modernize- (C++ idioms), cppcoreguidelines- . A .clang-tidy file in the solution folder chooses the checks for everyone. Making it routine Tools only help when they run all the time: 1. Warnings at level 4, as errors, from day one. 2. Code Analysis on every build in at least one configuration. 3. The test suite run under ASan regularly, and in continuous integration (lesson 17.08). 4. New warnings are fixed, not suppressed; when a suppression is genuinely right, it is narrow (one line, pragma warning(suppress: ...) ) with a comment saying why. The practice task writes the overflow-checked arithmetic that UBSan and the analyzers push you towards. Common mistakes !warning Turning tools on late in a project Hundreds of warnings at once get suppressed wholesale. Start clean and keep it clean. !warning Blanket suppressions pragma warning(disable: ...) for a whole file hides future bugs too. !warning Assuming a clean run means no bugs Sanitizers only see the paths that ran; analysers cannot see everything. Use all of them, plus tests. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the main difference between a sanitizer and static analysis? + A sanitizer checks while the program runs, on the paths executed; static analysis examines the source for problems on any path - Sanitizers are only for Linux - Static analysis requires running the program They complement each other. ? Which tool catches signed integer overflow as it happens? + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer - AddressSanitizer - Compiler warning C4244 ASan is about memory accesses. ? What does a SAL annotation like _Out_writes_z_(destSize) give the analyzer? + A description of the buffer the function writes, so it can check callers and the function itself - A runtime check - Faster code The Windows headers use these throughout.

title: Arithmetic that cannot overflow silently
body: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, and unsigned overflow wraps silently. Code that computes sizes from untrusted numbers must detect both. Write, without using any type wider than the inputs: - checkedAdd(a, b) for std::int32_t : the sum, or std::nullopt if it would overflow; - checkedMul(a, b) for std::uint64_t : the product, or std::nullopt if it would exceed the maximum; - allocationSize(count, elementSize, header) : header + count elementSize as std::uint64_t , or std::nullopt if any step overflows. Do not compute the overflowing result and then test it (that is already undefined for signed values). Check before the operation.

title: 17.03  Fuzzing
body: Fuzzing feeds a program huge numbers of automatically generated, mostly broken inputs and watches for crashes, hangs and sanitizer reports. Coverage-guided fuzzers such as libFuzzer learn which inputs reach new code and mutate those further, finding bugs no human would think to test. This lesson writes fuzz targets for Delve's parsers, runs them with MSVC's fuzzer support and AddressSanitizer, and minimises the crashing inputs. The idea Tests check the cases you thought of. Bugs live in the cases you did not: a level file with a 2-billion-character line, a save whose length field says 0xFFFFFFFF, a message cut off mid-header. A fuzzer generates such inputs automatically, millions per hour: Coverage guidance is what makes modern fuzzers effective: the compiler instruments the program to record which code each input reaches, and inputs that reach something new are kept and mutated further. The fuzzer gradually learns the format's structure (the magic number, the version field, valid section headers) without being told. Writing a fuzz target A fuzz target is one function that takes a block of bytes and passes them to the code under test: cpp-norun // fuzz_level.cpp: fuzz Delve's level parser (lesson 11.02's practice task) include <cstddef include <cstdint include <string include "level.h" extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t data, size_t size) { const std::string text(reinterpret_cast<const char (data), size); const auto level{ parseLevel(text) }; // must never crash, hang or trip a sanitizer if (level) { // Check invariants the parser promises: the result is self-consistent. if (level- tiles.size() != static_cast<size_t (level- width level- height)) __debugbreak(); } return 0; } Good fuzz targets: - target one parser or decoder of untrusted data: level files, saves (lessons 10.07, 11.06), INI settings (10.08), telemetry snapshots (12.04), IOCTL request structures (16.05), PE headers (9.02); - are deterministic and fast (thousands of runs per second); - check invariants as well as crashes: a successful parse should produce a consistent result; - do not touch the file system, network or global state. Running it with MSVC Visual Studio 2022 supports libFuzzer directly: 1. A new console project fuzz_level containing the target and the parser's source. 2. C/C++ → Command Line : /fsanitize=fuzzer /fsanitize=address (ASan makes memory bugs crash immediately instead of silently). 3. A corpus folder with a few valid level files as starting points. 4. Run: fuzz_level.exe corpus -max_total_time=600 The fuzzer prints progress ( cov: grows as it discovers code). On a crash it stops, prints the sanitizer report, and writes the input to a file such as crash-3f2a... . Running fuzz_level.exe crash-3f2a... reproduces it under the debugger. Minimising Fuzzer-found inputs are often large and noisy. Minimisation shrinks one to the smallest input that still fails, which usually makes the bug obvious. libFuzzer does it with -minimize_crash=1 ; the underlying idea is simple enough to write yourself, and the practice task does: repeatedly try removing parts of the input, keeping any removal after which it still fails. Fuzzing a driver's interface Lesson 16.10's test plan included fuzzing the driver from user mode: a program in the lab VM that opens the device and sends random control codes, lengths and buffer contents in a loop, with Driver Verifier on. Any bug check is a finding; the last request is logged before sending, so it can be reproduced. That is exactly how many real driver vulnerabilities are found, which is why driver authors should do it first. Common mistakes !warning Fuzzing without sanitizers Most memory bugs do not crash on their own. Combine fuzzing with ASan. !warning Slow targets A target doing file I/O or logging runs a hundred times slower and finds far less. !warning Fixing the crash but not adding the input to the tests Every fuzzer finding becomes a regression test (lesson 17.01). Knowledge check quiz ? What makes a coverage-guided fuzzer better than random inputs? + It keeps inputs that reach new code and mutates them further, gradually learning the input format - It uses a list of known bugs - It runs faster New coverage guides the search. ? Why run a fuzz target with AddressSanitizer? + So memory errors that would not crash on their own are detected immediately - To make it faster - Fuzzers require it to compile Silent overruns become clear failures. ? What does minimising a crashing input achieve? + The smallest input that still fails, which usually makes the cause obvious - A faster fuzzer - A fix for the bug Then add it as a regression test.

title: Minimise a failing input
body: A fuzzer found an input that makes a parser fail. Write minimise(input, fails) , which shrinks it to a smaller input that still fails, by greedy single-character removal: 1. Try removing the character at position 0, then 1, then 2, and so on, of the current input. 2. As soon as removing one gives an input for which fails still returns true, keep that shorter input and start again from position 0 . 3. When no single removal still fails, return the current input. fails(input) is guaranteed to be true for the original input. Also return how many times fails was called, so the cost can be compared with smarter methods. fails = "contains both 'x' and 'y'" minimise("abxcdye") - "xy"

title: 17.04  Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
match: 17.04 Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
body: Security bugs are ordinary bugs in code that handles input an attacker can control. This lesson collects the course's lessons into secure coding practice for C++: trust boundaries , the classic bug classes (buffer overruns, integer errors, use after free, path traversal, format strings, time-of-check to time-of-use), and the habits and safe building blocks that prevent them. Trust boundaries A trust boundary is any place where data crosses from something you do not control into something you do. Everything this course built has them: Boundary Untrusted side --- --- Files loaded by the game Level files, saves, settings, mods (lessons 10.07, 13.02) Network messages Other players, servers, anything on the internet Plugins and scripts Mod authors' code and data (lesson 13.07) Shared memory and pipes The other process (lesson 12.07) Command-line arguments and environment Whoever started the program A driver's IOCTLs Any user who can open the device (lesson 16.07) The rule is the same at every one: validate at the boundary , before the data is used for anything (sizes, indices, paths, allocations, decisions). Inside, code can rely on data being valid because it was checked once, at the edge. The classic bug classes Bug How it happens Prevention --- --- --- Buffer overrun Copying or indexing past a buffer's end with a length from input (lessons 2.08, 2.09) std::string , std::vector , std::span ; check lengths against the destination; .at() in debug paths Integer overflow and truncation count size wraps; a 64-bit length truncated to 32 bits; signed/unsigned mix-ups (lessons 1.02, 17.02) Checked arithmetic; consistent unsigned sizes; compiler warnings C4244, C4267, C4018 Use after free / dangling Keeping pointers to objects that can disappear (lessons 2.04, 3.10) Ownership through smart pointers; ids and handles instead of raw pointers Uninitialised memory Reading or sending memory never written, leaking its old contents (lesson 16.07) Always initialise; zero output structures Path traversal A file name like ..\..\Windows\system.ini from input reaches files outside the intended folder (lesson 13.02) Reject .. , absolute paths and drive letters; resolve and check the result stays under the base; the practice task Format string printf(userText) interprets % sequences in input Always printf("%s", text) ; prefer std::format with a constant format Time of check to time of use Data checked, then read again after it may have changed (lessons 15.02, 12.04) Copy once, then check and use the copy Injection Building commands, SQL or scripts by concatenating input Pass input as data (arguments, parameters), never as code Nearly every security advisory for C and C++ software falls in this table. Safe building blocks Modern C++ removes whole classes of these bugs if you let it: - std::span<T carries a pointer and a length together, so functions can never lose track of a buffer's size (lesson 2.07). - std::string_view for read-only text, with the lifetime caveat of lesson 2.04. - Containers instead of raw arrays and new . - std::optional and status returns instead of sentinel values that can be mistaken for data. - std::format instead of printf -family formatting. - RAII for every resource, so error paths cannot leak (lesson 2.04). Defence in depth No single measure is perfect, so layers are combined: 1. Correct code : validation at boundaries, safe building blocks. 2. Tools : warnings, analysis, sanitizers, fuzzing (lessons 17.02, 17.03). 3. Platform mitigations left on: ASLR (lesson 6.09), DEP and non-executable data (6.03), stack cookies (7.05), control-flow guard. They turn many exploitable bugs into crashes. 4. Least privilege : programs and tools that run with only the rights they need (lesson 6.08) limit what any remaining bug can do. Common mistakes !warning Validating deep inside the code instead of at the boundary Some path will skip the check. Validate where the data enters. !warning Trusting your own file formats Users and attackers can edit any file on their machine. !warning Turning mitigations off for convenience They cost almost nothing and defeat whole classes of attack. Knowledge check quiz ? Where should untrusted input be validated? + At the trust boundary where it enters, before it is used for anything - Wherever it is finally used - Only in Debug builds Then the inside of the program can rely on it. ? A mod asks the game to load ..\..\saves\other.sav . What bug class is this? + Path traversal - Format string - Integer overflow Reject parent-directory components and check the resolved path stays inside the mod's folder. ? Why use std::span for buffer parameters? + It carries the pointer and the length together, so the size cannot be lost or mismatched - It is faster than a pointer - It allocates memory Lost lengths are the root of many overruns.

title: Join paths safely
where: 17.04 Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
body: A mod asks for files by relative path. Write safeJoin(base, relative) , which returns base joined with relative , or std::nullopt if the request could reach outside base . Paths use \ or / as separators; the result uses \ . Reject (return std::nullopt ) if relative : - is empty; - is absolute: starts with \ or / , or has a drive letter ( C: ), or contains : anywhere (which on Windows also names alternate data streams); - contains any component that is .. ; - contains an empty component (two separators in a row such as a//b , or a trailing separator), or a component that ends with a space or a dot (Windows silently strips those, so secret.txt. would open secret.txt ), except the component . itself, which is simply skipped. Otherwise return base , a single \ , and the components joined with \ (skipping . components). If only . components remain, return base unchanged. safeJoin("C:\Game\mods\lantern", "textures/light.png") - "C:\Game\mods\lantern\textures\light.png" safeJoin("C:\Game\mods\lantern", "../../saves/a.sav") - nullopt

title: 17.05  Threat Modelling
body: A threat model is a structured answer to "what could go wrong, and what are we doing about it?" written before the code, not after the breach. This lesson walks through the four questions of threat modelling, draws a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, applies STRIDE to find threats systematically, and ranks them so effort goes where it matters. The worked example is Delve with mods, saves and an online leaderboard. The four questions Threat modelling sounds formal, but it comes down to four questions: 1. What are we building? A diagram of the parts and the data flowing between them. 2. What can go wrong? Threats, found systematically rather than by guessing. 3. What are we going to do about it? A mitigation, an acceptance, or a design change for each one. 4. Did we do a good job? Review it as the design changes, and check mitigations were really built. It takes an hour for a small project and saves weeks of fixes later, because design changes are cheap before the code exists. Step 1: a data-flow diagram Draw the processes, data stores, external parties and flows, and mark where trust changes: Trust boundaries in this diagram: between the mod folder and the game (anyone can write files there), between the player's machine and the server (the server cannot trust anything the client sends), and between the server and other players viewing scores (their browsers will render whatever names are stored). Step 2: STRIDE STRIDE is a checklist of six threat types. Walk every element and flow in the diagram and ask each question: Letter Threat Question Property it violates --- --- --- --- S Spoofing Can someone pretend to be another user or component? Authentication T Tampering Can someone change data or code they should not? Integrity R Repudiation Can someone deny doing something, with no way to prove otherwise? Accountability I Information disclosure Can someone read what they should not? Confidentiality D Denial of service Can someone stop it working for others? Availability E Elevation of privilege Can someone gain rights they should not have? Authorisation Step 3: threats and responses for Delve Element STRIDE Threat Response --- --- --- --- Mod folder → game T, E A malicious mod's data overflows a parser and runs code Validate at the boundary (17.04), fuzz the parsers (17.03), data-only mods by default, native plugins opt-in with a warning (13.07) Mod folder → game I A mod path like ..\..\ reads files outside its folder safeJoin (17.04's practice) Save files T A player edits their save Accept for single player: it is their game Game → leaderboard T, S A client submits an impossible score, or one in someone else's name Server-side validation and replay checks (17.06), accounts with tokens Leaderboard D One client floods submissions Rate limiting per account and address Leaderboard → other players T, E A player name containing a script runs in viewers' browsers Escape output; limit name characters Score database I Leaked email addresses Store only what is needed; access control on the database Game → leaderboard R A player disputes a ban Keep submitted replays and the server's decision log Note the save-file row: accepting a threat is a legitimate answer, when the impact falls only on the person causing it. Step 4: ranking Not every threat deserves the same effort. A simple ranking multiplies likelihood (1 to 5) by impact (1 to 5) and handles the highest scores first, with ties broken by whichever is cheapest to fix. Many teams use richer schemes, but any explicit ranking beats fixing whatever someone noticed last. The practice task implements one. Keeping it alive A threat model is a document in the repository next to the design notes. Update it when a feature adds a new data flow or trust boundary (an online feature, a plugin API, a new file format), and check the "response" column against the code during reviews. Common mistakes !warning Starting from attacks you have heard of STRIDE over a diagram finds the threats specific to your design, not just famous ones. !warning Treating every threat as "must fix" Some are accepted, some are cheap to fix, some need a design change. Rank and decide. !warning Writing it once A threat model of last year's design protects last year's design. Knowledge check quiz ? What does the T in STRIDE stand for, and which property does it violate? + Tampering, which violates integrity - Theft, which violates confidentiality - Timing, which violates availability Changing data or code without permission. ? Why is "accept" a valid response for players editing their own single-player saves? + The impact falls only on the person making the change - Saves cannot be edited - Accepting is always the best response Effort goes to threats that harm others. ? Where do trust boundaries appear on a data-flow diagram? + Wherever data passes between parts with different levels of trust, such as from the client to the server - Around every function - Only around the database Those are where validation is needed.

title: Rank the threats
body: Write rankThreats(threats) , which returns the threats' names in the order they should be handled: - by score ( likelihood impact ), highest first; - ties broken by lower cost first (cheaper fixes earlier); - remaining ties by name alphabetically. Threats marked accepted are left out. Likelihood and impact are 1 to 5; any threat with a value outside that range is a mistake in the threat model and is also left out.

title: 17.06  Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
match: 17.06 Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
body: This course taught how programs look from the inside, which is also how cheats and tampering work. This lesson takes the defender's side: why a game can never fully trust the client, why server authority is the foundation of fair online play, how to verify the integrity of your own files and updates with hashes and code signing, what client-side anti-tamper can and cannot do, and the legal, ethical and privacy limits that apply to both sides. The client is in the player's hands Every technique in chapters 5 to 16 works on a program running on your own machine: reading its memory, changing its code, injecting a DLL, inspecting its traffic. A player can do all of that to a game on their machine. That leads to the most important rule of game security: !important Never trust the client Anything that runs on the player's computer can be read and changed by the player. Decisions that affect other players must be made, or at least checked, somewhere the player does not control. Client-side protection can make tampering slower and more obvious; it cannot make it impossible. Fair play in online games rests on design first and detection second. Server authority In an authoritative server design, clients send inputs ("move forward", "fire at this direction") and the server runs the simulation and decides the results. A modified client can still send inputs, but it cannot directly set its health, teleport, or award itself a score. What the server validates: Check Example --- --- Physics limits A move longer than maximum speed times elapsed time is clamped or rejected (the practice task) Rates and cooldowns No more shots than the weapon's fire rate allows Visibility The server sends a player only what that player could legitimately see, so there is nothing hidden in memory to reveal Game rules Items can only be used if owned; doors only opened if unlocked Plausibility over time Statistics that are consistently beyond human limits are flagged for review, never banned automatically For single-score games like Delve's leaderboard, the equivalent is submitting a replay (the seed and the inputs) instead of a score; the server re-simulates it deterministically and computes the score itself (the leaderboard threat in lesson 17.05). Integrity of your own files Separately from cheating, you need to know the code and data you ship are the code and data that run, and that updates come from you: - Hash manifests : a list of every shipped file with its SHA-256 hash. The launcher or updater checks files against it, which catches corruption and incomplete updates (lesson 3.08's checksums, made cryptographic). - Code signing : an Authenticode signature on your executables and DLLs (and the manifest) proves who published them and that they were not changed. Windows shows the publisher and SmartScreen builds reputation from it; drivers must be signed to load at all (lesson 16.01). - Signed updates : an updater verifies the signature of a downloaded update before installing it, so a compromised download server cannot push malicious code. - Safe loading : load DLLs only from your own folder with full paths (lesson 13.04), so a planted DLL is not picked up instead. What client-side anti-tamper does Commercial games add protection on the client. Understanding its purpose, at a high level, helps you design around it and judge its trade-offs: Measure Purpose Limit --- --- --- Integrity checks of the game's own code and data Detect modified files or patched code Runs on the same machine it is protecting Obfuscation Make analysis (chapter 9) slower Slows, never prevents Detecting debuggers and injected modules Notice the tools of chapters 8 and 13 False positives on legitimate software Kernel-mode components Observe from a more privileged level Very high trust demanded from players; a driver bug crashes their machine (chapter 16) The cost side matters: kernel-level anti-cheat asks players to trust your code with full control of their computer, and some players reasonably refuse. Collect only what is needed, document what is collected, and remove the component when the game is uninstalled. The rules for both sides - Terms of service and the law apply. Modifying or analysing a game you do not own can break its licence, and creating or selling cheats for online games has led to lawsuits. Cheating in online games harms other players, and this course does not teach it. - Fair-play enforcement must be fair : decisions reviewed by humans, an appeal process, and evidence kept (the repudiation row in 17.05). - Privacy : anti-cheat that scans the player's machine is handling personal data and falls under laws such as the GDPR. - Single-player modding is a different matter: it harms no one, and many developers support it with official tools (chapter 13). Common mistakes !warning Trusting client-reported results "The client says it hit for 9999 damage" must never be believed. !warning Sending hidden information to clients If the client receives every enemy position, a modified client can show them. Send only what can be seen. !warning Relying on obfuscation instead of design Obfuscation buys time. Server authority removes whole classes of cheats. Knowledge check quiz ? Why can client-side protection never fully stop tampering? + It runs on the player's own machine, which they control completely - Because clients are always slower than servers - It can, if it is obfuscated enough Protection there can only raise the cost. ? In an authoritative-server design, what do clients send? + Their inputs, which the server validates and simulates to decide the results - Their positions and health, which the server trusts - Nothing; the server guesses The server owns the game state. ? What does code signing an update prove? + Who published it and that it has not been changed since signing - That it has no bugs - That it runs faster The updater checks the signature before installing.

title: Validate movement on the server
where: 17.06 Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
body: An authoritative server receives each client's reported position every tick and must not trust it. Write validateMove(previous, reported, dt, maxSpeed, walls) : - The allowed distance is maxSpeed dt plus a tolerance of 1% of it (network timing is never perfect). - If the reported move is within the allowed distance, the move is accepted at the reported position. - If it is further, the move is clamped : the position becomes previous moved towards reported by exactly maxSpeed dt (no tolerance). - Either way, if the resulting position is inside any wall rectangle ( x = left && x < right && y = top && y < bottom ), the move is rejected and the position stays previous . - A dt that is not positive, or a reported position that is not finite (NaN or infinity), is rejected . Return the outcome and the position the server will use.

title: 17.07  Performance Without Guessing
body: Programmers are famously bad at guessing where time goes. This lesson replaces guessing with measurement: frame budgets, profilers (Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool and sampling in general), microbenchmarks done properly, and the statistics that make timings trustworthy (medians and percentiles instead of averages). It ends with the common real causes of slow C++: cache misses, allocations, and work repeated every frame. Budgets first "Fast enough" needs a number. A game at 60 frames per second has 16.7 ms per frame for everything: input, simulation, rendering, audio, and the tools of chapter 12 if they are running. At 144 Hz it is 6.9 ms. A budget turns "it feels slow" into "the overlay takes 3.1 ms of our 16.7". For tools the budget is different (a memory scan should finish in under a second, an overlay should cost under 0.5 ms a frame), but it is still a number. Measure, then change one thing, then measure again Always measure Release builds (lesson 4.10: Debug builds can be ten times slower, and differently slow), on the same machine, with the same input, several times. Profilers A sampling profiler interrupts the program thousands of times a second and records which function was running. Functions that appear in many samples are where the time goes. In Visual Studio: Debug → Performance Profiler → CPU Usage , run the scenario, stop, and read the Hot Path and the list of functions sorted by Total CPU (including callees) and Self CPU (excluding them). Other useful tools: Tool Shows --- --- Visual Studio CPU Usage Where CPU time goes, by function and line Visual Studio Memory Usage Allocations and their call stacks Windows Performance Recorder and Analyzer Whole-system timelines: threads, waits, disk, GPU PIX GPU and frame timing for Direct3D games An in-game frame timer Per-system timings every frame, for regressions Microbenchmarks done properly Sometimes you want to compare two versions of one function. Timing it naively lies in several ways: cpp include <algorithm include <chrono include <iostream include <numeric include <vector volatile long long sink; // stops the optimiser removing the work long long sumVector(const std::vector<int & v) { return std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL); } int main() { std::vector<int data(1'000'000); std::iota(data.begin(), data.end(), 0); std::vector<double samples; for (int run{ 0 }; run < 25; ++run) { const auto start{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; sink = sumVector(data); const auto end{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; samples.push_back(std::chrono::duration<double, std::micro (end - start).count()); } std::sort(samples.begin(), samples.end()); std::cout << "min " << samples.front() << " us, median " << samples samples.size() / 2 << " us\n"; } varies min 212.4 us, median 231.9 us The rules it follows: - Repeat many times and look at the distribution; one run means nothing. - Use the result (here through a volatile variable) so the optimiser cannot delete the work. - Use steady_clock , which never jumps, not the wall clock. - Report the median and a high percentile (p95, p99), not just the mean: a single slow run caused by the operating system can pull the mean far away, while players feel the slow frames that the percentiles show. The practice task computes these. - Keep input sizes realistic: data that fits in the cache behaves completely differently from data that does not. The usual real causes When you do measure, the culprit in C++ is usually one of a short list: Cause Sign Typical fix --- --- --- Cache misses Time in simple loops over large data; pointer-heavy structures (lesson 2.06) Contiguous arrays, structure of arrays, smaller structs Allocations in the frame loop operator new and malloc high in the profile Reserve once, reuse buffers, pools (lesson 3.10) Repeated work The same computation or lookup every frame Cache the result; recompute only on change Algorithmic cost Time grows much faster than input size A better algorithm: hashing instead of searching, sorting once Waiting Low CPU but slow; threads blocked Profile waits (WPA); avoid blocking calls on the main thread Debug-only overhead Fast in Release Nothing to fix; measure Release Note what is not on the list: rewriting clear code into clever code with no measurement. That rarely helps and often hurts. Common mistakes !warning Profiling Debug builds You will optimise the wrong things. !warning Trusting one timing Run many times; report the median and a percentile. !warning Benchmarks the optimiser deletes If the result is unused, the compiler may remove the code and report it as free. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the frame budget at 60 frames per second? + About 16.7 milliseconds - 60 milliseconds - 1 millisecond 1000 ms divided by 60. ? Why report the median and p95 rather than only the mean? + A few unusually slow runs distort the mean, while the median shows the typical case and p95 the slow cases players feel - The mean is harder to compute - Percentiles are always smaller Distributions, not single numbers. ? Why store a benchmark's result in a volatile variable? + So the optimiser cannot remove the work because its result appears unused - To make it run faster - To avoid cache misses Unused results invite dead-code elimination.

title: Benchmark statistics
body: Write summarise(samples) for a list of timings in milliseconds. It returns: - min and max ; - median : the middle value after sorting, or the mean of the two middle values for an even count; - p95 : the nearest-rank 95th percentile: sort, then take the value at 1-based rank ceil(0.95 n) ; - trimmedMean : the mean after dropping the lowest 10% and highest 10% of the sorted values, where 10% is n / 10 rounded down (so with fewer than 10 samples nothing is dropped). An empty list returns all zeros. The input must not be modified.

title: 17.08  Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
match: 17.08 Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
body: A program is not finished when it works on your machine. This lesson covers what it takes to put a tool or game in other people's hands and keep it working: reproducible Release builds, versioning with semantic versions , crash reports with symbols kept for every release, installers and updates, documentation, licences, and the habits of maintenance (changelogs, issue tracking, and deciding what not to build). A reproducible Release build Anyone on the team, or a build server, should produce the same release from the same commit: - The build is one command or one button: Build → Batch Build or msbuild Delve.sln /p:Configuration=Release /p:Platform=x64 . - Dependencies are pinned: the SDL2 version from lesson 11.01 is checked in or fetched at a fixed version (vcpkg with a manifest and baseline does this). - Release settings are deliberate: optimisation on, warnings as errors, /guard:cf and other mitigations on (lesson 17.04), and /Zi with PDBs even for Release. - A continuous integration service (GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines) builds and runs the tests (17.01) on every push, so a broken build is noticed in minutes. Semantic versions A semantic version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tells users what an update means: Part Increase when Example --- --- --- MAJOR You make a change that breaks compatibility: an old save format no longer loads, a plugin API function changes 1.4.2 → 2.0.0 MINOR You add features compatibly 1.4.2 → 1.5.0 PATCH You fix bugs compatibly 1.4.2 → 1.4.3 Pre-releases add a suffix ( 2.0.0-beta.1 ) and sort before the final version. Versioning interfaces between components (lesson 12.06's telemetry protocol, lesson 13.07's plugin API) follows the same rule, which is why those had version fields. The practice task compares and bumps versions. Put the version in the executable's version resource (Add → Resource → Version) so it shows in the file's properties, in the crash report, and in the title or about screen. Crash reports and symbols Users will hit crashes you never saw. Lesson 8.04's minidumps are how you find out: 1. The program installs an unhandled-exception filter that writes a minidump with MiniDumpWriteDump and offers to send it. 2. For every release, you keep the exact PDBs produced by that build, in a symbol store ( symstore add ) or a folder named by version. 3. When a dump arrives, WinDbg or Visual Studio loads it with the matching symbols and shows the call stack and variables at the crash. Without the matching PDB, a dump is a list of addresses. Losing a release's symbols means losing the ability to debug its crashes. Installers and updates Option Suits --- --- A zip file with a portable folder Small tools; nothing to install or uninstall An MSIX package or an MSI (WiX) Applications that need Start menu entries, file associations, clean uninstall A store or launcher (Steam, itch.io, Microsoft Store) Games: it handles distribution, updates and signing Your own updater Only when nothing else fits; it must verify signatures (17.06) Whatever the method: code-sign the files, install per-user without administrator rights when possible (lesson 6.08), and keep settings and saves in the user's folders ( %APPDATA% , Saved Games ), not next to the program. Documentation Three documents cover most needs: - A README : what it is, how to install it, how to use the common features, system requirements. - A changelog : each version, with what was added, changed, fixed and removed, in plain language. - For anything with an interface others build on (a plugin API, a protocol, a driver's IOCTLs), a reference : every function or message, its parameters, errors and version. Licences Every dependency's licence must allow your use: SDL2 uses the zlib licence (very permissive), Dear ImGui is MIT, some libraries are GPL (which places conditions on your own code if you distribute it). List them in a third-party notices file. Choose a licence for your own code too, if you publish it; without one, others have no right to use it. Maintenance After release, most of the work is maintenance: - Track bugs and requests in an issue tracker , each with steps to reproduce, version and logs. - Fix with a regression test first (17.01), then the fix. - Release patches from a known commit, tagged with the version ( git tag v1.4.3 ). - Say no to features that do not fit. Each one is code to maintain forever, a lesson that applies with special force to low-level tools, where every new feature is also new attack surface (17.05). Common mistakes !warning Not keeping Release PDBs Crash reports become useless. !warning Breaking compatibility in a minor version Users and plugin authors trusted the version number. !warning Saving data next to the executable Program Files is not writable by normal users, and updates may replace the folder. Knowledge check quiz ? A change makes old save files fail to load. Which part of the version increases? + MAJOR - MINOR - PATCH It breaks compatibility. ? Why keep the PDB files of every release? + Crash dumps from users can only be read with the exact symbols from the build that crashed - Windows needs them to run the program - They make the program faster Without them a dump is just addresses. ? Where should a game store its saves? + In the user's folders, such as Saved Games or AppData - Next to the executable in Program Files - In the Windows folder Per-user, writable, and untouched by updates.

title: Compare and bump versions
where: 17.08 Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
body: Write three functions for semantic versions of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional pre-release suffix after a - (such as 2.0.0-beta.1 ): - parseVersion(text) : the version, or std::nullopt if the text is not three non-negative whole numbers separated by dots (each made only of digits, at least one, no leading zeros except 0 itself), optionally followed by - and a non-empty suffix. - compareVersions(a, b) : negative if a < b , zero if equal, positive if a b . Compare MAJOR, then MINOR, then PATCH numerically. If those are equal, a version with a suffix is lower than one without; two suffixes compare as plain strings. - bump(v, part) : "major" gives MAJOR+1.0.0 , "minor" gives MAJOR.MINOR+1.0 , "patch" gives MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+1 . The suffix is always removed. Return it formatted as text. compareVersions(1.10.0, 1.9.0) 0 (numeric, not text) compareVersions(2.0.0-beta.1, 2.0.0) < 0 bump(1.4.2, "minor") 1.5.0

title: 18.01  Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
match: 18.01 Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
body: The first capstone joins chapters 6, 12 and 14 into one polished tool: a read-only memory inspector for programs you built yourself , with a Dear ImGui interface showing the region map, a hex view with typed overlays, snapshots with change highlighting, and the telemetry channel from chapter 12. This lesson gives the specification, an architecture, the milestones in order, the acceptance tests and stretch goals. What you are building Xenon Inspector is a desktop tool for looking inside your own running programs while you develop them: Delve, the practice targets of lesson 9.10, and anything else you compile. It answers questions like "what does this struct look like in memory right now?", "which bytes changed when I picked up that item?" and "how is this program's address space laid out?". The ground rules from chapter 12 are part of the specification, not an afterthought: !important Scope - The inspector only opens processes whose executable lies under a folder you configure as your build output (for example D:\dev\bin ), or processes it starts itself from there. It refuses anything else, with a message explaining why. - It is read-only : it never writes to the target's memory. - It uses documented APIs only ( OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION PROCESS_VM_READ , VirtualQueryEx , ReadProcessMemory , the Tool Help snapshot functions) and needs no administrator rights. Features Panel Shows Built in --- --- --- Process picker Running processes under the build folder, with a Launch button for executables there 6.07, 12.01 Region map Every region: base, size, state, protection, type, and the module it belongs to; filters and sorting 6.04, 14.04 Hex view Bytes of a selected address range, 16 per row with ASCII; Go to address; follows a pointer on double-click 12.02 Typed overlay A struct definition (from a small text file) laid over the hex view, showing each field's name, type and value 2.06, 9.09 Snapshots Take a snapshot of a range, take another later, and list and highlight the changed ranges the practice task Telemetry If the target publishes chapter 12's telemetry channel, its live values in a table 12.04, 12.05 Settings Build folder, refresh rate, window layout, persisted 14.05 Architecture Keep the layers separate, as lesson 17.01 recommends: the struct parser and the snapshot diff are pure functions with unit tests; the process access layer is the only code that calls Windows; the panels only draw the model and send it commands. Then most of the program can be tested without a target running. Milestones Build it in order; each milestone is usable on its own. 1. Skeleton : the ImGui window from lesson 14.02 with an empty dock space, a settings file and the build-folder setting. 2. Process access : list processes, apply the scope check (resolve the executable path with QueryFullProcessImageNameW , then check it is under the build folder after normalising both), open with the minimum rights. Unit-test the path check with lesson 17.04's lessons about .. and case. 3. Region map : the VirtualQueryEx walk from lesson 6.04 on the target, shown in a sortable table with module names. 4. Hex view : read on demand only the visible rows, handle unreadable pages ( ReadProcessMemory fails or reads partially: show ?? ), and refresh at the configured rate. 5. Snapshots and diff : copy a range, compare later, list changed ranges, highlight them in the hex view. 6. Typed overlay : parse definitions such as struct Player { i32 health; f32 x; f32 y; u8 flags; } with natural alignment (lesson 2.05) and show the values. 7. Telemetry : connect to the target's telemetry channel if it exists, and show its version check from lesson 12.06. 8. Hardening : lesson 12.07's checklist: the target exiting at any moment, huge regions, invalid addresses typed by the user, and a fuzz test of the struct parser (17.03). Acceptance tests The inspector is done when: - it refuses a process outside the build folder, including one reached by a path with .. , a different case, or a short 8.3 name; - it shows Delve's region map and its main module's base matches the one Delve prints (lesson 6.09); - the overlay of Delve's Player struct shows the health dropping when a monster hits; - a snapshot diff around the inventory shows exactly the bytes that change when an item is picked up; - closing Delve while the inspector is reading it gives a clear message, not a crash; - the unit tests pass under AddressSanitizer; - it never opens a handle with write or operation rights (verify with Process Explorer's handle view). Stretch goals - Read the target's PDB with the DIA SDK or dbghelp to show real type names and fields instead of hand-written definitions. - A "watch list" of addresses with a plot of each value over time (lesson 14.04). - Export a snapshot and its overlay as a report for a bug ticket. Common mistakes !warning Reading huge ranges every frame Read only what is visible, and only at the refresh rate. !warning Mixing Windows calls into the UI code It makes the inspector untestable and the UI slow when a read blocks. !warning Loosening the scope check "just for testing" The rule is the feature. Keep test targets in the build folder. Knowledge check quiz ? Why is the process scope check done on the full executable path after normalising it? + So paths with .. , different case or short names cannot get around it - Because process names are always unique - To make it faster The same lessons as safe path joining. ? Why read only the visible rows of the hex view? + Reading large ranges from another process every frame is slow and unnecessary - ReadProcessMemory can only read 16 bytes - The target would crash Read what you show. ? Which access rights does the inspector need? + PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION and PROCESS_VM_READ - PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS - PROCESS_VM_WRITE and PROCESS_VM_OPERATION The least rights for a read-only tool.

title: Diff two snapshots
where: 18.01 Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
body: The inspector's snapshot panel compares two copies of the same memory range. Write diffSnapshots(before, after, base, mergeGap) , which returns the changed ranges as a list of { address, length } : - before and after are the bytes of the range starting at address base . If their sizes differ, only the common length is compared. - A changed byte is one where before i != after i . - Neighbouring changed bytes form one range. Two changed ranges separated by at most mergeGap unchanged bytes are merged into one range (which then includes the unchanged bytes between them), because a field that changed in two places reads better as one block. - Ranges are returned in address order. base 0x1000, before 00 00 00 00 00 00, after 00 11 00 22 00 00, mergeGap 0 - {0x1001,1} {0x1003,1} the same with mergeGap 1 - {0x1001,3}

title: 18.02  Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
match: 18.02 Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
body: The second capstone turns Delve into a game built to be modded, joining chapters 10, 11 and 13 with the security of chapter 17. Mods add data (levels, items, monsters), scripts and optional native plugins through a versioned API; a mod manager resolves load order and dependencies; the game survives broken mods. This lesson gives the specification, the mod format, the plugin API shape, milestones, acceptance tests and stretch goals. What you are building Delve: Open Depths is Delve with a mod system that strangers could use safely: - Data mods add or override levels, items, monsters and text, with no code at all (lesson 13.02). - Script mods add behaviour through the small scripting layer from lesson 10.08. - Native plugins are DLLs using a versioned C interface (lessons 13.03, 13.04), disabled by default and enabled per mod with a clear warning. - A mod manager screen lists installed mods, shows conflicts and missing dependencies, and lets the player enable, disable and reorder them. - The game never crashes because of a mod : bad data is rejected with a message, and a plugin that fails is disabled for the next start. The mod format Each mod is a folder under Mods\ with a manifest: ini ; Mods\lantern\mod.ini mod id = lantern name = The Lantern version = 1.2.0 api = 1 requires = core-items = 1.0.0 after = brighter-torches content items = data/items.ini levels = data/levels plugin = lantern.dll ; optional, native code Field Rules --- --- id Lower-case letters, digits and - ; unique version A semantic version (lesson 17.08) api The plugin and script API version it was built for; the game refuses mods for a newer major version requires Other mod ids, with optional minimum versions; a missing one disables this mod with a message after Soft ordering: load after these if present, without requiring them content paths Relative to the mod folder, passed through safeJoin (lesson 17.04) Load order Mods that override the same item need a deterministic order. Build a graph where an edge a → b means "a loads before b" (from requires and after ), then a topological sort , with alphabetical order breaking ties so the result never depends on folder listing order. A cycle is reported to the player, naming the mods in it, and those mods are disabled. The practice task implements this. The plugin API The native API follows lesson 13.07: a C interface with a version, a table of functions the game provides, and a table the plugin fills in. cpp-norun // delve_api.h, shipped to plugin authors define DELVE_API_VERSION 1 struct DelveHost // functions the game gives the plugin { uint32_t size; // sizeof(DelveHost), so fields can be added later void ( log)(const char text); int ( registerItem)(const char id, const char name, int value); int ( onEvent)(const char event, void ( handler)(const char payload)); }; struct DelvePlugin // functions the plugin gives the game { uint32_t size; const char id; void ( shutdown)(); }; // The one export every plugin provides: extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) int DelvePluginInit(uint32_t apiVersion, const DelveHost host, DelvePlugin out); Rules for the host side: - Check the apiVersion and each table's size before using it. - Load plugins only from their own mod folder, by full path, with LoadLibraryExW and LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 (lesson 13.04). - Never let a C++ exception or a structured exception cross the boundary: wrap every call into a plugin, and on failure disable the plugin and record it in Mods\disabled.ini . - Plugins run with the game's rights: the warning to the player says so plainly (lesson 17.06). Milestones 1. Manifests : find and parse every mod.ini , validate fields, report problems in a log and on screen. 2. Load order : dependency checks, the topological sort, cycle reports. 3. Data mods : item and level overrides applied in load order; later mods win; the debug menu (lesson 13.06) shows which mod defined each item. 4. Mod manager screen : enable, disable, reorder (which edits after hints in a user file, never the mod's own manifest), and show errors. 5. Scripts : event hooks ( onPickup , onLevelStart ) calling the script layer, with a time limit per call. 6. Native plugins : the API above, with the version and size checks and crash containment. 7. A sample mod pack : three small mods (a new item set, a new level, and a plugin that adds an achievement log) that exercise every feature, shipped with a short modding guide. 8. Hardening : fuzz the manifest and item parsers (lesson 17.03), and work through the threat model from lesson 17.05 for the mod folder. Acceptance tests - With the sample pack installed in any folder order, the load order is the same every time. - A mod requiring a missing mod is disabled with a message naming the missing id. - Two mods that require each other are both disabled with a message naming the cycle. - A manifest with a content path of ..\..\saves is refused. - A plugin built for API version 2 is refused by a version 1 game with a clear message. - A plugin that throws during DelvePluginInit is disabled, and the game starts normally the next time. - Removing every mod gives exactly the original game. Stretch goals - Hot reload of data mods while the game runs. - A mod.ini linter as a separate command-line tool for mod authors. - Packaging mods as a single zip file with a hash in the manifest, verified on load. Common mistakes !warning Load order that depends on the file system Folder listing order differs between machines. Sort explicitly. !warning Passing C++ types across the plugin boundary std::string and exceptions differ between compiler versions. Keep the API in C. !warning Letting one bad mod stop the game Report, disable, continue. Knowledge check quiz ? Why is alphabetical order used to break ties in the load order? + So the result is deterministic and does not depend on the order the folders were listed in - Because mods are always named alphabetically - To make loading faster The same mods must load the same way everywhere. ? Why does each API table start with its size ? + So new fields can be added later and the other side can tell which fields exist - To align the structure - Windows requires it A common pattern for versioned C interfaces. ? A plugin throws an exception during initialisation. What should the game do? + Catch it at the boundary, disable that plugin, record it, and carry on - Crash, so the player notices - Ignore it and keep calling the plugin Mods must not be able to break the game.

title: Mod load order
where: 18.02 Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
body: Write loadOrder(mods) . Each mod has an id , a list requires_ (mods that must be present and load first) and a list of after (mods that should load first if present ). Return: - order : the ids of the mods that can load, in load order; - disabled : the ids of mods that cannot load, sorted alphabetically. Rules: 1. A mod whose requires_ names a mod that is not in the list, or that is itself disabled, is disabled. Repeat until nothing more is disabled (disabling one mod can disable those that require it). 2. Among the remaining mods, requires_ and after entries naming present mods are edges "that one loads first". after entries naming absent mods are ignored. 3. Produce a topological order ; whenever several mods are ready, take the alphabetically smallest first. 4. Mods that cannot be ordered because they are in a cycle, or depend on a mod in a cycle, are disabled too.

title: 18.03  Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
match: 18.03 Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
body: The third capstone grows chapter 16's echo driver into XenonLog , a small, well-engineered driver and client pair that runs only in your lab virtual machine. The driver keeps a bounded in-kernel message log that clients append to and read back through versioned IOCTLs; the client is an ImGui tool with live statistics. The emphasis is engineering quality: validation, locking at the right IRQL, Driver Verifier, a fuzzing client, kernel debugging and a written design. What you are building XenonLog is a teaching driver: it does nothing a user-mode program could not, which is exactly why it is a good capstone. All the difficulty is in doing it correctly in kernel mode . - The driver ( XenonLog.sys ) creates \Device\XenonLog , keeps a ring buffer of up to 256 messages of up to 200 bytes each, and supports four control codes: append a message, read messages from a sequence number, get statistics, and clear. - The client ( XenonLogUI.exe ) is an ImGui window that sends messages, shows the log live, plots messages per second, and displays the driver's statistics and version. - The fuzzer ( XenonLogFuzz.exe ) sends random and malformed requests for hours with Driver Verifier enabled. !important Lab rules (from chapters 15 and 16) - Everything runs in the lab VM from lesson 15.08, with a snapshot taken before every test, test signing on in the VM only, and kernel debugging over the network from the host. - The driver touches only its own buffers . It never reads or writes another process's memory, never registers callbacks on other processes or threads, and never hides anything. Those are out of scope for this course. - It never ships outside the VM and is never installed on your everyday machine. The interface cpp-norun // xenonlog_ioctl.h, shared by the driver and its clients define XENONLOG_VERSION 1 define XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT 200 define XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE 0x8001 define IOCTL_XENONLOG_APPEND CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x801, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_WRITE_DATA) define IOCTL_XENONLOG_READ CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x802, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_DATA) define IOCTL_XENONLOG_STATS CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x803, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_DATA) define IOCTL_XENONLOG_CLEAR CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x804, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_WRITE_DATA) pragma pack(push, 8) struct XenonLogHeader { UINT32 version; UINT32 size; }; // every request starts with this struct XenonLogAppend { XenonLogHeader h; UINT32 length; CHAR text XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT ; }; struct XenonLogReadRequest { XenonLogHeader h; UINT64 fromSequence; UINT32 maxMessages; }; struct XenonLogMessage { UINT64 sequence; LARGE_INTEGER time; UINT32 processId; UINT32 length; CHAR text XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT ; }; struct XenonLogStats { XenonLogHeader h; UINT64 appended; UINT64 dropped; UINT64 rejected; UINT32 stored; }; pragma pack(pop) Every request carries a header with the interface version and the structure's size, as lesson 12.06 taught for user-mode protocols. The driver rejects a request whose header does not match before reading anything else. The practice task writes that validation as plain C++ that can be unit-tested outside the kernel. Engineering requirements Area Requirement From --- --- --- Validation Check input and output lengths for every code; validate the header; check length <= XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT and that length bytes fit in the input; count rejected requests 16.07, 17.04 Output Zero output buffers before filling; set Information to exactly the bytes written 16.07 Locking Protect the ring buffer with a spin lock or a fast mutex, choosing by the IRQL the code runs at; hold it only while copying 15.06 Memory Allocate the ring buffer once in DriverEntry from non-paged pool with a pool tag; free it in unload 15.04 Access The device's security descriptor allows administrators and the client group only; FILE_READ_DATA and FILE_WRITE_DATA in the control codes 16.04, 6.08 Cleanup Unload deletes the symbolic link and device and frees everything; no leaks reported by Driver Verifier's pool tracking 16.03 Analysis Builds with /W4 /WX and passes Code Analysis with the driver rule set 17.02 Milestones 1. Design document : a page describing the interface, the ring buffer's behaviour when full (oldest messages dropped and counted), locking, and the threat model from lesson 17.05 for the device interface. 2. User-mode core : the ring buffer and request validation as plain C++ with unit tests on the host (the practice task covers validation). 3. Driver skeleton : lesson 16.10's echo driver renamed, with the new device name and the four control codes returning STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED . 4. Append and read : the ring buffer in the driver, with locking and validation; a command-line client to test. 5. Statistics and clear . 6. ImGui client : live log, sending, statistics, a plot, and a clear message when the driver is not loaded. 7. Verification : Driver Verifier with standard settings plus pool tracking; a kernel debugging session stepping through an append; the fuzzer running for an hour without a bug check. 8. Write-up : the design document updated with what changed, test results, and one bug you found and how. Acceptance tests - Two clients appending at the same time never corrupt a message (check sequence numbers are unique and continuous). - Appending 1000 messages leaves the 256 newest, with dropped equal to 744. - A request with the wrong version, a wrong size , length of 201, or a too-small output buffer is rejected with STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER or STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL , and rejected increases. - The fuzzer runs for an hour with Driver Verifier on and no bug check. - Load, use, unload and reload ten times without a leak or bug check. - A standard user who is not in the client group cannot open the device. Stretch goals - Rewrite the driver with KMDF and compare the amount of code (lesson 16.10's note). - Add an event that the driver signals when new messages arrive, so the client waits instead of polling. - Write the ring buffer once and compile the same source into the unit tests and the driver. Common mistakes !warning Testing outside the VM One mistake costs a blue screen on the machine you work on. Use the lab. !warning Holding a spin lock while calling anything that can wait At raised IRQL that is an immediate bug check. Copy under the lock, do everything else outside it. !warning Validating the length field but not that the bytes are there length must fit inside the input buffer the I/O manager actually passed. Knowledge check quiz ? Why does every XenonLog request start with a version and a size? + So the driver can reject requests from mismatched or malicious clients before reading anything else - Windows requires it for all IOCTLs - To align the structures Check the header first. ? What happens when the ring buffer is full and a new message arrives? + The oldest message is dropped and the dropped count increases - The driver bug checks - The new message is silently ignored with no record Bounded memory, visible behaviour. ? Where must all XenonLog testing happen? + In the lab virtual machine with test signing and a snapshot - On your everyday machine with test signing on - Anywhere, since it is only a log The rules from chapters 15 and 16 do not change.

title: Validate an append request
where: 18.03 Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
body: XenonLog's append request must be checked before the driver uses it. Write the check as plain C++ so it can be unit-tested outside the kernel: validateAppend(input, inputLength) , where input points to the bytes the I/O manager passed and inputLength is how many there are. The layout (all little-endian, no padding): Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 version , must be 1 4 4 size , must equal inputLength 8 4 length of the text 12 length the text Return a Status : - TooSmall if inputLength is less than 12 (the header and length field), or input is null; - BadVersion if version is not 1; - BadSize if size is not equal to inputLength ; - TooLong if length is greater than 200; - Truncated if 12 + length is greater than inputLength ; - Ok otherwise, and also set text to the message. Check in exactly that order, and read the fields with std::memcpy (the input may not be aligned).

title: 18.04  Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
match: 18.04 Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
body: The last capstone applies chapter 9's reverse engineering, chapter 8's debugging and chapter 7's assembly to a program whose source you have not read, and turns the findings into a clear technical report. Targets are chosen so the analysis is legal and checkable: open-source programs you build yourself with the source set aside, practice programs published for analysis, and programs a classmate writes for you. The lesson covers choosing a target, the method, the report's structure and how to check your conclusions against the truth. Choosing a target The analysis must be legal and checkable . Good targets: Target Why it works --- --- An open-source program you compile yourself, in Release, then analyse without reading the source; the source is the answer key afterwards Legal under its licence; you can check every conclusion A practice program written for analysis (often called a "crackme" or reversing challenge) from a site whose rules allow it Made for this; usually comes with write-ups to compare A program a classmate or friend writes for you with a short brief ("a small file format and a checksum"), who keeps the source until you finish Realistic and fun; both of you learn One of your own old programs whose source you no longer remember Surprisingly instructive Not suitable: commercial software or games whose licence forbids reverse engineering, anything protected by anti-tamper (lesson 17.06), online games, and anything you would analyse to get around a protection or a payment. Lesson 9.01's ground rules apply unchanged. A good size is 50 to 500 KB of code: large enough to need a method, small enough to finish. A command-line tool with a file format (a compressor, an image converter, a small game with save files) is ideal. The method 1. Triage (lessons 9.02, 9.03): architecture, sections, imports (file, network, crypto, UI?), exported functions, strings. Write down hypotheses: "it reads .cfg files", "it uses zlib". 2. Run it in a VM or sandbox folder and watch with Process Monitor: files it opens, registry keys, what it prints. 3. Find the interesting code (lesson 9.08): from a string such as "invalid header" or an import such as CreateFileW , follow cross-references back to the functions that use them. 4. Understand it (lessons 9.04 to 9.06, 9.09, chapter 7): rename functions and variables in the disassembler as you go, reconstruct structs from field offsets, recognise loops, switches, vtables and library code. 5. Confirm dynamically (lesson 9.07): break on the function, check arguments and results match your reading, change an input byte and predict what happens. 6. Document : names, structures and the report below. Keep a lab notebook : every address, hypothesis, test and result, dated. It is what turns hours of clicking into a report. The report Section Contents --- --- Summary What the program does, in one paragraph, for someone who will not read further Target and method Exact file, version, hash, how it was obtained and why analysing it is permitted; tools used Architecture Main modules or components and how they interact, with a diagram Function map A table of the important functions: address, your name, purpose, confidence Data structures Reconstructed structs with offsets, sizes and field meanings File format or protocol A byte-level description, if the program has one, with an example decoded by hand Findings Anything notable: bugs, unsafe patterns (lesson 17.04), surprising design choices Verification How each major conclusion was confirmed, and what is still uncertain Comparison (open-source targets) What you got right, wrong and missed, once you read the source The confidence column matters: "high (confirmed in the debugger)", "medium (consistent with the code)", "low (a guess from the name of a string)". Honest uncertainty is what makes a report trustworthy. Acceptance criteria - The target is one of the permitted kinds, recorded with its hash and licence. - The function map covers the program's main path from main (or WinMain ) to its output, with at least 15 functions named. - At least two structures are reconstructed with every field's offset. - If the program has a file format, a small program of yours reads or writes it correctly (proof of understanding). - Every high-confidence claim has a recorded dynamic confirmation. - For an open-source target, the comparison section is honest about errors. Stretch goals - Write a script for your disassembler (Ghidra's Python or Java API) that applies your function names and struct definitions automatically, and include it. - Analyse two builds of the same program (Debug and Release, or two versions) and document what changed. - Turn the report into a short talk for classmates. Common mistakes !warning Reading everything in order Start from strings, imports and behaviour, and work towards the interesting code. !warning Not writing things down Without a notebook, you will analyse the same function twice. !warning Stating guesses as facts Give every conclusion a confidence and the evidence for it. Knowledge check quiz ? Why is an open-source program built yourself a good target? + Analysing it is permitted by its licence, and the source lets you check every conclusion afterwards - Open-source programs have no machine code - It is the only legal target An answer key, with permission. ? What is the best starting point for finding a program's interesting code? + Strings and imports, following cross-references back to the functions that use them - The first byte of the .text section - A random function Work from what you can observe. ? Why does the function map have a confidence column? + So readers know which conclusions were confirmed and which are educated guesses - To sort the table - It is a legal requirement Honest uncertainty makes a report trustworthy.

title: Name an address
where: 18.04 Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
body: While analysing a program, you keep a function map : each function's start address, size and the name you gave it. Write a small symboliser over it: - FunctionMap(entries) stores the entries. Entries may arrive in any order. If two entries overlap , the constructor keeps only the earlier of the two in the list given (the later one is discarded), since it was probably a mistake in the notes. - describe(address) returns: - "name" if the address is a function's first byte; - "name+0x1f" (offset in lower-case hex, no padding) if it is inside a function ( start <= address < start + size ); - "?" if it is in no function. - count() returns how many entries were kept. Make describe faster than checking every entry: sort the kept entries once and use a binary search ( std::upper_bound ).

title: Glossary
body: Terms from the lessons written so far, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is given in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Access violation The error Windows raises when a program reads or writes memory it is not allowed to touch, such as address 0. It stops the program. (1.03) Address The number of a byte in memory. A variable's address is the number of its first byte. Written in hexadecimal. (1.03) Address space layout randomisation A Windows security feature that loads programs at a different place in memory on each run. (1.03) Alignment The rule that a value should start at an address that is a multiple of its size, because the processor reads it fastest there. (1.03) Base plus offset Describing a location as "where something starts this time" plus a fixed distance, because absolute addresses change between runs. (1.03) Binary Base 2. Numbers written with only the digits 0 and 1. (1.02) Bit One binary digit: a switch that is on or off. (1.02) Byte Eight bits. The unit that memory is measured and numbered in. (1.02) Compiler The program that translates C++ into the processor's own instructions. (1.01) CPU The processor: the part that carries out instructions. (1.01) Decode The step of the cycle in which the CPU works out what a fetched instruction means. (1.01) Dereference To go to the address a pointer holds and use the value there. Written p . (1.03) Execute The step of the cycle in which the CPU carries out an instruction. (1.01) Fetch The step of the cycle in which the CPU copies the next instruction out of memory. (1.01) Heap The region of memory a program asks for while it runs. (1.03) Hexadecimal Base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F. One hex digit is exactly four bits. Written with 0x in front. (1.02) Instruction register The register that holds the instruction the CPU is currently working on. (1.01) Little-endian A byte order in which the lowest-value byte of a number is stored at the lowest address. PCs use it. (1.02) Memory (RAM) Where a running program and the values it is using are held. Emptied when the power goes off. (1.01) Null pointer A pointer holding address 0, meaning it is not aimed at anything. Written nullptr . (1.03) Overflow Going past the largest value a type can hold. Unsigned values wrap round to zero. (1.02) Padding Unused bytes the compiler leaves between values to keep them aligned. (1.03) Pointer A variable whose value is an address. (1.03) Pointer arithmetic Adding to or subtracting from a pointer. It moves by whole elements, not single bytes. (1.03) Process A program that has been loaded into memory and is running. (1.01) Program counter The register that holds the address of the next instruction to fetch. (1.01) Register A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. (1.01) Stack The region of memory that holds the local variables of functions that are currently running. (1.03) Storage Disks and SSDs: where files are kept for the long term. (1.01) Two's complement The way negative whole numbers are stored: the top bit is worth minus its usual amount. (1.02) Undefined behaviour Something the C++ language makes no promise about. The program may crash, misbehave, or appear to work. (1.02, 1.03)

title: 1.01  Immediate Mode versus Retained Mode
body: Most user-interface toolkits keep a tree of widget objects that you create once and update. Dear ImGui does the opposite - you describe the whole interface again every frame, as ordinary code, and it draws it. This lesson explains the idea, why it suits tools and debug views so well, and where its limits are. Two ways to build an interface Retained mode is what Windows Forms, Qt, HTML and Unity's UI Toolkit do. You create objects once - a window, a slider, a label - and the toolkit keeps them. To change what the user sees, you change the objects; to react to the user, you register callbacks: cpp-norun // retained mode (pseudo-code) auto slider = new Slider(window, "Speed", 0.0f, 10.0f); slider- setValue(player.speed); slider- onChanged( & (float v) { player.speed = v; }); // keep the copy and the real value in sync There are now two copies of the speed: player.speed and the slider's value. Keeping them in sync is your job, and most UI bugs live in that gap. Immediate mode is what Dear ImGui does. There are no widget objects for you to keep. Every frame, you call functions that describe the interface as it should be right now , and each call returns what the user did: cpp-norun // immediate mode: this runs every frame ImGui::Begin("Player"); ImGui::SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, 0.0f, 10.0f); // shows player.speed, writes to it if dragged if (ImGui::Button("Reset")) player.speed = 4.0f; // true on the frame it was clicked ImGui::End(); The slider reads player.speed directly and writes to it directly. There is no second copy, no callback, no "update the UI when the data changes". If the game changes the speed, the slider shows it next frame because it is drawn from the data again. Why tools love it - Interfaces are just code. Loops and if s produce lists and optional parts: for (auto& enemy : enemies) ImGui::Text(...) . When an enemy dies, it disappears from the list with no extra work. - Fast to write. A debug window for a new system is often ten lines, written in the system's own file. - Always in sync with the data, because it is drawn from it. - Drops into any engine. ImGui only produces triangles and textures to draw; a small back end feeds them to DirectX, OpenGL, Vulkan or Metal, and passes mouse and keyboard input in. That is why game studios use it for editors, debug overlays, profilers and in-house tools: those are exactly the interfaces where speed of writing matters more than polish. But ImGui does keep some state "Immediate mode" describes the API , not the library's insides. ImGui remembers what it must between frames: window positions and sizes, which tree nodes are open, which widget is being dragged, scroll positions, text being edited. It finds that state by each widget's ID , which it computes from the label you pass (lesson 1.05). That is the one rule you have to learn early. It also means the cost is real: building the UI runs your code every frame. For tools, that is a few hundred microseconds; for a game's main menu shown to players, a retained toolkit or a hand-made UI is often a better fit (lesson 6.03). Where immediate mode is not the best choice - Player-facing game UI with animation, art direction and controller navigation everywhere. - Large text documents or anything needing rich text layout. - Accessibility : screen readers and similar tools rely on a widget tree that ImGui does not expose. For the tools this course builds - inspectors, editors, profilers, consoles - it is excellent. Common mistakes !warning Copying values into the UI and back Pass pointers to the real data. SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, ...) needs no copy. !warning Trying to store widget objects There are none to store. If something should appear, call its function this frame; if not, don't. Knowledge check quiz ? What does ImGui::Button return? + true on the frame the button was clicked - A pointer to the button object - The button's ID Immediate-mode functions return what the user did this frame. ? A value changes in the game. What must you do so an ImGui slider shows the new value? + Nothing; the slider is drawn from the value again next frame - Call an update function on the slider - Register a callback There is no copy to keep in sync. ? Which of these is a poor fit for Dear ImGui? + A heavily styled main menu shown to players with a controller - A debug window listing every enemy - A property editor in a level editor Tools are its strength; polished player-facing UI usually is not.

title: Drawn from the data
body: In immediate mode the interface is rebuilt from the data every frame, so it can never be out of date. Write the text lines a debug window would show for a list of enemies: cpp struct Enemy { std::string name; int hp; }; std::vector<std::string enemyWindow(const std::vector<Enemy & enemies); - The first line is "Enemies alive: N" , counting enemies with hp 0 . - Then one line per living enemy, in order: "<name (<hp hp)" . - If none are alive, the second line is "(none)" . Call it twice with different data and you get two different "frames": nothing has to be updated or removed.

title: 1.02  Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11
match: 1.02 Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11
