body: Dear ImGui is a handful of source files you add to your project, plus a platform back end (input and windows) and a renderer back end (drawing). This lesson builds the standard Win32 + DirectX 11 program step by step, the same set-up as ImGui's own example. What you download Get Dear ImGui from its GitHub repository ( ocornut/imgui ). Use a release tag; for docking and multiple viewports (lesson 4.04), use the docking branch, which most tools do. You need: Files What they are --- --- imgui.cpp , imgui_draw.cpp , imgui_tables.cpp , imgui_widgets.cpp , imgui_demo.cpp The library itself imgui.h , imconfig.h , imgui_internal.h , imstb_ .h Its headers backends/imgui_impl_win32.cpp/.h Platform back end: Win32 window messages to ImGui input backends/imgui_impl_dx11.cpp/.h Renderer back end: ImGui's triangles to Direct3D 11 ImGui has no build system of its own on purpose: add these .cpp files to your Visual Studio project like your own. Then link d3d11.lib and d3dcompiler.lib (and dxgi.lib ). The shape of the program cpp-norun include "imgui.h" include "imgui_impl_win32.h" include "imgui_impl_dx11.h" include <d3d11.h // Forward-declared in imgui_impl_win32.h behind an if: declare it yourself. extern IMGUI_IMPL_API LRESULT ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler(HWND hWnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam); LRESULT CALLBACK WndProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { if (ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam)) return true; // ImGui sees input first switch (msg) { case WM_SIZE: / resize the swap chain buffers (see ImGui's example) / return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); } int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE instance, HINSTANCE, PWSTR, int) { // 1. A window and a Direct3D 11 device and swap chain (ordinary Win32 and D3D11 code). HWND hwnd = createWindow(instance, WndProc); createDeviceAndSwapChain(hwnd); // fills g_device, g_context, g_swapChain, g_renderTarget // 2. ImGui itself. IMGUI_CHECKVERSION(); ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableKeyboard; // arrow keys and Tab move between widgets ImGui::StyleColorsDark(); // 3. The two back ends. ImGui_ImplWin32_Init(hwnd); ImGui_ImplDX11_Init(g_device, g_context); // 4. The loop (lesson 1.03). bool running = true; while (running) { MSG msg; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; } if (!running) break; ImGui_ImplDX11_NewFrame(); ImGui_ImplWin32_NewFrame(); ImGui::NewFrame(); ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); // every widget ImGui has, to explore (lesson 1.06) ImGui::Render(); const float clear 4 = { 0.1f, 0.1f, 0.12f, 1.0f }; g_context- OMSetRenderTargets(1, &g_renderTarget, nullptr); g_context- ClearRenderTargetView(g_renderTarget, clear); ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData()); g_swapChain- Present(1, 0); // 1 = wait for vertical sync } // 5. Shut down in reverse order. ImGui_ImplDX11_Shutdown(); ImGui_ImplWin32_Shutdown(); ImGui::DestroyContext(); destroyDeviceAndWindow(); return 0; } The parts that are not ImGui (creating the window, the device, the swap chain, resizing) are copied almost word for word from examples/example_win32_directx11/main.cpp in the ImGui repository. Start from that file; it is the reference everyone uses. What each piece does - ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler turns Windows messages (mouse moves, clicks, keys, characters, focus) into ImGui input. It must run first in your window procedure. - ImGui::CreateContext makes the one object that holds all of ImGui's state. Most programs have exactly one. - ImGui_ImplWin32_Init and ImGui_ImplDX11_Init connect the context to the window and to the device. The DirectX back end creates its own shaders, a font texture and buffers. - In the loop, the two back ends' NewFrame calls feed ImGui the window size, time and input, then ImGui::NewFrame starts recording widgets. - ImGui::Render finishes the frame and produces draw data : lists of triangles, textures and clipping rectangles. The renderer back end draws them over your scene. In a game that already has a renderer In a real game, step 1 already exists. You add steps 2 and 3 after your device is created, call the three NewFrame functions at the start of your frame, and call ImGui::Render plus ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData after your scene is drawn, so ImGui appears on top. Lesson 2.05 deals with sharing the mouse and keyboard between ImGui and the game. Common mistakes !warning Not forwarding window messages Without ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler first in the window procedure, windows draw but nothing reacts to the mouse. !warning Forgetting the extern declaration imgui_impl_win32.h hides ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler behind an if 0 . Declare it yourself, as above. !warning Mismatched versions of imgui.h and the back ends Back ends must come from the same version of ImGui. IMGUI_CHECKVERSION() catches a header and a .cpp from different versions. Knowledge check quiz ? What does the renderer back end do? + Draws ImGui's triangles and textures with your graphics API - Reads the mouse and keyboard - Decides where widgets go The platform back end handles input; the renderer back end draws. ? Where must ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler be called? + At the start of your window procedure, so ImGui sees input first - Once, after creating the window - After ImGui::Render It turns every window message into ImGui input. ? When should a game draw ImGui? + After its own scene, so the interface appears on top - Before clearing the screen - In a separate window only ImGui's draw data is rendered over the finished frame.

title: Are the files all there?
where: 1.02 Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11
body: A Win32 + DirectX 11 project needs these Dear ImGui source files: imgui.cpp , imgui_draw.cpp , imgui_tables.cpp , imgui_widgets.cpp , imgui_impl_win32.cpp , imgui_impl_dx11.cpp . Write cpp std::vector<std::string missingImGuiFiles(const std::vector<std::string & projectFiles); Project files may include folders ( third_party/imgui/imgui.cpp , backends\imgui_impl_dx11.cpp ): only the name after the last / or \ counts, compared without regard to case. Return the missing required names, in the order listed above.

title: 1.03  The Frame and the Draw Data
match: 1.03 The Frame and the Draw Data
body: Every ImGui frame follows the same steps - input in, widgets described, draw data out. This lesson looks inside them, explains what draw data is, and covers the timing questions every tool runs into - frame rate, delta time, and only drawing when something changed. Inside a frame - Input in. The platform back end sets io.DisplaySize , io.DeltaTime , and queues input events (mouse position, buttons, keys, characters). - NewFrame. ImGui processes the events, decides which window is under the mouse, which widget is hovered , and clears last frame's draw lists. - Your code. Each widget function does three things at once: it lays itself out (takes space from the window's cursor), handles input (was it clicked?), and adds shapes to the window's draw list. It returns the result immediately. - Render. ImGui sorts windows by depth and collects every window's draw list into one ImDrawData . - Draw. The back end uploads vertices and indices to the GPU and issues one draw call per command. You can call widget functions anywhere between NewFrame and Render : in your game's update, in each system's own debug function, in a loop over entities. They all add to the same frame. Draw data cpp-norun ImDrawData data = ImGui::GetDrawData(); for (int n = 0; n < data- CmdListsCount; ++n) { const ImDrawList list = data- CmdLists n ; // one per window, roughly // list- VtxBuffer: vertices (position, texture coordinate, colour) // list- IdxBuffer: triangle indices for (const ImDrawCmd& cmd : list- CmdBuffer) { // cmd.ClipRect: scissor rectangle; cmd.TextureId: which texture; cmd.ElemCount: how many indices } } Everything ImGui draws, including text, is textured triangles. Text uses a font atlas : one texture containing every glyph, built at start-up (lesson 4.05). That is why ImGui is so portable: a back end only needs to draw coloured, textured triangles with scissor rectangles. You rarely touch draw data yourself, but it helps to know that ImGui::GetWindowDrawList() gives you the current window's draw list, so you can add your own lines, circles and text (useful for graphs and minimaps): cpp-norun ImDrawList draw = ImGui::GetWindowDrawList(); ImVec2 p = ImGui::GetCursorScreenPos(); draw- AddCircleFilled(ImVec2(p.x + 20, p.y + 20), 12.0f, IM_COL32(240, 180, 70, 255)); ImGui::Dummy(ImVec2(40, 40)); // reserve the space so the next widget goes below Delta time and frame rate ImGui needs to know how much time passed since the last frame ( io.DeltaTime ) for double-click detection, key repeat, blinking cursors and animations. The Win32 back end measures it with QueryPerformanceCounter . Your own code can read it too: cpp-norun ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); ImGui::Text("%.1f FPS (%.2f ms)", io.Framerate, 1000.0f / io.Framerate); io.Framerate is an average over the last 60 frames or so, so the number does not jump around. Tools that sleep A game redraws every frame anyway. A standalone tool (a level editor, an asset browser) does not need to burn a CPU core redrawing an unchanged screen at 144 Hz. Common approaches: - V-sync: Present(1, 0) waits for the display, capping the frame rate at its refresh rate. - Wait for input when idle: if nothing is animating, block in MsgWaitForMultipleObjects or WaitMessage until a message arrives, then draw a few frames (ImGui sometimes needs one or two extra frames to settle a layout). - Minimised: when IsIconic(hwnd) is true, sleep instead of drawing. The practice for this lesson has you write the "how many frames should I still draw?" logic a sleeping tool uses. Common mistakes !warning Calling widget functions before NewFrame or after Render ImGui asserts. Every widget call belongs between the two. !warning Assuming one frame is enough after input Some layouts settle over two frames (a window measuring its content). Draw a couple more frames after the last input. Knowledge check quiz ? What does a widget function do in one call? + Lays itself out, handles input, adds its shapes to the draw list, and returns the result - Only adds itself to a list to be processed later - Draws itself directly with Direct3D Layout, input and drawing happen together, immediately. ? Why can ImGui run on almost any graphics API? + It only needs textured, coloured triangles with scissor rectangles drawn - It contains a back end for every API inside imgui.cpp - It uses the operating system's drawing functions A back end is a small piece of code that draws ImDrawData. ? How should a standalone tool avoid using a full CPU core while idle? + Wait for input when nothing changes, and use v-sync - Lower the font size - Call ImGui::Render less often but NewFrame every time A tool only needs to redraw when something happens.

title: Only draw when something happens
where: 1.03 The Frame and the Draw Data
body: A standalone tool should not redraw an unchanged screen hundreds of times a second. Write the logic that decides, each time round the loop, whether to draw a frame or to sleep until the next input: cpp class IdleTracker { public: explicit IdleTracker(int settleFrames); // extra frames to draw after the last input void onInput(); // some input arrived void setAnimating(bool animating); // something on screen moves (a spinner, a live graph) bool shouldDraw(); // called once per loop iteration }; - shouldDraw returns true while animating, every time. - Otherwise, after onInput , it returns true for the next settleFrames calls (ImGui sometimes needs a frame or two to settle a layout), then false until the next input. - At the very start (before any input) it returns true for settleFrames calls too, so the first screen is drawn. - Input while frames are still pending starts the count again from settleFrames .

title: A steady frame rate
where: 1.03 The Frame and the Draw Data
body: io.Framerate is not the rate of the last frame, which jumps around: it averages the last frames. Write the same thing: cpp class FrameRate { public: explicit FrameRate(int window); // how many recent frames to average void add(double deltaSeconds); // one frame's duration double fps() const; // frames per second over the recent frames, 0 if none yet double averageMs() const; // average frame time in milliseconds, 0 if none yet }; fps() is the number of frames in the window divided by their total duration. Keep only the last window durations: when a new one arrives and the window is full, the oldest is dropped. Keep a running total rather than adding all durations up on every call.

title: 1.04  Windows, Text and Buttons
body: The first real interface - windows with Begin and End , every way of showing text, and buttons. Along the way you learn ImGui's rules for Begin / End pairs, what the boolean returned by Begin means, and how to open and close a window from code. A window cpp-norun ImGui::Begin("Stones"); // a window titled "Stones"; created the first time, remembered afterwards ImGui::Text("Hello from Xenon"); ImGui::End(); // ALWAYS called, whatever Begin returned The first time, ImGui creates the window with a default size and position; you can move and resize it, and it remembers (lesson 4.06 saves that to disk). Two Begin("Stones") calls in the same frame append to the same window , which is handy: different systems can add to one "Debug" window. Begin returns false when the window is collapsed (folded by its title-bar arrow) or entirely clipped. You may skip its contents then, to save time, but End must still be called: cpp-norun if (ImGui::Begin("Stones")) { expensiveStoneList(); // skipped while the window is collapsed } ImGui::End(); Begin / End is a different rule from most pairs in ImGui. For nearly everything else that starts with Begin ( BeginMenu , BeginTable , BeginPopup , BeginCombo ...), you call the matching End only if Begin returned true . Lesson 4.01 comes back to this; it is the most common beginner bug. A closable window Pass a pointer to a bool and the window gets a close button that sets it to false : cpp-norun static bool showStones = true; if (showStones) { if (ImGui::Begin("Stones", &showStones)) ImGui::Text("Close me with the x"); ImGui::End(); } From code, set showStones = true again (from a menu item, a key) to reopen it. Size and position cpp-norun ImGui::SetNextWindowPos(ImVec2(20, 20), ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); ImGui::SetNextWindowSize(ImVec2(320, 240), ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); ImGui::Begin("Stones"); SetNextWindow... applies to the next Begin . The condition says when: ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver only if the window has never been seen (not even in imgui.ini ), ImGuiCond_Once once per run, ImGuiCond_Always every frame (the user can then no longer move it). Use FirstUseEver for defaults. Window flags change behaviour: ImGuiWindowFlags_NoResize , NoMove , NoCollapse , AlwaysAutoResize (fits its content), NoTitleBar , MenuBar (lesson 4.01), and more, combined with . Text Function Shows --- --- ImGui::Text("Score %d", score) printf-style formatted text ImGui::TextUnformatted(text) Text as is, fastest, no % processing; takes a begin and optional end pointer ImGui::TextColored(ImVec4(1, 0.6f, 0.2f, 1), "Warning") Coloured text ImGui::TextDisabled("(none)") Greyed-out text ImGui::TextWrapped("long text...") Wraps at the window's edge ImGui::BulletText("item") A bullet point ImGui::LabelText("Label", "%d", value) Value with a label on the right, aligned like other widgets ImGui::SeparatorText("Section") A separator line with a title Text uses printf formatting: never pass user-provided text as the format string ( Text(name) ), because a % in it reads garbage. Use TextUnformatted(name) or Text("%s", name) . Buttons cpp-norun if (ImGui::Button("Add stone")) // true on the frame it was clicked (mouse released over it) stones.push_back(Stone{}); if (ImGui::Button("Clear", ImVec2(120, 0))) // width 120, default height stones.clear(); ImGui::SmallButton("x"); // no frame padding, for inline buttons ImGui::ArrowButton(" left", ImGuiDir_Left); // an arrow, no visible label A button counts as clicked when the mouse is pressed and released over it . Pressing, dragging away and releasing elsewhere does not click it. Lesson 1.05's practice and the next lessons look at how that works. Common mistakes !warning Calling End only when Begin returned true For windows, End is always called. For most other Begin functions, it is only called if Begin returned true. Learn the two rules. !warning Text(userString) A % in the string crashes or prints garbage. Use TextUnformatted. Knowledge check quiz ? Begin returns false because the window is collapsed. What must you still do? + Call End - Nothing - Call Begin again For windows, End is always paired with Begin. ? What does ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver mean for SetNextWindowSize? + Use this size only if the window has never existed, not even in the saved settings - Use it every frame - Use it the first time each frame It sets a default without overriding what the user chose. ? Why is ImGui::Text(name) with a player's name dangerous? + The name is used as a printf format string, so a % in it reads garbage - Text cannot show names - Names must be translated first Use TextUnformatted or Text("%s", name).

title: When is a button clicked?
body: A button is clicked when the mouse is pressed over it and released over it . Pressing, dragging off and releasing elsewhere does not click it; pressing elsewhere and releasing over it does not either. Write the logic ImGui's buttons use, over a sequence of frames: cpp struct Rect { float x, y, w, h; }; struct MouseFrame { float x, y; bool down; }; std::vector<int clickFrames(const Rect& button, const std::vector<MouseFrame & frames); For each frame i , the button: - is hovered if the mouse is inside the rectangle ( x <= mx < x + w and y <= my < y + h ); - becomes active on a frame where the mouse button goes down (it was up on the previous frame, or this is frame 0) while hovered; - stays active while the mouse button is held, wherever the mouse moves; - on the frame the mouse button goes up while it is active, it is clicked if the mouse is hovering it then; either way it stops being active. Return the indexes of the frames on which it was clicked.

title: 1.05  How ImGui Identifies Widgets
body: ImGui remembers a widget between frames by its ID , a number computed from the widget's label and the ID stack . Two widgets with the same ID in the same place behave as one, which is the classic "my second button does not work" bug. This lesson explains IDs, the and label rules, and PushID . The problem cpp-norun for (Stone& stone : stones) { ImGui::Text("%s", stone.name.c_str()); ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Delete")) remove(stone); // only the first one works! } Every button has the label "Delete". ImGui computes each widget's ID from its label, so all the buttons get the same ID. When you press the third one, ImGui thinks the widget with that ID is active, but the first button with that ID claims it. The result: only the first button works, or the wrong one reacts. How an ID is made An ID is a 32-bit hash. ImGui keeps an ID stack : a stack of seed values. Each widget's ID is the hash of its label, seeded with the value on top of the stack. Every window pushes its own seed (from its name), so a "Delete" button in window A and one in window B already differ. ID = hash(label, seed = top of the ID stack) To make widgets in a loop differ, push something unique onto the stack around each iteration: cpp-norun for (int i = 0; i < (int)stones.size(); ++i) { ImGui::PushID(i); // changes the seed for everything inside ImGui::Text("%s", stones i .name.c_str()); ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Delete")) toDelete = i; // now each has a different ID ImGui::PopID(); } PushID accepts an integer, a string, or a pointer ( PushID(&stone) is a good choice: the stone's address is unique and stable). Every PushID needs a PopID . Label tricks: and Labels do two jobs: the text shown and the source of the ID. Two markers separate them: - : everything after it is part of the ID but not shown . "Delete 3" shows "Delete" and hashes the whole string. " speed" shows nothing (a slider with no label). - : only the part from onward is used for the ID. "Score: 120 score" shows "Score: 120" and hashes just " score" , so the ID stays the same when the score changes. Useful for window titles that show changing text: Begin("Level 3 - 12 enemies LevelWindow") keeps its position and size even though the title changes. Label Shown Hashed for the ID --- --- --- "Delete" Delete Delete "Delete 3" Delete Delete 3 " speed" (nothing) speed "HP: 87 hp" HP: 87 hp The practice has you implement exactly this table, plus the stack, with a simple hash. When IDs matter IDs are how ImGui finds a widget's remembered state: whether it is hot (hovered) or active (being clicked or dragged), whether a tree node is open, a text box's cursor, a window's position. If two widgets share an ID, they share that state. If a widget's ID changes every frame (say its label contains a timer), it loses its state every frame: a tree node never stays open, a drag stops immediately. Debugging IDs - Tools, ID Stack Tool in the demo window, or ImGui::ShowIDStackToolWindow() , shows the ID stack under the mouse. - Recent versions of ImGui detect duplicate IDs in the same window and draw a warning over them ( io.ConfigDebugHighlightIdConflicts , on by default in debug builds). Common mistakes !warning Buttons with the same label in a loop Wrap each iteration in PushID / PopID, or add and a unique suffix. !warning A label that changes every frame The widget gets a new ID each frame and forgets its state. Use with a fixed part. !warning Forgetting PopID Every widget after it gets a different ID than intended. ImGui asserts at the end of the window. Knowledge check quiz ? Two buttons labelled "Delete" are drawn in the same window without PushID. What happens? + They share one ID, so clicking one can trigger the other or only the first works - ImGui renames the second automatically - Both work normally IDs come from labels; the same label gives the same ID. ? What is shown and what is hashed for the label "Gold: 50 gold"? + Shown "Gold: 50"; hashed " gold" - Shown "Gold: 50 gold"; hashed "Gold: 50" - Shown "gold"; hashed "Gold: 50" keeps the ID stable while the visible text changes. ? Why does PushID(&stone) work well in a loop? + The address is unique for each stone and stays the same between frames - Pointers are faster to hash - It shows the address on screen A good ID source is unique and stable.

title: Labels, IDs and the ID stack
match: Labels, IDs and the ID stack
body: Implement ImGui's label rules with a simpler hash. ImGui really uses a CRC32-based hash; here use FNV-1a , which is short to write: hash = seed XOR 2166136261 (both 32-bit unsigned) for each byte b of the text: hash = (hash XOR b) 16777619 (wrapping 32-bit arithmetic) Write cpp std::string displayText(const std::string& label); // what the widget shows std::string idText(const std::string& label); // the part of the label that is hashed uint32_t hashText(const std::string& text, uint32_t seed); class IdStack { public: explicit IdStack(uint32_t windowSeed); void push(const std::string& text); // like PushID(text): the new seed is hashText(text, current seed) void push(int n); // like PushID(int): the same as push(std::to_string(n)) void pop(); // never pops the window's seed uint32_t idOf(const std::string& label) const; // hashText(idText(label), current seed) }; The label rules: Label displayText idText --- --- --- "Delete" Delete Delete "Delete 3" Delete Delete 3 " speed" (empty) speed "HP: 87 hp" HP: 87 hp displayText is everything before the first (which also covers ). idText is the whole label, unless it contains : then it is the part from the first to the end.

title: 1.06  The Demo Window and the Debug Tools
match: 1.06 The Demo Window and the Debug Tools
body: Dear ImGui ships its best documentation as a program - ShowDemoWindow shows every widget with the code beside it. It also ships tools for finding your own bugs - the Metrics window, the ID Stack tool, the Item Picker and debug logs. This lesson shows how to use them all. ShowDemoWindow cpp-norun ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); One call opens a window that demonstrates almost every feature of ImGui: widgets, layout, tables, popups, drag and drop, styling, fonts. It is the real documentation : when you want to know how to do something, find it in the demo window, then open imgui_demo.cpp and search for the label you saw. The code you need is right there. The demo's "Tools" menu (top of the window) opens the other tools below. Keep imgui_demo.cpp in every project during development; it costs nothing until called. Leave the call out of shipping builds (lesson 6.03). The style editor cpp-norun ImGui::ShowStyleEditor(); Every size, rounding and colour of the current style, editable live. Tune a style here, then click "Export" to copy the C++ code that sets it (lesson 4.05). The Metrics/Debugger window cpp-norun ImGui::ShowMetricsWindow(); It shows ImGui's own state: every window with its position, size and draw list (how many vertices, how many draw commands), the active and hovered widget IDs, the ID stack, the font atlas, tables' internal state, and more. Hover a draw command and it highlights what it draws. Use it when: - the interface is slow (which window has thousands of vertices?); - something is drawn but you cannot see why (where is its clip rectangle?); - a window behaves oddly (what are its flags and size constraints?). The ID Stack tool cpp-norun ImGui::ShowIDStackToolWindow(); Hover any widget: it shows the ID stack for it, level by level - the window's seed, every PushID , the label - and the final ID. The fastest way to understand why two widgets clash (lesson 1.05). The Item Picker In the Metrics window, Tools, Item Picker : click any widget in your program, and ImGui stops in the debugger inside the code that drew it . When you have a complex tool and cannot find which of fifty functions draws a misbehaving checkbox, this finds it in one click. Debug log The Metrics window has a Debug Log section that records what ImGui does in categories you choose: focus changes, popups, navigation, I/O events, docking. Turn on "I/O" and you see every mouse and keyboard event the back end feeds in, which answers "is ImGui even receiving my input?". Assertions are your friends ImGui uses IM_ASSERT heavily: unmatched Begin / End , PushID / PopID , calls outside a frame, bad parameters. In a Debug build the debugger stops on the exact line, with a comment in the source explaining the rule you broke. Read the comment above the assert; it nearly always says what to do. You can route assertions to your own handler by defining IM_ASSERT in imconfig.h . Common mistakes !warning Guessing instead of looking When a widget misbehaves, the ID Stack tool, the Metrics window and the Item Picker usually find the cause in seconds. !warning Disabling assertions to make a crash go away The assert is reporting a real mistake that will cause worse problems later. Fix the pairing or the call order instead. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the quickest way to find example code for a widget you saw in ShowDemoWindow? + Search imgui_demo.cpp for the label shown in the demo - Read imgui.cpp from the top - Ask the Metrics window The demo is the documentation, with its source beside it. ? Which tool tells you why two widgets share an ID? + The ID Stack tool - The style editor - The font atlas viewer It shows each level of the stack for the hovered widget. ? You cannot find which function draws a misbehaving widget. What helps? + The Item Picker, which breaks into the debugger in the code that drew the clicked widget - Increasing the font size - Removing PushID calls It is in the Metrics window's Tools.

title: Check the pairs, like ImGui's asserts
match: Check the pairs, like ImGui's asserts
where: 1.06 The Demo Window and the Debug Tools
body: ImGui asserts when Begin / End and PushID / PopID calls do not pair up. Write a checker that reports the first mistake in one frame's calls: cpp struct Call { std::string name; bool result{ true }; }; // result: what a Begin... function returned std::string checkFrame(const std::vector<Call & calls); The calls are Begin , End , BeginChild , EndChild , BeginTable , EndTable , BeginMenu , EndMenu , PushID and PopID . The rules: - Begin and BeginChild : the matching End / EndChild is always required, whatever they returned. - BeginTable and BeginMenu : the matching end is required only if it returned true , and must not be called if it returned false . - PushID needs a PopID before the scope it was pushed in ends. - Ends must match the most recent open thing: EndTable when the innermost open item is a Begin window is wrong. Return the first problem as one of these messages (with the call's position i , counting from 0): - "<End... at <i has no matching <Begin... " : an end with nothing matching open, or that does not match the innermost open item; - "<End... at <i was called although <Begin... returned false" : ending a BeginTable / BeginMenu that returned false (when its end would be the next end of that type); - "missing <End... for <Begin... at <i " : the frame ended while something was still open (report the innermost one, with the position of its begin). Return "" when everything pairs up.

title: A tiny immediate-mode UI of your own
match: A tiny immediate-mode UI of your own
body: The best way to understand Dear ImGui is to write a very small version of it. Build a UI context that, like ImGui, lays widgets out, handles the mouse, remembers state by ID, and produces a list of things to draw. No graphics: the "draw list" is a list of strings a test can read. cpp struct Input { float mouseX{ -1 }, mouseY{ -1 }; bool mouseDown{ false }; }; class Ui { public: void beginFrame(const Input& input); void endFrame(); void label(const std::string& text); bool button(const std::string& label); bool checkbox(const std::string& label, bool value); void pushId(const std::string& id); void popId(); const std::vector<std::string & drawList() const; // what the last frame drew }; Layout. Widgets stack vertically. The first widget's top is at y = 0 ; every widget is 20 high and 100 wide at x = 0 , and the next widget starts 4 below the previous one (so tops at 0, 24, 48...). beginFrame resets the cursor to the top and clears the draw list. Drawing. Each widget adds one line to the draw list: - label : "text <shown text " - button : "button <shown text " , followed by hot if the mouse is over it and active if it is the active widget (both can appear, in that order) - checkbox : "checkbox <shown text x " or "... " (after any change this frame), then the same hot / active marks. The shown text follows lesson 1.05's rule. IDs. A widget's ID is its label's ID text (lesson 1.05, including ) combined with the current ID stack, which starts empty each frame. You may represent an ID simply as a string, the stack's entries and the ID text joined with / . Behaviour (lesson 1.04's practice): - A widget is hot if the mouse is inside its rectangle this frame. - If the mouse button goes down this frame over a widget, that widget becomes the active ID (only one widget can be active). - When the mouse button goes up , the active widget is clicked if the mouse is over it, and the active ID is cleared. button returns true on that frame; checkbox flips value and returns true . - The active ID lives between frames in the Ui object (it is ImGui's remembered state); everything else is rebuilt every frame. - If the active widget is not drawn in a frame at all, the active ID is cleared at endFrame (like ImGui, which forgets widgets that disappear).

title: 2.01  Sliders, Drags and Checkboxes
body: Most tool interfaces are numbers and switches. This lesson covers checkboxes, radio buttons, sliders and drags for floats, integers and vectors, how a slider maps the mouse to a value, logarithmic sliders, format strings, and how to know when a value changed or finished changing. Checkboxes and radio buttons cpp-norun ImGui::Checkbox("God mode", &settings.godMode); // bool static int difficulty = 1; ImGui::RadioButton("Easy", &difficulty, 0); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::RadioButton("Normal", &difficulty, 1); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::RadioButton("Hard", &difficulty, 2); // sets difficulty to 2 when chosen ImGui::CheckboxFlags("Collides", &body.flags, FLAG_COLLIDES); // one bit of an integer All of them return true on the frame the value changed. Sliders cpp-norun ImGui::SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, 0.0f, 20.0f); // drag the grab across the width ImGui::SliderFloat("Gravity", &world.gravity, 0.0f, 30.0f, "%.2f m/s^2"); // a format for the shown value ImGui::SliderInt("Lives", &player.lives, 0, 9); ImGui::SliderFloat3("Position", &player.pos.x, -100.0f, 100.0f); // three sliders for x, y, z ImGui::SliderAngle("Heading", &player.headingRadians); // stored in radians, shown in degrees A slider maps the mouse's position across its width to a value between min and max . With the grab's width taken out of the track, the mapping is simply linear: t = (mouseX - trackStart) / trackWidth clamped to 0..1 value = min + t (max - min) and back again to place the grab: t = (value - min) / (max - min) . For integer sliders the value is rounded to the nearest whole number. The practice writes both directions. Ctrl+click (or double-click) on a slider turns it into a text field so you can type an exact value. By default a typed value can go outside the range; pass ImGuiSliderFlags_AlwaysClamp to prevent that. Logarithmic sliders For values that span orders of magnitude (a light's intensity from 0.01 to 1000), a linear slider puts nearly all its width on the large numbers. ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic maps the position to the logarithm of the value instead, so 0.01 to 0.1 gets as much room as 100 to 1000: cpp-norun ImGui::SliderFloat("Intensity", &light.intensity, 0.01f, 1000.0f, "%.3f", ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic); Drags A drag changes the value by dragging horizontally, with no fixed track, so it suits values without natural limits: cpp-norun ImGui::DragFloat("Mass", &body.mass, 0.1f); // 0.1 per pixel dragged ImGui::DragFloat("Radius", &body.radius, 0.05f, 0.0f, 50.0f); // with optional limits ImGui::DragInt("Count", &spawner.count, 1.0f, 0, 1000); ImGui::DragFloat3("Scale", &obj.scale.x, 0.01f); ImGui::DragFloatRange2("Spawn delay", &spawner.minDelay, &spawner.maxDelay, 0.05f, 0.0f, 10.0f); Holding Shift while dragging moves faster, Alt slower. Drags are the most common number widget in professional tools because they take little space and work for any range. Knowing when a value changed Every widget returns true when it changed the value this frame. Tools often need more: cpp-norun if (ImGui::DragFloat("Height", &terrain.height, 0.1f)) terrain.rebuildPreview(); // every frame during the drag if (ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit()) // the drag ended and the value had changed undo.record("Change height"); // record ONE undo step for the whole drag (lesson 5.04) if (ImGui::IsItemActive()) { / being dragged right now / } The IsItem... functions ask about the widget just drawn: IsItemHovered , IsItemActive , IsItemActivated (started this frame), IsItemEdited , IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit . Format strings The format argument is printf-style and controls only what is shown : "%.0f" rounds the display, "%d px" adds a unit, "%.1f%%" shows a percent sign ( %% ). The stored value keeps its full precision. Common mistakes !warning A slider with min greater than or equal to max It cannot map anything. ImGui asserts in debug builds. !warning Recording an undo step on every frame of a drag One drag would create sixty undo steps a second. Use IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit. Knowledge check quiz ? A slider from 0 to 20 is 200 pixels wide. The mouse is 50 pixels from its start. What value does it set? + 5 - 50 - 2.5 t = 50 / 200 = 0.25, and 0 + 0.25 20 = 5. ? When should you use a drag instead of a slider? + For values with no natural limits, or where space is short - Never; drags are deprecated - Only for integers Drags change by a speed per pixel and need no track. ? How do you record one undo step for a whole drag? + Check ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit() after the widget - Use the widget's return value - Record in IsItemHovered It is true once, when the edit ends and the value changed.

title: Slider maths
body: Write the mapping a slider uses between the mouse and the value: cpp float valueFromMouse(float mouseX, float trackStart, float trackWidth, float minValue, float maxValue); float positionOf(float value, float trackStart, float trackWidth, float minValue, float maxValue); int intValueFromMouse(float mouseX, float trackStart, float trackWidth, int minValue, int maxValue); float logValueFromMouse(float mouseX, float trackStart, float trackWidth, float minValue, float maxValue); - valueFromMouse : t = (mouseX - trackStart) / trackWidth , clamped to 0..1; the value is min + t (max - min) . - positionOf : the reverse, the x position of the grab for a value; values outside the range are clamped to its ends. - intValueFromMouse : like valueFromMouse with the integer range, rounded to the nearest whole number. - logValueFromMouse : for a logarithmic slider (both limits above 0), t maps to the logarithm: value = min pow(max / min, t) . A track of width 0 or less always gives min (and positionOf gives trackStart ). valueFromMouse(150, 100, 200, 0, 20) == 5 logValueFromMouse(200, 100, 200, 0.01, 100) == 1 // halfway on a log scale from 0.01 to 100

title: 2.02  Text Input and Validation
body: Text fields in ImGui write into a buffer you own. This lesson covers InputText with character arrays and std::string , number fields, multi-line text, flags that restrict what can be typed, callbacks for custom filtering and completion, and validating a value before you accept it. InputText with a buffer cpp-norun static char name 64 = "Granite"; ImGui::InputText("Name", name, IM_ARRAYSIZE(name)); // edits the array in place ImGui edits your buffer directly and never writes more than its size (including the terminating zero). IM_ARRAYSIZE gives the number of elements of an array. InputText with std::string The file misc/cpp/imgui_stdlib.cpp (add it to your project) gives overloads that resize a std::string as you type: cpp-norun include "misc/cpp/imgui_stdlib.h" ImGui::InputText("Name", &stone.name); // std::string ImGui::InputTextMultiline("Notes", &level.notes, ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 120)); // full width, 120 high ImGui::InputTextWithHint(" search", "Search stones...", &search); // grey hint when empty -FLT_MIN as a width means "all the space up to the right edge"; it is ImGui's idiom for "fill". Number fields cpp-norun ImGui::InputInt("Count", &count); // with - and + buttons ImGui::InputInt("Count", &count, 0); // step 0: no buttons ImGui::InputFloat("Weight", &weight, 0.1f, 1.0f, "%.2f"); ImGui::InputScalar("Seed", ImGuiDataType_U64, &seed); // any numeric type Restricting what can be typed Flags filter characters as they are typed: Flag Allows --- --- ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsDecimal 0123456789.+- / ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsHexadecimal 0123456789ABCDEFabcdef ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsUppercase Turns letters to upper case ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsNoBlank No spaces or tabs ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsScientific Decimal plus e / E Others change behaviour: EnterReturnsTrue (return true only when Enter is pressed, ideal for a console), ReadOnly , Password (shows ), AutoSelectAll , EscapeClearsAll . Callbacks: custom filters, history, completion For anything the flags cannot do, pass a callback: cpp-norun int onlyIdentifierChars(ImGuiInputTextCallbackData data) { const ImWchar c = data- EventChar; const bool ok = (c = 'a' && c <= 'z') (c = 'A' && c <= 'Z') (c = '0' && c <= '9') c == '_'; return ok ? 0 : 1; // return 1 to reject the character } ImGui::InputText("Id", id, sizeof(id), ImGuiInputTextFlags_CallbackCharFilter, onlyIdentifierChars); ImGuiInputTextFlags_CallbackCompletion calls you when Tab is pressed (for auto-completing a console command), and CallbackHistory when Up or Down is pressed (for recalling previous commands). The console example in the demo window shows both. Validating a value Filtering stops characters ; validation checks the whole value . A common, friendly pattern: edit a copy, show what is wrong, and only apply it when it is valid and the edit is finished. cpp-norun static std::string editing = level.name; ImGui::InputText("Level name", &editing); const std::string problem = validateLevelName(editing); // "" if fine if (!problem.empty()) ImGui::TextColored(ImVec4(1, 0.4f, 0.4f, 1), "%s", problem.c_str()); if (ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit() && problem.empty()) level.name = editing; The practice writes validateLevelName and a character filter. Keyboard focus ImGui::SetKeyboardFocusHere() before a text field gives it the keyboard focus on that frame: useful when a search window or console opens. ImGui::IsItemFocused() tells whether the field has focus. Common mistakes !warning Passing sizeof of a pointer as the buffer size InputText("x", ptr, sizeof(ptr)) passes 8. Use the real buffer size, IM_ARRAYSIZE for arrays, or the std::string overload. !warning Applying invalid text immediately Edit a copy and apply when it validates, so half-typed values never reach your data. Knowledge check quiz ? Which flag makes InputText return true only when Enter is pressed? + ImGuiInputTextFlags_EnterReturnsTrue - ImGuiInputTextFlags_ReadOnly - ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsDecimal Ideal for console commands and search boxes. ? What does a CallbackCharFilter return to reject a character? + 1 - 0 - The character itself Returning nonzero discards the typed character. ? What is the difference between filtering and validating? + Filtering stops individual characters as they are typed; validating checks the whole value - They are the same thing - Validating happens in the back end A name can contain only allowed characters and still be invalid as a whole.

title: Validate a level name
body: Write the two checks a level-name field uses: cpp bool allowedChar(char32_t c); // the character filter: is this character allowed at all? std::string validateLevelName(const std::string& name, const std::vector<std::string & existing); allowedChar allows lower-case letters a - z , digits, _ and - . Everything else is filtered out as it is typed. validateLevelName checks the whole value and returns the first problem, or an empty string: 1. empty: "Give the level a name." 2. longer than 32 characters: "Keep the name to 32 characters." 3. a character allowedChar refuses (for text pasted in): "Use a-z, 0-9, _ and - only." 4. starts with - or _ : "Start the name with a letter or digit." 5. already in existing (exact match): "A level called <name already exists."

title: 2.03  Combo Boxes and List Boxes
body: Choosing one item from many is everywhere in tools - a material, a level, an enemy type. This lesson covers BeginCombo with Selectable , the simple Combo overloads, list boxes, filtering a long list as you type, and showing enums by name. BeginCombo and Selectable The flexible way to make a drop-down: cpp-norun static const char materials = { "Granite", "Basalt", "Slate", "Marble", "Limestone" }; static int current = 0; if (ImGui::BeginCombo("Material", materials current )) // the text shown when closed { for (int i = 0; i < IM_ARRAYSIZE(materials); ++i) { const bool selected = (i == current); if (ImGui::Selectable(materials i , selected)) current = i; if (selected) ImGui::SetItemDefaultFocus(); // keyboard navigation starts here } ImGui::EndCombo(); // only if BeginCombo returned true! } BeginCombo returns true while the drop-down is open; then you draw its contents and call EndCombo . If it returns false , you do not call EndCombo (lesson 1.04's second rule). Selectable is a full-width clickable row that can be shown as selected. You will use it in lists, tables and trees too. The simple overloads For a plain list of strings there is a one-line version: cpp-norun ImGui::Combo("Material", &current, materials, IM_ARRAYSIZE(materials)); ImGui::Combo("Quality", &quality, "Low\0Medium\0High\0\0"); // items separated by \0, ending with \0\0 Use BeginCombo when the items are not a simple array: a std::vector of objects, items with icons, items you want to filter. Enums by name A table of names next to the enum keeps a combo honest: cpp-norun enum class Weather { Clear, Rain, Snow, Fog, Count }; constexpr const char weatherNames = { "Clear", "Rain", "Snow", "Fog" }; static_assert(IM_ARRAYSIZE(weatherNames) == static_cast<int (Weather::Count)); int w = static_cast<int (level.weather); if (ImGui::Combo("Weather", &w, weatherNames, IM_ARRAYSIZE(weatherNames))) level.weather = static_cast<Weather (w); The static_assert fails the build if someone adds an enum value without a name. List boxes A list box is the same idea, always open, with a fixed height: cpp-norun if (ImGui::BeginListBox(" levels", ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 8 ImGui::GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing()))) { for (int i = 0; i < (int)levels.size(); ++i) if (ImGui::Selectable(levels i .name.c_str(), i == selectedLevel)) selectedLevel = i; ImGui::EndListBox(); } Size the height in lines ( GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing ) so it adapts to the font. Filtering long lists A list of 400 assets needs a search box. Keep a filter string, and only draw matching items: cpp-norun static std::string filter; ImGui::InputTextWithHint(" filter", "Filter...", &filter); for (const Asset& a : assets) if (matches(a.name, filter)) if (ImGui::Selectable(a.name.c_str(), &a == selected)) selected = &a; A good matches ignores case and lets the words of the filter appear anywhere, in any order: "rock big" matches "big_mossy_rock". The practice writes it. ImGui also ships ImGuiTextFilter for include/exclude filters, which lesson 5.02 uses. Common mistakes !warning Calling EndCombo when BeginCombo returned false ImGui asserts. EndCombo belongs inside the if. !warning Selectables with the same text They share an ID (lesson 1.05). PushID per item, or add and the index. Knowledge check quiz ? When is EndCombo called? + Only when BeginCombo returned true - Always, like End for windows - Never; it is automatic BeginCombo returns true while the drop-down is open. ? Why add a static_assert next to an enum's name table? + So the build fails if an enum value is added without a matching name - To speed up the combo - Because Combo requires it The table and the enum must stay the same length. ? How do you size a list box to show eight items? + 8 ImGui::GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing() as its height - ImVec2(0, 8) - It always shows eight Measuring in lines adapts to the font size.

title: Filter a long list
body: Write the matching a filter box above a long list uses, and the list it produces: cpp bool matches(const std::string& item, const std::string& filter); std::vector<int visibleItems(const std::vector<std::string & items, const std::string& filter); int keepSelection(const std::vector<int & visible, int selected); - matches : split the filter into words at spaces. The item matches if every word appears somewhere in it, in any order, ignoring upper and lower case. An empty filter (or one with only spaces) matches everything. - visibleItems : the indexes of the matching items, in order. - keepSelection : after the filter changes, keep the selected item if it is still visible; otherwise select the first visible item; if nothing is visible, return -1 . matches("big_mossy_rock", "rock BIG") == true matches("big_mossy_rock", "rock small") == false

title: 2.04  Colours and Colour Pickers
body: ImGui works with colours in two forms - four floats from 0 to 1 ( ImVec4 ) and one packed 32-bit integer ( ImU32 , built with IM_COL32 ). This lesson covers the colour widgets, converting between the forms and to HSV, and why packed colours store their bytes in the order they do. Colour widgets cpp-norun ImGui::ColorEdit3("Fog colour", &fog.color.x); // float 3 : r, g, b from 0 to 1 ImGui::ColorEdit4("Tint", &sprite.tint.x); // float 4 : with alpha ImGui::ColorPicker4("Sky", &sky.x); // the big picker with a hue wheel or square ImGui::ColorButton(" swatch", ImVec4(0.9f, 0.6f, 0.2f, 1.0f)); // a clickable swatch ColorEdit shows the colour as numbers with a swatch; click the swatch for a picker popup. Flags choose the details: ImGuiColorEditFlags_NoAlpha , DisplayHex , DisplayHSV , PickerHueWheel , Float (0..1 numbers instead of 0..255), HDR (values above 1). Two forms of colour ImVec4 : four floats, red, green, blue, alpha, each from 0 to 1. Widgets and styles use this form. ImU32 : four bytes packed into one 32-bit unsigned integer. Draw lists use this form, because millions of vertices each carry a colour and four bytes are much smaller than four floats. The macro builds one: cpp-norun ImU32 gold = IM_COL32(240, 180, 70, 255); // r, g, b, a from 0 to 255 draw- AddRectFilled(min, max, gold); With ImGui's default settings, IM_COL32(r, g, b, a) is (a << 24) (b << 16) (g << 8) r Red is in the lowest byte. Written in memory on a little-endian PC (lesson 1.02 of the gamedev course), the bytes are in the order R, G, B, A , which is exactly the vertex format the GPU reads. That is why it looks "backwards" as a hexadecimal number: opaque red is 0xFF0000FF . Converting between them: cpp-norun ImVec4 v = ImGui::ColorConvertU32ToFloat4(gold); ImU32 u = ImGui::ColorConvertFloat4ToU32(ImVec4(1, 0.5f, 0, 1)); // rounds to the nearest of 0..255 ImU32 w = ImGui::GetColorU32(ImGuiCol_Text); // a style colour, with the current alpha HSV Hue, saturation, value is a friendlier space for adjusting colours: change the hue to cycle through the rainbow while keeping brightness; lower the saturation to grey something out. cpp-norun float h, s, v; ImGui::ColorConvertRGBtoHSV(c.x, c.y, c.z, h, s, v); // all in 0..1, hue too h = std::fmod(h + 0.1f, 1.0f); // shift the hue ImGui::ColorConvertHSVtoRGB(h, s, v, c.x, c.y, c.z); A classic tool trick is to give each item a distinct colour from its index: hue = i 0.618034f modulo 1 (the golden ratio spreads them evenly), saturation 0.6, value 0.9. The practice writes the conversions. Hexadecimal colour codes Artists often paste colours as F0B446 or F0B446CC . Parsing them into an ImVec4 is a small, useful function, which the practice also has you write. Common mistakes !warning Building an ImU32 by hand in the wrong byte order 0xF0B446FF is not gold with full alpha in ImGui's layout. Use IM_COL32 or ColorConvertFloat4ToU32. !warning Passing 0-255 values to ColorEdit ColorEdit edits floats from 0 to 1. Convert when your data stores bytes. Knowledge check quiz ? What does IM_COL32(255, 0, 0, 255) equal with ImGui's default byte order? + 0xFF0000FF - 0xFFFF0000 - 0x00FF00FF Alpha in the top byte, then blue, green, and red in the lowest byte. ? Why do draw lists use ImU32 instead of ImVec4? + Four bytes per vertex colour is far smaller than four floats - ImVec4 cannot hold alpha - The GPU cannot read floats Every vertex carries a colour. ? Which colour space makes "rotate through the rainbow at the same brightness" easy? + HSV - Packed ImU32 - RGB Change only the hue.

title: Colour conversions
body: Write ImGui's colour conversions yourself: cpp struct Vec4 { float r, g, b, a; }; uint32_t col32(int r, int g, int b, int a); // like IM_COL32: (a << 24) (b << 16) (g << 8) r uint32_t toU32(const Vec4& c); // floats 0..1 to bytes, rounded to nearest, clamped Vec4 toVec4(uint32_t packed); // bytes to floats: byte / 255 void rgbToHsv(float r, float g, float b, float& h, float& s, float& v); // all in 0..1, hue too bool parseHex(const std::string& text, Vec4& out); // " RRGGBB" or " RRGGBBAA" - toU32 : each float is clamped to 0..1, multiplied by 255 and rounded to the nearest whole number ( + 0.5 then truncate). - rgbToHsv : v is the largest of r, g, b; s is (max - min) / max (0 when max is 0); hue is in sixths of a turn: if max is r, h = (g - b) / (max - min) ; if max is g, h = 2 + (b - r) / (max - min) ; if max is b, h = 4 + (r - g) / (max - min) ; then divide by 6 and add 1 if negative. For a grey (max equal to min) the hue is 0. - parseHex : a then exactly 6 or 8 hexadecimal digits (either case). Without alpha digits, alpha is 1. Anything else returns false .

title: 2.05  Sharing Input with Your Game
body: When ImGui runs on top of a game, the same click could mean "press this button" or "shoot". ImGui tells you which with io.WantCaptureMouse and io.WantCaptureKeyboard . This lesson shows how to route input correctly, read keys and the mouse through ImGui yourself, and add keyboard shortcuts to your tools. Who gets the click? Your game reads the mouse and keyboard too. Without care, typing a level name into a text field also walks the player around, and clicking a button also fires the gun. ImGui sets three flags every frame: Flag True when --- --- io.WantCaptureMouse The mouse is over an ImGui window, or ImGui is using it (dragging a slider that left the window) io.WantCaptureKeyboard An ImGui widget has keyboard focus (a text field, or keyboard navigation is active) io.WantTextInput A text field wants characters (on consoles and phones: show the on-screen keyboard) The rule is simple: ImGui first; the game only if ImGui does not want it. cpp-norun ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); if (!io.WantCaptureMouse) { if (mouse.leftPressed) player.shoot(mouse.worldPosition); camera.zoom(mouse.wheel); } if (!io.WantCaptureKeyboard) { player.move(keys.wasd()); } Read the flags after ImGui::NewFrame() and use them for this frame's game input. They are computed from last frame's layout, which is fine: windows do not move faster than a frame. Reading input through ImGui Your tool code can ask ImGui directly about keys and the mouse, using the same input the back end fed in: cpp-norun if (ImGui::IsKeyPressed(ImGuiKey_F5)) reloadLevel(); // pressed this frame (with key repeat by default) if (ImGui::IsKeyDown(ImGuiKey_LeftShift)) speed = 4.0f; // held if (ImGui::IsMouseClicked(ImGuiMouseButton_Right)) openMenuAt(ImGui::GetMousePos()); if (ImGui::IsMouseDragging(ImGuiMouseButton_Middle)) pan(ImGui::GetIO().MouseDelta); if (ImGui::IsMouseDoubleClicked(ImGuiMouseButton_Left)) focusSelection(); ImGuiKey_ values name every key independent of the platform: ImGuiKey_A , ImGuiKey_Escape , ImGuiKey_Delete , ImGuiKey_LeftCtrl , ImGuiMod_Ctrl (either Ctrl key). Keyboard shortcuts Recent versions of ImGui have a proper shortcut system that respects focus (a shortcut in one window does not fire while you type in another): cpp-norun if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_S)) saveLevel(); if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_Z)) undo(); if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiMod_Shift ImGuiKey_Z)) redo(); For a global shortcut that should work whichever window has focus, pass ImGuiInputFlags_RouteGlobal . Menu items show their shortcut text but do not trigger it by themselves (lesson 4.01). Tools often store shortcuts as text in a settings file: "Ctrl+Shift+S" . Parsing that text into modifiers and a key is a good small exercise, which the practice has you write. Gamepads With io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableGamepad and a back end that reports the gamepad (the Win32 back end supports XInput), the D-pad moves between widgets and A activates them. Useful for debug menus on a game being tested with a controller. Common mistakes !warning The game reading input before ImGui Typing in a text field moves the player. Check WantCaptureKeyboard before the game handles keys. !warning Checking the flags before NewFrame They are only updated in NewFrame. Check them after it. Knowledge check quiz ? The player is typing a level name in an ImGui text field. Which flag tells the game to ignore the keyboard? + io.WantCaptureKeyboard - io.WantCaptureMouse - io.WantTextInput only It is true while an ImGui widget has keyboard focus. ? The mouse is over an ImGui window and the player clicks. Should the game fire? + No; io.WantCaptureMouse is true - Yes; games always get the mouse - Only on a double click ImGui gets first claim on the input. ? Which call checks the shortcut Ctrl+S with ImGui's focus rules? + ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_S) - ImGui::IsKeyDown(ImGuiKey_S) - ImGui::MenuItem("Save", "Ctrl+S") MenuItem only shows the text; Shortcut detects the keys.

title: Who gets the input?
body: Each frame, decide which input the game may act on. Write cpp struct Frame { bool wantCaptureMouse; bool wantCaptureKeyboard; bool mouseClicked; std::vector<char keys; // keys pressed this frame }; struct GameInput { bool shoot{ false }; std::string moves; }; GameInput gameInput(const Frame& f); - The game shoots only if the mouse was clicked and ImGui does not want the mouse. - The game moves for each of w , a , s , d in keys , in order (other keys are ignored), only if ImGui does not want the keyboard. moves is those letters as a string.

title: Parse a shortcut
body: Tools store shortcuts as text, such as "Ctrl+Shift+S" . Write cpp struct Chord { bool ctrl{ false }, shift{ false }, alt{ false }; std::string key; }; bool parseShortcut(const std::string& text, Chord& out); std::string formatShortcut(const Chord& c); parseShortcut : - parts are separated by + ; spaces around them are ignored; names ignore case; - the modifiers are Ctrl (also Control ), Shift and Alt , each at most once; - exactly one part is the key, and it comes last : a single letter or digit (stored in upper case, "S" ), F1 to F12 , or one of Enter , Escape , Space , Tab , Delete (stored with that spelling); - anything else returns false . formatShortcut writes the modifiers in the order Ctrl, Shift, Alt, then the key, joined with + : "Ctrl+Shift+S" .

title: A developer console
body: Most games built with ImGui have a developer console: a text field where you type god , give gold 500 or teleport 12 40 , with history and Tab completion. ImGui gives you the text field and callbacks (lesson 2.02); write the logic behind them. cpp class Console { public: void addCommand(const std::string& name, std::function<std::string(const std::vector<std::string &) run); std::string execute(const std::string& line); // runs a line, returns what to print std::string historyUp(const std::string& current); // Up arrow: an older line std::string historyDown(const std::string& current); // Down arrow: a newer line std::string complete(const std::string& current); // Tab const std::vector<std::string & log() const; // everything printed so far }; Executing ( execute ): - Split the line into words on spaces; a part in double quotes is one word without its quotes ( say "hello there" gives say , hello there ). Empty input does nothing and returns "" . - The first word is the command name, matched without regard to case. Run it with the remaining words and return what it returns. - An unknown command returns Unknown command: <name . - Add plus the line to the log, then the result if it is not empty. Add the line to the history unless it is the same as the most recent history entry. - help is built in: it returns all command names, sorted, joined with ", " . History ( historyUp , historyDown ): like a terminal. Up from the edited line shows the newest history entry, then older ones; it stops at the oldest. Down goes back towards newer entries, and past the newest returns to the line that was being typed before Up was first pressed (the current argument at that first Up). execute resets the position. Completion ( complete ): complete the first word only, against the command names (and help ): - if exactly one name starts with it (ignoring case), return that name followed by a space; - if several do, return their longest common prefix (in lower case), or the input unchanged if that is no longer than the input, and add a log line listing the candidates sorted, joined with " " ; - if none do, return the input unchanged.

title: 3.01  Sizes, SameLine, Spacing and Groups
body: ImGui places widgets with a cursor that moves down after each one. This lesson shows how to control it - SameLine , item widths, spacing, indentation, groups, alignment and disabled sections - so a tool's window reads cleanly at any font size. The cursor Every window has a layout cursor . Each widget is placed at the cursor, then the cursor moves to the start of the next line. That is why widgets stack vertically by default. Everything in this lesson changes where the cursor goes, or how wide the next widget is. SameLine cpp-norun ImGui::Text("Stones:"); ImGui::SameLine(); // the next widget goes to the right of the last one ImGui::Text("%d", count); ImGui::SameLine(200.0f); // ...at x = 200 from the window's left edge ImGui::Button("Add"); ImGui::SameLine(0.0f, 2.0f); // default position, but only 2 pixels of spacing ImGui::Button("-"); Widths By default, widgets with a frame (sliders, inputs, combos) take about two thirds of the window width, leaving room for the label on the right. Change it: cpp-norun ImGui::SetNextItemWidth(120.0f); // the next widget only ImGui::DragFloat("Mass", &mass); ImGui::PushItemWidth(-FLT_MIN); // all following widgets: fill to the right edge ImGui::InputText(" notes", &notes); // (hide the label with , or it would be cut off) ImGui::PopItemWidth(); ImGui::PushItemWidth(ImGui::GetFontSize() 10); // ten "M" widths: scales with the font Prefer sizes based on GetFontSize() , GetFrameHeight() and GetContentRegionAvail() over fixed pixel numbers, so the tool still looks right when someone raises the font size or the display scale. cpp-norun const float avail = ImGui::GetContentRegionAvail().x; // width left on this line ImGui::Button("Half", ImVec2(avail 0.5f, 0)); // 0 height = the normal height Spacing, separators, indentation cpp-norun ImGui::Spacing(); // a little vertical space ImGui::Separator(); // a horizontal line ImGui::SeparatorText("Physics"); // a line with a title ImGui::Indent(); // move the left edge right (by the style's indent width) ImGui::Text("indented"); ImGui::Unindent(); ImGui::Dummy(ImVec2(0, 20)); // an invisible widget that takes space ImGui::NewLine(); // move to the next line, like pressing Enter Groups A group makes several widgets act as one item for layout: you can put the whole group on the same line as something else, and IsItemHovered asks about the whole group. cpp-norun ImGui::BeginGroup(); ImGui::Text("Player"); ImGui::Text("HP %d", hp); ImGui::Text("MP %d", mp); ImGui::EndGroup(); ImGui::SameLine(); // the next group sits to the right of the whole first group ImGui::BeginGroup(); ImGui::Text("Enemy"); ImGui::Text("HP %d", enemyHp); ImGui::EndGroup(); Alignment ImGui lays text from the top of the line. Next to a framed widget (a button, an input) plain text looks too high. Call ImGui::AlignTextToFramePadding() before such text to line it up with the frames on the same line. To right-align something, move the cursor yourself: cpp-norun const float w = ImGui::CalcTextSize("Delete").x + ImGui::GetStyle().FramePadding.x 2; ImGui::SameLine(ImGui::GetContentRegionMax().x - w); ImGui::Button("Delete"); CalcTextSize measures text with the current font. The practice uses that kind of measurement to lay out a row of buttons. Disabled sections cpp-norun ImGui::BeginDisabled(!level.loaded); // greyed out and not interactive while no level is loaded if (ImGui::Button("Save")) saveLevel(); ImGui::EndDisabled(); Better than hiding the button: the user sees it exists and why it cannot be used yet (add a tooltip, lesson 4.02). Common mistakes !warning Fixed pixel sizes everywhere They break at other font sizes and display scales. Measure from the font and the available width. !warning A full-width widget with a visible label The label is pushed off the right edge. Hide it with and put a Text in front instead. Knowledge check quiz ? Which call puts the next widget to the right of the previous one? + ImGui::SameLine() - ImGui::NewLine() - ImGui::Indent() SameLine moves the cursor back up to the end of the last item. ? What does a width of -FLT_MIN mean for PushItemWidth? + Fill up to the right edge of the window - No width at all - The default width It is ImGui's idiom for "all the space that is left". ? Why use BeginDisabled instead of hiding a button? + The user sees the action exists and that it cannot be used right now - Disabled buttons draw faster - Hidden buttons still receive clicks Make it clear why, with a tooltip.

title: Right-aligned buttons
body: Lay out a row of buttons aligned to the right edge of a window, the way dialog boxes put "Cancel Apply OK" at the bottom right. Text is measured with a fixed character width (a monospace font), so: buttonWidth(label) = label.size() charWidth + 2 framePadding Write cpp std::vector<float rightAlignedX(const std::vector<std::string & labels, float charWidth, float framePadding, float spacing, float contentMaxX, float contentMinX); It returns the left x position of each button, in the given order, so that: - the last button's right edge is exactly at contentMaxX ; - there are spacing pixels between neighbouring buttons; - if the row does not fit between contentMinX and contentMaxX , start the first button at contentMinX instead and let the row run off the right (never off the left). rightAlignedX({ "Cancel", "OK" }, 7, 4, 8, 400, 10) "Cancel" is 6 7+8 = 50 wide, "OK" is 2 7+8 = 22 wide, total 50 + 8 + 22 = 80 == { 320, 378 }

title: 3.02  Child Windows and Scrolling
body: A child window is a scrolling region inside a window - a list that scrolls while the buttons below it stay put, or a two-pane layout. This lesson covers BeginChild , sizing children to fill space, scrolling from code, auto-scrolling logs, and clipping so a list of a hundred thousand items costs nothing. BeginChild cpp-norun ImGui::BeginChild("stones", ImVec2(0, 200), ImGuiChildFlags_Borders); // full width, 200 high, with a border for (const Stone& s : stones) ImGui::Text("%s", s.name.c_str()); ImGui::EndChild(); // ALWAYS, like End if (ImGui::Button("Add")) addStone(); // stays below, not scrolled BeginChild / EndChild follow the window rule: EndChild is always called, whatever BeginChild returned. Sizes: 0 means "fill what is available", a positive number is a fixed size, a negative number means "fill, minus this much". So "a list that fills the window except for one row of buttons below it" is: cpp-norun const float footer = ImGui::GetFrameHeightWithSpacing(); // the height of one row of buttons ImGui::BeginChild("list", ImVec2(0, -footer), ImGuiChildFlags_Borders); // ... ImGui::EndChild(); ImGui::Button("Add"); Two panes side by side cpp-norun ImGui::BeginChild("left", ImVec2(200, 0), ImGuiChildFlags_Borders ImGuiChildFlags_ResizeX); // resizable drawLevelList(); ImGui::EndChild(); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::BeginChild("right"); // takes the rest drawLevelDetails(); ImGui::EndChild(); ImGuiChildFlags_ResizeX adds a handle on the child's right edge the user can drag. (Before version 1.90 the second argument of BeginChild was a bool border ; the flags replaced it.) Scrolling from code cpp-norun ImGui::SetScrollHereY(0.5f); // scroll so the current cursor position is in the middle ImGui::SetScrollY(0.0f); // to the top float y = ImGui::GetScrollY(), maxY = ImGui::GetScrollMaxY(); A log window wants to follow new lines, but only if the user has not scrolled up to read something: cpp-norun const bool atBottom = ImGui::GetScrollY() = ImGui::GetScrollMaxY(); // measure BEFORE adding lines for (const auto& line : log) ImGui::TextUnformatted(line.c_str()); if (atBottom) ImGui::SetScrollHereY(1.0f); // keep following Clipping long lists Drawing 100,000 lines every frame is slow even if only 30 are visible. ImGuiListClipper works out which items are on screen, so you only draw those, while the scroll bar still behaves as if all of them were there: cpp-norun ImGuiListClipper clipper; clipper.Begin((int)lines.size()); // all items have the same height while (clipper.Step()) for (int i = clipper.DisplayStart; i < clipper.DisplayEnd; ++i) ImGui::TextUnformatted(lines i .c_str()); The idea is simple arithmetic: with each item h pixels high, the scroll position y and the visible height H , the first visible item is floor(y / h) and the last is ceil((y + H) / h) . The clipper reserves empty space for the items above and below so the scroll bar is right. The practice writes this calculation. Clipping needs every item to have the same height . For variable heights, keep a prefix sum of heights and binary-search it, or group items into rows of equal height. Common mistakes !warning Calling EndChild only when BeginChild returned true Like End, EndChild is always called. !warning Auto-scroll that fights the user Check whether you were at the bottom before adding lines, and only follow then. !warning Drawing every line of a huge log Use ImGuiListClipper; the cost then depends on the window height, not the log length. Knowledge check quiz ? A child should fill the window except for 40 pixels of buttons below it. What height do you pass? + -40 - 40 - 0 Negative sizes mean "fill, minus this much". ? What must be true of the items for ImGuiListClipper to work? + They all have the same height - They are sorted - There are fewer than 1000 It computes the visible range from a fixed item height. ? With items 20 pixels high, scrolled to y = 1000, what is the first visible item? + 50 - 20 - 1000 floor(1000 / 20) = 50.

title: What the clipper draws
body: Write the calculation inside ImGuiListClipper : cpp struct Range { int start; int end; }; // draw items start .. end-1 Range visibleRange(int itemCount, float itemHeight, float scrollY, float viewHeight); float contentHeight(int itemCount, float itemHeight); bool shouldFollow(float scrollY, float scrollMaxY); - visibleRange : the first visible item is floor(scrollY / itemHeight) ; the end is ceil((scrollY + viewHeight) / itemHeight) . Clamp both to 0 .. itemCount . An item height of 0 or less, or no items, gives {0, 0} . - contentHeight : the total height the scroll bar must cover. - shouldFollow : a log keeps following new lines only if it was scrolled to the bottom: scrollY = scrollMaxY - 1 (allowing one pixel of rounding). visibleRange(100000, 20, 1000, 300) == { 50, 65 }

title: 3.03  Tables
body: Tables are ImGui's most capable layout tool - columns that resize, reorder, hide and sort, frozen header rows, scrolling with clipping, and alternate row backgrounds. This lesson builds an entity table step by step and explains sorting specs, the part most people find confusing. A basic table cpp-norun if (ImGui::BeginTable("entities", 3, ImGuiTableFlags_Borders ImGuiTableFlags_RowBg)) { ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Name"); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("HP", ImGuiTableColumnFlags_WidthFixed, 60.0f); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Position"); ImGui::TableHeadersRow(); for (const Entity& e : entities) { ImGui::TableNextRow(); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::TextUnformatted(e.name.c_str()); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d", e.hp); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%.1f, %.1f", e.x, e.y); } ImGui::EndTable(); // only if BeginTable returned true } BeginTable returns false when the table is clipped (scrolled out of view); then you skip it and do not call EndTable (lesson 1.04's second rule). Inside, any widget can go in any cell. Useful flags Flag Effect --- --- Resizable Drag column borders to resize Reorderable Drag headers to reorder columns Hideable Right-click the header to hide columns Sortable Click headers to sort (see below) ScrollY (with an outer size) The table scrolls; combine with TableSetupScrollFreeze(0, 1) to keep the header row visible RowBg Alternate row colours SizingFixedFit , SizingStretchProp ... How column widths are chosen The table remembers widths, order, visibility and sort per table ID, and saves them in imgui.ini (lesson 4.06). Scrolling a large table cpp-norun const ImVec2 outer(0, ImGui::GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing() 15); // 15 rows high if (ImGui::BeginTable("big", 3, ImGuiTableFlags_ScrollY ImGuiTableFlags_RowBg, outer)) { ImGui::TableSetupScrollFreeze(0, 1); // keep the first row (headers) visible / TableSetupColumn x3, TableHeadersRow / ImGuiListClipper clipper; clipper.Begin((int)rows.size()); while (clipper.Step()) for (int i = clipper.DisplayStart; i < clipper.DisplayEnd; ++i) { / TableNextRow, cells for rows i / } ImGui::EndTable(); } Sorting With ImGuiTableFlags_Sortable , clicking a header changes the table's sort specs . ImGui does not sort your data: it tells you what the user asked for, and you sort. cpp-norun if (ImGuiTableSortSpecs specs = ImGui::TableGetSortSpecs()) { if (specs- SpecsDirty) // the user changed the sort (or first frame) { std::sort(entities.begin(), entities.end(), & (const Entity& a, const Entity& b) { for (int n = 0; n < specs- SpecsCount; ++n) { const ImGuiTableColumnSortSpecs& s = specs- Specs n ; // ColumnIndex, SortDirection int cmp = compareColumn(a, b, s.ColumnIndex); // -1, 0 or 1 if (cmp != 0) return s.SortDirection == ImGuiSortDirection_Ascending ? cmp < 0 : cmp 0; } return false; }); specs- SpecsDirty = false; } } Call this after TableSetupColumn / TableHeadersRow and before the rows. Key points: - Sort only when SpecsDirty , not every frame. - With ImGuiTableFlags_SortMulti , Shift-clicking adds secondary sort columns: Specs 0 is the primary key, Specs 1 breaks its ties, and so on. The loop above handles any number. - Give each column a stable meaning with TableSetupColumn("Name", flags, width, userId) and compare by ColumnUserID if the columns can be reordered or hidden. The practice writes this multi-key comparison. Common mistakes !warning Sorting every frame Sort when SpecsDirty is set, then clear it. !warning Expecting ImGui to sort the data It only reports what the user clicked. Your data, your sort. Knowledge check quiz ? When BeginTable returns false, what do you do? + Skip the table and do not call EndTable - Call EndTable anyway - Call BeginTable again Tables follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule. ? With SortMulti, the user sorts by Team, then Shift-clicks HP. What is Specs 1 ? + HP, which breaks ties between rows with the same Team - Team - Nothing; only one key is allowed Specs are in order of priority. ? Who sorts the rows of an ImGui table? + Your code, using the sort specs when they are dirty - ImGui, automatically - The renderer back end ImGui reports the requested order; you apply it.

title: Sort by the table's specs
body: A sortable table hands you a list of sort specs, most important first. Sort the rows the way they ask: cpp struct Row { std::string name; std::string team; int hp; }; struct SortSpec { int column; bool ascending; }; // 0 = name, 1 = team, 2 = hp void sortRows(std::vector<Row & rows, const std::vector<SortSpec & specs); - Compare by the first spec's column; if equal, by the second's; and so on. - Text columns compare as plain strings; hp compares as a number. - Each spec has its own direction. - Rows equal in every spec keep their original order (use a stable sort). - No specs: leave the order alone.

title: 3.04  Trees and Selection
body: A scene hierarchy, a file browser and an asset list all need a tree and a selection that behaves like every other program - click to select, Ctrl+click to add, Shift+click for a range. This lesson covers TreeNode and its flags, building a tree from your data, and implementing multi-selection properly. Tree nodes cpp-norun if (ImGui::TreeNode("Level")) // true while open { ImGui::Text("child item"); if (ImGui::TreeNode("Props")) { ImGui::Text("rock"); ImGui::TreePop(); } ImGui::TreePop(); // only if TreeNode returned true } ImGui remembers whether each node is open by its ID (lesson 1.05), so two nodes with the same label in the same place open and close together. In a loop, use PushID or the TreeNode(ptr_id, fmt, ...) overload, which takes a pointer as the ID and a separate display text. TreeNodeEx and its flags cpp-norun ImGuiTreeNodeFlags flags = ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_OpenOnArrow // click the arrow to open, the label to select ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_OpenOnDoubleClick ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_SpanAvailWidth; // the whole row is clickable if (node.children.empty()) flags = ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_Leaf ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_NoTreePushOnOpen; if (isSelected(node.id)) flags = ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_Selected; const bool open = ImGui::TreeNodeEx((void )(intptr_t)node.id, flags, "%s", node.name.c_str()); if (ImGui::IsItemClicked() && !ImGui::IsItemToggledOpen()) // clicked the label, not the arrow select(node.id); - Leaf draws no arrow; with NoTreePushOnOpen you also skip TreePop for it. - DefaultOpen opens a node the first time it is seen. - ImGui::SetNextItemOpen(true) opens the next node from code: "reveal the selected object in the tree". Building a tree from your data Scene data is usually a flat list where each object knows its parent. Draw it recursively: cpp-norun void drawNode(const Scene& scene, int id) { const Object& o = scene.objects id ; ImGuiTreeNodeFlags flags = ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_OpenOnArrow ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_SpanAvailWidth; if (o.children.empty()) flags = ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_Leaf ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_NoTreePushOnOpen; const bool open = ImGui::TreeNodeEx((void )(intptr_t)id, flags, "%s", o.name.c_str()); if (open && !o.children.empty()) { for (int child : o.children) drawNode(scene, child); ImGui::TreePop(); } } The practice builds the "children of each node" lists from parent links and produces the order rows appear in, which is also what Shift+click ranges need. Selection that behaves Users expect: Action Result --- --- Click Select only this item; it becomes the anchor Ctrl+click Toggle this item, keep the others; it becomes the anchor Shift+click Select every item between the anchor and this one , in display order, replacing the selection Ctrl+Shift+click Add that range to the existing selection The anchor is the last item clicked without Shift. Ranges are measured in display order : the order rows appear on screen, which for a tree is depth-first over the open nodes. Store the selection as a set of stable IDs, never as row positions, so it survives sorting and filtering. Dear ImGui 1.91 added a full multi-select API ( BeginMultiSelect / EndMultiSelect ) that handles these rules, box-selection and keyboard navigation for you; writing the rules yourself once, as the practice does, makes it much easier to use well. Common mistakes !warning Selecting when the arrow was clicked Check IsItemToggledOpen so opening a node does not also select it. !warning Storing the selection as row numbers Rows change when the list is sorted, filtered or a node opens. Store IDs. Knowledge check quiz ? What does ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_OpenOnArrow change? + Only clicking the arrow opens the node, so clicking the label can select it - The node is always open - The arrow is hidden It separates opening from selecting. ? The anchor is item 3 and the user Shift+clicks item 7. What is selected? + Items 3 to 7 in display order, replacing the previous selection - Only item 7 - Items 3 and 7 Shift+click selects the range from the anchor. ? Why store selected items by ID rather than by row number? + Rows change with sorting, filtering and opening nodes; IDs do not - IDs take less memory - ImGui requires it The selection must survive changes to what is shown.

title: Rows of a tree
body: A scene is a flat list of objects, each knowing its parent ( -1 for a root).
