Write the order the tree's rows appear on screen: cpp struct Object { int id; int parent; std::string name; }; std::vector<int displayOrder(const std::vector<Object & objects, const std::set<int & open); - Roots come first-to-last in the order they appear in objects ; so do the children of each object. - A row is shown for every root, and for every child of an open object whose own row is shown (depth first: an object's children come right after it, before its next sibling). - Return the ids in row order. objects: 1 "Level" (root), 2 "Props" (parent 1), 3 "Rock" (parent 2), 4 "Lights" (parent 1), 5 "UI" (root) open {1} - 1, 2, 4, 5 open {1, 2} - 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 open {2} - 1, 5 (2 is open but its parent is closed, so it is not shown)

title: Click, Ctrl+click, Shift+click
body: Implement selection that behaves like every desktop program, over rows in display order (as produced above): cpp class Selection { public: void click(const std::vector<int & rows, int id, bool ctrl, bool shift); bool isSelected(int id) const; std::vector<int selected() const; // sorted by id int anchor() const; // -1 when there is none }; Action Result --- --- Click Select only id ; it becomes the anchor Ctrl+click Toggle id , keep the rest; it becomes the anchor Shift+click Replace the selection with every row from the anchor to id , inclusive, in rows order Ctrl+Shift+click Add that range to the current selection - With Shift but no anchor (or an anchor not in rows ), behave like a plain click (or a Ctrl+click, if Ctrl is held too). - Shift+click does not move the anchor, so the user can Shift+click again to change the range end.

title: 3.05  Tabs, Collapsing Headers and Tooltips
body: Tools have more settings than fit on one screen. This lesson covers the ways to organise them - collapsing headers, tab bars, and the old Columns API you will meet in existing code - plus tooltips and help markers, so every setting can explain itself. Collapsing headers A collapsing header is a full-width bar that hides or shows the section below it. Inspectors are usually a stack of them: cpp-norun if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Transform", ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_DefaultOpen)) { ImGui::DragFloat3("Position", &t.pos.x, 0.1f); ImGui::DragFloat3("Rotation", &t.rot.x, 1.0f); } if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Physics")) { ImGui::DragFloat("Mass", &body.mass, 0.1f, 0.0f, 1000.0f); } It is a tree node that does not push to the ID stack and needs no TreePop . Pass a bool as a second argument and it also gets a close button, handy for "remove this component" in an inspector. Tab bars cpp-norun if (ImGui::BeginTabBar("settings", ImGuiTabBarFlags_Reorderable)) { if (ImGui::BeginTabItem("Graphics")) { drawGraphics(); ImGui::EndTabItem(); } if (ImGui::BeginTabItem("Audio")) { drawAudio(); ImGui::EndTabItem(); } if (ImGui::BeginTabItem("Controls")) { drawControls(); ImGui::EndTabItem(); } ImGui::EndTabBar(); } Both pairs follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule. A bool open on BeginTabItem gives the tab a close button (an editor with one tab per open file). To switch to a tab from code, pass ImGuiTabItemFlags_SetSelected on that frame. The old Columns API Older code uses ImGui::Columns(2) , NextColumn() and Columns(1) to split a window into columns. It still works but is legacy : tables (lesson 3.03) do everything it did and more. When you meet Columns in an existing tool, consider converting it to a two-column table with ImGuiTableFlags_SizingStretchProp . Tooltips cpp-norun ImGui::DragFloat("Drag", &body.drag, 0.01f); ImGui::SetItemTooltip("Air resistance. 0 = none, 1 = moves through syrup."); // shown when the last item is hovered if (ImGui::IsItemHovered(ImGuiHoveredFlags_DelayNormal)) // a richer tooltip after a short delay { ImGui::BeginTooltip(); ImGui::Text("Drag curve"); ImGui::PlotLines(" curve", samples, IM_ARRAYSIZE(samples)); ImGui::EndTooltip(); } SetItemTooltip covers most cases. With BeginTooltip / EndTooltip you can put any widgets inside. The help marker A common pattern from the demo window: a small greyed "(?)" after a setting that shows an explanation when hovered: cpp-norun static void HelpMarker(const char text) { ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::TextDisabled("(?)"); if (ImGui::BeginItemTooltip()) { ImGui::PushTextWrapPos(ImGui::GetFontSize() 30.0f); // wrap at about 30 characters wide ImGui::TextUnformatted(text); ImGui::PopTextWrapPos(); ImGui::EndTooltip(); } } Wrapping long help text matters: an unwrapped tooltip can be wider than the screen. The practice writes a word-wrap function like the one ImGui uses for TextWrapped . Common mistakes !warning Calling EndTabItem for a tab that is not selected BeginTabItem returns true only for the visible tab. EndTabItem goes inside the if. !warning Tooltips with very long unwrapped text Push a text wrap position, or use TextWrapped. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the difference between CollapsingHeader and TreeNode? + CollapsingHeader does not push the ID stack and needs no TreePop - CollapsingHeader cannot be closed - TreeNode is always full width It is a header-style section toggle. ? Which call shows a simple tooltip for the widget just drawn? + ImGui::SetItemTooltip("...") - ImGui::BeginTooltip() with no checks - ImGui::Text in the same line It shows only when the last item is hovered. ? You find ImGui::Columns(2) in old code. What should you consider? + Converting it to a two-column table - Deleting it; it no longer compiles - Nothing; it is the recommended API Columns is legacy; tables replace it.

title: Wrap tooltip text
body: Long help text in a tooltip must wrap. Write the word wrap TextWrapped does, with widths counted in characters: cpp std::vector<std::string wrapText(const std::string& text, int width); - Words are separated by spaces. Put as many words on a line as fit in width characters, with one space between words. - A word longer than width goes on a line of its own, cut into pieces of width characters. - A newline \n in the text always starts a new line (an empty line between two \n stays as an empty line). - Several spaces in a row count as one. No line starts or ends with a space. - width below 1 is treated as 1. wrapText("Air resistance. 0 means none.", 12) == { "Air", "resistance.", "0 means", "none." }

title: An entity browser
body: Combine the milestone into the model behind a real tool window: a table of entities with a filter box, sortable columns, multi-selection and a clipped, scrolling body. cpp struct Entity { int id; std::string name; std::string team; int hp; }; struct SortSpec { int column; bool ascending; }; // 0 name, 1 team, 2 hp class EntityBrowser { public: explicit EntityBrowser(std::vector<Entity entities); void setFilter(const std::string& filter); // lesson 2.03's word matching on name and team void setSort(const std::vector<SortSpec & specs); // lesson 3.03 std::vector<int rows() const; // ids of visible entities, filtered and sorted void click(int id, bool ctrl, bool shift); // lesson 3.04's rules over rows() std::vector<int selected() const; // sorted ids std::vector<int visibleRows(float scrollY, float viewHeight, float rowHeight) const; // lesson 3.02, ids void removeSelected(); // deletes the selected entities int count() const; // entities left }; Rules: - rows() holds the entities whose name or team match the filter, sorted by the specs (stable; with no specs, in the original order). - The selection is by id and survives filtering and sorting. Selected entities that the filter hides stay selected. - click uses the current rows() as display order for Shift ranges. - visibleRows returns the ids of the rows the clipper would draw for that scroll position. - removeSelected deletes every selected entity, including hidden ones, and clears the selection and the anchor.

title: 4.01  Menus and Shortcuts
body: A main menu bar turns a pile of windows into an application - File, Edit, View, Tools. This lesson covers menu bars in the main viewport and in windows, menu items with checkmarks and shortcut text, the Begin/End rule for menus, and wiring the shortcuts so they actually work. The main menu bar cpp-norun if (ImGui::BeginMainMenuBar()) // across the top of the screen { if (ImGui::BeginMenu("File")) { if (ImGui::MenuItem("New level", "Ctrl+N")) newLevel(); if (ImGui::MenuItem("Open...", "Ctrl+O")) openDialog(); if (ImGui::MenuItem("Save", "Ctrl+S", false, level.dirty)) save(); // disabled when nothing changed ImGui::Separator(); if (ImGui::MenuItem("Quit", "Alt+F4")) running = false; ImGui::EndMenu(); } if (ImGui::BeginMenu("View")) { ImGui::MenuItem("Stones", nullptr, &showStones); // a checkmark bound to a bool ImGui::MenuItem("Log", nullptr, &showLog); ImGui::EndMenu(); } ImGui::EndMainMenuBar(); } This is the pair rule you met in lesson 1.04: BeginMainMenuBar / EndMainMenuBar and BeginMenu / EndMenu are only ended if their Begin returned true . A closed menu returns false , so its EndMenu is skipped. MenuItem has two useful forms: - MenuItem(label, shortcut, selected, enabled) returns true when clicked; selected draws a checkmark, enabled = false greys it out. - MenuItem(label, shortcut, bool selected) toggles the bool when clicked: the standard "show window" switch. Menus can nest: a BeginMenu inside another opens a sub-menu. A menu bar inside a window cpp-norun ImGui::Begin("Level editor", nullptr, ImGuiWindowFlags_MenuBar); if (ImGui::BeginMenuBar()) { if (ImGui::BeginMenu("Edit")) { / ... / ImGui::EndMenu(); } ImGui::EndMenuBar(); } // window contents ImGui::End(); Shortcut text is only text The second argument of MenuItem ("Ctrl+S") is only displayed . Clicking the menu item works; pressing Ctrl+S does nothing unless you also check the keys. Do that once, outside the menu code, so the shortcut works even when the menu is closed: cpp-norun if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_S, ImGuiInputFlags_RouteGlobal)) save(); A tidy approach is a table of commands : each has a name, a shortcut, an "is it available" check and an action. The menu draws from the table, the shortcut handler checks the table, and a command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, like editors have) can list it too. The practice builds that table, including detecting two commands that claim the same shortcut. Keyboard navigation in menus With ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableKeyboard , pressing Alt focuses the menu bar, arrow keys move through it, Enter activates and Escape closes, the way desktop applications behave. Common mistakes !warning Calling EndMenu when BeginMenu returned false ImGui asserts. EndMenu goes inside the if. !warning Expecting the shortcut text to work by itself It is a label. Check the keys with Shortcut or IsKeyPressed. !warning Two commands on the same shortcut Only one will ever run, depending on which is checked first. Detect clashes when you build the command table. Knowledge check quiz ? BeginMenu("File") returns false because the menu is closed. What do you do? + Skip its items and do not call EndMenu - Call EndMenu anyway - Call BeginMenu again next frame with a different label Menus follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule. ? What does the "Ctrl+S" argument of MenuItem do? + It is shown next to the item; it does not detect the keys - It registers a global shortcut - It sends Ctrl+S to the window Detect the shortcut separately. ? Which MenuItem form toggles a bool when clicked? + MenuItem(label, shortcut, &flag) - MenuItem(label) - MenuItem(label, shortcut, false, true) Ideal for showing and hiding windows.

title: A command table
body: Menus, shortcuts and a command palette work best from one table of commands. Write it: cpp struct Command { std::string name; // "File/Save" std::string shortcut; // "Ctrl+S", or "" for none (already in a normal form: modifiers Ctrl, Shift, Alt in that order) std::function<bool() enabled; // may be empty: always enabled std::function<void() run; }; class Commands { public: void add(Command c); std::vector<std::string clashes() const; // "Ctrl+S: File/Save, Edit/Select" for each shortcut used twice or more bool press(const std::string& shortcut); // run the command with this shortcut, if any is enabled std::vector<std::string menu(const std::string& top) const; // items under a top-level menu }; - clashes : one line per shortcut used by two or more commands, in alphabetical order of shortcut; the command names in the order they were added, joined with ", " . - press : among commands with this shortcut, run the first added one that is enabled and return true ; return false if none is enabled or none has it. - menu("File") : for each command whose name starts with File/ , in order added, the text after File/ , followed by " " and the shortcut if it has one, and (disabled) if its enabled returns false right now.

title: 4.02  Popups, Context Menus and Modals
body: Popups are small windows that appear on request and close when you click elsewhere - right-click menus, pickers, confirmations. This lesson explains ImGui's popup model (open by ID, draw every frame while open), context menus on items and windows, modal dialogs that block the rest of the interface, and the classic "unsaved changes" confirmation. Opening and drawing are separate A popup has an ID, like a widget. You open it once, in reaction to something, and you draw it every frame with BeginPopup , which returns true only while it is open: cpp-norun if (ImGui::Button("Pick a stone")) ImGui::OpenPopup("stone picker"); // once, on click if (ImGui::BeginPopup("stone picker")) // every frame { for (const char s : { "Granite", "Basalt", "Slate" }) if (ImGui::Selectable(s)) chosen = s; // a Selectable closes the popup ImGui::EndPopup(); // only if BeginPopup returned true } The popup closes by itself when the user clicks outside it, presses Escape, or clicks a Selectable / MenuItem inside it. Close it from code with ImGui::CloseCurrentPopup() inside the popup. Both calls must be made with the same ID stack : an OpenPopup inside a PushID(i) opens a popup that BeginPopup can only find inside the same PushID(i) . This is the most common popup bug, and a direct consequence of lesson 1.05. Context menus Right-click menus have shortcuts that do the opening for you: cpp-norun ImGui::Selectable(stone.name.c_str()); if (ImGui::BeginPopupContextItem()) // right-click on the item just drawn { if (ImGui::MenuItem("Rename")) startRename(stone); if (ImGui::MenuItem("Delete")) deleteStone(stone); ImGui::EndPopup(); } if (ImGui::BeginPopupContextWindow(nullptr, ImGuiPopupFlags_MouseButtonRight ImGuiPopupFlags_NoOpenOverItems)) { // right-click on empty space in the window if (ImGui::MenuItem("Add stone")) addStone(); ImGui::EndPopup(); } Modals A modal popup blocks interaction with everything behind it until it is closed, and dims the background. Use it for decisions that must be made before continuing: cpp-norun if (wantsToQuit && level.dirty) ImGui::OpenPopup("Unsaved changes"); ImGui::SetNextWindowPos(ImGui::GetMainViewport()- GetCenter(), ImGuiCond_Appearing, ImVec2(0.5f, 0.5f)); if (ImGui::BeginPopupModal("Unsaved changes", nullptr, ImGuiWindowFlags_AlwaysAutoResize)) { ImGui::Text("Save changes to %s before quitting?", level.name.c_str()); if (ImGui::Button("Save", ImVec2(100, 0))) { save(); quit(); ImGui::CloseCurrentPopup(); } ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Don't save", ImVec2(100, 0))) { quit(); ImGui::CloseCurrentPopup(); } ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Cancel", ImVec2(100, 0))) { wantsToQuit = false; ImGui::CloseCurrentPopup(); } ImGui::EndPopup(); } SetNextWindowPos with the pivot (0.5, 0.5) and ImGuiCond_Appearing centres the dialog each time it appears. Passing a bool as the second argument gives the modal a close button. The unsaved-changes flow "Quit", "New level" and "Open level" all have the same shape: if there are unsaved changes, ask first; then do the action only if the user saved or chose not to. A small state machine keeps it correct: remember the pending action , open the modal, and when a button is pressed run (or drop) the pending action. The practice builds it. Common mistakes !warning OpenPopup and BeginPopup under different ID stacks The popup is opened but never found. Call both at the same PushID level. !warning Calling OpenPopup every frame The popup reopens and resets constantly. Open it once, in response to an event. !warning Using a modal for information Modals interrupt. Use them for decisions only; show information in a tooltip or a log. Knowledge check quiz ? How often do you call OpenPopup and BeginPopup? + OpenPopup once when it should open; BeginPopup every frame - Both every frame - Both once Opening is an event; drawing happens every frame while open. ? OpenPopup("menu") is called inside PushID(3), BeginPopup("menu") outside it. What happens? + The popup never appears, because the IDs differ - It works normally - ImGui opens two popups Popup IDs follow the ID stack. ? When should you use a modal popup? + For a decision that must be made before continuing, such as saving unsaved changes - For every message - For tooltips Modals block everything else until answered.

title: The unsaved-changes dialog
body: "New level", "Open level" and "Quit" must all ask about unsaved changes first. Write the state machine behind the modal: cpp class Guard { public: explicit Guard(std::function<bool() save); // save returns false if saving failed void setDirty(bool dirty); void request(const std::string& action); // "new", "open" or "quit" bool dialogOpen() const; // should the modal be open this frame? void answer(const std::string& choice); // "save", "discard" or "cancel" std::vector<std::string done() const; // actions that went ahead, in order }; - request while not dirty : the action goes ahead at once (added to done ). - request while dirty: the action becomes pending and the dialog opens. A second request while the dialog is already open replaces the pending action. - answer("save") : call save . If it succeeds, the document is no longer dirty and the pending action goes ahead. If it fails, the dialog stays open and nothing happens. - answer("discard") : the pending action goes ahead; the document is treated as not dirty any more. - answer("cancel") : the pending action is dropped; still dirty. - Every answer except a failed save closes the dialog. Answers while the dialog is closed do nothing.

title: 4.03  Drag and Drop
body: Dragging an asset onto a slot, reordering a list, moving an object to another parent in a tree - ImGui's drag and drop works between any two items with a typed payload . This lesson covers sources, targets, payload types, reordering a list by dragging, and re-parenting in a tree without creating loops. Source and target Any item can be a drag source and any item a drop target . They talk through a payload : a small block of bytes with a type name. cpp-norun // The source: an asset in the browser ImGui::Selectable(asset.name.c_str()); if (ImGui::BeginDragDropSource()) { ImGui::SetDragDropPayload("ASSET", &asset.id, sizeof(asset.id)); // copied by ImGui ImGui::Text("%s", asset.name.c_str()); // drawn under the mouse while dragging ImGui::EndDragDropSource(); } // The target: a texture slot in the inspector ImGui::Button(material.texture.empty() ? "(drop a texture)" : material.texture.c_str(), ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 0)); if (ImGui::BeginDragDropTarget()) { if (const ImGuiPayload p = ImGui::AcceptDragDropPayload("ASSET")) // non-null on the frame of the drop { const int id = static_cast<const int (p- Data); material.texture = assets.byId(id).name; } ImGui::EndDragDropTarget(); } Both Begin... functions follow the "End only if Begin returned true" rule. The type string (up to 32 characters) lets a target accept only what it understands: a texture slot accepts "ASSET" , ignores "ENTITY" . While dragging, matching targets highlight automatically. The payload is copied , so pass small, stable things: an id, an index, never a pointer to something that may move or be deleted during the drag. Reordering a list A list where each row is both a source and a target can be reordered by dragging: cpp-norun for (int i = 0; i < (int)layers.size(); ++i) { ImGui::PushID(i); ImGui::Selectable(layers i .name.c_str()); if (ImGui::BeginDragDropSource()) { ImGui::SetDragDropPayload("LAYER", &i, sizeof(i)); ImGui::Text("%s", layers i .name.c_str()); ImGui::EndDragDropSource(); } if (ImGui::BeginDragDropTarget()) { if (const ImGuiPayload p = ImGui::AcceptDragDropPayload("LAYER")) pendingMove = { static_cast<const int (p- Data), i }; // apply after the loop ImGui::EndDragDropTarget(); } ImGui::PopID(); } if (pendingMove) { moveItem(layers, pendingMove- from, pendingMove- to); pendingMove.reset(); } Apply the move after the loop: changing the vector while iterating over it would skip or repeat rows. "Move item from from to to " means: take the item out, and insert it so it ends up at index to . The practice writes moveItem . Re-parenting in a tree Dropping a tree node on another node makes it a child of that node. One rule protects the data: a node may not be dropped onto itself or onto any of its own descendants , which would make a loop (the node would become its own ancestor) and detach that whole branch from the tree. Check the ancestry before accepting: cpp-norun bool isAncestor(const Scene& s, int maybeAncestor, int node) // walk up the parent links ImGui can help the user too: AcceptDragDropPayload with ImGuiDragDropFlags_AcceptBeforeDelivery lets you peek at the payload while hovering and show a "not allowed" cursor or tooltip before the drop. The practice implements the re-parenting rule. Dragging from outside The Win32 back end does not deliver files dragged from Explorer as ImGui payloads. Handle WM_DROPFILES (after DragAcceptFiles(hwnd, TRUE) ) in your window procedure, and act on the files directly, for example importing them into the asset browser. Common mistakes !warning A pointer in the payload The data may move or be deleted during the drag. Use ids or indexes. !warning Changing a container while drawing it Record the move and apply it after the loop. !warning Allowing a node to become its own descendant Check ancestry before re-parenting, or part of the tree disappears into a loop. Knowledge check quiz ? What is a drag-and-drop payload's type string for? + So a target only accepts payloads it understands - To choose the cursor - To name the window "ASSET" and "ENTITY" payloads go to different targets. ? Why apply a list reorder after the loop that draws the list? + Changing the vector while iterating over it skips or repeats items - ImGui requires all drops at the end of the frame - It is faster Record the move, then apply it once the loop is done. ? Node A is the parent of B, and B the parent of C. Can A be dropped onto C? + No; A would become a descendant of itself - Yes - Only if C has no children Check that the target is not the dragged node or one of its descendants.

title: Move an item in a list
match: Move an item in a list
body: Dragging a row of a reorderable list onto another row moves it there. Write cpp template <typename T void moveItem(std::vector<T & items, int from, int to); Take the item at from out and insert it so that it ends up at index to (counted in the final list). Indexes outside the list, or from == to , change nothing. { A, B, C, D, E }, from 1 to 3 - { A, C, D, B, E } { A, B, C, D, E }, from 4 to 0 - { E, A, B, C, D }

title: Re-parent without loops
body: Dropping a scene object onto another in the tree makes it a child of that object. Write cpp bool isAncestor(const std::map<int, int & parentOf, int ancestor, int node); bool reparent(std::map<int, int & parentOf, int node, int newParent); parentOf maps every object to its parent; roots map to -1 . - isAncestor(a, n) : is a the parent of n , or its parent's parent, and so on up to the root? An object is not its own ancestor. - reparent(node, newParent) : refuse (return false , change nothing) if newParent is node itself or a descendant of node , or if either is not in the map (except newParent == -1 , which makes node a root). Otherwise set the parent and return true .

title: 4.04  Docking and Multiple Viewports
body: With the docking branch, windows snap into each other as tabs and splits - the layout of every modern editor - and with multiple viewports they can leave the main window and become real operating-system windows. This lesson turns both on, builds a dockspace over the whole screen, creates a default layout from code, and explains how dock nodes split space. Turning it on Docking lives on Dear ImGui's docking branch (lesson 1.02). Enable it once after creating the context: cpp-norun ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_DockingEnable; io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_ViewportsEnable; // optional: windows may leave the main window Now drag any window by its title bar onto another: a docking overlay appears with targets for "as a tab", "split left", "split right", "split top", "split bottom". Hold Shift while dragging to dock only when you want to (set io.ConfigDockingWithShift = true ). A dockspace over the whole screen Editors fill the application window with one big dockspace that other windows dock into: cpp-norun ImGui::NewFrame(); ImGui::DockSpaceOverViewport(0, ImGui::GetMainViewport(), ImGuiDockNodeFlags_PassthruCentralNode); drawMenuBar(); // a main menu bar sits above the dockspace drawSceneWindow(); drawInspector(); drawLog(); ImGuiDockNodeFlags_PassthruCentralNode leaves the empty central area transparent, so your 3D scene drawn behind ImGui shows through it and receives clicks there. How docking splits space A dockspace is a tree of dock nodes . Each node is either a leaf , holding one or more windows as tabs, or a split , holding two child nodes side by side (horizontal) or one above the other (vertical) with a ratio : root (split left/right, ratio 0.2) ├── left: Scene tree 20% of the width └── right (split top/bottom, ratio 0.75) ├── top: Viewport Game tabs, 75% of the height └── bottom: Log Profiler tabs, 25% Every node's rectangle is computed from its parent's: the first child gets ratio of the size along the split axis, the second gets the rest. The practice computes these rectangles, which is exactly the arithmetic ImGui does every frame. A default layout from code The first time a user opens your editor, it should not be a pile of floating windows. The DockBuilder API (in imgui_internal.h ) builds a layout: cpp-norun include "imgui_internal.h" void buildDefaultLayout(ImGuiID dockspace) { ImGui::DockBuilderRemoveNode(dockspace); ImGui::DockBuilderAddNode(dockspace, ImGuiDockNodeFlags_DockSpace); ImGui::DockBuilderSetNodeSize(dockspace, ImGui::GetMainViewport()- Size); ImGuiID left, right; ImGui::DockBuilderSplitNode(dockspace, ImGuiDir_Left, 0.2f, &left, &right); ImGuiID bottom, centre; ImGui::DockBuilderSplitNode(right, ImGuiDir_Down, 0.25f, &bottom, &centre); ImGui::DockBuilderDockWindow("Scene", left); ImGui::DockBuilderDockWindow("Viewport", centre); ImGui::DockBuilderDockWindow("Log", bottom); ImGui::DockBuilderFinish(dockspace); } Call it when the dockspace has no saved layout yet ( ImGui::DockBuilderGetNode(id) == nullptr before the first DockSpace call), and from a "Reset layout" menu item. After that, imgui.ini remembers whatever the user arranged (lesson 4.06). Multiple viewports With ViewportsEnable , dragging a window outside the application window turns it into a real operating-system window, so tools can spread over several monitors. Your loop needs two more calls after rendering the main window: cpp-norun ImGui::Render(); ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData()); if (io.ConfigFlags & ImGuiConfigFlags_ViewportsEnable) { ImGui::UpdatePlatformWindows(); // create, move, resize OS windows ImGui::RenderPlatformWindowsDefault(); // render and present each one } g_swapChain- Present(1, 0); Coordinates then become desktop coordinates rather than window coordinates, which matters if you place windows yourself: use ImGui::GetMainViewport()- Pos as the origin. Common mistakes !warning Using docking functions on the master branch They do not exist there. Use the docking branch, as most tools do. !warning Rebuilding the default layout every frame The user's arrangement is wiped every frame. Build it only when there is none, or on request. Knowledge check quiz ? What is a dock node? + Either a leaf holding windows as tabs, or a split holding two child nodes with a ratio - A separate operating-system window - A kind of table A dockspace is a tree of them. ? A split node 1000 pixels wide, split left/right with ratio 0.2. How wide is the left child? + 200 pixels - 800 pixels - 20 pixels The first child gets ratio times the size along the split axis. ? What does ImGuiDockNodeFlags_PassthruCentralNode do? + Leaves the empty centre of the dockspace transparent so the scene behind shows through and gets clicks - Hides all docked windows - Docks every window into the centre Editors draw the 3D view there.

title: Where each dock node goes
body: A dockspace is a tree of nodes. Compute every leaf's rectangle, as ImGui does each frame: cpp struct Rect { float x, y, w, h; }; struct DockNode { std::string name; // for a leaf: the window docked there; for a split: unused char split{ 0 }; // 0 for a leaf; 'x' = left/right, 'y' = top/bottom float ratio{ 0.5f }; // share of the first child along the split axis std::vector<DockNode children; // exactly 2 for a split }; std::vector<std::pair<std::string, Rect layout(const DockNode& root, const Rect& area, float splitterSize); - A leaf takes its whole rectangle. - A split 'x' gives the first child the left part and the second the right part; 'y' gives the first the top and the second the bottom. - Between the two children is a splitter of splitterSize pixels. The space shared out is size along the axis - splitterSize : the first child gets ratio of it (rounded down to a whole pixel with floor ), the second gets the rest. - Return every leaf, depth first, first child before second, with its rectangle. root: split x, ratio 0.2, children leaf "Scene", split y ratio 0.75 leaf "Viewport", leaf "Log" area {0, 0, 1004, 704}, splitter 4 Scene {0, 0, 200, 704} Viewport {204, 0, 800, 525} Log {204, 529, 800, 175}

title: 4.05  Styling, Fonts and Icons
body: The default look is fine for debug views, but a tool people use all day deserves care. This lesson covers the style object, colours and sizes, temporary style changes with Push/Pop, loading fonts at the right size for the display's scale, and merging an icon font so buttons can show symbols. The style All sizes and colours live in one ImGuiStyle : cpp-norun ImGuiStyle& style = ImGui::GetStyle(); ImGui::StyleColorsDark(); // start from a built-in theme: Dark, Light or Classic style.WindowRounding = 4.0f; style.FrameRounding = 3.0f; style.FramePadding = ImVec2(8, 5); style.ItemSpacing = ImVec2(8, 6); style.ScrollbarSize = 12.0f; style.Colors ImGuiCol_WindowBg = ImVec4(0.09f, 0.10f, 0.12f, 1.0f); style.Colors ImGuiCol_Header = ImVec4(0.95f, 0.70f, 0.27f, 0.35f); style.Colors ImGuiCol_HeaderHovered = ImVec4(0.95f, 0.70f, 0.27f, 0.55f); There are about 55 colours ( ImGuiCol_Text , Button , ButtonHovered , ButtonActive , FrameBg , CheckMark , SliderGrab ...) and dozens of sizes. Tune them live with the style editor (lesson 1.06), then press "Export" to copy the code. A good theme usually comes from a small palette: a background, a slightly lighter panel, an accent, and the same accent at three strengths for normal, hovered and active. The practice generates such a theme from one accent colour. Temporary changes cpp-norun ImGui::PushStyleColor(ImGuiCol_Button, ImVec4(0.8f, 0.2f, 0.2f, 1.0f)); ImGui::PushStyleVar(ImGuiStyleVar_FrameRounding, 8.0f); if (ImGui::Button("Delete level")) confirmDelete(); ImGui::PopStyleVar(); ImGui::PopStyleColor(); Every Push needs a Pop (with a count: PopStyleColor(2) pops two). Scaling for the display On a 4K laptop at 200% scale, a 13-pixel font is unreadable. Get the window's scale and apply it to both the font size and the style: cpp-norun const float scale = ImGui_ImplWin32_GetDpiScaleForHwnd(hwnd); // 1.0 at 96 DPI, 1.5 at 144, 2.0 at 192 style.ScaleAllSizes(scale); // paddings, roundings, spacing io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf", 15.0f scale); Load the font at the real size rather than scaling a small font up, which looks blurry. (ImGui 1.92 added dynamic font sizes, which handles much of this for you; the idea is the same.) Fonts cpp-norun ImFont body = io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf", 16.0f); ImFont mono = io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/JetBrainsMono-Regular.ttf", 15.0f); // ... ImGui::PushFont(mono); ImGui::TextUnformatted(logText); ImGui::PopFont(); The first font added becomes the default. Fonts are rasterised into the font atlas texture (lesson 1.03) when the back end builds it; add them before the first NewFrame . Icon fonts Icon fonts such as Font Awesome or Material Symbols put pictures in Unicode's "private use" area. Merge one into your text font so a single label can mix words and icons: cpp-norun io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf", 16.0f); ImFontConfig config; config.MergeMode = true; // add these glyphs to the previous font config.GlyphMinAdvanceX = 16.0f; // icons all the same width static const ImWchar iconRange = { 0xE000, 0xF8FF, 0 }; // the private use area io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/fa-solid-900.ttf", 14.0f, &config, iconRange); ImGui::Button("\xef\x83\x87 Save"); // U+F0C7 (a floppy disk in Font Awesome) as UTF-8 ImGui strings are UTF-8 . A code point above U+007F is written as two to four bytes; U+F0C7 becomes EF 83 87 . Projects usually use a header with named constants ( ICON_FA_FLOPPY_DISK ) generated for the icon font. The practice has you write the UTF-8 encoder. Common mistakes !warning Scaling a small font up instead of loading it at the right size The text is blurry. Load fonts at the size they will be drawn. !warning Mismatched Push and Pop counts ImGui asserts at the end of the frame. Pop as many as you pushed. !warning Writing non-ASCII text in a source file without UTF-8 Save source files as UTF-8 (and compile with /utf-8) or write the bytes as escapes. Knowledge check quiz ? What does style.ScaleAllSizes(2.0f) change? + Paddings, spacings, roundings and other sizes, but not the font - Only the font size - The window size Load the font at the scaled size separately. ? Why merge an icon font into the text font? + So one string can mix words and icons without switching fonts - To make the atlas smaller - Because icon fonts cannot be loaded alone MergeMode adds the icon glyphs to the previous font. ? How many bytes does the code point U+F0C7 take in UTF-8? + Three - One - Two Code points from U+0800 to U+FFFF use three bytes.

title: UTF-8 for icons
body: ImGui labels are UTF-8. To put an icon's code point into a label, encode it. Write cpp std::string utf8(char32_t codePoint); std::vector<char32_t decodeUtf8(const std::string& text); utf8 encodes one code point: Code point Bytes --- --- U+0000 to U+007F 0xxxxxxx U+0080 to U+07FF 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800 to U+FFFF 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000 to U+10FFFF 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx The x bits are the code point's bits, highest first. Surrogates (U+D800 to U+DFFF) and anything above U+10FFFF are not valid: encode them as U+FFFD (the replacement character) instead. decodeUtf8 turns a string back into code points. A byte that does not start a valid sequence (or a sequence cut short) decodes as U+FFFD and decoding continues with the next byte. utf8(U'A') == "A" utf8(0xF0C7) == "\xEF\x83\x87" (Font Awesome's floppy disk)

title: A theme from one colour
body: A good theme uses one accent colour at three strengths. Write cpp struct Color { float r, g, b, a; }; Color withAlpha(Color c, float a); Color lighten(Color c, float amount); // move each channel towards 1 by amount (0..1) Color darken(Color c, float amount); // move each channel towards 0 by amount (0..1) std::vector<Color accentStates(Color accent); // { normal, hovered, active } - lighten(c, t) : each of r, g, b becomes x + (1 - x) t ; darken(c, t) : x (1 - t) . Alpha is unchanged. - accentStates : normal is the accent at alpha 0.40; hovered is the accent at alpha 0.60; active is the accent lightened by 0.15 at alpha 1.0.

title: 4.06  Saving Settings and Layouts
body:
ImGui saves window positions, sizes, docking and table layouts to imgui.ini by itself. This lesson explains that file, how to move it, how to store your own tool's settings in the same file with a settings handler , and how to save and restore named layouts. imgui.ini By default ImGui writes imgui.ini in the working directory a few seconds after something changes, and reads it at start-up: ini Window Stones Pos=60,40 Size=320,260 Collapsed=0 DockId=0x00000002,0 Table 0x8A4C2B11,4 Column 0 Weight=1.0000 Visible=1 Order=0 Sort=0v Column 1 Width=60 Visible=1 Order=1 Docking Data DockSpace ID=0x3BC79352 Window=0x4647B76E Pos=0,19 Size=1280,701 Split=X DockNode ID=0x00000001 Parent=0x3BC79352 SizeRef=256,701 Selected=0x8B1D2D3A DockNode ID=0x00000002 Parent=0x3BC79352 SizeRef=1022,701 CentralNode=1 It is a simple text format: Type Name section headers, then Key=Value lines. Where it goes The working directory is a bad place: it changes with how the program is started. Put it in the user's settings folder: cpp-norun static std::string iniPath = settingsFolder() + "\xenon_editor_imgui.ini"; // e.g. under %APPDATA% io.IniFilename = iniPath.c_str(); // the string must outlive ImGui: keep it static or global io.IniSavingRate = 2.0f; // seconds of quiet before saving Set io.IniFilename = nullptr to turn saving off, and save or load yourself with ImGui::SaveIniSettingsToMemory() and ImGui::LoadIniSettingsFromMemory(text) , for example to keep the layout inside your own project file. Your own settings in the same file A settings handler lets your tool save its own data as more sections of imgui.ini , so window layout and tool settings live and load together: cpp-norun ImGuiSettingsHandler handler; handler.TypeName = "XenonEditor"; handler.TypeHash = ImHashStr("XenonEditor"); handler.ReadOpenFn = (ImGuiContext , ImGuiSettingsHandler , const char name) - void { return std::strcmp(name, "Options") == 0 ? &g_options : nullptr; // which object receives the lines }; handler.ReadLineFn = (ImGuiContext , ImGuiSettingsHandler , void entry, const char line) { auto o = static_cast<Options (entry); int v; if (std::sscanf(line, "GridSize=%d", &v) == 1) o- gridSize = v; else if (std::sscanf(line, "Snap=%d", &v) == 1) o- snap = v != 0; }; handler.WriteAllFn = (ImGuiContext , ImGuiSettingsHandler h, ImGuiTextBuffer out) { out- appendf(" %s Options 
", h- TypeName); out- appendf("GridSize=%d
Snap=%d

", g_options.gridSize, g_options.snap ? 1 : 0); }; ImGui::AddSettingsHandler(&handler); // before the first NewFrame (the ini is read then) When your settings change, call ImGui::MarkIniSettingsDirty() so ImGui saves soon. Because the format is so simple, reading and writing it yourself is easy too. The practice writes a small reader that turns the file into sections of key-value pairs, and a writer that puts them back, keeping sections it does not understand untouched. Named layouts Editors often let users save layouts by name: "Level design", "Animation", "Debugging". With SaveIniSettingsToMemory and LoadIniSettingsFromMemory , a layout is just a string: cpp-norun layouts "Animation" = ImGui::SaveIniSettingsToMemory(); // save the current arrangement ImGui::LoadIniSettingsFromMemory(layouts "Animation" .c_str()); // switch to it (at the start of a frame) Common mistakes !warning A temporary string for io.IniFilename ImGui keeps the pointer. A temporary dies and ImGui reads freed memory. Keep it in a static or global. !warning Adding a settings handler after the first frame The ini file has already been read, so your section is ignored. Add handlers before the first NewFrame. Knowledge check quiz ? Why should imgui.ini not stay in the working directory? + The working directory depends on how the program is started, so settings appear lost - ImGui cannot write there - It is slower Use a fixed per-user settings folder. ? What does a settings handler let you do? + Store your tool's own settings as sections of the same ini file - Change ImGui's colours - Save draw data Your data then loads and saves together with the layout. ? How do you implement named layouts? + Keep strings from SaveIniSettingsToMemory and apply one with LoadIniSettingsFromMemory - Copy imgui.ini by hand - Call the DockBuilder every frame A layout is the ini text.

title: Read and write imgui.ini
body: Write a reader and writer for the ini format ImGui uses, that keeps sections it does not understand untouched: cpp struct Section { std::string type; // "Window" std::string name; // "Stones" std::vector<std::string lines; // the lines inside, as written (without the newline) }; std::vector<Section readIni(const std::string& text); std::string writeIni(const std::vector<Section & sections); std::string getValue(const Section& s, const std::string& key); // "" if missing void setValue(Section& s, const std::string& key, const std::string& value); - readIni : a section starts with a line Type Name . The type and name are between the brackets; the name may itself contain (for example Table 0x8A4C2B11,4 ), so the name ends at the last of the line. Every following line, up to the next header, belongs to the section, except empty lines, which are dropped. Lines before the first header are ignored. Lines may end with \r\n . - writeIni : each section as Type Name , then its lines, then one empty line, all separated by \n . - getValue(s, "Size") : the text after = on the first line that starts with Size= . - setValue : replace the first Key= line's value, or append Key=value if there is none.

title: A command palette
where: Menus, Popups, Docking and Style projects
body: Code editors open a command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P: type a few letters of any command and it appears at the top. Write the search behind one, for the command table from lesson 4.01's practice. cpp class Palette { public: void add(const std::string& name); // "File/Save Level" void ran(const std::string& name); // the user ran this command (it becomes the most recent) int score(const std::string& query, const std::string& name) const; // -1 when it does not match std::vector<std::string search(const std::string& query, std::size_t limit) const; }; Matching and scoring ( score ), ignoring upper and lower case: - Every character of the query must appear in the name in order (not necessarily next to each other): "svl" matches "File/Save Level" . Spaces in the query are ignored. - Match each query character at the earliest position after the previous match (left to right, no backtracking). If some character cannot be found, the score is -1 . - Each matched character scores 1 , plus 5 if it comes right after the previous matched character, plus 8 if it is at the start of a word : the first character of the name, a character after a space, / , _ or - , or an upper-case letter right after a lower-case one (in the original spelling: "saveLevel" , the L ). - An empty query (or only spaces) scores 0 for every name. Searching ( search ): the names with a score of 0 or more, best first; ties go to the more recently run command (commands never run come after those that were); then alphabetical. Return at most limit names. add "File/Save Level", "File/Save As", "View/Show Stats", "Edit/Select All" score("sl", "File/Save Level") = (1 + 8) + (1 + 8) = 18 (S and L both start words) score("sl", "Edit/Select All") = (1 + 8) + 1 = 10 (the l of Select follows an unmatched e: no bonus)

title: 5.01  Plots and Live Graphs
body: A number that changes every frame is hard to read; a graph of its last few seconds is easy. This lesson covers ImGui's built-in PlotLines and PlotHistogram , the ring buffer that feeds them, scaling and statistics, drawing your own graph with the draw list, and when to reach for the ImPlot library. Built-in plots cpp-norun static float frameTimes 120 = {}; static int offset = 0; frameTimes offset = ImGui::GetIO().DeltaTime 1000.0f; // this frame, in ms offset = (offset + 1) % IM_ARRAYSIZE(frameTimes); ImGui::PlotLines("Frame ms", frameTimes, IM_ARRAYSIZE(frameTimes), offset, nullptr, 0.0f, 33.3f, ImVec2(0, 80)); ImGui::PlotHistogram("Enemies per room", roomCounts, roomCount, 0, nullptr, 0.0f, FLT_MAX, ImVec2(0, 60)); Arguments: label, values, count, values_offset , overlay text, scale min, scale max, size. Pass FLT_MAX for the scale and ImGui fits it to the data each frame. The values_offset is the key to live graphs: the array is a ring buffer where the newest value overwrites the oldest, and the offset tells PlotLines where the oldest value now is, so the graph scrolls from left to right without shifting the whole array every frame. A ring buffer class Wrap that pattern so every graph in your tools can use it: cpp-norun template <std::size_t N class History { public: void push(float v) { m_data m_next = v; m_next = (m_next + 1) % N; if (m_count < N) ++m_count; } int offset() const { return m_count < N ? 0 : static_cast<int (m_next); } // where the oldest sample is int count() const { return static_cast<int (m_count); } const float data() const { return m_data.data(); } // plus min(), max(), average() for the overlay text private: std::array<float, N m_data{}; std::size_t m_next{ 0 }, m_count{ 0 }; }; Before the buffer is full, the samples are in 0 .. count-1 and the offset is 0. After it fills, the oldest sample is wherever the next write will go. The practice writes this class with its statistics, which go well in the overlay: "avg 16.7 ms max 21.3" . Smoothing Raw values jitter. Two cheap smoothers: - Moving average over the last N samples (the ring buffer has them). - Exponential smoothing : smoothed += (value - smoothed) k with k around 0.1, which reacts quickly but filters noise, and needs no buffer. Show the raw graph and the smoothed number together. Your own graph with the draw list For anything the built-ins do not do (several lines in one graph, thresholds, labels), draw it yourself: cpp-norun ImDrawList dl = ImGui::GetWindowDrawList(); const ImVec2 p0 = ImGui::GetCursorScreenPos(); const ImVec2 size(ImGui::GetContentRegionAvail().x, 100); dl- AddRectFilled(p0, ImVec2(p0.x + size.x, p0.y + size.y), IM_COL32(20, 22, 28, 255)); // the 16.6 ms (60 fps) budget line const float budgetY = p0.y + size.y (1.0f - 16.6f / 33.3f); dl- AddLine(ImVec2(p0.x, budgetY), ImVec2(p0.x + size.x, budgetY), IM_COL32(240, 180, 70, 160)); // the data as a polyline: map sample i to x and value to y std::vector<ImVec2 pts; for (int i = 0; i < history.count(); ++i) { / x = p0.x + i size.x / (N - 1); y = p0.y + size.y (1 - value / maxValue) / } dl- AddPolyline(pts.data(), (int)pts.size(), IM_COL32(120, 200, 255, 255), ImDrawFlags_None, 1.5f); ImGui::Dummy(size); // reserve the space in the layout Mapping a value to a pixel row is the same linear mapping as a slider (lesson 2.01), upside down: larger values are higher on screen, which means smaller y . ImPlot For serious charts (axes with ticks, zoom and pan, legends, many series, scatter plots, heat maps), use ImPlot ( epezent/implot ), a companion library built on ImGui: cpp-norun if (ImPlot::BeginPlot("Frame time")) { ImPlot::SetupAxes("frame", "ms"); ImPlot::PlotLine("cpu", cpuMs, count, 1.0, 0.0, 0, offset); ImPlot::PlotLine("gpu", gpuMs, count, 1.0, 0.0, 0, offset); ImPlot::EndPlot(); } It needs its own context ( ImPlot::CreateContext() after ImGui's). Common mistakes !warning Shifting the whole array every frame Use a ring buffer and pass the offset; nothing needs to move. !warning Auto-scaling a graph that should be compared over time FLT_MAX rescales every frame, so a spike shrinks everything else. Fix the scale for budgets like frame time. Knowledge check quiz ? What is the values_offset argument of PlotLines for? + It says where the oldest sample of a ring buffer is, so the graph scrolls without moving data - It moves the graph on screen - It skips the first values Pass the ring buffer's write position once it is full. ? A ring buffer of 120 samples is full and its next write position is 37. Where is the oldest sample? + At index 37 - At index 0 - At index 36 The next write will overwrite the oldest sample. ? When should you use ImPlot instead of PlotLines? + When you need axes, zooming, legends or several series - Never; it is slower - Only for histograms PlotLines is a quick single-series sparkline.

title: A history for live graphs
body: Write the ring buffer that feeds PlotLines , with the statistics for its overlay: cpp class History { public: explicit History(int capacity); void push(float value); int count() const; // samples stored, up to capacity int offset() const; // index of the oldest sample (0 until the buffer is full) float at(int i) const; // the i-th oldest sample, 0 = oldest float average() const; // 0 when empty float maximum() const; // 0 when empty std::string overlay() const; // "avg 16.7 max 21.3", one decimal each }; float smooth(float previous, float value, float k); // exponential smoothing: previous + (value - previous) k at(i) must give samples in order from oldest to newest, whether or not the buffer has wrapped round.

title: 5.02  A Log Window with Filters
body: Every engine prints far more log lines than anyone can read. A good log window lets you filter by severity and by text, follows new lines without fighting the user, colours errors, and copes with a million lines. This lesson builds one with ImGuiTextFilter , a level filter and the list clipper. The data Keep log entries as data, not one big string, so they can be filtered: cpp-norun enum class Level { Trace, Info, Warning, Error }; struct LogEntry { double time; Level level; std::string category; std::string text; }; class Log { public: void add(Level level, std::string category, std::string text); const std::vector<LogEntry & entries() const; void clear(); private: std::vector<LogEntry m_entries; // or a ring buffer with a maximum size std::mutex m_mutex; // other threads log too }; Log calls come from many threads (loading, audio, networking). Protect the container with a mutex, or have each thread push into a lock-free queue that the UI thread drains once per frame. ImGuiTextFilter ImGui ships a small text filter with a useful syntax: cpp-norun static ImGuiTextFilter filter; filter.Draw("Filter (\"inc,-exc\")", 240.0f); for (const LogEntry& e : log.entries()) if (filter.PassFilter(e.text.c_str())) ImGui::TextUnformatted(e.text.c_str()); The filter text is a comma-separated list of words: - texture shows lines containing "texture"; - texture,shader shows lines containing either ; - -vsync hides lines containing "vsync"; - -missing,texture shows texture lines except those containing "missing". The terms are checked in order , and the first one that matches the line decides: an exclusion that matches hides the line, an inclusion that matches shows it. So order matters: with texture,-missing , a line "texture missing" matches texture first and is shown. Put exclusions first. Spaces around terms are ignored and matching ignores case. If no term matches, the line passes only if the filter has no inclusions at all. The practice reimplements these exact rules. Severity and category Add check boxes for levels and a combo for categories, and combine them with the text filter: cpp-norun static bool showLevel 4 = { false, true, true, true }; // hide Trace by default ImGui::Checkbox("Info", &showLevel 1 ); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::Checkbox("Warnings", &showLevel 2 ); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::Checkbox("Errors", &showLevel 3 ); Each line then passes if its level is shown, its category matches, and the text filter passes. Drawing a million lines Filtering every line every frame is fine for thousands, not for millions. Keep a list of the indexes of matching entries, rebuild it only when the filter changes, and append to it as new entries arrive (checking only the new ones). Then draw it with the clipper (lesson 3.02): cpp-norun ImGuiListClipper clipper; clipper.Begin((int)visible.size()); while (clipper.Step()) for (int row = clipper.DisplayStart; row < clipper.DisplayEnd; ++row) { const LogEntry& e = entries visible row ; ImGui::PushStyleColor(ImGuiCol_Text, colourFor(e.level)); ImGui::TextUnformatted(e.text.c_str()); ImGui::PopStyleColor(); } Follow new lines only when the user was at the bottom (lesson 3.02), and offer "Copy" ( ImGui::SetClipboardText ) and "Clear" buttons. Common mistakes !warning Logging from other threads into a vector without a lock Two threads pushing at once corrupt it. Lock, or queue and drain on the UI thread. !warning Filtering the whole log every frame Rebuild the visible index list only when the filter changes; append for new lines. Knowledge check quiz ? Which lines does the filter "-missing,texture" show? + Lines containing "texture" but not "missing" - Lines containing "texture" or "missing" - Only lines containing both Terms are checked in order: the exclusion comes first, then the inclusion. ? With the filter "texture,-missing", is the line "texture missing" shown? + Yes: "texture" matches first and decides - No: the exclusion always wins - Only if the filter is empty The first matching term decides, so put exclusions first. ? A filter contains only "-vsync". What passes? + Every line that does not contain "vsync" - Nothing - Only lines containing "vsync" With no inclusions, everything not excluded passes. ? How does a log window stay fast with a million entries? + Keep an index list of matching entries, update it incrementally, and draw it with the clipper - Draw every line each frame - Limit the log to 100 lines The cost then depends on the window height and the new lines.

title: ImGuiTextFilter's rules
body: Reimplement ImGui's text filter exactly: cpp class TextFilter { public: explicit TextFilter(const std::string& text); bool pass(const std::string& line) const; }; - The filter text is split at commas into terms ; spaces at the start and end of each term are removed; empty terms are ignored. - A term starting with - is an exclusion (the rest of it is the text to look for); any other term is an inclusion . A lone - is ignored. - pass(line) : if there are no terms, every line passes. Otherwise check the terms in order , looking for each one's text inside the line without regard to case : the first term found decides: an exclusion returns false , an inclusion returns true . - If no term is found in the line: the line passes only if there are no inclusions at all. "-missing,texture" "texture loaded" - true; "texture missing" - false; "shader" - false "texture,-missing" "texture missing" - true (texture is found first) "-vsync" "frame done" - true; "vsync on" - false

title: Keep the visible lines up to date
match: Keep the visible lines up to date
body: Filtering a huge log every frame is too slow. Keep a list of the indexes of lines that pass, update it only for new lines, and rebuild it only when the filter changes: cpp class FilteredLog { public: void add(const std::string& line); void setFilter(const std::string& filter); // rebuilds the visible list const std::vector<int & visible() const; // indexes of passing lines, in order int checks() const; // how many times a line was tested against the filter }; Use lesson 5.02's filter rules (write them again, or reuse your TextFilter ). checks counts every test of one line against the filter, so the tests can see that adding a line costs one check and that changing the filter costs one check per line, not more.

title: 5.03  A Property Inspector
body: An inspector shows and edits the properties of whatever is selected. Writing one widget call per field for every type gets tedious; describing each type's fields once, as data, lets one function draw an inspector for anything. This lesson builds that property table , handles editing several selected objects at once, and shows "mixed" values. By hand first cpp-norun void inspect(Light& l) { ImGui::DragFloat3("Position", &l.pos.x, 0.1f); ImGui::ColorEdit3("Colour", &l.color.x); ImGui::SliderFloat("Intensity", &l.intensity, 0.0f, 100.0f, "%.1f", ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic); ImGui::Checkbox("Casts shadows", &l.shadows); } Perfectly fine for three types. With forty component types, and the same fields needing undo, saving and copy-paste, a description of the fields pays off. Describing fields as data cpp-norun enum class Kind { Float, Int, Bool, Color3, Vec3, String }; struct Field { const char name; Kind kind; std::size_t offset; // where the field is inside the object (offsetof) float min = 0, max = 0; // for sliders; 0, 0 means "a drag with no limits" }; static const Field lightFields = { { "Position", Kind::Vec3, offsetof(Light, pos) }, { "Colour", Kind::Color3, offsetof(Light, color) }, { "Intensity", Kind::Float, offsetof(Light, intensity), 0.0f, 100.0f }, { "Casts shadows", Kind::Bool, offsetof(Light, shadows) }, }; One function then draws any object described this way: cpp-norun bool inspect(void object, std::span<const Field fields) { bool changed = false; for (const Field& f : fields) { void p = static_cast<char (object) + f.offset; switch (f.kind) { case Kind::Float: changed = f.max f.min ? ImGui::SliderFloat(f.name, (float )p, f.min, f.max) : ImGui::DragFloat(f.name, (float )p, 0.1f); break; case Kind::Int: changed = ImGui::DragInt(f.name, (int )p); break; case Kind::Bool: changed = ImGui::Checkbox(f.name, (bool )p); break; case Kind::Color3: changed = ImGui::ColorEdit3(f.name, (float )p); break; case Kind::Vec3: changed = ImGui::DragFloat3(f.name, (float )p, 0.1f); break; case Kind::String: changed = ImGui::InputText(f.name, (std::string )p); break; } } return changed; } The same table drives saving (write each field by name), loading, copy and paste, and undo (record which field changed and its old value). That is a small reflection system; big engines generate these tables from their source code. offsetof is only guaranteed for standard-layout types (plain structs without virtual functions or mixed access); keep component data like that. Editing several objects at once When the user selects five lights and changes the intensity, all five should change. Show each field once: - if all selected objects have the same value, show it normally; - if they differ , show it as mixed (ImGui's ImGuiItemFlags_MixedValue draws a dash in a checkbox, and you can display "--" in a number field); - when the user edits it, write the new value to every selected object. For drags, the most useful behaviour is often relative: dragging position by +2 moves every object by +2, keeping their arrangement. The practice computes the shown values for a multi-selection. Common mistakes !warning Editing only the first selected object Users expect the change to apply to everything selected. !warning Using offsetof on a class with virtual functions It is not guaranteed to work. Keep inspectable data in plain structs. Knowledge check quiz ? Why describe a type's fields in a table? + One table drives the inspector, saving, loading, copy and paste and undo for every type - Tables draw faster - ImGui requires it It is a small reflection system. ? Three selected lights have intensities 5, 5 and 8. What should the intensity field show? + A mixed value, such as "--" - 5 - 6 Values that differ are shown as mixed until edited. ? What does offsetof(Light, intensity) give? + The byte position of intensity inside a Light - The size of intensity - The value of intensity Add it to the object's address to reach the field.

title: Mixed values in an inspector
body: With several objects selected, each field shows one value or "mixed". Write cpp struct Object { int id; std::map<std::string, double fields; }; std::string shownValue(const std::vector<Object & selected, const std::string& field); void setAll(std::vector<Object & selected, const std::string& field, double value); void addAll(std::vector<Object & selected, const std::string& field, double delta); - shownValue : "--" if the values differ between the selected objects; otherwise the common value written with std::to_string and trailing zeros after the decimal point removed (and the point too if nothing is left after it): 5 , 2.5 , -0.125 . An object without the field does not count; if no selected object has it (or nothing is selected), return "" . - setAll writes the value into every selected object that has the field. - addAll adds delta to the field of every selected object that has it (a relative drag: their differences stay the same).

title: 5.04  Undo and Redo for Tools
body: No one trusts an editor without undo. This lesson builds the classic command pattern undo stack, explains why redo history is cleared by a new edit, shows how to merge the sixty small changes of one drag into one step using ImGui's item queries, and how to mark a document as saved. Commands Every change to the document is an object that knows how to do and undo itself: cpp-norun struct Change { virtual ~Change() = default; virtual void apply(Level& level) = 0; virtual void revert(Level& level) = 0; virtual std::string label() const = 0; // shown in Edit Undo "Move rock" }; struct SetIntensity final : Change { int lightId; float before, after; void apply(Level& l) override { l.light(lightId).intensity = after; } void revert(Level& l) override { l.light(lightId).intensity = before; } std::string label() const override { return "Change intensity"; } }; Two stacks undo stack: create rock move rock change colour <- top: the most recent change redo stack: - Do a change: apply it, push it on the undo stack, and clear the redo stack . - Undo : pop from the undo stack, revert it, push it on the redo stack. - Redo : pop from the redo stack, apply it, push it back on the undo stack. Why clear redo on a new change? After undoing "change colour", the redo stack holds it. If the user now moves a tree, the colour change belonged to a history that no longer exists: redoing it on top of the new state could make no sense. Every editor you know behaves this way. One drag, one undo step A slider drag changes the value every frame. Recording each frame would make one drag sixty undo steps. Use ImGui's item queries (lesson 2.01): cpp-norun static float before; if (ImGui::IsItemActivated()) before = light.intensity; // the drag started: remember the old value ImGui::SliderFloat("Intensity", &light.intensity, 0, 100); // edits live, for immediate feedback if (ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit()) // the drag ended with a change undo.record(std::make_unique<SetIntensity (light.id, before, light.intensity)); // record, do not re-apply Note record , not apply : the value is already set. Another approach is merging : when a new change has the same target as the top of the stack and arrives within a short time, combine them into one (keeping the oldest before and the newest after ). Text editors use merging for typing. Saved and dirty The document is dirty (has unsaved changes) when the undo stack differs from what it was at the last save. Remember a saved marker : the size of the undo stack at save time (or a pointer to the top change). - After saving, the marker equals the current position: not dirty. - Undoing back to the saved point makes it clean again, which a simple dirty = true flag cannot do. - If a new change clears redo history that included the saved point, the saved state can never be reached again: always dirty until saved. The practice builds the whole stack with labels, the saved marker and a limit on how many steps are kept. Groups "Delete 40 selected objects" is 40 changes but one action for the user. Put several changes into a group that applies them in order and reverts them in reverse order, and push the group as one step. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to clear redo after a new change Redo then applies a change from an abandoned history. !warning A change that stores pointers to objects Deleting and undoing recreates the object at a new address. Store ids. !warning Reverting a group in the same order it was applied Later changes may depend on earlier ones. Revert in reverse. Knowledge check quiz ? The user undoes twice, then makes a new change. What happens to the redo stack? + It is cleared - It keeps both changes - The new change goes onto it Those changes belong to a history that no longer exists. ? How do you record one undo step for a whole slider drag? + Remember the value in IsItemActivated and record the change in IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit - Record a change every frame - Record nothing; drags cannot be undone One step from the value before to the value after. ? Why does a saved marker work better than a dirty flag? + Undoing back to the saved state makes the document clean again - It uses less memory - It saves automatically Compare the current position with the position at the last save.

title: An undo stack
body: Write the undo stack a tool uses, with labels, a saved marker, groups and a size limit: cpp struct Change { std::string label; std::function<void() apply; std::function<void() revert; }; class UndoStack { public: explicit UndoStack(int limit); // keep at most this many undo steps void push(Change c); // the change has ALREADY been applied: just record it void pushGroup(const std::string& label, std::vector<Change changes); // already applied, one step bool undo(); // false if nothing to undo bool redo(); // false if nothing to redo std::string undoLabel() const; // "Undo <label ", or "" if nothing to undo std::string redoLabel() const; // "Redo <label ", or "" void markSaved(); bool dirty() const; }; - push and pushGroup clear the redo history. - A group undoes by reverting its changes in reverse order, and redoes by applying them in order. - When the undo history would exceed limit , the oldest step is dropped. - dirty() is false right after markSaved() , and becomes false again if the user undoes or redoes back to exactly that point. If the saved point is lost for good (it was in redo history that a new change cleared, or it was dropped by the limit), the document stays dirty until the next save. A new stack is not dirty.

title: An undoable inspector
body: Combine lessons 5.03 and 5.04 into the model behind a real inspector: several objects selected, fields shown as one value or mixed, drags that edit live but create one undo step, undo and redo, and a dirty flag for the title bar. cpp class Inspector { public: void addObject(int id, std::map<std::string, double fields); void select(std::vector<int ids); // ids that do not exist are ignored std::string shown(const std::string& field) const; // lesson 5.03's rules over the selection void beginEdit(const std::string& field); // like IsItemActivated: a drag starts void editValue(const std::string& field, double value); // every frame of the drag: write live void endEdit(); // like IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit bool undo(); bool redo(); std::string undoLabel() const; // "Undo Change range" or "" (see below) double value(int id, const std::string& field) const; // NaN if the object or field does not exist void markSaved(); bool dirty() const; }; Editing. - beginEdit(field) remembers the current value of field for every selected object that has it. - editValue(field, v) writes v to that field on every selected object that has it, immediately, so the view updates during the drag. - endEdit() records one undo step that takes every affected object from its remembered value to its current value. If nothing changed (every value is what it was), it records nothing. - editValue called without a beginEdit for that field (a checkbox click, a value typed in) applies and records its own one-step change at once. - The step's label is Change <field for one object, or Change <field (<n objects) for several. - The selection at the time of the edit is part of the step: undoing after the selection changed still restores the right objects. Undo, redo and dirty follow lesson 5.04's practice (a new step clears redo; dirty compares the current position with the saved one; there is no limit here).

title: 6.01  Project: A Level Editor
body: Build a tile-based level editor with Dear ImGui - a docked layout with a viewport, a tile palette, an inspector and a log; painting, erasing, rectangle and flood-fill tools; panning and zooming; undo and redo; and saving to a text file. This lesson is the plan, the key pieces of code, and the order to build them in. What you build Xenon Level Editor ┌ File Edit View Tools ───────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ┌ Palette ┐ ┌ Viewport ─────────────────────────┐ ┌ Inspector ┐ │ │ │ grass │ │ the tile map, drawn with the │ │ tile 12,7 │ │ │ │ stone │ │ draw list; pan with the middle │ │ kind:stone│ │ │ │ water │ │ button, zoom with the wheel │ │ ... │ │ │ │ ... │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └─────────┘ └───────────────────────────────────┘ └───────────┘ │ │ ┌ Log ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Everything in it comes from earlier lessons; this project is about putting them together well. The pieces and where they come from Piece Lessons --- --- Win32 + DX11 host, docking, default layout 1.02, 4.04 Main menu with File, Edit, View and a command table 4.01 Palette as a list of selectables with colour swatches 2.03, 2.04 Viewport drawn with the draw list 1.03, 5.01 Tools: paint, erase, rectangle, flood fill this lesson's practice Undo and redo, one step per stroke 5.04 Inspector for the tile under the mouse 5.03 Unsaved-changes guard on New, Open, Quit 4.02 Log window 5.02 Settings and layout saved in the ini 4.06 The viewport: from screen to tiles and back The viewport needs a camera : a pan offset (where the map's origin is on screen) and a zoom (pixels per tile). cpp-norun struct Camera { ImVec2 pan{ 0, 0 }; float zoom{ 32.0f }; }; // zoom = pixels per tile ImVec2 tileToScreen(const Camera& c, ImVec2 origin, float tx, float ty) { return ImVec2(origin.x + c.pan.x + tx c.zoom, origin.y + c.pan.y + ty c.zoom); } // and the reverse, screenToTile, for the mouse Zooming around the mouse feels right only if the tile under the mouse stays under the mouse: remember which tile it is before changing the zoom, then adjust the pan so it is back under the cursor. The practice writes these functions; they are the same maths any 2D editor or map view uses. Drawing only what is visible matters for big maps: compute the visible range of tiles from the viewport rectangle (lesson 3.02's clipper idea in 2D) and loop over just those. cpp-norun ImGui::Begin("Viewport"); const ImVec2 origin = ImGui::GetCursorScreenPos(); const ImVec2 size = ImGui::GetContentRegionAvail(); ImGui::InvisibleButton("canvas", size, ImGuiButtonFlags_MouseButtonLeft ImGuiButtonFlags_MouseButtonMiddle); const bool hovered = ImGui::IsItemHovered(); ImDrawList dl = ImGui::GetWindowDrawList(); dl- PushClipRect(origin, ImVec2(origin.x + size.x, origin.y + size.y), true); // draw visible tiles, the grid, the hovered tile's outline, the rectangle tool's preview dl- PopClipRect(); if (hovered && ImGui::IsMouseDragging(ImGuiMouseButton_Middle)) camera.pan += ImGui::GetIO().MouseDelta; if (hovered && ImGui::GetIO().MouseWheel != 0) zoomAround(camera, ImGui::GetMousePos(), ImGui::GetIO().MouseWheel); ImGui::End(); InvisibleButton covering the canvas gives you hover, active and clicks for the whole area, and stops the window from being dragged when you paint. Tools and undo Each tool turns mouse input into changes to tiles : - Paint and Erase : while the left button is held, set the tile under the mouse. Collect every tile changed during the stroke, with its old value, and record one undo step when the button is released (lesson 5.04's "one drag, one step"). - Rectangle : show a preview while dragging; on release, fill the rectangle as one step. - Flood fill : replace the connected region of the clicked tile's kind with the new kind, as one step. Use an explicit stack or queue, not recursion: a large region would overflow the call stack. The file format A readable text format makes levels easy to diff in version control: xenon-level 1 size 40 24 palette . grass, stone, ~ water tiles ........................................ ... .........~~~~~................... One character per tile, rows top to bottom, with a version number on the first line (lesson 3.05) so a future editor can read old files. The project at the end of this milestone has you write the editor's core: map, tools, undo and file format. Order to build in 1. Host, docking, menu, empty windows: it runs. 2. Map data, the viewport drawing it, pan and zoom. 3. Paint and erase with the palette, then undo for them. 4. Save and load, the dirty flag in the title, the unsaved-changes guard. 5. Rectangle and flood fill. 6. Inspector, log, settings.

title: The editor's camera
body: Write the camera maths for a 2D editor viewport: cpp struct Vec2 { float x, y; }; struct Camera { Vec2 pan{ 0, 0 }; float zoom{ 32 }; }; // zoom: pixels per tile Vec2 tileToScreen(const Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 tile); Vec2 screenToTile(const Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 screen); void zoomAround(Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 mouse, float factor, float minZoom, float maxZoom); void visibleTiles(const Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 size, int mapW, int mapH, int& x0, int& y0, int& x1, int& y1); - tileToScreen : origin + pan + tile zoom (for each of x and y). - screenToTile : the reverse: (screen - origin - pan) / zoom . - zoomAround : multiply the zoom by factor , clamped to minZoom..maxZoom , and change pan so that the point under mouse (in tile coordinates, before the zoom) is still under mouse afterwards. - visibleTiles : the range of whole tiles that touch the viewport rectangle ( origin to origin + size ): x0 = floor of the left edge in tiles, x1 = ceil of the right edge (exclusive end), likewise for y, each clamped to 0..mapW or 0..mapH .

title: 6.02  Project: An In-Game Profiler
body: Build a profiler that runs inside your game - scoped timers you sprinkle through the code, a per-frame tree of where the time went with total and self times, a frame-time graph with the budget line, and a flame view drawn with the draw list. This lesson covers measuring, collecting, aggregating and showing the data. Measuring with scopes A zone is a named span of time. Mark zones with a small RAII object that records a begin event when constructed and an end event when destroyed: cpp-norun class Zone { public: explicit Zone(const char name) : m_name{ name } { Profiler::get().begin(m_name, now()); } ~Zone() { Profiler::get().end(m_name, now()); } private: const char m_name; }; // Two steps, so __LINE__ is replaced by the number before the names are joined. define PROFILE_JOIN2(a, b) a b define PROFILE_JOIN(a, b) PROFILE_JOIN2(a, b) define PROFILE_ZONE(name) Zone PROFILE_JOIN(profileZone, __LINE__){ name } void updateEnemies() { PROFILE_ZONE("updateEnemies"); for (auto& e : enemies) { PROFILE_ZONE("think"); e.think(); } } now() should be a high-resolution clock: QueryPerformanceCounter on Windows, or std::chrono::steady_clock . The string is a literal, so storing the pointer is fine and cheap. Zones nest naturally: "think" begins and ends inside "updateEnemies". Recording only begin and end events, in order, captures the whole tree. From events to a tree At the end of a frame, the events of that frame form a list like: begin frame 0 begin update 10 begin physics 12 end physics 40 begin think 41 end think 52 begin think 52 end think 60 end update 61 begin render 61 end render 150 end frame 152 Walk them with a stack : a begin pushes a new node as a child of the top of the stack; an end pops it and stores its duration. Each node's total time is its own duration; its self time is the total minus its children's totals: the time spent in that zone's own code. Zones with the same name under the same parent (the two "think" zones) are usually merged into one row with a call count. The practice builds exactly this. frame 152.0 ms self 12.0 update 51.0 self 4.0 physics 28.0 think 19.0 (2 calls) render 89.0 Showing it - A table tree (lessons 3.03 and 3.04): name, total, self, calls, with tree nodes in the first column and sorting by total or self. - A frame graph (lesson 5.01): the last few hundred frame times with the 16.6 ms line; clicking a bar pauses on that frame to inspect its tree. - A flame view : each zone as a bar whose x position and width are its start and duration in the frame, and whose row is its nesting depth. Draw it with AddRectFilled and AddText , coloured by name (the golden-ratio hue trick from lesson 2.04 keeps colours stable per name). Hover a bar for a tooltip with the exact numbers. Threads Zones on other threads (loading, audio, job workers) need their own event lists: give each thread its own buffer ( thread_local ) and merge them at the end of the frame, showing one lane per thread in the flame view. Keep the profiler cheap - Two clock reads and two small writes per zone: keep zones out of loops that run millions of times, or profile a sample of them. - No memory allocation per event: pre-allocate the event buffer. - Compile zones out of shipping builds: define PROFILE_ZONE(name) to nothing (lesson 6.03). Professional tools such as Tracy and Optick follow this design and add network streaming, GPU timing and much more; after this project you will know how to read them.

title: Where did the frame go?
body: Turn one frame's profiler events into the rows of a profiler table: cpp struct Event { bool begin; std::string name; double time; }; // time in milliseconds std::vector<std::string profileRows(const std::vector<Event & events); - Walk the events with a stack. A begin starts a zone inside the zone on top of the stack; an end finishes the zone on top (its name will match). - Zones with the same name under the same parent are merged into one row: their totals add up and their call count increases. Merging also merges their children, by name. - A row's total is the sum of its zones' durations; its self time is its total minus the totals of its children. - Rows are listed depth first: a zone, then its children in the order they first appeared, then its next sibling. Each row is two spaces of indentation per level of depth, then: <name total <t self <s with one decimal place each, followed by (<n calls) when merged from more than one zone. frame 0..152: update 10..61 (physics 12..40, think 41..52, think 52..60), render 61..150 frame total 152.0 self 12.0 update total 51.0 self 4.0 physics total 28.0 self 28.0 think total 19.0 self 19.0 (2 calls) render total 89.0 self 89.0 An end event with an empty stack, or events left open at the end, make the result the single line unbalanced events .

title: 6.03  ImGui in a Game You Ship
match: 6.03 ImGui in a Game You Ship
body: Dear ImGui is a development tool first. Before a game ships, decide what happens to the debug interface - compile it out, hide it behind a key, or keep a few tools for players - and check what it costs. This lesson covers build switches, performance, security and licensing.
