Three choices Choice When How --- --- --- Compile it out Most shipped games A build switch removes every debug window and the ImGui calls Hidden behind a key or a flag Games tested by others, early access Present but not drawn until a debug key or a command-line flag Keep some tools for players Modding tools, level editors shipped with the game Treated as real product UI: styled, tested, translated A build switch Give your project a configuration flag, say XENON_DEV_TOOLS , defined in Debug and in an internal "Development" configuration, and not in Shipping: cpp-norun if XENON_DEV_TOOLS drawDebugWindows(); ImGui::ShowMetricsWindow(&showMetrics); endif Keep tool code in its own files ( debug_ui/ .cpp ) so the shipping build can leave whole files out. If the game uses ImGui for nothing else, the shipping build need not link ImGui at all, which also removes the font atlas and its texture memory. What it costs Measure before guessing: - CPU : building the UI runs your code every frame. Debug windows that loop over every entity are the usual culprits; use the clipper and only build windows that are open (lesson 1.04's Begin return value). - GPU : usually tiny, a few draw calls. Watch for thousands of custom draw-list primitives. - Memory : the font atlas (a few megabytes with large fonts and icon fonts), plus vertex buffers. - Input : if a debug window has keyboard focus, the game must not react to keys (lesson 2.05). In a shipping build with hidden tools, make sure nothing can grab focus while hidden. The Metrics window (lesson 1.06) shows vertex counts per window. Security and cheating Debug tools that edit memory, spawn items or teleport are cheats in a multiplayer game. In anything online: - compile them out of client builds, rather than hiding them; - never trust the client: the server decides what is allowed, whatever the client's interface can do. Licensing Dear ImGui is under the MIT licence : free to use in commercial games, provided the licence text is included with the software (usually in an "open source licences" screen or file). The same goes for ImPlot and most companion libraries; check each one's licence. Fonts have their own licences (Font Awesome Free and most Google Fonts allow embedding with attribution). Checklist - Shipping configuration builds without XENON_DEV_TOOLS and runs. - No debug window can be opened in a shipping build by any key combination. - Debug-only assets (tool fonts, icon fonts) are not in the shipping package. - Licence texts for every library and font are included. - For a game with shipped tools: those windows are styled, scale with the display, work with a controller if the game does, and are translated. Knowledge check quiz ? What should happen to cheat-like debug tools in an online game's client? + They should be compiled out, and the server must not trust the client anyway - Hidden behind a secret key - Left in; players will not find them Hiding is not enough; and the server decides what is allowed. ? What does the MIT licence require when you ship Dear ImGui? + Including the licence text with the software - Paying a fee - Publishing your game's source code It is a permissive licence. ? Why put debug UI code in its own files? + So the shipping build can leave whole files out - Because ImGui requires it - To make them load faster A build switch is cleaner at the file level.

title: The level editor's core
body: Write the core of lesson 6.01's level editor: the map, the four tools, undo and redo, and the file format. The ImGui part on top of it (palette, viewport, menus) is then a thin layer that calls these functions. cpp class Level { public: Level(int width, int height, char fill); int width() const; int height() const; char at(int x, int y) const; // ' ' outside the map void strokeBegin(); // mouse pressed with the paint or erase tool void strokePaint(int x, int y, char tile); // every frame while held: set one tile (outside the map: ignored) void strokeEnd(); // mouse released: one undo step for the whole stroke void rectangle(int x0, int y0, int x1, int y1, char tile); // corners in any order, both included, one step void floodFill(int x, int y, char tile); // the connected region (4 directions) of that tile's kind, one step bool undo(); bool redo(); bool dirty() const; void markSaved(); std::string save() const; static bool load(const std::string& text, Level& out); }; Steps. Each stroke, rectangle or fill is one undo step holding, for every tile it changed, the old and the new character. A step that changes nothing is not recorded. A new step clears redo; dirty works like lesson 5.04's practice (a new level is not dirty). Rectangles and fills clip to the map. A flood fill on a tile that already has the new kind does nothing. Use an explicit stack or queue for the fill, not recursion. The file format ( save ): lines separated by \n : xenon-level 1 size <width <height tiles <height lines of exactly width characters load accepts exactly this (lines may end with \r\n ), with version 1 only, a width and height from 1 to 1000, and the right number of rows of the right length; otherwise it returns false and leaves out unchanged. A loaded level has empty undo history and is not dirty.

title: Cheat Sheet - Dear ImGui
body: The frame cpp-norun ImGui_ImplDX11_NewFrame(); ImGui_ImplWin32_NewFrame(); ImGui::NewFrame(); // ... your UI ... ImGui::Render(); ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData()); Before your game uses input: if (!ImGui::GetIO().WantCaptureMouse) { ... } , likewise WantCaptureKeyboard . Windows Code Does --- --- if (ImGui::Begin("Name", &open, flags)) { ... } ImGui::End(); A window; End always runs ImGui::SetNextWindowSize(ImVec2(400, 300), ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); Size on first use only ImGui::BeginChild("id", ImVec2(0, 200), ImGuiChildFlags_Borders); ... title: Common Errors
body: Message or symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- Assertion "Missing End()" or "Mismatched Begin/End calls" End was skipped when Begin returned false, or an early return left a scope open Always call End after Begin ; pair every Push and Pop 1.04 Assertion about the ID stack ("PushID/PopID mismatch") A PushID without a PopID on some path Pop on every path; keep pushes and pops in one function 1.05 Clicking one button triggers another, or only the first of several works Several widgets with the same label in the same scope share an ID suffix or PushID(i) around each row 1.05 A text box loses its contents or focus every frame Its label changes each frame, so its ID changes Put the changing part before 1.05 Nothing appears, but there is no error Render or the backend draw call is missing, or the window is off screen Check the frame order; delete imgui.ini 1.03 An assertion about WithinFrameScope A widget called outside NewFrame ... Render Submit UI only during a frame 1.03 The game moves when you drag a slider or type in a box Game input ignores WantCaptureMouse and WantCaptureKeyboard Check them before handling input 2.05 TreePop assertion, or children drawn at the wrong indent TreePop called when TreeNode returned false, or not at all Call TreePop only inside if (TreeNode(...)) 3.04 A long list makes the frame slow Every row is submitted even when not visible ImGuiListClipper 3.02 A popup never opens OpenPopup and BeginPopup used different IDs, often in different ID scopes Call both in the same scope with the same string 4.02 A modal opens and closes at once, or cannot be closed OpenPopup is called every frame Call it once, on the event 4.02 Drag and drop does nothing The payload type strings differ, or the payload is the wrong size One shared constant for the type; check DataSize 4.03 Docking does not work ImGuiConfigFlags_DockingEnable not set, or the master branch is used instead of the docking branch Use the docking branch; set the flag 4.04 Text is blurry or shows "?" boxes Font loaded at the wrong size, or glyph ranges missing for the characters Load at the display size; add the ranges you need 4.05 A font change has no effect The font was added after the atlas was built Add fonts before the first frame, or rebuild the atlas 4.05 Windows reset their layout every start IniFilename is nullptr , or the program runs from another folder Give the ini file a full path 4.06 A drag creates hundreds of undo steps One step is recorded per frame of the drag Record on IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit 5.04 Stack overflow in a flood fill Recursive fill on a large region Explicit stack or queue 6.01

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Backend The code that connects ImGui to a platform (input, window, clock: imgui_impl_win32 ) and a renderer (drawing: imgui_impl_dx11 ). ImGui itself does neither. (1.02) Begin / End The pair that opens and closes a window. End must always be called, even when Begin returns false. (1.04) BeginChild A scrolling region inside a window with its own size, border and scroll position. (3.02) Clipper ImGuiListClipper : tells you which rows of a long list are visible so you submit only those. (3.02) Collapsing header A full-width header that shows or hides the widgets after it, without indenting them. (3.05) Command list A list of draw commands (vertices, indices, texture, clip rectangle) that the renderer backend turns into GPU draw calls. (1.03) Context ImGuiContext : all of ImGui's state. Created with CreateContext , destroyed with DestroyContext . (1.02) Dear ImGui A C++ immediate-mode GUI library for tools and debug UI, by Omar Cornut. (1.01) Docking The docking-branch feature that lets windows be docked into each other as tabs and splits, arranged by a dock space. (4.04) Dock space An area that windows can be docked into; DockSpaceOverViewport makes the whole main window one. (4.04) DockBuilder The internal API for building a default dock layout in code on first run. (4.04) Drag and drop source / target A widget that starts a drag with a typed payload, and a widget that accepts payloads of a matching type. (4.03) Draw data ImDrawData : everything ImGui wants drawn this frame, produced by Render . (1.03) Draw list ImDrawList : the list of shapes a window draws, which you can add lines, rectangles, circles and text to yourself. (1.03, 5.01) Font atlas One texture holding every glyph of every loaded font at its size. (4.05) Frame One pass of NewFrame , your UI code, Render and drawing the draw data. ImGui rebuilds the UI every frame. (1.03) Hot, active, focused The widget under the mouse, the widget being pressed or dragged, and the widget receiving keyboard input. (1.01) ID The number ImGui uses to tell widgets apart, hashed from the label and the ID stack. (1.05) ID stack PushID / PopID : scopes that make the same label unique in different places, such as rows of a list. (1.05) Immediate mode A GUI style where the program describes the UI from its own data every frame, and the library keeps almost no widget objects. (1.01) ini file imgui.ini : where ImGui saves window positions, sizes, docking and table settings, and where your own settings handlers can save more. (4.06) and In a label, hides what follows but keeps it in the ID; makes only what follows the ID, so the visible text can change. (1.05) Item The last widget submitted; IsItemHovered , IsItemActive , IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit and friends ask about it. (1.04) Metrics window ShowMetricsWindow : ImGui's own debug view of windows, draw lists and IDs. (1.06) Modal A popup that blocks the rest of the UI until it is closed, such as a confirmation dialog. (4.02) Multiple viewports The feature that lets ImGui windows leave the main window and become real OS windows. (4.04) Payload The typed data carried by a drag and drop. (4.03) Popup A window opened with OpenPopup and shown with BeginPopup , closing when you click elsewhere. (4.02) Retained mode A GUI style where the library keeps a tree of widget objects that the program creates, changes and destroys. (1.01) Selectable A widget that can be highlighted as selected, used for lists and menus. (2.03) Self time In a profiler, a zone's total time minus the time spent in its child zones. (6.02) Settings handler ImGuiSettingsHandler : your own section in the ini file, read and written by callbacks. (4.06) Style ImGuiStyle : sizes, roundings and colours for every widget. (4.05) Table BeginTable : columns with headers, resizing, reordering, sorting and scrolling. (3.03) Text filter ImGuiTextFilter : a box where the user types comma-separated terms, with - for exclusions, to filter lines. (5.02) Tree node A widget that expands to show indented children; TreePop closes its scope. (3.04) Undo step One user action recorded as the change needed to undo and redo it; a whole drag is one step. (5.04) WantCaptureMouse / WantCaptureKeyboard Flags ImGui sets when it is using the mouse or keyboard, so the game should ignore them. (2.05) Zone In a profiler, a named span of time marked by a begin and an end event. (6.02)

title: 1.01  What a Process Is
body: A process is a running program's container - a private address space, a table of handles, a security token, one or more threads and an exit code. Process IDs and handles, why processes cannot see each other's memory, and why that isolation is the reason inter-process communication needs special tools. A container for a running program When you start a program, Windows creates a process : not the code itself, but everything the running code needs and owns. Part What it is --- --- Address space a private range of virtual addresses (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 6.04) holding the program, its DLLs, heaps and stacks Threads the things that actually execute; a process has at least one Handle table the kernel objects it has opened: files, pipes, events, other processes Access token who it runs as, and what it is allowed to do Environment and command line text handed over at start-up Exit code a number left behind when it ends Every process has a process ID (PID), a number unique among running processes. PIDs are reused after a process is gone, so a PID alone is not a safe long-term reference to "that process". Isolation Each process has its own address space. The address 0x2C409610 in one process and the same number in another refer to entirely different memory, or to nothing. A bug in one program cannot overwrite another program's variables, and a crash ends only the process that crashed. That isolation is the whole reason this course exists. Two threads in one process share memory and can talk by just writing variables (with care). Two processes cannot: everything they exchange has to go through something the operating system provides and both can reach: - a pipe carrying bytes from one to the other; - a file mapping that the kernel maps into both address spaces; - a socket , even when both ends are on the same machine; - named kernel objects (events, mutexes, semaphores) for signalling; - window messages , for programs with windows; - plain files , and higher layers built on the above (COM, RPC). Handles to processes To do anything with another process, you need a handle to it, with the access you ask for: cpp-norun HANDLE process{ OpenProcess(SYNCHRONIZE PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, FALSE, pid) }; if (process) { WaitForSingleObject(process, INFINITE); // wait until it ends DWORD code{}; GetExitCodeProcess(process, &code); CloseHandle(process); } A process handle is better than a PID for keeping track of a process: while you hold the handle, the process object stays valid (even after the process ends, so you can read its exit code), and its PID cannot be reused for another process. When you start a child yourself, CreateProcessW gives you its handle directly. Threads, processes and jobs - A thread runs code inside a process. Several threads share the process's memory and handles. - A process owns resources and isolates them from other processes. - A job object groups processes so they can be managed together: limits on memory or CPU, and ending them all at once (lesson 1.03). When should work be split across processes instead of threads? When isolation is worth the cost of communication: a crash in a plugin should not take down the editor; an untrusted file parser should run with fewer rights; a long build should continue even if the window closes. Browsers run each site in its own process for exactly these reasons. Lifetime A process ends when its last thread ends, when it calls ExitProcess , or when another process ends it with TerminateProcess . Windows then closes every handle it had open, which matters for IPC: a pipe whose other end belonged to a process that died is closed, and a mutex it owned is released as abandoned (lesson 4.03). Good IPC code always plans for the other side disappearing without warning.

title: Handles outlive PIDs
body: PIDs are reused, handles are not (lesson 1.01). Model that difference: a tracker that hands out tickets , like handles, each referring to one particular run of a process even after its PID has been given to another. cpp class Tracker { public: void started(std::uint32_t pid, const std::string& name); void exited(std::uint32_t pid, std::uint32_t code); int open(std::uint32_t pid); bool isRunning(int ticket) const; std::optional<std::string nameOf(int ticket) const; std::optional<std::uint32_t exitCodeOf(int ticket) const; }; - started records that a process with this PID and name is now running. (The PID is never in use twice at the same time.) - exited records that the currently running process with that PID ended with code . An unknown PID is ignored. - open returns a new ticket (0, 1, 2, ...) for the process currently running with that PID, or -1 if none is. - A ticket keeps referring to the same process: nameOf and exitCodeOf answer for it even after it exits and its PID is reused. exitCodeOf is std::nullopt while it runs; any unknown ticket gives std::nullopt and isRunning false.

title: 1.02  Starting Processes Well
body: Everything that goes into a new process besides its command line - the environment block and how to build one, the working directory, which handles it inherits and how to limit them to exactly the ones you mean, and the creation flags that matter. More than a command line The Win32 API course (lesson 5.03) covered CreateProcessW , quoting arguments and waiting for the result. A child process inherits much more than its arguments from the call that creates it, and getting the rest right is what makes launching helpers reliable: cpp-norun BOOL CreateProcessW( LPCWSTR application, // nullptr: take it from the command line LPWSTR commandLine, // writable buffer LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, BOOL inheritHandles, // may the child inherit handles at all? DWORD flags, // CREATE_NO_WINDOW, CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, ... LPVOID environment, // nullptr: a copy of ours LPCWSTR currentDirectory, // nullptr: ours LPSTARTUPINFOW startup, // standard handles, window settings, attributes LPPROCESS_INFORMATION info); // the handles and IDs of the new process and its thread The environment block Every process has a set of environment variables ( PATH , TEMP , your own settings). By default a child gets a copy of the parent's. To give it a different set, pass an environment block : one buffer of NAME=value strings, each ending with a zero, the whole block ending with an extra zero. text A=1\0Path=C:\Tools;C:\Windows\System32\0TEMP=C:\Temp\0\0 Rules that matter: - With CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT the block is UTF-16 ( wchar_t ); use it always. - Windows expects the variables sorted by name, ignoring case . Names are case-insensitive: Path and PATH are the same variable, and a block must not contain both. - A block replaces the whole environment. Start from the parent's ( GetEnvironmentStringsW ), change what you need, and keep SystemRoot , Path and TEMP , which many programs need to work at all. Passing settings to a helper through environment variables is common and simple; but they are visible to anything that can inspect the process, so never put secrets in them. The working directory Relative paths in the child, and the order it searches for some files, depend on its current directory . By default it inherits yours, which is often not what you want (your own current directory can be anything the user chose). Pass the directory explicitly, usually the folder of the tool or of the project it works on. Handle inheritance A kernel object handle can be marked inheritable . If inheritHandles is TRUE , the child receives a copy of every inheritable handle the parent has, at the same values. That is how a child gets the ends of pipes for its standard streams (lesson 1.04). The danger is "every". In a multi-threaded program, another thread may create an inheritable handle at the same moment, and it leaks into your child; the child then keeps a pipe or file open that you expected to close, and the other end never sees end-of-file. The fix is to name the exact handles to inherit with an attribute list : cpp-norun SIZE_T size{}; InitializeProcThreadAttributeList(nullptr, 1, 0, &size); std::vector<std::byte storage(size); auto list{ reinterpret_cast<LPPROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST (storage.data()) }; InitializeProcThreadAttributeList(list, 1, 0, &size); HANDLE inherit { childStdin, childStdout }; UpdateProcThreadAttribute(list, 0, PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST, inherit, sizeof(inherit), nullptr, nullptr); STARTUPINFOEXW si{ { sizeof(si) } }; si.lpAttributeList = list; CreateProcessW(nullptr, cmd.data(), nullptr, nullptr, TRUE, EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, env.data(), directory.c_str(), &si.StartupInfo, &pi); DeleteProcThreadAttributeList(list); Now only those two handles are passed, whatever else is inheritable. Creation flags Flag Effect --- --- CREATE_NO_WINDOW a console program runs without opening a console window CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE give it its own console window CREATE_SUSPENDED create it with its main thread paused, for example to add it to a job before it runs (lesson 1.03) CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT the environment block is UTF-16 EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT startup is a STARTUPINFOEXW with an attribute list BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS run it at lower priority, good for background work

title: Environment blocks
body: Build and edit the environment block a child process receives (lesson 1.02). Here it is a std::string of NAME=value entries, each followed by a zero byte, with one more zero at the end (the real block is UTF-16, with exactly the same layout). cpp using Variables = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string ; std::string buildBlock(const Variables& vars); Variables parseBlock(const std::string& block); std::string withVariable(const std::string& block, const std::string& name, const std::string& value); std::string withoutVariable(const std::string& block, const std::string& name); - buildBlock sorts the variables by name ignoring case (compare the names with every letter in upper case), and if two names are the same ignoring case, keeps only the last one given. An empty list gives a block of two zeros. - parseBlock reads the entries back in order, splitting each at its first = after the first character (Windows keeps hidden entries like =C:=C:\Work , whose names start with = ). - withVariable returns a new block with the variable set (replacing any existing one with the same name ignoring case, and keeping the spelling of the new name); withoutVariable removes it.

title: 1.03  Waiting, Exit Codes and Jobs
body: Knowing how a child process ended - waiting with timeouts, exit code conventions and the NTSTATUS codes a crash leaves behind - and job objects that group processes, end them all at once and limit what they can use. Waiting A process handle becomes signalled when the process ends, so every wait function works on it: cpp-norun switch (WaitForSingleObject(process, 30'000)) // up to 30 seconds { case WAIT_OBJECT_0: / it ended / break; case WAIT_TIMEOUT: / still running: decide whether to keep waiting or end it / break; case WAIT_FAILED: / bad handle: GetLastError() / break; } Always choose a timeout. A child that hangs (waiting for input it will never get, stuck on a dialog box, deadlocked) would otherwise freeze the parent for ever. WaitForMultipleObjects waits for any of several processes (up to 64 handles) at once. Exit codes GetExitCodeProcess gives the code a process ended with. While it is still running it returns STILL_ACTIVE (259), which is one reason not to use 259 as a real exit code, and why you should check the process has really ended before trusting the value. Conventions: Code Usually means --- --- 0 success 1, 2, ... small numbers the program's own errors (documented by each tool: robocopy uses 0 to 7 for success!) 0xC0000005 access violation: it crashed 0xC0000409 stack buffer overrun or fail-fast: the /GS check or abort style termination 0xC00000FD stack overflow 0xC0000374 heap corruption 0xC000013A ended with Ctrl+C 0x40010004 ended by a debugger 0xE06D7363 an unhandled C++ exception ( msc in its last three bytes) Codes starting with 0xC are NTSTATUS error values: the process did not choose to exit, Windows ended it after an unhandled exception. A supervisor that restarts helpers (milestone 6) needs to tell "the job failed" (a small code) from "the program crashed" (an NTSTATUS), and log them differently. Ending a process TerminateProcess(process, code) ends a process immediately: no destructors, no flushing of files, no clean-up of any kind. It is a last resort. Prefer asking the process to stop through your own channel (a "quit" message on a pipe, an event it watches), waiting a few seconds, and only then terminating. Job objects A job object groups processes. Its most useful features: Kill on close. End every process in the job when the last handle to the job closes, including when your process crashes: cpp-norun HANDLE job{ CreateJobObjectW(nullptr, nullptr) }; JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION info{}; info.BasicLimitInformation.LimitFlags = JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE; SetInformationJobObject(job, JobObjectExtendedLimitInformation, &info, sizeof(info)); // start each helper with CREATE_SUSPENDED, then: AssignProcessToJobObject(job, pi.hProcess); ResumeThread(pi.hThread); Without this, helper processes outlive a crashed parent and pile up in Task Manager. Children that the helpers start themselves join the job automatically. Limits. A job can cap memory per process or for the whole job, CPU time, CPU rate, and the number of active processes. A build tool can use them to stop one runaway compiler from taking the whole machine. Accounting. QueryInformationJobObject reports the total CPU time, I/O and peak memory of everything in the job, which is a simple way to measure what a group of processes really cost.

title: Reading exit codes
body: Turn a child process's exit code into something a person or a supervisor can act on (lesson 1.03): cpp bool crashed(std::uint32_t code); std::string describeExit(std::uint32_t code); - crashed is true for NTSTATUS error codes: those whose top two bits are both set ( 0xC0000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF ). - describeExit returns: Code Text --- --- 0 success 259 still running 0xC0000005 crashed: access violation 0xC00000FD crashed: stack overflow 0xC0000409 crashed: stack buffer overrun or fail-fast 0xC0000374 crashed: heap corruption 0xC000013A stopped with Ctrl+C any other crash code crashed: 0xC0001234 (8 uppercase hex digits) 0xE06D7363 unhandled C++ exception anything else failed with code N (in decimal)

title: 1.04  Talking Through Standard Streams
body:
The simplest channel between a parent and a child - its standard input, output and error redirected to pipes - and the deadlocks waiting for anyone who reads them carelessly, plus line-based protocols over stdio as used by language servers and many tools. Three streams for free Every process has three standard handles: input , output and error . A console program reads from the first and writes to the others. When you start a program, you can connect any of them to a pipe you hold the other end of, and you have a two-way channel with no extra setup on the child's side: it just uses std::cin and std::cout . That is why so many tools talk this way: compilers report errors on stderr, git writes results on stdout, and language servers (the processes behind code completion in editors) exchange JSON messages over stdin and stdout. Wiring it up cpp-norun SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES inheritable{ sizeof(inheritable), nullptr, TRUE }; HANDLE inRead, inWrite, outRead, outWrite; CreatePipe(&inRead, &inWrite, &inheritable, 0); // parent writes inWrite - child reads inRead CreatePipe(&outRead, &outWrite, &inheritable, 0); // child writes outWrite - parent reads outRead SetHandleInformation(inWrite, HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT, 0); // the parent's ends must NOT be inherited SetHandleInformation(outRead, HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT, 0); STARTUPINFOW si{ sizeof(si) }; si.dwFlags = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES; si.hStdInput = inRead; si.hStdOutput = outWrite; si.hStdError = outWrite; // or a third pipe, to keep errors apart CreateProcessW(/ ... / TRUE / inherit /, CREATE_NO_WINDOW, / ... / &si, &pi); CloseHandle(inRead); // the child has its own copies now CloseHandle(outWrite); // essential: otherwise reading outRead never ends Closing the parent's copies of the child's ends is the step people forget. A pipe reports end-of-file to the reader only when every write handle is closed; if the parent still holds outWrite , reading outRead waits for ever after the child exits. Likewise, when the parent has nothing more to send, it closes inWrite , and the child's next read sees end-of-file. Many tools read until end of input before they start working. The deadlock Pipes have a fixed buffer, typically a few kilobytes. A writer whose pipe is full blocks until the reader takes something out. That creates a classic deadlock: 1. The parent writes a large input to the child's stdin, all of it, before reading anything. 2. The child reads a little, then writes a lot of output, filling its stdout pipe. 3. The child blocks writing; the parent blocks writing; neither ever reads. The same happens with stdout and stderr on two pipes: the parent reads stdout to the end while the child blocks writing to a full stderr. The rule: read every output pipe continuously while also writing . In practice, read each output pipe on its own thread (or use overlapped I/O, lesson 2.05), collecting what arrives, and write input on another. Lines and encodings Output arrives in arbitrary chunks, not lines: one read can return half a line, or three and a half. To process line by line, keep a buffer per stream, append each chunk, and take out complete lines (ending in 
 , with a  before it on Windows) as they appear; whatever is left waits for the next chunk. The final partial line is complete only when the stream reaches end-of-file. Console programs write in the console's code page or in UTF-8; when you capture them you receive raw bytes and must decode them yourself. Many tools let you choose ( git -c core.quotepath=off , Python's PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 ); for your own helpers, always write UTF-8. Protocols over stdio Stdio becomes a real protocol once both sides agree on message boundaries. Two common choices: - One message per line (JSON Lines, for example): simple, as long as messages never contain a raw newline. - Headers then a body of known length , as the Language Server Protocol does: text Content-Length: 52
 
 {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize",...} The reader parses headers up to the blank line, then reads exactly Content-Length bytes. Milestone 2 builds framing like this properly. !warning A child that writes anything else to stdout (a debug printf , a library's warning) corrupts a stdout protocol. Send logs to stderr, or to a file.

title: Lines from a stream
body:
Output from a child arrives in arbitrary chunks (lesson 1.04). Collect it into lines, one collector per stream: cpp class LineCollector { public: void add(std::string_view chunk); void finish(); std::vector<std::string take(); std::size_t pending() const; }; - add appends a chunk. Every 
 ends a line; a  directly before it is dropped (Windows line endings), and so is a lone  at the very end of a line. Lines do not include their 
 . - finish is called at end-of-file: whatever is left becomes a last line, unless nothing is left. - take returns the complete lines collected so far, in order, and forgets them. - pending is the number of bytes waiting for the end of their line. A 
 split across two chunks (  at the end of one, 
 at the start of the next) must still give one line ending, not a stray  .

title: 1.05  Choosing an IPC Method
body: A map of the ways processes communicate on Windows - pipes, shared memory, sockets, kernel objects, window messages, files, COM and RPC - compared on speed, simplicity, who can connect and what happens when one side dies, with a guide to choosing. Many tools, different jobs Every IPC method moves data or signals between address spaces through the kernel, but they differ a great deal in what they are good at. The rest of the course covers each in depth; this lesson is the map. Method Moves Strengths Weaknesses --- --- --- --- Anonymous pipe a byte stream, one way trivial for parent and child; stdio only between related processes Named pipe a byte or message stream, two way any two processes on the machine (or network); per-client connections; access control Windows-specific API Shared memory (file mapping) nothing: both see the same bytes fastest by far, no copying you build every structure and all synchronisation yourself Socket (loopback TCP, AF_UNIX) a byte stream same code works across a network; every language has it some overhead; open ports need care Events, mutexes, semaphores signals, not data waiting without spinning; combine with shared memory carry no data Window messages ( WM_COPYDATA ) small messages easy between GUI programs needs windows and a message loop; blocked between privilege levels Files anything simple, survives restarts slow; coordinating readers and writers is hard COM, RPC method calls rich, typed interfaces heavy machinery to learn and debug Questions that decide Are the processes related? A parent and the child it starts can share anonymous pipes or inherited handles. Unrelated programs need a name both know: a named pipe, a named mapping, a port number. How much data, how often? A few messages a second: any method. Megabytes per frame (a video stream, a game's state for an external tool): shared memory , with a small signal to say "new data". Copying through a pipe costs time per byte; shared memory costs nothing per byte once mapped. Request and response, or a stream? Pipes and sockets fit conversations naturally. Shared memory suits "latest state" and ring buffers of records. What if one side dies? Pipes and sockets tell you : the other end is closed and reads fail. Shared memory does not: a dead writer leaves the last data in place and a mutex abandoned (lesson 4.03). Anything built on shared memory needs its own liveness checks, such as watching the other process's handle. Across machines later? If there is any chance, use sockets from the start; the protocol is then the same locally and remotely. Who may connect? Named pipes and kernel objects carry Windows security descriptors (lesson 5.05); TCP ports on localhost are open to every local process, so the protocol must check who is talking. Common combinations - Editor and language server : stdio pipes with length-framed JSON messages. - Game and external debug tool : shared memory holding the game's state, plus an event or a seqlock so the tool reads consistent snapshots; a named pipe for commands back to the game. - Single-instance app : a named mutex to detect the running copy, a named pipe or WM_COPYDATA to hand it the new command line. - Browser : one process per site, communicating with the main process over named pipes with a custom message system, shared memory for rendered frames. - Background service and its settings app : a named pipe with an access control list allowing only the user's session. The shape of every IPC design Whatever the method, a robust design has the same parts, which the following milestones build one by one: 1. Discovery : how the two sides find each other (a name, an inherited handle, a port). 2. Framing : where each message begins and ends. 3. Format : how values are encoded so both sides agree. 4. Flow : who speaks when; requests, responses, events. 5. Failure : timeouts, the other side vanishing, bad input. 6. Security : who is allowed to connect, and never trusting what arrives.

title: Running a compiler from an editor
match: Running a compiler from an editor
body: An editor runs the compiler as a child process and shows its errors in a list, the way Visual Studio, VS Code and the Xenon desktop app do. Build the part that turns the child's captured output and exit code into a result the editor can display. cpp enum class Stream { Out, Err }; struct Chunk { Stream stream; std::string bytes; }; struct Diagnostic { std::string file; int line; int column; // 0 when the message has none std::string severity; // "error", "warning" or "note" std::string code; // "C2065", or "" when the message has none std::string message; }; struct BuildResult { std::vector<std::string outLines, errLines; std::vector<Diagnostic diagnostics; int errors, warnings; bool succeeded; std::string status; }; std::optional<Diagnostic parseDiagnostic(const std::string& line); BuildResult collect(const std::vector<Chunk & chunks, std::uint32_t exitCode); parseDiagnostic understands the MSVC and Clang styles: text C:\src\game.cpp(12,5): error C2065: 'hp': undeclared identifier C:\src\game.cpp(40): warning C4244: 'argument': conversion from 'double' to 'int' src/main.cpp:7:3: error: expected ';' after expression src/main.cpp:9:1: note: to match this '{' The file ends where ( or : starts the line number (but a drive letter's colon, as in C:\ , is part of the file). The severity is error , warning or note ; an MSVC code (a letter followed by digits) may follow it; the message is what remains after : . Anything else is std::nullopt . collect splits each stream's chunks into lines separately (the rules of practice 1.04, with a final partial line at the end), parses every line of both streams in stream order (all of Out first, then Err ) as diagnostics, counts errors and warnings, and sets the result: - succeeded is true when the exit code is 0 and there are no errors; - status is succeeded , failed: N errors (always the plural), or for a crash code (top two bits set) compiler crashed: 0xC0000005 (8 uppercase hex digits). A failure with no error lines is failed: exit code N .

title: 2.01  Anonymous Pipes
body: The one-way byte channel behind standard streams - creating a pipe, its buffer and what happens when it fills, end-of-file and broken pipes, peeking without blocking, and passing pipe ends to a child. Two ends, one direction CreatePipe makes an anonymous pipe : a buffer in the kernel with a read end and a write end , each a handle. cpp-norun HANDLE readEnd{}, writeEnd{}; if (!CreatePipe(&readEnd, &writeEnd, nullptr, 64 1024)) // ask for a 64 KB buffer throw std::runtime_error("CreatePipe failed"); const char message { "hello" }; DWORD n{}; WriteFile(writeEnd, message, 5, &n, nullptr); // into the pipe char buffer 16 ; ReadFile(readEnd, buffer, sizeof(buffer), &n, nullptr); // n == 5 Bytes come out in the order they went in, with no boundaries: two writes of 5 bytes may be read as one read of 10, or as reads of 3 and 7. For two-way communication, use two pipes. "Anonymous" means it has no name: the only way for another process to use it is to be given a handle to one end, by inheritance when it starts (lesson 1.04) or by DuplicateHandle . That makes anonymous pipes ideal between a parent and its children, and useless between unrelated programs (lesson 2.02). When the buffer fills The buffer size passed to CreatePipe is a suggestion (0 means a default of a few kilobytes). When it is full, WriteFile blocks until the reader takes data out. When it is empty, ReadFile blocks until data arrives. Blocking is what makes simple pipe code correct, and also what causes the deadlocks of lesson 1.04 when both sides wait on each other. To find out without blocking whether data is waiting, use PeekNamedPipe (it works on anonymous pipes too): cpp-norun DWORD available{}; if (PeekNamedPipe(readEnd, nullptr, 0, nullptr, &available, nullptr) && available 0) / a ReadFile of up to available bytes returns at once /; End-of-file and broken pipes How each side learns that the other has finished: Situation What the other side sees --- --- every write handle is closed, buffer empty ReadFile fails with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE (109): this is end-of-file for a pipe the read handle is closed WriteFile fails with ERROR_NO_DATA (232) ("the pipe is being closed") Note " every write handle": any copy of the write end left open anywhere, in the parent or inherited by another child, keeps the reader waiting. Close your copies of ends you do not use, immediately. Treat ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE on a read as a normal, expected end of the conversation, not as an error to report. Sizes and speed Each ReadFile and WriteFile is a call into the kernel and a copy of the data. Many tiny writes are slow; batch output into larger writes (a few kilobytes) where you can. Anonymous pipes on Windows are actually implemented as named pipes with generated names, so everything about performance in the next lessons applies to them too. Inside one process Pipes also work between threads of one process, which is occasionally handy for code that already speaks in handles. But between threads, a std::queue with a mutex and condition variable is simpler and faster: pipes earn their keep crossing process boundaries.

title: A pipe that behaves like the real one
match: A pipe that behaves like the real one
body: Model an anonymous pipe's rules (lesson 2.01) so they can be tested: a bounded buffer, end-of-file only when every writer is closed, and broken pipes. cpp enum class Status { Ok, WouldBlock, EndOfFile, BrokenPipe }; struct ReadResult { Status status; std::string data; }; class Pipe { public: explicit Pipe(std::size_t capacity); int openWriter(); void closeWriter(int writer); void closeReader(); Status write(int writer, std::string_view data, std::size_t& accepted); ReadResult read(std::size_t maxBytes); std::size_t available() const; }; - The pipe starts with one writer, number 0, and one reader. openWriter adds another writer handle (as duplicating or inheriting one does) and returns its number (1, 2, ...). - write with a closed or unknown writer returns BrokenPipe . If the reader is closed, it also returns BrokenPipe and accepts nothing. Otherwise it accepts as many bytes as fit in the free space, sets accepted , and returns Ok if it accepted everything, or WouldBlock if some did not fit (a real pipe would block until there was room). - read returns up to maxBytes bytes in order with Ok . With nothing buffered, it returns EndOfFile if every writer is closed, otherwise WouldBlock . - available is the number of buffered bytes, like PeekNamedPipe .

title: 2.02  Named Pipes
body: Pipes any program can find by name - creating a server instance, waiting for a client to connect, connecting as a client and handling a busy server, byte and message modes, disconnecting, and the rules for pipe names. A pipe with a name A named pipe is created by a server under a name such as \\.\pipe\xenon-indexer . Any program on the machine that knows the name can connect as a client . Each connection is a private, two-way channel between the server and that one client. The server cpp-norun HANDLE pipe{ CreateNamedPipeW( LR"(\\.\pipe\xenon-indexer)", PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, // read and write PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE PIPE_WAIT // message mode (below) PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS, // this machine only PIPE_UNLIMITED_INSTANCES, // how many clients at once 64 1024, 64 1024, // out and in buffer sizes 0, // default client wait timeout nullptr) }; // security: lesson 5.05 if (pipe == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) / GetLastError() /; if (!ConnectNamedPipe(pipe, nullptr) && GetLastError() != ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED) / failed /; // a client is connected: ReadFile / WriteFile on pipe CreateNamedPipeW creates one instance : a single connection slot. ConnectNamedPipe waits until a client connects to it. ( ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED means a client connected between the create and the connect call, which is success.) To serve another client at the same time you create another instance (lesson 2.04). When the conversation ends, DisconnectNamedPipe drops the client and the same instance can ConnectNamedPipe again; or close it. The client cpp-norun HANDLE pipe{}; for (;;) { pipe = CreateFileW(LR"(\\.\pipe\xenon-indexer)", GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr); if (pipe != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) break; if (GetLastError() != ERROR_PIPE_BUSY) / no server: ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (2) / return; if (!WaitNamedPipeW(LR"(\\.\pipe\xenon-indexer)", 2000)) return; // every instance busy: wait up to 2 s } DWORD mode{ PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE }; SetNamedPipeHandleState(pipe, &mode, nullptr, nullptr); // read whole messages too The client opens the pipe like a file. Two errors matter: ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND means no server is running (start it, or report that), and ERROR_PIPE_BUSY means the server exists but every instance is in use, so wait with WaitNamedPipeW and try again. Another client can win the race after the wait, which is why it is a loop. Byte mode and message mode - Byte mode ( PIPE_TYPE_BYTE ): a stream like an anonymous pipe. Boundaries are lost. - Message mode ( PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE with PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE on the reading side): each WriteFile is one message, and each ReadFile returns at most one message. If your buffer is too small, the read returns what fits and fails with ERROR_MORE_DATA ; keep reading to get the rest of the same message. Message mode is convenient, but it is Windows-only and ties your protocol to pipes. Many programs use byte mode with their own framing (lesson 2.03), which then works unchanged over sockets too. Names - Local pipes are \\.\pipe\ followed by the name. Remote ones are \\server\pipe\name (blocked by PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS , which you should set unless you need them). - The name part may contain any character except \ . The whole string can be up to 256 characters. Names are not case-sensitive . - Names are global to the machine: two programs, or two users, choosing \\.\pipe\server collide. Make names specific: product, purpose, and usually the user or session ( \\.\pipe\xenon-indexer-S-1-5-21-... or a per-user random suffix stored where the client can find it). - A name that another program created first can be squatted : your client might connect to an impostor. Lesson 5.05 covers how to guard against it.

title: Pipe names
body: Apply the naming rules of lesson 2.02: cpp bool validPipeName(const std::string& name); bool samePipe(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); std::string pipeNameFor(const std::string& product, const std::string& purpose, const std::string& user); - validPipeName : the name starts with \\.\pipe\ or \\SERVER\pipe\ (a server name of letters, digits, - , _ or . , not empty), the part after pipe\ is not empty and contains no \ , and the whole string is at most 256 characters. The word pipe may be in any case. - samePipe : two names refer to the same pipe if they are equal ignoring case. - pipeNameFor builds \\.\pipe\product-purpose-user in lower case, replacing every character that is not a letter or digit in each part with _ .

title: 2.03  Message Framing
body: Turning a byte stream into messages - length prefixes and why they beat delimiters for binary data, choosing the size and byte order of the length, refusing absurd lengths, reading exactly N bytes, and recovering when the other side sends nonsense. Streams have no boundaries A pipe in byte mode, a TCP socket and stdio all deliver a stream : bytes in order, with no record of how they were written. If one side writes "hello" and then "world", the other may read "hellow" and "orld". A program that exchanges messages must therefore mark where each one ends. That is framing . Three ways to frame Method How Good for Problem --- --- --- --- delimiter end each message with \n (or \0 ) text, line-based protocols the delimiter cannot appear inside a message without escaping fixed size every message is N bytes very simple records wastes space; inflexible length prefix each message starts with its length binary data, anything the reader must trust the length Length prefixes are the usual choice for program-to-program protocols. A message is sent as: text length: 4 bytes, little-endian payload: length bytes 05 00 00 00 68 65 6C 6C 6F - "hello" Choosing the length field - Size : 2 bytes allows 64 KB messages, 4 bytes up to 4 GB. 4 bytes is the common default. - Byte order : say which, and stick to it. Little-endian matches x86 and ARM; network protocols traditionally use big-endian. It matters only that both sides agree. - What it counts : the payload only, or the whole frame including the length? Document it; the bug where one side counts the header and the other does not is a classic. Reading a frame On a stream, a single read may return part of a header, a header and part of a payload, or several frames at once. The robust pattern keeps a buffer (lesson 6.03 of the Reverse Engineering course used it for a protocol): 1. Append whatever arrives to the buffer. 2. While the buffer holds at least a header: read the length; if the whole frame is there, take it out and handle it; otherwise wait for more. When you know how much you need and are happy to block, a "read exactly N bytes" helper is simpler: cpp-norun bool readExactly(HANDLE pipe, void buffer, DWORD size) { auto at{ static_cast<char (buffer) }; while (size 0) { DWORD got{}; if (!ReadFile(pipe, at, size, &got, nullptr) got == 0) return false; // closed or failed at += got; size -= got; } return true; } std::uint32_t length{}; if (!readExactly(pipe, &length, 4) length MAX_MESSAGE) return false; std::vector<char payload(length); if (!readExactly(pipe, payload.data(), length)) return false; Never trust a length The length comes from the other process, which may be buggy, old, or hostile. A length of 0xFFFFFFFF must not make you allocate 4 GB. Always: - enforce a maximum message size that suits your protocol (a few megabytes at most for most uses) and treat anything larger as a protocol error; - decide what a length of 0 means (an empty message, or an error); - on any framing error, close the connection . After a bad length you no longer know where the next frame starts, so there is nothing safe to continue with. Message mode instead Named pipes in message mode (lesson 2.02) do the framing for you: one write is one message. The reading side still has to handle messages larger than its buffer, by reading again after ERROR_MORE_DATA and joining the pieces. It also still needs a maximum size. And everything breaks the day the protocol moves to a socket, which is why many designs frame by hand even on pipes.

title: Length-prefixed frames
body: Frame messages on a byte stream with a 4-byte little-endian length prefix (lesson 2.03): cpp std::vector<std::uint8_t frame(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & payload); class Deframer { public: explicit Deframer(std::uint32_t maxMessage); void feed(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t next(); bool failed() const; }; struct MessageRead { std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes; bool moreData; }; std::vector<MessageRead readInMessageMode(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & message, std::size_t bufferSize); - frame returns the 4-byte length of the payload followed by the payload. - Deframer : feed appends received bytes; next returns the next complete payload, or std::nullopt if more bytes are needed. A length above maxMessage is a protocol error: the deframer becomes failed , discards everything, and from then on next always returns std::nullopt and feed ignores input. A length of 0 is an empty message. - readInMessageMode shows how a message-mode pipe read loop (lesson 2.02) sees one message: successive reads of at most bufferSize bytes, each marked moreData (the ERROR_MORE_DATA case) except the last. An empty message is one read of 0 bytes.

title: 2.04  Serving Many Clients
body: A pipe server that handles several clients at once - one instance per client, the accept loop with a thread per connection, keeping an instance always listening, identifying who connected, limits, and shutting the server down cleanly. One instance per client A named pipe instance is one connection. To serve several clients at the same time, the server creates several instances of the same name. The standard shape is an accept loop : cpp-norun for (;;) { HANDLE instance{ CreateNamedPipeW(name, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, PIPE_TYPE_BYTE PIPE_WAIT PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS, PIPE_UNLIMITED_INSTANCES, 65536, 65536, 0, &security) }; if (instance == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) break; const BOOL connected{ ConnectNamedPipe(instance, nullptr) GetLastError() == ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED }; if (!connected) { CloseHandle(instance); continue; } std::thread{ serveClient, instance }.detach(); // serveClient reads, replies, and closes the handle } Each loop iteration creates a fresh instance and waits on it, so as soon as one client is handed to its thread, the next client can connect. Between ConnectNamedPipe returning and the next CreateNamedPipeW , there is a moment with no free instance; a client arriving then gets ERROR_PIPE_BUSY , waits with WaitNamedPipeW (lesson 2.02) and gets in. Some servers keep two or more instances listening to make that window smaller. Thread per client A thread per client is the simplest correct design: each thread runs straightforward blocking code (read a request, handle it, write a reply) and closes its instance when the client disconnects ( ReadFile fails with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE ). It is the right choice for tens of clients. For hundreds or thousands, the threads' stacks and scheduling cost too much, and overlapped I/O with a completion port (lesson 2.05) serves them all with a few threads. Shared state that client threads touch (a list of connected clients, a cache) needs a mutex, like any multi-threaded code. Limits nMaxInstances (the fourth argument) caps how many instances may exist. With a cap of 4, a fifth client keeps getting ERROR_PIPE_BUSY until one of the four disconnects. Set a cap that matches what your server can handle, and give clients a sensible wait and retry policy. Who connected? A server can ask about the process at the other end: cpp-norun ULONG clientPid{}; GetNamedPipeClientProcessId(instance, &clientPid); // the client's PID and, with care, run code in the client's security context with ImpersonateNamedPipeClient (lesson 5.05). The PID is useful for logging and for watching the client process; it is not proof of who the client is, since PIDs can be reused and any program may connect. Access control on the pipe itself is the real gate. Shutting down The accept loop above blocks in ConnectNamedPipe , so how does it ever stop? Common answers: - Set a "stopping" flag, then connect to your own pipe as a client: the blocked ConnectNamedPipe returns, the loop sees the flag and exits. - Use overlapped ConnectNamedPipe (lesson 2.05) and wait on both the connection event and a "stop" event. - CancelIoEx(instance, nullptr) from another thread cancels the pending connect. Then tell each client thread to finish: close their handles (their reads fail) or set a flag they check between messages, and wait for them to end before the program exits.

title: Instances and clients
body: Model a named pipe server's instances (lesson 2.04): how many are listening, which are connected, and what a client trying to connect experiences. cpp enum class Connect { Connected, Busy, NoServer }; class PipeServer { public: explicit PipeServer(int maxInstances); bool createInstance(); Connect clientConnects(std::uint32_t pid, int& instance); void clientDisconnects(int instance); void closeInstance(int instance); int listening() const; std::vector<std::uint32_t clients() const; }; - Instances are numbered 0, 1, 2, ... in the order created. createInstance adds a listening instance; it returns false (and creates nothing) if maxInstances instances already exist. - clientConnects : if no instance exists at all, NoServer (like ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND ). If none is listening, Busy (like ERROR_PIPE_BUSY ). Otherwise the lowest-numbered listening instance becomes connected to that client, instance is set to its number, and the result is Connected . - clientDisconnects makes a connected instance listen again (like DisconnectNamedPipe and a new ConnectNamedPipe ). - closeInstance removes an instance, whatever its state; its number is not reused. - clients lists the PIDs of connected clients in instance order.

title: 2.05  Overlapped I/O and Completion Ports
body: Doing pipe I/O without blocking a thread per operation - FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, OVERLAPPED structures and events, ERROR_IO_PENDING, GetOverlappedResult, and I/O completion ports that let a few threads serve thousands of connections as state machines. Asking now, finding out later Blocking I/O ties up a thread while it waits. Overlapped I/O starts an operation and returns at once; the result arrives later. To use it, open or create the handle with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED (for a pipe server, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED ), and pass an OVERLAPPED structure to each call: cpp-norun OVERLAPPED ov{}; ov.hEvent = CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr); // signalled when the operation completes char buffer 4096 ; if (!ReadFile(pipe, buffer, sizeof(buffer), nullptr, &ov)) { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_IO_PENDING) / a real failure /; // ... the read is in progress; do other work, or wait ... } DWORD got{}; if (GetOverlappedResult(pipe, &ov, &got, TRUE / wait /)) { / got bytes are in buffer / } Rules that bite: - The OVERLAPPED and the buffer must stay alive and untouched until the operation completes . Putting them on the stack of a function that returns while the read is pending is a classic memory corruption. - One OVERLAPPED per outstanding operation. - An operation may complete immediately (the call returns TRUE ); handle that path too. - CancelIoEx(handle, &ov) cancels a pending operation; you must still wait for its completion (with ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED ) before freeing the buffer. With an event per operation, one thread can wait for many with WaitForMultipleObjects , up to 64 handles. Beyond that, use a completion port. I/O completion ports An I/O completion port (IOCP) is a queue that collects the completions of many handles. Associate each handle with the port and a key of your choosing (usually a pointer to the connection's state): cpp-norun HANDLE port{ CreateIoCompletionPort(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, nullptr, 0, 0) }; CreateIoCompletionPort(pipe, port, reinterpret_cast<ULONG_PTR (connection), 0); // associate Then start overlapped operations as usual (no event needed), and have a few worker threads pull completions: cpp-norun for (;;) { DWORD bytes{}; ULONG_PTR key{}; OVERLAPPED ov{}; const BOOL ok{ GetQueuedCompletionStatus(port, &bytes, &key, &ov, INFINITE) }; auto connection{ reinterpret_cast<Connection (key) }; if (!ok bytes == 0 && connection- expectingData()) { connection- close(); continue; } connection- onCompleted(ov, bytes); // advance its state machine, start the next operation } PostQueuedCompletionStatus adds your own items to the queue, which is how you wake the workers to shut down. Connections as state machines With completions arriving one at a time, each connection is no longer a thread running top to bottom; it is a state machine that reacts to each completion and starts the next operation: text read 4 header bytes complete READING_HEADER --------------------------- READING_BODY (start a read of length bytes) ^ write complete body complete: handle the request +------------- WRITING <-----------------+ (start writing the reply) Each state knows which operation it is waiting for and how many bytes it still needs (a read may return fewer bytes than asked; then it simply reads again for the rest). This is more code than a thread per client, but a handful of worker threads can serve thousands of connections, and the same design works for sockets: it is how high-performance Windows servers are written. For smaller servers the Windows thread pool API ( CreateThreadpoolIo ) wraps completion ports for you, and C++ libraries such as Asio provide the same model portably.

title: A connection as a state machine
match: A connection as a state machine
body: Write the state machine of lesson 2.05: one connection served with overlapped I/O, reacting to completions one at a time. Requests are framed with a 4-byte little-endian length; the reply to each request is the request's bytes reversed, framed the same way. cpp enum class Op { Read, Write, Close }; struct Request { Op op; std::size_t size; std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; class Connection { public: explicit Connection(std::uint32_t maxMessage); Request start(); Request onRead(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); Request onWritten(std::size_t bytes); int served() const; }; Each call returns the next operation to start : - Read with size : read up to size bytes; the result comes back through onRead (it may be fewer bytes). - Write with data : write these bytes; onWritten reports how many were written (it may be fewer; then write the rest). - Close : the connection is finished. The flow: start asks to read the 4-byte header. While the header is incomplete, keep asking for the missing bytes. A length above maxMessage means Close . Then read the body (asking for exactly the bytes still missing). With the whole body, write the framed reply; when all of it is written, count one served request and ask for the next header. An onRead with 0 bytes means the client disconnected: Close .

title: A log collector
body: Several helper processes send log records to one collector over a named pipe, one connection each, in byte mode with their own framing. Build the collector's core: per-client reassembly, validation, disconnects in the middle of a record, and draining records by level. Each record on the wire is: text length: 2 bytes, little-endian level: 1 byte text: length - 1 bytes so length counts the level byte and the text. cpp struct Record { int client; std::uint32_t pid; std::uint8_t level; std::string text; }; class LogCollector { public: int connect(std::uint32_t pid); void received(int client, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); void disconnected(int client); std::vector<Record drain(std::uint8_t minLevel); bool isConnected(int client) const; int partialDropped() const; int protocolErrors() const; }; - connect registers a new client connection from process pid and returns its id (0, 1, 2, ...). - received appends bytes from that client and extracts every complete record, in order. Records from different clients are kept in the order they completed . Bytes for an unknown or disconnected client are ignored. - A record whose length is 0 or greater than 1025, or whose level is above 5, is a protocol error : count it, drop the client's buffered bytes and disconnect the client (as the server would close a misbehaving connection). Records completed before the error are kept. - disconnected : the client is gone; if it had an incomplete record buffered, count one partial drop . - drain returns every collected record with level = minLevel , in order, and forgets all collected records (lower levels are discarded).

title: 3.01  File Mappings
body: Shared memory on Windows - a named file mapping backed by the page file, views mapped into each process at different addresses, sizes and page rounding, Local and Global names, who creates and who opens, and when the memory goes away. The fastest channel there is Every method so far copies data: from the sender into the kernel, and from the kernel into the receiver. Shared memory copies nothing. The kernel maps the same physical pages into two (or more) processes' address spaces; a byte written by one is immediately visible to the other. On Windows, shared memory is a file mapping object. It can be backed by a real file (lesson 3.04) or, for pure IPC, by the page file: cpp-norun constexpr DWORD SIZE{ 64 1024 }; // The creator (often the server, or whichever process starts first) HANDLE mapping{ CreateFileMappingW(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, // page-file backed: no real file &security, // who may open it (lesson 5.05) PAGE_READWRITE, 0, SIZE, // size: high and low 32 bits LR"(Local\xenon-telemetry)") }; const bool existed{ GetLastError() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS }; // someone created it first void view{ MapViewOfFile(mapping, FILE_MAP_READ FILE_MAP_WRITE, 0, 0, SIZE) }; // ... use view as SIZE bytes of memory ... UnmapViewOfFile(view); CloseHandle(mapping); cpp-norun // Another process HANDLE mapping{ OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, LR"(Local\xenon-telemetry)") }; const void view{ MapViewOfFile(mapping, FILE_MAP_READ, 0, 0, 0) }; // 0: map all of it CreateFileMappingW with a name opens the existing object if it already exists (and sets ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS ), so it serves both sides when either might start first. OpenFileMappingW only opens, failing with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND if nobody created it. Different addresses The view appears at some address in each process, chosen independently: 0x1F0000 in one, 0x2A0000 in the other. The bytes are the same; the addresses are not. That one fact shapes everything you put into shared memory (lesson 3.02): a pointer stored in shared memory is meaningless to the other process . Sizes and pages Memory is mapped in whole pages (4 KB), so a mapping's real size is rounded up to a page. A view's starting offset must be a multiple of the allocation granularity , 64 KB on Windows ( GetSystemInfo reports it). Pages are committed lazily: a 1 GB page-file mapping costs nothing until its pages are touched, then each touched page costs RAM or page file. The size is given as two 32-bit halves because mappings can be larger than 4 GB: high word size 32 , low word size & 0xFFFFFFFF . Names: Local and Global Kernel object names (mappings, and the events and mutexes of milestone 4) live in a namespace per session : - Local\name (or just name ): visible only within the current login session. The usual choice for programs on a user's desktop. - Global\name : visible across sessions, so a service in session 0 and a desktop program can share it. Creating global objects needs the SeCreateGlobalPrivilege right, which services and administrators have. After the prefix the name may not contain another backslash. As with pipe names, choose names that will not collide: product, purpose, and a user or session identifier. Lifetime A mapping exists as long as any process holds a handle to it or has a view mapped. When the last one is gone, a page-file mapping and its contents vanish. So: - If the creator exits while another process still has it open, the data stays. - If every process closes it, the next process to create it gets fresh, zeroed memory. A page-file mapping always starts zeroed, which is useful: an all-zero header can mean "not yet initialised" (lesson 3.02). What it does not give you Shared memory moves no messages and sends no signals. It does not tell a reader that new data has arrived, it does not stop two writers from colliding, and it does not tell you when the other process has died. Every one of those must be built on top: atomics and ring buffers (lesson 3.03), events (milestone 4), seqlocks (lesson 3.05), and watching the other process's handle.

title: Mapping arithmetic
body: The numbers behind CreateFileMappingW and MapViewOfFile (lessons 3.01 and 3.04): cpp struct ViewPlan { std::uint64_t viewOffset; std::uint64_t delta; std::uint64_t viewLength; }; std::uint64_t pagesFor(std::uint64_t bytes); std::pair<std::uint32_t, std::uint32_t splitSize(std::uint64_t size); ViewPlan planView(std::uint64_t fileOffset, std::uint64_t length); bool validObjectName(const std::string& name); - pagesFor : how many 4096-byte pages hold bytes (0 bytes need 0 pages). - splitSize gives the high and low 32-bit halves a mapping size is passed as. - planView : to read length bytes at fileOffset , the view must start at a multiple of 65 536: viewOffset is the offset rounded down, delta how far into the view the data starts, viewLength is delta + length . - validObjectName : a name for a mapping, event or mutex is either a plain name, or Local\ or Global\ followed by a name; the name part must not be empty and must not contain \ . The whole string is at most 260 characters.

title: 3.02  Laying Out Shared Data
body: What may live in shared memory and what may not - offsets instead of pointers, fixed-size types instead of std::string and std::vector, a header with a magic number, version and size, safe initialisation when either side may start first, and lock-free atomics. The rules A block of shared memory is seen by several processes, at different addresses, possibly built by different versions of your program, possibly by different compilers. So everything in it must mean the same thing to all of them: 1. No pointers. Store offsets from the start of the block instead, and turn them into pointers locally: base + offset . 2. No types that own heap memory. A std::string or std::vector placed in shared memory holds a pointer to its own process's heap. Use fixed-size arrays ( char name 64 ) or offsets to data inside the block. 3. Fixed-size types. std::uint32_t , std::int64_t , float : never long (4 bytes on Windows, 8 on Linux) or size_t (different in 32- and 64-bit processes). 4. Explicit layout. Put members in a stable order, use static_assert on sizes and offsets, and remember padding (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 3.01). 5. No virtual functions , which would put a vtable pointer in the block. cpp-norun struct TelemetryHeader { std::uint32_t magic; // 'XTEL': this really is our block std::uint32_t version; // the layout version std::uint32_t size; // total bytes the creator made std::uint32_t ready; // 0 until the creator has finished initialising std::uint64_t firstSample; // offset of the sample table std::uint32_t sampleCount; std::uint32_t reserved; }; static_assert(sizeof(TelemetryHeader) == 32); A header first Begin every shared block with a header like that: - A magic number confirms the block is what you think: a stale mapping from an old version, or an unrelated program using the same name, is caught at once. - A version lets a newer reader refuse, or adapt to, an older layout. - A size stops a reader from trusting offsets that point past the end. Check every offset against it before use: the other process may be buggy, or hostile. Offsets instead of pointers A linked structure in shared memory stores offsets. A node at offset 0 is impossible (the header is there), so 0 can mean "none": cpp-norun struct Node { std::uint64_t next; std::int32_t value; std::uint32_t pad; }; template <typename T T at(std::byte base, std::uint64_t offset) { return offset ? reinterpret_cast<T (base + offset) : nullptr; } for (Node n{ at<Node (base, header- first) }; n; n = at<Node (base, n- next)) { / ... / } Because offsets are relative to the block, the structure is correct in every process however its view is placed. (The same idea is how memory-mapped file formats and pointer-free serialisation libraries such as FlatBuffers work.) Initialising safely Both processes may start at nearly the same moment. The creator (the one that did not get ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS ) fills in the header and the data, and sets ready last . Every other process waits until ready is set before trusting anything. Because a page-file mapping starts zeroed, ready == 0 reliably means "not yet". For this to be safe, ready must be written and read as an atomic with release and acquire ordering, so the data written before it is visible once it is seen: cpp-norun auto ready{ reinterpret_cast<std::atomic<std::uint32_t (&header- ready) }; ready- store(1, std::memory_order_release); // creator, after filling everything in while (ready- load(std::memory_order_acquire) == 0) Sleep(1); // others (with a timeout in real code) Atomics in shared memory std::atomic<T works across processes only if it is lock-free : a lock-based fallback uses a lock inside each process's own runtime, which the other process cannot see. For 32- and 64-bit integers on x64 they always are; check with static_assert(std::atomic<std::uint64_t ::is_always_lock_free) . Construct them in place in the block (with placement new, or by relying on the zeroed memory for types whose zero state is valid), and never put std::mutex in shared memory; use the named kernel objects of milestone 4 instead.

title: A list that works at any address
match: A list that works at any address
body: Build a linked list inside a block of bytes using offsets instead of pointers (lesson 3.02), so that a copy of the block placed anywhere else, as another process's view would be, still works. cpp class SharedList { public: static constexpr std::uint32_t MAGIC{ 0x5453494C }; // "LIST" explicit SharedList(std::vector<std::byte & block); void create(); bool valid() const; bool push(std::int32_t value); std::vector<std::int32_t values() const; std::uint32_t count() const; }; The block starts with a 24-byte header, followed by nodes of 16 bytes each: Header offset Field --- --- 0 std::uint32_t magic 4 std::uint32_t count 8 std::uint64_t offset of the first node (0 = none) 16 std::uint64_t offset where the next node will be placed Node offset Field --- --- 0 std::uint64_t offset of the next node (0 = none) 8 std::int32_t value 12 4 bytes of padding - create writes a fresh header: magic, count 0, no first node, next free offset 24. - valid checks the block is big enough for a header and holds the magic. - push adds a node holding value at the end of the list, placing it at the next free offset; if the block has no room for another node it returns false and changes nothing. - values walks the list from the first node. It must never read outside the block: a next offset that is not inside the block (or not a whole node from the end) stops the walk. - Read and write the fields with std::memcpy at byte offsets. The tests copy the whole block into a different vector and read it there.

title: 3.03  Ring Buffers
body: A queue in shared memory without locks - a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer with a write counter and a read counter, power-of-two capacities, detecting full and empty, acquire and release ordering, and what to do when the buffer is full. A queue made of a circle To stream messages through shared memory (a game sending events to an external debug tool, an audio engine passing samples), you need a queue that two processes can use at once without a lock. The standard answer is a ring buffer : an array of slots used in a circle, with two counters. text tail (next to read) head (next to write) slots: . A B C D . . . - The producer writes a slot at head , then advances head . - The consumer reads the slot at tail , then advances tail . - Each counter is written by only one side. That is what makes it work without locks: there is never a moment where both sides write the same variable. This is a single-producer, single-consumer (SPSC) ring. With several producers or consumers you need more machinery (compare-and-swap loops, or a lock); keep one writer and one reader per ring, and use several rings if needed. Counters that only grow Store head and tail as ever-increasing counters, not as slot indexes. Then: - the number of items is head - tail ; - empty is head == tail ; - full is head - tail == capacity ; - the slot for counter n is n % capacity , or n & (capacity - 1) when the capacity is a power of two , which is why ring sizes almost always are. With unsigned 32- or 64-bit counters, head - tail stays correct even when the counters wrap past their maximum, as long as the capacity is less than the wrap-around range. The code cpp-norun struct RingHeader { std::atomic<std::uint32_t head; // written only by the producer std::atomic<std::uint32_t tail; // written only by the consumer std::uint32_t capacity; // a power of two }; bool push(RingHeader h, std::uint32_t slots, std::uint32_t value) { const std::uint32_t head{ h- head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) }; // our own counter const std::uint32_t tail{ h- tail.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; // the consumer's if (head - tail == h- capacity) return false; // full slots head & (h- capacity - 1) = value; // write the slot first, h- head.store(head + 1, std::memory_order_release); // then publish it return true; } std::optional<std::uint32_t pop(RingHeader h, std::uint32_t slots) { const std::uint32_t tail{ h- tail.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) }; const std::uint32_t head{ h- head.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; // see the slots written before it if (head == tail) return std::nullopt; // empty const std::uint32_t value{ slots tail & (h- capacity - 1) }; h- tail.store(tail + 1, std::memory_order_release); // hand the slot back return value; } The ordering is the important part. The producer writes the slot before publishing the new head with release ; the consumer reads head with acquire before reading the slot. That pair guarantees the consumer never sees an advanced head without the slot's data. The same pairing in the other direction guarantees the producer never overwrites a slot the consumer is still reading. When the ring is full The producer has to choose a policy: - Fail and let the caller decide (the code above). Good for commands, which must not be lost. - Drop the new item and count the loss : good for telemetry and logs, where a live process must never wait for a slow observer. Keep a "dropped" counter in the header so the consumer can report the gap. - Wait : spin briefly, then wait on an event the consumer signals (milestone 4). Only when the producer can afford to block. Avoiding false sharing head and tail sit next to each other but are written by different processes on different cores. Each write invalidates the other core's copy of the 64-byte cache line containing both, which slows everything down. Put them on separate cache lines with alignas(64) padding. The counters are tiny; the padding is cheap.

title: A lock-free ring buffer
body: Build the single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer of lesson 3.03 over a block of memory. The producer and the consumer each make their own Ring object over the same block, as two processes would over one mapping. cpp struct alignas(64) RingHeader { std::atomic<std::uint32_t head; char pad1 60 ; std::atomic<std::uint32_t tail; char pad2 60 ; std::uint32_t capacity; std::atomic<std::uint32_t dropped; }; class Ring { public: Ring(void memory, std::uint32_t capacity, bool create); bool push(std::uint32_t value); void pushOrDrop(std::uint32_t value); std::optional<std::uint32_t pop(); std::uint32_t size() const; std::uint32_t dropped() const; }; The memory holds a RingHeader followed by capacity slots of std::uint32_t (the tests provide a block large enough and aligned to 64). - With create true, the constructor sets up the header (placement new or plain stores): head 0, tail 0, the capacity, dropped 0. Otherwise it uses the header that is there.
