The capacity is a power of two. - push adds a value, or returns false if the ring is full. pushOrDrop adds it, or counts it in dropped if full. - pop removes the oldest value, or gives std::nullopt if empty. - size is head - tail . - Use acquire and release ordering exactly as in the lesson. The tests include a real producer thread and consumer thread.

title: 3.04  Memory-Mapped Files
body: Mapping a real file into memory - reading huge files as if they were arrays, views of part of a file and the 64 KB granularity rule, writing through a mapping and flushing it, growing a mapped file, sharing a mapped file between processes, and the errors that arrive as exceptions. A file as memory A file mapping can be backed by a real file instead of the page file. Then the file's contents appear in memory, and reading memory reads the file: cpp-norun HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; LARGE_INTEGER size{}; GetFileSizeEx(file, &size); HANDLE mapping{ CreateFileMappingW(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY, 0, 0, nullptr) }; // 0, 0: the file's size const auto data{ static_cast<const std::uint8_t (MapViewOfFile(mapping, FILE_MAP_READ, 0, 0, 0)) }; std::span<const std::uint8_t bytes{ data, static_cast<std::size_t (size.QuadPart) }; // parse bytes directly: no ReadFile, no buffer, no copy Pages are read from disk only when first touched, so mapping a 2 GB file is instant, and reading only its index touches only the index's pages. Parsers for big binary formats (game assets, databases, the PE files of the Reverse Engineering course) often work this way: the file is the data structure, navigated by offsets. Views of part of a file A 64-bit process can map even very large files whole. When you need only a window (a 32-bit process, or a file larger than you want mapped), map a view of part of it. The view's starting offset must be a multiple of the allocation granularity (64 KB): text want bytes 100 000 to 100 499 aligned start = 100 000 rounded down to 65 536 = 65 536 delta = 100 000 - 65 536 = 34 464 map from 65 536 for 34 464 + 500 bytes; the data starts delta bytes into the view Writing Open the file and mapping for writing ( GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE , PAGE_READWRITE , FILE_MAP_WRITE ) and writes to memory become writes to the file. The operating system writes changed pages back to disk in its own time; FlushViewOfFile(view, 0) starts it now, and FlushFileBuffers(file) waits until it is on the disk, which matters for anything that must survive a power cut. A mapping cannot make a file bigger than the size it was created with. To append, close the views and mapping, extend the file ( SetFilePointerEx and SetEndOfFile , or create the mapping with a larger size, which extends the file), and map again. Programs that grow mapped files usually extend in large steps (doubling) to avoid remapping constantly. Sharing a mapped file Two processes mapping the same file see each other's writes immediately, through the same pages, exactly like a page-file mapping, and the data also persists in the file afterwards. This is how some databases share their data between processes. Coordinating writers still needs the synchronisation of milestone 4. Errors become exceptions With ReadFile , a disk error is a return value. With a mapped file, the error happens when you touch a page, inside an ordinary memory access, so it arrives as a structured exception, EXCEPTION_IN_PAGE_ERROR : a file on a network share that disappears, a USB drive pulled out, a file truncated by another process. Code that maps files it does not fully control wraps access in __try / __except , or prefers ReadFile for such files. Mapped files also hold the file open: it cannot be deleted while mapped, which surprises users of tools that leave mappings around.

title: Indexing a mapped file
body: A mapped file is just a span of bytes (lesson 3.04). Navigate one without copying it. The file holds records, each a 4-byte little-endian length followed by that many bytes: cpp struct Index { std::vector<std::size_t offsets; bool truncated; }; Index buildIndex(std::span<const std::uint8_t file); std::span<const std::uint8_t recordAt(std::span<const std::uint8_t file, const Index& index, std::size_t i); std::optional<std::size_t findRecord(std::span<const std::uint8_t file, const Index& index, std::string_view text); - buildIndex walks the file from the start and records the offset of each record's data (just after its length). If a length runs past the end of the file, it stops there and sets truncated (a file cut short by a crash, or corrupt). Trailing bytes too short for a length also count as truncated. - recordAt returns a view of record i 's data inside the file (no copy), or an empty span for an index out of range. - findRecord returns the number of the first record whose bytes equal text .

title: 3.05  Seqlocks and Snapshots
body: Publishing a state that changes constantly, such as a game's player positions for an external tool - why readers can see torn data, double buffering, and the seqlock - a sequence counter that lets readers detect a write in progress and retry without ever blocking the writer. The problem: torn reads A game updates a block of shared state every frame: player position, health, the current level. An external tool (an overlay, a stats panel, a test harness) reads it whenever it likes. If the tool reads while the game is halfway through writing, it can see the new x with the old y: a torn read , a state that never existed. A lock would fix it, but a lock lets a slow reader stall the game, which is exactly what must not happen. We want: the writer never waits; readers always get a consistent snapshot, retrying if needed. Double buffering Keep two copies of the state and an index saying which one is current. The writer fills the other copy, then flips the index (atomically, with release ordering). Readers read the index (acquire), then copy that buffer. It is simple, but not quite safe on its own: a reader that is slow enough could still be copying buffer A when the writer, two frames later, starts filling A again. It works when readers are known to be fast compared with the update rate; otherwise add a check, which leads to the seqlock. The seqlock A seqlock pairs the data with a sequence counter : - The writer increments the counter (it becomes odd : "writing"), writes the data, then increments it again ( even : "stable"). - A reader reads the counter; if it is odd, a write is in progress, try again. Otherwise it copies the data, then reads the counter again. If the counter changed, a write happened during the copy, so the copy may be torn: try again. cpp-norun // writer: never waits seq.store(s + 1, std::memory_order_relaxed); // odd: writing std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release); copyIn(data, state); seq.store(s + 2, std::memory_order_release); // even: stable // reader: retries instead of blocking anyone for (;;) { const std::uint32_t before{ seq.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; if (before & 1) continue; // writer is busy State copy{ copyOut(data) }; std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire); if (seq.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == before) return copy; // nothing changed meanwhile } The writer never blocks, readers never block the writer, and a reader only retries in the rare case that it overlapped a write. Linux uses seqlocks for the system clock for exactly these reasons. Doing it correctly in C++ The data is read while it may be being written, which is a data race and undefined behaviour if the data is ordinary memory, however carefully the counter is checked afterwards. The clean way is to store the payload in atomic words and copy it word by word with relaxed atomic loads and stores; the fences then order those against the counter. That is what the practice does: the state is any trivially copyable struct, copied into and out of an array of std::atomic<std::uint64_t . Requirements and limits: - One writer at a time. Several writers need a lock among themselves (they can still let readers use the seqlock). - The state must be trivially copyable: plain numbers and arrays, no pointers into a process's heap. - Readers must cope with retrying; under constant updates of a huge state they could retry several times, so keep the published state small.

title: A seqlock
body: Build the seqlock of lesson 3.05 for any trivially copyable state, storing the payload in atomic words so that reading during a write is not undefined behaviour: cpp template <typename T class SeqLock { public: static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T ); void write(const T& value); std::optional<T tryRead() const; T read() const; std::uint32_t sequence() const; }; - write (one writer only): increment the sequence (now odd), copy the value into the words with relaxed atomic stores, increment the sequence again (now even). Use the fences from the lesson. - tryRead makes one attempt: if the sequence is odd, or changes during the copy, return std::nullopt ; otherwise the copied value. - read retries tryRead until it succeeds. - sequence returns the current counter (twice the number of completed writes when nothing is writing). - Before the first write, reads return a value-initialised T .

title: A message ring in shared memory
match: A message ring in shared memory
body: Lesson 3.03's ring carries fixed-size numbers. Real messages vary in size. Build a single-producer, single-consumer ring of variable-size messages inside one block of memory, as a game would use to stream events to an external tool through a file mapping. cpp class MessageRing { public: static constexpr std::uint32_t MAGIC{ 0x474E4952 }; // "RING" static std::size_t bytesNeeded(std::uint32_t capacity); MessageRing(void memory, std::uint32_t capacity, bool create); bool valid() const; bool send(std::span<const std::uint8_t payload); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t receive(); std::uint64_t pending() const; }; Layout. The block starts with a header, then capacity bytes of data area. capacity is a power of two and at least 64. The header holds the magic, the capacity, and two std::atomic<std::uint64_t counters on separate cache lines: head (total bytes ever written to the data area) and tail (total bytes ever consumed). bytesNeeded returns the header's size plus capacity . With create false, the object reads the capacity from the header; valid checks the magic. Records. A message is written at data position head % capacity as a 4-byte length followed by the payload, the whole record padded to a multiple of 8 bytes. Because every record starts at a multiple of 8, there are always at least 8 bytes before the end of the data area. Wrapping. If a record does not fit in the space before the end of the data area, the producer writes a wrap marker (length 0xFFFFFFFF ) at the current position, counts the rest of the data area as used, and writes the record at the start. A record never straddles the end. send returns false, changing nothing, if the payload is longer than capacity / 2 - 4 bytes, or if there is not enough free space ( capacity - (head - tail) ) for the record plus any wrap padding. It writes the record then publishes the new head with release ordering. receive returns std::nullopt when empty. It skips a wrap marker (moving tail to the start of the next lap), reads the record, and publishes the new tail with release ordering. pending is head - tail .

title: 4.01  Named Kernel Objects
body: Events, mutexes and semaphores that several processes can open by name - creating versus opening, ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS, the session namespaces, signalled and non-signalled states, and why a kernel object outlives the handle that made it until the last handle closes. Synchronisation that crosses processes std::mutex and std::condition_variable work between threads of one process. Between processes you use kernel objects : objects that live in the Windows kernel, reached through handles, and that can be given a name so another process can open the same one. Object Create Open Used for --- --- --- --- event CreateEventW OpenEventW "something happened": new data, stop now mutex CreateMutexW OpenMutexW exclusive access to a shared resource semaphore CreateSemaphoreW OpenSemaphoreW allow up to N at once waitable timer CreateWaitableTimerW OpenWaitableTimerW signal at a time or interval Processes, threads, file mappings and pipes are kernel objects too, which is why the same wait functions work on all of them. Create or open The usual pattern is for both sides to call Create... with the same name: cpp-norun HANDLE ready{ CreateEventW(&security, FALSE, FALSE, LR"(Local\xenon-telemetry-ready)") }; if (!ready) / failed: GetLastError() /; const bool someoneElseCreatedIt{ GetLastError() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS }; If the object exists, Create... opens it instead (and the creation parameters, such as the initial state, are ignored), so it does not matter which process starts first. Open... fails with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND if the object does not exist, which is what you want when only one side should create it (a client must not create the server's objects). ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS is how a single-instance application detects a copy already running (lesson 6.01). Note that GetLastError() must be read immediately after the call, and that the call succeeds in that case. Names and namespaces Kernel object names follow the rules from lesson 3.01: Local\ (the default) within the session, Global\ across sessions. Names share one namespace across object types: an event and a mutex cannot both be called xenon-lock (the second create fails with ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE ). Choose specific names, and prefix them with your product and purpose. Signalled or not Every waitable kernel object is either signalled or non-signalled , and the wait functions block until an object is signalled: Object Signalled when --- --- event it has been set (lesson 4.02) mutex nobody owns it semaphore its count is above zero process, thread it has ended waitable timer its time has come Some objects change state when a wait succeeds on them (a mutex becomes owned, a semaphore's count drops, an auto-reset event resets); others stay signalled (a process stays ended). Lifetime A kernel object exists as long as any process holds a handle to it. When the last handle closes, the object, and its name, are gone. Practical consequences: - If the creator exits but another process still has the object open, the object stays and keeps its state. - A process that crashes has all its handles closed by Windows, so it cannot leave objects behind for ever. - To keep an object available between runs you need some process to hold it open, typically a long-running service. Security Every named object can carry a security descriptor saying who may open it and with which rights. The default allows the creating user and administrators, which is usually right for Local\ objects. Objects shared with a service or another user need an explicit descriptor (lesson 5.05). And because anyone allowed can create an object with your name first , a client should check it really talks to your server, not an impostor.

title: A namespace of kernel objects
body: Model how named kernel objects are created, opened and destroyed (lesson 4.01): cpp enum class Kind { Event, Mutex, Semaphore }; enum class Result { Created, Opened, NotFound, WrongType }; class ObjectNamespace { public: Result create(Kind kind, const std::string& name, int& handle); Result open(Kind kind, const std::string& name, int& handle); void close(int handle); bool exists(const std::string& name) const; int handleCount(const std::string& name) const; }; - Handles are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... and never reused. Each successful create or open returns a new handle to the object. - create : if no object has that name, it makes one and returns Created . If an object of the same kind exists, it opens it and returns Opened (the ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS case). If an object of a different kind has the name, WrongType and no handle. - open : like create, but returns NotFound instead of creating. - Names are compared ignoring case . - close releases a handle; when an object's last handle closes, the object and its name are gone. Closing an unknown or already closed handle does nothing. - handleCount is the number of open handles to the named object (0 if none).

title: 4.02  Events and Waiting
body: Signalling between processes with events - auto-reset versus manual-reset, SetEvent and ResetEvent, the lost-wakeup trap and how to avoid it, WaitForMultipleObjects for waiting on several things at once, and the return values every wait must check. An event is a flag the kernel can wait on An event is a kernel object with two states, set (signalled) and reset (non-signalled). A process waits on it with WaitForSingleObject ; another process sets it with SetEvent . The waiting thread uses no CPU while it waits. cpp-norun // producer, after putting a message in the shared ring buffer ring.send(message); SetEvent(dataReady); // consumer for (;;) { if (WaitForSingleObject(dataReady, 1000) == WAIT_TIMEOUT) { / check the producer is alive / continue; } while (auto m{ ring.receive() }) handle( m); } Shared memory carries the data; the event carries the "look now". Together they give a fast channel that neither spins nor polls. Auto-reset and manual-reset The second argument of CreateEventW chooses the kind: Kind When set When a wait succeeds --- --- --- auto-reset ( FALSE ) wakes one waiting thread the event resets itself manual-reset ( TRUE ) wakes all waiting threads stays set until someone calls ResetEvent - Use auto-reset for "there is work": each set lets one waiter through. - Use manual-reset for a state that everyone should see: "shutting down", "initialisation complete". Once set, every current and future wait returns at once. Events do not count Setting an auto-reset event that is already set does nothing: two SetEvent calls before the consumer wakes up still wake it only once. An event is a flag, not a counter. That is fine as long as the consumer, once woken, processes everything that is waiting (the while loop above), not just one item. If you need to count, use a semaphore (lesson 4.03). The lost wakeup The classic bug is checking for work and then waiting, with a gap between: cpp-norun if (ring.empty()) // 1. consumer sees nothing { // 2. producer sends and calls SetEvent ResetEvent(dataReady); // 3. consumer clears the signal it never saw WaitForSingleObject(dataReady, INFINITE); // 4. waits for ever, with a message waiting } The safe pattern never resets a manual event while data may be waiting, and always re-checks the data after waking : with an auto-reset event, wait first, then drain everything; with timeouts on every wait, a missed signal costs at most one timeout instead of a hang. Waiting for several things A consumer usually needs to wake for more than one reason: new data, or "stop", or "the producer process died". WaitForMultipleObjects waits on up to 64 handles at once: cpp-norun HANDLE handles { stopEvent, producerProcess, dataReady }; switch (const DWORD r{ WaitForMultipleObjects(3, handles, FALSE, 5000) }) { case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 0: return; // stop requested case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 1: reportProducerDied(); return; // its process handle became signalled case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 2: drain(); break; // data ready case WAIT_TIMEOUT: break; // nothing in 5 s default: / WAIT_FAILED or WAIT_ABANDONED_0 + i (lesson 4.03) / break; } With bWaitAll FALSE , it returns when any is signalled and tells you which (the lowest index if several are). Put the most important handle first: if stop and data arrive together, stop wins. Waiting on the other process's handle alongside your event is how a shared-memory channel learns that its peer has gone, which shared memory alone never tells you. Check every wait Return Meaning --- --- WAIT_OBJECT_0 + i object i is signalled WAIT_TIMEOUT the time ran out WAIT_ABANDONED_0 + i object i is a mutex whose owner died (lesson 4.03) WAIT_FAILED an error, such as an invalid handle: GetLastError() Code that treats every non-timeout return as success sooner or later acts on an abandoned mutex or a closed handle as if all were well.

title: Auto-reset, manual-reset and waiting for several
match: Auto-reset, manual-reset and waiting for several
body: Model events and WaitForMultipleObjects (lesson 4.02): cpp class Event { public: explicit Event(bool manualReset, bool initiallySet = false); void set(); void reset(); bool isSet() const; bool tryWait(); }; struct Waitable { Event event; bool processEnded; }; std::optional<std::size_t waitAny(std::vector<Waitable & objects); - tryWait is a wait with a zero timeout: if the event is set it succeeds, and an auto-reset event resets itself; a manual-reset event stays set. If not set, it returns false. - set and reset change the state; setting an event that is already set does nothing more (events do not count). - waitAny is WaitForMultipleObjects with "any" and a zero timeout: each entry is either an event ( event not null) or a process handle ( event null; signalled when processEnded ). It returns the lowest index that is signalled, consuming an auto-reset event at that index only, or std::nullopt if none is.

title: 4.03  Mutexes, Semaphores and Abandonment
body: Exclusive access across processes with a named mutex - ownership, recursion, releasing, and WAIT_ABANDONED when the owner died holding it - and semaphores for limiting how many can do something at once. A mutex across processes A named mutex gives exclusive access to something several processes share: a block of shared memory with a structure too large for atomics, a log file, a device. cpp-norun HANDLE lock{ CreateMutexW(&security, FALSE, LR"(Local\xenon-settings-lock)") }; switch (WaitForSingleObject(lock, 2000)) { case WAIT_OBJECT_0: editSharedSettings(); ReleaseMutex(lock); break; case WAIT_ABANDONED: // We own it now, but the previous owner died while holding it: the data may be half-written. repairOrResetSharedSettings(); ReleaseMutex(lock); break; case WAIT_TIMEOUT: / someone has held it for 2 s: report, retry later / break; } A successful wait makes the calling thread the owner; only that thread may ReleaseMutex . A Win32 mutex is recursive : the owner can wait on it again without blocking, and must release it once per successful wait. Releasing a mutex you do not own fails with ERROR_NOT_OWNER . A kernel mutex costs a system call per wait and release, far more than a std::mutex within a process. Use it for coarse operations (edit the settings block, append a record), not in a tight loop. Abandonment What if a process crashes while holding the mutex? A std::mutex in shared memory would stay locked for ever. A kernel mutex is better: when its owning thread ends, Windows releases it and marks it abandoned , and the next successful wait returns WAIT_ABANDONED instead of WAIT_OBJECT_0 . That return means: you now own the mutex, but whatever it protected may be inconsistent , because the dead owner may have stopped halfway through an update. Do not treat it as plain success. Validate the shared data (checksums and version numbers in the shared header pay for themselves here), repair or reinitialise it, and carry on. The abandoned state is cleared once reported, so only the first waiter gets the warning. Semaphores A semaphore holds a count between 0 and a maximum. A successful wait takes one from the count (blocking while it is 0); ReleaseSemaphore(handle, n, &previous) adds n . cpp-norun // At most 4 builds may run at once, across every process that opens this name HANDLE slots{ CreateSemaphoreW(nullptr, 4, 4, LR"(Local\xenon-build-slots)") }; if (WaitForSingleObject(slots, INFINITE) == WAIT_OBJECT_0) { runBuild(); ReleaseSemaphore(slots, 1, nullptr); } Unlike a mutex, a semaphore has no owner : any thread or process may release it. That makes it suitable for producer and consumer counting (the producer releases one per item, the consumer waits once per item), and means there is no abandonment : if a process dies holding a "slot", the count is lost for good. A watchdog that tracks which processes took slots, or a design where slots are tied to process handles, guards against that. Choosing Need Use --- --- exclusive access, must survive a crashed owner mutex (and handle WAIT_ABANDONED ) at most N at once semaphore count items between a producer and a consumer semaphore "something happened" or "a state is now true" event fast exclusive access inside one process std::mutex

title: Mutex ownership and abandonment
body: Model a Win32 mutex and semaphore (lesson 4.03) with a zero-timeout wait: cpp enum class Wait { Acquired, Abandoned, Timeout }; class Mutex { public: Wait tryWait(int thread); bool release(int thread); void threadEnded(int thread); std::optional<int owner() const; }; class Semaphore { public: Semaphore(int initial, int maximum); bool tryWait(); bool release(int count); int count() const; }; Mutex - If unowned, a wait makes thread the owner with a recursion count of 1 and returns Acquired , or Abandoned if the mutex was abandoned (the abandoned mark is then cleared). - If thread already owns it, the count goes up and the result is Acquired . - If another thread owns it, Timeout . - release by the owner lowers the count, freeing the mutex at 0; it returns false (and changes nothing) for a thread that does not own it. - threadEnded : if that thread owns the mutex, it becomes unowned and abandoned . Semaphore - tryWait takes one from the count if it is above 0. - release adds count unless that would exceed the maximum: then it returns false and changes nothing.

title: 4.04  Window Messages Between Programs
body: Programs with windows can talk through messages - finding another program's window, WM_COPYDATA for sending a block of data, registered message numbers, message-only windows, SendMessage versus PostMessage, and the privilege boundary UIPI puts in the way. Messages are already IPC Every window receives messages through its message loop (Win32 API course, lesson 1.03), and a program can send messages to another program's windows. For two desktop programs that both have windows, this is the simplest IPC there is: no pipes, no shared memory, and the message arrives in the receiver's normal message loop on its UI thread. Finding the window The sender needs the receiver's window handle ( HWND ): cpp-norun HWND target{ FindWindowW(L"XenonMainWindowClass", nullptr) }; // by window class name Give your windows a distinctive class name so they can be found reliably; titles change with documents and languages. Background programs without a visible window create a message-only window ( CreateWindowExW with parent HWND_MESSAGE ): it has no screen presence, cannot be enumerated by accident, but can be found with FindWindowExW(HWND_MESSAGE, nullptr, className, nullptr) and receives messages. WM_COPYDATA Ordinary messages carry only two numbers ( wParam and lParam ), and a pointer in them would be meaningless in the other process. WM_COPYDATA is the exception: Windows copies a block of data into the receiver for the duration of the message. cpp-norun // sender const std::wstring path{ LR"(C:\Projects\demo.xproj)" }; COPYDATASTRUCT cds{}; cds.dwData = 1; // your own "message type" cds.cbData = static_cast<DWORD ((path.size() + 1) sizeof(wchar_t)); cds.lpData = const_cast<wchar_t (path.c_str()); DWORD_PTR result{}; SendMessageTimeoutW(target, WM_COPYDATA, reinterpret_cast<WPARAM (myWindow), reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (&cds), SMTO_ABORTIFHUNG, 2000, &result); // receiver, in the window procedure case WM_COPYDATA: { const auto cds{ reinterpret_cast<const COPYDATASTRUCT (lParam) }; if (cds- dwData == 1 && cds- cbData = sizeof(wchar_t) && cds- cbData % sizeof(wchar_t) == 0) openProject(std::wstring(static_cast<const wchar_t (cds- lpData), cds- cbData / sizeof(wchar_t) - 1)); return TRUE; } Rules: - The data is valid only while the receiver handles the message . Copy what you need before returning. - WM_COPYDATA must be sent , not posted, because the copy only lives during the call. Use SendMessageTimeoutW with a timeout so a hung receiver cannot hang the sender. - Validate everything: dwData , the size, and the content. Any program on the desktop can send you WM_COPYDATA . Registered messages For simple notifications without data ("reload your settings"), define your own message number. Numbers from WM_APP up are private to one program; to agree on a number between programs, register a name: cpp-norun const UINT reloadMessage{ RegisterWindowMessageW(L"Xenon.ReloadSettings") }; // same number in every process PostMessageW(HWND_BROADCAST, reloadMessage, 0, 0); // tell every top-level window SendMessage and PostMessage - PostMessageW puts the message in the receiver's queue and returns immediately. Fire and forget; works only with plain numbers. - SendMessageW waits until the receiver has processed the message and returns its result. If the receiver is hung, so is the sender, which is why cross-process sends should always be SendMessageTimeoutW . UIPI: the privilege boundary User Interface Privilege Isolation stops a process from sending most messages to a window of a process running at a higher integrity level . A normal program cannot send WM_COPYDATA to a program running as administrator: the message is silently dropped. The elevated program can allow specific messages with ChangeWindowMessageFilterEx(hwnd, WM_COPYDATA, MSGFLT_ALLOW, nullptr) , after which it must treat every such message as coming from a less trusted sender. When not to use messages Window messages need a window and a message loop on both sides, run on the UI thread (so heavy work blocks the interface), and are limited to one desktop. For services, background workers, large data or high rates, use pipes or shared memory. For "hand a file to the running instance of my editor", they are perfect.

title: Packing WM_COPYDATA
body: Build and check the data of a WM_COPYDATA message (lesson 4.04) that asks a running editor to open a file. On Windows the path is UTF-16, wchar_t ; here it is std::u16string , which has the same 2-byte characters on every compiler. cpp struct CopyData { std::uint64_t type; std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes; }; constexpr std::uint64_t OPEN_FILE{ 1 }; CopyData openFileMessage(const std::u16string& path); std::optional<std::u16string readOpenFile(const CopyData& message); - openFileMessage puts the path's characters into bytes , each as 2 little-endian bytes, followed by a terminating zero character (2 zero bytes), with type OPEN_FILE . - readOpenFile accepts only messages that any program could have sent, so it checks everything: type must be OPEN_FILE ; the size must be even and at least 4 bytes (one character and the terminator); the last character must be the terminating zero; no other character may be zero; the path may be at most 32 767 characters. It returns the path without the terminator, or std::nullopt .

title: 4.05  Deadlocks and Timeouts
body: How cooperating processes get stuck waiting for each other - lock-order deadlocks, request-reply deadlocks over pipes, waiting for a peer that died - and the disciplines that prevent them - a global lock order, timeouts on every wait, never holding a lock across IPC, and watchdogs. Stuck for ever A deadlock is a set of threads or processes each waiting for something only another of them can provide. Nothing crashes, nothing logs an error; the programs simply stop responding. Across processes they are harder to find than within one, because no single debugger sees both sides. Lock-order deadlocks Two processes and two named mutexes: text Process A: lock "settings", then lock "cache" Process B: lock "cache", then lock "settings" If A takes "settings" and B takes "cache" at the same moment, each then waits for the other's mutex, for ever. Drawn as a wait-for graph (an arrow from each waiter to the holder of what it wants), a deadlock is a cycle : A waits for B, B waits for A. The fix is a global lock order : give every lock a rank and always take them in increasing order, in every process. Then a cycle cannot form, because every arrow points "up" the ranking. Writing the order down (in the code next to the names) is the cheapest deadlock prevention there is. Request-reply deadlocks Locks are not the only thing you wait for. Over pipes: - Both sides send a large message at the same time, before reading. Both pipes fill, both writes block, neither side ever reads (the stdio version was in lesson 1.04). - A server, while handling client A's request, calls into client A (a callback), while client A is blocked waiting for the reply to its request. - Process A sends a WM_COPYDATA to B while B is blocked in SendMessageW to A. The disciplines that prevent these: - Never hold a lock while doing IPC. Copy what you need, release, then send or wait. A lock held across a pipe write turns a slow peer into a frozen one. - Read continuously. A side that may need to receive while it is sending must read on another thread or with overlapped I/O. - Avoid synchronous calls back into the caller. Make callbacks asynchronous (post a message, queue an event) or design the protocol so only one side initiates requests. Waiting for the dead A process that died while you wait for its reply, its event or its mutex is the most common "deadlock" of all. Kernel objects help (pipes break, mutexes are abandoned), but an event that a dead process will never set just stays unset. - Time out every wait. INFINITE belongs only where something else (a stop event, a process handle in the same WaitForMultipleObjects ) guarantees an end. After a timeout, check whether the peer is alive (wait on its process handle with 0 timeout) before deciding to wait again or give up. - Include the peer's process handle in multi-object waits (lesson 4.02). - Use a watchdog for long-running systems: each worker updates a heartbeat (a counter in shared memory, or a periodic message); a supervisor that sees no heartbeat for a few seconds treats the worker as hung, ends it and starts another (lesson 6.02). Finding a deadlock When it happens anyway: 1. Attach a debugger to each stuck process and look at every thread's call stack: you will see each waiting in WaitForSingleObject , ReadFile or SendMessage . 2. Find out what each is waiting for: which handle, which object name. Process Explorer's handle view (and the "wait chain" view in Resource Monitor's Analyze Wait Chain) shows which objects each process has and who holds what. 3. Draw the wait-for graph. The cycle is the bug; the fix is usually an ordering rule or a lock released before an IPC call.

title: Finding deadlocks
body: Given who holds which lock and who is waiting for which, find a deadlock (lesson 4.05), and check an acquisition sequence against a lock order: cpp using Holders = std::map<std::string, std::string ; // lock - process holding it using Waits = std::map<std::string, std::string ; // process - lock it is waiting for std::optional<std::vector<std::string findDeadlock(const Holders& holders, const Waits& waits); std::optional<std::string orderViolation(const std::vector<std::string & locksTaken, const std::map<std::string, int & rank); - findDeadlock builds the wait-for graph: a process waiting for a lock waits for that lock's holder. If there is a cycle, it returns the processes in the cycle in waiting order (each waits for the next, the last for the first), starting with the alphabetically smallest process in the cycle. Otherwise std::nullopt . A process waiting for a free lock, or for a lock held by a process that is not waiting, is not deadlocked. - orderViolation takes the locks one process acquires, in order (it holds them all), and returns the first lock taken while a lock of equal or higher rank is already held, or std::nullopt if the order is respected. Locks missing from rank are not checked.

title: A lock manager
body: Build a lock service for a group of cooperating processes: named recursive locks with a declared order, fair queues of waiters, refusal of requests that would deadlock, and correct handling of a process that dies holding locks. It brings milestone 4 together in one model. cpp enum class Outcome { Acquired, AcquiredAbandoned, Waiting, Deadlock, OrderViolation }; using Grant = std::pair<int, Outcome ; // (process, how it got the lock) class LockManager { public: void setRank(const std::string& lock, int rank); Outcome acquire(int process, const std::string& lock); std::vector<Grant release(int process, const std::string& lock); std::vector<Grant processDied(int process); std::optional<int owner(const std::string& lock) const; std::vector<std::string held(int process) const; std::vector<int waiters(const std::string& lock) const; }; acquire checks, in this order: 1. If process already owns lock : its recursion count goes up; Acquired . 2. Order : if the lock has a rank and the process holds any other ranked lock of equal or higher rank: OrderViolation (nothing changes). 3. If the lock is free: the process owns it with count 1; Acquired , or AcquiredAbandoned if its last owner died holding it (that mark is then cleared). 4. Deadlock : if waiting would close a cycle (the owner, directly or through a chain of waiting processes, is waiting for a lock process holds): Deadlock (it does not wait). 5. Otherwise the process joins the end of the lock's queue: Waiting . A process waits for at most one lock at a time. release lowers the owner's count (doing nothing for a non-owner); at zero the lock passes to the first waiter in its queue, who gets it with count 1. It returns the grants made (empty or one), as Acquired . processDied removes the process from every queue, and releases every lock it owned completely (whatever the count). Each such lock passes to its first waiter with AcquiredAbandoned , or, if nobody waits, stays free but marked abandoned for the next acquirer. It returns the grants in order of lock name. held lists a process's locks sorted by name; waiters a lock's queue in order.

title: 5.01  Sockets on One Machine
body: Using sockets for local IPC - Winsock start-up, a TCP server bound to 127.0.0.1 and never to every interface, letting the system choose a port and publishing it in a file, Unix domain sockets on Windows, and how sockets compare with named pipes. Why sockets locally Named pipes are Windows-specific. Sockets are everywhere: every language, every operating system, the same API whether the other end is in the next process or on another continent. Many tools use a local socket for IPC: debuggers' remote protocols, language tooling, local web dashboards, game editors talking to a running game. The Networking course covers sockets in depth; this lesson covers what is special about using them on one machine . A loopback server cpp-norun WSADATA wsa{}; WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2, 2), &wsa); // once per process SOCKET listener{ socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_TCP) }; sockaddr_in addr{}; addr.sin_family = AF_INET; addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_LOOPBACK); // 127.0.0.1 only addr.sin_port = htons(0); // 0: let the system pick a free port bind(listener, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), sizeof(addr)); listen(listener, SOMAXCONN); int length{ sizeof(addr) }; getsockname(listener, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), &length); const unsigned short port{ ntohs(addr.sin_port) }; // the port it actually got SOCKET client{ accept(listener, nullptr, nullptr) }; // wait for a connection // recv / send on client , with the framing of lesson 2.03 Three choices matter for local IPC: 1. Bind to 127.0.0.1 (loopback), never to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces). Bound to everything, your private IPC endpoint is reachable from the network, and Windows Firewall asks the user whether to allow it. Bound to loopback, only local processes can connect and no prompt appears. 2. Let the system choose the port (port 0). Fixed port numbers collide with other programs and with a second copy of your own. 3. Publish the port where the client can find it: a small file in the user's profile ( %LOCALAPPDATA%\Xenon\agent.port ) holding the port, the server's PID, and a random token the client must present (lesson 5.05). The client reads the file, connects to 127.0.0.1:port , and proves it read the file by sending the token. Unix domain sockets on Windows Windows 10 (version 1803) and later support AF_UNIX stream sockets: socket endpoints that are paths in the file system instead of ports. cpp-norun include <afunix.h SOCKET s{ socket(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0) }; sockaddr_un addr{}; addr.sun_family = AF_UNIX; strcpy_s(addr.sun_path, R"(C:\Users\sam\AppData\Local\Xenon\agent.sock)"); bind(s, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), sizeof(addr)); Advantages: no ports at all, and access is controlled by the file's permissions : put it in a folder only the user can read and other users cannot connect. Code written for Linux and macOS (which have had Unix sockets for decades) ports with little change. Delete the socket file before binding again ( bind fails if it exists) and when shutting down. Sockets versus named pipes Named pipe Loopback TCP AF_UNIX --- --- --- --- Portable Windows only everywhere Windows 10+, Linux, macOS Who can connect controlled by a security descriptor any local process controlled by file permissions Discovery a name you choose a port, published somewhere a path Message mode yes no (frame yourself) no Client identity GetNamedPipeClientProcessId , impersonation nothing built in limited Across machines yes (SMB) yes no For a Windows-only program that wants strong access control, named pipes remain a good choice. For anything that might be portable, or that a tool in another language must talk to, prefer sockets, and design the security in from the start.

title: Loopback endpoints and port files
body: Lesson 5.01's server binds to loopback on a system-chosen port and publishes it in a file. Write both sides of that file, and the checks a client makes: cpp struct Endpoint { std::string host; std::uint16_t port; }; struct PortFile { std::uint16_t port; std::uint32_t pid; std::string token; }; bool isLoopback(const std::string& host); std::optional<Endpoint parseEndpoint(const std::string& text); std::string writePortFile(const PortFile& f); std::optional<PortFile readPortFile(const std::string& text); - isLoopback : localhost (any case), ::1 , or an IPv4 address 127.a.b.c with each part 0 to 255. - parseEndpoint reads host:port or ::1 :port (IPv6 in brackets). The port is 1 to 65535, digits only. The host must be loopback; anything else gives std::nullopt . - writePortFile writes three lines: port=50123 , pid=4120 , token=... , each ending in \n . - readPortFile reads them back in any order, ignoring blank lines and \r ; all three keys must appear exactly once, the port must be valid, the pid a number, and the token 32 lowercase hex characters.

title: 5.02  Designing a Message Protocol
body: The decisions behind a protocol two programs will speak for years - a handshake with a magic number and version, an envelope with type, id, flags and length, kinds of messages, version negotiation, error replies, and writing it all down. A protocol is a contract Two programs talking over a pipe or a socket depend on a set of agreements: what bytes come first, what each message means, what happens when one side is newer than the other. That contract is the protocol , and it outlives the code: once two released versions of your programs speak it, changing it means staying compatible. A little design up front saves years of trouble. The handshake The first exchange on a new connection should establish that both sides speak the same protocol: text client - server HELLO magic "XIPC", version 2.3, client name "xenon-editor" server - client WELCOME version 2.1, server name "xenon-agent", capabilities - A magic number catches connections from something that is not your client at all (a port scanner, an old program on a reused port, a browser) before you try to parse its bytes as messages. - A version lets both sides agree on the dialect. A common scheme: the major version changes when old and new cannot talk at all; the minor version changes when features are added compatibly. Both sides use the same major and the lower of the two minors, and simply avoid features newer than that. - Capabilities (a list of feature names or flag bits) are an alternative or complement to minor versions: "I support compression and batch requests". If the handshake fails, say why (a message with an error code, if possible) and close the connection. The envelope Every message after the handshake shares one outer structure, the envelope , so that any message can be framed, routed and logged without understanding its payload: Field Size Purpose --- --- --- length 4 frame length (lesson 2.03) type 1 or 2 what kind of message flags 1 bits such as "this is a reply", "this is an error" id 4 matches replies to requests (lesson 5.04) payload rest type-specific content (lesson 5.03) Kinds of messages Almost every protocol needs the same three kinds: - Requests : "do this and tell me the result". Carry an id. - Responses : the result of one request, carrying its id; either a success with data or an error with a code and a message. - Events (notifications): sent without being asked, such as "file changed" or "build finished". No reply expected. Keep error replies structured: a numeric code that programs can act on ("not found", "bad argument", "busy", "not supported in this version") plus a human-readable message for logs. Rules that keep a protocol healthy - Unknown message types : reply "not supported" (for requests) or ignore (for events). Never crash, never close the connection. - Unknown fields : skip them, if the encoding allows (lesson 5.03). This is what lets a newer sender add fields that an older receiver ignores. - Limits : maximum message size, maximum outstanding requests, maximum string lengths. Write them in the specification and enforce them. - Text or binary? Text (JSON) is easy to debug and to speak from any language; binary is compact and fast. JSON lines or JSON with a length header (like the Language Server Protocol) are fine for most tools; reach for binary when messages are frequent or large. - Write it down. A short specification (one page with the envelope, the message types and their payloads, versions and limits) is worth more than any amount of "the code is the documentation", especially when the other side is written by someone else or in another language.

title: Handshake and envelope
body: Implement the opening of lesson 5.02's protocol: the handshake, version negotiation, and the envelope every later message uses. cpp struct Version { std::uint16_t major, minor; }; struct Envelope { std::uint8_t type; std::uint8_t flags; std::uint32_t id; std::vector<std::uint8_t payload; }; std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeHello(Version v); std::optional<Version decodeHello(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::optional<Version negotiate(Version client, const std::vector<Version & serverSupports); std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeEnvelope(const Envelope& e); std::optional<Envelope decodeEnvelope(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); - A hello is 8 bytes: X I P C , then the major and minor versions as 2-byte little-endian numbers. decodeHello checks the length and the magic. - negotiate : the server supports one or more major versions, each with its highest minor. If it supports the client's major, the result is that major with the lower of the two minors; otherwise std::nullopt . - An envelope is type (1 byte), flags (1 byte), id (4 bytes little-endian), then the payload. decodeEnvelope needs at least those 6 bytes.

title: 5.03  Serialising Data
body: Turning values into bytes both sides read the same way - fixed-width little-endian numbers, length-prefixed UTF-8 strings, variable-length integers and zigzag encoding, tag-length-value records that let new fields be added without breaking old readers, and when to use JSON or a library instead. Never send a struct's memory The tempting shortcut is send(socket, &settings, sizeof(settings)) . It breaks as soon as anything differs between the two sides: padding between members, the size of long , a std::string member (a pointer into the sender's heap), a newer version with an added field. Serialise instead: write each value in a defined byte format, and read it back the same way. Building blocks Fixed-width integers , in a stated byte order. Little-endian is the usual choice for new protocols between PCs: cpp-norun void putU32(std::vector<std::uint8_t & out, std::uint32_t v) { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 4; ++i) out.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t (v (8 i))); } Strings as a length followed by the bytes, in UTF-8 (convert from Windows' UTF-16 at the edge). Never rely on a terminating zero in the data. Booleans as one byte, 0 or 1; reject other values on reading. Floating point as the IEEE bit pattern ( std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t (f) ), which every modern machine shares. Variable-length integers Most numbers in messages are small (ids, counts, lengths), so spending 8 bytes on each is wasteful. A varint (LEB128) uses 7 bits per byte, with the top bit saying "more bytes follow": text 1 - 01 127 - 7F 128 - 80 01 (low 7 bits 0000000 with "more", then 1) 300 - AC 02 (300 = 0b10_0101100: 0101100 more = 0xAC, then 10 = 0x02) Small numbers take one byte, large ones up to ten. Negative numbers would always take ten bytes, so signed values are first zigzag-encoded , mapping 0, −1, 1, −2, 2, ... to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...: (n << 1) ^ (n 63) . Protocol Buffers uses exactly these two tricks. Readers must reject varints that are too long (more than 10 bytes) or that overflow, since the bytes come from another process. Tag, length, value For messages that will grow over time, write each field as a tag (which field), a length (how many bytes), and the value . A reader that meets a tag it does not know skips length bytes and carries on: text field 1 (name): 01 05 41 64 61 4D 73 tag 1, 5 bytes, "AdaMs" field 2 (volume): 02 01 4B tag 2, 1 byte, varint 75 field 9 (new!): 09 02 xx xx an old reader skips these 2 bytes This is what makes schema evolution possible: a newer sender adds fields; an older receiver ignores them; a newer receiver handles their absence from an older sender with defaults. The rules: never reuse a tag number for a different meaning, never change a field's type, and treat every field as optional. Or use JSON, or a library - JSON is self-describing text: easy to read in logs, available in every language, naturally tolerant of extra fields. It is slower and bigger, and numbers lose precision beyond 2^53. Excellent for tools and control messages. - Protocol Buffers , FlatBuffers , MessagePack and Cap'n Proto give compact binary formats, code generation from a schema, and the evolution rules above, already tested. For a large or long-lived protocol, a library beats a home-made format. Writing the building blocks yourself once, as this lesson's practice does, is still the best way to understand what those libraries do and to debug their output in a hex dump.

title: Varints and tagged fields
body: Write the serialisation building blocks of lesson 5.03 and use them for a message that can grow new fields: cpp void putVarint(std::vector<std::uint8_t & out, std::uint64_t value); std::optional<std::uint64_t getVarint(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & in, std::size_t& at); std::uint64_t zigzag(std::int64_t n); std::int64_t unzigzag(std::uint64_t z); struct Settings { std::optional<std::string name; std::optional<std::int64_t volume; std::optional<bool fullscreen; }; std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeSettings(const Settings& s); std::optional<Settings decodeSettings(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); - putVarint writes LEB128: 7 bits at a time, lowest first, top bit set on every byte except the last. getVarint reads one at at and moves at past it; it fails (returning std::nullopt ) if the bytes run out or the value would need more than 10 bytes. - zigzag maps 0, -1, 1, -2, 2 ... to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ...; unzigzag undoes it. - encodeSettings writes each field that is present, in tag order, as: tag (varint), length (varint), value. Tag 1 name : the UTF-8 bytes. Tag 2 volume : a varint of its zigzag. Tag 3 fullscreen : one byte, 0 or 1. - decodeSettings reads fields in any order. Unknown tags are skipped using their length. It fails on a truncated field, a field whose value does not fill its length exactly, a boolean other than 0 or 1, or a field that appears twice.

title: 5.04  Requests, Responses and Events
body: The flow of a conversation - request ids that match responses to requests, many requests in flight at once, timeouts and cancellation, events the server sends unasked, what ordering a stream does and does not guarantee, and safe retries. One at a time is too slow The simplest client sends a request and waits for the response before sending the next. That works, but a slow request (indexing a large project) blocks every quick one behind it, and every request pays the full round trip. Real protocols let several requests be in flight at once, which needs a way to tell responses apart. Correlation ids Each request carries an id chosen by the sender, unique among its outstanding requests (a counter is fine). The response carries the same id. The client keeps a table of pending requests: text id 41 findSymbol("Player") sent at 10.000 s id 42 formatFile("a.cpp") sent at 10.002 s id 43 ping sent at 10.003 s <- response id 43 "pong" (answered first: it was quick) <- response id 41 3 results <- response id 42 error "file locked" When a response arrives, the client looks up its id, removes the entry and delivers the result to whoever is waiting: a callback, a promise, or a coroutine. A response with an unknown id (late, after a timeout; or a bug) is logged and dropped. JSON-RPC 2.0, used by the Language Server Protocol, is exactly this: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":41,"method":"findSymbol","params":{...}} and a response {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":41,"result":...} , with notifications having no id . Timeouts and cancellation Every pending request needs a deadline . A periodic check (or a timer) finds requests past their deadline, removes them from the table and reports a timeout to the caller. If the server answers later, the response no longer matches anything and is dropped. A timeout on the client does not stop the work on the server. For expensive requests, add a cancel message ( cancel id 41 ) that the server uses to abandon the work. It may still send a response (a result or a "cancelled" error), and the client must cope with either. Events The server often needs to speak first: a file changed on disk, a build finished, a log line. These are events (notifications): a message type with no id and no response. Clients subscribe to the events they want, so a server does not flood clients with messages they will ignore. Events and responses share one connection, so the client's reading loop dispatches each incoming message by kind: response (match the id) or event (call the subscriber). Ordering A single stream (one pipe or TCP connection) delivers messages in the order they were sent . That gives useful guarantees: two events sent in order arrive in order, and a response sent after an event arrives after it. It does not mean responses come back in the order requests were sent, if the server handles requests concurrently. Design so that clients never depend on response order, only on ids. Across several connections there is no ordering at all. Retries and idempotency After a timeout or a dropped connection, the client may not know whether the server performed a request. Retrying is safe only if the request is idempotent : doing it twice has the same effect as once ( setVolume(70) , getStatus ). For requests that are not ( appendLog , createFile ), either let the server recognise a repeated request by a request key chosen by the client and return the original result, or report the uncertainty to the user instead of retrying blindly.

title: Pending requests
body: Keep the client's table of requests in flight (lesson 5.04): ids, deadlines, matching responses, and timeouts. cpp struct Done { std::uint32_t id; std::string method; std::string outcome; }; class PendingRequests { public: explicit PendingRequests(std::uint32_t maxInFlight); std::optional<std::uint32_t send(const std::string& method, std::uint64_t now, std::uint64_t timeout); std::optional<Done response(std::uint32_t id, const std::string& result); std::vector<Done expire(std::uint64_t now); std::vector<Done connectionLost(); std::size_t inFlight() const; }; - send gives the request the next id (1, 2, 3, ... never reused) and a deadline of now + timeout , and returns its id; if maxInFlight requests are already pending it returns std::nullopt and uses no id. - response completes the pending request with that id, returning it with outcome set to result ; an unknown id (late or bogus) returns std::nullopt . - expire completes every request whose deadline is at or before now , with outcome timeout , in id order. - connectionLost completes every pending request with outcome connection lost , in id order.

title: 5.05  Securing Local Communication
body: Local IPC is an attack surface - other users, other programs and even web pages can reach it. Access control on pipes and objects, preventing pipe squatting, checking which program you are talking to, tokens for localhost sockets, the Host header against DNS rebinding, validating every message, and the dangers of impersonation. "Local" is not "safe" It is tempting to assume that anything talking to your local pipe or port is your own program. It is not: - Other users on the same machine (a shared PC, a terminal server) can reach Global\ objects, pipes with default permissions, and every localhost port. - Any program the user runs, including malware with no special rights, can connect to the user's own pipes and ports. - Web pages in a browser can make requests to http://127.0.0.1:port and, with tricks such as DNS rebinding, read the answers. A local IPC endpoint that performs actions (run a build, write a file, read settings) is a privilege boundary. Design it like one. Access control on pipes and objects Named pipes, mappings, events and mutexes accept a security descriptor that lists who may open them. Written in SDDL (Security Descriptor Definition Language): cpp-norun // Only the current user (the owner) and SYSTEM may connect; nothing inherited from defaults. PSECURITY_DESCRIPTOR sd{}; ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptorW(L"D:P(A;;GA;;;OW)(A;;GA;;;SY)", SDDL_REVISION_1, &sd, nullptr); SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa{ sizeof(sa), sd, FALSE }; HANDLE pipe{ CreateNamedPipeW(name, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE, / ... /, &sa) }; LocalFree(sd); D:P is a protected list of permissions; (A;;GA;;;OW) allows ( A ) all access ( GA ) to the object's owner ( OW ); SY is the system account. For a service that desktop programs must reach, allow the specific group or user that should connect, not "Everyone". Pipe squatting A malicious program can create your pipe name before your server starts, and your client then connects to the impostor and sends it whatever it sends the real server. Defences: - The server creates its first instance with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE : if the name already exists, creation fails and the server knows something is wrong instead of silently sharing the name. - The client verifies the server: GetNamedPipeServerProcessId gives the server's PID; check that process's image path (and, for high-value cases, its code signature) is your server's. - Use names that include something an attacker cannot predict, such as a random value from a file only the user can read. Tokens for sockets Localhost TCP ports have no access control at all. The usual defence is a secret token : the server generates a random token at start-up ( BCryptGenRandom , at least 128 bits), writes it with the port into a file in the user's profile (readable only by that user), and requires every client to send it first. Compare tokens in constant time (examine every byte, whatever the first mismatch), so the comparison's timing cannot leak how many leading bytes were right. Browsers and DNS rebinding If your local server speaks HTTP, any web page can try to talk to it. Browsers' same-origin rules stop a page reading responses from 127.0.0.1 directly, but DNS rebinding gets around that: an attacker's domain first resolves to their server and then to 127.0.0.1 , so the browser thinks the page and your local server share an origin. Defences: - Check the Host header : accept only localhost:PORT or 127.0.0.1:PORT . A rebinding attack arrives with the attacker's domain in Host . - Check the Origin header on requests that change anything, and refuse unknown origins. - Require the token as well; a web page cannot read the user's token file. Validate everything, assume nothing Every byte from the other side is untrusted input: lengths (lesson 2.03), message types, string contents, paths. A path from a client must be checked before use (no .. escaping an allowed folder, no device names); a request to run something must never become a command line built from client text. Treat a local client with the same suspicion as a network client. Impersonation, carefully A pipe server can call ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to act with the client's rights, which is how a service safely opens a file on behalf of a user: Windows checks the user's permissions, not the service's. The danger runs the other way: a client that connects to a malicious server lets that server impersonate the client. Clients of pipes they do not fully trust should open them with SECURITY_SQOS_PRESENT SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION in CreateFileW 's flags, which lets the server identify the client but not act as it.

title: Guarding a localhost endpoint
body: A local tool exposes a small HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:PORT . Write the checks from lesson 5.05 that every request must pass before it is handled: cpp struct Request { std::string method; // "GET", "POST", ... std::map<std::string, std::string headers; // header names in lower case }; bool constantTimeEquals(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); std::string checkRequest(const Request& r, std::uint16_t port, const std::string& token); - constantTimeEquals : false if the lengths differ; otherwise it compares every byte, combining the differences, and only decides at the end (no early return on the first mismatch). - checkRequest returns "ok" or the reason for refusing, checking in this order: 1. host must be exactly localhost:PORT or 127.0.0.1:PORT : else "bad host" (the DNS rebinding defence). 2. For any method other than GET , an origin header, if present, must be http://localhost:PORT or http://127.0.0.1:PORT : else "bad origin" . 3. authorization must be Bearer followed by the token, compared in constant time: else "bad token" .

title: A small RPC layer
body: Put milestone 5 together: a remote procedure call layer that lets one process call named methods in another, with ids, errors, timeouts and events. The transport (a pipe or socket with framing) is left out: messages are passed as byte vectors, one per frame. Wire format. Every message is: a type byte ( 1 request, 2 response, 3 error, 4 event), a 4-byte little-endian id, then fields. A string is a 2-byte little-endian length and that many bytes. A list is a 1-byte count followed by that many strings. Type Fields after the id --- --- request method name (string), arguments (list) response result (string) error message (string) event event name (string), arguments (list); its id is 0 cpp using Message = std::vector<std::uint8_t ; using Method = std::function<std::string(const std::vector<std::string &) ; class RpcServer { public: void method(const std::string& name, Method fn); Message handle(const Message& incoming); Message event(const std::string& name, const std::vector<std::string & args); }; class RpcClient { public: Message call(const std::string& method, const std::vector<std::string & args, std::uint64_t now, std::uint64_t timeout, std::uint32_t& id); void handle(const Message& incoming); std::optional<std::string result(std::uint32_t id); std::optional<std::string error(std::uint32_t id); std::vector<std::uint32_t expire(std::uint64_t now); std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::vector<std::string takeEvents(); }; Server. method registers a handler. handle decodes a request and returns the reply: a response with the handler's result; an error unknown method NAME ; an error with the exception's message if the handler throws std::invalid_argument ; or, if the bytes are not a well-formed request (wrong type, truncated, leftover bytes), an error with id 0 and message malformed message . event encodes an event. Client. call gives the request the next id (from 1), remembers it with a deadline of now + timeout , sets id and returns the encoded request. handle decodes a message from the server: a response or error for a pending id completes that request (anything for an unknown id is ignored); an event is queued. Malformed messages are ignored. result and error return a completed request's outcome once , then forget it. expire removes and returns, in id order, pending requests whose deadline is at or before now . takeEvents returns the queued events in order and clears them.

title: 6.01  A Single-Instance Application
body: Making a second launch hand its work to the copy already running - a named mutex to detect the first instance, forwarding the command line through a pipe or WM_COPYDATA, resolving relative paths with the sender's folder, bringing the window to the front, and the races when two copies start at once. One copy, many launches Double-click a document while your editor is open, and the user expects the document to open in the running editor , not in a second copy. The pattern is common enough to have a name: a single-instance application . It combines three pieces from this course: a named kernel object to detect the first instance, an IPC channel to hand over the command line, and window activation. Detecting the first instance cpp-norun const std::wstring name{ LR"(Local\Xenon.Editor.)" + currentUserSid() }; // per user HANDLE instance{ CreateMutexW(nullptr, FALSE, name.c_str()) }; const bool primary{ GetLastError() != ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS }; // keep instance open for the whole life of the primary: its existence is the signal The first process creates the mutex and becomes the primary ; every later one sees ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS and becomes a secondary . The mutex is never locked; only its existence matters, and because Windows closes it when the primary exits (even by crashing), a stale "running" signal cannot survive. Choose the scope with the name: Local\ plus the user's identity gives one instance per user per session, which is usually right. A global name would make two users on one machine fight over one instance. Forwarding the command line The secondary must hand its arguments to the primary and exit. Either channel works: - WM_COPYDATA to the primary's window (lesson 4.04): simple, if the primary has a window and runs at the same integrity level. - A named pipe the primary listens on (milestone 2): works for background processes too, and lets the primary reply ("opened", or an error). What to send is not just the arguments. Relative paths ( notes.md , ..\docs\a.md ) mean something only relative to the secondary's current folder, which the primary does not share. Send the secondary's current directory along with the arguments, and let the primary resolve paths against it (or resolve them before sending). Bringing the window forward Windows restricts which process may steal the foreground, so that background programs cannot pop up over what the user is doing. The secondary was just launched by the user, so it may set the foreground, and it can pass that right on: cpp-norun AllowSetForegroundWindow(primaryPid); // in the secondary, before forwarding // the primary, on receiving the request: if (IsIconic(window)) ShowWindow(window, SW_RESTORE); SetForegroundWindow(window); Without that, the primary's window just flashes in the taskbar. The races - Two launches at once. Both call CreateMutexW at nearly the same moment; the kernel guarantees exactly one creates it. But the secondary may try to forward before the primary has created its pipe or window. The secondary must retry for a short while (a second or two) before giving up. - The primary is shutting down. The secondary forwards to a primary that is about to exit, and the request is lost. Have the primary close the mutex first when shutting down, so new launches become primaries themselves, and accept that a request arriving during shutdown may need a retry. - The primary is hung. Forwarding with a timeout ( SendMessageTimeoutW , or a pipe with a timeout) lets the secondary tell the user, or start anyway as a second instance, rather than hanging too.

title: Forwarding a command line
body: A second launch of a single-instance editor forwards its arguments and its current folder to the running copy (lesson 6.01). Write the encoding of that request and the primary's resolution of the files to open: cpp struct Forwarded { std::string cwd; std::vector<std::string args; }; std::string encodeForward(const Forwarded& f); std::optional<Forwarded decodeForward(const std::string& text); std::string resolvePath(const std::string& cwd, const std::string& path); std::vector<std::string filesToOpen(const Forwarded& f); - encodeForward writes cwd , then each argument, each followed by a zero byte ( '\0' ); decodeForward reads them back. Text that is empty or does not end with a zero is malformed. - resolvePath uses Windows rules with \ : a path starting with a drive ( C:\ ) or \\ (a network path) is already absolute; otherwise it is joined to cwd . Then . parts are removed and .. removes the previous part (never going above the drive or the \\server\share ). The result never ends with \ unless it is just a drive root ( C:\ ). - filesToOpen takes the arguments that are not options (options start with - or / ) and resolves each against cwd , keeping their order and skipping exact duplicates of a path already listed (compare ignoring case).

title: 6.02  Worker Processes
body: Doing work in separate processes on purpose - isolating crashes, using several cores, running with fewer rights - and the supervisor that starts workers, watches their heartbeats, restarts them with exponential backoff, and stops trying when they keep crashing. Why split work into processes Threads are cheaper, so why would a program start extra worker processes ? Because a process gives things a thread cannot: - Crash isolation. A worker parsing an untrusted file, running a third-party plugin, or compiling user code can crash without taking the main program with it. The main program reports the failure and starts a new worker. - Memory isolation. A worker that leaks or fragments its heap can simply be restarted from time to time. - Fewer rights. A worker can run with a restricted token or inside an AppContainer, so even a compromised worker can do little. Browsers render every site in such a sandboxed process. - Parallelism without shared state. Workers that share nothing need no locks between them. The cost is communication: everything a worker needs must be sent to it, and results sent back, through the channels of this course. The supervisor A process that starts and watches workers is a supervisor . Its jobs: 1. Start each worker, inside a job object so they all end if the supervisor dies (lesson 1.03), with a channel to talk to it. 2. Watch it: wait on its process handle to learn the moment it exits, and on a heartbeat (a regular "still alive" message, or a counter it increments in shared memory) to detect a worker that is alive but hung. 3. Stop it gracefully when asked: send "stop", wait a few seconds, then TerminateProcess if needed. 4. Restart it when it fails, according to a policy. A restart policy Restarting immediately and for ever is a bad policy: a worker that crashes at start-up (a missing file, a bad configuration) would restart hundreds of times a second, filling logs and burning CPU. Good supervisors use: - Exponential backoff : wait 1 s before the first restart, then 2 s, 4 s, 8 s... up to a maximum (say 60 s). Transient problems get quick retries; persistent ones stop hammering the system. - A reset after success : if the worker ran for a good while (say 5 minutes) before failing, the next restart starts again from 1 s; it was a one-off failure, not a crash loop. - Giving up : if it has crashed, say, 5 times within 10 minutes, stop restarting, mark the feature unavailable and tell the user (or an administrator). A human needs to look. - Clean exits are not failures : a worker that exits with code 0 because it finished its job is not restarted. Windows services have this built in (the "Recovery" tab of a service's properties sets first, second and later failure actions with delays); your own supervisor implements the same idea. Heartbeats and hangs A hung worker is worse than a crashed one: its process handle never signals. A heartbeat closes the gap. The worker sends one every second, for example; the supervisor treats three seconds without one as a hang, terminates the worker (it is not going to stop gracefully) and handles it like a crash, with a distinct reason in the log. The heartbeat must come from the worker's real work loop , not from a separate timer thread that keeps ticking while the work is stuck. Logging Every start, exit (with its exit code described as in lesson 1.03), restart delay and give-up should be logged with the worker's name and PID. Crash loops are diagnosed from these logs, often long after the fact.

title: A restart policy
body: Decide what a supervisor does when a worker exits (lesson 6.02). Times are in seconds. cpp struct Decision { bool restart; std::uint64_t at; std::string reason; }; class RestartPolicy { public: void started(std::uint64_t now); Decision exited(std::uint32_t exitCode, std::uint64_t now); bool gaveUp() const; }; - started records that the worker (re)started at now . - exited decides: - exit code 0: no restart, reason finished . - Otherwise it is a failure. Remember the time of the failure. If there have been 5 failures within the last 600 seconds (counting this one, times now - 600 to now inclusive), give up: no restart, reason crash loop , and gaveUp stays true; any later exit is also answered with crash loop . - If the worker had run for 300 seconds or more since its last start, the delay resets to 1 second. - Otherwise the delay is 1 second for the first failure and doubles with each failure in a row, up to 60 seconds. - Restart at now + delay , reason restart in Ns .

title: 6.03  Plugins in Separate Processes
body: Running extensions out of process, as editors and browsers do - the host and plugin protocol, manifests and API version compatibility, subscribing plugins to events, timeouts for slow plugins, disabling misbehaving ones, and what isolation does and does not protect. In-process and out-of-process plugins The DLLs course built plugins as DLLs loaded into the host: fast, direct function calls, but a plugin that crashes or corrupts memory takes the host down with it, and a plugin cannot be stopped without stopping the host. Out-of-process plugins run in their own processes and talk to the host through IPC. VS Code runs every extension in a separate extension host process; browsers run extensions and every site in separate processes; audio workstations can run plugins "sandboxed". The host survives any plugin failure, can stop a plugin at any moment, and can give plugins fewer rights than itself. The price is that every interaction is a message: calls are slower, data must be serialised, and the plugin API must be designed as a protocol (milestone 5) rather than as C++ interfaces. The manifest Each plugin ships a manifest the host reads before starting anything: json { "name": "word-count", "version": "1.4.0", "api": "2.3", "entry": "word-count.exe", "events": "documentSaved", "selectionChanged" , "commands": "wordCount.show" } From it the host decides whether the plugin is compatible (API major version equal, minor version not newer than the host's: the rules of lesson 5.02), which events to send it, and which commands it provides, all without running its code. A host that starts plugins only when one of their events or commands is first needed (lazy activation) starts fast even with many plugins installed. The conversation A typical host and plugin protocol: 1. The host starts the plugin process (with a pipe on its stdio, or a named pipe whose name it passes as an argument) in a job object. 2. Handshake : versions and capabilities. 3. The host sends events the plugin subscribed to; the plugin sends requests to the host API (read the document, show a message) and gets responses. 4. The host sends commands the user invoked; the plugin replies. 5. On shutdown, a "deactivate" message, a short wait, then termination. Slow and broken plugins Plugins will misbehave, and the host must stay responsive whatever they do: - Every request to a plugin has a timeout. A command that takes too long is reported to the user as failed; the host does not wait for ever. - Count failures per plugin. After several timeouts or crashes in a short period, disable the plugin and tell the user which one it was, so they know what to update or remove. - Do not let one plugin block another. Each plugin has its own connection and queue; a busy plugin delays only its own messages. (VS Code puts all extensions in one host process, which is a compromise: one heavy extension slows the others, but the editor itself stays responsive.) What isolation protects, and what it does not A separate process protects the host from a plugin's crashes, hangs and memory corruption . It does not stop a plugin from doing harm with the rights it has: a plugin process running as the user can read the user's files, whatever API the host offers it. Real protection from untrusted plugins needs a restricted process (a low-integrity token, an AppContainer, a job object with UI restrictions) that cannot reach files or the network directly, so everything must go through the host's API, which can check each request. Browsers do exactly that for web content.

title: A plugin host's bookkeeping
body: Decide which plugins a host may load, which ones receive each event, and when to disable a misbehaving one (lesson 6.03): cpp struct Manifest { std::string name; int apiMajor; int apiMinor; std::vector<std::string events; }; class PluginHost { public: PluginHost(int apiMajor, int apiMinor); bool load(const Manifest& m); std::vector<std::string route(const std::string& event) const; bool reportTimeout(const std::string& plugin, std::uint64_t now); std::vector<std::string enabled() const; }; - load accepts a plugin only if its API major equals the host's and its API minor is not newer than the host's, and no plugin of the same name (ignoring case) is loaded. It returns whether it was loaded. - route lists the enabled plugins subscribed to event , in the order they were loaded. The event name in a manifest subscribes to everything. - reportTimeout records a timeout for a plugin; if it has had 3 timeouts within 60 seconds (times now - 60 to now ), it is disabled. It returns true if this report disabled it. Disabled plugins are never routed to, and reports about them or unknown plugins return false. - enabled lists enabled plugin names in load order.

title: 6.04  Testing and Debugging IPC
