body: Making communicating programs testable - keeping the protocol logic separate from the transport, in-memory transports and fault injection, golden transcripts, logging both sides with ids and times, and the tools for seeing handles, pipes and traffic, including debugging two processes at once. Separate logic from transport IPC code is hard to test when the protocol logic is tangled with ReadFile , WriteFile and real processes. Structure it in layers, as every practice in this course has: - a transport that moves bytes (a pipe, a socket, shared memory); - framing that turns bytes into messages; - protocol logic that turns messages into actions and replies. Then the framing and the logic can be unit-tested with byte vectors and no processes at all, running in milliseconds. A thin integration test checks that the real transport is wired up correctly. Fault injection The bugs that matter in IPC appear only under conditions that rarely happen on a developer's machine. Make them happen on purpose with a fault-injecting transport used in tests: - deliver messages split into small chunks, and several joined into one read (the deframer must not care); - delay messages, and deliver responses out of order ; - drop the connection halfway through a message; - kill the peer process in the middle of an exchange; - send garbage : random bytes, absurd lengths, unknown types. Deterministic patterns (split every frame into 3-byte pieces) are easier to debug than random ones; a seeded random generator gives variety while keeping failures reproducible. Golden transcripts Record the messages of a known-good session as text, one per line ("client to server: REQUEST id=1 method=open path=a.md"), and keep it as a golden transcript . A test replays the client side and compares the server's replies with the transcript. To keep it stable, normalise fields that legitimately change (timestamps, generated ids) before comparing. When a change alters the protocol on purpose, regenerate the golden file and review the diff; when it does so by accident, the test catches it. Logging both sides When something goes wrong between two processes, you need both sides' view. Log every message sent and received with: - a timestamp (milliseconds, from a monotonic clock), - the direction and the peer (client id, PID), - the message id and type. With ids in both logs, lining up the two sides is mechanical: find request 41 in the client log and in the server log, and the gap between them is the time it spent in the pipe and the queue. Tools - Process Explorer : the lower pane's handle view shows every pipe, event, mutex and mapping a process has open, by name. "Find Handle or DLL" finds which process holds an object. - Sysinternals PipeList ( pipelist.exe ): every named pipe on the machine with instance counts. (In PowerShell: Get-ChildItem \\.\pipe\ .) - Process Monitor : pipe operations appear as file operations on \Device\NamedPipe\... . - Wireshark with the Npcap loopback adapter captures localhost TCP traffic. - Resource Monitor , CPU tab, "Analyze Wait Chain": shows what a hung process is waiting for, including another process. Debugging two processes Visual Studio can debug several processes in one session: start the server under the debugger, then Debug Attach to Process for the client (or set both as startup projects in the solution's properties). Breakpoints in both work, and the Processes window switches between them. For child processes started by your program, Microsoft's Child Process Debugging Power Tool extension attaches automatically. Remember that stopping one side at a breakpoint makes the other side's timeouts fire; raise timeouts in debug builds, or expect them.

title: Golden transcripts
body: Compare a recorded session against a golden transcript (lesson 6.04), after normalising the fields that change from run to run: cpp std::string normalise(const std::string& line, std::map<std::string, std::string & ids); std::optional<std::string firstDifference(const std::vector<std::string & golden, const std::vector<std::string & actual); A transcript line looks like +12ms c s REQUEST id=41 method=open path=a.md . - normalise : - drops a leading timestamp token (one that starts with + and ends with ms ); - replaces the value of every id= field with a stable name: the first distinct id seen becomes 1 , the next 2 , and so on, using the ids map so the same id gets the same name on every line; - leaves everything else as it is, with single spaces between tokens. - firstDifference normalises both transcripts (each with its own id map) and compares line by line. It returns std::nullopt if they match, or a description: line N: expected "...", got "..." (normalised lines, N counting from 1), or for different lengths line N: expected "...", got end of transcript / line N: expected end of transcript, got "..." .

title: 6.05  Case Studies
body: How real systems combine the techniques of this course - a multi-process browser, an editor and its language servers, a game and its live editor link, a Windows service with a tray application - and the questions to ask when designing your own. A browser A modern browser such as Chrome or Edge runs as many processes: one browser process (the window, tabs, network, storage), a renderer process per site (running its HTML, CSS and JavaScript), a GPU process , and utility processes for audio, network and storage. - Isolation : a crash or exploit in one site's renderer is contained; renderers run in a strict sandbox with almost no rights. - Communication : named pipes carrying a custom message system (Mojo) with typed interfaces generated from definition files. - Shared memory : rendered frames and large data move through shared memory, with only small messages over the pipes. - Supervision : a crashed renderer shows the "Aw, Snap!" page; the browser process carries on. Every idea from this course is there: processes for isolation, pipes for messages, shared memory for bulk data, protocol design with versioned interfaces, and security at every boundary. An editor and its language servers VS Code and many other editors get code intelligence from language servers : separate processes, one per language, speaking the Language Server Protocol. - Transport : usually the server's stdin and stdout (lesson 1.04), with Content-Length framing. - Protocol : JSON-RPC 2.0, with requests and ids (completion, go to definition), notifications (document changed), and capabilities negotiated in an initialize handshake (lesson 5.02). - Independence : the server can be written in any language, by anyone, and work with any editor that speaks the protocol. That is the strongest argument for a documented, language-neutral protocol. A game and its live editor Game engines often connect a running game to an editor or debug tool: change a value in the editor and see it in the game at once. - Discovery : the game listens on a loopback port (or named pipe) and announces itself through a port file, or the editor launches the game with the endpoint on the command line. - Commands : a request and response protocol over a socket or pipe: set this property, spawn this object, reload this asset. - Telemetry : frame times, memory and object counts streamed back, or published in shared memory with a seqlock so the tool never slows the game (lesson 3.05). - Robustness : either side can restart; the connection is re-established automatically, and the game never blocks waiting for the tool. A service and its tray application A Windows service runs in session 0 under its own account; the user's tray icon runs in the user's session. They cannot share windows or Local\ objects, so: - the service creates a named pipe with a security descriptor that allows the interactive users (lesson 5.05); - the tray application connects as a client, sends commands (pause, settings), and receives events (status changes); - the service impersonates the client when it must act with the user's rights, and validates every request, because any program the user runs can connect. Designing your own Faced with a new system, walk through the questions this course has raised: 1. Which processes, and why? Isolation, rights, crash containment, or just separate products? 2. Who finds whom? Inherited handles, names, port files, command-line arguments. 3. Which channel? Pipes or sockets for messages, shared memory for bulk or latest-state data, events and mutexes for signalling. 4. What is the protocol? Handshake, envelope, versioning, requests, responses and events, limits. 5. What fails, and how do you notice? Timeouts, process handles, heartbeats, abandoned mutexes. 6. Who could abuse it? Access control, tokens, validation, impersonation. 7. How will you test and debug it? Layers, fault injection, transcripts, logs with ids. The project that ends this course answers all seven for one complete system.

title: A client and server
body: The final project: the server of a small multi-user workspace chat, as it would run behind a named pipe or loopback socket, with every concern of the course in it: a handshake with a version, validation of everything a client sends, rate limiting, events to other clients, clean handling of clients that quit or vanish. The transport is left out: the server receives one text line at a time from a client and returns the lines to send, and to whom. cpp struct Out { int client; std::string line; }; class ChatServer { public: int connect(); std::vector<Out receive(int client, const std::string& line, std::uint64_t nowMs); std::vector<Out disconnect(int client); std::vector<std::string users() const; }; connect registers a new connection and returns its id (1, 2, 3, ...). A client starts not joined . receive handles one line. First, for any line from an open connection: - more than 512 characters: reply ERROR line too long ; - rate limit : if this client has already sent 5 lines in the last 1000 ms (lines at times greater than now - 1000 ), reply ERROR slow down and do nothing else. Every line received counts, including refused ones. Then the command is the text up to the first space; the rest (after that one space) is its argument: Line Before joining After joining --- --- --- HELLO 1 name join (below) ERROR already joined SAY text ERROR say hello first others get FROM name text ; empty text: ERROR empty message ; text over 200 characters: ERROR message too long TELL name text ERROR say hello first that user gets PRIVATE sender text ; unknown user: ERROR no such user name ; missing text: ERROR usage: TELL name text WHO ERROR say hello first USERS a,b,c (all joined names) QUIT BYE , connection closed BYE , others get LEFT name , connection closed anything else ERROR unknown command X ERROR unknown command X Joining with HELLO version name : a version other than 1 gets ERROR unsupported version and the connection is closed . A name must be 1 to 16 characters of letters, digits, _ and - ( ERROR bad name ) and not already used, ignoring case ( ERROR name taken ). On success the client gets WELCOME name and every other joined client gets JOINED name . Replies to the sender come first, then messages to others in client id order. "Others" means joined clients other than the sender. Names in USERS and users are sorted ignoring case. A closed or unknown connection: receive and disconnect return nothing. disconnect is a connection that vanished: if the client had joined, the others get LEFT name .

compare names 2.02 Client gets ERROR_PIPE_BUSY every instance is in use WaitNamedPipeW and retry; create more instances 2.04 Memory corruption with overlapped I/O the OVERLAPPED or buffer went out of scope while pending keep them alive until completion 2.05 Shared data is garbage in the other process a pointer or std::string was stored in shared memory store offsets and fixed-size data 3.02 A reader sees half-updated state torn read seqlock or double buffering 3.05 CreateMutexW fails with ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE another kind of object already has that name use distinct names 4.01 A consumer sleeps although data is waiting lost wakeup; event reset after the data arrived drain all work after each wake; time out waits 4.02 A wait returns WAIT_ABANDONED the mutex's owner died while holding it validate or repair the shared data 4.03 WM_COPYDATA never arrives the receiver runs elevated (UIPI) ChangeWindowMessageFilterEx in the receiver, or use a pipe 4.04 Two processes hang waiting for each other lock-order or request-reply deadlock global lock order; no locks held across IPC; timeouts 4.05 Firewall prompt when the app starts the server bound to 0.0.0.0 bind to 127.0.0.1 5.01 A web page can trigger your local API localhost has no access control token, Host and Origin checks 5.05 A worker restarts hundreds of times no backoff on a crash loop exponential backoff and give up 6.02

title: Glossary
body: Abandoned mutex : a mutex whose owning thread ended while holding it; the next wait returns WAIT_ABANDONED . (4.03) Anonymous pipe : an unnamed one-way pipe, shared by inheritance or duplication. (2.01) Auto-reset event : an event that resets itself when it releases one waiter. (4.02) Backoff : waiting longer after each failure before retrying. (6.02) Correlation id : a number in a request that its response carries back. (5.04) Deadlock : processes or threads each waiting for something another of them holds. (4.05) Envelope : the common outer structure of every message in a protocol. (5.02) Environment block : a child's environment variables as NAME=value strings ending in zeros. (1.02) Event (kernel) : a kernel object that is set or reset, used to signal. (4.02) Exit code : the number a process leaves when it ends. (1.03) File mapping : a kernel object that maps the same memory into several processes. (3.01) Framing : marking where each message begins and ends in a byte stream. (2.03) Handshake : the first exchange of a connection, agreeing on protocol and version. (5.02) Heartbeat : a regular "still alive" signal from a worker. (6.02) Idempotent : safe to perform twice with the same effect as once. (5.04) Instance (pipe) : one connection slot of a named pipe. (2.02) I/O completion port : a queue collecting completions of overlapped operations. (2.05) Job object : a group of processes managed and limited together. (1.03) Manual-reset event : an event that stays set until explicitly reset. (4.02) Message mode : a named pipe mode where each write is one message. (2.02) Named pipe : a pipe any process can open by name. (2.02) Overlapped I/O : starting an operation that completes later, without blocking. (2.05) Pipe squatting : creating another program's pipe name first to intercept its clients. (5.05) Ring buffer : a fixed array used as a circular queue. (3.03) Semaphore : a kernel object with a count, allowing up to N at once. (4.03) Seqlock : a sequence counter that lets readers detect concurrent writes and retry. (3.05) Single-instance application : a program whose later launches hand their work to the running copy. (6.01) Supervisor : a process that starts, watches and restarts workers. (6.02) Tag-length-value : a field encoding that lets readers skip unknown fields. (5.03) Torn read : reading part of an old state and part of a new one. (3.05) UIPI : User Interface Privilege Isolation, blocking messages to higher-integrity windows. (4.04) Varint : a variable-length integer encoding using 7 bits per byte. (5.03) WM_COPYDATA : the window message that copies a block of data to another process. (4.04)

title: 1.01  Java and the JDK: Your First Program
match: 1.01 Java and the JDK: Your First Program
body: What Java is and how it runs - source code, the compiler, bytecode and the JVM - installing the JDK, the shape of a Java program with a class and a main method, printing with System.out, comments, compiling and running from the command line, and reading compiler errors. Java Java is one of the most widely used programming languages: university courses, Android apps, banking and business systems, big-data tools and many games servers are written in it. It is statically typed (every variable has a fixed type, checked before the program runs) and object-oriented (programs are built from classes and objects, milestone 3). How Java runs The compiler javac turns your source code into bytecode : instructions for the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), not for any real processor. The JVM runs that bytecode on whatever computer it is installed on, compiling the busiest parts to fast machine code while the program runs. That is Java's motto: write once, run anywhere . The JDK (Java Development Kit) contains the compiler, the JVM and the standard library. Install a current LTS version (Java 21 or 25) from adoptium.net or oracle.com. The practice editor here compiles and runs your code on Java 25 for you. Your first program java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println("Hello, Xenon!"); System.out.println(2 + 3); } } Every part matters: - public class Main declares a class named Main . All Java code lives inside classes. A public class must be in a file with the same name: Main.java . - public static void main(String args) is the main method , where the program starts. args holds any command-line arguments. - System.out.println(...) prints a line. System.out.print(...) prints without moving to a new line. - Statements end with ; , and braces { } group code into blocks. - Java is case-sensitive : system.out.println does not exist. Compiling and running bash javac Main.java creates Main.class java Main runs it (class name, without .class) java Main.java since Java 11: compile and run a single file in one step IDEs such as IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code with the Java extensions, and Eclipse do this for you with a Run button, and underline errors as you type. Java 25 also accepts a shorter form for small programs, with no class written out: java-norun void main() { IO.println("Hello from a compact source file"); } This course uses the full form, which every Java version and every course you will meet uses. Comments java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { // A comment to the end of the line. / A comment that can span lines. / System.out.println("Comments are ignored by the compiler."); } / A Javadoc comment: tools turn these into documentation pages. / static void documented() { } } Compiler errors The compiler checks the whole program before it runs. An error names the file, line and problem: text Main.java:3: error: ';' expected System.out.println("Hello") ^ Main.java:4: error: cannot find symbol System.out.printn("Hi"); ^ symbol: method printn(String) Fix the first error first: the others are often caused by it. "cannot find symbol" almost always means a typo or a missing import.

title: Input and output
where: 1.01 Java and the JDK: Your First Program
body: Write a program that asks for a name and a birth year with a Scanner , then greets the person and says how old they turn in 2026: Name? Ada Birth year? 1990 Hello, Ada! In 2026 you turn 36. The prompts are printed with System.out.print (no line break). Read both answers with nextLine() and convert the year with Integer.parseInt .

title: 1.02  Variables and Primitive Types
body: Declaring and assigning variables, the eight primitive types and their ranges, literals, var, constants with final, primitive versus reference types, widening and narrowing conversions with casts, integer overflow, and naming conventions. Variables A variable is a named place that holds a value of one type , fixed when it is declared: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int count = 3; double price = 2.50; boolean done = false; char grade = 'A'; // one character, in single quotes String name = "Ada"; // text, in double quotes (a class, not a primitive) count = count + 1; // fine: still an int // count = "four"; // error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int var total = count price; // var: the compiler infers double final int MAX_PLAYERS = 4; // final: cannot be assigned again System.out.println(name + ": " + count + " x " + price + " = " + total + ", max " + MAX_PLAYERS + ", " + grade + " " + done); } } A local variable must be assigned before it is read; reading an unassigned one is a compile error ("variable might not have been initialized"). The primitive types Type Size Range / precision Literal --- --- --- --- byte 8 bits -128 to 127 (byte) 10 short 16 bits -32 768 to 32 767 (short) 10 int 32 bits about ±2.1 billion 42 , 1_000_000 , 0xFF long 64 bits about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ 42L float 32 bits about 7 digits 3.14f double 64 bits about 15 digits 3.14 , 1e-9 char 16 bits one UTF-16 character 'a' , '\n' boolean true or false true Use int for whole numbers, long when they may exceed two billion (milliseconds, file sizes, populations), double for measurements, and boolean for yes/no. For money, use long cents or java.math.BigDecimal : double cannot store 0.1 exactly. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2); // 0.30000000000000004 System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE); int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE; big = big + 1; // overflows silently System.out.println(big); // -2147483648 System.out.println(Math.addExact(5, 6)); // throws ArithmeticException on overflow instead long population = 8_100_000_000L; // too big for int: needs long and the L suffix System.out.println(population); } } Primitive and reference types The eight primitives hold their value directly. Every other type (String, arrays, your own classes) is a reference type : the variable holds a reference to an object. Assigning a reference copies the reference, so both variables see the same object: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = 1; int b = a; // a copy of the value b = 2; System.out.println(a); // 1 int x = {1, 2, 3}; int y = x; // the same array y 0 = 99; System.out.println(x 0 ); // 99 } } A reference variable can also be null : no object at all. Using it then throws a NullPointerException . Conversions Converting to a wider type is automatic (no information can be lost); converting to a narrower type needs a cast and may lose information: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int i = 42; long l = i; // widening: automatic double d = i; // widening: automatic int back = (int) 3.99; // narrowing: cast, cuts off to 3 byte small = (byte) 300; // wraps around: 44 char c = (char) ('a' + 1); int code = 'A'; // a char is a number: 65 System.out.println(l + " " + d + " " + back + " " + small + " " + c + " " + code); System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("123") + 1); // text to number System.out.println(Double.parseDouble("2.5") 2); System.out.println(String.valueOf(42) + "!"); // number to text } } Names Java naming conventions: camelCase for variables and methods ( totalPrice ), PascalCase for classes ( ShoppingCart ), and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants ( MAX_PLAYERS ). Choose names that say what a value means: secondsElapsed , not s .

title: Types and conversions
body: Complete the static methods in Solution : java static double toCelsius(double fahrenheit) // (F - 32) 5 / 9 static double average(int a, int b, int c) // the exact average: average(1, 2, 2) is 1.666... static int parseOrDefault(String text, int fallback) // the whole number in text (spaces around allowed), or fallback static long toCents(double euros) // euros as whole cents, rounded: 19.99 gives 1999, 0.29 gives 29

title: 1.03  Operators and Math
body: Arithmetic with integer division and remainder, compound assignment and increment, comparison and logical operators with short-circuiting, the ternary operator, precedence, the Math class, and comparing doubles safely. Arithmetic java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = 17, b = 5; System.out.println(a + b); // 22 System.out.println(a - b); // 12 System.out.println(a b); // 85 System.out.println(a / b); // 3: int / int is integer division System.out.println(a % b); // 2: the remainder System.out.println(a / 5.0); // 3.4: a double operand makes it a double division System.out.println((double) a / b); System.out.println(-17 / 5); // -3: rounds toward zero System.out.println(-17 % 5); // -2: the sign follows the left side System.out.println(Math.floorMod(-17, 5)); // 3: always 0 to 4 } } minutes / 60 and minutes % 60 split minutes into hours and the rest. n % 2 == 0 tests for even numbers. Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException ; double division by zero gives Infinity or NaN . Watch out for + with strings: once a String is involved, + joins text. "Total: " + 2 + 3 is "Total: 23" ; write "Total: " + (2 + 3) . Assignment shortcuts java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int score = 10; score += 5; // 15 score = 2; // 30 score -= 1; // 29 score++; // 30 score--; // 29 System.out.println(score); int i = 5; System.out.println(i++); // prints 5, then i becomes 6 System.out.println(++i); // i becomes 7, then prints 7 } } Comparisons and logic Operator Meaning --- --- == , != Equal, not equal (for primitives) < , <= , , = Ordering && And (short-circuit) \ \ Or (short-circuit) ! Not java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int age = 20; boolean hasTicket = true; boolean canEnter = age = 18 && hasTicket; boolean discount = age < 12 age = 65; System.out.println(canEnter + " " + discount + " " + !canEnter); String name = null; if (name != null && name.length() 3) System.out.println("long name"); // safe: && stops early System.out.println(age = 18 ? "adult" : "minor"); // the ternary operator } } && and short-circuit : the right side is only evaluated when needed, which makes the null check above safe. Conditions must be boolean : if (count) does not compile in Java. For objects, == compares references (is it the same object?), not contents. Strings are compared with equals (lesson 1.04). Precedence , / , % before + , - ; then comparisons; then && ; then ; then ?: ; then assignment. Use parentheses when in doubt. Math java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(Math.sqrt(16)); // 4.0 System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 10)); // 1024.0 System.out.println(Math.abs(-3.5)); // 3.5 System.out.println(Math.max(3, 9)); // 9 System.out.println(Math.round(2.5)); // 3: rounds halves up, returns long System.out.println(Math.round(-2.5)); // -2 System.out.println(Math.floor(-2.5) + " " + Math.ceil(2.1)); // -3.0 3.0 System.out.println(Math.clamp(15, 0, 10)); // 10 (Java 21+) System.out.println(Math.PI); System.out.println((int) (Math.random() 6) + 1 0); // a dice roll 1-6 } } Comparing doubles Because of rounding, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false . Compare floating-point numbers with a tolerance: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { double x = 0.1 + 0.2; System.out.println(x == 0.3); // false System.out.println(Math.abs(x - 0.3) < 1e-9); // true } }

title: Operators
body: Complete the methods: java static boolean isLeapYear(int year) // divisible by 4, except centuries, except every 400 years static String clock(int minutes) // minutes after midnight as "h:mm": 125 is "2:05" static int coins(int cents, int coin) // how many coins of that size fit into cents static boolean canVote(int age, boolean isCitizen, boolean isRegistered) // 18 or over, citizen and registered clock wraps around the day: 1440 is "0:00" again, and negative minutes count back from midnight ( -30 is "23:30" ).

title: 1.04  Strings and Input
body: Working with String - its common methods, immutability, comparing with equals instead of ==, escapes and text blocks, formatting with printf and String.format - and reading keyboard input with Scanner, including the nextInt/nextLine trap. Strings A String is a sequence of characters. Strings are immutable : methods return new strings and never change the original. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String s = " Ada Lovelace "; String t = s.trim(); System.out.println(" " + t + " " + t.length()); System.out.println(t.toUpperCase() + " " + t.toLowerCase()); System.out.println(t.charAt(0) + " " + t.charAt(t.length() - 1)); System.out.println(t.substring(4) + " " + t.substring(0, 3)); // from 4 / from 0 up to 3 System.out.println(t.indexOf("Love") + " " + t.indexOf('z')); // position, or -1 System.out.println(t.contains("Love") + " " + t.startsWith("Ada") + " " + t.endsWith("x")); System.out.println(t.replace("Ada", "Augusta")); System.out.println(String.join("-", t.split(" "))); System.out.println("ha".repeat(3) + " " + "".isEmpty() + " " + " ".isBlank()); } } Method Gives --- --- length() , charAt(i) Number of characters, the character at index i (from 0) substring(start) , substring(start, end) Part of the string (end excluded) indexOf(x) , lastIndexOf(x) Position, or -1 toUpperCase() , toLowerCase() , trim() , strip() New strings contains , startsWith , endsWith , isEmpty , isBlank Tests replace(a, b) , split(regex) , String.join(sep, parts) Change, split, join equals , equalsIgnoreCase , compareTo Comparisons equals, not == == on objects asks "is this the same object ?". Two strings with the same text can be different objects, so always compare text with equals : java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String a = "hello"; String b = new String("hello"); System.out.println(a == b); // false: different objects System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true: same text System.out.println("Hello".equalsIgnoreCase(a)); System.out.println("apple".compareTo("banana") < 0); // alphabetical order } } "hello" == "hello" sometimes happens to be true (Java reuses identical literals), which makes the bug hard to notice. Use equals every time. Escapes and text blocks java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println("Tab:\tQuote:\" Backslash:\\ Newline:\nnext line"); String json = """ { "name": "Ada", "langs": "Java", "C" } """; // a text block (Java 15+): no escaping needed System.out.print(json); } } Formatting printf and String.format use format specifiers : java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String name = "Tea"; double price = 2.5; int qty = 3; System.out.printf("%s x%d = %.2f%n", name, qty, price qty); // %n: a new line System.out.printf(" %-10s %8.2f %05d %n", name, price, 42); // left-aligned, width 8, zero-padded String line = String.format("%,d people", 1234567); System.out.println(line); System.out.println("%s is %d".formatted("Ada", 36)); } } Specifier For --- --- %s Any value as text %d Whole numbers %.2f Decimals with 2 places %10s , %-10s Right / left aligned in 10 characters %05d , %,d Zero-padded, thousands separators %n A line break Reading input with Scanner java import java.util.Scanner; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in); System.out.print("What is your name? "); String name = in.nextLine(); System.out.print("Your age? "); int age = in.nextInt(); System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "! Next year you will be " + (age + 1) + "."); } } import java.util.Scanner; at the top of the file makes the Scanner class available. nextLine() reads a whole line, nextInt() and nextDouble() read the next number, and hasNextInt() / hasNextLine() check what comes next. The classic trap : nextInt() reads the number but leaves the line break after it. A nextLine() right after returns that empty rest of the line. Either call an extra nextLine() after the number, or read every line with nextLine() and convert it with Integer.parseInt(line.trim()) , which is what this course does.

title: Working with strings
body: Complete the methods: java static String initials(String fullName) // "ada king lovelace" gives "A.K.L." static int countWord(String text, String word) // whole-word matches, ignoring case static String censor(String text, String word) // every match of word (ignoring case) replaced by of the same length static String priceLine(String item, double price) // item left in 12 characters, price right in 8 with 2 decimals - initials ignores extra spaces. - countWord("The cat and the hat. THE end", "the") is 3: words are separated by anything that is not a letter. - censor("Darn, DARN it", "darn") gives " , it" ; it replaces inside words too ( "darned" becomes " ed" ). - priceLine("Tea", 2.5) is "Tea 2.50" . Use String.format(Locale.ROOT, ...) so the decimal point is . everywhere.

title: 1.05  Control Flow
body: Making decisions with if and else, the classic switch statement and the modern switch expression with arrows, loops with while, do-while, for and the enhanced for, break and continue, labelled breaks for nested loops, and input loops with a sentinel. if and else java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int temperature = 23; if (temperature = 30) { System.out.println("Hot"); } else if (temperature = 18) { System.out.println("Pleasant"); } else { System.out.println("Cold"); } } } Always use braces, even for one statement: without them, only the first line belongs to the if , however it is indented. switch The modern switch expression (Java 14+) uses arrows, needs no break , and produces a value: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int day = 6; String kind = switch (day) { case 6, 7 - "weekend"; case 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - "weekday"; default - "not a day"; }; System.out.println(kind); String command = "stop"; switch (command) { case "go", "start" - System.out.println("Starting"); case "stop" - System.out.println("Stopping"); default - System.out.println("Unknown command"); } } } You will also meet the classic form with colons. There, each case falls through into the next unless it ends with break , a frequent source of bugs: java-norun switch (command) { case "go": System.out.println("Starting"); break; // without this, "Stopping" would print too case "stop": System.out.println("Stopping"); break; default: System.out.println("Unknown"); } Prefer the arrow form in new code. while and do-while java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int n = 27, steps = 0; while (n != 1) { n = (n % 2 == 0) ? n / 2 : 3 n + 1; steps++; } System.out.println(steps + " steps"); int tries = 0; do { tries++; // runs at least once } while (tries < 3); System.out.println(tries); } } for loops java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { System.out.print(i + " "); } System.out.println(); String names = {"Ada", "Grace", "Linus"}; for (String name : names) { // the enhanced for: every item System.out.println(name.toUpperCase()); } for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++) { // nested loops: a times table for (int col = 1; col <= 4; col++) { System.out.printf("%4d", row col); } System.out.println(); } } } Use the classic for when you need the index or count; the enhanced for ( for (Type x : collection) ) when you just need every item. break and continue java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int numbers = {4, 7, -1, 12, 0, 9}; int sum = 0; for (int x : numbers) { if (x < 0) continue; // skip this one if (x == 0) break; // stop the loop sum += x; } System.out.println(sum); // 23 outer: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++) { if (i j == 6) { System.out.println("found " + i + " x " + j); break outer; // leaves both loops } } } } } Input loops A common pattern reads until a special sentinel value or the end of input: java import java.util.Scanner; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in); int total = 0; while (in.hasNextLine()) { String line = in.nextLine().trim(); if (line.equals("done")) break; try { total += Integer.parseInt(line); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("Not a number: " + line); } } System.out.println("Total: " + total); } } try / catch handles text that is not a number; exceptions are covered fully in lesson 4.04.

title: Guess the number
body: Write the game "guess the number". So that it can be tested, the secret number is the first line of input; then each line is a guess: Secret? 37 Guess 1-100: 50 Too high. Guess 1-100: 25 Too low. Guess 1-100: abc Please enter a whole number. Guess 1-100: 0 Out of range. Guess 1-100: 37 Correct! You needed 3 guesses. - Print Secret? and read the secret, then repeat: print Guess 1-100: , read a line, and answer. - Text that is not a whole number gives Please enter a whole number. and a number outside 1 to 100 gives Out of range. ; neither counts as a guess. - When the guess is right, print Correct! You needed N guesses. ( 1 guess for one) and stop. - If the input ends before the right guess, print Out of guesses. The number was N.

title: A report card
body: Write a program that reads exam results, one student per line as <name <score , until an empty line or the end of the input, and prints a report: Ada 92 Grace 78 Linus 64 Bob 41 Alan 78 gives Ada 92 A Grace 78 C Linus 64 D Bob 41 F Alan 78 C Students: 5 Average: 70.60 Highest: Ada (92) Lowest: Bob (41) Grades: A=1 B=0 C=2 D=1 F=1 Rules: - A line is a name (one word) and a whole-number score from 0 to 100, separated by spaces (extra spaces are fine). Any other line prints Skipping: <the line as typed and is ignored. - Each student line is the name left-aligned in 12 characters, the score right-aligned in 3, two spaces and the grade: 90 and above A , 80 B , 70 C , 60 D , below 60 F . - After the input: the count, the average with 2 decimals (with a . : use Locale.ROOT ), the highest and lowest (the first one on a tie) and how many of each grade. - With no valid students, print only No students. - Do it without arrays or lists (they come in milestone 2): keep running totals as you read.

title: 2.01  Methods
body: Defining static methods with parameters and return types, void methods, calling methods, pass-by-value for primitives and references, overloading, variable-length arguments, local variables and scope, returning early, and designing small methods that do one thing. Defining methods A method is a named block of code with parameters and a return type . Until classes and objects arrive in milestone 3, our methods are static : they belong to the class and are called by name. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(area(3, 4)); System.out.println(describe("Ada", 36)); greet("Grace"); System.out.println(isEven(10) + " " + isEven(7)); } static double area(double width, double height) { return width height; } static String describe(String name, int age) { return name + " (" + age + ")"; } static void greet(String name) { // void: returns nothing System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!"); } static boolean isEven(int n) { return n % 2 == 0; } } Every path through a non-void method must return a value of the declared type; the compiler checks this ("missing return statement"). A return can come early to stop the method at once: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(grade(95) + grade(72) + grade(-5)); } static String grade(int score) { if (score < 0 score 100) return "?"; if (score = 90) return "A"; if (score = 70) return "C"; return "F"; } } Pass by value Java always passes copies of values . For a primitive, the method gets a copy of the number; changing the parameter does not change the caller's variable. For an object, the method gets a copy of the reference : it can change the object the reference points to, but not make the caller's variable point somewhere else. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int n = 1; addOne(n); System.out.println(n); // 1: addOne changed its own copy int numbers = {1, 2, 3}; doubleAll(numbers); System.out.println(numbers 0 ); // 2: the array itself was changed replace(numbers); System.out.println(numbers 0 ); // 2: replacing the parameter does not affect the caller } static void addOne(int x) { x = x + 1; } static void doubleAll(int values) { for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) values i = 2; } static void replace(int values) { values = new int {100, 200}; } } Overloading Methods may share a name when their parameter lists differ. The compiler picks the closest match: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(max(3, 9)); System.out.println(max(2.5, 1.5)); System.out.println(max(4, 8, 6)); System.out.println(sum() + " " + sum(1, 2, 3) + " " + sum(new int {10, 20})); } static int max(int a, int b) { return a b ? a : b; } static double max(double a, double b) { return a b ? a : b; } static int max(int a, int b, int c) { return max(max(a, b), c); } static int sum(int... numbers) { // varargs: any number of ints, as an array int total = 0; for (int n : numbers) total += n; return total; } } Scope A variable exists from its declaration to the end of the block { } it is declared in. Parameters and variables of one method are invisible to other methods; the only way to share values is to pass them as arguments and return results. Good methods - One method, one job, named with a verb: calculateTotal , isValid , printReport . - Prefer methods that return results over methods that print them: a returned value can be tested, printed, or used in further calculations. - Keep methods short. If you need a comment to explain a section of a method, that section probably wants to be its own method.

title: Writing methods
body: Complete the static methods in Solution : java static boolean isPrime(int n) // true for 2, 3, 5, 7, ...; false for anything below 2 static int gcd(int a, int b) // greatest common divisor (Euclid's algorithm); gcd(0, 0) is 0 static int digitSum(long n) // sum of the decimal digits, ignoring a minus sign static double area(double radius) // a circle static double area(double width, double height) // a rectangle (an overload) static String repeat(String s, int times, String separator) // "ab", 3, "-" gives "ab-ab-ab" isPrime should only try divisors up to the square root of n . gcd works for negative numbers too and always returns a value of 0 or more.

title: 2.02  Arrays
body: Creating arrays with new and initializers, indexing and length, default values, looping over arrays, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, the java.util.Arrays helpers (toString, sort, fill, copyOf, equals, binarySearch), copying versus sharing, two-dimensional arrays, and classic array algorithms. Creating arrays An array holds a fixed number of values of one type. Its length is set when it is created and never changes: java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int scores = new int 5 ; // five zeros scores 0 = 90; scores 4 = 75; String days = {"Mon", "Tue", "Wed"}; // an initializer double prices = new double {2.5, 4.0}; System.out.println(scores.length + " " + days.length); System.out.println(days days.length - 1 ); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(scores)); // 90, 0, 0, 0, 75 System.out.println(scores); // I@1b6d3586: not the contents! } } Indexes run from 0 to length - 1 . Using any other index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException . New arrays are filled with default values : 0 , 0.0 , false , '\u0000' , or null for objects. Printing an array directly shows its type and an identity code; use Arrays.toString . Looping java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int data = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42}; int sum = 0, max = data 0 ; for (int x : data) { // every value sum += x; if (x max) max = x; } System.out.println(sum + " " + max + " " + (double) sum / data.length); for (int i = data.length - 1; i = 0; i--) { // with indexes: backwards System.out.print(data i + " "); } System.out.println(); } } The Arrays class java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {5, 2, 9, 1}; Arrays.sort(a); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); System.out.println(Arrays.binarySearch(a, 5)); // index 2: needs a sorted array int longer = Arrays.copyOf(a, 6); // copy, padded with zeros int part = Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, 3); // indexes 1 and 2 int sevens = new int 3 ; Arrays.fill(sevens, 7); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(longer) + Arrays.toString(part) + Arrays.toString(sevens)); System.out.println(Arrays.equals(a, new int {1, 2, 5, 9}) + " " + (a == new int {1, 2, 5, 9})); System.out.println(Arrays.stream(a).sum()); } } == on arrays compares references; Arrays.equals compares contents. Copying versus sharing Arrays are objects: assigning one array variable to another shares the same array. java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {1, 2, 3}; int same = a; // the same array int copy = a.clone(); // a new array with the same values same 0 = 99; System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a) + " " + Arrays.toString(copy)); } } Two dimensions java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int grid = new int 3 4 ; // 3 rows of 4 grid 1 2 = 7; for (int row : grid) System.out.println(Arrays.toString(row)); int triangle = {{1}, {1, 1}, {1, 2, 1}}; // rows may have different lengths System.out.println(triangle 2 .length + " " + Arrays.deepToString(triangle)); } } A 2D array is an array of arrays: grid.length is the number of rows and grid r .length the length of row r . Classic algorithms Many exam questions are small array algorithms. Two examples: java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int values = {3, 8, 1, 9, 4}; reverse(values); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(values)); System.out.println(indexOf(values, 1) + " " + indexOf(values, 7)); } static void reverse(int a) { for (int i = 0, j = a.length - 1; i < j; i++, j--) { int tmp = a i ; a i = a j ; a j = tmp; } } static int indexOf(int a, int target) { // linear search for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (a i == target) return i; } return -1; } }

title: Array algorithms
body: Complete the methods. None of them may change the arrays they are given. java static int rotate(int values, int k) // every item k places to the right, wrapping around; k may be negative or large static int secondLargest(int values) // the second-largest distinct value static int runningTotals(int values) // {1, 2, 3} gives {1, 3, 6} static int transpose(int m) // rows become columns static int mergeSorted(int a, int b) // two sorted arrays into one sorted array, in one pass - secondLargest({5, 9, 9, 2}) is 5. With fewer than two distinct values it throws IllegalArgumentException . - transpose of a 2 × 3 matrix is 3 × 2. You may assume every row has the same length (and that there is at least one row).

title: 2.03  ArrayList and Wrapper Types
body: The growable ArrayList - adding, getting, setting, removing, searching and sorting - the List interface, wrapper classes like Integer and Double, autoboxing and its traps (remove by index or value, == on Integers, null unboxing), List.of, and iterating while removing safely. ArrayList An ArrayList is a list that grows and shrinks as needed. The type in angle brackets says what it holds: java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String names = new ArrayList< (); names.add("Grace"); names.add("Ada"); names.add(0, "Ken"); // insert at index 0 names.set(1, "Linus"); // replace index 1 System.out.println(names + " " + names.size()); System.out.println(names.get(0) + " " + names.contains("Ada") + " " + names.indexOf("Ada")); names.remove("Ken"); // by value names.remove(0); // by index Collections.addAll(names, "Barbara", "Margaret"); Collections.sort(names); System.out.println(names); System.out.println(names.isEmpty()); } } Declare variables with the interface type List<String and create an ArrayList< () : the rest of the code then works with any kind of list. < (the diamond) lets the compiler fill in the type. Array ArrayList --- --- int a = new int 5 ; List<Integer list = new ArrayList< (); a.length list.size() a i , a i = x list.get(i) , list.set(i, x) fixed size add , remove , grows as needed holds primitives holds objects only Wrapper types Collections hold objects, not primitives. Each primitive has a wrapper class : Integer , Double , Boolean , Character , Long ... Java converts automatically between them ( autoboxing and unboxing ): java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Integer numbers = new ArrayList< (); numbers.add(5); // int 5 is boxed into an Integer numbers.add(10); int first = numbers.get(0); // unboxed back to int int total = 0; for (int n : numbers) total += n; System.out.println(first + " " + total); System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("42") + Integer.MAX_VALUE % 10 + " " + Character.isDigit('7')); } } Three traps to know: java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Integer list = new ArrayList< (List.of(10, 20, 30)); list.remove(1); // removes INDEX 1 (the 20), not the value 1 list.remove(Integer.valueOf(30)); // removes the VALUE 30 System.out.println(list); Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; System.out.println(a == b); // false: two different Integer objects System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true: compare wrapper values with equals Integer missing = null; try { int n = missing; // unboxing null throws NullPointerException } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("cannot unbox null"); } } } Fixed lists and copies List.of(1, 2, 3) makes an unmodifiable list: add and set throw UnsupportedOperationException . It is ideal for constants and test data. To get a list you can change, copy it: new ArrayList< (List.of(1, 2, 3)) . Removing while looping Removing items inside an enhanced for over the same list throws ConcurrentModificationException . Loop backwards with indexes, or use removeIf : java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Integer values = new ArrayList< (List.of(4, 7, 10, 13, 16)); for (int i = values.size() - 1; i = 0; i--) { if (values.get(i) % 2 == 1) values.remove(i); } System.out.println(values); values.removeIf(v - v 12); // a lambda (lesson 6.01): remove what matches System.out.println(values); } }

title: Working with ArrayList
body: Complete the methods: java static List<Integer withoutDuplicates(List<Integer values) // a new list, first occurrences kept, in order static void removeNegatives(List<Integer values) // changes the given list in place static List<String longWords(List<String words, int minLength) // words with at least minLength letters, upper-cased static List<Integer positionsOf(List<String items, String target) // every index where target appears (equals) static double average(List<Integer values) // 0.0 for an empty list; null items are skipped

title: 2.04  Recursion
body: Methods that call themselves - base cases and recursive cases, how the call stack works, tracing factorial and Fibonacci, recursion on arrays and strings, the cost of naive recursion and memoization, StackOverflowError, and when to prefer a loop. A method that calls itself A recursive method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive method needs: 1. a base case that is answered directly, without recursion; 2. a recursive case that moves toward the base case. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(factorial(5)); System.out.println(sumTo(100)); System.out.println(power(2, 10)); } static long factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; // base case return n factorial(n - 1); // recursive case: a smaller problem } static int sumTo(int n) { return n == 0 ? 0 : n + sumTo(n - 1); } static long power(long base, int exp) { if (exp == 0) return 1; long half = power(base, exp / 2); // halves the problem each time return exp % 2 == 0 ? half half : half half base; } } The call stack Each call gets its own stack frame holding its parameters and local variables. factorial(4) waits for factorial(3) , which waits for factorial(2) , and so on; when the base case returns, the waiting calls finish in reverse order: text factorial(4) 4 factorial(3) 3 factorial(2) 2 factorial(1) 1 <- base case 2 1 = 2 3 2 = 6 4 6 = 24 Without a base case (or with one that is never reached), calls pile up until the stack runs out of space and Java throws StackOverflowError . Recursion on arrays and strings Recursion fits problems that contain smaller copies of themselves. Pass indexes to work on part of an array without copying it: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(reverse("recursion")); System.out.println(isPalindrome("racecar") + " " + isPalindrome("java")); int sorted = {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91}; System.out.println(binarySearch(sorted, 23, 0, sorted.length - 1)); System.out.println(countDigits(90210)); } static String reverse(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) return s; return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0); } static boolean isPalindrome(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) return true; return s.charAt(0) == s.charAt(s.length() - 1) && isPalindrome(s.substring(1, s.length() - 1)); } static int binarySearch(int a, int target, int lo, int hi) { if (lo hi) return -1; // nothing left: not found int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (a mid == target) return mid; if (a mid < target) return binarySearch(a, target, mid + 1, hi); return binarySearch(a, target, lo, mid - 1); } static int countDigits(int n) { return n < 10 ? 1 : 1 + countDigits(n / 10); } } Repeated work and memoization The direct recursive Fibonacci is elegant and terribly slow: fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2) , which recompute the same values again and again, roughly 1.6ⁿ calls in total. Memoization stores each answer the first time it is computed: java import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; public class Main { static int calls = 0; static final Map<Integer, Long memo = new HashMap< (); public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(slowFib(25) + " after " + calls + " calls"); calls = 0; System.out.println(fastFib(90) + " after " + calls + " calls"); } static long slowFib(int n) { calls++; return n < 2 ? n : slowFib(n - 1) + slowFib(n - 2); } static long fastFib(int n) { calls++; if (n < 2) return n; Long known = memo.get(n); if (known != null) return known; long result = fastFib(n - 1) + fastFib(n - 2); memo.put(n, result); return result; } } Recursion or a loop? Anything recursive can be written with a loop, and vice versa. Use recursion when the problem is naturally recursive: trees (lesson 5.05), nested structures, divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort and quicksort (lesson 5.02), and exploring all combinations. Use a loop for simple repetition such as summing an array: it is clearer and cannot overflow the stack.

title: Recursion
body: Write these with recursion (no loops): java static String toBinary(int n) // 10 gives "1010", 0 gives "0"; n is 0 or more static int countPaths(int rows, int cols) // paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down static List<String permutations(String s) // every ordering of the characters, sorted, without repeats static List<String hanoi(int n, char from, char to, char via) // the moves to shift n discs, like "A- C" - countPaths(3, 3) is 6. It must be fast for countPaths(16, 16) (155117520): remember answers you have already worked out. - permutations("aba") is "aab", "aba", "baa" . - hanoi(2, 'A', 'C', 'B') is "A- B", "A- C", "B- C" .

title: 2.05  Strings in Depth
body: Characters as numbers and the Character class, walking through strings, why repeated concatenation is slow and how StringBuilder fixes it, string comparison and sorting, splitting with regular expressions, a first look at Pattern and Matcher, and converting between strings, chars and numbers. Characters A char is a 16-bit number that stands for a character. Arithmetic on chars works on those numbers: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { char c = 'b'; System.out.println((int) c); // 98 System.out.println((char) (c + 1)); // c System.out.println('7' - '0'); // 7: a digit character to its value System.out.println(Character.isLetter(c) + " " + Character.isDigit('7') + " " + Character.isWhitespace(' ')); System.out.println(Character.toUpperCase(c) + " " + Character.isUpperCase('Q')); System.out.println((char) ('a' + 25)); // z } } c - 'a' gives a letter's position in the alphabet (0 for a ), which is the trick behind Caesar ciphers and letter counts. Walking through a string java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String text = "Hello, World 2026!"; int letters = 0, digits = 0, upper = 0; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { char ch = text.charAt(i); if (Character.isLetter(ch)) letters++; if (Character.isDigit(ch)) digits++; if (Character.isUpperCase(ch)) upper++; } System.out.println(letters + " letters, " + digits + " digits, " + upper + " capitals"); int counts = new int 26 ; for (char ch : text.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) { if (ch = 'a' && ch <= 'z') counts ch - 'a' ++; } System.out.println("l appears " + counts 'l' - 'a' + " times"); } } StringBuilder Strings are immutable, so s += x creates a brand-new string and copies everything each time. In a loop that is slow (quadratic). A StringBuilder is a mutable buffer: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { sb.append(i); if (i < 5) sb.append(", "); } System.out.println(sb); sb.insert(0, " ").append(" "); sb.reverse(); System.out.println(sb + " " + sb.length()); sb.setLength(0); // clear it sb.append("caesar").setCharAt(0, 'C'); System.out.println(sb.toString()); } } Method Does --- --- append(x) Add to the end (returns the builder, so calls chain) insert(i, x) , deleteCharAt(i) , delete(a, b) Insert and remove setCharAt(i, c) , reverse() Change in place length() , charAt(i) , toString() Read Comparing and sorting compareTo orders strings by character codes: all capitals come before all lower-case letters ( "Zoe" before "adam" ). For human ordering ignore case: java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String names = new ArrayList< (List.of("bob", "Alice", "carol", "Bob")); names.sort(null); // natural (code) order System.out.println(names); names.sort(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER); System.out.println(names); System.out.println("apple".compareTo("apricot") < 0); } } Regular expressions split , matches and replaceAll take regular expressions , a small language for text patterns: Pattern Matches --- --- \\d , \\s , \\w A digit, a white-space character, a word character aeiou , ^0-9 One of these / anything but these + , , ? , {2,4} One or more, zero or more, optional, 2 to 4 times ^ , $ Start, end In Java source, each backslash is written twice: the regex \d+ is the string "\\d+" . java import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(String.join(" ", "a, b;c d".split(" ,;\\s +"))); System.out.println("2026-03-14".matches("\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}")); System.out.println("call 555-1234 or 555-9876".replaceAll("\\d{3}-\\d{4}", "<number ")); Matcher m = Pattern.compile("(\\w+)@(\\w+\\.\\w+)").matcher("ada@math.org, grace@navy.mil"); while (m.find()) System.out.println(m.group(1) + " at " + m.group(2)); } } Converting From To Code --- --- --- String int / double Integer.parseInt(s) , Double.parseDouble(s) number String String.valueOf(n) , Integer.toString(n) , "" + n String char s.toCharArray() char String new String(chars) , String.valueOf(chars) char String String.valueOf(c) , Character.toString(c) int binary / hex text Integer.toBinaryString(n) , Integer.toHexString(n)

title: Strings and characters
body: Complete the methods: java static String caesar(String text, int shift) // shift letters through the alphabet, keeping case; other characters unchanged static boolean isAnagram(String a, String b) // same letters in any order, ignoring case, spaces and punctuation static String compress(String s) // "aaabccdddd" gives "a3bc2d4" static String capitalizeWords(String s) // "the QUICK brown" gives "The Quick Brown"; single spaces in the result - caesar("Hello, World!", 3) is "Khoor, Zruog!" ; shifts can be negative or larger than 26. - compress writes a count only when a character repeats; when the compressed text would not be shorter, it returns the original.

title: Tic-tac-toe
body: Write a two-player game of tic-tac-toe on a 3 × 3 board. Players type their moves as row column (each 1 to 3): X to move: 2 2 . . . ---+---+--- . X . ---+---+--- . . . O to move: 1 1 O . . ---+---+--- . X . ---+---+--- . . . X to move: ... Rules: - X moves first; players alternate. Print X to move: (or O to move: ) before reading each line. - A line that is not two whole numbers prints Enter row and column, like 2 3 ; numbers outside 1 to 3 print Out of range ; a square that is already used prints Taken . After any of these, the same player tries again. - After each valid move, print the board as shown: each row is a b c , rows are separated by ---+---+--- , and empty squares are . . - When a player gets three in a row (across, down or diagonally), print X wins! (or O wins! ) and stop. When the board is full without a winner, print Draw. and stop. - If the input ends before the game is over, print Game abandoned.

title: 3.01  Classes and Objects
body: Defining your own classes with fields, constructors and instance methods, creating objects with new, the this reference, references and null, toString, object identity versus equality, and how to design a class around the data it owns. A class A class is a blueprint: it describes the data an object holds ( fields ) and what it can do ( methods ). Each object made from it with new is an instance with its own copy of the fields. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Counter clicks = new Counter("clicks"); Counter errors = new Counter("errors"); clicks.increment(); clicks.increment(); errors.increment(); System.out.println(clicks.describe()); System.out.println(errors.describe()); clicks.reset(); System.out.println(clicks); // uses toString } } class Counter { private final String name; // fields: every Counter has its own private int count; // starts at 0 Counter(String name) { // the constructor: runs when new Counter(...) is called this.name = name; } void increment() { count++; } void reset() { count = 0; } int getCount() { return count; } String describe() { return name + ": " + count; } @Override public String toString() { return "Counter " + name + "=" + count + " "; } } - new Counter("clicks") allocates an object and runs the constructor , which has the class's name and no return type. - Methods without static are instance methods : they run on one object and use its fields. - this is the object the method or constructor is running on. this.name = name copies the parameter into the field with the same name. - Overriding toString decides how the object prints. @Override asks the compiler to check that you really are overriding a method. Several classes can live in one file, but only one can be public , and it gives the file its name. In larger programs each class gets its own file. Objects are references A variable of a class type holds a reference to an object. Assigning it copies the reference: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = a; // the same object Point c = new Point(1, 2); // a different object with the same values b.x = 10; System.out.println(a.x); // 10 System.out.println(a == b); // true: same object System.out.println(a == c); // false: different objects System.out.println(a.equals(c)); // false too: Object.equals compares identity unless overridden Point nothing = null; try { System.out.println(nothing.x); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NullPointerException: there is no object"); } } } class Point { int x, y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } To make equals compare contents , a class must override equals (and hashCode ; lesson 4.02). Records (lesson 3.05) do that automatically. Methods that work with other objects Methods can take and return objects, including objects of their own class: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Fraction half = new Fraction(1, 2); Fraction third = new Fraction(1, 3); Fraction sum = half.plus(third); System.out.println(half + " + " + third + " = " + sum); System.out.println(new Fraction(6, 8)); } } class Fraction { private final int num, den; Fraction(int num, int den) { if (den == 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("denominator is zero"); int g = gcd(Math.abs(num), Math.abs(den)); int sign = den < 0 ? -1 : 1; this.num = sign num / g; this.den = sign den / g; } Fraction plus(Fraction other) { return new Fraction(num other.den + other.num den, den other.den); } private static int gcd(int a, int b) { return b == 0 ? Math.max(a, 1) : gcd(b, a % b); } @Override public String toString() { return num + "/" + den; } } Fraction keeps its fields final : once made, a fraction never changes, and plus returns a new fraction. Immutable objects like this (and String ) are simple to reason about and safe to share. Designing a class Ask: what data belongs together, and what operations keep that data correct? A BankAccount owns a balance and offers deposit and withdraw , which refuse to make it invalid. A class with good methods means the rest of the program never has to repeat those rules.

title: A shopping cart class
body: Write a class ShoppingCart that keeps prices in whole cents: java ShoppingCart cart = new ShoppingCart(); cart.add("Tea", 250, 2); // name, unit price in cents, quantity cart.add("Cake", 425, 1); cart.add("tea", 250, 1); // the same item (names ignore case): quantity becomes 3, the first name is kept cart.itemCount(); // 4: total quantity cart.totalCents(); // 1175 cart.remove("TEA"); // true; false if not in the cart cart.receipt(); // see below - add throws IllegalArgumentException for a blank name, a negative price or a quantity below 1. Adding an existing item with a different price also throws. - receipt() lists the items in the order they were first added, one per line, as <name x<qty <line total with euros and 2 decimals ( Tea x3 7.50 ), then Total: <total . Lines end with \n . An empty cart gives just Total: 0.00\n . Keep the items in a private list; you may write a small private helper class for an item, nested inside ShoppingCart . The class lives in ShoppingCart.java : in Java, a top-level class goes in a file with its own name.

title: 3.02  Encapsulation, Constructors and static
body: Access modifiers and why fields should be private, getters and setters with validation, constructor overloading and this(...), immutable classes with final fields, static fields and methods, static factory methods, constants, and when a class should be a utility class. Encapsulation Encapsulation means an object guards its own data: fields are private , and the only way to change them is through methods that keep them valid. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { BankAccount acc = new BankAccount("Ada", 100); acc.deposit(50); System.out.println(acc.withdraw(500)); // false: refused System.out.println(acc.getBalance()); try { acc.deposit(-10); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("refused: " + e.getMessage()); } // acc.balance = -1000; // error: balance has private access } } class BankAccount { private final String owner; private long balance; // in cents would be safer for money; whole euros keep the example short BankAccount(String owner, long opening) { this.owner = owner; deposit(opening); } BankAccount(String owner) { this(owner, 0); // calls the other constructor } void deposit(long amount) { if (amount < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative deposit"); balance += amount; } boolean withdraw(long amount) { if (amount < 0 amount balance) return false; balance -= amount; return true; } long getBalance() { return balance; } String getOwner() { return owner; } } Modifier Visible to --- --- private Only this class (none) Classes in the same package protected The same package and subclasses public Everyone Make fields private , offer methods for what callers need, and only add a setter when changing a field is really part of the class's job; then validate in the setter. Constructors A class can have several constructors (overloading). One can call another with this(...) as its first statement, so the setup logic lives in one place. If you write no constructor, Java provides an empty one; as soon as you write any constructor, that free one disappears. Immutable classes A class whose fields are all final and set only in the constructor is immutable . Immutable objects cannot be changed by accident, are safe to share between parts of a program and between threads, and make good map keys. String , Integer and LocalDate are immutable; records (lesson 3.05) are the short way to write your own. static A static field belongs to the class, not to any object: there is exactly one, shared by all instances. A static method has no this and can use only static fields and its parameters. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Ticket a = new Ticket(); Ticket b = new Ticket(); System.out.println(a.getNumber() + " " + b.getNumber() + " issued: " + Ticket.issued()); Temperature t = Temperature.fromFahrenheit(212); System.out.println(t.celsius() + " " + Temperature.ABSOLUTE_ZERO); System.out.println(MathUtil.clamp(15, 0, 10)); } } class Ticket { private static int next = 1; // shared by all tickets private final int number; Ticket() { number = next++; } int getNumber() { return number; } static int issued() { return next - 1; } } class Temperature { static final double ABSOLUTE_ZERO = -273.15; // a constant: static final, UPPER_CASE private final double celsius; private Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; } // private: use the factory methods static Temperature fromCelsius(double c) { return new Temperature(c); } static Temperature fromFahrenheit(double f) { return new Temperature((f - 32) 5 / 9); } double celsius() { return celsius; } } final class MathUtil { private MathUtil() { } // a utility class: no instances static int clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) { return Math.max(lo, Math.min(hi, v)); } } - Static factory methods like Temperature.fromFahrenheit have descriptive names, unlike constructors, and can validate or reuse objects. List.of , Integer.valueOf and LocalDate.of are examples. - static final fields are constants . - A utility class ( Math , Arrays , Collections ) has only static methods and a private constructor. - Avoid mutable static fields outside of small cases like counters: shared state makes programs hard to test and reason about.

title: An immutable time class
body: Write an immutable final class Time for times of day, with static factories and constants: java static final Time MIDNIGHT, NOON static Time of(int hour, int minute) // IllegalArgumentException outside 0-23 / 0-59 static Time parse(String text) // "9:05" or "09:05"; anything else: IllegalArgumentException Time plusMinutes(int minutes) // a NEW time, wrapping around midnight; minutes may be negative int minutesUntil(Time later) // minutes going forward: 23:00 to 01:00 is 120 boolean isBefore(Time other) String toString() // "09:05" boolean equals(Object o), int hashCode() // equal when hour and minute are equal - The constructor is private; the fields are private final . - parse trims spaces; the hour has one or two digits and the minute exactly two.

title: 3.03  Inheritance and Polymorphism
body: Extending a class with extends, calling the superclass constructor with super, overriding methods and @Override, protected members, dynamic dispatch and polymorphism, the Object class with toString, equals and hashCode, casting with instanceof patterns, final, and when to prefer composition. extends A class can extend one other class, its superclass , inheriting its fields and methods and adding or changing some: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Employee staff = { new Employee("Ada", 4000), new Manager("Grace", 5000, 3), new Intern("Linus", 1200, 6), }; double total = 0; for (Employee e : staff) { System.out.println(e.describe()); // each object answers in its own way total += e.monthlyCost(); } System.out.println("Total: " + total); } } class Employee { private final String name; protected final double salary; // visible to subclasses Employee(String name, double salary) { this.name = name; this.salary = salary; } String getName() { return name; } double monthlyCost() { return salary; } String describe() { return name + " costs " + monthlyCost(); } } class Manager extends Employee { private final int reports; Manager(String name, double salary, int reports) { super(name, salary); // must be the first statement this.reports = reports; } @Override double monthlyCost() { return super.monthlyCost() + 200 reports; } @Override String describe() { return super.describe() + " (manages " + reports + ")"; } } class Intern extends Employee { private final int months; Intern(String name, double stipend, int months) { super(name, stipend); this.months = months; } @Override String describe() { return getName() + " is an intern for " + months + " months"; } } - super(...) runs the superclass constructor; it must come first. If you leave it out, Java calls super() with no arguments. - Overriding : a subclass method with the same signature replaces the inherited one. @Override makes the compiler check that it really overrides something (a typo would otherwise create a new method silently). - super.method() calls the superclass's version. Polymorphism A variable of type Employee can refer to a Manager . When a method is called, Java uses the version of the actual object's class, decided at run time ( dynamic dispatch ). So describe() in Employee calls monthlyCost() , and for a manager that is the manager's version. Code written for Employee works for every subclass, including ones written later. The Object class Every class extends Object , directly or indirectly, and inherits toString , equals and hashCode . Override them to give your class sensible behaviour: java import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.Set; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Book a = new Book("Dune", 1965); Book b = new Book("Dune", 1965); System.out.println(a + " " + a.equals(b)); Set<Book shelf = new HashSet< (); shelf.add(a); shelf.add(b); System.out.println(shelf.size()); // 1: equal books count once } } class Book { private final String title; private final int year; Book(String title, int year) { this.title = title; this.year = year; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { if (this == o) return true; if (!(o instanceof Book other)) return false; return year == other.year && title.equals(other.title); } @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(title, year); } @Override public String toString() { return title + " (" + year + ")"; } } The rule: objects that are equal must have equal hash codes. Override both together, or HashSet and HashMap will misbehave (lesson 4.02). instanceof and casting instanceof checks an object's type; the pattern form also gives you a variable of that type: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Object things = {"text", 42, 3.5, new int {1, 2}}; for (Object o : things) { if (o instanceof String s) System.out.println("a string of length " + s.length()); else if (o instanceof Integer i && i 40) System.out.println("a big int " + i); else System.out.println("something else: " + o.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } The old form, ((String) o).length() , casts explicitly and throws ClassCastException if the object is not that type. Many instanceof checks in a row usually mean a method should be overridden instead. final A final class cannot be extended ( String is final); a final method cannot be overridden. Use final for classes not designed for inheritance. Composition over inheritance Inheritance means "is a": a Manager is an Employee . When the relationship is "has a" (a Car has an Engine ), hold the other object in a field instead: composition . It is more flexible, since you can swap the part, and avoids deep hierarchies that are hard to change. Java allows only one superclass, but any number of interfaces (next lesson).

title: Bank accounts with inheritance
body: Build a small hierarchy, one class per file ( Account.java , SavingsAccount.java , CheckingAccount.java ). Money is in whole cents ( long ). java class Account // Account(String owner, long balance) String getOwner(), long getBalance() void deposit(long amount) // IllegalArgumentException if amount <= 0 boolean withdraw(long amount) // false (and no change) if amount <= 0 or not allowed long available() // how much can be withdrawn now: the balance void monthEnd() // nothing for a plain account String toString() // "<Kind <owner : <balance in euros, 2 decimals ", Kind is the class's simple name class SavingsAccount extends Account // SavingsAccount(String owner, long balance, double yearlyRate) monthEnd(): adds interest of balance yearlyRate / 12, rounded to the nearest cent class CheckingAccount extends Account // CheckingAccount(String owner, long balance, long overdraftLimit) available(): balance + overdraftLimit withdraw(...): allowed up to available(); every successful withdrawal also costs a fee of 25 cents monthEnd(): if the balance is negative, charges 2% of the overdrawn amount, rounded to the nearest cent withdraw in Account should use available() , so that CheckingAccount only needs to override available() and add its fee. The fee may take the balance further below zero.

title: 3.04  Interfaces and Abstract Classes
body: Abstract classes and abstract methods, interfaces as contracts, implementing several interfaces, default and static interface methods, programming to an interface, the built-in Comparable and Iterable, functional interfaces as a preview of lambdas, and choosing between an interface and an abstract class. Abstract classes An abstract class cannot be instantiated. It holds shared code and declares abstract methods , without bodies, that every concrete subclass must implement: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Shape shapes = {new Circle(1), new Rectangle(2, 3), new Circle(0.5)}; double total = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) { System.out.println(s.describe()); total += s.area(); } System.out.printf("Total area: %.2f%n", total); // new Shape("x"); // error: Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated } } abstract class Shape { private final String name; protected Shape(String name) { this.name = name; } abstract double area(); // no body: subclasses must provide it String describe() { return String.format("%s with area %.2f", name, area()); } // shared code } class Circle extends Shape { private final double r; Circle(double r) { super("circle"); this.r = r; } @Override double area() { return Math.PI r r; } } class Rectangle extends Shape { private final double w, h; Rectangle(double w, double h) { super("rectangle"); this.w = w; this.h = h; } @Override double area() { return w h; } } Interfaces An interface is a contract: a list of methods a class promises to provide.
