A class implements any number of interfaces: java import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Notifier channels = List.of(new EmailNotifier("ada@example.com"), new SmsNotifier("+3161234")); for (Notifier n : channels) { if (n.isAvailable()) n.send("Your order has shipped"); } Notifier quiet = new EmailNotifier("not-an-address"); quiet.sendAll(List.of("a", "b")); // a default method } } interface Notifier { boolean isAvailable(); void send(String message); default void sendAll(List<String messages) { // a default method: implementers get it for free if (!isAvailable()) { System.out.println("not available"); return; } for (String m : messages) send(m); } } class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { private final String address; EmailNotifier(String address) { this.address = address; } public boolean isAvailable() { return address.contains("@"); } public void send(String message) { System.out.println("email to " + address + ": " + message); } } class SmsNotifier implements Notifier { private final String number; SmsNotifier(String number) { this.number = number; } public boolean isAvailable() { return number.startsWith("+"); } public void send(String message) { System.out.println("sms to " + number + ": " + message); } } Interface methods are public automatically, so implementing methods must be public too. Interfaces can also have static methods and constants, but no instance fields. Program to an interface Declare variables and parameters with interface types ( List , Notifier ), and create concrete classes ( ArrayList , SmsNotifier ) in one place. Code that depends only on the interface works with any implementation, including test fakes, and the implementation can change without touching it. Built-in interfaces Comparable<T gives a class a natural order , used by Collections.sort , Arrays.sort , TreeSet and TreeMap : java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Version versions = new ArrayList< (List.of(new Version(1, 10), new Version(1, 2), new Version(0, 9))); Collections.sort(versions); System.out.println(versions); } } class Version implements Comparable<Version { private final int major, minor; Version(int major, int minor) { this.major = major; this.minor = minor; } @Override public int compareTo(Version other) { // negative, zero or positive if (major != other.major) return Integer.compare(major, other.major); return Integer.compare(minor, other.minor); } @Override public String toString() { return major + "." + minor; } } Other everyday interfaces: Iterable<T (usable in an enhanced for), Comparator<T (an external ordering, lesson 4.03), Runnable (a task for a thread, lesson 6.04), and AutoCloseable (try-with-resources, lesson 4.05). An interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface ; a lambda can implement it in one line (lesson 6.01): Comparator<String byLength = (a, b) - a.length() - b.length(); Interface or abstract class? Interface Abstract class --- --- A capability that unrelated classes share ( Comparable , Notifier ) A family of closely related classes sharing code and state ( Shape ) A class can implement many A class can extend only one No instance fields Fields and constructors Prefer interfaces; reach for an abstract class when subclasses really share state and code. Often both: an interface for the contract and an abstract class with a partial implementation.

title: Text filters behind an interface
body: Write an interface and several implementations that clean up text, plus a pipeline that combines them. The project has three files: java // TextFilter.java interface TextFilter { String apply(String text); default String name() { return getClass().getSimpleName(); } } // Filters.java: the simple filters, as static nested classes class Filters { static class Trim implements TextFilter // removes spaces at both ends and collapses runs of spaces to one static class LowerCase implements TextFilter static class ReplaceWords implements TextFilter // ReplaceWords(Map<String, String replacements): whole words, case-sensitive static class MaxLength implements TextFilter // MaxLength(int max): cuts to max characters, ending with "..." when cut } // Pipeline.java class Pipeline implements TextFilter, Iterable<TextFilter Pipeline add(TextFilter filter) // returns this, so calls can be chained String apply(String text) // applies every filter in order String name() // "Pipeline Trim, LowerCase " - new Filters.ReplaceWords(Map.of("teh", "the")) turns "teh cat ate teh fish" into "the cat ate the fish" , but leaves "tehran" alone. Words are separated by single spaces. - MaxLength throws IllegalArgumentException for a max below 3. - A Pipeline is itself a TextFilter , so pipelines can contain pipelines.

title: 3.05  Records, Enums and Sealed Types
body: Modern Java data modelling - records with compact constructors and value equality, enums with fields, methods and switch, EnumMap, sealed interfaces that list their implementations, and pattern matching in switch with record patterns for exhaustive handling of every case. Records A record is a class for plain data. One line gives you private final fields, a constructor, accessors, and equals , hashCode and toString based on the values: java import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = new Point(1, 2); System.out.println(a + " " + a.equals(b) + " " + a.x()); // accessors are x() and y() Set<Point set = new HashSet< (Set.of(a)); System.out.println(set.contains(b)); // true: value equality System.out.println(a.plus(new Point(10, 10))); System.out.println(new Range(3, 7).length()); try { new Range(5, 1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } } record Point(int x, int y) { Point plus(Point other) { return new Point(x + other.x, y + other.y); } // records can have methods } record Range(int start, int end) { Range { // a compact constructor: validation if (start end) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start after end: " + start + " " + end); } int length() { return end - start; } } Records are immutable : to "change" one, create a new one. Use them for values that are compared, stored in sets and maps, returned from methods, and passed between parts of a program. Enums An enum is a type with a fixed set of named values. Enums can have fields, constructors and methods: java import java.util.EnumMap; import java.util.Map; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Planet home = Planet.EARTH; System.out.printf("%s: %.2f m/s2%n", home, home.surfaceGravity()); for (Planet p : Planet.values()) System.out.print(p.name().toLowerCase() + " "); System.out.println(); System.out.println(Planet.valueOf("MARS").ordinal()); Map<Planet, Integer visits = new EnumMap< (Planet.class); visits.merge(Planet.MARS, 1, Integer::sum); visits.merge(Planet.MARS, 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(visits); Level level = Level.WARN; String colour = switch (level) { case DEBUG, INFO - "grey"; case WARN - "orange"; case ERROR - "red"; }; // no default needed: every constant is covered System.out.println(colour + " " + level.isAtLeast(Level.INFO)); } } enum Planet { MERCURY(3.303e23, 2.4397e6), EARTH(5.976e24, 6.37814e6), MARS(6.421e23, 3.3972e6); private final double mass, radius; Planet(double mass, double radius) { this.mass = mass; this.radius = radius; } double surfaceGravity() { return 6.67300e-11 mass / (radius radius); } } enum Level { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; boolean isAtLeast(Level other) { return compareTo(other) = 0; } } Use enums instead of int or String codes for fixed sets: directions, card suits, order states, log levels. The compiler then rejects invalid values, and a switch can be checked for completeness. Sealed types A sealed interface or class lists exactly which classes may implement or extend it. Together with records, that models data that is "one of these kinds": java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Shape shapes = {new Circle(1), new Square(2), new Rect(2, 3)}; for (Shape s : shapes) System.out.printf("%s - %.2f%n", s, area(s)); System.out.println(describe(new Rect(4, 4)) + ", " + describe(new Rect(2, 5))); } static double area(Shape s) { return switch (s) { // pattern matching for switch case Circle c - Math.PI c.r() c.r(); case Square sq - sq.side() sq.side(); case Rect(double w, double h) - w h; // a record pattern takes the record apart }; // exhaustive: every permitted type is covered } static String describe(Shape s) { return switch (s) { case Rect(double w, double h) when w == h - "a square-shaped rectangle"; // a guard case Rect r - "a rectangle"; default - "another shape"; }; } } sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Rect { } record Circle(double r) implements Shape { } record Square(double side) implements Shape { } record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape { } Because the compiler knows every possible Shape , the switch in area needs no default . If someone adds Triangle to the permits list, every switch that does not handle it stops compiling, showing exactly what to update. This style, data as records and behaviour as functions that switch over them, complements classic object-oriented polymorphism.

title: Expressions with sealed records
body: Model arithmetic expressions as a sealed interface whose cases are records nested inside it, and write three operations with pattern matching, all in Expr.java : java sealed interface Expr { record Num(double value) implements Expr { } record Var(String name) implements Expr { } record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { } record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { } record Neg(Expr inner) implements Expr { } static double eval(Expr e, Map<String, Double vars) // IllegalArgumentException("unknown variable x") when missing static String show(Expr e) // fully parenthesised, see below static Expr simplify(Expr e) } Records nested in a sealed interface are its permitted subtypes automatically; from outside they are written Expr.Num , Expr.Add ... show : numbers without a trailing .0 when whole ( 2 , 2.5 ), variables by name, (a + b) , (a b) , and -a for negation. For example show(new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Var("x"), new Num(3)))) is "(2 + (x 3))" . simplify works bottom-up (simplify the parts first), then applies these rules: - Add : both numbers → their sum; 0 + e or e + 0 → e - Mul : both numbers → their product; 0 e or e 0 → Num(0) ; 1 e or e 1 → e - Neg : of a number → the negated number; Neg(Neg(e)) → e Use switch with patterns, with no default , so the compiler checks every case is handled.

title: Cards and poker hands
body: Model a deck of playing cards with enums and records, and rank five-card poker hands. Each type goes in its own file, named after it, as in any Java project: Suit.java , Rank.java , Card.java , Deck.java , Category.java , HandValue.java and Poker.java . java enum Suit { CLUBS, DIAMONDS, HEARTS, SPADES } // symbols C, D, H, S enum Rank { TWO, THREE, ..., TEN, JACK, QUEEN, KING, ACE } // symbols 2-9, T, J, Q, K, A record Card(Rank rank, Suit suit) // toString: "AS", "TH", "2C"; static Card parse(String) class Deck // a full 52-card deck enum Category { HIGH_CARD, PAIR, TWO_PAIR, THREE_OF_A_KIND, STRAIGHT, FLUSH, FULL_HOUSE, FOUR_OF_A_KIND, STRAIGHT_FLUSH } record HandValue(Category category, List<Rank tiebreak) implements Comparable<HandValue class Poker static List<Card parseHand(String text) // "AS KD 7H 7C 2S" static HandValue evaluate(List<Card five) static int compare(String hand1, String hand2) // positive if hand1 wins, negative if hand2 wins, 0 for a tie Cards and deck - Card.parse("QH") gives the queen of hearts; anything else (wrong length, unknown symbol) throws IllegalArgumentException . Symbols are upper case. - new Deck() has 52 different cards in order: suits in enum order, and within each suit ranks from two to ace. size() , deal() (removes and returns the top card, the first one; IllegalStateException when empty) and shuffle(Random random) (use Collections.shuffle(list, random) ). Evaluating a hand (exactly 5 different cards, else IllegalArgumentException ): - Categories from lowest to highest as in the enum. A straight is five consecutive ranks; the ace can also be low in A 2 3 4 5 (a five-high straight). A flush is five cards of one suit. - tiebreak lists the ranks that decide between two hands of the same category, most important first: ranks ordered by how many times they occur (more first), then by rank (higher first). So 7H 7C AS KD 2S (a pair) gives SEVEN, ACE, KING, TWO , and KS KH 4D 4C KC (full house) gives KING, FOUR . For straights and straight flushes it is just the highest card, with FIVE for the ace-low straight. - HandValue.compareTo compares the category first, then the tiebreak lists rank by rank.

title: 4.01  Generics
body: Type parameters on classes, interfaces and methods, why generics replaced Object and casts, bounded types with extends, wildcards with ? extends and ? super (PECS), type erasure and its limits, and writing your own generic container. Why generics Before generics (Java 5), a list held Object s. Every read needed a cast, and putting the wrong type in was only discovered when the program crashed: java-norun List names = new ArrayList(); // a "raw" list names.add("Ada"); names.add(42); // nothing stops this String first = (String) names.get(0); String second = (String) names.get(1); // ClassCastException at run time With a type parameter , List<String holds only strings, the compiler checks every add , and no casts are needed. Mistakes become compile errors. A generic class java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Box<String name = new Box< ("Ada"); Box<Integer age = new Box< (36); String n = name.get(); // no cast int a = age.get() + 1; System.out.println(n + " " + a + " " + name.map(String::length).get()); Pair<String, Integer entry = new Pair< ("apples", 4); System.out.println(entry + " " + entry.swap()); } } class Box<T { private final T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } <R Box<R map(java.util.function.Function<T, R f) { return new Box< (f.apply(value)); } // a generic method } record Pair<A, B (A first, B second) { Pair<B, A swap() { return new Pair< (second, first); } } By convention, type parameters are single capital letters: T (type), E (element), K / V (key/value), R (result). Type arguments must be reference types: Box<int is not allowed, use Box<Integer . Generic methods A method can have its own type parameters, written before the return type. The compiler infers them from the arguments: java import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(last(List.of("a", "b", "c"))); System.out.println(last(List.of(1, 2, 3))); System.out.println(max(List.of(4, 9, 2)) + " " + max(List.of("pear", "apple"))); } static <T T last(List<T items) { return items.get(items.size() - 1); } static <T extends Comparable<T T max(List<T items) { // a bounded type parameter T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) if (item.compareTo(best) 0) best = item; return best; } } T extends Comparable<T means "any T that can be compared with itself", which is what lets the body call compareTo . Wildcards A List<Integer is not a List<Number , even though Integer is a Number . (If it were, you could add a Double to a list of integers through the List<Number variable.) Wildcards express "a list of some type": java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Integer ints = List.of(1, 2, 3); List<Double doubles = List.of(1.5, 2.5); System.out.println(sum(ints) + " " + sum(doubles)); List<Number numbers = new ArrayList< (); List<Object objects = new ArrayList< (); addOnes(numbers, 2); addOnes(objects, 1); System.out.println(numbers + " " + objects); } static double sum(List<? extends Number values) { // read Numbers from it double total = 0; for (Number n : values) total += n.doubleValue(); return total; } static void addOnes(List<? super Integer target, int count) { // write Integers into it for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(1); } } The rule of thumb is PECS : Producer Extends, Consumer Super . A parameter you only read from takes ? extends T ; one you only write to takes ? super T . Collections.copy(List<? super T dest, List<? extends T src) uses both. Type erasure Generics exist only at compile time: the compiler checks the types and then erases them, so at run time a List<String is just a List . Consequences: - new T() and new T 10 are not allowed (the type is unknown at run time). - x instanceof List<String is not allowed; x instanceof List<? is. - You cannot overload f(List<String ) and f(List<Integer ) : after erasure they are the same.

title: Generic methods and types
body: Write a generic record and generic static methods: java // Pair.java record Pair<A, B (A first, B second) { static <A, B Pair<A, B of(A first, B second) Pair<B, A swap() } // Generics.java class Generics { static <T extends Comparable<? super T T max(Collection<T items) // NoSuchElementException when empty static double sum(Collection<? extends Number numbers) static void fill(List<? super Integer target, int from, int to) // adds from, from+1, ..., to-1 static <K, V Map<V, List<K invert(Map<K, V map) // keys grouped by value static <T List<Pair<T, T pairs(List<T items) // a, b, c, d gives (a, b), (c, d) ; an odd last item is dropped } The bound on max must also accept LocalDate , which implements Comparable<ChronoLocalDate rather than Comparable<LocalDate . invert returns a LinkedHashMap and keeps both the values and each list of keys in the order the map gives them, so with a LinkedHashMap or TreeMap input the result is predictable.

title: 4.02  The Collections Framework
body: The interfaces and implementations of java.util - List, Set, Map, Queue and Deque with ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue - choosing between them, iterating, counting and grouping with maps, the equals and hashCode contract, and immutable collections. The big picture Program to the interface ( List , Set , Map ) and pick the implementation for its performance and ordering. Need Use --- --- A sequence, access by index ArrayList Unique items, fast contains HashSet (no order), LinkedHashSet (insertion order), TreeSet (sorted) Look up by key HashMap (no order), LinkedHashMap (insertion order), TreeMap (sorted keys) A stack or a queue ArrayDeque Always take the smallest (or largest) next PriorityQueue LinkedList is rarely the right choice: ArrayList and ArrayDeque are faster for almost everything. Sets java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String words = List.of("pear", "apple", "pear", "fig", "apple"); System.out.println(new HashSet< (words)); // some order System.out.println(new LinkedHashSet< (words)); // first-seen order System.out.println(new TreeSet< (words)); // sorted Set<Integer a = new TreeSet< (Set.of(1, 2, 3, 4)); Set<Integer b = Set.of(3, 4, 5); Set<Integer both = new TreeSet< (a); both.retainAll(b); // intersection Set<Integer either = new TreeSet< (a); either.addAll(b); // union a.removeAll(b); // difference System.out.println(both + " " + either + " " + a); System.out.println(new HashSet< (words).add("fig")); // false: already there } } Maps java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Map<String, Integer ages = new HashMap< (); ages.put("Ada", 36); ages.put("Grace", 85); ages.put("Ada", 37); // replaces System.out.println(ages.get("Ada") + " " + ages.get("Bob") + " " + ages.getOrDefault("Bob", -1)); System.out.println(ages.containsKey("Grace") + " " + ages.size()); String text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"; Map<String, Integer counts = new TreeMap< (); for (String w : text.split(" ")) counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum); // counting System.out.println(counts); Map<Character, List<String byLetter = new TreeMap< (); for (String w : List.of("apple", "avocado", "banana", "cherry")) { byLetter.computeIfAbsent(w.charAt(0), k - new ArrayList< ()).add(w); // grouping } System.out.println(byLetter); for (Map.Entry<String, Integer e : counts.entrySet()) { if (e.getValue() 1) System.out.print(e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue() + " "); } System.out.println(); } } map.get(missing) returns null , and unboxing that null into an int throws NullPointerException . Use getOrDefault , containsKey , or merge / computeIfAbsent . Queues and stacks java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Deque<String stack = new ArrayDeque< (); stack.push("a"); stack.push("b"); stack.push("c"); System.out.println(stack.pop() + " " + stack.peek()); // c b: last in, first out Queue<String queue = new ArrayDeque< (); queue.offer("first"); queue.offer("second"); System.out.println(queue.poll() + " " + queue.size()); // first 1: first in, first out PriorityQueue<Integer pq = new PriorityQueue< (List.of(5, 1, 4, 2)); StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(); while (!pq.isEmpty()) out.append(pq.poll()).append(' '); // always the smallest next System.out.println(out); } } equals and hashCode HashSet and HashMap find objects by hashCode() first, then confirm with equals() . For your own classes used as keys or set members: - override both equals and hashCode , using the same fields; - objects that are equals must have the same hashCode ; - do not change those fields while the object is in a hash set or map key (it would be filed under the old hash). Records do all of this for you, which makes them ideal keys. TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo (or a Comparator ) instead, and treat items that compare as 0 as duplicates. Iterating and removing All collections work with the enhanced for . To remove while iterating, use removeIf(...) or an explicit Iterator and its remove() ; removing through the collection itself during a for loop throws ConcurrentModificationException . Immutable collections List.of , Set.of and Map.of create unmodifiable collections; List.copyOf(list) makes an unmodifiable copy. Returning unmodifiable views ( Collections.unmodifiableList(items) ) from a class protects its internal lists from outside changes.

title: Choosing collections
body: Write these methods in Text.java , each with the collection that fits: java class Text { static List<String topWords(String text, int n) // the n most frequent words, ties alphabetical static Character firstUnique(String s) // the first character that appears exactly once, or null static SortedMap<Integer, List<String byLength(List<String words) // lengths sorted; words in input order, no repeats static boolean isBalanced(String s) // brackets ( ) { } properly nested; other characters ignored } - Words in topWords are runs of letters, compared in lower case. - byLength( "fig", "pear", "kiwi", "fig", "plum" ) is {3= fig , 4= pear, kiwi, plum } .

title: 4.03  Comparable, Comparator and Sorting
body: Natural ordering with Comparable, external orderings with Comparator, building comparators with comparing, thenComparing, reversed and nullsFirst, sorting lists and arrays, stability, sorted collections with custom orderings, the compareTo contract, and common mistakes like subtracting to compare. Natural order: Comparable A class that implements Comparable<T has a natural order : compareTo returns a negative number when this comes first, zero when equal, positive when this comes after. Strings, numbers and dates already have one. java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Student students = new ArrayList< (List.of( new Student("Grace", 88), new Student("Ada", 95), new Student("Linus", 88))); Collections.sort(students); // uses compareTo System.out.println(students); } } record Student(String name, int score) implements Comparable<Student { @Override public int compareTo(Student other) { return name.compareTo(other.name); // natural order: by name } } Other orders: Comparator A Comparator is an ordering kept outside the class, so one class can be sorted many ways. The Comparator helper methods build them from the fields to compare: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Student students = new ArrayList< (List.of( new Student("Grace", 88, 2), new Student("Ada", 95, 1), new Student("Linus", 88, 1), new Student("Barbara", 72, 3))); students.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::score).reversed() .thenComparing(Student::name)); // by score, highest first; ties by name System.out.println(students); students.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::year).thenComparing(Student::score, Comparator.reverseOrder())); System.out.println(students); Comparator<String byLength = Comparator.comparingInt(String::length); List<String words = new ArrayList< (List.of("kiwi", "fig", "banana", "pear")); words.sort(byLength.thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())); System.out.println(words); } } record Student(String name, int score, int year) { } Builder Meaning --- --- Comparator.comparing(f) , comparingInt(f) , comparingDouble(f) Compare by a key .thenComparing(g) Break ties with a second key .reversed() The opposite order Comparator.naturalOrder() , reverseOrder() Natural order and its reverse Comparator.nullsFirst(c) , nullsLast(c) Allow nulls Student::score is a method reference : shorthand for the lambda s - s.score() (lesson 6.01). Sorting java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int nums = {5, 3, 9, 1}; Arrays.sort(nums); // primitives: natural order only Integer boxed = {5, 3, 9, 1}; Arrays.sort(boxed, Comparator.reverseOrder()); // objects: any comparator System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums) + " " + Arrays.toString(boxed)); List<String names = new ArrayList< (List.of("bob", "Alice", "carol")); names.sort(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER); System.out.println(names); TreeSet<String byLength = new TreeSet< (Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(s - s)); byLength.addAll(List.of("pear", "fig", "banana", "kiwi")); System.out.println(byLength + " first=" + byLength.first()); } } Sorting objects in Java ( List.sort , Collections.sort , Arrays.sort on objects) is stable : equal items keep their relative order. That is what makes sorting by one key and then another work as expected. The compareTo contract A correct comparison must be consistent: if a < b then b a ; if a < b and b < c then a < c ; and ideally compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals is true (a TreeSet treats compare-0 items as duplicates). A classic bug is comparing by subtraction: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = Integer.MIN_VALUE, b = 1; System.out.println(a - b 0); // true: the subtraction overflows, so the order is wrong System.out.println(Integer.compare(a, b)); // -1: correct } } Always use Integer.compare , Double.compare , or the Comparator builders.

title: Sorting with comparators
body: Employees are records: java // Employee.java record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) { } Write the queries in Staff.java using Comparator builders ( comparing , thenComparing , reversed ): java class Staff { static List<Employee bySalary(List<Employee staff) // highest salary first, ties by name static List<Employee byDeptThenAge(List<Employee staff) // department A-Z, then youngest first, then name static Map<String, Employee oldestPerDept(List<Employee staff) // TreeMap by department; ties: the earlier name static List<String topEarners(List<Employee staff, int n) // names of the n best paid, ties by name } None of the methods may change the list they are given.

title: 4.04  Exceptions
body: Throwing and catching exceptions, the exception hierarchy, checked versus unchecked exceptions and the throws clause, multi-catch, finally, try-with-resources, custom exception classes with causes, stack traces, and good practice for validating arguments and handling errors. throw and catch When a method cannot do its job it throws an exception. The exception travels up the call stack until a catch block handles it; if none does, the program stops and prints a stack trace . java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String inputs = {"42", "abc", "-5"}; for (String input : inputs) { try { int age = parseAge(input); System.out.println("age " + age); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("'" + input + "' is not a number"); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } } static int parseAge(String text) { int age = Integer.parseInt(text); // may throw NumberFormatException if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age cannot be negative: " + age); return age; } } Catch blocks are tried in order, so put specific types first: NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException , so the other order would not compile (the second catch could never run). The hierarchy - Unchecked exceptions ( RuntimeException and its subclasses) usually mean a bug or bad argument. The compiler does not force you to handle them. - Checked exceptions (other Exception subclasses, like IOException ) are problems a correct program can still meet: a missing file, a lost connection. A method that may throw one must declare it with throws , and callers must catch it or declare it too. - Error s are serious problems of the JVM itself; do not catch them. java import java.io.IOException; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try { System.out.println(loadSetting("theme")); System.out.println(loadSetting("missing")); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("could not load: " + e.getMessage()); } } static String loadSetting(String key) throws IOException { // callers must deal with IOException if (key.equals("missing")) throw new IOException("no setting " + key); return "dark"; } } finally and try-with-resources finally runs whether or not an exception happened, for clean-up. For anything that must be closed (files, connections), try-with-resources closes it automatically, even if an exception is thrown: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try (Resource a = new Resource("first"); Resource b = new Resource("second")) { System.out.println("using both"); throw new IllegalStateException("something failed"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage()); } finally { System.out.println("finally runs too"); } } } class Resource implements AutoCloseable { private final String name; Resource(String name) { this.name = name; System.out.println("open " + name); } @Override public void close() { System.out.println("close " + name); } // closed in reverse order } Any class implementing AutoCloseable works in a try-with-resources statement. Your own exceptions Create an exception class when callers need to recognise your specific problem. Pass the original exception as the cause when you wrap one: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try { Config.port("80x"); } catch (ConfigException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage() + " <- caused by " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } class ConfigException extends Exception { // checked ConfigException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); } } class Config { static int port(String text) throws ConfigException { try { return Integer.parseInt(text); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { throw new ConfigException("bad port '" + text + "'", e); } } } Extend RuntimeException instead for exceptions that signal programming errors, so callers are not forced to catch them. Good practice - Validate arguments early with clear messages: Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name") , if (qty < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be at least 1: " + qty) . - Catch only what you can handle , where you can do something useful. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch ; at least log it. - Do not use exceptions for normal control flow : check with hasNextInt() , containsKey() or Optional (lesson 6.03) when a missing value is normal. - Read stack traces from the top : the first line names the exception and message; the first at line in your own code is usually where to look.

title: A config parser with exceptions
body: Parse simple configuration text such as server settings port = 8080 host = example.org debug = true into a map, reporting problems with your own checked exception: java // ConfigException.java class ConfigException extends Exception { ConfigException(int line, String message) // getMessage(): "line <n : <message " ConfigException(int line, String message, Throwable cause) int line() } // Config.java class Config { static Map<String, String parse(List<String lines) throws ConfigException static int getInt(Map<String, String config, String key, int min, int max) throws ConfigException } parse : - skips blank lines and lines starting with (after trimming); - every other line must be key = value (one = ; spaces around key and value are trimmed); else ConfigException(n, "expected key = value") ; - keys are non-empty and made of letters, digits, . and _ ; else "bad key" ; - a key defined twice: "duplicate key <key " ; - line numbers count from 1; the result keeps the order of the file. - A null list throws NullPointerException (a bug in the caller, not a config problem). getInt reports problems with line 0: a missing key gives "missing <key " , a value that is not a whole number gives "<key is not a number" with the NumberFormatException as the cause, and a number outside min..max gives "<key must be between <min and <max " .

title: 4.05  Files and I/O
body:
Reading and writing text files with java.nio.file - Path and Files, readString, readAllLines, lines and write, BufferedReader and BufferedWriter for large files, character encodings, directories and walking them, handling IOException, parsing CSV records, and the older java.io classes you will still meet. Path and Files Modern Java uses java.nio.file : a Path names a file, and the Files class does the work: java import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file. ; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { Path file = Path.of("notes.txt"); Files.writeString(file, "first line
second line
"); Files.writeString(file, "appended
", StandardOpenOption.APPEND); String all = Files.readString(file); List<String lines = Files.readAllLines(file); System.out.println(all.length() + " characters, " + lines.size() + " lines, last: " + lines.get(lines.size() - 1)); Files.write(Path.of("numbers.txt"), List.of("1", "2", "3")); long sum = 0; try (var stream = Files.lines(Path.of("numbers.txt"))) { // lazy: one line at a time sum = stream.mapToLong(Long::parseLong).sum(); } System.out.println(sum + " " + Files.exists(file) + " " + Files.size(file)); } } main declares throws IOException here to keep the example short; real programs catch it where they can report the problem. Paths and directories java import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file. ; import java.util.stream.Stream; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { Path dir = Path.of("data", "2026"); Files.createDirectories(dir); // all missing levels; fine if it exists Path report = dir.resolve("report.csv"); // data/2026/report.csv Files.writeString(report, "id,total
1,9.50
"); System.out.println(report.getFileName() + " in " + report.getParent()); try (Stream<Path all = Files.walk(Path.of("data"))) { all.filter(Files::isRegularFile).forEach(p - System.out.println("found " + p.toString().replace('\', '/'))); } Files.copy(report, dir.resolve("backup.csv"), StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING); Files.delete(dir.resolve("backup.csv")); } } Build paths with Path.of(a, b, c) and resolve , never by gluing strings with / or \ : the separator differs between systems. Large files: buffered readers and writers readAllLines loads the whole file into memory. For big files, read line by line with a BufferedReader , and write with a BufferedWriter , both in try-with-resources: java import java.io. ; import java.nio.file. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { Path log = Path.of("log.txt"); try (BufferedWriter out = Files.newBufferedWriter(log)) { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { out.write("entry " + i); out.newLine(); } } // closing flushes the buffer to disk int count = 0; try (BufferedReader in = Files.newBufferedReader(log)) { String line; while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { if (line.endsWith("3") line.endsWith("5")) count++; } } System.out.println(count); } } Text is stored as bytes using an encoding . Files methods use UTF-8 by default, which handles every language; pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly when using older APIs. Errors File operations fail for reasons outside your program. The specific exceptions tell you why: java import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try { String text = Files.readString(Path.of("settings.ini")); System.out.println(text); } catch (NoSuchFileException e) { System.out.println("no settings file: using defaults"); } catch (AccessDeniedException e) { System.out.println("not allowed to read " + e.getFile()); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("could not read settings: " + e.getMessage()); } } } Reading records A common task is reading structured lines into objects. Keep parsing in its own method, and decide what to do with bad lines: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String lines = List.of("name,score", "Ada,95", "Grace,abc", "Linus,72", ""); List<Result results = new ArrayList< (); List<String problems = new ArrayList< (); for (int i = 1; i < lines.size(); i++) { String line = lines.get(i); if (line.isBlank()) continue; String f = line.split(","); try { results.add(new Result(f 0 .trim(), Integer.parseInt(f 1 .trim()))); } catch (NumberFormatException ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { problems.add("line " + (i + 1) + ": " + line); } } System.out.println(results); System.out.println(problems); } } record Result(String name, int score) { } catch (A B e) is a multi-catch : one handler for several exception types. Real CSV can contain quoted commas; use a library such as Apache Commons CSV for files you do not control. The older java.io You will meet older code using java.io.File , FileReader , FileWriter and Scanner(new File(...)) . They still work; Path and Files are the modern replacements with better error messages. file.toPath() and path.toFile() convert between them.

title: Working with files
body: Write file utilities with java.nio.file : java // Summary.java record Summary(int lines, int words, long characters, String longestLine) { } // FileTools.java class FileTools { static Summary summarize(Path file) throws IOException static int copyMatching(Path in, Path out, String needle) throws IOException static List<String findByExtension(Path dir, String extension) throws IOException } - summarize : the number of lines, words (runs of non-white-space characters), characters (the file size in characters, line breaks included), and the longest line (the first one on a tie; "" for an empty file). - copyMatching writes the lines of in that contain needle (ignoring case) to out , creating missing parent directories, and returns how many lines it wrote. Read and write line by line with a BufferedReader and BufferedWriter in try-with-resources. - findByExtension lists every regular file under dir (in subfolders too) whose name ends with . + extension (ignoring case), as paths relative to dir with / separators, sorted.

title: An inventory with files
body: Build a shop's stock system that loads and saves CSV files, with collections for fast lookups, comparators for reports and a checked exception for bad data. One type per file: java // Item.java record Item(String sku, String name, int quantity, long priceCents) // compact constructor validates // InventoryException.java class InventoryException extends Exception // InventoryException(int line, String message) int line() // getMessage(): "line <n : <message " // Inventory.java class Inventory { void add(Item item) // IllegalArgumentException("duplicate sku <sku ") if the sku exists Item find(String sku) // null when unknown; skus ignore case void restock(String sku, int amount) // amount = 1; NoSuchElementException("no item <sku ") when unknown void sell(String sku, int amount) // amount = 1; IllegalStateException("only <n left") when short long totalValueCents() List<Item lowStock(int threshold) // quantity below threshold; lowest quantity first, then sku List<Item search(String term) // name contains term, ignoring case; sorted by name, then sku List<Item all() // sorted by sku void save(Path file) throws IOException static Inventory load(Path file) throws IOException, InventoryException } Items : sku is 3 to 12 letters, digits or - , stored in upper case; name is not blank and is trimmed; quantity is 0 or more; priceCents is 0 or more. A record's compact constructor checks this and throws IllegalArgumentException (it may also normalise the values it is given). Files are CSV with a header line sku,name,quantity,price . Prices are written in euros with 2 decimals ( 2.50 ). Names never contain commas. Example: sku,name,quantity,price TEA-01,Green tea,40,2.50 MUG-01,Large mug,3,8.00 - save writes the header and then all() in sku order, creating missing parent folders. - load reads such a file. A missing file lets the IOException through. It throws InventoryException for: a wrong header ( line 1: bad header ), a line without exactly 4 fields ( wrong number of fields ), a quantity or price that is not a number ( bad number , with the NumberFormatException as the cause), an item the record rejects (its message, with the IllegalArgumentException as the cause), and a duplicate sku ( duplicate sku <SKU ). Blank lines are skipped. Line numbers count from 1 (the header).

title: 5.01  Algorithm Analysis and Big O
body: How to compare algorithms independently of computers - counting basic steps, Big O notation and the common growth classes from O(1) to O(2^n), analysing loops, nested loops and halving, best, worst and average cases, the costs of Java's collection operations, measuring with System.nanoTime, and space complexity. Counting steps How fast is an algorithm? Timing it depends on the computer, the JVM warming up and what else is running. Instead we count how the number of basic steps grows with the size of the input, n . java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int data = new int 1000 ; for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) data i = i; System.out.println(contains(data, 999) + " " + hasDuplicate(data) + " " + binarySearch(data, 999)); } static boolean contains(int a, int target) { // up to n comparisons: O(n) for (int x : a) if (x == target) return true; return false; } static boolean hasDuplicate(int a) { // about n n/2 comparisons: O(n²) for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a i == a j ) return true; return false; } static int binarySearch(int a, int target) { // halves the range each step: O(log n) int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) 1; if (a mid == target) return mid; if (a mid < target) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1; } return -1; } } Big O Big O describes the growth rate, ignoring constant factors and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 20 steps is O(n²) , because for large n the n² term dominates everything else. Class Name Example n = 1 000 n = 1 000 000 --- --- --- --- --- O(1) constant array index, HashMap.get 1 1 O(log n) logarithmic binary search 10 20 O(n) linear one loop over the data 1 000 1 000 000 O(n log n) linearithmic merge sort, Arrays.sort 10 000 20 000 000 O(n²) quadratic nested loops over the data 1 000 000 10¹² (hours) O(2ⁿ) exponential trying every subset, naive Fibonacci 10³⁰¹ forever The difference between O(n log n) and O(n²) is the difference between a program that sorts a million items in a fraction of a second and one that takes days. Analysing code - Simple statements are O(1). - A loop that runs n times around O(1) work is O(n). - Nested loops multiply: an O(n) loop inside an O(n) loop is O(n²). - Sequential parts add, and the biggest wins: O(n) followed by O(n²) is O(n²). - A loop that halves (or doubles) its range each step is O(log n). - A method call costs whatever that method costs: calling an O(n) method inside an O(n) loop is O(n²). That last rule hides many slow programs: java-norun for (String word : words) { // n times if (!unique.contains(word)) { // ArrayList.contains is O(n): the whole loop is O(n²) unique.add(word); } } // With a HashSet, contains is O(1) on average, and the loop is O(n). Best, worst and average Linear search finds the target immediately in the best case (it is first), checks everything in the worst case (it is last or missing), and about half in the average case. Big O usually describes the worst case, because that is the guarantee. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in its worst case; merge sort is O(n log n) always. Costs of Java's collections Operation ArrayList LinkedList HashMap / HashSet TreeMap / TreeSet --- --- --- --- --- get by index O(1) O(n) - - add at the end O(1) amortised O(1) - - insert / remove at the front O(n) O(1) - - contains / find by key O(n) O(n) O(1) average O(log n) add / remove by key - - O(1) average O(log n) iterate in sorted order - - no order O(n) "Amortised O(1)" means that occasionally an add costs O(n), when the array is full and must be copied into a bigger one, but spread over many adds the average is constant (lesson 5.04 builds such a list). Measuring Analysis predicts; measurement confirms. System.nanoTime() measures elapsed time: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { for (int n : new int {2_000, 4_000, 8_000}) { List<Integer list = new ArrayList< (); Set<Integer set = new HashSet< (); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { list.add(i); set.add(i); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int found = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (list.contains(n - 1 - i)) found++; // O(n²) in total long t1 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (set.contains(n - 1 - i)) found++; // O(n) in total long t2 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("n=%d list=%d ms set=%d ms (%d)%n", n, (t1 - t0) / 1_000_000, (t2 - t1) / 1_000_000, found); } } } Doubling n roughly quadruples the list time (quadratic) and roughly doubles the set time (linear). Small timings are noisy: the JVM compiles hot code while running, so measure repeatedly with large inputs, or use a benchmarking tool such as JMH. Space Algorithms also use memory . Making a copy of the input is O(n) extra space; a few variables are O(1); recursion uses stack space proportional to its depth (O(log n) for binary search written recursively, O(n) for a recursive sum).

title: Make it fast
body: The starter's methods give the right answers but are O(n²). Rewrite each one to be O(n) (or O(n log n)), so that the tests with 200 000 numbers finish in time: java class Fast { static boolean hasDuplicate(int a) // any value twice? static int twoSum(int sorted, int target) // indexes {i, j}, i < j, with sorted i + sorted j == target, or null static int longestRun(int a) // length of the longest run of consecutive equal values static int countDistinct(int a) } For twoSum the array is sorted ascending; return the pair with the smallest i (and for that i , the smallest j ).

title: 5.02  Searching and Sorting
body: Linear and binary search with their invariants and the overflow-safe midpoint, the simple sorts (selection and insertion) and why they are O(n²), divide and conquer with merge sort and quicksort, stability, choosing a pivot, and what Java's own sorts use. Searching Linear search checks every item: O(n), but it works on any list. Binary search needs a sorted array and halves the range each step: O(log n). java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int sorted = {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91}; for (int target : new int {23, 2, 91, 7}) System.out.print(binarySearch(sorted, target) + " "); System.out.println(); } static int binarySearch(int a, int target) { int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1; // the target, if present, is always in a lo..hi while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; // not (lo + hi) / 2: that can overflow for huge arrays if (a mid == target) return mid; if (a mid < target) lo = mid + 1; // the target is to the right else hi = mid - 1; // the target is to the left } return -1; } } The comment on the first line is the loop's invariant : a statement that is true before every round. Binary search is famously easy to get subtly wrong (infinite loops, off-by-one bounds); keeping the invariant in mind is how to get it right. Arrays.binarySearch and Collections.binarySearch do it for you. Simple sorts Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining item and swaps it into place. Insertion sort takes each item and slides it left into the sorted part, like sorting playing cards in your hand: java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {29, 10, 14, 37, 13}; selectionSort(a); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); int b = {5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3}; insertionSort(b); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(b)); } static void selectionSort(int a) { for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) { int min = i; for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a j < a min ) min = j; int tmp = a i ; a i = a min ; a min = tmp; } } static void insertionSort(int a) { for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) { int key = a i ; int j = i - 1; while (j = 0 && a j key) { a j + 1 = a j ; // shift bigger items right j--; } a j + 1 = key; } } } Both are O(n²) in the worst case. Insertion sort is O(n) on data that is already nearly sorted, which is why fast library sorts use it for small pieces. Merge sort Divide and conquer : split the array in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves in one pass. There are log n levels of splitting and each level does O(n) merging work, so merge sort is O(n log n) in every case. It needs O(n) extra space and is stable (equal items keep their order). java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10}; mergeSort(a, 0, a.length); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); } static void mergeSort(int a, int from, int to) { // sorts a from..to) if (to - from < 2) return; int mid = (from + to) 1; mergeSort(a, from, mid); mergeSort(a, mid, to); int merged = new int to - from ; int i = from, j = mid, k = 0; while (i < mid && j < to) merged k++ = a i <= a j ? a i++ : a j++ ; // <= keeps it stable while (i < mid) merged k++ = a i++ ; while (j < to) merged k++ = a j++ ; System.arraycopy(merged, 0, a, from, merged.length); } } Quicksort Quicksort picks a pivot , partitions the array so smaller items come before it and larger after, and recursively sorts both sides. It sorts in place and is very fast in practice: O(n log n) on average, but O(n²) when the pivots are consistently bad (for example, always the first item of already sorted data). Choosing the middle item or a random one avoids the common bad cases. java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70}; quickSort(a, 0, a.length - 1); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); } static void quickSort(int a, int lo, int hi) { if (lo = hi) return; int pivot = a (lo + hi) 1 ; int i = lo, j = hi; while (i <= j) { // Hoare-style partition while (a i < pivot) i++; while (a j pivot) j--; if (i <= j) { int t = a i ; a i = a j ; a j = t; i++; j--; } } quickSort(a, lo, j); quickSort(a, i, hi); } } Java's own sorts Call Algorithm Stable --- --- --- Arrays.sort(int ) and other primitives Dual-pivot quicksort Not needed (equal numbers are identical) Arrays.sort(Object ) , List.sort , Collections.sort TimSort (merge sort + insertion sort, fast on partly sorted data) Yes Use the library sorts in real programs. Writing the algorithms yourself is how you learn the ideas they rely on: divide and conquer, invariants, and analysing recursive work.

title: Sorting algorithms
body: Implement sorting yourself (no Arrays.sort , Collections.sort or List.sort ): java class Sorts { static void insertionSort(int a) // in place static int mergeSort(int a) // returns a new sorted array; a is unchanged static long countInversions(int a) // pairs i < j with a i a j , in O(n log n) static <T void stableSort(List<T list, Comparator<? super T cmp) // a stable merge sort of the list, in place } countInversions measures how far an array is from sorted: {2, 4, 1, 3, 5} has 3 (2 1, 4 1, 4 3). Count them while merge sorting: when an item from the right half is taken before the remaining items of the left half, it forms an inversion with each of them. The tests use 100 000 numbers, too many for an O(n²) count.

title: 5.03  Linked Lists
body: Building a singly linked list from nodes - adding at the front and back with a tail reference, getting by index, removing, reversing in place, iterating with Iterator, the edge cases of empty and one-element lists, doubly linked lists and sentinel nodes, and comparing linked lists with array lists. Nodes and links A linked list stores each item in a node that also holds a reference to the next node. The list keeps a reference to the first node, the head ; the last node's next is null . Adding at the front is O(1): make a new node point at the old head. There is no indexing in O(1): reaching item i means following i links. A singly linked list java import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { MyList<String list = new MyList< (); list.addLast("b"); list.addFirst("a"); list.addLast("c"); list.addLast("d"); System.out.println(list + " size " + list.size() + " get(2)=" + list.get(2)); list.remove("c"); list.reverse(); System.out.println(list); for (String s : list) System.out.print(s.toUpperCase()); System.out.println(); } } class MyList<T implements Iterable<T { private static class Node<T { T value; Node<T next; Node(T value, Node<T next) { this.value = value; this.next = next; } } private Node<T head, tail; private int size; void addFirst(T value) { head = new Node< (value, head); if (tail == null) tail = head; // the list was empty size++; } void addLast(T value) { Node<T node = new Node< (value, null); if (tail == null) head = tail = node; // the list was empty else { tail.next = node; tail = node; } size++; } T get(int index) { if (index < 0 index = size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("index " + index); Node<T n = head; for (int i = 0; i < index; i++) n = n.next; return n.value; } boolean remove(T value) { Node<T prev = null; for (Node<T n = head; n != null; prev = n, n = n.next) { if (n.value.equals(value)) { if (prev == null) head = n.next; else prev.next = n.next; // unlink if (n == tail) tail = prev; size--; return true; } } return false; } void reverse() { Node<T prev = null, cur = head; tail = head; while (cur != null) { Node<T next = cur.next; cur.next = prev; // turn the arrow around prev = cur; cur = next; } head = prev; } int size() { return size; } public Iterator<T iterator() { return new Iterator< () { private Node<T next = head; public boolean hasNext() { return next != null; } public T next() { if (next == null) throw new NoSuchElementException(); T v = next.value; next = next.next; return v; } }; } @Override public String toString() { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(" "); for (Node<T n = head; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.value).append(n.next != null ? ", " : ""); return sb.append(" ").toString(); } } Points to notice: - Node is a private static nested class : it is part of the list's implementation, invisible outside. - Keeping a tail reference makes addLast O(1) instead of walking the whole list. - Every method that changes the list must handle the edge cases : the empty list, a one-node list, and changes at the head or the tail. Most linked-list bugs live there; draw the boxes and arrows on paper for each case. - Implementing Iterable lets the list work with the enhanced for . Reversing in place reverse walks the list once with three references ( prev , cur , next ) and turns each link around: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. It is a classic interview question because it tests exactly the pointer handling above. Doubly linked lists A doubly linked node also points to the previous node. Removing a node you already hold becomes O(1) (no need to find its predecessor), and the list can be walked backwards. java.util.LinkedList is doubly linked. Many implementations use a sentinel (dummy) node at both ends, so that the first and last real nodes are not special cases. Linked list or array list? ArrayList Linked list --- --- --- get(i) O(1) O(n) add/remove at the front O(n) O(1) add at the end O(1) amortised O(1) with a tail memory compact array one object per item, with extra references cache friendliness excellent poor In practice ArrayList (and ArrayDeque for queues) win almost every benchmark, because modern processors are very fast at reading consecutive memory. Linked structures matter as building blocks : queues, hash table buckets, adjacency lists in graphs, and trees, which are linked lists with more than one next .

title: A linked list of ints
body: Write a singly linked list from scratch, with a private nested Node class and head and tail references (no java.util collections inside): java class IntLinkedList { void addFirst(int value) void addLast(int value) int removeFirst() // NoSuchElementException when empty int get(int index) // IndexOutOfBoundsException outside 0..size-1 int indexOf(int value) // first index, or -1 int removeAll(int value) // removes every node holding value; returns how many void reverse() // in place, O(n), no new nodes int middle() // the middle value, the second of the two middles for an even size; one pass int size() String toString() // " 1, 2, 3 " } middle must walk the list once, using two references that move at different speeds; removeAll must also keep tail correct, so that addLast still works afterwards.

title: 5.04  Stacks, Queues and Hash Tables
body: Implementing a growable array list with amortised O(1) appends, a stack and its uses (undo, bracket matching, expression evaluation), a circular-buffer queue, and a hash table with chaining - hash functions, buckets, load factor and resizing - and why equals and hashCode matter. A growable array ArrayList is an array with spare room. When the array is full, it allocates a bigger one (typically 1.5 or 2 times bigger) and copies everything: java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { IntList list = new IntList(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) list.add(i i); System.out.println(list.size() + " " + list.get(19) + " capacity " + list.capacity()); } } class IntList { private int data = new int 4 ; private int size; void add(int value) { if (size == data.length) data = Arrays.copyOf(data, data.length 2); // grow: O(n), but rarely data size++ = value; } int get(int i) { if (i < 0 i = size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException(i); return data i ; } int size() { return size; } int capacity() { return data.length; } } Because the capacity doubles, adding n items copies at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n items in total: amortised O(1) per add. Stacks A stack is last in, first out: push on top, pop from the top, peek at the top, all O(1). Stacks undo actions, track nested structure, and evaluate expressions: java import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(evalPostfix("3 4 + 2 ")); // (3 + 4) 2 System.out.println(evalPostfix("5 1 2 + 4 + 3 -")); // 5 + (1 + 2) 4 - 3 } static int evalPostfix(String expr) { Deque<Integer stack = new ArrayDeque< (); for (String tok : expr.split(" ")) { switch (tok) { case "+", "-", " ", "/" - { int b = stack.pop(), a = stack.pop(); // note the order stack.push(switch (tok) { case "+" - a + b; case "-" - a - b; case " " - a b; default - a / b; }); } default - stack.push(Integer.parseInt(tok)); } } return stack.pop(); } } The method-call stack itself (lesson 2.04) is the same idea: each call is pushed, and returning pops it. Queues A queue is first in, first out: offer at the back, poll from the front. A circular buffer implements it in an array without shifting: front and back indexes move forward and wrap around. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { RingQueue q = new RingQueue(3); q.offer(1); q.offer(2); q.offer(3); System.out.println(q.poll() + " " + q.poll()); q.offer(4); q.offer(5); // wraps around the end of the array StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(); while (!q.isEmpty()) out.append(q.poll()).append(' '); System.out.println(out); } } class RingQueue { private final int data; private int front, size; RingQueue(int capacity) { data = new int capacity ; } boolean offer(int x) { if (size == data.length) return false; // full data (front + size) % data.length = x; size++; return true; } int poll() { if (size == 0) throw new IllegalStateException("empty"); int x = data front ; front = (front + 1) % data.length; size--; return x; } boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; } } Queues schedule work fairly (print jobs, requests, breadth-first search in graphs). Hash tables A hash table finds a key in O(1) on average. A hash function turns the key into a number; that number modulo the array length chooses a bucket . Different keys can land in the same bucket (a collision ); with chaining , each bucket holds a small list of entries. java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { HashTable<String, Integer ages = new HashTable< (); ages.put("Ada", 36); ages.put("Grace", 85); ages.put("Ada", 37); for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) ages.put("user" + i, i); System.out.println(ages.get("Ada") + " " + ages.get("Bob") + " size " + ages.size() + " buckets " + ages.buckets()); } } class HashTable<K, V { private record Entry<K, V (K key, V value) { } private List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V table = newTable(8); private int size; private static <K, V List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V newTable(int n) { List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V t = new ArrayList< (n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) t.add(new LinkedList< ()); return t; } private int indexFor(K key, int buckets) { return Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), buckets); // hashCode may be negative } V get(K key) { for (Entry<K, V e : table.get(indexFor(key, table.size()))) { if (e.key().equals(key)) return e.value(); } return null; } void put(K key, V value) { LinkedList<Entry<K, V bucket = table.get(indexFor(key, table.size())); for (var it = bucket.listIterator(); it.hasNext(); ) { if (it.next().key().equals(key)) { it.set(new Entry< (key, value)); return; } // replace } bucket.add(new Entry< (key, value)); size++; if (size table.size() 3 / 4) resize(); // load factor 0.75 } private void resize() { List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V bigger = newTable(table.size() 2); for (LinkedList<Entry<K, V bucket : table) for (Entry<K, V e : bucket) bigger.get(indexFor(e.key(), bigger.size())).add(e); table = bigger; } int size() { return size; } int buckets() { return table.size(); } } - The load factor is entries ÷ buckets. Keeping it below about 0.75 (by doubling and re-inserting everything) keeps buckets short, so get and put stay O(1) on average. - A poor hash function that sends many keys to the same bucket turns the table into a linked list: O(n). Java's HashMap even turns long buckets into small trees to limit the damage. - This is why keys must have consistent equals and hashCode (lesson 4.02): hashCode picks the bucket, equals finds the entry inside it.

title: A min-stack and a hash set
match: A min-stack and a hash set
body: Write two data structures from scratch. java // MinStack.java: a stack of ints that also reports its minimum, every operation O(1) class MinStack { void push(int x) int pop() // NoSuchElementException when empty int peek() int min() // the smallest value currently in the stack boolean isEmpty() } // IntHashSet.java: a set of ints using an array of buckets with chaining class IntHashSet { boolean add(int x) // false if already present boolean contains(int x) boolean remove(int x) // false if absent int size() int capacity() // the number of buckets: starts at 8, doubles when size would exceed 0.75 x capacity } Use arrays and your own node classes; java.util collections are not allowed inside these classes (exceptions are fine). Negative numbers must work in the hash set.

title: 5.05  Trees and Binary Search Trees
body: Trees and their vocabulary, binary trees, the binary search tree property, recursive insert, search and delete including the two-child case, in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order traversal, height and balance, why balanced trees like Java's TreeMap guarantee O(log n), and heaps for priority queues. Trees A tree is made of nodes connected by edges, with one root at the top. Each node has zero or more children ; nodes without children are leaves . The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. File systems, HTML pages, organisation charts and parsed expressions (practice 3.05) are trees. In a binary tree every node has at most two children, left and right . Binary search trees A binary search tree (BST) keeps this property at every node: everything in the left subtree is smaller, and everything in the right subtree is larger. Searching follows one path down, discarding half the tree at each step when the tree is balanced: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Bst tree = new Bst(); for (int x : new int {50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 30}) tree.insert(x); System.out.println(tree.inOrder() + " size " + tree.size() + " height " + tree.height()); System.out.println(tree.contains(60) + " " + tree.contains(65) + " min " + tree.min()); tree.delete(30); // a node with two children tree.delete(80); // a leaf System.out.println(tree.inOrder() + " " + tree.preOrder() + " " + tree.levelOrder()); } } class Bst { private static class Node { int key; Node left, right; Node(int key) { this.key = key; } } private Node root; private int size; void insert(int key) { root = insert(root, key); } private Node insert(Node n, int key) { if (n == null) { size++; return new Node(key); } if (key < n.key) n.left = insert(n.left, key); else if (key n.key) n.right = insert(n.right, key); return n; // duplicates are ignored } boolean contains(int key) { Node n = root; while (n != null) { if (key == n.key) return true; n = key < n.key ? n.left : n.right; } return false; } int min() { if (root == null) throw new NoSuchElementException(); Node n = root; while (n.left != null) n = n.left; return n.key; } void delete(int key) { root = delete(root, key); } private Node delete(Node n, int key) { if (n == null) return null; if (key < n.key) n.left = delete(n.left, key); else if (key n.key) n.right = delete(n.right, key); else { if (n.left == null) { size--; return n.right; } // zero or one child: replace by the child if (n.right == null) { size--; return n.left; } Node successor = n.right; // two children: take the smallest key on the right while (successor.left != null) successor = successor.left; n.key = successor.key; n.right = delete(n.right, successor.key); } return n; } int size() { return size; } int height() { return height(root); } private int height(Node n) { return n == null ? -1 : 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right)); } List<Integer inOrder() { List<Integer out = new ArrayList< (); inOrder(root, out); return out; } private void inOrder(Node n, List<Integer out) { if (n == null) return; inOrder(n.left, out); out.add(n.key); inOrder(n.right, out); // left, node, right: sorted } List<Integer preOrder() { List<Integer out = new ArrayList< (); preOrder(root, out); return out; } private void preOrder(Node n, List<Integer out) { if (n == null) return; out.add(n.key); preOrder(n.left, out); preOrder(n.right, out); // node first: copies the shape } List<Integer levelOrder() { // breadth first, with a queue List<Integer out = new ArrayList< (); Deque<Node queue = new ArrayDeque< (); if (root != null) queue.add(root); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { Node n = queue.poll(); out.add(n.key); if (n.left != null) queue.add(n.left); if (n.right != null) queue.add(n.right); } return out; } } Recursive methods that return the (possibly new) subtree, like insert and delete , avoid special cases for the root: root = insert(root, key) . Deleting Deleting has three cases: 1. a leaf : just remove it; 2. a node with one child : replace it by that child; 3. a node with two children : copy in its in-order successor (the smallest key in its right subtree), then delete the successor from the right subtree, which has at most one child. Traversals Order Visits Typical use --- --- --- In-order left, node, right A BST's keys in sorted order Pre-order node, left, right Copying or printing the tree's structure Post-order left, right, node Deleting a tree, evaluating an expression tree Level-order level by level, with a queue Shortest paths in unweighted trees, printing by depth Balance A BST's operations take time proportional to its height . Random insertions give a height of about 2 log n, but inserting keys in sorted order makes every node a right child: the "tree" becomes a linked list and everything is O(n). Self-balancing trees fix this by restructuring (rotating) nodes during insertions and deletions so the height stays O(log n). Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees : their get , put and remove are O(log n) guaranteed, and they iterate in sorted order. Heaps A binary heap is a different tree property: every parent is smaller than (or equal to) its children, so the minimum is always at the root. It is stored compactly in an array (the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 ), and both adding and removing the minimum are O(log n). Java's PriorityQueue is a binary heap; heap sort and Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm are built on one.

title: A binary search tree map
body: Write a generic map backed by an (unbalanced) binary search tree: java class TreeMapLite<K extends Comparable<K , V { void put(K key, V value) // adds, or replaces the value of an existing key V get(K key) // null when absent boolean containsKey(K key) boolean remove(K key) // false when absent; handles nodes with 0, 1 and 2 children int size() int height() // -1 for an empty tree, 0 for a single node List<K keys() // in sorted order K floorKey(K key) // the greatest key <= key, or null int countBetween(K lo, K hi) // keys with lo <= key <= hi, without visiting subtrees that cannot contain any } null keys throw NullPointerException .

title: An LRU cache
body: A least-recently-used (LRU) cache keeps a limited number of entries; when it is full, adding a new one evicts the entry that was used longest ago. Web browsers, databases and operating systems all use one. Every operation must be O(1) , which needs two structures working together: - a HashMap from key to node, for finding an entry in O(1); - a doubly linked list of nodes in order of use, most recent at the front, for moving and evicting in O(1). Write the list yourself (no LinkedHashMap , LinkedList or ArrayDeque ): java // LruCache.java class LruCache<K, V { LruCache(int capacity) // capacity = 1, else IllegalArgumentException V get(K key) // null when absent; a hit makes the entry the most recent void put(K key, V value) // adds or replaces (and makes it the most recent); evicts when full boolean remove(K key) int size() List<K keys() // most recent first void onEvict(BiConsumer<K, V listener) // called with each evicted entry (not for remove or replace) Stats stats() } // Stats.java record Stats(long hits, long misses, long evictions) { double hitRate() // hits / (hits + misses), or 0 when there were no gets }

title: 6.01  Lambdas and Functional Interfaces
body: Passing behaviour as a value - functional interfaces, lambda syntax, method references, the java.util.function interfaces (Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction, UnaryOperator), composing functions, effectively final captured variables, and lambdas with the collections API (forEach, removeIf, replaceAll, sort, computeIfAbsent). Behaviour as a value A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. A lambda is a short way to write an object that implements it: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Comparator<String byLength = (a, b) - Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()); // a lambda Runnable hello = () - System.out.println("hello"); hello.run(); List<String words = new ArrayList< (List.of("banana", "fig", "cherry", "kiwi")); words.sort(byLength); System.out.println(words); Calculator add = (x, y) - x + y; // our own functional interface Calculator power = (x, y) - { // a block body needs return int result = 1; for (int i = 0; i < y; i++) result = x; return result; }; System.out.println(add.apply(2, 3) + " " + power.apply(2, 10)); } } @FunctionalInterface interface Calculator { int apply(int x, int y); } Lambda syntax: (parameters) - expression , or (parameters) - { statements; } . Parameter types are inferred; a single parameter needs no parentheses: s - s.length() . @FunctionalInterface asks the compiler to check that the interface has exactly one abstract method. The standard functional interfaces java.util.function provides interfaces for the common shapes, so you rarely define your own: Interface Method Shape Example --- --- --- --- Function<T, R R apply(T t) T to R String::length BiFunction<T, U, R R apply(T t, U u) two inputs to R (a, b) - a + b Predicate<T boolean test(T t) a yes/no question s - s.isEmpty() Consumer<T void accept(T t) uses a value System.out::println Supplier<T T get() makes a value ArrayList::new UnaryOperator<T T apply(T t) T to T s - s.trim() BinaryOperator<T T apply(T a, T b) two Ts to T Integer::sum Primitive versions ( IntPredicate , ToIntFunction , IntBinaryOperator ...) avoid boxing in performance-sensitive code. Method references When a lambda only calls an existing method, a method reference says the same more briefly: java import java.util. ; import java.util.function. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Function<String, Integer length = String::length; // an instance method of the argument Function<String, Integer parse = Integer::parseInt; // a static method Consumer<Object print = System.out::println; // an instance method of a specific object Supplier<List<String newList = ArrayList::new; // a constructor BinaryOperator<Integer sum = Integer::sum; print.accept(length.apply("hello") + parse.apply("41") + sum.apply(1, 0)); List<String list = newList.get(); list.add("made by a supplier"); print.accept(list); } } Composing functions The functional interfaces have default methods for combining them: java import java.util.function. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Function<Integer, Integer doubleIt = x - x 2; Function<Integer, Integer addTen = x - x + 10; System.out.println(doubleIt.andThen(addTen).apply(5)); // (5 2) + 10 = 20 System.out.println(doubleIt.compose(addTen).apply(5)); // (5 + 10) 2 = 30 Predicate<String notEmpty = s - !s.isEmpty(); Predicate<String shortWord = s - s.length() < 5; Predicate<String keep = notEmpty.and(shortWord.negate()); System.out.println(keep.test("banana") + " " + keep.test("fig") + " " + keep.test("")); } } Capturing variables A lambda can use local variables from the surrounding code only if they are effectively final (never reassigned after initialisation): java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int threshold = 3; // effectively final: fine to capture List<String words = List.of("a", "abcd", "ab", "abcdef"); words.stream().filter(w - w.length() threshold).forEach(System.out::println); // int count = 0; // words.forEach(w - count++); // error: count is not effectively final int count = {0}; // a common workaround; a stream's count() is better words.forEach(w - count 0 ++); System.out.println(count 0 ); } } Lambdas with collections Many collection methods take functions: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String names = new ArrayList< (List.of("ada", "", "grace", "linus", "")); names.removeIf(String::isEmpty); names.replaceAll(s - Character.toUpperCase(s.charAt(0)) + s.substring(1)); names.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.reverseOrder())); names.forEach(n - System.out.print(n + " ")); System.out.println(); Map<Integer, List<String byLength = new TreeMap< (); for (String n : names) byLength.computeIfAbsent(n.length(), k - new ArrayList< ()).add(n); byLength.forEach((len, group) - System.out.println(len + ": " + group)); Map<String, Integer stock = new HashMap< (Map.of("tea", 3)); stock.merge("tea", 2, Integer::sum); stock.computeIfPresent("tea", (k, v) - v 4 ? v - 4 : v); System.out.println(stock); } }

title: Functions as values
body: Write helpers that take and return functions, in Funcs.java : java class Funcs { static <T UnaryOperator<T pipeline(List<UnaryOperator<T steps) // applies the steps left to right static <T Predicate<T allOf(List<Predicate<T tests) // true when every test passes (true for none) static <T, R Function<T, R memoize(Function<T, R f) // calls f once per distinct argument static Supplier<Integer counter(int start, int step) // each get() returns the next value: start, start+step, ... static <T Map<Boolean, List<T split(List<T items, Predicate<T test) // {true= matching , false= others }, order kept } Each call to counter or memoize returns an independent function with its own state.

title: 6.02  The Stream API
body: Processing data declaratively with streams - creating streams, intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit), terminal operations (collect, toList, count, reduce, anyMatch, min, max), primitive streams and summary statistics, Collectors for grouping, partitioning, joining and mapping, laziness, and when a loop is clearer. A pipeline A stream is a sequence of values flowing through a pipeline of operations. It describes what to compute, not how to loop: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String words = List.of("stream", "lambda", "java", "list", "map", "filter", "java"); List<String result = words.stream() .filter(w - w.length() 3) // keep some .map(String::toUpperCase) // transform each .distinct() // drop repeats .sorted() // order .toList(); // collect (Java 16+) System.out.println(result); System.out.println(words.stream().filter(w - w.startsWith("l")).count()); } } A pipeline has a source ( list.stream() , Arrays.stream(array) , Stream.of(...) , IntStream.range(0, 10) , Files.lines(path) ), any number of intermediate operations that return a new stream, and one terminal operation that produces a result.
