Intermediate Does --- --- filter(pred) Keeps matching items map(f) , mapToInt(f) Transforms each item flatMap(f) Replaces each item by a stream of items, flattened distinct() , sorted() , sorted(cmp) Removes repeats, sorts limit(n) , skip(n) , takeWhile(p) , dropWhile(p) Cuts the stream peek(f) Looks at items as they pass (for debugging) Terminal Gives --- --- toList() , collect(...) A collection forEach(f) Runs f on each item count() , sum() , average() , min() , max() Numbers (some as Optional ) anyMatch , allMatch , noneMatch Booleans findFirst() , findAny() An Optional item reduce(identity, op) Combines all items into one Numbers IntStream , LongStream and DoubleStream have arithmetic built in: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100).sum()); System.out.println(IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).filter(n - n % 2 == 0).map(n - n n).boxed().toList()); int scores = {72, 95, 88, 61, 79}; IntSummaryStatistics stats = Arrays.stream(scores).summaryStatistics(); System.out.println(stats.getMin() + " " + stats.getMax() + " " + stats.getAverage()); System.out.println(Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc").mapToInt(String::length).sum()); System.out.println(Stream.iterate(1, x - x 2).limit(10).reduce(0, Integer::sum)); } } Collectors collect with the Collectors helpers builds maps, groups and strings: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Person people = List.of( new Person("Ada", "London", 36), new Person("Grace", "New York", 85), new Person("Linus", "Helsinki", 55), new Person("Alan", "London", 41)); Map<String, List<String byCity = people.stream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, TreeMap::new, Collectors.mapping(Person::name, Collectors.toList()))); System.out.println(byCity); Map<String, Long countByCity = people.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, Collectors.counting())); System.out.println(new TreeMap< (countByCity)); Map<Boolean, List<String over50 = people.stream() .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(p - p.age() 50, Collectors.mapping(Person::name, Collectors.toList()))); System.out.println(over50); String names = people.stream().map(Person::name).sorted().collect(Collectors.joining(", ", " ", " ")); double avgAge = people.stream().collect(Collectors.averagingInt(Person::age)); Map<String, Integer ageByName = people.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Person::name, Person::age)); Optional<Person oldest = people.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age)); System.out.println(names + " " + avgAge + " " + ageByName.get("Linus") + " " + oldest.map(Person::name).orElse("-")); } } record Person(String name, String city, int age) { } toMap throws if two items have the same key; pass a merge function as a third argument to combine them. flatMap java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String lines = List.of("the quick brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy dog"); List<String words = lines.stream() .flatMap(line - Arrays.stream(line.split(" "))) // each line becomes many words .distinct() .toList(); System.out.println(words.size() + " " + words); } } Laziness Intermediate operations do nothing until a terminal operation runs, and then items flow through one at a time. That allows infinite sources with limit , and lets findFirst stop early. A stream can be used once ; calling a second terminal operation on it throws IllegalStateException . Stream lambdas should not change shared state (no adding to an outside list in map ); use collectors instead. parallelStream() splits work across cores, but only helps for large, CPU-heavy, side-effect-free pipelines. Streams or loops? Streams shine for transform-filter-collect pipelines and grouping. A plain loop is often clearer when you need indexes, early exits with complex conditions, checked exceptions, or several results at once. Use whichever reads better.

title: Stream queries
body: Books are records: java // Book.java record Book(String title, String author, int year, int pages, List<String genres) { } Answer each question in Shelf.java with one stream pipeline (no loops): java class Shelf { static List<String titlesBy(List<Book books, String author) // sorted by year, then title static Map<String, Double averagePagesByGenre(List<Book books) // TreeMap: genre - average pages static Map<Integer, Long countByDecade(List<Book books) // TreeMap: 1960 - 3, ... static List<String genresByPopularity(List<Book books) // most books first, ties alphabetical static Optional<Book longestBefore(List<Book books, int year) // most pages among books before year static String authorsLine(List<Book books) // distinct authors, sorted, "A; B; C" }

title: 6.03  Optional and Modern Java
body: Representing maybe-missing values with Optional and its methods (map, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent), when not to use it, and a tour of modern Java features - var, text blocks, switch expressions and pattern matching, records and sealed types together, the java.time date API, and immutable collections. Optional null as "no value" causes NullPointerException s far from where the null came from. Optional<T makes "maybe missing" part of a method's type, so callers must decide what to do: java import java.util. ; public class Main { static final Map<String, String EMAILS = Map.of("ada", "ada@example.com", "bob", ""); public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(findEmail("ada").orElse("no email")); System.out.println(findEmail("zed").orElse("no email")); String domain = findEmail("ada") .map(e - e.substring(e.indexOf('@') + 1)) // transform if present .orElse("unknown"); System.out.println(domain); findEmail("bob").ifPresentOrElse(e - System.out.println("send to " + e), () - System.out.println("bob has none")); try { String e = findEmail("zed").orElseThrow(() - new NoSuchElementException("no email for zed")); } catch (NoSuchElementException ex) { System.out.println(ex.getMessage()); } } static Optional<String findEmail(String user) { return Optional.ofNullable(EMAILS.get(user)).filter(e - !e.isBlank()); } } Method Does --- --- Optional.of(x) , ofNullable(x) , empty() Create (of throws for null) isPresent() , isEmpty() Test map(f) , flatMap(f) , filter(p) Transform, keeping "missing" missing orElse(v) , orElseGet(supplier) A default ( orElseGet computes it only when needed) orElseThrow() , orElseThrow(supplier) The value, or an exception ifPresent(f) , ifPresentOrElse(f, g) Act on it Streams return Optional from findFirst , min and max . Use Optional as a return type for "maybe nothing". Do not use it for fields or parameters, do not call get() without checking (use orElseThrow() to make the intent clear), and never return null from a method declared to return an Optional . Modern Java in one place Java has changed a lot since Java 8. Code written today looks like this: java import java.time. ; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit; import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { var orders = List.of( // var: inferred local types new Order("A-1", new Paid(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 1), 4999)), new Order("A-2", new Pending()), new Order("A-3", new Refunded("damaged", 1250))); for (var order : orders) System.out.println(order.id() + ": " + describe(order.status())); String report = """ Orders: %d Generated: %s """.formatted(orders.size(), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 14).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_DATE)); // a text block System.out.print(report); LocalDate due = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1); // java.time: immutable dates System.out.println(due + " " + due.getDayOfWeek() + " " + ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1), due)); Duration d = Duration.ofMinutes(135); System.out.println(d.toHours() + "h " + d.toMinutesPart() + "m"); } static String describe(Status s) { return switch (s) { // pattern matching over a sealed type case Paid(LocalDate on, long cents) when cents 10_000 - "large payment on " + on; case Paid(LocalDate on, long cents) - "paid %d.%02d on %s".formatted(cents / 100, cents % 100, on); case Pending p - "waiting for payment"; case Refunded(String reason, long cents) - "refunded (" + reason + ")"; }; } } sealed interface Status permits Paid, Pending, Refunded { } record Paid(LocalDate on, long cents) implements Status { } record Pending() implements Status { } record Refunded(String reason, long cents) implements Status { } record Order(String id, Status status) { } Feature Since Lesson --- --- --- Lambdas, streams, Optional , java.time 8 6.01, 6.02, here var for local variables 10 here List.of , Map.of , Set.of 9 2.03 Switch expressions with - 14 1.05 Text blocks """ 15 1.04 Records, instanceof patterns 16 3.05, 3.03 Sealed types 17 3.05 Pattern matching for switch, record patterns 21 3.05 Virtual threads 21 6.04 Unnamed variables _ , compact source files 22, 25 java.time Use java.time for dates and times (never the old Date and Calendar ): Class Holds --- --- LocalDate , LocalTime , LocalDateTime A date / time / both, without a time zone ZonedDateTime , Instant A moment in time, with a zone / in UTC Duration , Period An amount of time / of days, months, years DateTimeFormatter Formatting and parsing All are immutable: date.plusDays(1) returns a new date.

title: Optional and java.time
body: A staff directory keeps people by id. Write it with Optional for everything that may be missing, and dates with java.time : java // Person.java record Person(String id, String name, String managerId, String city, LocalDate born) { } // managerId and city may be null // Directory.java class Directory { Directory(List<Person people) Optional<Person find(String id) Optional<String managerName(String id) // the name of the person's manager, if both exist String cityOf(String id) // the city, or "unknown" when the person or the city is missing Optional<Person oldest() static int age(LocalDate born, LocalDate today) // whole years static long daysUntilBirthday(LocalDate born, LocalDate today) // 0 on the birthday; Feb 29 birthdays count on Feb 28 in other years } Use map , flatMap , filter and orElse rather than isPresent() and get() .

title: 6.04  Threads and Concurrency
body: Running work at the same time - threads and Runnable, joining, race conditions and why count++ is unsafe, synchronized and locks, atomic variables and concurrent collections, ExecutorService and Future, CompletableFuture, virtual threads, deadlock, and the rule of sharing as little mutable state as possible. Threads The practice sandbox runs every program on a single thread, so the examples in this lesson are for reading and for running with your own JDK ( java Main.java ). The practice task shows how concurrent code is designed so that its logic can be tested without real threads. A thread is an independent path of execution. A program starts with one ( main ); more threads let it use several processor cores, or keep working while one task waits: java-norun public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() - { for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) System.out.println("worker " + i); }); worker.start(); // runs at the same time as main System.out.println("main continues"); worker.join(); // wait for it to finish System.out.println("worker finished"); } } start() begins the new thread; calling run() directly would just run the code on the current thread. The order of output from different threads is not guaranteed. Race conditions When threads share mutable data, their steps interleave unpredictably. count++ is really read, add one, write back; two threads can read the same old value, and one increment is lost: java-norun import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class Main { static int unsafeCount = 0; static int syncCount = 0; static final AtomicInteger atomicCount = new AtomicInteger(); static synchronized void incrementSync() { syncCount++; } public static void main(String args) throws InterruptedException { Runnable work = () - { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) { unsafeCount++; // a race incrementSync(); // one thread at a time atomicCount.incrementAndGet(); // an atomic hardware operation } }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.println((unsafeCount <= 200_000) + " " + syncCount + " " + atomicCount.get()); } } synchronized lets only one thread at a time run the method (or a synchronized (lock) { ... } block) for the same lock object, and makes changes visible to the next thread that takes the lock. AtomicInteger , AtomicLong and LongAdder do single-variable updates without locks. Thread-safe collections ArrayList and HashMap are not safe for concurrent changes. Use the java.util.concurrent collections: Instead of Use --- --- HashMap ConcurrentHashMap (with merge , compute for atomic updates) ArrayList with rare writes CopyOnWriteArrayList a queue between threads ArrayBlockingQueue , LinkedBlockingQueue Executors Creating threads by hand is low level. An ExecutorService keeps a pool of threads and runs tasks you submit; Callable tasks return a result through a Future : java-norun import java.util. ; import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { List<Future<Long results = new ArrayList< (); for (int part = 0; part < 4; part++) { long from = part 250_000L, to = from + 250_000; results.add(pool.submit(() - sumOfSquares(from, to))); // a Callable<Long } long total = 0; for (Future<Long f : results) total += f.get(); // waits for each result System.out.println(total == sumOfSquares(0, 1_000_000)); } // closing waits for the tasks and shuts the pool down } static long sumOfSquares(long from, long to) { long s = 0; for (long i = from; i < to; i++) s += i i % 1000; return s; } } Splitting work so that each task computes its own result, and combining the results at the end, avoids shared mutable state entirely. That is the safest kind of concurrency. CompletableFuture and virtual threads CompletableFuture chains asynchronous steps: java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { CompletableFuture<String user = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - slow("Ada", 100)); CompletableFuture<Integer score = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - slow(42, 100)); String summary = user.thenCombine(score, (u, s) - u + " scored " + s) .exceptionally(e - "failed: " + e.getMessage()) .join(); System.out.println(summary); try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { // Java 21: virtual threads for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) { int n = i; executor.submit(() - slow(n, 10)); // ten thousand cheap threads } } System.out.println("10 000 waiting tasks done"); } static <T T slow(T value, long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return value; } } Virtual threads (Java 21) are very cheap threads managed by the JVM. They make it practical to give each waiting task (a web request, a database call) its own thread, written as simple blocking code. Deadlock and other dangers - Deadlock : thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Both wait forever. Always take locks in the same order, and hold them briefly. - Visibility : without synchronisation, a change made by one thread may never be seen by another. Use volatile for simple flags, or locks and atomics. - InterruptedException : it means someone asked the thread to stop. Do not swallow it; finish up, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() . The best concurrency advice is to avoid sharing mutable state: use immutable objects (records), give each task its own data, and communicate through concurrent queues or futures. Testable concurrent code Code that creates its own threads is hard to test: the results depend on timing. Instead, let the caller pass in an Executor (the interface behind every thread pool). Production code passes a real pool; a test passes Runnable::run , which runs each task immediately on the calling thread, so the result is the same every time: java-norun static long sumInChunks(int data, int chunks, Executor executor) { List<CompletableFuture<Long parts = new ArrayList< (); for (int c = 0; c < chunks; c++) { int from = c data.length / chunks, to = (c + 1) data.length / chunks; parts.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - sum(data, from, to), executor)); } return parts.stream().mapToLong(CompletableFuture::join).sum(); } sumInChunks(data, 8, Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)); // in the program sumInChunks(data, 8, Runnable::run); // in a test: deterministic

title: Concurrent code you can test
body: Concurrent code is easiest to test when it does not create threads itself but receives an Executor . The program passes a thread pool; a test passes Runnable::run , which runs every task at once on the calling thread. Write: java // Parallel.java class Parallel { static <T List<T runAll(List<Callable<T tasks, Executor executor) throws Exception static long sumInChunks(int data, int chunks, Executor executor) } // SafeCounter.java: a counter that many threads may update at the same time class SafeCounter { void increment() void add(long n) long get() long getAndReset() // returns the current value and sets it to 0, as one atomic step } - runAll submits every task to the executor (one execute call per task, in order) and returns their results in task order. If tasks fail, it throws the exception of the first failing task in the list (the original exception, not a wrapper). - sumInChunks splits data into chunks consecutive parts of nearly equal size ( chunks from 1 up; never more chunks than items, except that an empty array gives 0), sums each part as its own task on the executor, and adds the part sums. chunks below 1 throws IllegalArgumentException . - SafeCounter must be correct when used from many threads: use AtomicLong (or LongAdder , or synchronized ).

title: 6.05  Project: A Complete Program
body: How a real Java program is organised - packages and the folder layout, access across packages, Maven and Gradle with a pom.xml or build.gradle, dependencies, unit tests with JUnit 5, building a runnable JAR, and the plan for the final project, a command-driven event planner. Packages Real programs put classes into packages , named like reversed domain names, matching the folder structure: text planner/ pom.xml (or build.gradle) src/main/java/ com/example/planner/ App.java package com.example.planner; model/Event.java package com.example.planner.model; model/Schedule.java io/CommandParser.java package com.example.planner.io; src/test/java/ com/example/planner/model/ScheduleTest.java java-norun package com.example.planner.model; // first line of the file import java.time.LocalDateTime; // imports come after the package line import java.util.List; public record Event(String title, LocalDateTime start, int minutes) { } - A class in another package is used with an import (or its full name, com.example.planner.model.Event ). - public members are visible everywhere; members without a modifier are visible only inside their own package. This lets a package hide its helper classes. - Each public class lives in a file with its name, in the folder of its package. Build tools Maven and Gradle compile the code, download libraries, run the tests and package the program. With Maven, a pom.xml describes the project: xml <project <modelVersion 4.0.0</modelVersion <groupId com.example</groupId <artifactId planner</artifactId <version 1.0.0</version <properties <maven.compiler.release 25</maven.compiler.release </properties <dependencies <dependency <groupId org.junit.jupiter</groupId <artifactId junit-jupiter</artifactId <version 5.11.4</version <scope test</scope </dependency </dependencies </project bash mvn compile compile src/main/java mvn test run the tests in src/test/java mvn package build target/planner-1.0.0.jar java -cp target/planner-1.0.0.jar com.example.planner.App Gradle does the same with a build.gradle (or build.gradle.kts ) script: gradle build , gradle test , gradle run . IDEs import either kind of project directly. Unit tests with JUnit JUnit 5 is the standard Java test framework. Test classes mirror the main classes' packages: java-norun package com.example.planner.model; import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test; import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions. ; class ScheduleTest { @Test void overlappingEventsAreRejected() { Schedule s = new Schedule(); s.add(new Event("Lunch", at(12, 0), 60)); assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () - s.add(new Event("Call", at(12, 30), 15))); } @Test void eventsAreListedInTimeOrder() { Schedule s = new Schedule(); s.add(new Event("Late", at(18, 0), 30)); s.add(new Event("Early", at(9, 0), 30)); assertEquals(List.of("Early", "Late"), s.titles()); } } assertEquals(expected, actual) , assertTrue , assertThrows and @ParameterizedTest work like the checkEq and checkThrows you have used throughout this course. The final project The project for this milestone is an event planner that reads commands, keeps a schedule, refuses overlapping events, and answers questions about free time. It brings the course together: Part Uses --- --- Event record with validation records, java.time (3.05, 6.03) Schedule with sorted events collections, comparators, exceptions (4.02 to 4.04) Free-slot search and the daily summary algorithms over sorted data, streams (5.02, 6.02) Command loop with error messages parsing, exceptions, switch (1.05, 4.04) Build it in layers, testing each before the next: the record, then the schedule's add and list, then overlaps, then free slots, then the commands. Keep the rules in Schedule and the input handling in Main , so the rules can be tested without typing commands. Where to go next - Web services with Spring Boot or Quarkus, which build on everything here: classes, interfaces, collections, exceptions and streams. - Android apps (with Kotlin or Java). - Data structures and algorithms in more depth: graphs, dynamic programming and balanced trees, in this site's DSA course. - Concurrency in depth with "Java Concurrency in Practice", and modern Java features as each release adds them.

title: Parsing planner commands
body: The final project reads commands like add 2026-03-14 09:00 90 Team meeting . Parse a line into a sealed command type, so the rest of the program can switch over it: java // Command.java sealed interface Command { record Add(LocalDateTime start, int minutes, String title) implements Command { } record Remove(String title) implements Command { } record Day(LocalDate date) implements Command { } record Free(LocalDate date, int minutes) implements Command { } record Summary() implements Command { } record Quit() implements Command { } record Invalid(String message) implements Command { } static Command parse(String line) } Input Result --- --- add <yyyy-MM-dd <HH:mm <minutes <title... Add ; the title is the rest of the line, words joined by single spaces remove <title... Remove day <yyyy-MM-dd Day free <yyyy-MM-dd <minutes Free summary , quit Summary , Quit The command word ignores case and extra spaces. Problems give Invalid with one of these messages: - Usage: add <date <time <minutes <title (and likewise Usage: remove <title , Usage: day <date , Usage: free <date <minutes ) for missing or extra arguments; summary and quit ignore extra words; - Bad date or time when a date or time does not parse (strict yyyy-MM-dd and HH:mm , so 2026-02-30 is bad); - Minutes must be between 5 and 720 for a number outside that range, and Bad number for text that is not a whole number; - Unknown command: <word for anything else, and Empty line for a blank line.

title: An event planner
body: Build a command-driven event planner. It reads one command per line until quit or the end of the input, keeps a schedule, refuses overlapping events, and finds free time. Commands are parsed by Command.parse from practice 6.05, which is already in the project ( Command.java ). The program is four files: Main.java (the command loop), Event.java , Schedule.java and Command.java . add 2026-03-14 09:00 90 Team meeting add 2026-03-14 12:00 60 Lunch add 2026-03-14 10:00 30 Call day 2026-03-14 free 2026-03-14 60 summary quit prints Added: 2026-03-14 09:00-10:30 Team meeting Added: 2026-03-14 12:00-13:00 Lunch Overlaps with Team meeting (09:00-10:30) Saturday 2026-03-14 09:00-10:30 Team meeting 12:00-13:00 Lunch Free: 08:00-09:00 2 events, 2h 30m planned Busiest day: 2026-03-14 (2 events) Bye. Event is a record Event(String title, LocalDateTime start, int minutes) with end() and a method telling whether it overlaps another event (they overlap when each starts before the other ends; one ending exactly when the next starts is fine). Commands (no prompts): Command Output --- --- add Added: <date <HH:mm -<HH:mm <title , or Overlaps with <title (<HH:mm -<HH:mm ) naming the earliest-starting event it overlaps remove <title Removes the earliest event with that title (ignoring case): Removed: <title as stored , or No event called <title day <date The day name and date ( Saturday 2026-03-14 ), then each event starting that day in time order as <HH:mm -<HH:mm <title , or Nothing planned. free <date <minutes The earliest gap of at least that many minutes between 08:00 and 18:00 that day, as Free: <HH:mm -<HH:mm (the whole gap), or No free slot of <minutes minutes on <date . Any event overlapping the window counts, including its parts outside the window. summary <n events, <h h <m m planned ( 1 event for one) and Busiest day: <date (<n events) (the earliest on a tie), or just No events. invalid input The Invalid message from Command.parse quit Ends the loop The program always ends by printing Bye.

title: Common Errors
body: Compiler errors Message Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- ';' expected A missing semicolon, often at the end of the line before Add it 1.01 cannot find symbol A typo, wrong case ( system.out ), a missing import, or a variable used outside its block Check spelling and case; add the import ; declare it in the right scope 1.01 class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.java The public class and file name differ Rename the file or the class 1.01 incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int Assigning a value of the wrong type Convert with Integer.parseInt , or fix the type 1.02 incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int A narrowing conversion without a cast Cast (int) x , or use Math.round 1.02 integer number too large A big literal without L 8_100_000_000L 1.02 variable x might not have been initialized Reading a local variable before every path assigns it Initialise it when declared 1.02 missing return statement A path through a non-void method ends without return Return (or throw) on every path 2.01 bad operand types for binary operator '&&' / incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean Using a number as a condition Compare: if (n != 0) 1.03 non-static method m() cannot be referenced from a static context Calling an instance method from main without an object Create an object, or make the method static 3.02 X is abstract; cannot be instantiated new on an abstract class or interface Create a concrete subclass 3.04 X is not abstract and does not override abstract method m() A class misses an interface or abstract method Implement it (public, same signature) 3.04 unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown Calling a method that throws a checked exception try / catch it, or add throws IOException 4.04 local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final A lambda uses a variable that is reassigned Don't reassign it, or use a stream result or an AtomicInteger 6.01 the switch expression does not cover all possible input values A switch over a sealed type or enum misses a case Add the case (or a default ) 3.05 generic array creation / cannot select from a type variable Trying new T or T.class Use a List<T , or pass a Class<T 4.01 Exceptions at run time Exception Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- NullPointerException Using a member of null : an unset field, a missing map key, unboxing a null Initialise fields; check map results; use getOrDefault or Optional 3.01 ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException / IndexOutOfBoundsException An index equal to length / size() or negative Indexes run from 0 to length - 1 2.02 NumberFormatException Integer.parseInt on text that is not a whole number Catch it, or check the input first 1.04 InputMismatchException Scanner.nextInt() met text Read lines and parse them 1.04 ArithmeticException: / by zero Integer division by 0 Check the divisor 1.03 ConcurrentModificationException Changing a collection inside an enhanced for over it removeIf , an Iterator 's remove , or loop backwards with indexes 2.03 UnsupportedOperationException Changing a List.of(...) or other unmodifiable collection Copy it: new ArrayList< (List.of(...)) 2.03 ClassCastException A cast to a type the object does not have Use instanceof patterns 3.03 StackOverflowError Recursion without a reachable base case Fix the base case, or use a loop 2.04 NoSuchElementException next() past the end, Optional.get() on empty, Scanner out of input Check hasNext , use orElse , check hasNextLine 6.03 IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon Using a stream twice Create a new stream each time 6.02 NoSuchFileException A wrong path or missing file Check the path; Files.exists ; handle the IOException 4.05 IllegalArgumentException (your own) A method received a bad argument Read the message; fix the caller 4.04 Wrong results without an error Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- 7 / 2 is 3 Integer division Use 7 / 2.0 or a cast 1.03 "Total: " + 1 + 2 prints Total: 12 + joins strings left to right Parenthesise the sum 1.03 Two equal strings are not == == compares references equals 1.04 nextLine() returns "" after nextInt() The line break was left in the input Read whole lines and parse 1.04 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 Binary floating point Compare with a tolerance; use long cents or BigDecimal for money 1.02 A large int became negative Overflow Use long , or Math.addExact 1.02 An array prints as I@1b6d3586 Arrays have no readable toString Arrays.toString(a) 2.02 list.remove(1) removed the wrong item On a List<Integer it removes index 1 list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) 2.03 Two Integer s with the same value are not == == compares wrapper objects equals 2.03 A HashSet holds "duplicates" of your objects equals overridden without hashCode (or neither) Override both, or use a record 4.02 A sort comparator gives a wrong order for big numbers Comparing by subtraction overflows Integer.compare or Comparator.comparingInt 4.03 A classic switch runs several cases Missing break (fall-through) Use the arrow form case X - 1.05 A counter updated from threads is too low A race condition AtomicInteger , synchronized , or no shared state 6.04 A written file is empty or cut off The writer was not closed or flushed try-with-resources 4.05

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Abstract class A class that cannot be instantiated; it shares code and declares abstract methods subclasses must implement. (3.04) Access modifier public , protected , private or none (package-private): who may use a member. (3.02) Amortised O(1) Usually constant time, with rare expensive steps that average out, like ArrayList.add . (5.04) Array A fixed-size, indexed sequence of values of one type. (2.02) ArrayList A list backed by an array that grows as needed. (2.03) Autoboxing Automatic conversion between a primitive and its wrapper, such as int and Integer . (2.03) Base case The input a recursive method answers directly, without calling itself. (2.04) Big O Notation for how an algorithm's work grows with input size, ignoring constants. (5.01) Binary search Finding a value in a sorted array by halving the range each step: O(log n). (5.02) Binary search tree A binary tree where left subtrees hold smaller keys and right subtrees larger ones. (5.05) Bytecode The instructions javac produces for the Java Virtual Machine. (1.01) Cast An explicit conversion, such as (int) 3.9 . (1.02) Checked exception An exception that must be caught or declared with throws , such as IOException . (4.04) Class A blueprint for objects: fields, constructors and methods. (3.01) Collection The interface of groups of objects: lists, sets and queues. (4.02) Comparable The interface giving a class its natural order through compareTo . (3.04) Comparator An ordering kept outside the compared class. (4.03) Constructor Code that initialises a new object; it has the class's name and no return type. (3.01) Deadlock Threads waiting forever for locks the others hold. (6.04) Dynamic dispatch Choosing which overridden method to run from the object's actual class at run time. (3.03) Effectively final A local variable never reassigned, which lambdas may capture. (6.01) Encapsulation Keeping an object's data private and changing it only through its methods. (3.02) Enhanced for for (T x : collection) : a loop over every item. (1.05) Enum A type with a fixed set of named constants, which can have fields and methods. (3.05) equals / hashCode Value equality and its matching hash; overridden together. (3.03) Exception An object thrown to signal an error, caught with try / catch . (4.04) ExecutorService A pool of threads that runs submitted tasks. (6.04) Field A variable that belongs to an object (or to the class, if static). (3.01) final Cannot be reassigned (variables), overridden (methods) or extended (classes). (1.02) Functional interface An interface with exactly one abstract method, implementable by a lambda. (6.01) Garbage collector The JVM part that frees objects no longer referenced. (1.01) Generics Type parameters such as List<String , checked at compile time. (4.01) Hash table An array of buckets indexed by hash code, giving O(1) average lookup. (5.04) Immutable Cannot change after creation, like String , records and LocalDate . (3.02) Inheritance A class extending another and reusing its members. (3.03) Interface A contract of methods that implementing classes provide. (3.04) Invariant A condition that stays true, such as at the start of every loop round. (5.02) Iterator An object that walks through a collection with hasNext and next . (5.03) JDK / JVM The Java Development Kit (compiler, tools, library) / the Java Virtual Machine that runs bytecode. (1.01) Lambda A short anonymous function: x - x 2 . (6.01) Linked list Nodes that each hold a value and a reference to the next node. (5.03) Load factor Entries divided by buckets in a hash table; kept low by resizing. (5.04) Map Key-to-value lookup: HashMap , TreeMap , LinkedHashMap . (4.02) Memoization Storing results of earlier calls to avoid recomputing them. (2.04) Merge sort Divide-and-conquer sort: split, sort halves, merge; O(n log n), stable. (5.02) Method A named block of code with parameters and a return type. (2.01) Method reference Shorthand for a lambda calling one method: String::length . (6.01) NullPointerException Thrown when a member of null is used. (3.01) Object An instance of a class; also the root class of all classes. (3.01) Optional A container for a value that may be absent, used as a return type. (6.03) Overloading Several methods with the same name and different parameters. (2.01) Overriding A subclass replacing an inherited method. (3.03) Package A named group of classes matching a folder, such as com.example.app . (6.05) Pass by value Java copies argument values; for objects, it copies the reference. (2.01) Pattern matching Testing and taking apart values with instanceof and switch patterns. (3.05) Polymorphism Code written for a supertype working with any subtype's behaviour. (3.03) Primitive type One of the eight value types: int , long , double , boolean , char , byte , short , float . (1.02) Queue First in, first out: offer at the back, poll from the front. (4.02) Race condition A bug where the result depends on how threads' steps interleave. (6.04) Record A concise immutable data class with generated equals, hashCode and toString. (3.05) Recursion A method calling itself on a smaller problem. (2.04) Reference type A type whose variables hold references to objects. (1.02) Scanner The class that reads text input, such as from System.in . (1.04) Sealed type An interface or class that lists the only classes allowed to implement or extend it. (3.05) Set A collection without duplicates: HashSet , TreeSet , LinkedHashSet . (4.02) Stack Last in, first out: push , pop , peek . (5.04) Stable sort A sort that keeps equal items in their original order. (4.03) static Belonging to the class rather than to an instance. (3.02) Stream A pipeline of operations over a sequence of values. (6.02) StringBuilder A mutable buffer for building strings efficiently. (2.05) switch expression switch with - arms that produces a value. (1.05) synchronized Lets only one thread at a time run a block for the same lock. (6.04) Text block A multi-line string between """ delimiters. (1.04) Thread An independent path of execution. (6.04) try-with-resources try (Resource r = ...) , which closes the resource automatically. (4.04) Type erasure Generic types being removed after compile-time checking. (4.01) Unchecked exception A RuntimeException , which need not be declared or caught. (4.04) var Declares a local variable whose type the compiler infers. (6.03) Wildcard ? in a generic type: List<? extends Number . (4.01) Wrapper class The object version of a primitive: Integer , Double , Boolean ... (2.03)

title: 1.01  What JavaScript Is and Running It
match: 1.01 What JavaScript Is and Running It
body: JavaScript is the language every web browser runs, and with Node.js it runs on servers and in tools too. This lesson explains where it runs, how it is executed, the console, and how TypeScript relates to it. The language of the web Every web browser contains a JavaScript engine. HTML describes a page, CSS styles it, and JavaScript makes it do things: respond to clicks, check forms, fetch data, draw, play games. Because every browser runs it, it is the most widely deployed programming language there is. JavaScript also runs outside the browser: Where Engine / runtime Used for --- --- --- Browsers V8 (Chrome, Edge), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari) Web pages and apps Node.js , Deno, Bun V8 or JavaScriptCore Servers, command-line tools, build tools Desktop apps Electron (VS Code, Discord, this site's desktop app) Apps built with web technology How it runs Like Python, JavaScript is not compiled ahead of time by you. The engine parses your code and runs it, compiling hot parts to machine code on the fly ( just-in-time compilation ), which makes modern JavaScript fast. A first program javascript console.log("Hello, Xenon!"); console.log("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3); console.log( 1, 2, 3 , { name: "Ada", age: 36 }); console.log prints its arguments separated by spaces; arrays and objects are shown in a readable form. Press Run to try it. Statements end with a semicolon. JavaScript inserts missing semicolons automatically in most places, but the rules have surprising corners, so this course always writes them. Running it yourself - In a browser : open the developer tools (F12), choose the Console tab, and type JavaScript; it runs on the current page. - With Node.js : install it from nodejs.org, save code in hello.js , and run node hello.js . Running node alone opens an interactive prompt. An editor such as VS Code understands JavaScript out of the box and shows errors as you type. Comments javascript // a comment to the end of the line / a comment over several lines / const answer = 42; // the meaning of everything JavaScript and TypeScript TypeScript is JavaScript with types added: you write let count: number = 0 , and a checker tells you before running that count = "ten" is a mistake. TypeScript compiles to plain JavaScript by removing the types, so it runs everywhere JavaScript does. Most large JavaScript projects today are written in TypeScript. This course teaches JavaScript first (milestones 1-4), then TypeScript on top (milestone 5); everything you learn about JavaScript applies to TypeScript unchanged.

title: Your first program
where: 1.01 What JavaScript Is and Running It
body: Change the program so it prints exactly: Hello, Xenon! 2 + 3 = 5 The second line must be calculated: print the text 2 + 3 = and the value of 2 + 3 .

title: 1.02  Values, Variables and Types
body: JavaScript's types - number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, symbol and objects - declaring variables with const and let (and why not var), typeof, and how values are copied or shared. Declaring variables javascript const name = "Ada"; // cannot be reassigned let score = 10; // can be reassigned score = score + 5; console.log(name, score); Use const by default and let only when the variable really must change. The old var has confusing rules (function scope, hoisting): never use it in new code. const means the name cannot be pointed at another value. If the value is an object or array, its contents can still change: javascript const list = 1, 2 ; list.push(3); // fine: the same array, changed console.log(list); // list = ; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable The types Type Examples Notes --- --- --- number 42 , 3.14 , -0 , NaN , Infinity One type for whole and fractional numbers (64-bit floats) bigint 9007199254740993n Arbitrarily large whole numbers string "hi" , 'hi' , hi Text boolean true , false undefined undefined A variable with no value yet, a missing property null null "Deliberately nothing" symbol Symbol("id") Unique keys (advanced) object { a: 1 } , 1, 2 , functions, dates Everything else javascript console.log(typeof 42, typeof "x", typeof true, typeof undefined, typeof 10n); console.log(typeof {}, typeof , typeof null, typeof function () {}); Two famous oddities: typeof null is "object" (a historical bug that cannot be fixed), and arrays are objects too; use Array.isArray(x) to check for an array. Numbers All numbers are 64-bit floating point, so whole numbers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (about 9 × 10¹⁵), and decimal fractions are approximate ( 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 , exactly as in Python's lesson 1.04). Invalid arithmetic gives NaN ("not a number"), which is not even equal to itself: test it with Number.isNaN(x) . undefined and null javascript let pending; console.log(pending); // undefined: declared but not assigned const user = { name: "Ada" }; console.log(user.email); // undefined: no such property const selected = null; // "no selection", on purpose Treat undefined as "not set" and null as "set to nothing". Both are falsy, and x == null is true for both (one of the few good uses of == , lesson 1.03). Copying and sharing Primitive values (numbers, strings, booleans...) are copied; objects and arrays are shared by reference: javascript let a = 5; let b = a; b += 1; // a is still 5 const p = { x: 1 }; const q = p; q.x = 99; // p.x is also 99: one object, two names const r = { ...p }; // a (shallow) copy r.x = 0; console.log(a, p.x, r.x); Naming Variables and functions use camelCase ; classes use PascalCase ; constants that are true configuration values are often UPPER_CASE . Names are case-sensitive.

title: What type is it?
body: Write two functions: javascript function describeType(value) { } // "null", "array", or what typeof says function copyWith(obj, key, value) { } // a NEW object: obj's properties plus key set to value; obj unchanged describeType(null) is "null" and describeType( 1 ) is "array" (fixing typeof 's two oddities); everything else is typeof value .

title: 1.03  Operators, Comparisons and Conversions
body: Arithmetic and assignment operators, strict versus loose equality, truthiness, the logical operators and the nullish operators ?? and ?., and converting between strings and numbers without surprises. Arithmetic Operator Meaning Example --- --- --- + - / Add, subtract, multiply, divide 7 / 2 is 3.5 % Remainder (keeps the sign of the left side) -7 % 3 is -1 Power 2 10 is 1024 ++ , -- Add or subtract 1 count++ += , -= , = , ... Update total += price Whole-number division is Math.trunc(a / b) (towards zero) or Math.floor(a / b) (down). Note % differs from Python for negative numbers. Strict equality Always compare with === and !== : equal value and type. javascript console.log(1 === 1, 1 === "1", "a" === "a"); // true false true console.log(1 == "1", 0 == "", null == undefined); // true true true: loose equality converts types Loose == converts its operands with complicated rules ( == false is true). The one common use is x == null , which is true for both null and undefined . Objects (including arrays) are equal only if they are the same object: 1 === 1 is false . Truthiness In conditions, these values are falsy : false , 0 , -0 , 0n , "" , null , undefined , NaN . Everything else is truthy, including "0" , "false" , and {} . Logical operators && and return one of their operands , not necessarily true or false : javascript console.log("" "default"); // "default": the first truthy value console.log("Ada" && "admin"); // "admin": the first falsy value, or the last console.log(!0, !!"text"); // true true: !! converts to a boolean a b is often used for defaults, but it replaces every falsy value, including 0 and "" . The nullish operators only react to null and undefined : javascript const volume = 0; console.log(volume 50); // 50: wrong, 0 was a real value console.log(volume ?? 50); // 0: ?? only replaces null and undefined const user = { profile: null }; console.log(user.profile?.email); // undefined instead of a TypeError console.log(user.settings?.theme ?? "light"); ?. (optional chaining) stops and gives undefined if the left side is null or undefined . Converting Want Use Watch out --- --- --- Number from text Number("42") Number("") is 0 ; Number("4x") is NaN Whole number from text parseInt("42px", 10) Reads until the first non-digit: 42 ; always pass the base 10 Decimal from text parseFloat("3.5kg") 3.5 Text from a number String(42) , ${42} , (3.14159).toFixed(2) toFixed returns a string Boolean Boolean(x) or !!x Truthiness rules above + with a string concatenates : "5" + 3 is "53" , while "5" - 3 is 2 . Convert explicitly before doing arithmetic on text from forms or files.

title: Conversions and defaults
body: Write three functions: javascript function toNumber(text) { } // the number in text, or null if it is not a number function volumeOr(volume, fallback) { } // volume, unless it is null or undefined (0 is a real volume!) function setting(user, key, fallback) { } // user.settings key , or fallback when anything on the way is missing toNumber ignores spaces around the number and accepts decimals and a minus sign, but returns null for an empty or blank text and for anything that Number cannot convert (such as "4x" ).

title: 1.04  Strings and Template Literals
body: Working with text - template literals with ${} expressions, indexing and length, the most useful string methods, splitting and joining, padding and formatting numbers, and Unicode characters. Three kinds of quotes javascript const single = 'It\'s'; const double = "She said \"hi\""; const name = "Ada"; const template = Hello, ${name}! 2 + 3 = ${2 + 3} ; console.log(single, double, template); Template literals (backticks) insert any expression with ${...} and can span several lines. Use them whenever text and values are mixed. Reading strings javascript const word = "JavaScript"; console.log(word.length, word 0 , word.at(-1), word.slice(4), word.slice(0, 4), word.slice(-6)); at(-1) counts from the end; slice(start, end) takes a part (end not included; negative values count from the end). Strings are immutable : methods return new strings. Useful methods Method Example Gives --- --- --- toUpperCase , toLowerCase "Ada".toUpperCase() "ADA" trim , trimStart , trimEnd " hi ".trim() "hi" includes , startsWith , endsWith "photo.png".endsWith(".png") true indexOf "banana".indexOf("na") 2 ( -1 if absent) split "a,b,c".split(",") "a", "b", "c" replace , replaceAll "a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+") "a+b+c" repeat "ab".repeat(3) "ababab" padStart , padEnd "7".padStart(3, "0") "007" replace with a string replaces only the first match; use replaceAll (or a regular expression with the g flag, lesson 2.02's practice) for all. Joining a list: "a", "b" .join(", ") is "a, b" . Formatting numbers javascript const price = 1234.5; console.log(price.toFixed(2)); // "1234.50" console.log(price.toLocaleString("en-US")); // "1,234.5" console.log(price.toLocaleString("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" })); console.log(String(5).padStart(3, " "), (0.256 100).toFixed(1) + "%"); Intl.NumberFormat and toLocaleString format numbers, currencies and dates for a language and region. Comparing strings < and compare strings by character codes: "Zebra" < "apple" is true because capitals come first. For human sorting, use a.localeCompare(b) (lesson 2.02 uses it with sort ). Unicode JavaScript strings are UTF-16 (the Win32 course's lesson 1.02 explains the encoding). "é".length is 1, but an emoji such as "😀".length is 2 , because it is stored as two code units. To count or walk characters properly, use ...text or for (const ch of text) , which handle such pairs: javascript const text = "hi 😀"; console.log(text.length, ...text .length); // 5 4

title: Text helpers
body: Write four string functions: javascript function titleCase(text) { } // "the lord of the rings" - "The Lord Of The Rings" (words separated by single spaces) function truncate(text, max) { } // at most max characters; if cut, the last character is "…" function countChars(text) { } // the number of characters, counting an emoji as one function receiptLine(item, price) { } // item padded to 12 characters, price with 2 decimals right-aligned in 8 truncate("Hello, world", 6) is "Hello…" ; text that fits is returned unchanged. receiptLine("tea", 2.5) is "tea 2.50" .

title: 1.05  Control Flow
body: Making decisions and repeating work - if and else, the conditional operator, switch, for loops in their three forms, while and do-while, break and continue, and labelled loops. if and else javascript const temperature = 18; if (temperature < 0) { console.log("Freezing"); } else if (temperature < 15) { console.log("Cold"); } else { console.log("Mild or warm"); } Conditions go in parentheses, blocks in braces. Braces are optional for a single statement, but always writing them avoids a classic bug when a second line is added later. The conditional operator chooses between two values: javascript const age = 20; const label = age = 18 ? "adult" : "minor"; console.log(label); switch switch compares one value against several cases with === : javascript function dayType(day) { switch (day) { case "Sat": case "Sun": return "weekend"; case "Mon": return "start of the week"; default: return "weekday"; } } console.log(dayType("Sun"), dayType("Wed")); Without return or break , execution falls through into the next case. That is useful for grouping cases ( "Sat" and "Sun" above) and a bug when forgotten. for loops javascript for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // counting console.log("round", i); } const fruits = "apple", "pear", "plum" ; for (const fruit of fruits) { // the VALUES of an array (or string, Map, Set...) console.log(fruit); } const scores = { ada: 95, grace: 88 }; for (const key in scores) { // the KEYS of an object console.log(key, scores key ); } Use for...of for arrays and strings; for...in is for object keys only (on arrays it gives the indexes as strings, which is rarely what you want). To get indexes with for...of : for (const i, fruit of fruits.entries()) . while and do...while javascript let n = 27; let steps = 0; while (n !== 1) { n = n % 2 === 0 ? n / 2 : 3 n + 1; steps++; } console.log(steps); let attempt = 0; do { attempt++; } while (attempt < 3); // the body runs at least once console.log(attempt); break and continue break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next round. In nested loops, a label says which loop to leave: javascript outer: for (let row = 0; row < 3; row++) { for (let col = 0; col < 3; col++) { if (row col === 2) { console.log("found at", row, col); break outer; } } }

title: Loops and switches
body: Write three functions: javascript function fizzBuzz(n) { } // array for 1..n: "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" of 5, "FizzBuzz" of both, else the number as a string function dayType(day) { } // "Sat"/"Sun" - "weekend", "Mon"-"Fri" - "weekday", anything else - "unknown" (use switch) function collatzSteps(n) { } // steps to reach 1: halve even numbers, 3n + 1 for odd ones (use while)

title: A receipt printer
body: Write formatReceipt(items, tipPercent) , which turns a list of items into the text of a receipt: javascript formatReceipt( { name: "Green tea", price: 2.5, qty: 2 }, { name: "Chocolate cake", price: 4.25, qty: 1 }, , 10) Green tea x2 5.00 Chocolate cake 4.25 --------------------------- Subtotal 9.25 Tip 10% 0.93 Total 10.18 Rules: - Each item line is the name, followed by x<qty when the quantity is more than 1, padded on the right to 19 characters, then the line total (price × qty) with 2 decimals right-aligned in 8 characters. Names longer than 19 characters (with the quantity) are cut to 18 characters plus … . - Then a line of 27 dashes, then Subtotal , Tip <percent % and Total lines in the same layout. The tip is the subtotal × percent / 100, rounded to cents ; the total is subtotal + tip. - With a tip of 0, the tip line is left out. - To avoid floating-point errors, work in whole cents: Math.round(price 100) . - Items with a quantity of 0 or less are skipped. If no items are left, the receipt is just No items . - Lines are joined with \n (no newline at the end).

title: 2.01  Functions
body: Function declarations, function expressions and arrow functions, parameters with defaults, rest parameters and spread, returning values, functions as values, and callbacks. Three ways to write a function javascript function area(width, height) { // declaration: usable anywhere in its scope return width height; } const perimeter = function (w, h) { // expression assigned to a variable return 2 (w + h); }; const square = x = x x; // arrow function: short form for one expression const describe = (w, h) = { const a = area(w, h); return ${w}x${h} has area ${a} ; }; console.log(area(3, 4), perimeter(3, 4), square(5), describe(2, 3)); Arrow functions with one expression return it automatically; with braces they need return . To return an object literal from a one-line arrow, wrap it in parentheses: () = ({ ok: true }) . A function without return returns undefined . Parameters Missing arguments are undefined ; extra ones are ignored. Default values apply when an argument is undefined : javascript function greet(name, greeting = "Hello") { return ${greeting}, ${name}! ; } console.log(greet("Ada"), greet("Ada", "Hi")); A rest parameter collects any number of arguments into an array; spread does the reverse: javascript function total(...numbers) { return numbers.reduce((sum, n) = sum + n, 0); } const prices = 3, 4, 5 ; console.log(total(1, 2), total(...prices), Math.max(...prices)); For functions with many options, pass one object and destructure it (lesson 2.03): function connect({ host, port = 443, timeout = 10 }) . Calls then name every option. Functions are values Functions can be stored, passed and returned like any value. A function passed to another function is a callback : javascript function repeat(times, action) { for (let i = 0; i < times; i++) action(i); } repeat(3, i = console.log("round", i)); const operations = { double: x = x 2, negate: x = -x }; console.log(operations.double(21), operations "negate" (5)); The array methods of lesson 2.02 ( map , filter , sort ) and all asynchronous code (milestone 4) are built on callbacks. Pure functions A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, and it changes nothing outside itself. Pure functions are the easiest to test and reuse; keep reading files, printing and changing shared data at the edges of a program, and the logic in pure functions in between. Hoisting Function declarations are hoisted: they can be called before the line that defines them. Functions assigned to const cannot, because the variable does not exist yet ("temporal dead zone"). Define helpers before use, or rely on declarations deliberately.

title: Functions that take functions
body: Write three functions: javascript function average(...numbers) { } // the average of any number of arguments; 0 when there are none function applyTimes(f, times, start) { } // f applied times times: applyTimes(x = x 2, 3, 1) is 8 function compose(...fns) { } // a function that applies fns right to left: compose(f, g)(x) is f(g(x)) compose() with no functions returns a function that gives back its argument unchanged.

title: 2.02  Arrays and Array Methods
body: Creating and changing arrays, and the methods that make array code short and clear - map, filter, reduce, find, some and every, includes, sort with a compare function, slice versus splice, flat and flatMap, and which methods change the array. Basics javascript const fruits = "apple", "pear" ; fruits.push("plum"); // add at the end fruits.unshift("fig"); // add at the start const last = fruits.pop(); // remove from the end console.log(fruits, last, fruits.length, fruits.includes("pear"), fruits.indexOf("pear")); Transforming without loops Method Returns --- --- map(f) A new array of f(item) for each item filter(f) A new array of the items where f(item) is truthy reduce(f, start) One value built up from all items find(f) / findIndex(f) The first matching item / its index ( undefined / -1 if none) some(f) / every(f) Whether any / all items match forEach(f) Nothing: just runs f on each item javascript const orders = { item: "tea", qty: 2, price: 2.5 }, { item: "cake", qty: 1, price: 4 }, { item: "mug", qty: 3, price: 8 }, ; const totals = orders.map(o = o.qty o.price); const big = orders.filter(o = o.qty o.price 5).map(o = o.item); const sum = totals.reduce((acc, t) = acc + t, 0); console.log(totals, big, sum, orders.find(o = o.item === "cake"), orders.some(o = o.qty 2)); Chaining filter then map then reduce reads like a description of the result. The callbacks also receive the index as a second argument: map((item, i) = ...) . Sorting sort() changes the array and, without arguments, compares items as strings : 10, 9, 1 .sort() gives 1, 10, 9 . Always give numbers a compare function, which returns a negative number when a comes first: javascript const nums = 10, 9, 1, 100 ; console.log( ...nums .sort((a, b) = a - b)); // ascending const people = { name: "bob", age: 30 }, { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "carol", age: 30 } ; people.sort((a, b) = a.age - b.age a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); console.log(people.map(p = p.name)); // by age, then name a.localeCompare(b) compares text the way people expect. chains criteria: if the first difference is 0, the second decides. toSorted() returns a sorted copy instead of changing the array. Changing versus copying Changes the array Returns a new array --- --- push , pop , shift , unshift map , filter , concat splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) slice(start, end) sort , reverse , fill toSorted , toReversed , with(i, value) Copy an array with ...arr or arr.slice() . Code that does not change its inputs is easier to reason about: prefer the right-hand column. Nested arrays javascript console.log( 1, 2 , 3 , .flat()); // 1, 2, 3 console.log( "a b", "c" .flatMap(s = s.split(" "))); // "a", "b", "c" const grid = Array.from({ length: 2 }, () = Array(3).fill(0)); // 2 separate rows of 3 zeros Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) = ...) builds an array of n computed items.

title: Array methods
body: Each function takes an array of products like { name: "Mug", price: 8, stock: 3, tags: "kitchen" } and must not change it: javascript function inStockNames(products) { } // names of products with stock 0, in their original order function stockValue(products) { } // the sum of price stock over all products function cheapestFirst(products) { } // a NEW array sorted by price, then by name ignoring case function allTags(products) { } // every tag used, once each, sorted alphabetically

title: 2.03  Objects and Destructuring
body: Objects as collections of named values - creating and reading them, dot and bracket access, adding and deleting properties, shorthand and computed names, Object.keys, values and entries, spread and copying, and destructuring objects and arrays. Object literals javascript const book = { title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, "page count": 412, // names with spaces need quotes }; console.log(book.title, book "page count" ); book.rating = 5; // add delete book.year; // remove console.log(book, "year" in book, book.missing); // undefined for missing properties Use dot access for fixed names and brackets when the name is in a variable: book field . Shorthand and computed names javascript const title = "Dune"; const year = 1965; const field = "genre"; const entry = { title, year, field : "sci-fi", describe() { return ${this.title} (${this.year}) ; } }; console.log(entry, entry.describe()); { title } is short for { title: title } ; field uses the variable's value as the name; describe() {...} is a method. Looping over an object javascript const scores = { ada: 95, grace: 88, linus: 72 }; console.log(Object.keys(scores), Object.values(scores)); for (const name, score of Object.entries(scores)) { console.log( ${name}: ${score} ); } const curved = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(scores).map(( n, s ) = n, s + 5 )); console.log(curved); Object.entries and Object.fromEntries turn an object into key, value pairs and back, so array methods can transform objects. Copying and merging Spread copies properties into a new object; later properties win: javascript const defaults = { theme: "light", size: 12 }; const user = { size: 14 }; const settings = { ...defaults, ...user, wrap: true }; console.log(settings); Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared. structuredClone(obj) makes a deep copy. Destructuring Destructuring takes values out of objects and arrays into variables: javascript const person = { name: "Ada", age: 36, address: { city: "London" } }; const { name, age: years, email = "none", address: { city } } = person; console.log(name, years, email, city); const first, second = 0, ...others = 10, 20, 30, 40 ; console.log(first, second, others); let a = 1, b = 2; a, b = b, a ; // swap console.log(a, b); age: years renames; = "none" gives a default when the property is undefined ; nested patterns reach inside. It is especially useful in parameters: javascript function formatUser({ name, age, city = "unknown" }) { return ${name}, ${age}, ${city} ; } console.log(formatUser({ name: "Grace", age: 85 }));

title: Objects and destructuring
body: Write three functions: javascript function mergeSettings(defaults, user) { } // a new object: defaults overridden by user; neither input changes function invert(obj) { } // swap keys and values: { a: "x" } becomes { x: "a" } function summary({ name, age, city = "unknown", ...rest }) { } summary returns a string like "Ada (36) from London, 2 more fields" . When age is missing, leave out (36) ; the count is the number of other fields, with field for 1 and fields otherwise; when there are none, leave out the comma part. mergeSettings also merges one level deeper: if both have a plain object (not an array) under the same key, such as colors , the result has both sets of inner properties.

title: 2.04  Scope and Closures
body: Where variables live - block scope with let and const, function scope, the scope chain, closures that remember variables, private state with closures, and the classic closure-in-a-loop bug that let fixes. Block scope let and const are visible only inside the block (the braces) where they are declared: javascript const x = "outer"; { const x = "inner"; // a different variable, hiding the outer one inside this block console.log(x); } console.log(x); for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) { } // console.log(i); // ReferenceError: i only exists inside the loop When a name is used, JavaScript looks in the current block, then the enclosing ones, then the function, then the module and global scope: the scope chain . Closures A function remembers the variables of the scope where it was created , even after that scope has finished. A function together with those variables is a closure : javascript function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return () = ++count; } const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter(); console.log(a(), a(), a(), b()); // 1 2 3 1: separate counts count cannot be reached from outside except through the returned function: closures give private state . Modules of functions Closures can bundle several functions around shared private data: javascript function createStack() { const items = ; return { push(x) { items.push(x); }, pop() { return items.pop(); }, get size() { return items.length; }, }; } const s = createStack(); s.push(1); s.push(2); console.log(s.pop(), s.size); // 2 1: items itself is unreachable Classes (lesson 3.01) with private fields do the same job; both styles are common. The loop bug With var , there is one variable for the whole loop, so every callback sees its final value. let creates a new binding for each iteration: javascript const fns = ; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() = i); console.log(fns.map(f = f())); // 0, 1, 2 ; with var it would be 3, 3, 3 Functions that make functions Closures let you configure a function once and use it many times: javascript const multiplier = n = x = x n; const double = multiplier(2); const triple = multiplier(3); console.log(double(5), triple(5)); function once(fn) { let done = false, result; return (...args) = { if (!done) { done = true; result = fn(...args); } return result; }; } const init = once(() = { console.log("initialising"); return 42; }); console.log(init(), init()); // prints "initialising" only once

title: Closures
body: Write three functions that use closures: javascript function makeCounter(start = 0, step = 1) { } // returns { next(), reset(), value() } function memoize(f) { } // returns a function giving f's result, computing each argument only once function makeLimiter(limit) { } // returns a function that wraps another so it runs at most limit times - next() adds step and returns the new value; value() returns the current value; reset() goes back to start . - The memoized function takes one argument; for an argument it has seen before it returns the stored result without calling f again. - makeLimiter(2)(f) gives a function that calls f with its arguments the first 2 times and returns undefined after that. Each wrapped function has its own count.

title: 2.05  Maps, Sets and JSON
body: Map for key-value data with any key type and reliable ordering, Set for unique values, when to use them instead of plain objects and arrays, grouping with Map and Object.groupBy, and converting data to and from JSON text. Map A Map stores key-value pairs. Unlike a plain object, its keys can be any value (numbers, objects), it remembers insertion order, and it has a size: javascript const stock = new Map(); stock.set("apples", 4).set("pears", 0); stock.set("apples", stock.get("apples") + 1); console.log(stock.get("apples"), stock.has("plums"), stock.size); for (const fruit, count of stock) console.log(fruit, count); stock.delete("pears"); console.log( ...stock.keys() , Object.fromEntries(stock)); Counting with a Map: javascript const words = "the cat and the hat".split(" "); const counts = new Map(); for (const w of words) counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1); console.log(counts); Use a Map when keys are data (user names, ids) and change at run time; use a plain object for a fixed set of named fields (a record). Set A Set holds unique values with fast has : javascript const tags = new Set( "js", "web", "js" ); tags.add("ts"); console.log(tags.size, tags.has("web"), ...tags ); const unique = ...new Set( 3, 1, 3, 2, 1 ) ; console.log(unique); const a = new Set( 1, 2, 3 ), b = new Set( 2, 3, 4 ); console.log( ...a .filter(x = b.has(x))); // intersection Recent engines also have a.union(b) , a.intersection(b) and a.difference(b) . Objects in Maps and Sets are compared by identity : new Set( {}, {} ).size is 2. Grouping Object.groupBy (and Map.groupBy ) group items by a key function: javascript const people = { name: "Ada", team: "red" }, { name: "Bob", team: "blue" }, { name: "Cy", team: "red" } ; const byTeam = Object.groupBy(people, p = p.team); console.log(Object.keys(byTeam), byTeam.red.map(p = p.name)); In older environments, the same is a few lines with reduce or a loop and a Map. JSON JSON is the text format of web APIs, written exactly like JavaScript literals (with double-quoted keys): javascript const order = { id: 7, items: "tea", "cake" , paid: true, note: null }; const text = JSON.stringify(order); console.log(text); console.log(JSON.stringify(order, null, 2)); // pretty-printed const back = JSON.parse(text); console.log(back.items 1 , back.paid); JSON has strings, numbers, booleans, null , arrays and objects. undefined and functions are left out, Date objects become strings, and Maps and Sets become {} : convert them first ( Object.fromEntries(map) , ...set ). JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid text (lesson 3.03 shows how to handle it).

title: Maps, Sets and JSON
body: Write four functions: javascript function wordFrequencies(text) { } // a Map from lower-case word to count, in first-seen order function topWords(text, n) { } // the n most frequent words as word, count pairs; ties keep first-seen order function saveState(state) { } // JSON text for { tags: Set, scores: Map, name } that loadState can read back function loadState(text) { } // the original shape: a Set, a Map and the name Words are runs of letters and apostrophes ( / a-z' +/g on the lower-case text).

title: A gradebook
body: Write gradebook(records) , which turns a list of raw score records into a report object. Each record is { student, subject, score } : javascript gradebook( { student: "Ada", subject: "maths", score: 92 }, { student: "Bob", subject: "maths", score: 61 }, { student: "Ada", subject: "art", score: 78 }, { student: "Bob", subject: "art", score: 85 }, { student: "Cy", subject: "maths", score: 47 }, ) returns javascript { students: { name: "Ada", average: 85, grade: "B", subjects: { maths: 92, art: 78 } }, { name: "Bob", average: 73, grade: "C", subjects: { maths: 61, art: 85 } }, { name: "Cy", average: 47, grade: "F", subjects: { maths: 47 } }, , subjects: { maths: { average: 66.67, best: "Ada" }, art: { average: 81.5, best: "Bob" } }, top: "Ada", } Rules: - Clean the data first : skip records whose score is not a number between 0 and 100 (inclusive), or whose student or subject is not a non-empty string. Trim names and subjects; subjects are compared in lower case ( "Maths" and "maths" are the same subject, reported as "maths" ). - If the same student has several records for one subject, the last one counts. - A student's average is the mean of their subject scores, rounded to 2 decimals ( Math.round(x 100) / 100 ). Grades from the unrounded average: 90 and above A , 80 B , 70 C , 60 D , below 60 F . - students is sorted by average, highest first; ties by name alphabetically. subjects inside each student keeps first-seen order. - In the report's subjects , keys appear in first-seen order; average is the mean of that subject's scores rounded to 2 decimals, and best is the student with the highest score (on a tie, the one whose name comes first alphabetically). - top is the first student in students , or null when there are none. - The function must not change records .

title: 3.01  Classes
body: Defining classes with constructors, fields and methods, private fields with , getters and setters, static members, inheritance with extends and super, overriding methods, instanceof, and when a plain object or function is simpler. A class A class describes a kind of object: the data each one holds and what it can do. javascript class Account { owner; // a public field balance = 0; // a private field: only code inside the class can use it constructor(owner, opening = 0) { this.owner = owner; this.deposit(opening); } deposit(amount) { if (amount < 0) throw new RangeError("deposit must not be negative"); this. balance += amount; return this; // returning this allows chaining } get balance() { // read like a property: acc.balance return this. balance; } toString() { return ${this.owner}: ${this. balance.toFixed(2)} ; } } const acc = new Account("Ada", 10); acc.deposit(5).deposit(2.5); console.log(acc.balance, String(acc)); // acc. balance // SyntaxError outside the class new Account(...) creates an object and runs constructor with this set to it. Inside methods, this is the object the method was called on. Getters, setters and static members javascript class Temperature { celsius; constructor(celsius) { this. celsius = celsius; } get fahrenheit() { return this. celsius 9 / 5 + 32; } set fahrenheit(f) { this. celsius = (f - 32) 5 / 9; } static fromFahrenheit(f) { const t = new Temperature(0); t.fahrenheit = f; return t; } static count = 0; } const t = Temperature.fromFahrenheit(212); console.log(t.fahrenheit); t.fahrenheit = 32; console.log(t.fahrenheit); A setter runs code when a property is assigned, which is the place to validate. Static members belong to the class itself, not to each object: Temperature.fromFahrenheit , Math.max , Number.isInteger . Static factory methods like fromFahrenheit give alternative ways to build an object. Inheritance extends makes a class that starts with everything of another. The child's constructor must call super(...) before using this : javascript class Shape { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } area() { return 0; } describe() { return ${this.name} with area ${this.area().toFixed(1)} ; } } class Circle extends Shape { constructor(r) { super("circle"); this.r = r; } area() { return Math.PI this.r 2; } // overrides Shape's area } class Square extends Shape { constructor(side) { super("square"); this.side = side; } area() { return this.side 2; } describe() { return super.describe() + " (a square)"; } // extends the parent's version } const shapes = new Circle(1), new Square(2) ; for (const s of shapes) console.log(s.describe()); console.log(shapes 0 instanceof Circle, shapes 0 instanceof Shape, shapes 0 instanceof Square); describe in Shape calls this.area() , which runs the child's version: each object answers in its own way ( polymorphism ). When to use a class Use a class when many objects share behaviour and keep state that must stay consistent (a bank account, a game entity, a connection). For plain data, an object literal is enough; for a single operation, a function is enough. Prefer shallow hierarchies: one level of extends is common, three is usually a sign that composition (an object holding other objects) fits better.

title: A class with private state
body: Write a class Inventory that keeps item counts: javascript const inv = new Inventory(); inv.add("apple", 3).add("pear").add("apple", 2); // add(name, count = 1) returns this inv.remove("apple", 4); // returns true; false (and no change) if there are not enough inv.count("apple"); // 1; 0 for unknown items inv.total; // a getter: the sum of all counts (2 here) inv.names(); // names with a count above 0, sorted Inventory.from({ tea: 2, cake: 1 }); // a static factory building an Inventory from an object - The counts are stored in a private field, so inv.items and similar do not exist. - add and remove throw a RangeError when count is not a positive whole number. - An item whose count reaches 0 is removed completely. Then write class LimitedInventory extends Inventory , built with new LimitedInventory(max) , whose add throws a RangeError with the message full when the total would go above max ; otherwise it adds as usual.

title: 3.02  Prototypes and this
body: How JavaScript objects really share behaviour - the prototype chain under classes, Object.create, own versus inherited properties, the four rules for this, losing this when passing methods, and fixing it with arrow functions and bind. The prototype chain Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype . When a property is not found on an object, JavaScript looks on its prototype, then that object's prototype, and so on: the prototype chain . javascript const animal = { speak() { return ${this.name} makes a sound ; } }; const dog = Object.create(animal); // dog's prototype is animal dog.name = "Rex"; console.log(dog.speak()); // found on animal, run with this = dog console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal); console.log(Object.hasOwn(dog, "name"), Object.hasOwn(dog, "speak")); Classes are built on this: methods live once on ClassName.prototype , and every instance links to it. javascript class Point { constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } length() { return Math.hypot(this.x, this.y); } } const p = new Point(3, 4); console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(p) === Point.prototype, Object.keys(p), p.length()); Object.keys shows only an object's own properties ( x , y ); length is inherited. Arrays get map from Array.prototype , and everything ends at Object.prototype , whose prototype is null . Never add methods to built-in prototypes ( Array.prototype.sum = ... ): it can clash with future versions of the language and with other code. What this is this is decided when a function is called , not where it is written: Call this --- --- obj.method() obj new Fn() the new object fn.call(x, ...) / fn.apply(x, ... ) / a bind(x) copy x fn() on its own undefined (in modules and classes) Arrow functions do not have their own this ; they use the this of the code around them. Losing this Taking a method out of its object and calling it later loses this . This happens whenever a method is passed as a callback: javascript class Timer { constructor() { this.ticks = 0; } tick() { this.ticks++; } } const timer = new Timer(); const f = timer.tick; try { f(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name, e.message); } 1, 2, 3 .forEach(() = timer.tick()); // fix 1: an arrow function calling the method 1, 2 .forEach(timer.tick.bind(timer)); // fix 2: bind makes a copy with this fixed console.log(timer.ticks); A third fix is a class field holding an arrow function: tick = () = { this.ticks++; }; . Each instance then gets its own copy with this fixed, which is convenient for event handlers (milestone 6). call, apply and bind javascript function introduce(greeting, punctuation) { return ${greeting}, I am ${this.name}${punctuation} ; } const ada = { name: "Ada" }; console.log(introduce.call(ada, "Hi", "!")); console.log(introduce.apply(ada, "Hello", "." )); const adaIntro = introduce.bind(ada, "Hey"); console.log(adaIntro("?")); bind can also fix leading arguments, as "Hey" here.

title: Prototypes and this
