(2.04) CommonJS Node's older module system, with require and module.exports . (3.05) Concurrency limit Running at most N asynchronous tasks at the same time, for example with a worker pool. (4.05) const Declares a variable that cannot be reassigned (its object can still change). (1.02) CORS The browser rule that a page may read responses from another site only if that site allows it. (4.04) Debounce Running a function once the calls to it have stopped for a while. (4.05) Default export The one unnamed export of a module, imported without braces. (3.05) Destructuring Taking values out of objects and arrays into variables: const { name } = user . (2.03) devDependency A package needed only while developing or building, such as a test runner. (6.04) Discriminated union A union whose variants share a tag property with different literal types, such as kind . (5.03) DOM The tree of objects a browser builds from HTML, which JavaScript reads and changes. (6.01) Enum A TypeScript set of named constants that also exists at run time. (5.05) Error-first callback Node's callback style: (err, value) = ... , with err null on success. (4.01) ES module A file with its own scope that shares values with export and import . (3.05) Event delegation Handling events of many child elements with one listener on a parent. (6.02) Event loop The mechanism that runs queued tasks and microtasks one at a time when the call stack is empty. (4.01) Exhaustive check Assigning to never in a switch's default, so that unhandled variants fail to compile. (5.03) fetch The function that makes HTTP requests and returns a promise for a Response. (4.04) FormData An object collecting a form's named fields; all values are strings. (6.02) Generator A function that produces values one at a time with yield , pausing between them. (3.04) Generic A function, interface or class with a type parameter, such as first<T (items: T ): T . (5.04) Getter / setter Methods that run when a property is read ( get ) or assigned ( set ). (3.01) Hoisting Function declarations being usable before the line that defines them. (2.01) Immutability Not changing existing values; building new ones instead, as update does. (6.05) Inference TypeScript working out a type from a value, so it need not be written. (5.01) Interface A named description of an object's shape. (5.02) Iterable An object with a Symbol.iterator () method, usable in for...of and spread. (3.04) JSON The text format for data, written like JavaScript literals with double-quoted keys. (2.05) keyof The union of a type's property names. (5.04) let Declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned. (1.02) Literal type A type allowing one exact value, such as "up" or 3 . (5.03) Lock file package-lock.json : the exact version of every installed package. (6.04) localStorage Per-site string storage in the browser that survives reloads. (6.03) Map A collection of key-value pairs with keys of any type, in insertion order. (2.05) Microtask A callback, such as a promise reaction, that runs as soon as the current code finishes, before the next task. (4.01) Migration Converting stored data from an older version's shape to the current one. (6.03) Narrowing TypeScript working out a more exact type after a check such as typeof x === "string" . (5.03) never The type with no values: code that cannot be reached. (5.03) npm Node's package manager, which installs packages and runs scripts from package.json . (6.04) Nullish null or undefined , the values that ?? and ?. look for. (1.03) Optional chaining a?.b : stops and gives undefined when a is null or undefined. (1.03) Parameter property A TypeScript constructor parameter with public , private or readonly that also declares the property. (5.05) Polymorphism Different classes answering the same method call in their own way. (3.01) Private field A class field whose name starts with , reachable only inside the class. (3.01) Promise An object standing for a result that arrives later: pending, then fulfilled or rejected. (4.02) Prototype The object another object falls back to for properties it does not have itself. (3.02) Pure function A function whose result depends only on its arguments and that changes nothing outside itself. (2.01) Rest parameter ...args in a function definition: collects the remaining arguments into an array. (2.01) Scope The region of code where a variable can be used. (2.04) Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers, where a major change may break code. (6.04) Set A collection of unique values. (2.05) Spread ...x in a call, array or object literal: expands its items or properties. (2.01) State The data that describes everything an app shows; the page is rendered from it. (6.01) Strict equality === : equal without type conversion. (1.03) Structural typing TypeScript comparing types by their shape rather than their name. (5.02) Template literal A string in backticks that can contain ${expressions} and line breaks. (1.04) this The object a function was called on, decided at call time. (3.02) Throttle Running a function at most once per period. (4.05) Truthy / falsy How a value counts in a condition; the falsy values are false , 0 , "" , null , undefined and NaN . (1.02) Tuple A TypeScript array type with a fixed length and a type per position: string, number . (5.01) Type alias A name for any type: type Id = string \ number . (5.02) Type assertion value as Type : telling the compiler to treat a value as a type without checking. (5.03) Type guard A function returning x is T , which narrows its argument when it returns true. (5.03) TypeScript JavaScript with type annotations, checked by a compiler and then removed. (5.01) typeof The operator giving a value's type as a string, such as "number" . (1.02) Union type A \ B : a value that is one of several types. (5.03) unknown The TypeScript type for any value that must be checked before use. (5.01) Utility type A built-in generic that transforms a type: Partial , Pick , Omit , Record . (5.05) XSS Cross-site scripting: injected HTML or script running in a page, often through innerHTML . (6.01)

title: 1.01  User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
match: 1.01 User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
body: What the kernel is, why the processor separates user mode from kernel mode, what drivers are for, and why a bug in a driver takes the whole machine down. This lesson also sets the rules for the course - everything happens in a virtual machine. Two privilege levels The processor runs code at different privilege levels . Windows uses two: User mode Kernel mode --- --- --- Who runs there Applications, services, most of Windows' own programs The kernel, the executive, the HAL and drivers Memory Its own process's address space only All of memory, every process, the hardware A crash Ends that one process Stops the whole machine: a bug check (blue screen) Errors Exceptions, error codes Must be handled perfectly; there is no one to clean up User-mode code cannot touch the hardware or another process's memory; when it needs something the system provides (reading a file, creating a window), it makes a system call , and the processor switches to kernel mode to run trusted code on its behalf, then switches back. What lives in the kernel Drivers are modules that run in kernel mode, loaded by the system, to extend it: a driver for a graphics card or a USB device, a file system, a network filter, an antivirus filter. They follow the same rules as the rest of the kernel and have the same power. Why drivers are different Everything in the Win32 API course still applies in spirit, but a kernel driver adds rules that user-mode code never sees: - No safety net : dereferencing a bad pointer, leaking memory, or holding a lock too long affects the whole machine, and a crash stops everything with a bug check. - No C++ runtime as you know it : no exceptions, no new without care, no standard library containers, no printf . Drivers are written in C or a careful subset of C++. - Interrupt levels (IRQLs, lesson 3.02) decide what code may do at any moment: some code may not wait, may not touch pageable memory, may not even call most functions. - Everything coming from user mode is hostile until checked : a driver is a door into the kernel, and an unchecked buffer is a security hole for the whole system (lesson 2.05). Most of the time, the right answer is not to write a driver : user-mode services, ETW, Windows' built-in APIs and user-mode driver frameworks cover far more than people expect (lesson 5.04). This course is about understanding the kernel and building drivers correctly when they are needed. The rules of this course 1. Everything runs in a virtual machine (lesson 1.02). Never load a test driver on the computer you work on. 2. The drivers in this course echo, count and log : they talk to their own user-mode client and observe documented events. They never read or write other processes' memory, never hide anything, and never try to get around any of Windows' protections. 3. Test drivers are loaded with test signing , Microsoft's documented mechanism for driver development, enabled only inside the virtual machine. How the practice works Compiler Explorer runs ordinary programs, not drivers. So the practice checks the logic that goes inside drivers in plain C++: the I/O control codes, the kernel's string type, buffer validation, linked lists, ring buffers, IRQL rules. Each practice declares the few kernel types it needs, exactly as the WDK headers do.

title: Reading NTSTATUS values
where: 1.01 User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
body: Kernel functions return an NTSTATUS : the top two bits are the severity (0 success, 1 informational, 2 warning, 3 error), bits 16-27 the facility and the low 16 bits the code. Write the helpers a driver and its user-mode client use: cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; bool ntSuccess(NTSTATUS s); // NT_SUCCESS: s = 0 std::string severity(NTSTATUS s); // "success", "informational", "warning" or "error" std::string statusName(NTSTATUS s); // a few well-known names, else "0x%08X" std::uint32_t toWin32Error(NTSTATUS s); // what GetLastError shows in user mode Known names: 0x00000000 STATUS_SUCCESS, 0x00000103 STATUS_PENDING, 0x80000005 STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW, 0xC0000002 STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED, 0xC000000D STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER, 0xC0000010 STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST, 0xC0000022 STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED, 0xC0000023 STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0xC000009A STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES. Unknown ones are printed as 0x and 8 upper-case hex digits. toWin32Error maps: SUCCESS → 0, PENDING → 997, BUFFER_OVERFLOW → 234, NOT_IMPLEMENTED → 1, INVALID_PARAMETER → 87, INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST → 1, ACCESS_DENIED → 5, BUFFER_TOO_SMALL → 122, INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES → 1450; anything else → 317.

title: 1.02  Building a Safe Lab
body: Setting up the virtual machine where every driver in this course runs - Hyper-V or VMware, snapshots, test signing inside the VM only, kernel debugging over the network with KDNET, and a routine that makes crashes cheap. Two machines Driver development uses two machines: Machine Role --- --- Host (your computer) Visual Studio, the WDK, WinDbg. Builds the driver and debugs the target. Never loads test drivers. Target (a virtual machine) Runs Windows with test signing and a kernel debugger attached. Loads the driver. Crashes are expected. Hyper-V (built into Windows 10/11 Pro and later) or VMware Workstation both work. Give the VM 2 processors (synchronisation bugs only show up with more than one), 4 GB of memory and a fresh Windows installation of the same version you target. Snapshots Take a snapshot (Hyper-V calls it a checkpoint) once the VM is set up: Windows installed, updated, debugging configured. Before each test session, you can go back to it in seconds. A driver that corrupts the system, or a VM that no longer boots, costs nothing. Test signing, in the VM only Windows only loads drivers signed by Microsoft (lesson 5.04). For development, Microsoft provides test signing : the WDK signs your driver with a test certificate, and a machine in test-signing mode accepts it. Inside the VM , from an administrator command prompt: cpp-norun bcdedit /set testsigning on and restart. Test signing requires Secure Boot to be off for that VM (in Hyper-V: the VM's Settings Security uncheck Enable Secure Boot). The desktop then shows "Test Mode" in a corner as a reminder. Never do this on your own computer: it is a development setting for a machine that exists to be crashed. Kernel debugging with KDNET A kernel debugger stops the whole target machine, lets you inspect it, and catches crashes before the blue screen. KDNET runs it over the network: 1. On the host, find its IP address ( ipconfig ) and choose a port from 50000 to 50039. 2. Copy kdnet.exe and VerifiedNICList.xml from the WDK ( C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64 ) to the VM. 3. In the VM, as administrator: kdnet.exe <host-ip <port . It enables debugging and prints a key like 1.2.3.4 . Restart the VM. 4. On the host: WinDbg File Attach to kernel Net, enter the port and the key. When the VM boots, WinDbg connects. Break (Ctrl+Break) freezes the whole VM at once, and g lets it run again. Lesson 1.05 uses this connection. The routine 1. Build the driver on the host (lesson 1.03). 2. Copy the .sys file (and its .inf or .cat , if any) to the VM through a shared folder. 3. Load it (lesson 1.04), with WinDbg attached and showing DbgPrint output. 4. If it crashes, WinDbg stops at the bug check: run !analyze -v , read the call stack, fix the code. 5. Restore the snapshot if the VM is in a bad state. Why bother Kernel bugs are expensive in the real world: a crashing driver can take down thousands of machines at once. The lab makes every one of your mistakes cheap and visible, and the debugger makes them understandable. Professionals work exactly this way.

title: Checking the debugger settings
body: Before restarting the VM for kernel debugging, a helper script checks the KDNET settings from lesson 1.02 and prints the command for the host. Write it: cpp struct Kdnet { std::string host; int port{ 0 }; std::string key; }; bool parseSettings(const std::string& text, Kdnet& out, std::string& error); std::string hostCommand(const Kdnet& k); // "windbg -k net:port=50005,key=1.2.3.4" The text is name=value pairs separated by spaces, in any order: host= , port= and key= , each exactly once. Rules, checked in this order with these errors: 1. a pair without = , or an unknown or repeated name: "bad setting: <the pair " 2. any of the three missing: "missing host" , "missing port" or "missing key" (checked in that order) 3. host must be an IPv4 address: four numbers 0-255 without leading zeros ( 0 itself is fine): "bad host" 4. port must be a number from 50000 to 50039: "port must be 50000-50039" 5. key must be four parts separated by dots, each 1 to 13 characters from 0-9 and a-z (lower case): "bad key"

title: 1.03  The Windows Driver Kit
body: Installing Visual Studio with the Windows Driver Kit, creating a driver project, what is different about building a driver, the kernel's types and calling conventions, and the kernel's string type UNICODE_STRING. Installing On the host : 1. Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload, plus the individual components MSVC (latest) Spectre-mitigated libraries for x64. 2. The Windows SDK and the Windows Driver Kit (WDK) of the same version, from Microsoft's "Download the WDK" page, including the Visual Studio extension. After installation, Visual Studio has project templates such as Kernel Mode Driver, Empty (KMDF) and Empty WDM Driver . KMDF and WDM Model What it is --- --- WDM (Windows Driver Model) The underlying model: you handle IRPs, device objects and power yourself KMDF (Kernel-Mode Driver Framework) A framework on top of WDM that handles the boilerplate, power management and Plug and Play correctly UMDF The same framework for drivers that run in user mode Microsoft recommends KMDF (or UMDF) for new hardware drivers. This course uses small WDM drivers that are not tied to hardware ("software drivers"), because they show plainly how the kernel's I/O model works; everything you learn carries over to KMDF, which wraps the same objects. What is different about the build - The output is a .sys file: a PE image like a DLL, loaded into kernel space. - No C runtime: the driver links against ntoskrnl.exe (and a few other kernel modules) instead. include <ntddk.h replaces <windows.h . - Warnings are errors, and code analysis runs on every build (lesson 5.02). - The build signs the driver with a test certificate automatically (Driver Signing Test Sign). - C++ is allowed, but without exceptions or RTTI, and with new only if you define it yourself on top of the pool allocator (lesson 3.01). Kernel types The kernel has its own type names, close to Win32's: Type Meaning --- --- NTSTATUS The result of almost every kernel function: STATUS_SUCCESS (0), or an error such as STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ; check with NT_SUCCESS(status) ULONG , USHORT , UCHAR , ULONG_PTR 32, 16, 8-bit unsigned, pointer-sized unsigned PVOID , PCHAR Pointers PDRIVER_OBJECT , PDEVICE_OBJECT , PIRP The kernel's objects (milestone 2) UNICODE_STRING The kernel's string (below) NTSTATUS values have a severity in the top two bits: 0 success, 1 informational, 2 warning, 3 error. So every error is negative as a 32-bit signed number, and NT_SUCCESS is just status = 0 . UNICODE_STRING The kernel does not use null-terminated strings. It uses a counted UTF-16 string: cpp-norun typedef struct _UNICODE_STRING { USHORT Length; // bytes in use, NOT characters, NOT including any null USHORT MaximumLength; // bytes in the buffer PWSTR Buffer; // may not be null-terminated! } UNICODE_STRING; UNICODE_STRING name = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING copy; RtlInitUnicodeString(&copy, L"literal"); // only for null-terminated literals if (RtlEqualUnicodeString(&a, &b, TRUE)) { ... } // TRUE: ignore case Three facts cause most bugs: 1. Lengths are in bytes. A string of 5 characters has Length = 10 . 2. The buffer is not necessarily null-terminated. Passing Buffer to anything that expects a C string reads past the end. Always use Length . 3. The maximum length is a USHORT , so a string is at most 32 767 characters. Printing one uses the %wZ format, which reads the counted structure: DbgPrint("name: %wZ\n", &name); . The practice implements the copy, append, compare and prefix functions on this structure.

title: UNICODE_STRING
body: Write the kernel's counted string functions from lesson 1.03 (simplified versions of the Rtl functions): cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_SUCCESS = 0; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000023u); struct UNICODE_STRING { std::uint16_t Length; std::uint16_t MaximumLength; char16_t Buffer; }; void initString(UNICODE_STRING& s, const char16_t nullTerminated); // RtlInitUnicodeString void copyString(UNICODE_STRING& dest, const UNICODE_STRING& src); // RtlCopyUnicodeString NTSTATUS appendString(UNICODE_STRING& dest, const UNICODE_STRING& src); // RtlAppendUnicodeStringToString bool equalStrings(const UNICODE_STRING& a, const UNICODE_STRING& b, bool ignoreCase); bool isPrefix(const UNICODE_STRING& prefix, const UNICODE_STRING& s, bool ignoreCase); std::u16string toStd(const UNICODE_STRING& s); // only the first Length bytes - Lengths are in bytes. initString points Buffer at the given text, sets Length to its length in bytes without the null, and MaximumLength to that plus 2. A null pointer gives an empty string (all zero). - copyString copies as many whole characters as fit into dest 's buffer ( MaximumLength ), and sets dest.Length ; if there is room for another character, it also writes a null after the copy (not counted in Length ). - appendString adds src after dest 's text if the result fits in dest.MaximumLength , else changes nothing and returns STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL . - Case-insensitive comparison only needs to fold a - z to upper case here.

title: 1.04  A First Driver
body: The smallest driver - DriverEntry and an Unload routine that frees everything - printing with DbgPrintEx, loading and unloading it as a service with sc.exe, and what happens to each step inside the kernel. DriverEntry Every driver has an entry point, DriverEntry , called once when the driver is loaded. It receives the driver object the I/O manager created for it, and the path of its registry key: cpp-norun include <ntddk.h void XenonUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driverObject) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(driverObject); DbgPrintEx(DPFLTR_IHVDRIVER_ID, DPFLTR_INFO_LEVEL, "XenonHello: unloaded\n"); } extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driverObject, PUNICODE_STRING registryPath) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(registryPath); driverObject- DriverUnload = XenonUnload; DbgPrintEx(DPFLTR_IHVDRIVER_ID, DPFLTR_INFO_LEVEL, "XenonHello: loaded\n"); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } - extern "C" because the kernel looks the function up by its plain name. - Setting DriverUnload makes the driver unloadable ; without it, it stays until the machine restarts. - Returning a failure status from DriverEntry means the driver is not loaded at all, and the kernel will not call Unload , so DriverEntry must clean up everything it did before failing. The golden rule of Unload Everything the driver creates (device objects, symbolic links, memory, registered callbacks, timers, threads) must be undone in Unload , in reverse order. A driver that leaves a callback registered and is then unloaded leaves the kernel pointing at code that no longer exists: the next call crashes the machine. Milestone 2 onwards builds drivers whose Unload mirrors DriverEntry step by step. Seeing DbgPrint output DbgPrintEx messages go to the kernel debugger (WinDbg on the host, lesson 1.02). By default the INFO level is filtered out; enable it once in the VM's registry or from WinDbg: cpp-norun ed nt!Kd_IHVDRIVER_Mask 0xF Without a debugger attached, the Sysinternals tool DebugView (run as administrator, Capture Kernel enabled) shows the same messages inside the VM. Loading as a service A software driver is installed as a kernel service . In the VM, as administrator: cpp-norun sc create XenonHello type= kernel binPath= C:\Drivers\XenonHello.sys sc start XenonHello :: DriverEntry runs: "XenonHello: loaded" sc stop XenonHello :: Unload runs: "XenonHello: unloaded" sc delete XenonHello (The space after each = is required by sc .) The service lives under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\XenonHello , which is the registryPath passed to DriverEntry : drivers keep their configuration there. If sc start fails with error 577, the driver's signature was not accepted: check that test signing is on in the VM and the driver was test-signed by the build. What happens inside 1. sc start asks the Service Control Manager , which asks the kernel to load the driver. 2. The I/O manager maps the .sys file into kernel memory, checks its signature, resolves its imports against ntoskrnl.exe , creates a DRIVER_OBJECT , and calls DriverEntry . 3. sc stop makes the I/O manager call DriverUnload , then unmap the image. In WinDbg, lm m XenonHello shows the loaded module, and bp XenonHello!DriverEntry (set before sc start ) stops in your code so you can step through it.

title: Setting up and tearing down
body: Lesson 1.04's golden rule: Unload undoes everything DriverEntry did, in reverse order, and a DriverEntry that fails undoes what it already did. Write a small helper that enforces this, and that driver code can be written against: cpp class Setup { public: void done(const std::string& step, std::function<void() undo); // a step succeeded; remember how to undo it void rollback(); // undo every remembered step, newest first, once std::size_t count() const; }; std::vector<std::string runDriverEntry(const std::vector<std::string & steps, int failAt, std::vector<std::string & log); - Setup::rollback calls the undo functions in reverse order and forgets them, so a second call does nothing. count is how many steps are remembered. - runDriverEntry simulates a DriverEntry : for each step in order, if its index equals failAt , it logs "fail <step " , rolls back, and returns an empty list; otherwise it logs "do <step " and remembers an undo that logs "undo <step " . If all steps succeed, it returns the steps that Unload must undo, in the order Unload must undo them (newest first), without undoing anything yet.

title: 1.05  Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
body: Using WinDbg on the VM - breaking in, symbols, breakpoints in your driver, inspecting structures, reading a bug check with !analyze, and the handful of commands you will use every day. Symbols first A debugger without symbols shows addresses; with them it shows function names, types and source lines. Set the symbol path once (in WinDbg's settings or with a command) to Microsoft's symbol server plus your build folder: cpp-norun .sympath srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols;C:\Projects\XenonHello\x64\Debug .reload Your driver's .pdb (built next to the .sys ) gives your function names and source lines. Everyday commands Command Does --- --- g Go: let the target run Ctrl+Break Break in: freeze the whole target lm / lm m Xenon List loaded modules bp XenonHello!XenonDispatch Breakpoint on a function bu XenonHello!DriverEntry Breakpoint that waits for the module to load bl , bc List / clear breakpoints p , t , gu Step over, step into, step out k / kb Call stack dv Local variables dt nt!_UNICODE_STRING addr Show a structure at an address dx Explore objects with the data model ( dx @$curprocess ) !analyze -v Explain a bug check Reading a crash When the driver crashes, the target stops with a bug check and WinDbg shows something like: cpp-norun Fatal System Error: 0x000000d1 (0xFFFFA00012345678, 0x0000000000000002, 0x0000000000000000, 0xFFFFF80123456789) !analyze -v explains it: - The bug check code : 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (touched pageable or invalid memory at a high IRQL, lesson 3.02), 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA (a bad pointer), 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION , 0xC4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION (lesson 5.01), 0xCE DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS . - The parameters : for 0xD1 , the address that was touched, the IRQL, whether it was a read or a write, and the instruction's address. - The faulting module and stack : which driver, which function, which line. Most crashes in your own driver are found in a minute this way: the stack ends in your function, the source line shows the bad pointer. Crash dumps Without a live debugger, Windows writes a dump on a bug check ( C:\Windows\MEMORY.DMP or minidumps in C:\Windows\Minidump ). Open it in WinDbg (File Open dump file) and run the same !analyze -v . Configure "Kernel memory dump" in the VM's System Properties Startup and Recovery. Debugging habits - Put a DbgPrintEx at the start and end of every dispatch routine while developing; remove or quieten them later (lesson 4.02). - Set bu breakpoints before loading the driver, so DriverEntry can be stepped through. - When something "randomly" crashes, turn on Driver Verifier for your driver (lesson 5.01): it turns hidden bugs into immediate, explained crashes.

title: Reading a bug check
body: Parse the line WinDbg prints when the VM stops on a bug check (lesson 1.05), and explain the common ones: cpp struct BugCheck { std::uint32_t code; std::uint64_t p 4 ; }; bool parseBugCheck(const std::string& line, BugCheck& out); std::string bugCheckName(std::uint32_t code); std::string explain(const BugCheck& b); The line looks like Fatal System Error: 0x000000d1 (0xFFFFA00012345678,0x0000000000000002,0x0000000000000000,0xFFFFF80123456789) , possibly with spaces after the commas; the code and parameters are hexadecimal with 0x , in either case. Anything that does not have exactly this shape (with four parameters) fails. Names: 0x0A IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION, 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA, 0x7E SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED, 0xC4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION, 0xCE DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS, 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL; others UNKNOWN_BUG_CHECK . explain : - 0xD1 and 0x0A : "<read write execute of 0x<p0 at IRQL <p1 " where p2 is 0 read, 1 write, 8 execute (anything else access ), and p0 is printed as 16 upper-case hex digits; - 0x50 : "<read write of invalid address 0x<p0 " with p1 0 for read, anything else write; - others: the name.

title: Names in the kernel
body: The kernel and user mode name the same things differently. A driver creates \Device\XenonEcho , links it as \??\XenonEcho , and its client opens \\.\XenonEcho ; C:\Notes is \??\C:\Notes to the kernel; the driver's registry path is \REGISTRY\MACHINE\... while regedit shows HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\... . Write the conversions a driver and its tools need (milestone 2 uses them): cpp bool validBaseName(const std::string& base); std::string deviceName(const std::string& base); // "\Device\<base " std::string linkName(const std::string& base); // "\??\<base " std::string userPath(const std::string& base); // "\\.\<base " std::string win32ToNt(const std::string& path); std::string ntToWin32(const std::string& nt); std::string serviceName(const std::string& registryPath); std::string userRegistryPath(const std::string& registryPath); - validBaseName : 1 to 32 characters, letters and digits only, starting with a letter. The three name functions return "" for an invalid base. - win32ToNt : C:\x (a drive letter, colon and backslash) → \??\C:\x ; \\server\share\x → \??\UNC\server\share\x ; \\.\Name → \??\Name ; \\?\C:\x → \??\C:\x ; \\?\UNC\server\x → \??\UNC\server\x . Anything else (relative paths, C:x , \x ) cannot be converted without a current directory: return "" . - ntToWin32 reverses it: \??\UNC\... → \\... ; \??\C:\... (a drive) → C:\... ; \??\Name (anything else after \??\ ) → \\.\Name ; \DosDevices\ is the same as \??\ (in any letter case); \Device\... → \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\... ; anything else → "" . - serviceName : for a path starting with \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ then CurrentControlSet or ControlSet followed by three digits, then \Services\<name (and nothing after the name), return the name; else "" . Comparisons ignore case; the name keeps its case. - userRegistryPath : \REGISTRY\MACHINE\rest → HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\rest , \REGISTRY\USER\rest → HKEY_USERS\rest (prefix case ignored, rest unchanged); else "" .

title: 2.01  Device Objects and Symbolic Links
body: A driver is reached through a device object. This lesson creates one with IoCreateDevice, gives it a symbolic link so user mode can open it as \\.\XenonEcho, secures it so only administrators can, and deletes both in Unload. Drivers and devices A driver object represents the loaded code. A device object represents something requests can be sent to. A user-mode program never talks to a driver directly: it opens a device , and the I/O manager routes its requests to the driver that owns that device. Device objects live in the kernel's object namespace under \Device . User mode cannot see that directory directly; it sees \?? (shown to Win32 as \\.\ ), so the driver creates a symbolic link there pointing at its device. Project m01 built these names. Creating them in DriverEntry cpp-norun UNICODE_STRING deviceName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING linkName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\??\\XenonEcho"); extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING) { PDEVICE_OBJECT device = nullptr; NTSTATUS status = IoCreateDeviceSecure(driver, 0, &deviceName, FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, FALSE, &SDDL_DEVOBJ_SYS_ALL_ADM_ALL, nullptr, &device); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) return status; status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&linkName, &deviceName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) { IoDeleteDevice(device); return status; } // undo step 1 device- Flags = DO_BUFFERED_IO; // lesson 2.04 device- Flags &= ~DO_DEVICE_INITIALIZING; // ready for requests driver- DriverUnload = XenonUnload; // dispatch routines: lesson 2.02 return STATUS_SUCCESS; } void XenonUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver) { IoDeleteSymbolicLink(&linkName); // reverse order IoDeleteDevice(driver- DeviceObject); } Note how practice 1.04's rule shows up: when the symbolic link fails, DriverEntry deletes the device it already created, and Unload deletes the link, then the device. Who may open it By default a device object can be opened by anyone. A driver that does something only administrators should be able to trigger must say so: - IoCreateDeviceSecure with an SDDL string sets the device's security descriptor: SDDL_DEVOBJ_SYS_ALL_ADM_ALL allows only SYSTEM and Administrators. Even for a teaching driver, this is the right habit. - FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN makes the I/O manager check that security for every open, including opens of names "under" the device ( \\.\XenonEcho\anything ), which otherwise skip the check. Lesson 5.03 comes back to device security; an unprotected device is one of the most common driver vulnerabilities. Exclusive and multiple devices The Exclusive argument ( FALSE above) allows several handles at once. A driver can create several device objects (they form a list starting at driver- DeviceObject ), each with its own name, and use the device extension (the second argument, a size) to keep per-device data, reached later as device- DeviceExtension . Seeing them In the VM, the Sysinternals tool WinObj shows the object namespace: \Device\XenonEcho and the link \GLOBAL??\XenonEcho (where \?? resolves for most processes). In WinDbg, !devobj \Device\XenonEcho and !drvobj XenonEcho show the objects and their dispatch routines.

title: Who may open the device
body: Lesson 2.01 protects the device with an SDDL string such as D:P(A;;GA;;;SY)(A;;GA;;;BA) . Write a small version of the check Windows makes when someone opens it: cpp struct Ace { bool allow; std::uint32_t rights; std::string trustee; }; bool parseDacl(const std::string& sddl, std::vector<Ace & out); bool accessCheck(const std::vector<Ace & dacl, const std::vector<std::string & groups, std::uint32_t desired); parseDacl reads D: optionally followed by flags ( P , AI ; ignored), then ACEs in parentheses: (type;flags;rights;;;trustee) with exactly six fields. The type is A (allow) or D (deny); flags are ignored; rights are GA (all: 0x10000000 ), GR (read: 0x80000000 ), GW (write: 0x40000000 ), GX (execute: 0x20000000 ), any concatenation of them ( GRGW ), or a hex number 0x... ; the trustee is a two-letter alias such as SY , BA , WD , AU , IU . Anything else fails. accessCheck : the caller belongs to groups (aliases). Expand GA in each ACE to GR GW GX first. Walk the ACEs in order , considering only those whose trustee is one of the caller's groups: a deny ACE that covers any desired right that is not yet granted denies access at once; an allow ACE grants its rights. Access is allowed when every desired right has been granted. An empty DACL allows nothing.

title: 2.02  IRPs and Dispatch Routines
body: Every request to a driver arrives as an IRP - an I/O request packet. This lesson explains what an IRP holds, the stack locations, dispatch routines for create, close, read and write, completing a request, and why every IRP must be completed exactly once. The I/O request packet When a user-mode program calls CreateFileW , ReadFile , WriteFile , DeviceIoControl or CloseHandle on a device, the I/O manager builds an IRP and passes it to the driver. An IRP carries: Part What --- --- Major function What kind of request: IRP_MJ_CREATE , IRP_MJ_CLOSE , IRP_MJ_READ , IRP_MJ_WRITE , IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL , IRP_MJ_CLEANUP , ... Parameters Depending on the major function: the length to read, the control code, buffer lengths Buffers The user's data, passed in one of three ways (lesson 2.04) IoStatus The result to return: Status and Information (usually the number of bytes transferred) Each driver in a stack of drivers (filters above a device driver) gets its own stack location in the IRP with its own parameters; IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp) returns the current driver's. Dispatch routines The driver object has a table of dispatch routines , one per major function, filled in DriverEntry : cpp-norun driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CREATE = XenonCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CLOSE = XenonCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_READ = XenonRead; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_WRITE = XenonWrite; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = XenonDeviceControl; Unset entries point to a default that fails the request with STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST . Completing a request cpp-norun NTSTATUS CompleteIrp(PIRP irp, NTSTATUS status, ULONG_PTR information) { irp- IoStatus.Status = status; irp- IoStatus.Information = information; IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return status; // the dispatch routine returns the same status } NTSTATUS XenonCreateClose(PDEVICE_OBJECT, PIRP irp) { return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, 0); // opening and closing always succeed } NTSTATUS XenonWrite(PDEVICE_OBJECT device, PIRP irp) { auto stack = IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp); const ULONG length = stack- Parameters.Write.Length; // with buffered I/O, the data is in irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer (lesson 2.04) auto ext = static_cast<XenonExtension (device- DeviceExtension); ext- bytesWritten += length; // a counter: this driver only counts return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, length); } Information is what the user sees as "bytes written" or "bytes read". IoCompleteRequest hands the IRP back to the I/O manager, which copies results to user mode and wakes the waiting thread. Exactly once Every IRP a driver receives must be completed exactly once , or passed on to another driver, or marked pending and completed later: - Never completed: the user's thread waits forever, and the process cannot exit ("hangs in kill"). - Completed twice: the IRP is freed and then used again, which crashes the system (Driver Verifier catches it, bug check 0xC4 ). - Touched after completing: the IRP may already be freed; read anything you need before calling IoCompleteRequest . A driver that cannot finish a request at once (waiting for data, for example) calls IoMarkIrpPending(irp) , returns STATUS_PENDING , and completes it later from another context. Pending IRPs must be cancellable ( IoSetCancelRoutine , or better, cancel-safe queues IoCsqInitialize ), and all of them must be completed before the driver unloads, or the system bug-checks with 0xCE . Create, cleanup and close - IRP_MJ_CREATE : a handle is being opened. The driver can refuse it (return an error). - IRP_MJ_CLEANUP : the last handle to a file object was closed; cancel that file object's pending requests here. - IRP_MJ_CLOSE : the file object itself is going away (after all references are gone). The practice simulates a dispatch table and checks the exactly-once rule.

title: Completing every IRP exactly once
body: Write a miniature I/O manager that calls dispatch routines and checks lesson 2.02's rules, the way Driver Verifier does: cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_SUCCESS = 0, STATUS_PENDING = 0x103; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000010u); enum Major { IRP_MJ_CREATE = 0, IRP_MJ_CLOSE = 2, IRP_MJ_READ = 3, IRP_MJ_WRITE = 4, IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = 14, IRP_MJ_MAXIMUM = 28 }; struct Irp { int major; NTSTATUS status{ 0 }; std::uint64_t information{ 0 }; int completions{ 0 }; bool markedPending{ false }; }; void completeIrp(Irp& irp, NTSTATUS status, std::uint64_t information); // IoCompleteRequest void markPending(Irp& irp); // IoMarkIrpPending using Dispatch = std::function<NTSTATUS(Irp&) ; class IoManager { public: void setDispatch(int major, Dispatch d); std::string send(Irp& irp); }; - completeIrp stores the status and information and counts a completion; markPending sets the flag. - Majors without a dispatch routine (or outside 0 .. IRP_MJ_MAXIMUM - 1 ) are completed with STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST and information 0 by the I/O manager itself. - send calls the routine and returns a verdict, checking in this order: - "completed twice" if completed more than once; - if the routine returned STATUS_PENDING : "pending without mark" if not marked pending, "pending but completed" if it was also completed (in this model, pending IRPs are completed later), else "pending" ; - "not completed" if not completed; - "status mismatch" if the returned status differs from the IRP's status; - otherwise "ok" .

title: 2.03  IOCTLs and a User-Mode Client
body: Device I/O controls are a driver's private API. This lesson defines control codes with CTL_CODE, shares them in a header between driver and client, handles IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL, and writes the user-mode client that calls DeviceIoControl. Control codes Read and write move bytes; anything else a driver offers ("give me your statistics", "reset the counter", "echo this back") is an I/O control (IOCTL). Each has a 32-bit control code built with the CTL_CODE macro: cpp-norun define CTL_CODE(DeviceType, Function, Method, Access) \ (((DeviceType) << 16) ((Access) << 14) ((Function) << 2) (Method)) Field Bits Meaning --- --- --- Device type 31-16 FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN (0x22) for software drivers; values from 0x8000 are for vendors Required access 15-14 FILE_ANY_ACCESS (0), FILE_READ_DATA (1), FILE_WRITE_DATA (2), or both (3) Function 13-2 Your number; 0x800 and up for your own codes Method 1-0 How buffers are passed: METHOD_BUFFERED (0), METHOD_IN_DIRECT (1), METHOD_OUT_DIRECT (2), METHOD_NEITHER (3) The access field matters for security: the I/O manager checks that the handle was opened with that access before the request reaches the driver. An IOCTL that changes state should require FILE_WRITE_DATA . The practice packs and unpacks these fields. A shared header Driver and client must agree on the codes and on the layout of the data, so they share one header: cpp-norun // XenonEchoIoctl.h - included by the driver and the client pragma once define XENON_DEVICE 0x8000 define IOCTL_XENON_ECHO CTL_CODE(XENON_DEVICE, 0x800, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS) define IOCTL_XENON_GET_STATS CTL_CODE(XENON_DEVICE, 0x801, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_DATA) define IOCTL_XENON_RESET CTL_CODE(XENON_DEVICE, 0x802, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_WRITE_DATA) struct XenonStats { ULONG size; // sizeof(XenonStats): lets the structure grow in later versions ULONG echoes; ULONGLONG bytesWritten; }; The size field at the start is a common versioning trick: a newer driver can tell an older client's smaller structure apart and fill only what it knows. The driver side cpp-norun NTSTATUS XenonDeviceControl(PDEVICE_OBJECT device, PIRP irp) { auto stack = IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp); auto& p = stack- Parameters.DeviceIoControl; auto ext = static_cast<XenonExtension (device- DeviceExtension); void buffer = irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer; // METHOD_BUFFERED: one buffer for input and output switch (p.IoControlCode) { case IOCTL_XENON_ECHO: if (p.OutputBufferLength < p.InputBufferLength) return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0); InterlockedIncrement(&ext- echoes); return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, p.InputBufferLength); // the data is already in place: echoed case IOCTL_XENON_GET_STATS: { if (p.OutputBufferLength < sizeof(XenonStats)) return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0); auto s = static_cast<XenonStats (buffer); s- size = sizeof(XenonStats); s- echoes = ext- echoes; s- bytesWritten = ext- bytesWritten; return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, sizeof(XenonStats)); } case IOCTL_XENON_RESET: ext- echoes = 0; ext- bytesWritten = 0; return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, 0); } return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST, 0); } Every length is checked before the buffer is used. Lesson 2.05 explains why that check is the most important line in the function. The client cpp-norun HANDLE device = CreateFileW(L"\\\\.\\XenonEcho", GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr); if (device == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { / 2: driver not loaded; 5: not an administrator / } char message = "hello, kernel"; char reply 64 = {}; DWORD returned = 0; if (DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_XENON_ECHO, message, sizeof(message), reply, sizeof(reply), &returned, nullptr)) printf("echoed %lu bytes: %s\n", returned, reply); XenonStats stats{}; DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_XENON_GET_STATS, nullptr, 0, &stats, sizeof(stats), &returned, nullptr); CloseHandle(device); returned is the IRP's Information . When the driver fails a request, DeviceIoControl returns FALSE and GetLastError holds the Win32 translation of the NTSTATUS (practice 1.01: STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL becomes 122).

title: Control codes
body: Write CTL_CODE and its inverse from lesson 2.03, and the access check the I/O manager makes before an IOCTL reaches the driver: cpp struct Ioctl { std::uint32_t deviceType, access, function, method; }; std::uint32_t ctlCode(std::uint32_t deviceType, std::uint32_t function, std::uint32_t method, std::uint32_t access); Ioctl decode(std::uint32_t code); std::string describe(std::uint32_t code); bool accessAllowed(std::uint32_t code, std::uint32_t handleAccess); // handleAccess: bit 0 read, bit 1 write - ctlCode is (deviceType << 16) (access << 14) (function << 2) method . - describe gives "device 0x8000, function 0x800, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS" : hex in upper case with at least 4 digits for the device and 3 for the function, method names METHOD_BUFFERED , METHOD_IN_DIRECT , METHOD_OUT_DIRECT , METHOD_NEITHER , access names FILE_ANY_ACCESS (0), FILE_READ_DATA (1), FILE_WRITE_DATA (2), FILE_READ_DATA FILE_WRITE_DATA (3). - accessAllowed : every access bit the code requires must be in handleAccess .

title: 2.04  Buffered, Direct and Neither I/O
body: The three ways user buffers reach a driver - the I/O manager copying through a system buffer, locking the user's pages with an MDL, or handing over raw user addresses - with their costs, their rules, and why METHOD_NEITHER is best avoided. The problem A user buffer lives at a user-mode address of one particular process. The driver may run in another thread's context, at a raised IRQL where paging is impossible, or later when that process is gone. So a raw user pointer is not something a driver can simply use. Windows offers three ways to hand data across. Buffered I/O The I/O manager allocates a system buffer in kernel memory (non-paged), copies the user's input into it before calling the driver, and copies the output back to the user after the request completes: --- --- Driver sees irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer For IOCTLs One buffer of max(input length, output length) : input at the start, output written over it Cost Two copies Safety Excellent: the driver never touches user memory Use it for small requests (up to a few kilobytes), which is most IOCTLs. Its one trap: input and output share the buffer, so read all of the input you need before writing output. Direct I/O For large transfers, copying is wasteful. With direct I/O , the I/O manager locks the user's pages in memory and describes them with an MDL (memory descriptor list); the driver maps them into kernel space: cpp-norun PVOID data = MmGetSystemAddressForMdlSafe(irp- MdlAddress, NormalPagePriority MdlMappingNoExecute); if (!data) return CompleteIrp(irp, STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES, 0); For METHOD_IN_DIRECT / OUT_DIRECT IOCTLs, the input buffer is still buffered ( SystemBuffer ) and the output buffer comes as the MDL. The data is not copied, but the user process can change it while the driver reads it (it is the user's memory), so the driver must not read a value twice and assume it is the same. Neither I/O METHOD_NEITHER gives the driver the raw user addresses ( Parameters.DeviceIoControl.Type3InputBuffer and irp- UserBuffer ) and does nothing else. The driver must then: - run in the requesting thread's context (be the top driver, called directly); - probe the addresses with ProbeForRead / ProbeForWrite inside __try / __except , because the user can pass any address, including kernel addresses; - capture (copy) the data into its own memory before using it, because another user thread can change it at any moment ("double fetch" bugs). Many serious driver vulnerabilities come from METHOD_NEITHER handled carelessly. Use buffered I/O unless there is a measured reason not to; this course's drivers never use neither I/O. Read and write The device object's flags choose the method for IRP_MJ_READ and IRP_MJ_WRITE : DO_BUFFERED_IO or DO_DIRECT_IO (set in DriverEntry , lesson 2.01). IOCTLs choose per control code, in the method bits. Summary Method Input Output Use for --- --- --- --- METHOD_BUFFERED SystemBuffer SystemBuffer (same) Small requests: almost all IOCTLs METHOD_IN_DIRECT / OUT_DIRECT SystemBuffer MDL Large data transfers METHOD_NEITHER raw user pointer raw user pointer Avoid The practice computes, for a request, how big the system buffer is and what each side sees.

title: Where the buffers are
body: For an IOCTL with a given method and lengths, work out what lesson 2.04 says the driver receives: cpp struct BufferPlan { std::uint32_t systemBufferSize; // 0 if there is no system buffer bool inputInSystemBuffer; bool outputInSystemBuffer; bool outputAsMdl; bool rawUserPointers; }; BufferPlan planFor(std::uint32_t method, std::uint32_t inLength, std::uint32_t outLength); std::uint32_t bytesCopiedBack(std::uint32_t method, std::uint32_t outLength, std::uint64_t information); - METHOD_BUFFERED (0): one system buffer of max(in, out) bytes holds the input and receives the output. - METHOD_IN_DIRECT (1) and METHOD_OUT_DIRECT (2): the input (if any) is in a system buffer of in bytes; the output buffer (if out 0 ) comes as an MDL. - METHOD_NEITHER (3): no system buffer; raw user pointers. - bytesCopiedBack : only buffered I/O copies output back: min(information, outLength) . The direct methods wrote straight into the user's pages (0 copied), and neither I/O copies nothing either.

title: 2.05  Validating Everything From User Mode
body: A driver is a door into the kernel, and everything coming through it must be treated as hostile. This lesson lists the checks every request needs - lengths, alignment, structure versions, counts and offsets, integer overflow - and how to write handlers that cannot be tricked. The threat model Any program that can open the device can send any bytes with any lengths, in any order, from many threads at once. A bug that a normal client would never trigger is still reachable by a program written to trigger it. In the kernel, such a bug is not a crash of one program: it can crash the machine or, worse, let a program gain kernel privileges. That is why device security (lesson 2.01) and validation go together. The checks For every request, in this order: 1. Lengths : is the input at least the size of the header? Is the output large enough for the answer? Compare against sizeof the structure, never trust a length field inside the data alone. 2. Version and size fields : if the structure has a size (lesson 2.03), it must be at least the oldest supported size and at most the buffer length. 3. Counts and offsets inside the data : "an array of count entries follows" must satisfy header + count × entrySize <= length , computed without overflow . 4. Enumerations and flags : unknown values are rejected, not ignored; reserved fields must be zero (so they can be used later). 5. Strings : counted, not null-terminated (lesson 1.03); a length must be even for UTF-16 and within the buffer. Only after all checks pass does the handler use the data. Integer overflow The classic mistake: cpp-norun // count comes from the user if (sizeof(Header) + req- count sizeof(Entry) inputLength) return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER; // WRONG With a huge count , the multiplication wraps around to a small number, the check passes, and the loop reads far past the buffer. Check without overflowing: cpp-norun if (inputLength < sizeof(Header)) return STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL; const SIZE_T room = inputLength - sizeof(Header); if (req- count room / sizeof(Entry)) return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER; // division cannot overflow The kernel's ntintsafe.h has RtlULongMult , RtlSizeTAdd and friends that report overflow; use them for any arithmetic on user-supplied values. Read once With direct or neither I/O, the user can change the buffer while the driver reads it. A value read twice can differ between the check and the use ("time of check to time of use"). Copy the header into a local variable once , validate the copy, and use only the copy. With buffered I/O this cannot happen, which is another reason to prefer it. Fail closed - Return an error for anything unexpected, without partially doing the work. - Set Information to 0 on failure, so no uninitialised bytes are copied back to user mode. When returning data, never return more bytes than were written: copying back uninitialised kernel memory leaks information (zero output buffers first with RtlZeroMemory , or use pool allocations that zero memory, lesson 3.01). - Keep each handler small: one IOCTL, one function, with all checks at the top. Testing like an attacker Test every IOCTL with: zero lengths, lengths of 1, lengths one short of the structure, huge counts, counts that overflow, wrong versions, unknown flags, and many threads at once. Practice 2.05 and project m02 do exactly that against a request validator; lesson 5.01's Driver Verifier and lesson 5.02's tools check the real driver.

title: A request that cannot be tricked
match: A request that cannot be tricked
body: Validate a variable-length request the way lesson 2.05 says: the input buffer holds a header followed by count entries: cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_SUCCESS = 0; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC000000Du); constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000023u); constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_REVISION_MISMATCH = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000059u); struct Header { std::uint32_t size; std::uint32_t version; std::uint32_t count; std::uint32_t flags; }; // 16 bytes struct Entry { std::uint32_t id; std::uint32_t value; }; // 8 bytes NTSTATUS parseRequest(const std::uint8_t input, std::uint32_t inputLength, std::vector<Entry & out); In this order: 1. inputLength < sizeof(Header) → STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL . 2. Copy the header once ( std::memcpy into a local) and use only the copy from then on. 3. size must equal sizeof(Header) , else STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER . 4. version must be 1 or 2, else STATUS_REVISION_MISMATCH . 5. flags may only use bits 0 and 1; any other bit set → STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER . 6. The entries must fit: count entries of 8 bytes after the header, within inputLength , checked without overflow ; else STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER . Trailing bytes after the entries are allowed. 7. Version 1 requests may have at most 16 entries; more → STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER . On success, out receives the entries (copied with memcpy , since the buffer may not be aligned). On any failure, out is left empty.

title: The echo driver's requests
body: Write the request handling of the XenonEcho driver from milestone 2, in plain C++ with a simulated IRP, so it can be tested against every kind of bad input before it ever runs in the VM. In the driver, dispatch is called by the dispatch routines; here the tests build the IRPs exactly as the I/O manager would for METHOD_BUFFERED . cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_SUCCESS = 0; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC000000Du); constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000010u); constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000022u); constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000023u); enum Major { IRP_MJ_CREATE = 0, IRP_MJ_CLOSE = 2, IRP_MJ_READ = 3, IRP_MJ_WRITE = 4, IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = 14 }; constexpr std::uint32_t ctl(std::uint32_t fn, std::uint32_t access) { return (0x8000u << 16) (access << 14) (fn << 2); } constexpr std::uint32_t IOCTL_ECHO = ctl(0x800, 0), IOCTL_GET_STATS = ctl(0x801, 1), IOCTL_RESET = ctl(0x802, 2), IOCTL_SET_NAME = ctl(0x803, 2), IOCTL_GET_NAME = ctl(0x804, 1); struct Irp { int major; std::uint32_t code{ 0 }; // device control only std::vector<std::uint8_t systemBuffer; // max(inLength, outLength) bytes, input copied in std::uint32_t inLength{ 0 }, outLength{ 0 }; std::uint32_t handleAccess{ 3 }; // bit 0 read, bit 1 write NTSTATUS status{ 0 }; std::uint64_t information{ 0 }; int completions{ 0 }; }; class EchoDevice { public: void dispatch(Irp& irp); std::uint32_t echoes() const; std::uint64_t bytesWritten() const; std::u16string name() const; }; Every IRP is completed exactly once (set status and information , and count one completion). On any failure, information is 0. - IRP_MJ_CREATE and IRP_MJ_CLOSE succeed. IRP_MJ_WRITE counts inLength bytes towards bytesWritten and returns that length as information. Any other major (including read) is STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST . - Device control : first the access check the I/O manager would make: if the code's access bits (14-15) are not all in handleAccess , STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED . Then: - IOCTL_ECHO : the output must be at least as long as the input ( STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL otherwise). The data is already in the system buffer, so echoing is just counting one echo and returning inLength as information. - IOCTL_GET_STATS : needs 16 bytes of output: writes size (16, uint32 ), echoes ( uint32 ) and bytesWritten ( uint64 ), little-endian, and returns 16. - IOCTL_RESET : sets both counters to 0. - IOCTL_SET_NAME : input is a header { uint32 size; uint32 length; } then length bytes of UTF-16. Fewer than 8 bytes of input is STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL ; size must be 8, length even, at most 64, and within the input (checked without overflow), else STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER . Copy the header once before checking it. - IOCTL_GET_NAME : writes uint32 length then the name's bytes; the output must hold 4 + length bytes ( STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL otherwise), and the information is 4 + length . - Any other code: STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST .

title: 3.01  Kernel Memory: Pools and Tags
body: Drivers allocate from the kernel's pools - paged and non-paged - with ExAllocatePool2, tag every allocation, free everything they allocate, and use tags and PoolMon to find leaks. This lesson also defines operator new and delete for kernel C++. Two pools The kernel's general-purpose heap is the pool , in two kinds: Pool Can be paged out? Use when --- --- --- Non-paged ( POOL_FLAG_NON_PAGED ) Never The memory is touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above (lesson 3.02), in DPCs, with spin locks held Paged ( POOL_FLAG_PAGED ) Yes Only touched at PASSIVE_LEVEL / APC_LEVEL ; most configuration and bookkeeping Non-paged memory is a limited resource (it always occupies physical RAM), so use paged pool when the rules allow. Touching paged memory at a raised IRQL is the classic 0xD1 bug check: the page might not be in memory, and the page fault cannot be handled at that level. Allocating cpp-norun constexpr ULONG XENON_TAG = 'nriC'; // shows as "Cirn" in tools (stored little-endian) auto entry = static_cast<LogEntry (ExAllocatePool2(POOL_FLAG_NON_PAGED, sizeof(LogEntry), XENON_TAG)); if (!entry) return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES; // allocations CAN fail: always check // ... use it ... ExFreePoolWithTag(entry, XENON_TAG); ExAllocatePool2 (Windows 10 2004 and later) zeroes the memory by default, which prevents leaking old data to user mode (lesson 2.05). The older ExAllocatePoolWithTag does not zero; older code must call RtlZeroMemory itself. Pool tags Every allocation carries a 4-character tag . Written as a multi-character constant, it is stored in memory in reverse, so 'nriC' appears as Cirn in the tools; the practice converts between the two. Tags let you: - see how much memory your driver uses, with the Sysinternals-like PoolMon tool (in the WDK) or WinDbg's !poolused 2 Cirn ; - find a leak : a tag whose count keeps growing; - find what owns a corrupted block: !pool <address shows the tag of the allocation around an address. Use distinct tags for different kinds of allocations ( Cirn for log entries, CirB for buffers) so a leak points straight at its source. Freeing everything Pool memory is not freed when the driver unloads. Leaked memory stays allocated until the machine restarts, and Driver Verifier (lesson 5.01) bug-checks with 0xC4 when a driver unloads with allocations still outstanding. Pair every allocation with a free on every path, including error paths, which is what RAII classes are for. C++ in the kernel Kernel C++ has no default operator new . Define one that takes the pool and tag, and pair it with delete : cpp-norun void __cdecl operator new(size_t size, POOL_FLAGS flags, ULONG tag) { return ExAllocatePool2(flags, size, tag); // returns nullptr on failure: callers must check } void __cdecl operator delete(void p, size_t) { if (p) ExFreePool(p); } auto ctx = new (POOL_FLAG_PAGED, XENON_TAG) Context{}; if (!ctx) return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES; delete ctx; A small UniquePool<T class (a unique_ptr look-alike that frees with the tag) removes most leaks by construction. No exceptions exist in the kernel, so "out of memory" is always a null pointer to check, never an exception. Stack space Kernel threads have small stacks: about 12 KB on x64 (versus 1 MB in user mode). Never put large arrays or structures on the stack in a driver; allocate them from the pool. Deep recursion is out of the question.

title: Pool tags and a leak tracker
match: Pool tags and a leak tracker
body: Write lesson 3.01's tag conversions, and a tracker like the one Driver Verifier keeps for a driver's allocations: cpp std::uint32_t tagValue(const std::string& shown); // "Cirn" - the ULONG the code writes as 'nriC' std::string tagText(std::uint32_t tag); // and back; non-printable bytes shown as '.' class PoolTracker { public: int allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::uint32_t tag); // returns a handle 1, 2, 3...; 0 for 0 bytes (failure) std::string free(int handle, std::uint32_t tag); // "ok", "unknown", "double free" or "tag mismatch" std::size_t bytesInUse(std::uint32_t tag) const; std::vector<std::string leaks() const; // "<tag text : <n allocation(s), <bytes bytes", sorted by tag text }; - Tags : the tag is 4 characters stored in memory in the order shown, and read as a little-endian 32-bit number: "Cirn" is 'C' 'i' << 8 'r' << 16 'n' << 24 . Shorter strings are padded with spaces; longer ones use the first 4 characters. - free : a handle never allocated is "unknown" ; one already freed is "double free" ; a live one freed with a different tag is "tag mismatch" and stays allocated. "ok" frees it. - leaks lists every tag with live allocations: "Cirn: 2 allocations, 96 bytes" ( allocation when 1).

title: 3.02  IRQL
body: The interrupt request level decides what kernel code may do at each moment. This lesson explains PASSIVE, APC, DISPATCH and device levels, what is forbidden at each, how the documentation states each function's IRQL, and how to raise and lower it correctly. Levels, not threads Every processor runs at an IRQL (interrupt request level) at every moment. Code running at a given IRQL can only be interrupted by something at a higher IRQL. The levels that matter to drivers: IRQL Value Who runs there --- --- --- PASSIVE_LEVEL 0 Normal threads, DriverEntry , most dispatch routines, work items APC_LEVEL 1 Asynchronous procedure calls; code holding a fast mutex DISPATCH_LEVEL 2 DPCs, timers' DPCs, code holding a spin lock; the thread scheduler itself Device IRQLs (DIRQL) 3+ Hardware interrupt service routines The two big rules At DISPATCH_LEVEL and above, the scheduler cannot run on that processor. Therefore: 1. No waiting. Anything that might block (waiting on an event with a timeout other than zero, acquiring a mutex, KeDelayExecutionThread ) is forbidden: there is no one to switch to while waiting. 2. No page faults. Touching pageable memory (paged pool, pageable code, user buffers) is forbidden: resolving a page fault needs to wait for the disk. This is bug check 0xD1 / 0x0A . Breaking either rule does not always crash at once: if the page happens to be in memory, nothing goes wrong, until one day it is not. That is why Driver Verifier (lesson 5.01) forces pages out to make these bugs reproducible. Reading the documentation Every kernel function's documentation ends with a line such as IRQL: <= DISPATCH_LEVEL or IRQL: PASSIVE_LEVEL . That is the highest IRQL at which it may be called. Some examples: Function Maximum IRQL --- --- ExAllocatePool2 (non-paged) DISPATCH_LEVEL ExAllocatePool2 (paged) APC_LEVEL KeAcquireSpinLock DISPATCH_LEVEL ExAcquireFastMutex APC_LEVEL ZwCreateFile , registry functions PASSIVE_LEVEL IoCompleteRequest DISPATCH_LEVEL KeSetEvent (Wait = FALSE) DISPATCH_LEVEL Static analysis (lesson 5.02) checks annotations such as _IRQL_requires_max_(DISPATCH_LEVEL) against your code paths. The practice writes a small checker for a call path. Raising and lowering cpp-norun KIRQL old; KeRaiseIrql(DISPATCH_LEVEL, &old); // now nothing on this CPU can preempt us // ... very short work on non-paged data ... KeLowerIrql(old); // always back to exactly where we were You may only raise with KeRaiseIrql and only lower with KeLowerIrql to the value you saved. Most drivers never call these directly: acquiring a spin lock raises to DISPATCH_LEVEL , and releasing it lowers back (lesson 3.03). KeGetCurrentIrql() tells you where you are; NT_ASSERT(KeGetCurrentIrql() <= APC_LEVEL) at the top of a function documents and checks its requirement in debug builds. PAGED_CODE() does the same for functions placed in pageable sections. Where dispatch routines run Dispatch routines for a top-level software driver run at PASSIVE_LEVEL in the context of the calling thread, so they may wait and allocate paged memory. Completion routines, DPCs and timer callbacks run at DISPATCH_LEVEL . A function called from both kinds of places must obey the stricter rules.

title: An IRQL checker
body: Static analysis follows each code path and checks lesson 3.02's rules. Write a small version that walks a list of operations, keeps track of the IRQL, and reports the first problem: cpp std::string checkPath(int startIrql, const std::vector<std::string & ops); // "" if the path is fine Operations: - "raise N" : KeRaiseIrql to N; N must not be lower than the current IRQL. Saves the old IRQL on a stack. - "lower" : KeLowerIrql back to the most recently saved IRQL (pops it). - "spin acquire" / "spin release" : acquiring is allowed at IRQL 2 or below, raises to 2 and saves the old IRQL; releasing restores it. - "mutex acquire" / "mutex release" : a fast mutex, allowed at IRQL 1 or below, raises to 1 and saves; releasing restores. - "call <function " for these functions, with their maximum IRQL: ExAllocatePool2Paged 1, ExAllocatePool2NonPaged 2, ZwCreateFile 0, KeSetEvent 2, IoCompleteRequest 2, KeWaitForSingleObject 1 (waiting), RtlCopyMemory 31. - "touch paged" : reading paged memory, allowed below 2. Problems, as "step <n : <message " with steps counted from 1: - an operation above its maximum: "<what at IRQL <current (max <max )" , where <what is the function name, spin acquire , mutex acquire or touch paged ; - "raise to <N from <current " when raising lower; "release without acquire" for a release (or lower ) with nothing saved, or that does not match the most recent acquire kind (a spin release while a mutex is the latest, and so on); - "unknown operation" for anything else. After all operations, if something is still held: "end: <k lock(s) or raise(s) still held" ; if the IRQL is not back to startIrql , "end: IRQL <current , expected <start " (checked after the first). An empty string means the path is correct.

title: 3.03  Locks in the Kernel
body: Protecting shared data in a driver - interlocked operations, spin locks and queued spin locks, fast mutexes, executive resources for many readers, and how IRQL decides which lock you may use. This lesson also covers deadlocks and lock ordering in the kernel. Why drivers need locks A driver's dispatch routines can run on several processors at once (several threads calling DeviceIoControl ), and a DPC can run at the same time as a dispatch routine. Shared data, such as the echo driver's counters or the log driver's buffer, must be protected, exactly as in user mode (the Win32 course's lesson 5.04), but the choice of lock depends on the IRQL. Interlocked operations For a single number, interlocked functions are the cheapest and work at any IRQL on non-paged data: cpp-norun InterlockedIncrement(&ext- echoes); InterlockedExchangeAdd64(&ext- bytesWritten, length); LONG previous = InterlockedCompareExchange(&ext- state, Running, Idle); // only if it was Idle Spin locks A spin lock protects data used at DISPATCH_LEVEL (or from both passive code and DPCs). Acquiring it raises the IRQL to DISPATCH_LEVEL and, if another processor holds it, spins (busy-waits) until it is free: cpp-norun KSPIN_LOCK lock; // in non-paged memory; KeInitializeSpinLock(&lock) once KIRQL old; KeAcquireSpinLock(&lock, &old); // short, non-blocking work on non-paged data KeReleaseSpinLock(&lock, old); Because other processors may be spinning, hold spin locks for microseconds : no allocation of paged memory, no waiting, no calling out to unknown code. Queued spin locks ( KeAcquireInStackQueuedSpinLock ) are fairer and scale better on many processors; prefer them for anything contended. Fast mutexes At PASSIVE_LEVEL , a waiting thread can sleep instead of spinning. A fast mutex does that and raises to APC_LEVEL while held: cpp-norun FAST_MUTEX mutex; // ExInitializeFastMutex(&mutex) ExAcquireFastMutex(&mutex); // work that may touch paged memory and take a while ExReleaseFastMutex(&mutex); Fast mutexes are not recursive: acquiring one twice on the same thread deadlocks it. Executive resources When many threads read and few write, an ERESOURCE ( ExAcquireResourceSharedLite / ExAcquireResourceExclusiveLite , inside KeEnterCriticalRegion ) lets readers share. Push locks ( FltAcquirePushLockShared in filter drivers) are a lighter alternative. Choosing Data is used at Lock --- --- Any IRQL, single value Interlocked DISPATCH_LEVEL (DPCs, timers) or mixed Spin lock (queued) PASSIVE_LEVEL only, short sections Fast mutex PASSIVE_LEVEL , mostly reads ERESOURCE or push lock Deadlocks in the kernel The user-mode rules hold, with harsher consequences: a deadlock freezes the system or bug-checks it. Take locks in a fixed order everywhere; never acquire a spin lock while holding another unless that order is documented and always the same; never wait for something while holding a spin lock. Driver Verifier's deadlock detection records the order in which your driver takes locks and reports any cycle, even one that has not deadlocked yet; the practice builds that detector.

title: Deadlock detection
body: Driver Verifier's deadlock detection records the order in which locks are taken and reports a possible deadlock as soon as two code paths take the same locks in opposite orders, even if they have not actually deadlocked yet. Write it: cpp class LockOrder { public: std::string acquire(int thread, const std::string& lock); // "" or a problem std::string release(int thread, const std::string& lock); }; - Each thread has its own stack of held locks. - acquire while holding other locks records an order "A before B" from every held lock A to the new lock B. Before recording, if B can already reach A through recorded orders (B before ... before A), return "possible deadlock: B - ... - A - B" : the existing chain from B to A (the shortest, choosing names alphabetically when several are as short), followed by the new lock again. The lock is still acquired. - Acquiring a lock the thread already holds returns "recursive acquire: <lock " and does not acquire it again. - release of a lock the thread does not hold returns "release of unheld lock: <lock " . Releasing a lock that is held but not the most recent is allowed (it is removed from wherever it is).

title: 3.04  DPCs, Timers and Work Items
body: Deferring work in the kernel - DPCs run soon at DISPATCH_LEVEL, kernel timers fire DPCs once or periodically, and work items move work back to PASSIVE_LEVEL in a system thread. This lesson also covers making sure all of them are finished before Unload. Why defer Code at a high IRQL must be quick and may not wait. When it needs to do more (process data, allocate paged memory, write a file), it defers the work to a lower IRQL: DPCs A deferred procedure call runs a function at DISPATCH_LEVEL soon, on some processor. Hardware drivers queue one from their interrupt routine; software drivers mostly meet DPCs through timers. cpp-norun KDPC dpc; KeInitializeDpc(&dpc, XenonDpcRoutine, context); // once KeInsertQueueDpc(&dpc, nullptr, nullptr); // run it soon; returns FALSE if already queued A DPC runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL : the rules of lesson 3.02 apply, so only non-paged data, spin locks, no waiting. Timers A kernel timer queues a DPC when it expires, once or periodically: cpp-norun KTIMER timer; KeInitializeTimerEx(&timer, NotificationTimer); LARGE_INTEGER due; due.QuadPart = -10'000'000LL; // NEGATIVE = relative, in 100 ns units: 1 second from now KeSetTimerEx(&timer, due, 1000 / period in ms, 0 for once /, &dpc); // ... KeCancelTimer(&timer); Due times are in 100-nanosecond units : negative values are relative to now, positive values are absolute system times (the FILETIME of the Win32 course's lesson 2.03). Getting the sign or the unit wrong is a classic bug: a positive "10 seconds" means a date in January 1601, which has long passed, so the timer fires at once. The practice converts and checks these values. Work items To get back to PASSIVE_LEVEL (to allocate paged memory, write a file, call a registry function), queue a work item ; a system worker thread runs it: cpp-norun PIO_WORKITEM item = IoAllocateWorkItem(deviceObject); IoQueueWorkItem(item, XenonWorkRoutine, DelayedWorkQueue, context); // in XenonWorkRoutine (PASSIVE_LEVEL): do the work, then IoFreeWorkItem(item) IoAllocateWorkItem ties the work item to the device object, which keeps the driver loaded until the work item has finished: older APIs without that link let a driver unload while its work routine was still running. Shutting down cleanly Unload must guarantee that none of these will run again afterwards, or the kernel will call into unloaded code: 1. Cancel periodic timers: KeCancelTimer . 2. Wait for DPCs that may already be queued or running: KeFlushQueuedDpcs() . 3. Wait for outstanding work items: keep a count (or rundown protection, ExWaitForRundownProtectionRelease ) and wait until it reaches zero. 4. Only then free the memory they use. This order matters: freeing a context before the last DPC has finished is a use-after-free in the kernel. A periodic job The log driver of milestone 4 uses all three: a periodic timer's DPC moves events from a non-paged buffer, counts them, and when there are enough, queues a work item that runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL . Project m03 builds the counting and buffering core.

title: Timers and a clean unload
body: Write the timer arithmetic of lesson 3.04, and a checker for the order of the clean-up steps in Unload : cpp std::int64_t relativeDue(std::int64_t milliseconds); // for KeSetTimerEx: negative, 100 ns units std::int64_t msUntilFire(std::int64_t due, std::int64_t nowFileTime); // 0 if already due int firesBetween(std::int64_t firstMs, int periodMs, std::int64_t fromMs, std::int64_t toMs); std::string checkUnload(const std::vector<std::string & steps); - relativeDue(1000) is -10 000 000 . For zero or negative milliseconds the formula would give 0 or a positive number, which means an absolute time long past: return -1 instead (the smallest relative wait). - msUntilFire : a negative due is relative: -due / 10000 milliseconds (rounded down). A positive one is an absolute FILETIME: (due - now) / 10000 if in the future, else 0. - firesBetween : a timer first fires at firstMs and then every periodMs (0 means once). How many times does it fire with fromMs < t <= toMs ? - checkUnload : the steps are names among cancel timer , flush dpcs , wait work items , free context , delete link , delete device . Rules, reported as the first broken one: flush dpcs must come after cancel timer ( "flush dpcs before cancel timer" ); free context must come after both flush dpcs and wait work items ( "free context before flush dpcs" / "free context before wait work items" , checked in that order); delete device must come after delete link ( "delete device before delete link" ); every one of the six must appear exactly once ( "missing <step " / "twice <step " , checked first, in the list order above). "" if all is well.

title: 3.05  Lists in the Kernel
body: The kernel's own data structures - intrusive doubly linked lists with LIST_ENTRY and CONTAINING_RECORD, singly linked lists, interlocked lists, lookaside lists for fixed-size allocations, and ring buffers for logs. Intrusive lists The kernel has no std::list . Its lists are intrusive : the link lives inside the object, as a LIST_ENTRY member: cpp-norun typedef struct _LIST_ENTRY { struct _LIST_ENTRY Flink; struct _LIST_ENTRY Blink; } LIST_ENTRY; struct LogItem { LIST_ENTRY link; // the list goes through here LARGE_INTEGER time; ULONG processId; }; LIST_ENTRY head; // the list itself: a LIST_ENTRY that points to itself when empty InitializeListHead(&head); InsertTailList(&head, &item- link); if (!IsListEmpty(&head)) { PLIST_ENTRY e = RemoveHeadList(&head); LogItem oldest = CONTAINING_RECORD(e, LogItem, link); // from the link back to the object } The list is circular : the head's Flink is the first element, its Blink the last, and the last element's Flink points back to the head. An empty list is a head that points to itself. CONTAINING_RECORD subtracts the member's offset from the link's address to find the object around it. An object can be in several lists at once with several LIST_ENTRY members. No allocation happens when inserting or removing: the object already contains its link. That is exactly what the kernel wants: inserting at DISPATCH_LEVEL under a spin lock never fails and never allocates. The practice implements these functions and checks the list's invariants. Walking and removing cpp-norun for (PLIST_ENTRY e = head.Flink; e != &head; ) { LogItem item = CONTAINING_RECORD(e, LogItem, link); e = e- Flink; // advance BEFORE removing if (tooOld(item)) { RemoveEntryList(&item- link); ExFreePoolWithTag(item, XENON_TAG); } } Lists are not thread-safe: protect them with a lock (lesson 3.03), or use ExInterlockedInsertTailList with a spin lock for simple queues. Singly linked and interlocked lists SINGLE_LIST_ENTRY is a one-way list (a stack: PushEntryList , PopEntryList ). Interlocked singly linked lists ( SLIST_HEADER , InterlockedPushEntrySList ) are lock-free stacks that work at any IRQL, useful for passing items between a DPC and a worker. Lookaside lists Allocating many objects of the same size from the pool is relatively slow.
