A lookaside list keeps freed blocks of one size for reuse: cpp-norun LOOKASIDE_LIST_EX lookaside; ExInitializeLookasideListEx(&lookaside, nullptr, nullptr, NonPagedPoolNx, 0, sizeof(LogItem), XENON_TAG, 0); auto item = static_cast<LogItem (ExAllocateFromLookasideListEx(&lookaside)); ExFreeToLookasideListEx(&lookaside, item); ExDeleteLookasideListEx(&lookaside); // in Unload, after freeing every item Ring buffers A log that must never grow without limit uses a ring buffer : a fixed array where new entries overwrite the oldest when it is full. Two indexes (where to write next, how many are stored) and a lock are all it needs, and it never allocates after start-up. The log driver of milestone 4 stores events this way and counts how many were dropped because nobody read them in time.

title: LIST_ENTRY
body: Implement the kernel's intrusive list functions from lesson 3.05 exactly as wdm.h defines them, plus CONTAINING_RECORD and a checker for the list's links: cpp struct LIST_ENTRY { LIST_ENTRY Flink; LIST_ENTRY Blink; }; void InitializeListHead(LIST_ENTRY head); bool IsListEmpty(const LIST_ENTRY head); void InsertHeadList(LIST_ENTRY head, LIST_ENTRY entry); void InsertTailList(LIST_ENTRY head, LIST_ENTRY entry); bool RemoveEntryList(LIST_ENTRY entry); // true if the list is empty afterwards LIST_ENTRY RemoveHeadList(LIST_ENTRY head); // the head itself if the list was empty LIST_ENTRY RemoveTailList(LIST_ENTRY head); int checkList(const LIST_ENTRY head); // number of entries, or -1 if any link is inconsistent define CONTAINING_RECORD(address, type, field) \ reinterpret_cast<type (reinterpret_cast<char (address) - offsetof(type, field)) - The list is circular: an empty list's head points to itself in both directions. - RemoveEntryList unlinks the entry from its neighbours and returns whether Flink == Blink for those neighbours afterwards (which is "the list is now empty" when the entry was the only one). - checkList walks forward from the head: for every entry e , e- Flink- Blink must be e , and it must come back to the head within 100 000 steps; it returns the number of entries (not counting the head), or -1.

title: The log driver's ring buffer
body: The log driver of milestone 4 records events (a process started, a thread exited) from callbacks that may run on any processor, and a user-mode viewer reads them with an IOCTL. Write its core: a fixed-size ring buffer that never allocates after start-up, gives every event a sequence number, overwrites the oldest events when full, tells a reader how many it missed, and packs events into the IOCTL's output buffer. cpp struct Event { std::uint64_t seq; std::uint64_t time; std::uint32_t pid; std::uint32_t kind; }; class EventRing { public: explicit EventRing(std::size_t capacity); std::uint64_t push(std::uint64_t time, std::uint32_t pid, std::uint32_t kind); std::size_t size() const; std::uint64_t overwritten() const; std::vector<Event read(std::uint64_t afterSeq, std::size_t maxCount, std::uint64_t& missed) const; std::uint32_t serialize(std::uint64_t afterSeq, std::uint8_t out, std::uint32_t outLength) const; }; - push stores an event with the next sequence number (1, 2, 3, ...) and returns it. When the buffer holds capacity events, the oldest is overwritten (and counted by overwritten ). It is called from many threads at once: protect the ring with a lock (a spin lock in the driver, std::mutex here). The storage is allocated once, in the constructor. - read returns, oldest first, up to maxCount events with a sequence number greater than afterSeq . missed is how many events after afterSeq are no longer in the buffer (overwritten before this reader got them): oldest seq - afterSeq - 1 when that is positive, else 0. - serialize writes, for the viewer's IOCTL_LOG_READ , a 16-byte header { uint32 count; uint32 missed; uint64 lastSeq; } followed by count records of 24 bytes ( seq , time as uint64 , pid , kind as uint32 ), little-endian, as many as fit in outLength . lastSeq is the last record's sequence number, or afterSeq if there is none, so the viewer can pass it back next time. It returns the number of bytes written, or 0 if outLength is less than 16.

title: 4.01  Process and Thread Notifications
body: Windows lets drivers observe system events through documented callbacks - process creation and exit, thread creation and exit, and image loads. This lesson registers them, explains the context they run in and what information they carry, and keeps the course's log driver strictly an observer. Documented observation points Security products, monitoring tools and system utilities need to know what happens on the machine. Instead of guessing, Windows provides notification callbacks , documented functions that call a driver when: Callback Registered with Called when --- --- --- Process PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx A process is created or exits Thread PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine A thread is created or exits Image load PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine An executable or DLL is mapped into a process They are the supported way to observe these events. The log driver in this milestone uses the process and thread callbacks to record events into project m03's ring buffer (with one more field, extra : the parent's id for a process start, the thread's id for thread events), and a user-mode viewer displays them. It observes only: it does not change, block or reach into any process. The process callback cpp-norun void XenonProcessNotify(PEPROCESS process, HANDLE processId, PPS_CREATE_NOTIFY_INFO info) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(process); LARGE_INTEGER now; KeQuerySystemTimePrecise(&now); if (info) // non-null: the process is being created g_ring.push(now.QuadPart, HandleToULong(processId), KindProcessStart, HandleToULong(info- ParentProcessId)); else // null: the process is exiting g_ring.push(now.QuadPart, HandleToULong(processId), KindProcessExit, 0); } // DriverEntry: status = PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx(XenonProcessNotify, FALSE); // FALSE: register // Unload: PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx(XenonProcessNotify, TRUE); // TRUE: remove PS_CREATE_NOTIFY_INFO describes the new process: its parent's id, the image file name, and the command line (as UNICODE_STRING s that are only valid during the callback: copy what you keep). The Ex version requires the driver to be linked with /INTEGRITYCHECK , which the project settings provide. The thread callback cpp-norun void XenonThreadNotify(HANDLE processId, HANDLE threadId, BOOLEAN create) { g_ring.push(now(), HandleToULong(processId), create ? KindThreadStart : KindThreadExit, HandleToULong(threadId)); } Where callbacks run - Process and thread callbacks run at PASSIVE_LEVEL (thread callbacks sometimes at APC_LEVEL ), synchronously in the creating or exiting thread. Every process creation on the machine waits for your callback to return. - So callbacks must be fast : record a few numbers into a non-paged ring buffer under a spin lock (or interlocked operations) and return. No file writing, no waiting, no allocation if avoidable. - Many callbacks run at once on different processors: the ring buffer's lock (project m03) is essential. The unload rule, again A registered callback is a pointer the kernel will keep calling. Unload must remove every callback before anything else is freed; if removal fails (or is forgotten), the next process creation calls into unloaded memory and the machine bug-checks. Practice 1.04 and 3.04's checkers enforce exactly this order: unregister callbacks, then flush, then free. Process ids and times Process and thread ids are reused once a process has exited, so the viewer identifies processes by (id, start time) rather than id alone. KeQuerySystemTimePrecise returns a FILETIME-style UTC time (100 ns units since 1601, the Win32 course's lesson 2.03), which the viewer converts for display.

title: A process table from events
body: The log viewer turns lesson 4.01's process events into a table of running processes and a tree. Write it, remembering that process ids are reused: cpp struct ProcEvent { bool start; std::uint32_t pid; std::uint32_t parent; std::uint64_t time; }; class ProcessTable { public: void apply(const ProcEvent& e); int alive() const; int unknownExits() const; std::vector<std::string tree() const; std::string lifetime(std::uint32_t pid) const; }; - start : records a new process (pid, parent id, start time). If a process with the same pid is still recorded as running (its exit event was lost), it is first marked as ended at this time. - exit : the running process with that pid gets its exit time. An exit for a pid that is not running is counted by unknownExits and otherwise ignored. - tree lists the running processes as lines of the pid, indented two spaces per level. A process's parent is the running process whose pid is its parent id and which started no later than it; without one, it is at the top level. Siblings (and top-level processes) are in order of start time, then pid; children follow their parent directly (depth first). - lifetime describes the most recent process with that pid: "running" , "ran <ms ms" (times are in 100 ns units, rounded down), or "unknown" .

title: 4.02  Logging and Tracing from a Driver
match: 4.02 Logging and Tracing from a Driver
body: Getting information out of a driver without slowing the system down - DbgPrintEx levels and filters, rate limiting, WPP software tracing, and TraceLogging with ETW, which lets tools like WPR and WPA record a driver's events alongside the rest of the system. DbgPrintEx, carefully DbgPrintEx (lesson 1.04) is the first tool, but it has costs: - It formats text in the kernel, which is slow compared with recording a few numbers. - Output is filtered by component and level : DbgPrintEx(DPFLTR_IHVDRIVER_ID, DPFLTR_ERROR_LEVEL, ...) is always shown, INFO_LEVEL only when the filter mask allows it. - A message in a hot path (a callback called for every thread creation) can flood the debugger and slow the whole VM to a crawl. Use it for errors and rare events, and rate-limit anything that can repeat: at most a few messages per second, then one summary ("suppressed 1 204 similar messages"). The practice builds a token-bucket limiter. Levels and keywords Good driver logging distinguishes: Level Use --- --- Critical / Error Something failed and the driver cannot do its job Warning Unexpected but handled (a request rejected by validation) Information Important state changes (loaded, device created) Verbose Detailed tracing for debugging, off by default Keywords are bit flags for areas of the driver ( 0x1 I/O requests, 0x2 callbacks, 0x4 memory). A trace session enables a level and a keyword mask, and the driver checks both before formatting anything, so disabled events cost almost nothing. WPP software tracing WPP (Windows software trace preprocessor) turns DoTraceMessage(FLAG_IO, "length %d", len) calls into compact binary events at build time: only the arguments are recorded, and the format strings live in the .pdb . Tracing is enabled per driver from outside ( tracelog , TraceView ), and the cost when disabled is a single flag check. Many Microsoft drivers trace this way; the WDK templates set it up. TraceLogging and ETW ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the system-wide, high-speed tracing infrastructure that Windows itself uses. TraceLogging is the simplest way for a driver to write ETW events, with self-describing fields: cpp-norun include <TraceLoggingProvider.h TRACELOGGING_DEFINE_PROVIDER(g_provider, "Xenon.Log", (0x5c1f0a8e, 0x9b0a, 0x4c1d, 0x8f, 0x3e, 0x1a, 0x2b, 0x3c, 0x4d, 0x5e, 0x6f)); // your own GUID TraceLoggingRegister(g_provider); // DriverEntry TraceLoggingWrite(g_provider, "ProcessStart", TraceLoggingLevel(TRACE_LEVEL_INFORMATION), TraceLoggingKeyword(0x2), TraceLoggingUInt32(pid, "ProcessId"), TraceLoggingUInt32(parentPid, "ParentId")); TraceLoggingUnregister(g_provider); // Unload Record a session with WPR (Windows Performance Recorder) using a profile that enables Xenon.Log , and open the trace in WPA (Windows Performance Analyzer): your events appear on the same timeline as CPU usage, disk I/O and every other system event. That makes ETW far more powerful than a private log. Which one when Need Use --- --- Errors you want to see while developing DbgPrintEx at error level Detailed debugging traces WPP or TraceLogging at verbose level Events other tools should see, with timing TraceLogging (ETW) A product feature (the user sees the events) Your own channel: a ring buffer and an IOCTL (lesson 4.03) The course's log driver uses its own ring buffer because the viewer is part of the "product"; it would also be good practice to emit the same events with TraceLogging.

title: Rate-limited logging
where: 4.02 Logging and Tracing from a Driver
body: Write the two filters of lesson 4.02 that keep driver logging cheap: the level-and-keyword check, and a token-bucket rate limiter for messages from hot paths. cpp bool enabled(int level, std::uint64_t keywords, int sessionLevel, std::uint64_t sessionMask); class RateLimiter { public: RateLimiter(int perSecond, int burst); std::string log(std::int64_t nowMs, const std::string& message); }; - enabled : levels are numbers where smaller is more important (1 critical ... 5 verbose); an event is enabled when its level is at most sessionLevel and it has no keywords, or shares at least one keyword bit with sessionMask . - RateLimiter : a bucket holds up to burst tokens and starts full; it refills at perSecond tokens per second, continuously. Each message costs one token. If a token is available, log returns the message, prefixed by "(<n suppressed) " if n messages were suppressed since the last one that got through; otherwise it counts the message as suppressed and returns "" . Use integer arithmetic: keep the bucket in thousandths of a token (a message costs 1000), and add elapsedMs perSecond thousandths per elapsed millisecond. Time never goes backwards in the tests.

title: 4.03  Designing a Log Driver
body: Putting milestones 2 to 4 together - the XenonLog driver records process and thread events into a ring buffer, a secured device offers one read IOCTL, and a user-mode viewer polls it, resumes where it stopped and shows what was lost. This lesson is the design, the protocol and the order to build it. The pieces Part From --- --- Device, symbolic link, security (administrators only) 2.01 Dispatch, IOCTL, validation 2.02 - 2.05, project m02 Non-paged storage, spin lock 3.01 - 3.03 Ring buffer with sequence numbers (project m03's record plus extra ) 3.05, project m03 Callbacks 4.01 Rate-limited debug output 4.02 The protocol One IOCTL does the work: cpp-norun define IOCTL_LOG_READ CTL_CODE(0x8001, 0x800, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_DATA) struct LogReadRequest { ULONG size; ULONG reserved; ULONGLONG afterSeq; }; // input: 16 bytes // output: { ULONG count; ULONG missed; ULONGLONG lastSeq; } // + count x { ULONGLONG seq; ULONGLONG time; ULONG pid; ULONG kind; ULONG extra; ULONG reserved; } // 32 bytes The viewer keeps lastSeq and passes it back as afterSeq each time, so it never sees an event twice and always learns how many it missed. Because the request carries the position, the driver keeps no per-reader state: two viewers can read independently, and a viewer that crashes leaves nothing behind. The input has a size and a reserved field that must be zero (lesson 2.05), so the request can grow later. Design decisions - Fixed memory : the ring buffer is allocated once in DriverEntry (non-paged, for example 4096 events). Callbacks never allocate, so they cannot fail and are fast. - Losing events is acceptable, slowing the system is not : when the viewer reads too slowly, old events are overwritten and the viewer reports "N events lost". A design that blocked process creation until the viewer caught up would be unacceptable. - Short locks : the callback holds the spin lock only to copy 32 bytes into a slot. Serializing for the IOCTL copies the events out under the lock, then formats outside it. - Security : only administrators can open the device (lesson 2.01); the IOCTL requires read access; the driver reports only process and thread ids and times, not command lines or other data from inside processes. Unload, in order 1. Unregister the thread callback, then the process callback (no new events). 2. Delete the symbolic link, then the device (no new requests; open handles keep the device until closed). 3. Free the ring buffer. Practice 3.04's checker, extended with the callbacks, describes exactly this order. The viewer The user-mode viewer (a console program or the Win32 course's list view) runs a loop: send IOCTL_LOG_READ with the last sequence number, parse the reply, append lines, sleep 200 ms (or wait for a notification event, project m03's stretch goal). It keeps a table of processes seen (id and start time to parent and first-seen time), formats times as local time, and shows " N events lost " when missed is not zero. Project m04 writes the viewer's logic. Order to build in 1. The driver with only the device and a stub IOCTL that returns an empty reply; the viewer connects and prints "0 events". 2. The ring buffer with a test IOCTL that pushes fake events; the viewer shows them. 3. The process callback; then the thread callback. 4. Driver Verifier on (lesson 5.01) while starting and stopping many programs; fix everything it reports. 5. The viewer's process table, filters and lost-event display.

title: The read request
body: Write both ends of lesson 4.03's IOCTL_LOG_READ request: the viewer builds it, the driver validates it and works out how many 32-byte records fit in the reply. cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_SUCCESS = 0; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC000000Du); constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000023u); std::vector<std::uint8_t buildReadRequest(std::uint64_t afterSeq); // { u32 size = 16; u32 reserved = 0; u64 afterSeq } NTSTATUS validateReadRequest(const std::uint8_t input, std::uint32_t inLength, std::uint32_t outLength, std::uint64_t& afterSeq); std::uint32_t recordsThatFit(std::uint32_t outLength); validateReadRequest , in this order: input shorter than 16 bytes, or output shorter than the 16-byte reply header → STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL ; size not 16 or reserved not 0 → STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ; otherwise afterSeq is set and the result is success. recordsThatFit is how many whole 32-byte records follow the 16-byte header (0 if not even the header fits).

title: The log viewer
body: Write the logic of XenonLogView , the user-mode viewer of lesson 4.03's log driver: parse the driver's replies safely (a user-mode program must not trust a driver's output blindly either), turn events into readable lines, follow process lifetimes, report lost events, and filter. cpp struct Record { std::uint64_t seq, time; std::uint32_t pid, kind, extra; }; struct Reply { std::uint32_t missed{ 0 }; std::uint64_t lastSeq{ 0 }; std::vector<Record records; }; enum Kind : std::uint32_t { ProcessStart = 1, ProcessExit = 2, ThreadStart = 3, ThreadExit = 4 }; bool parseReply(const std::uint8_t data, std::uint32_t length, Reply& out); std::string clockTime(std::uint64_t fileTime); // "HH:MM:SS.mmm" (UTC) class Viewer { public: void apply(const Reply& reply); std::uint64_t nextAfter() const; void filterPid(std::uint32_t pid); // 0: show everything std::vector<std::string lines() const; std::string summary() const; }; parseReply : a 16-byte header { u32 count; u32 missed; u64 lastSeq } then count records of 32 bytes { u64 seq; u64 time; u32 pid; u32 kind; u32 extra; u32 reserved } . It fails if the length is below 16 or does not hold count records (checked without overflow), if the sequence numbers are not strictly increasing, or if lastSeq is not the last record's sequence number (when there are records). Extra bytes after the records are allowed. clockTime formats the time of day of a FILETIME (100 ns units since 1601, UTC): hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds. Viewer : apply adds, in order: - " <n events lost " first if missed 0 ; - one line per record: "<clock start <pid (parent <extra )" , "<clock exit <pid " followed by " after <ms ms" if this viewer saw that process start (the most recent start of that pid), "<clock thread start <pid /<extra " , "<clock thread exit <pid /<extra " , and "<clock event <kind for <pid " for unknown kinds. nextAfter is the highest lastSeq applied so far (start: 0). lines returns all lines, or with a pid filter, only the lines for that pid (lost-event lines are always shown). summary is "<a started, <b exited, <c threads, <d lost" , counting process starts, process exits, thread starts and lost events.

title: 5.01  Driver Verifier
body: Driver Verifier makes hidden driver bugs crash immediately and explain themselves - special pool for overruns and use-after-free, forced IRQL checking, pool tracking for leaks, I/O verification, deadlock detection and low-resources simulation. This lesson turns it on in the VM and reads what it reports. Bugs that hide Many driver bugs do not crash when they happen: an overrun writes into a neighbouring allocation that nobody reads for an hour; a paged buffer touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL happens to be resident; a leak grows slowly. Driver Verifier , built into Windows, watches selected drivers and makes those bugs fail immediately and loudly , with bug check 0xC4 and a parameter that says exactly what went wrong. Turning it on (in the VM) cpp-norun verifier /standard /driver XenonLog.sys :: the standard checks for one driver verifier /query :: what is enabled and current counters verifier /reset :: turn it off (takes effect after restart) Restart the VM after enabling. From then on, every load of XenonLog.sys runs under Verifier. Only verify your own drivers: verifying system drivers slows the machine and is not your concern. And never leave it on outside the lab. What the standard checks do Check Catches --- --- Special pool Each allocation on its own page, right against an inaccessible guard page: an overrun faults at the exact instruction; freed memory is made inaccessible, so use-after-free faults too Force IRQL checking Pageable memory is made non-resident whenever the IRQL is raised, so touching it at DISPATCH_LEVEL crashes every time, not occasionally Pool tracking Every allocation is recorded; unloading with allocations outstanding is a bug check listing them I/O verification IRPs completed twice, completed with bad status, freed while in use, or left pending at unload Deadlock detection Lock order violations (practice 3.03), even when no deadlock happened Security checks User-mode addresses used without probing, kernel addresses passed from user mode Miscellaneous checks Freeing memory that contains active timers, DPCs or locks Optional: low resources simulation ( /faults ) makes random allocations fail, which tests every if (!p) return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES; path that otherwise never runs. Reading a Verifier bug check cpp-norun DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION (c4) Arg1: 0000000000000062, A driver has forgotten to free its pool allocations prior to unloading. Arg2: ffffd30a1c2e3f20, name of the driver having the issue. Arg3: ffffd30a1d4b6010, verifier internal structure with driver information. Arg4: 0000000000000003, total of (paged+nonpaged) allocations that weren't freed. !analyze -v decodes the first argument (the kind of violation), and !verifier 3 XenonLog.sys lists the outstanding allocations with their tags and the stacks that allocated them: the leak points straight at its source. For special-pool crashes, the call stack ends at the instruction that overran. A testing routine With Verifier on, exercise the driver hard: start and stop it repeatedly, run the viewer while starting and stopping hundreds of programs, send every IOCTL with bad inputs (practice 5.02's fuzzer), close handles while requests are pending. A driver that survives this under Verifier is in good shape. Project m05 builds a special-pool simulator to see exactly how overruns, use-after-free and leaks are caught.

title: Every failure path
body: Driver Verifier's low-resources simulation makes allocations fail to exercise error paths. Do it systematically: run an initialisation function once for each allocation it makes, failing exactly that one, and check that every failure path cleans up. cpp class Allocator { public: explicit Allocator(int failAt); // the failAt-th allocation (0-based) fails; -1: none fail int allocate(std::size_t bytes); // a handle 0, or 0 on failure void free(int handle); int outstanding() const; // allocated and not freed int calls() const; // allocate calls made }; using Init = std::function<bool(Allocator&, std::vector<int & kept) ; std::string checkFailurePaths(const Init& init); init must return false and free everything when an allocation fails; when it succeeds it returns true and puts the handles it keeps in kept (as DriverEntry keeps its device and buffers). checkFailurePaths : 1. Run init with no failures. It must succeed, otherwise return "fails without injected failures" . Count its allocation calls n . Free everything in kept ; if anything is still outstanding, return "leak on success" . 2. For i from 0 to n - 1 : run init with allocation i failing. It must return false ( "succeeded although allocation <i failed" ) and leave nothing outstanding ( "leak when allocation <i fails" ). 3. Return "all <n failure paths clean" .

title: 5.02  Static Analysis and Testing
body: Finding driver bugs before they run - SAL annotations, Code Analysis for drivers, CodeQL with Microsoft's driver queries, the Static Driver Verifier idea, unit-testing driver logic in user mode, and fuzzing IOCTL handlers. Annotations SAL (source annotation language) tells the compiler's analysis what a function expects: cpp-norun _IRQL_requires_max_(DISPATCH_LEVEL) NTSTATUS XenonPush(_Inout_ Ring ring, _In_reads_bytes_(length) const void data, _In_ ULONG length); _IRQL_requires_(PASSIVE_LEVEL) _Must_inspect_result_ NTSTATUS XenonLoadSettings(_In_ PUNICODE_STRING registryPath, _Out_ Settings settings); With annotations, analysis can report: a function called at a higher IRQL than it allows, a buffer read beyond its declared length, an _Out_ parameter not set on every success path, a result ignored. The WDK's headers are annotated throughout, which is why analysis finds so much in driver code. Code Analysis and CodeQL - Code Analysis for drivers ( /analyze with the driver rule sets, enabled by default in WDK projects): checks IRQL rules, annotation contracts, pool tagging, missing NT_SUCCESS checks, and common C mistakes on every build. Treat its warnings as errors. - CodeQL with Microsoft's Windows driver query suite: deeper, whole-program queries; required for drivers submitted for Windows certification. Run it from the command line or in CI on every change. - Static Driver Verifier (older WDK versions): model-checks the driver against rules for the use of kernel APIs, such as "a spin lock is always released" or "an IRP is completed once on every path". The ideas live on in CodeQL's rules. Test the logic in user mode Most of a driver is ordinary logic: parsing requests, validating, ring buffers, state machines. Writing it as plain, kernel-independent C++ with a thin kernel layer around it lets you unit-test it in user mode , quickly and with every tool available, which is exactly what every practice in this course has done. The kernel layer (dispatch routines that call the tested functions) stays small enough to review line by line. Fuzzing A fuzzer sends huge numbers of generated inputs to a handler and checks that nothing goes wrong. For an IOCTL handler, "wrong" means: a crash or exception, information larger than the output buffer, information not 0 on failure, an IRP not completed exactly once, or memory touched outside the buffers. Two kinds: - Generation : build inputs from the protocol's description with interesting values (0, 1, maximum, one less than the structure size, huge counts) in each field. - Mutation : start from valid requests and flip bits, change lengths, splice requests together. Run the handler under the fuzzer in user mode first (with the address sanitizer, /fsanitize=address , which catches overruns like special pool), then against the real driver in the VM under Driver Verifier. The practice writes a deterministic fuzzer harness. A test plan for a driver 1. Unit tests for the logic, in user mode, on every build. 2. Code Analysis on every build; CodeQL in CI. 3. Fuzz every IOCTL in user mode with the sanitizer. 4. In the VM with Verifier: load and unload loops, the real workload, the fuzzer against the device, low-resources simulation. 5. Multiple processors in the VM, and many threads in the tests.

title: A fuzzing harness
body: Write a deterministic fuzzer for IOCTL handlers like the ones in this course (lesson 5.02), and the invariant checks it applies to every call: cpp struct Result { std::int32_t status; std::uint64_t information; int completions; }; using Handler = std::function<Result(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & input, std::uint32_t outLength) ; class Lcg { public: explicit Lcg(std::uint32_t seed); std::uint32_t next(); // state = state 1664525 + 1013904223 (mod 2^32); returns the new state }; std::vector<std::uint8_t makeInput(Lcg& rng); std::string fuzz(const Handler& handler, int iterations, std::uint32_t seed); Every random number below is rng.next() 16 , the upper 16 bits: the low bits of this kind of generator repeat with a very short period (the lowest two bits cycle every 4 numbers), so next() % 4 would never produce the same choice twice in a row. makeInput draws, in this order: a length % 41 (0 to 40 bytes), then for each byte a choice % 4 : 0 → 0x00 , 1 → 0xFF , 2 → 0x10 , 3 → a random byte & 0xFF . (Small, edge-case-heavy values find more bugs than uniform noise.) fuzz runs iterations times: make an input, draw an output length % 65 , call the handler, and check, in this order: 1. the handler threw: "iteration <i : exception" ; 2. completions != 1 : "iteration <i : completed <n times" ; 3. failure ( status < 0 ) with information not 0: "iteration <i : information on failure" ; 4. success with information greater than outLength : "iteration <i : information exceeds output" . It returns the first problem, or "<iterations iterations, no problems" . Iterations count from 0. One Lcg drives the whole run.

title: 5.03  Secure Driver Design
body: Drivers run with full kernel privilege, so a flaw in one is a flaw in the whole system. This lesson lists the classic driver vulnerabilities - unprotected devices, unchecked buffers, METHOD_NEITHER, arbitrary memory access interfaces, information leaks, missing access checks - and the design rules that prevent them. Why driver security matters A program that can talk to a driver talks to the kernel. If the driver can be made to do something it should not, any program that can open the device gains that power. Vulnerable drivers, including legitimately signed ones, are regularly abused to gain kernel privileges, which is why Windows now ships a vulnerable driver blocklist and why Microsoft's driver security guidance is long. Designing a driver securely is part of writing it at all. The classic flaws Flaw What goes wrong Prevention --- --- --- Unprotected device Any user, even a low-privilege one, can open it and send requests IoCreateDeviceSecure with a strict SDDL; FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN (lesson 2.01) Missing access bits in IOCTLs A read-only handle can trigger state changes FILE_WRITE_DATA (or FILE_READ_DATA ) in each control code (lesson 2.03) Unchecked lengths and counts Reads and writes beyond buffers, integer overflow Lesson 2.05's checks, every time METHOD_NEITHER mistakes Unprobed user pointers, kernel addresses accepted, double fetches Use buffered I/O (lesson 2.04) Generic "read/write memory" or "call function" interfaces Turns the driver into a tool for anyone to control the kernel Never offer them; each IOCTL does one specific, safe thing Information leaks Uninitialised bytes, kernel addresses or other processes' data returned to user mode Zero buffers, return only what you wrote, never return pointers Trusting the caller Acting on a process id, handle or path supplied by user mode without checking that caller's rights Check the requestor's rights, open objects with the caller's access mode Race conditions State checked and then used after another thread changed it Locks around state; copy user input once Design rules 1. Minimise the interface. Every IOCTL is attack surface. Offer the fewest, narrowest operations that do the job. The log driver offers exactly one, and it only reads its own ring buffer. 2. Least privilege. Only the accounts that need the device can open it; only the handles that need write access can change state. 3. Validate everything, fail closed (lesson 2.05). 4. Never expose kernel addresses or raw memory. No IOCTL should accept or return a kernel pointer, an arbitrary address, a physical address, or a port number to read and write. 5. Do not act on other processes on a caller's behalf. A driver that opens, reads or modifies another process because a user-mode request asked it to is a privilege escalation waiting to happen. The drivers in this course never touch other processes at all. 6. Keep it small and reviewed. Less kernel code is less risk: do the complex parts in a user-mode service and keep the driver minimal. 7. Test as an attacker would (lesson 5.02), under Driver Verifier (lesson 5.01). Reviewing a driver A security review walks every entry point (each dispatch routine, each IOCTL, each callback) and asks: who can reach it? What can they control? What does the code assume about that input? What happens with the worst input at the worst time? The practice turns this checklist into a small audit tool for a driver's description.

title: A security audit
body: Turn lesson 5.03's checklist into an audit of a driver's description: cpp struct IoctlSpec { std::string name; int method; int access; bool changesState; bool checksLengths; bool returnsPointers; bool takesAddress; }; struct DriverSpec { bool secureDevice; bool secureOpen; bool zeroesOutput; std::vector<IoctlSpec ioctls; }; std::vector<std::string audit(const DriverSpec& d); Findings, in this order (driver-wide first, then for each IOCTL in order, its findings in the order listed): - "device can be opened by anyone" if not secureDevice ; - "opens below the device skip the security check" if not secureOpen ; - "output buffers are not zeroed" if not zeroesOutput ; - for each IOCTL, prefixed with "<name : " : - "METHOD_NEITHER" if method == 3 ; - "changes state without write access" if changesState and the access lacks bit 1 ( FILE_WRITE_DATA is 2); - "lengths not checked" if not checksLengths ; - "returns kernel pointers" if returnsPointers ; - "accepts an address to access" if takesAddress .

title: 5.04  Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver
match: 5.04 Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver
body: How real drivers reach users - driver packages, INF files and catalogs, Microsoft's attestation and HLK signing through the Partner Center, Windows Update - and the alternatives that make most drivers unnecessary: user-mode services, ETW, UMDF and existing system features. Why everything must be signed Since Windows 10 version 1607, new kernel drivers load only when signed by Microsoft . A developer's own certificate is not enough: the driver is submitted to Microsoft, which signs it. Test signing (lesson 1.02) exists only for development machines. This requirement is a cornerstone of Windows security: it means every driver on a normal machine is traceable to a registered company, and drivers found to be malicious or vulnerable can be revoked and blocked. The driver package A driver is shipped as a package : File Purpose --- --- XenonLog.sys The driver XenonLog.inf Installation instructions: where files go, services and registry entries, version XenonLog.cat A catalog: hashes of the package's files, signed A minimal INF for a software driver: cpp-norun Version Signature = "$WINDOWS NT$" Class = System ClassGuid = {4d36e97d-e325-11ce-bfc1-08002be10318} Provider = %ProviderName% DriverVer = 11/15/2026,1.0.0.0 CatalogFile = XenonLog.cat PnpLockdown = 1 DestinationDirs DefaultDestDir = 13 ; the driver store DefaultInstall.NTamd64 CopyFiles = XenonLog.Files DefaultInstall.NTamd64.Services AddService = XenonLog,, XenonLog.Service XenonLog.Service ServiceType = 1 ; kernel driver StartType = 3 ; on demand ErrorControl = 1 ServiceBinary = %13%\XenonLog.sys ; ... XenonLog.Files , Strings DriverVer (date and four-part version) decides which of several packages Windows prefers; InfVerif (in the WDK) checks the INF for errors. The practice parses and checks the Version section. Getting Microsoft's signature Through the Partner Center (Windows Hardware Dev Center), with an EV code-signing certificate identifying your company: - Attestation signing : submit the package (signed with your EV certificate); Microsoft checks it and signs it. It loads on client Windows. Fast, no hardware tests. - HLK certification : run the Hardware Lab Kit tests and submit the results; required for Windows Server and for distribution through Windows Update with the "certified" status. Drivers must also pass the driver CodeQL checks (lesson 5.02) and the HVCI (memory integrity) compatibility requirements: no writable-and-executable memory, for example. Distribution Signed packages are installed with pnputil /add-driver XenonLog.inf /install , an installer that calls DiInstallDriver , or published through Windows Update for hardware drivers. Updating a driver means a new package with a higher DriverVer . When not to write a driver Every driver adds risk to every machine it runs on, needs Microsoft's signature, and is much harder to write and update than user-mode code. Before writing one, check the alternatives: Need Use instead --- --- Watching process creation, file and registry activity ETW providers (Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process and others), Windows Defender's and Sysmon's existing logging Talking to a USB device WinUSB or a UMDF user-mode driver Background work with system rights A Windows service Network filtering Windows Filtering Platform from user mode where possible Performance data ETW, performance counters This course's log driver is a teaching project: in practice, a user-mode program subscribing to the kernel's ETW process events gives the same information without any driver at all. Knowing how the kernel works is valuable for debugging, performance work and security; writing kernel code should be the last option, taken with everything this course has covered.

title: Checking an INF's Version section
where: 5.04 Signing, Distribution and When Not to Write a Driver
body: Write a small part of what InfVerif checks (lesson 5.04): read the Version section of an INF file, validate it, and compare DriverVer values. cpp struct DriverVer { int month, day, year; int v 4 ; }; struct VersionInfo { std::string signature, cls, provider, catalog; DriverVer ver; }; bool parseDriverVer(const std::string& text, DriverVer& out); // "11/15/2026,1.0.0.0" std::vector<std::string checkVersion(const std::string& inf, VersionInfo& out); int compareDriverVer(const DriverVer& a, const DriverVer& b); // -1, 0, 1: date first, then version The INF : lines ( \r\n allowed); ; starts a comment to the end of the line; blank lines are ignored; Name starts a section (names are case-insensitive); in a section, key = value with spaces around keys and values trimmed and keys compared ignoring case. Only Version matters here. parseDriverVer : MM/DD/YYYY,a.b.c.d with a valid date (month 1-12, day within the month, leap years counted, year 1900 or later), and four version parts 0-65535; the version part may also have fewer parts ( 1.2 ), the rest being 0. No spaces. checkVersion returns the problems found, in this order, or an empty list: - "no Version section" (then nothing else is checked); - "Signature must be $WINDOWS NT$" unless it is exactly that, ignoring case and with or without surrounding quotes; - "missing Class" , "missing Provider" , "missing CatalogFile" for each one that is absent or empty; - "bad DriverVer" if absent or invalid. It fills out with what it found (quotes around the signature removed).

title: How special pool catches bugs
body: Build a model of Driver Verifier's special pool (lesson 5.01) to see exactly how it turns silent memory bugs into immediate, explained failures. Each allocation gets its own page, placed so its last byte is right before an inaccessible guard page; the unused start of the page is filled with a pattern that is checked when the block is freed; freed pages become inaccessible. cpp class SpecialPool { public: explicit SpecialPool(std::size_t pageSize); int allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::uint32_t tag); std::string write(int handle, std::size_t offset, std::size_t length); std::string read(int handle, std::size_t offset, std::size_t length) const; void underrun(int handle, std::size_t bytesBefore); std::string free(int handle, std::uint32_t tag); int pagesInUse() const; std::vector<std::string unloadReport() const; }; - allocate returns handles 1, 2, 3, ... for 1 <= bytes <= pageSize (else 0, which is a failed allocation). The block occupies the last bytes bytes of a page of pageSize bytes; every byte before it is filled with 0xAA . - write and read describe an access to length bytes starting offset bytes into the block. In bounds: "" . An access that goes past the block's end touches the guard page and faults at once: "overrun by <n bytes" for a write, "read past the end by <n bytes" for a read, where n is how far past the end the access reaches. An access to a freed block: "write to freed memory" / "read of freed memory" . An unknown handle: "unknown handle" . (A successful write stores nothing in this model; only the bounds matter.) - underrun simulates a bug that writes bytesBefore bytes just before the block (into the fill area; at most the size of the fill area). It does not fault: special pool can only notice it later. - free : "unknown handle" , "double free" , or "tag mismatch" (the block stays allocated). Otherwise the page is released and becomes inaccessible, and the result is "ok" , or "underrun detected" if the fill pattern before the block was changed. - unloadReport lists the blocks never freed, grouped by tag, sorted by the tag's text (practice 3.01): "Cirn: 2 allocations, 96 bytes" ; empty if nothing leaked.

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- APC_LEVEL IRQL 1: asynchronous procedure calls run here; holding a fast mutex raises to it. (3.02) Attestation signing Microsoft signing a driver package submitted through the Partner Center, without hardware tests. (5.04) Bug check The system stopping because kernel code failed; the blue screen, with a code and four parameters. (1.05) Buffered I/O The I/O manager copying user data through a kernel system buffer. (2.04) Callback (notification) A driver function registered with a documented API, called on events such as process creation. (4.01) Catalog (.cat) A signed list of hashes of a driver package's files. (5.04) CONTAINING_RECORD Computes the address of a structure from the address of one of its members. (3.05) CTL_CODE The macro that builds an IOCTL's 32-bit code from device type, function, method and access. (2.03) Device object The object requests are sent to; a driver creates one and names it under \Device. (2.01) Direct I/O Locking the user's pages and describing them with an MDL instead of copying. (2.04) DISPATCH_LEVEL IRQL 2: DPCs and spin-lock holders run here; no waiting, no paged memory. (3.02) Dispatch routine The driver function that handles one kind of IRP (create, read, device control...). (2.02) DPC Deferred procedure call: a function queued to run soon at DISPATCH_LEVEL. (3.04) Driver object The object representing a loaded driver, with its dispatch table and Unload routine. (1.04) Driver Verifier A built-in tool that checks selected drivers and makes their bugs fail immediately. (5.01) DriverEntry A driver's entry point, called once when it is loaded. (1.04) ETW Event Tracing for Windows: the system-wide high-speed tracing infrastructure. (4.02) Fast mutex A lock for PASSIVE_LEVEL code that sleeps instead of spinning. (3.03) INF The text file that describes how to install a driver package. (5.04) IOCTL An I/O control request: a driver's own operations, sent with DeviceIoControl. (2.03) IRP I/O request packet: the structure carrying one request to a driver. (2.02) IRQL Interrupt request level: decides what code may run and do on a processor at a moment. (3.02) KDNET Kernel debugging over the network between host and target. (1.02) KMDF / UMDF Microsoft's kernel-mode and user-mode driver frameworks on top of WDM. (1.03) LIST_ENTRY The kernel's intrusive doubly linked list link. (3.05) Lookaside list A cache of freed fixed-size blocks for fast reuse. (3.05) MDL Memory descriptor list: describes the physical pages of a locked buffer. (2.04) METHOD_NEITHER Passing raw user pointers to the driver; best avoided. (2.04) Non-paged pool Kernel memory that is never paged out; required at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above. (3.01) NTSTATUS The 32-bit result of kernel functions; negative means failure. (1.03) Paged pool Kernel memory that can be paged out; only for PASSIVE_LEVEL and APC_LEVEL code. (3.01) PASSIVE_LEVEL IRQL 0: normal thread execution; everything is allowed. (3.02) Pending IRP A request marked pending and completed later; must be cancellable and finished before unload. (2.02) Pool tag Four characters attached to each pool allocation, used to find leaks and owners. (3.01) SAL Source annotation language: annotations that let analysis check buffers, IRQLs and results. (5.02) SDDL Security descriptor definition language, used to say who may open a device. (2.01) Special pool Verifier's allocator that puts each block against a guard page to catch overruns. (5.01) Spin lock A lock that busy-waits at DISPATCH_LEVEL; held only briefly. (3.03) Symbolic link A name in \?? that points to a device so user mode can open it as \\.\Name. (2.01) Test signing A development mode that loads drivers signed with a test certificate; only in the lab VM. (1.02) UNICODE_STRING The kernel's counted UTF-16 string, with lengths in bytes. (1.03) Unload The routine that undoes everything DriverEntry did, in reverse order. (1.04) WDK Windows Driver Kit: headers, libraries, tools and templates for building drivers. (1.03) WinDbg Microsoft's debugger, used for kernel debugging and crash dumps. (1.05) Work item Work queued to run at PASSIVE_LEVEL in a system worker thread. (3.04)

title: 1.01  What Lua Is and Running Code
match: 1.01 What Lua Is and Running Code
body: Where Lua came from and where it runs today (games, editors, databases, network tools), how a Lua program runs from top to bottom, print, comments, and how to read an error message. A language made to live inside programs Lua (Portuguese for moon ) was created in 1993 at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro by Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo and Waldemar Celes. They needed a small language that engineers could use to configure and script their programs, and they built one that fits in a few hundred kilobytes, starts instantly and is written in plain C. That design is why Lua turns up inside so many other programs. A program written in C or C++ embeds Lua: it carries the Lua interpreter along, and lets users write Lua scripts that call into it. You have probably used Lua without knowing: Where What Lua does there --- --- Roblox Its scripting language, Luau, grew out of Lua 5.1 World of Warcraft Every add-on and interface mod is Lua LÖVE, Defold, Solar2D Whole 2D games are written in Lua Neovim Its configuration and plugins are Lua Redis Scripts that run inside the database nginx (OpenResty), HAProxy Request handling in web servers Wireshark Protocol decoders Adobe Lightroom Much of the application itself This course teaches Lua 5.4 , the current standard version. What you learn carries over directly to Luau, LuaJIT and every embedded Lua; lesson 6.05 lists the differences. The first program lua print("Hello, Lua!") Hello, Lua! Press Run on any example in these lessons to run it yourself. print writes its arguments and ends the line. A Lua program is a list of statements run from the top down; there is no main to write. print takes any number of values and separates them with a tab : lua print("one", 2, 3.5) print() print("after an empty line") one 2 3.5 after an empty line Statements may end with ; , but nobody writes it. Line breaks do not matter to Lua either; you could put two statements on one line. Write one per line, indented with four spaces where something is inside something else. Comments lua -- Two dashes start a comment that runs to the end of the line. print("code") -- after code, too -- A long comment spans several lines. print("done") code done When something goes wrong Lua reads the whole file before it runs anything. A syntax error stops it from starting at all, and the message names the file, the line and what was wrong near where: lua-norun print("Hello" print("again") text main.lua:2: ')' expected (to close '(' at line 1) near 'print' The mistake is on line 1 (a missing ) ), but Lua only notices when it reaches line 2. Look at the line named and the line before it. A run-time error happens while the program runs. Everything before it has already happened: lua print("first") print(10 + nil) print("never printed") first lua: main.lua:2: attempt to perform arithmetic on a nil value stack traceback: main.lua:2: in main chunk The stack traceback lists where the program was, newest first. For now, the first line is the one to read: main.lua:2 and what went wrong. !tip Lua is case-sensitive print , Print and PRINT are three different names. Only the first one exists.

title: Your first program

body: Change the program so that it prints exactly these two lines: Hello, Xenon! Lua is ready. Press Run to try it, then Check .

title: 1.02  Values, Variables and Types
body: Lua's eight types and the type function, nil as "no value", local variables and why every variable should be local, assigning several variables at once, and swapping two values. Values have types, variables do not A variable in Lua is a name for a value. The value has a type; the variable does not, so the same variable can hold a number now and a string later: lua local x = 42 print(x, type(x)) x = "forty-two" print(x, type(x)) 42 number forty-two string type(v) returns the type's name as a string. Lua has eight types: Type Examples Used for --- --- --- nil nil "no value here" boolean true , false yes or no number 42 , 3.14 , -7 integers and decimals string "text" , 'text' text, and any bytes table {1, 2, 3} , {name = "Ada"} lists, dictionaries, records, objects: everything else function print , function() end code you can call userdata an open file data owned by C code thread a coroutine lesson 6.03 The first five come up on every page of this course. Tables get all of milestone 2. nil nil means "nothing". A variable that was never given a value holds nil , and so does a table field that does not exist: lua local score print(score) print(type(nil)) print(undefined_name) nil nil nil Reading a name nobody created is not an error in Lua: it is simply nil . That is convenient, and it is also how a typo hides: pirnt would be nil , and the error only appears when you try to call it. local Write local the first time you introduce a variable: lua local name = "Ada" local year = 1843 print(name .. " wrote the first program in " .. year) Ada wrote the first program in 1843 Without local , the assignment creates a global variable, visible to the whole program, including every other file and library it loads. Globals are slower and invite clashes between unrelated parts of a program. Lesson 3.05 covers scope in full; until then the rule is simple: !important Every new variable starts with local local count = 0 , never just count = 0 . The only things you make global on purpose are functions a task asks for by name. Names are letters, digits and _ , not starting with a digit. They are case-sensitive. A few words are reserved: text and break do else elseif end false for function goto if in local nil not or repeat return then true until while Several at once One assignment can set several variables. The values on the right are all worked out first, then assigned: lua local a, b, c = 1, 2, 3 print(a, b, c) local x, y = 10 -- y gets nil: there is no second value print(x, y) local p, q = 1, 2, 3 -- the extra 3 is dropped print(p, q) a, b = b, a -- swap, with no temporary variable print(a, b) 1 2 3 10 nil 1 2 2 1 Booleans true and false , the results of comparisons: lua local adult = 20 = 18 print(adult, type(adult), not adult) true boolean false Lesson 1.05 shows how decisions use them, and a rule that surprises people from other languages: in Lua, 0 and "" count as true . Only false and nil are false.

Rewrite it so that: - every variable is declared with local , - the two values are swapped with one multiple assignment, without temp , - it prints the same three lines as now. right left string nil number 3

title: 1.03  Numbers and Arithmetic
body: Integers and floats inside the one number type, the operators including / and // and ^, how % works with negatives, the math library, converting with tonumber and tostring, and rounding. Two kinds of number Every number has type number , but Lua 5.4 keeps two subtypes apart: whole-number integers (64-bit) and floats (decimals, 64-bit doubles). math.type tells them apart: lua print(math.type(3), math.type(3.0), math.type(1e3)) print(3 == 3.0) integer float float true An integer and a float with the same value are equal. The difference shows when you print them: a float always prints with a decimal point, so 3.0 prints as 3.0 . The operators Operator Meaning Example Result --- --- --- --- + - add, subtract, multiply 7 6 42 / division, always a float 7 / 2 , 6 / 2 3.5 , 3.0 // floor division: round down 7 // 2 , -7 // 2 3 , -4 % remainder 7 % 3 1 ^ power, always a float 2 ^ 10 1024.0 - negation -x lua print(7 / 2, 6 / 2, 7 // 2, 7.5 // 2) print(2 ^ 10, 10 % 3, -7 // 2, -7 % 3) 3.5 3.0 3 3.0 1024.0 1 -4 2 Integer operations stay integers ( + - // % with two integers). As soon as a float takes part, or you use / or ^ , the result is a float. // rounds down , towards minus infinity, so -7 // 2 is -4 , not -3 . % matches it: the result has the sign of the divisor, and a == (a // b) b + a % b always holds. That makes n % 2 == 0 a reliable even test, also for negative n . Precedence is the one from school: ^ first (and it groups right to left, 2^3^2 is 2^9 ), then unary minus and not , then / // % , then + - . Use brackets whenever it is not obvious. !warning -2 ^ 2 is -4.0 ^ binds tighter than the minus in front, so this is -(2 ^ 2) . Write (-2) ^ 2 for 4.0. The math library lua print(math.floor(3.7), math.ceil(3.2), math.abs(-5)) print(math.max(4, 9, 2), math.min(4, 9, 2)) print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi) print(math.maxinteger) print(math.fmod(7, 3), math.tointeger(5.0)) 3 4 5 9 2 4.0 3.1415926535898 9223372036854775807 1 5 math.floor and math.ceil return integers when they can. math.huge is infinity, and math.random(1, 6) gives a random whole number from 1 to 6. Integers wrap around past math.maxinteger (it becomes the most negative integer); floats do not wrap but lose precision past about 2^53. Text to number and back Input arrives as text. tonumber turns a string into a number, or gives nil if it cannot: lua print(tonumber("42"), tonumber("3.5"), tonumber(" 12 ")) print(tonumber("12abc"), tonumber("ff", 16), tonumber("1e2")) print(tostring(42) .. "!") 42 3.5 12 nil 255 100.0 42! Lua also converts on its own in arithmetic: "10" + 1 is 11 . Do not rely on that; convert input explicitly with tonumber and check for nil . Rounding and showing decimals There is no math.round . Round to the nearest whole number with math.floor(x + 0.5) . To show a number with a fixed number of decimals, use string.format : lua local price = 2.5 3.3333 print(price) print(string.format("%.2f", price)) print(math.floor(price + 0.5)) print(string.format("%d items", 3)) 8.33325 8.33 8 3 items %.2f means "a float with two decimals", %d a whole number. Lesson 4.04 covers every format. !warning %d needs a whole number string.format("%d", 3.5) is an error: "number has no integer representation". 3.0 is fine.

title: Seconds to a clock
body: Read a whole number of seconds and print it as hours, minutes and seconds, H:MM:SS . Minutes and seconds always have two digits; hours have as many as they need. Seconds? 3725 1:02:05 The prompt is Seconds? with a space after the question mark, written with io.write so the answer stays on the same line.

title: 1.04  Strings and Input
body:
Writing strings with quotes, escapes and long brackets, joining with .., the length operator , strings never changing, io.write versus print, and reading input with io.read and its formats. Writing strings Single and double quotes mean the same; pick the one that avoids escaping: lua local a = "It's fine" local b = 'She said "hi"' local c = "Tab:	Newline:
Backslash: \ Quote: "" print(a) print(b) print(c) It's fine She said "hi" Tab: Newline: Backslash: \ Quote: " A long string between and spans lines and takes everything literally, with no escapes. If the text itself contains , put the same number of = signs in both brackets: == ... == . lua local poem = Roses are red, the moon is "Lua". print(poem) Roses are red, the moon is "Lua". (A line break straight after is skipped.) Joining and measuring .. joins two strings. Numbers are turned into text automatically; anything else must go through tostring : lua local name = "Ada" local greeting = "Hello, " .. name .. "!" print(greeting) print("Total: " .. 3 4) print("Ready: " .. tostring(true)) print( greeting, "") Hello, Ada! Total: 12 Ready: true 11 0 gives a string's length in bytes . For plain English text that is the number of letters; for letters outside ASCII it is more (lesson 4.05). !warning Joining nil is an error "Hi " .. nil stops the program: "attempt to concatenate a nil value". It usually means a variable was never set, or input ran out. Strings never change. Every operation that seems to change one, like string.upper , returns a new string: lua local word = "lua" local loud = string.upper(word) print(word, loud, word:upper()) lua LUA LUA word:upper() is a shorter way of writing string.upper(word) . Milestone 4 uses it everywhere. print and io.write print adds tabs between values and a newline at the end. io.write writes exactly what you give it, nothing more, which is what you want for prompts and for building a line in pieces: lua io.write("Loading") io.write(".", ".", ".") io.write(" done
") io.write("Answer: ", 42, "
") Loading... done Answer: 42 Reading input io.read reads from the keyboard (standard input). Its argument says what to read: Call Reads Gives at the end of input --- --- --- io.read() or io.read("l") the next line, without its newline nil io.read("n") a number, skipping spaces and newlines before it nil (also if the text is not a number) io.read("L") the next line, with its newline nil io.read("a") everything that is left "" lua io.write("Your name? ") local name = io.read() io.write("Your age? ") local age = io.read("n") print("Hello, " .. name .. ". Next year you are " .. age + 1 .. ".") When you press Run , a console opens under the code and the program waits there for you to type each answer and press Enter. Several formats in one call return several values: local a, b = io.read("n", "n") reads two numbers from the same line or from two lines. !tip Reading a line, then a number io.read("n") leaves the rest of its line unread. If you read a number and then want the next full line, read once more with io.read() to finish the number's line first. Reading every line with io.read() and converting with tonumber avoids the problem.

title: A receipt line
body: Read three lines: an item's name, a quantity (a whole number) and a unit price (may have decimals). Print the receipt line: the quantity, x , the item, a colon, and the total with two decimals. Item? tea Quantity? 3 Price? 2.5 3 x tea: 7.50 The prompts are Item? , Quantity? and Price? (with a space after the question mark). The item's name can contain spaces.

title: Shout it

title: 1.05  Making Decisions
body: if, elseif and else, the comparison operators with ~= for "not equal", what counts as true (everything except false and nil), and, or and not and what they return, and the x or default idiom. if lua local temperature = 31 if temperature 30 then print("Hot") elseif temperature 15 then print("Mild") else print("Cold") end Hot if condition then ... end . Any number of elseif branches (one word), an optional else , and one end that closes the whole statement. The conditions are tested in order and only the first true branch runs. Comparing Operator Meaning --- --- == equal ~= not equal (not != ) < <= = order lua print(1 == 1.0, "a" == "a", 1 == "1") print(3 ~= 4, "apple" < "banana", "Z" < "a") true true false true true true Values of different types are never equal: 1 == "1" is false . Strings compare letter by letter by their byte values, so all capitals come before all lower-case letters. Comparing a number with a string using < is an error. What counts as true Lua's rule is short: false and nil are false. Everything else is true , including 0 , "" and an empty table. lua if 0 then print("0 is true") end if "" then print("empty text is true") end if nil then print("never") else print("nil is false") end 0 is true empty text is true nil is false !warning Coming from Python, C or JavaScript if count then does not test whether count is zero. It tests whether count exists. Write if count 0 then or if count ~= 0 then . and, or, not lua local age, member = 20, false if age = 18 and not member then print("Adult, not a member") end if age < 12 or age 65 then print("Discount") else print("Full price") end Adult, not a member Full price and and or stop as soon as the answer is known, and they return one of their operands , not just true or false : - a and b gives a if a is false or nil, otherwise b . - a or b gives a if a is true (anything but false/nil), otherwise b . lua print(nil or "default", "set" or "default") print(nil and "x", 5 and "x") print(false or nil, not nil, not 0) default set nil x nil true false That gives two idioms you will see in all Lua code: lua local name = nil local shown = name or "anonymous" -- a default for a missing value local score = 72 local result = score = 50 and "pass" or "fail" -- like a ? b : c print(shown, result) anonymous pass !warning The and-or trick fails when the middle value is false cond and false or "x" gives "x" even when cond is true, because true and false is false , and then or picks "x" . Use a full if when the "true" value can be false or nil . Checking input tonumber and io.read("n") give nil for bad input. Test for it before using the value: lua local answer = tonumber("12x") if answer == nil then print("That is not a number.") elseif answer % 2 == 0 then print(answer .. " is even") else print(answer .. " is odd") end That is not a number. if not answer then says the same as if answer == nil then here, since a number is never false .
