title: A pocket calculator
body: Write a calculator for one sum. It asks for a number, an operation and a second number, then prints the result: First number? 7 Operation (+ - / // % ^)? / Second number? 2 7 / 2 = 3.5 - The operations are + - / // % ^ . Read the operation as a whole line. - Print the result as Lua prints it: 7 // 2 = 3 , 2 ^ 10 = 1024.0 , 1.5 + 1 = 2.5 . - If either number is not a number, print That is not a number. and nothing else. - If the operation is not one of the seven, print Unknown operation: <what was typed . - / , // and % by zero print Cannot divide by zero. - After the result, print a second line describing it: The result is a whole number. when it is a whole number (also 1024.0 ), otherwise The result has decimals. Ask all three questions before printing any message, even when the first answer is already wrong.

title: 2.01  Loops
body: The numeric for loop with its start, stop and step, while and repeat-until, break, skipping to the next round with goto continue, and the loop variable belonging to the loop. The numeric for lua for i = 1, 5 do io.write(i, " ") end print() for i = 10, 1, -3 do io.write(i, " ") end print() for x = 0, 1, 0.25 do io.write(x, " ") end print() 1 2 3 4 5 10 7 4 1 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 (The third loop counts in floats, because its step is a float. io.write writes a float like 0.0 as plain 0 ; print and tostring would show 0.0 .) for i = start, stop, step do ... end . The step is 1 when left out, and may be negative. Both ends are included : for i = 1, 5 runs five times. The start, stop and step are worked out once, before the first round, so changing them inside the loop has no effect. A loop that cannot start does not run at all: for i = 5, 1 do runs zero times (the step is +1, and 5 is already past 1). The loop variable is local to the loop . After end it is gone, and assigning to it inside the loop does not change the number of rounds. lua local total = 0 for n = 1, 100 do total = total + n end print(total) 5050 while while repeats as long as its condition is true, checking it before each round: lua local n, steps = 27, 0 while n ~= 1 do if n % 2 == 0 then n = n // 2 else n = 3 n + 1 end steps = steps + 1 end print(steps) 111 repeat ... until repeat checks its condition after each round, so the body always runs at least once. It stops when the condition becomes true: lua local value = 1 repeat value = value 3 until value 100 print(value) 243 A local declared inside the body is still visible in the until condition, which makes repeat natural for "ask until the answer is valid": lua-norun local age repeat io.write("Age? ") age = tonumber(io.read()) until age and age = 0 break break leaves the innermost loop at once: lua for i = 2, 100 do if i i 50 then print("first square over 50: " .. i i) break end end first square over 50: 64 Skipping a round Lua has no continue . Use goto with a label at the end of the body: lua for i = 1, 10 do if i % 3 ~= 0 then goto continue end io.write(i, " ") ::continue:: end print() 3 6 9 ::continue:: is a label ; goto continue jumps to it. The name is your choice, but continue is what everyone writes. Often an if around the rest of the body reads just as well. Loops inside loops lua for row = 1, 3 do local line = "" for col = 1, 4 do line = line .. row col .. "\t" end print(line) end 1 2 3 4 2 4 6 8 3 6 9 12 break leaves only the inner loop. To leave both, put the loops in a function and return , or use a flag. Reading until input ends io.read() returns nil when there is no more input, which ends a while loop neatly: lua-norun local count = 0 local line = io.read() while line do count = count + 1 line = io.read() end print(count .. " lines") Lesson 6.02 shows the shorter for line in io.lines() do .

title: A multiplication square
body: Read a whole number n from 1 to 12 and print an n by n multiplication square. Every number takes 4 characters, right-aligned ( string.format("%4d", value) ), and each row is one line. Size? 4 1 2 3 4 2 4 6 8 3 6 9 12 4 8 12 16 If the number is outside 1 to 12, print Size must be 1 to 12.

title: Collatz steps
body: Read a whole number n greater than 0. Repeat: if n is even, halve it; if it is odd, make it 3n + 1. Stop at 1. Print every number on one line separated by spaces, starting with n itself, then the number of steps on a second line. Start? 6 6 3 10 5 16 8 4 2 1 8 steps

title: 2.02  Tables as Lists
body: The table as Lua's only data structure, lists that start at index 1, the length operator, adding and removing with table.insert and table.remove, ipairs, and why holes in a list break . One structure for everything Lua has exactly one way to group values: the table . A table maps keys to values. Used with the keys 1, 2, 3 and so on, it is a list (an array); with other keys it is a dictionary, a record or an object. This lesson is about lists. lua local fruits = { "apple", "banana", "cherry" } print(fruits 1 , fruits 3 , fruits) print(fruits 4 ) apple cherry 3 nil !important Lists start at 1 The first item is fruits 1 , the last is fruits fruits . fruits 0 is nil. Every library function counts from 1 too. t is the list's length. Reading past the end is not an error, it is nil . Changing a list lua local t = { 10, 20, 30 } t 2 = 25 -- replace t t + 1 = 40 -- add at the end table.insert(t, 50) -- add at the end table.insert(t, 1, 5) -- insert at position 1, the rest move up print(table.concat(t, ", ")) local last = table.remove(t) -- remove the last, and return it local first = table.remove(t, 1) -- remove position 1, the rest move down print(first, last, table.concat(t, ", ")) 5, 10, 25, 30, 40, 50 5 50 10, 25, 30, 40 table.concat(t, sep) joins a list of strings or numbers into one string. It is the quickest way to print a list; print(t) only shows something like table: 0x55d0c8a3e2a0 . Looping over a list lua local scores = { 72, 95, 64 } for i = 1, scores do print(i, scores i ) end for i, score in ipairs(scores) do print("score " .. i .. " is " .. score) end 1 72 2 95 3 64 score 1 is 72 score 2 is 95 score 3 is 64 ipairs(t) gives each position and its value, in order, from 1 until the first nil . Use _ for a value you do not need: for _, score in ipairs(scores) . Do not insert into or remove from a list while looping over it forwards; positions move under you. Loop backwards ( for i = t, 1, -1 ) when removing. Building a list lua local squares = {} for n = 1, 6 do squares squares + 1 = n n end print(table.concat(squares, " ")) local evens = {} for _, n in ipairs(squares) do if n % 2 == 0 then table.insert(evens, n) end end print( evens, table.concat(evens, " ")) 1 4 9 16 25 36 3 4 16 36 Holes A list must not have holes : nil in the middle. Setting an item to nil does not remove it from a list; it makes a hole, and then may give either end of the hole, and ipairs stops at it: lua local t = { "a", "b", "c", "d" } t 2 = nil for i, v in ipairs(t) do print(i, v) end 1 a To remove an item, use table.remove . To mark one as missing, store false or a special value, not nil . Tables are values you share A variable holds a reference to a table, not a copy. Two variables can name the same table: lua local a = { 1, 2, 3 } local b = a b 1 = 99 print(a 1 , a == b) print({ 1, 2 } == { 1, 2 }) 99 true false == on tables asks "the same table?", not "the same contents?". Lesson 2.05 shows how to copy and compare by content.

title: List tools
body: Fill in four functions that work on lists of numbers. None of them may change the list they are given. lua-norun sum(list) -- the total; 0 for an empty list largest(list) -- the biggest value, or nil for an empty list reversed(list) -- a NEW list with the items in the opposite order without(list, value) -- a NEW list with every item equal to value left out lua-norun sum({ 3, 4, 5 }) -- 12 largest({ 3, 9, 2 }) -- 9 reversed({ 1, 2, 3 }) -- { 3, 2, 1 } without({ 1, 2, 1, 3 }, 1) -- { 2, 3 }

title: 2.03  Tables as Dictionaries
body: Tables with any keys, the dot shorthand for string keys, records, adding and removing with nil, pairs and its order, counting and grouping, and using a table as a set. Any value can be a key A table's keys do not have to be 1, 2, 3. Any value except nil can be a key, most often a string: lua local ages = { "Ada" = 36, "Grace" = 85 } ages "Linus" = 21 -- add ages "Ada" = 37 -- replace ages "Grace" = nil -- remove print(ages "Ada" , ages "Grace" , ages "Nobody" ) 37 nil nil Setting a key to nil removes it: a table never stores nil values. Reading a key that is not there gives nil , so if ages name then tests whether a key exists. The dot shorthand When a key is a string that is a valid name, t.name means exactly t "name" , and in a constructor name = value means "name" = value : lua local book = { title = "Programming in Lua", year = 2016, pages = 388 } print(book.title, book "year" ) book.edition = 4 local field = "pages" print(book field , book.field) Programming in Lua 2016 388 nil The last line shows the classic mistake: book.field is the key "field" , not the value of the variable field . Use brackets when the key is in a variable. A table used like this is a record : one thing with named parts. Lists of records are the bread and butter of Lua programs: lua local people = { { name = "Ada", born = 1815 }, { name = "Alan", born = 1912 }, } for _, p in ipairs(people) do print(p.name .. " was born in " .. p.born) end Ada was born in 1815 Alan was born in 1912 A constructor can mix both kinds: { "a", "b", sep = ", " } has 1 , 2 and sep . pairs pairs(t) visits every key and value in a table: lua local stock = { apples = 4, pears = 0, plums = 12 } local total = 0 for fruit, count in pairs(stock) do total = total + count end print(total) 16 !warning pairs has no order The order of pairs is not the order you wrote the keys in, and may differ from run to run. When order matters, collect the keys in a list and sort it (next lesson), or keep a list beside the table. ipairs is for the list part (1, 2, 3... in order); pairs is for everything. t counts only the list part: stock above is 0. Counting and grouping Two patterns that come up all the time: lua local words = { "the", "cat", "and", "the", "hat" } local counts = {} for _, w in ipairs(words) do counts w = (counts w or 0) + 1 end print(counts.the, counts.cat, counts.dog) local by_letter = {} for _, w in ipairs(words) do local first = w:sub(1, 1) by_letter first = by_letter first or {} table.insert(by_letter first , w) end print(table.concat(by_letter.t, " "), by_letter.c) 2 1 nil the the 1 (counts w or 0) + 1 uses the or default from lesson 1.05: a missing count starts at 0. Sets A table whose values are all true is a set : it answers "is this in it?" instantly, however big it is. lua local vowels = { a = true, e = true, i = true, o = true, u = true } local text, n = "programming in lua", 0 for i = 1, text do if vowels text:sub(i, i) then n = n + 1 end end print(n .. " vowels") local seen = {} for _, w in ipairs({ "b", "a", "b", "c", "a" }) do seen w = true end local unique = 0 for _ in pairs(seen) do unique = unique + 1 end print(unique .. " different") 6 vowels 3 different To count the entries of a non-list table you have to loop with pairs ; does not count them.

title: Counting words
body: Fill in three functions for a word-counting tool. The words arrive already split, as a list of strings. lua-norun count_words(words) -- a table: word - how many times it appears most_common(counts) -- the word with the highest count and that count (two results); -- ties go to the word that comes first alphabetically; nil for an empty table unique_sorted(words) -- a list of the different words, sorted alphabetically lua-norun local counts = count_words({ "b", "a", "b" }) -- { b = 2, a = 1 } most_common(counts) -- "b", 2 unique_sorted({ "b", "a", "b" }) -- { "a", "b" }

title: 2.04  The Table Library
body: table.sort with and without a comparison function, sorting records and sorting by several keys, sorting a dictionary's keys for ordered output, table.concat, table.unpack and table.pack, and table.move. table.sort table.sort(t) sorts a list in place (it changes t and returns nothing), smallest first: lua local nums = { 5, 2, 9, 1, 7 } table.sort(nums) print(table.concat(nums, " ")) local names = { "lua", "C", "Rust", "ada" } table.sort(names) print(table.concat(names, " ")) 1 2 5 7 9 C Rust ada lua Strings sort by byte value, so capitals come first. For any other order, pass a comparison function : it gets two items and returns true when the first must come before the second. lua local nums = { 5, 2, 9, 1, 7 } table.sort(nums, function(a, b) return a b end) print(table.concat(nums, " ")) local names = { "lua", "C", "Rust", "ada" } table.sort(names, function(a, b) return a:lower() < b:lower() end) print(table.concat(names, " ")) 9 7 5 2 1 ada C lua Rust function(a, b) ... end written right inside the call is a function without a name; lesson 3.03 explains it. For now, read it as "the rule for the order". !warning The rule must be strict Return a < b , never a <= b . With <= two equal items each claim to come first, and table.sort can fail with "invalid order function for sorting". table.sort is also not stable: equal items may swap places. Sorting records lua local people = { { name = "Grace", age = 85 }, { name = "Ada", age = 36 }, { name = "Linus", age = 36 }, } table.sort(people, function(a, b) if a.age ~= b.age then return a.age < b.age end -- first by age return a.name < b.name -- then by name end) for _, p in ipairs(people) do print(p.age, p.name) end 36 Ada 36 Linus 85 Grace Comparing the first key and only falling back to the second when they are equal sorts by several keys at once, and also makes the order of equal ages predictable. Ordered output from a dictionary pairs has no order, so to print a dictionary sorted, collect its keys, sort them, then look each one up: lua local stock = { plums = 12, apples = 4, pears = 7 } local keys = {} for k in pairs(stock) do keys keys + 1 = k end table.sort(keys) for _, k in ipairs(keys) do print(k, stock k ) end apples 4 pears 7 plums 12 concat, unpack, pack, move lua local parts = { "2026", "11", "16" } print(table.concat(parts, "-")) print(table.concat(parts, "", 2, 3)) -- only items 2 to 3 print(table.unpack({ 10, 20, 30 })) local a, b = table.unpack({ 10, 20, 30 }) print(a + b) print(math.max(table.unpack({ 4, 9, 2 }))) local packed = table.pack("x", nil, "z") print(packed.n, packed 1 , packed 3 ) local src, dst = { 1, 2, 3 }, { "a", "b", "c", "d" } table.move(src, 1, 3, 2, dst) -- copy src 1..3 into dst from position 2 print(table.concat(dst, " ")) 2026-11-16 1116 10 20 30 30 9 3 x z a 1 2 3 - table.unpack(t) turns a list into separate values: what you need to pass a list to a function that takes separate arguments, like math.max . - table.pack(...) does the opposite and records the count in n , which matters when some values are nil . - table.move(a, from, to, at, b) copies a range, into another table or within the same one. table.concat only joins strings and numbers. A list containing true or a table is an error: convert with tostring first.

title: A leaderboard
body: Players are records such as { name = "Ada", score = 120 } . Fill in: lua-norun rank(players) -- sorts the list in place: highest score first, equal scores by name (A to Z), -- and returns the same table top(players, n) -- a NEW list of the names of the n best players (fewer if there are not n) sorted_keys(t) -- the keys of any table whose keys are strings, as a sorted list leaderboard(players) -- one string: "1. Ada 120" lines joined with "\n", in ranked order

title: 2.05  Nested Tables and Copies
body: Tables inside tables for grids and data, references and what really gets copied, shallow and deep copies, comparing tables by content, and printing a nested table so you can see it. Tables inside tables A table's values can be tables, which gives you any shape of data you need: lua local grid = { { 1, 2, 3 }, { 4, 5, 6 }, } print(grid 2 3 , grid, grid 1 ) local game = { player = { name = "Ada", hp = 30, items = { "sword", "lamp" } }, level = 3, } print(game.player.name, game.player.items 2 , game.player.items) game.player.hp = game.player.hp - 5 print(game.player.hp) 6 2 3 Ada lamp 2 25 Building a grid takes a loop for the rows and one for the columns. Every row must be its own table: lua local rows, cols = 3, 4 local board = {} for r = 1, rows do board r = {} for c = 1, cols do board r c = "." end end board 2 3 = " " for r = 1, rows do print(table.concat(board r )) end .... .. . .... What gets copied Assigning a table, passing it to a function or storing it inside another table never copies it . Every one of those is the same table: lua local row = { 0, 0, 0 } local bad = { row, row, row } -- the same row three times bad 1 1 = 9 print(bad 1 1 , bad 2 1 , bad 3 1 ) 9 9 9 Numbers, strings and booleans behave like separate copies (they cannot be changed in place anyway); tables and functions are shared. Copying A shallow copy makes a new table with the same keys and values. Nested tables inside are still shared: lua local function shallow_copy(t) local copy = {} for k, v in pairs(t) do copy k = v end return copy end local a = { 1, 2, inner = { 3 } } local b = shallow_copy(a) b 1 = 100 b.inner 1 = 300 print(a 1 , a.inner 1 ) 1 300 A deep copy copies the nested tables too. It calls itself for every table it meets (a function calling itself is recursion , lesson 3.04): lua local function deep_copy(t) if type(t) ~= "table" then return t end local copy = {} for k, v in pairs(t) do copy k = deep_copy(v) end return copy end local a = { 1, inner = { 2, deeper = { 3 } } } local b = deep_copy(a) b.inner.deeper 1 = 99 print(a.inner.deeper 1 , b.inner.deeper 1 ) 3 99 This simple version is fine for data. It does not handle a table that contains itself, and it does not copy metatables (milestone 5). Comparing by content == asks whether two tables are the same table. To ask whether they hold the same things, compare key by key, in both directions: lua local function same(a, b) if type(a) ~= "table" or type(b) ~= "table" then return a == b end for k, v in pairs(a) do if not same(v, b k ) then return false end end for k in pairs(b) do if a k == nil then return false end end return true end print(same({ 1, { 2, 3 } }, { 1, { 2, 3 } }), same({ 1, 2 }, { 1, 2, 3 })) true false The test kit's check_eq compares tables exactly this way, which is why your practice tests can say check_eq(result, { 1, 2, 3 }) . Seeing a nested table print(t) shows only an address. While you work, a small function that writes a table out helps a lot: lua local function show(v) if type(v) ~= "table" then return type(v) == "string" and string.format("%q", v) or tostring(v) end local parts = {} for _, item in ipairs(v) do parts parts + 1 = show(item) end local keys = {} for k in pairs(v) do if not (math.type(k) == "integer" and k = 1 and k <= v) then keys keys + 1 = k end end table.sort(keys, function(x, y) return tostring(x) < tostring(y) end) for _, k in ipairs(keys) do parts parts + 1 = tostring(k) .. " = " .. show(v k ) end return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ", ") .. "}" end print(show({ 1, "two", { 3 }, name = "Ada", ok = true })) {1, "two", {3}, name = "Ada", ok = true} Keep a function like this in your toolbox; you will reuse it in later practice.

title: Grids and copies
body: Fill in four functions for nested tables: lua-norun make_grid(rows, cols, fill) -- a list of rows, each a list of cols copies of fill; every row its own table transpose(grid) -- a NEW grid whose rows are the old columns deep_copy(t) -- a copy that shares no table with t, at any depth (values that are not tables are returned as they are) equal(a, b) -- true when a and b have the same contents at every depth lua-norun transpose({ { 1, 2, 3 }, { 4, 5, 6 } }) -- { { 1, 4 }, { 2, 5 }, { 3, 6 } } equal({ 1, { 2 } }, { 1, { 2 } }) -- true Assume tables never contain themselves.

title: A grade book
body: Write a program that collects students' scores and prints a report. It first asks how many students there are, then for each one their name and their score (a whole number from 0 to 100). Then it prints the report: the students ranked by score (highest first, equal scores by name A to Z), each with a letter grade, then the class average and how many got each grade. Students? 3 Name? Grace Score? 88 Name? Ada Score? 95 Name? Alan Score? 88 Report 1. Ada 95 A 2. Alan 88 B 3. Grace 88 B Average: 90.3 A: 1 B: 2 C: 0 D: 0 F: 0 - Grades: A for 90 and over, B 80-89, C 70-79, D 60-69, F below 60. - Each report line is string.format("%2d. %-10s %3d %s", position, name, score, grade) . - The average has one decimal. - A score that is not a whole number from 0 to 100 prints Invalid score, try again. and asks for that score again ( Score? ). - With 0 students, print Report , No students. and nothing else.

title: 3.01  Functions
body: Defining functions with function ... end, local functions, parameters and return, returning several values and where the extra values go, and functions that return nothing. Defining and calling lua local function greet(name) return "Hello, " .. name .. "!" end print(greet("Ada")) print(greet("Lua")) Hello, Ada! Hello, Lua! local function name(parameters) ... end defines a function. return hands a value back to the caller and leaves the function at once. A function is defined when Lua runs the definition, so define it above the code that calls it. Like variables, functions should be local unless something else needs to find them by name. In the practice tasks, the functions the task names are global ( function greet(name) ) so the tests can call them. Parameters A parameter is a local variable that starts with the value the caller passed. Lua does not check how many arguments you pass: missing ones are nil , extra ones are dropped. lua local function describe(name, age) return name .. " is " .. tostring(age) end print(describe("Ada", 36)) print(describe("Ada")) print(describe("Ada", 36, "ignored")) Ada is 36 Ada is nil Ada is 36 The next lesson uses this to give parameters default values. Returning several values A function can return several values, and the caller can take as many as it wants: lua local function min_max(list) local lo, hi = list 1 , list 1 for _, v in ipairs(list) do if v < lo then lo = v end if v hi then hi = v end end return lo, hi end local lo, hi = min_max({ 4, 9, 2, 7 }) print(lo, hi) local just_lo = min_max({ 4, 9, 2, 7 }) print(just_lo) 2 9 2 Lua's own functions do this too: string.find returns a start and an end, pcall returns a success flag and a result. Where the extra values go Every value of a call is kept only when the call is the last item in a list (of arguments, of a table constructor, of a return ). Anywhere else, the call is cut down to its first value: lua local function two() return 1, 2 end print(two()) -- 1 2 print(two(), "x") -- 1 x : not last, so only the first value print("x", two()) -- x 1 2 print((two())) -- 1 : brackets cut it to one value local t = { two(), two() } print( t) -- 3 : {1, 1, 2} 1 2 1 x x 1 2 1 3 Functions that return nothing A function without return , or with a plain return , returns no values. Using its result gives nil : lua local function log(message) print(" log " .. message) end local result = log("started") print(result) log started nil !warning Printing is not returning A function that prints its answer cannot be used in a calculation. When a task says "returns", use return ; the tests read the returned value, not the printed text. return must be the last statement in its block. To leave a function early from the middle, put it inside an if , which is the usual way anyway: lua local function sign(n) if n 0 then return 1 end if n < 0 then return -1 end return 0 end print(sign(-5), sign(0), sign(8)) -1 0 1

title: Several results
body: Write three functions that each return more than one value, or a value worked out in steps: lua-norun stats(list) -- three results: the smallest value, the largest, and the mean (average); nil for an empty list clamp(x, lo, hi) -- x, but no lower than lo and no higher than hi divmod(a, b) -- two results: a // b and a % b lua-norun stats({ 4, 9, 2 }) -- 2, 9, 5.0 clamp(15, 0, 10) -- 10 divmod(17, 5) -- 3, 2

title: 3.02  Optional and Variable Arguments
body: Default values with or, when or is wrong for booleans, functions that take any number of arguments with ..., select and table.pack, and named arguments passed in a table. Defaults A missing argument is nil , and x or default replaces nil : lua local function repeat_text(text, times, sep) times = times or 2 sep = sep or " " local parts = {} for i = 1, times do parts i = text end return table.concat(parts, sep) end print(repeat_text("ha")) print(repeat_text("ha", 3)) print(repeat_text("ha", 3, "-")) ha ha ha ha ha ha-ha-ha !warning or swallows false verbose = verbose or true makes verbose true even when the caller passed false . For a boolean (or any parameter where false is meaningful), test for nil: if verbose == nil then verbose = true end . Any number of arguments Three dots as the last parameter collect every extra argument. Inside the function, ... stands for all of them: lua local function sum(...) local total = 0 for _, n in ipairs({ ... }) do total = total + n end return total end print(sum(), sum(5), sum(1, 2, 3, 4)) 0 5 10 { ... } packs them into a list. Named parameters can come first: local function printf(format, ...) . lua local function printf(format, ...) io.write(string.format(format, ...)) end printf("%s has %d items, %.1f%% full\n", "bag", 3, 37.5) bag has 3 items, 37.5% full Passing ... on to another function forwards every value unchanged. ( %% in a format is a literal % .) nil among the arguments { ... } and ipairs stop at the first nil , so they lose arguments after one. When nil can be an argument, use select or table.pack : lua local function count(...) return select(" ", ...) end print(count(1, nil, 3), count()) local function show_all(...) local args = table.pack(...) for i = 1, args.n do io.write(i, "=", tostring(args i ), " ") end print() end show_all("a", nil, "c") print(select(2, "a", "b", "c")) 3 0 1=a 2=nil 3=c b c - select(" ", ...) is the number of arguments, nils included. - select(n, ...) gives argument n and everything after it . - table.pack(...) gives a table with the count in its field n . Named arguments When a function has many optional settings, take a single table and read fields from it. The call reads almost like a sentence, and you can leave out anything: lua local function make_window(options) local title = options.title or "Untitled" local width = options.width or 640 local height = options.height or 480 return title .. " (" .. width .. "x" .. height .. ")" end print(make_window({ title = "Editor", width = 1024 })) print(make_window{ height = 200 }) Editor (1024x480) Untitled (640x200) When a function's only argument is a table constructor or a string literal, the brackets can be left out: make_window{ ... } , print "hi" . You will see this in configuration files and in libraries. Use it sparingly in your own code.

title: Optional and many arguments
body: Write four functions: lua-norun greet(name, greeting) -- "Hello, Ada!"; greeting defaults to "Hello", name to "there" join(sep, ...) -- every argument after sep, turned into text with tostring and joined with sep; -- nil arguments count too: join("-", 1, nil, 3) is "1-nil-3" count_args(...) -- how many arguments were passed, nils included pad(options) -- options.text padded with spaces to options.width (default 10); -- options.align is "left" (default) or "right"; text longer than width is unchanged lua-norun pad{ text = "hi", width = 5 } -- "hi " pad{ text = "hi", width = 5, align = "right" } -- " hi"

title: 3.03  Functions as Values and Closures
body: Functions are values you can store, pass and return, anonymous functions, writing map, filter and reduce, closures that remember the variables around them, counters and factories, and the loop variable being fresh each round. Functions are values local function add(a, b) ... end is a shorter way of writing local add = function(a, b) ... end . A function is a value of type function , like a number or a table, so it can be stored in variables and tables, passed to other functions and returned from them: lua local function double(x) return x 2 end local twice = double print(twice(21), type(double)) local ops = { add = function(a, b) return a + b end, mul = function(a, b) return a b end, } print(ops.add(2, 3), ops "mul" (2, 3)) 42 function 5 6 A function written without a name ( function(a, b) ... end ) is an anonymous function . You met one already as the comparison passed to table.sort . Functions that take functions A function that takes or returns another function is a higher-order function. The three classic ones work on lists: lua local function map(list, f) local out = {} for i, v in ipairs(list) do out i = f(v) end return out end local function filter(list, keep) local out = {} for _, v in ipairs(list) do if keep(v) then out out + 1 = v end end return out end local function reduce(list, f, start) local acc = start for _, v in ipairs(list) do acc = f(acc, v) end return acc end local nums = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 } print(table.concat(map(nums, function(x) return x x end), " ")) print(table.concat(filter(nums, function(x) return x % 2 == 0 end), " ")) print(reduce(nums, function(a, b) return a + b end, 0)) 1 4 9 16 25 36 2 4 6 21 Lua has none of these built in; programs write them (or take them from a library) when they want them. Closures A function can use the local variables of the function it was written inside, even after that outer function has returned. The inner function together with the variables it remembers is a closure : lua local function make_counter() local count = 0 return function() count = count + 1 return count end end local a = make_counter() local b = make_counter() print(a(), a(), a()) print(b()) 1 2 3 1 Each call of make_counter creates a new count , and the returned function keeps it alive. a and b have separate counters. The remembered variables are called upvalues . Closures are how Lua code keeps private state without objects: lua local function make_multiplier(factor) return function(x) return x factor end end local triple = make_multiplier(3) local half = make_multiplier(0.5) print(triple(7), half(7)) 21 3.5 Shared, not copied A closure shares the variable itself, not a copy of its value. Two closures made in the same call share the same variable: lua local function make_account(balance) local function deposit(n) balance = balance + n end local function get() return balance end return deposit, get end local deposit, get = make_account(100) deposit(25) deposit(5) print(get()) 130 The loop variable of a for is a new local in every round, so closures made in a loop each remember their own value: lua local buttons = {} for i = 1, 3 do buttons i = function() return "button " .. i end end print(buttons 1 (), buttons 3 ()) button 1 button 3 (In some languages every one of those would say "button 3". In Lua each round has its own i .)

title: Functions that take and make functions
match: Functions that take and make functions
body: Write five higher-order functions: lua-norun map(list, f) -- a new list of f(item) for every item filter(list, keep) -- a new list of the items for which keep(item) is true reduce(list, f, start) -- f(f(f(start, a), b), c)... for the items a, b, c; start when the list is empty compose(f, g) -- a function that returns f(g(x)) make_counter(start, step) -- a function that returns start the first time it is called, -- then start + step, start + 2 step...; step defaults to 1 lua-norun local inc_then_double = compose(function(x) return x 2 end, function(x) return x + 1 end) inc_then_double(4) -- 10 local c = make_counter(10, 5) c(), c(), c() -- 10, 15, 20

title: 3.04  Recursion
body: Functions that call themselves, the base case, why a local recursive function needs local function, walking nested tables, speeding up repeated work with memoisation, and Lua's proper tail calls. A function that calls itself A recursive function solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of the same problem. It needs a base case that stops, and every other call must move towards it: lua local function factorial(n) if n <= 1 then return 1 end -- base case return n factorial(n - 1) -- a smaller problem end print(factorial(5), factorial(20)) 120 2432902008176640000 local function factorial matters here. It declares the local name first, then the function, so the body can see factorial . Written as local factorial = function(n) ... factorial(n - 1) ... end , the name inside refers to a global factorial that does not exist yet, and the call fails. Without a base case (or with one the calls never reach) the program fails with "stack overflow" after about 200,000 nested calls. Walking nested data Recursion fits data that contains smaller versions of itself, like tables in tables: lua local function sum_all(t) local total = 0 for _, v in pairs(t) do if type(v) == "table" then total = total + sum_all(v) else total = total + v end end return total end print(sum_all({ 1, 2, { 3, 4, { 5 } }, { 6 } })) local function depth(t) if type(t) ~= "table" then return 0 end local deepest = 0 for _, v in pairs(t) do deepest = math.max(deepest, depth(v)) end return deepest + 1 end print(depth({ 1, { 2, { 3 } } }), depth({}), depth(5)) 21 3 1 0 A tree of files and folders, a menu with sub-menus, a parsed expression: the shape is always "a value, or a table of more of the same". Remembering answers The direct recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values over and over, so it gets slow very fast: lua local calls = 0 local function slow_fib(n) calls = calls + 1 if n < 2 then return n end return slow_fib(n - 1) + slow_fib(n - 2) end print(slow_fib(25), calls) 75025 242785 Memoisation stores each answer in a table the first time and looks it up afterwards: lua local memo = {} local function fib(n) if n < 2 then return n end if memo n then return memo n end local result = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) memo n = result return result end print(fib(25), fib(90)) 75025 2880067194370816120 From hundreds of thousands of calls down to about a hundred. Tail calls When a function's very last action is return f(args) , Lua does not keep the current call around while f runs: it replaces it. Such a tail call uses no extra stack, so a tail-recursive function can run any number of times: lua local function count_down(n) if n == 0 then return "done" end return count_down(n - 1) -- a tail call end print(count_down(1000000)) done return n f(n - 1) is not a tail call (the multiplication still has to happen afterwards), and neither is return (f(x)) or f(x); return . Only return f(args) exactly.

title: Recursive functions
body: Write four functions, each one calling itself: lua-norun sum_digits(n) -- the sum of the decimal digits of a whole number n = 0: sum_digits(4096) is 19 to_binary(n) -- the binary digits of a whole number n = 0 as a string: to_binary(10) is "1010", to_binary(0) is "0" flatten(list) -- a new flat list of every value in list and in the lists inside it, in order paths(rows, cols) -- the number of ways from the top-left to the bottom-right corner of a rows x cols grid, -- moving only right or down paths(r, c) is paths(r - 1, c) + paths(r, c - 1) , and 1 when r or c is 1. The tests ask for paths(17, 17) , which takes far too long unless the function remembers answers it has already worked out.

title: 3.05  Scope, Globals and Blocks
body: Where a local is visible, blocks and do ... end, shadowing, how globals live in the table _G, why a typo creates a global, the const and close attributes of Lua 5.4, and keeping a file's names private. A local lives in its block A local variable is visible from the line after its declaration to the end of the block it is in. Every then ... end , loop body, function body and do ... end is a block: lua local x = "outer" do local x = "inner" -- a new x, hiding the outer one local y = 1 print(x, y) end print(x, y) inner 1 outer nil do ... end makes a block on its own, which is useful to keep helper variables from leaking. The inner x shadows the outer one: same name, different variable. Shadowing is legal but confusing; prefer new names. Globals are a table A name that is not a local is a global , and globals are simply fields of a table called _G : lua score = 10 -- no local: a global print(_G.score, _G "score" ) _G.level = 3 print(level) print(type(_G.print), _G.math.pi 3) 10 10 3 function true print , math , string , table and the rest of the standard library are globals too: entries in _G . That has a consequence: lua local function total(list) sum = 0 -- forgot local for _, v in ipairs(list) do sum = sum + v end return sum end print(total({ 1, 2, 3 }), sum) 6 6 sum leaked out of the function into the whole program. A second function using its own sum would silently trample this one. Misspell a variable ( totl = totl + 1 ) and you get a global, plus an "arithmetic on a nil value" error much later. !tip Finding accidental globals Run luac -l -p file.lua (shipped with Lua) and look for SETTABUP lines: each one writes a global. Editors with a Lua language server underline undefined globals as you type. Lesson 5.02 shows how to make reading a missing global an error. Locals are also faster than globals: a local lives in a register, a global is a table lookup every time. That is why Lua code often starts with local insert = table.insert . const and close Lua 5.4 adds two attributes for locals: lua local LIMIT <const = 100 print(LIMIT 2) -- LIMIT = 5 would not compile: attempt to assign to const variable 'LIMIT' 200 <const makes assigning to the variable a compile-time error. <close is for resources: when the block ends, Lua calls the value's __close metamethod, so a file or lock is released even if an error happens. Lesson 6.04 uses it with files. Private names in a file A file is a block too. A local at the top of a file is visible to the rest of that file and to nothing else. A module (lesson 5.05) keeps its helpers local and hands out only what it returns: lua-norun -- shapes.lua local function square(x) return x x end -- private helper local M = {} function M.circle_area(r) return math.pi square(r) end return M Upvalues and blocks together A block can create private state for a function, with no global and no outer variable involved: lua local next_id do local last = 0 next_id = function() last = last + 1 return "id" .. last end end print(next_id(), next_id(), last) id1 id2 nil last is invisible outside the do block, but the closure keeps it alive.

title: Leaking globals
body: These two functions give the right answers, but every variable inside them is accidentally global: after one call, total , count , best and the others are visible to the whole program, and a second function using the same names would trample them. Fix them so that the only globals they create are the two functions themselves.

title: A function toolkit
body: Build a small library of tools that wrap other functions, the kind every larger Lua program ends up with. Write them as fields of a module table and return it: lua-norun local fn = {} -- ... return fn Function Returns --- --- fn.memoize(f) a function like f (one argument) that calls f only once per different argument, and gives the remembered result after that, even when the result is nil or false fn.once(f) a function that calls f the first time (with its arguments, returning all its results) and afterwards returns those same results without calling f fn.partial(f, ...) a function that calls f with the given arguments first, followed by its own arguments fn.pipe(...) a function that passes its argument through every given function from left to right; with no functions it returns its argument unchanged fn.count_calls(f) two results: a function that calls f and passes back all its results, and a function that returns how many times it has been called lua-norun local add = function(a, b, c) return a + b + (c or 0) end fn.partial(add, 1)(2) -- 3 fn.partial(add, 1, 2)(3) -- 6 fn.pipe(math.abs, math.sqrt)(-16) -- 4.0

title: 4.01  The String Library
body: Method syntax s:upper(), sub with positive and negative positions, upper, lower, rep, reverse, byte and char, find with plain text, and walking through a string character by character. Method syntax Every string function lives in the table string , and every string knows it. So string.upper(s) can be written s:upper() : the colon passes the string as the first argument. lua local s = "Hello, Lua" print(string.upper(s), s:upper(), s:lower()) print(("abc"):rep(3), ("abc"):rep(3, "-"), s:reverse()) print(s:len(), s) HELLO, LUA HELLO, LUA hello, lua abcabcabc abc-abc-abc auL ,olleH 10 10 A string literal needs brackets around it before the colon: ("abc"):rep(3) . sub: pieces of a string s:sub(i, j) returns the characters from position i to j , both included , counting from 1. Negative positions count from the end: -1 is the last character. lua local s = "programming" print(s:sub(1, 3), s:sub(4), s:sub(-4), s:sub(-4, -2)) print(s:sub(5, 5), s:sub(20), s:sub(3, 1) == "") pro gramming ming min r true sub never fails: positions past the end are clamped, and an empty range gives "" . To get one character, use s:sub(i, i) . Characters and their codes s:byte(i) gives the numeric code of the byte at position i ; string.char turns codes back into text: lua print(("A"):byte(), ("abc"):byte(1, 3)) print(string.char(72, 105, 33)) local shifted = {} for i = 1, "HAL" do shifted i = string.char(("HAL"):byte(i) + 1) end print(table.concat(shifted)) 65 97 98 99 Hi! IBM Walking through a string lua local word = "banana" local count = 0 for i = 1, word do if word:sub(i, i) == "a" then count = count + 1 end end print(count) local reversed = {} for i = word, 1, -1 do reversed reversed + 1 = word:sub(i, i) end print(table.concat(reversed)) 3 ananab Building a new string by .. -ing one character at a time works but copies the whole string each time. For anything long, collect the pieces in a table and table.concat once at the end. find s:find(text, start, true) looks for text and returns where it starts and ends, or nil : lua local s = "one, two, three" print(s:find("two", 1, true)) print(s:find("four", 1, true)) print(s:find(",", 6, true)) print(s:find(".", 1, true), s:find(".")) 6 8 nil 9 9 nil 1 1 The fourth argument true means plain search. Without it, the text is a pattern (next lesson), where . means "any character", which is why the last find(".") matched at 1. Always pass 1, true when you are searching for literal text that might contain . % - + ? ( ) ^ $ . Using find to split at a separator: lua local function split_once(s, sep) local at = s:find(sep, 1, true) if not at then return s, nil end return s:sub(1, at - 1), s:sub(at + sep) end print(split_once("key=value", "=")) print(split_once("no separator", "=")) key value no separator nil Comparing and testing lua local a, b = "Lua", "lua" print(a == b, a:lower() == b:lower()) print(("hello"):sub(1, 2) == "he", ("file.txt"):sub(-4) == ".txt") false true true true

title: String helpers
body: Write five small string functions with the string library (no patterns needed yet): lua-norun capitalize(s) -- first character upper case, the rest lower case: "hELLO" - "Hello" starts_with(s, prefix) -- true when s begins with prefix (prefix may contain any characters, such as "." or "%") ends_with(s, suffix) -- true when s ends with suffix count_char(s, c) -- how many times the one-character string c appears in s is_palindrome(s) -- true when s reads the same backwards, ignoring case and everything that is not a letter lua-norun is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama") -- true starts_with("v1.2", "v1.") -- true

title: 4.02  Patterns
body: Lua patterns as a small alternative to regular expressions, the character classes %d %a %s %w and friends, sets in square brackets, the repeat signs + - ?, anchors, captures, and string.match. A small language for text Lua does not have regular expressions. It has patterns , which do most of the same work with a much smaller set of rules. string.match(s, pattern) returns the first part of s that matches, or nil : lua print(("order 66 shipped"):match("%d+")) print(("hello"):match("%d+")) print(("Version 5.4.7"):match("%d+%.%d+")) 66 nil 5.4 Character classes Class Matches Upper case = the opposite --- --- --- . any character %a letters %A not a letter %d digits 0-9 %D %l / %u lower / upper case letters %s whitespace (space, tab, newline) %S %w letters and digits %W %p punctuation %P %x hex digits % also escapes the special characters: %. is a real dot, %% a real percent sign, %- a real minus. (Lua uses % where other languages use \ .) A set in square brackets matches one character from it: aeiou a vowel, %w_ a letter, digit or underscore, 0-9a-f a range. ^... matches any character not in the set: ^, anything but a comma. Repeats Sign Means --- --- + one or more, as many as possible zero or more, as many as possible - zero or more, as few as possible ? optional: zero or one lua local s = "<b bold</b and <i it</i " print(s:match("<. ")) -- greedy: as much as possible print(s:match("<.- ")) -- lazy: as little as possible print(("-42"):match("^-?%d+$"), ("4-2"):match("^-?%d+$")) <b bold</b and <i it</i <b -42 nil Repeat signs apply to one character class only. Lua patterns cannot repeat a group: there is no (ab)+ . When you need that, use a loop or a real parser. Anchors ^ at the start of a pattern means "only at the start of the text", $ at the end means "only at the end". With both, the whole text must match, which is how you validate input: lua local function is_whole_number(s) return s:match("^%d+$") ~= nil end local function is_name(s) return s:match("^ %a_ %w_ $") ~= nil end print(is_whole_number("123"), is_whole_number("12a"), is_whole_number("")) print(is_name("player_1"), is_name("1player")) true false false true false Captures Brackets mark captures : the parts you want back. match then returns each capture instead of the whole match: lua local date = "2026-11-16" local y, m, d = date:match("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)") print(y, m, d, tonumber(m) + 1) local key, value = (" volume = 11 "):match("^%s (%w+)%s =%s (.-)%s $") print(" " .. key .. " ", " " .. value .. " ") print(("John Smith"):match("(%a+) (%a+)")) 2026 11 16 12 volume 11 John Smith Captures are always strings: convert numbers with tonumber . %s (.-)%s $ is the standard way to capture something with the spaces around it trimmed. Trimming on its own is so common it is worth writing once: lua local function trim(s) return (s:match("^%s (.-)%s $")) end print(" " .. trim(" padded text ") .. " ") padded text find works with patterns too and returns the position followed by the captures: lua print(("x = 10"):find("(%d+)")) 5 6 10

title: Validating and parsing
body: Write four functions with string.match and patterns: lua-norun trim(s) -- s without spaces, tabs and newlines at either end is_identifier(s) -- true when s is a valid Lua name: a letter or _, then letters, digits or _ parse_time(s) -- "HH:MM" (hour with 1 or 2 digits, minutes with exactly 2) - two numbers, hour and minute; -- nil when the text is not in that form or the hour is over 23 or the minutes over 59 parse_setting(line) -- "key = value" - key, value, both trimmed; the key is an identifier, the value anything -- (it may be empty); nil when the line has no = or the key is not an identifier lua-norun parse_time("9:05") -- 9, 5 parse_time("24:00") -- nil parse_setting(" volume = 11 ") -- "volume", "11" parse_setting("title=My Game") -- "title", "My Game" Do not check whether is_identifier names a reserved word.

title: 4.03  gmatch and gsub
body:
Looping over every match with gmatch, splitting text into words, lines and fields, replacing with gsub using a string, %1 captures, a table or a function, counting replacements, and %f for whole words. gmatch: every match s:gmatch(pattern) gives every match in turn, for use in a for loop: lua local text = "The quick brown fox, the lazy dog." local words = {} for word in text:gmatch("%a+") do words words + 1 = word:lower() end print( words, table.concat(words, " ")) for key, value in ("a=1, b=22, c=333"):gmatch("(%w+)=(%w+)") do io.write(key, "- ", value, " ") end print() 7 the quick brown fox the lazy dog a- 1 b- 22 c- 333 With captures in the pattern, each round gets the captures. Splitting Lua has no split function; gmatch with a "not the separator" set does it: lua local function split(s, sep) local out = {} for field in (s .. sep):gmatch("(.-)" .. sep:gsub("%p", "%%%0")) do out out + 1 = field end return out end local parts = split("red,green,,blue", ",") print( parts, table.concat(parts, " ")) for line in ("first
second
third"):gmatch(" ^
 +") do io.write("<", line, " ") end print() local nums = {} for n in ("4 8 15 16"):gmatch("%S+") do nums nums + 1 = tonumber(n) end print( nums, nums 3 + nums 4 ) 4 red green blue <first <second <third 4 31 The split function keeps empty fields ( ,, gives "" ): adding one separator at the end makes every field end with a separator, and (.-) then takes each field up to it. sep:gsub("%p", "%%%0") escapes punctuation in the separator so that "." means a real dot. When you only need the non-empty pieces, ^, + and %S+ are simpler. gsub: replacing s:gsub(pattern, replacement) returns a new string with every match replaced, and the number of replacements: lua print(("hello world"):gsub("o", "0")) print(("hello world"):gsub("o", "0", 1)) local cleaned = ("too many spaces"):gsub("%s+", " ") print(cleaned) hell0 w0rld 2 hell0 world 1 too many spaces The optional fourth argument limits the number of replacements. Because gsub returns two values, print(s:gsub(...)) shows the count too; assign to one variable, or wrap it in brackets, to keep only the string. Using the captures In the replacement string, %1 is the first capture, %2 the second, %0 the whole match: lua print(("2026-11-16"):gsub("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)", "%3/%2/%1")) print(("John Smith"):gsub("(%a+) (%a+)", "%2, %1")) print(("cat dog"):gsub("%a+", "<%0 ")) 16/11/2026 1 Smith, John 1 <cat <dog 2 A table or a function as the replacement With a table , each match is looked up in it; a match with no entry is left alone. With a function , it is called with the captures and its result is used (returning nil or false keeps the original): lua local vars = { name = "Ada", lang = "Lua" } print((("Hi $name, welcome to $lang. $missing stays."):gsub("%$(%w+)", vars))) local function title_case(s) return (s:gsub("(%a)(%a )", function(first, rest) return first:upper() .. rest:lower() end)) end print(title_case("the LORD of the rings")) print((("1 2 3 4"):gsub("%d+", function(n) return tostring(tonumber(n) 10) end))) Hi Ada, welcome to Lua. $missing stays. The Lord Of The Rings 10 20 30 40 Templates, escaping, renaming: almost every text tool in Lua is a gsub with a function. Counting The second result of gsub makes counting easy. Replace each match with itself ( "%0" ) or with anything, and keep only the count: lua local text = "she sells sea shells" local _, s_count = text:gsub("s", "s") local _, words = text:gsub("%S+", "") print(s_count, words) 6 4 Whole words %f set is a frontier : it matches the empty position where the previous character is not in the set and the next one is. %f %w word%f %W finds word only as a whole word: lua local s = "cat concat cat's catalogue" print((s:gsub("%f %w cat%f %W ", "DOG"))) DOG concat DOG's catalogue

body: Write four functions: lua-norun split(s, sep) -- the pieces of s between each sep, keeping empty pieces; sep is plain text -- (it may be "." or "%" and means that character); split("a,,b", ",") is { "a", "", "b" } words(s) -- the words of s in lower case, as a list; a word is a run of letters and apostrophes fill(template, values) -- every {name} in template replaced by tostring(values name ); -- a {name} with no value is left as it is title_case(s) -- the first letter of every word upper case, the rest of the word lower case lua-norun words("Don't PANIC, it's fine.") -- { "don't", "panic", "it's", "fine" } fill("{who} has {n} items", { who = "Ada", n = 3 }) -- "Ada has 3 items" title_case("the LORD of the rings") -- "The Lord Of The Rings"

title: 4.04  string.format and Building Text
body: The format directives %d %s %f %x %q, width, padding, alignment and precision, lining up a table of text, building long strings with a buffer table, and turning values into text with tostring and %q. string.format string.format(template, ...) fills the template's directives with the values, in order: lua print(string.format("%s is %d years old", "Ada", 36)) print(string.format("Pi is about %.3f", math.pi)) print(string.format("%d%% done", 75)) print(("%s = %s"):format("x", 10)) Ada is 36 years old Pi is about 3.142 75% done x = 10 Directive Shows Example Result --- --- --- --- %d a whole number ("%d"):format(42) 42 %f a float, 6 decimals by default ("%.2f"):format(2/3) 0.67 %g a number, short form ("%g"):format(0.5) 0.5 %e scientific notation ("%.1e"):format(12345) 1.2e+04 %x / %X hexadecimal ("%x"):format(255) ff %o octal ("%o"):format(8) 10 %c the character with that code ("%c"):format(65) A %s any value as text (calls tostring) ("%s"):format(true) true %q a value as Lua source (quoted string) ("%q"):format('a"b') "a\"b" %% a literal % Width, padding and alignment A number between % and the letter sets a minimum width . The value is padded on the left with spaces; - pads on the right instead; 0 pads numbers with zeros: lua print(string.format(" %5d %-5d %05d ", 42, 42, 42)) print(string.format(" %8.2f %-8s %3s ", 3.14159, "left", "toolong")) print(string.format("%02d:%02d:%02d", 7, 5, 9)) 42 42 00042 3.14 left toolong 07:05:09 The width is a minimum: longer values are never cut. %.3s does cut a string to 3 characters. Lining up columns Widths make text tables line up: lua local items = { { "Tea", 3, 2.5 }, { "Sandwich", 1, 6.25 }, { "Cake", 2, 3.0 }, } local total = 0 print(string.format("%-10s %3s %8s", "Item", "Qty", "Total")) for _, item in ipairs(items) do local name, qty, price = item 1 , item 2 , item 3 total = total + qty price print(string.format("%-10s %3d %8.2f", name, qty, qty price)) end print(string.rep("-", 23)) print(string.format("%-14s %8.2f", "Sum", total)) Item Qty Total Tea 3 7.50 Sandwich 1 6.25 Cake 2 6.00 ----------------------- Sum 19.75 Building long text Joining strings with .. in a loop copies the growing string every time: fine for ten pieces, slow for ten thousand. The Lua way is a buffer : collect the pieces in a table and join them once. lua local buffer = {} for i = 1, 5 do buffer buffer + 1 = string.format("line %d", i) end local text = table.concat(buffer, "\n") print(text) print( text) line 1 line 2 line 3 line 4 line 5 34 Values as text tostring turns any value into text. %q turns a string into Lua source that reads back as the same string, escapes and all, which is how you save data that Lua can load again: lua print(tostring(12), tostring(1.5), tostring(nil), tostring(false)) local tricky = 'She said "hi"\nthen left' print(string.format("%q", tricky)) print(string.format("%q", 1/3)) 12 1.5 nil false "She said \"hi\"\ then left" 0x1.5555555555555p-2 %q writes a newline as a backslash followed by a real newline, and floats in hexadecimal so that the exact value survives.

title: An order summary
body: Read order lines until a line that is just end (or until the input runs out). Each line is name,quantity,price , for example Tea,3,2.50 . Print a table with the columns lined up, then the total: Tea,3,2.50 Sandwich,1,6.25 Cake slice,2,3 end Item Qty Price Total Tea 3 2.50 7.50 Sandwich 1 6.25 6.25 Cake slice 2 3.00 6.00 Total 19.75 - The header and rows use string.format("%-12s %6s %8s %8s", ...) for the header and "%-12s %6d %8.2f %8.2f" for each row; the total line is "%-12s %24.2f" with the word Total . - Spaces around the commas are allowed and ignored ( Tea , 3 , 2.50 ). - A line that does not have that form prints Skipped: <the line at the point it is read, before the table, and is left out. - With no valid lines at all, print only No orders. (after any Skipped: lines). There is no prompt.

title: 4.05  UTF-8 and Bytes
body: Lua strings as bytes, why counts bytes not letters, UTF-8 in brief, the utf8 library with len, char, codepoint and codes, taking characters safely, and the \u escape. Strings are bytes A Lua string is a sequence of bytes , any bytes at all. Lua does not know about letters, accents or alphabets. For English text one byte is one letter, so you never notice. For anything else you do: lua local word = "café" print( word, word:upper(), word:sub(1, 4)) 5 CAFé caf� é takes two bytes, so the length is 5; upper changes only the ASCII letters; and sub(1, 4) cut the é in half, leaving a broken byte that shows as � . UTF-8 in one paragraph Almost all text today is UTF-8 . Every character (every Unicode code point ) is stored as 1 to 4 bytes: plain ASCII as one byte with the same value as always, é as two, € and most Asian scripts as three, emoji as four. A program that treats the text as bytes still works for copying, joining, searching for ASCII, and comparing. It goes wrong when it counts, cuts or reverses. The utf8 library Lua 5.3 and later include utf8 for exactly those cases: lua local word = "café" print(utf8.len(word)) print(utf8.char(72, 233, 8364, 128512)) print(utf8.codepoint("é"), utf8.codepoint("A€", 1, -1)) for pos, code in utf8.codes("añ€") do print(pos, code, utf8.char(code)) end 4 Hé€😀 233 65 8364 1 97 a 2 241 ñ 4 8364 € Function Does --- --- utf8.len(s) number of characters, or nil plus a position if s is not valid UTF-8 utf8.char(...) the characters with these code points utf8.codepoint(s, i, j) the code points of the characters starting between byte i and j utf8.codes(s) loop over the characters: byte position and code point utf8.offset(s, n) the byte position where character n starts utf8.charpattern a pattern matching one UTF-8 character Working character by character utf8.charpattern with gmatch gives the characters as strings, which makes counting, reversing and cutting safe: lua local function chars(s) local out = {} for ch in s:gmatch(utf8.charpattern) do out out + 1 = ch end return out end local list = chars("¡Olé!") print( list, table.concat(list, " ")) local reversed = {} for i = list, 1, -1 do reversed reversed + 1 = list i end print(table.concat(reversed)) local function first_chars(s, n) local stop = utf8.offset(s, n + 1) return stop and s:sub(1, stop - 1) or s end print(first_chars("café crème", 4), first_chars("hi", 10)) 5 ¡ O l é ! !élO¡ café hi utf8.offset(s, n + 1) is the byte where character n + 1 starts, so everything before it is the first n characters. Escapes \u{XXXX} puts a code point into a string literal as UTF-8; \xXX puts in one byte; \ddd one byte in decimal: lua print("\u{48}\u{E9}\u{20AC}", "\x41\x42", "\65\66") print( "\u{20AC}") Hé€ AB AB 3 Bytes are useful too Because a string can hold any bytes, Lua strings also carry binary data: file contents, network packets, images. string.pack and string.unpack write and read numbers as raw bytes in a given layout: lua local packed = string.pack("<i4 i2", 1000, -2) print( packed, packed:byte(1, -1)) print(string.unpack("<i4 i2", packed)) 6 232 3 0 0 254 255 1000 -2 7 < means little-endian, i4 a 4-byte integer, i2 a 2-byte one. unpack returns the values and then the position after them. (The Computer Fundamentals and C courses explain endianness and two's complement, which is why -2 is 254 255.)

title: UTF-8 safe text
body: Write four functions that treat text as characters, not bytes, so they work for any language: lua-norun char_count(s) -- the number of characters in the UTF-8 text s reverse_text(s) -- s with its characters in the opposite order (not its bytes) truncate(s, n) -- the first n characters of s followed by "…" when s has more than n characters; s itself otherwise is_ascii(s) -- true when every byte of s is below 128 lua-norun char_count("café") -- 4 ( "café" is 5) reverse_text("añb") -- "bña" truncate("crème brûlée", 5) -- "crème…"

title: A text report
body: Read a whole text from the input and print a report about it: in The cat sat on the mat. A different cat and the end. gives Lines: 3 Words: 12 Characters: 53 Longest word: different (9) Average word length: 3.2 Top words: the 3 cat 2 a 1 and 1 different 1 - Lines : the number of lines (a last line without a newline still counts; empty input has 0 lines). - Words : a word is a run of letters and apostrophes, compared in lower case ( The and the are the same word). - Characters : the number of UTF-8 characters in the whole text, newlines included. - Longest word : the longest word (in characters) and its length; when several are equally long, the one that appears first. - Average word length : in characters, one decimal. - Top words : the five most common words, most common first, ties in alphabetical order. Each line is two spaces, the word padded with spaces to 8 characters, one more space and the count; a word longer than 8 characters pushes its count along. Fewer than five lines when there are fewer different words. Count the padding in characters: string.format("%-8s", "crème") pads by bytes and would add one space too few. - With no words at all, print the first three lines and then No words. Read everything at once with io.read("a") .

title: 5.01  Metatables and Operators
body: What a metatable is, setmetatable and getmetatable, giving tables arithmetic with __add and friends, comparisons with __eq, __lt and __le, __tostring, __len, __concat and __call, and sharing one metatable between many tables. Changing what operators do Adding two tables is normally an error. A metatable is an ordinary table that changes how another table behaves: it holds metamethods , functions with special names that Lua calls when an operation would otherwise fail or needs a decision. lua local mt = {} mt.__add = function(a, b) return { x = a.x + b.x, y = a.y + b.y } end local p = setmetatable({ x = 1, y = 2 }, mt) local q = setmetatable({ x = 10, y = 20 }, mt) local r = p + q print(r.x, r.y, getmetatable(p) == mt) 11 22 true setmetatable(t, mt) gives t the metatable mt and returns t , so it fits on one line with the constructor. getmetatable(t) reads it back. When Lua sees p + q and p is not a number, it looks for __add in p 's metatable, then in q 's, and calls the first one it finds with both operands. A small vector type The usual pattern: one metatable for all values of the type, and a function that makes new ones. lua local Vec = {} Vec.__index = Vec -- explained in the next lesson local function vec(x, y) return setmetatable({ x = x, y = y }, Vec) end Vec.__add = function(a, b) return vec(a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y) end Vec.__sub = function(a, b) return vec(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y) end Vec.__mul = function(a, b) if type(a) == "number" then return vec(a b.x, a b.y) end if type(b) == "number" then return vec(a.x b, a.y b) end return a.x b.x + a.y b.y -- two vectors: the dot product end Vec.__unm = function(a) return vec(-a.x, -a.y) end Vec.__eq = function(a, b) return a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y end Vec.__tostring = function(a) return "(" .. a.x .. ", " .. a.y .. ")" end Vec.__len = function(a) return math.sqrt(a.x a.x + a.y a.y) end local a, b = vec(3, 4), vec(1, 2) print(tostring(a + b), tostring(a - b), tostring(2 b), tostring(-a)) print(a b, a, a == vec(3, 4), a ~= b) print(a) (4, 6) (2, 2) (2, 4) (-3, -4) 11 5.0 true true (3, 4) print calls tostring , which uses __tostring , so a vector prints nicely. __eq is only asked when both sides are tables (or both userdata); a ~= b is simply not (a == b) . The metamethods Key Called for --- --- __add __sub __mul __div __mod __pow __unm __idiv + - / % ^ , unary - , // __band __bor __bxor __shl __shr __bnot the bitwise operators & \ ~ << ~ __concat .. __len __eq __lt __le == , < (and ), <= (and = ) __call calling the table like a function __tostring tostring and print __index __newindex reading and writing missing keys (next lesson) __close __gc __mode __name __metatable resources, garbage collection, weak tables, names, protection Comparisons and sorting With __lt , values can be compared with < , which also lets table.sort sort them without a comparison function: lua local Money = {} local function money(cents) return setmetatable({ cents = cents }, Money) end Money.__lt = function(a, b) return a.cents < b.cents end Money.__le = function(a, b) return a.cents <= b.cents end Money.__tostring = function(m) return string.format("$%d.%02d", m.cents // 100, m.cents % 100) end Money.__concat = function(a, b) return tostring(a) .. tostring(b) end local prices = { money(450), money(99), money(1200) } table.sort(prices) print(prices 1 .. " < " .. prices 2 .. " < " .. prices 3 ) print(money(5) <= money(5), money(7) money(3)) $0.99 < $4.50 < $12.00 true true __concat receives the two operands, one of which may be a string, which is why it calls tostring on both. Calling a table __call makes a table callable. The table itself arrives as the first argument: lua local greeter = setmetatable({ greeting = "Hello" }, { __call = function(self, name) return self.greeting .. ", " .. name .. "!" end, }) print(greeter("Ada")) greeter.greeting = "Hi" print(greeter("Lua")) Hello, Ada! Hi, Lua! Only tables (from Lua) From Lua code you can set metatables on tables only. Strings share one metatable set by the library, which is what makes s:upper() work: its __index is the string table. lua print(getmetatable("").__index == string) true

title: A vector type
body: Make 2D vectors behave like numbers. Vec(x, y) makes a vector: a table { x = x, y = y } with a shared metatable VecMeta that gives it these operations: Expression Result --- --- a + b , a - b a new vector, added or subtracted part by part a 3 , 3 a a new vector, both parts multiplied by the number a b (two vectors) the dot product, a.x b.x + a.y b.y , a number -a a new vector pointing the other way a == b true when both parts are equal a the length, math.sqrt(x^2 + y^2) tostring(a) "(3, 4)" Every vector made by Vec (and every vector the operations return) must have VecMeta as its metatable.

title: 5.02  __index and __newindex
body: Default values for missing keys, __index as a table and as a function, rawget and rawset, watching and blocking writes with __newindex, read-only tables, catching typos in globals, and weak tables. When a key is missing Reading a key that a table does not have normally gives nil . If the table's metatable has __index , Lua asks it instead. __index as a table: Lua looks the key up in that table (and, if that table has its own __index , keeps going): lua local defaults = { colour = "grey", size = 10, visible = true } local button = setmetatable({ colour = "red" }, { __index = defaults }) print(button.colour, button.size, button.visible, button.missing) button.size = 14 print(button.size, defaults.size) red 10 true nil 14 10 The table keeps its own values; only missing keys fall back to defaults . Writing goes into the table itself, never into defaults . This one mechanism is the whole basis of classes and inheritance in Lua (next two lessons). __index as a function: Lua calls it with the table and the key, and uses what it returns: lua local squares = setmetatable({}, { __index = function(t, n) local value = n n rawset(t, n, value) -- remember it, so next time it is a plain field return value end, }) print(squares 12 , squares 3 , rawget(squares, 12), rawget(squares, 5)) 144 9 144 nil rawget(t, k) and rawset(t, k, v) read and write without metamethods. They are how a metamethod reaches the table itself without calling itself again. When a key is new __newindex runs when you assign to a key the table does not have yet (assigning to an existing key never calls it): lua local log = {} local watched = setmetatable({}, { __newindex = function(t, key, value) log log + 1 = key .. "=" .. tostring(value) rawset(t, key, value) end, }) watched.a = 1 watched.b = 2 watched.a = 10 -- a already exists: no call print(table.concat(log, " "), watched.a) a=1 b=2 10 Read-only tables To catch every write, keep the real data elsewhere and give out an empty proxy whose __index reads from the data and whose __newindex refuses: lua local function read_only(data) return setmetatable({}, { __index = data, __newindex = function(_, key) error("cannot change " .. tostring(key), 2) end, __len = function() return data end, }) end local days = read_only({ "Mon", "Tue", "Wed" }) print(days 2 , days) local ok, err = pcall(function() days 1 = "Sun" end) print(ok, err) Tue 3 false main.lua:11: cannot change 1 pcall runs a function and catches its error instead of stopping the program (lesson 6.01). error(message, 2) blames the line that did the writing, not the line inside the metamethod. Catching typos in globals Globals live in the table _G , and _G can have a metatable too. This makes reading or creating an unknown global an error, which catches misspelled variable names at once: lua setmetatable(_G, { __newindex = function(_, name) error("assigning undeclared global '" .. name .. "'", 2) end, __index = function(_, name) error("reading undeclared global '" .. name .. "'", 2) end, }) local count = 0 print(pcall(function() cuont = count + 1 end)) print(pcall(function() return totl end)) false main.lua:7: assigning undeclared global 'cuont' false main.lua:8: reading undeclared global 'totl' Real projects use a version of this (often called strict.lua ), or a language server that reports undefined globals as you type. Weak tables A table normally keeps everything in it alive. __mode = "k" makes its keys weak , "v" its values, "kv" both: the garbage collector may remove an entry when nothing else refers to that key or value. A weak-keyed table is how you attach extra data to objects without keeping them alive forever: lua local extra = setmetatable({}, { __mode = "k" }) local obj = {} extra obj = "notes about obj" print(extra obj ) obj = nil collectgarbage() local n = 0 for _ in pairs(extra) do n = n + 1 end print(n) notes about obj 0

title: Defaults, counters and read-only tables
body: Write three functions with __index and __newindex : lua-norun with_defaults(t, defaults) -- gives t a metatable so that a key missing from t is read from defaults; returns t. -- Writing to t still writes to t, never to defaults. default_table(value) -- a new empty table where reading any missing key gives value (nothing is stored by reading) read_only(t) -- a proxy: reading works like t (also ), but assigning any key raises the error -- "attempt to change a read-only table" lua-norun local counts = default_table(0) counts.apples = counts.apples + 1 -- counts.apples is 1; counts.pears is still 0

title: 5.03  Classes and Objects
body: Methods and the colon, self, the class pattern with a metatable whose __index is the class, a constructor called new, keeping methods shared and data per object, and the dot-versus-colon mistake. Methods and self A table can hold functions that work on that table. Lua passes the table explicitly, as a parameter named self by convention, and the colon writes that for you: lua local account = { owner = "Ada", balance = 100 } function account.deposit(self, amount) -- the long way self.balance = self.balance + amount end function account:withdraw(amount) -- the colon adds self self.balance = self.balance - amount end account.deposit(account, 50) -- the long way account:withdraw(30) -- the colon passes account as self print(account.balance) 120 function t:name(args) means function t.name(self, args) , and t:name(args) means t.name(t, args) . That is all the colon does. A class One account is easy. For many, put the methods in one table, the class , and give every object a metatable whose __index is the class. Each object holds only its own data; a missing key (a method name) falls back to the class: lua local Account = {} Account.__index = Account function Account.new(owner, balance) local self = setmetatable({}, Account) self.owner = owner self.balance = balance or 0 return self end function Account:deposit(amount) if amount <= 0 then error("deposit must be positive", 2) end self.balance = self.balance + amount return self.balance end function Account:report() return string.format("%s has %d", self.owner, self.balance) end local a = Account.new("Ada", 100) local b = Account.new("Grace") a:deposit(25) b:deposit(10) print(a:report()) print(b:report()) print(a.deposit == b.deposit, rawget(a, "deposit")) Ada has 125 Grace has 10 true nil The pieces: - Account is both the class (it holds the methods) and the objects' metatable. - Account.__index = Account sends every missing key, every method name, to the class. - Account.new is the constructor: it makes a table, sets the metatable, fills in the fields. - Methods are defined once; every object shares them. new is called with a dot ( Account.new(...) ) because it does not work on an existing object. Some code writes Account:new(...) and uses self as the class inside; both styles are common. Metamethods in the class Because the class is the metatable, metamethods go in the same table: lua local Point = {} Point.__index = Point function Point.new(x, y) return setmetatable({ x = x, y = y }, Point) end function Point:distance_to(other) return math.sqrt((self.x - other.x) ^ 2 + (self.y - other.y) ^ 2) end function Point.__tostring(p) return "Point(" .. p.x .. ", " .. p.y .. ")" end function Point.__eq(a, b) return a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y end local p, q = Point.new(0, 0), Point.new(3, 4) print(p, q, p:distance_to(q), p == Point.new(0, 0)) Point(0, 0) Point(3, 4) 5.0 true Dot or colon? !danger The most common object bug in Lua Calling a method with a dot, a.deposit(25) , passes 25 as self and nothing as amount , and the error is confusing: "attempt to index a number value (local 'self')". Methods are called with a colon: a:deposit(25) . lua local Counter = {} Counter.__index = Counter function Counter.new() return setmetatable({ n = 0 }, Counter) end function Counter:add() self.n = self.n + 1 end local c = Counter.new() print(pcall(c.add)) -- like c.add() : self is nil c:add() print(c.n) false main.lua:4: attempt to index a nil value (local 'self') 1 Private data Fields of a table are visible to anyone who has the table. When a value must stay private, keep it in a closure instead of a field. Each object then carries its own functions, which costs more memory but nothing outside can reach the data: lua local function new_stack() local items = {} -- private: only the functions below see it return { push = function(v) items items + 1 = v end, pop = function() return table.remove(items) end, size = function() return items end, } end local s = new_stack() s.push(1); s.push(2); s.push(3) print(s.pop(), s.size(), s.items) 3 2 nil These are called with a dot: they are closures, not methods, and need no self .

title: A bank account class
body: Write a class Account with a metatable whose __index is the class itself: Method Does --- --- Account.new(owner, balance) a new account; balance defaults to 0 acc:deposit(amount) adds the amount and returns the new balance; an amount of 0 or less raises an error containing amount must be positive acc:withdraw(amount) takes the amount out and returns the new balance; an amount of 0 or less raises the same error; more than the balance raises an error containing insufficient funds and changes nothing acc:balance() the balance acc:history() a list of strings, one per successful deposit or withdrawal, oldest first: "deposit 50" , "withdraw 20" tostring(acc) "Account(Ada, 130)" Each account has its own balance and history.

title: 5.04  Inheritance
body: Making a subclass whose missing keys fall back to its base class, calling the base constructor and overridden methods, polymorphism with one loop over different kinds of object, checking what an object is, and when composition is simpler. A chain of __index A subclass is a class whose own missing keys fall back to another class. Since a class is just a table, give it a metatable whose __index is the base class: lua local Animal = {} Animal.__index = Animal function Animal.new(name, sound) return setmetatable({ name = name, sound = sound or "..." }, Animal) end function Animal:speak() return self.name .. " says " .. self.sound end function Animal:describe() return self.name .. " is an animal" end local Dog = setmetatable({}, { __index = Animal }) -- Dog falls back to Animal Dog.__index = Dog -- dogs fall back to Dog function Dog.new(name, trick) local self = Animal.new(name, "woof") -- build the Animal part self.trick = trick return setmetatable(self, Dog) -- then make it a Dog end function Dog:describe() -- override return Animal.describe(self) .. " that can " .. self.trick end function Dog:fetch() return self.name .. " fetches the ball" end local cat = Animal.new("Tom", "meow") local rex = Dog.new("Rex", "roll over") print(cat:speak()) print(rex:speak()) -- found in Animal print(rex:describe()) -- Dog's own version print(rex:fetch()) print(cat.fetch) Tom says meow Rex says woof Rex is an animal that can roll over Rex fetches the ball nil Looking up rex:speak : not in rex , so try Dog (rex's metatable's __index ); not in Dog , so try Animal (Dog's metatable's __index ); found. Any depth works the same way. Calling the base class Lua has no super . Call the base class's function by name and pass self yourself: Animal.describe(self) . The same goes for the constructor: Dog.new calls Animal.new to fill in the shared fields, then sets the metatable to Dog . One loop, many kinds Polymorphism : code that calls obj:area() works for any object that has an area method, whatever its class: lua local Shape = {} Shape.__index = Shape function Shape:describe() return string.format("%s with area %.2f", self.kind, self:area()) end local Circle = setmetatable({}, { __index = Shape }) Circle.__index = Circle function Circle.new(r) return setmetatable({ kind = "circle", r = r }, Circle) end function Circle:area() return math.pi self.r ^ 2 end local Rect = setmetatable({}, { __index = Shape }) Rect.__index = Rect function Rect.new(w, h) return setmetatable({ kind = "rectangle", w = w, h = h }, Rect) end function Rect:area() return self.w self.h end local shapes = { Circle.new(1), Rect.new(2, 3), Circle.new(0.5) } local total = 0 for _, s in ipairs(shapes) do print(s:describe()) total = total + s:area() end print(string.format("total %.2f", total)) circle with area 3.14 rectangle with area 6.00 circle with area 0.79 total 9.93 Shape:describe calls self:area() , which runs whichever area the actual object has. What is this object? There is no built-in instanceof . Walk up the chain of metatables: lua local Base = {} Base.__index = Base local Child = setmetatable({}, { __index = Base }) Child.__index = Child local function is_a(obj, class) local mt = getmetatable(obj) while mt do if mt == class then return true end local parent = getmetatable(mt) mt = parent and parent.__index end return false end local c = setmetatable({}, Child) print(is_a(c, Child), is_a(c, Base), is_a({}, Base), is_a(setmetatable({}, Base), Child)) true true false false Often a simpler question is better: "can it do what I need?", if obj.area then . A helper for classes Writing the two __index lines for every class gets old.
