Errors Winsock reports errors through WSAGetLastError() , with codes from 10000 up. The ones you meet constantly: Code Name Usually means --- --- --- 10035 WSAEWOULDBLOCK a non-blocking socket has nothing to do yet (lesson 2.04): not an error 10054 WSAECONNRESET the other side reset the connection (crashed, or closed abruptly) 10053 WSAECONNABORTED your side aborted it (often a timeout inside Windows) 10060 WSAETIMEDOUT connecting or sending timed out 10061 WSAECONNREFUSED nothing is listening on that port 10065 WSAEHOSTUNREACH no route to that machine 10048 WSAEADDRINUSE the port you tried to bind is taken Network code must expect every one of these at any moment: the network is the least reliable thing your program touches. Closing closesocket(s) releases the socket. If unsent data is still buffered, Windows keeps trying to deliver it in the background. To tell the other side "I have finished sending" while still receiving its reply, call shutdown(s, SD_SEND) first; the other side's recv then returns 0 once it has read everything (lesson 2.02).

title: What a socket error means
body: Turn WSAGetLastError() codes into decisions (lesson 2.01): cpp enum class Action { TryAgainLater, Reconnect, GiveUp }; std::string errorName(int code); Action actionFor(int code); - errorName gives the name for these codes, and WSA error N for any other: Code Name --- --- 10004 WSAEINTR 10035 WSAEWOULDBLOCK 10048 WSAEADDRINUSE 10051 WSAENETUNREACH 10053 WSAECONNABORTED 10054 WSAECONNRESET 10060 WSAETIMEDOUT 10061 WSAECONNREFUSED 10065 WSAEHOSTUNREACH - actionFor : WSAEINTR and WSAEWOULDBLOCK mean try again later ; a lost connection ( WSAECONNABORTED , WSAECONNRESET , WSAETIMEDOUT ) means reconnect ; a server that is not there or not reachable ( WSAECONNREFUSED , WSAENETUNREACH , WSAEHOSTUNREACH ) also means reconnect (later, with backoff); anything else, including WSAEADDRINUSE , means give up and report it.

title: 2.02  A TCP Client and Server
body:
The server side - bind, listen and accept - a complete echo server and client, sending everything with a loop, reading until a whole message has arrived, closing gracefully with shutdown, and the TIME_WAIT state that sometimes stops a server restarting. The server's calls cpp-norun SOCKET listener{ socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_TCP) }; sockaddr_in addr{}; addr.sin_family = AF_INET; addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY); // every interface (127.0.0.1 for local only) addr.sin_port = htons(7777); // htons: byte order, lesson 2.03 if (bind(listener, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), sizeof(addr)) == SOCKET_ERROR) { / port in use? / } listen(listener, SOMAXCONN); // start accepting; queue pending connections for (;;) { sockaddr_in from{}; int fromLength{ sizeof(from) }; SOCKET client{ accept(listener, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&from), &fromLength) }; if (client == INVALID_SOCKET) break; serve(client); // one client at a time, for now closesocket(client); } - bind claims an address and port. - listen turns the socket into a listening socket. The operating system completes handshakes on its own and queues the new connections. - accept takes the next connection from the queue and returns a new socket for it. The listening socket keeps listening. This server handles one client at a time; lesson 2.04 fixes that. Sending everything send may accept fewer bytes than you gave it, so real code always loops: cpp-norun bool sendAll(SOCKET s, const char data, int length) { while (length 0) { const int sent{ send(s, data, length, 0) }; if (sent == SOCKET_ERROR) return false; data += sent; length -= sent; } return true; } Receiving whole messages Likewise, one recv returns whatever has arrived. A line-based protocol reads into a buffer and takes out complete lines: cpp-norun std::string buffer; char chunk 4096 ; for (;;) { const int got{ recv(s, chunk, sizeof(chunk), 0) }; if (got <= 0) break; // closed (0) or error buffer.append(chunk, static_cast<std::size_t (got)); for (std::size_t end{ buffer.find('
') }; end != std::string::npos; end = buffer.find('
')) { handleLine(buffer.substr(0, end)); buffer.erase(0, end + 1); } } The same shape with a length prefix instead of 
 handles binary messages. A test that sends one short message over loopback will seem to work without the loop, because small messages usually arrive in one piece locally; across a real network, they do not. Closing gracefully Closing a TCP connection properly is a small dance: 1. The side that has finished sending calls shutdown(s, SD_SEND) : a FIN goes out. 2. The other side's recv returns 0 after it has read everything. It sends whatever it still has, then shuts down its own sending. 3. The first side's recv returns 0. Both call closesocket . Calling closesocket while data from the peer is still unread makes Windows send a reset instead, and the peer may lose the last data it sent you. A client that sends a request and then shutdown(SD_SEND) to say "that is all" (as many simple protocols do) gets the full reply reliably. TIME_WAIT After a connection closes, the side that closed first keeps a record of it for a while (up to a few minutes) in the TIME_WAIT state, so that stray delayed packets of the old connection are not mistaken for a new one. A consequence: a server that is stopped and immediately restarted can fail to bind its port with WSAEADDRINUSE , because old connections are still in TIME_WAIT. On Windows, SO_REUSEADDR has dangerous semantics (it allows another program to bind the same port too); use SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE to protect a server's port, and design restarts to tolerate a short wait.

title: Partial sends and receives
body: A fake socket behaves like a real one under load: each send accepts only part of what you give it, and each recv returns whatever chunk came next. Write the loops from lesson 2.02 against it: cpp class FakeSocket { public: FakeSocket(std::size_t maxPerSend, std::vector<std::string incoming); int send(const char data, int length); int recv(char buffer, int size); const std::string& wire() const; void breakConnection(); }; bool sendAll(FakeSocket& s, const std::string& data); std::optional<std::string recvExactly(FakeSocket& s, std::size_t count, std::string& leftover); std::optional<std::string recvLine(FakeSocket& s, std::string& leftover); The FakeSocket is given (it is in the starter): send accepts at most maxPerSend bytes and returns how many, or -1 after breakConnection ; recv returns the next incoming chunk (split to fit the buffer), 0 when there are no more chunks, or -1 after breakConnection . - sendAll sends every byte, looping; false if send fails. - recvExactly returns exactly count bytes, first using bytes already in leftover , then reading; extra bytes read beyond count go back into leftover . If the stream ends or fails first, std::nullopt . - recvLine returns the next line without its \n (and without a \r before it), keeping any bytes after it in leftover ; std::nullopt if the stream ends first (a partial line stays in leftover ).

title: 2.03  Byte Order and Packet Layouts
body: Network byte order is big-endian - htons, htonl and their inverses, writing and reading binary headers field by field, fields smaller than a byte packed into bit fields, why a C++ struct is the wrong tool for a wire format, and the Internet checksum. Big-endian on the wire Internet protocols write multi-byte numbers big-endian : most significant byte first. This is network byte order . A port number 7777 ( 0x1E61 ) goes on the wire as 1E 61 . Your x86 or ARM processor stores it little-endian, as 61 1E . Every number in a protocol header must be converted. The socket API provides the conversions: Function Converts --- --- htons 16-bit, host to network htonl 32-bit, host to network ntohs , ntohl network to host That is why lesson 2.02 wrote addr.sin_port = htons(7777) : the sockaddr_in structure holds the port in network order. Forgetting the conversion is a classic bug: the server listens on port 24862 ( 0x611E ) instead of 7777. Writing headers field by field The portable way to write a binary format is byte by byte, with shifts, which gives the same result on every machine whatever its own byte order: cpp-norun void put16(std::vector<std::uint8_t & out, std::uint16_t v) { out.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t (v 8)); // big-endian: high byte first out.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t (v)); } std::uint16_t get16(const std::uint8_t p) { return static_cast<std::uint16_t ((p 0 << 8) p 1 ); } Your own protocols can choose little-endian (the IPC course did); when you implement a standard protocol, follow its specification, which for internet protocols almost always says big-endian. Bit fields Some header fields are smaller than a byte. The first byte of an IPv4 header holds two 4-bit numbers: the version (4) in the high half and the header length in 32-bit words in the low half: text byte 0: 0100 0101 - version 4, header length 5 words (20 bytes) = 0x45 Read and write them with shifts and masks: cpp-norun const int version{ p 0 4 }; const int headerLength{ (p 0 & 0x0F) 4 }; const std::uint8_t first{ static_cast<std::uint8_t ((4 << 4) 5) }; TCP's flags (SYN, ACK, FIN...) are single bits of one byte, tested with masks such as flags & 0x02 for SYN. Why not a struct? It is tempting to declare a C++ struct matching a header and memcpy or cast the packet to it. Every one of these breaks it: - Padding : the compiler may insert bytes between fields to align them. - Byte order : the struct's integers are in host order. - C++ bit fields : their order within a byte is implementation-defined. - Alignment : casting a packet buffer to a struct pointer can read misaligned data, and is an aliasing violation. Real network code does use structs with pragma pack(1) and careful conversions, but reading and writing fields explicitly, as above, is clearer and always correct. The Internet checksum IPv4, TCP, UDP and ICMP headers carry a 16-bit checksum so that corrupted packets can be detected. It is computed the same way everywhere (RFC 1071): 1. Treat the data as a sequence of 16-bit big-endian words (pad an odd final byte with a zero). 2. Add them all up using one's complement addition: whenever the sum overflows 16 bits, add the carry back into the low 16 bits. 3. The checksum is the bitwise NOT of the result. To verify , run the same sum over the data including the checksum field: a correct packet gives 0xFFFF before the final NOT (zero after it). It is a weak checksum, catching most single errors but not reordered words; TLS and application-level hashes protect data properly.

title: A big-endian header and its checksum
match: A big-endian header and its checksum
body: Pack and unpack a small binary header in network byte order, with bit fields, and compute the Internet checksum (lesson 2.03): cpp struct Header { std::uint8_t version; // 0..15 std::uint8_t type; // 0..15 std::uint16_t length; std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint16_t checksum; }; std::uint16_t internetChecksum(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & data); std::vector<std::uint8_t pack(Header h, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & payload); std::optional<Header unpack(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet, std::vector<std::uint8_t & payload); Layout (10 bytes, then the payload): byte 0 holds version in its high 4 bits and type in its low 4 bits; byte 1 is reserved and always 0; then length (bytes 2-3), sequence (bytes 4-7) and checksum (bytes 8-9), each big-endian. (The checksum sits at an even offset on purpose: the Internet checksum works on 16-bit words, so its field must be one of them.) - internetChecksum is RFC 1071: sum the data as 16-bit big-endian words (an odd last byte is padded with a zero), folding carries back in, and return the bitwise NOT. - pack sets length to 10 + payload size, writes the header with checksum 0, appends the payload, computes the checksum over everything and writes it into its field. (The length and checksum you pass are ignored.) - unpack fails if the packet is shorter than 10 bytes, if byte 1 is not 0, if length does not equal the packet's size, or if the checksum does not verify (the checksum computed over the whole packet, checksum field included, must be 0). Otherwise it returns the header and puts the payload in payload .

title: 2.04  Serving Many Connections
body: Moving beyond one client at a time - thread per connection and its limits, non-blocking sockets and WSAEWOULDBLOCK, an event loop built on select or WSAPoll, per-connection buffers for reading and writing, and when to reach for I/O completion ports. The problem Lesson 2.02's server serves one client at a time: while it waits in recv for client A, client B is stuck in the accept queue. There are two classic ways out. Thread per connection Accept, then hand each client socket to a new thread running blocking code. Simple, and fine for dozens of clients. With thousands, the threads' memory (each has a stack) and context switching dominate, and shared state needs locks everywhere. Non-blocking sockets and an event loop A socket can be put in non-blocking mode: cpp-norun u_long nonBlocking{ 1 }; ioctlsocket(s, FIONBIO, &nonBlocking); Then recv , send , accept and connect never wait. If they cannot do anything right now, they fail with WSAEWOULDBLOCK , which is not an error, just "nothing yet". On its own that turns waiting into busy polling; combined with a call that waits until any socket is ready , it gives an efficient single-threaded server: an event loop . cpp-norun std::vector<WSAPOLLFD fds; // the listener, then one entry per client for (;;) { WSAPoll(fds.data(), static_cast<ULONG (fds.size()), 1000); // wait up to 1 s for anything for (WSAPOLLFD& f : fds) { if (f.revents & POLLRDNORM) { / readable: accept (listener) or recv (client) / } if (f.revents & POLLWRNORM) { / writable: send queued data / } if (f.revents & (POLLERR POLLHUP)) { / close it / } } } select is the older, more widespread form of the same idea (on Windows it handles 64 sockets per call unless you raise FD_SETSIZE ); WSAPoll is the Windows version of Unix's poll . Per-connection state In an event loop no function can wait for "the rest of the message", so each connection keeps its own state: - an input buffer : bytes received so far; after each recv , take out every complete message and handle it, leaving any partial one; - an output queue : bytes waiting to be sent. Never call send in a loop until everything goes: when it returns WSAEWOULDBLOCK or sends only part, keep the rest and ask to be told when the socket is writable ( POLLWRNORM ), then send more. text recv - append to input - extract messages - handle - append replies to output writable - send as much of output as the socket takes - keep the rest The output queue also needs a limit : a client that never reads would otherwise make the server buffer replies for ever. When a queue grows too large, stop reading from that client, or disconnect it. Fairness One busy client must not starve the others. Read a bounded amount per client per loop iteration, handle a bounded number of messages, then move on. The same applies to expensive work: an event loop must never do anything slow (a disk read, a heavy computation) inline, or every client waits. Push slow work to worker threads and post the result back to the loop. Scaling further For thousands of busy connections on Windows, I/O completion ports (the IPC course, lesson 2.05) are the high-performance model: overlapped WSARecv / WSASend on every socket, completions collected by a few worker threads. Libraries such as Asio (C++), libuv (behind Node.js) and the Windows thread pool hide most of the detail.

title: An event loop's connections
body: Write the per-connection logic of lesson 2.04's event loop for a line-based "shout" server: every line a client sends is answered with the same line in upper case. The loop itself is simulated: it tells you when a connection has bytes to read, and when it can write and how many bytes the socket will take. cpp class Loop { public: explicit Loop(std::size_t maxQueued); int accept(); void readable(int id, const std::string& bytes); std::string writable(int id, std::size_t capacity); bool wantsWrite(int id) const; bool isOpen(int id) const; std::size_t queued(int id) const; }; - accept opens a connection and returns its id (1, 2, ...). - readable appends bytes to the connection's input; every complete line (ending in \n , with an optional \r before it) is answered by appending the upper-cased line plus \n to its output queue. A line QUIT closes the connection after its queued output has been written (no more input is read). If the output queue would grow beyond maxQueued bytes, the client is not reading its replies: the connection is closed at once and its queue dropped. - writable returns up to capacity bytes from the front of the queue (what send accepted) and removes them. When a closing connection's queue becomes empty, it is closed. - wantsWrite is true while the queue is not empty (the loop then asks for POLLWRNORM ). - Closed or unknown connections: readable does nothing, writable returns "" , isOpen is false.

title: 2.05  UDP Sockets
body: Sending and receiving datagrams - sendto and recvfrom, connected UDP sockets, size limits, coping with loss, duplication and reordering, a request with timeouts and retries, checking who an answer came from, Windows' connection-reset quirk, and broadcast. Datagrams A UDP socket sends and receives whole datagrams , each with its own destination: cpp-norun SOCKET s{ socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, IPPROTO_UDP) }; sockaddr_in to{}; to.sin_family = AF_INET; to.sin_port = htons(9000); inet_pton(AF_INET, "192.168.1.50", &to.sin_addr); sendto(s, packet, packetLength, 0, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&to), sizeof(to)); char buffer 1500 ; sockaddr_in from{}; int fromLength{ sizeof(from) }; const int got{ recvfrom(s, buffer, sizeof(buffer), 0, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&from), &fromLength) }; // got bytes from address from : exactly one datagram No listen , no accept , no connection: a server just bind s a port and receives datagrams from anyone. Each recvfrom returns exactly one datagram, never part of one and never two. If your buffer is too small, the rest of that datagram is discarded ( WSAEMSGSIZE ). A UDP socket can also be connected with connect : no packets are exchanged, but send and recv then go to and come only from that one peer, which is convenient for clients. Size A datagram can in theory be 65 507 bytes, but anything larger than the path's MTU is fragmented at the IP level, and losing any fragment loses the whole datagram. Keep datagrams under about 1200 bytes of payload to be safe on almost every path (QUIC uses this limit). Larger data is split by your own protocol (milestone 5). Loss, duplication and reordering Every datagram may be lost, may arrive twice, or may arrive after one sent later. Code using UDP must handle all three: - Loss : anything that must arrive needs a timeout and a resend (and so an acknowledgement). - Duplicates : give each datagram a sequence number and ignore numbers already seen. - Reordering : use the sequence numbers to discard stale data or to put things back in order. On a quiet local network losses are rare, which makes untested UDP code look correct. Test with simulated loss (Windows tools such as clumsy drop and delay packets on purpose). A request with retries The simplest reliable pattern over UDP is a query: send a request, wait for the answer, resend if it does not come. DNS works this way: 1. Send the request, with a random id . 2. Wait up to a timeout (say 500 ms). 3. If nothing arrives, resend, doubling the timeout each time, up to a few attempts. 4. Accept an answer only if it comes from the address and port you sent to and carries your id . Anything else is ignored: a stray packet, a late answer to an earlier attempt, or an attacker trying to slip in a forged reply. A Windows quirk When a datagram is sent to a port where nothing listens, the target replies with an ICMP "port unreachable". On Windows, the next recvfrom on your socket then fails with WSAECONNRESET , even though UDP has no connections. A server receiving from many clients must ignore that error (or disable the behaviour with the SIO_UDP_CONNRESET ioctl) instead of treating it as fatal. Broadcast A datagram to 255.255.255.255 (or the subnet's broadcast address, lesson 1.02) reaches every device on the local network, after enabling SO_BROADCAST on the socket. Games use this to find servers on a LAN: the client broadcasts "any servers?" and each server answers with its name and port. Routers do not forward broadcasts, so it only works locally; multicast groups extend the idea in a more controlled way.

title: A UDP query with retries
body: Write the client side of lesson 2.05's request with retries, as a state machine driven by time and by arriving datagrams: cpp struct Endpoint { std::uint32_t address; std::uint16_t port; }; enum class Status { Waiting, Answered, Failed }; class UdpQuery { public: UdpQuery(Endpoint server, std::uint16_t id, int attempts, std::uint64_t firstTimeout); std::uint64_t start(std::uint64_t now); std::optional<std::uint64_t onTimer(std::uint64_t now); void onDatagram(Endpoint from, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & data, std::uint64_t now); Status status() const; int sends() const; std::vector<std::uint8_t answer() const; }; - start sends the first request and returns the time its timeout expires: now + firstTimeout . - onTimer is called when that time comes. If still waiting: if fewer than attempts requests have been sent, it sends again and returns the new expiry, with the timeout doubled each time ( firstTimeout , then 2×, 4×...); otherwise the query has failed and it returns std::nullopt . If already answered or failed, std::nullopt . - onDatagram accepts a datagram as the answer only while waiting, only if it comes from the server's address and port, and only if its first two bytes are the id, big-endian. The answer is the rest of the datagram. Anything else is ignored. - sends counts requests sent.

title: A key-value server
body: Build the core of a small networked key-value store, in the style of Redis's text protocol, running on lesson 2.04's event loop: per-connection buffers, partial writes, limits, and a shared store all clients see. Protocol. Each request is one line (ending \n , optional \r before it), words separated by single spaces: Request Reply --- --- SET key value +OK (the value is everything after key , and may contain spaces) GET key $value , or -ERR no such key DEL key :1 if it existed, :0 otherwise INCR key :N after adding 1 (a missing key counts as 0); -ERR not a number if the value is not an integer KEYS a,b,c (all keys, sorted), or when empty QUIT +BYE , then the connection closes once that reply is written anything else -ERR unknown command Every reply ends with \n . Keys are 1 to 64 characters with no spaces; a request with a missing or bad key, or a missing value for SET , gets -ERR bad request . A line longer than 1024 bytes (or 1024 bytes of input without a line end) closes the connection at once. cpp class KvServer { public: explicit KvServer(std::size_t maxQueued); int accept(); void readable(int id, const std::string& bytes); std::string writable(int id, std::size_t capacity); bool isOpen(int id) const; std::size_t keyCount() const; }; The event loop calls readable with bytes received and writable with how many bytes the socket can take (returning what was sent), exactly as in practice 2.04, including closing a client whose unsent replies would exceed maxQueued bytes.

title: 3.01  How HTTP Works
body:
The protocol of the web as plain text over TCP - a request line, headers and an optional body; a status line, headers and a body in reply - methods, status codes, the headers that matter, persistent connections, and where HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ. Text over a connection HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol on top of TCP. A client opens a connection (to port 80, or 443 for HTTPS) and sends a request : text GET /courses/networking HTTP/1.1
 Host: xenon.justloofy.dev
 User-Agent: my-client/1.0
 Accept: text/html
 
 - The request line : a method , the target (path and query), and the version. - Headers : Name: value lines. - A blank line ( 
 alone) ends the headers. - Then an optional body , for methods that send data. The server answers with a response in the same shape: text HTTP/1.1 200 OK
 Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
 Content-Length: 1532
 
 <!doctype html ... (exactly 1532 bytes) You can speak it by hand: curl -v https://example.com shows both sides, and over plain HTTP even telnet example.com 80 and typing the request works. Methods Method Means Body Safe to repeat? --- --- --- --- GET fetch a resource no yes HEAD like GET, headers only no yes POST submit data, create something, run an action yes no PUT replace a resource with this body yes yes (idempotent) PATCH change part of a resource yes not necessarily DELETE remove a resource usually no yes (idempotent) OPTIONS ask what is allowed (used by browsers' CORS checks) no yes "Safe to repeat" is the idempotency of the IPC course's lesson 5.04: browsers and proxies retry GETs freely, but never a POST without asking. Status codes The first digit says the class: Class Meaning Common codes --- --- --- 1xx information 101 Switching Protocols (WebSockets) 2xx success 200 OK , 201 Created , 204 No Content 3xx go elsewhere 301 Moved Permanently , 302 Found , 304 Not Modified 4xx the client's fault 400 Bad Request , 401 Unauthorized , 403 Forbidden , 404 Not Found , 429 Too Many Requests 5xx the server's fault 500 Internal Server Error , 502 Bad Gateway , 503 Service Unavailable Clients should handle a code by its class when they do not know it specifically: an unknown 4xx is treated like 400. Headers that matter Header Purpose --- --- Host which website on this server (required in HTTP/1.1: one IP serves many sites) Content-Length the body's size in bytes Transfer-Encoding: chunked the body comes in pieces of announced size (lesson 3.02) Content-Type what the body is: text/html , application/json , image/png Connection: close close the connection after this response Location where a 3xx redirect points; where a 201 created something Cache-Control , ETag , If-None-Match caching and conditional requests (304) Authorization credentials, such as Bearer <token Cookie / Set-Cookie state the browser keeps for a site Header names are case-insensitive ( content-length is the same header); values are not. Connections HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default: after a response, the same connection carries the next request, saving a TCP (and TLS) handshake each time. That only works if each side knows exactly where every message ends, which is why every response needs a Content-Length or chunked encoding, or must close the connection to mark its end. On one HTTP/1.1 connection requests are answered in order , one at a time, so browsers open several connections per site to load pages in parallel. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 HTTP/2 keeps the same methods, status codes and headers but sends them as binary frames , compresses headers, and multiplexes many requests over one connection at once. HTTP/3 does the same over QUIC (UDP), so a lost packet delays only its own request (lesson 1.04). Programs usually get both from a library; the meaning of requests and responses is the HTTP/1.1 you see here.

title: Status lines
body: Build and read HTTP status lines (lesson 3.01): cpp struct Status { std::string version; int code; std::string reason; }; std::string reasonFor(int code); std::string statusLine(int code); std::optional<Status parseStatusLine(const std::string& line); std::string classOf(int code); - reasonFor : OK for 200, Created 201, No Content 204, Moved Permanently 301, Found 302, Not Modified 304, Bad Request 400, Unauthorized 401, Forbidden 403, Not Found 404, Method Not Allowed 405, Too Many Requests 429, Internal Server Error 500, Service Unavailable 503; anything else Unknown . - statusLine is HTTP/1.1 CODE REASON\r\n . - parseStatusLine reads VERSION CODE REASON (the reason may contain spaces, or be empty after the second space), where the version starts with HTTP/ , and the code is exactly three digits from 100 to 599. A trailing \r\n or \r is ignored. - classOf : informational (1xx), success , redirect , client error , server error , or invalid outside 100 to 599.

title: 3.02  Parsing HTTP Messages
body:
Reading HTTP from a byte stream - finding the end of the headers, splitting the start line and headers, case-insensitive names, finding the body's length from Content-Length or chunked transfer encoding, and the limits and strictness that keep a parser safe. In two stages An HTTP message arrives on a TCP stream in arbitrary chunks (lesson 2.02), so a parser works in two stages: 1. The head : collect bytes until the first 

 . Everything before it is the start line and headers. 2. The body : decide from the headers how many bytes the body has, and collect exactly that many. Anything after the end of the body belongs to the next message on the connection. The start line and headers Split the head into lines at 
 . The first line is the request line ( METHOD TARGET VERSION , separated by single spaces) or, in a response, the status line ( VERSION CODE REASON ). Each following line is a header: text Content-Type: text/plain - name "Content-Type", value "text/plain" - The name is everything before the first : . It must not be empty or contain spaces. - The value is everything after it, with spaces and tabs trimmed from both ends. - Names are case-insensitive : store them in lower case and look them up that way. - A header can appear more than once ( Set-Cookie often does). For most headers repeats are combined with commas; keep them all and let each use decide. How long is the body? The rules, in order: 1. Responses to HEAD , and 1xx , 204 and 304 responses never have a body. 2. If Transfer-Encoding: chunked is present, the body is chunked (below). 3. Otherwise, if Content-Length is present, the body is exactly that many bytes. 4. Otherwise a request has no body, and a response body runs until the server closes the connection. A message with both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length , or with two different Content-Length values, is ambiguous and must be rejected : front-end proxies and back-end servers that resolve such ambiguity differently are the cause of request smuggling attacks. Chunked transfer encoding When a server does not know the length in advance (a page generated as it goes), it sends the body in chunks , each preceded by its size in hexadecimal , ending with a zero-size chunk: text 4
 Wiki
 6
 pedia 
 D
 in

chunks.
 0
 
 That body is Wikipedia in

chunks. : 4 + 6 + 13 bytes. Each size line may carry extensions after a ; , which you ignore. After the zero chunk come optional trailer headers and a final empty line. Limits and strictness An HTTP parser takes input from anyone on the internet, so it must be strict and bounded: - Limit the head (8 KB is common) and the number of headers; reply 431 or close beyond that. - Limit the body you will accept; reply 413 Payload Too Large . - Reject malformed lines, a Content-Length that is not a plain decimal number, negative or absurd sizes, and the ambiguous combinations above, with 400 Bad Request . - Do not "fix" bad input; a lenient parser behind a strict one (or the other way round) is exactly how smuggling works. For real servers, use a well-tested parser library (llhttp, the one inside Node.js, or your framework's); writing one, as the practice does, teaches what they check and why.

title: Headers and the body's length
body: Parse the head of an HTTP request and decide how its body is delimited (lesson 3.02): cpp struct Head { std::string method, target, version; std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string headers; // names in lower case, in order }; enum class BodyKind { None, Length, Chunked, Invalid }; struct Body { BodyKind kind; std::size_t length; }; std::optional<Head parseHead(const std::string& head); std::vector<std::string headerValues(const Head& h, const std::string& name); Body requestBody(const Head& h); - parseHead takes everything before the blank line. Lines are separated by \r\n . The request line is exactly three parts separated by single spaces, with a version starting HTTP/ . Each header line has a name (non-empty, no spaces or tabs) before its first : , and a value with spaces and tabs trimmed from both ends; names are stored in lower case. Any malformed line makes the whole head invalid. - headerValues returns every value of a header (compare names ignoring case), in order. - requestBody : - Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length both present, or several Content-Length values that are not all identical: Invalid . - Transfer-Encoding present: Chunked if its value is exactly chunked (ignoring case), otherwise Invalid . - Content-Length present: it must be 1 to 15 digits only, else Invalid ; then Length with that value (0 is allowed). - Neither: None .

title: 3.03  URLs and Encoding
body: The parts of a URL - scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment - percent-encoding and which characters need it, query strings and form encoding, and resolving a relative link against a base URL. The parts of a URL text https://xenon.justloofy.dev:8443/courses/net%20working?tab=lessons&sort=new part-2 \___/ \_________________/ \__/\____________________/ \__________________/ \____/ scheme host port path query fragment Part Notes --- --- scheme http , https , ws , ftp ... case-insensitive host a name or address; IPv6 addresses go in brackets: http:// ::1 :8080/ port optional; defaults to 80 for http, 443 for https path starts with / ; / if absent query after ? ; usually name=value pairs joined with & fragment after ; never sent to the server , used by the browser to jump within a page A URL can also contain user:password@ before the host. Never use it: the credentials end up in logs and histories. For an HTTP request, the client sends the path and query as the request target ( GET /courses/net%20working?tab=lessons HTTP/1.1 ) and the host and port in the Host header. Percent-encoding URLs may only contain a limited set of characters. Anything else is percent-encoded : each byte of its UTF-8 encoding written as % and two hex digits. text space - %20 é (C3 A9) - %C3%A9 / - %2F (when it is part of a name, not a separator) The characters that never need encoding are the unreserved ones: letters, digits, - , . , _ and ~ . Others are reserved because they have meaning in URLs ( / ? & = : @ and more); they must be encoded when used as data. When building a URL from user input, encode every part that comes from outside; when parsing one, decode each part after splitting it at its separators, so an encoded %2F stays part of a name instead of becoming a path separator. Decoding must reject broken sequences: a % not followed by two hex digits. Accepting them sloppily has been the cause of many security bugs (a check passes on the encoded form, then the decoded form means something else). Query strings and forms A query string is a list of name=value pairs separated by & . HTML forms submit their fields the same way (as the body of a POST with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded ), with one quirk: in form encoding a space is written + , so + itself must be sent as %2B . When parsing form data or queries, turn + into a space before percent-decoding. text q=networking+basics&level=2&tag=c%2B%2B - q = "networking basics", level = "2", tag = "c++" The same name can appear several times ( tag=a&tag=b ); keep all of them in order. Relative URLs Links in a page are often relative to the page's own URL (the base ). Resolving href against https://site/a/b/page.html : href Result --- --- other.html https://site/a/b/other.html (same folder) ../up.html https://site/a/up.html /root.html https://site/root.html (from the host) //cdn.site/x.js https://cdn.site/x.js (same scheme) https://other/x itself: already absolute ?page=2 https://site/a/b/page.html?page=2 The path rules are the same . and .. folding as file paths (the IPC course's lesson 6.01), with / instead of \ .

title: URLs, percent-encoding and query strings
body: Take URLs apart and handle their encoding (lesson 3.03): cpp struct Url { std::string scheme, host; int port; std::string path, query, fragment; }; std::optional<Url parseUrl(const std::string& text); std::string percentEncode(const std::string& text); std::optional<std::string percentDecode(const std::string& text); std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string parseQuery(const std::string& query); - parseUrl handles scheme://host :port /path ?query fragment . The scheme (letters, digits, + , - , . , starting with a letter) is returned in lower case; the host in lower case, with an IPv6 host written in brackets returned without them. The port defaults to 80 for http and 443 for https (0 for any other scheme when absent); a port must be digits from 1 to 65535. The path is / when absent. Query and fragment exclude their ? and . The parts stay percent-encoded. A missing :// , an empty host, or a bad port gives std::nullopt . - percentEncode leaves letters, digits, - , . , _ and ~ as they are and writes every other byte as % and two uppercase hex digits. - percentDecode turns %XY (either case) back into the byte; a % not followed by two hex digits gives std::nullopt . - parseQuery splits at & into name=value pairs (a pair without = has an empty value; empty pieces are skipped), turns + into a space, then percent-decodes both sides; a pair that fails to decode is skipped.

title: 3.04  A Tiny Web Server
body:
Putting the milestone together - routing requests by method and path with parameters, serving static files with the right Content-Type, building correct responses, and the path traversal attack that a naive file server falls for and how to stop it. The loop A web server is the event loop of lesson 2.04 with HTTP as its protocol: 1. Accept connections; read bytes into each connection's buffer. 2. When a whole request has arrived (lesson 3.02), route it to a handler. 3. The handler produces a response: status, headers, body. 4. Serialise the response into the connection's output queue. 5. Keep the connection for the next request, unless either side asked to close. Routing A router maps a method and a path pattern to a handler. Patterns often contain parameters : text GET / - home page GET /courses/{id} - one course; id from the path GET /courses/{id}/lessons/{lesson} POST /api/progress - save progress Matching splits the path at / , compares segment by segment, and collects {name} segments as parameters (percent-decoded, lesson 3.03). Useful rules: - If a path matches a route but not with this method, reply 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header listing the methods that would work, rather than 404. - Prefer exact segments over parameters when both match ( /courses/new before /courses/{id} ), or order routes so the specific one is tried first. - Unknown paths get 404 . Responses A correct response always includes a status line, a Content-Length (or chunked encoding), and a Content-Type when there is a body: cpp-norun std::string response{ "HTTP/1.1 " + std::to_string(status) + " " + reason(status) + "
" }; response += "Content-Type: " + type + "
"; response += "Content-Length: " + std::to_string(body.size()) + "
"; response += "
"; response += body; Content-Type for files comes from the extension: .html is text/html; charset=utf-8 , .css text/css , .js text/javascript , .json application/json , .png image/png , .svg image/svg+xml , and unknown types application/octet-stream . Also send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff so browsers trust that type instead of guessing. Path traversal A naive static file server maps a URL path straight onto a folder: GET /images/logo.png serves C:\site\public\images\logo.png . Now someone requests: text GET /../../Windows/win.ini GET /images/..%2F..%2F..%2Fsecret.txt GET /images/..\..\config.json If the server joins those to its folder without care, it serves files outside the public folder: configuration, source code, keys. This is path traversal , one of the oldest web vulnerabilities. Defend in layers: 1. Percent-decode the path once , then reject anything containing \ , a NUL byte, or a : (drive letters and Windows alternate data streams). 2. Split at / and resolve . and .. yourself; reject any request whose .. would climb above the root, rather than silently clamping it. 3. Reject segments Windows treats specially: names ending in . or a space, and device names such as CON , NUL or COM1 . 4. As a last check, compute the final absolute path and verify it is still inside the public folder (with std::filesystem::weakly_canonical on the real path). 5. Never serve hidden or dot files ( .env , .git ) unless intended. The practice builds exactly this check. What a tiny server is for A small server like this is useful for local tools (a dashboard for your game's stats, a documentation viewer) and for learning. For anything facing the internet, use a mature server or framework, and put TLS in front (next lesson): they have already handled the thousands of edge cases this milestone only touches.

title: A router and a safe file path
match: A router and a safe file path
body: Build the two decisions at the heart of lesson 3.04's tiny web server: cpp struct Match { int status; std::string handler; std::map<std::string, std::string params; std::string allow; }; class Router { public: void add(const std::string& method, const std::string& pattern, const std::string& handler); Match route(const std::string& method, const std::string& path) const; }; std::optional<std::string safeRelativePath(const std::string& urlPath); Router - A pattern is a path split at / ; a segment {name} matches any non-empty segment and captures it (percent-decoded; a segment that fails to decode does not match). - route compares the path, segment by segment, with every route. Routes with exact segments are preferred over parameters: among the routes that match, choose the one with the most exact segments, and on a tie the one added first. - Result: status 200 with the handler and parameters; if routes match the path but none for this method, status 405 and allow listing their methods, in the order added, joined by , ; otherwise 404. safeRelativePath turns a URL path into a path relative to the public folder, or refuses it: - The path must start with / . Percent-decode it once (refuse on failure). - Refuse any \ , : or byte 0 in the decoded path. - Split at / , ignore empty and . segments, let .. remove the previous segment, and refuse if a .. has nothing to remove. - Refuse segments that start with . (hidden files), end with . or a space, or whose name before the first . is a Windows device name: con , prn , aux , nul , com1 to com9 , lpt1 to lpt9 (any case). - Return the remaining segments joined with / ; an empty result becomes index.html .

title: 3.05  HTTPS and TLS
body: What TLS adds to a connection - encryption, integrity and server authentication - certificates and the chain of trust, how hostnames are matched including wildcards, the handshake in outline, SNI, and why you always use a library for it. Three promises Plain HTTP travels as readable text: anyone on the path (the café's Wi-Fi, an internet provider, a compromised router) can read it and change it. TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor of SSL) wraps a TCP connection and adds three guarantees: - Confidentiality : the data is encrypted; observers see only sizes and timing. - Integrity : any change in transit is detected and the connection fails. - Authentication : the client knows it is talking to the real server for that name, not an impostor. HTTPS is simply HTTP inside TLS, on port 443. Everything in this milestone applies unchanged inside the encrypted channel. Certificates Authentication rests on certificates . A server's certificate contains its public key and the names it is valid for, signed by a certificate authority (CA). The client checks: 1. The signature chain: the server's certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA that the operating system or browser trusts. 2. The certificate is within its validity dates and not revoked. 3. The name : the host the client meant to reach is listed in the certificate's subject alternative names. Then, during the handshake, the server proves it holds the private key matching the certificate's public key. An attacker can copy a certificate (it is public) but not the private key. Free, automated certificates from Let's Encrypt made HTTPS the norm; there is no reason to serve anything public over plain HTTP. Matching names Name checking is where many home-made implementations fail. The rules (RFC 6125) for each name in the certificate: - Compare case-insensitively . - An exact name matches only itself: xenon.justloofy.dev matches xenon.justloofy.dev . - A wildcard .justloofy.dev matches exactly one label in its place: xenon.justloofy.dev yes; justloofy.dev no (no label); a.b.justloofy.dev no (two labels). - The wildcard must be the entire leftmost label : .dev style names that cover a whole public suffix are refused by clients, and partial wildcards like x .example.com should be refused too. - IP addresses are matched against IP entries, never against wildcards. The handshake in outline TLS 1.3, the current version, needs one round trip: 1. ClientHello : supported versions and ciphers, a key share, and the server name it wants ( SNI , below). 2. ServerHello with the server's key share; from both shares each side computes the same secret keys. Then, already encrypted, the certificate, a signature proving key ownership, and "finished". 3. The client checks the certificate and signature, sends its own "finished", and application data flows. Resumed connections can even send data in the first flight (0-RTT), with care about replays. SNI One IP address often hosts many HTTPS sites, but the certificate must be chosen before any HTTP is exchanged. So the ClientHello carries the hostname in the Server Name Indication extension. It is sent in clear text (Encrypted Client Hello is being deployed to fix that), which is why packet captures, and network filters, can see which site a TLS connection is for even though they cannot see the pages. Milestone 4's practice extracts it. Use a library TLS involves careful cryptography, certificate parsing, chain building, revocation, and dozens of past attacks that implementations must avoid. Never write your own. On Windows: - WinHTTP or WinINet : HTTPS requests with one API, using the system's certificate store. - SChannel : the system TLS implementation for your own sockets. - OpenSSL , BoringSSL or mbedTLS : cross-platform libraries. - Higher-level HTTP libraries (libcurl, cpp-httplib with OpenSSL) handle it for you. And never "fix" a certificate error by turning verification off. That removes the authentication guarantee entirely and leaves the encryption protecting your traffic for an attacker.

title: Certificate name matching
body: Write the hostname check every TLS client performs (lesson 3.05): cpp bool nameMatches(const std::string& certificateName, const std::string& host); bool certificateMatches(const std::vector<std::string & names, const std::string& host); - nameMatches compares ignoring case. A trailing dot on either side is ignored ( example.com. ). - A name without matches only the same host. - A wildcard is allowed only as the whole leftmost label ( .example.com ). It matches exactly one non-empty label in that position: a.example.com yes; example.com and a.b.example.com no. - Wildcards are refused (never match) if the rest of the name has fewer than two labels ( .com , ), and anywhere else ( x .example.com , a. .example.com ) never matches. - A host that is an IPv4 address (four dot-separated numbers) never matches a wildcard. - certificateMatches is true if any of the certificate's names matches.

title: A streaming HTTP parser
body:
Build the request side of an HTTP/1.1 server: a parser that takes bytes as they arrive from a connection and produces complete requests, with chunked bodies, pipelining, keep-alive and the limits of lesson 3.02, plus a correct response builder. cpp using Headers = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string ; struct Request { std::string method, target, version; Headers headers; std::string body; bool keepAlive; }; class RequestParser { public: RequestParser(std::size_t maxHead, std::size_t maxBody); void feed(const std::string& bytes); std::optional<Request next(); bool failed() const; int errorStatus() const; std::size_t pending() const; }; std::string buildResponse(int status, const Headers& headers, const std::string& body); The head. It ends at the first 

 . If no terminator has arrived and more than maxHead bytes are buffered, or the head is longer than maxHead , the parser fails with 431 . The head is parsed as in practice 3.02 (names in lower case, values trimmed), except that the version must be exactly HTTP/1.0 or HTTP/1.1 . Any malformed head fails with 400 . The body. Decided as in practice 3.02: an invalid combination fails with 400 ; Content-Length larger than maxBody fails with 413 . A chunked body is a series of chunks: a size line of 1 to 8 hex digits (optionally followed by ; and an extension, which is ignored) ending 
 , that many bytes, and 
 ; a size of 0 ends the chunks, and is followed by optional trailer lines and an empty line ( 
 ). Malformed chunks fail with 400 ; a decoded body larger than maxBody fails with 413 . Keep-alive. For HTTP/1.1 it is true unless a Connection header contains the token close ; for HTTP/1.0 it is false unless a Connection header contains keep-alive (tokens are separated by commas, compared ignoring case and surrounding spaces). The parser. feed appends bytes; next returns the next complete request (several can be waiting, pipelined) or std::nullopt if more bytes are needed. Once failed, the parser ignores further input and next always gives std::nullopt ; errorStatus says why (0 while not failed). pending is the number of buffered bytes not yet consumed. buildResponse writes HTTP/1.1 CODE REASON
 (reasons as in practice 3.01), each header as Name: value
 in order, then Content-Length: N
 unless the status is 1xx, 204 or 304 (which have no body: the body is then left out), then 
 and the body.

title: 4.01  Packet Capture
body: Seeing the actual packets - capturing with Wireshark and Npcap, capture filters versus display filters, the pcap file format with its global and per-packet headers, and the rules about what you may capture. Seeing what is really sent Everything in this course so far has been described from the program's point of view. A packet capture shows what actually crossed the wire: every header, every retransmission, every byte. When a networked program misbehaves, a capture is usually the fastest way to find out whether the bug is in the client, the server, or the network. Tools - Wireshark : the standard graphical capture and analysis tool. It decodes thousands of protocols, shows each packet's layers as a tree, and can follow whole conversations. - Npcap : the capture driver Wireshark installs on Windows. Enable its "loopback" support to capture traffic to 127.0.0.1 , which never touches a real network card. - tshark and dumpcap : Wireshark's command-line tools, for capturing on servers and scripting. - pktmon : built into Windows 10 and later ( pktmon start --capture ), writing captures that Wireshark can open after conversion ( pktmon etl2pcap ). Two kinds of filter Capture filters decide what is recorded at all, in the BPF syntax of libpcap. They keep files small on busy networks: text host 192.168.1.50 tcp port 7777 udp and port 53 not port 3389 Display filters decide what Wireshark shows from a capture, using its own field names, and can be changed freely afterwards: text ip.addr == 192.168.1.50 tcp.port == 7777 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 dns.qry.name contains "justloofy" http.request.method == "POST" tcp.analysis.retransmission tls.handshake.extensions_server_name Capture broadly, filter the display narrowly: you cannot recover packets a capture filter dropped. The pcap file format Captures are saved as pcap files (or the newer pcapng , which Wireshark uses by default and can convert). The classic pcap format is simple, which is why every tool supports it: A 24-byte global header: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 magic number: 0xA1B2C3D4 (microsecond timestamps) or 0xA1B23C4D (nanoseconds) 4 2 + 2 version, 2.4 8 4 time zone correction (always 0) 12 4 timestamp accuracy (always 0) 16 4 snapshot length : the most bytes stored per packet 20 4 link type : 1 means Ethernet frames The magic number also tells you the byte order of the file: read as little-endian it is 0xA1B2C3D4 on files written by little-endian machines; if it reads as 0xD4C3B2A1 , every field in the file is big-endian. Then, for each packet, a 16-byte record header and the packet bytes: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 timestamp, seconds 4 4 timestamp, microseconds (or nanoseconds) 8 4 captured length : bytes stored in the file 12 4 original length : bytes the packet really had When a packet was longer than the snapshot length, only the first bytes are stored and the captured length is smaller than the original. Decoders must cope with truncated packets. What you may capture Capturing traffic is reading other people's communication when it is not yours. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to examine, only the traffic you need, and treat captures as sensitive data: they can contain passwords sent without encryption, cookies, and private messages. Deleting a capture you no longer need is good practice.

title: Reading a pcap file
body: Read a classic pcap capture file (lesson 4.01): its global header and its packet records, in either byte order. cpp struct PcapInfo { bool bigEndian; bool nanoseconds; std::uint32_t snapLength; std::uint32_t linkType; }; struct PcapPacket { std::uint32_t seconds; std::uint32_t fraction; std::uint32_t originalLength; std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; std::optional<PcapInfo readHeader(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); std::optional<std::vector<PcapPacket readPackets(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); - readHeader needs at least 24 bytes. Read the first 4 bytes as a little-endian number: 0xA1B2C3D4 is a little-endian file with microsecond timestamps, 0xA1B23C4D little-endian with nanoseconds, 0xD4C3B2A1 big-endian with microseconds and 0x4D3CB2A1 big-endian with nanoseconds. Any other magic fails. The major version (bytes 4-5, in the file's byte order) must be 2. Then fill in the snapshot length (bytes 16-19) and the link type (bytes 20-23). - readPackets reads the header, then every record up to the end of the file: a 16-byte record header (seconds, fraction of a second, captured length, original length, all in the file's byte order) and captured length bytes of data. fraction is the microseconds or nanoseconds field as stored. It fails if the header is bad, a record header or its data runs past the end of the file, or the captured length is greater than the snapshot length or the original length. A file with no records gives an empty list.

title: 4.02  Ethernet and IP Headers
body: Decoding the first layers of a captured packet - the Ethernet frame with MAC addresses and EtherType, the IPv4 header field by field with its options and checksum, fragments, and the fixed 40-byte IPv6 header. Ethernet A captured Ethernet frame starts with a 14-byte header: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 6 destination MAC address 6 6 source MAC address 12 2 EtherType : what follows MAC addresses are written as six hex bytes separated by colons: 3c:22:fb:12:9a:01 . The EtherType values you will meet: EtherType Protocol --- --- 0x0800 IPv4 0x86DD IPv6 0x0806 ARP (finding the MAC address for an IP on the local network) 0x8100 a VLAN tag: 4 more bytes, then the real EtherType (The frame check sequence at the end of the frame is usually not included in captures.) IPv4 The IPv4 header follows at offset 14: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 bits version: 4 0 4 bits IHL : header length in 32-bit words (5 = 20 bytes, more if options) 1 1 DSCP and ECN (priority and congestion marking) 2 2 total length : header plus data, in bytes 4 2 identification (shared by the fragments of one packet) 6 3 bits + 13 bits flags (bit 1: don't fragment, bit 2: more fragments) and fragment offset in 8-byte units 8 1 TTL 9 1 protocol : 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP 10 2 header checksum 12 4 source address 16 4 destination address 20 ... options, if IHL 5 All big-endian. Decoding rules: - The transport header starts at IHL × 4 bytes, not always 20. - Use the total length to know where the IP data ends: Ethernet pads small frames to 60 bytes, and those padding bytes are not part of the packet. - The checksum covers the header only (lesson 2.03's algorithm over IHL × 4 bytes): a correct header sums to zero. - A packet with the "more fragments" flag or a non-zero fragment offset is a fragment : only the first fragment carries the TCP or UDP header; the others carry continuation data. A decoder that treats every fragment as starting with a TCP header reads garbage. IPv6 IPv6 has a fixed 40-byte header, simpler to parse: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 bits version: 6 0 8 bits + 20 bits traffic class and flow label 4 2 payload length (everything after the 40-byte header) 6 1 next header : 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 58 ICMPv6, or an extension header 7 1 hop limit (IPv6's TTL) 8 16 source address 24 16 destination address There is no header checksum (the layers above have their own), and optional information comes as a chain of extension headers , each naming the next, which a full decoder must walk before it reaches TCP or UDP.

title: Ethernet and IPv4 headers
body: Decode the first two layers of a captured frame (lesson 4.02). cpp struct Ipv4 { std::uint8_t headerLength; // in bytes std::uint16_t totalLength; std::uint16_t id; bool dontFragment; bool moreFragments; std::uint16_t fragmentOffset; // in bytes std::uint8_t ttl; std::uint8_t protocol; std::uint32_t source; std::uint32_t destination; bool checksumOk; }; std::string macToString(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & frame, std::size_t offset); std::string ipToString(std::uint32_t ip); std::optional<std::uint16_t etherType(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & frame, std::size_t& payloadOffset); std::optional<Ipv4 parseIpv4(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet); - macToString writes the six bytes starting at offset as lower-case hex pairs separated by colons ( 3c:22:fb:12:9a:01 ), or returns an empty string if they do not fit. - ipToString writes dotted decimal: 0xC0A80001 is 192.168.0.1 . - etherType returns the EtherType at bytes 12-13 and sets payloadOffset to 14. If it is a VLAN tag ( 0x8100 ), the real EtherType is at bytes 16-17 and the payload starts at 18. It fails if the frame is too short for what it needs. - parseIpv4 decodes an IPv4 header at the start of packet . It fails if the packet is shorter than 20 bytes, the version is not 4, the header length is under 20 or longer than the packet, or the total length is less than the header length or more than the packet's size (a packet may be longer than its total length: that is Ethernet padding). The fragment offset is converted to bytes. checksumOk says whether the Internet checksum over the header comes out as 0; a bad checksum does not make the parse fail.

title: 4.03  TCP and UDP Headers
body: The transport headers byte by byte - UDP's eight bytes, TCP's ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, data offset, flags, window and options such as MSS and window scaling - and the pseudo-header both checksums cover. UDP The UDP header is 8 bytes, all big-endian: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 source port 2 2 destination port 4 2 length : header plus data 6 2 checksum (0 in IPv4 means "not computed") That is everything UDP adds to IP (lesson 1.04). TCP The TCP header is 20 bytes plus options: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 source port 2 2 destination port 4 4 sequence number : the number of the first data byte (or of the SYN) 8 4 acknowledgement number : the next byte expected, valid when ACK is set 12 4 bits data offset : header length in 32-bit words (5 to 15) 13 8 bits flags 14 2 window : free receive buffer space 16 2 checksum 18 2 urgent pointer (almost never used) 20 ... options, up to data offset × 4 The flags byte, from the most significant bit: Bit Value Flag Means --- --- --- --- 7 0x80 CWR congestion window reduced 6 0x40 ECE congestion seen (ECN) 5 0x20 URG urgent pointer valid 4 0x10 ACK the acknowledgement number is valid 3 0x08 PSH push this data to the application now 2 0x04 RST reset: abort the connection 1 0x02 SYN synchronise: open a connection 0 0x01 FIN finished sending The payload starts at data offset × 4 , and its length is the IP data length minus that. A SYN or FIN with no data still uses up one sequence number, which is why the handshake's acknowledgements are "seq + 1". Options Options are type-length-value records (type 0 ends the list, type 1 is a one-byte padding "no-op"): Kind Name Purpose --- --- --- 2 MSS the largest segment this side will accept (lesson 1.01) 3 window scale multiply the 16-bit window by 2^n, for fast networks 4 SACK permitted selective acknowledgements may be used 5 SACK which ranges beyond a gap have arrived 8 timestamps for measuring round trips and protecting against wrapped sequence numbers Most appear only in the SYN and SYN-ACK, where the two sides negotiate them. The checksum and the pseudo-header TCP and UDP checksums use the Internet checksum (lesson 2.03), computed over: 1. a pseudo-header : source address, destination address, a zero byte, the protocol number, and the TCP or UDP length (for IPv4: 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 bytes); 2. the TCP or UDP header (with the checksum field as zero when computing it); 3. the data, padded with a zero byte if its length is odd. Including the addresses means a packet delivered to the wrong machine or port fails its checksum. To verify a received segment, run the sum over the pseudo-header and the whole segment including its checksum: a correct one comes out as zero. In captures taken on the sending machine, Wireshark often reports TCP checksums as wrong: modern network cards compute them in hardware ( checksum offloading ) after the capture point, so the captured packet still has a blank or partial checksum. Wireshark's "Validate TCP checksum" option is off by default for this reason.

title: TCP headers and the transport checksum
match: TCP headers and the transport checksum
body: Decode a TCP header with its options, name its flags, and compute the checksum TCP and UDP use (lesson 4.03). cpp struct Tcp { std::uint16_t sourcePort; std::uint16_t destinationPort; std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint32_t acknowledgement; std::uint8_t headerLength; // in bytes std::uint8_t flags; std::uint16_t window; std::optional<std::uint16_t mss; std::optional<std::uint8_t windowScale; bool sackPermitted; }; std::optional<Tcp parseTcp(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & segment); std::string flagNames(std::uint8_t flags); std::uint16_t transportChecksum(std::uint32_t source, std::uint32_t destination, std::uint8_t protocol, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & segment); - parseTcp fails if the segment is shorter than 20 bytes, or the header length (data offset × 4) is under 20 or longer than the segment. It then walks the options between byte 20 and the end of the header: kind 0 ends the list, kind 1 is a single padding byte, and any other kind has a length byte that counts the kind and length bytes too. A length under 2, or an option that would run past the header, makes the parse fail. Record MSS (kind 2, length 4), window scale (kind 3, length 3) and SACK permitted (kind 4, length 2); skip other kinds. - flagNames lists the set flags from bit 0 upwards, separated by commas: FIN, SYN, RST, PSH, ACK, URG, ECE, CWR . So 0x12 is "SYN,ACK" and no flags is "" . - transportChecksum runs the Internet checksum over the IPv4 pseudo-header (source, destination, a zero byte, the protocol, and the segment's length as 16 bits) followed by the segment, padding an odd last byte with zero. With the segment's checksum field set to zero it gives the value to write there; over a received segment it gives 0 when the checksum is right.

title: 4.04  Following a TCP Conversation
body: Turning a list of captured segments into the conversation they carry - identifying a connection by its addresses and ports, relative sequence numbers, the handshake, data in both directions, retransmissions and duplicates, and how connections end with FIN or RST. One connection among many A capture interleaves packets from every connection on the machine. A single TCP connection is identified by its four-tuple : the two IP addresses and the two ports. Packets in one direction have it as (A, portA, B, portB); replies have it reversed. A tracker uses a canonical key (the lower endpoint first, say) so both directions land in the same conversation. Relative sequence numbers Each side's initial sequence number (ISN) is random, so raw numbers like 3141592653 are hard to read. Wireshark shows relative numbers by default: the sequence number minus that side's ISN. The SYN is relative 0, the first data byte relative 1 (the SYN used up one number), and the relative number of any byte is its position in the stream plus one. Do the same in your own tools. Reading a conversation text direction flags rel seq rel ack len 1 client- server SYN 0 0 2 server- client SYN,ACK 0 1 0 3 client- server ACK 1 1 0 4 client- server PSH,ACK 1 1 75 request 5 server- client ACK 1 76 1448 response, part 1 6 server- client ACK 1449 76 1448 part 2 7 client- server ACK 76 2897 0 8 server- client FIN,ACK 2897 76 0 9 client- server FIN,ACK 76 2898 0 10 server- client ACK 2898 77 0 - Packets 1 to 3 are the handshake. - The client sent 75 bytes (4); the server acknowledged them (ack 76 in packet 5) and sent 2 896 bytes in two segments. - Each FIN takes one sequence number, so the final acknowledgements are one more than the data. Retransmissions and duplicates When a segment is lost, the sender sends the same bytes again later. In a capture this appears as a segment whose sequence range has already been seen . Wireshark flags these as TCP Retransmission ; duplicate acknowledgements (the same ack number repeated, often three times before a fast retransmit) as TCP Dup ACK . To reassemble the byte stream, as "Follow TCP Stream" does, take each direction's segments in sequence order , keep only bytes not already placed, and stop at any gap (a segment never captured). The result is exactly what each program read with recv , which makes reading application protocols (next lesson) possible. How connections end - FIN in both directions, each acknowledged: an orderly close (lesson 2.02). - RST : an abort. A RST in reply to a SYN means connection refused : nothing listens on that port. A RST in the middle of a conversation usually means a program crashed or closed with unread data, or a firewall killed the connection. - Nothing : a connection that simply stops, often because one side vanished; it is eventually timed out by keep-alives or by the application. Counting how each connection in a capture ended is often the quickest diagnosis of "it sometimes disconnects".

title: Following TCP conversations
body: Group captured TCP segments into conversations, rebuild each direction's byte stream the way "Follow TCP Stream" does, count retransmissions, and say how each connection ended (lesson 4.04). cpp constexpr std::uint8_t FIN{ 0x01 }, SYN{ 0x02 }, RST{ 0x04 }, PSH{ 0x08 }, ACK{ 0x10 }; struct Segment { std::uint32_t sourceIp; std::uint16_t sourcePort; std::uint32_t destinationIp; std::uint16_t destinationPort; std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint8_t flags; std::string data; }; class Tracker { public: void add(const Segment& s); std::size_t conversations() const; std::string stream(std::uint32_t fromIp, std::uint16_t fromPort, std::uint32_t toIp, std::uint16_t toPort) const; int retransmissions() const; std::string state(std::uint32_t ipA, std::uint16_t portA, std::uint32_t ipB, std::uint16_t portB) const; }; - A conversation is one pair of endpoints (address and port), whichever direction a segment goes. Each direction is tracked separately, by its sender. - A direction's initial sequence number comes from its first SYN. Data in a segment at sequence n belongs at stream offset n - (ISN + 1) , computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic so it works across the wrap from 0xFFFFFFFF to 0 . Data in the SYN itself, data from a direction whose SYN was not seen, and data that would reach past offset 1 << 24 (16 MiB) are ignored. - The first copy of each byte wins. A segment with data in which every byte had already arrived counts as one retransmission . - stream returns the bytes sent from the first endpoint to the second, from offset 0 up to the first gap; an unknown conversation gives "" . - state describes the conversation between the two endpoints, in either order: "none" if there is no such conversation; "refused" if a RST came from a side that never sent a SYN; "reset" for any other RST; "closed" if both sides sent a FIN; otherwise "open" .

title: 4.05  Reading Protocols in Captures
body: Going up the stack in a capture - DNS queries and answers over UDP, plain HTTP in a reassembled TCP stream, and TLS, where only the handshake is readable - the record layer, the ClientHello, and the server name in its SNI extension. DNS DNS messages travel in single UDP datagrams to and from port 53 (lesson 1.03). The 12-byte header: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 id: matches answers to questions 2 2 flags: the top bit ( QR ) is 0 for a query, 1 for a response; the low 4 bits are the response code (0 OK, 3 no such name) 4 2 number of questions 6 2 number of answers 8 2 number of authority records 10 2 number of additional records The question follows: a name in label format, a 2-byte type and a 2-byte class. Answers repeat the name (usually as a compression pointer back to the question), then type, class, a 4-byte TTL, a 2-byte data length and the data (4 bytes for an A record). In a capture, DNS tells you which names a program looked up and what it was told, often the first clue to what it is doing. HTTP Plain HTTP (port 80, or your own local server) is readable once the TCP stream is reassembled: the request line, headers and body of lesson 3.01, in clear text. That is also why it should not be used for anything private. TLS: only the handshake Almost all web traffic is HTTPS, and a capture shows its content only as encrypted application data . But the start of the handshake is readable, and it says a lot. TLS sends records : Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 1 content type: 22 handshake, 23 application data, 21 alert 1 2 legacy version ( 03 01 or 03 03 ) 3 2 length of the record's data The first record from the client is a handshake record containing a ClientHello : Field Size --- --- handshake type 1 (1 = ClientHello) length 3 client version 2 random 32 session id 1-byte length, then that many bytes cipher suites 2-byte length, then 2 bytes per suite compression methods 1-byte length, then the methods extensions 2-byte length, then extensions: each a 2-byte type, 2-byte length, and data Extension type 0 is server name indication (lesson 3.05). Its data is a 2-byte list length, then entries of a 1-byte name type (0 = host name), a 2-byte length and the name. So from a capture you can learn, for each TLS connection, which hostname it was for, which versions and cipher suites the client offered, and the certificate the server sent (in TLS 1.2; TLS 1.3 encrypts it). This is how network monitoring tools label encrypted traffic, and why Encrypted Client Hello is being introduced. When it does not decode Real traffic is messier than tables: a ClientHello split across two TCP segments, records that span segments, protocols on unusual ports, QUIC traffic over UDP 443 that Wireshark decodes only partly. A robust decoder checks every length against the bytes actually available and reports "truncated" or "not this protocol" rather than reading past the end. The practice holds you to that.

title: The server name in a TLS ClientHello
match: The server name in a TLS ClientHello
body: Read the first bytes a TLS client sends and find the version, the cipher suites it offers, and the hostname in its server name indication extension, checking every length on the way (lesson 4.05). cpp struct ClientHello { std::uint16_t version; std::vector<std::uint16_t cipherSuites; std::optional<std::string serverName; }; std::optional<ClientHello parseClientHello(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & stream); stream is the start of the client's reassembled TCP stream. Parse: 1. The record : content type 22 (handshake), a 2-byte version (ignored), a 2-byte length, and that many bytes. The ClientHello must be inside this one record; bytes after the record are ignored. 2. The handshake message : type 1 (ClientHello) and a 3-byte length; the message must fit in the record. 3. The ClientHello : a 2-byte version, 32 random bytes, a session id (1-byte length and bytes), cipher suites (2-byte length, then 2 bytes each: an odd length is an error) and compression methods (1-byte length and bytes). 4. The extensions , if any bytes are left in the message: a 2-byte total length, then extensions of a 2-byte type, a 2-byte length and that many bytes. In extension type 0, the data is a 2-byte list length and then entries of a 1-byte name type, a 2-byte length and the name. The first entry of name type 0 is the server name. Every length must fit inside whatever contains it: a field that runs past its record, message, extension list or extension makes the whole parse fail. A ClientHello with no server name succeeds with serverName empty.

title: A packet dissector
body: Build a small tcpdump : give it a pcap file and it prints one line per packet, decoding Ethernet, IPv4, TCP, UDP and DNS, and saying plainly when a packet is truncated or malformed instead of reading past its end. cpp std::string dissect(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & frame); std::vector<std::string dissectFile(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & pcap); Ethernet. A frame shorter than 14 bytes is truncated . One VLAN tag ( 0x8100 ) is allowed, as in practice 4.02. Then, by EtherType: EtherType Line --- --- 0x0806 ARP 0x86DD IP6 next header N, length L , from the IPv6 header's next header and payload length; truncated if the 40-byte header does not fit 0x0800 the IPv4 rules below anything else ethertype 0x88cc, length 60 : four lower-case hex digits and the frame's size IPv4. If fewer than 20 bytes follow the Ethernet header, the line is truncated . If the version is not 4, the header length is under 20, or the total length is less than the header length, it is malformed . If the header is longer than the bytes available, truncated . Otherwise the IP data is the bytes after the header, up to the total length or the end of the captured frame, whichever comes first (a capture's snapshot length may have cut the packet short, and Ethernet padding is not data). L , the data length, is always total length - header length , whatever was captured. A and B below are the source and destination in dotted decimal, a and b the source and destination ports. Packet Line --- --- fragment offset not 0 IP A B: fragment offset O, length L , O in bytes TCP (6) IP A.a B.b: Flags F , seq S, ack K, win W, length P UDP (17) IP A.a B.b: UDP, length P , or a DNS summary ICMP (1) IP A B: ICMP, length L anything else IP A B: proto N, length L A packet whose IP header checksum is wrong still decodes, and its line ends with bad checksum . TCP. If fewer than 20 bytes of TCP header were captured: IP A B: truncated . If the TCP header length is under 20 or longer than L: IP A B: malformed . If the header (options included) was not all captured: IP A B: truncated . The flags are written as letters in the order S (SYN), F (FIN), R (RST), P (PSH), U (URG), then . for ACK, or none if there are none: so a SYN-ACK is S. . The , ack K part appears only when ACK is set. P is L - TCP header length . Only the headers need to have been captured, not the data. UDP. If fewer than 8 bytes were captured: IP A B: truncated . If the UDP length is under 8 or more than L: IP A.a B.b: malformed . P is UDP length - 8 . If either port is 53, try to read DNS from the UDP data (up to the UDP length or the end of what was captured): at least a 12-byte header, at least one question, and a question name made of plain labels (no compression pointers) followed by 4 bytes of type and class, all inside the data. The root name is written . . Then the line is IP A.a B.b: followed by: - DNS query NAME if the QR bit is 0; - DNS response NAME, no such name if the response code is 3; - otherwise DNS response NAME, 1 answer or DNS response NAME, N answers . If the DNS cannot be read, the line is the ordinary UDP, length P . dissectFile reads a pcap file in either byte order, with microsecond or nanosecond timestamps (practice 4.01). If the header is bad or the link type is not 1 (Ethernet), it returns no lines. For each complete record it adds T and the record's dissect line, where T is the time since the first packet as seconds with six decimals ( 0.750100 ; nanoseconds are cut to microseconds, and a time earlier than the first packet shows as 0.000000 ). An incomplete record at the end is left out.

title: 5.01  Why Games Use UDP
body: Why real-time games build their own protocol on UDP instead of using TCP - head-of-line blocking, the newest state making old data worthless - what a game protocol adds on top, virtual connections with timeouts, and testing under simulated loss and delay. TCP's promise is the problem TCP delivers every byte, in order. For a web page that is exactly right. For a game sending the player positions 30 or 60 times a second, it is a trap: - When one segment is lost, every later byte waits until the lost one is retransmitted, at least one round trip later, often more. Positions that arrived perfectly well sit in the receive buffer, unusable. This is head-of-line blocking , and it turns a single lost packet into a visible freeze. - The data being waited for is already out of date . By the time the position from 100 ms ago is resent, three newer positions exist. Nobody wants the old one. - TCP also slows down on loss (congestion control) and may combine small writes (Nagle's algorithm, disabled with TCP_NODELAY ), both of which add delay a game would rather not have. UDP delivers each datagram independently: some are lost, some are duplicated, some arrive out of order, but nothing waits for anything else. A game takes that and adds only what it needs. What a game protocol adds Over the next lessons you build the usual pieces: Piece Purpose Lesson --- --- --- sequence numbers tell newer from older packets, discard duplicates 5.02 acknowledgements learn which packets arrived, cheaply 5.03 round-trip time know how long to wait before resending 5.04 reliable messages the few things that must arrive (chat, "player joined", a purchase) 5.04 fragmentation send a block bigger than one packet 5.05 The key idea: most data is unreliable and newest-wins (positions, inputs, animation state), and only some messages need to be reliable. A game protocol lets each kind travel the way it needs. A virtual connection UDP has no connections, so the protocol makes its own: - Every packet starts with a protocol id (a fixed number such as a hash of the game name and version).
