Packets without it are dropped at once: stray traffic, port scanners, an old version of the game. - A connection is just "the address and port I hear from". The server keeps a table keyed by address and port. - Connecting uses a small handshake, often with a random salt from each side, so a forged source address cannot create a connection. Real games add encryption and a token from a login server. - Both sides send something at a steady rate (even an empty packet), and a connection that has heard nothing for a few seconds is timed out. There is no FIN: silence is how a UDP connection ends. Testing on a bad network A protocol that works on 127.0.0.1 with no loss proves nothing. Test with simulated conditions: - Latency : hold each packet for, say, 100 ms before delivering it. - Jitter : vary that delay, which also reorders packets. - Loss : drop a share of packets, 1 % to 10 % (and sometimes bursts). - Duplication : occasionally deliver a packet twice. You can put a simulator inside your own code between "send" and the socket, which makes the tests repeatable, or use tools such as clumsy on Windows or tc netem on Linux to degrade real traffic. Make the simulator deterministic (a fixed pattern or a seeded generator), so a failure can be repeated.

title: A deterministic bad network
body: Build the network simulator the rest of this milestone tests against (lesson 5.01): it delays packets, drops some and reorders others, always in the same way, so a failing test can be repeated. cpp class LinkSimulator { public: LinkSimulator(double latency, std::vector<bool dropPattern, std::vector<double extraDelay); void send(double now, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet); std::vector<std::vector<std::uint8_t receive(double now); std::size_t inFlight() const; int dropped() const; }; Number the packets passed to send from 0, counting dropped ones too. Packet k : - is dropped if dropPattern is not empty and dropPattern k % dropPattern.size() is true; - otherwise is delivered at now + latency + extra , where extra is extraDelay k % extraDelay.size() , or 0 if extraDelay is empty. receive(now) removes and returns every packet whose delivery time is at or before now , earliest delivery first; packets due at the same time come out in the order they were sent. inFlight is the number of packets waiting, and dropped the number dropped so far.

title: 5.02  Sequence Numbers That Wrap
body: Numbering packets with a small counter that wraps around - comparing sequence numbers correctly across the wrap with half-range arithmetic, the signed difference between two numbers, and discarding duplicates and stale packets with a sliding window. A number on every packet Every packet carries a sequence number that the sender increments each time. Receivers use it to tell which packet is newer, to drop duplicates, and (next lesson) to say which ones arrived. Bytes on the wire are precious, so the number is usually 16 bits . At 60 packets a second it wraps from 65 535 back to 0 every 18 minutes. Comparing with a plain a b fails at the wrap: packet 2 is newer than packet 65 534, though 2 < 65 534. Half-range comparison Treat the numbers as points on a circle. a is newer than b if going forward from b to a is less than half way round : cpp-norun bool sequenceGreater(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b) { return (a b && a - b < 32768) (a < b && b - a 32768); } An equivalent and shorter form uses the signed difference: subtract in 16-bit unsigned arithmetic and reinterpret as a signed 16-bit number. cpp-norun int sequenceDifference(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b) { return static_cast<std::int16_t (static_cast<std::uint16_t (a - b)); } cpp-norun sequenceDifference(5, 3) // 2: 5 is two packets newer sequenceDifference(2, 65534) // 4: across the wrap sequenceDifference(65534, 2) // -4 Exactly half way round (a difference of 32 768) is ambiguous; it never matters in practice because no protocol keeps that many packets in flight. This is the same "serial number arithmetic" TCP uses for its 32-bit sequence numbers (RFC 1982). Duplicates and stale packets Because UDP may duplicate and reorder, a receiver keeps a little history: - the latest sequence number seen so far; - which of the recent numbers before it have also been seen, usually as a bit per number for the last 32 to 256. When a packet arrives: Difference from latest Meaning Action --- --- --- positive newer than anything seen accept; slide the window forward zero, or already marked duplicate drop negative, inside the window late but new accept, mark it seen negative, beyond the window too old to judge drop For newest-wins data (positions), you can go further and ignore any packet older than the latest , since its state is stale anyway; reliable messages inside it must still be processed, which is why the decision belongs to each kind of data, not to the packet.

title: Wrapping sequence numbers
body: Compare 16-bit sequence numbers across the wrap and filter out duplicates and stale packets (lesson 5.02). cpp int sequenceDifference(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b); bool sequenceGreater(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b); class DuplicateFilter { public: bool accept(std::uint16_t sequence); std::optional<std::uint16_t latest() const; }; - sequenceDifference is a - b computed in 16 bits and read as a signed 16-bit number: from -32768 to 32767. - sequenceGreater is true when a is newer than b : their difference is positive. (Exactly half way round counts as greater in neither direction.) - DuplicateFilter remembers the latest sequence number accepted and which of the 256 numbers ending at it (latest - 255 to latest) have been seen. accept returns true and records the number if it has not been seen: the first number ever, a newer one (which becomes the latest), or an older one inside the window that is not yet marked. It returns false for a number already seen or one 256 or more behind the latest. latest is empty until something is accepted.

title: 5.03  Acknowledgement Bitfields
body: Telling the sender which packets arrived without sending a packet per acknowledgement - the latest received number plus a 32-bit field for the ones before it, why the redundancy survives loss, and how the sender turns acks into "delivered" events. Acknowledging cheaply TCP acknowledges bytes cumulatively and retransmits itself. A game protocol wants something different: the sender should simply learn which packets arrived , so it can decide what, if anything, to resend. And since both sides are sending packets all the time anyway, acknowledgements ride along in the header of every packet ( piggybacking ) instead of getting packets of their own. The usual header: Field Size Meaning --- --- --- sequence 16 bits this packet's number ack 16 bits the most recent sequence number received from the other side ackBits 32 bits bit i set means packet ack - 1 - i was also received So every packet acknowledges 33 packets at once. Redundancy beats loss Suppose the other side receives packets 100 to 140 except 137. Its next packets all say: text ack = 140, ackBits: bit 2 clear (137 missing), every other bit of the 32 set It sends this many times a second. Even if most of its packets are lost, any one that gets through tells you the whole story of the last 33 packets. An acknowledgement is lost for good only if the other side's packets are lost for more than about half a second in a row at 60 packets a second, and by then the connection is in trouble anyway. The receiving side Keep latest and bits . When a packet with sequence s arrives (using d = sequenceDifference(s, latest) from lesson 5.02): - d 0 : the new latest is s . The old latest becomes bit d - 1 , and every old bit moves up by d (bits shifted past 31 are forgotten). If d 32 , the old history is gone completely. - d < 0 : set bit -d - 1 , if it is below 32. - d == 0 : a duplicate; nothing changes. Watch out for shifting a 32-bit value by 32 or more: in C++ that is undefined behaviour, so handle d = 32 separately or shift a 64-bit value. The sending side The sender remembers what it put in each packet it sent (a ring buffer of the last few hundred, indexed by sequence % size ). When an ack and ackBits arrive, it walks the 33 numbers they cover. Each that is marked received and was not acknowledged before becomes a "delivered" event: - reliable messages in that packet are done and need no resending; - the time between sending and the ack is a round-trip sample (next lesson); - a packet still unacknowledged long after newer ones were acked was almost certainly lost . Each packet must produce its "delivered" event once , though it will be acknowledged by dozens of incoming packets.

title: Acks with a bitfield
body: Build both halves of piggybacked acknowledgements (lesson 5.03): the receiver's ack and ackBits , and the sender's "which of my packets were delivered". cpp class ReceivedPackets { public: void record(std::uint16_t sequence); std::uint16_t ack() const; std::uint32_t ackBits() const; }; class SentPackets { public: void sent(std::uint16_t sequence); std::vector<std::uint16_t onAck(std::uint16_t ack, std::uint32_t ackBits); }; ReceivedPackets. Before anything is recorded, ack is 0 and ackBits is 0. The first recorded number becomes the ack with no bits. After that, with d the signed difference between the new number and the current ack (practice 5.02): - d 0 : the new number becomes the ack; the old ack becomes bit d - 1 and every old bit moves up by d ; bits that would pass bit 31 are dropped; - d < 0 : set bit -d - 1 if it is below 32, otherwise ignore the number; - d == 0 : nothing changes. SentPackets remembers every sequence number passed to sent that has not yet been acknowledged. onAck looks at ack and at ack - 1 - i for each set bit i ; each of those still waiting is now acknowledged and stops waiting. It returns them oldest first (the one furthest behind ack first, ack last), and a packet is never returned twice. Sending the same number again (after the counter wraps) makes it wait again.

title: 5.04  Round Trips and Resending
body: Measuring how long a round trip takes and smoothing it, the retransmission timeout from RFC 6298 with backoff and Karn's rule, and building reliable ordered messages on top of unreliable packets - message ids, resending until acknowledged, and delivering in order. Measuring the round trip The time from sending a packet to receiving its acknowledgement is a round-trip time (RTT) sample. Single samples are noisy (the other side may wait a few milliseconds before sending its next packet), so protocols keep a smoothed estimate. TCP's method, from RFC 6298, works well for games too: text first sample R: srtt = R rttvar = R / 2 each later R: rttvar = 3/4 · rttvar + 1/4 · srtt - R srtt = 7/8 · srtt + 1/8 · R timeout: rto = srtt + 4 · rttvar (clamped to a minimum and maximum) srtt is the smoothed RTT, the number to show the player as "ping". rttvar measures how much it varies; adding four times it to the timeout means a slow-but-normal round trip is not mistaken for a loss. - Before any sample, use a safe initial timeout (TCP uses 1 second). - When a timeout fires and you resend, double the timeout (exponential backoff ), up to the maximum, so a broken connection is not flooded. The next real sample resets it. - Karn's rule : never take a sample from something that was resent, because you cannot tell whether the ack is for the first copy or the second. With per-packet acks (lesson 5.03) this is easy: each packet is sent once, and only resent messages travel in new packets. Reliable messages Some things must arrive: chat, "you picked up the key", a match result. On top of unreliable packets: 1. Give each reliable message an increasing message id (16 bits, compared as in lesson 5.02). 2. Keep it in a send queue until it is acknowledged. 3. Each time you build a packet, include queued messages that were never sent , or were sent longer ago than the timeout . Remember which message ids went into which packet. 4. When the packet is acknowledged (lesson 5.03), the messages in it are done: remove them from the queue. On the receiving side: - Messages may arrive out of order (a resent message overtakes nothing, but a later one may arrive first) and more than once. - Keep the id of the next message to deliver . A message with that id is delivered at once, followed by any buffered ones that now follow it. A later id is buffered. An earlier id is a duplicate and is dropped. If order does not matter (each message independent), deliver immediately and only drop duplicates: that avoids one lost message holding back the others, the same head-of-line problem as TCP but chosen only where it is needed. Many games run several channels : unreliable, reliable unordered and reliable ordered. Resending is expensive Every resend uses bandwidth that newer data could have used. Keep reliable messages small and rare, send state (positions) unreliably, and if something important is large, send it once reliably and then send changes. The next lesson deals with sizes.

title: Round-trip time and the resend timeout
match: Round-trip time and the resend timeout
body: Estimate the round-trip time and the retransmission timeout the way RFC 6298 does (lesson 5.04). cpp class RttEstimator { public: RttEstimator(double minRto, double maxRto); void sample(double rtt); double srtt() const; double rttvar() const; double rto() const; void backoff(); }; - Before any sample, srtt and rttvar are 0 and rto is 1000 (milliseconds), clamped to minRto, maxRto . - The first sample R sets srtt = R and rttvar = R / 2 . - Each later sample sets rttvar = 0.75 rttvar + 0.25 srtt - R (using the old srtt ), then srtt = 0.875 srtt + 0.125 R . - After every sample, rto = srtt + 4 rttvar , clamped to minRto, maxRto . - backoff doubles rto , up to maxRto . The next sample replaces the backed-off value.

title: 5.05  Fragmentation and Bandwidth
body: Keeping packets under the path MTU, why IP fragmentation is avoided, splitting large blocks into fragments and reassembling them with ids, counts and timeouts, budgeting bandwidth per connection, and choosing what to send when it does not all fit. How big can a packet be? An Ethernet frame carries 1 500 bytes of IP packet (lesson 1.01). Paths through tunnels, VPNs and mobile networks carry less. If a UDP datagram is too big, IP fragments it, and then: - losing any fragment loses the whole datagram, so the loss rate multiplies; - some routers and firewalls drop fragments altogether; - with IPv6, routers do not fragment at all. So games keep every datagram under a safe size, typically 1 200 bytes of payload (the same limit QUIC uses), and split large data themselves. Your own fragments To send a block larger than one packet (a map, a full snapshot, a file), split it into fragments , each sent in its own packet with a small header: Field Size Meaning --- --- --- block id 16 bits which block this belongs to fragment index 8 bits 0 to count - 1 fragment count 8 bits how many fragments the block has The receiver keeps a reassembly buffer per block id: which fragments have arrived and their bytes. When all count are there, the block is complete. Rules that make it robust: - Check everything : index below count, count above zero, the same count in every fragment of a block, a fragment size within limits. A wrong value is a dropped packet, never an out-of-range write. - Ignore duplicates of fragments already present. - Time out incomplete blocks, and limit how many are in progress, so a lost fragment or a malicious sender cannot use up memory. - If the block must arrive, either resend the missing fragments (using acks) or resend the whole block reliably. A neat scheme is to make each fragment a reliable message. A bandwidth budget A connection cannot send as much as it likes: the player's upload may be a few hundred kilobits per second, and a server sends to many players. Decide a budget per connection, for example 256 kbit/s, which at 60 packets a second is about 530 bytes per packet. When everything does not fit: - Give each kind of data a priority . Things that have not been sent for a while gain priority (an accumulator : each tick, add each object's priority to its score; send the highest scores; reset the score of what was sent). Far-away objects get a lower priority, so they update less often but are never starved. - Send reliable messages first, but cap them so they cannot crowd out state entirely. - Watch round-trip time and loss: when they climb, the path is congested. Sending less (fewer packets a second, or smaller ones) is kinder to the network and usually improves the game, too.

title: Splitting and reassembling blocks
body: Send blocks larger than one packet as fragments, and put them back together safely on the other side (lesson 5.05). cpp struct Fragment { std::uint16_t block; std::uint8_t index; std::uint8_t count; std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; std::vector<Fragment split(std::uint16_t block, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & data, std::size_t maxFragment); class Reassembler { public: explicit Reassembler(double timeout); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t add(const Fragment& f, double now); void expire(double now); std::size_t pending() const; }; split cuts data into pieces of maxFragment bytes (the last may be shorter), numbered from 0, each knowing the total count. Empty data is one empty fragment. If maxFragment is 0 or more than 255 fragments would be needed, it returns no fragments. Reassembler keeps the blocks in progress, keyed by block id. add first calls expire(now) , then: - drops the fragment (returning nothing and changing nothing) if its count is 0, its index is not below its count, its data is longer than 1200 bytes, or a block with the same id is in progress with a different count; - ignores a fragment whose index has already arrived for that block; - starts a new block if none is in progress with that id, unless 16 blocks are already in progress, in which case the fragment is dropped; a block's timer starts with its first fragment; - when a block has all its fragments, removes it and returns its data in index order. expire(now) removes every block whose first fragment arrived more than timeout before now . pending is the number of blocks in progress.

title: A reliable channel over unreliable packets
match: A reliable channel over unreliable packets
body: Build the reliability layer of a game protocol: one endpoint of a connection that sends a packet every tick, acknowledges the other side's packets with a bitfield, and carries reliable, ordered messages that are resent until they are known to have arrived. The tests connect two endpoints through a link that loses, delays and repeats packets, and check that every message arrives once and in order. cpp class ReliableEndpoint { public: explicit ReliableEndpoint(double resendAfter); bool send(const std::string& message); std::vector<std::uint8_t update(double now); void receive(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet); std::vector<std::string take(); std::size_t unacked() const; }; The packet (all numbers big-endian): Bytes Field --- --- 0-1 sequence 2-3 ack 4-7 ack bits 8 message count then, per message message id (2 bytes), length (2 bytes), the bytes Sending. send queues a message, giving it the next message id (0, 1, 2 ..., wrapping at 65 536), and returns true; a message longer than 1 000 bytes is refused with false. unacked is the number of queued messages not yet acknowledged. update(now) builds and returns exactly one packet, every time it is called, even with no messages in it: - its sequence number is the next one (0 for the first packet, then 1, 2, ...); - ack and ack bits describe the packets received from the other side, exactly as in practice 5.03; before any packet has been received they are 65 535 and 0 (the other side's numbers start at 0, so this acknowledges nothing); - it then goes through the queue in id order and includes each message that has never been sent, or was last sent resendAfter or more before now . It stops at the first such message that would make the packet larger than 1 200 bytes, or when the packet already holds 255 messages. Each included message is marked as sent at now ; - it remembers which messages went into this sequence number. Receiving. receive first checks the whole packet: at least 9 bytes, every message fits, and nothing is left over. A malformed packet is ignored completely. Otherwise: 1. Record its sequence number for your own acks (practice 5.03). 2. Read its ack and ack bits . Each of your packets they acknowledge for the first time is delivered: every message in it is acknowledged and leaves the queue (it may be in several packets; the first ack is enough). 3. Deliver its messages in order: keep the id of the next message to deliver (starting at 0). A message whose id is that one or up to 1 023 after it (by the signed difference of practice 5.02) is buffered if it is not already; anything else is a duplicate or nonsense and is dropped. Then, as long as the next id is buffered, move it to the delivered list and advance. take returns the messages delivered since the last call, in order, and clears that list.

title: 6.01  The Authoritative Server
body: How multiplayer games are organised - the server owns the truth and clients send only inputs, why that is the basis of fair play, the fixed tick with an accumulator, tick numbers as the shared clock, and choosing tick and send rates. Who decides what happened? In a multiplayer game, several machines each run a copy of the world, and their copies drift apart: messages take time, packets are lost, clocks differ. Someone has to decide what really happened. Almost every modern action game uses an authoritative server : - The server runs the real simulation. Its state is the truth. - Clients send only their inputs ("move left, jump, fire at this angle"), never results ("I am now here", "I hit him for 100"). - The server applies the inputs, simulates, and sends the resulting state back to every client, which shows it. This is also the foundation of fair play: a modified client can send odd inputs, but it cannot declare that it teleported or that its shot hit. The server validates every input : movement is limited to what the rules allow (a move vector longer than 1 is clamped, not trusted), a player cannot fire faster than the weapon allows, and actions are checked against the server's own state. The alternatives have their places: peer-to-peer lockstep (every machine runs the same deterministic simulation from everyone's inputs, common in strategy games with thousands of units) and client authority for casual cooperative games where cheating does not matter. This milestone builds the server-authoritative model. The tick The server simulates in fixed steps called ticks , for example 60 per second (a step of 16.67 ms) or 20 to 30 for slower games. Fixed steps make physics stable and the simulation reproducible: the same inputs give the same results. Real time does not arrive in neat steps, so a loop accumulates elapsed time and runs as many ticks as fit: cpp-norun accumulator += elapsed; while (accumulator = step) { simulateOneTick(); accumulator -= step; } alpha = accumulator / step; // how far we are towards the next tick, for smooth drawing If the machine falls far behind (a long pause, a debugger stop), running hundreds of ticks to catch up makes things worse: each slow frame causes even more ticks the next frame. Cap the ticks per frame and drop the rest of the backlog. Clients run the same loop, drawing with alpha to blend between the last two simulated states, so motion is smooth on a 144 Hz screen while the simulation runs at 60. Tick numbers are the clock Every snapshot the server sends carries its tick number , and every input a client sends carries a sequence number (and often the tick it was made for). These numbers, not wall-clock times, are how the two sides talk about time: - "This snapshot is the world at tick 4 512." - "The last input of yours I applied was number 917." - "When you fired, you were seeing the world at tick 4 505." (lesson 6.05) Tick rate and send rate The server need not send a snapshot every tick. Typical choices: simulate at 60, send snapshots at 20 to 60, and clients send inputs every tick (often several inputs per packet, for redundancy against loss, as in milestone 5). Higher rates feel more responsive and cost bandwidth and server CPU per player; many games pick 30 or 64 and tune from there.

title: The fixed tick and input checks
match: The fixed tick and input checks
body: Write the two pieces every authoritative server starts with (lesson 6.01): a fixed-timestep accumulator that never spirals, and a check that keeps movement input inside the rules. cpp class FixedStep { public: FixedStep(std::int64_t step, int maxSteps); int advance(std::int64_t elapsed); double alpha() const; std::int64_t ticks() const; std::int64_t dropped() const; }; std::pair<float, float clampMove(float x, float y); Times are whole microseconds, so the arithmetic is exact. - advance adds elapsed (a negative value counts as 0) to the accumulator and returns how many ticks to run now: the number of whole steps in the accumulator, which it removes. If that is more than maxSteps , it returns maxSteps and throws away the extra whole steps too, keeping only the remainder below one step; the time thrown away is added to dropped . - alpha is the accumulator divided by the step, from 0 up to (not including) 1. - ticks is the total number of ticks returned so far. - clampMove returns a move vector a server can trust: if either part is not finite (infinity or NaN) the move is (0, 0) ; if its length is more than 1 it is scaled down to length 1; otherwise it is returned unchanged.

title: 6.02  Snapshots and Delta Compression
body: Sending the world to clients efficiently - what goes in a snapshot, quantising floats into a few bits, sending only what changed against a baseline the client has acknowledged, change masks, and what happens when packets are lost. A snapshot A snapshot is the server's world state at one tick, as one client needs to see it: for each relevant entity, an id and the fields that matter (position, angle, health, animation). Sending it all, every time, is simple and robust: each snapshot stands alone, so a lost one does not matter. It is also big. Thirty players with 20 bytes each is 600 bytes, times 60 snapshots a second, times 30 clients: over 8 Mbit/s of upload for one server. Two techniques shrink it dramatically. Quantisation A float is 4 bytes with far more precision than a game needs. If the map is 0 to 1 000 units wide, storing the position as a 16-bit integer gives steps of 1 000 / 65 535 ≈ 0.015 units, invisible on screen: cpp-norun std::uint16_t quantize(float v, float min, float max) { const float t{ (std::clamp(v, min, max) - min) / (max - min) }; return static_cast<std::uint16_t (std::lround(t 65535.0f)); } float dequantize(std::uint16_t q, float min, float max) { return min + (max - min) (q / 65535.0f); } The same idea everywhere: an angle in 8 or 10 bits, health as a byte, a boolean as a single bit. The error is at most half a step. Crucially, the server simulates with the quantised values too (or rounds its state the same way), so client and server agree exactly on what was sent. Delta compression Most of the world does not change from one snapshot to the next: a player standing still, a door that is closed. So send only the difference against a snapshot the client already has: - The client acknowledges the snapshots it receives (milestone 5's acks). - The server keeps the last few dozen snapshots per client and encodes each new one against the latest one the client acknowledged , the baseline . - For each entity it writes the id and a change mask , one bit per field, followed by only the fields whose bit is set. Unchanged entities are left out entirely; new entities have every bit set; removed ones get a "removed" marker. The client reconstructs the new snapshot by copying the baseline and applying the changes. A typical scene shrinks from hundreds of bytes to tens. When packets are lost Delta compression against an acknowledged baseline stays correct under loss: if snapshots 101 to 103 are lost, the server simply keeps encoding against 100 (the last one acknowledged) until a newer one is acknowledged. Deltas grow a little while packets are being lost, and shrink again once acks get through. What must never happen is encoding against a snapshot the client might not have. Then the client applies changes to the wrong base and its world is silently wrong. If there is no usable baseline (a new client, or a baseline too old to keep), send a full snapshot.

title: Quantised snapshots and deltas
body: Shrink snapshots the way lesson 6.02 describes: quantise floats into 16 bits, and encode a snapshot as the changes from a baseline the client already has. cpp struct Entity { std::uint16_t id; std::uint16_t x; std::uint16_t y; std::uint8_t angle; std::uint8_t health; }; std::uint16_t quantize(float value, float min, float max); float dequantize(std::uint16_t q, float min, float max); std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeDelta(const std::vector<Entity & baseline, const std::vector<Entity & current); std::optional<std::vector<Entity decodeDelta(const std::vector<Entity & baseline, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & delta); Quantising. quantize clamps the value to min, max , maps it to 0..65 535 and rounds to the nearest integer (halves away from zero, as std::lround does); NaN gives 0. dequantize maps back: min + (max - min) q / 65535 . The delta format. Snapshots are lists of entities sorted by id, each id once. A delta is a 2-byte entry count, then the entries in increasing id order, each a 2-byte id, a 1-byte mask , and the fields the mask names, in this order (all numbers big-endian): Mask bit Field --- --- 0x01 x, 2 bytes 0x02 y, 2 bytes 0x04 angle, 1 byte 0x08 health, 1 byte 0x80 removed, alone, with no fields encodeDelta writes one entry for each id that is in current but differs from the baseline (only the changed fields), each id new in current (mask 0x0F ), and each id in the baseline missing from current (mask 0x80 ). Unchanged entities are left out. decodeDelta starts from the baseline and applies the entries, returning the new snapshot sorted by id. It fails if the data is truncated or has bytes left over, the ids are not strictly increasing, a mask is 0 or uses other bits, a removal is combined with other bits or names an id not in the baseline, or an entry for an id not in the baseline is not a full 0x0F .

title: 6.03  Interpolation
body: Making other players move smoothly from snapshots that arrive 20 to 60 times a second with jitter and loss - rendering a little in the past, blending between the two snapshots around the render time, the size of the delay, and limited extrapolation. The problem Snapshots arrive 20 to 60 times a second, unevenly (jitter), and some are lost. If a client simply placed every other player at the position from the latest snapshot, they would jump from point to point, stutter when a snapshot arrived late, and freeze when one was lost. Render in the past The standard answer is entity interpolation : show other entities slightly in the past, at renderTime = now - delay , and blend between the two snapshots on either side of that time. text snapshots: t=100 t=150 t=200 t=250 ^ renderTime = 175 position = snapshot150 + (snapshot200 - snapshot150) · (175 - 150) / (200 - 150) Because the render time is behind the newest snapshot, the client usually already holds the snapshot after it, so it can always blend smoothly. The delay is chosen to cover the gap between snapshots plus some jitter, typically two snapshot intervals : about 100 ms at 20 snapshots a second (Counter-Strike's long-standing default), less at higher rates. If one snapshot is lost, the client blends across the wider gap and nobody notices. The cost is that other players are seen where they were about 100 ms ago, plus half the round trip. That is why the next two lessons exist: prediction for your own player, lag compensation for hitting others. Times and buffers - Use the server's tick numbers (or times derived from them), not the time each snapshot happened to arrive: arrival times include jitter, which is exactly what interpolation is meant to hide. - Keep a short buffer of recent snapshots per entity, sorted by time, and drop ones older than the render time needs. - Ignore a snapshot older than the newest one held: it arrived out of order and adds nothing. - Clients keep their idea of "now in server ticks" by tracking the latest snapshot tick and advancing it with their own clock, nudging it gently when snapshots arrive earlier or later than expected. When snapshots stop If the render time passes the newest snapshot (several are lost in a row), there is nothing to blend towards. Options: - Hold the last position: safe, but the entity freezes. - Extrapolate from the last two snapshots' velocity for a short time (dead reckoning), then hold. A little extrapolation hides a short gap; a lot shows players running into walls and snapping back when the truth arrives. Limit it to about one snapshot interval. Interpolate other values the same way: angles (taking the short way round), animation times. Discrete values (alive or dead, which weapon) simply switch when the render time passes their snapshot.

title: An interpolation buffer
body: Show a remote player smoothly from irregular snapshots by rendering a fixed delay in the past and blending between snapshots (lesson 6.03). cpp struct Snapshot { double time; double x; double y; }; class Interpolator { public: Interpolator(double delay, double maxExtrapolation); void add(const Snapshot& s); std::optional<std::pair<double, double positionAt(double now) const; std::size_t buffered() const; }; - add stores a snapshot unless its time is not newer than the newest one already stored (an out-of-order arrival), keeping at most the 32 newest. - positionAt renders at t = now - delay : - with no snapshots, there is no position; - at or before the oldest snapshot, the oldest position; - between two stored snapshots, the straight-line blend of the two around t ; - after the newest snapshot: with only one snapshot, its position; otherwise continue at the velocity between the two newest snapshots for t - newest time , but for no longer than maxExtrapolation , then hold there. - buffered is the number of snapshots stored.

title: 6.04  Prediction and Reconciliation
body: Hiding latency for your own player - running your inputs immediately with the same simulation code as the server, keeping the inputs not yet confirmed, and when the server's state arrives, resetting to it and replaying the rest; plus smoothing corrections and what cannot be predicted. The delay you feel With a pure authoritative server, pressing a key does nothing until the input reaches the server, is simulated, and the result comes back: a full round trip, 50 to 150 ms. Movement feels like wading through syrup. Client-side prediction The client already knows its own inputs and has the same movement code as the server. So it applies each input immediately to its own player and shows the result, without waiting: 1. Make an input, give it the next sequence number, and send it to the server. 2. Simulate it locally at once, exactly as the server will. 3. Keep it in a list of pending inputs: sent, but not yet confirmed. When nothing unexpected happens, the server computes exactly the same positions a round trip later, and the prediction was perfect. Reconciliation Each snapshot tells the client its player's authoritative state and the sequence number of the last input the server applied . That state is in the past: inputs sent since then are still on their way. So the client: 1. Drops pending inputs with sequence numbers up to the last applied one: they are confirmed. 2. Resets its player to the authoritative state. 3. Replays the remaining pending inputs on top of it, with the same simulation. The result is the present again, now based on the truth. If the prediction was right, nothing visibly changes. If something the client could not know happened (another player pushed it, the server rejected a move, an explosion knocked it back), the replay starts from the corrected state and the player ends up where they really are. text client predicted: inputs 1..10 applied, at x = 100 snapshot arrives: server applied up to 7, x = 70 (no surprises) reconcile: drop 1..7, reset to 70, replay 8, 9, 10 → x = 100 (no change) snapshot arrives: server applied up to 7, x = 40 (hit by something at input 5) reconcile: drop 1..7, reset to 40, replay 8, 9, 10 → x = 70 (correction of -30) Making it work well - Same code, same results. The client must run exactly the server's movement code with the same inputs and tick length, and ideally the same quantisation (lesson 6.02). Any difference shows as constant small corrections. - Smooth the corrections. Instead of snapping the camera, move the displayed position towards the corrected one over a few frames, while the simulated position snaps at once. - Ignore old snapshots. A snapshot that confirms fewer inputs than one already applied arrived out of order: drop it. - Predict only what is yours. Your movement and your weapon's animation are predicted. Other players are interpolated (lesson 6.03), and anything that decides the game, such as hits, damage and pickups, waits for the server.

title: Prediction and reconciliation
body: Make your own player respond instantly: predict each input locally, keep the unconfirmed ones, and when the server's state arrives, reset to it and replay them (lesson 6.04). cpp struct Input { std::uint32_t sequence; float moveX; float moveY; }; struct PlayerState { float x; float y; }; PlayerState simulate(PlayerState s, const Input& in, float speed, float dt); class PredictedPlayer { public: PredictedPlayer(PlayerState start, float speed, float dt); Input applyInput(float moveX, float moveY); void onServerState(std::uint32_t lastProcessed, PlayerState authoritative); PlayerState state() const; std::size_t pending() const; }; - simulate is the movement code the client and server share. It clamps the move vector to length 1 (as in practice 6.01: a non-finite part makes the move zero), then moves by move speed dt in each axis. - applyInput makes the next input (sequence numbers start at 1), simulates it on the current state at once, keeps it as pending, and returns it so it can be sent. - onServerState reconciles. It ignores a state whose lastProcessed is lower than one already reconciled. Otherwise it drops every pending input with a sequence number up to lastProcessed , sets the state to authoritative , and replays the remaining pending inputs in order.

title: 6.05  Lag Compensation
body: Making hits fair when every player sees others in the past - the server keeping a short history of positions, rewinding targets to the moment the shooter saw, testing the shot there, limiting the rewind, and the trade-offs it creates for the player being shot. Aiming at the past Thanks to interpolation (lesson 6.03), a client sees other players where they were about 100 ms ago, plus the time its own input takes to reach the server. A player who aims perfectly at a running enemy on their screen and fires would miss if the server tested the shot against where the enemy is now : by the time the shot arrives, the enemy has moved on. Players would have to aim ahead by an amount that changes with their ping. Nobody wants that. Rewinding the world Lag compensation makes the server test the shot against what the shooter actually saw: 1. The server keeps a history of every player's position (and hitbox) for each of the last few hundred milliseconds of ticks. 2. The fire input says which tick the shooter was seeing : the render time of its interpolation, as a tick number (it can be fractional, between two snapshots). 3. The server rewinds the other players to that tick, interpolating between the two recorded ticks around it, just as the client did. 4. It tests the shot (a ray, the bullet's path) against those rewound positions, then puts everything back. If the shooter's screen showed a hit, the server agrees. The shooter's own position comes from the present, since that is known exactly. Limits The client says which tick it saw, so the server must not trust it blindly: - Clamp the rewind to a maximum, typically 200 ms to 1 second. A client claiming to see the world 3 seconds ago gets the oldest allowed tick instead, so a laggy or dishonest client cannot rewrite history far back. - Reject ticks in the future (newer than the server's current tick). - Check the claimed tick against what the server knows about that client's latency; a value that jumps around is suspicious. The trade-off Lag compensation favours the shooter . The player being shot sometimes feels it is unfair: they reached cover on their screen, then died anyway, because on the shooter's screen (100 ms behind) they had not yet. This "shot around the corner" effect grows with the shooter's latency, which is the main reason for capping the rewind. Every shooter game tunes this balance; some reduce compensation for players with very high ping. Lag compensation is for instant hits (hitscan weapons). Slow projectiles, such as rockets and arrows, are usually simulated on the server from the moment they are fired, sometimes with a small head start to make up for the shooter's latency.

title: Rewinding for hits
body: Build the server side of lag compensation (lesson 6.05): a history of a player's positions per tick, a limit on how far a shot may rewind, and the hit test. cpp class PositionHistory { public: explicit PositionHistory(std::size_t capacity); void record(std::int64_t tick, double x, double y); std::optional<std::pair<double, double at(double tick) const; }; double rewindTick(double claimed, std::int64_t now, int maxRewind); bool segmentHitsCircle(double ox, double oy, double dx, double dy, double range, double cx, double cy, double radius); - record adds a position for a tick that must be newer than the last recorded one (otherwise it is ignored), keeping only the newest capacity entries. - at gives the position at a tick, which may be fractional. Outside the range from the oldest to the newest recorded tick there is no answer. Inside it, blend in a straight line between the recorded ticks either side (ticks may have gaps); at a recorded tick, its position. - rewindTick limits the tick a client claims it was seeing to between now - maxRewind and now . - segmentHitsCircle tests a shot from (ox, oy) in direction (dx, dy) (any length; a zero direction never hits) for range units against a circle: it hits if the closest point of that segment to the centre is within radius .

title: A multiplayer movement core
body: Build the heart of a small multiplayer action game: an authoritative server that applies players' inputs each tick, sends snapshots and decides hits with lag compensation, and a client that predicts its own movement, reconciles with the server, and interpolates everyone else. The tests run both through a link with several ticks of delay. cpp struct Input { std::uint32_t sequence; int moveX; int moveY; }; struct PlayerSnapshot { int id; int x; int y; std::uint32_t lastInput; }; struct Snapshot { std::int64_t tick; std::vector<PlayerSnapshot players; }; class GameServer { public: explicit GameServer(int speed); int addPlayer(int x, int y); void receiveInput(int player, const Input& in); void teleport(int player, int x, int y); void tick(); Snapshot snapshot() const; int hitscan(int shooter, double viewTick, double dirX, double dirY, double range, double radius) const; }; class GameClient { public: GameClient(int playerId, int speed, int x, int y); Input makeInput(int moveX, int moveY); void receiveSnapshot(const Snapshot& s); std::pair<int, int position() const; std::size_t pendingInputs() const; std::optional<std::pair<double, double remotePosition(int playerId, double tick) const; }; The world. Positions are whole numbers in an arena from 0 to 1 000 on both axes; every position is clamped into it. Movement , shared by server and client: clamp moveX and moveY to -1..1 each, then add move speed to each axis and clamp to the arena. (Integers make prediction exact, as lesson 6.02 recommends.) The server. - addPlayer gives ids 1, 2, 3 ... and places the player (clamped), with last input 0. - receiveInput queues an input for a known player, unless its sequence number is not above the player's last applied input, the same number is already queued, or 64 inputs are already queued. - teleport moves a known player (clamped). It stands for anything the server does that a client cannot predict. - tick advances the tick number (from 0 to 1, and so on). Then, for each player in id order, it applies every queued input in sequence order, recording the last one applied, and empties the queue. Finally it records every player's position for this tick in a history that keeps the last 64 ticks. - snapshot is the current tick and every player, in id order. - hitscan tests an instant shot (lesson 6.05). The shooter must exist and the direction must not be zero. The view tick is clamped to between tick - 32 and the current tick. Each other player is rewound to that tick from the history, blending between the recorded ticks either side of a fractional tick; a player not recorded at those ticks is skipped. The shot starts at the shooter's current position, goes range units along the direction, and hits a player if the closest point of that segment is within radius of them. Return the id of the hit player nearest the shooter along the shot (the lower id on a tie), or 0. The client. - makeInput makes the next input (sequence numbers from 1) with both parts clamped to -1..1, applies it to the predicted position at once, keeps it as pending and returns it. - receiveSnapshot ignores a snapshot whose tick is not newer than the newest one already received. For the client's own player it reconciles (lesson 6.04): drop pending inputs up to the player's last applied input, take the server's position, and replay the rest. Every other player's position is stored with the snapshot's tick, keeping the 32 newest per player. - remotePosition interpolates another player (lesson 6.03) at a tick, which may be fractional: before their oldest stored tick it is the oldest position, after the newest the newest, and in between a straight blend. A player never seen (including the client's own) has no position.

title: Glossary
body: ACK : the TCP flag meaning the acknowledgement number is valid; generally, a message saying data arrived. (1.04, 4.03) Ack bitfield : 32 bits after an ack number saying which of the previous 32 packets also arrived. (5.03) ARP : the protocol that finds the MAC address for an IP address on the local network. (4.02) Authoritative server : a server whose simulation is the truth; clients send only inputs. (6.01) Backoff : waiting longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling. (5.04) Baseline : the earlier snapshot a delta is encoded against. (6.02) Big-endian : most significant byte first; the network byte order. (2.03) Byte stream : what TCP delivers: bytes in order, with no message boundaries. (2.02) Capture filter : a BPF expression deciding which packets are recorded. (4.01) Checksum : a value computed over data to detect corruption; the Internet checksum is a one's-complement sum of 16-bit words. (2.03) Chunked encoding : an HTTP body sent as hex-sized pieces ending with a zero-size chunk. (3.02) CIDR : writing a network as address and prefix length, such as 192.168.1.0/24 . (1.02) ClientHello : the first TLS handshake message, listing versions, cipher suites and extensions. (4.05) Delta compression : sending only what changed against a baseline. (6.02) Display filter : a Wireshark expression deciding which captured packets are shown. (4.01) DNS : the system that turns names into addresses. (1.03) EtherType : the Ethernet header field saying which protocol follows. (4.02) Extrapolation : guessing a position beyond the newest snapshot from its velocity. (6.03) FIN : the TCP flag meaning "I have finished sending". (1.04) Fixed timestep : simulating in equal ticks regardless of frame time. (6.01) Fragment : a piece of a packet or block too big to send whole. (4.02, 5.05) Handshake : the opening exchange of a connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for TCP. (1.04) Head-of-line blocking : later data waiting for a lost earlier piece. (5.01) Header : the fixed fields at the start of a packet or message. (1.01) IHL : the IPv4 header length, in 32-bit words. (4.02) Interpolation : blending between two snapshots around a render time in the past. (6.03) Jitter : variation in delay between packets. (5.01) Keep-alive : reusing an HTTP connection for several requests. (3.01) Lag compensation : rewinding other players to the time the shooter saw before testing a hit. (6.05) Latency : the time a packet takes to arrive; the round trip is there and back. (1.04) Loopback : the address of your own machine, 127.0.0.1 or ::1 . (1.02) MAC address : the six-byte hardware address of a network interface. (4.02) MSS : maximum segment size, the largest TCP payload a side accepts. (1.01, 4.03) MTU : the largest packet a link carries. (1.01) NAT : a router rewriting private addresses and ports to its public address. (1.02) pcap : the classic capture file format. (4.01) Port : a 16-bit number choosing which program on a machine receives the data. (1.04) Prediction : applying your own inputs immediately instead of waiting for the server. (6.04) Pseudo-header : the addresses, protocol and length included in TCP and UDP checksums. (4.03) Quantisation : storing a value in fewer bits at a fixed step. (6.02) Reconciliation : resetting to the server's state and replaying unconfirmed inputs. (6.04) Retransmission : sending data again because it, or its acknowledgement, was lost. (4.04) Routing table : prefixes and next hops; the longest matching prefix wins. (1.05) RST : the TCP flag that aborts a connection; in reply to a SYN, "connection refused". (4.04) RTO : retransmission timeout, how long to wait for an ack before resending. (5.04) RTT : round-trip time. (5.04) Sequence number : a counter on each packet or byte, used to order and acknowledge. (1.04, 5.02) Snapshot : the world state at one server tick. (6.02) SNI : server name indication, the hostname a TLS client sends in its ClientHello. (3.05, 4.05) Socket : an endpoint for sending and receiving network data. (2.01) Subnet mask : the bits of an address that name the network. (1.02) SYN : the TCP flag that opens a connection. (1.04) Tick : one step of a fixed-timestep simulation. (6.01) TLS : the protocol that encrypts and authenticates a connection; the S in HTTPS. (3.05) TTL : time to live, a hop count decremented by each router. (1.05) UDP : the transport that sends independent datagrams with no delivery guarantee. (1.04)

title: 1.01  Memory Is a Row of Bytes
match: 1.01 Memory Is a Row of Bytes
body:
A program's memory is one long row of bytes, each with a number called its address. Every variable occupies a few of those bytes, sizeof says how many, and & gives the address of the first one. Addresses are written in hexadecimal and change from run to run. One long row Everything a running program works with, its variables, its strings, its arrays, even its own machine code, sits in memory . To the program, memory looks like one very long row of bytes. Each byte holds a number from 0 to 255, and each byte has its own number too: its address . text address 0x1000 0x1001 0x1002 0x1003 0x1004 0x1005 0x1006 0x1007 value 2A 00 00 00 48 69 00 FF That is the whole model. There are no "variables" in memory, no types, no names: only bytes with addresses. Variables, types and names are how your code decides to read those bytes. A variable is a few bytes When you write int score{ 42 }; , the compiler sets aside a few bytes somewhere in that row and agrees with itself that those bytes are score . How many bytes depends on the type, and sizeof tells you: cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "char: " << sizeof(char) << '
'; std::cout << "short: " << sizeof(short) << '
'; std::cout << "int: " << sizeof(int) << '
'; std::cout << "long long: " << sizeof(long long) << '
'; std::cout << "float: " << sizeof(float) << '
'; std::cout << "double: " << sizeof(double) << '
'; std::cout << "int : " << sizeof(int ) << '
'; } On a 64-bit Windows program you get 1, 2, 4, 8, 4, 8 and 8. char is 1 by definition; the others are set by the platform, which is why code that cares uses the fixed-width types from <cstdint : std::uint8_t , std::int32_t , std::uint64_t and friends always have the size in their name. The last line matters for this whole course: an address is itself a number that takes 8 bytes in a 64-bit program, whatever it points at. & gives an address The & operator in front of a variable gives the address of its first byte: cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 42 }; double ratio{ 0.75 }; char grade{ 'A' }; std::cout << "score is at " << &score << " and takes " << sizeof(score) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "ratio is at " << &ratio << " and takes " << sizeof(ratio) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "grade is at " << static_cast<void (&grade) << '
'; } Two things to notice: - Addresses are printed in hexadecimal , because a 64-bit address in decimal is a long unreadable number. 0x000000E5B1AFF8A4 is easier to compare by eye than 986 316 798 116. - For grade we had to cast to void . std::cout treats a char as the start of a text string and would try to print characters from that address until it found a zero byte. void means "just an address", and prints as one. Run it twice and the addresses change. Windows places the stack, the heap and the program itself at a random position every time it starts ( address space layout randomisation , ASLR), so a bug cannot rely on a fixed address. The distances between your variables usually stay the same; the starting point moves. Bigger values span several bytes A 4-byte int occupies four consecutive addresses, and &score is the address of the lowest of them. Which byte holds which part of the number is the byte order . Every x86 and ARM computer you will use is little-endian : the least significant byte comes first. demo-bytes value: 305419896 order: little So the int 0x12345678 is stored as 78 56 34 12 . This looks backwards on paper and is completely natural to the processor: the byte at the variable's address is always the lowest part, whatever the size. Looking at the bytes You can look at any object's bytes with a pointer to unsigned char , the one type C++ guarantees may view the bytes of anything. Pointers are the next lesson, so for now read this as "start at the object's address and read one byte at a time": cpp include <cstdio int main() { int value{ 0x12345678 }; const unsigned char bytes{ reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char (&value) }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < static_cast<int (sizeof(value)); ++i) std::printf("byte %d: %02X
", i, bytes i ); } It prints 78 , 56 , 34 , 12 . You will write a full hex dump of any object in this milestone's project. !tip A debugger's Memory window shows exactly this row of bytes. In Visual Studio, while stopped at a breakpoint, open Debug Windows Memory Memory 1 and type &score in the address box. Watching the bytes change as you step is the fastest way to build a picture of memory.

title: Byte by byte
where: 1.01 Memory Is a Row of Bytes
body: A little-endian computer stores the lowest byte of a number at the lowest address. Write the two directions of that rule for a 32-bit number, using shifts and masks (no pointers yet): cpp std::array<std::uint8_t, 4 toLittleEndian(std::uint32_t value); std::uint32_t fromLittleEndian(const std::array<std::uint8_t, 4 & bytes); - toLittleEndian(0x12345678) gives { 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12 } : element 0 is the byte that would sit at the variable's address. - fromLittleEndian puts them back together, so fromLittleEndian(toLittleEndian(x)) == x for every x .

title: 1.02  Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses
match: 1.02 Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses
body:
A pointer is an ordinary variable whose value is an address. Its type says what kind of value lives at that address. Declaring, initialising and printing pointers, nullptr for "no address", and why int and double are different types even though both are 8 bytes. Storing an address The last lesson printed addresses with & . A pointer is a variable that stores one: cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 42 }; int where{ &score }; // where holds the address of score std::cout << "score lives at " << &score << '
'; std::cout << "where holds " << where << '
'; // the same number std::cout << "where itself is at " << &where << '
'; // a different address: where is a variable too } Read int where as "where is a pointer to an int". It is an 8-byte variable like any other: it has its own address ( &where ), its own bytes, and a value. The value just happens to be an address. demo-pointers title: where holds the address of one of these ints values: 42, 7, 19, 64, 3 Click the boxes in the demo. The pointer never contains 42 or 7; it contains the address of the box it aims at. The type says what is at the address int , double and char are all 8 bytes and all hold an address, yet they are different types and do not mix: cpp-norun int score{ 42 }; double ratio{ 0.5 }; int p{ &score }; // fine double q{ &ratio }; // fine int r{ &ratio }; // error: cannot convert double to int The type is the instruction for reading the address: int says "at this address start 4 bytes that form an int". If the compiler let you aim an int at a double , reading through it would take the first 4 of the double's 8 bytes and call them an int, which is nonsense. So the compiler refuses unless you explicitly ask with a cast, which this course will only do for looking at raw bytes (lesson 2.05). Where the star goes All of these declare the same thing: cpp-norun int a; int a; int a; This course writes int a because the star is part of the type. But beware: in a declaration of several names, the star belongs to each name separately. cpp-norun int a, b; // a is int , b is a plain int! int c, d; // both pointers Declare one pointer per line and the trap never bites. nullptr: no address at all A pointer that does not point anywhere yet should hold nullptr : cpp-norun int target{ nullptr }; // points at nothing if (target == nullptr) { / nothing chosen yet / } if (!target) { / the same test, shorter / } nullptr is an address that is never a valid object (address 0 on every system you will meet). It is the pointer equivalent of "none". Old code uses NULL or 0 ; nullptr is the modern spelling and cannot be mistaken for the integer 0. !warning A pointer declared without a value, int p; , holds whatever bytes happened to be in its memory: a random address. Using it reads or writes some arbitrary place. Always initialise pointers, to a real address or to nullptr . Pointers can change A pointer is a variable, so it can be pointed somewhere else: cpp include <iostream int main() { int red{ 1 }, green{ 2 }, blue{ 3 }; int chosen{ &red }; std::cout << chosen << '
'; chosen = &blue; // now it holds blue's address std::cout << chosen << '
'; chosen = nullptr; // and now nothing std::cout << chosen << '
'; // prints 0000000000000000 (void)green; } Changing chosen never changes red , green or blue . It only changes which address chosen holds. Changing the value at the address is the next lesson. Addresses can be compared Two pointers of the same type can be compared with == and != : they are equal when they hold the same address, that is, when they point at the same object. This is how you ask "are these the same thing?" rather than "do these hold equal values?": cpp-norun int a{ 5 }, b{ 5 }; int p{ &a }; int q{ &a }; int r{ &b }; // p == q: true, same object. p == r: false, different objects, even though a == b.

title: Choosing with pointers
where: 1.02 Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses
body: Write functions that take and return pointers , without copying any of the ints: cpp int pickLarger(int a, int b); bool sameObject(const int a, const int b); int firstNonNull(int a, int b, int c); - pickLarger returns whichever pointer points at the larger value; if the values are equal it returns a . If one of the two is nullptr it returns the other one, and if both are, nullptr . - sameObject is true when both point at the same object (the same address), not when the values are merely equal. Two nullptr s count as the same. - firstNonNull returns the first of its arguments that is not nullptr , or nullptr if all three are.

title: 1.03  Dereferencing
body:
The operator follows a pointer to the object at its address, to read it or to write it. Two pointers to one object see each other's writes. The - operator reaches a member through a pointer, and const can protect either the pointer or the value it points at. Following the address in front of a pointer means "the object at this address". This is called dereferencing : cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 42 }; int p{ &score }; std::cout << p << '
'; // read through p: 42 p = 100; // write through p std::cout << score << '
'; // 100: score itself changed p += 5; std::cout << score << '
'; // 105 } p is not a copy of score . It is score , reached by its address. Anything you can do to score , you can do to p . The star now has two jobs, and context tells them apart: Where Meaning --- --- In a declaration: int p p is a pointer to int In an expression: p the int that p points at & and undo each other: &score is score , and & p is p . Two names for one object When two pointers hold the same address, a write through one is seen through the other. Programmers call this aliasing : cpp include <iostream int main() { int health{ 100 }; int shown{ &health }; // what the health bar reads int damage{ &health }; // what the combat code changes damage -= 30; std::cout << shown << '
'; // 70: same object } This is the main reason pointers exist: several parts of a program can work on one object instead of each holding its own copy. Arrows for members For a pointer to a struct or class, ( p).member reaches a member. The brackets are needed because . binds tighter than , and that is ugly enough that C++ has a shorthand: p- member . cpp include <iostream include <string struct Player { std::string name; int health; }; int main() { Player hero{ "Ada", 100 }; Player p{ &hero }; ( p).health -= 10; // works p- health -= 10; // the same, and what everyone writes std::cout << p- name << " has " << p- health << '
'; // Ada has 80 } Dereferencing nullptr A pointer holding nullptr points at no object, so p has nothing to reach. On Windows reading address 0 makes the processor raise an access violation and the program is stopped: cpp-norun int p{ nullptr }; p = 5; // crash: Exception thrown: write access violation. p was nullptr. So code that might receive nullptr must check first: if (p) p = 5; . Lesson 1.05 covers this and the other kinds of bad pointer in detail. const and pointers A pointer involves two things that could be read-only: the object it points at, and the pointer variable itself. const can protect either, depending on which side of the star it sits: cpp-norun int score{ 42 }; int other{ 7 }; const int a{ &score }; // pointer to const int: a = 1 is an error, a = &other is fine int const b{ &score }; // const pointer to int: b = 1 is fine, b = &other is an error const int const c{ &score }; // neither can change Read right to left: int const b is "b is a const pointer to int"; const int a is "a is a pointer to an int that is const". The first form, pointer to const , is the one you use all the time. A function that only reads through a pointer takes const T , which both documents and enforces that it will not change the caller's object. !note const int does not make score constant. score can still be changed directly or through another pointer. It only means this pointer is not allowed to change it.

title: Damage and healing through pointers
body: A game passes its players around by pointer, so every system changes the same Player : cpp struct Player { int health; int maxHealth; int armour; }; void damage(Player p, int amount); void heal(Player p, int amount); void healBoth(Player a, Player b, int amount); int totalHealth(const Player a, const Player b); - damage : armour soaks up damage first and is used up by it; whatever is left comes off health, which never goes below 0. Damage of 0 or less does nothing. - heal adds to health, but never above maxHealth . Healing of 0 or less does nothing. - healBoth heals both players. If a and b are the same player, it is healed only once. - totalHealth adds up both players' health; if both pointers are the same player, it is counted once. It takes const Player because it only reads. All four use - to reach the members.

title: 1.04  Pointers as Parameters
body:
C++ passes arguments by copying them, so a function cannot change the caller's variables, unless it receives their addresses. Out-parameters, swap, returning several results, optional parameters with nullptr, and when a reference is the better choice. Functions get copies When you call a function, each argument is copied into the function's parameter. Changing the parameter changes the copy: cpp include <iostream void heal(int health) { health += 25; // changes the local copy only } int main() { int health{ 50 }; heal(health); std::cout << health << '
'; // still 50 } The health inside heal is a separate variable in heal 's stack frame (lesson 4.02 shows the frames). It vanishes when the function returns. demo-stack title: heal gets a copy call main main starts with its own health. local health = 50 call heal health=50 heal gets a new frame with a COPY of the value. set health = 75 Only the copy changes. return heal's frame, and the copy, are gone. return 0 main's health is still 50. Passing the address If the function receives the address instead, it can reach the caller's variable: cpp include <iostream void heal(int health) { health += 25; // follow the address to the caller's variable } int main() { int health{ 50 }; heal(&health); // pass where health is, not what it is std::cout << health << '
'; // 75 } The pointer is still copied, but a copy of an address points at the same place. This is how C, and lots of Windows API functions, let a function change things in its caller. The classic: swap cpp include <iostream void swapInts(int a, int b) { const int old{ a }; a = b; b = old; } int main() { int left{ 1 }, right{ 2 }; swapInts(&left, &right); std::cout << left << ' ' << right << '
'; // 2 1 } Without pointers (or references) swap cannot be written at all. Out-parameters A function returns one value, but sometimes it has several results. A common pattern returns success or failure and writes the results through pointers, called out-parameters : cpp-norun // Splits "12:45" into hours and minutes. Returns false if the text is not a time. bool parseTime(const std::string& text, int hours, int minutes); int h{}, m{}; if (parseTime("12:45", &h, &m)) { / use h and m / } The Windows API is full of these: GetExitCodeProcess(process, &exitCode) returns success as a BOOL and the exit code through a pointer. Modern C++ often prefers returning a struct or a std::optional , but you will read out-parameters constantly. Optional parameters A pointer parameter can be nullptr , which gives a natural way to say "I do not want this result": cpp-norun void stats(const int values, int count, int minOut, int maxOut) { // ... work out lo and hi ... if (minOut) minOut = lo; // the caller may not want the minimum if (maxOut) maxOut = hi; } stats(data, 10, nullptr, &largest); // only interested in the maximum The rule that follows: if a parameter may be nullptr, check before writing through it . If it may not, say so in the function's comment, or better, use a reference. References: pointers that cannot be null A C++ reference ( int& ) is an address too, under the hood, but with three differences: it must be bound to an object when created, it can never be re-pointed, and it cannot be null. You use it without or & : cpp-norun void heal(int& health) { health += 25; } heal(health); // no & at the call So which to use? Use When --- --- T& the function always needs an object to change const T& the function only reads a large object and wants to avoid a copy T "no object" is a valid answer (nullptr), or the code talks to a C API const T the same, read only This course uses pointers almost everywhere, because pointers are the subject. In your own C++ code, prefer references when null is not meaningful.

title: Out-parameters
body: Write three functions that hand results back through pointers: cpp void sort3(int a, int b, int c); bool parseTime(const std::string& text, int hours, int minutes); void minMax(const int values, int count, int minOut, int maxOut); - sort3 rearranges the three ints so that a <= b <= c . - parseTime reads text of the form H:MM or HH:MM (hours 0 to 23, minutes 00 to 59, minutes always two digits). On success it writes the numbers through hours and minutes and returns true. On failure it returns false and writes nothing . Either out-pointer may be nullptr , meaning the caller does not want that number. - minMax finds the smallest and largest of count values ( values i reads the i-th). Either out-pointer may be nullptr . If count is 0 or less, nothing is written.

title: 1.05  Null, Dangling and Wild Pointers
body: The three kinds of bad pointer - null, dangling and wild - what each one is, what happens when you follow it, why the crash often appears far from the bug, and the habits that keep pointers valid. A pointer is only as good as its address A pointer can hold any 64-bit number. Only some of those numbers are the address of an object that exists right now. Following any other is undefined behaviour : the C++ standard says nothing about what happens, and in practice the result ranges from an immediate crash to silently wrong data a minute later. There are three ways a pointer goes bad. 1. Null pointers A pointer holding nullptr says honestly "I point at nothing". Following it is still a bug, but the friendliest one: address 0 and the pages around it are never mapped on Windows, so the processor stops the program at once. text Exception thrown: read access violation. p was nullptr. A crash at the bad line, naming the variable, is the best case. Small addresses near zero, like 0x0000000000000018 , mean the same thing: something did p- member with p null, and 0x18 was that member's offset. 2. Dangling pointers A dangling pointer holds the address of an object that used to exist: cpp-norun int makeScore() { int score{ 42 }; return &score; // score dies when the function returns } int p{ makeScore() }; // p dangles: the memory is still there, the object is not cpp-norun int data{ new int{ 7 } }; delete data; // the object is gone data = 8; // use after free: data still holds the old address cpp-norun std::vector<int v{ 1, 2, 3 }; int first{ &v 0 }; v.push_back(4); // the vector may move its elements to a bigger block first = 10; // first may now point into freed memory Dangling pointers are the worst kind, because the address is plausible . The memory is still mapped, often still holds the old value, so reading through it seems to work, until something else reuses that memory. Then you read someone else's data, or write into it, and the crash happens later, somewhere unrelated. !danger "It printed the right value" does not prove a pointer is valid. A dangling pointer often reads the old value for a while. Tools like AddressSanitizer (lesson 4.05) catch these at the moment they happen. 3. Wild pointers A wild pointer was never given a valid value at all: cpp-norun int p; // uninitialised: holds whatever bytes were on the stack p = 5; // writes to a random address In a debug build MSVC fills uninitialised stack memory with 0xCC bytes, so the pointer is 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC and the crash is immediate and recognisable. Learn the debug fill patterns; they tell you what went wrong at a glance: Value MSVC debug meaning --- --- 0xCCCCCCCC uninitialised stack memory 0xCDCDCDCD heap memory from new / malloc , never written 0xDDDDDDDD heap memory that was freed 0xFDFDFDFD the guard bytes just before and after a heap block 0xFEEEFEEE memory freed back to the Windows heap A pointer value of 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD means "this pointer was read out of freed memory": a use after free one step removed. Out of bounds is the fourth way A pointer can also start valid and be moved off the end of its object, which is the subject of the next milestone. Reading one element past an array reads whatever is next in memory; writing there corrupts it. Habits that keep pointers valid - Initialise every pointer , to an object or nullptr . Never int p; . - Check pointers that may be null before following them, and document which ones may be. - Never return the address of a local variable. Return the value, or memory that outlives the function. - Set a pointer to nullptr after delete if the variable lives on, so a later mistake is a clean null crash instead of a use after free. - Do not keep pointers into a vector across operations that grow it. Keep an index instead. - Know who owns the object a pointer points at, and how long it lives (milestone 4).

title: Handles that know when they dangle
match: Handles that know when they dangle
body: A raw pointer cannot tell whether its object still exists. Game engines often hand out handles instead: an index into a table plus a generation number. When a slot is freed its generation goes up, so an old handle to it no longer matches and is recognised as dangling. cpp struct Handle { int index; unsigned generation; }; class Pool { public: Handle create(int value); bool destroy(Handle h); int get(Handle h); int alive() const; }; - create stores the value and returns its handle. It reuses the lowest-numbered free slot if there is one; otherwise it adds a new slot at the end. A new slot starts at generation 0. - destroy frees the slot if the handle is valid, adds 1 to that slot's generation and returns true. For an invalid handle (out of range, slot already free, or wrong generation) it does nothing and returns false. - get returns a pointer to the stored value for a valid handle, or nullptr for an invalid one. - alive counts the slots in use. A handle { index, generation } is valid when index is inside the table, that slot is in use, and its generation equals the handle's.

title: A memory inspector
body: Build the two halves of a memory viewer like the one in a debugger: a hex dump of any bytes, and readers that turn bytes back into numbers. cpp std::string hexDump(const void data, std::size_t size, std::uint64_t baseAddress); std::uint64_t readLittleEndian(const unsigned char bytes, int count); std::int32_t readInt32(const unsigned char bytes); hexDump shows size bytes starting at data , 16 per line. Each line is: - the address of its first byte, baseAddress plus the offset, as 8 uppercase hex digits; - two spaces; - for each of the 16 positions: one extra space before position 8, then either the byte as 2 uppercase hex digits and a space, or 3 spaces when the data has run out; - a space, then , then the 16 bytes (or fewer on the last line) as characters, with any byte outside 32 to 126 shown as . , then . Every line ends with \n . Zero bytes give an empty string. For example 16 bytes of Hello, pointers! at 0x1000 : text 00001000 48 65 6C 6C 6F 2C 20 70 6F 69 6E 74 65 72 73 21 Hello, pointers! Because it takes const void , it can dump anything: hexDump(&someStruct, sizeof(someStruct), 0) . Inside, view the bytes through a const unsigned char . readLittleEndian combines count bytes (1 to 8), lowest first, into one number. readInt32 reads 4 bytes as a signed 32-bit number, so FF FF FF FF is -1 .

title: 2.01  Arrays Are Consecutive Memory
body:
An array is its elements placed one after another with no gaps, so element i sits at the start address plus i times the element size. An array's name turns into a pointer to its first element when passed to a function, which is why the function loses the length and sizeof stops working. Side by side An array is the simplest data structure there is: its elements stored one after another , with nothing in between. cpp include <iostream int main() { int scores 5 { 90, 72, 85, 64, 99 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 5; ++i) std::cout << "scores " << i << " is at " << &scores i << '
'; } Each address is 4 more than the last, because each int is 4 bytes. That gives the one formula that every array access uses: address of element i = address of element 0 + i × size of one element demo-pointers title: five ints, four bytes apart values: 90, 72, 85, 64, 99 This is why indexing is fast: reaching scores 1000 is one multiplication and one addition, not a walk past 999 others. And it is why arrays start at 0: element 0 is at the start plus 0. The name becomes a pointer In almost every expression, an array's name turns into a pointer to its first element. This is called decay : cpp-norun int scores 5 { 90, 72, 85, 64, 99 }; int p{ scores }; // the same as &scores 0 std::cout << p; // 90 Decay is what happens when you pass an array to a function. These three declarations all mean exactly the same thing, a pointer: cpp-norun int sum(int values 5 , int count); int sum(int values , int count); int sum(int values, int count); The 5 in the first one is ignored. The function receives an address and nothing else, so it cannot know how long the array is . That is why C-style functions always take a count alongside the pointer, and why so many bugs are "the count was wrong". sizeof after decay sizeof on a real array gives the size of the whole array. On a decayed pointer it gives the size of a pointer: cpp include <iostream void show(int values ) { std::cout << "inside: " << sizeof(values) << '
'; // 8: just a pointer } int main() { int scores 5 {}; std::cout << "outside: " << sizeof(scores) << '
'; // 20: five ints std::cout << "count: " << sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores 0 ) << '
'; show(scores); } The compiler warns about sizeof on an array parameter for exactly this reason. Inside the function, the count has to come from the caller. In modern C++, std::size(scores) gives the count of a real array and refuses to compile on a pointer, which is safer than the division. Indexing is pointer arithmetic values i is defined as (values + i) : "start at values , move i elements along, and follow". The next lesson takes that apart. For now it explains a curiosity: because addition does not care about order, i values also compiles and means the same. Do not write it; just know that is arithmetic on an address. No bounds checking Nothing stops scores 5 or scores -1 . The formula happily computes an address outside the array and the program reads or writes whatever is there: another variable, a return address, padding. In a debug build MSVC's runtime checks may catch a write just past a local array when the function returns: text Run-Time Check Failure 2 - Stack around the variable 'scores' was corrupted. That message means "something wrote past the end of scores ", and the culprit ran some time before the message appeared. Arrays of other things The formula works for any element type. An array of 3 double s has elements 8 bytes apart.
