body: Tuples are fixed sequences for values that belong together - coordinates, records, several return values. This lesson covers creating them, unpacking with , swapping, and when to choose a tuple over a list. Tuples A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed: written with parentheses (or just commas): python point = (3, 4) person = ("Ada", 1815, "London") single = (42,) the comma makes it a tuple; (42) is just 42 print(point 0 , len(person), person 1: ) Tuples support indexing, slicing, in , len , count and index , but not append or item assignment. When to use a tuple List Tuple --- --- Many items of the same kind that may change: a list of scores A fixed group of values with different meanings: a point, a date, a record Grows and shrinks Fixed size Cannot be a dictionary key Can be a dictionary key (if its items can) A good rule: if the position of an item has a meaning (index 0 is the name, index 1 the year), it is a tuple; if all items mean the same thing, it is a list. Unpacking Assigning a tuple (or any sequence) to several names unpacks it: python name, year, city = ("Ada", 1815, "London") x, y = (3, 4) a, b = b_and_a = (1, 2) print(name, year, x + y) The number of names must match, unless one name has a , which collects the rest into a list: python first, rest = 1, 2, 3, 4 body, last = "hello" head, _, tail = range(10) print(first, rest, body, last, head, tail) _ is the conventional name for a value you do not need. Swapping and multiple return values python a, b = 1, 2 a, b = b, a swap, no temporary variable def min_max(values): return min(values), max(values) returns one tuple low, high = min_max( 3, 9, 1 ) print(low, high) Unpacking in loops is where it is used most: python for name, score in ("Ada", 95), ("Grace", 88) : print(name, score) Named tuples When a tuple has many fields, positions become hard to remember. collections.namedtuple (or dataclasses, lesson 4.04) gives them names: python from collections import namedtuple Point = namedtuple("Point", "x", "y" ) p = Point(3, 4) print(p.x, p.y, p)

title: Points as tuples
body: Work with points stored as (x, y) tuples: python def parse_point(text): ... "3,4" or " 3 , -4 " - (3, 4) / (3, -4) as ints def distance(p, q): ... straight-line distance between two points def closest(points, target): ... the point nearest to target (the first one on a tie); None for no points def bounds(points): ... ((min_x, min_y), (max_x, max_y)) of all points

title: 2.05  Dictionaries and Sets
body: Looking things up by key with dictionaries - creating, reading with get, updating, looping over items, counting and grouping - and sets for unique values and fast membership, with union, intersection and difference. Dictionaries A dictionary maps keys to values , and finds a value by its key instantly, however big it is: python ages = {"Ada": 36, "Grace": 85} print(ages "Ada" ) 36 ages "Linus" = 21 add ages "Ada" = 37 replace del ages "Grace" remove print(ages, len(ages), "Ada" in ages) Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples); values can be anything. Dictionaries keep the order in which keys were added. Reading safely d key raises KeyError for a missing key. When a key may be missing, use get with a default: python stock = {"apples": 4} print(stock.get("pears", 0)) 0 print(stock.get("apples", 0)) 4 Looping python prices = {"tea": 2.5, "cake": 3.0} for item in prices: keys print(item) for item, price in prices.items(): pairs print(f"{item}: {price:.2f}") print(list(prices.values()), sum(prices.values())) Counting and grouping Two patterns come up constantly: python words = "the cat and the hat".split() counts = {} for w in words: counts w = counts.get(w, 0) + 1 print(counts) {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'and': 1, 'hat': 1} by_length = {} for w in words: by_length.setdefault(len(w), ).append(w) print(by_length) {3: 'the', 'cat', 'and', 'the', 'hat' } setdefault(key, default) returns the value for the key, inserting the default first if it is missing. collections.Counter and defaultdict (lesson 5.04) make both even shorter. Sets A set holds unique values, in no particular order, with very fast in : python seen = {"Ada", "Grace"} seen.add("Ada") no effect: already there print(len(seen), "Grace" in seen) unique = set( 3, 1, 3, 2, 1 ) remove duplicates print(sorted(unique)) 1, 2, 3 Sets do maths with other sets: Operation Meaning --- --- a \ b Union: in either a & b Intersection: in both a - b Difference: in a but not b a ^ b In exactly one of them a <= b a is a subset of b python monday = {"Ada", "Grace", "Linus"} tuesday = {"Grace", "Barbara"} print(monday & tuesday, monday - tuesday, monday tuesday) {} is an empty dictionary ; an empty set is set() . Choosing a collection Need Use --- --- Ordered items, by position list A fixed record tuple Look up by a key dict Unique values, membership tests set Testing x in some_list checks every item; x in some_set is instant. For large collections that you search often, that difference is huge.

title: Counting words
body: Write the core of a word-frequency tool: python def word_counts(text): ... dict of word - count; words are lower-cased, with .,!?;:"' removed from their ends def top_words(counts, n): ... the n most common (word, count) pairs: highest count first, ties in alphabetical order def shared_letters(a, b): ... sorted list of the letters (a-z, ignoring case) that appear in both words Words are separated by whitespace; a "word" that is empty after removing punctuation is ignored.

title: A to-do list
body: Write an interactive to-do list. It reads commands after the prompt until quit : Command Does Prints --- --- --- add <text Adds a task (the rest of the line, spaces kept) Added <n : <text list Shows every task, numbered from 1 <n . <text or <n . x <text ; Nothing to do. if there are none done <n Marks task n as done Done: <text undo <n Marks task n as not done Undone: <text remove <n Deletes task n (later tasks move up) Removed: <text clear Deletes every finished task Cleared <k task(s). quit Ends Bye! <k of <n done. - An empty line does nothing. Commands are not case-sensitive ( ADD , List ), but the task text keeps its case. - add without text prints Nothing to add. - For done , undo and remove : if n is not a whole number, print Not a number: <n ; if there is no such task, print No task <n ; without n , print Which task? . - Anything else prints Unknown command: <word . add buy milk Added 1: buy milk add Call Ada Added 2: Call Ada done 1 Done: buy milk list 1. x buy milk 2. Call Ada quit Bye! 1 of 2 done.

title: 3.01  Functions
body: Packaging code under a name - def, parameters and return values, returning several values, functions without a return, docstrings, and why small functions with one job make programs easier to change and test. Defining a function python def area(width, height): """Return the area of a width x height rectangle.""" return width height print(area(3, 4)) 12 print(area(2.5, 2)) 5.0 - def names the function and its parameters . - The indented body runs each time the function is called . - return sends a value back and ends the function at once. - The string right after the def line is the docstring : help(area) shows it, and editors display it. A function must be defined before the line that calls it runs, but it can call functions defined later in the file, as long as they exist by the time the call happens. Return values A function without return (or with a bare return ) returns None : python def greet(name): print(f"Hello, {name}!") result = greet("Ada") print(result) None Mixing up "prints" and "returns" is a classic mistake: a function that prints its answer cannot be used in a calculation. Prefer functions that return values and leave printing to the code that calls them. Return several values as a tuple and unpack them (lesson 2.04): python def stats(values): return min(values), max(values), sum(values) / len(values) low, high, mean = stats( 4, 8, 6 ) print(low, high, mean) Early returns Returning early keeps the main path of a function unindented: python def describe(age): if age < 0: return "invalid" if age < 13: return "child" if age < 18: return "teenager" return "adult" Why functions - Name a piece of logic, so the code reads as a series of steps. - Reuse it instead of copying it. - Test it on its own: every unit test in this course calls functions. - Change it in one place. A good function does one thing, has a name that says what (a verb: load_scores , is_valid ), and is short enough to read at a glance. If you need "and" to describe it, it may be two functions. Functions are values A function is an object like any other: it can be stored in a variable, put in a list, or passed to another function: python def shout(text): return text.upper() + "!" def whisper(text): return text.lower() + "..." for style in shout, whisper : print(style("Hello")) Lesson 5.03 uses this for sorting with key functions.

title: A weather line
body: Build a forecast line from small functions that each do one thing: python def to_fahrenheit(celsius): ... celsius 9 / 5 + 32 def describe(celsius): ... "freezing" (<= 0), "cold" (< 15), "mild" (< 25), "hot" otherwise def forecast_line(day, celsius): ... "Mon: 18.0°C / 64.4°F (mild)": one decimal for both temperatures forecast_line must use the other two functions.

title: 3.02  Parameters and Arguments
body: The flexible ways Python passes values to functions - positional and keyword arguments, default values and the mutable default trap, args and kwargs, keyword-only and positional-only parameters, and unpacking arguments. Positional and keyword arguments Arguments can be passed by position or by name : python def describe(name, age, city): return f"{name}, {age}, from {city}" print(describe("Ada", 36, "London")) print(describe(city="London", name="Ada", age=36)) any order print(describe("Ada", city="London", age=36)) positional first, then keywords Keyword arguments make calls readable when there are several values of the same type: resize(width=800, height=600) cannot be confused. Default values Parameters can have defaults, used when the argument is left out: python def greet(name, greeting="Hello", punctuation="!"): return f"{greeting}, {name}{punctuation}" print(greet("Ada")) print(greet("Ada", "Hi")) print(greet("Ada", punctuation=".")) Parameters with defaults come after those without. The mutable default trap Default values are created once , when the function is defined. A list or dictionary default is shared between all calls: python def add_item(item, basket= ): WRONG: one list for every call basket.append(item) return basket print(add_item("apple")) 'apple' print(add_item("pear")) 'apple', 'pear' surprise! The fix is None as the default and a new list inside: python def add_item(item, basket=None): if basket is None: basket = basket.append(item) return basket Any number of arguments args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary: python def total( numbers): return sum(numbers) def tag(name, attributes): parts = " ".join(f'{k}="{v}"' for k, v in attributes.items()) return f"<{name} {parts} " print(total(1, 2, 3)) print(tag("img", src="cat.png", alt="A cat")) The reverse, unpacking , spreads a list or dictionary into arguments: python values = 1, 2, 3 print(total( values)) options = {"greeting": "Hi", "punctuation": "?"} print(greet("Ada", options)) Keyword-only and positional-only A in the parameter list makes everything after it keyword-only ; a / makes everything before it positional-only : python def connect(host, port, /, , timeout=10, retries=3): return f"{host}:{port} timeout={timeout} retries={retries}" print(connect("example.org", 443, timeout=5)) Keyword-only parameters are good for options ( timeout , reverse ): callers must name them, so calls stay readable and the order can change later. Arguments are references Python passes references to objects. A function can change a mutable argument (a list, a dictionary) and the caller sees it, but assigning a new value to the parameter name does not affect the caller's variable. Documenting whether a function changes its arguments ("sorts the list in place") avoids surprises.

title: Flexible parameters
body: Write four functions that use lesson 3.02's parameter features: python def format_price(amount, currency="€", decimals=2, , thousands=False): ... def average( numbers): ... None when called with no numbers def merged(defaults, overrides): ... a NEW dict: defaults updated with the overrides def add_tag(tag, tags=None): ... appends tag to tags (or to a new list) and returns the list - format_price(1234.5) is "1234.50 €" ; format_price(1234.5, "$", 0) is "1234 $" (rounded); with thousands=True the number has commas: "1,234.50 €" . - merged must not change defaults . - add_tag must not share a list between calls that do not pass one.

title: 3.03  Scope and Closures
body: Where names live - local and global scope, the LEGB lookup order, global and nonlocal, functions defined inside functions, closures that remember values, and lambda expressions. Local and global A name assigned inside a function is local : it exists only while the function runs and does not affect a name outside with the same spelling: python count = 10 def reset(): count = 0 a new LOCAL name; the global count is untouched return count reset() print(count) 10 Names are looked up in the order L ocal, E nclosing functions, G lobal (the module), B uilt-in ( print , len ): the LEGB rule. Reading a global inside a function works; assigning to it creates a local, unless you say otherwise. global and nonlocal python total = 0 def add(n): global total total += n add(5) print(total) 5 global is rarely a good idea: functions that change globals are hard to test and reason about. Pass values in and return results instead. nonlocal does the same for a variable of an enclosing function, which is how closures keep state (below). A common error: reading a variable that is assigned later in the same function raises UnboundLocalError , because the assignment makes it local for the whole function. Functions inside functions A function can define another function, which can see the outer function's names: python def make_greeter(greeting): def greet(name): return f"{greeting}, {name}!" return greet hello = make_greeter("Hello") howdy = make_greeter("Howdy") print(hello("Ada"), howdy("Grace")) greet remembers greeting even after make_greeter has returned. A function together with the variables it remembers is a closure . Closures with state With nonlocal , a closure can update what it remembers: python def make_counter(): count = 0 def next_value(): nonlocal count count += 1 return count return next_value counter = make_counter() print(counter(), counter(), counter()) 1 2 3 Each call to make_counter creates a separate count . For anything larger, a class (lesson 4.01) is usually clearer. lambda A lambda is a small anonymous function written as an expression: lambda parameters: expression . It is handy where a short function is passed to another: python square = lambda x: x x print(square(7)) pairs = ("Ada", 36), ("Grace", 85), ("Linus", 21) print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda pair: pair 1 )) Keep lambdas to one simple expression; anything more deserves a def with a name. A closure trap Closures remember variables , not values. Lambdas made in a loop all see the loop variable's final value: python funcs = lambda: i for i in range(3) print( f() for f in funcs ) 2, 2, 2 funcs = lambda i=i: i for i in range(3) a default captures the current value print( f() for f in funcs ) 0, 1, 2

title: Functions that remember
body: Write three closure factories: python def make_counter(start=0, step=1): ... returns a function; each call returns the next value: start, start + step, ... def make_averager(): ... returns a function f(x) that adds x and returns the average of all values so far def memoize(func): ... returns a function that calls func only once per argument, remembering results The function returned by memoize must also have an attribute calls counting how many times func really ran: set it with wrapper.calls = 0 and update it as wrapper.calls += 1 .

title: 3.04  Modules and Packages
body: Splitting a program into files - modules and import, the forms of import, the __name__ == "__main__" idiom, packages, how Python finds modules, the standard library, and installing third-party packages with pip in a virtual environment. Modules Every .py file is a module . Another file can import it to use its functions and variables: python geometry.py import math def circle_area(r): return math.pi r r python main.py import geometry print(geometry.circle_area(2)) The forms of import: Form Use as --- --- import geometry geometry.circle_area(2) import geometry as geo geo.circle_area(2) from geometry import circle_area circle_area(2) from geometry import Everything public; avoid: it hides where names come from A module's code runs once , the first time it is imported; later imports reuse it. The main guard When a file is run directly, its __name__ is "__main__" ; when it is imported, __name__ is the module's name. That lets a file be both a module and a script: python geometry.py def circle_area(r): return 3.14159 r r if __name__ == "__main__": print(circle_area(2)) only when run as a script, not on import Put demonstration and start-up code under this guard so importing the module has no side effects. Packages A package is a folder of modules (traditionally with an __init__.py file): shapes/ __init__.py circles.py polygons.py python from shapes.circles import area from shapes import polygons __init__.py runs when the package is imported and can import the most useful names, so users can write from shapes import area . How imports are found Python searches the folder of the script being run first, then the standard library, then installed packages ( sys.path lists the folders). Naming your own file like a standard module ( random.py , json.py ) shadows the real one: import random then imports your file, with confusing errors. The standard library Python comes "with batteries included": math , random , datetime , pathlib , json , csv , re , collections , itertools , statistics , urllib , sqlite3 and many more. Look there first: milestone 6 uses several of them. python import random, statistics rolls = random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(1000) print(statistics.mean(rolls)) Third-party packages Thousands more packages live on PyPI (the Python Package Index) and are installed with pip . Use a virtual environment per project, so each project has its own packages and versions: python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate (Windows; source .venv/bin/activate on Linux and macOS) pip install requests pip freeze requirements.txt (record the versions; pip install -r requirements.txt restores them)

title: The standard library
body: Use modules from the standard library (lesson 3.04) instead of writing everything yourself: python def roll_dice(count, sides, seed): ... a list of count rolls from 1 to sides, using random.Random(seed) def summary(values): ... (mean, median, mode) using the statistics module def days_between(start, end): ... days from start to end, dates written "YYYY-MM-DD", using datetime def is_prime(n): ... True for primes; use math.isqrt for the square root random.Random(seed) makes a generator that always produces the same sequence for the same seed; call its randint(1, sides) once per roll.

title: 3.05  Files and Paths
body:
Reading and writing text files safely with with-blocks, reading line by line, encodings, appending, working with paths using pathlib, listing and finding files, and the difference between text and binary files. Opening files with with python with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write("first line
") f.write("second line
") with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f: text = f.read() print(text) The with block closes the file when it ends, even if an error happens inside. Always use it. Mode Meaning --- --- "r" Read (the default); error if missing "w" Write: creates the file, empties it if it exists "a" Append: writes at the end "x" Create: error if it already exists "rb" , "wb" Binary (bytes instead of text) Always pass encoding="utf-8" for text: the default depends on the computer, and a file written on one machine can be unreadable on another. Reading line by line A file object is iterable, one line at a time, which works for files of any size: python with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write("apples 3
pears 5

plums 2
") total = 0 with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f: for line in f: line = line.strip() remove the "
" (and spaces) if not line: continue skip blank lines name, count = line.split() total += int(count) print(total) f.read() reads everything as one string; f.readlines() gives a list of lines (with their 
 ); f.read().splitlines() gives lines without them. Writing write takes a string and does not add a new line; print(..., file=f) does: python scores = {"Ada": 95, "Grace": 88} with open("scores.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: for name, score in scores.items(): print(f"{name},{score}", file=f) Paths with pathlib pathlib.Path represents a path and has methods for everything you do with files: python from pathlib import Path folder = Path("reports") folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True) create if missing report = folder / "2026-11.txt" / joins path parts on every system report.write_text("total: 42
", encoding="utf-8") print(report.exists(), report.name, report.stem, report.suffix, report.parent) print(report.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) for path in sorted(folder.glob(" .txt")): files matching a pattern; rglob searches subfolders print(path.name, path.stat().st_size, "bytes") Path.home() is the user's home folder, Path.cwd() the current folder, and path.resolve() the full absolute path. When files are missing Opening a missing file for reading raises FileNotFoundError . Check first with path.exists() or handle the error (lesson 4.05). Paths in a script are relative to the current working directory , not to the script's folder; Path(__file__).parent is the script's own folder when you need files next to it. Text and binary Text files are decoded into str using an encoding; binary files ( "rb" ) give bytes , for images, zip files and anything that is not text. Path.read_bytes() and write_bytes() are the binary versions.

title: Saving and loading scores
body: Store a dictionary of scores in a text file, one name,score per line, and read it back: python def save_scores(path, scores): ... writes the scores sorted by name; replaces the file def load_scores(path): ... dict name - int score; skips blank lines and lines that are not "name,number"; {} if the file is missing def add_score(path, name, score): ... appends one line to the file (creating it if needed) Names may contain spaces; spaces around the name and the number are ignored. A line like Ada,abc or just text is skipped. Write files as UTF-8.

title: A grade book
body: Write a small grade-book module: read students' marks from a file, compute statistics, and write an aligned report. python def parse_line(line): ... "Ada Lovelace: 90, 85, 77" - ("Ada Lovelace", 90, 85, 77 ); None if not valid def load(path): ... dict name - list of marks, from every valid line, in file order def average(marks): ... rounded to one decimal; None for no marks def letter(avg): ... "A" = 90, "B" = 80, "C" = 70, "D" = 60, else "F"; "-" for None def report(book): ... the report text (below) def save_report(path, book): ... writes report(book) to path Lines : a name, a colon, then marks separated by commas. Spaces around everything are ignored. Marks are whole numbers from 0 to 100. A line with no colon, an empty name, or any mark that is not a valid number is invalid ( None ); a line with a name and no marks after the colon is valid with an empty list. Blank lines are skipped. A name that appears again replaces the earlier marks. The report , one line per student sorted by average (highest first; students without marks last; ties by name), then a summary: Name Avg Grade Grace Hopper 92.0 A Ada Lovelace 84.0 B Linus - - 3 students, class average 88.0 - The name column is as wide as the longest name or the word Name , whichever is longer, plus 3 spaces; the average is right-aligned in 4 characters ( - when there are no marks); then 2 spaces and the grade. The header uses the same widths ( Avg right-aligned in 4). - The class average is the average of the students' averages (students without marks are left out), with one decimal, or - if no student has marks. - Every line ends with a new line.

title: 4.01  Classes and Objects
body: Bundling data and behaviour together - defining a class, __init__ and self, attributes and methods, class attributes, keeping an object valid, properties, and when a class is better than a dictionary or a few functions. A class is a new type A class describes a kind of object: what data it holds ( attributes ) and what it can do ( methods ). Each instance has its own data: python class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner, balance=0): self.owner = owner self.balance = balance def deposit(self, amount): self.balance += amount def describe(self): return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance:.2f}" a = BankAccount("Ada") b = BankAccount("Grace", 100) a.deposit(25) print(a.describe(), " ", b.describe()) - __init__ runs when an instance is created and sets up its attributes. - self is the instance the method is working on. a.deposit(25) is the same as BankAccount.deposit(a, 25) . - Attributes are created by assigning to self.something . Class names use CapitalisedWords ; methods follow function naming ( lower_case ). Keeping objects valid A class can protect its data so the object never gets into a nonsense state: python class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner, balance=0): if balance < 0: raise ValueError("balance cannot be negative") self.owner = owner self._balance = balance def withdraw(self, amount): if amount <= 0: raise ValueError("amount must be positive") if amount self._balance: raise ValueError("insufficient funds") self._balance -= amount @property def balance(self): return self._balance acct = BankAccount("Ada", 50) acct.withdraw(20) print(acct.balance) 30: read like an attribute A leading underscore ( _balance ) means "internal: do not touch from outside"; Python does not enforce it, but everyone respects it. A property exposes a value for reading while the class controls how it changes. raise (lesson 4.05) refuses invalid requests. Class attributes Attributes defined in the class body belong to the class , shared by all instances: python class Dice: sides = 6 shared def __init__(self): self.rolls = per instance print(Dice.sides, Dice().sides) Use class attributes for constants and defaults; never for mutable data that each instance should have its own copy of (the same trap as mutable default arguments, lesson 3.02). Methods that do not need an instance python class Temperature: def __init__(self, celsius): self.celsius = celsius @classmethod def from_fahrenheit(cls, f): another way to create an instance return cls((f - 32) 5 / 9) @staticmethod def is_valid(celsius): just a function kept with the class return celsius = -273.15 print(Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212).celsius, Temperature.is_valid(-300)) When to write a class Use a class when data and the operations on it belong together and the data has rules (an account's balance cannot go negative). For a few related values with no behaviour, a dictionary, tuple or dataclass (lesson 4.04) is simpler. For a single operation, a function is enough.

title: A bank account
body: Write a BankAccount class that can never get into an invalid state: python class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner, balance=0): ... ValueError if balance < 0 balance a read-only property def deposit(self, amount): ... ValueError unless amount 0 def withdraw(self, amount): ... ValueError unless 0 < amount <= balance def transfer(self, other, amount): ... withdraw here, deposit there; nothing changes if it fails def history(self): ... list of ("deposit" "withdraw", amount) in order, a copy The opening balance is not part of the history. A transfer appears as a withdraw in this account's history and a deposit in the other's.

title: 4.02  Special Methods
body: Making your classes behave like built-in types - __repr__ and __str__ for printing, __eq__ and ordering, arithmetic operators, __len__, __getitem__ and __iter__ for containers, __contains__, and __hash__ for use in sets and as keys. Methods Python calls for you Methods with double underscores on both sides ("dunder" methods) are called by Python's own syntax: You write Python calls --- --- repr(x) , the REPL, debugging x.__repr__() str(x) , print(x) , f-strings x.__str__() (falls back to __repr__ ) x == y x.__eq__(y) x < y x.__lt__(y) x + y , x y x.__add__(y) , x.__mul__(y) len(x) x.__len__() x i x.__getitem__(i) for item in x x.__iter__() item in x x.__contains__(item) hash(x) , sets, dict keys x.__hash__() A vector python import math class Vector: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y def __repr__(self): return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})" def __eq__(self, other): if not isinstance(other, Vector): return NotImplemented return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y) def __add__(self, other): return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y) def __mul__(self, k): return Vector(self.x k, self.y k) def __rmul__(self, k): k v, when k is on the left return self k def __abs__(self): return math.hypot(self.x, self.y) v = Vector(3, 4) print(v + Vector(1, 1), 2 v, abs(v), v == Vector(3, 4)) __repr__ should look like the code that would create the object: it is what you see when debugging. Returning NotImplemented (not raising) from __eq__ lets Python try the other side or fall back to "not equal". Containers A class that holds items can support len , indexing, in and loops: python class Playlist: def __init__(self, songs): self._songs = list(songs) def __len__(self): return len(self._songs) def __getitem__(self, index): return self._songs index slices work too, because lists support them def __iter__(self): return iter(self._songs) def __contains__(self, song): return song in self._songs p = Playlist("Intro", "Theme", "Outro") print(len(p), p 1 , p -1 , "Theme" in p, s.upper() for s in p ) Ordering and hashing Defining __eq__ and __lt__ , plus functools.total_ordering , gives all six comparisons, so sorted() works on your objects. An object used in a set or as a dictionary key needs __hash__ consistent with __eq__ (equal objects must have equal hashes); a class that defines __eq__ without __hash__ becomes unhashable, which is correct for mutable objects. Dataclasses (lesson 4.04) write most of this for you.

title: Money that behaves
body: Write a Money class stored as whole cents, with the special methods of lesson 4.02: python m = Money(1250, "EUR") repr(m) "Money(1250, 'EUR')" str(m) "12.50 EUR" m + Money(5, "EUR") Money(1255, 'EUR'); adding different currencies raises ValueError m 3, 3 m Money(3750, 'EUR') m == Money(1250, "EUR"), m < Money(1300, "EUR") comparing different currencies raises ValueError {m, Money(1250, "EUR")} one element: equal money has equal hashes sum( ... , Money(0, "EUR")) works because + works Negative amounts print with a minus sign: Money(-5, "USD") is "-0.05 USD" . Comparing Money with something that is not Money using == gives False .

title: 4.03  Inheritance and Protocols
body: Sharing behaviour between classes - subclasses, overriding methods, super(), abstract base classes, and Python's duck typing, where any object with the right methods will do. This lesson also says when composition is better than inheritance. Subclasses A subclass inherits everything from its base class and can add or override methods: python class Shape: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def area(self): return 0.0 def describe(self): return f"{self.name} with area {self.area():.2f}" class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self, width, height): super().__init__("rectangle") let the base class set up its part self.width, self.height = width, height def area(self): overrides Shape.area return self.width self.height class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, radius): super().__init__("circle") self.radius = radius def area(self): return 3.141592653589793 self.radius 2 for shape in Rectangle(3, 4), Circle(1) : print(shape.describe()) describe is written once, in Shape , and calls whichever area the actual object has: this is polymorphism . isinstance(shape, Shape) is true for both. super() super() gives access to the base class's version of a method, most often to extend __init__ or to add to a method rather than replace it: python class LoggedRectangle(Rectangle): def area(self): result = super().area() print(f"area computed: {result}") return result Abstract base classes When a base class only describes what subclasses must provide, make it abstract so it cannot be used by mistake: python from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Exporter(ABC): @abstractmethod def export(self, rows): """Return the rows as text.""" class CsvExporter(Exporter): def export(self, rows): return "\n".join(",".join(map(str, row)) for row in rows) print(CsvExporter().export( (1, 2), (3, 4) )) Exporter() would raise TypeError: abstract methods are missing Duck typing Python does not require a shared base class. If an object has the methods that are used, it works: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck...". len() works on anything with __len__ ; a function that calls .write(text) works with a file, a StringIO , or your own class with a write method. python import io def save_report(out, lines): for line in lines: out.write(line + "\n") buffer = io.StringIO() save_report(buffer, "a", "b" ) works with any object that has write() print(repr(buffer.getvalue())) typing.Protocol (lesson 5.05) lets you describe such a "duck" for type checkers without inheritance. Composition over inheritance Inheritance means "is a": a circle is a shape. When the relationship is "has a" (a car has an engine), store the other object in an attribute instead: composition . It is more flexible (the engine can be swapped) and avoids deep class hierarchies that are hard to change. A good rule: inherit only when the subclass truly can be used everywhere the base class can.

title: A family of shapes
body: Write a small class hierarchy: python class Shape(ABC): abstract: area() and perimeter() are abstract methods def describe(self): ... "<Name : area 12.00, perimeter 14.00", with the class name class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self, width, height) class Square(Rectangle): def __init__(self, side) a square IS a rectangle class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, radius) use math.pi def largest(shapes): ... the shape with the greatest area (the first one on a tie); None for an empty list def total_area(shapes): ... works for any objects that have an area() method, shapes or not Shape() itself must raise TypeError (it is abstract). describe is written only once, in Shape ; type(self).__name__ gives the class name.

title: 4.04  Dataclasses and Enums
body: Less boilerplate for data-holding classes - @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, with defaults, field(default_factory), ordering, frozen instances and __post_init__ validation - and Enum for a fixed set of named values. Dataclasses Many classes mostly hold data. Writing __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ by hand for them is tedious; @dataclass generates them from annotated fields: python from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Book: title: str author: str year: int tags: list str = field(default_factory=list) a NEW list per instance read: bool = False b = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965) b.tags.append("sci-fi") print(b) print(b == Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965, "sci-fi" )) The type annotations ( str , int ) document the fields; Python does not check them at run time. Fields with defaults come after fields without. Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults: a plain = is refused for exactly the reason of lesson 3.02. Options Option Effect --- --- @dataclass(order=True) Adds < , <= , , = comparing fields in order, so instances sort @dataclass(frozen=True) Instances cannot be changed after creation, and become hashable @dataclass(slots=True) Uses less memory per instance python @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True) class Version: major: int minor: int patch: int = 0 print(sorted( Version(2, 0), Version(1, 9, 3), Version(1, 10) )) releases = {Version(1, 0): "first"} frozen: usable as a key Validation __post_init__ runs after the generated __init__ and can check or compute fields: python @dataclass class Rectangle: width: float height: float def __post_init__(self): if self.width <= 0 or self.height <= 0: raise ValueError("sides must be positive") @property def area(self): return self.width self.height print(Rectangle(2, 3).area) Dataclasses are ordinary classes: they can have methods and properties, and inherit. Enums An enum is a fixed set of named values, much safer than strings like "red" that can be misspelt: python from enum import Enum, auto class Status(Enum): TODO = auto() DOING = auto() DONE = auto() s = Status.DOING print(s, s.name, s.value, s is Status.DOING) print( status.name for status in Status ) print(Status "DONE" , Status(1)) by name, by value Enums are compared with is or == , can be iterated, and work well with match (lesson 1.05). StrEnum and IntEnum make members that also behave as strings or numbers, handy when the values are written to files.

title: Tasks as dataclasses
body: Model tasks with a dataclass and an enum: python class Priority(Enum): HIGH = 1; NORMAL = 2; LOW = 3 @dataclass class Task: title: str priority: Priority = Priority.NORMAL tags: list str = field(default_factory=list) done: bool = False def parse_task(text): ... "Write report !high work urgent" - Task("Write report", Priority.HIGH, "work", "urgent" ) def sort_tasks(tasks): ... a new list: not done first, then by priority (HIGH first), then title def with_tag(tasks, tag): ... the tasks that have the tag (compared ignoring case) In parse_task , words starting with are tags (stored without , in lower case, in order, without duplicates); a word !high , !normal or !low (any case) sets the priority; everything else forms the title, words joined by single spaces. An unknown !word raises ValueError .

title: 4.05  Errors and Exceptions
body: Handling what goes wrong - reading tracebacks, try and except, catching specific exceptions, else and finally, raising your own errors, custom exception classes, and the difference between asking permission and asking forgiveness. Exceptions and tracebacks When something goes wrong, Python raises an exception . If nothing handles it, the program stops with a traceback : Traceback (most recent call last): File "main.py", line 3, in <module print(average( )) File "main.py", line 2, in average return sum(values) / len(values) ZeroDivisionError: division by zero Read it from the bottom : the last line says what happened ( ZeroDivisionError ) and why; the lines above show the chain of calls, ending at the line that failed. Common exceptions: Exception Typical cause --- --- ValueError Right type, wrong value: int("abc") TypeError Wrong type: "a" + 1 KeyError Missing dictionary key IndexError List index out of range AttributeError Misspelt attribute or method, or None where an object was expected FileNotFoundError Opening a missing file ZeroDivisionError Division by zero try and except python text = input("A number: ") try: number = int(text) except ValueError: print("That was not a whole number.") else: print("Twice that is", number 2) runs only if there was no exception finally: print("Done.") always runs Catch specific exceptions. A bare except: (or except Exception: ) also hides bugs such as misspelt names, and makes problems silently disappear. Several kinds can share a handler, and the exception object can be inspected: python for raw in "12", "x", None : try: print(int(raw) 2) except (ValueError, TypeError) as e: print("skipping:", e) Raising exceptions A function that cannot do its job should raise rather than return a strange value: python def withdraw(balance, amount): if amount <= 0: raise ValueError(f"amount must be positive, got {amount}") if amount balance: raise ValueError("insufficient funds") return balance - amount The caller decides what to do: show a message, retry, or let it stop the program. Your own exception classes For errors specific to your program, define a class deriving from Exception , so callers can catch exactly them: python class ConfigError(Exception): """The configuration file is invalid.""" def read_port(settings): if "port" not in settings: raise ConfigError("missing port") return int(settings "port" ) try: read_port({}) except ConfigError as e: print("Config problem:", e) raise NewError(...) from e inside an except keeps the original exception attached as the cause, which makes the traceback tell the whole story. Asking forgiveness Python style often prefers trying and handling the failure ( EAFP : easier to ask forgiveness than permission) over checking first ( LBYL : look before you leap): python counts = {"a": 1} try: value = counts "b" except KeyError: value = 0 Checking first can be wrong anyway: a file that exists when you check can be deleted before you open it. For simple cases, dict.get and str.isdigit are clearer than either.

title: Reading records safely
body: Read records like Ada,36,ada@example.org from lines of text, collecting errors instead of crashing: python class InvalidRecord(Exception): ... def parse_record(line): ... - (name, age, email); raises InvalidRecord with a message def load_records(lines): ... - (records, errors); errors are "line N: <message ", N counting from 1 parse_record checks, in order, and raises InvalidRecord with these messages: - not exactly three comma-separated fields: "expected 3 fields, got N" - an empty name (after stripping spaces): "missing name" - an age that is not a whole number: "age is not a number: <text " (use int() and catch its ValueError , re-raising as InvalidRecord with from ) - an age outside 0-150: "age out of range: <age " - an email without exactly one @ with text on both sides: "invalid email: <text " Fields are stripped of surrounding spaces. load_records skips blank lines (they are not errors).

title: An inventory system
body: Write the stock-keeping core of a small shop: products as dataclasses, an Inventory class that behaves like a container, its own exception types, and order processing that reports problems instead of stopping. python class InventoryError(Exception): ... class UnknownProduct(InventoryError): ... str(e) is "unknown product: <sku " class OutOfStock(InventoryError): ... str(e) is "only <n of <sku left" @dataclass class Product: sku: str name: str price_cents: int quantity: int = 0 class Inventory: def add_product(self, product): ... ValueError if the sku already exists def restock(self, sku, amount): ... UnknownProduct / ValueError if amount <= 0 def take(self, sku, amount): ... UnknownProduct / ValueError / OutOfStock; returns the product def __len__(self): ... number of products def __contains__(self, sku): ... def __iter__(self): ... products in sku order @property def total_value(self): ... sum of price x quantity, in cents def low_stock(self, threshold): ... skus with quantity < threshold, in sku order def process_orders(inventory, orders): ... orders: list of (sku, amount); returns a list of report lines process_orders handles each order in turn and adds one line: "OK <sku x<amount " when it succeeded, or "FAILED <sku x<amount : <message " with the exception's message for any InventoryError or ValueError . A failed order changes nothing. After the orders, it adds "<k of <n orders filled" . take with amount <= 0 raises ValueError("amount must be positive") ; restock the same.

title: 5.01  Comprehensions
body: Building lists, dictionaries and sets in one readable expression - list comprehensions with conditions, nested comprehensions, dictionary and set comprehensions, conditional expressions inside them, and when a plain loop is clearer. List comprehensions A very common loop builds a new list from an old one: python squares = for n in range(1, 6): squares.append(n n) A list comprehension says the same in one expression: python squares = n n for n in range(1, 6) print(squares) 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 Read it as " n × n for each n in the range". The parts are: the expression to collect, then for name in iterable . Filtering An if at the end keeps only some items: python words = "apple", "Kiwi", "banana", "fig", "Cherry" long_words = w for w in words if len(w) 4 capitalised = w for w in words if w 0 .isupper() print(long_words, capitalised) To transform some items rather than drop them, put a conditional expression (lesson 1.05) at the front: python numbers = 3, -1, 4, -5 print( n if n = 0 else 0 for n in numbers ) 3, 0, 4, 0 if at the end filters; if ... else at the front chooses a value. Nested loops Several for clauses work like nested loops, read left to right: python pairs = (x, y) for x in range(3) for y in range(3) if x != y grid = 0 4 for _ in range(3) 3 separate rows of 4 zeros flat = cell for row in 1, 2 , 3, 4 for cell in row print(pairs :3 , flat) Dictionary and set comprehensions python words = "apple", "fig", "banana" lengths = {w: len(w) for w in words} dict initials = {w 0 for w in words} set inverted = {v: k for k, v in {"a": 1, "b": 2}.items()} print(lengths, initials, inverted) Generator expressions With parentheses instead of brackets, the same syntax makes a generator that produces items one at a time without building a list (lesson 5.02). Passed straight to a function, the extra parentheses can be dropped: python print(sum(n n for n in range(1_000_000))) print(any(w.startswith("b") for w in "apple", "banana" )) print(max(len(w) for w in "apple", "fig", "banana" )) When not to use one Comprehensions are for building a collection. If the loop's job is a side effect (printing, writing files), use a plain for . If the expression needs several steps or nested conditions, a loop with good variable names is clearer than a comprehension that has to be read three times. A good rule: one for , at most one condition, one short expression.

title: One-line collections
body: Write each function body as a single return with a comprehension: python def squares_of_evens(numbers): ... 4, 16 for 1, 2, 3, 4 def word_lengths(words): ... {"fig": 3, "apple": 5} def initials(names): ... sorted list of the distinct first letters, upper-case def transpose(matrix): ... rows become columns: 1, 2 , 3, 4 - 1, 3 , 2, 4 def flatten(lists): ... 1, 2 , , 3 - 1, 2, 3 All rows of a matrix have the same length; an empty matrix transposes to an empty list.

title: 5.02  Iterators and Generators
body: How for loops really work - iterables and iterators, iter and next, writing generator functions with yield, lazy pipelines that process data of any size, infinite sequences, and yield from. The iteration protocol A for loop works with any iterable : lists, strings, dictionaries, files, ranges. Behind the scenes it asks the iterable for an iterator with iter() and calls next() on it until it raises StopIteration : python it = iter( 10, 20, 30 ) print(next(it), next(it), next(it)) next(it) now would raise StopIteration: the loop's signal to stop An iterator is used up once it has been walked through; a list can be iterated again and again because each for gets a fresh iterator. Generator functions A function containing yield is a generator function . Calling it does not run the body; it returns a generator, and each next() runs the body up to the next yield : python def countdown(n): print("starting") while n 0: yield n n -= 1 print("done") for value in countdown(3): print(value) The function's local variables survive between yield s, so generators are an easy way to write iterators without a class. Lazy pipelines Generators produce values on demand . That lets you process data far larger than memory, one item at a time, by chaining small steps: python def read_numbers(lines): for line in lines: line = line.strip() if line: yield int(line) def only_even(numbers): for n in numbers: if n % 2 == 0: yield n lines = "4", "", "7", "10", "3" could be a file with millions of lines print(sum(only_even(read_numbers(lines)))) 14 No intermediate list is ever built: each number flows through the whole pipeline before the next is read. Infinite sequences A generator can go on forever; the consumer decides when to stop: python import itertools def fibonacci(): a, b = 0, 1 while True: yield a a, b = b, a + b print(list(itertools.islice(fibonacci(), 10))) itertools.islice takes the first n items; next(gen) takes one. yield from yield from other yields every item of another iterable, which makes recursive generators short: python def flatten(items): for item in items: if isinstance(item, list): yield from flatten(item) else: yield item print(list(flatten( 1, 2, 3, 4 , 5 ))) Iterators in the standard library Many built-ins return lazy iterators rather than lists: range , enumerate , zip , map , filter , reversed , dictionary views, and file objects. Wrap one in list(...) when you really need all the items at once, for example to index them or loop over them twice.

title: Generators
body: Write four generator functions (each must use yield ): python def chunks(items, size): ... yields lists of size items; the last one may be shorter def running_total(numbers): ... yields the sum so far after each number def primes(): ... yields 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... forever def take(n, iterable): ... yields the first n items (fewer if the iterable ends) chunks must work with any iterable, including another generator, and must not read more items than it needs.

title: 5.03  Sorting, Key Functions and Lambdas
body: Putting things in order - sorted and sort with key functions, sorting by several criteria, stable sorting, reverse order per field, operator.itemgetter and attrgetter, min and max with keys, and structural pattern matching on sequences. Key functions sorted(items, key=f) sorts by f(item) instead of the items themselves. key takes any function of one argument: python words = "banana", "Apple", "cherry", "fig" print(sorted(words)) 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'fig' : capitals first print(sorted(words, key=str.lower)) case-insensitive print(sorted(words, key=len)) by length: 'fig', 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry' min and max take a key too: max(words, key=len) is the longest word. Several criteria Return a tuple from the key: tuples compare item by item, so the second item breaks ties of the first: python people = ("Ada", 36), ("Grace", 85), ("Alan", 36), ("Bob", 85) print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p 1 , p 0 ))) by age, then name To sort one field descending and another ascending, negate the number: key=lambda p: (-p 1 , p 0 ) is "oldest first, then by name". For text fields that cannot be negated, use stability (below). Stable sorting Python's sort is stable : items with equal keys keep their original order. That allows sorting in several passes, least important key first : python people = ("Ada", 36), ("Grace", 85), ("Alan", 36), ("Bob", 85) by_name = sorted(people, key=lambda p: p 0 , reverse=True) names Z-A result = sorted(by_name, key=lambda p: p 1 ) then ages ascending, names stay Z-A print(result) operator helpers operator.itemgetter and attrgetter build key functions that are clearer and a little faster than lambdas: python from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter from dataclasses import dataclass rows = {"name": "Ada", "score": 95}, {"name": "Bob", "score": 72} print(sorted(rows, key=itemgetter("score"), reverse=True)) @dataclass class Player: name: str level: int team = Player("Ada", 7), Player("Bob", 3) print(sorted(team, key=attrgetter("level"))) Sorting your own objects Objects without a key need __lt__ (lesson 4.02) or @dataclass(order=True) (lesson 4.04) to be sortable. A key function is usually better: it does not fix one "natural" order for a class that can be sorted many ways. match on sequences match (lesson 1.05) can also take sequences apart by shape, which helps when processing commands or records: python def describe(command): match command.split(): case "go", direction : return f"going {direction}" case "take", items if items: return f"taking {', '.join(items)}" case "quit" "exit" : return "bye" case _: return "unknown" for c in "go north", "take key lamp", "exit", "dance" : print(describe(c)) Each case matches the list's length and literal words, binds the other positions to names, and can add a guard with if .

title: Sorting it out
body: Write sorting and matching helpers: python def leaderboard(players): ... players: list of {"name": ..., "score": ...}; score descending, then name ascending (case-insensitive) def sort_versions(versions): ... "1.10", "1.2", "1.9.1", "1.2.0" - numeric order; equal versions keep their order def longest_words(text, n): ... the n longest distinct words (lower-cased), longest first, ties alphabetical def describe(command): ... uses match (below) describe returns: "going <dir " for go <dir ; "taking <a , <b " for take followed by one or more items; "bye" for quit or exit ; "unknown" otherwise (including take with no items). Words are separated by spaces.

title: 5.04  The Standard Library Toolbox
body: The modules that make everyday code short - collections (Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple), itertools (chain, groupby, product, combinations, accumulate), functools (lru_cache, partial, reduce) and a few more worth knowing. collections Counter counts things: python from collections import Counter words = "the cat and the hat and the bat".split() counts = Counter(words) print(counts "the" , counts "dog" ) 3 0: missing keys count as 0 print(counts.most_common(2)) ('the', 3), ('and', 2) print(Counter("hello") + Counter("world")) counters add up defaultdict creates missing values automatically, which makes grouping one line: python from collections import defaultdict by_letter = defaultdict(list) for word in "apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry" : by_letter word 0 .append(word) print(dict(by_letter)) deque is a list with fast adding and removing at both ends, ideal for queues and "the last N items": python from collections import deque recent = deque(maxlen=3) for page in "home", "about", "shop", "cart" : recent.append(page) print(list(recent)) 'about', 'shop', 'cart' queue = deque( "a", "b" ) queue.appendleft("z") print(queue.popleft(), queue) itertools Function Gives --- --- chain(a, b) The items of a, then of b islice(it, n) The first n items groupby(sorted_items, key) Runs of consecutive items with the same key product(a, b) Every pair (nested loops) permutations(xs, r) , combinations(xs, r) Orderings, selections accumulate(xs) Running totals count(start) , cycle(xs) , repeat(x) Infinite sequences pairwise(xs) Overlapping pairs: (a, b), (b, c), ... python from itertools import groupby, combinations, accumulate, pairwise scores = sorted( ("Ada", "A"), ("Bob", "B"), ("Cy", "A") , key=lambda s: s 1 ) for grade, group in groupby(scores, key=lambda s: s 1 ): print(grade, name for name, _ in group ) print(list(combinations("ABC", 2))) print(list(accumulate( 3, 1, 4, 1 ))) 3, 4, 8, 9 print( b - a for a, b in pairwise( 1, 4, 9, 16 ) ) groupby only groups consecutive items: sort by the same key first. functools python from functools import lru_cache, partial, reduce @lru_cache(maxsize=None) remembers results: a ready-made version of practice 3.03's memoize def ways(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2) print(ways(80)) int_from_binary = partial(int, base=2) a function with some arguments filled in print(int_from_binary("1011")) print(reduce(lambda a, b: a b, 1, 2, 3, 4 )) 24: combine items pairwise A few more Module For --- --- statistics mean , median , mode , stdev random choice , shuffle , sample , seeded generators string Constants such as ascii_letters , digits textwrap Wrapping and indenting text heapq Priority queues: always pop the smallest bisect Searching and inserting in sorted lists

title: Using the toolbox
body: Use collections , itertools and functools from lesson 5.04: python def top_letters(text, n): ... the n most common letters (a-z, ignoring case) as (letter, count); ties alphabetical def by_extension(filenames): ... dict extension - sorted names; files without a dot go under ""; extensions lower-case def moving_average(values, window): ... list of the averages of each full window of consecutive values def staircases(n): ... ways to climb n steps taking 1 or 2 at a time; fast for n = 200 (use lru_cache) moving_average( 1, 2, 3, 4 , 2) is 1.5, 2.5, 3.5 ; a window larger than the list gives . Use a deque(maxlen=window) . The extension is the part after the last dot.

title: 5.05  Type Hints and Testing
body: Making Python code safer as it grows - type hints for functions, collections and optional values, checking them with mypy or Pyright, Protocols for duck typing - and automated tests with assert, pytest, fixtures and parametrised tests. Type hints Type hints say what types a function expects and returns. Python ignores them when running; editors and type checkers use them to find mistakes before the code runs: python def average(values: list float ) - float: return sum(values) / len(values) def find_user(users: dict str, int , name: str) - int None: return users.get(name) print(average( 1.0, 2.5 ), find_user({"ada": 1}, "bob")) Hint Means --- --- int , str , float , bool That type list int , dict str, float , set str , tuple int, str Collections with their item types tuple int, ... A tuple of any length of ints X \ None An X or None Callable int , str ( from collections.abc import Callable ) A function from int to str Iterable str , Iterator int Anything you can loop over / an iterator With hints, find_user(users, "bob") + 1 is reported by the checker: the result may be None . Running mypy main.py or using Pyright (built into VS Code's Python extension) checks a whole project. Protocols typing.Protocol describes a "duck" (lesson 4.03) for the type checker, without requiring inheritance: python from typing import Protocol class HasArea(Protocol): def area(self) - float: ... def total_area(shapes: list HasArea ) - float: return sum(s.area() for s in shapes) Any class with an area() method returning a float is accepted. Tests with assert The simplest test is a function full of assert s: python def slug(title: str) - str: return "-".join(title.lower().split()) def test_slug(): assert slug("Hello World") == "hello-world" assert slug(" many spaces ") == "many-spaces" assert slug("") == "" test_slug() print("all good") The practice on this site works the same way: @test functions with check_eq , or plain test_... functions with assert . pytest pytest ( pip install pytest ) finds every test_ .py file and every test_ function in it, runs them, and reports failures with the values involved: tests/test_slug.py::test_slug PASSED tests/test_money.py::test_add FAILED assert add(2, 3) == 6 where 5 = add(2, 3) Two features make tests short: python import pytest @pytest.mark.parametrize("title, expected", ("Hello World", "hello-world"), (" A b ", "a-b"), ("", ""), ) def test_slug(title, expected): assert slug(title) == expected def test_bad_age_raises(): with pytest.raises(ValueError): int("forty") Fixtures provide prepared objects to tests by naming them as parameters ( tmp_path gives a fresh temporary folder, for testing file code). What to test Test the behaviour callers rely on: normal cases, edge cases (empty input, zero, the largest value, a single item), and error cases (what is raised). Write a test for every bug you fix, so it cannot come back. Small pure functions, which take arguments and return results without printing or reading files, are the easiest to test: one more reason to write code that way.

title: Typed and tested
body: Write two functions with type hints , exactly as shown, so a type checker (and the tests) can read them: python def slugify(title: str) - str: ... "Hello, World!" - "hello-world" def parse_duration(text: str) - int: ... "1h30m" - 5400 seconds slugify : lower-case; every run of characters that are not letters or digits becomes one - ; no - at either end. parse_duration : a sequence of number-and-unit parts with units h , m , s (any case), in that order, each at most once, no spaces: "45s" , "2h" , "1h5s" , "90m" . Anything else (empty text, an unknown unit, a unit twice or out of order, a missing number, leftover characters) raises ValueError .

title: A log analyser
body: Analyse web-server log lines with a generator pipeline, Counter and key-function sorting: 2026-11-15T10:00:01 GET /home 200 532ms 2026-11-15T10:00:07 GET /search 500 1200ms python @dataclass(frozen=True) class Entry: time: str "2026-11-15T10:00:01" method: str path: str status: int ms: int def parse_lines(lines): ... a generator of Entry; skips blank lines, lines starting with , and malformed lines def summarize(entries): ... a dict (below) def report(summary): ... the report text (below) parse_lines expects exactly five space-separated fields; the status must be a whole number and the duration a whole number followed by ms . Anything else is skipped silently. It must be a generator ( yield ). summarize returns a dictionary with: - "requests" : the number of entries; - "server_errors" : entries with status 500 or more; "client_errors" : 400 to 499; - "by_status" : a list of (status, count) pairs sorted by status; - "slowest" : the three slowest (ms, path) pairs, slowest first, ties by path; - "busiest_minute" : (minute, count) for the minute (the time's first 16 characters) with the most requests, the earliest on a tie, or None for no entries; - "average_ms" : a dict path to average duration, rounded to one decimal. report produces lines ending in \n : Requests: 6 Server errors: 1, client errors: 1 Status codes: 200 x4, 404 x1, 500 x1 Slowest: /search 1200ms, /home 532ms, /home 316ms Busiest minute: 2026-11-15T10:00 (4 requests) Average by path: /about 120.0 ms /home 316.0 ms /missing 15.0 ms /search 1200.0 ms The status-code and slowest lines list nothing after the colon when empty ( Status codes: with nothing after). The busiest line reads Busiest minute: none without entries. In "Average by path", paths are sorted, left-aligned in a column as wide as the longest path plus 3, and the average is right-aligned in 6 characters with one decimal, then ms .

title: 6.01  Text Processing and Regular Expressions
body: Finding and extracting patterns in text with the re module - the pattern language, search, findall and fullmatch, groups and named groups, substitution, flags, and when plain string methods are the better tool. What regular expressions are for String methods (lesson 2.01) find fixed text. A regular expression describes a pattern : "a date like 2026-11-15", "an email address", "a word followed by a number". The re module searches for patterns, extracts parts of them and replaces them. Always write patterns as raw strings ( r"..." ), so backslashes reach re unchanged. The pattern language Pattern Matches --- --- abc The text abc . Any character except a new line \d , \w , \s A digit, a word character (letter, digit, _ ), whitespace \D , \W , \S Anything but those aeiou , a-z0-9 , ^, One character from a set, a range, or not in the set , + , ? Zero or more, one or more, zero or one of what precedes {3} , {2,4} Exactly 3, between 2 and 4 ^ , $ Start, end (of the text, or of each line with re.M ) \b A word boundary a\ b a or b ( ) A group: captures the part it matches \. , \( A literal dot or parenthesis and + are greedy (they take as much as possible); ? and +? take as little as possible. Searching python import re text = "Orders: 1042 on 2026-11-15, 1043 on 2026-11-16." print(re.findall(r" (\d+)", text)) '1042', '1043' : the group's text m = re.search(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", text) the first match, or None if m: print(m.group(0), m.group(1), m.groups()) print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", "2026-11-15"))) the WHOLE text must match Function Returns --- --- re.search(p, s) First match anywhere, or None re.match(p, s) Match at the start only re.fullmatch(p, s) Match of the whole string: use it for validation re.findall(p, s) List of matches (or of groups) re.finditer(p, s) Match objects one by one, with positions re.split(p, s) Split at matches re.sub(p, repl, s) Replace matches Named groups Names make complicated patterns readable: python import re line = "2026-11-15 10:42:07 ERROR disk full" pattern = re.compile(r"(?P<date \S+) (?P<time \S+) (?P<level A-Z +) (?P<message . )") m = pattern.match(line) print(m "level" , "-", m "message" , m.groupdict()) re.compile builds the pattern once, which is tidier (and a little faster) when it is used many times. Replacing python import re print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too many spaces")) collapse whitespace print(re.sub(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", r"\3/\2/\1", "2026-11-15")) 15/11/2026: groups in the replacement print(re.sub(r"\d+", lambda m: str(int(m.group()) 2), "3 apples, 10 pears")) Flags re.I ignores case, re.M makes ^ and $ match at every line, re.S lets . match new lines too, and re.X allows spaces and comments inside the pattern for long expressions. When not to use them Regular expressions are compact but hard to read. For fixed text, in , startswith , split and replace are clearer. For structured formats such as CSV, JSON and HTML, use a real parser (lesson 6.02): patterns for them break on the first unusual input. Test patterns on examples, including ones that should not match.

title: Patterns in text
body: Use the re module for four jobs: python def find_emails(text): ... sorted, distinct, lower-cased addresses found anywhere in the text def to_iso_dates(text): ... every DD/MM/YYYY date rewritten as YYYY-MM-DD; the rest unchanged def is_hex_colour(text): ... " 1a2B3c" or " fff": a and exactly 3 or 6 hex digits, nothing else def parse_log(line): ... dict with date, time, level, message; None if the line does not fit - An email here is: one or more of letters, digits, . , _ , % , + , - ; an @ ; then one or more parts of letters, digits and - separated by dots, ending in a dot and 2 or more letters. - Dates have 1 or 2 digit days and months: 5/1/2026 becomes 2026-01-05 (pad with zeros). - Log lines look like 2026-11-15 10:42:07 ERROR disk full : a date, a time, a level of capital letters, and a message (the rest, at least one character).

title: 6.02  CSV and JSON
body:
The two data formats you meet everywhere - reading and writing CSV with the csv module (quoting, DictReader and DictWriter, converting types), and JSON with the json module (loading, dumping, pretty printing, and what maps to what). CSV CSV (comma-separated values) is how spreadsheets and databases exchange tables: name,city,score Ada,London,95 "Hopper, Grace",New York,88 Splitting lines on commas breaks on the second row: a field that contains a comma is quoted . The csv module handles quoting, embedded quotes and line breaks correctly: python import csv, io data = 'name,city,score
Ada,London,95
"Hopper, Grace",New York,88
' reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)) with a real file: open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") rows = list(reader) print(rows 1 "name" , rows 1 "score" ) Hopper, Grace 88 total = sum(int(r "score" ) for r in rows) every field is TEXT: convert it print(total) csv.reader gives each row as a list; csv.DictReader uses the header row to give dictionaries, which is clearer. Open CSV files with newline="" so the module can handle line endings itself. Writing: python import csv, io out = io.StringIO() writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames= "name", "score" ) writer.writeheader() writer.writerow({"name": "Hopper, Grace", "score": 88}) writer.writerows( {"name": "Ada", "score": 95} ) print(out.getvalue()) The writer adds quotes where needed. Spreadsheets in some countries use ; as the separator: pass delimiter=";" . JSON JSON is the format of web APIs and many configuration files. It maps directly to Python values: JSON Python --- --- object {...} dict array ... list string str number int or float true / false True / False null None python import json text = '{"name": "Ada", "languages": "en", "fr" , "active": true, "manager": null}' person = json.loads(text) text - Python print(person "languages" 1 , person "active" , person "manager" ) person "score" = 95 print(json.dumps(person)) Python - text print(json.dumps(person, indent=2, sort_keys=True)) With files, json.load(f) and json.dump(obj, f, indent=2) read and write directly. Pass ensure_ascii=False to write accented characters as they are rather than as é escapes. Only these types can be written. Dates, sets, tuples (written as lists) and your own classes need converting first, for example with dataclasses.asdict(obj) or a default= function. Keys of JSON objects are always strings: a dict with int keys comes back with string keys. Errors in data Real files contain surprises: missing columns, empty fields, numbers with spaces, invalid JSON. Validate as you convert (lesson 4.05): json.loads raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError ) with the line and column of the problem; for CSV, check each row and collect errors rather than stopping at the first one. The final project does exactly that.

title: CSV in, JSON out
body: Convert between the formats of lesson 6.02: python def read_people(csv_text): ... - (people, errors): people is a list of {"name": str, "age": int, "city": str} def to_json(people): ... pretty JSON: indent 2, keys sorted, non-ASCII characters kept as they are def write_csv(people): ... CSV text with the header name,age,city and one row per person (lines end with \n) read_people reads CSV with a header row (the columns may be in any order; extra columns are ignored). A row whose age is not a whole number is skipped and reported as "row N: bad age <text " , where N counts the data rows from 1. Missing columns in the header: return ( , "missing column: <name " ) for the first missing of name , age , city . Use the csv module (names and cities may contain commas and quotes).

title: 6.03  Dates and Times
body: Working with dates and times in Python - date, time, datetime and timedelta, parsing and formatting with ISO 8601 and strftime, date arithmetic, time zones with zoneinfo, and measuring durations with time.perf_counter. The types python from datetime import date, time, datetime, timedelta d = date(2026, 11, 15) t = time(14, 30) dt = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 14, 30, 5) print(d, t, dt, d.weekday(), d.isoweekday(), d.strftime("%A")) print(date.today(), datetime.now()) weekday() is 0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday. All these objects are immutable: methods such as replace return new ones. Parsing and formatting ISO 8601 ( 2026-11-15 , 2026-11-15T14:30:05 ) is the unambiguous standard format: use it for files and data. python from datetime import date, datetime d = date.fromisoformat("2026-11-15") dt = datetime.fromisoformat("2026-11-15T14:30:05") print(dt.isoformat(), d.isoformat()) For other formats, strptime parses and strftime formats with codes: Code Meaning Example --- --- --- %Y / %y Year 2026 / 26 %m / %d Month / day, two digits 11 / 15 %B / %b Month name / short November / Nov %A / %a Weekday name / short Sunday / Sun %H / %I / %p Hour (24 h) / hour (12 h) / AM-PM 14 / 02 / PM %M / %S Minutes / seconds 30 / 05 python from datetime import datetime dt = datetime.strptime("15/11/2026 14:30", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M") print(dt.strftime("%A %d %B %Y, %H:%M")) print(f"{dt:%Y-%m-%d}") format codes work inside f-strings too Month and day names depend on the system language; for fixed output, prefer numbers. Arithmetic Subtracting dates gives a timedelta ; adding a timedelta moves a date: python from datetime import date, timedelta start = date(2026, 11, 15) print(start + timedelta(days=30)) print((date(2026, 12, 25) - start).days, "days to go") week = start + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(7) print( d.strftime("%a") for d in week ) timedelta has days, seconds and microseconds; there is no "add one month" because months differ in length: compute it explicitly (practice 6.03). Time zones A datetime without time zone information is naive : it just says "14:30" without saying where. For events that people in different places see, attach a zone with zoneinfo : python from datetime import datetime from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo meeting = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 14, 30, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/London")) print(meeting.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))) print(meeting.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC")).isoformat()) Store times in UTC, convert to local time only for display (the Win32 course's lesson 2.03 gives the same advice). On Windows, pip install tzdata provides the zone database. Measuring durations For timing code, use time.perf_counter() , a high-resolution clock that never jumps: python import time start = time.perf_counter() total = sum(i i for i in range(200_000)) print(f"took {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f} s") Never time code with datetime.now() : the wall clock can be adjusted while the program runs.

title: Calendar arithmetic
body: timedelta has no months or years, so write the calendar helpers yourself (with datetime.date ): python def add_months(d, n): ... same day n months later (or earlier); clamp to the month's last day def age_on(birthday, day): ... whole years old on day def workdays_between(start, end): ... Monday-Friday dates d with start <= d < end def next_weekday(d, weekday): ... the first date AFTER d with that weekday (0 = Monday) add_months(date(2026, 1, 31), 1) is date(2026, 2, 28) ; add_months(date(2024, 3, 31), -1) is date(2024, 2, 29) . Someone born on 29 February is a year older on 1 March in non-leap years (they have not had a 29 February yet on 28 February). workdays_between returns 0 when end <= start .

title: 6.04  Automation Scripts
body: Turning Python code into tools you run every day - command-line arguments with argparse, exit codes, reading from standard input, working through folders of files safely, running other programs with subprocess, and logging what a script did. A script's shape A useful script has a main function, reads its arguments, does its work, and exits with a status: python import argparse import sys def main(argv=None): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Count lines in text files.") parser.add_argument("files", nargs="+", help="files to count") parser.add_argument("--min", type=int, default=0, help="only show files with at least this many lines") parser.add_argument("-q", "--quiet", action="store_true", help="print only the total") args = parser.parse_args(argv) total = 0 for name in args.files: try: with open(name, encoding="utf-8") as f: count = sum(1 for _ in f) except OSError as e: print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr) return 1 total += count if not args.quiet and count = args.min: print(f"{count:6} {name}") print(f"{total:6} total") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main()) Running python count.py --help prints a help text generated from the definitions; wrong arguments give a clear error. Passing argv explicitly to main makes the script easy to test: main( "notes.txt", "--quiet" ) . argparse in brief Definition Command line --- --- add_argument("path") A required positional argument add_argument("files", nargs="+") One or more add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10) An option with a value add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true") A flag add_argument("--mode", choices= "fast", "safe" ) Only these values Exit codes and streams By convention, exit code 0 means success and anything else failure; other programs and scripts (and CI systems) rely on it. Write results to standard output and messages and errors to standard error ( print(..., file=sys.stderr) ), so results can be redirected to a file ( python count.py .txt counts.txt ) without the errors mixed in. Reading standard input makes a script work in pipelines: for line in sys.stdin: . Working through files safely Automation often changes many files at once, so build in safety: python from pathlib import Path def rename_photos(folder, dry_run=True): for i, path in enumerate(sorted(Path(folder).glob(" .jpg")), start=1): target = path.with_name(f"photo-{i:03}.jpg") if target.exists(): print(f"skip {path.name}: {target.name} exists") continue print(f"{path.name} - {target.name}") if not dry_run: path.rename(target) - A dry run that only prints what would happen, as the default. - Never overwrite without checking. - Work on a copy first; keep backups. - Log every change (below), so it can be undone. Running other programs subprocess.run starts another program and waits for it. Pass the command as a list (no shell, no quoting problems: the Win32 course's lesson 5.03 explains why quoting is hard): python import subprocess, sys result = subprocess.run( sys.executable, "--version" , capture_output=True, text=True) print(result.returncode, result.stdout.strip() or result.stderr.strip()) check=True raises an exception if the program fails. Avoid shell=True with any text that comes from users or files. Logging For scripts that run unattended, the logging module records what happened with times and levels, to the screen and a file: python import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s") log = logging.getLogger("backup") log.info("copied %d files", 42) log.warning("skipped %s: locked", "notes.docx") Scheduling To run a script every day, use the system's scheduler: Task Scheduler on Windows (action: python.exe , argument: the script's full path), cron on Linux and macOS. Use full paths everywhere, because scheduled tasks do not start in your usual folder.

title: A command-line tool
body: Write the main function of a small wordstat tool with argparse , so it can be run as a script and tested by calling main( ... ) : usage: wordstat -h --top N --ignore-case files files ... - For each file, in the order given, print <file : <lines lines, <words words . - With --top N (default 0: off), then print top words: and the N most common words over all files, one per line as <word <count , most common first, ties alphabetical. With --ignore-case , words are lower-cased before counting. Words are what str.split() gives. - If a file cannot be read, print wordstat: cannot read <file to standard error , skip it, and at the end return exit code 1; otherwise return 0. - main(argv) takes the arguments as a list (without the program name) and returns the exit code; it does not call sys.exit .

title: 6.05  Project: A Data Report Tool
body: Bring the whole course together in a command-line tool that reads sales data from CSV, validates it, groups and summarises it by month and product, and writes a text report and a JSON file. This lesson is the design, the structure and the order to build it in. What it does python sales_report.py sales.csv --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-06-30 --json summary.json Sales report 2026-01-01 to 2026-06-30 Rows: 1 204 read, 1 198 used, 6 rejected (see errors below) Month Orders Revenue 2026-01 201 12 450.50 2026-02 188 11 980.00 ... Top products 1. Green tea 3 120.00 2. Mug 2 400.00 ... Errors line 17: quantity is not a number: "two" ... The input is a CSV file with a header date,product,quantity,unit_price .
