The pieces and where they come from Piece Lessons --- --- Reading CSV with DictReader, converting fields 6.02 Validating rows, collecting errors with line numbers 4.05, practice 4.05 A dataclass for a sale 4.04 Filtering by date range 6.03 Grouping by month and product 2.05, 5.04 ( defaultdict , Counter ) Sorting the top products 5.03 Aligned text output 1.03 (format specifications) JSON output 6.02 Command-line arguments, exit codes, stderr 6.04 Tests for every function 5.05 Structure Keep the tool in small, testable functions, with input and output only at the edges: python def read_rows(lines) - tuple list Sale , list str : ... parse and validate def in_range(sales, start, end) - list Sale : ... def by_month(sales) - dict str, tuple int, float : ... month - (orders, revenue) def top_products(sales, n) - list tuple str, float : ... def format_report(...) - str: ... def main(argv=None) - int: ... the only function that touches files read_rows takes lines rather than a path, so tests can pass a list of strings; main opens the file and passes open(path) to it. The final project of this milestone is exactly these functions, checked by tests. Money Revenue is a sum of quantity × unit_price . Floats can show tiny errors over thousands of rows (lesson 1.04). Either round only when displaying, or work in whole cents ( round(float(price) 100) ), or use decimal.Decimal for exact decimal arithmetic. The project uses cents. Order to build in 1. read_rows with tests for good rows, each kind of bad row, and blank lines. 2. by_month and top_products , tested on a few hand-made sales. 3. format_report , compared against an expected text in a test. 4. main with argparse; try it on a real CSV exported from a spreadsheet. 5. Date filtering and JSON output. 6. Run it on messy data: an extra column, a missing header, a different delimiter, an empty file; make each fail clearly. Where to go next With this course you can write scripts and tools for almost any everyday task. From here: - Data analysis : pandas for tables, matplotlib for charts, Jupyter notebooks for exploring. - Web : requests to call APIs, Flask or FastAPI to build them. - Automation of the desktop and browser : openpyxl for Excel files, playwright for web pages. - Speed : profile first ( cProfile ), then reach for better algorithms (the DSA course) before anything else.

title: The sales report tool
body: Write the functions of lesson 6.05's report tool. The input is CSV with a header date,product,quantity,unit_price : python @dataclass(frozen=True) class Sale: day: date product: str quantity: int cents: int unit price in cents def read_sales(lines): ... - (sales, errors) def in_range(sales, start, end): ... sales with start <= day <= end (either bound may be None) def by_month(sales): ... {"2026-01": (orders, revenue_cents), ...} in month order def top_products(sales, n): ... (product, revenue_cents), ... highest first, ties by name def money(cents): ... 1234567 - "12 345.67" (thin groups of three with spaces) def format_report(sales, errors, n): ... the report text (below) read_sales takes an iterable of lines (a list of strings or an open file) and uses the csv module. For each data row (numbered from 1), the first problem found is reported as "row N: <message " and the row skipped: bad date <text (not ISO YYYY-MM-DD ), missing product , bad quantity <text (not a whole number greater than 0), bad price <text (not a number with at most two decimals and at least 0). A price like 4.5 is 450 cents. Spaces around fields are ignored. A row with the wrong number of fields is wrong number of fields . If the header is not exactly date,product,quantity,unit_price (ignoring spaces and case), return ( , "bad header" ) . Revenue is quantity × cents . format_report produces: Sales: 4 rows, 2 rejected Month Orders Revenue 2026-01 2 34.00 2026-02 2 1 210.50 Top products 1. Mug 1 200.00 2. Green tea 34.00 Errors row 3: bad quantity two row 5: missing product - The month table's rows are built as f"{month:<7}{orders: 10}{money(rev): 14}" , under the header f"{'Month':<7}{'Orders': 10}{'Revenue': 14}" . - Top products: the first n , as f" {i}. {product:<12}{money(rev): 12}" . - The Errors section only appears if there are errors. Every line ends with \n .

title: Cheat Sheet - Python
body: Basics python name = input("Name? ") always a str age = int(input("Age? ")) convert print(f"{name} is {age}", end="\n") f-string print(f"{3.14159:.2f} {1234567:,} {'x': 5} {7:03}") Operators --- --- / // % Division (float), floor division, remainder, power == != < in is None Comparisons and or not Logic (short-circuit) a if cond else b Conditional expression Strings Code Gives --- --- s 0 , s -1 , s 1:4 , s ::-1 Index, last, slice, reversed s.lower() , .upper() , .title() , .strip() Case, trimmed s.split(",") , ", ".join(items) Split, join s.replace(a, b) , s.find(x) , s.count(x) Replace, position (-1), count s.startswith(x) , s.isdigit() , x in s Tests Collections python xs = 3, 1, 2 ; xs.append(4); xs.sort(); last = xs.pop() t = (1, "a"); a, b = t; first, rest = xs d = {"a": 1}; d "b" = 2; d.get("z", 0); for k, v in d.items(): ... s = {1, 2}; s.add(3); s & {2, 3}; s {9}; s - {1} Need Use --- --- Ordered, changeable list Fixed record tuple , namedtuple , @dataclass Lookup by key dict ( Counter , defaultdict ) Unique values set Queue / last N collections.deque Loops python for i, x in enumerate(xs, start=1): ... for a, b in zip(xs, ys): ... for n in range(10, 0, -2): ... while True: if done: break squares = x x for x in xs if x 0 lookup = {k: len(k) for k in words} Functions python def f(a, b=2, args, key=None, kwargs) - int: """Docstring.""" return a + b lambda x: x 2 sorted(items, key=lambda r: (-r.score, r.name)) Never use a mutable default ( = ): use None and create inside. Classes python from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Item: name: str tags: list str = field(default_factory=list) class Account: def __init__(self, owner): self._balance = 0 @property def balance(self): return self._balance def __repr__(self): return f"Account({self._balance})" Errors python try: n = int(text) except ValueError as e: print("bad:", e) else: ... finally: ... raise ValueError("message") class MyError(Exception): pass Files python from pathlib import Path with open("f.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f: for line in f: ... Path("out.txt").write_text("hi\n", encoding="utf-8") for p in Path(".").glob(" .csv"): ... Data formats python import csv, json rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("a.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8"))) data = json.loads(text); text = json.dumps(data, indent=2) import re re.findall(r"\d+", s); re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", s); re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s) from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta date.fromisoformat("2026-11-15") + timedelta(days=7) Scripts python import argparse, sys def main(argv=None): p = argparse.ArgumentParser() p.add_argument("path"); p.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5) args = p.parse_args(argv) return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())

re-indent the block 1.05 SyntaxError: invalid syntax at if x = 5: = used for comparison == 1.05 SyntaxError: '(' was never closed A missing bracket, often on the line before the error Check brackets and quotes on the previous lines 1.01 TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str Adding text and a number str(n) , or an f-string 1.02 TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str' input() used as a number int(input()) 1.03 The input 5 doubled prints 55 Multiplying the text from input Convert with int() first 1.03 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False Floats are approximate math.isclose , or whole cents 1.04 if x == 1 or 2: is always true or 2 is on its own and truthy if x in (1, 2): 1.05 IndexError: list index out of range Index past the end (remember the last is len - 1 ) Check the length; use for item in xs 2.02 Changing one list changes another Two names for the same list, or 0 3 2 copy() , or a comprehension for nested lists 2.02 KeyError: 'name' Missing dictionary key d.get(key, default) , or in first 2.05 A function's default list keeps old items Mutable default argument None default, new list inside 3.02 UnboundLocalError Assigning to a name that is also read in the function before the assignment Pass it in and return it; global / nonlocal only if really needed 3.03 NameError: name 'x' is not defined Typo, or used before it was assigned or imported Check spelling and order 3.01 A function prints None No return (or printing instead of returning) return the value 3.01 ModuleNotFoundError Package not installed in this environment, or a typo pip install ... in the active virtual environment 3.04 Your module behaves strangely on import Your file is named like a standard module ( random.py ) Rename the file 3.04 FileNotFoundError Wrong path, or relative to a different working folder Path(__file__).parent / name , check exists() 3.05 UnicodeDecodeError reading a file Wrong or default encoding encoding="utf-8" (or the file's real encoding) 3.05 AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ... A function returned None (for example xs.sort() ) sorted(xs) , or check for None 2.02, 4.05 TypeError: __init__() missing 1 required positional argument Creating an object without all arguments, or forgetting self Pass the arguments; def method(self, ...) 4.01 TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' A list used as a dict key or set item Use a tuple 2.04 A generator gives nothing the second time Generators can be iterated once Convert to a list, or create it again 5.02 itertools.groupby splits groups Data not sorted by the group key Sort by the same key first 5.04 json.decoder.JSONDecodeError Invalid JSON (trailing comma, single quotes) Fix the data; the message gives line and column 6.02 CSV fields split wrongly Splitting lines by hand Use the csv module 6.02 A regular expression matches too much Greedy . . ? , or a narrower character class 6.01

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Abstract base class A class that only describes methods subclasses must provide; it cannot be instantiated. (4.03) Argument A value passed to a function when it is called. (3.01) Attribute A value stored on an object, reached with a dot: account.owner . (4.01) Bytecode The compact form the interpreter turns source code into before running it. (1.01) Class A description of a kind of object: its data and its methods. (4.01) Closure A function together with variables from an enclosing function that it still uses. (3.03) Comprehension An expression that builds a list, dict or set from an iterable: x x for x in xs . (5.01) CSV Comma-separated values: a text format for tables. (6.02) Dataclass A class whose __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ are generated from annotated fields. (4.04) Decorator A @name line above a function or class that wraps or registers it: @property , @dataclass . (4.01) Dictionary A mapping from keys to values with fast lookup. (2.05) Docstring The string right after a def or class line, describing it. (3.01) Duck typing Using any object that has the needed methods, whatever its class. (4.03) Dunder method A special method such as __len__ that Python calls for built-in syntax. (4.02) Dynamic typing Values have types, names do not; a name can refer to values of any type. (1.02) Enum A fixed set of named values. (4.04) Exception An object raised when something goes wrong; it stops the program unless handled. (4.05) f-string A string with f before it, where {expressions} are inserted and formatted. (1.03) Falsy / truthy Counting as false (0, "", None, empty collections) or true in a condition. (1.02) Generator A function with yield that produces values one at a time, on demand. (5.02) Immutable Cannot be changed after creation: strings, tuples, numbers, frozen dataclasses. (2.01) Inheritance A class taking the attributes and methods of a base class. (4.03) Interpreter The program that reads and runs Python code directly. (1.01) Iterable / iterator Something you can loop over / the object that produces its items one at a time. (5.02) JSON A text format for nested data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false, null. (6.02) Key function A function passed as key= that decides how items are compared when sorting. (5.03) Keyword argument An argument passed by name: greet(name="Ada") . (3.02) Lambda A small anonymous function written as an expression. (3.03) List An ordered, changeable sequence. (2.02) Method A function defined in a class and called on an instance. (4.01) Module A .py file whose names can be imported. (3.04) Mutable Can be changed in place: lists, dictionaries, sets, most objects. (2.02) Package A folder of modules. (3.04) Parameter A name in a function's definition that receives an argument. (3.01) PEP 8 Python's style guide: naming, spacing, layout. (1.02) pip The tool that installs packages from PyPI. (3.04) Property A method used like an attribute, for controlled reading (and writing). (4.01) Protocol A description of the methods an object needs, for type checkers. (5.05) Regular expression A pattern that describes text to search for or extract. (6.01) REPL The interactive prompt that runs one line at a time and shows results. (1.01) Scope Where a name is visible: local, enclosing, global, built-in (LEGB). (3.03) Set An unordered collection of unique values with fast membership tests. (2.05) Slice A part of a sequence: xs start:stop:step . (2.01) Traceback The report printed for an unhandled exception, read from the bottom. (4.05) Tuple A fixed, unchangeable sequence for values that belong together. (2.04) Type hint An annotation such as - int that tools use to check types. (5.05) Unpacking Assigning the items of a sequence to several names at once. (2.04) Virtual environment A folder with its own Python packages for one project. (3.04)

title: 1.01  What raylib Is and Setting It Up
match: 1.01 What raylib Is and Setting It Up
body: raylib is a small C library for making games - windows, drawing, input, sound and 3D in a few hundred plain functions. This lesson explains what it does and does not do, installs it with vcpkg, and runs a first window in Visual Studio. A library, not an engine raylib is a C library by Ramon Santamaria for learning and making games. It gives you functions; you write the game: raylib does You do --- --- Open a window, run at a frame rate Decide what happens each frame Draw shapes, textures, text, 3D models Keep the game's data: positions, scores, levels Read keyboard, mouse, gamepad and touch Turn input into movement and actions Load and play sounds and music Decide when to play them Basic collision tests and maths helpers Collision response, physics, AI, menus An engine such as Unity or Godot gives you an editor, a scene tree, physics and a component system, and you fit your game into them. With raylib nothing is hidden: every pixel on screen is there because your code drew it this frame. That is why it is a good way to learn how games actually work, and it is enough for complete, polished 2D and small 3D games. raylib is written in C99, so its API is plain functions and structs: Vector2 , Rectangle , Color , Texture2D . It works fine from C++, and the course uses C++ for everything around it. Installing with vcpkg The simplest way on Windows is vcpkg , Microsoft's C++ package manager: cpp-norun git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat C:\dev\vcpkg\vcpkg integrate install C:\dev\vcpkg\vcpkg install raylib:x64-windows integrate install makes every Visual Studio project find vcpkg's headers and libraries automatically. Then create a new Console App (C++) project, set the platform to x64 , and replace the code with: cpp-norun include "raylib.h" int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "My first raylib window"); SetTargetFPS(60); while (!WindowShouldClose()) // Esc or the close button { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); DrawText("Hello, raylib!", 280, 200, 32, DARKGRAY); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); } Press F5: a window opens with the text in it, and closes with Esc. If the build cannot find raylib.h , check that the platform is x64 (vcpkg installed the x64 version) and that integrate install was run. !note Other ways work too: the raylib Windows installer comes with its own compiler and editor, and CMake projects can fetch raylib with FetchContent . The code in this course is the same whichever you use. Hiding the console window A console app opens a black console next to the game, which is handy for printf debugging. For a release build, set Linker System SubSystem to Windows and Linker Advanced Entry Point to mainCRTStartup , so main still runs but no console appears. raylib's cheatsheet raylib's website has a one-page cheatsheet listing every function by module: rcore (window, input, timing), rshapes , rtextures , rtext , rmodels , raudio . Keep it open while you work; the function names are descriptive enough that it is often all you need. The examples page has more than a hundred small programs, each a single file, that show one feature each. How the practice works Compiler Explorer, which runs the practice on this site, has no window or GPU. So the practice checks the game logic you would put around raylib's calls: movement, collision, animation timing, cameras, tile maps, pathfinding. Each practice declares the few raylib types it needs, such as struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; , exactly as raylib does, so the code moves into a real raylib project unchanged.

title: The frame budget
where: 1.01 What raylib Is and Setting It Up
body: SetTargetFPS(60) gives each frame a budget of 1000 / 60 = 16.7 milliseconds for input, update and drawing. Write three small helpers a game's debug overlay uses: cpp double frameBudgetMs(int fps); // 1000 / fps; 0 when fps <= 0 (no limit) int framesFor(double seconds, int fps); // how many frames that many seconds takes, rounded to the nearest std::string fpsLabel(double frameTimeSeconds); // "60 FPS (16.7 ms)" fpsLabel shows the frames per second as 1 / frameTime rounded to the nearest whole number, and the frame time in milliseconds with one decimal place. A frame time of 0 or less gives "-- FPS" .

title: 1.02  The Game Loop
body: Every game is a loop that reads input, updates the world and draws it, many times a second. This lesson takes raylib's loop apart - what BeginDrawing and EndDrawing do, why the screen is cleared every frame, and how to keep update and drawing apart. Input, update, draw A film shows 24 still pictures a second; a game makes its pictures as it goes. Each picture is a frame , and each frame the game does three things: 1. Input : which keys are down, where the mouse is. 2. Update : move things, check collisions, change scores and timers. 3. Draw : show the world as it is now. At 60 frames per second that happens every 16.7 ms. The game's state lives in variables that survive from frame to frame; the loop changes them a little each time. cpp-norun include "raylib.h" int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "Moving square"); SetTargetFPS(60); float x = 100.0f; // state: survives between frames while (!WindowShouldClose()) { // Input and update if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT)) x += 4.0f; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_LEFT)) x -= 4.0f; // Draw BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); DrawRectangle(static_cast<int (x), 200, 50, 50, MAROON); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); } What the raylib calls do Call Does --- --- InitWindow(w, h, title) Opens the window and creates the OpenGL context: call it before anything that loads or draws SetTargetFPS(60) Makes EndDrawing wait so frames come no faster than 60 a second WindowShouldClose() True once Esc or the close button was pressed BeginDrawing() Starts the frame's drawing ClearBackground(c) Fills the whole frame with one colour EndDrawing() Shows the finished frame (swaps buffers), waits for the target frame rate, and polls input for the next frame CloseWindow() Closes the window and frees the context Note the last point about EndDrawing : raylib reads the keyboard and mouse there, so IsKeyPressed reports what happened since the previous frame. Why clear every frame? The game draws into a back buffer while the screen shows the front buffer; EndDrawing swaps them. The back buffer still holds an old frame, so without ClearBackground the new frame is drawn over old pictures and moving things leave trails. Clear first, then draw everything that should be visible, back to front: later drawing covers earlier drawing. Keep update and draw apart It is tempting to move things inside the drawing code. Keep them apart instead: cpp-norun struct Game { float x{ 100 }; int score{ 0 }; }; void update(Game& g) { if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT)) g.x += 4.0f; } void draw(const Game& g) { DrawRectangle(static_cast<int (g.x), 200, 50, 50, MAROON); } while (!WindowShouldClose()) { update(game); BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); draw(game); EndDrawing(); } draw takes the game by const& : it can look but not change. This split pays off again and again: you can pause by skipping update , run the update twice as fast for testing, or test update without a window at all, which is exactly what the practice on this site does.

title: Update apart from draw
body: Split a tiny game into an update that changes the state and a draw that only describes what to show: cpp struct Input { bool left; bool right; bool pausePressed; }; struct Game { float x{ 100 }; bool paused{ false }; int frames{ 0 }; }; void update(Game& g, const Input& in); std::vector<std::string draw(const Game& g); update - pausePressed toggles paused , always. - While paused, nothing else changes. - Otherwise: right adds 4 to x , left subtracts 4 (both: no movement); x stays within 0..750 ; frames goes up by one. draw returns the draw calls in order, as text: 1. "clear RAYWHITE" 2. "rect <x 200 50 50" with x as a whole number (truncated, like static_cast<int ) 3. "text frames <frames " 4. and only while paused, last: "text PAUSED"

title: 1.03  Coordinates, Shapes and Colours
body: Where things go on the screen and how to draw them - raylib's coordinate system with y pointing down, Vector2 and Rectangle, the shape functions, colours with alpha, and centring things on the screen. Screen coordinates The top-left corner of the window is (0, 0) . x grows to the right and y grows downwards , in pixels. In an 800 × 450 window the bottom-right pixel is (799, 449) . (0,0) ──────────── x ──────────▶ (800,0) │ y (400,225) is the centre │ ▼ (0,450) Y pointing down surprises people used to maths graphs: "up" on screen means subtracting from y, and gravity adds to y. The basic types cpp-norun typedef struct Vector2 { float x; float y; } Vector2; typedef struct Rectangle { float x; float y; float width; float height; } Rectangle; // x, y = top-left corner typedef struct Color { unsigned char r, g, b, a; } Color; C++ can build them with braces: Vector2 p{ 100, 50 } , Rectangle r{ 10, 10, 64, 32 } , Color sky{ 135, 206, 235, 255 } . raylib has named colours ( RED , DARKBLUE , RAYWHITE , BLANK for fully transparent) and helpers such as Fade(RED, 0.5f) for half-transparent red. Shapes Function Draws --- --- DrawPixel(x, y, c) One pixel DrawLine(x1, y1, x2, y2, c) / DrawLineEx(a, b, thick, c) A line DrawRectangle(x, y, w, h, c) / DrawRectangleRec(rect, c) A filled rectangle from its top-left corner DrawRectangleLinesEx(rect, thick, c) A rectangle's outline DrawRectangleRounded(rect, roundness, segments, c) Rounded corners DrawCircle(cx, cy, r, c) / DrawCircleV(centre, r, c) A filled circle from its centre DrawTriangle(a, b, c, colour) A triangle (points counter-clockwise) DrawPoly(centre, sides, radius, rotation, c) A regular polygon Rectangles are placed by their top-left corner, circles by their centre. Mixing the two up is the most common reason a shape is "half a size off". Centring To centre a rectangle of size w × h in the window: cpp-norun const float x = (GetScreenWidth() - w) / 2.0f; const float y = (GetScreenHeight() - h) / 2.0f; Text works the same way with MeasureText(text, fontSize) , which returns the width in pixels: cpp-norun const char title = "GAME OVER"; const int width = MeasureText(title, 48); DrawText(title, (GetScreenWidth() - width) / 2, 180, 48, RED); Colours and alpha a is the alpha (opacity): 255 is solid, 0 is invisible. Drawing a half-transparent black rectangle over the whole screen is the classic "paused" dim. To mix two colours, interpolate each channel: r = a.r + (b.r - a.r) t , which raylib's ColorLerp does (raylib 5.5). Drawing order Shapes drawn later appear on top. A frame is usually drawn in layers: background, world, effects, then the interface on top of everything.

title: Placing things on screen
body: Write the helpers for putting shapes where you mean them: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Color { unsigned char r, g, b, a; }; Rectangle centred(int screenW, int screenH, float w, float h); // a w x h rectangle in the middle of the screen Rectangle circleBounds(Vector2 centre, float radius); // the square around a circle Vector2 rectCentre(Rectangle r); Color colorLerp(Color a, Color b, float t); // each channel a + (b - a) t, rounded; t clamped to 0..1

title: 1.04  Frame Time and Smooth Movement
body: Moving "4 pixels a frame" runs twice as fast on a 120 Hz screen. This lesson moves things in units per second using the frame time, adds velocity and acceleration, normalises diagonal movement, and keeps big frame-time spikes from breaking the game. Pixels per frame is a trap In lesson 1.02 the square moved 4 pixels a frame. With SetTargetFPS(60) that is 240 pixels a second, but on a slow computer at 30 frames a second it is 120, and with the frame rate unlocked on a fast one it could be 1000. The game's speed depends on the computer. The fix is to measure time. GetFrameTime() returns the seconds the last frame took (about 0.0167 at 60 FPS), often called dt (delta time). Movement becomes units per second × dt : cpp-norun const float speed = 240.0f; // pixels per second const float dt = GetFrameTime(); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT)) x += speed dt; Now the square moves 240 pixels a second at any frame rate: smaller steps when frames are short, bigger when they are long. Velocity and acceleration Real movement has velocity (how fast, in pixels per second) and acceleration (how fast the velocity changes): cpp-norun struct Body { Vector2 pos; Vector2 vel; }; void step(Body& b, Vector2 accel, float dt) { b.vel.x += accel.x dt; b.vel.y += accel.y dt; b.pos.x += b.vel.x dt; b.pos.y += b.vel.y dt; } This is semi-implicit Euler integration: change the velocity first, then move with the new velocity. It is simple and stable enough for almost every game. A car that speeds up while you hold a key, a ship that drifts, and a falling ball all come from these two lines. Friction or drag slows things down. A simple version multiplies the velocity by a factor each second: vel = pow(0.1f, dt) keeps 10 % of the speed per second regardless of the frame rate. Multiplying by a fixed 0.9f every frame would again depend on the frame rate. Diagonals are too fast Holding right and down adds speed on both axes: the length of (1, 1) is 1.41, so diagonal movement is 41 % faster. Normalise the input direction to length 1 before scaling it: cpp-norun Vector2 dir{ 0, 0 }; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_D)) dir.x += 1; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_A)) dir.x -= 1; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_S)) dir.y += 1; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_W)) dir.y -= 1; const float len = std::sqrt(dir.x dir.x + dir.y dir.y); if (len 0) { dir.x /= len; dir.y /= len; } pos.x += dir.x speed dt; pos.y += dir.y speed dt; raylib's raymath.h has Vector2Normalize , Vector2Scale , Vector2Add and many more for exactly this. Spikes When you drag the window or the program pauses in the debugger, the next frame time can be a whole second. Objects then jump through walls. Clamp dt to a sensible maximum, such as 1/20 s: the game slows down briefly instead of breaking. cpp-norun const float dt = std::min(GetFrameTime(), 0.05f); Milestone 3 goes further with fixed time steps , which make physics behave the same at every frame rate. Timers Many game rules are timers: a power-up lasting 5 seconds, a shot every 0.25 s. Keep a float that counts down by dt: cpp-norun cooldown -= dt; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_SPACE) && cooldown <= 0) { shoot(); cooldown += 0.25f; } if (cooldown < 0) cooldown = 0; Adding the period back ( += 0.25f ) instead of setting it keeps the average rate exact even when frames do not divide the period evenly.

title: Moving by the second
body: Write the movement pieces of lesson 1.04: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; Vector2 inputDirection(bool up, bool down, bool left, bool right); // length 1, or (0, 0) float clampDt(float dt); // at most 0.05, never below 0 void step(Vector2& pos, Vector2& vel, Vector2 accel, float drag, float dt); class Shooter { public: explicit Shooter(float period); int update(bool fireHeld, float dt); // how many shots this frame }; - inputDirection : up is negative y, right is positive x; opposite keys cancel. - step : semi-implicit Euler with drag: first vel += accel dt , then vel = pow(drag, dt) (drag is the fraction of speed kept per second), then pos += vel dt . - Shooter : holding fire shoots once immediately, then once every period seconds. The cooldown counts down by dt every frame; while fire is held and the cooldown is at or below zero, a shot is fired and period is added to the cooldown (several shots in one long frame are possible). When fire is not held, the cooldown stops at zero instead of going negative.

title: 1.05  Keyboard, Mouse and Gamepad Input
body: Reading every kind of input raylib supports - keys held and pressed, typed characters, the mouse and its wheel, and gamepads with their sticks and dead zones - and mapping them to game actions so players can rebind them. Down, pressed, released Function True when --- --- IsKeyDown(KEY_SPACE) The key is held this frame IsKeyPressed(KEY_SPACE) The key went down since the last frame (once per press) IsKeyReleased(KEY_SPACE) The key went up since the last frame IsKeyUp(KEY_SPACE) The key is not held IsKeyPressedRepeat(KEY_LEFT) The key's auto-repeat fired, as in a text box Use Down for continuous actions (moving, accelerating) and Pressed for one-off actions (jumping, shooting once, opening a menu). Using IsKeyDown for a menu choice moves the selection every frame the key is held, which is 60 items a second. Keys are named KEY_A ... KEY_Z , KEY_ZERO ... KEY_NINE , KEY_LEFT , KEY_ENTER , KEY_LEFT_SHIFT and so on, by their position on a US keyboard. For typed text (names, chat) use GetCharPressed() , which returns Unicode characters one by one in a loop, respecting the keyboard layout and Shift: cpp-norun for (int c = GetCharPressed(); c != 0; c = GetCharPressed()) if (c = 32 && c < 127 && name.size() < 12) name += static_cast<char (c); if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_BACKSPACE) && !name.empty()) name.pop_back(); The mouse Function Gives --- --- GetMousePosition() A Vector2 in window pixels GetMouseDelta() How far it moved since the last frame IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) Click, once (also Down, Released) GetMouseWheelMove() Wheel movement this frame, positive away from you SetMouseCursor(MOUSE_CURSOR_POINTING_HAND) Changes the cursor shape DisableCursor() / EnableCursor() Hides and locks the cursor, for 3D cameras A button is a rectangle plus a click test: CheckCollisionPointRec(GetMousePosition(), rect) && IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) . Gamepads raylib numbers gamepads from 0 and uses positional button names so code works for Xbox and PlayStation pads alike: cpp-norun if (IsGamepadAvailable(0)) { const float lx = GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, GAMEPAD_AXIS_LEFT_X); // -1 .. 1 const float ly = GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, GAMEPAD_AXIS_LEFT_Y); if (IsGamepadButtonPressed(0, GAMEPAD_BUTTON_RIGHT_FACE_DOWN)) jump(); // A on Xbox, Cross on PlayStation } Dead zones A stick at rest rarely reads exactly 0; it drifts by a few hundredths, which would make the character creep. Apply a dead zone : treat small values as zero, and rescale the rest so movement still starts smoothly from zero. cpp-norun float deadZone(float v, float dz) { if (std::fabs(v) < dz) return 0.0f; return (v - std::copysign(dz, v)) / (1.0f - dz); // dz..1 becomes 0..1 } A better version uses the stick's length (a radial dead zone) so diagonal movement is not cut off differently from straight movement; the practice builds both pieces. Actions, not keys Game code should not ask "is W down?" but "is the player moving up?". Map actions to any number of inputs: cpp-norun enum class Action { Left, Right, Jump, Pause }; struct Binding { Action action; int key; int gamepadButton; }; bool actionPressed(Action a, const std::vector<Binding & bindings) { for (const auto& b : bindings) if (b.action == a && (IsKeyPressed(b.key) IsGamepadButtonPressed(0, b.gamepadButton))) return true; return false; } Now a settings screen can change the bindings, and the game code never changes.

title: Sticks and bindings
body: Two pieces of an input layer: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; Vector2 radialDeadZone(Vector2 stick, float dz); enum class Action { Left, Right, Jump, Pause }; class Bindings { public: void bind(Action a, int key); // a key belongs to at most one action void unbind(int key); bool down(Action a, const std::set<int & keysDown) const; std::vector<int keysFor(Action a) const; // in increasing order }; radialDeadZone : take the stick's length. Below dz , the result is (0, 0) . Otherwise keep the direction and rescale the length from dz..1 to 0..1 ; a length above 1 (sticks can report slightly more on diagonals) counts as 1. Bindings : an action can have any number of keys. Binding a key that already belongs to another action moves it to the new one, so one key never does two things. down is true if any of the action's keys is in keysDown .

title: Two-paddle tennis
body: Write the whole game logic of a two-player paddle-and-ball game. The raylib part is then a dozen lines: read the keys, call update , draw two rectangles, a circle and the score. cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Game { Rectangle left{ 30, 185, 10, 80 }, right{ 760, 185, 10, 80 }; Vector2 ball{ 400, 225 }, vel{ 300, 0 }; float radius{ 8 }; int leftScore{ 0 }, rightScore{ 0 }; int winner{ 0 }; // 0 while playing, 1 left won, 2 right won }; void update(Game& g, float leftDir, float rightDir, float dt); // dirs: -1 up, 0, 1 down float computerDir(const Rectangle& paddle, Vector2 ball); The field is 800 × 450. Each call of update , in this order: 1. If there is a winner, nothing happens. 2. Paddles move at 360 pixels per second in their direction and stay inside the field ( 0 <= y and y + height <= 450 ). 3. The ball moves by vel dt . 4. Walls : if the ball's top goes above 0, put it back at y = radius and make vel.y positive; likewise at the bottom ( y = 450 - radius , vel.y negative). 5. Paddles : the ball hits a paddle when the circle overlaps the paddle's rectangle (closest point test) and it is moving towards that paddle. On a hit: - the new speed is min(speed 1.05, 900) where speed is the length of vel ; - offset = (ball.y - paddle centre y) / (height / 2) , clamped to -1..1 ; - the angle is offset 60 degrees, and vel = (±speed·cos, speed·sin) with x pointing away from the paddle; - the ball is pushed out to touch the paddle's face: x = paddle.x + width + radius for the left one, paddle.x - radius for the right one. 6. Scoring : when the ball is completely past the left edge ( x + radius < 0 ) the right player scores, and past the right edge ( x - radius 800 ) the left player scores. The ball then goes back to (400, 225) with vel = (300, 0) towards the player who lost the point ( -300 if the left player lost). The first to 5 wins. computerDir steers a paddle towards the ball: 1 if the ball is more than 10 pixels below the paddle's centre, -1 if more than 10 above, else 0 .

title: 2.01  Textures and Sprites
body: Loading images onto the GPU as textures, drawing them whole or in part, scaling, rotating and tinting them with DrawTexturePro, the origin point, flipping, and loading and unloading assets at the right time. Images and textures raylib has two kinds of picture: Type Lives in Use --- --- --- Image Main memory (CPU) Loading, editing pixels, generating pictures Texture2D Video memory (GPU) Drawing, every frame Most of the time you load a file straight into a texture: cpp-norun Texture2D player = LoadTexture("assets/player.png"); // after InitWindow // ... game loop: DrawTexture(player, 100, 200, WHITE); UnloadTexture(player); // before CloseWindow LoadTexture needs the OpenGL context, so it must come after InitWindow , and UnloadTexture before CloseWindow . Loading inside the game loop every frame is a classic mistake: it re-reads the file and allocates video memory 60 times a second. Paths are relative to the working directory , which in Visual Studio is the project folder, not the folder of the .exe . Call ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()) at start-up and copy the assets next to the program, and the same paths work everywhere. Drawing Function Draws --- --- DrawTexture(tex, x, y, tint) The whole texture at its own size DrawTextureV(tex, pos, tint) The same with a Vector2 DrawTextureEx(tex, pos, rotation, scale, tint) Rotated (degrees) and scaled DrawTextureRec(tex, source, pos, tint) Part of the texture (the source rectangle) DrawTexturePro(tex, source, dest, origin, rotation, tint) Part of it, into any rectangle, rotated around origin The tint multiplies every pixel's colour: WHITE leaves it as it is, RED keeps only the red channel, and Fade(WHITE, 0.5f) makes it half transparent. Flashing a sprite white when it is hit or red when it is low on health is one tint away. DrawTexturePro This one function does everything, so it is worth understanding: cpp-norun const Rectangle source{ 0, 0, 32, 32 }; // which part of the texture, in texture pixels const Rectangle dest{ pos.x, pos.y, 64, 64 }; // where on screen, and how big const Vector2 origin{ 32, 32 }; // pivot, relative to dest's top-left DrawTexturePro(tex, source, dest, origin, angleDegrees, WHITE); - dest.x, dest.y is where the origin ends up on screen. With origin at the centre of dest , pos is the sprite's centre and rotation spins it around its middle. - A negative source width flips the picture horizontally; a negative height flips it vertically. That is how one "facing right" picture serves for both directions. Pixel art Small pixel-art sprites scaled up look blurry with the default bilinear filtering. Set point filtering for crisp pixels: cpp-norun SetTextureFilter(tex, TEXTURE_FILTER_POINT); and scale by whole numbers (2×, 3×, 4×) so every source pixel becomes the same number of screen pixels. Keeping assets together As soon as there are more than a few textures, keep them in one place that loads everything at start-up and unloads it at the end: cpp-norun struct Assets { Texture2D player, tiles, enemy; void load() { player = LoadTexture("assets/player.png"); / ... / } void unload() { UnloadTexture(player); / ... / } }; Lesson 6.02 adds a cache keyed by file name, so the same picture is never loaded twice.

title: Crisp pixels on any screen
body: A pixel-art game is drawn at a small native size, such as 320 × 180, and scaled up by a whole number so every pixel stays square. Write the helpers: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; int pixelScale(int screenW, int screenH, int nativeW, int nativeH); // the largest whole scale that fits, at least 1 Rectangle letterbox(int screenW, int screenH, int nativeW, int nativeH); // the scaled picture, centred, whole-pixel position Rectangle spriteSource(Rectangle frame, bool facingLeft); // negative width to flip Rectangle spriteDest(Vector2 centre, float w, float h, float scale); // a dest rectangle for an origin at the centre - letterbox : size is native × scale; x and y centre it, rounded down to whole pixels. - spriteDest : with DrawTexturePro 's origin at (w scale / 2, h scale / 2) , the dest rectangle's x and y are the centre itself, and its size is w scale by h scale .

title: 2.02  Sprite Sheets and Animation
body: Animation is a sequence of frames shown one after another. This lesson cuts frames out of a sprite sheet, plays them at their own speed using a timer, handles looping and one-shot animations, and switches between animations as a character's state changes. Sprite sheets A sprite sheet is one texture holding many frames in a grid. A 4-frame walk cycle of 32 × 32 frames is a 128 × 32 picture. Loading one texture instead of many is faster to draw and easier to manage. The source rectangle of frame i in a sheet with columns frames per row: cpp-norun Rectangle frameRect(int i, int columns, float w, float h) { return { (i % columns) w, (i / columns) h, w, h }; } Playing frames over time An animation shows each frame for a while, then moves to the next. Count time, not game frames, so the animation runs at the same speed at any frame rate (lesson 1.04): cpp-norun struct Animation { int first, count; // frames first .. first + count - 1 in the sheet float fps; // animation frames per second bool loop; }; struct Animator { const Animation anim{ nullptr }; float time{ 0 }; void play(const Animation& a) { if (anim != &a) { anim = &a; time = 0; } } void update(float dt) { time += dt; } int frame() const { int i = static_cast<int (time anim- fps); i = anim- loop ? i % anim- count : std::min(i, anim- count - 1); return anim- first + i; } bool finished() const { return !anim- loop && time anim- fps = anim- count; } }; Notice play only restarts when the animation changes : calling play(walk) every frame while walking must not restart the walk at frame 0 each frame, which would freeze it on the first picture. Looping and one-shot animations - Looping : idle, walk, run. The frame wraps around with % . - One-shot : attack, hurt, death. It stops on the last frame, and finished() tells the game to go back to idle (or to remove the enemy). Some animations need events at a particular frame: the sword's hit should only count on frame 3 of the attack, and a footstep sound should play on frames 1 and 3 of the walk. Check when the frame number changes to a given value, not while it is that value, or the sound plays every game frame. Choosing the animation from the state The character's state picks the animation: cpp-norun if (attacking) animator.play(attackAnim); else if (!onGround) animator.play(jumpAnim); else if (fabs(vel.x) 1) animator.play(walkAnim); else animator.play(idleAnim); animator.update(dt); Rectangle src = frameRect(animator.frame(), 8, 32, 32); if (facingLeft) src.width = -src.width; // lesson 2.01's flip DrawTexturePro(sheet, src, { pos.x, pos.y, 64, 64 }, { 32, 64 }, 0, WHITE); The order of the checks is a priority list: an attack overrides everything, jumping overrides walking. Lesson 4.04 turns this into a proper state machine . Frame timing that varies Hand-made animations often hold some frames longer than others: the wind-up of an attack is slow, the strike is fast. Store a duration per frame instead of one fps , and find the current frame by walking through the durations; the practice does this.

title: An animator with timed frames
body: Write an animator where every frame has its own duration, and that reports animation events: cpp struct Animation { std::vector<float durations; bool loop; }; // one duration (seconds) per frame class Animator { public: void play(const Animation a); // restarts only if a is a different animation std::vector<int update(float dt); // the frames entered during this update, in order int frame() const; // current frame index, 0-based bool finished() const; // one-shot animation past its last frame's end }; - After play , the current frame is 0, and frame 0 counts as entered by the next update (so an event on frame 0 fires once). - update(dt) adds dt to the time and returns every frame whose start time was passed during this update (including frame 0 right after play ). A looping animation wraps around, so a long dt can enter the same frames again: report each entry in order. - A one-shot animation stays on its last frame. finished becomes true when the time reaches the total of all durations; no more frames are entered after that. Example: durations { 0.1, 0.2, 0.1 } looping, so the frames start at 0, 0.1 and 0.3, and the loop comes back to frame 0 at 0.4. update(0.05) → {0} ; update(0.1) → {1} (time 0.15); update(0.2) → {2} (time 0.35); update(0.1) → {0} (time 0.45).

title: 2.03  Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
match: 2.03 Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
body: Drawing text with raylib's default font and with your own fonts, measuring and aligning it, formatting numbers with TextFormat, and building the interface a small game needs - a score display, health bar, buttons and a menu you can use with keys or the mouse. Drawing text cpp-norun DrawText("Score", 20, 20, 24, DARKGRAY); // default font, size in pixels DrawText(TextFormat("Score: %05d", score), 20, 50, 24, DARKGRAY); // printf-style formatting TextFormat works like printf and returns a const char to a buffer inside raylib. The buffer is reused (raylib keeps a few), so use the result straight away; do not store the pointer. Your own fonts The default font is small pixel art. For anything else, load a TrueType font at the size you will draw it: cpp-norun Font title = LoadFontEx("assets/Kenney Future.ttf", 64, nullptr, 0); // 64 px glyphs, default characters SetTextureFilter(title.texture, TEXTURE_FILTER_BILINEAR); DrawTextEx(title, "XENON QUEST", { 200, 80 }, 64, 2, WHITE); // size and letter spacing // ... UnloadFont(title); A font is a texture of glyphs (an atlas ) plus their positions. Drawing at a very different size from the loaded size looks blurry when bigger and grainy when smaller, so load each size you use a lot. For characters beyond basic Latin (accents, other alphabets), pass the list of code points you need. Measuring and aligning MeasureText(text, size) (default font) and MeasureTextEx(font, text, size, spacing) give the size of a text in pixels. With them you can align anything: Alignment x --- --- Left x Centre x - width / 2 Right x - width Score displays are usually right-aligned, so the digits do not shift left and right when the number gets longer. A health bar cpp-norun void healthBar(Rectangle r, float hp, float maxHp) { const float t = std::clamp(hp / maxHp, 0.0f, 1.0f); DrawRectangleRec(r, DARKGRAY); DrawRectangleRec({ r.x, r.y, r.width t, r.height }, t 0.3f ? LIME : RED); DrawRectangleLinesEx(r, 2, BLACK); } A nice touch is a second, slower bar behind it that catches up with the real value, so the player sees how much damage was just taken. Buttons and menus An interface for a small game needs only buttons: cpp-norun bool button(Rectangle r, const char label) { const bool hover = CheckCollisionPointRec(GetMousePosition(), r); DrawRectangleRec(r, hover ? SKYBLUE : LIGHTGRAY); const int w = MeasureText(label, 20); DrawText(label, static_cast<int (r.x + (r.width - w) / 2), static_cast<int (r.y + (r.height - 20) / 2), 20, BLACK); return hover && IsMouseButtonReleased(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT); } This is an immediate-mode button, like the Dear ImGui course's: it is drawn and checked in the same call. For a menu that works with keys and gamepads as well, keep a selected index , move it with up and down (wrapping around), and activate with Enter; hovering the mouse over an item also selects it. raylib also comes with raygui , a single-header immediate-mode GUI library in the same style, with sliders, checkboxes and text boxes, when a game needs more than buttons. Interface coordinates The interface is drawn after the world and outside any camera (lesson 4.01), in screen coordinates, so it stays put while the world scrolls. Anchor it to the screen's edges or centre rather than fixed positions so it still fits when the window is resized.

title: Menus and wrapped text
where: 2.03 Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
body: Two interface pieces: cpp std::vector<std::string wrapText(const std::string& text, int maxWidth, int charWidth); class Menu { public: void add(const std::string& label, bool enabled = true); void move(int delta); // -1 up, +1 down: next enabled item, wrapping around void hover(int index); // the mouse is over an item: select it if enabled int selected() const; // -1 if no item is enabled std::string line(int index) const; // " Label" when selected, " Label" otherwise, " (Label)" when disabled }; wrapText splits on spaces into lines no wider than maxWidth pixels, each character being charWidth wide (a fixed-width font). Words are kept whole and separated by one space; a word wider than a line on its own is put on its own line anyway. Several spaces in a row count as one, and an empty text gives no lines. Menu : the first enabled item added becomes selected. move skips disabled items and wraps from the last to the first and back; if no item is enabled it does nothing.

title: 2.04  Sound and Music
body: Playing sound effects and streaming music with raylib's audio module - the audio device, Sound versus Music, volume and pitch, playing the same sound many times at once, a little random variation, and volume settings in decibels and percentages. The audio device Audio has its own start and end, like the window: cpp-norun InitWindow(800, 450, "Sound"); InitAudioDevice(); // load sounds and music, run the game ... CloseAudioDevice(); CloseWindow(); Sound and Music Type Loaded Use --- --- --- Sound Completely into memory Short effects: jumps, hits, coins. Starts instantly Music Streamed from the file in small pieces Long tracks and ambience. Little memory cpp-norun Sound jump = LoadSound("assets/jump.wav"); Music theme = LoadMusicStream("assets/theme.ogg"); PlayMusicStream(theme); while (!WindowShouldClose()) { UpdateMusicStream(theme); // every frame, or the music stutters and stops if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_SPACE)) PlaySound(jump); // ... } UnloadSound(jump); UnloadMusicStream(theme); UpdateMusicStream refills the stream's buffer. Forget it and the music plays a fraction of a second and stops: the most common audio bug in raylib games. WAV and OGG are the usual formats; OGG is much smaller for music. Volume and pitch SetSoundVolume(s, 0.5f) , SetSoundPitch(s, 1.2f) and SetMusicVolume(m, v) change one sound; SetMasterVolume(v) changes everything. Pitch 2.0 is an octave up and plays twice as fast. Variation : hearing exactly the same footstep fifty times sounds mechanical. Vary the pitch a little each time: cpp-norun SetSoundPitch(step, 0.9f + GetRandomValue(0, 20) / 100.0f); // 0.9 .. 1.1 PlaySound(step); The same sound many times PlaySound on a Sound that is already playing restarts it. For rapid gunfire or many coins collected at once, that cuts each sound off. Make a few aliases that share the same sample data and play them in turn: cpp-norun Sound coin = LoadSound("assets/coin.wav"); Sound coinVoices 4 ; for (Sound& v : coinVoices) v = LoadSoundAlias(coin); int next = 0; // to play: PlaySound(coinVoices next ); next = (next + 1) % 4; // at the end: UnloadSoundAlias for each, then UnloadSound(coin) Volume settings players understand Loudness is heard roughly logarithmically: halving the amplitude ( 0.5 ) sounds only a little quieter, about -6 decibels. A volume slider that maps 0-100 % straight to amplitude feels like it does nothing for most of its range and then drops suddenly at the bottom. A better mapping is through decibels, for example 0 % = silent and 1-100 % spread over -40 dB to 0 dB: cpp-norun float sliderToAmplitude(int percent) { if (percent <= 0) return 0.0f; const float db = -40.0f (1.0f - percent / 100.0f); return std::pow(10.0f, db / 20.0f); } Keep separate music and effects volumes (and multiply each by a master volume) so players can turn the music down without losing the effects. Sound and gameplay Sound is feedback. Each important event deserves one: jumping, landing, hitting, being hit, collecting, a menu choice, a level complete. Playing them from the place in the code where the event happens, not from the drawing code, keeps them in time with the game even when frames are dropped.

title: Volumes and voices
body: The sound settings and a pool of voices: cpp float sliderToAmplitude(int percent); // 0 - 0; 1..100 - -40 dB .. 0 dB float effectiveVolume(int master, int channel); // both sliders, multiplied as amplitudes class VoicePool { public: explicit VoicePool(int voices); int play(float now, float length); // returns the voice used int playing(float now) const; // how many voices are still sounding at time now }; - sliderToAmplitude : percent is clamped to 0..100 . 0 is silence; otherwise db = -40 (1 - percent / 100) and the amplitude is 10^(db / 20) . - effectiveVolume is sliderToAmplitude(master) sliderToAmplitude(channel) . - VoicePool::play : a voice is free at time now if it never played or its sound ended ( start + length <= now ). Use the lowest-numbered free voice; if none is free, steal the one that started earliest (lowest number on a tie). The voice records now and length .

title: 2.05  Screens and Game States
body: A finished game has a title screen, the game itself, a pause menu, a game-over screen and transitions between them. This lesson organises a game into screens - first with an enum and a switch, then with screen objects on a stack - and fades smoothly from one to the next. One loop, many screens A whole game runs in the same loop, but what the loop does depends on which screen is showing: cpp-norun enum class Screen { Title, Playing, Paused, GameOver }; Screen screen = Screen::Title; while (!WindowShouldClose()) { switch (screen) { case Screen::Title: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_ENTER)) { resetGame(); screen = Screen::Playing; } break; case Screen::Playing: updateGame(); if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_P)) screen = Screen::Paused; if (lives == 0) screen = Screen::GameOver; break; case Screen::Paused: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_P)) screen = Screen::Playing; break; case Screen::GameOver: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_ENTER)) screen = Screen::Title; break; } BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(BLACK); switch (screen) { / draw each screen / } EndDrawing(); } This is a state machine : a set of states, one current state, and transitions triggered by events. For a small game an enum and two switches is perfectly fine. Screens as objects As screens grow, each switch case becomes a hundred lines. Give each screen its own class: cpp-norun class Scene { public: virtual ~Scene() = default; virtual void update(float dt) = 0; virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual bool coversBelow() const { return true; } // a pause menu does not }; A stack of screens The pause menu shows the game behind it, frozen. A stack of scenes handles that naturally: - push : put a scene on top (open the pause menu). - pop : remove the top (close it, back to the game). - replace : swap the top for another (title to game). Only the top scene is updated. Drawing starts from the highest scene that covers what is below it and goes up to the top, so the frozen game is drawn first and the menu over it. cpp-norun void drawStack(const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Scene & stack) { std::size_t first = stack.size() - 1; while (first 0 && !stack first - coversBelow()) --first; for (std::size_t i = first; i < stack.size(); ++i) stack i - draw(); } Changing the stack while a scene's update is running (the pause scene pops itself) would destroy the object whose function is running. Instead, scenes request changes, and the stack applies them after the update has finished; the practice builds exactly this. Transitions Cutting straight from one screen to the next is abrupt. A fade is simple: draw a black rectangle over everything with an alpha that rises from 0 to 255, switch the screen when it is fully black, and let it fall back to 0: cpp-norun // fade goes 0 - 1 over 0.3 s, then the screen changes, then 1 - 0 over 0.3 s DrawRectangle(0, 0, GetScreenWidth(), GetScreenHeight(), Fade(BLACK, fade)); While a transition runs, ignore input, or a quick player can press Enter twice and skip two screens. Resetting the game "Play again" must reset everything : score, lives, level, timers, positions, enemies, particles. Keep all of a play-through's state in one struct and reset it by assigning a fresh one: game = Game{}; . Leftover state from the previous round is a very common bug.

title: A stack of scenes
body: Write the scene stack from lesson 2.05. Scenes are described by a name and whether they cover what is below them; requests made during an update are applied afterwards: cpp struct Scene { std::string name; bool coversBelow; }; class SceneStack { public: void push(Scene s); // requests: queued, applied by apply() void pop(); void replace(Scene s); // pop the top and push s (on an empty stack: just push) void clear(); // remove every scene void apply(); // carry out the queued requests in order, then forget them std::string top() const; // "" if empty std::vector<std::string drawOrder() const; // bottom to top, starting at the highest covering scene std::size_t size() const; }; - pop on an empty stack does nothing. - drawOrder starts at the highest scene with coversBelow == true (or the bottom scene if none covers) and lists up to the top.

title: Brick breaker
body: Write the logic of a brick-breaking game: a grid of bricks with hit points, a paddle, a ball that starts on the paddle, lives and score. With it, lesson 2.03's interface, lesson 2.04's sounds and lesson 2.05's screens make a complete game. cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Brick { Rectangle r; int hp; }; struct Game { std::vector<Brick bricks; Rectangle paddle{ 350, 420, 100, 12 }; Vector2 ball{ 400, 414 }, vel{ 0, 0 }; float radius{ 6 }; bool stuck{ true }; // the ball sits on the paddle until launched int lives{ 3 }, score{ 0 }; bool gameOver{ false }; }; Game makeGame(const std::vector<std::string & rows); void launch(Game& g); void update(Game& g, float paddleDir, float dt); // paddleDir: -1 left, 0, 1 right int bricksLeft(const Game& g); makeGame : each character of each row is a brick slot: . is empty, 1 to 9 is a brick with that many hit points. Bricks are 60 × 20 with no gaps; the slot in row r , column c is at x = 40 + 60c , y = 40 + 20r . Only real bricks are stored, in row order then column order. launch : if the ball is stuck, it leaves the paddle with velocity (0, -360) . update , in this order: 1. Nothing happens once the game is over. 2. The paddle moves at 480 px/s and stays inside the 800-pixel-wide field. 3. A stuck ball sits on the paddle, centred: (paddle.x + width/2, paddle.y - radius) . Nothing else happens. 4. The ball moves; it bounces off the left, right and top walls (put it back at radius from the wall and make the velocity point away from it). 5. Paddle : if the ball moves down and overlaps the paddle (circle against rectangle), it is aimed like lesson 1's paddles but upwards: offset = (ball.x - paddle centre x) / (width/2) clamped to -1..1 , angle = offset 60° , vel = (speed·sin, -speed·cos) keeping the speed, and ball.y = paddle.y - radius . 6. Bricks : the first brick (in stored order) with hit points left that overlaps the ball is hit, and only that one. It loses a hit point: destroyed bricks score 10, others 1. The ball bounces off the side of the brick with the smaller overlap: with ox and oy the overlaps of the ball's bounding square and the brick on each axis, if ox < oy it bounces horizontally ( vel.x points away from the brick's centre and the ball moves ox away), otherwise vertically (the same with y and oy ). 7. Lost ball : when ball.y - radius 450 , a life is lost. With lives left, the ball is stuck on the paddle again (placed as in step 3); at zero lives the game is over. bricksLeft counts bricks with hit points left.

title: 3.01  Detecting Collisions
body: The collision tests 2D games are built on - point in rectangle, rectangle against rectangle, circle against circle and circle against rectangle - how each one works, raylib's functions for them, and choosing the right shape for each object. Shapes stand in for sprites Testing every pixel of two sprites against each other is slow and rarely what you want. Games give each object a simple collision shape , usually a little smaller than its picture so near misses feel fair: Shape Good for --- --- Axis-aligned rectangle ( AABB ) Characters, tiles, platforms, pickups Circle Balls, bullets, round enemies, anything that rotates Point The mouse, a bullet's tip "Axis-aligned" means the rectangle is not rotated: its sides are parallel to x and y. That makes every test a few comparisons. Point in rectangle cpp-norun bool pointInRect(Vector2 p, Rectangle r) { return p.x = r.x && p.x < r.x + r.width && p.y = r.y && p.y < r.y + r.height; } raylib: CheckCollisionPointRec(p, r) . There is also CheckCollisionPointCircle and CheckCollisionPointTriangle . Rectangle against rectangle Two rectangles overlap unless one is completely to the left, right, above or below the other: cpp-norun bool rectsOverlap(Rectangle a, Rectangle b) { return a.x < b.x + b.width && b.x < a.x + a.width && a.y < b.y + b.height && b.y < a.y + a.height; } raylib: CheckCollisionRecs(a, b) , and GetCollisionRec(a, b) returns the overlapping rectangle itself, whose width and height lesson 3.02 uses to push objects apart. Use < rather than <= so that rectangles that only touch (one's right edge exactly at the other's left edge) do not count as overlapping. A character standing exactly on top of a floor tile should not be "inside" it. Circle against circle Two circles overlap when the distance between their centres is less than the sum of the radii. Compare squared distances to avoid the square root: cpp-norun bool circlesOverlap(Vector2 a, float ra, Vector2 b, float rb) { const float dx = b.x - a.x, dy = b.y - a.y, r = ra + rb; return dx dx + dy dy < r r; } raylib: CheckCollisionCircles(a, ra, b, rb) . Circle against rectangle Find the point of the rectangle closest to the circle's centre by clamping the centre to the rectangle on each axis; the shapes overlap when that point is inside the circle: cpp-norun bool circleRect(Vector2 c, float r, Rectangle rect) { const float nx = std::clamp(c.x, rect.x, rect.x + rect.width); const float ny = std::clamp(c.y, rect.y, rect.y + rect.height); const float dx = c.x - nx, dy = c.y - ny; return dx dx + dy dy < r r; } If the centre is inside the rectangle, the closest point is the centre itself and the distance is 0. raylib: CheckCollisionCircleRec(c, r, rect) . The two projects so far used this test. Lines and rays CheckCollisionLines(a1, a2, b1, b2, &point) tests two line segments and gives the crossing point: useful for lasers, line of sight, and fast bullets (lesson 3.02). The maths behind it is a pair of cross products, which the practice writes. Who collides with whom Not everything needs to test against everything. Write down the pairs that matter: player with enemies, player with pickups, player's bullets with enemies, enemies' bullets with the player, everything with walls. Many games give each object a layer and a mask (bit flags) and test a pair only if one's mask contains the other's layer.

title: The four collision tests
body: Write the collision tests of lesson 3.01, and the segment test for lasers and fast bullets: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; bool pointInRect(Vector2 p, Rectangle r); bool rectsOverlap(Rectangle a, Rectangle b); // touching edges do not count bool circlesOverlap(Vector2 a, float ra, Vector2 b, float rb); // touching does not count bool circleRect(Vector2 c, float r, Rectangle rect); // touching does not count bool segmentsCross(Vector2 a1, Vector2 a2, Vector2 b1, Vector2 b2, Vector2 where); - pointInRect : the left and top edges are inside, the right and bottom edges are not. - segmentsCross : true if the segments a1-a2 and b1-b2 cross at a single point (parallel segments never count); then where is that point (when where is not null). With d = (a2 - a1) × (b2 - b1) (the 2D cross product x1 y2 - y1 x2 ), the crossing is at a1 + t (a2 - a1) where t = ((b1 - a1) × (b2 - b1)) / d and u = ((b1 - a1) × (a2 - a1)) / d , and both t and u must be in 0..1 .

title: 3.02  Resolving Collisions
body: Knowing two things overlap is half the job; the other half is deciding what happens. This lesson pushes objects apart along the shortest way out, moves one axis at a time so characters slide along walls, and stops fast objects from tunnelling through thin walls. Detection and response When the player walks into a wall, the overlap test says "yes". The response decides what happens: stop, slide along it, bounce, take damage. For solid things the response is to separate the objects so they no longer overlap. The shortest way out For two overlapping rectangles, the overlap is itself a rectangle ( GetCollisionRec ). Push the moving object out along the axis where the overlap is smaller : that is the shortest way out, called the minimum translation vector . cpp-norun void pushOut(Rectangle& mover, Rectangle wall) { const Rectangle o = GetCollisionRec(mover, wall); if (o.width == 0 o.height == 0) return; if (o.width < o.height) mover.x += (mover.x < wall.x) ? -o.width : o.width; // out left or right else mover.y += (mover.y < wall.y) ? -o.height : o.height; // out up or down } The brick breaker of milestone 2 used this idea for the ball. It has one weakness: at a corner, when the overlap is nearly square, it can pick the wrong axis, and a character walking along a floor made of tiles can "catch" on the seam between two tiles. One axis at a time The fix used by almost every 2D platformer is to move and resolve each axis separately : cpp-norun // 1. Move horizontally, then resolve horizontally only. player.x += vel.x dt; for (const Rectangle& wall : walls) if (CheckCollisionRecs(player, wall)) { if (vel.x 0) player.x = wall.x - player.width; // hit a wall on the right else if (vel.x < 0) player.x = wall.x + wall.width; vel.x = 0; } // 2. Then vertically. player.y += vel.y dt; onGround = false; for (const Rectangle& wall : walls) if (CheckCollisionRecs(player, wall)) { if (vel.y 0) { player.y = wall.y - player.height; onGround = true; } // landed else if (vel.y < 0) player.y = wall.y + wall.height; // bumped the head vel.y = 0; } Because each step only moved along one axis, the direction of that movement says exactly which side was hit. The player slides along walls naturally: blocked on x, still free on y. And "landed on something" falls out for free as onGround . Tunnelling A bullet moving 1200 pixels a second moves 20 pixels a frame at 60 FPS. A wall 8 pixels thick can be completely between two frames' positions, so the overlap test never sees it: the bullet tunnels through. Fixes, from simplest: 1. Clamp the frame time (lesson 1.04) and keep walls at least as thick as anything moves in a frame. 2. Sub-steps : split a big movement into several small ones, each no longer than the smallest object. 3. Sweep : test the path, not just the end point. For a small bullet, test the segment from the old position to the new one against each wall ( CheckCollisionLines against its edges), and take the nearest hit. For a moving box, the swept AABB test computes the time t between 0 and 1 at which it first touches the other box. Bouncing and sliding With the normal of the surface (the direction it faces, such as (0, -1) for a floor), other responses are one line each: Response Velocity --- --- Stop v = 0 Slide Remove the part along the normal: v -= dot(v, n) n Bounce Reflect: v -= 2 dot(v, n) n , times a bounciness below 1

title: Move and slide
body: Write the axis-separated movement of lesson 3.02, and the bounce and slide responses: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Hits { bool left{ false }, right{ false }, ceiling{ false }, ground{ false }; }; Hits moveAndSlide(Rectangle& box, Vector2& vel, float dt, const std::vector<Rectangle & walls); Vector2 slide(Vector2 v, Vector2 normal); // v - dot(v, n) n Vector2 bounce(Vector2 v, Vector2 normal, float bounciness); // (v - 2 dot(v, n) n), then the part along n times bounciness moveAndSlide 1. Move box.x by vel.x dt . For every wall the box now overlaps (touching does not count): moving right, put the box's right side at the wall's left side ( right = true ); moving left, its left side at the wall's right side ( left = true ). Then vel.x = 0 . With several walls, the box ends at the nearest stop. 2. The same for y: moving down sets ground , moving up sets ceiling , then vel.y = 0 . bounce : reflect, then scale only the component along the normal by bounciness , keeping the sliding component as it is. The normal has length 1.

title: 3.03  Gravity, Jumping and Game Feel
body: Jumping that feels good is designed, not simulated. This lesson derives gravity and jump speed from the height and time you want, then adds the tricks platformers rely on - variable jump height, faster falling, coyote time, jump buffering and acceleration on the ground and in the air. Gravity is acceleration Gravity adds to the vertical velocity every frame (y points down, so it is positive): cpp-norun vel.y += gravity dt; vel.y = std::min(vel.y, maxFallSpeed); // terminal velocity: falls stay readable A jump sets the vertical velocity upwards once: vel.y = -jumpSpeed . Design the jump, then compute the numbers Guessing gravity = 1500, jumpSpeed = 600 and tweaking forever is the slow way. Decide what you want instead: how high (in pixels) and how long the rise takes (in seconds). Physics gives the rest: gravity = 2 height / time² jumpSpeed = 2 height / time A jump of 96 pixels (three 32-pixel tiles) rising in 0.4 s needs gravity = 1200 px/s² and jumpSpeed = 480 px/s. Change the height and the jump still takes 0.4 s; change the time and it still reaches 96 pixels. Level designers can then rely on "the player can jump three tiles". Variable jump height Players expect a tap to make a small hop and holding the button to jump high. When the button is released while still rising, cut the upward speed: cpp-norun if (IsKeyReleased(KEY_SPACE) && vel.y < 0) vel.y = 0.5f; Falling faster Real jumps are symmetrical, but they feel floaty. Most platformers use stronger gravity on the way down (1.5 to 2 times), which makes jumps feel snappy and landings decisive: cpp-norun const float g = vel.y 0 ? gravity 1.8f : gravity; Coyote time When a player runs off a ledge and presses jump a moment too late, a strict game says "you are in the air, no jump". It feels unfair, because the player saw themselves on the ledge. Coyote time allows a jump for a short time (about 0.1 s) after leaving the ground: cpp-norun if (onGround) coyote = 0.1f; else coyote -= dt; Jump buffering The opposite case: the player presses jump a moment before landing. Remember the press for a short time and jump as soon as it becomes possible: cpp-norun if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_SPACE)) buffer = 0.1f; else buffer -= dt; if (buffer 0 && coyote 0) { vel.y = -jumpSpeed; buffer = 0; coyote = 0; } Both timers must be cleared when the jump happens, or one press makes two jumps. Running Instant full speed feels stiff; slow acceleration feels like ice. Move the horizontal velocity towards the target speed by a maximum change per second, with different rates for speeding up, slowing down and turning, and less control in the air: cpp-norun float approach(float v, float target, float maxDelta) { if (v < target) return std::min(v + maxDelta, target); return std::max(v - maxDelta, target); } const float target = inputX runSpeed; const float rate = onGround ? (inputX != 0 ? accel : decel) : airAccel; vel.x = approach(vel.x, target, rate dt); Feel is the sum of small things None of these is realistic, and all of them are in nearly every good platformer. Add the small extras too: a puff of dust on landing, a squash of the sprite, a short sound. Lesson 4.03 builds the particles.

title: A jump that feels right
body: Write the pieces of lesson 3.03: cpp float gravityFor(float height, float riseTime); // 2h / t² float jumpSpeedFor(float height, float riseTime); // 2h / t float approach(float v, float target, float maxDelta); struct Jumper { float coyote{ 0 }, buffer{ 0 }; }; bool wantsJump(Jumper& j, bool onGround, bool pressed, float dt, float window); float cutJump(float velY, bool released); - approach moves v towards target by at most maxDelta (which is never negative) and never past it. - wantsJump , called once per frame, in this order: 1. coyote becomes window when on the ground, otherwise it goes down by dt ; 2. buffer becomes window when jump was pressed this frame, otherwise it goes down by dt ; 3. if both are above zero, both are set to zero and the function returns true (jump now). - cutJump halves the vertical speed when the button was released while still rising ( velY < 0 ); otherwise returns it unchanged.

title: 3.04  Fixed Time Steps
body: Physics that depends on the frame time behaves slightly differently at every frame rate. A fixed time step runs the simulation in equal steps whatever the frame rate - this lesson builds the accumulator loop, guards against the spiral of death, and interpolates between steps for smooth drawing. Variable steps are not quite the same Multiplying by dt (lesson 1.04) makes speeds right on average, but the results still differ with the frame rate. A jump simulated in steps of 1/30 s reaches a slightly different height from the same jump in steps of 1/144 s, and collision against thin objects depends on how far things move per step. For a puzzle or platformer where a jump must clear exactly three tiles, or for replays and networked games where every computer must compute the same thing, that is not good enough. The accumulator Run the simulation in fixed steps, such as 1/60 s, however long the frame took. Keep the left-over time for the next frame: cpp-norun const float step = 1.0f / 60.0f; float accumulator = 0.0f; while (!WindowShouldClose()) { accumulator += GetFrameTime(); while (accumulator = step) { updatePhysics(step); // always the same dt accumulator -= step; } draw(); } At 144 FPS most frames run zero steps or one; at 30 FPS each frame runs two. The simulation itself always sees exactly 60 steps a second. The spiral of death If one step takes longer to compute than step of real time, each frame adds more time to the accumulator than the steps remove, frames get slower, and the game freezes completely. Limit the number of steps per frame (or clamp the frame time), accepting that the game slows down instead: cpp-norun accumulator += std::min(GetFrameTime(), 0.25f); int steps = 0; while (accumulator = step && steps < 5) { updatePhysics(step); accumulator -= step; ++steps; } Smooth drawing with interpolation With a 60 Hz simulation on a 144 Hz screen, some frames show the same physics state twice and the motion looks slightly jerky. After the loop, accumulator / step is how far (0 to 1) the real time is between the last step and the next one. Keep the previous state and draw between the two: cpp-norun const float alpha = accumulator / step; const Vector2 drawPos = { prev.x + (curr.x - prev.x) alpha, prev.y + (curr.y - prev.y) alpha }; This draws up to one step behind the newest state, which is not noticeable, and every frame shows a slightly different position. Input with fixed steps Read input once per frame, but let the steps use it. One-off presses need care: if a frame runs zero steps, a jump press in that frame must not be lost; if it runs two , it must not jump twice. Store the press in a flag that the first step consumes. Which approach to use Approach Use when --- --- Variable dt , clamped Simple games where small differences do not matter Fixed step Platformers, physics puzzles, anything with replays or networking Fixed step + interpolation The same, on high-refresh screens

title: The fixed-step loop
body: Write the accumulator of lesson 3.04 as a class, with the spiral-of-death guard and a one-off press that steps consume: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; class FixedStep { public: FixedStep(float step, int maxSteps); int advance(float frameTime); // how many steps to run this frame float alpha() const; // accumulator / step after advance void press(); // a one-off input this frame bool takePress(); // true once per press, for the first step that asks }; Vector2 lerp(Vector2 a, Vector2 b, float t); - advance clamps the frame time to at most 0.25 s, adds it to the accumulator, and counts steps while the accumulator holds at least one step, subtracting a step each time. When maxSteps is reached, the accumulator is set to 0 (the game slows down rather than freezing). - press sets a flag; takePress returns it and clears it. A press in a frame with no steps is still there for the next frame's first step.

title: 3.05  Spatial Grids for Many Objects
body: Testing every object against every other is n squared - fine for 50 objects, hopeless for 5000. A uniform grid puts each object in the cells it touches and only tests objects that share a cell. This lesson builds one, rebuilds it every frame, and avoids testing pairs twice. Every pair is too many With n objects there are n(n-1)/2 pairs. For 100 objects that is 4950 tests a frame: no problem. For 5000 bullets and enemies it is 12.5 million, many times the frame budget. Most of those pairs are on opposite sides of the screen and could never touch. The idea of broad phase collision is to cheaply find the pairs that might touch, and only run the real test (the narrow phase ) on them. A uniform grid Divide the world into square cells , a bit bigger than a typical object. Each cell keeps a list of the objects that overlap it: cpp-norun struct Grid { float cellSize; int cols, rows; std::vector<std::vector<int cells; // object indices per cell int cellX(float x) const { return std::clamp(static_cast<int (std::floor(x / cellSize)), 0, cols - 1); } int cellY(float y) const { return std::clamp(static_cast<int (std::floor(y / cellSize)), 0, rows - 1); } void insert(int id, Rectangle r) { for (int cy = cellY(r.y); cy <= cellY(r.y + r.height); ++cy) for (int cx = cellX(r.x); cx <= cellX(r.x + r.width); ++cx) cells cy cols + cx .push_back(id); } }; An object overlapping a cell boundary is put in every cell it touches, so neighbours across a boundary still meet in some cell. Using it Each frame: 1. Clear the cells (keep the vectors' memory; just clear() each). 2. Insert every object. 3. For each cell, test each pair of objects in that cell . Two objects that share several cells would be tested several times, once in each. Avoid duplicates by testing a pair only when a < b and recording tested pairs in a set, or, faster, only in the cell that contains the top-left corner of their overlap. For a query ("which enemies are within the explosion?"), look only in the cells the query area covers, and collect each object once. Choosing the cell size - Too small: big objects are in many cells, and inserting costs more than it saves. - Too large: many objects per cell, back towards n squared. - A cell about twice the size of a typical object is a good start. Measure with a profiler and adjust.
