Other structures Structure Good when --- --- Uniform grid Objects of similar size spread over a bounded world: most 2D games Spatial hash The same, but the world is unbounded: cells are keys in a hash map Quadtree Sizes vary a lot, or objects cluster in a few places Sort and sweep Objects mostly spread along one axis, as in side-scrollers Static and moving things Walls and tiles never move, so do not put them in the per-frame grid: a tile map is already a grid (lesson 4.02), and you can look up the tiles under an object directly from its position. Only moving objects need inserting every frame.

title: A uniform grid
body: Write the broad phase of lesson 3.05: cpp struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; class SpatialGrid { public: SpatialGrid(float cellSize, int cols, int rows); void clear(); void insert(int id, Rectangle r); std::vector<int query(Rectangle area) const; // ids of objects overlapping area, sorted, each once std::vector<std::pair<int, int overlappingPairs() const; // (a, b) with a < b, sorted, each once int testsMade() const; // narrow-phase tests in the last overlappingPairs }; - An object goes into every cell its rectangle touches. Cell coordinates are floor(x / cellSize) , clamped to the grid; the far edge uses the rectangle's right and bottom ( x + width , y + height ). - query looks only in the cells the area covers, and returns objects whose rectangles really overlap the area (touching does not count). - overlappingPairs tests each pair of objects that share a cell, once only, and keeps those whose rectangles really overlap. testsMade counts how many distinct pairs were tested.

title: Platformer physics
body: Write the complete movement of a platformer character on a tile map: running with acceleration, a designed jump with variable height, coyote time and buffering, stronger gravity when falling, and axis-separated collision against solid tiles. This is the heart of every platformer; drawing it in raylib is a sprite at box.x, box.y . cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Level { std::vector<std::string rows; }; // ' ' solid, anything else empty; tiles are 32 x 32 struct Input { float x{ 0 }; bool jumpPressed{ false }, jumpReleased{ false }; }; struct Player { Rectangle box{ 0, 0, 24, 30 }; Vector2 vel{ 0, 0 }; bool onGround{ false }; float coyote{ 0 }, buffer{ 0 }; }; bool solidAt(const Level& level, int tx, int ty); void step(Player& p, const Level& level, const Input& in, float dt); solidAt : inside the map, ' ' is solid. Outside the map, left, right and above are solid (walls the player cannot leave through); below the map is empty, so the player can fall out. step , in this order (the numbers come from lesson 3.03: a 96-pixel jump rising in 0.4 s): 1. Run : move vel.x towards in.x 200 (lesson 3.03's approach ) by rate dt , where rate is 1600 on the ground with input, 2000 on the ground without input, and 900 in the air. 2. Jump : coyote becomes 0.1 on the ground, else goes down by dt ; buffer becomes 0.1 when jump was pressed, else goes down by dt . If both are above zero: vel.y = -480 , both timers become 0, and onGround becomes false. 3. Variable height : if jump was released and vel.y < 0 , halve vel.y . 4. Gravity : add 1200 dt , or 2160 dt while falling ( vel.y 0 ), then limit vel.y to at most 600. 5. Move x and resolve against the solid tiles the box overlaps (touching does not count), stopping at the nearest one as in practice 3.02; vel.x = 0 when blocked. 6. Move y and resolve the same way. onGround is true exactly when this step landed on something. The tiles a box overlaps run from floor(x / 32) to ceil((x + width) / 32) - 1 , and likewise for y.

title: 4.01  Cameras and Scrolling Worlds
body: A world bigger than the screen needs a camera. This lesson uses raylib's Camera2D - target, offset, zoom and rotation - converts between screen and world coordinates, and makes the camera follow the player smoothly with a dead zone, look-ahead, limits at the level's edges and screen shake. World and screen coordinates So far everything was drawn in screen coordinates. A level 5000 pixels wide does not fit, so objects get world coordinates, and a camera decides which part of the world is on screen. cpp-norun Camera2D camera{}; camera.target = player.pos; // the world point the camera looks at camera.offset = { GetScreenWidth() / 2.0f, GetScreenHeight() / 2.0f }; // where that point appears on screen camera.rotation = 0.0f; camera.zoom = 1.0f; BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(SKYBLUE); BeginMode2D(camera); drawWorld(); // in world coordinates EndMode2D(); drawInterface(); // in screen coordinates, on top EndDrawing(); Everything between BeginMode2D and EndMode2D is transformed: a world point p appears on screen at (p - target) zoom + offset (plus rotation). Putting offset at the screen's centre keeps the target in the middle. Converting The mouse is in screen coordinates; to click on the world, convert: cpp-norun const Vector2 mouseWorld = GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), camera); const Vector2 labelPos = GetWorldToScreen2D(enemy.pos, camera); // e.g. a name above an enemy in the interface Following the player camera.target = player.pos works, but the camera jerks with every small movement. Better cameras: - Smoothing : move the target part of the way towards the player each frame. Like friction in lesson 1.04, make it independent of the frame rate: target += (player - target) (1 - pow(0.001f, dt)) . - Dead zone : the camera does not move while the player stays inside a box around the screen's centre; it moves only enough to keep the player in the box. Small movements no longer shake the view. - Look-ahead : aim a little ahead of the player in the direction they are moving or facing, so they see more of what is coming. - Platformer vertical rule : many platformers only move the camera vertically when the player lands, so jumps do not bounce the view. Staying inside the level The camera should not show the void beyond the level's edges. After moving it, clamp the target so the visible area stays inside the level: cpp-norun const float halfW = GetScreenWidth() / 2.0f / camera.zoom; const float halfH = GetScreenHeight() / 2.0f / camera.zoom; camera.target.x = std::clamp(camera.target.x, halfW, levelWidth - halfW); camera.target.y = std::clamp(camera.target.y, halfH, levelHeight - halfH); If the level is smaller than the screen, centre it instead (the clamp range would be empty). Zoom Zooming around the mouse, as in the ImGui course's level editor, keeps the point under the mouse fixed: convert the mouse to world coordinates, change the zoom, and set offset to the mouse and target to that world point. Screen shake A short shake on a hit or explosion makes it feel powerful. Keep a trauma value between 0 and 1 that events add to and that decays over time; offset the camera by a random amount proportional to trauma² : cpp-norun trauma = std::max(0.0f, trauma - dt 1.5f); const float shake = trauma trauma; camera.offset = { centre.x + shake 12 randomMinus1To1(), centre.y + shake 12 randomMinus1To1() }; Squaring makes small trauma barely visible and large trauma strong. Always provide an option to turn shake off: some players get motion sickness. Parallax Background layers that move slower than the world make a cheap illusion of depth: draw a far layer with a camera whose target is target 0.2 , a nearer one with 0.5 , then the world at 1 .

title: A camera that follows well
body: Write the camera helpers of lesson 4.01 (no rotation): cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Camera2D { Vector2 offset, target; float rotation, zoom; }; Vector2 worldToScreen(Vector2 p, const Camera2D& c); // (p - target) zoom + offset Vector2 screenToWorld(Vector2 p, const Camera2D& c); Vector2 deadZone(Vector2 target, Vector2 player, float halfW, float halfH); Vector2 smoothTowards(Vector2 from, Vector2 to, float keepPerSecond, float dt); Vector2 clampToLevel(Vector2 target, float screenW, float screenH, float zoom, float levelW, float levelH); - deadZone : the player may be up to halfW and halfH away from the target on each axis; if further, the target moves just enough to bring the player back to the edge of that box. - smoothTowards : the remaining distance shrinks to keepPerSecond of itself each second: from + (to - from) (1 - keepPerSecond^dt) . - clampToLevel : the visible area is screenW / zoom by screenH / zoom around the target. Keep it inside 0..levelW and 0..levelH . On an axis where the level is smaller than the visible area, centre on the level instead.

title: 4.02  Tile Maps and Levels
body: Most 2D levels are grids of tiles. This lesson stores a tile map, draws only the visible part from a tile sheet, loads levels from text files, places objects such as the player's start and enemies from the same file, and picks wall tiles automatically from their neighbours. A grid of numbers A tile map is a 2D grid where each cell holds a tile number: 0 for empty, 1 for grass, 2 for stone and so on. A 200 × 30 level is only 6000 small numbers, and collision is a direct lookup (the platformer of milestone 3 used exactly this). cpp-norun struct TileMap { int width, height, tileSize; std::vector<int tiles; // row by row int at(int x, int y) const { return (x < 0 y < 0 x = width y = height) ? 0 : tiles y width + x ; } }; A flat std::vector indexed with y width + x is faster and simpler than a vector of vectors. Drawing from a tile sheet Tile pictures come from one texture, a tile sheet , like a sprite sheet. Tile n is the n -th cell (lesson 2.02's frameRect ). Draw only the tiles the camera can see, as the ImGui level editor did: cpp-norun const Vector2 tl = GetScreenToWorld2D({ 0, 0 }, camera); const Vector2 br = GetScreenToWorld2D({ (float)GetScreenWidth(), (float)GetScreenHeight() }, camera); const int x0 = std::max(0, (int)std::floor(tl.x / map.tileSize)), x1 = std::min(map.width - 1, (int)std::floor(br.x / map.tileSize)); const int y0 = std::max(0, (int)std::floor(tl.y / map.tileSize)), y1 = std::min(map.height - 1, (int)std::floor(br.y / map.tileSize)); for (int y = y0; y <= y1; ++y) for (int x = x0; x <= x1; ++x) if (const int t = map.at(x, y); t != 0) DrawTextureRec(sheet, frameRect(t, sheetColumns, 16, 16), { (float)x 16, (float)y 16 }, WHITE); At high zoom, thin lines can appear between tiles because of rounding. Draw at whole-pixel positions, use point filtering, and give the tile sheet a 1-pixel border around each tile ( extrusion ) if it still happens. Levels from text files A text file is the easiest level format to make and to change: level 1 size 40 12 legend stone, = grass, ~ water, P player, E enemy, C coin ....................................... ..............C.C.C.................... ...P...........====.........E.......... ==========.......................====== ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Load it line by line: header lines first, then the grid. Letters for objects (P, E, C) are not tiles: when loading, record their positions in lists (player start, enemy spawns, coins) and put an empty tile in the map. One file then describes both the terrain and what is in it. For bigger projects, the free Tiled editor saves maps as JSON or XML with layers and object lists; the loader is longer but the idea is the same. Several layers Real levels have layers: a background layer drawn behind the player, the solid layer for collision, a decoration layer in front. Each is its own grid of the same size. Only the solid layer is used for collision. Auto-tiling Choosing the right edge and corner pieces for every wall by hand is tedious. Auto-tiling chooses them: for each solid cell, look at its four neighbours and build a 4-bit number, one bit per side: bit 0: solid above bit 1: solid right bit 2: solid below bit 3: solid left The number (0 to 15) picks one of 16 tile pictures: 0 is a lone block, 15 is a solid interior, 5 (above and below) is a vertical column piece, and so on. Paint just "solid" in the level file and the loader draws proper edges. Using all eight neighbours (for inner corners) gives 47 or 256 variations with the same idea.

title: Loading a level file
body: Load lesson 4.02's text level format and auto-tile it: cpp struct Point { int x, y; }; struct LevelData { int width{ 0 }, height{ 0 }; std::vector<std::string grid; // only ' ', '=' and '.' are left in it Point player{ -1, -1 }; std::vector<Point enemies, coins; }; bool loadLevel(const std::string& text, LevelData& out, std::string& error); int wallMask(const LevelData& level, int x, int y); // 4-bit auto-tile number, -1 for a non-wall The format , one item per line ( \r\n endings allowed): - Lines starting with followed by a space, and empty lines, are comments, but only before the grid. - size W H (both 1 to 500) must come before the grid. Other header lines (such as legend ... ) are ignored. - Then exactly H lines of exactly W characters. and = are walls, . is empty, P is the player start (exactly one), E an enemy and C a coin; those letters become . in the grid. Any other character is an error. Errors return false with one of these messages: "missing size" , "bad size" , "wrong row count" , "row N has the wrong length" (N counting from 1), "unknown tile 'X' in row N" , "no player start" , "more than one player start" . wallMask : for a wall cell, bit 0 is set if the cell above is a wall, bit 1 right, bit 2 below, bit 3 left. Cells outside the map are not walls.

title: 4.03  Particles and Effects
body: Dust, sparks, smoke and explosions are particles - many small, short-lived objects. This lesson builds a particle system with a fixed pool, emitters with randomised properties, values that change over a particle's life, and additive blending, plus the small effects that make a game feel alive. What a particle is A particle is a tiny object with a position, a velocity, a lifetime and a look. Hundreds of them, each living a second or less, make dust when landing, sparks when hitting, smoke from a chimney or an explosion. cpp-norun struct Particle { Vector2 pos, vel; float life, maxLife; // seconds left, and at birth float size; Color color; }; Each frame, every living particle moves (often with gravity or drag), its life goes down by dt , and it is drawn. When life reaches 0 it is dead. A pool, not new and delete Creating and destroying hundreds of objects per second with new , or push_back and erase on a vector, wastes time. Use a fixed pool : - A std::vector<Particle with a fixed capacity, such as 2000. - An integer count of living particles, all at the front. - Spawning writes into slot count and increments it (if the pool is full, either skip or overwrite the oldest). - Killing particle i copies the last living particle into slot i and decrements count ("swap and pop"); order does not matter for particles. No memory is allocated after start-up, and updating walks one tight array. Emitters An emitter creates particles with randomised properties: cpp-norun void burst(Pool& pool, Vector2 at, int n) { for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { const float angle = GetRandomValue(0, 359) DEG2RAD; const float speed = GetRandomValue(60, 180); pool.spawn({ at, { std::cos(angle) speed, std::sin(angle) speed }, 0.6f, 0.6f, 4.0f, ORANGE }); } } A burst emits many at once (explosion, landing dust). A continuous emitter emits a rate per second, carrying the fraction over to the next frame like the shooter in lesson 1.04, so 30 particles per second is exactly 30 at any frame rate. Changing over a lifetime Particles look much better when their properties change as they age. With t = 1 - life / maxLife going from 0 at birth to 1 at death: Property Typical change --- --- Size Grows (smoke) or shrinks (sparks): lerp(startSize, endSize, t) Colour Yellow to red to grey: interpolate between colour stops Alpha Fades out near the end: alpha = 1 - t , or 1 - t² to stay solid longer Speed Slows with drag Blending Draw fire, sparks, magic and lights with additive blending: colours add up, so overlapping particles glow brighter instead of covering each other: cpp-norun BeginBlendMode(BLEND_ADDITIVE); for (const Particle& p : pool.alive()) DrawCircleV(p.pos, p.size, p.color); EndBlendMode(); Smoke and dust use normal (alpha) blending, which darkens and covers. Small effects with a big impact - Hit flash : draw the sprite white for 0.05 s when hit (tint, lesson 2.01). - Hit stop : freeze the game for 2 or 3 frames on a heavy hit. - Squash and stretch : scale the sprite a little on jumping and landing. - Screen shake (lesson 4.01). - Floating numbers : damage values that rise and fade, which are particles with text. These are often called juice : none of them change the rules, all of them change how the game feels.

title: A particle pool
body: Write lesson 4.03's particle pool and a continuous emitter: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Particle { Vector2 pos, vel; float life, maxLife; }; class ParticlePool { public: explicit ParticlePool(int capacity); bool spawn(const Particle& p); // false when full void update(float dt, Vector2 gravity); // move, age, remove the dead int count() const; const Particle& at(int i) const; // 0 .. count() - 1 }; float fadeAlpha(const Particle& p); // 1 at birth, 0 at death: 1 - t² with t = 1 - life / maxLife class Emitter { public: explicit Emitter(float perSecond); int emit(float dt); // how many to spawn this frame }; - update , for each living particle: vel += gravity dt , pos += vel dt , life -= dt ; particles whose life is now <= 0 are removed with swap and pop (the last living particle moves into the removed one's slot, so check that slot again). - fadeAlpha is clamped to 0..1 . - Emitter::emit adds perSecond dt to a running total and returns the whole part of it, keeping the fraction for later frames.

title: 4.04  Enemies and State Machines
body: Enemies that patrol, notice the player, chase, attack and give up feel smart, but are a handful of states and the rules for moving between them. This lesson builds enemy behaviour as a finite state machine with enter and exit actions, timers, line of sight, and a little randomness. States Describe an enemy's behaviour as states , each with its own simple behaviour: State Does Leaves when --- --- --- Patrol Walks between two points Sees the player → Chase Chase Runs towards the player Close enough → Attack; lost sight for 3 s → Return Attack Plays the attack, damages on one frame Animation finished → Chase Return Walks back to the patrol route Arrived → Patrol; sees the player → Chase Hurt Knocked back, briefly helpless 0.3 s passed → Chase Each state is easy to write and test on its own, and the diagram is something a designer can read and change. In code cpp-norun enum class State { Patrol, Chase, Attack, Return, Hurt }; struct Enemy { State state{ State::Patrol }; float timer{ 0 }; Vector2 pos; / ... / }; void enter(Enemy& e, State s) { e.state = s; e.timer = 0; // time spent in the new state if (s == State::Attack) e.anim.play(attackAnim); // enter actions } void update(Enemy& e, const World& w, float dt) { e.timer += dt; switch (e.state) { case State::Patrol: walkTowards(e, e.patrolPoints e.nextPoint , dt); if (canSee(e, w.player)) enter(e, State::Chase); break; case State::Chase: walkTowards(e, w.player.pos, dt); if (distance(e.pos, w.player.pos) < 24) enter(e, State::Attack); else if (canSee(e, w.player)) e.lastSeen = e.timer; else if (e.timer - e.lastSeen 3) enter(e, State::Return); break; // ... } } Going through enter for every change is what makes this robust: there is exactly one place where a state starts, so its timer is always reset and its animation always started. Changes from outside (the player hits the enemy) also go through enter(e, State::Hurt) . Seeing the player "Sees the player" is usually three tests, cheapest first: 1. Distance : within the sight range? 2. Angle : within the field of view in front of the enemy? With the facing direction f and the direction to the player d (both normalised), dot(f, d) cos(halfAngle) . 3. Line of sight : no wall in between? Walk along the line through the tile map, or test the segment against walls (practice 3.01). Making it feel alive - Reaction time : wait 0.3 s after spotting the player before chasing, and show a "!" above the enemy. It is fairer and more readable. - Telegraphing : an attack has a wind-up the player can see and react to. - Variety : give each enemy slightly different speeds and timers, randomised at spawn, so a group does not move in lockstep. Beyond state machines When state machines grow to dozens of states, games move to hierarchical state machines (states inside states), behaviour trees or utility AI (score every possible action and pick the best). For most small games, a state machine like this one is all you need.

title: An enemy brain
body: Write the state machine of lesson 4.04 and the field-of-view test: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; bool inView(Vector2 pos, Vector2 facing, Vector2 target, float range, float halfAngleDegrees); enum class State { Patrol, Alert, Chase, Attack, Return, Hurt }; struct Senses { bool seesPlayer; float distance; bool attackFinished; bool atPatrolRoute; bool wasHit; }; struct Brain { State state{ State::Patrol }; float timer{ 0 }; float unseen{ 0 }; }; void think(Brain& b, const Senses& s, float dt); std::string name(State s); // "Patrol", "Alert", ... inView : the target is within range (inclusive) and within halfAngleDegrees of the facing direction ( facing has length 1). A target exactly at pos is in view. think : first timer += dt . A hit ( wasHit ) always enters Hurt , from any state, even Hurt itself. Otherwise, by state: State Changes to --- --- Patrol Alert if it sees the player Alert Chase once timer = 0.3 (the reaction time) Chase Attack if distance < 24 ; otherwise counts unseen up by dt while not seeing the player (back to 0 when seeing them) and goes to Return when unseen = 3 Attack Chase when attackFinished Return Chase if it sees the player; Patrol when atPatrolRoute Hurt Chase once timer = 0.3 Entering a state sets timer and unseen to 0. At most one change happens per call.

title: 4.05  Pathfinding on a Grid
body: Walking straight at the player gets enemies stuck on walls. This lesson finds paths around obstacles on a tile map - breadth-first search for equal costs, A with a heuristic for speed, costs for different terrain, and flow fields when many enemies chase one target. The problem An enemy in a maze cannot just walk towards the player: the straight line goes through walls. It needs a path : a list of tiles from where it is to where it wants to be, around the obstacles. A tile map is already a graph : each walkable tile is a node, connected to its walkable neighbours (4 directions, or 8 with diagonals). Breadth-first search BFS explores tiles in order of distance from the start, like a ripple spreading in water: cpp-norun std::vector<int came(map.width map.height, -1); // where each tile was reached from std::queue<int frontier; frontier.push(start); came start = start; while (!frontier.empty()) { const int cur = frontier.front(); frontier.pop(); if (cur == goal) break; for (int next : neighbours(cur)) if (came next == -1 && walkable(next)) { came next = cur; frontier.push(next); } } // walk back from goal to start through came , then reverse When every step costs the same, the first time BFS reaches the goal it has found a shortest path. The came array records how each tile was reached; following it backwards from the goal gives the path. A BFS explores in all directions, even away from the goal. A\ explores the most promising tiles first. For each tile it knows: - g : the cost of the best path found so far from the start; - h : a heuristic , an estimate of the cost from the tile to the goal; - f = g + h : the estimated cost of a path through this tile. A always expands the tile with the smallest f next, using a priority queue ( std::priority_queue with a comparison on f ). With 4-direction movement, the Manhattan distance dx + dy is the standard heuristic. As long as the heuristic never overestimates the real cost, A still finds a shortest path, usually after exploring far fewer tiles than BFS. Terrain costs Swamp could cost 3 to cross and road 1. Then the cheapest path is not always the shortest, and BFS no longer works: use Dijkstra's algorithm (A with h = 0 ) or A with the costs added to g . The heuristic must use the cheapest possible cost per step so it still never overestimates. Following a path - Recompute the path only every half second or when the target moves to another tile, not every frame. - Move towards the next tile's centre; when close enough, move on to the one after. - Smooth it: skip waypoints when there is a clear line of sight to a later one, so enemies walk diagonally across open rooms instead of zig-zagging along grid lines. Many enemies, one target Fifty enemies chasing the player would run fifty searches. A flow field runs one: a BFS (or Dijkstra) from the player outwards over the whole map, storing each tile's distance. Each enemy then simply steps to its neighbour with the smallest distance. The cost no longer depends on the number of enemies, which is how tower defence and swarm games handle hundreds of units.

title: Paths and flow fields
body: Write lesson 4.05's breadth-first search and a flow field on a map of strings, where is a wall and anything else is walkable: cpp struct Cell { int x, y; }; std::vector<Cell findPath(const std::vector<std::string & map, Cell start, Cell goal); std::vector<std::vector<int flowField(const std::vector<std::string & map, Cell target); Cell nextStep(const std::vector<std::vector<int & field, Cell from); - Movement is in 4 directions, and neighbours are always tried in the order up, right, down, left . Cells outside the map are walls. - findPath returns the cells from start to goal , both included, of a shortest path; with the neighbour order above, BFS gives one particular path, and that is the one expected. It returns an empty vector if there is no path or either end is a wall; start == goal gives just that cell. - flowField gives every cell's number of steps to target (BFS from the target), -1 for walls and unreachable cells. - nextStep returns the neighbour (in the same order) with the smallest non-negative distance that is smaller than the distance at from ; if there is none, from itself.

title: A dungeon crawler
body: Write the rules of a small turn-based dungeon game: the player walks a tile map, collects coins and reaches the exit, while enemies chase them using a flow field (lesson 4.05) and fight when adjacent. Click-to-travel uses a weighted path through swamp. Drawing it in raylib is a tile map (lesson 4.02) and a few sprites. cpp struct Cell { int x, y; }; struct Enemy { Cell pos; int hp; }; class Dungeon { public: explicit Dungeon(const std::vector<std::string & rows); bool move(int dx, int dy); // the player's turn; false if no turn was taken bool wait(); // pass a turn; false once the game is over std::vector<Cell travelPath(Cell to) const; Cell player() const; int hp() const; int coins() const; int coinsLeft() const; const std::vector<Enemy & enemies() const; bool won() const; bool lost() const; }; The map : wall, . floor, ~ swamp (walkable), P the player's start, E an enemy (2 hit points), C a coin, X the exit; the letters stand on floor. The player has 3 hit points. A player turn ( move ): nothing happens and false is returned if the game is over or the target is a wall. If an enemy is on the target cell, the player attacks it (it loses 1 hit point and disappears at 0) and stays put; otherwise the player moves there and picks up a coin if there is one. If the player is now on the exit with no coins left, the game is won and the enemies do not act. wait is a turn that does nothing on the player's side. The enemies' turn , after every player turn, one enemy at a time in their original order: 1. If it is next to the player (4 directions), it attacks: the player loses 1 hit point. At 0 the game is lost and the remaining enemies do not act. 2. Otherwise, if its walking distance to the player (BFS through everything but walls) is at most 8, it steps to the neighbour with the smallest distance that is smaller than its own, trying up, right, down, left in that order and skipping cells with another enemy. Otherwise it stays. Compute the distances once per enemies' turn, from the player's cell, before any enemy moves. travelPath returns the cheapest path from the player to to , both included, where entering a floor cell costs 1 and entering swamp costs 3 (Dijkstra or A ). Enemies are ignored. A wall or unreachable target gives an empty path. Any cheapest path is accepted.

title: 5.01  A First 3D Scene
body: raylib draws 3D as easily as 2D. This lesson sets up a Camera3D, explains 3D coordinates and perspective, draws cubes, spheres, planes and a grid, loads and draws models, and introduces the vectors and matrices that move things in 3D. Three axes 3D adds a third axis. raylib uses a right-handed, y-up system: Axis Points --- --- x Right y Up (not down, as on the 2D screen) z Towards the viewer Positions are Vector3 { x, y, z } , in whatever unit you choose; most games use 1 unit = 1 metre , which makes gravity 9.81 and a person about 1.8 tall. The camera A 3D camera is defined by where it is, what it looks at and which way is up: cpp-norun Camera3D camera{}; camera.position = { 6.0f, 4.0f, 6.0f }; // where the eye is camera.target = { 0.0f, 0.5f, 0.0f }; // the point it looks at camera.up = { 0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f }; // which way is up camera.fovy = 45.0f; // vertical field of view, in degrees camera.projection = CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE; // or CAMERA_ORTHOGRAPHIC Perspective makes far things smaller, like a real eye; the field of view is how wide the view is (45-70° is typical). Orthographic keeps sizes constant regardless of distance, which suits strategy and isometric games; then fovy is the height of the view in world units. Drawing cpp-norun BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); BeginMode3D(camera); DrawPlane({ 0, 0, 0 }, { 20, 20 }, LIGHTGRAY); // a floor DrawCube({ 0, 0.5f, 0 }, 1, 1, 1, RED); // centre and size DrawCubeWires({ 0, 0.5f, 0 }, 1, 1, 1, MAROON); DrawSphere({ 2, 1, 0 }, 0.5f, BLUE); DrawCylinder({ -2, 0, 0 }, 0.3f, 0.3f, 1.5f, 16, GREEN); DrawGrid(20, 1.0f); // a helpful reference grid EndMode3D(); DrawFPS(10, 10); // 2D on top, as usual EndDrawing(); Note that 3D shapes are placed by their centre : a 1 × 1 × 1 cube standing on the floor has its centre at y = 0.5. Models Real objects come from 3D files. raylib loads glTF ( .glb / .gltf , the best choice), OBJ, IQM, VOX and M3D: cpp-norun Model tree = LoadModel("assets/tree.glb"); // meshes, materials and textures DrawModel(tree, { 3, 0, -2 }, 1.0f, WHITE); // position, uniform scale, tint DrawModelEx(tree, pos, { 0, 1, 0 }, angleDegrees, { 1, 1, 1 }, WHITE); // rotated around an axis UnloadModel(tree); glTF files can also contain animations : LoadModelAnimations and UpdateModelAnimation play them. Free models in this format are available from sites such as Kenney and Quaternius. Vectors in 3D raymath.h has everything for Vector3 : Vector3Add , Vector3Subtract , Vector3Scale , Vector3Length , Vector3Normalize , Vector3DotProduct and Vector3CrossProduct . - The dot product a · b = a b cos θ measures how much two directions agree: 1 for the same direction (when normalised), 0 for perpendicular, -1 for opposite. It answers "is the enemy in front of me?". - The cross product a × b is a vector perpendicular to both. From a "forward" direction and "up", forward × up gives "right", which is how cameras find their sideways direction. Matrices Objects are placed with a transform : scale, then rotate, then translate. raylib represents it as a 4 × 4 Matrix ( MatrixScale , MatrixRotateY , MatrixTranslate , combined with MatrixMultiply ). DrawModelEx builds it for you; you need matrices yourself for things like a sword attached to a hand, where the child's transform is multiplied by the parent's. Lighting The shapes above are drawn with flat colours, without light. Lighting needs a shader (lesson 5.04); raylib's examples include a basic lighting shader ( shaders_basic_lighting ) that most projects start from.

title: Vectors in three dimensions
body: Write the 3D vector helpers raymath gives you, to see how they work: cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; float dot(Vector3 a, Vector3 b); Vector3 cross(Vector3 a, Vector3 b); float length(Vector3 v); Vector3 normalize(Vector3 v); // (0, 0, 0) stays (0, 0, 0) float angleBetween(Vector3 a, Vector3 b); // in degrees, 0 if either is zero Vector3 rotateY(Vector3 v, float degrees); // x' = x cos + z sin, z' = -x sin + z cos Vector3 transformPoint(Vector3 p, float scale, float yawDegrees, Vector3 translate); // scale, then rotate, then move cross(a, b) = (a.y b.z - a.z b.y, a.z b.x - a.x b.z, a.x b.y - a.y b.x) . Clamp the cosine to -1..1 before acos , because rounding can push it slightly outside.

title: 5.02  Moving in 3D
body: Walking around a 3D world - raylib's built-in camera modes, then a first-person controller of your own with yaw and pitch from the mouse, movement relative to where you look, gravity and jumping, and a third-person camera that orbits the player. The built-in camera modes raylib can move a camera for you: cpp-norun DisableCursor(); // hide and lock the mouse while (!WindowShouldClose()) { UpdateCamera(&camera, CAMERA_FIRST_PERSON); // WASD + mouse // ... draw } Modes are CAMERA_FREE , CAMERA_ORBITAL , CAMERA_FIRST_PERSON and CAMERA_THIRD_PERSON . They are fine for trying things out, but a game needs its own controller: collision, gravity, rebindable keys and its own feel. UpdateCameraPro takes movement and rotation you computed yourself. Yaw and pitch A first-person view is described by two angles: - Yaw : turning left and right, around the y axis. The mouse's x movement changes it. - Pitch : looking up and down. The mouse's y movement changes it, clamped to about ±89° so the view never flips over the top. From the angles, the direction you look in: cpp-norun const Vector3 forward{ std::cos(pitch) std::sin(yaw), std::sin(pitch), std::cos(pitch) std::cos(yaw), }; camera.position = eye; camera.target = Vector3Add(eye, forward); Mouse look: yaw -= GetMouseDelta().x sensitivity; pitch -= GetMouseDelta().y sensitivity; . Sensitivity is a setting players expect, along with "invert Y". Moving where you look Walking uses the flat forward direction: the yaw only, so looking at the floor does not make you walk slower or dig into the ground: cpp-norun const Vector3 flatForward{ std::sin(yaw), 0, std::cos(yaw) }; const Vector3 right{ -std::cos(yaw), 0, std::sin(yaw) }; // forward x up, for this yaw Vector3 wish{ 0, 0, 0 }; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_W)) wish = Vector3Add(wish, flatForward); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_S)) wish = Vector3Subtract(wish, flatForward); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_D)) wish = Vector3Add(wish, right); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_A)) wish = Vector3Subtract(wish, right); if (Vector3Length(wish) 0) wish = Vector3Normalize(wish); // lesson 1.04's diagonal fix, in 3D Then the 2D ideas carry over unchanged: acceleration towards wish speed , gravity on y, jumping with coyote time and a buffer, and the eye at about 1.7 units above the feet. Collision with the world The simplest world is boxes (walls, crates, platforms) and the player is a box or a vertical capsule . Resolving one axis at a time (lesson 3.02) works in 3D exactly as in 2D, with three axes instead of two: move on x and push out, then z, then y (landing sets "on ground"). raylib's CheckCollisionBoxes(a, b) tests two BoundingBox es ( min and max corners). A third-person camera A third-person camera orbits the player at a distance, using the same yaw and pitch: cpp-norun const Vector3 offset{ distance std::cos(pitch) std::sin(yaw), distance std::sin(pitch), distance std::cos(pitch) std::cos(yaw), }; camera.target = Vector3Add(player.pos, { 0, 1.5f, 0 }); // look at the shoulders, not the feet camera.position = Vector3Subtract(camera.target, offset); // behind, along the view direction If a wall comes between the camera and the player, cast a ray from the target towards the camera (lesson 5.03) and move the camera in front of the wall, or the player sees the inside of the wall. Smooth the camera's movement (lesson 4.01's smoothTowards works per axis in 3D).

title: Looking and walking in 3D
body: Write the maths of lesson 5.02's controller. Angles are in degrees: cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; Vector3 lookDirection(float yaw, float pitch); // (cos p sin y, sin p, cos p cos y) float clampPitch(float pitch); // -89 .. 89 float wrapYaw(float yaw); // into 0 <= yaw < 360 Vector3 wishDirection(float yaw, bool forward, bool back, bool left, bool right); Vector3 orbitPosition(Vector3 target, float yaw, float pitch, float distance); - wishDirection uses the flat forward (sin y, 0, cos y) and right (-cos y, 0, sin y) ; forward and back add and subtract the forward direction, right and left the right direction; the sum is normalised (or (0, 0, 0) ). - orbitPosition is target - lookDirection(yaw, pitch) distance : behind the target along the view.

title: 5.03  Picking and 3D Collision
body: Clicking on things in 3D, shooting, line of sight and camera collision all ask one question - what does this ray hit first? This lesson turns the mouse into a ray, tests rays against planes, spheres and boxes, and adds sphere and box collision for moving objects. Rays A ray is a start point and a direction: Ray { Vector3 position; Vector3 direction; } . Points along it are position + direction t for t = 0 . Every "what is in this direction?" question is a ray test: Question Ray from Direction --- --- --- What did the player click? The camera Through the mouse position What does the gun hit? The muzzle or the eye The aim Can the enemy see the player? The enemy's eyes Towards the player (with the distance as a limit) Is the floor below me? The feet Straight down The mouse as a ray cpp-norun const Ray ray = GetScreenToWorldRay(GetMousePosition(), camera); // raylib 5 (older: GetMouseRay) const RayCollision hit = GetRayCollisionBox(ray, crateBox); if (hit.hit) { / hit.point, hit.normal, hit.distance / } raylib has GetRayCollisionSphere , GetRayCollisionBox , GetRayCollisionMesh (exact, per triangle, slower), GetRayCollisionTriangle and GetRayCollisionQuad . To pick among many objects, test them all and keep the hit with the smallest distance . Ray against a plane The ground plane y = h is hit where position.y + direction.y t = h : cpp-norun if (direction.y != 0) { t = (h - position.y) / direction.y; if (t = 0) hit = position + direction t; } That is how strategy games turn a click into a point on the ground to move units to. Ray against a sphere Substitute the ray into the sphere equation p - centre ² = r² and solve the quadratic in t . With m = position - centre and a normalised direction d : b = m · d , c = m · m - r² ; if c 0 and b 0 the ray starts outside and points away (no hit); otherwise, with disc = b² - c , there is no hit when disc < 0 , and the first hit is at t = -b - sqrt(disc) (or 0 if that is negative, meaning the ray starts inside). Ray against a box: the slab method An axis-aligned box is the overlap of three slabs (between two x planes, two y planes, two z planes). For each axis, compute where the ray enters and leaves that slab; the ray is inside the box between the latest entry and the earliest exit: cpp-norun float tmin = 0, tmax = INFINITY; for each axis a: if (d a == 0) { if (p a < min a p a max a ) no hit; } else { float t1 = (min a - p a ) / d a , t2 = (max a - p a ) / d a ; if (t1 t2) swap(t1, t2); tmin = max(tmin, t1); tmax = min(tmax, t2); if (tmin tmax) no hit; } hit at tmin The axis that produced the final tmin is the face that was hit, which gives the normal for bullet holes or ricochets. The practice writes this test. Moving objects - Sphere against sphere : centres closer than the sum of the radii, exactly as circles in 2D. - Box against box : overlap on all three axes ( CheckCollisionBoxes ). - Sphere against box : clamp the centre into the box for the closest point, as in 2D ( CheckCollisionBoxSphere ). For level geometry that is not boxes, raylib's GetRayCollisionMesh and a few rays (down for the floor, forward for walls) are often enough for a small game; larger games use a physics library such as Jolt or Bullet.

title: What does the ray hit?
body: Write lesson 5.03's ray tests. Ray directions have length 1: cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; struct Ray { Vector3 position, direction; }; struct BoundingBox { Vector3 min, max; }; struct Hit { bool hit{ false }; float distance{ 0 }; Vector3 point{ 0, 0, 0 }, normal{ 0, 0, 0 }; }; Hit rayPlaneY(Ray r, float height); // the horizontal plane y = height, from either side Hit raySphere(Ray r, Vector3 centre, float radius); Hit rayBox(Ray r, BoundingBox b); int pickNearest(Ray r, const std::vector<BoundingBox & boxes); // index of the nearest box hit, -1 for none - Hits only count at distance = 0 . A ray starting inside a sphere or a box hits at distance 0. - rayPlaneY 's normal is (0, 1, 0) when the ray comes from above and (0, -1, 0) from below; a ray parallel to the plane misses. - raySphere 's normal is from the centre to the hit point, normalised (for a ray starting inside, leave it (0, 0, 0) ). - rayBox uses the slab method. The normal points out of the face that was entered: the axis whose entry distance was the final tmin , with the sign opposite to the ray's direction on that axis. Starting inside, the normal is (0, 0, 0) .

title: 5.04  Shaders
body: Shaders are small programs that run on the GPU for every vertex and every pixel. This lesson explains vertex and fragment shaders, writes GLSL fragment shaders for raylib, passes values in with uniforms, and builds a flash effect, a dissolve and a simple light. Programs on the GPU Everything raylib draws goes through two small programs on the graphics card: raylib's default shaders just position vertices with the camera and multiply the texture colour by the tint. Writing your own fragment shader (also called a pixel shader) lets you change how every pixel looks: flashes, outlines, dissolves, lighting, water, colour grading. They are written in GLSL , a C-like language. A first fragment shader raylib on desktop uses OpenGL 3.3, so shaders start with version 330 : cpp-norun // flash.fs version 330 in vec2 fragTexCoord; // from raylib's default vertex shader in vec4 fragColor; // the tint uniform sampler2D texture0; // the texture being drawn uniform float flash; // our own value: 0 = normal, 1 = white out vec4 finalColor; void main() { vec4 texel = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord) fragColor; finalColor = vec4(mix(texel.rgb, vec3(1.0), flash), texel.a); } mix(a, b, t) is linear interpolation, vec3 / vec4 are vectors, and .rgb / .a pick components. The shader runs for every pixel of the sprite, in parallel. Using it from raylib cpp-norun Shader shader = LoadShader(nullptr, "assets/flash.fs"); // nullptr: keep the default vertex shader const int flashLoc = GetShaderLocation(shader, "flash"); // each frame: const float amount = hitTimer 0 ? 1.0f : 0.0f; SetShaderValue(shader, flashLoc, &amount, SHADER_UNIFORM_FLOAT); BeginShaderMode(shader); DrawTexturePro(sprite, src, dest, origin, 0, WHITE); EndShaderMode(); UnloadShader(shader); A uniform is a value that is the same for every pixel of one draw call: a time, a colour, a position. Look its location up once with GetShaderLocation , then set it every frame with SetShaderValue . Other types are SHADER_UNIFORM_VEC2 , VEC3 , VEC4 and INT , and SetShaderValueTexture passes extra textures. A dissolve A dissolve makes an object burn away. Read a noise texture, and throw away pixels whose noise value is below a threshold that rises from 0 to 1: cpp-norun uniform sampler2D noise; uniform float threshold; void main() { vec4 texel = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord) fragColor; float n = texture(noise, fragTexCoord).r; if (n < threshold) discard; // this pixel is not drawn float edge = smoothstep(threshold, threshold + 0.05, n); // 0 at the edge, 1 inside finalColor = vec4(mix(vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.1), texel.rgb, edge), texel.a); // glowing orange edge } A point light Simple lighting in 2D: brighten pixels near a light and darken the rest: cpp-norun uniform vec2 lightPos; // in screen pixels uniform float radius; void main() { vec4 texel = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord) fragColor; float d = distance(gl_FragCoord.xy, lightPos); float light = clamp(1.0 - d / radius, 0.15, 1.0); finalColor = vec4(texel.rgb light, texel.a); } gl_FragCoord is the pixel's position in the window, but with y measured from the bottom , so pass screenHeight - y for the light's y. Forgetting that flips the light upside down. Debugging shaders A shader that fails to compile is reported in raylib's log (the console window) with a line number, and raylib falls back to the default shader. When a result is wrong, output intermediate values as colours: finalColor = vec4(vec3(n), 1.0); shows the noise as grey levels. Shaders are calculations on numbers, so the maths behind them (interpolation, distances, smoothstep) can be tested on the CPU first, which is what this lesson's practice does.

title: Shader maths on the CPU
body: A fragment shader is a function from a pixel's inputs to its colour. Write lesson 5.04's shaders as C++ functions, with GLSL's built-ins: cpp struct Vec3 { float r, g, b; }; float mixf(float a, float b, float t); // a + (b - a) t Vec3 mix3(Vec3 a, Vec3 b, float t); float clampf(float x, float lo, float hi); float smoothstep(float e0, float e1, float x); // t = clamp((x - e0) / (e1 - e0), 0, 1); t² (3 - 2t) Vec3 flash(Vec3 texel, float amount); // towards white bool dissolve(Vec3 texel, float noise, float threshold, Vec3& out); float pointLight(float fragX, float fragY, float lightX, float lightY, float screenH, float radius); - dissolve : returns false (the pixel is discarded) when noise < threshold . Otherwise edge = smoothstep(threshold, threshold + 0.05, noise) and out = mix3({1, 0.5, 0.1}, texel, edge) . - pointLight : the fragment is in OpenGL coordinates (y from the bottom); the light is in raylib coordinates (y from the top). Convert the light's y, then return clamp(1 - distance / radius, 0.15, 1) . - smoothstep also works with e0 e1 (falling instead of rising), which the vignette in lesson 5.05 uses.

title: 5.05  Render Textures and Post-Processing
body: Drawing into a texture instead of the screen opens up a lot - pixel-perfect scaling, minimaps, split screens, and post-processing effects applied to the whole frame such as vignettes, colour grading, blur and scanlines. Drawing into a texture A render texture is a texture you can draw into, like an off-screen window: cpp-norun RenderTexture2D target = LoadRenderTexture(320, 180); // each frame: BeginTextureMode(target); ClearBackground(BLACK); drawWorld(); // everything goes into the texture EndTextureMode(); BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(BLACK); // draw the texture to the screen; the source height is NEGATIVE because OpenGL textures are upside down DrawTexturePro(target.texture, { 0, 0, 320, -180 }, letterboxRect, { 0, 0 }, 0, WHITE); EndDrawing(); UnloadRenderTexture(target); The negative source height is the one thing everyone forgets: without it, the whole picture is upside down. Pixel-perfect scaling This is the clean way to make a pixel-art game: draw everything at the native resolution (320 × 180) into a render texture with point filtering, then draw that texture scaled up by a whole number, centred, with black bars (the letterbox from practice 2.01). Every pixel is the same size whatever the window size, and the mouse is mapped back with the inverse of the same scale and offset. Other uses Use How --- --- Minimap Draw the level from above with a second camera into a small texture, show it in a corner Split screen One render texture per player, each with its own camera, side by side Mirrors, security cameras Draw the scene from another camera into a texture used on an object Caching Draw something expensive once (a big static background) and reuse the texture Post-processing Post-processing is a shader applied to the whole finished frame: draw the world into a render texture, then draw that texture to the screen inside BeginShaderMode . The fragment shader sees every pixel of the frame: cpp-norun // vignette.fs: darken towards the edges version 330 in vec2 fragTexCoord; uniform sampler2D texture0; out vec4 finalColor; void main() { vec3 c = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord).rgb; float d = distance(fragTexCoord, vec2(0.5)); // 0 in the centre, about 0.7 in the corners c = smoothstep(0.8, 0.3, d); // fade from 1 to 0 between 0.3 and 0.8 finalColor = vec4(c, 1.0); } Common effects: - Vignette (above): focuses the eye on the centre. - Colour grading : adjust brightness, contrast and saturation, or tint the whole frame for mood (blue at night, red when low on health). - Grey scale : dot(c, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) gives the perceived brightness, used for a "game over" or flashback look. - Blur : average neighbouring pixels; done in two passes (horizontal, then vertical) for speed, often to put a menu over a blurred game. - Scanlines and curvature : an old CRT look. - Bloom : blur only the bright parts and add them back, so lights glow. raylib's examples include a dozen post-processing shaders ( shaders_postprocessing ) to start from. Keep it optional Post-processing costs a full-screen pass per effect, and some effects (blur, shake, flashing) bother some players. Give each strong effect a setting, and keep the interface outside the effect by drawing it after the post-processed frame.

title: Post-processing a frame
body: Write lesson 5.05's effects on a small grey-scale picture, and the mouse mapping for a letterboxed render texture: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; float luminance(float r, float g, float b); // 0.299 r + 0.587 g + 0.114 b float vignette(float u, float v); // smoothstep(0.8, 0.3, distance from (0.5, 0.5)) std::vector<float blur3(const std::vector<float & image, int w, int h); bool screenToNative(Vector2 mouse, Rectangle shown, int nativeW, int nativeH, int& px, int& py); - blur3 is a 3-tap box blur in two passes: first horizontal (each pixel becomes the average of itself and its left and right neighbours), then vertical on the result. At the edges, a missing neighbour is replaced by the nearest pixel ( clamp to edge ). The image is stored row by row. - screenToNative : shown is where the native-resolution picture is drawn on screen. Return the native pixel under the mouse ( floor of the scaled position) and true , or false if the mouse is outside shown (its right and bottom edges are outside). - vignette : use the same smoothstep as practice 5.04.

title: A first-person arena
body: Write the core of a small first-person target-shooting game: mouse look, walking relative to the view, gravity and jumping, collision against box-shaped walls in three dimensions, and shooting with a ray that walls block. In raylib it is drawn with DrawCube for the walls and targets and a Camera3D at the player's eye. cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; struct Box { Vector3 min, max; }; struct Target { Box box; int hp; }; struct Keys { bool forward{ false }, back{ false }, left{ false }, right{ false }, jump{ false }; }; struct Player { Vector3 feet{ 0, 0, 0 }; Vector3 vel{ 0, 0, 0 }; float yaw{ 0 }, pitch{ 0 }; // degrees bool onGround{ false }; }; void look(Player& p, float mouseDx, float mouseDy, float sensitivity); Vector3 eye(const Player& p); Vector3 viewDirection(const Player& p); void walk(Player& p, const std::vector<Box & walls, const Keys& k, float dt); int shoot(const Player& p, const std::vector<Box & walls, std::vector<Target & targets); look : yaw -= mouseDx sensitivity , wrapped into 0 <= yaw < 360 ; pitch -= mouseDy sensitivity , clamped to -89..89 . eye is the feet plus 1.6 up. viewDirection is practice 5.02's lookDirection(yaw, pitch) . walk , in this order: 1. The wish direction from the keys, using the flat forward and right directions of practice 5.02, normalised; vel.x and vel.z become the wish direction times 5 (metres per second). 2. If jump is held and the player is on the ground, vel.y = 7 . 3. Gravity: vel.y -= 20 dt . 4. Move along x, then z, then y, each followed by collision with the walls. The player's box is feet.x ± 0.3 , feet.z ± 0.3 , and feet.y to feet.y + 1.8 ; touching does not count as overlapping. Blocked on x or z, the player stops at the wall's face (0.3 from it) and that velocity becomes 0. On y, moving down onto a box lands on its top ( onGround ), moving up stops the head at its bottom; vel.y becomes 0. Several walls: the nearest stop, as in practice 3.02. 5. onGround is true exactly when this step landed. shoot casts a ray from the eye along the view direction against all walls and all targets with hit points left (practice 5.03's slab test). If the nearest hit is a target, it loses a hit point and its index is returned; otherwise (a wall or nothing) -1 .

title: 6.01  Saving Progress and Settings
body: Players expect a game to remember their settings, their progress and their best scores. This lesson chooses what to save and where, writes simple versioned text formats, saves safely so a crash never destroys a save, and keeps a high-score table. What to save Kind Examples When --- --- --- Settings Volumes, key bindings, window mode, screen shake on or off When changed Progress Levels unlocked, items collected, the current level and checkpoint At checkpoints, level ends and on quit Records High scores, best times, statistics When a record changes Save data , not objects: the level number and the player's health, not the Player object with its texture handles and pointers. Loading then rebuilds the objects from the data. Where Never write next to the .exe : on Windows, a game installed in Program Files is not allowed to. Each user has a folder for this, %APPDATA% (for example C:\Users\Sam\AppData\Roaming\YourGame\ ): cpp-norun include <cstdlib include <filesystem std::filesystem::path saveFolder() { const char appData = std::getenv("APPDATA"); // Windows std::filesystem::path dir = appData ? appData : "."; dir /= "XenonQuest"; std::filesystem::create_directories(dir); return dir; } On Linux the convention is ~/.local/share/<game , on macOS ~/Library/Application Support/<game . A simple format A text file of key=value lines is readable, easy to debug and easy to extend: version=2 music=70 effects=85 fullscreen=0 key.jump=32 Rules that keep it robust: - Defaults first : start from default settings and overwrite only the keys that are present and valid. A missing or damaged line then simply keeps its default, and new settings added in an update work with old files. - Validate and clamp every value: a volume of 900 or a key code of -5 must not reach the game. - Ignore unknown keys , so an older game can read a newer file. - Version the file, so a later version can convert old data (a migration ). Saving safely If the game crashes or the power fails halfway through writing, the save file is cut off and the player loses everything. Write to a temporary file first, then replace the old one in a single step: cpp-norun void saveSafely(const std::filesystem::path& file, const std::string& text) { const auto temp = file.string() + ".tmp"; { std::ofstream out{ temp, std::ios::binary }; out << text; } // closed (flushed) at the brace std::filesystem::rename(temp, file); // replaces the old file } A rename within one folder is atomic on Windows and Linux: afterwards there is either the complete old file or the complete new one. Keeping the previous save as save.bak adds another layer of protection. Detecting damage A checksum stored with the data detects files that were cut off or damaged: compute a number from the content (such as FNV-1a, a few lines of code), write it on the last line, and when loading, recompute it and compare. On a mismatch, fall back to the backup or to defaults, and tell the player rather than crashing. A checksum is not protection against cheating: anyone can recompute it. For a single-player game that is fine; let players edit their saves if they want to. High scores A high-score table is a sorted list with a maximum length: cpp-norun struct Score { std::string name; int points; }; void addScore(std::vector<Score & table, Score s) { auto pos = std::find_if(table.begin(), table.end(), & (const Score& t) { return s.points t.points; }); table.insert(pos, s); // after equal scores: earlier players keep their place if (table.size() 10) table.pop_back(); } Ask for the name (lesson 1.05's typed text) only when the score actually makes it into the table.

title: A settings file
body: Read and write lesson 6.01's settings file: cpp struct Settings { int music{ 70 }, effects{ 85 }; // 0 .. 100 bool fullscreen{ false }; bool shake{ true }; int jumpKey{ 32 }; // 1 .. 512 }; Settings parseSettings(const std::string& text); std::string writeSettings(const Settings& s); parseSettings starts from the defaults and reads key=value lines ( \r\n allowed): - music and effects : whole numbers, clamped to 0..100 ; - fullscreen and shake : 0 or 1 (anything else is ignored); - key.jump : a whole number from 1 to 512 (out of range is ignored); - version must be 1 or 2 if present; a file with any other version is ignored completely (defaults). Version 1 files stored the volumes as 0..10 , so for them music and effects are multiplied by 10; - spaces around keys and values are trimmed; unknown keys, lines without = , and values that are not whole numbers (such as 7x ) are ignored. writeSettings writes version 2, in this order, each line ending in \n : version=2 music=70 effects=85 fullscreen=0 shake=1 key.jump=32

title: 6.02  Packaging a Finished Game
body: Turning a project that runs on your computer into a game anyone can download - release builds, loading assets reliably, an asset cache, the window and icon, testing on a clean machine, a web build with Emscripten, and publishing on itch.io. A release build Switch Visual Studio to Release . Debug builds are often ten times slower and need debug runtime DLLs that players do not have. Then: - Static runtime : set C/C++ Code Generation Runtime Library to /MT , so the game does not need the Visual C++ Redistributable installed. With vcpkg, use the x64-windows-static triplet so raylib is linked in too, and the game is a single .exe plus its assets. - No console : SubSystem Windows with entry point mainCRTStartup (lesson 1.01). - Icon : add a resource file ( .rc ) with an .ico for the file's icon in Explorer, and call SetWindowIcon(LoadImage("icon.png")) for the title bar. Assets that always load The classic bug of a first release: it works in Visual Studio, but double-clicking the .exe shows a black window, because the assets are loaded relative to the working directory , which is now different. Fix it once at start-up: cpp-norun ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()); // relative paths now start next to the .exe and make the build copy the assets folder next to the .exe (a post-build step, or CMake's file(COPY ...) ). Check every load: a missing texture has an id of 0 ( IsTextureValid in raylib 5.5). Show a clear message ("assets/player.png is missing") instead of an invisible player. An asset cache When several objects use the same texture, load it once and share it: cpp-norun class TextureCache { public: Texture2D get(const std::string& path) { auto it = m_textures.find(path); if (it != m_textures.end()) return it- second; Texture2D t = LoadTexture(path.c_str()); m_textures.emplace(path, t); return t; } ~TextureCache() { for (auto& path, t : m_textures) UnloadTexture(t); } // before CloseWindow private: std::unordered_map<std::string, Texture2D m_textures; }; Normalise the paths used as keys ( assets/./player.png and assets/player.png are the same file), and destroy the cache before CloseWindow , since unloading needs the graphics context. Reference counting lets the cache free textures a level no longer uses; the practice builds it. Test on a clean machine Your computer has Visual Studio, vcpkg and every DLL; players' computers do not. Before publishing, run the game from a zip on a computer (or a fresh Windows virtual machine, or Windows Sandbox) that has never seen your development tools. Check the window size on a small laptop screen and a big monitor, a gamepad, and that settings and saves end up in %APPDATA% . A web build raylib compiles to WebAssembly with Emscripten , so the game runs in a browser with nothing to install. The main loop must give control back to the browser every frame, so it becomes a function: cpp-norun if defined(PLATFORM_WEB) include <emscripten/emscripten.h endif void frame() { update(); draw(); } int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "Game"); if defined(PLATFORM_WEB) emscripten_set_main_loop(frame, 0, 1); // the browser calls frame() else SetTargetFPS(60); while (!WindowShouldClose()) frame(); endif CloseWindow(); } Build raylib for the web ( make PLATFORM=PLATFORM_WEB ), compile with emcc ... -s USE_GLFW=3 --preload-file assets , and you get an .html , a .js , a .wasm and a .data file with the assets. Browsers only start audio after the player clicks, so show a "click to start" screen first. Publishing itch.io is the usual home for small games: upload the Windows zip and the web build (as a zip with index.html , set to "playable in the browser"), add screenshots, a short description and the controls. A short GIF of gameplay does more than any description. Use version numbers in the zip names and keep a changelog.

title: A reference-counted asset cache
body: Write lesson 6.02's asset cache, with the loading and unloading done by functions you pass in (in a real game they call LoadTexture and UnloadTexture ): cpp std::string normalizePath(const std::string& path); class AssetCache { public: AssetCache(std::function<int(const std::string&) load, std::function<void(int) unload); ~AssetCache(); // unloads everything still loaded int acquire(const std::string& path); // the asset's handle; loads it on first use void release(const std::string& path); // one fewer user; unloads at zero int users(const std::string& path) const; // 0 if not loaded std::size_t loaded() const; }; normalizePath : backslashes become / ; empty parts and . parts are removed; .. removes the part before it (a .. with nothing before it is kept); letters become lower case (Windows file names ignore case). So Assets\\.\\sprites//../Player.PNG is assets/player.png . AssetCache : every function normalises the path first, so different spellings of the same file share one asset. acquire calls load only the first time (or again after the asset was fully released) and counts users. release on an asset that is not loaded does nothing. A load result of 0 means it failed: it is not cached, and acquire returns 0.

title: 6.03  Project: A Complete Small Game
body: Put the whole course together into one finished game - choosing a scope you can finish, the order to build it in, data-driven waves and levels, the polish that makes it feel complete, and a checklist for release. The example is a top-down arena survival game. Finishing is the skill Most first games are never finished: the idea grows faster than the code. The goal of this project is a small game that is complete : a title screen, a game that starts, gets harder and ends, a game-over screen with a score, settings that are remembered, sound, and a build someone else can play. The example here is an arena survival game: the player moves around a single arena with the keyboard or a gamepad and shoots in the direction they aim; enemies arrive in waves; each wave is harder; the score is the number of waves survived and enemies defeated. It uses almost every lesson, and is small enough to finish in a few weekends. Choose your own idea if you prefer, but keep it to one mechanic, one screen-sized world and one goal . The pieces and where they come from Piece Lessons --- --- Loop, frame time, input with bindings 1.02 - 1.05 Sprites and animations for the player and enemies 2.01, 2.02 Interface: score, health bar, wave number, menus 2.03 Sounds with variation, music, volume settings 2.04 Title, game, pause and game-over screens with fades 2.05 Circle collisions, a grid for many bullets and enemies 3.01, 3.05 Fixed time step 3.04 Camera with shake 4.01 Particles for hits and deaths 4.03 Enemy state machine: approach, wind-up, charge 4.04 Flow field so enemies go around obstacles 4.05 Post-processing: a vignette, a red flash when hurt 5.04, 5.05 Settings and high scores saved safely 6.01 Release and web builds 6.02 Waves as data Hard-coding "wave 3 has five chargers" makes balancing slow. Describe waves as data in a text file that the game reads: time kind count interval wave 1 0 walker 4 1.0 6 walker 4 0.5 wave 2 0 walker 6 0.6 3 charger 2 2.0 Each line is a spawn group : starting at time seconds into the wave, spawn count enemies of kind , one every interval seconds. The game asks "which enemies spawn between the last frame and this one?" and the answer comes straight from the data. You can rebalance without recompiling, and even reload the file while the game runs. The practice builds this spawner. Difficulty should rise in steps with pauses between them: tension, then relief. After the hand-made waves, generate more by scaling counts and shortening intervals. Order to build in 1. The toy : a player that moves and shoots in an empty arena. Make it feel good before anything else: speed, acceleration, the bullet's speed, a sound and a particle burst for every shot. 2. Something to shoot : one enemy type, collision, health, dying. 3. A game : waves from the data file, a score, losing. 4. Screens : title, pause, game over with the score, play again (reset everything, lesson 2.05). 5. Variety : a second and a third enemy type with different behaviour. 6. Polish : shake, hit flash, hit stop, death particles, music, a vignette. 7. Remembering : settings and the high-score table. 8. Release : icon, release build, clean-machine test, web build, itch.io page. At every step the game runs, and you can stop and still have something to show. The release checklist - It starts with a title screen and can be quit from the menu. - Every input has a keyboard and a gamepad binding, and the controls are shown somewhere. - Pause works and stops everything, including timers and spawns. - Play again resets everything. - Music and effects volumes are separate, saved, and applied at start-up. - Screen shake and flashes can be turned off. - The window can be resized or made fullscreen, and the game still fits. - Settings and scores are in %APPDATA% , saved safely. - It runs from a zip on a clean machine. - Someone who has never seen it played it without your help. The last one matters most: watch a friend play without saying anything. Every place they hesitate is something to make clearer.

title: Waves from data
body: Write lesson 6.03's data-driven wave spawner: cpp struct Spawn { double time; std::string kind; }; class Waves { public: bool load(const std::string& text, std::string& error); int count() const; // number of waves std::vector<Spawn schedule(int wave) const; // every spawn of a wave (1-based), sorted by time std::vector<std::string spawnsBetween(int wave, double from, double to) const; // spawns with from < time <= to double length(int wave) const; // time of the wave's last spawn, 0 if none }; The format : lines starting with and empty lines are ignored. wave N starts wave N, and waves must be numbered 1, 2, 3... in order. Every other line inside a wave is a group: time kind count interval (time and interval are decimal numbers, count a whole number of at least 1, interval at least 0). A group spawns count enemies of kind at time , time + interval , time + 2 × interval , ... Errors ( load returns false and leaves the previous waves in place): "line N: expected wave 2" (the wrong number), "line N: group outside a wave" , "line N: bad group" (N counting all lines from 1). schedule sorts by time; spawns at the same time keep the order of their groups in the file, then their order in the group. An unknown wave number gives no spawns.

title: Saves that survive
body:
Write the save system a finished game needs: a readable, versioned save file with a checksum, migration from the previous version, a fallback to the backup when the main save is damaged, and the high-score table. cpp struct Score { int points; std::string name; }; struct SaveData { int level{ 1 }; int coins{ 0 }; std::vector<std::string unlocked; // area names, in the order they were unlocked std::vector<Score scores; // best first, at most 5 }; enum class LoadResult { Ok, Missing, Damaged, TooNew }; std::uint32_t fnv1a(const std::string& text); std::string writeSave(const SaveData& s); LoadResult loadSave(const std::string& text, SaveData& out); int chooseSave(const std::string& primary, const std::string& backup, SaveData& out); int addScore(std::vector<Score & table, const std::string& name, int points); fnv1a is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash: start at 2166136261 ; for each byte, XOR it in, then multiply by 16777619 (arithmetic wraps around at 2³²). The file (version 2), lines ending in 
 : xenon-save 2 level 3 coins 120 unlocked forest,caves score 1200 Sam score 900 Alex Smith checksum 1a2b3c4d unlocked lists the areas separated by commas (the line is written even when empty: unlocked , with nothing after the space). Each score line is the points then the name (which may contain spaces). The last line is checksum followed by the FNV-1a hash of everything before it (all the earlier lines with their 
 ), as 8 lower-case hex digits. loadSave : - An empty text is Missing . - The first line must be xenon-save N . N greater than 2 is TooNew ; N must be 1 or 2. - The checksum line must be last and must match; otherwise, or for any line that cannot be read, the result is Damaged . Lines may end with 
 (the checksum is computed over the text as stored, so a file with 
 endings hashes them too). - Version 1 files had gold instead of coins and no unlocked line: load them into the version 2 data. - Unknown lines are ignored, so later versions can add lines. level must be at least 1 and coins at least 0, or it is Damaged . - Only on Ok is out changed. chooseSave loads the primary text into out and returns 1; if that is not Ok , it tries the backup and returns 2; if neither loads, out becomes a default SaveData and it returns 0. addScore inserts a score into the table, best first, after existing equal scores, keeps at most 5, and returns the new score's rank (1 to 5), or 0 if it did not make the table.

title: Cheat Sheet - raylib
body: The skeleton cpp-norun include "raylib.h" int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "Game"); InitAudioDevice(); SetTargetFPS(60); ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()); // load assets here while (!WindowShouldClose()) { const float dt = GetFrameTime(); // update BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); // draw EndDrawing(); } // unload assets here CloseAudioDevice(); CloseWindow(); } Window and time Function Does --- --- SetConfigFlags(FLAG_WINDOW_RESIZABLE \ FLAG_VSYNC_HINT \ FLAG_MSAA_4X_HINT) Before InitWindow GetScreenWidth() , GetScreenHeight() Window size ToggleFullscreen() , ToggleBorderlessWindowed() Fullscreen modes GetFrameTime() , GetTime() , GetFPS() Seconds per frame, seconds since start, frames per second GetRandomValue(min, max) Random whole number, both included Input Function True or gives --- --- IsKeyDown(KEY_A) / IsKeyPressed / IsKeyReleased Held / went down / went up GetCharPressed() Next typed character, 0 when none left GetMousePosition() , GetMouseDelta() , GetMouseWheelMove() Mouse IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) Click IsGamepadAvailable(0) , GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, GAMEPAD_AXIS_LEFT_X) Gamepad stick, -1..1 IsGamepadButtonPressed(0, GAMEPAD_BUTTON_RIGHT_FACE_DOWN) A / Cross DisableCursor() , EnableCursor() Lock the mouse for 3D Shapes and text Function Draws --- --- DrawRectangleRec(rect, c) , DrawRectangleLinesEx(rect, thick, c) Rectangle from its top-left corner DrawCircleV(centre, r, c) Circle from its centre DrawLineEx(a, b, thick, c) , DrawTriangle(a, b, c, colour) Line, triangle DrawText(text, x, y, size, c) , MeasureText(text, size) Default font DrawTextEx(font, text, pos, size, spacing, c) , MeasureTextEx(...) Your font TextFormat("Score: %d", score) printf-style text (do not keep the pointer) Fade(c, 0.5f) , ColorLerp(a, b, t) Transparency, mixing Textures Function Does --- --- LoadTexture(path) , UnloadTexture(t) After InitWindow / before CloseWindow SetTextureFilter(t, TEXTURE_FILTER_POINT) Crisp pixel art DrawTexturePro(t, src, dest, origin, rotation, tint) Part of a texture, scaled, rotated; negative src.width flips LoadRenderTexture(w, h) , BeginTextureMode(rt) ... EndTextureMode() Draw into a texture; draw it with a negative source height Sound Function Does --- --- LoadSound(path) , PlaySound(s) , LoadSoundAlias(s) Short effects; aliases play over each other SetSoundVolume(s, v) , SetSoundPitch(s, p) , SetMasterVolume(v) Volume 0..1, pitch 1 = normal LoadMusicStream(path) , PlayMusicStream(m) , UpdateMusicStream(m) Streamed music; update every frame Collision Function Tests --- --- CheckCollisionRecs(a, b) , GetCollisionRec(a, b) Rectangles, and their overlap CheckCollisionCircles(c1, r1, c2, r2) , CheckCollisionCircleRec(c, r, rect) Circles CheckCollisionPointRec(p, rect) Point CheckCollisionLines(a1, a2, b1, b2, &point) Segments CheckCollisionBoxes(a, b) , GetRayCollisionBox(ray, box) 3D boxes and rays Cameras cpp-norun Camera2D cam{ / offset / { 400, 225 }, / target / player, / rotation / 0, / zoom / 1 }; BeginMode2D(cam); / world / EndMode2D(); // then the interface Vector2 world = GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), cam); Camera3D cam3{ { 6, 4, 6 }, { 0, 0.5f, 0 }, { 0, 1, 0 }, 45, CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE }; BeginMode3D(cam3); DrawCube({ 0, 0.5f, 0 }, 1, 1, 1, RED); DrawGrid(20, 1); EndMode3D(); Ray ray = GetScreenToWorldRay(GetMousePosition(), cam3); Shaders cpp-norun Shader sh = LoadShader(nullptr, "effect.fs"); // default vertex shader int loc = GetShaderLocation(sh, "amount"); SetShaderValue(sh, loc, &amount, SHADER_UNIFORM_FLOAT); BeginShaderMode(sh); / draw / EndShaderMode(); BeginBlendMode(BLEND_ADDITIVE); / glowing things / EndBlendMode(); Game maths Formula Use --- --- pos += vel dt; vel += accel dt (velocity first) Movement vel = pow(keepPerSecond, dt) Frame-rate independent drag gravity = 2h / t² , jumpSpeed = 2h / t A jump of height h rising in t seconds v - 2 dot(v, n) n Bounce off a surface with normal n (p - target) zoom + offset World to screen (2D camera, no rotation)

title: Common Errors
body: Message or symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- cannot open source file "raylib.h" vcpkg installed for another platform, or not integrated Set the platform to x64; run vcpkg integrate install 1.01 LNK2019 for InitWindow or other raylib functions raylib's library is not linked Use vcpkg's integration, or add raylib.lib plus winmm.lib 1.01 A crash or black texture when loading at start-up LoadTexture called before InitWindow Load assets after InitWindow 2.01 Textures are white or missing when started outside Visual Studio Relative paths and a different working directory ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()) and copy the assets next to the .exe 2.01, 6.02 Moving objects leave trails The frame is not cleared ClearBackground at the start of every frame 1.02 The game runs faster on a fast screen Movement per frame instead of per second Multiply by GetFrameTime() 1.04 Diagonal movement is too fast The direction is not normalised Normalise the input direction 1.04 A menu choice jumps several items per key press IsKeyDown used for a one-off action IsKeyPressed 1.05 The character creeps with the gamepad untouched Stick drift A dead zone 1.05 An animation is stuck on its first frame play restarts the animation every frame Restart only when the animation changes 2.02 The music plays for a moment and stops UpdateMusicStream is not called every frame Call it every frame 2.04 A rapidly repeated sound cuts itself off PlaySound restarts a Sound that is playing Sound aliases 2.04 "Play again" starts with old enemies or score State not reset Reset the whole game state: game = Game{}; 2.05 Characters catch on the seams between floor tiles Collision resolved on both axes at once Move and resolve one axis at a time 3.02 Bullets pass through thin walls Tunnelling Clamp dt, sub-steps or a swept test 3.02 Jumps reach different heights on different computers Variable time step A fixed time step 3.04 The game freezes after a slow frame The spiral of death Limit steps per frame or clamp the frame time 3.04 The interface scrolls with the world Drawn inside BeginMode2D Draw it after EndMode2D 2.03, 4.01 Clicks select the wrong object in a scrolled world Mouse position used without the camera GetScreenToWorld2D 4.01 Thin lines between tiles when zoomed Rounding and filtering at tile edges Whole-pixel positions, point filtering, extruded tile sheets 4.02 The view flips when looking straight up Pitch not clamped Clamp pitch to ±89° 5.02 A render texture is drawn upside down OpenGL textures are flipped Negative source height 5.05 A light shader's light is mirrored vertically gl_FragCoord measures y from the bottom Pass screenHeight - y 5.04 Shader changes have no effect The shader failed to compile and raylib fell back to the default Read the compile error in the log 5.04 Settings or saves are not written in Program Files Windows does not allow writing there Save in %APPDATA% 6.01 No sound in the web build Browsers start audio only after a user action A "click to start" screen 6.02

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- A\ A path search that expands the most promising cell first, using the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost remaining. (4.05) AABB Axis-aligned bounding box: a rectangle (or box in 3D) whose sides are parallel to the axes. (3.01) Accumulator In a fixed-step loop, the real time that has passed but has not been simulated yet. (3.04) Additive blending Drawing where colours add up, so overlaps glow brighter; used for fire, sparks and light. (4.03) Alpha A colour's opacity, 0 (invisible) to 255 (solid). In interpolation, how far between two steps the current time is. (1.03, 3.04) Atlas One texture holding many smaller pictures, such as the glyphs of a font or the tiles of a level. (2.03) Auto-tiling Choosing a wall's picture automatically from which of its neighbours are walls. (4.02) BFS Breadth-first search: explores cells in order of distance, finding shortest paths when every step costs the same. (4.05) Broad phase The cheap first step of collision detection that finds which pairs might touch. (3.05) Camera2D / Camera3D raylib's descriptions of which part of the world is shown and how. (4.01, 5.01) Checksum A number computed from a file's contents and stored with it, to detect damage. (6.01) Coyote time A short time after leaving a ledge during which a jump is still allowed. (3.03) Dead zone A range of input treated as zero (stick drift), or a box the player can move in without the camera following. (1.05, 4.01) Delta time (dt) The time the last frame took, used to make movement per second instead of per frame. (1.04) Dot product a · b : how much two directions agree; for normalised vectors, the cosine of the angle between them. (5.01) Emitter Something that creates particles, in bursts or at a steady rate.
