(4.03) Emscripten The compiler that turns C and C++ into WebAssembly so a game runs in a browser. (6.02) Fixed time step Simulating in equal steps regardless of the frame rate. (3.04) Flow field A grid of distances to one target, which any number of units can follow downhill. (4.05) Fragment shader A GPU program that runs once per pixel and chooses its colour. (5.04) Frame One pass of input, update and draw. (1.02) Game loop The loop every game runs: read input, update the world, draw it. (1.02) Jump buffering Remembering a jump press for a short time so it happens as soon as the player lands. (3.03) Juice Small effects that change how a game feels but not its rules: shake, flashes, particles, sounds. (4.03) Letterbox Scaling a picture to fit the screen and filling the rest with bars. (2.01, 5.05) Migration Converting data saved by an older version of the game into the current format. (6.01) Minimum translation vector The shortest move that separates two overlapping shapes. (3.02) Narrow phase The exact collision test, run only on the pairs the broad phase found. (3.05) Normal A direction perpendicular to a surface, pointing out of it. (3.02, 5.03) Parallax Background layers moving slower than the world to suggest depth. (4.01) Particle A small, short-lived object with a position, velocity and lifetime. (4.03) Pitch / yaw Looking up and down / turning left and right. (5.02) Pool A fixed block of pre-allocated objects reused instead of creating and destroying them. (4.03) Post-processing A shader applied to the whole finished frame. (5.05) Ray A start point and a direction; ray tests answer "what is in this direction?". (5.03) Render texture A texture you can draw into instead of the screen. (5.05) Semi-implicit Euler Updating velocity from acceleration first, then position from the new velocity. (1.04) Shader A small program that runs on the GPU for every vertex or pixel. (5.04) Slab method Testing a ray against a box as the overlap of three pairs of parallel planes. (5.03) Sound alias A second Sound that shares another's sample data, so both can play at once. (2.04) Spatial grid Cells that list the objects inside them, so only nearby objects are tested against each other. (3.05) Spiral of death Simulation steps taking longer than real time, making each frame slower than the last. (3.04) Sprite sheet One texture holding the frames of animations in a grid. (2.02) State machine A set of states, exactly one of them current, and the events that move between them. (2.05, 4.04) Swap and pop Removing an element by moving the last one into its place, when order does not matter. (4.03) Telegraphing Showing that an attack is coming so the player can react. (4.04) Texture2D A picture in video memory, ready to draw. (2.01) Tile map A grid of tile numbers describing a level. (4.02) Tint A colour multiplied into every pixel of a drawn texture. (2.01) Trauma A 0 to 1 value that events add to, driving screen shake. (4.01) Tunnelling A fast object passing completely through a thin one between two frames. (3.02) Uniform A value passed to a shader that is the same for every pixel of a draw call. (5.04) Working directory The folder relative paths start from; often not the folder of the .exe. (2.01, 6.02)

title: 1.01  What Reverse Engineering Is
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: Reverse engineering is working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. Why people do it - debugging, security, compatibility, preservation, learning - the ground rules about what you may examine, and how this course keeps every target your own. Working backwards A compiler turns source code into machine code and throws most of the meaning away: names of local variables, comments, the structure of classes, often whole functions that it inlined. Reverse engineering is working backwards from what is left, the machine code, the data, the program's behaviour, to an understanding of how it works. You already do a little of it every time you debug a Release build and the debugger shows assembly instead of your source, or when you read a crash dump. This course turns that into a skill. Why people do it - Debugging without source. A crash inside a library you only have as a DLL, a driver, or an old build of your own program whose source has changed since. - Security. Finding vulnerabilities so they can be fixed; analysing malware to understand what it does and how to detect and remove it; checking that a program does what its makers say. - Compatibility and interoperability. Reading a file format or protocol so your program can open the files or talk to the device. Wine, LibreOffice's support for old document formats and many game mods began this way. - Preservation. Keeping old software running after its company is gone: emulators, source ports of classic games, recovered file formats. - Learning. Seeing what the compiler really made of your code is the best way to understand optimisation, calling conventions and C++ objects. The ground rules Reverse engineering is a tool, and like any tool the question is what you point it at. Before you examine any program, ask: 1. Is it mine? Programs you wrote and compiled are always fine to take apart. Most of this course works on exactly those. 2. Do I have permission? Practice targets made to be reversed (crackmes, CTF challenges, this course's targets), bug bounty programs with published rules, and work your employer or client authorised in writing. 3. What does the licence say, and the law where I live? Many end-user licences forbid reverse engineering. Some countries give limited rights to do it anyway for interoperability or security research; the details differ by country and change over time. When it matters, the answer comes from a lawyer, not a forum post. 4. Does it affect other people? Anything that touches an online service, another player, or another person's computer or data is off limits without explicit permission, whatever the technique. This course never goes near defeating copy protection, cheating in online games, bypassing anti-cheat or anti-debugging systems, or getting into systems you do not own. Those are not only against the rules of the services involved; they hurt the people on the other side. !note Every target in this course is either a program you build yourself in Visual Studio or a practice target the course provides: byte arrays, simulated memory, file formats and a tiny virtual machine designed to be taken apart. What you need to know already You should be comfortable with C++ and have seen some x64 assembly: registers, mov , add , cmp , jumps, call and ret . The Assembly course or milestone 7 of the Game Development course covers that. Milestone 2 here starts with a refresher aimed at reading rather than writing. The Pointers and Memory course is useful background too: reverse engineering is mostly memory, offsets and pointers. How the course works Each lesson describes how the work is done with real tools on real programs, and the practice turns the core of each technique into code you write and test: parsing a PE file, finding functions, rebuilding a call stack, scanning memory, encoding jumps, disassembling instructions. By the end you will have written small versions of most of the tools you use.

title: 1.02  The Tools of the Trade
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: Disassemblers and decompilers for static analysis, debuggers for dynamic analysis, hex editors, PE viewers and system monitors - what each kind of tool does, the free ones worth installing, and a first look at your own program in each. Two ways of looking Reverse engineering has two halves that you switch between all the time: - Static analysis : reading the program without running it. Its file, its machine code, its strings and data. - Dynamic analysis : running it and watching. Stepping through code, inspecting memory, recording what it touches. Static analysis sees everything but has to guess what values things have. Dynamic analysis sees real values but only the paths the program actually takes. Each answers the other's questions. Disassemblers and decompilers A disassembler turns machine code back into assembly text. A decompiler goes a step further and produces C-like pseudocode. Both build a database of the program: functions, cross-references, names and comments that you add as you understand things. Tool Notes --- --- Ghidra free and open source (from the NSA), disassembler and decompiler, scripting in Java and Python IDA Free the long-time industry standard; the free version decompiles x64 using a cloud service Binary Ninja modern, scriptable; a free cloud version Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) not for binaries, but the best way to learn what source compiles into Decompiler output is a guess. It is usually close, sometimes wrong, and never has your original names. Treat it as a map, and check important details in the disassembly. Debuggers A debugger runs a program under control: breakpoints, single-stepping, viewing and changing registers and memory. Tool Notes --- --- Visual Studio debugger best with source and symbols; shows disassembly too (Debug Windows Disassembly) x64dbg free, open source, made for working without source; the usual choice for reversing on Windows WinDbg Microsoft's debugger; powerful command language, crash dumps, kernel debugging Looking at files and bytes - A hex editor (HxD, or ImHex, which also understands file structures) shows a file's raw bytes. - A PE viewer (PE-bear, CFF Explorer, or dumpbin /headers /imports from Visual Studio's Developer Command Prompt) shows the structure of .exe and .dll files: headers, sections, imports. - Strings tools (Sysinternals strings , or the strings window in Ghidra and x64dbg) list readable text in a file. Error messages and file names in a program tell you a lot before you read a single instruction. Watching behaviour The Sysinternals tools from Microsoft are essential: - Process Monitor records every file, registry and network operation a process makes. - Process Explorer shows each process's DLLs, handles, threads and memory. - API Monitor (third party) logs calls to Windows API functions with their arguments. A first look at your own program Build a small program in Visual Studio in Release configuration, so the optimiser has done its work: cpp-norun include <cstdio int score(int hits, int misses) { return hits 10 - misses 3; } int main(int argc, char ) { std::printf("score: %d\n", score(argc 4, argc)); } Then: 1. Open the .exe in a PE viewer and find its sections and its imports. You will see printf is not imported directly; the C runtime DLL ( ucrtbase.dll or vcruntime140.dll plus api-ms-win-crt- ) is. 2. Run strings on it: score: %d is there, among many strings from the runtime. 3. Open it in Ghidra or x64dbg and find main . You may find score has disappeared entirely: the optimiser inlined it and folded the arithmetic. That is the first lesson of reverse engineering: the binary is what the compiler made, not what you wrote. Keep the PDB (the symbol file Visual Studio writes beside the .exe ) out of the way when you practise. With it, every tool shows your function names; without it, you see what a reverse engineer normally sees.

title: Comparing two builds
body: A hex editor's compare view is one of the most used tools in reversing: build your program twice with one small change and compare the files to see exactly which bytes the change touched. Write its core: cpp struct Change { std::size_t offset; std::size_t length; }; std::vector<Change diffBytes(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & before, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & after); std::string describe(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & before, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & after, Change c); - diffBytes returns the runs of consecutive differing bytes, in order. If one file is longer, everything past the end of the shorter one counts as different (joined to a run that reaches the end of the shorter one). - describe formats one change as 0xOFFSET: BEFORE - AFTER : the offset in uppercase hex without padding, then the bytes of each side as two uppercase hex digits separated by spaces. A byte position that a side does not have is shown as -- . text 0x1A: 74 05 - EB 05 0x40: -- -- - 90 C3

title: 1.03  Inside a PE File
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: Every .exe and .dll on Windows is a Portable Executable - a DOS header pointing at the PE headers, a file header, an optional header with the entry point, image base and data directories, and a table of sections. RVAs versus file offsets, and how to convert between them. One format for every program Windows programs and libraries, .exe , .dll , .sys , all use the Portable Executable (PE) format. It tells the Windows loader how to map the file into memory, where execution starts, which DLLs and functions it needs, and where everything is. Reading it is the first thing every reverse engineering tool does. text file offset 0 +---------------------------+ DOS header ("MZ") e_lfanew at 0x3C - PE headers DOS stub "This program cannot be run in DOS mode." e_lfanew +---------------------------+ "PE\0\0" signature File header (20 bytes) machine, number of sections Optional header (240) entry point, image base, data directories Section table 40 bytes per section +---------------------------+ .text (code) .rdata (constants, imports) .data (globals) .pdata, .rsrc, .reloc ... +---------------------------+ All numbers are little-endian. Every structure here is in winnt.h under names like IMAGE_DOS_HEADER and IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 . The DOS header The file starts with the two bytes 4D 5A , "MZ", a leftover from MS-DOS that every PE still carries. Of the DOS header's fields only one still matters: the 4-byte e_lfanew at offset 0x3C , the file offset of the real PE headers. The NT headers At e_lfanew are the bytes 50 45 00 00 , "PE" and two zeros. Then: The file header ( IMAGE_FILE_HEADER , 20 bytes): Offset Size Field --- --- --- +0 2 Machine : 0x8664 for x64, 0x14C for 32-bit x86, 0xAA64 for ARM64 +2 2 NumberOfSections +4 4 TimeDateStamp : when it was linked (or a hash, in reproducible builds) +16 2 SizeOfOptionalHeader : 0xF0 for 64-bit images +18 2 Characteristics : flags such as "is a DLL" (0x2000) The optional header ( IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 , despite the name always present) starts right after it. The fields you will use most: Offset Size Field --- --- --- +0 2 Magic : 0x20B means 64-bit (PE32+), 0x10B 32-bit +16 4 AddressOfEntryPoint : where execution starts, as an RVA +24 8 ImageBase : the preferred load address, typically 0x140000000 for an .exe +32 4 SectionAlignment : sections start on multiples of this in memory (0x1000) +36 4 FileAlignment : and on multiples of this in the file (0x200) +56 4 SizeOfImage : total size once loaded +70 2 DllCharacteristics : flags such as ASLR-compatible (0x40) +112 16 × 8 the data directories Each data directory is an RVA and a size pointing at a table the loader needs. The important ones by index: 0 exports, 1 imports, 2 resources, 3 exceptions ( .pdata ), 5 base relocations, 6 debug information, 12 the import address table. Sections The section table follows the optional header: NumberOfSections entries of 40 bytes ( IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER ): Offset Size Field --- --- --- +0 8 Name , padded with zeros: .text , .rdata , .data ... +8 4 VirtualSize : size in memory +12 4 VirtualAddress : where it starts in memory, as an RVA +16 4 SizeOfRawData : size in the file +20 4 PointerToRawData : where it starts in the file +36 4 Characteristics : code (0x20), read (0x40000000), write (0x80000000), execute (0x20000000) The usual sections: .text for code (read + execute), .rdata for constants, strings and import tables (read only), .data for globals (read + write), .pdata for exception unwinding information, .rsrc for resources such as icons, .reloc for relocations. A section can be bigger in memory than in the file: .data holds zero-initialised globals that take no space on disk, so its VirtualSize exceeds its SizeOfRawData and the loader fills the rest with zeros. RVAs and file offsets Almost every address inside a PE is a relative virtual address (RVA): an offset from wherever the image is loaded in memory. Loaded at ImageBase , the real address is ImageBase + RVA ; with ASLR, the actual base differs each run, but RVAs stay the same. Reading the file instead of memory, you need to turn an RVA into a file offset. Find the section that contains it, then: file offset = RVA − section.VirtualAddress + section.PointerToRawData text .rdata: VirtualAddress 0x3000, PointerToRawData 0x1E00 RVA 0x3450 - 0x3450 - 0x3000 + 0x1E00 = 0x2250 in the file If the RVA falls in the part of a section beyond SizeOfRawData (the zero-filled tail), it has no bytes in the file at all. RVAs below the first section point into the headers, which are mapped at the same offsets in the file.

title: Reading the PE headers
body: Read the headers of a 64-bit PE file from its bytes (lesson 1.03), and convert RVAs to file offsets: cpp struct Section { std::string name; std::uint32_t virtualAddress, virtualSize, rawPointer, rawSize, characteristics; }; struct Headers { std::uint16_t machine; std::uint32_t entryPoint; std::uint64_t imageBase; std::vector<Section sections; }; std::optional<Headers readHeaders(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); std::optional<std::uint32_t rvaToOffset(const Headers& h, std::uint32_t rva); readHeaders returns std::nullopt unless the file starts with MZ , has the PE\0\0 signature at e_lfanew (offset 0x3C), and an optional header magic of 0x20B , with every header inside the file. The section table starts right after the optional header, whose size is in the file header. Section names are up to 8 characters, without the zero padding. rvaToOffset finds the section with virtualAddress <= rva < virtualAddress + virtualSize and returns rva - virtualAddress + rawPointer , or std::nullopt if no section contains it or the RVA is past the section's rawSize (in its zero-filled tail).

title: 1.04  Imports, Exports and Relocations
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: How a PE says which DLL functions it needs - import descriptors, the import name table and the import address table the loader fills in - how a DLL publishes its own functions in the export directory, and the base relocations that let an image load at any address. Imports tell a story A program reaches Windows and other libraries through imported functions. The import table lists every DLL and every function the program asked the linker for. Before reading any code, the imports alone tell you a great deal: - CreateFileW , ReadFile , WriteFile : it works with files. - RegOpenKeyExW , RegSetValueExW : it reads or writes the registry. - WSAStartup , connect , send , recv (from ws2_32.dll ): it talks over the network. - CreateProcessW , OpenProcess , ReadProcessMemory : it starts or inspects other processes. - Very few imports, just LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress : it looks up what it needs at run time, which hides its intentions from this kind of reading. The import directory Data directory 1 points at an array of import descriptors ( IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR , 20 bytes each), one per DLL, ending with one that is all zeros: Offset Field --- --- +0 OriginalFirstThunk : RVA of the import name table (INT) +12 Name : RVA of the DLL's name, a zero-terminated string such as KERNEL32.dll +16 FirstThunk : RVA of the import address table (IAT) The INT is an array of 8-byte entries (in 64-bit images), ending with a zero entry. Each entry says which function is wanted: - If the top bit is set ( 0x8000000000000000 ), the low 16 bits are an ordinal : the function's number in the DLL's export table. - Otherwise it is the RVA of an IMAGE_IMPORT_BY_NAME : a 2-byte hint (a guess at the function's position in the DLL's name list) followed by the function's name as a zero-terminated string. In the file, the IAT holds the same entries as the INT. When the program loads, the loader looks up each function in its DLL and overwrites each IAT entry with the function's real address . Calls to imported functions in the code are indirect calls through the IAT: nasm-norun call qword ptr rip+0x1A2B ; the IAT slot for CreateFileW That is why a disassembler can label such calls by name: it knows which IAT slot holds which import. Exports A DLL publishes its own functions in the export directory (data directory 0, IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY ): Offset Field --- --- +12 Name : RVA of the DLL's own name +16 Base : the ordinal of the first function, usually 1 +20 NumberOfFunctions +24 NumberOfNames +28 AddressOfFunctions : RVA of an array of function RVAs +32 AddressOfNames : RVA of an array of name RVAs, sorted alphabetically +36 AddressOfNameOrdinals : RVA of an array of 2-byte indexes into the functions array Finding a function by name, as GetProcAddress does: search the sorted names; at the same position in the name-ordinals array is an index; at that index in the functions array is the function's RVA. A function can also be exported by ordinal only, with no name. If a function's RVA points inside the export directory itself, it is a forwarder : the "address" is really a string such as NTDLL.RtlAllocateHeap , telling the loader to look in another DLL. Many kernel32.dll exports are forwarded this way. Base relocations Code contains some absolute addresses, for example a pointer to a global stored in a table. They are computed assuming the image loads at ImageBase . With ASLR it usually loads elsewhere, so each such address must be adjusted by the difference. The base relocation table (data directory 5, usually the .reloc section) lists every place that needs it, grouped by 4 KB page: a block header with the page's RVA and the block size, then 2-byte entries whose top 4 bits are a type (10, IMAGE_REL_BASED_DIR64 , for a 64-bit address) and low 12 bits an offset within the page. The loader adds actualBase - ImageBase to the 8 bytes at each location. x64 code itself mostly uses RIP-relative addressing ( rip+0x1234 ), which needs no relocation at all; relocations are mostly for pointers stored in data. That is one reason x64 programs relocate cheaply. For a reverse engineer this matters when comparing a running program with its file: bytes at relocated locations differ between the two by exactly the load difference, and tools (and the byte patterns of milestone 4) must allow for it.

title: Looking up exports
body: Do what GetProcAddress does, on a DLL image already loaded in memory (so every RVA is simply an index into image ): cpp struct Export { std::uint32_t rva; std::string forwarder; }; std::string dllName(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & image, std::uint32_t dirRva); std::optional<Export findByName(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & image, std::uint32_t dirRva, std::uint32_t dirSize, std::string_view name); std::optional<Export findByOrdinal(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & image, std::uint32_t dirRva, std::uint32_t dirSize, std::uint32_t ordinal); The export directory at dirRva is laid out as in lesson 1.04 ( Name at +12, Base at +16, NumberOfFunctions at +20, NumberOfNames at +24, then the three array RVAs at +28, +32 and +36). - dllName reads the zero-terminated name. - findByName finds the name in the sorted names array with a binary search (compare as std::strcmp would), takes the 2-byte index at the same position of the name-ordinals array, and returns the function RVA at that index. - findByOrdinal uses ordinal - Base as the index into the functions array. - In both, a missing name, an index outside the functions array or a function RVA of 0 gives std::nullopt . If the function RVA lies inside the export directory ( dirRva <= rva < dirRva + dirSize ), it is a forwarder : set forwarder to the string at that RVA.

title: 1.05  Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
match: 1.05 Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: The first half hour with an unknown program - strings in ASCII and UTF-16, imports and exports, the compiler and runtime it was built with, the PDB path in its debug directory, resources, section entropy and the signs of packing - before reading any code. Look before you read Opening an unknown program straight in a disassembler and starting at the entry point is the slow way. A short triage first tells you what kind of program it is, what it is likely to do, and where to start reading. Everything here is static and quick. Strings Text in a program is often its most informative content: error messages, file names, registry keys, URLs, format strings, debug messages left in by the developers. Windows programs store text in two encodings, and you need both: - ASCII / UTF-8 : one byte per character, 48 65 6C 6C 6F for "Hello". - UTF-16LE : two bytes per character, the Windows "wide" strings used by every W function: 48 00 65 00 6C 00 6C 00 6F 00 . A strings tool scans the file for runs of printable characters (usually at least 4 or 5 long) in both forms. In a disassembler, each string becomes a landmark: find "Invalid licence file" and look at the code that refers to it, and you are in the licence check; find %s\\saves\\slot%d.dat and you have found the save code. Imports and exports The import table (lesson 1.04) is a summary of capabilities. Sort the imports by DLL and read the list: DLL Suggests --- --- ws2_32.dll , winhttp.dll , wininet.dll network advapi32.dll (Reg , Crypt ) registry, services, older cryptography bcrypt.dll , ncrypt.dll cryptography d3d11.dll , dxgi.dll , opengl32.dll graphics user32.dll (CreateWindowEx, GetMessage) a window and a message loop dbghelp.dll symbol handling, crash dumps A DLL's exports are its whole public interface, often with descriptive names. Compiler and runtime How a program was built changes what its code looks like, so identify it early: - Rich header : MSVC-linked files have an undocumented block between the DOS stub and the PE header (the word Rich marks its end) listing the tool versions used. - Imports of the runtime : vcruntime140.dll and api-ms-win-crt- mean Visual C++ 2015 or later; msvcrt.dll with MinGW-style names means GCC; libstdc++ names mean GCC or Clang with the GNU library. - Characteristic code : MSVC's __security_check_cookie calls at function ends (the /GS check from the Pointers and Memory course), its exception tables in .pdata . - Programs written in .NET are a different world: a tiny native stub and a large block of .NET metadata and bytecode, best opened with a .NET decompiler (ILSpy, dnSpy) instead. The debug directory Data directory 6 points at debug information. For MSVC builds it usually contains a CodeView record with the path of the PDB file as it was on the build machine: text C:\Users\dev\source\repos\Inventory\x64\Release\Inventory.pdb That gives you the project's name and sometimes the developer's folder layout. If the matching PDB is available (Microsoft publishes them for Windows' own DLLs on its symbol server), every tool can show real function names: always look before working without them. Resources The .rsrc section holds icons, dialogs, menus, string tables, version information (product name, company, version number), and sometimes whole embedded files. Resource Hacker or PE viewers list them. Entropy and packing Entropy measures how random a block of bytes looks, from 0 bits per byte (all the same byte) to 8 (perfectly random). Ordinary machine code sits around 5 to 6.5; text lower; compressed or encrypted data close to 8. A section with entropy near 8, together with very few imports and an entry point outside .text , usually means the program is packed : compressed or encrypted, with a small stub that unpacks the real code at run time. Packers are used to make programs smaller and, often, to make them harder to analyse; malware uses them heavily. Static analysis of a packed file mostly sees the stub; the real code appears only in memory, after it unpacks. Shannon entropy over a block of bytes: H = − Σ p(b) × log₂ p(b), over the byte values b that occur, where p(b) is how often b occurs divided by the block size. A triage checklist 1. File type, 32 or 64 bit, .exe or .dll, native or .NET. 2. Compiler and runtime. 3. Sections: names, sizes, permissions, entropy. Anything writable and executable is unusual. 4. Imports, grouped by DLL. Exports, if a DLL. 5. Strings, both encodings, skimmed for landmarks. 6. Debug directory and PDB path; are symbols available? 7. Resources and version information. Write down what you find. The next step, reading code, starts from these landmarks.

title: Strings and entropy
where: 1.05 Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
body: Two triage tools from lesson 1.05: cpp struct FoundString { std::size_t offset; std::string text; bool wide; }; std::vector<FoundString findStrings(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, std::size_t minLength); double entropy(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, std::size_t begin, std::size_t size); findStrings finds text of at least minLength characters, where a character is a printable byte from 0x20 to 0x7E: - ASCII strings: runs of printable bytes. - Wide (UTF-16LE) strings: runs of pairs "printable byte, then 0x00", starting at any offset. text holds just the characters ( "Wide" , not the zeros), and wide is true. - Results are sorted by offset; at the same offset an ASCII string comes first. Report each whole run once, not the shorter runs inside it. entropy is the Shannon entropy in bits per byte of size bytes starting at begin : -sum(p log2(p)) over the byte values present, where p is that value's count divided by size . An empty range has entropy 0.

title: A PE inspector
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format projects
body: Build the core of a PE viewer like PE-bear or dumpbin : load a 64-bit PE file from its bytes, list its sections, find which section an RVA belongs to, and list every import. cpp struct Section { std::string name; std::uint32_t virtualAddress, virtualSize, rawPointer, rawSize, characteristics; }; struct Import { std::string dll; std::string function; std::uint16_t ordinal; }; class PeFile { public: bool load(std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes); std::uint32_t entryPoint() const; std::uint64_t imageBase() const; const std::vector<Section & sections() const; std::optional<std::uint32_t rvaToOffset(std::uint32_t rva) const; std::string sectionOf(std::uint32_t rva) const; std::string permissions(const Section& s) const; std::vector<Import imports() const; }; - load keeps the bytes and reads the headers as in lesson 1.03; it returns false (and the object holds nothing) for anything that is not a valid 64-bit PE. - rvaToOffset as in the practice; sectionOf names the section containing an RVA, or returns "" . - permissions gives three characters for a section: r or - , w or - , x or - (read 0x40000000, write 0x80000000, execute 0x20000000). - imports reads the import directory (data directory 1, whose RVA is at offset 120 of the optional header): one descriptor of 20 bytes per DLL, until an all-zero one. For each, read the DLL name, then the 8-byte thunks of its import name table ( OriginalFirstThunk , or FirstThunk when that is 0) until a zero thunk. A thunk with the top bit set is an import by ordinal ( function empty, ordinal the low 16 bits); otherwise it is the RVA of a 2-byte hint and the name ( ordinal 0). Imports are listed in file order. Any RVA that cannot be turned into a file offset stops the reading cleanly, returning what was read so far.

title: 2.01  x64 for Readers
body: The x64 you need to read compiled code rather than write it - registers and their smaller parts, the handful of instructions that make up most programs, flags and conditional jumps, and the Microsoft x64 calling convention that tells you where every argument and return value is. Reading, not writing Writing assembly means choosing instructions. Reading it means recognising patterns quickly, and compiled code uses a surprisingly small set of them. This lesson is a refresher aimed at reading the output of MSVC, in the Intel syntax that Visual Studio, x64dbg, WinDbg and Ghidra all show: destination first. nasm-norun mov rax, qword ptr rcx+10h ; rax = the 8 bytes at rcx + 0x10 (Disassemblers write hex either as 10h or 0x10 . They mean the same.) Registers Sixteen 64-bit general registers. Each has smaller views of its low part: 64 32 16 8 Usual role in compiled code --- --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al return value, scratch rcx ecx cx cl 1st argument, this rdx edx dx dl 2nd argument rbx ebx bx bl kept across calls rsp esp sp spl stack pointer rbp ebp bp bpl kept across calls, sometimes frame pointer rsi , rdi esi , edi kept across calls; string copies r8 , r9 r8d , r9d r8w r8b 3rd and 4th arguments r10 , r11 scratch r12 to r15 kept across calls Plus rip , the instruction pointer, and sixteen 128-bit xmm0 to xmm15 registers for floating point and SIMD. One rule catches everyone: writing a 32-bit register clears the top 32 bits of the 64-bit one. mov eax, 1 sets all of rax to 1, and xor eax, eax is the compiler's favourite way to zero rax (it is shorter than xor rax, rax ). Writing 8 or 16-bit parts leaves the rest alone. The instructions you will see most Instruction Does --- --- mov a, b copy movzx , movsx , movsxd copy a small value into a bigger register, zero- or sign-extending lea a, expr compute the address expression, without reading memory; also used for arithmetic: lea eax, rcx+rcx 4 is eax = ecx 5 add , sub , imul , neg , inc , dec arithmetic and , or , xor , not , shl , shr , sar bits; sar is a signed shift, often division by a power of two cmp a, b compute a - b , set the flags, keep nothing else test a, b compute a & b , set the flags; test eax, eax asks "is eax zero (or negative)?" jcc target jump if a condition holds (table below) jmp target jump always call target , ret function call and return push , pop save and restore registers on the stack cmovcc , setcc conditional move or set a byte from the flags, without jumping Flags and conditional jumps cmp and test set flags; the conditional jump that follows reads them. The jump names say whether the comparison was signed or unsigned , which tells you the type of the variables: Signed Unsigned After cmp a, b , jumps if --- --- --- jl jb a < b jle jbe a <= b jg ja a b jge jae a = b je / jz a == b jne / jnz a != b jl / jg mean the source compared int s; jb / ja mean unsigned , sizes or pointers. A bounds check written as one unsigned comparison, cmp ecx, 10; jae out_of_range , catches negative indexes too, because they look huge when unsigned. The Microsoft x64 calling convention Every function call on 64-bit Windows follows one convention, so you always know where the arguments are: - The first four arguments go in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , or in xmm0 to xmm3 if they are float or double . The position counts, not the type: in f(int a, double b, int c) , a is in rcx , b in xmm1 , c in r8 . - Further arguments go on the stack. The caller always reserves 32 bytes of shadow space just above the return address for the callee to save the four register arguments in, so the 5th argument is at rsp+28h on entry to the function (8 for the return address, 0x20 of shadow space), the 6th at rsp+30h , and so on. - The return value comes back in rax , or xmm0 for floating point. - rax , rcx , rdx , r8 to r11 and xmm0 to xmm5 are volatile : a call may destroy them. rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 to r15 and xmm6 to xmm15 are non-volatile : a function that uses them must save and restore them, which is exactly what its prologue's pushes are. - For a member function, this is the hidden first argument, in rcx . So when you see a call, look just before it for writes to rcx , rdx , r8 and r9 : those are its arguments. Just after it, a read of eax or rax is using its result. nasm-norun mov r8d, 3 ; third argument: 3 lea rdx, rsp+40h ; second argument: the address of a local mov rcx, rbx ; first argument: whatever rbx holds call ReadConfig test eax, eax ; did it return 0? je failed

title: Where are the arguments?
body: Apply the Microsoft x64 calling convention (lesson 2.01): cpp enum class Kind { Integer, Floating }; std::vector<std::string argumentLocations(const std::vector<Kind & args); std::string returnLocation(Kind result); bool isVolatile(const std::string& reg); - argumentLocations gives where each argument is on entry to the function. Position decides the register: the first four go in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 if they are integers or pointers, or xmm0 to xmm3 if floating point. Later arguments are on the stack: the 5th at rsp+0x28 , the 6th at rsp+0x30 , and so on in steps of 8, whatever their kind. - returnLocation is rax for integers and xmm0 for floating point. - isVolatile is true for registers a call may destroy: rax , rcx , rdx , r8 to r11 , and xmm0 to xmm5 . Everything else ( rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , rsp , r12 to r15 , xmm6 to xmm15 ) is non-volatile.

title: 2.02  Recognising Functions
body: Where functions start and end in a binary without symbols - prologues that save registers and reserve stack, epilogues, leaf functions, int3 padding, the .pdata table that lists every function, thunks and tail calls, and following the C runtime's start-up code to main. No labels in machine code A .exe does not record where one function ends and the next begins. The bytes run on; only the call instructions and a few tables tell you where functions are. Disassemblers find functions with a mix of the evidence below, and when they get it wrong (and they sometimes do) you need to recognise the signs yourself. Prologues A function that calls others or uses non-volatile registers starts by setting itself up: nasm-norun mov qword ptr rsp+8 , rbx ; save rbx in the shadow space the caller reserved push rdi ; save rdi sub rsp, 30h ; reserve stack: 0x20 shadow space for calls it makes, plus locals The common forms in MSVC output: Bytes Instruction --- --- 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx (save to shadow space) 40 53 push rbx with a do-nothing REX prefix, used so the instruction is 2 bytes for hot-patching 55 , 56 , 57 push rbp , push rsi , push rdi 41 54 ... 41 57 push r12 ... push r15 48 83 EC 28 sub rsp, 28h (small frame) 48 81 EC 50 01 00 00 sub rsp, 150h (large frame) The stack must be 16-byte aligned at every call . On entry the return address has just been pushed, so rsp is 8 more than a multiple of 16; that is why frames are odd multiples of 8 when nothing else is pushed: sub rsp, 28h , 38h , 48h . Functions with large local arrays first call __chkstk (it touches each new page of stack in order, for the guard page of the Pointers and Memory course). Functions with buffers start with the /GS cookie: mov rax, __security_cookie ; xor rax, rsp; mov rsp+... , rax , and end with the matching check. Epilogues The end undoes the start, in reverse: nasm-norun mov rbx, qword ptr rsp+40h ; restore rbx (8 + 30h + 8 further up now) add rsp, 30h pop rdi ret There can be several epilogues in one function, one per return , or one shared epilogue that every path jumps to. Leaf functions A function that calls nothing and needs no non-volatile registers needs no frame at all: nasm-norun lea eax, rcx+rdx 2 ; return a + b 2 ret Small leaf functions are common, and they often have no recognisable prologue. In Release builds many of them disappear entirely, inlined into their callers. int3 padding MSVC starts functions on 16-byte boundaries and fills the gaps between them with CC bytes, the int3 breakpoint instruction. A run of CC s after a ret or a jmp is a reliable sign that a new function follows. ( CC can also appear inside an instruction, as part of an immediate or displacement, so it is evidence, not proof.) .pdata: the list of functions On x64 Windows there is a better source. The exception directory (data directory 3, the .pdata section) holds a RUNTIME_FUNCTION entry for every function that has a frame: three RVAs, the function's start, its end, and its unwind information. Windows needs these to unwind the stack for exceptions and to walk call stacks in a debugger, so they are always present and always right. Disassemblers use them first; leaf functions without frames are the only ones missing. The unwind information also records exactly what the prologue does (which registers were pushed, how big the frame is), which is how a debugger rebuilds a call stack without frame pointers. Thunks and tail calls - A thunk is a tiny function that only jumps somewhere else: jmp qword ptr __imp_CreateFileW for an import, or a stub that adjusts this and jumps to the real member function. - A tail call is a function ending with jmp OtherFunction instead of call and ret : the optimiser reuses the frame. Do not mistake that jmp for a jump inside the same function. Finding main The entry point in the PE header is not your main . In an MSVC program it is mainCRTStartup , which sets up the C runtime, runs global constructors and then calls main . A reliable route: from the entry point, follow the jump to __scrt_common_main_seh ; near its end it calls _get_initial_narrow_environment , __p___argv and __p___argc and then a function with those results in r8 , rdx and ecx : that call is main(argc, argv, envp) . For a GUI program it is WinMain , called with the instance handle in rcx . With practice, finding main takes a minute.

title: Finding functions in raw code
body: Find likely function starts in a block of MSVC x64 machine code with no symbols, using the two kinds of evidence from lesson 2.02: cpp bool looksLikePrologue(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at); std::vector<std::size_t findFunctions(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code); looksLikePrologue is true when the bytes at at begin with one of these ( ?? is any byte), with every byte of the pattern inside the buffer: Pattern Instruction --- --- 55 , 53 , 56 , 57 push rbp , push rbx , push rsi , push rdi 40 53 , 40 55 , 40 56 , 40 57 the same pushes with a REX prefix 41 54 , 41 55 , 41 56 , 41 57 push r12 to push r15 48 83 EC ?? sub rsp, imm8 48 81 EC ?? ?? ?? ?? sub rsp, imm32 48 89 ?? 24 ?? or 4C 89 ?? 24 ?? where the third byte's bits match 01 ??? 100 saving a register at rsp+imm8 findFunctions returns, in increasing order, every offset that is a candidate and looks like a prologue. Offset 0 is always a candidate; so is any offset whose byte is not CC but the byte before it is CC (the end of int3 padding).

title: 2.03  Branches, Loops and Switches
body: What if, else, && and , for and while loops and switch statements compile into, how to read a function as a graph of basic blocks, and the jump tables that big switch statements become. Basic blocks Inside a function, code runs straight down until a jump. A basic block is a run of instructions with one way in (its first instruction) and one way out (its last). Every disassembler shows a function as a graph of blocks joined by arrows, the control flow graph , and reading that graph is most of reading a function. A new block starts: - at the function's first instruction; - at every jump target; - right after every jump or ret (the fall-through of a conditional jump, or simply code that something else jumps to). A call does not end a block: the call returns and execution carries on. if and else The compiler usually inverts the condition and jumps over the "then" part: cpp-norun if (health <= 0) die(); else heal(5); nasm-norun test ecx, ecx ; health in ecx jg else_part ; NOT (health <= 0): skip the then part call die jmp done else_part: mov ecx, 5 call heal done: When you read test / cmp followed by a jump, the jump is usually the opposite of the condition in the source. && and Short-circuit operators become a chain of jumps. if (a 0 && b 0) f(); jumps past f as soon as either test fails: nasm-norun test ecx, ecx jle skip test edx, edx jle skip call f skip: jumps into the body as soon as one test succeeds. Two jumps to the same place mean && ; a jump into the body followed by a test of the next condition means . Loops A for or while loop has a backwards jump: a jump to an address earlier in the function. That is the quickest way to spot a loop in a listing. cpp-norun for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) total += values i ; Optimised compilers usually test once before the loop and then use a do-while shape with the test at the bottom, which saves a jump per iteration: nasm-norun xor eax, eax ; total test edx, edx ; count <= 0? skip the loop entirely jle done xor r8d, r8d ; i top: add eax, dword ptr rcx+r8 4 inc r8 cmp r8, rdx jl top ; backwards: the loop done: ret Recognise the parts: initialisation before, the body, the increment, the compare and the backward jump. Optimised loops are often unrolled (the body repeated several times per jump) or vectorised (SIMD instructions handling four or eight elements at once), with a small extra loop for the leftovers. Switch statements A switch with a few cases becomes a chain of comparisons. A switch with many cases over a dense range of values becomes a jump table : an array of addresses indexed by the value. nasm-norun sub ecx, 1 ; cases 1..5: make the index start at 0 cmp ecx, 4 ja default_case ; unsigned: also catches values below 1 lea rdx, __ImageBase ; the module's base address movsxd rcx, ecx mov eax, dword ptr rdx+rcx 4+3A40h ; table of 32-bit RVAs at RVA 0x3A40 add rax, rdx ; RVA + base = address of the case jmp rax MSVC stores the table as RVAs (4 bytes each) and adds the image base, so the table needs no relocations. Reading the table gives you the address of every case. The ja before it handles every value outside the table, including negative ones, with one unsigned comparison. Conditional moves Small if s are often compiled without jumps at all: nasm-norun cmp ecx, edx mov eax, edx cmovl eax, ecx ; eax = (ecx < edx) ? ecx : edx - std::min cmovcc and setcc ( setl al : set al to 1 if less) are branch-free, so they leave the control flow graph simpler than the source was.

title: Basic blocks
body: Split a function's instructions into basic blocks and connect them, as a disassembler does before drawing a graph (lesson 2.03). Instructions are given already decoded: cpp enum class Op { Plain, Call, Jump, Branch, Return }; struct Insn { std::uint32_t address; std::uint32_t length; Op op; std::uint32_t target; }; struct Block { std::uint32_t start; std::uint32_t end; std::vector<std::uint32_t successors; }; std::vector<Block basicBlocks(const std::vector<Insn & code); code is in address order with no gaps. Jump is an unconditional jmp , Branch a conditional jump, Call a call (its target is another function), Return a ret . target only matters for Jump and Branch . - A block starts at the first instruction, at every Jump / Branch target that is one of the instructions, and at the instruction after any Jump , Branch or Return . - A block's end is the address just past its last instruction. - Successors : a block ending in Jump goes to its target; one ending in Branch goes to its target and falls through to the next instruction; one ending in Return has none; any other block falls through to the next block. A target outside the function (a tail call) is not a successor. Successors are sorted with no duplicates, and fall-through past the last instruction does not count. - Blocks are returned sorted by start.

title: 2.04  Data in Machine Code
body: Recognising locals, globals, struct members, arrays and strings in disassembly - what the addressing modes reveal, how sizes and signedness show the types, floating point in xmm registers, and rebuilding a struct by collecting every offset the code uses. Addresses tell you what the data is Every memory operand in x64 has the form base + index scale + displacement , and the shape of it is a strong hint about the data being reached: Operand Usually means --- --- rsp+40h , rbp-10h a local variable or spilled value in the current frame rip+1A2Bh (shown as a name like dword_140005000 ) a global or a constant in the image rcx+18h a member at offset 0x18 of the struct rcx points at rax+rdx 4 element rdx of an array of 4-byte things starting at rax rax+rdx 8+10h element rdx of an array of 8-byte things that starts at offset 0x10 of a struct rcx+rdx byte rdx of a buffer, or an array of 1-byte things The scale (1, 2, 4 or 8) is the element size. A stride that is not a power of two shows up as a multiplication first: imul rdx, rdx, 1Ch then rax+rdx is an array of 28-byte structs. Sizes and signedness The size of a memory access gives the size of the field: Access Size --- --- byte ptr , al , movzx eax, byte ptr 1 word ptr , ax 2 dword ptr , eax 4 qword ptr , rax 8 Signedness shows in how a small value is widened and compared: - movsx / movsxd (sign-extend) and jl / jg mean signed: char , short , int . - movzx (zero-extend) and jb / ja mean unsigned: unsigned char , bool , uint16_t , sizes. An 8-byte value that is later used as rax+... is a pointer. One that is passed to printf with %llu is a number. Floating point float and double live in xmm registers and use their own instructions: Instruction Means --- --- movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+10h load a float movsd xmm0, qword ptr rcx+10h load a double addss , mulss , subsd , divsd ... arithmetic; ss = single (float), sd = double comiss , ucomisd compare, then ja / jb (floating point compares use the unsigned conditions) cvtsi2ss , cvttss2si int to float, float to int (truncating) So a 4-byte field read with movss is a float , not an int . Strings and constants Code that uses a string literal loads its address with a RIP-relative lea : nasm-norun lea rcx, rip+2F1Ah ; disassemblers show: lea rcx, aSaveFailedS "Save failed: %s" call printf That is how the strings you found in triage (lesson 1.05) lead you to code: ask the disassembler for cross-references to the string, and it lists every instruction that loads its address. Floating-point constants also live in .rdata : mulss xmm0, dword ptr __real@3f000000 is "multiply by 0.5" (0x3F000000 is the bits of 0.5f, readable with lesson 2.05's bit tricks from the Pointers and Memory course). Rebuilding a struct Without source, you reconstruct a struct by collecting every access through the same pointer. Suppose in a function where rcx is a Player you see: nasm-norun mov eax, dword ptr rcx+0Ch ; 4 bytes at 0x0C movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+10h ; a float at 0x10 movss xmm1, dword ptr rcx+14h ; a float at 0x14 movzx edx, byte ptr rcx+18h ; an unsigned byte at 0x18 mov r8, qword ptr rcx+20h ; 8 bytes at 0x20, used later as r8+... : a pointer Written down as a struct, with gaps kept as padding: cpp-norun struct Player { std::uint8_t unknown_00 0x0C ; std::int32_t field_0C; float field_10; float field_14; // two floats in a row: probably x, y std::uint8_t field_18; // compared with 0 and 1 elsewhere: a bool std::uint8_t pad_19 7 ; Thing field_20; }; Then you rename fields as you learn what they are: field_10 and field_14 are written by the movement code, so they become x and y . Every disassembler lets you define such structs and apply them, so the listing shows rcx+Player.x instead of rcx+10h . The reconstruction grows as you read more functions that use the same struct, and its size usually comes from the new or malloc call that creates it: mov ecx, 30h; call operator new means the object is 0x30 bytes.

title: Rebuilding a struct from accesses
body: Turn a list of memory accesses seen through one pointer into a C++ struct definition, as lesson 2.04 does by hand: cpp struct Access { std::uint32_t offset; std::uint32_t size; bool isFloat; bool isSigned; }; std::string recoverStruct(const std::string& name, std::vector<Access accesses, std::uint32_t totalSize); - Sort accesses by offset. Accesses at the same offset merge into one field: the largest size wins, and it is floating point if any of them was, signed if any was. - An access that starts inside the previous field is ignored. - Field types: size 1 std::int8_t / std::uint8_t , 2 std::int16_t / std::uint16_t , 4 std::int32_t / std::uint32_t or float , 8 std::int64_t / std::uint64_t or double . Signed types when isSigned ; float / double when isFloat . - Fields are named field_ and the offset as at least two uppercase hex digits: field_0C , field_1A0 . - A gap before a field, or between the last field and totalSize , becomes std::uint8_t pad_XX n ; with XX the gap's offset written the same way. The output is exactly: text struct Player { std::uint8_t pad_00 12 ; std::int32_t field_0C; float field_10; }; with four spaces before each member and a newline after every line, including the last.

title: 2.05  C++ in Machine Code
body: How C++ features look once compiled by MSVC - this in rcx, constructors that install the vtable pointer, virtual calls through vtable slots, RTTI and the type names it leaves in the binary, name mangling, and the layouts of std::string and std::vector. Methods are functions with this A member function is an ordinary function with a hidden first argument, this , so in MSVC x64 it arrives in rcx . Code that reads rcx+... at the top of a function and never sets rcx first is usually a method reading its own members: nasm-norun Player::takeDamage: sub dword ptr rcx+0Ch , edx ; this- health -= amount ret Ordinary arguments shift up one place: the first visible argument is in rdx , the second in r8 . Constructors install the vtable A class with virtual functions has a hidden pointer at offset 0 to its class's vtable (lesson 3.05 of the Pointers and Memory course). The constructor writes it before anything else: nasm-norun Archer::Archer: lea rax, Archer:: vftable' ; the address of Archer's table in .rdata mov qword ptr rcx , rax ; this- vptr = &table mov dword ptr rcx+8 , 64h ; this- health = 100 mov rax, rcx ; constructors return this ret A derived class's constructor calls the base constructor first (which writes the base vtable) and then overwrites offset 0 with its own. Finding every place that stores a particular vtable address finds every constructor of that class. The vtable itself, in .rdata , is an array of function addresses: listing it gives you every virtual function of the class, in declaration order. Virtual calls A call through a vtable is unmistakable: nasm-norun mov rax, qword ptr rcx ; the object's vtable pointer call qword ptr rax+18h ; slot 3 (0x18 / 8) of the table The displacement divided by 8 is the slot number . To find which function runs, find the object's actual class (its constructor, or the vtable pointer seen in memory in a debugger) and read that slot of its table. The same call can reach different functions for different objects; that is the point of virtual functions, and it is why static analysis alone sometimes cannot say where a call goes. RTTI If run-time type information is on (the default in MSVC; /GR ), every polymorphic class leaves its name in the binary. Just before each vtable (at vftable - 8 ) is a pointer to a Complete Object Locator , which leads to a type descriptor containing the mangled class name: text .?AVArcher@@ class Archer .?AVUnit@Game@@ class Game::Unit .?AUVec3@@ struct Vec3 These strings survive even in Release builds with no PDB, so searching a binary for .?AV lists its polymorphic classes, and the locator next to each vtable tells you which class the table belongs to. Ghidra and IDA read RTTI automatically and name vtables and classes for you. Name mangling C++ allows overloading, so the linker needs a unique name for each function. MSVC encodes the scope, name and signature into a decorated name: Decorated Means --- --- ?update@Player@@QEAAXM@Z public: void Player::update(float) ?attack@Enemy@Game@@QEAAHH@Z public: int Game::Enemy::attack(int) ??0Player@@QEAA@XZ Player::Player(void) : the constructor ??1Player@@UEAA@XZ virtual Player::~Player(void) : the destructor The pieces after ? up to @@ are the name and then its enclosing scopes, innermost first. ??0 and ??1 mark constructors and destructors. The undname tool from Visual Studio decodes any of them fully. You meet decorated names in exports, in imports from C++ DLLs, and in RTTI. Standard library layouts Recognising standard containers in memory saves a lot of time. In MSVC's Release builds: std::string is 32 bytes: Offset Holds --- --- 0x00 either the text itself (up to 15 characters, the small string buffer) or a pointer to it on the heap 0x10 the size 0x18 the capacity: 15 while the text is inline So code that does cmp qword ptr rcx+18h , 0Fh and then picks between rcx and rcx is reading a std::string 's text: "if the capacity is above 15, follow the pointer". std::vector<T is three pointers, 24 bytes: first element, one past the last element, end of the allocated capacity. Its size is (end - begin) / sizeof(T) , which compiles to a subtraction and a shift or division: sub rax, rcx; sar rax, 3 is the size of a vector of 8-byte elements. std::unique_ptr<T is just the pointer; std::shared_ptr<T is two pointers, object then control block. Debug builds add checking members and change these layouts; always reverse the build configuration that you actually have.

title: Virtual calls and decorated names
body: Two everyday jobs when reading C++ binaries (lesson 2.05). Memory is simulated as a map from 8-aligned addresses to 8-byte values: cpp using Memory = std::map<std::uint64_t, std::uint64_t ; int slotOf(std::uint32_t displacement); std::optional<std::uint64_t virtualTarget(const Memory& m, std::uint64_t object, std::uint32_t displacement); std::optional<std::string classOf(const Memory& m, const std::map<std::uint64_t, std::string & locators, std::uint64_t object); std::string undecorate(const std::string& name); - slotOf turns the displacement in call qword ptr rax+disp into a slot number ( 0x18 is slot 3). - virtualTarget does what a virtual call does: read the vtable pointer at object , then the function address at vtable + displacement . Any missing value, or a vtable pointer of 0, gives std::nullopt . - classOf reads the vtable pointer at object , then the locator pointer stored just before the table (at vtable - 8 ), and looks that locator up in locators to get the class name. - undecorate turns an MSVC decorated name into its qualified name: - ?name@Scope1@Scope2@@... becomes Scope2::Scope1::name (the parts after ? up to @@ are the name, then scopes innermost first; everything after @@ is ignored). - ??0Class@...@@... is a constructor: ...::Class::Class . ??1Class@...@@... is a destructor: ...::Class::~Class . - A name not starting with ? is returned unchanged.

title: A control flow graph with loops
match: A control flow graph with loops
body: Build the analysis behind a disassembler's graph view: basic blocks, which blocks can be reached at all, which jumps go backwards, and the natural loops they form. cpp enum class Op { Plain, Call, Jump, Branch, Return }; struct Insn { std::uint32_t address; std::uint32_t length; Op op; std::uint32_t target; }; struct Block { std::uint32_t start; std::uint32_t end; std::vector<std::uint32_t successors; }; struct Loop { std::uint32_t header; std::vector<std::uint32_t body; }; class Graph { public: explicit Graph(const std::vector<Insn & code); const std::vector<Block & blocks() const; std::optional<std::uint32_t blockOf(std::uint32_t address) const; std::vector<std::uint32_t predecessors(std::uint32_t block) const; std::vector<std::uint32_t unreachable() const; std::vector<std::pair<std::uint32_t, std::uint32_t backEdges() const; std::vector<Loop loops() const; }; - Blocks follow exactly the rules of the practice in lesson 2.03. Blocks are identified by their start address. - blockOf gives the start of the block containing an address ( start <= address < end ), or std::nullopt . - predecessors lists, sorted, the blocks that have the given block as a successor. - unreachable lists, sorted, blocks that cannot be reached by following successors from the first block. (Code after a ret that nothing jumps to is often a sign of a misidentified function or a jump table you have not resolved.) - backEdges lists every edge from - to whose target block starts at or before the source block's start, sorted by from then to . In compiled code these are the loops' jumps back to the top. - loops : for each block that is the target of at least one back edge (the loop header ), the body is the header plus every block from which some back-edge source can be reached by walking predecessors without passing through the header. Bodies are sorted; loops are sorted by header.

title: 3.01  How Debuggers Work
body: A debugger is an ordinary program using the Windows debugging API - debug events, software breakpoints made from a single int3 byte, single-stepping with the trap flag, the four hardware breakpoint registers, and first- and second-chance exceptions. A program that controls another A debugger is not magic built into Windows; it is a program that uses a documented API. It either starts the target with CreateProcessW(..., DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS, ...) or attaches to a running one with DebugActiveProcess(pid) . From then on, whenever something interesting happens in the target, Windows freezes every thread of the target and reports a debug event to the debugger: cpp-norun DEBUG_EVENT event{}; while (WaitForDebugEvent(&event, INFINITE)) { switch (event.dwDebugEventCode) { case CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: / the process started: its image base, entry point / break; case LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT: / a DLL loaded: its base address / break; case EXCEPTION_DEBUG_EVENT: / a breakpoint, a single step, or a real crash / break; case EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: return; } ContinueDebugEvent(event.dwProcessId, event.dwThreadId, DBG_CONTINUE); // let it run again } While the target is frozen, the debugger reads and writes its memory ( ReadProcessMemory , WriteProcessMemory ) and its registers ( GetThreadContext , SetThreadContext ). Everything a debugger shows you comes from those four calls. Software breakpoints: one byte To stop at an address, the debugger overwrites the first byte of the instruction there with 0xCC , the one-byte int3 instruction, after saving the original byte. text before: 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx armed: CC 89 5C 24 08 int3 (and garbage after it) When the target executes int3 , the processor raises a breakpoint exception, Windows freezes the process, and the debugger gets an EXCEPTION_DEBUG_EVENT with code EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT (0x80000003). Then it must clean up carefully: 1. int3 has already executed, so rip points one byte past the breakpoint. Set rip back by one. 2. Write the original byte back, so the real instruction can run. 3. To keep the breakpoint for next time, it cannot simply write CC back now: the instruction has not run yet. So it sets the trap flag and continues; after exactly one instruction the processor stops again with a single-step exception; the debugger re-writes CC and continues normally. When the debugger shows you memory, it shows the saved original bytes , not the CC s, so you never see them. But the program can: code that reads its own bytes (a checksum of its code, for example) sees a CC where a breakpoint is set. That is one reason the next kind exists. Single-stepping Bit 8 of the EFLAGS register is the trap flag (TF). When it is set, the processor raises a single-step exception ( EXCEPTION_SINGLE_STEP , 0x80000004) after executing one instruction. "Step into" is: set TF, continue, wait for the event. "Step over" a call is: put a temporary breakpoint on the instruction after the call and run. Hardware breakpoints The processor has four debug registers , DR0 to DR3 , each holding an address, and a control register DR7 that says for each one: - whether it is enabled; - what triggers it: execute , write , or read or write ; - how many bytes it covers: 1, 2, 4 or 8. When the condition is met, the processor raises a single-step exception and DR6 says which one fired. Because nothing in memory changes, hardware breakpoints are invisible to code that checksums itself, and they can do something software breakpoints cannot: stop when data is written or read. A data breakpoint ("break when this address is written") is the tool of lesson 3.03. There are only four, and they are per thread: the debugger sets them in every thread's context. Exceptions: first and second chance Breakpoints are exceptions, but so are real errors. When any exception happens in a debugged process, the debugger hears about it first (a first-chance exception) and can choose: - DBG_CONTINUE : "I handled it" (used for its own breakpoints); - DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED : "pass it to the program's own handlers". If the program's own handlers (C++ catch , __try / __except ) do not handle it either, the debugger is told a second time, second chance , just before the process would die. Many programs throw and catch exceptions in normal operation, which is why debuggers let you choose which first-chance exceptions stop and which only get logged.

title: Software breakpoints
body: Manage software breakpoints over a block of code the way a debugger does (lesson 3.01). The code is a byte buffer; address base + i is byte i . cpp class Breakpoints { public: Breakpoints(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::uint64_t base); bool set(std::uint64_t address); bool remove(std::uint64_t address); bool isSet(std::uint64_t address) const; std::vector<std::uint8_t view() const; std::optional<std::uint64_t onBreakpoint(std::uint64_t& rip); void onSingleStep(); }; - set saves the original byte and writes 0xCC . Setting one that is already set, or an address outside the code, returns false. - remove writes the original byte back. False if there is no breakpoint there. - view returns the code as the user should see it: with the original bytes in place of every CC you wrote. - onBreakpoint is called when the target stops on an int3 with rip already past it. If rip - 1 is one of your breakpoints: move rip back by one, put the original byte back so the instruction can run, remember that this breakpoint must be re-armed , and return its address. Otherwise (an int3 that was in the program itself) return std::nullopt and change nothing. - onSingleStep is called after the target has executed that one instruction: write 0xCC again for the breakpoint waiting to be re-armed, if it is still set.

title: 3.02  Tracing Execution
body: Following what a program actually does - stepping into, over and out, rebuilding the call stack from return addresses, naming addresses as module plus symbol plus offset, conditional and logging breakpoints, and recording traces. Getting to the interesting code Static analysis gives you a map; dynamic analysis tells you which roads are travelled. The usual way in is a breakpoint on something you can name: - an imported function the behaviour must use: CreateFileW for "it opens a file", send for "it sends a message"; - the code that references a string you found in triage; - an exported function of a DLL. When it stops, the call stack tells you how the program got there, and the caller is usually the code you want. Step into, over and out Command Usual key Does --- --- --- Step into F7 (x64dbg), F11 (VS) run one instruction; follow calls into the function Step over F8 (x64dbg), F10 (VS) run one instruction; run a whole call as one step Run to return Ctrl+F9 (x64dbg), Shift+F11 (VS) run until the current function returns Run to cursor F4 run until a chosen instruction Stepping over a call to a library function you do not care about, and out of functions you have seen enough of, keeps you in the code that matters. The call stack Every call pushes a return address, so at any moment the stack holds a chain of addresses back through every active function. Turning that into a list of frames is unwinding : - With frame pointers : some code keeps rbp pointing at the saved rbp of the caller, with the return address just above it. Then the stack is a linked list: rbp is the caller's rbp , rbp+8 the return address. Follow it until rbp is 0. - Without frame pointers , which is the usual case for optimised x64 Windows code, the debugger uses the unwind information in .pdata (lesson 2.02): for each function it knows how far rsp moved and where registers were saved, so it can compute the caller's rsp and find the return address. This is why x64 call stacks on Windows are reliable even in Release builds. text frame return address as shown 0 00007FF6 1A2B1074 game!Player::takeDamage+0x14 1 00007FF6 1A2B3410 game!Combat::resolve+0x80 2 00007FF6 1A2B5E2C game!World::update+0x21C 3 00007FF6 1A2B0F90 game!main+0x50 Naming addresses Raw addresses change every run (ASLR), so debuggers show them as module!symbol+offset : the module the address is in, the nearest symbol at or below it, and the distance. Without symbols, module+offset : game.exe+0x1074 , which is the same every run, because it is an RVA (lesson 1.03). Always record addresses this way in your notes; an absolute address from yesterday's session means nothing today. Conditional and logging breakpoints A breakpoint on CreateFileW in a program that opens hundreds of files is useless unless it stops only on the one you care about. Debuggers let you attach a condition : - x64dbg: streq(utf16(rcx), "C:\\Saves\\slot1.dat") , or a simpler test on a register such as rdx == 0xC0000000 . - Visual Studio: a condition in C++ syntax on variables when you have symbols. - WinDbg: bp kernel32!CreateFileW ".if (...) {} .else {gc}" . A logging breakpoint (a tracepoint in Visual Studio) prints a message and continues without stopping: "CreateFileW {utf16@rcx}" logs every file the program opens with its name, which is often all you need. Traces A trace records every instruction executed (or every call, or every block) between two points. x64dbg's trace recording and WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging go further: TTD records a whole run so you can step backwards through it, put a data breakpoint on a value and run backwards to see who last wrote it. For a hard question ("where did this wrong value come from?"), a recorded trace turns hours of re-running into minutes. Traces are large: millions of instructions per second of execution. Trace small windows, between two breakpoints around the behaviour you care about.

title: Rebuilding a call stack
body: Walk a call stack through frame pointers and name every address as module!symbol+offset (lesson 3.02). Memory is simulated as a map from address to 8-byte value. cpp using Memory = std::map<std::uint64_t, std::uint64_t ; struct Symbol { std::uint32_t rva; std::string name; }; struct Module { std::string name; std::uint64_t base; std::uint32_t size; std::vector<Symbol symbols; }; std::vector<std::uint64_t walkStack(const Memory& m, std::uint64_t rip, std::uint64_t rbp, int maxFrames); std::string describe(const std::vector<Module & modules, std::uint64_t address); walkStack returns rip followed by the return address of each frame: while rbp is not 0 and fewer than maxFrames addresses have been collected, read the return address at rbp + 8 and the caller's rbp at rbp . Stop if either read is missing, if the return address is 0, or if the next rbp is not higher than the current one (a stack only grows down, so a frame pointer going down means a corrupt chain). describe names an address: - in a module, with a symbol at or below its RVA: module!symbol+0x1a (offset in lowercase hex), or module!symbol when the offset is 0. Use the nearest symbol below (symbols may be listed in any order); - in a module with no symbol below it: module+0x1a2 (the RVA); - in no module: 0x7ff61a2b1074 , the address itself.

title: 3.03  Finding Where Data Lives
body: Locating a value in a running program you built - value scanning by narrowing a set of candidate addresses, the types and alignments to search for, then a data breakpoint to find the code that writes it, and working back from that code to the structure and the pointer path that reach it. The problem You can see a number on the screen of your own game: the player has 87 health. Where in memory is it, and which code changes it? You have no symbols, or the value is deep inside objects created at run time. Three steps answer it: scan for the value, watch the address to find the code, then walk back from the code to the structures around it. Value scanning A value scanner (the tool you build in this milestone's project) reads all of the process's readable, writable memory and keeps a list of candidate addresses: 1. First scan : every address where the 4 bytes equal 87. In a real program that is thousands of hits. 2. Change the value in the program (take some damage: 87 becomes 72). 3. Next scan : of the previous candidates, keep only those that now hold 72. 4. Repeat until one or a few addresses remain. When you do not know the exact value (a health bar with no number), scan for unknown first (every address is a candidate), then narrow with changed , unchanged , increased and decreased scans: lose health, scan "decreased"; do nothing, scan "unchanged"; heal, scan "increased". To scan efficiently you have to guess the type and alignment right: Value Likely stored as Alignment --- --- --- health, ammo, score int32_t (sometimes int16_t or a float ) 4 position, speed, a fraction float (or double ) 4 (8) money in a big game int64_t or double 8 a flag bool or a byte 1 Compilers align members (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 3.01), so scanning only at multiples of the size is both faster and avoids false hits from overlapping bytes. Floats are compared with a tolerance, because the shown value is rounded: 87 on screen may be 86.99997 in memory. !note Do this on your own programs: the debug build of a game you are writing, or the sample programs of the Game Development course. Online games, and games that forbid it, are off limits. Data breakpoints: who writes this? Once you have the address, set a hardware write breakpoint on it (lesson 3.01): in x64dbg, right-click the address in the dump, Breakpoint Hardware, Write, Dword; in Visual Studio, Debug New Breakpoint Data Breakpoint. Then take damage again. The debugger stops on the instruction just after the write: nasm-norun game.exe+0x2A1F: sub dword ptr rbx+1Ch , eax ; the write game.exe+0x2A22: mov ecx, dword ptr rbx+1Ch ; <- execution stops here Now you know the code ( game.exe+0x2A1F ), and the operand tells you more: rbx points at the object that contains the health, and health is at offset 0x1C in it. So: object address = health address − 0x1C That one fact turns a lone address into a structure. Other accesses through rbx in the same function are other members of the same object, and reverse engineering the struct begins (lesson 2.04). Walking back to a stable path The health address changes every time you start the game, because the player object is created on the heap. To find it again next time you need a pointer path from something stable (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 3.03): 1. You know the object's address (health − 0x1C). Scan memory for pointers with that value: 8-byte values equal to the object address. Those are the places that point at the player. 2. For each one, find what contains it: perhaps a World object's player array at offset 0x28. 3. Repeat from that object until you reach a static address inside the module's image: game.exe+0x51A8 . The result is a path such as game.exe+0x51A8 → 0x28 → 0x1C that finds the health in every run. Tools automate this as a pointer scan : from the target, search backwards for chains of pointers within some offset limit (the Pointers and Memory course's milestone 3 project built exactly that engine). With your own program you can also just read the source, but doing it by hand once makes it clear what every debugger and memory tool is doing.

title: Who writes this address?
body: A trace has recorded every memory write a program made, with the instruction that made it. Answer the questions of lesson 3.03: cpp struct Write { std::uint64_t rip; std::uint64_t address; std::uint32_t size; std::string operand; }; std::vector<std::uint64_t whatWrites(const std::vector<Write & trace, std::uint64_t address, std::uint32_t size); std::optional<std::int64_t displacementOf(const std::string& operand); std::vector<std::uint64_t objectCandidates(const std::vector<Write & trace, std::uint64_t address); - whatWrites lists the instructions ( rip ) whose write overlaps the bytes address to address + size - 1 , each once, in the order they first appear in the trace. - displacementOf reads the displacement from a memory operand in disassembler style: rbx+0x1C gives 0x1C, rax-0x8 gives -8, rbx gives 0, rax+rcx 4+0x10 gives 0x10. Numbers are 0x hex. If there is no ... it returns std::nullopt . - objectCandidates takes every write that covers exactly address (starts at it) and works out the object's start as address - displacement ; it returns the distinct results in increasing order. Operands with an index register (a ) are skipped, because their displacement is not a member offset.

title: 3.04  Watching Behaviour from Outside
body: Learning what a program does without a debugger - Process Monitor's file and registry log and its filters, API Monitor, network captures with Wireshark, Event Tracing for Windows, and Sysmon - and reading their logs systematically. Behaviour first Before reading a program's code you can learn a lot by just watching it from outside: which files it opens, which registry keys it reads, which servers it talks to, which processes it starts. Behavioural analysis needs no understanding of the code, is hard for a program to notice, and often answers the question outright: "where does it keep its settings?" is answered by one Process Monitor capture. Process Monitor Process Monitor (Sysinternals, procmon.exe ) records every file system, registry, process and thread event on the system, with the process, the path, the result and details. A capture is enormous, so the skill is filtering (Filter Filter...): - Process Name is Inventory.exe then Include: only your target. - Operation is WriteFile : only writes. - Path contains \Saves\ : only one folder. - Result is NAME NOT FOUND : things the program looked for and did not find, which reveals optional configuration files, missing DLLs and plugins it would load if they existed. Useful columns and tools: Path , Result , Detail (offsets and lengths of reads and writes); Tools File Summary and Registry Summary to count accesses per path; double-click an event to see its call stack (with symbols for system DLLs), which shows the code in the program that caused it. Logs can be saved as CSV (File Save, Comma-Separated Values), which is the format of this lesson's practice: text "Time of Day","Process Name","PID","Operation","Path","Result","Detail" "10:14:02.1234567","Inventory.exe","4120","CreateFile","C:\Users\sam\AppData\Roaming\Inventory\config.ini","SUCCESS","Desired Access: Generic Read" API Monitor API Monitor (rohitab.com) logs calls to Windows API functions with their arguments and return values : every RegQueryValueExW with the key and value name, every connect with the address. It shows what Process Monitor cannot see, such as calls that do not touch files or the registry (cryptography, window messages, time). Network captures Wireshark captures network traffic and decodes hundreds of protocols. Filters such as ip.addr == 192.168.1.20 && tcp.port == 7777 narrow it to one conversation; Follow TCP Stream shows the whole exchange as text or hex. For a program's own custom protocol you see only bytes, which is where lesson 6.03 picks up. Encrypted traffic (HTTPS, TLS) shows only the handshake and sizes, unless the program is yours and you can log its keys. Event Tracing for Windows ETW is the logging system built into Windows itself: the kernel and many components publish events (process starts, image loads, network, disk, the .NET runtime...). Tools such as Windows Performance Recorder, PerfView and logman capture them with very little overhead.
