Sysmon (Sysinternals) is a service that logs selected ETW-based events to the Windows event log permanently: process creation with full command lines and hashes, network connections, file creation. Security teams use it constantly, and it is a good way to watch a program over hours. Reading logs systematically Behaviour logs are only useful if you summarise them. A good habit for each capture: 1. Filter to the target process (and its children: the PID of processes it started). 2. List the distinct files written, files read, registry keys read and written, and network endpoints. 3. Note the failures ( NAME NOT FOUND , ACCESS DENIED ): they show what the program expected to exist. 4. Record the sequence of the important operations: what it reads at start-up, what it writes when you press Save. The practice builds exactly that summary from a Process Monitor CSV.

title: Summarising a Process Monitor log
body: Turn a Process Monitor capture saved as CSV (lesson 3.04) into the summary you would write by hand: cpp struct Event { std::string time, process, pid, operation, path, result, detail; }; struct Summary { std::vector<std::string filesRead, filesWritten, keysRead, keysWritten, notFound; }; std::vector<std::string splitCsvLine(const std::string& line); std::vector<Event parseLog(const std::string& csv); Summary summarise(const std::vector<Event & events, const std::string& process); - splitCsvLine splits one CSV line into fields. Fields may be wrapped in double quotes; inside quotes, commas are part of the field and "" stands for one " . - parseLog skips the header line and blank lines and turns each other line of 7 fields into an Event (lines with a different number of fields are skipped). - summarise looks only at events of process and fills each list with distinct paths, sorted: - filesRead : operation ReadFile with result SUCCESS ; - filesWritten : operation WriteFile with result SUCCESS ; - keysRead : RegQueryValue with result SUCCESS ; - keysWritten : RegSetValue with result SUCCESS ; - notFound : any operation with result NAME NOT FOUND .

title: 3.05  Comparing Runs
body: Differential analysis - snapshot memory before and after an action and diff it, compare which code ran with and without a feature (code coverage diffing), compare files a program wrote, and use time travel debugging to answer questions backwards. Change one thing, compare the rest Many reverse engineering questions have the form "what part of the program handles X?". The most efficient way to answer them is not to read more code, but to run the program twice , once doing X and once not, and compare. Whatever differs is about X. This is differential analysis , and it works on memory, on code coverage and on files. Memory snapshots Take a snapshot of a region of memory (an object, a heap, a whole module's data section), do one thing in the program, and take another. The diff shows exactly which bytes the action changed: text before jump: ... 00 00 C8 42 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 ... after jump: ... 00 00 F0 42 00 00 A0 41 00 00 00 00 ... ^ y position ^ vertical ^ on ground: 100.0 - speed 1 - 0 120.0 0 - 20.0 Read changed 4-byte groups both as integers and as floats: 00 00 C8 42 is the float 100.0, which is far more meaningful than the integer 1 120 403 456. Changes by small, sensible amounts are interesting; values that change on every snapshot whatever you do (timers, frame counters, random state) are noise that you learn to filter out by taking a third snapshot without doing anything. Code coverage diffing The same idea applies to code. Record which basic blocks execute (a coverage tool, a trace, or the Lighthouse plugin for Ghidra and IDA with coverage files from DynamoRIO's drcov ) during two runs: 1. Run A: start the program, open the menu, close it. 2. Run B: start the program, open the menu, press the button you are curious about , close it. Blocks executed in B but not in A are the code for that button. A function with a thousand blocks often has only a dozen in the difference, and that is where to start reading. File diffing When a program writes files, compare them across small changes. Save a game, move one step, save again, and diff the two save files (lesson 1.02's practice): the bytes that changed hold the position. Change the player's name and save again: the bytes that changed are the name, and the bytes before them are often its length. Lesson 6.02 builds a whole file format this way. Time travel debugging WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging (TTD) records an entire run of a program into a trace file. Afterwards you can replay it in the debugger and move both forwards and backwards : - g- runs backwards to the previous breakpoint. - A data breakpoint plus g- finds the last write to a value before the current moment: "who set this to the wrong value?" is answered in one command. - Queries such as dx @$cursession.TTD.Calls("kernel32!CreateFileW") list every call to a function anywhere in the recording, with arguments. Recording slows the program down a great deal and produces large files, so record the shortest run that shows the behaviour. For your own programs' hardest bugs, TTD is often the fastest tool there is.

title: Diffing memory snapshots
body: Compare two snapshots of the same block of memory, taken before and after an action (lesson 3.05), and report the 4-byte values that changed, read both as integers and as floats: cpp struct Changed { std::uint64_t address; std::int32_t beforeInt, afterInt; float beforeFloat, afterFloat; }; std::vector<Changed changedDwords(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & before, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & after, std::uint64_t base); std::vector<Changed withoutNoise(const std::vector<Changed & changes, const std::vector<Changed & noise); bool looksLikeFloat(float value); - changedDwords compares the two snapshots (the same size) 4 bytes at a time, at offsets 0, 4, 8, ...; every group where any byte differs is reported with its address ( base + offset ) and its values before and after, read little-endian as std::int32_t and as float . A trailing group of fewer than 4 bytes is ignored. - withoutNoise removes every change whose address also appears in noise (changes seen in a snapshot pair taken while doing nothing), keeping the order. - looksLikeFloat is a plausibility check: true for 0 and for finite values whose absolute value is between 0.0001 and 1 000 000. Tiny or enormous values usually mean the bytes are not really a float.

title: A value scanner
body: Build the engine of a memory value scanner (lesson 3.03). It works on snapshots : a list of memory regions copied out of a process (in a real tool, with VirtualQueryEx and ReadProcessMemory on your own program; here they are given). cpp struct Region { std::uint64_t base; std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes; }; using Snapshot = std::vector<Region ; enum class Type { Int32, Float, Double }; enum class Compare { Exact, Changed, Unchanged, Increased, Decreased, IncreasedBy, DecreasedBy }; class Scanner { public: explicit Scanner(Type type); void firstScan(const Snapshot& memory, double value); void firstScanUnknown(const Snapshot& memory); void nextScan(const Snapshot& memory, Compare how, double value = 0); std::vector<std::uint64_t results() const; std::optional<double read(const Snapshot& memory, std::uint64_t address) const; }; - The size and alignment of a value are 4 for Int32 and Float , 8 for Double . Only addresses that are multiples of the alignment, with all the value's bytes inside one region, are ever results. - read reads the value at an address as the scanner's type (little-endian), or std::nullopt if it is not readable. - firstScan finds every such address whose value equals value . Integers must match exactly; floats and doubles match when they differ from value by at most 0.001. It replaces any earlier results. - firstScanUnknown makes every readable aligned address a result. - nextScan keeps only the results for which the comparison holds between the value now (in memory ) and the value at the previous scan ; results that can no longer be read are dropped: - Exact : now equals value (with the same tolerance as firstScan ); - Changed / Unchanged : now differs from / equals the previous value (exactly, for every type); - Increased / Decreased : now is greater / less than the previous value; - IncreasedBy / DecreasedBy : now minus previous (or previous minus now) equals value , with the tolerance for floats. - Every scan remembers the current values for the next comparison. - results returns the addresses in increasing order.

title: 4.01  Patching Instructions
body: Changing a compiled program's behaviour by changing its bytes - turning a conditional jump into an unconditional one, inverting a condition, filling instructions with nops - in the file or in memory, on programs you built yourself, and what breaks when you do. Why patch your own programs Patching means changing a program's machine code directly instead of recompiling it. On your own software it has real uses: - Testing a hypothesis while reversing: "if I skip this check, does the crash go away?" answers a question in seconds. - Working around a bug in a build you cannot rebuild right now: an old release, a build machine that no longer exists, a tool whose source was lost. - Learning : seeing exactly which bytes encode which instructions makes disassembly far less mysterious. The practice targets here are programs you compile yourself. Build a small test program with a check you can find, for example: cpp-norun include <cstdio include <cstring bool debugMenuAllowed(const char build) { return std::strcmp(build, "internal") == 0; } int main() { if (debugMenuAllowed("release")) std::puts("debug menu on"); else std::puts("debug menu off"); } Compile it in Release, find the comparison in x64dbg (search for the string "debug menu off" and follow the cross-reference), and change the outcome without touching the source. The simplest patches The decision is almost always a conditional jump right after a test or cmp : nasm-norun call debugMenuAllowed test al, al je short off_branch ; 74 0C lea rcx, aDebugMenuOn Three standard edits: Goal Change Bytes --- --- --- always take the jump je becomes jmp 74 0C becomes EB 0C never take the jump replace it with nops 74 0C becomes 90 90 take it in the opposite case je becomes jne 74 0C becomes 75 0C The short conditional jumps are 70 to 7F , and each condition and its opposite differ only in the lowest bit : 74 je / 75 jne, 7C jl / 7D jge, 72 jb / 73 jae. So flipping bit 0 inverts any of them. The 6-byte near forms are 0F 80 to 0F 8F , with the same rule on the second byte. 90 is nop , the one-byte "do nothing". Longer nops exist ( 66 90 , 0F 1F 00 , up to 15 bytes), and compilers use them to pad loops, but a run of 90 s works fine for patching. Patch whole instructions A patch must leave the processor reading valid instructions. Replacing a 2-byte jump with a 5-byte one overwrites the next 3 bytes, which belong to another instruction, and the processor will then decode garbage. Rules: - Keep the patch the same length as what it replaces, padding with nop s. - If you need more room, use a code cave (lesson 4.03). - Always check the original bytes before patching: if they are not what you expect, you are looking at a different build, and patching blindly will break it. In the file or in memory In memory (in the debugger, or with WriteProcessMemory ): instant, undone when the program restarts. Code pages are read+execute, so a program patching memory needs VirtualProtect to make the page writable first, and FlushInstructionCache afterwards. Debuggers do this for you. In the file : permanent. Convert the instruction's address to a file offset (the RVA conversion of lesson 1.03: address − image base − section RVA + section file offset), and change the bytes there. x64dbg can write all your memory patches back to a copy of the file (File Patch file). What breaks - Code signing : a signed .exe or .dll no longer matches its signature after any change. Windows and antivirus software treat it as unsigned. Drivers simply refuse to load. - Integrity checks inside the program (checksums of its own code) will notice. - Updates replace the file and your patch is gone; and the next build of a program has different addresses, which is what lesson 4.05 is about. Keep the original file, record every patch (address, original bytes, new bytes, why), and patch copies.

title: Safe patches
body: Write the patch operations of lesson 4.01, each checking what it is about to overwrite: cpp struct Patch { std::size_t offset; std::vector<std::uint8_t original; std::vector<std::uint8_t replacement; }; bool apply(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const Patch& p); bool revert(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const Patch& p); std::optional<Patch forceJump(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t offset); std::optional<Patch invertJump(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t offset); Patch nopOut(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t offset, std::size_t length); - apply writes replacement only if original and replacement have the same length, the bytes fit, and the bytes at offset are exactly original ; it returns whether it did. revert does the reverse (checks for replacement , writes original ). - forceJump makes the conditional jump at offset always taken: - short 7x dd becomes EB dd ; - near 0F 8x dd dd dd dd becomes 90 E9 dd dd dd dd (a nop, then a jump with the same displacement, which still reaches the same target because the jmp ends where the jcc did). - Anything else gives std::nullopt . - invertJump flips the condition: the lowest bit of the 7x byte, or of the 8x byte after 0F . - nopOut makes a patch replacing length bytes with 90 s. The patches returned carry the current bytes as original , so they can be applied and reverted.

title: 4.02  Encoding Jumps and Calls
body: How x64 encodes jumps and calls - short and near relative jumps, conditional jumps, relative calls, why the displacement counts from the end of the instruction, the 2 GB limit, and the absolute jumps used when a target is further away. Relative, from the end Almost every jump and call on x64 is relative : the instruction holds a signed distance, the displacement , and the target is target = address of the next instruction + displacement The distance is counted from the end of the jump, not its start, because by the time the processor uses it, rip already points past the instruction. Instruction Bytes Length Displacement --- --- --- --- jmp short EB dd 2 8-bit, −128 to +127 jmp near E9 dd dd dd dd 5 32-bit jcc short 70+cc dd 2 8-bit jcc near 0F 80+cc dd dd dd dd 6 32-bit call E8 dd dd dd dd 5 32-bit Example: a jmp at 0x1400010A0 to 0x140001200 : text next instruction = 0x1400010A0 + 5 = 0x1400010A5 displacement = 0x140001200 - 0x1400010A5 = 0x15B bytes = E9 5B 01 00 00 Backwards jumps have negative displacements in two's complement: EB FE is a jump to itself (−2), an infinite loop; E9 00 00 00 00 jumps to the next instruction, which does nothing. Because displacements are relative, a block of code containing only relative jumps between its own instructions can be moved anywhere and still works; a relative jump or call to outside the block points somewhere else once it is moved. That fact drives lessons 4.03 and 4.04. The 2 GB limit A 32-bit displacement reaches about ±2 GB. Inside one module that is plenty. But code you allocate at run time with VirtualAlloc may land anywhere in the 128 TB address space, too far for E9 . Then you need an absolute jump: nasm-norun ; 14 bytes: jump to the 8-byte address stored right after the instruction FF 25 00 00 00 00 jmp qword ptr rip+0 xx xx xx xx xx xx xx xx ; the absolute target address nasm-norun ; 12 bytes, but it destroys rax 48 B8 xx xx xx xx xx xx xx xx mov rax, imm64 FF E0 jmp rax The first form changes no registers, which is why hooking libraries use it. Alternatively, allocate your new code within 2 GB of the module ( VirtualAlloc with an address hint near it), so a 5-byte E9 reaches it. Calls through memory Calls to imported functions are not relative calls to the function; they are indirect calls through the import address table: nasm-norun FF 15 xx xx xx xx call qword ptr rip+disp32 ; the IAT slot The displacement here gives the address of the slot , also counted from the end of the instruction (6 bytes long); the slot holds the function's address. Virtual calls are FF 50 xx / FF 90 xx xx xx xx ( call qword ptr rax+disp ) and friends. Encoding in code Choosing the shortest encoding that reaches: cpp-norun std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeJump(std::uint64_t from, std::uint64_t to) { const std::int64_t shortDisp{ static_cast<std::int64_t (to - (from + 2)) }; if (shortDisp = -128 && shortDisp <= 127) return { 0xEB, static_cast<std::uint8_t (shortDisp) }; const std::int64_t nearDisp{ static_cast<std::int64_t (to - (from + 5)) }; if (nearDisp = INT32_MIN && nearDisp <= INT32_MAX) { / E9 + 4 bytes of nearDisp, little-endian / } / otherwise FF 25 00 00 00 00 + 8 bytes of to / } Note that the two candidate displacements are computed from different ends: from + 2 for the short form, from + 5 for the near one.

title: Encoding and decoding jumps
body: Encode jumps and calls between two addresses, and decode where a branch goes (lesson 4.02): cpp std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeJump(std::uint64_t from, std::uint64_t to); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeCall(std::uint64_t from, std::uint64_t to); std::optional<std::uint64_t branchTarget(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at, std::uint64_t address); - encodeJump returns the shortest jump at address from that reaches to : EB + 8-bit displacement if it fits, else E9 + 32-bit displacement if it fits, else the 14-byte absolute form FF 25 00 00 00 00 followed by to as 8 little-endian bytes. Remember each relative form counts from its own end. - encodeCall returns E8 + 32-bit displacement, or std::nullopt if the target is out of range. - branchTarget decodes the branch at code at , which is at address address , and returns its target: EB , E9 , E8 , 70 - 7F and 0F 80 - 0F 8F . Displacements are signed. Anything else, or bytes running past the end of code , gives std::nullopt .

title: 4.03  Code Caves
body: When a patch needs more room than the instructions it replaces - finding unused space in a binary, jumping out to it with a detour, running the overwritten instructions there, and jumping back - plus adding a section or allocating memory instead. When a patch does not fit Turning a je into a jmp fits in the same two bytes. Adding behaviour does not: logging a value, adding a check, calling a function. You need somewhere to put new code. A code cave is unused space in the program where new code can live, reached by a jump from the original code. Where caves are - Padding between functions : MSVC aligns functions to 16 bytes and fills the gaps with CC (lesson 2.02). Each gap is small (up to 15 bytes) but there are many. - The end of a section : sections are padded in the file to a multiple of FileAlignment (0x200) with zeros, and in memory to SectionAlignment (0x1000). The space between a section's VirtualSize and its padded size is mapped with the section's permissions, so in .text it is executable. In the file, it is the bytes between VirtualSize and SizeOfRawData . - A new section : a PE editor (CFF Explorer, or a few lines of code) can add a section with read+execute permissions and as much room as you like, updating NumberOfSections and SizeOfImage . - At run time : VirtualAlloc a page of executable memory, preferably within 2 GB of the module so 5-byte jumps reach it (lesson 4.02). To find caves in a section, look for runs of 00 or CC at least as long as the code you need, preferably not directly after real code (a run of zeros can be a legitimate array of zeros that something reads). The detour Say you want to log every value passed to a function in your own program, at an instruction in the middle of it: nasm-norun 140001A30: 8B 47 1C mov eax, dword ptr rdi+1Ch 140001A33: 2B C3 sub eax, ebx 140001A35: 89 47 1C mov dword ptr rdi+1Ch , eax 140001A38: ... A 5-byte jmp to the cave must overwrite whole instructions, so it takes the first two (3 + 2 = 5 bytes, exactly; with other lengths, the leftover bytes become nop s). Those overwritten instructions are called the stolen bytes , and the cave must run them, or the program loses them: nasm-norun ; at 140001A30, the patch: E9 xx xx xx xx jmp cave ; in the cave: cave: ; ... your new code: save registers, call a logger, restore registers ... 8B 47 1C mov eax, dword ptr rdi+1Ch ; the stolen instructions, 2B C3 sub eax, ebx ; exactly as they were E9 xx xx xx xx jmp 140001A35 ; back to the next original instruction Rules that keep a detour correct: 1. Steal whole instructions : at least 5 bytes' worth, rounded up to the next instruction boundary. 2. Do not steal a jump target : if any other code jumps into the middle of the stolen range, that jump now lands inside your jmp . Check the cross-references for each stolen address. 3. Relocate relative instructions : a stolen call , jmp or jcc , or any instruction with a RIP-relative operand ( mov eax, rip+... ), means something else once it runs at the cave's address. Its displacement must be recalculated for the new location, or the instruction replaced. 4. Preserve state : your new code must save and restore every register and the flags it changes ( pushfq / popfq ), and keep the stack 16-byte aligned before any call . Planning the stolen bytes Given the lengths of the instructions at the patch point, the number of bytes to steal is the smallest sum of whole instructions that reaches 5: text lengths 3, 2, 3, ... - steal 5 (two instructions) lengths 2, 2, 4, ... - steal 8 (three instructions; 3 nops after the jmp) lengths 7, ... - steal 7 (one instruction; 2 nops) Your disassembler (or the one you build in milestone 5) gives the lengths.

title: Planning a detour
body: Plan a code cave detour (lesson 4.03): find caves, decide how many bytes to steal, and build the cave's code. cpp struct Cave { std::size_t offset; std::size_t length; }; std::vector<Cave findCaves(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t minLength); std::optional<std::size_t bytesToSteal(const std::vector<std::size_t & instructionLengths, std::size_t needed); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t buildCave(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & stolen, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & newCode, std::uint64_t caveAddress, std::uint64_t returnAddress); - findCaves lists runs of the same filler byte, 0x00 or 0xCC , at least minLength long, in order. A run is one byte value only (a run of CC s next to a run of 00 s is two caves). - bytesToSteal takes the lengths of the instructions at the patch point, in order, and returns the total length of the fewest whole instructions that add up to at least needed bytes, or std::nullopt if they never do. - buildCave returns the bytes placed at caveAddress : newCode , then the stolen instructions unchanged, then an E9 jump back to returnAddress . If the stolen bytes start a relative branch or call ( E8 , E9 , EB , 70 - 7F or 0F 8x as the first byte of the stolen bytes) it returns std::nullopt , because copying them unchanged would break them; so does a jump back that does not fit in 32 bits.

title: 4.04  Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
match: 4.04 Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
body: Redirecting calls to a function so your code runs first - import address table hooks, inline hooks with a trampoline that still calls the original, libraries that do it safely, and using hooks for instrumentation, logging and testing in software you build. What a hook is A hook makes calls to a function go to your code instead, usually so your code can do something and then call the original. Inside your own software, hooks are a practical tool: - Instrumentation : count and time every call to an allocator or a file function without changing the call sites. - Logging : record the arguments of every call to a third-party library you only have as a DLL. - Testing : make a system function fail on purpose ( CreateFileW returns "access denied") to test error handling. - Fixing : replace a buggy function in a library you cannot rebuild. Profilers, debuggers, crash reporters and the Windows compatibility layer all hook functions. Everything here is about functions in your own process or programs you build. IAT hooks Calls to imported functions go through the import address table (lesson 1.04): call qword ptr IAT slot . Change the slot , and every call from that module goes to your function instead: cpp-norun using CreateFileWFn = HANDLE (WINAPI )(LPCWSTR, DWORD, DWORD, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, DWORD, DWORD, HANDLE); static CreateFileWFn realCreateFileW{ nullptr }; HANDLE WINAPI loggingCreateFileW(LPCWSTR name, DWORD access, DWORD share, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa, DWORD disposition, DWORD flags, HANDLE templ) { std::wprintf(L"opening %s\n", name); return realCreateFileW(name, access, share, sa, disposition, flags, templ); // the original } // Find the slot for CreateFileW in this module's import table, then: DWORD old; VirtualProtect(slot, sizeof(void ), PAGE_READWRITE, &old); realCreateFileW = reinterpret_cast<CreateFileWFn ( slot); slot = reinterpret_cast<void (&loggingCreateFileW); VirtualProtect(slot, sizeof(void ), old, &old); IAT hooks are simple and safe: one pointer changes, no code is rewritten. Their limit is scope: they catch calls from the module whose table you changed , not calls from other DLLs, and not calls made through GetProcAddress . Inline hooks and trampolines An inline hook patches the first bytes of the target function itself, so every caller is caught. It is the detour of lesson 4.03 at a function's start: text target function, before: after: 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 ,rbx E9 xx xx xx xx jmp yourFunction 57 push rdi 57 push rdi 48 83 EC 20 sub rsp,20h 48 83 EC 20 sub rsp,20h To still call the original, you build a trampoline : a small block of executable memory holding the stolen instructions followed by a jump back to the rest of the original: text trampoline: 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx ; stolen bytes E9 xx xx xx xx jmp target+5 ; continue the original Your function calls the trampoline whenever it wants the original behaviour. Everything from lesson 4.03 applies: steal whole instructions, relocate RIP-relative ones, and do not overwrite a jump target. Two more problems are specific to hooking a live process: - Other threads may be executing the bytes you are overwriting. Suspend the other threads while you write, and check none of them is stopped inside the stolen range. - Distance : the trampoline must be within 2 GB for 5-byte jumps, or you need the 14-byte absolute form at the function start, which steals more bytes. Use a library Writing a robust inline hook engine means a full instruction-length decoder, relocation of every RIP-relative instruction form, thread handling and more. In practice use one of: - Microsoft Detours (MIT licence): the reference implementation, used by Microsoft's own tools. - MinHook (BSD licence): small, simple API ( MH_CreateHook , MH_EnableHook ). Understanding what they do, as in this lesson, is what lets you debug them when a hook misbehaves.

title: Hooks on paper
where: 4.04 Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
body: Work out the bytes a hooking library writes (lesson 4.04), for a function at a known address: cpp struct InlineHook { std::vector<std::uint8_t patch; // written over the start of the target function std::vector<std::uint8_t trampoline; // placed at the trampoline address }; std::optional<InlineHook planHook(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & functionStart, const std::vector<std::size_t & lengths, std::uint64_t target, std::uint64_t hook, std::uint64_t trampolineAt); std::uint64_t hookIat(std::vector<std::uint64_t & iat, std::size_t slot, std::uint64_t replacement); planHook : the target function starts at address target ; functionStart holds its first bytes and lengths the lengths of its first instructions. - Steal the fewest whole instructions covering at least 5 bytes. If they are not all available in functionStart , return std::nullopt . - patch is an E9 jump from target to hook , followed by 90 s to fill the rest of the stolen bytes. - trampoline is the stolen bytes unchanged, then an E9 jump from the end of those bytes (at trampolineAt + stolen ) back to target + stolen . - If a stolen instruction starts with a relative branch or call ( E8 , E9 , EB , 70 - 7F , 0F 80 - 0F 8F ), or any jump does not fit in 32 bits, return std::nullopt . hookIat replaces the address in an import address table slot and returns the old one, so the hook can call the original.

title: 4.05  Byte Patterns That Survive Rebuilds
body: Every new build moves code around, so fixed addresses break. Byte patterns with wildcards find the same code in any build - which bytes to keep and which to wildcard, keeping a pattern unique, scanning efficiently, and resolving the RIP-relative address inside a match. Addresses do not survive a rebuild A patch or a pointer path recorded as game.exe+0x2A1F is correct for exactly one build. Change one line of source, rebuild, and functions shift by a few bytes; everything after them moves. Debug tooling for your own game, patch scripts for an old build, and analysis notes all need a way to find "the same code" in a different build. The instructions themselves change much less than their addresses. A byte pattern (also called a signature, or an AOB, "array of bytes") describes the code by its bytes, with wildcards for the bytes that vary between builds. Which bytes vary Take the instruction that subtracts damage from health: nasm-norun 2B C3 sub eax, ebx 89 47 1C mov dword ptr rdi+1Ch , eax 48 8B 0D 6A 2F 01 00 mov rcx, qword ptr rip+12F6Ah ; a global E8 F5 03 00 00 call UpdateHud - Opcodes and registers ( 2B C3 , 89 47 , 48 8B 0D , E8 ): change only if the compiler chooses differently, which is rare for unchanged source. - Struct offsets ( 1C ): change only if the struct changes. - RIP-relative displacements ( 6A 2F 01 00 ) and call/jump displacements ( F5 03 00 00 ): change with almost every build, because they are distances to other code and data that moved. - Absolute addresses in data: change with every build and every relocation. So the pattern is: text 2B C3 89 47 1C 48 8B 0D ?? ?? ?? ?? E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? Making it unique A pattern is only useful if it matches exactly once in the module. Short patterns of common instruction sequences match hundreds of places. Tools that generate signatures (plugins for x64dbg, IDA and Ghidra) start at the instruction you want and keep adding the following instructions, wildcarding the displacements, until the pattern is unique. Good habits: - Prefer patterns built from distinctive instructions: uncommon struct offsets, unusual immediates. - Keep them short enough to survive small code changes nearby; 15 to 30 bytes is typical. - Record the offset of the instruction you care about within the pattern ("the patch goes 2 bytes into the match"). - Check uniqueness again after every rebuild; the build that breaks a pattern is the one that tells you to make a better one. Scanning The simplest scanner compares the pattern at every position, skipping wildcard positions: cpp-norun for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i + pattern.size() <= bytes.size(); ++i) { bool match{ true }; for (std::size_t k{ 0 }; k < pattern.size() && match; ++k) match = !pattern k .has_value() bytes i + k == pattern k ; if (match) hits.push_back(i); } That is fast enough for one module of a few megabytes. Scan only executable sections ( .text ) for code patterns; it is quicker and avoids accidental matches in data. Faster scanners first look for the pattern's rarest fixed byte with memchr , or use SIMD to compare 16 or 32 bytes at once. Resolving what a match points at Often the pattern finds an instruction that refers to what you want: a global variable, a function. The wildcards hide the displacement, but once you have a match you can read it and compute the target, exactly as the processor does: text match at game.exe+0x2A1F: 48 8B 0D 6A 2F 01 00 mov rcx, rip+0x12F6A instruction starts at match + 5, is 7 bytes long, displacement at its byte 3 target = (address of the instruction + 7) + 0x12F6A The same for a call ( E8 , 5 bytes, displacement at byte 1). This is how a pattern finds a global or function in every build: the pattern survives, and the displacement inside it tells you where the thing is this time.

title: A pattern scanner
body: Build the byte pattern tools of lesson 4.05: cpp using Pattern = std::vector<std::optional<std::uint8_t ; std::optional<Pattern parsePattern(const std::string& text); std::vector<std::size_t findAll(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, const Pattern& pattern); std::optional<std::uint64_t ripTarget(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, std::size_t instruction, std::size_t length, std::size_t displacementAt, std::uint64_t base); - parsePattern reads tokens separated by spaces: two hex digits (either case) for a byte, ?? or ? for a wildcard. Anything else, or no tokens at all, gives std::nullopt . - findAll returns every offset where the pattern matches, in order (matches may overlap). - ripTarget : the instruction at offset instruction of bytes (loaded at address base ) is length bytes long and holds a signed 32-bit displacement at byte displacementAt of the instruction. Return the address it refers to: the address just past the instruction plus the displacement. If the bytes run out, return std::nullopt .

title: A patch engine
body: Bring lessons 4.01 and 4.05 together into a small patching tool for builds of your own programs: patches written in a text file, located by offset or by a byte pattern so they survive rebuilds, checked before anything is written, and applied all together or not at all. The patch file looks like this: text patches for Inventory.exe skip-intro offset: 0x1A40 original: 74 0C replacement: EB 0C no-cooldown pattern: 2B C3 89 47 ?? 48 8B 0D at: 2 original: 89 47 1C replacement: 90 90 90 cpp struct PatchSpec { std::string name; std::optional<std::size_t offset; std::string pattern; std::size_t at{ 0 }; std::vector<std::uint8_t original, replacement; }; class PatchSet { public: bool parse(const std::string& text, std::string& error); const std::vector<PatchSpec & patches() const; std::optional<std::size_t locate(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const PatchSpec& p) const; std::vector<std::string check(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code) const; bool applyAll(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code) const; bool revertAll(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code) const; }; parse reads the file line by line (blank lines and lines starting with are ignored; spaces around keys and values are trimmed). name starts a patch. Keys: offset (hex with 0x , or decimal), pattern (lesson 4.05's syntax), at (decimal, default 0), original and replacement (hex bytes). On a problem it returns false with error set: - line N: unknown key for a key it does not know, and line N: key outside a patch for a key before the first name ; - line N: bad bytes for an original or replacement that is not all two-digit hex bytes; - patch NAME: needs offset or pattern when a patch has neither, or both; - patch NAME: original and replacement differ when they are empty or not the same length. locate returns the patch's offset: its offset , or for a pattern, the position of its only match plus at . No match or more than one match gives std::nullopt . check returns the problems that would stop applyAll , in this order, each patch in file order: NAME: not found (cannot locate), NAME: original bytes differ (the bytes there are not original , or would run past the end), then for each pair of located patches whose byte ranges overlap, A and B overlap (A before B in the file). applyAll writes every replacement if check finds nothing, and returns whether it did. revertAll puts back every original , but only if every patch currently holds its replacement ; otherwise it changes nothing and returns false.

title: 5.01  How x64 Instructions Are Encoded
body: The layout of an x64 instruction - legacy prefixes, the REX prefix, one to three opcode bytes, the ModRM and SIB bytes that describe operands, displacements and immediates - and how to work out an instruction's length, the first job of any disassembler. Variable length x64 instructions are between 1 and 15 bytes long, and nothing marks where one ends: you only know an instruction's length by decoding it. That is why a disassembler that starts one byte off produces nonsense, and why the first thing any disassembler, hooking library or patch tool needs is a length decoder . Every instruction has the same overall shape, with most parts optional: text legacy prefixes REX opcode ModRM SIB displacement immediate 0-4 bytes 0-1 1-3 0-1 0-1 0, 1, 2 or 4 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 Prefixes Legacy prefixes modify the instruction: 66 switches the operand size from 32 to 16 bits, F2 and F3 are the rep prefixes (and select different SSE instructions), F0 is lock , and segment overrides ( 64 for fs: , 65 for gs: ) appear in code that reads thread-local data. The REX prefix is a byte from 40 to 4F that must come directly before the opcode . Its low four bits are flags: Bit Name Effect --- --- --- 3 ( 8 ) W 64-bit operand size 2 ( 4 ) R adds 8 to the ModRM reg field: reach r8 to r15 1 ( 2 ) X adds 8 to the SIB index field 0 ( 1 ) B adds 8 to the ModRM rm field, the SIB base field, or a register in the opcode 48 (W only) is by far the most common byte in x64 code: it turns mov eax, ecx into mov rax, rcx . 40 with no flags still matters: it changes the meaning of 8-bit registers ( spl , bpl instead of ah , ch ), and MSVC uses 40 53 for push rbx so the instruction is 2 bytes long. Opcodes Most common instructions have a one-byte opcode . Some encode a register in the opcode itself: 50 +r is push r , 58 +r is pop r , B8 +r is mov r, imm (with REX.B selecting r8 to r15 ). Two-byte opcodes start with the escape byte 0F : 0F 84 is near je , 0F B6 is movzx , 0F 1F is the long nop . Three-byte opcodes start 0F 38 or 0F 3A (mostly SIMD). ModRM Instructions with a register or memory operand have a ModRM byte after the opcode, split into three fields: text 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 mod reg rm - reg : a register operand (or, for some opcodes, an extension of the opcode: 83 /5 means "opcode 83 with reg field 5", which is sub ). - mod and rm together describe the other operand: mod rm Operand Extra bytes --- --- --- --- 11 any the register rm none 00 101 rip + disp32 4 00 100 SIB SIB (+4 if the SIB base is 101 ) 00 other rm none 01 100 SIB + disp8 SIB + 1 01 other rm + disp8 1 10 100 SIB + disp32 SIB + 4 10 other rm + disp32 4 Register numbers: 0 rax , 1 rcx , 2 rdx , 3 rbx , 4 rsp , 5 rbp , 6 rsi , 7 rdi , and 8 to 15 for r8 to r15 with a REX bit. SIB When rm is 100 in a memory form, a SIB byte follows, for base + index scale : text scale index base scale: 00=1, 01=2, 10=4, 11=8 An index of 100 (without REX.X) means no index ; that is how rsp+8 is encoded, since rsp cannot be an index. A base of 101 with mod 00 means no base, disp32 instead. A worked example 4C 8B 44 24 28 : text 4C REX: 0100 1100 - W=1, R=1 8B opcode: mov reg, r/m 44 ModRM: 01 000 100 - mod 01 (disp8), reg 000 (+8 from R = r8), rm 100 (SIB follows) 24 SIB: 00 100 100 - scale 1, index 100 (none), base 100 (rsp) 28 disp8: 0x28 = mov r8, qword ptr rsp+0x28 (5 bytes) Immediates Constants embedded in the instruction come last: 1 byte for 83 /x ib and short jumps, 4 bytes for 81 /x id , C7 /0 id and E8 / E9 displacements, and 8 bytes only for mov r64, imm64 ( 48 B8 + 8 bytes). With the 66 prefix, the 4-byte immediates of 81 and C7 become 2 bytes. Putting it together, an instruction's length is: prefixes + REX + opcode bytes + ModRM (if any) + SIB (if any) + displacement + immediate. The practice writes exactly that for a useful subset.

title: An instruction length decoder
body: Write the length decoder at the heart of every disassembler and hooking library (lesson 5.01), for a common subset of x64: cpp std::size_t instructionLength(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at); It returns the length of the instruction starting at code at , or 0 if the bytes are not in the subset or run out before the instruction ends. 1. Prefixes : any number of 66 , F2 , F3 , then optionally one REX byte ( 40 - 4F ). 2. Opcode and what follows it: Opcode Then --- --- 50 - 5F , 90 , C3 , CC nothing 70 - 7F , EB 1-byte displacement E8 , E9 4-byte displacement B8 - BF 4-byte immediate, or 8 with REX.W 01 03 29 2B 31 33 39 3B 63 85 89 8B 8D ModRM 83 ModRM, then 1-byte immediate 81 , C7 ModRM, then 4-byte immediate (2 bytes with a 66 prefix) 0F 80 - 0F 8F 4-byte displacement 0F 1F , 0F B6 , 0F B7 , 0F BE , 0F BF ModRM 3. ModRM (lesson 5.01's table): mod 11 adds nothing; otherwise rm 100 adds a SIB byte (and 4 more bytes if the SIB base is 101 with mod 00); mod 00 with rm 101 adds 4; mod 01 adds 1; mod 10 adds 4.

title: 5.02  Writing a Disassembler
body: From bytes to text - table-driven decoding, naming registers and building memory operands, formatting immediates and branch targets, linear sweep versus recursive descent, telling code from data, and the real libraries (Zydis, Capstone) behind every tool. Decoding and formatting A disassembler does two jobs for each instruction: 1. Decode : read prefixes, opcode, ModRM, SIB, displacement and immediate into a structure: which operation, which registers, which memory expression, which constant. This also gives the length. 2. Format : turn that structure into text in a chosen syntax: mov rax, qword ptr rcx+0x10 (Intel, as MSVC and x64dbg show it) or movq 0x10(%rcx), %rax (AT&T, as GDB and objdump show by default). Keeping them separate pays off: analysis code (a control flow graph, a pattern generator) wants the structure, not the text. Tables x86 has hundreds of opcodes, so real decoders are table-driven : an array indexed by opcode byte saying what follows (ModRM or not, immediate size, operand roles) and the mnemonic. A small decoder for common instructions is a table like this: Opcode Form Mnemonic --- --- --- 01 / 03 r/m, reg / reg, r/m add 29 / 2B r/m, reg / reg, r/m sub 31 / 33 r/m, reg / reg, r/m xor 39 / 3B r/m, reg / reg, r/m cmp 85 r/m, reg test 89 / 8B r/m, reg / reg, r/m mov 8D reg, m lea 83 /0 /4 /5 /7 r/m, imm8 add and sub cmp 81 /0 /4 /5 /7 r/m, imm32 the same with a 32-bit immediate C7 /0 r/m, imm32 mov B8 +r reg, imm32 (imm64 with REX.W) mov 50 +r / 58 +r reg push / pop E8 / E9 / EB rel32 / rel32 / rel8 call / jmp / jmp 70 +cc / 0F 80 +cc rel8 / rel32 jo jno jb jae je jne jbe ja js jns jp jnp jl jge jle jg C3 , CC , 90 none ret , int3 , nop With just these, most of a typical function decodes. Operands Registers depend on the operand size: with REX.W the 64-bit names ( rax , ..., r15 ), otherwise the 32-bit ones ( eax , ..., edi , r8d , ..., r15d ). Registers inside a memory operand are addresses, so they always use the 64-bit names: dword ptr rbp-0x4 , never ebp-0x4 . Memory operands are built from the ModRM and SIB fields: base, then +index scale , then the displacement as +0x10 or -0x8 , all in brackets. A size keyword in front says how many bytes are accessed: qword ptr , dword ptr , word ptr , byte ptr . lea takes no size keyword, because it accesses no memory. Immediates for arithmetic are sign-extended: 83 C0 FF is add eax, -0x1 , not add eax, 0xff . Branch targets are shown as absolute addresses, computed from the instruction's address, its length and its displacement (lesson 4.02), because that is what a reader needs. Linear sweep and recursive descent How do you choose where to decode? - Linear sweep decodes from the start of a section to the end, each instruction right after the previous one. Simple, and it sees everything, but when it meets data inside code (a jump table, padding, a literal pool), it decodes it as nonsense instructions, and may stay out of step for a few instructions afterwards. objdump works this way. - Recursive descent starts at known entry points (the entry point, exports, .pdata functions) and follows the code: decode until a ret or jmp , and queue every branch and call target. It never decodes data by mistake, but misses code that is only reached indirectly (through function pointers, vtables, jump tables), unless it resolves those too. Ghidra, IDA and Binary Ninja combine this with many heuristics. When a byte does not decode as any known instruction, a disassembler shows it as data, db 0x0f , and moves on by one byte. Use a library for real work A complete x86-64 decoder covers thousands of instruction forms, AVX-512, and many corner cases. For your own tools use a library: - Zydis : fast, thorough, C, MIT licence; decodes into a detailed structure and formats Intel or AT&T. - Capstone : many architectures (x86, ARM, MIPS...), C with bindings for Python and other languages, BSD licence. - iced (Rust and .NET): very complete, also encodes. Writing a small one yourself, as this milestone's project does, is how you learn what those libraries give you, and how to read their output when it surprises you.

title: Formatting operands
body: Turn a ModRM byte (with its SIB and displacement) into the two operand strings a disassembler prints (lesson 5.02): cpp struct Operands { std::string reg; std::string rm; std::size_t length; }; std::optional<Operands decodeModRm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at, std::uint8_t rex, int bits); std::string registerName(int number, int bits); - registerName gives register number (0 to 15) at a size: 64 bits rax rcx rdx rbx rsp rbp rsi rdi r8 ... r15 ; 32 bits eax ecx edx ebx esp ebp esi edi r8d ... r15d . - decodeModRm reads the ModRM byte at code at . rex is the REX byte (or 0); bits (32 or 64) is the operand size. - reg is register ( reg field + 8 if REX.R) at bits . - If mod is 11, rm is register ( rm field + 8 if REX.B) at bits . - Otherwise rm is a memory operand: dword ptr (or qword ptr for 64 bits), then , the base, +index scale if there is an index, the displacement, . Base and index are always 64-bit names; REX.B extends the base (or rm ), REX.X the index. The displacement is written +0x1c or -0x8 (lowercase hex), and left out when it is 0 and there is a base. - mod 00 with rm 101 is rip+0x10 (always with its displacement, even 0, signed). - A SIB index of 100 (without REX.X) means no index. A SIB base of 101 with mod 00 means no base: then the displacement is printed as 0x10 with no + if it comes first ( 0x10 , rcx 4+0x10 ). - length counts the ModRM byte, SIB and displacement. - Running out of bytes gives std::nullopt .

title: 5.03  Reading a Process's Memory Map
body: Seeing a running process the way debuggers do, with documented Windows APIs - opening a process with the right access rights, walking its address space with VirtualQueryEx, understanding states, protections and types, listing its modules, and reading memory safely. The documented way in Debuggers, profilers, Process Explorer and memory scanners all look at other processes through a handful of documented Windows functions. Using them on your own programs is how you build inspection tools for them, such as an external stats viewer for a game you are developing (the Game Development course builds one). First, open the process with only the access you need: cpp-norun HANDLE process{ OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION PROCESS_VM_READ, FALSE, pid) }; if (!process) { / GetLastError(): 5 = access denied / } Windows checks the request against the target's security. You can open processes running as your own user; processes of other users, services and protected processes (antivirus, DRM, system processes) refuse. That is the security boundary working as intended. Walking the address space VirtualQueryEx describes the region of pages containing an address. Starting at 0 and jumping from region to region walks the whole address space: cpp-norun MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; for (std::uintptr_t at{ 0 }; VirtualQueryEx(process, reinterpret_cast<void (at), &info, sizeof(info)) == sizeof(info); at = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t (info.BaseAddress) + info.RegionSize) { // info.BaseAddress, info.RegionSize, info.State, info.Protect, info.Type, info.AllocationBase } Each region is a run of pages with identical attributes: Field Values --- --- State MEM_FREE (0x10000), MEM_RESERVE (0x2000), MEM_COMMIT (0x1000) Protect PAGE_NOACCESS 0x01, PAGE_READONLY 0x02, PAGE_READWRITE 0x04, PAGE_WRITECOPY 0x08, PAGE_EXECUTE 0x10, PAGE_EXECUTE_READ 0x20, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE 0x40, PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY 0x80, plus the modifier PAGE_GUARD 0x100 Type MEM_IMAGE (a mapped .exe or .dll), MEM_MAPPED (a mapped file or shared memory), MEM_PRIVATE (heap, stacks, VirtualAlloc ) AllocationBase the start of the VirtualAlloc (or mapping) this region belongs to One allocation often shows up as several regions: an image is one allocation with a region per section ( .text as PAGE_EXECUTE_READ , .data as PAGE_READWRITE ...), and a thread stack is one reservation with a committed part, a guard page and a reserved remainder. Grouping regions by AllocationBase reassembles them. PAGE_WRITECOPY is how image pages that are writable start out: shared between processes until one writes, then copied for that process alone. Modules To list loaded modules with their names and base addresses: cpp-norun HANDLE snap{ CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPMODULE TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32, pid) }; MODULEENTRY32W entry{ sizeof(entry) }; for (BOOL ok{ Module32FirstW(snap, &entry) }; ok; ok = Module32NextW(snap, &entry)) { // entry.szModule, entry.modBaseAddr, entry.modBaseSize, entry.szExePath } CloseHandle(snap); ( EnumProcessModulesEx with GetModuleBaseNameW is the other route.) With the module list you can turn any address into module+offset (lesson 3.02), and the module's base plus an RVA into a real address. Reading memory cpp-norun std::uint32_t health{}; SIZE_T got{}; if (ReadProcessMemory(process, reinterpret_cast<void (address), &health, sizeof(health), &got) && got == sizeof(health)) { // use health } Rules that keep a reader robust: - Check every read. Memory can be freed between your query and your read; ReadProcessMemory then fails (error 299, partial copy). - Only read committed, readable regions. Skip PAGE_NOACCESS and PAGE_GUARD regions; touching a guard page would change the target's behaviour. - Read in large chunks when scanning (a whole region at a time), not one value per call: each call is a trip into the kernel. - The target keeps running. Values can change between reads; a consistent snapshot needs the target paused ( DebugActiveProcess , or suspending its threads). Writing ( WriteProcessMemory , needing PROCESS_VM_WRITE PROCESS_VM_OPERATION ) and creating threads in another process are what debuggers do to your own programs; outside your own software, they are exactly what security software watches for.

title: Making sense of a memory map
match: Making sense of a memory map
body: Process the region list VirtualQueryEx returns (lesson 5.03) into what a memory viewer shows: cpp struct RegionInfo { std::uint64_t base, size, allocationBase; std::uint32_t state, protect, type; }; struct Allocation { std::uint64_t base, size; std::uint32_t type; int regions; }; struct ModuleInfo { std::string name; std::uint64_t base, size; }; std::string protection(std::uint32_t protect); bool readable(const RegionInfo& r); std::vector<Allocation allocations(const std::vector<RegionInfo & regions); std::string label(const std::vector<ModuleInfo & modules, std::uint64_t address); - protection turns a Protect value into rwx style: 0x01 --- , 0x02 r-- , 0x04 rw- , 0x08 rw- , 0x10 --x , 0x20 r-x , 0x40 rwx , 0x80 rwx ; if the PAGE_GUARD bit 0x100 is also set, add guard . Any other base value gives ? . - readable is true for regions that are committed ( MEM_COMMIT = 0x1000), not guard pages, and whose protection allows reading ( r in the string above). - allocations groups non-free regions ( MEM_FREE = 0x10000 are skipped) by allocationBase , in order of base: each allocation's base is the allocation base, size runs from there to the end of its last region, type is its first region's type, and regions counts them. - label names an address: name+0x1a2 (lowercase hex offset from the module's base) inside a module, otherwise 0x and the address in lowercase hex.

title: 5.04  Symbols and PDB Files
body: What a PDB holds, how a binary names its exact PDB through a GUID and age, symbol servers and the path layout they use, public versus private symbols, and turning addresses into names with DbgHelp - including Microsoft's symbols for Windows itself. Names live in a separate file When MSVC links a program it writes the machine code into the .exe and the names into a separate PDB (program database) file: function names and addresses, global variables, types and struct layouts, local variables, source file and line information. The .exe itself contains almost none of it, which is why stripped binaries are hard to read. With the matching PDB, every tool in this course shows names: call stacks, disassembly, crash dumps. Always check whether one is available before working without it. Which PDB matches? A PDB is only useful for the exact build it came from. The .exe records which one it needs in a CodeView record in its debug directory (lesson 1.05): Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 signature RSDS 4 16 GUID: a unique id generated at link time 20 4 age: incremented by incremental relinks 24 ... PDB file name or path, zero-terminated (UTF-8) The PDB contains the same GUID and age. Tools refuse a PDB whose GUID or age differs, even if the file name matches: a PDB from yesterday's build of the same project describes different addresses. Symbol servers A symbol server is a store of PDBs indexed by that GUID and age, so a debugger can fetch exactly the right one. The path inside the store is: text <pdb name /<GUID <age /<pdb name Inventory.pdb/3F2504E04F8911D39A0C0305E82C33011/Inventory.pdb The GUID is written as 32 uppercase hex digits in a specific order: its first field as a 32-bit number, the next two as 16-bit numbers, then its last 8 bytes in order; the age follows in hex with no leading zeros. Microsoft publishes PDBs for Windows' own DLLs on its public server. Point your tools at it with the _NT_SYMBOL_PATH environment variable: text srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols ( C:\Symbols is a local cache.) Then call stacks through ntdll.dll , kernel32.dll and user32.dll show real function names. For your own builds, keep every released build's PDBs in a store of your own (the symstore tool from the Windows SDK adds them), and every crash report from a user can be read with names, even months later. Public and private symbols - Private symbols , the full PDB your build creates, include types, local variables and line numbers. - Public symbols contain only the names and addresses of functions and globals. Microsoft's server mostly has these. They are created with the linker's /PDBSTRIPPED option, which is what you would ship if you publish symbols for your own product without giving away its structure. DbgHelp Windows' DbgHelp library ( dbghelp.dll ) loads symbols and answers questions about them; it is what WinDbg and many crash reporters use: cpp-norun SymSetOptions(SYMOPT_UNDNAME SYMOPT_DEFERRED_LOADS); SymInitialize(process, nullptr / use _NT_SYMBOL_PATH /, TRUE / load every module /); char buffer sizeof(SYMBOL_INFO) + MAX_SYM_NAME {}; auto symbol{ reinterpret_cast<SYMBOL_INFO (buffer) }; symbol- SizeOfStruct = sizeof(SYMBOL_INFO); symbol- MaxNameLen = MAX_SYM_NAME; DWORD64 displacement{}; if (SymFromAddr(process, address, &displacement, symbol)) std::printf("%s+0x%llx\n", symbol- Name, displacement); // Player::update+0x1a Other useful calls: SymFromName (name to address), SymGetLineFromAddr64 (address to source line), StackWalk64 (unwinding), and MiniDumpWriteDump for writing crash dumps that you later open with these same symbols. Without any PDB, you still have the export names, RTTI class names (lesson 2.05), and whatever names you recover and add in your disassembler's database, which is effectively a PDB you write by hand.

title: Finding the right PDB
body: Read a binary's CodeView record and work out where its PDB lives on a symbol server (lesson 5.04): cpp struct CodeView { std::array<std::uint8_t, 16 guid; std::uint32_t age; std::string path; }; std::optional<CodeView parseCodeView(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & record); std::string pdbName(const std::string& path); std::string guidText(const std::array<std::uint8_t, 16 & guid); std::string symbolServerPath(const CodeView& cv); - parseCodeView reads the record: RSDS , the 16 GUID bytes, a 4-byte little-endian age, then the PDB path up to a zero byte (or the end). Anything shorter than 24 bytes or with another signature gives std::nullopt . - pdbName is the file name part of the path: everything after the last \ or / . - guidText formats a GUID the symbol server's way: the first 4 bytes as one little-endian 32-bit number (8 hex digits), the next 2 as a little-endian 16-bit number (4 digits), the next 2 the same, then the last 8 bytes one by one (2 digits each). Uppercase, no separators: 32 characters. - symbolServerPath is name/GUIDAGE/name , with the age in uppercase hex without leading zeros.

title: 5.05  Scripting Your Analysis
body: Automating the repetitive parts of reverse engineering - scripting Ghidra, IDA and x64dbg, Python with pefile and Capstone for batch work, generating byte signatures automatically, and keeping your findings in a form you can reuse on the next build. Do it once by hand, then script it Reverse engineering has a lot of repetition: renaming every function that calls a logging function after the string it logs, finding every use of a struct, re-finding fifty functions in a new build. Anything you do more than a few times is worth a script, and every serious tool has a scripting interface. Ghidra Ghidra runs scripts written in Java or Python (Jython, or real Python 3 with the Ghidrathon or PyGhidra extensions) from its Script Manager. A script sees the whole program database: python-norun Rename every function that references a string beginning " net " after that string. from ghidra.program.model.symbol import SourceType for s in currentProgram.getListing().getDefinedData(True): text = s.getValue() if not isinstance(text, str) or not text.startswith(" net "): continue for ref in getReferencesTo(s.getAddress()): f = getFunctionContaining(ref.getFromAddress()) if f and f.getName().startswith("FUN_"): f.setName("net_" + text 6: .split() 0 , SourceType.USER_DEFINED) FUN_ is Ghidra's prefix for unnamed functions, so the check keeps names you already chose. Ghidra also has a headless mode ( analyzeHeadless ) that imports, analyses and runs scripts over many binaries without the user interface: the way to process a hundred builds. IDA and x64dbg - IDAPython gives the same kind of access in IDA ( idautils.Functions() , idc.set_name , cross-references), and IDA Free supports it in recent versions. - x64dbg has a simple command script language ( bp , run , log , conditional commands) for automating debugging sessions, and a plugin SDK in C++ for anything bigger, such as a plugin that logs every call to a function with formatted arguments. - WinDbg has JavaScript extensions and its data model ( dx ) for querying a session like a database. Python outside the tools For batch work on files, plain Python with two libraries goes a long way: python-norun import pefile, capstone pe = pefile.PE("Inventory.exe") text = next(s for s in pe.sections if s.Name.startswith(b".text")) code = text.get_data() base = pe.OPTIONAL_HEADER.ImageBase + text.VirtualAddress md = capstone.Cs(capstone.CS_ARCH_X86, capstone.CS_MODE_64) for insn in md.disasm(code :64 , base): print(f"{insn.address:x} {insn.mnemonic} {insn.op_str}") for entry in pe.DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT: print(entry.dll.decode(), imp.name.decode() for imp in entry.imports if imp.name ) pefile parses everything in milestone 1; Capstone disassembles as in lesson 5.02. Together they answer questions such as "which of these 200 builds import WinHttpOpen ?" in seconds. Generating signatures The byte patterns of lesson 4.05 are tedious to make by hand. A signature generator automates the recipe: 1. Start at the instruction you care about. 2. Add whole instructions one at a time, writing their bytes into the pattern but wildcarding the bytes that change between builds: RIP-relative and branch displacements, absolute addresses. 3. After each instruction, scan the module. When the pattern matches exactly once, stop. 4. If it grows past a length limit before becoming unique, give up and try starting from a nearby instruction instead. The decoder from this milestone supplies the instruction lengths and tells you which bytes are displacements. The practice writes this generator. Keeping findings Your understanding of a program is an asset: names, struct layouts, comments, signatures. Keep it in a form that survives: - Save the disassembler database and export names and types (Ghidra can export to C headers; IDA to .idc or .h ). - Keep a text file of signatures with what each one finds, so a new build can be re-labelled by running them. - For your own programs, the PDB is the real answer: archive it with every build.

title: A signature generator
body: Automate lesson 4.05's patterns as described in lesson 5.05: grow a pattern one instruction at a time, wildcarding the bytes that change between builds, until it is unique. cpp struct Insn { std::size_t offset; std::size_t length; std::size_t variableAt; std::size_t variableLength; }; std::string toPattern(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const std::vector<Insn & insns); std::size_t countMatches(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const std::string& pattern); std::optional<std::string makeSignature(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const std::vector<Insn & insns, std::size_t first, std::size_t maxBytes); insns describes consecutive instructions: each one's offset and length, and which of its bytes vary between builds ( variableLength bytes starting variableAt bytes into the instruction; variableLength 0 means none). - toPattern writes the bytes of the given instructions as a pattern: uppercase two-digit hex, ?? for variable bytes, separated by single spaces. - countMatches counts the places in code where a pattern of that form matches (overlapping matches count). - makeSignature starts with instruction number first and adds the following instructions one at a time; as soon as the pattern matches exactly once, it returns it. If adding the next instruction would make the pattern longer than maxBytes bytes, or the instructions run out, it returns std::nullopt .

title: A small x64 disassembler
body: Combine the length decoder and the operand formatter of this milestone into a working disassembler for the common instructions of lesson 5.02, using a linear sweep: cpp struct Line { std::uint64_t address; std::size_t length; std::string text; }; std::vector<Line disassemble(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::uint64_t base); Start at offset 0 and decode one instruction after another. Each Line has the instruction's address ( base + offset), its length and its text. A byte that does not start a known instruction (or an instruction cut off by the end of code ) becomes db 0x0f (two lowercase hex digits) with length 1, and decoding continues at the next byte. (Look at the test that does this: the bytes after an unknown instruction can decode as something plausible but wrong, exactly the weakness of linear sweep from lesson 5.02.) The subset. An optional REX prefix ( 40 - 4F ), then: Opcode Text --- --- 50 +r / 58 +r push r64 / pop r64 (REX.B adds 8) C3 , CC , 90 ret , int3 , nop E8 / E9 rel32, EB rel8 call TARGET / jmp TARGET 70 +cc rel8, 0F 80 +cc rel32 jCC TARGET with cc names o no b ae e ne be a s ns p np l ge le g 01 29 31 39 85 89 add sub xor cmp test mov rm , reg 03 2B 33 3B 8B add sub xor cmp mov reg , rm 8D lea reg , memory without the size keyword 83 /0 /4 /5 /7 ib add and sub cmp rm , IMM (8-bit, sign-extended) 81 /0 /4 /5 /7 id the same with a 32-bit signed immediate C7 /0 id mov rm , IMM (32-bit signed) B8 +r mov r32, IMM (32-bit, unsigned); with REX.W mov r64, IMM (64-bit) Formatting follows lesson 5.02 and the practice of 5.02: operand size 64 with REX.W, else 32; register and memory operands exactly as decodeModRm produced them ( qword ptr rbp-0x8 , rip+0x10 ...). Immediates are 0x plus lowercase hex, with - in front of negative ones ( -0x1 ). Branch and call targets are absolute addresses: 0x and lowercase hex of the address after the instruction plus the signed displacement. A ModRM reg field not listed for 83 , 81 or C7 makes the instruction unknown.

title: 6.01  A Method for Unknown Programs
body: How to approach a program you know nothing about without getting lost - start from a question, triage, find landmarks, form a hypothesis, test it dynamically, write it down, and know when to stop reading and switch technique. The trap The beginner's approach to an unknown binary is to open it at the entry point and read. After two hours you have understood the C runtime's start-up code in detail and know nothing about the program. Real programs are millions of instructions; nobody reads them all. Experienced reverse engineers read a tiny fraction, chosen carefully. Start from a question Every session needs a concrete goal, written down before you start: - "Where does it store its settings, and in what format?" - "Why does it crash when the file name contains a space?" - "How does the save file encode the player's inventory?" - "What does this DLL's exported Init function expect as its arguments?" A question tells you what you can ignore, which is almost everything. The loop 1. Triage (lesson 1.05): what is it, how was it built, what does it import, which strings does it contain? Ten minutes. 2. Find landmarks related to the question: strings ("Save failed"), imports ( CreateFileW , RegSetValueExW ), exports, RTTI class names, behaviour seen in Process Monitor. Each landmark leads to code through cross-references. 3. Form a hypothesis : "this function parses the save file; its first argument is the file contents; rcx+8 is the item count". 4. Test it dynamically : put a breakpoint there, trigger the behaviour, check the registers and memory against your guess. Change an input (a different save) and predict the change. 5. Record what you learned : rename the function, define the struct, add a comment, note the evidence. 6. Repeat , each answer raising the next, smaller question. Static reading suggests; dynamic testing confirms. A claim that has not been checked in a debugger, or against a second sample, is still a guess. Mark it as one. Top down and bottom up - Top down : start from a high-level landmark (the save command in the menu) and descend into the functions it calls until you reach the detail you need. - Bottom up : start from a low-level landmark (the call to WriteFile ) and climb the call stack to find who decided what to write. Bottom up is usually faster for questions about data; top down for questions about behaviour. Switch whenever you stall. Recognise library code A large part of any program is library code: the C runtime, the C++ standard library, compression, image loading, JSON parsing. Do not reverse it. Recognise it and name it: - Ghidra's Function ID and IDA's FLIRT signatures name known library functions automatically. - Strings give libraries away: inflate 1.2.13 Copyright , stb_image , error messages of well-known libraries. - Constants give algorithms away: 0x67452301 starts MD5 and SHA-1, 0xEDB88320 is CRC-32's polynomial, 0x9E3779B9 appears in TEA and in hash functions. Once you know a function is memcpy or zlib's inflate , you know its arguments and can step over it. Keep notes Write as you go, in the disassembler's database and in a plain notes file: - the question, and what you have concluded so far; - each finding with its evidence : address (as module+offset ), what you saw, how you confirmed it; - open questions and things you assumed. Notes make the work resumable tomorrow, shareable with someone else, and checkable when a new build arrives. Know when to switch If you have read the same function for an hour, stop and change technique: run it with different inputs and watch, diff two runs (lesson 3.05), look for a library signature, or find a different landmark. Reverse engineering is mostly choosing the right next small question.

title: A triage report
body: Turn the facts gathered in triage (lessons 1.05 and 6.01) into the warnings an analyst writes at the top of their notes: cpp struct SectionFacts { std::string name; double entropy; bool write; bool execute; }; struct Facts { std::vector<SectionFacts sections; int importCount; std::string entrySection; bool hasDebugInfo; }; std::vector<std::string triageFlags(const Facts& f); Return the flags that apply, in exactly this order: Flag When --- --- "no imports" importCount is 0 "few imports" importCount is 1 to 9 "high entropy: NAME" a section's entropy is above 7.2 (one flag per such section, in section order) "writable code: NAME" a section is both writable and executable (one per section) "entry outside .text" entrySection is not .text "probably packed" at least one high-entropy section and fewer than 10 imports "symbols may be available" hasDebugInfo is true

title: 6.02  Reversing a File Format
body: Working out an undocumented binary file format from samples - collecting files from controlled changes, magic numbers and versions, lengths and counts, offsets, byte order, strings, checksums and compression - and proving your understanding by writing a parser that reads every sample and a writer the program accepts. Why formats Formats are where reverse engineering pays off most often in practice: opening old save files, converting a tool's project files, reading a device's logs, importing a game's levels into an editor you are writing. And a format can often be worked out from files alone , with the code only consulted to settle doubts. Collect samples with controlled changes The single most useful technique is to make the program write files that differ in one known way : - Save twice with nothing changed: the bytes that differ are timestamps, random ids or counters. - Change the player's name from "Ada" to "Adam": the name's bytes appear, and something nearby probably grows by one (a length). - Add one item to the inventory: a count goes up by one, and a block of bytes is inserted. - Change one number you can see (gold 100 to 101): find 64 becoming 65 , and you know the field's position, size and byte order. Diff each pair (lesson 1.02's tool) and write down every observation. Twenty careful samples beat a thousand random ones. What to look for Magic numbers. Most formats start with a fixed signature: PK (zip), \x89PNG , RIFF , MZ . A custom format often starts with a readable tag like SAVE or GMDT . Versions. A small number near the start that never changes between your samples, but differs in files from an older version of the program. Lengths and counts. A number just before a variable-length thing: a byte or two before a string that equals its length, a count before a list. Changing the thing changes the number. Offsets. A number that equals the position of something else in the file: a table of contents. Check whether values in the header match positions where blocks start. Byte order. 64 00 00 00 is little-endian 100; 00 00 00 64 big-endian. A value you control, such as gold, settles it. Floats. Positions and fractions are often float s: four bytes that read as nonsense integers but sensible floats ( 00 00 C8 42 is 100.0). Strings. Length-prefixed, zero-terminated, fixed-size padded with zeros, ASCII or UTF-16. Checksums. If every change, however small, also changes a few bytes at the end (or the start), that is probably a checksum, and the program rejects files whose checksum does not match. Try the usual suspects over the rest of the file: a plain byte sum, CRC-32, Adler-32. A search for the CRC-32 constant 0xEDB88320 in the code confirms it. Compression and encryption. A block with entropy near 8 (lesson 1.05) is compressed or encrypted. Try decompressing with zlib (zlib streams usually start 78 9C or 78 DA ); otherwise find the code that reads the block. Writing it down Describe the format as a table of fields, then turn it into a parser : Offset Size Field Evidence --- --- --- --- 0 4 magic SAVE same in all samples 4 2 version, little-endian 2 in all current samples, 1 in an old one 6 1 name length 3 for "Ada", 4 for "Adam" ... Tools help: ImHex has a pattern language that overlays your field definitions on the bytes as you write them, highlighting fields so mistakes are obvious; Kaitai Struct describes formats in YAML and generates parsers in many languages. Proving it Your understanding is complete when: 1. Your parser reads every sample without leftovers or errors, and the values make sense. 2. Your writer produces a file from scratch that the program accepts and loads correctly. 3. Changing a field with your writer changes the right thing in the program. The practice is exactly this, for a small save file format.

title: A save file from samples
body: A small game the course provides writes save files in an undocumented format. You made it save four times with controlled changes (lesson 6.02): text A the start of a game: player "Ada", level 3, standing at x 100, y -2.5, carrying 5 of item 7 53 41 56 45 02 00 03 41 64 61 03 00 00 00 C8 42 00 00 20 C0 01 07 00 05 34 04 00 00 B the same, after renaming the player to "Adam" 53 41 56 45 02 00 04 41 64 61 6D 03 00 00 00 C8 42 00 00 20 C0 01 07 00 05 A2 04 00 00 C A, after picking up 1 of item 300 53 41 56 45 02 00 03 41 64 61 03 00 00 00 C8 42 00 00 20 C0 02 07 00 05 2C 01 01 63 04 00 00 D A, after levelling up to 4 and moving to x 101 53 41 56 45 02 00 03 41 64 61 04 00 00 00 CA 42 00 00 20 C0 01 07 00 05 37 04 00 00 Your notes so far: - The file always starts 53 41 56 45 , then 02 00 in every sample. - The name's bytes are preceded by a byte that equals its length. - The last four bytes change whenever anything changes. Adding up every byte before them gives the same number. - Floats are 4 bytes, little-endian ( 00 00 C8 42 is 100.0). Work out the rest from the samples, then write a reader and a writer: cpp struct Item { std::uint16_t id; std::uint8_t quantity; }; struct Save { std::string name; std::uint16_t level; float x, y; std::vector<Item items; }; std::optional<Save parseSave(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); std::vector<std::uint8_t writeSave(const Save& save); parseSave returns std::nullopt for a file with the wrong magic, a version other than 2, a wrong checksum, too few bytes for what the header announces, or bytes left over after the checksum. writeSave produces exactly the bytes the game would.

title: 6.03  Reversing a Network Protocol
body: Working out a custom protocol between a client and a server you run yourself - capturing the traffic, finding how messages are framed in a TCP stream, identifying message types, sequence numbers and fields, handling partial messages, and writing a dissector to decode captures automatically. The setting A protocol is a file format that arrives in pieces over time. The techniques of lesson 6.02 apply, plus the problem of splitting a stream into messages. Typical legitimate cases: the protocol of an old multiplayer game whose servers are gone, so a community server can be written; a device on your desk with its own control protocol; a debugging tool's link to your own game, which you wrote years ago and documented poorly. Work with a client and server you run yourself : capture traffic between them on your own machine or network. Other people's services, accounts and traffic are not yours to analyse. Capturing Wireshark captures the traffic (lesson 3.04). For a TCP connection, Follow TCP Stream shows each direction's bytes in order; save each direction as raw bytes for analysis. Do several captures with controlled actions, as with files: connect and disconnect; connect, send one chat message, disconnect; move one step left; move one step right. If the traffic is encrypted (TLS), the capture shows nothing useful. With your own client you can log the plaintext before encryption, or find the send function in the client and put a logging breakpoint there. Framing TCP delivers a stream of bytes , not messages: one send of 20 bytes may arrive as 20 bytes, or as 7 then 13, or glued to the next message. So every protocol over TCP has a framing rule that says where each message ends. The common ones: Framing Looks like --- --- length prefix every message starts with its length (often 2 or 4 bytes, often big-endian) delimiter messages end with \n or \r\n (text protocols: HTTP headers, SMTP, IRC) fixed size every message is N bytes type then known size a type byte, and each type has a fixed length To find a length prefix, look at the first bytes of each message and compare with the message's length: 00 0B followed by 11 bytes, 00 05 followed by 5. Watch whether the length counts itself or not. Inside a message Once messages are separated: - Type : an early byte with few distinct values, which correlates with actions (always 02 when you move, 03 when you chat). - Sequence numbers : a field that increases by one with every message in a direction. Gaps tell you about lost or filtered messages; the server's acknowledgements often echo them. - Fields : decoded as in a file format. Movement messages hold small signed numbers ( FF FF is −1 in 16 bits); chat messages hold a length and text. - Variable-length integers (varints): bytes with the top bit meaning "more follows", common in modern formats such as Protocol Buffers. Replaying a captured message, or sending a hand-made one from a small script, to your server and watching its reaction confirms what a field means. Partial messages A decoder must not assume messages arrive whole. It keeps a buffer, appends whatever arrives, and repeatedly takes a complete message from the front while enough bytes are present, leaving any partial tail for next time: cpp-norun buffer.insert(buffer.end(), received.begin(), received.end()); while (buffer.size() = 2) { const std::size_t length{ static_cast<std::size_t ((buffer 0 << 8) buffer 1 ) }; if (buffer.size() < 2 + length) break; // wait for the rest handle(std::span(buffer).subspan(2, length)); buffer.erase(buffer.begin(), buffer.begin() + 2 + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t (length)); } This same loop appears in every network program, and it is half of the Networking course's work too. Dissectors When you understand the protocol, teach Wireshark: a dissector written in Lua (a few dozen lines) decodes your protocol's messages in every capture, showing types, sequence numbers and fields by name. It turns future debugging of the protocol from hex reading into reading.

title: Decoding a captured protocol
