body: Captures between a small game client and server that the course provides showed this structure (lesson 6.03): every message is a 2-byte big-endian length (of everything after it), a 1-byte type , a 4-byte big-endian sequence number , then a payload: Type Name Payload --- --- --- 1 HELLO 1-byte name length, then the name 2 MOVE 2-byte big-endian signed dx, then dy 3 CHAT 2-byte big-endian text length, then the text 4 BYE nothing Write the decoder for a TCP stream, where messages can arrive split or joined: cpp struct Message { std::uint8_t type; std::uint32_t sequence; std::vector<std::uint8_t payload; }; class Decoder { public: void feed(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::vector<Message take(); std::size_t pending() const; }; std::string describe(const Message& m); std::vector<std::uint32_t missing(const std::vector<Message & messages); - feed adds received bytes; take returns every complete message received so far (in order) and removes them, leaving any incomplete tail; pending is how many bytes are waiting. A message whose length is below 5 cannot hold a type and a sequence: skip its whole frame. - describe formats: 7 HELLO Ada , 8 MOVE dx=3 dy=-1 , 9 CHAT gg , 10 BYE , and 11 TYPE 9 (2 bytes) for unknown types or payloads that do not match their type. - missing lists the sequence numbers skipped between consecutive messages (7, 8, 11 is missing 9 and 10), in order.

title: 6.04  Writing It Up
body: Turning an analysis into something others can use - the structure of a good report, evidence and reproducibility, annotated databases and headers, clean-room reimplementation, and handling security findings responsibly through coordinated disclosure. Analysis nobody can use is wasted The output of reverse engineering is understanding, and understanding that lives only in your head disappears. Whether it is for a teammate, your future self, or the maintainers of software you found a bug in, the work ends with writing it up. The shape of a report A useful report answers, in this order: 1. Summary : the question and the answer, in a few sentences. Many readers stop here. 2. Scope : exactly what was analysed: file name, version, hash (SHA-256), date, and which parts. 3. Findings : one section each, with the claim, the evidence (addresses as module+offset , disassembly excerpts, captured bytes, screenshots) and how confident you are. 4. How to reproduce : the steps someone else follows to see the same thing. 5. Open questions : what you did not resolve, and what you assumed. Evidence and reproduction are what separate a finding from an opinion. "The save file has a CRC-32 at offset 0x7C" is a claim; "changing any byte changes offset 0x7C–0x7F; the value matches crc32(bytes 0..0x7C)) in all 23 samples; the loader at game.exe+0x4A1B0 compares it and shows Corrupt save on mismatch" is a finding. Artefacts Alongside the report, keep what lets someone continue the work: - The disassembler database with your names, types and comments. - Headers for recovered structures, exported from the database or written by hand. - Parsers and scripts that encode the knowledge in executable form: a format parser is its own specification, and its tests are your evidence. - Signatures (lesson 4.05) for the important functions, so the work transfers to the next version. Reimplementation A common end goal is a new program that does what the old one did: a file converter, a replacement server, a source port of an old game. When rights matter, teams use a clean-room process: one person reverse engineers and writes a specification describing behaviour and formats; another, who never sees the original code, implements from the specification. That keeps the new code from being a copy of the old. Whether that is needed depends on the situation and the law; when it matters, take advice before starting. Security findings If your analysis turns up a vulnerability, in your own program or in software you were authorised to examine, the responsible path is coordinated disclosure : 1. Report it privately to the maintainers (a security contact, SECURITY.md , a bug bounty programme), with enough detail to reproduce and fix it. 2. Give them reasonable time to release a fix; 90 days is a common default. 3. Publish details only after a fix is available, or by agreement. Never test a vulnerability against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. Bug bounty programmes publish their rules precisely so that research within them is welcome.

title: 6.05  Where to Go Next
body: Places to keep practising legally - crackmes and CTF reversing challenges, open-source programs compiled yourself, the FLARE-On challenge, malware analysis training in safe labs - the books and courses worth your time, and what reverse engineering work looks like as a job. Keep practising on targets made for it Reverse engineering is learned by doing, and there is plenty to do legally: - Your own programs. Build open-source programs (or your own projects) in Release without the PDB, reverse a function, then compare with the source. It is the best feedback loop there is: you can always check your answer. - Crackmes. Small programs written to be reversed, with a password or key to find, sorted by difficulty: crackmes.one has thousands. This milestone's capstone is one. - CTF challenges. Capture the Flag competitions have "reversing" and "pwn" categories; past challenges with write-ups are archived (CTFtime lists events). picoCTF is aimed at beginners. - FLARE-On. An annual reversing challenge from Google's Mandiant FLARE team, with a dozen or so levels of increasing difficulty and published solutions. - Old games and software with official modding or source releases. Many classic games had their source released; comparing their binaries with the source is excellent practice. Malware analysis, safely Analysing malware is one of the main professional uses of these skills, and it must be done in an isolated lab: a virtual machine with no shared folders, a snapshot to restore, and no network (or a simulated one such as INetSim). Training material comes with prepared samples. Do not go looking for live malware to practise on, and never run a sample outside the lab. Books and courses - Practical Malware Analysis (Sikorski and Honig): the classic on static and dynamic analysis of Windows programs. - Practical Reverse Engineering (Dang, Gazet, Bachaalany): x86, x64, ARM and the Windows kernel. - The Ghidra Book (Eagle and Nance): using Ghidra in depth. - Windows Internals (Yosifovich and others): what the operating system does underneath everything in milestones 3 and 5. - OpenSecurityTraining2's free courses on x86-64 architecture, assembly and debuggers. The work itself Reverse engineering skills are used in several kinds of job: - Malware analysis and threat intelligence : understanding what malicious software does, to detect and remove it. - Vulnerability research : finding security bugs in software, for vendors, security firms or bug bounties. - Compatibility and interoperability : emulators, file converters, drivers for hardware with poor documentation. - Game development and modding : engine programmers reading compiler output, tools programmers working with old assets, modding communities working with official tools. - Software maintenance : every company has a program whose source was lost. All of them value the same things: careful method, notes with evidence, and judgement about what is appropriate to examine. What this course gave you You can read a PE file, find your way through x64 code compiled from C and C++, drive a debugger and know what it is doing underneath, find where data lives and what changes it, patch and hook your own programs, and you have written your own versions of a PE inspector, a control flow graph, a value scanner, a patch engine and a disassembler. The capstone puts it all to work on a program you have never seen.

title: A crackme on a tiny virtual machine
match: A crackme on a tiny virtual machine
body: The capstone. The course provides a program for a small virtual machine , the kind of thing crackmes and CTF challenges use: a "licence check" that prints OK for a correct key and NO otherwise. You have its bytecode and, from reversing the interpreter, its instruction set. Build the tools, then use them to find every key it accepts. The machine : eight 32-bit unsigned registers r0 - r7 (all 0 at the start), two flags eq and lt (false at the start), a program counter starting at 0, a read-only input string and an output string. Opcode Bytes Instruction Effect --- --- --- --- 00 1 halt stop 01 4 movi rA, imm16 rA = imm ( 01 A lo hi ) 02 3 mov rA, rB rA = rB 03 3 add rA, rB rA += rB 04 3 sub rA, rB rA -= rB 05 3 xor rA, rB rA ^= rB 06 3 mul rA, rB rA = rB 07 4 andi rA, imm16 rA &= imm 08 3 cmp rA, rB eq = rA == rB , lt = rA < rB 09 / 0A / 0B / 0C 3 jmp / je / jne / jl addr16 jump always / if eq / if not eq / if lt 0D 3 in rA, rB rA = input character at index rB , or 0 past the end 0E 2 out rA append the character rA & 0xFF to the output All arithmetic wraps at 32 bits; 16-bit values are little-endian. cpp struct VmLine { std::uint16_t address; std::string text; }; struct VmResult { std::string output; bool halted; bool error; int steps; }; std::vector<VmLine disassembleVm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & program); VmResult runVm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & program, const std::string& input, int maxSteps); std::vector<std::string findKeys(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & program); - disassembleVm works through the program from address 0. Texts: halt , movi r0, 0x30 , andi r0, 0xffff (immediates in lowercase hex), add r1, r7 , jl 0x0065 (jump targets as four lowercase hex digits), in r4, r1 , out r6 . An unknown opcode, a register number above 7, or an instruction cut off by the end becomes db 0xNN for that one byte, and disassembly continues at the next. - runVm executes. Every executed instruction, halt included, counts one step. It stops on halt ( halted true), on an error ( error true: an unknown opcode or bad register, an instruction running off the end of the program, or the program counter leaving the program), or after maxSteps steps (neither flag set). - findKeys runs the program on every 4-digit input from 0000 to 9999 (with a limit of 10 000 steps) and returns, in order, those whose output is exactly OK . Use your disassembler to read the program and understand the check before you brute-force it: the key space here is tiny, but the method of reading the bytecode is the point.

body: Problem Usual cause What to do Lesson --- --- --- --- Disassembly is nonsense after a certain point data inside code (a jump table, padding) decoded as instructions, or decoding started mid-instruction find where real code resumes; mark the data as data; use recursive descent 5.02 A function you wrote is missing from the binary inlined by the optimiser look in its callers; compare with a Debug build 1.02 Addresses from yesterday no longer match ASLR moved the module record and use module+offset 3.02 Addresses from the old build no longer match the program was rebuilt use byte patterns with wildcards 4.05 A breakpoint never hits the code runs in another thread, another module copy, or before you attached break on module load; start the program under the debugger 3.01 Memory shows CC where code should be your own software breakpoint, seen through a raw read read through the debugger, which hides them 3.01 A scan finds thousands of results wrong type or alignment, or too few narrowing scans change the value and rescan; try float; scan aligned only 3.03 The value is found but resets every run it lives on the heap find what writes it, the object base, then a pointer path 3.03 A patched program crashes immediately a patch overwrote part of the next instruction patch whole instructions, pad with nops 4.01 A detour crashes in the cave a stolen relative instruction was copied unchanged, or registers and flags were not preserved relocate or refuse relative instructions; save state 4.03 A hook works for some calls but not others an IAT hook only covers the module whose table changed hook other modules' tables, or use an inline hook 4.04 A pattern matches many places not distinctive enough add instructions until it is unique 4.05 The PDB is refused GUID or age does not match this build find the PDB from the exact build; use a symbol server 5.04 ReadProcessMemory fails with error 299 the region was freed or is not fully readable re-query the map; read only committed readable regions 5.03 A section has entropy near 8 and few imports the program is packed analyse the unpacked code in memory, in a lab if it is not yours 1.05 A file format has bytes that change on every save timestamps, counters or a checksum take two saves with no change to separate them 6.02

title: Glossary
body: Basic block : a run of instructions with one way in and one way out. (2.03) Calling convention : the rules for where arguments and return values go; on 64-bit Windows, rcx rdx r8 r9 and rax . (2.01) Code cave : unused space in a program used to hold new code reached by a jump. (4.03) CodeView record : the debug directory entry naming a binary's PDB by path, GUID and age. (5.04) Control flow graph : a function drawn as basic blocks connected by the jumps between them. (2.03) Cross-reference : a place in the code that refers to an address, such as a call to a function or a load of a string. (2.04) Data breakpoint : a hardware breakpoint that stops when data at an address is written or read. (3.01) Decompiler : a tool that reconstructs C-like source from machine code. (1.02) Detour : a jump from original code to new code, which runs the overwritten instructions and jumps back. (4.03) Disassembler : a tool that turns machine code into assembly text. (1.02) Dynamic analysis : studying a program while it runs. (1.02) Export : a function or variable a DLL makes available by name or ordinal. (1.04) Forwarder : an export that points at a function in another DLL. (1.04) Hook : redirecting calls to a function so other code runs first. (4.04) IAT : import address table, filled by the loader with the addresses of imported functions. (1.04) Leaf function : a function that calls nothing and often has no stack frame. (2.02) Linear sweep : disassembling from the start of a section to the end, one instruction after another. (5.02) Mangling (decoration) : encoding a C++ name's scope and signature into a linker symbol. (2.05) ModRM : the byte describing an instruction's register and memory operands. (5.01) Packed : compressed or encrypted, with a stub that restores the real code at run time. (1.05) PDB : program database: the symbols, types and line information for a build. (5.04) PE : Portable Executable, the format of Windows .exe and .dll files. (1.03) Pointer path : a stable base and a list of offsets that reaches a value on the heap. (3.03) Recursive descent : disassembling by following control flow from known entry points. (5.02) REX prefix : the byte from 0x40 to 0x4F that selects 64-bit operands and registers r8 to r15. (5.01) RTTI : run-time type information, which leaves class names in the binary. (2.05) RVA : relative virtual address: an offset from the module's load address. (1.03) Signature (pattern) : bytes with wildcards that find the same code in different builds. (4.05) Static analysis : studying a program without running it. (1.02) Stolen bytes : the original instructions overwritten by a hook or detour's jump. (4.03) Thunk : a tiny function that only jumps somewhere else. (2.02) Trampoline : the stolen bytes plus a jump back, used to call the original of a hooked function. (4.04) Triage : the first quick survey of an unknown binary. (1.05) Vtable : a class's table of virtual function addresses. (2.05)

title: 1.01  Rust and Cargo: Your First Program
match: 1.01 Rust and Cargo: Your First Program
body: What Rust is for and what makes it different, installing it with rustup, creating and running a project with Cargo, the shape of a program with fn main, printing with println! and format strings, comments, and how to read the compiler's unusually helpful error messages. Rust Rust is a systems language: it compiles to fast machine code with no garbage collector, like C and C++, so it suits operating systems, browsers, game engines, command-line tools, servers and embedded devices. What makes it different is that the compiler proves memory safety : no dangling pointers, no use-after-free, no data races between threads. The rules that guarantee this (ownership and borrowing, milestone 2) are checked when you compile, so they cost nothing when the program runs. The price is a stricter compiler. Rust programmers say they "fight the borrow checker" at first; the compiler's messages are excellent, and the bugs it stops are the ones that are hardest to find in other languages. Installing and Cargo Install Rust with rustup from rust-lang.org. It provides rustc (the compiler) and Cargo , the build tool and package manager you use for everything: bash cargo new hello a new project folder with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs cd hello cargo run compile and run (debug build) cargo build --release an optimised build in target/release cargo check type-check quickly without producing a program Cargo.toml describes the project and its dependencies ( crates , from crates.io). The practice editor here compiles your code on Rust 1.99 (edition 2024) for you. Your first program rust fn main() { println!("Hello, Xenon!"); let name = "Ada"; let year = 1815; println!("{name} was born in {year}."); println!("{} + {} = {}", 2, 3, 2 + 3); } - fn main() is where the program starts. Functions are declared with fn . - println! prints a line. The ! means it is a macro , not a function: macros can take a format string and a variable number of arguments, checked at compile time. - {} in the format string is filled by the next argument; {name} uses a variable of that name directly. - Statements end with ; . Blocks are in braces. Formatting rust fn main() { let pi = 3.14159265; let item = "tea"; println!(" {pi:.2} "); // 2 decimals: 3.14 println!(" {item: 8} {item:<8} {item:^8} "); // right, left, centred in 8 println!(" {:05} {:+} {:x} {:b} ", 42, 7, 255, 5); // zero-padded, sign, hex, binary println!("{:?}", vec! 1, 2, 3 ); // {:?} is the Debug format: for developers eprintln!("this goes to standard error"); let s = format!("{item} costs {:.2}", 2.5); // format! builds a String instead of printing println!("{s}"); } Comments rust // A line comment. / A block comment. / /// A documentation comment for the item below; cargo doc turns these into web pages. fn main() { println!("comments are ignored"); } Compiler errors Rust's error messages show the code, point at the problem and often suggest the fix: text error E0384 : cannot assign twice to immutable variable x -- src/main.rs:3:5 2 let x = 5; - first assignment to x 3 x = 6; ^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable help: consider making this binding mutable 2 let mut x = 5; +++ Read the first error first, and read the help: lines: they are usually right. rustc --explain E0384 prints a long explanation of any error code.

title: Input and output
where: 1.01 Rust and Cargo: Your First Program
body: Write a program that reads a name and a birth year (one per line), then greets the person and says how old they turn in 2026: Name? Ada Birth year? 1990 Hello, Ada! In 2026 you turn 36. Print the prompts with print! (no line break), read each answer with read_line , and trim it. Parse the year with parse::<i32 () .

title: 1.02  Variables, Mutability and Types
body: let and mut, why variables are immutable by default, shadowing, constants, the scalar types (integers of every size, floats, bool, char), type inference and annotations, integer overflow in debug and release builds, conversions with as and From, and tuples and arrays. let and mut Variables are immutable by default. Add mut to allow changes: rust fn main() { let x = 5; // x = 6; // error: cannot assign twice to immutable variable let mut count = 0; count += 1; count += 1; println!("{x} {count}"); } Immutability by default means that when you read let total = ... , you know total never changes afterwards. Mark a variable mut only when it must change. Shadowing A new let with the same name shadows the old variable. Unlike mut , it can change the type, which is handy for converting a value in steps: rust fn main() { let input = " 42 "; let input = input.trim(); // &str let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap(); // now an i32 let input = input 2; println!("{input}"); } Constants rust const MAX_PLAYERS: u32 = 4; // a constant: type required, known at compile time const SECONDS_PER_DAY: u64 = 24 60 60; fn main() { println!("{MAX_PLAYERS} {SECONDS_PER_DAY}"); } Scalar types Type Holds --- --- i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 , i128 Signed integers ( i32 is the default) u8 , u16 , u32 , u64 , u128 Unsigned integers (0 and up) isize , usize Pointer-sized integers; usize is used for indexes and lengths f32 , f64 Floating point ( f64 is the default) bool true or false char One Unicode character, 4 bytes: 'a' , 'é' , '🦀' rust fn main() { let a = 42; // inferred i32 let b: u8 = 255; let big = 1_000_000_000_000i64; let ratio = 0.75; // f64 let crab = '🦀'; let ok = a 40 && b == 255; println!("{a} {b} {big} {ratio} {crab} {ok}"); println!("{} {}", i32::MAX, u64::MAX); println!("{}", 7 / 2); // 3: integer division println!("{}", 7.0 / 2.0); // 3.5 println!("{}", -7 % 3); // -1 println!("{}", (-7i32).rem_euclid(3)); // 2 } Overflow If an integer operation overflows, a debug build panics ("attempt to add with overflow"); a release build wraps around. When wrapping or saturating is what you want, say so: rust fn main() { let x: u8 = 250; println!("{:?}", x.checked_add(10)); // None: would overflow println!("{}", x.wrapping_add(10)); // 4 println!("{}", x.saturating_add(10)); // 255 println!("{:?}", x.checked_add(5)); // Some(255) } Converting between types Rust never converts numbers implicitly; let y: i64 = x; with x: i32 is an error. Convert explicitly: rust fn main() { let small: i32 = 300; let wide: i64 = small.into(); // lossless: From / Into let wide2 = i64::from(small); let truncated = small as u8; // as: may lose information (300 becomes 44) let f = small as f64 / 7.0; let back = 3.99_f64 as i32; // 3: truncates toward zero let checked: Result<u8, _ = u8::try_from(small); // Err: does not fit println!("{wide} {wide2} {truncated} {f:.3} {back} {checked:?}"); } Prefer into() / from() for conversions that can never fail, try_from when they might, and as only when you really want truncation. Tuples and arrays rust fn main() { let point: (i32, f64, &str) = (3, 4.5, "label"); let (x, y, name) = point; // destructuring println!("{x} {y} {name} {}", point.0); let days = "Mon", "Tue", "Wed" ; // an array: fixed length, one type let zeros = 0; 5 ; // five zeros println!("{} {:?} {}", days 1 , zeros, days.len()); // days 10 ; // panics at run time: index out of bounds }

title: Numeric types
body: Write these functions in solution.rs : rust fn to_celsius(fahrenheit: f64) - f64 // (F - 32) 5 / 9 fn average(a: i32, b: i32, c: i32) - f64 // exact: average(1, 2, 2) is 1.666... fn to_cents(euros: f64) - i64 // rounded to the nearest cent: 19.99 gives 1999 fn add_volume(volume: u8, change: i16) - u8 // stays within 0..=100 whatever the change fn checked_area(width: u32, height: u32) - Option<u32 // None if the product overflows u32

title: 1.03  Functions and Expressions
body: Declaring functions with typed parameters and return types, statements versus expressions, returning the last expression without a semicolon, blocks as expressions, early return, unit (), and why Rust has no function overloading or default arguments. Functions rust fn main() { println!("{}", area(3.0, 4.0)); greet("Grace"); println!("{}", is_even(10)); let (q, r) = divide(17, 5); println!("{q} remainder {r}"); } fn area(width: f64, height: f64) - f64 { width height // no semicolon: this is the returned value } fn greet(name: &str) { // no return type: returns () ("unit") println!("Hello, {name}!"); } fn is_even(n: i32) - bool { n % 2 == 0 } fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) - (i32, i32) { (a / b, a % b) // a tuple returns two values } Every parameter needs a type; the return type follows - . Functions can be defined in any order. Names use snake_case . Statements and expressions Rust is an expression language : almost everything produces a value. - An expression evaluates to a value: 5 , a + b , if ... {} else {} , a block { ... } , a function call. - A statement does something and has no value: let x = 5; , or any expression followed by ; . The last expression in a block, without a semicolon, is the block's value: rust fn main() { let y = { let x = 3; x x + 1 // the block's value }; let sign = if y 5 { "big" } else { "small" }; // if is an expression too println!("{y} {sign}"); } Adding a ; after the last expression turns it into a statement, and the block's value becomes () . That is the most common error for newcomers: text error E0308 : mismatched types fn square(x: i32) - i32 { --- expected i32 because of return type x x; - help: remove this semicolon to return this value Early return return leaves a function early, typically after checking for a special case: rust fn main() { println!("{} {} {}", grade(95), grade(72), grade(-5)); } fn grade(score: i32) - char { if !(0..=100).contains(&score) { return '?'; } match score { 90..=100 = 'A', 70..=89 = 'C', _ = 'F', } } 0..=100 is an inclusive range ; 0..100 excludes the end. match (lesson 2.05) picks a branch by pattern. No overloading, no defaults Rust has no function overloading and no default parameter values. Give different functions different names ( area_circle , area_rect ), or use an Option parameter, a struct of options, or a trait (milestone 4). This keeps every call unambiguous.

title: Functions and expressions
body: Write these functions; use expressions (an if or block as the last expression) rather than return where you can: rust fn is_leap_year(year: i32) - bool fn clock(minutes: i32) - String // minutes after midnight as "h:mm": 125 is "2:05"; wraps around, -30 is "23:30" fn digit_sum(n: i64) - u32 // ignoring the sign fn gcd(a: u64, b: u64) - u64 // Euclid; gcd(0, 0) is 0 fn sign_word(x: f64) - &'static str // "negative", "zero" or "positive"

title: 1.04  Control Flow
body: if and else as expressions, loop with break values, while, for over ranges and collections, labelled breaks, a first look at match with ranges and multiple patterns, and choosing the right loop. if rust fn main() { let temperature = 23; if temperature = 30 { println!("Hot"); } else if temperature = 18 { println!("Pleasant"); } else { println!("Cold"); } let label = if temperature % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }; println!("{label}"); } The condition must be a bool : if count { } does not compile. Braces are required; parentheses around the condition are not used. loop, while and for rust fn main() { // loop runs until break; break can return a value let mut n = 27u64; let mut steps = 0; let result = loop { if n == 1 { break steps; } n = if n % 2 == 0 { n / 2 } else { 3 n + 1 }; steps += 1; }; println!("{result} steps"); // while: repeat while a condition holds let mut countdown = 3; while countdown 0 { print!("{countdown} "); countdown -= 1; } println!("lift-off"); // for: over a range or a collection for i in 1..=5 { print!("{} ", i i); } println!(); let names = "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" ; for (index, name) in names.iter().enumerate() { println!("{index}: {name}"); } for i in (0..10).rev().step_by(3) { print!("{i} "); } println!(); } for is the most common loop: it cannot go out of bounds and needs no index variable. enumerate() adds the index when you need it. break and continue rust fn main() { let numbers = 4, 7, -1, 12, 0, 9 ; let mut sum = 0; for x in numbers { if x < 0 { continue; } if x == 0 { break; } sum += x; } println!("{sum}"); 'outer: for i in 0..5 { for j in 0..5 { if i j == 6 { println!("found {i} x {j}"); break 'outer; // leaves both loops } } } } match match compares a value against patterns , in order, and must cover every possible value: rust fn main() { for day in 1, 6, 7, 9 { let kind = match day { 1..=5 = "weekday", 6 7 = "weekend", _ = "not a day", // _ matches anything else }; println!("{day}: {kind}"); } } If you leave out the _ arm, the compiler refuses: "non-exhaustive patterns". This exhaustiveness check catches forgotten cases at compile time. match becomes much more powerful with enums (lesson 2.05). Choosing a loop Situation Loop --- --- Over a collection or a range for Until a condition becomes false while Until something inside decides (retry, read until done) loop with break

title: Loops
body: Write these with loops: rust fn fizzbuzz(n: u32) - Vec<String // "1", "2", "Fizz", ..., "FizzBuzz", up to n fn collatz_steps(n: u64) - u32 // steps for n to reach 1 (n / 2 when even, 3n + 1 when odd); 0 for n = 1 fn primes_below(n: u32) - Vec<u32 // in order; use a sieve fn first_square_above(limit: u64) - u64 // the smallest perfect square strictly greater than limit Use loop , while and for where each fits best; collatz_steps can use loop with break returning the count.

title: 1.05  Strings and Input
body: The two string types - owned String and borrowed &str - and when to use each, common string methods, building strings with push_str and format!, reading lines from standard input, parsing numbers with parse and handling failure, and a first taste of Result and unwrap. String and &str Rust has two main string types: - String is an owned , growable string stored on the heap. You can change it. - &str (a "string slice") is a borrowed view of string data that lives somewhere else: in the program itself (string literals), or inside a String . rust fn main() { let literal: &str = "hello"; // a borrowed view of text in the program let mut owned: String = String::from("hello"); // owned, growable owned.push_str(", world"); owned.push('!'); let view: &str = &owned; // borrow a String as &str println!("{literal} {owned} {view} {}", owned.len()); let built = format!("{} has {} characters", literal, literal.len()); let joined = "a", "b", "c" .join("-"); let upper = owned.to_uppercase(); // methods that change text return a new String println!("{built} {joined} {upper}"); } Functions that only read text take &str : they then accept both literals and &String . Functions that keep text (store it in a struct) take String . Milestone 2 explains why. String methods Code Gives --- --- s.len() , s.is_empty() Length in bytes , emptiness s.trim() , s.to_lowercase() , s.to_uppercase() Trimmed slice, new Strings s.contains("x") , s.starts_with("x") , s.find("x") Tests, Option position s.replace("a", "b") A new String s.split(',') , s.split_whitespace() , s.lines() Iterators over pieces s.chars() , s.chars().rev().collect::<String () Characters, reversed s.parse::<i32 () A Result with the number or an error rust fn main() { let line = " Ada Lovelace, 1815 , mathematician "; let parts: Vec<&str = line.split(',').map( p p.trim()).collect(); println!("{:?}", parts); let year: i32 = parts 1 .parse().unwrap(); println!("{}", year + 200); let words: Vec<&str = "the quick brown fox".split_whitespace().collect(); println!("{} words, first {}", words.len(), words 0 ); println!("{}", "racecar".chars().rev().collect::<String ()); } .map( p p.trim()) applies a closure (an inline function, lesson 5.01) to each piece; collect() gathers the results into a Vec . Strings are UTF-8, so you cannot index them by position ( s 0 does not compile): a character may take several bytes. Use chars() (lesson 3.02 explains the details). Reading input rust use std::io; fn main() { let mut name = String::new(); println!("What is your name?"); io::stdin().read_line(&mut name).expect("could not read input"); let name = name.trim(); // read_line keeps the line break let mut age_text = String::new(); io::stdin().read_line(&mut age_text).expect("could not read input"); match age_text.trim().parse::<u32 () { Ok(age) = println!("Hello, {name}! Next year you will be {}.", age + 1), Err(_) = println!("Hello, {name}! That age is not a number."), } } - read_line(&mut name) appends the line (including its \n ) to name and returns a Result : reading can fail. - parse::<u32 () returns Ok(number) or Err(error) . match handles both. - .expect("message") and .unwrap() take the value out of an Ok , and panic (stop the program) on an Err . They are fine in quick programs and for errors that "cannot happen"; real error handling comes in lesson 3.04. To read every line until the input ends: rust use std::io::{self, BufRead}; fn main() { let mut total = 0; for line in io::stdin().lock().lines() { let line = line.unwrap(); if let Ok(n) = line.trim().parse::<i64 () { total += n; } } println!("total {total}"); } if let Ok(n) = ... runs the block only when the pattern matches: a short match with one interesting arm.

title: A temperature converter
body: Write a program that reads lines like 20 C , 68 F or 300 K until the input ends, and converts each to all three scales: 20 C 68.5 f abc C -500 C done prints 20.00 C = 68.00 F = 293.15 K 20.28 C = 68.50 F = 293.43 K Cannot read: abc C Below absolute zero: -500 C Cannot read: done Converted 2 values - A line is a number and a unit ( C , F or K , either case), separated by white space. Empty lines are skipped. - A line whose number does not parse, or that does not have exactly two parts, prints Cannot read: <line as typed ; an unknown unit prints Unknown unit in: <line ; a temperature below absolute zero (0 K) prints Below absolute zero: <line . - Each value is printed with two decimals. Celsius to Fahrenheit is C × 9/5 + 32 ; Kelvin is C + 273.15 . - At the end, print Converted N values .

title: A number converter
body: Write a program that converts numbers between bases and to Roman numerals, one command per line: bin 10 hex 255 oct 8 dec 0x1F dec 0b1010 roman 1994 quit prints 10 = 0b1010 255 = 0xff 8 = 0o10 0x1F = 31 0b1010 = 10 1994 = MCMXCIV Commands (the command word ignores case; extra spaces are fine): Command Does --- --- bin <n , hex <n , oct <n n is a decimal u64 ; prints <n = 0b... , 0x... (lower case) or 0o... dec <text text is decimal, or has a 0b , 0o or 0x prefix (prefix and hex digits in either case); prints <text = <decimal roman <n n from 1 to 3999; prints the Roman numeral, or Roman numerals go from 1 to 3999 quit Stops (so does the end of the input) Errors: a value that does not parse prints Not a number: <value ; a missing or extra value prints Usage: <command <value ; an unknown command prints Unknown command: <word . Blank lines are skipped. Do the conversions yourself with loops and arithmetic: no {:b} / {:x} / {:o} formatting and no from_str_radix .

title: 2.01  Ownership and Moves
body: The three ownership rules, the stack and the heap, how String owns heap memory and frees it when dropped, moves versus copies, the Copy trait for simple values, clone for explicit deep copies, ownership through function calls and return values, and why this replaces both garbage collection and manual free. Who frees the memory? Every program must give memory back when it is done with it. C and C++ make the programmer call free / delete (forgetting leaks memory; freeing twice or too early corrupts it). Java, C and Python use a garbage collector, which costs run time. Rust takes a third way: the compiler tracks ownership and inserts the clean-up itself, exactly once, at a point it can prove is safe. The rules 1. Every value has exactly one owner : a variable, a struct field, a vector slot... 2. There is only one owner at a time. 3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed). rust fn main() { { let s = String::from("hello"); // s owns a heap buffer holding "hello" println!("{s}"); } // s goes out of scope: the buffer is freed here // println!("{s}"); // error: s does not exist here } Stack and heap Values with a fixed, known size (integers, bool , char , tuples of those) live on the stack and are trivially cheap to copy. A String or Vec is a small struct on the stack (a pointer, a length, a capacity) that points to a buffer on the heap , whose size can change. Copying the small struct is cheap; copying the heap buffer is not, and two owners of one buffer would both try to free it. Moves So, assigning a String (or Vec , or any type that owns heap data) moves ownership. The old variable can no longer be used: rust-norun let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1; // the ownership moves to s2; nothing is copied on the heap println!("{s1}"); // error E0382 : borrow of moved value: s1 The compiler message explains exactly this, and points at the line where the move happened. After a move, only s2 will free the buffer, so it is freed once. Copy types Simple stack-only types implement the Copy trait: assignment copies them, and the original stays usable: rust fn main() { let a = 5; let b = a; // i32 is Copy: a is still valid let p = (1.5, true); let q = p; // a tuple of Copy types is Copy println!("{a} {b} {:?} {:?}", p, q); } Integers, floats, bool , char , shared references &T , and tuples and arrays of Copy types are Copy . String , Vec and Box are not. clone To really duplicate heap data, call .clone() . It is explicit on purpose: a deep copy may be expensive, and you can see it in the code. rust fn main() { let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1.clone(); // a second, independent buffer println!("{s1} {s2}"); } Ownership and functions Passing a value to a function moves (or copies) it, just like assignment. Returning a value moves it out to the caller: rust fn main() { let name = String::from("Ada"); let n = 42; take(name); // name moves into the function // println!("{name}"); // error: value moved copy_it(n); // n is copied: still usable println!("{n}"); let made = make_greeting("Grace"); // ownership moves out to made let back = give_back(made); // in and out again println!("{back}"); } fn take(s: String) { println!("took {s}"); } // s is dropped here fn copy_it(x: i32) { println!("copied {x}"); } fn make_greeting(name: &str) - String { format!("Hello, {name}!") } fn give_back(s: String) - String { s } Moving values in and out of every function would be tedious. The next lesson's borrowing lets a function use a value without taking it.

title: Ownership in function signatures
body: The starter does not compile: the tests keep using values after passing them to these functions, which moves them. Change the signatures (and bodies) so each function borrows when it only needs to read, and takes ownership only when it really keeps or changes the value: rust fn report(names: ...) - String // "3 names: Ada, Grace, Linus"; "no names" when empty fn longest(a: ..., b: ...) - String // a copy of the longer text (the first on a tie) fn shout(text: String) - String // takes ownership: upper-cases the text in place and adds "!" fn add_suffix(names: ..., suffix: &str) // appends suffix to every name in the vector, in place Read the tests to see how each function is called.

title: 2.02  References and Borrowing
body: Using values without taking ownership - shared references &T and mutable references &mut T, the borrowing rules (many readers or one writer), why they prevent data races and invalid pointers, non-lexical lifetimes, dangling references the compiler refuses, and dereferencing with . Borrowing A reference lets code use a value without owning it. Creating one is called borrowing : rust fn main() { let s = String::from("hello world"); let n = length(&s); // lend s; we keep ownership println!("{s} has {n} bytes"); // s is still ours } fn length(text: &String) - usize { // &String: a reference to a String text.len() } // the reference goes away; nothing is dropped &s creates a shared reference ; the function can read through it but not change the value. Mutable references To let a function change a value, lend it a mutable reference , &mut . Both the variable and the borrow must be marked mutable: rust fn main() { let mut s = String::from("hello"); add_world(&mut s); let mut count = 0; bump(&mut count); bump(&mut count); println!("{s} {count}"); } fn add_world(text: &mut String) { text.push_str(", world"); } fn bump(n: &mut i32) { n += 1; // dereferences: change the value the reference points to } The borrowing rules At any moment, a value can have either : - any number of shared references &T , or - exactly one mutable reference &mut T , but not both. And a reference must never outlive the value it points to. rust-norun let mut v = vec! 1, 2, 3 ; let first = &v 0 ; // a shared borrow of v v.push(4); // error E0502 : cannot borrow v as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable println!("{first}"); This rule prevents a real bug: push may move the vector's buffer to a bigger allocation, leaving first pointing at freed memory. In C++ the equivalent code compiles and corrupts memory at run time; in Rust it does not compile. Across threads, the same rule rules out data races (milestone 6). Borrows end when last used A borrow lasts until its last use , not until the end of the block, so code like this is fine: rust fn main() { let mut scores = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum(); // a shared borrow, used here and finished scores.push(total); // now a mutable borrow is fine let last = scores.last().unwrap(); // shared borrow println!("{last} {}", scores.len()); // more shared borrows: fine together } No dangling references A function cannot return a reference to something it created, because that value is dropped when the function ends: rust-norun fn dangle() - &String { // error E0106 : missing lifetime specifier let s = String::from("hi"); &s // s is dropped here: the reference would point at freed memory } Return the owned value instead: fn no_dangle() - String { String::from("hi") } . Lesson 4.04 explains the lifetimes the compiler uses to check this. &str and &String &String coerces to &str automatically ( deref coercion ), so functions that only read text should take &str and accept both: rust fn shout(text: &str) - String { text.to_uppercase() + "!" } fn main() { let owned = String::from("hey"); println!("{} {}", shout(&owned), shout("you")); }

title: Borrowing
body: Write these functions with the right kind of reference: rust fn add_score(scores: &mut Vec<u32 , score: u32) - usize // adds the score, returns the new count fn best<'a (scores: &'a u32 ) - Option<&'a u32 // a reference to the highest score (the first on a tie) fn normalize(words: &mut String ) // trims and lower-cases each word in place fn swap_ends(values: &mut i32 ) // swaps the first and last items (if there are at least two) fn count_starting(words: & String , prefix: &str) - usize // ignoring case The 'a in best says the returned reference points into scores ; lesson 4.04 explains it.

title: 2.03  Slices
body: Borrowing part of a collection with slices - string slices &str and their byte ranges, array and vector slices & T , ranges in indexing, slice methods (len, first, last, split_at, chunks, windows, contains, iter), mutable slices &mut T , and writing functions that take slices to accept arrays, vectors and parts of them. String slices A slice is a reference to a contiguous part of a collection. &s start..end borrows bytes start up to (not including) end : rust fn main() { let s = String::from("hello world"); let hello: &str = &s 0..5 ; let world = &s 6.. ; // to the end let all = &s .. ; // the whole string println!(" {hello} {world} {all} "); println!("{}", first_word("the quick brown fox")); } fn first_word(text: &str) - &str { match text.find(' ') { Some(i) = &text ..i , None = text, } } first_word returns a slice into its argument, without copying. The borrow checker makes sure the original string outlives the slice: you cannot clear the String while a slice of it is in use. String slice ranges are in bytes , and must fall on character boundaries. &"héllo" 0..2 panics, because é takes two bytes and the range cuts it in half. For text from users, prefer chars() and the string methods (lesson 3.02). Array and vector slices & T is a slice of any sequence of T : part of an array, part of a vector, or all of either. rust fn main() { let array = 3, 8, 1, 9, 4 ; let vector = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; println!("{} {} {}", sum(&array), sum(&vector), sum(&array 1..3 )); println!("{:?}", largest(&array)); println!("{:?}", largest(& )); } fn sum(values: & i32 ) - i32 { let mut total = 0; for v in values { total += v; } total } fn largest(values: & i32 ) - Option<i32 { let mut best = values.first()?; // ? returns None early for an empty slice for &v in values { if v best { best = v; } } Some(best) } Write functions that only read a sequence to take & T (and text as &str ): they then work with arrays, vectors and sub-ranges alike, and never need to own the data. Slice methods rust fn main() { let data = 5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 7 ; println!("{} {:?} {:?} {}", data.len(), data.first(), data.last(), data.contains(&4)); let (left, right) = data.split_at(2); println!("{left:?} {right:?}"); for pair in data.windows(2) { print!("{} ", pair 1 - pair 0 ); // differences between neighbours } println!(); for chunk in data.chunks(4) { print!("{chunk:?} "); } println!(); println!("{:?}", data.iter().position( &x x == 2)); let mut sorted = data; // arrays are Copy when their items are sorted.sort(); println!("{sorted:?} {:?}", sorted.binary_search(&7)); } Mutable slices &mut T lets a function change the items in place, without being able to change the length: rust fn main() { let mut v = vec! 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ; double_all(&mut v 1..4 ); reverse_in_place(&mut v); println!("{v:?}"); } fn double_all(values: &mut i32 ) { for x in values.iter_mut() { x = 2; } } fn reverse_in_place(values: &mut i32 ) { let n = values.len(); for i in 0..n / 2 { values.swap(i, n - 1 - i); } }

title: Slices
body: Return slices that point into the input instead of building new strings or vectors: rust fn first_word(text: &str) - &str // up to the first space; the whole text if there is none fn last_word(text: &str) - &str // after the last space, ignoring trailing spaces fn trim_zeros(values: & i32 ) - & i32 // without leading and trailing zeros fn max_window_sum(values: & i32 , k: usize) - Option<i32 // the largest sum of k neighbours; None if k is 0 or too big fn split_on(values: & i32 , separator: i32) - Vec<& i32 // like str::split, for numbers split_on(& 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 0, 4 , 0) gives 1 , 2, 3 , , 4 .

title: 2.04  Structs and Methods
body: Defining structs with named fields, tuple structs and unit structs, creating them with field init shorthand and update syntax, methods in impl blocks with &self, &mut self and self, associated functions like new, deriving Debug, Clone and PartialEq, and privacy with pub. Structs A struct groups named values into one type: rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Book { title: String, author: String, year: u16, pages: u32, } fn main() { let dune = Book { title: String::from("Dune"), author: String::from("Frank Herbert"), year: 1965, pages: 412, }; println!("{} by {} ({})", dune.title, dune.author, dune.year); println!("{dune:?}"); // needs derive(Debug) println!("{dune: ?}"); // pretty-printed let messiah = Book { title: String::from("Dune Messiah"), year: 1969, ..dune.clone() }; // update syntax println!("{} {}", messiah.title, messiah == dune); } derive(...) asks the compiler to generate standard behaviour: Debug for {:?} printing, Clone for .clone() , PartialEq for == (lesson 4.03 covers these traits). A struct owns its fields. A field of type String means each Book owns its text, which is usually what you want; fields holding references need lifetimes (lesson 4.04). Methods Methods are defined in an impl block. The first parameter says how the method uses the value: rust derive(Debug) struct Counter { name: String, count: u32, } impl Counter { fn new(name: &str) - Counter { // an associated function: no self, called as Counter::new Counter { name: name.to_string(), count: 0 } } fn increment(&mut self) { // &mut self: may change the struct self.count += 1; } fn describe(&self) - String { // &self: only reads it format!("{}: {}", self.name, self.count) } fn into_name(self) - String { // self: takes ownership; the counter is used up self.name } } fn main() { let mut clicks = Counter::new("clicks"); clicks.increment(); clicks.increment(); println!("{}", clicks.describe()); let name = clicks.into_name(); println!("{name}"); // clicks.describe(); // error: clicks was moved by into_name } First parameter Meaning Use for --- --- --- &self Borrows the value to read it Getters, calculations &mut self Borrows it to change it Updating fields self Takes ownership Turning it into something else none An associated function Constructors like new The method call clicks.increment() borrows clicks mutably for you; there is no need to write (&mut clicks).increment() . Inside methods, Self is the type being implemented. Tuple structs and unit structs rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Meters(f64); // a tuple struct: a named wrapper derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Point(i32, i32); struct Marker; // a unit struct: no fields impl Meters { fn to_feet(self) - f64 { self.0 3.28084 } } fn main() { let height = Meters(1.8); let p = Point(3, 4); let _m = Marker; println!("{:.2} {:?} {}", height.to_feet(), p, p.0 + p.1); } Wrapping a number in a tuple struct ( Meters , UserId ) makes the compiler stop you mixing up values that have the same underlying type: the newtype pattern. Privacy Fields and methods are private to their module unless marked pub . Inside one file's module that does not matter; once code is split into modules (lesson 3.05), keep fields private and expose methods, so that a struct's rules (like a non-negative balance) cannot be broken from outside.

title: A struct with methods
body: Write a Rectangle struct with methods: rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Rectangle { x: f64, y: f64, width: f64, height: f64 } // (x, y) is the top-left corner impl Rectangle { fn new(x: f64, y: f64, width: f64, height: f64) - Option<Rectangle // None for a width or height <= 0 fn square(x: f64, y: f64, side: f64) - Option<Rectangle fn area(&self) - f64 fn perimeter(&self) - f64 fn is_square(&self) - bool fn contains_point(&self, px: f64, py: f64) - bool // edges count as inside fn overlaps(&self, other: &Rectangle) - bool // touching edges do not count fn scale(&mut self, factor: f64) // keeps the corner, scales the size fn into_square(self) - Rectangle // a square with the same corner and the smaller side } y grows downwards, as on a screen: the bottom edge is at y + height .

title: 2.05  Enums, Option and match
body: Enums whose variants carry data, methods on enums, matching with destructuring and exhaustiveness, Option instead of null and its everyday methods (unwrap_or, map, and_then, ?), if let and let else, and modelling states so invalid ones cannot be represented. Enums with data An enum lists the possible variants of a type. Unlike enums in many languages, each Rust variant can hold its own data: rust derive(Debug) enum Shape { Circle { radius: f64 }, Rectangle { width: f64, height: f64 }, Triangle(f64, f64, f64), } impl Shape { fn area(&self) - f64 { match self { Shape::Circle { radius } = std::f64::consts::PI radius radius, Shape::Rectangle { width, height } = width height, Shape::Triangle(a, b, c) = { let s = (a + b + c) / 2.0; // Heron's formula (s (s - a) (s - b) (s - c)).sqrt() } } } } fn main() { let shapes = vec! Shape::Circle { radius: 1.0 }, Shape::Rectangle { width: 2.0, height: 3.0 }, Shape::Triangle(3.0, 4.0, 5.0), ; for s in &shapes { println!("{s:?} has area {:.2}", s.area()); } } match destructures each variant, binding its fields to names. The match must be exhaustive : add a variant to Shape and every match that does not handle it stops compiling, showing you exactly where to update the code. Option instead of null Rust has no null . A value that may be missing has type Option<T : rust-norun enum Option<T { Some(T), None, } You must handle None before you can use the value, so "forgot to check for null" bugs cannot happen: rust fn find_index(names: & &str , target: &str) - Option<usize { for (i, name) in names.iter().enumerate() { if name == target { return Some(i); } } None } fn main() { let names = "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" ; match find_index(&names, "Grace") { Some(i) = println!("found at {i}"), None = println!("not found"), } let i = find_index(&names, "Bob").unwrap_or(999); println!("{i}"); let len = find_index(&names, "Linus").map( i names i .len()); // transform if present println!("{len:?}"); } Method Gives --- --- unwrap_or(default) , unwrap_or_default() The value, or a default map(f) Some(f(v)) , or None and_then(f) Chains a step that itself returns an Option filter(p) None unless the value passes ok_or(err) Converts to a Result (lesson 3.04) is_some() , is_none() Tests unwrap() , expect("msg") The value, or a panic : use only when None is impossible Inside a function that returns Option , the ? operator returns None early: let first = values.first()?; . if let and let else When only one variant matters, if let is shorter than a full match , and let ... else handles the "otherwise bail out" case: rust fn parse_pair(text: &str) - Option<(i32, i32) { let Some((a, b)) = text.split_once(',') else { return None; // let-else: must leave the function }; let a = a.trim().parse().ok()?; let b = b.trim().parse().ok()?; Some((a, b)) } fn main() { if let Some((x, y)) = parse_pair("3, 4") { println!("{x} + {y} = {}", x + y); } println!("{:?} {:?}", parse_pair("7,x"), parse_pair("nothing")); } Make invalid states unrepresentable Enums let the type itself rule out impossible combinations. Instead of a struct with a status string and optional fields that only sometimes make sense, model each state: rust derive(Debug) enum Order { Draft { items: Vec<String }, Paid { items: Vec<String , amount_cents: u64 }, Shipped { tracking: String }, } fn describe(order: &Order) - String { match order { Order::Draft { items } if items.is_empty() = "an empty draft".to_string(), Order::Draft { items } = format!("a draft with {} items", items.len()), Order::Paid { amount_cents, .. } = format!("paid {}.{:02}", amount_cents / 100, amount_cents % 100), Order::Shipped { tracking } = format!("shipped, tracking {tracking}"), } } fn main() { let orders = Order::Draft { items: vec! }, Order::Paid { items: vec! "tea".into() , amount_cents: 1250 }, Order::Shipped { tracking: "ZX81".into() }, ; for o in &orders { println!("{}", describe(o)); } } A shipped order has a tracking number and a draft does not, by construction. if after a pattern is a guard ; .. ignores the remaining fields.

title: A robot driven by an enum
match: A robot driven by an enum
body: A robot on a grid follows commands. Write the types and functions: rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) enum Direction { North, East, South, West } derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) enum Command { Forward(u32), Turn(Turn), Say(String) } derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) enum Turn { Left, Right } derive(Debug) struct Robot { x: i32, y: i32, facing: Direction, log: Vec<String } fn parse_command(line: &str) - Option<Command impl Robot { fn new() - Robot // at (0, 0) facing North, empty log fn apply(&mut self, command: &Command) } - parse_command accepts forward <n , left , right and say <text (the text is the rest of the line, trimmed and non-empty), ignoring case for the command word; anything else is None . - Moving north is y + 1 , east x + 1 , south y - 1 , west x - 1 . Turning changes direction by 90 degrees. - Say adds "(<x , <y ) <text " to the log. Use match for every decision.

title: A to-do list
body: Write a to-do list manager that reads commands, one per line, until quit or the end of the input: add high Buy milk add Write report add low Water plants done 2 list stats prints Added 1: Buy milk Added 2: Write report Added 3: Water plants Completed 2 1 (high) Buy milk 3 (low) Water plants x 2 (normal) Write report 3 tasks: 1 done, 2 open (1 high) Command Does --- --- add high\ low <text Adds a task with that priority ( normal when the second word is not high or low ); ids count from 1 and are never reused. Prints Added <id : <text done <id Completed <id , or <id is already done undo <id Reopened <id , or <id is not done remove <id Removed <id list Open tasks first, by priority (high, normal, low) then id, as <id (<priority ) <text ; then done tasks by id as x ... ; or Nothing to do. when there are no tasks stats <n tasks: <d done, <o open (<h high) , where high counts open high-priority tasks quit Stops Errors: an id that is not a number prints Not a number: <text ; an unknown id prints No task <id ; a missing argument prints Usage: <command <id (or Usage: add high low <text ); anything else prints Unknown command: <word . Command words ignore case; blank lines are skipped.

title: 3.01  Vectors
body: Vec<T in depth - creating with vec! and Vec::new, pushing, popping, inserting and removing, indexing versus get, iterating by reference, by mutable reference and by value, sorting and deduplicating, retain, extend and drain, capacity, and the borrow rules that apply to vectors. Creating and growing A Vec<T is a growable array on the heap: Rust's most used collection. rust fn main() { let mut v: Vec<i32 = Vec::new(); v.push(3); v.push(1); v.push(4); let mut w = vec! 1, 5, 9, 2, 6 ; // the vec! macro let zeros = vec! 0; 4 ; println!("{v:?} {w:?} {zeros:?} len={} cap ={}", v.len(), v.capacity()); let last = w.pop(); // Some(6) w.insert(0, 100); // shifts everything right: O(n) let removed = w.remove(1); // returns the removed item w.extend( 7, 7, 8 ); println!("{last:?} {removed} {w:?}"); } Reading items Indexing with v i panics when i is out of range; v.get(i) returns an Option instead: rust fn main() { let v = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; println!("{}", v 1 ); match v.get(10) { Some(x) = println!("found {x}"), None = println!("no item 10"), } println!("{:?} {:?} {}", v.first(), v.last(), v.contains(&20)); if let first, .., last = v.as_slice() { // a slice pattern println!("{first}..{last}"); } } Use indexing when an out-of-range index would be a bug, and get when it is a normal possibility (user input, searching). Iterating rust fn main() { let mut scores = vec! 72, 95, 88 ; for s in &scores { // borrow each item: s is &i32 print!("{s} "); } println!(); for s in &mut scores { // borrow each item mutably: s is &mut i32 s += 5; } let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum(); let doubled: Vec<i32 = scores.iter().map( s s 2).collect(); println!("{scores:?} {total} {doubled:?}"); for s in scores { // by value: the vector is moved and consumed print!("{s} "); } println!(); // println!("{scores:?}"); // error: scores was moved by the loop } Loop Item type The vector afterwards --- --- --- for x in &v / v.iter() &T Unchanged, still usable for x in &mut v / v.iter_mut() &mut T Changed in place for x in v / v.into_iter() T Moved, gone Changing in bulk rust fn main() { let mut v = vec! 5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 8, 8, 2 ; v.sort(); // in place v.dedup(); // removes consecutive repeats println!("{v:?}"); v.retain( &x x % 2 == 1 x 4); // keep the matching items println!("{v:?}"); let mut words = vec! "pear", "Fig", "apple" ; words.sort_by_key( w w.to_lowercase()); println!("{words:?}"); let mut nums = vec! 3.2, 1.5, 2.7 ; nums.sort_by( a, b a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap()); // f64 has no total order: sort_by let drained: Vec<f64 = nums.drain(..2).collect(); println!("{drained:?} {nums:?}"); v.clear(); println!("{} {}", v.is_empty(), v.capacity() 0); } f64 cannot use sort() because NaN makes the order partial; sort_by with partial_cmp (or f64::total_cmp ) says how to compare. Vectors and the borrow rules While you hold a reference into a vector, you cannot push to it (lesson 2.02): pushing may move the whole buffer. Collect what you need first, or work with indexes: rust fn main() { let mut v = vec! 1, 2, 3 ; let first = v 0 ; // copy the value out (i32 is Copy), no borrow kept v.push(first 10); let len = v.len(); v.push(len as i32); println!("{v:?}"); } Capacity A vector keeps spare room and doubles its capacity when it runs out, so push is amortised O(1). If you know the final size, Vec::with_capacity(n) avoids repeated growth.

title: Working with vectors
body: Write these functions: rust fn running_totals(values: & i32 ) - Vec<i32 // 1, 2, 3 gives 1, 3, 6 fn remove_negatives(values: &mut Vec<i32 ) // in place, keeping the order fn merge_sorted(a: & i32 , b: & i32 ) - Vec<i32 // two sorted slices into one sorted vector, in one pass fn top_n(values: & i32 , n: usize) - Vec<i32 // the n largest, largest first (fewer if there are fewer) fn unique_in_order(values: & i32 ) - Vec<i32 // without repeats, first occurrences kept, in order

title: 3.02  Strings in Depth
body:
How Rust strings really work - UTF-8 bytes, chars and why there is no indexing by position, char_indices and safe slicing, building strings with push, push_str, + and format!, splitting, trimming and searching, case conversion, parsing, and converting between String, &str, char and bytes. UTF-8 A String is a vector of bytes that is always valid UTF-8 . ASCII characters take one byte, but others take two, three or four: rust fn main() { for s in "hello", "héllo", "日本", "🦀" { println!("{s}: {} bytes, {} chars", s.len(), s.chars().count()); } let word = "naïve"; for (byte_index, c) in word.char_indices() { print!("{byte_index}:{c} "); } println!(); println!("{:?}", word.as_bytes()); } That is why s 0 does not compile: a byte position is not a character position, and returning half a character would be wrong. Use: - s.chars() to go through characters (Unicode scalar values); - s.char_indices() to get each character with its byte position, for slicing safely; - s.bytes() when you really work with raw bytes (protocols, ASCII-only formats). s.chars().nth(i) finds the i-th character, but it walks from the start: O(i). If you need random access, collect into a Vec<char first. User-perceived characters can be several char s (an e plus a combining accent, or an emoji with a skin tone). For full text segmentation, the unicode-segmentation crate splits grapheme clusters . Building strings rust fn main() { let mut s = String::with_capacity(32); s.push_str("Hello"); s.push(','); s += " world"; // += takes a &str let greeting = s.clone() + "!"; // + takes ownership of the left side let parts = vec! "a", "b", "c" ; let joined = parts.join("/"); let repeated = "ab".repeat(3); let built = format!("{greeting} {joined} {repeated} {}", 42); println!("{built}"); let from_chars: String = 'R', 'u', 's', 't' .iter().collect(); let reversed: String = "stressed".chars().rev().collect(); println!("{from_chars} {reversed}"); } Searching, splitting and trimming rust fn main() { let text = " name=Ada; lang=Rust;year=2026 "; let t = text.trim(); println!("{:?} {:?}", t.find("lang"), t.find('z')); for pair in t.split(';').map(str::trim).filter( p !p.is_empty()) { if let Some((key, value)) = pair.split_once('=') { println!("{key} - {value}"); } } println!("{:?}", "a,b,,c".split(',').collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{:?}", "one two	three
".split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{:?}", "line1
line2
line3".lines().collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{}", "Hello".to_lowercase() == "hello"); println!("{}", "Straße".eq_ignore_ascii_case("STRASSE")); // false: ASCII-only comparison println!("{:?}", "x=1".strip_prefix("x=")); println!("{}", "cat".replace('c', "b")); } Converting From To Code --- --- --- &str String s.to_string() , String::from(s) , s.to_owned() String &str &s , s.as_str() number String n.to_string() , format!("{n}") &str number s.parse::<i32 () (a Result ) char String c.to_string() char digit c.to_digit(10) (an Option<u32 ) digit char char::from_digit(7, 10) Vec<u8 String String::from_utf8(bytes) (a Result : bytes may be invalid UTF-8) Slicing safely String slices use byte ranges and panic if a range cuts a character in half. To take "the first n characters" safely, find the byte position with char_indices : rust fn first_chars(s: &str, n: usize) - &str { match s.char_indices().nth(n) { Some((byte_index, _)) = &s ..byte_index , None = s, } } fn main() { println!("{}", first_chars("héllo wörld", 4)); println!("{}", first_chars("hi", 10)); }

title: Unicode strings
body: Write these text functions. They must work for any language, not just ASCII: rust fn capitalize_words(text: &str) - String // "élan VITAL" gives "Élan Vital"; words separated by single spaces in the result fn is_palindrome(text: &str) - bool // ignoring case and anything that is not alphanumeric fn truncate(text: &str, max_chars: usize) - String // at most max_chars characters; if cut, the last one is "…" fn run_lengths(text: &str) - String // "aaabcc" gives "a3bc2"; works on characters, not bytes fn reverse_words(text: &str) - String // "one two three" gives "three two one" truncate("Grüße aus Köln", 6) is "Grüße…" ; if the text fits, it is returned unchanged; max_chars 0 gives "" .

title: 3.03  HashMap and HashSet
body: Key-value lookups with HashMap - insert, get, contains_key, remove, iterating, and the entry API for counting and grouping - unique values with HashSet and its set operations, ordered alternatives BTreeMap and BTreeSet, ownership of keys and values, and which key types are allowed. HashMap HashMap<K, V maps keys to values with O(1) average lookup. It lives in std::collections : rust use std::collections::HashMap; fn main() { let mut ages: HashMap<String, u32 = HashMap::new(); ages.insert("Ada".to_string(), 36); ages.insert("Grace".to_string(), 85); ages.insert("Ada".to_string(), 37); // replaces; insert returns Some(36) println!("{:?}", ages.get("Ada")); // Some(37): look up with &str println!("{}", ages.get("Bob").copied().unwrap_or(0)); println!("{}", ages.contains_key("Grace")); if let Some(age) = ages.get_mut("Grace") { age += 1; } ages.remove("Ada"); for (name, age) in &ages { // order is unspecified println!("{name}: {age}"); } println!("{}", ages.len()); } A HashMap<String, ... can be looked up with a &str , so you do not need to allocate a String just to search. Inserting moves the key and value into the map: the map owns them. Values that are Copy (numbers) are copied in. The entry API Counting and grouping need "insert if missing, then update". The entry API does it in one lookup: rust use std::collections::HashMap; fn main() { let text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"; let mut counts: HashMap<&str, usize = HashMap::new(); for word in text.split_whitespace() { counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1; } let mut sorted: Vec<(&str, usize) = counts.into_iter().collect(); sorted.sort_by( a, b b.1.cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0))); // by count, then word println!("{sorted:?}"); let words = "apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry" ; let mut by_letter: HashMap<char, Vec<&str = HashMap::new(); for w in words { by_letter.entry(w.chars().next().unwrap()).or_default().push(w); } let mut letters: Vec<_ = by_letter.keys().collect(); letters.sort(); for l in letters { println!("{l}: {:?}", by_letter l ); } } Entry method Does --- --- entry(k).or_insert(v) Inserts v if missing; returns &mut V entry(k).or_insert_with(f) Same, computing the value only when needed entry(k).or_default() Inserts V::default() (0, empty vec...) if missing entry(k).and_modify(f).or_insert(v) Updates an existing value, or inserts map &key panics when the key is missing; use it only when the key must exist. HashSet HashSet<T holds unique values with fast membership tests: rust use std::collections::HashSet; fn main() { let mut seen = HashSet::new(); for tag in "rust", "cli", "rust", "web" { if !seen.insert(tag) { // insert returns false for duplicates println!("duplicate: {tag}"); } } let a: HashSet<i32 = 1, 2, 3, 4 .into_iter().collect(); let b: HashSet<i32 = 3, 4, 5 .into_iter().collect(); let mut both: Vec<_ = a.intersection(&b).copied().collect(); let mut either: Vec<_ = a.union(&b).copied().collect(); let mut only_a: Vec<_ = a.difference(&b).copied().collect(); both.sort(); either.sort(); only_a.sort(); println!("{both:?} {either:?} {only_a:?} {}", a.contains(&2)); } Ordered maps and sets HashMap and HashSet iterate in an unpredictable order. When order matters (printing, ranges, smallest or largest key), use BTreeMap and BTreeSet , which keep keys sorted (O(log n) operations): rust use std::collections::BTreeMap; fn main() { let mut scores = BTreeMap::new(); for (name, score) in ("linus", 72), ("ada", 95), ("grace", 88) { scores.insert(name, score); } println!("{scores:?}"); // sorted by key println!("{:?} {:?}", scores.first_key_value(), scores.last_key_value()); for (name, s) in scores.range("b".."h") { // keys from "b" up to "h" println!("{name} {s}"); } } Keys A key type must implement Eq and Hash (for HashMap ) or Ord (for BTreeMap ). Strings, integers, char , bool , tuples of those, and your own types with derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash) all work. f64 does not (NaN breaks equality); use an integer representation instead.

title: Maps and sets
body: Write these with HashMap , HashSet and BTreeMap : rust fn word_counts(text: &str) - HashMap<String, usize // lower-case words: runs of letters and ' fn top_words(text: &str, n: usize) - Vec<(String, usize) // most frequent first, ties alphabetical fn group_anagrams(words: & &str ) - Vec<Vec<String // groups in order of first appearance, words in input order fn first_unique_char(text: &str) - Option<char fn letter_histogram(text: &str) - BTreeMap<char, usize // lower-case letters only, sorted The tests need use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap, HashSet}; at the top of your file.

title: 3.04  Error Handling with Result
body: Recoverable errors with Result<T, E and unrecoverable ones with panic!, handling results with match, unwrap_or, map_err and and_then, propagating errors with the ? operator, writing your own error enums with Display and std::error::Error, converting errors with From so ? works across types, Box<dyn Error for quick programs, and when to panic. Two kinds of errors - Recoverable errors are expected possibilities: a file is missing, input is not a number. Functions return Result<T, E : Ok(value) or Err(error) . - Unrecoverable errors are bugs: an index past the end, a broken invariant. The program calls panic! , which stops the thread with a message. rust-norun enum Result<T, E { Ok(T), Err(E), } Handling a Result rust fn parse_age(text: &str) - Result<u32, String { let age: u32 = text.trim().parse().map_err( _ format!("'{text}' is not a number"))?; if age 150 { return Err(format!("{age} is not a realistic age")); } Ok(age) } fn main() { for input in "42", "abc", "200" { match parse_age(input) { Ok(age) = println!("age {age}"), Err(message) = println!("error: {message}"), } } let age = parse_age("x").unwrap_or(0); let doubled = parse_age("21").map( a a 2); println!("{age} {doubled:?}"); } Method Gives --- --- match / if let Ok(v) Full control unwrap_or(v) , unwrap_or_default() , unwrap_or_else(f) A fallback value map(f) , map_err(f) Transform the value / the error and_then(f) Chain a step that may also fail ok() Convert to an Option , dropping the error unwrap() , expect("why") The value, or a panic The ? operator ? after a Result means: if it is Err , return that error from the current function now; otherwise unwrap the Ok value. It turns error plumbing into one character: rust use std::num::ParseIntError; fn sum_line(line: &str) - Result<i64, ParseIntError { let mut total = 0; for part in line.split(',') { total += part.trim().parse::<i64 ()?; // stops at the first bad number } Ok(total) } fn main() { println!("{:?}", sum_line("1, 2, 3")); println!("{:?}", sum_line("1, two, 3")); } ? works in functions returning Result (or Option ), including main if it returns Result<(), E . Your own error type For a library or a larger program, define an error enum that lists what can go wrong, implement Display for messages, and From so ? converts other errors into yours: rust use std::fmt; use std::num::ParseIntError; derive(Debug) enum ConfigError { Missing(String), BadNumber { key: String, source: ParseIntError }, OutOfRange { key: String, value: i64 }, } impl fmt::Display for ConfigError { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { match self { ConfigError::Missing(key) = write!(f, "missing setting '{key}'"), ConfigError::BadNumber { key, source } = write!(f, "'{key}' is not a number ({source})"), ConfigError::OutOfRange { key, value } = write!(f, "'{key}' = {value} is out of range"), } } } impl std::error::Error for ConfigError {} fn get_port(settings: & (&str, &str) ) - Result<u16, ConfigError { let (_, text) = settings.iter().find( (k, _) k == "port") .ok_or_else( ConfigError::Missing("port".into()))?; let value: i64 = text.parse().map_err( e ConfigError::BadNumber { key: "port".into(), source: e })?; u16::try_from(value).map_err( _ ConfigError::OutOfRange { key: "port".into(), value }) } fn main() { for settings in vec! ("port", "8080") , vec! , vec! ("port", "eighty") , vec! ("port", "70000") { match get_port(&settings) { Ok(p) = println!("port {p}"), Err(e) = println!("error: {e}"), } } } With impl From<ParseIntError for ConfigError , a plain text.parse()? would convert automatically. The thiserror crate generates all of this from attributes, and anyhow offers a catch-all error type for applications. Box<dyn Error for quick programs When you just want ? to work with any error type, return Result<T, Box<dyn std::error::Error : rust use std::error::Error; fn run() - Result<i32, Box<dyn Error { let n: i32 = "41".parse()?; // ParseIntError converts automatically if n < 0 { return Err("negative".into()); // a &str converts too } Ok(n + 1) } fn main() { match run() { Ok(v) = println!("{v}"), Err(e) = println!("error: {e}"), } } When to panic Panic for bugs : a condition that should be impossible if the code is correct, a violated precondition in a function documented to panic, or in tests and quick experiments. Return a Result for anything the caller or the user can cause and handle. unwrap() in production code is a promise that it can never fail; expect("reason") documents why.

title: Parsing durations with Result
body: Parse durations such as 1h30m , 45s or 2h5m10s into seconds, with your own error type: rust derive(Debug, PartialEq) enum DurationError { Empty, // "duration is empty" MissingNumber(char), // "unit 'm' has no number" MissingUnit(String), // "number 12 has no unit" UnknownUnit(char), // "unknown unit 'x'" Overflow, // "duration is too long" } impl std::fmt::Display for DurationError { ... } // the messages above fn parse_duration(text: &str) - Result<u64, DurationError fn total(texts: & &str ) - Result<u64, DurationError // sum of several durations; the first error wins fn format_duration(seconds: u64) - String // 5410 gives "1h30m10s"; 0 gives "0s" - Units are d (days), h , m and s , each after a whole number; parts may come in any order and repeat ( 1m1m is 120). Spaces around the text are ignored. - Use checked_mul and checked_add so huge numbers give Overflow instead of wrapping; a number too big for u64 is also Overflow . - total must use ? .

title: 3.05  Modules, Crates and Tests
body: Organising code with mod, pub and use, privacy rules for items and struct fields, splitting modules into files, packages, library and binary crates, adding dependencies from crates.io with Cargo.toml, and writing unit tests with test , assert macros and cargo test, plus integration tests and documentation tests. Modules A module groups related items and controls what is visible outside it. Everything is private by default; pub makes it visible to the parent module and beyond: rust mod geometry { pub struct Point { pub x: f64, pub y: f64, } pub fn distance(a: &Point, b: &Point) - f64 { (square(a.x - b.x) + square(a.y - b.y)).sqrt() } fn square(v: f64) - f64 { v v } // private: only usable inside geometry pub mod shapes { use super::Point; // super: the parent module pub struct Circle { pub center: Point, pub radius: f64 } impl Circle { pub fn area(&self) - f64 { std::f64::consts::PI self.radius self.radius } } } } use geometry::shapes::Circle; use geometry::{distance, Point}; fn main() { let a = Point { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }; let b = Point { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 }; println!("{}", distance(&a, &b)); let c = Circle { center: b, radius: 1.0 }; println!("{:.3} at ({}, {})", c.area(), c.center.x, c.center.y); // geometry::square(2.0); // error: function square is private } - Paths use :: . crate:: starts at the crate's root, super:: at the parent, self:: at the current module. - use brings a path into scope so you can write the short name. - A pub struct can still have private fields: then code outside the module cannot build it directly and must use its constructor, which keeps its rules intact. Files In a real project each module usually has its own file: text src/ main.rs mod geometry; (tells Cargo to load src/geometry.rs) geometry.rs pub mod shapes; geometry/ shapes.rs mod geometry; with a semicolon means "the module's code is in geometry.rs (or geometry/mod.rs )". Packages and crates - A crate is a unit of compilation: a binary crate (with main , from src/main.rs ) or a library crate (from src/lib.rs ). - A package is a folder with Cargo.toml ; it can contain a library and any number of binaries. Dependencies come from crates.io: toml package name = "wordcount" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" dependencies clap = { version = "4", features = "derive" } serde = { version = "1", features = "derive" } cargo add clap --features derive edits the file for you. Cargo.lock records exact versions; commit it for applications. Unit tests Tests live next to the code, in a module that is only compiled for cargo test : rust-norun pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) - i32 { a + b } pub fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) - i32 { if b == 0 { panic!("division by zero"); } a / b } cfg(test) mod tests { use super:: ; test fn adds_small_numbers() { assert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5); } test fn negative_numbers() { assert!(add(-2, -3) < 0, "expected a negative sum"); assert_ne!(add(-1, 1), 1); } test should_panic(expected = "division by zero") fn dividing_by_zero_panics() { divide(1, 0); } test fn returns_result() - Result<(), String { let n: i32 = "42".parse().map_err( e format!("{e}"))?; assert_eq!(n, 42); Ok(()) } } bash cargo test build and run every test cargo test negative only tests whose name contains "negative" cargo test -- --nocapture show println! output from passing tests Because the tests module is a child of the module it tests, it can test private functions too. Integration tests go in a tests/ folder next to src/ and use the crate only through its public API, like a user would. Documentation tests are code examples inside /// comments, which cargo test compiles and runs, so examples in the documentation never go stale. The practice tasks in this course use the same idea with a small kit: test("name", { check_eq(actual, expected); }) .

title: A module with private state
