body: Write a module bank whose Account keeps its balance private, so the only way to change it is through methods that keep it valid: rust mod bank { derive(Debug, PartialEq) pub enum BankError { InvalidAmount, InsufficientFunds { needed: u64, available: u64 }, SameAccount } pub struct Account { / private: id, owner, balance in cents / } impl Account { pub fn open(id: u32, owner: &str) - Account pub fn id(&self) - u32 pub fn owner(&self) - &str pub fn balance(&self) - u64 pub fn deposit(&mut self, cents: u64) - Result<(), BankError // 0 is InvalidAmount pub fn withdraw(&mut self, cents: u64) - Result<(), BankError // InsufficientFunds when short } pub fn transfer(from: &mut Account, to: &mut Account, cents: u64) - Result<(), BankError // nothing changes on error pub mod report { pub fn summary(accounts: & super::Account ) - String // "3 accounts, total 12.34" } } - transfer between accounts with the same id fails with SameAccount ; an amount of 0 with InvalidAmount . - summary writes the total in euros with 2 decimals.

title: A gradebook report
body: Write a program that reads exam results as CSV from standard input and prints a report. The first line is the header name,subject,score ; each other line is one result: name,subject,score Ada,maths,92 Bob,maths,61 Ada,art,78 Bob,art,85 Cy,maths,abc Cy,maths,47 prints line 6: bad score 'abc' Students: Ada 85.0 B (2 results) Bob 73.0 C (2 results) Cy 47.0 F (1 result) Subjects: art avg 81.5 best Bob (85) maths avg 66.7 best Ada (92) Errors: 1 Rules: - A wrong header prints error: bad header and stops at once. Blank lines are skipped. - Each line has exactly 3 comma-separated fields, trimmed. Problems are printed as they are read , as line <n : <message (the header is line 1), and the line is skipped: expected 3 fields , empty name , empty subject , bad score '<text ' (not a whole number), score <n out of range (not 0 to 100). - Students are listed by average (highest first), then by name. Each line: two spaces, the name left-aligned in 10 characters, the average right-aligned in 5 with one decimal, a space, the grade (90 A , 80 B , 70 C , 60 D , else F , using the unrounded average), and (<n results) ( 1 result for one). - Subjects are listed by name. Each line: two spaces, the subject left-aligned in 10 characters, avg <average with one decimal , two spaces, and best <name (<score ) for the highest score (on a tie, the name that sorts first). - Last, Errors: <count . With no valid results at all, print No data. instead of the two lists (but still the errors before it and the count after it).

title: 4.01  Generics
body: Writing code once for many types - generic functions with type parameters and trait bounds, where clauses, generic structs and enums like Option and Result, impl blocks for generic types and for specific types, const generics for array sizes, and monomorphization, which makes generics cost nothing at run time. Generic functions A function with a type parameter works for many types. Without a bound , the body can do almost nothing with a T ; bounds say what the type must support: rust fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy (items: & T ) - Option<T { let mut best = items.first()?; for &item in items { if item best { best = item; } } Some(best) } fn describe<T: std::fmt::Debug (label: &str, value: T) - String { format!("{label}: {value:?}") } fn main() { println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", largest(& 3, 9, 2 ), largest(& 1.5, -2.0 ), largest(& 'x', 'b' )); println!("{:?}", largest::<i32 (& )); println!("{}", describe("point", (3, 4))); println!("{}", describe("list", vec! "a", "b" )); } T: PartialOrd + Copy means "any type that can be compared with < and copied". The compiler checks the bounds where the function is defined, so a generic function either works for every allowed type or does not compile at all. where clauses Long bound lists read better in a where clause: rust use std::fmt::Display; fn join_all<T, U (items: & T , extra: U) - String where T: Display, U: Display + Clone, { let mut out: Vec<String = items.iter().map( i i.to_string()).collect(); out.push(extra.to_string()); out.join(", ") } fn main() { println!("{}", join_all(& 1, 2, 3 , "and more")); } Generic structs and enums Vec<T , Option<T , Result<T, E and HashMap<K, V are generic types from the standard library. Your own types can be too: rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Pair<T { first: T, second: T, } impl<T: PartialOrd Pair<T { fn larger(&self) - &T { if self.first = self.second { &self.first } else { &self.second } } } impl<T Pair<T { fn swap(self) - Pair<T { Pair { first: self.second, second: self.first } } } impl Pair<f64 { // only for Pair<f64 fn distance(&self) - f64 { (self.first - self.second).abs() } } derive(Debug) enum Tree<T { Leaf(T), Node(Box<Tree<T , Box<Tree<T ), } fn count_leaves<T (t: &Tree<T ) - usize { match t { Tree::Leaf(_) = 1, Tree::Node(l, r) = count_leaves(l) + count_leaves(r), } } fn main() { let p = Pair { first: 3, second: 8 }; println!("{} {:?}", p.larger(), p.clone().swap()); println!("{}", Pair { first: 1.5, second: 4.0 }.distance()); let t = Tree::Node(Box::new(Tree::Leaf("a")), Box::new(Tree::Node(Box::new(Tree::Leaf("b")), Box::new(Tree::Leaf("c"))))); println!("{}", count_leaves(&t)); } impl<T Pair<T applies to every Pair ; impl<T: PartialOrd Pair<T only when T can be compared; impl Pair<f64 only for one concrete type. Box (lesson 5.04) puts the recursive tree parts on the heap. Const generics Types can also be parameterised by values , most often array lengths: rust fn sum_all<const N: usize (values: i32; N ) - i32 { let mut total = 0; for v in values { total += v; } total } derive(Debug) struct Grid<const W: usize, const H: usize { cells: u8; W ; H , } fn main() { println!("{} {}", sum_all( 1, 2, 3 ), sum_all( 10; 5 )); let g = Grid::<3, 2 { cells: 0; 3 ; 2 }; println!("{:?}", g); } Zero-cost The compiler generates a separate, fully optimised copy of a generic function for each concrete type it is used with ( monomorphization ). largest::<i32 and largest::<f64 are as fast as hand-written versions. The cost is compile time and binary size, not run time.

title: Generic types and functions
body: Write a generic stack and two generic functions: rust derive(Debug, Default) struct Stack<T { items: Vec<T } impl<T Stack<T { fn new() - Self fn push(&mut self, item: T) fn pop(&mut self) - Option<T fn peek(&self) - Option<&T fn len(&self) - usize fn is_empty(&self) - bool } impl<T: std::fmt::Display Stack<T { fn render(&self) - String // bottom to top, " 1 2 3 "; " " when empty } fn min_max<T: PartialOrd + Copy (items: & T ) - Option<(T, T) fn dedup_sorted<T: PartialEq + Clone (items: & T ) - Vec<T // drops consecutive repeats

title: 4.02  Traits
body: Defining shared behaviour with traits, implementing them for your types and for existing ones, default methods, traits as parameters with impl Trait and generic bounds, returning impl Trait, associated types and constants, supertraits, the orphan rule, and blanket implementations. A trait A trait names a set of methods that types can implement: shared behaviour, like an interface in other languages. rust trait Shape { fn area(&self) - f64; fn name(&self) - String; fn describe(&self) - String { // a default method: implementers may keep it format!("{} with area {:.2}", self.name(), self.area()) } } struct Circle { radius: f64 } struct Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) - f64 { std::f64::consts::PI self.radius self.radius } fn name(&self) - String { "circle".to_string() } } impl Shape for Rect { fn area(&self) - f64 { self.w self.h } fn name(&self) - String { "rectangle".to_string() } fn describe(&self) - String { format!("a {}x{} rectangle", self.w, self.h) } // override } fn main() { println!("{}", Circle { radius: 1.0 }.describe()); println!("{}", Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }.describe()); } Traits as parameters A function can accept any type implementing a trait. Three spellings mean the same thing for one parameter: rust trait Shape { fn area(&self) - f64; } struct Square(f64); impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) - f64 { self.0 self.0 } } struct Circle(f64); impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) - f64 { 3.14159 self.0 self.0 } } fn print_area(s: &impl Shape) { // impl Trait in argument position println!("{:.2}", s.area()); } fn total_area<S: Shape (shapes: & S ) - f64 { // a generic bound: all items the same type shapes.iter().map( s s.area()).sum() } fn bigger<'a (a: &'a impl Shape, b: &'a impl Shape) - f64 { a.area().max(b.area()) } fn main() { print_area(&Square(2.0)); println!("{}", total_area(& Square(1.0), Square(2.0) )); println!("{:.2}", bigger(&Square(1.0), &Circle(1.0))); } A Vec<S with S: Shape holds one concrete shape type. To mix circles and squares in one list you need trait objects (lesson 4.05). Returning impl Trait - impl Trait returns some type that implements the trait without naming it, which is how functions return iterators and closures: rust fn evens(limit: u32) - impl Iterator<Item = u32 { (0..limit).filter( n n % 2 == 0) } fn adder(n: i32) - impl Fn(i32) - i32 { move x x + n } fn main() { println!("{:?}", evens(10).collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{}", adder(5)(10)); } Implementing traits for existing types You can implement your own trait for types you did not write, including i32 and String : rust trait Shout { fn shout(&self) - String; } impl Shout for str { fn shout(&self) - String { self.to_uppercase() + "!" } } impl Shout for i32 { fn shout(&self) - String { format!("{}!!!", self) } } fn main() { println!("{} {}", "hello".shout(), 42.shout()); } The orphan rule : you may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. You cannot implement the standard library's Display for the standard library's Vec , which prevents two crates from giving conflicting implementations. Wrap the type in your own struct (the newtype pattern) when you need to. Associated types and constants A trait can require a type or a constant from its implementers. Iterator uses an associated type for its items: rust trait Unit { const SYMBOL: &'static str; const PER_METER: f64; fn from_meters(m: f64) - f64 { m Self::PER_METER } } struct Feet; impl Unit for Feet { const SYMBOL: &'static str = "ft"; const PER_METER: f64 = 3.28084; } struct Centimeters; impl Unit for Centimeters { const SYMBOL: &'static str = "cm"; const PER_METER: f64 = 100.0; } fn show<U: Unit (meters: f64) - String { format!("{:.1} {}", U::from_meters(meters), U::SYMBOL) } fn main() { println!("{} {}", show::<Feet (1.8), show::<Centimeters (1.8)); } Supertraits and blanket implementations A trait can require another ( trait Named: std::fmt::Display { ... } ). And an implementation can cover every type that meets a bound: the standard library implements ToString for every T: Display , which is why anything printable has .to_string() .

title: Traits for scoring words
body: A word game can score words in different ways. Write a trait and three implementations: rust trait Scorer { const NAME: &'static str; fn score(&self, word: &str) - u32; fn total(&self, words: & &str ) - u32 { ... } // default: the sum of the scores } struct LengthScorer; // one point per character struct VowelScorer { bonus: u32 } // bonus points per vowel (a e i o u, either case), 1 per other letter struct LetterScorer; // Scrabble letter values, ignoring case; non-letters score 0 fn best_word<'a, S: Scorer (scorer: &S, words: & &'a str ) - Option<&'a str // highest score, the first on a tie fn describe<S: Scorer (scorer: &S, word: &str) - String // "<NAME : <word scores <n " Scrabble values: 1 for A E I L N O R S T U, 2 for D G, 3 for B C M P, 4 for F H V W Y, 5 for K, 8 for J X, 10 for Q Z.

title: 4.03  The Standard Traits
body: The traits every Rust type should know - Debug and Display for printing, Clone and Copy, PartialEq and Eq, PartialOrd and Ord for comparing and sorting, Hash for map keys, Default, From and Into for conversions, FromStr for parsing, and operator overloading with Add and friends - which to derive and which to write by hand. Deriving Many standard traits can be derived : the compiler writes the obvious implementation field by field. rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord, Default) struct Version { major: u32, minor: u32, patch: u32, } fn main() { let a = Version { major: 1, minor: 10, patch: 0 }; let b = Version { major: 1, minor: 2, patch: 7 }; let c = a; // Copy: a is still usable println!("{:?} {} {}", a, a == c, a b); // Ord compares fields in order: major, minor, patch let mut list = vec! a, b, Version::default() ; list.sort(); println!("{list:?}"); let mut set = std::collections::HashSet::new(); set.insert(a); // Hash + Eq: usable as a key println!("{}", set.contains(&c)); } Trait Gives Derive when --- --- --- Debug {:?} printing Almost always Clone .clone() The type can be duplicated Copy Implicit copies on assignment Small, stack-only types (all fields Copy ) PartialEq , Eq == Values have meaningful equality ( Eq if it is total: not for floats) PartialOrd , Ord < , sorting There is a natural order (field order decides) Hash Use as HashMap / HashSet key Together with Eq Default Type::default() Every field has a sensible empty value Display Display ( {} ) is for users and is never derived; write it: rust use std::fmt; struct Money { cents: i64 } impl fmt::Display for Money { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_ ) - fmt::Result { let sign = if self.cents < 0 { "-" } else { "" }; let c = self.cents.abs(); write!(f, "{sign}{}.{:02} EUR", c / 100, c % 100) } } fn main() { let m = Money { cents: -1250 }; println!("{m}"); let s = m.to_string(); // ToString comes free with Display println!(" {s: 14} "); } Conversions: From, Into, TryFrom, FromStr rust use std::str::FromStr; derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Celsius(f64); derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Fahrenheit(f64); impl From<Fahrenheit for Celsius { fn from(f: Fahrenheit) - Self { Celsius((f.0 - 32.0) 5.0 / 9.0) } } derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8); impl FromStr for Rgb { type Err = String; fn from_str(s: &str) - Result<Self, Self::Err { let hex = s.strip_prefix(' ').ok_or("missing ")?; if hex.len() != 6 { return Err(format!("expected 6 hex digits, got {}", hex.len())); } let part = i: usize u8::from_str_radix(&hex i..i + 2 , 16).map_err( e e.to_string()); Ok(Rgb(part(0)?, part(2)?, part(4)?)) } } fn main() { let c: Celsius = Fahrenheit(212.0).into(); // Into comes free with From println!("{c:?}"); println!("{:?} {:?}", " ff8800".parse::<Rgb (), "ff8800".parse::<Rgb ()); } Implement From (never Into directly); x.into() then works too. Implementing From<YourError for AppError is what lets ? convert errors (lesson 3.04). FromStr makes "...".parse::<YourType () work. Operator overloading Operators are traits in std::ops : implementing Add gives your type + : rust use std::ops::{Add, Mul, Neg}; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Vec2 { x: f64, y: f64 } impl Add for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn add(self, o: Vec2) - Vec2 { Vec2 { x: self.x + o.x, y: self.y + o.y } } } impl Mul<f64 for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn mul(self, k: f64) - Vec2 { Vec2 { x: self.x k, y: self.y k } } } impl Neg for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn neg(self) - Vec2 { Vec2 { x: -self.x, y: -self.y } } } fn main() { let a = Vec2 { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }; let b = Vec2 { x: 0.5, y: -1.0 }; println!("{:?}", a + b 2.0 + -a); } Overload operators only where the meaning is obvious (vectors, money, matrices).
