Everything comes from one header: cpp-norun define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN // leave out rarely used parts, compiles faster define NOMINMAX // stop windows.h from defining min and max macros include <windows.h NOMINMAX matters in C++: without it, std::min and std::max collide with macros of the same name and produce baffling errors. The type names Windows has its own names for types, from a time before standard sized integers: Windows Meaning Standard C++ --- --- --- BYTE , WORD , DWORD 8, 16, 32-bit unsigned uint8_t , uint16_t , uint32_t BOOL An int used as true/false (not bool ) int UINT , LONG , ULONGLONG Unsigned int, 32-bit signed, 64-bit unsigned WPARAM , LPARAM , LRESULT Pointer-sized message parameters and results uintptr_t , intptr_t WCHAR , LPCWSTR , LPWSTR UTF-16 character, const and mutable string pointers wchar_t , const wchar_t HANDLE , HWND , HDC , HINSTANCE Handles (below) The LP prefix means "long pointer", a leftover from 16-bit Windows; C means const and W means wide (UTF-16). Handles A handle is an opaque value that refers to an object the system owns: a window ( HWND ), a file ( HANDLE ), a brush ( HBRUSH ), a module ( HMODULE ). You never look inside it; you pass it back to functions. Each kind is closed with its own function: Handle Created by Closed by --- --- --- File, thread, process, event CreateFileW , CreateThread , CreateEventW ... CloseHandle Window CreateWindowExW DestroyWindow GDI objects (pens, brushes, fonts, bitmaps) CreatePen , CreateSolidBrush ... DeleteObject Device context from GetDC GetDC ReleaseDC Loaded DLL LoadLibraryW FreeLibrary Forgetting to close handles is a leak : Task Manager's "Handles" and "GDI objects" columns show it growing. In C++, wrap each handle in a small RAII class (or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter), so it is closed automatically: cpp-norun struct HandleCloser { void operator()(HANDLE h) const { if (h && h != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) CloseHandle(h); } }; using UniqueHandle = std::unique_ptr<void, HandleCloser ; UniqueHandle file{ CreateFileW(L"notes.txt", GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr) }; Note the trap in that deleter: some functions return nullptr on failure, but CreateFileW returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (-1). Always check the documentation's "Return value" section. Errors Most functions report failure in their return value ( FALSE , nullptr , INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE ) and store a detailed error code for the calling thread, which GetLastError() returns. Call it immediately : any later API call may overwrite it. cpp-norun HANDLE h = CreateFileW(L"missing.txt", GENERIC_READ, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr); if (h == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { const DWORD error = GetLastError(); // 2 = ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND // ... } Common codes: 2 file not found, 3 path not found, 5 access denied, 32 sharing violation (another program has the file open), 87 invalid parameter, 183 already exists. Error codes to messages FormatMessageW turns a code into the system's text, in the user's language: cpp-norun std::wstring errorText(DWORD code) { wchar_t buffer = nullptr; const DWORD n = FormatMessageW(FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM FORMAT_MESSAGE_IGNORE_INSERTS, nullptr, code, 0, reinterpret_cast<wchar_t (&buffer), 0, nullptr); std::wstring text = n ? std::wstring(buffer, n) : L"Unknown error"; LocalFree(buffer); while (!text.empty() && (text.back() == L'\r' text.back() == L'\n')) text.pop_back(); // it ends in a line break return text; } COM-based APIs (lesson 3.02 onwards) return an HRESULT instead: negative means failure ( FAILED(hr) ), and HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(code) converts a Win32 error into one. The practice decodes both. Reading the documentation Every function has a page on Microsoft Learn with the same sections: the syntax (with in , out and in, optional on each parameter), return value (what failure looks like and whether GetLastError is set), remarks (the details that matter), and requirements (the header, the library to link, and the minimum Windows version). Read the remarks: they hold most of the surprises.

title: HRESULTs and error codes
body: An HRESULT is a 32-bit value: the top bit is set for failure, bits 16-26 are the facility (7 means "a Win32 error code"), and the low 16 bits are the code . Write the helpers: cpp using DWORD = std::uint32_t; using HRESULT = std::int32_t; bool failed(HRESULT hr); HRESULT hresultFromWin32(DWORD error); int facility(HRESULT hr); // (hr 16) & 0x7FF int code(HRESULT hr); // hr & 0xFFFF std::string describe(HRESULT hr); std::string trimLineBreaks(std::string text); - hresultFromWin32 works like the Windows macro: 0 stays 0 (success); any other code becomes 0x80000000 (7 << 16) (error & 0xFFFF) . - describe gives "S_OK" for 0, "0x80070005 (Win32 error 5)" for a failure with facility 7, "0x80004005" for other failures, and "success 0x00000001" for other successes (hex with 8 lower-case digits). - trimLineBreaks removes every \r and \n from the end of a message, as FormatMessageW leaves them there.

title: 1.02  Strings on Windows
body: Windows uses UTF-16 internally, while files and the web mostly use UTF-8. This lesson explains the W and A versions of functions, wchar_t and L"" literals, surrogate pairs, converting between UTF-8 and UTF-16, and the UTF-8 code page option. W and A Most API functions that take text come in two versions: - CreateFileW , MessageBoxW , SetWindowTextW : W for wide, taking UTF-16 strings ( const wchar_t ). - CreateFileA , MessageBoxA : A for ANSI, taking 8-bit strings in the system's legacy code page. CreateFile without a letter is a macro that picks one depending on whether UNICODE is defined. Modern code calls the W functions explicitly: the A versions convert to UTF-16 internally anyway, and with a legacy code page they lose every character that page cannot represent (try a Japanese file name on an English system). wchar_t and L"..." On Windows, wchar_t is 16 bits and holds one UTF-16 code unit . String literals with an L prefix are wide: L"Grüße" . std::wstring is the matching string class. UTF-16 and surrogate pairs Unicode has more than a million possible code points; 16 bits hold 65 536 values. UTF-16 encodes: - code points up to U+FFFF (all common scripts) as one 16-bit unit; - code points above U+FFFF (emoji, rare scripts) as two units, a surrogate pair : a high surrogate 0xD800-0xDBFF followed by a low surrogate 0xDC00-0xDFFF . U+1F600 (😀): subtract 0x10000 → 0xF600, 20 bits: 0000 1111 0110 0000 0000 high = 0xD800 + (top 10 bits) = 0xD83D low = 0xDC00 + (low 10 bits) = 0xDE00 So wcslen counts code units, not characters: an emoji has length 2. Cursor movement in a text editor must skip both halves of a pair. UTF-8 UTF-8 encodes each code point in 1 to 4 bytes: Code points Bytes --- --- U+0000 - U+007F 0xxxxxxx U+0080 - U+07FF 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800 - U+FFFF 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000 - U+10FFFF 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx ASCII text is unchanged, which is why UTF-8 is the standard for files, the web and most libraries. Converting MultiByteToWideChar and WideCharToMultiByte convert, called twice: once to get the size, once to convert: cpp-norun std::wstring widen(std::string_view utf8) { if (utf8.empty()) return {}; const int n = MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), (int)utf8.size(), nullptr, 0); if (n == 0) throw std::runtime_error("invalid UTF-8"); std::wstring out(n, L'\0'); MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), (int)utf8.size(), out.data(), n); return out; } std::string narrow(std::wstring_view utf16) { if (utf16.empty()) return {}; const int n = WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, WC_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf16.data(), (int)utf16.size(), nullptr, 0, nullptr, nullptr); std::string out(n, '\0'); WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, WC_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf16.data(), (int)utf16.size(), out.data(), n, nullptr, nullptr); return out; } A good rule for a program: keep strings in UTF-8 ( std::string ) inside the program and in files, and convert to UTF-16 at the boundary, right where you call a W function. The practice writes these conversions by hand, to understand exactly what happens to every byte, including invalid input. Invalid input Not every byte sequence is valid UTF-8, and not every wchar_t sequence is valid UTF-16 (a lone surrogate is invalid, and Windows file names can contain them). The usual answer is to replace each invalid part with U+FFFD (�, the replacement character) rather than fail or, worse, silently drop data. The UTF-8 code page Since Windows 10 version 1903, an application manifest (lesson 6.02) can set activeCodePage to UTF-8 . The A functions then take UTF-8, and fopen , std::ifstream and the console understand UTF-8 paths. It is a good option for porting code from Linux; for new Windows code, the W functions remain the clearest choice.

title: UTF-8 and UTF-16 by hand
body: Write the two conversions MultiByteToWideChar and WideCharToMultiByte do, replacing invalid input with U+FFFD: cpp std::u16string utf8ToUtf16(const std::string& utf8); std::string utf16ToUtf8(const std::u16string& utf16); std::size_t codePoints(const std::u16string& utf16); // characters, counting a surrogate pair once UTF-8 to UTF-16 : decode each sequence (lesson 1.02's table) and encode the code point as one unit, or as a surrogate pair above U+FFFF. A sequence is invalid if the lead byte is not a valid lead (a continuation byte 10xxxxxx , or 0xF8 and above), a continuation byte is missing, the value is overlong (could have been encoded in fewer bytes), it is a surrogate (U+D800-U+DFFF), or it is above U+10FFFF. For an invalid sequence, output one U+FFFD and continue with the byte after the lead byte . UTF-16 to UTF-8 : a high surrogate followed by a low surrogate is one code point; a surrogate on its own becomes U+FFFD (encoded as EF BF BD ).

title: 1.03  Windows, Classes and the Message Loop
match: 1.03 Windows, Classes and the Message Loop
body: The smallest real Windows program - registering a window class, creating a window, running the message loop, and writing the window procedure that handles messages. This lesson builds it line by line and explains each step. The whole program cpp-norun define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN define NOMINMAX include <windows.h LRESULT CALLBACK WndProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (msg) { case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); // ends the message loop return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); // default handling for everything else } int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE instance, HINSTANCE, PWSTR commandLine, int showCommand) { // 1. Describe a kind of window. WNDCLASSEXW wc{ sizeof(wc) }; wc.lpfnWndProc = WndProc; wc.hInstance = instance; wc.hCursor = LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_ARROW); wc.hbrBackground = reinterpret_cast<HBRUSH (COLOR_WINDOW + 1); wc.lpszClassName = L"XenonMainWindow"; if (!RegisterClassExW(&wc)) return 1; // 2. Create one. HWND hwnd = CreateWindowExW(0, L"XenonMainWindow", L"Hello, Windows", WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, 800, 500, nullptr, nullptr, instance, nullptr); if (!hwnd) return 1; ShowWindow(hwnd, showCommand); // 3. Run the message loop. MSG msg; while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { TranslateMessage(&msg); // turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages DispatchMessageW(&msg); // calls the window procedure } return static_cast<int (msg.wParam); } In Visual Studio, create a Windows Desktop Application (or an empty project with SubSystem set to Windows) so wWinMain is the entry point. Step 1: the window class A window class describes a kind of window: which window procedure handles its messages, its cursor, its background brush, its icon. Every window belongs to a class. RegisterClassExW registers it under a name, once per program. Buttons, edit boxes and list boxes are windows of classes Windows registers for you ( L"BUTTON" , L"EDIT" ), which is how controls work (lesson 2.05). COLOR_WINDOW + 1 is an odd convention: a system colour index plus one, cast to a brush, tells Windows to paint the background in the user's window colour. Step 2: creating the window CreateWindowExW takes the extended style, class name, title, style , position, size, parent, menu, instance and a user pointer. WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW is the usual top-level window with a title bar, border, and minimise, maximise and close buttons. CW_USEDEFAULT lets Windows choose the position. The size includes the border and title bar. To get a client area (the inside) of exactly 800 × 500, compute the outer size first with AdjustWindowRectEx (or AdjustWindowRectExForDpi , lesson 3.04). Step 3: the message loop Windows does not call your code directly when something happens. It puts a message in your thread's message queue : a key was pressed, the mouse moved, the window must be repainted. The loop takes messages out one by one: - GetMessageW waits until there is a message and returns it. It returns 0 for WM_QUIT (the loop ends) and -1 on error, which is why the loop tests 0 rather than just "true". - TranslateMessage creates character messages from key messages (lesson 2.01). - DispatchMessageW calls the window procedure of the window the message is for. Step 4: the window procedure The window procedure ( WndProc ) is called with each message: the window, the message number ( WM_... ), and two parameters whose meaning depends on the message. It returns a result whose meaning also depends on the message. Anything you do not handle goes to DefWindowProcW , which implements standard behaviour: moving and resizing the window, the system menu, closing on Alt+F4, and so on. Forgetting to call it for unhandled messages gives a window that cannot even be moved. Closing Clicking the close button sends WM_CLOSE ; the default handling calls DestroyWindow , which sends WM_DESTROY . The main window handles WM_DESTROY by calling PostQuitMessage(0) , which posts WM_QUIT , which makes GetMessageW return 0 and the loop end. To ask "save changes?" before closing, handle WM_CLOSE and only call DestroyWindow if the user agrees.

title: Window sizes and positions
where: 1.03 Windows, Classes and the Message Loop
body: Lesson 1.03's CreateWindowExW takes the outer size of a window, but programs think in client sizes. Write simplified versions of the sizing helpers: cpp struct RECT { long left, top, right, bottom; }; struct Frame { int border; int caption; int menu; }; // thickness in pixels; 0 for "none" RECT adjustWindowRect(RECT client, Frame f); // like AdjustWindowRectEx RECT centredIn(RECT work, int width, int height); RECT keepOnScreen(RECT window, RECT work); - adjustWindowRect : the border surrounds the window on all four sides; the caption and then the menu bar are above the client area, inside the border. - centredIn : a rectangle of that size centred in work (the monitor's area without the taskbar), rounding the left and top down (towards minus infinity). - keepOnScreen : if the window is larger than the work area on an axis, it shrinks to the work area's size on that axis; then it moves (keeping its size) the least distance needed to be entirely inside. Remember that right and bottom are exclusive: width is right - left .

title: 1.04  Messages in Depth
body: How messages really flow - posted versus sent messages, the order of messages when a window is created and destroyed, how WPARAM and LPARAM pack several values, storing per-window data, and custom messages of your own. Posted and sent There are two ways a message reaches a window procedure: Posted Sent --- --- --- Function PostMessageW SendMessageW Goes Into the queue; the loop dispatches it later Straight to the window procedure (on its thread) Returns Immediately, before it is handled After it is handled, with the procedure's result Typical Input, WM_PAINT , WM_TIMER , WM_QUIT , your own notifications WM_CREATE , WM_SIZE , WM_SETTEXT , asking a control a question SendMessageW is a function call through the window system. If the window belongs to another thread, the calling thread waits while that thread processes the message, which is how two threads can deadlock : each waiting for the other to answer. Use PostMessageW from worker threads (lesson 5.04). Some messages are never really in the queue: WM_PAINT , WM_TIMER and WM_MOUSEMOVE are produced on demand when the queue is otherwise empty, and repeated ones are combined. Ten invalidations before the next paint give one WM_PAINT . A window's life Creating a window sends, in order (among others): WM_NCCREATE , WM_NCCALCSIZE , WM_CREATE , then WM_SIZE and WM_MOVE as it gets its position, and WM_SHOWWINDOW when it is shown. Destroying it sends WM_DESTROY and, last of all, WM_NCDESTROY . "NC" means non-client : the frame and title bar. WM_CREATE is where a window creates its child controls and resources; WM_DESTROY is where it frees them. Packed parameters WPARAM and LPARAM are just numbers; each message defines what they hold. Often two 16-bit values are packed into one parameter: cpp-norun case WM_SIZE: { const int width = LOWORD(lParam); // low 16 bits const int height = HIWORD(lParam); // high 16 bits // wParam: SIZE_MAXIMIZED, SIZE_MINIMIZED, SIZE_RESTORED return 0; } case WM_LBUTTONDOWN: { const int x = GET_X_LPARAM(lParam); // from <windowsx.h ; SIGNED const int y = GET_Y_LPARAM(lParam); return 0; } Use GET_X_LPARAM rather than LOWORD for mouse positions: with several monitors, a position can be negative , and LOWORD would turn -1 into 65535. MAKELPARAM(lo, hi) packs two values for sending. The practice writes these macros as functions. Data for each window The window procedure is a free function, but a window usually belongs to a C++ object. The standard pattern passes this as the last argument of CreateWindowExW , picks it up in WM_NCCREATE , and stores it in the window with SetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWLP_USERDATA, ...) : cpp-norun class MainWindow { public: static LRESULT CALLBACK Proc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { MainWindow self = nullptr; if (msg == WM_NCCREATE) { self = static_cast<MainWindow (reinterpret_cast<CREATESTRUCTW (lParam)- lpCreateParams); self- m_hwnd = hwnd; SetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWLP_USERDATA, reinterpret_cast<LONG_PTR (self)); } else self = reinterpret_cast<MainWindow (GetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWLP_USERDATA)); return self ? self- handle(msg, wParam, lParam) : DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); } private: LRESULT handle(UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam); // an ordinary member function HWND m_hwnd{}; }; // CreateWindowExW(..., instance, this); Messages before WM_NCCREATE (there is at least WM_GETMINMAXINFO ) arrive while the pointer is not yet stored, hence the null check. Your own messages For messages of your own, use numbers from WM_APP (0x8000) to 0xBFFF within your application: cpp-norun constexpr UINT WM_APP_SEARCH_DONE = WM_APP + 1; PostMessageW(hwnd, WM_APP_SEARCH_DONE, count, 0); // from a worker thread: "the search finished" WM_USER (0x0400 and up) is reserved for a window class's own private messages; controls use that range, so do not send WM_USER messages to windows you did not write. Between programs, RegisterWindowMessageW(L"name") gives a number unique across the system.

title: Packing message parameters
body: Write lesson 1.04's parameter macros as functions, on 64-bit Windows types: cpp using WPARAM = std::uint64_t; using LPARAM = std::int64_t; using UINT = std::uint32_t; LPARAM makeLParam(int lo, int hi); // the low 16 bits of each, packed into the low 32 bits int loWord(LPARAM v); // unsigned: 0 .. 65535 int hiWord(LPARAM v); int getX(LPARAM v); // signed: -32768 .. 32767, like GET_X_LPARAM int getY(LPARAM v); std::string messageRange(UINT msg); messageRange names the range a message number belongs to: "system" below 0x0400 ( WM_USER ), "class" from 0x0400 to 0x7FFF , "app" from 0x8000 ( WM_APP ) to 0xBFFF , "registered" from 0xC000 to 0xFFFF , and "reserved" above.

title: 1.05  Painting with GDI
body: Windows asks a window to paint itself with WM_PAINT. This lesson handles it with BeginPaint and EndPaint, draws lines, shapes and text with GDI, manages pens, brushes and fonts without leaking them, and invalidates just the part of the window that changed. Windows does not remember your pixels When a window is uncovered, restored or resized, the system does not keep a copy of what was in it. It marks the area as invalid and sends WM_PAINT : the window must draw itself again. So every program keeps its state (the text, the shapes, the score) and paints from it, exactly like a game draws each frame from its data. WM_PAINT cpp-norun case WM_PAINT: { PAINTSTRUCT ps; HDC dc = BeginPaint(hwnd, &ps); // ps.rcPaint: the invalid rectangle RECT client; GetClientRect(hwnd, &client); DrawTextW(dc, L"Hello, GDI", -1, &client, DT_CENTER DT_VCENTER DT_SINGLELINE); EndPaint(hwnd, &ps); // validates the area return 0; } Always pair BeginPaint with EndPaint , even if you draw nothing: EndPaint marks the area valid. Without it, Windows keeps sending WM_PAINT forever and the program uses a whole CPU core. HDC is a device context : a drawing surface with its current pen, brush, font and colours. Outside WM_PAINT you can get one with GetDC / ReleaseDC , but painting belongs in WM_PAINT . Drawing Function Draws --- --- MoveToEx(dc, x, y, nullptr) , LineTo(dc, x, y) Lines with the current pen Rectangle(dc, l, t, r, b) , Ellipse , RoundRect , Polygon Outlined with the pen, filled with the brush FillRect(dc, &rect, brush) A filled rectangle, no outline TextOutW(dc, x, y, text, len) , DrawTextW(...) Text; DrawTextW can wrap and align in a rectangle SetTextColor , SetBkMode(dc, TRANSPARENT) Text colour, and no background box behind text Colours are COLORREF values made with RGB(r, g, b) . Note the byte order: RGB stores red in the lowest byte ( 0x00BBGGRR ), the opposite of the RRGGBB order in HTML. The practice packs and unpacks them. Coordinates are in pixels from the client area's top-left corner. A RECT 's right and bottom are exclusive : {0, 0, 10, 10} covers pixels 0 to 9. Pens, brushes and fonts GDI objects are selected into the device context, and the previous object must be put back before you delete yours: cpp-norun HPEN pen = CreatePen(PS_SOLID, 3, RGB(200, 40, 40)); HBRUSH brush = CreateSolidBrush(RGB(250, 230, 120)); HGDIOBJ oldPen = SelectObject(dc, pen); HGDIOBJ oldBrush = SelectObject(dc, brush); Ellipse(dc, 50, 50, 200, 150); SelectObject(dc, oldBrush); // put the originals back SelectObject(dc, oldPen); DeleteObject(brush); // now safe to delete DeleteObject(pen); Deleting an object while it is still selected fails silently, and the object leaks. A program that leaks a brush per paint eventually reaches the per-process limit of 10 000 GDI objects and stops drawing altogether. GetStockObject(BLACK_PEN) , WHITE_BRUSH and friends are system objects that never need deleting. Creating the pens and brushes you use often once, in WM_CREATE , is both faster and safer. Repainting what changed When the program's state changes, it does not paint directly. It invalidates the affected area and lets the next WM_PAINT do the work: cpp-norun InvalidateRect(hwnd, &changedRect, TRUE); // TRUE: erase the background first InvalidateRect(hwnd, nullptr, TRUE); // the whole client area Several invalidations before the next paint are combined into one region, and the paint's ps.rcPaint is the bounding rectangle of all of them; a careful program draws only what intersects it. UpdateWindow(hwnd) paints immediately instead of waiting for the queue to empty. Background erasing before each paint causes flicker on resizing; lesson 4.01 removes it with double buffering.

title: Colours and invalid rectangles
body: Two pieces of GDI painting: cpp using COLORREF = std::uint32_t; struct RECT { long left, top, right, bottom; }; COLORREF rgb(int r, int g, int b); // like the RGB macro: 0x00BBGGRR int getR(COLORREF c); int getG(COLORREF c); int getB(COLORREF c); bool fromHtml(const std::string& html, COLORREF& out); // " RRGGBB" or " RGB", hex in either case std::string toHtml(COLORREF c); // " rrggbb" in lower case bool isEmpty(RECT r); // no area bool intersect(RECT a, RECT b, RECT& out); // false (and out empty {0,0,0,0}) if they do not overlap RECT unite(RECT a, RECT b); // bounding rectangle; an empty rectangle is ignored class InvalidArea { public: void invalidate(RECT r); // empty rectangles do nothing bool needsPaint() const; RECT bounds() const; // {0,0,0,0} when nothing is invalid void validate(); // what EndPaint does }; RGB doubles each digit: f80 is ff8800 . Anything else (missing , wrong length, a non-hex digit) is rejected.

title: A model of the message queue
match: A model of the message queue
body: Build a small model of how Windows delivers messages, to understand exactly what the message loop of lesson 1.03 sees: posted and sent messages, WM_QUIT , WM_PAINT that keeps coming until the window is validated, timers whose missed ticks combine, and destroying windows. cpp using HWND = int; using UINT = std::uint32_t; using WPARAM = std::uint64_t; using LPARAM = std::int64_t; using LRESULT = std::int64_t; constexpr UINT WM_DESTROY = 0x0002, WM_PAINT = 0x000F, WM_CLOSE = 0x0010, WM_QUIT = 0x0012, WM_TIMER = 0x0113, WM_APP = 0x8000; struct MSG { HWND hwnd; UINT message; WPARAM wParam; LPARAM lParam; }; class Desktop { public: using Proc = std::function<LRESULT(Desktop&, HWND, UINT, WPARAM, LPARAM) ; HWND createWindow(Proc proc); bool isWindow(HWND hwnd) const; bool destroyWindow(HWND hwnd); LRESULT sendMessage(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM w, LPARAM l); bool postMessage(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM w, LPARAM l); void postQuitMessage(int code); void invalidate(HWND hwnd); void validate(HWND hwnd); void setTimer(HWND hwnd, UINT id, int periodMs); void killTimer(HWND hwnd, UINT id); void advance(int ms); bool peekMessage(MSG& out); int run(); LRESULT defWindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM w, LPARAM l); }; Windows : createWindow returns handles 1, 2, 3, ... in order. destroyWindow first sends WM_DESTROY to the window, then removes it together with its timers, its invalid state and the messages still posted to it; it returns false for something that is not a window. Sending and posting : sendMessage calls the window procedure straight away and returns its result (0 for a non-window). postMessage queues the message (false for a non-window). postQuitMessage remembers that a quit was requested, with its code. peekMessage removes and returns the next message, in this order (a simplified version of the real order): 1. the oldest posted message; 2. WM_QUIT (hwnd 0, wParam = the code) if a quit was requested; the request is then forgotten; 3. WM_PAINT for the lowest-numbered invalid window. It is not removed by being returned: the window stays invalid, and keeps getting WM_PAINT , until validate is called; 4. WM_TIMER ( wParam = the timer id) for a due timer: one whose next time is at or before the clock. With several due, the one due earliest (then the lower window, then the lower id). Returning it sets the timer's next time to now + period , so ticks missed while the program was busy become a single WM_TIMER . setTimer (re)starts a timer that is first due one period from now; the clock starts at 0 and only advance moves it. run is the message loop: peek a message; on WM_QUIT , return its code; otherwise call the window procedure (if the window still exists). If no message is available, return -1 (a real loop would wait forever). defWindowProc : WM_CLOSE destroys the window, WM_PAINT validates it; it returns 0.

title: 2.01  Keyboard Input
body: Keys arrive as WM_KEYDOWN and WM_KEYUP with virtual-key codes, text arrives as WM_CHAR after TranslateMessage. This lesson explains the difference, the information packed into lParam, auto-repeat, modifier keys, system keys and keyboard focus. Keys and characters Pressing Shift+A produces several messages: Message Means wParam --- --- --- WM_KEYDOWN Shift went down VK_SHIFT WM_KEYDOWN A went down 'A' (the virtual key) WM_CHAR The character "A" was typed L'A' (a UTF-16 unit) WM_KEYUP A went up 'A' WM_KEYUP Shift went up VK_SHIFT Key messages tell you which physical key moved, as a virtual-key code : 'A' to 'Z' , '0' to '9' , VK_LEFT , VK_RETURN , VK_F5 , VK_CONTROL and so on. They are for commands : arrows to move, Delete to delete, F5 to refresh. Character messages tell you which text the user typed, after the keyboard layout, Shift, Caps Lock and dead keys (é from ´ then e) are applied. They are for text input . TranslateMessage in the message loop makes them; leave it out and no WM_CHAR ever arrives. Characters above U+FFFF arrive as two WM_CHAR messages, one per surrogate (lesson 1.02). Never build text from WM_KEYDOWN : it knows nothing about layouts, so a French or German user gets the wrong letters. What lParam holds For key messages, lParam packs details of the keystroke: Bits Meaning --- --- 0 - 15 Repeat count (auto-repeat may combine several) 16 - 23 Scan code (the physical key's hardware code) 24 Extended key (right Ctrl, right Alt, arrow keys of the separate block, Insert/Delete ...) 29 Context code: Alt was down (for WM_SYSKEYDOWN ) 30 Previous key state: 1 if the key was already down (this is an auto-repeat) 31 Transition state: 0 for down, 1 for up Bit 30 is the useful one: holding a key sends WM_KEYDOWN again and again, and bit 30 tells a first press apart from repeats. A game-style "jump once per press" checks it. The practice decodes all the fields. Modifier keys To know whether Ctrl or Shift is held when a key arrives, ask: cpp-norun const bool ctrl = GetKeyState(VK_CONTROL) < 0; // high bit set = down const bool shift = GetKeyState(VK_SHIFT) < 0; GetKeyState gives the state as of the message being processed , which is what you want inside a window procedure. GetAsyncKeyState gives the state right now, which may differ if the program is behind; it is for polling, not for handling messages. Left and right versions exist ( VK_LSHIFT , VK_RSHIFT ) when it matters. System keys Keys pressed with Alt held, and F10, arrive as WM_SYSKEYDOWN / WM_SYSKEYUP / WM_SYSCHAR instead. DefWindowProcW uses them for the menu (Alt opens it, Alt+F opens File) and for Alt+F4. If you handle Alt combinations yourself, still pass the messages you do not use to DefWindowProcW , or Alt+F4 stops working. Focus Keyboard messages go to the window with the keyboard focus : one window in the system at a time. Clicking a control gives it the focus; SetFocus(hwnd) moves it in code. A window learns it gained or lost focus through WM_SETFOCUS and WM_KILLFOCUS : a text editor creates its caret ( CreateCaret , ShowCaret ) on the first and destroys it on the second. When a top-level window is reactivated, it should give the focus back to the control that had it, which dialogs do automatically (lesson 3.01).

title: Inside a key message
body: Decode and build the lParam of WM_KEYDOWN and WM_KEYUP (lesson 2.01's table), and name virtual keys: cpp using LPARAM = std::int64_t; struct KeyInfo { int repeat; int scanCode; bool extended; bool altDown; bool wasDown; bool released; }; KeyInfo decodeKey(LPARAM lParam); LPARAM encodeKey(const KeyInfo& k); bool isFirstPress(LPARAM lParam); // a key-down that is not an auto-repeat std::string keyName(int vk); keyName : 'A' - 'Z' and '0' - '9' are themselves; 0x70 - 0x87 are F1 - F24 ; 0x08 Backspace, 0x09 Tab, 0x0D Enter, 0x1B Esc, 0x20 Space, 0x21 PageUp, 0x22 PageDown, 0x23 End, 0x24 Home, 0x25 Left, 0x26 Up, 0x27 Right, 0x28 Down, 0x2D Insert, 0x2E Delete; anything else "0x" and two upper-case hex digits (such as 0xBA ).

title: 2.02  Mouse Input and Capture
body: Handling clicks, double-clicks, movement and the wheel, the modifier flags that come with them, capturing the mouse during a drag, knowing when the mouse leaves, setting the cursor, and hit-testing your own shapes. Mouse messages Message When --- --- WM_LBUTTONDOWN / UP , WM_RBUTTON... , WM_MBUTTON... , WM_XBUTTON... A button changes WM_LBUTTONDBLCLK A second click soon after the first (only if the class has CS_DBLCLKS ) WM_MOUSEMOVE The mouse moved over the client area WM_MOUSEWHEEL , WM_MOUSEHWHEEL The wheel turned (vertically, horizontally) WM_MOUSELEAVE The mouse left the window (after you asked for it) The position is in lParam , in client coordinates, read with GET_X_LPARAM / GET_Y_LPARAM (lesson 1.04). wParam holds flags for what else is down: MK_LBUTTON , MK_RBUTTON , MK_SHIFT , MK_CONTROL , MK_MBUTTON . A double-click arrives as down, up, double-click , up: the first click is delivered as an ordinary click first. Design double-click actions so the single click before them does no harm (select on click, open on double-click). The wheel WM_MOUSEWHEEL is different from the others: its position is in screen coordinates (convert with ScreenToClient ), and the amount is in the high word of wParam , signed, in multiples of WHEEL_DELTA (120) per notch: cpp-norun case WM_MOUSEWHEEL: { m_wheelRemainder += GET_WHEEL_DELTA_WPARAM(wParam); const int notches = m_wheelRemainder / WHEEL_DELTA; m_wheelRemainder -= notches WHEEL_DELTA; scrollLines(-notches 3); return 0; } Precision touchpads send small values such as 15 or 30. Accumulating the remainder, as above, keeps slow scrolling working instead of throwing every small movement away. The practice writes this accumulator. Capturing the mouse When the user presses the button inside your window and drags outside it, WM_MOUSEMOVE and the button-up go to whatever window is under the mouse, not yours. A drag (moving a slider, selecting text, drawing a line) needs capture : cpp-norun case WM_LBUTTONDOWN: SetCapture(hwnd); m_dragging = true; m_start = pointFrom(lParam); return 0; case WM_MOUSEMOVE: if (m_dragging) { m_end = pointFrom(lParam); InvalidateRect(hwnd, nullptr, FALSE); } return 0; case WM_LBUTTONUP: if (m_dragging) { ReleaseCapture(); } return 0; case WM_CAPTURECHANGED: m_dragging = false; return 0; // capture lost, for any reason While captured, every mouse message comes to your window, even from outside it, with positions that can be negative or beyond the client size. Handle WM_CAPTURECHANGED to end the drag cleanly: the system can take capture away (an Alt+Tab, a pop-up), and then no button-up will ever arrive. Knowing when the mouse leaves To highlight something on hover, you need to know when the mouse leaves . Ask for one WM_MOUSELEAVE with TrackMouseEvent , and ask again after each one: cpp-norun case WM_MOUSEMOVE: if (!m_tracking) { TRACKMOUSEEVENT t{ sizeof(t), TME_LEAVE, hwnd, 0 }; TrackMouseEvent(&t); m_tracking = true; } updateHover(pointFrom(lParam)); return 0; case WM_MOUSELEAVE: m_tracking = false; clearHover(); return 0; The cursor The class's cursor ( wc.hCursor ) is shown by default. To change it depending on what is under the mouse (a resize arrow over a splitter, a hand over a link), handle WM_SETCURSOR : cpp-norun case WM_SETCURSOR: if (LOWORD(lParam) == HTCLIENT && overSplitter()) { SetCursor(LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_SIZEWE)); return TRUE; } break; // let DefWindowProcW set the normal cursor Hit-testing The window only tells you a point; deciding what is under it is your job: test the point against your shapes from the topmost down, and the first hit wins. Rectangles use lesson 1.05's exclusive right and bottom edges; circles compare squared distances.

title: Wheels, hits and drags
body: Three pieces of mouse handling from lesson 2.02: cpp struct Shape { int id; bool circle; int x, y, w, h; }; // circle: centre (x, y), radius w class Wheel { public: int add(int delta); // whole notches (WHEEL_DELTA = 120) to act on now, keeping the rest }; int hitTest(const std::vector<Shape & shapes, int x, int y); // topmost = last in the list; -1 for none class Drag { public: explicit Drag(int threshold); void down(int x, int y); void move(int x, int y); bool up(int x, int y); // true if this ended a real drag (not a click) void captureLost(); // the drag is cancelled bool dragging() const; // past the threshold and not ended std::string state() const; // "idle", "pressed" or "dragging" }; - Wheel::add accumulates the signed delta and returns the whole notches in it, rounding towards zero, keeping the remainder (with its sign). - hitTest : rectangles are x .. x + w , y .. y + h with exclusive right and bottom; circles include points at a distance up to the radius. Return the id of the topmost shape containing the point. - Drag : after down it is "pressed". A move farther than threshold pixels from the down point on either axis (strictly more) makes it "dragging", and it stays dragging until up or captureLost . up returns true only if it was dragging, and returns to "idle". Moves while idle do nothing.

title: 2.03  Timers and the Clock
body: Doing things later or repeatedly with SetTimer and WM_TIMER, why timers are not precise, measuring time with QueryPerformanceCounter, the system clock and time zones, and running animation without freezing the interface. SetTimer A timer sends WM_TIMER to a window repeatedly: cpp-norun constexpr UINT_PTR TIMER_BLINK = 1; SetTimer(hwnd, TIMER_BLINK, 500, nullptr); // every 500 ms // ... case WM_TIMER: if (wParam == TIMER_BLINK) { m_caretVisible = !m_caretVisible; invalidateCaret(); } return 0; // ... KillTimer(hwnd, TIMER_BLINK); // e.g. in WM_DESTROY Calling SetTimer again with the same window and id restarts that timer with the new period. A one-shot "do this in two seconds" is a timer that kills itself in its first WM_TIMER . Timers are not precise WM_TIMER is a low-priority message, generated only when the queue has nothing else (like WM_PAINT , lesson 1.04's practice model): - The default resolution is about 15.6 ms : a 10 ms timer fires roughly every 15.6 ms. - If the program is busy, ticks are combined : after a 2-second pause, a 100 ms timer fires once, not twenty times. - So never count ticks to measure time. A countdown that does remaining -= 100 on each tick runs slow; one that checks the real clock is always right. Measuring time For measuring durations, use the high-resolution counter: cpp-norun LARGE_INTEGER frequency, start, now; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&frequency); // counts per second, fixed at boot QueryPerformanceCounter(&start); // ... work ... QueryPerformanceCounter(&now); const double seconds = double(now.QuadPart - start.QuadPart) / double(frequency.QuadPart); It is monotonic (never jumps backwards) and has sub-microsecond resolution. std::chrono::steady_clock is the portable way to the same counter. To convert counts to milliseconds without overflow or loss of precision, split into whole seconds and the remainder; the practice does exactly that. GetTickCount64() gives milliseconds since boot at the 15.6 ms resolution: fine for timeouts, too coarse for measuring. Wall-clock time The time of day is a different thing: it can jump when the user changes the clock, the computer syncs with a time server, or daylight saving changes. - GetSystemTimeAsFileTime gives the current time in UTC as a FILETIME : 100-nanosecond intervals since 1 January 1601 . - FileTimeToSystemTime breaks it into year, month, day, hour ...; SystemTimeToTzSpecificLocalTime converts UTC to local time. - Store and compare times in UTC, and convert to local time only to show them. Converting between FILETIME and Unix time (seconds since 1970) is a fixed offset: 11 644 473 600 seconds between 1601 and 1970. Animation Animating with a timer: on each WM_TIMER , compute the animation's state from the elapsed real time , not from the number of ticks, and invalidate. Then it runs at the right speed whatever the timer actually does: cpp-norun case WM_TIMER: { const double t = secondsSince(m_animStart); m_offset = easeOut(std::min(t / 0.25, 1.0)) m_distance; if (t = 0.25) KillTimer(hwnd, TIMER_ANIM); InvalidateRect(hwnd, nullptr, FALSE); return 0; } For smooth animation at the display's refresh rate, draw with Direct2D (milestone 4) and use DwmFlush or the swap chain's frame timing rather than WM_TIMER . Never block the loop Sleep(2000) in a window procedure freezes the whole window for two seconds: no painting, no input, and after about five seconds Windows marks it "Not responding". Anything that takes time goes to a timer (if it can be split into small steps) or a worker thread (lesson 5.04).

title: Counters and calendars
body: Write the time conversions of lesson 2.03: cpp std::int64_t countsToMicroseconds(std::int64_t counts, std::int64_t frequency); std::int64_t fileTimeToUnixMs(std::uint64_t fileTime); // 100 ns units since 1601-01-01 UTC std::uint64_t unixMsToFileTime(std::int64_t unixMs); std::string formatUtc(std::uint64_t fileTime); // "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" - countsToMicroseconds must not overflow for large counts (such as a counter of 10 000 000 per second after 30 days of uptime): split the counts into whole seconds and the remainder before multiplying. Round down. - Between 1601 and 1970 there are 11 644 473 600 seconds. fileTimeToUnixMs rounds down to the millisecond (towards minus infinity for times before 1970). - formatUtc converts the file time to a date and time in the Gregorian calendar (leap years: divisible by 4, except centuries, except every 400 years). Times are never before 1601.

title: 2.04  Menus, Accelerators and Resources
body: Adding a menu bar and context menus, handling WM_COMMAND, enabling and checking items as the program's state changes, keyboard shortcuts with accelerator tables, and the resource file that holds menus, icons, strings and version information. Resources A resource file ( .rc ) describes data that is compiled into the .exe : menus, icons, cursors, dialogs, string tables, version information. Visual Studio has editors for them; the text format is simple: cpp-norun // resource.h define IDR_MAINMENU 101 define IDR_ACCEL 102 define IDI_APP 103 define ID_FILE_NEW 40001 define ID_FILE_OPEN 40002 define ID_FILE_SAVE 40003 define ID_FILE_EXIT 40004 define ID_VIEW_STATUS 40010 // app.rc include "resource.h" IDI_APP ICON "app.ico" IDR_MAINMENU MENU BEGIN POPUP "&File" BEGIN MENUITEM "&New\tCtrl+N", ID_FILE_NEW MENUITEM "&Open...\tCtrl+O", ID_FILE_OPEN MENUITEM "&Save\tCtrl+S", ID_FILE_SAVE MENUITEM SEPARATOR MENUITEM "E&xit", ID_FILE_EXIT END POPUP "&View" BEGIN MENUITEM "&Status Bar", ID_VIEW_STATUS, CHECKED END END & marks the letter underlined for Alt navigation (Alt, F, S saves). \t separates the shortcut text shown on the right; it is only text: the shortcut itself comes from the accelerator table below. "..." means the item opens a dialog before doing anything. Load the menu by giving the class wc.lpszMenuName = MAKEINTRESOURCEW(IDR_MAINMENU) , or with LoadMenuW and SetMenu . WM_COMMAND Choosing a menu item sends WM_COMMAND with the item's id in LOWORD(wParam) : cpp-norun case WM_COMMAND: switch (LOWORD(wParam)) { case ID_FILE_NEW: newDocument(); return 0; case ID_FILE_SAVE: save(); return 0; case ID_FILE_EXIT: SendMessageW(hwnd, WM_CLOSE, 0, 0); return 0; // the same path as the close button } break; HIWORD(wParam) tells where the command came from: 0 for a menu, 1 for an accelerator, or a notification code for a control (lesson 2.05). Keeping items up to date "Save" should be greyed out when there is nothing to save, and "Status Bar" should show a check mark when the bar is visible. Update the items just before the menu opens, in WM_INITMENUPOPUP , from the program's state: cpp-norun case WM_INITMENUPOPUP: { HMENU menu = reinterpret_cast<HMENU (wParam); EnableMenuItem(menu, ID_FILE_SAVE, MF_BYCOMMAND (m_doc.dirty ? MF_ENABLED : MF_GRAYED)); CheckMenuItem(menu, ID_VIEW_STATUS, MF_BYCOMMAND (m_statusVisible ? MF_CHECKED : MF_UNCHECKED)); return 0; } Deriving the menu's state from the program's state every time, instead of updating items whenever something changes, means they can never get out of step. Context menus Right-clicking sends WM_CONTEXTMENU (also sent by the Menu key and Shift+F10, with position -1, -1: then show the menu at the selection instead): cpp-norun case WM_CONTEXTMENU: { HMENU menu = CreatePopupMenu(); AppendMenuW(menu, MF_STRING, ID_EDIT_CUT, L"Cu&t"); AppendMenuW(menu, MF_STRING, ID_EDIT_COPY, L"&Copy"); TrackPopupMenu(menu, TPM_RIGHTBUTTON, GET_X_LPARAM(lParam), GET_Y_LPARAM(lParam), 0, hwnd, nullptr); DestroyMenu(menu); return 0; } Accelerators An accelerator table maps key combinations to command ids, so Ctrl+S sends the same WM_COMMAND as the menu item: cpp-norun IDR_ACCEL ACCELERATORS BEGIN "N", ID_FILE_NEW, VIRTKEY, CONTROL "O", ID_FILE_OPEN, VIRTKEY, CONTROL "S", ID_FILE_SAVE, VIRTKEY, CONTROL VK_F5, ID_VIEW_REFRESH, VIRTKEY END The message loop translates them before anything else: cpp-norun HACCEL accel = LoadAcceleratorsW(instance, MAKEINTRESOURCEW(IDR_ACCEL)); while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { if (!TranslateAcceleratorW(hwnd, accel, &msg)) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } } Accelerator tables can also be built at run time with CreateAcceleratorTableW , which lets users choose their own shortcuts. Parsing a shortcut such as "Ctrl+Shift+S" into key and modifier flags, and spotting two commands with the same shortcut, is the practice. Strings and versions A string table keeps user-visible text out of the code ( LoadStringW(instance, IDS_TITLE, ...) ), which is how a program is translated. A VERSIONINFO resource gives the file version, product name and copyright shown in the file's Properties dialog.

title: Shortcuts and mnemonics
body: Parse and print keyboard shortcuts for a run-time accelerator table, find conflicts, and read menu mnemonics: cpp struct Shortcut { int key{ 0 }; bool ctrl{ false }, shift{ false }, alt{ false }; }; bool parseShortcut(const std::string& text, Shortcut& out); std::string formatShortcut(const Shortcut& s); std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string conflicts(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string & commands); char mnemonic(const std::string& menuText); parseShortcut : parts separated by + , case-insensitive, any order of modifiers; the last part is the key. Modifiers are Ctrl (or Control ), Shift and Alt , each at most once. Keys are a letter or digit (stored as its upper-case character code), F1 - F12 ( 0x70 onwards), and Delete (0x2E), Insert (0x2D), Home (0x24), End (0x23), PageUp (0x21), PageDown (0x22), Left (0x25), Up (0x26), Right (0x27), Down (0x28), Enter (0x0D), Esc (0x1B), Space (0x20), Tab (0x09). Spaces around parts are allowed. Anything else fails. formatShortcut writes Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Key in that order with the names above ( F5 , PageUp , S ). conflicts takes (command, shortcut text) pairs and returns each pair of command names whose shortcuts are the same, in the order of the first command, then the second. Shortcuts that do not parse are ignored. mnemonic : the upper-case letter after the first single & in a menu item's text ( && is a literal ampersand), or 0 if there is none.

title: 2.05  Standard Controls
body: Buttons, check boxes, edit boxes, list boxes and combo boxes are child windows of classes Windows provides. This lesson creates them, talks to them with messages, handles their notifications, gives them the right font, and moves the keyboard focus between them with Tab. Controls are windows A control is a child window of a predefined class. Create it in the parent's WM_CREATE with WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE , and give it an id in the menu parameter: cpp-norun constexpr int IDC_NAME = 1001, IDC_ADD = 1002, IDC_LIST = 1003, IDC_SHOUT = 1004; case WM_CREATE: { const auto instance = reinterpret_cast<CREATESTRUCTW (lParam)- hInstance; CreateWindowExW(WS_EX_CLIENTEDGE, L"EDIT", L"", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP ES_AUTOHSCROLL, 10, 10, 200, 24, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_NAME), instance, nullptr); CreateWindowExW(0, L"BUTTON", L"&Add", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP BS_DEFPUSHBUTTON, 220, 10, 80, 24, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_ADD), instance, nullptr); CreateWindowExW(0, L"BUTTON", L"&Shout", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP BS_AUTOCHECKBOX, 10, 44, 200, 24, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_SHOUT), instance, nullptr); CreateWindowExW(WS_EX_CLIENTEDGE, L"LISTBOX", L"", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP WS_VSCROLL LBS_NOTIFY, 10, 78, 290, 200, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_LIST), instance, nullptr); return 0; } Class Control Common styles --- --- --- BUTTON Push button, check box, radio button, group box BS_PUSHBUTTON , BS_DEFPUSHBUTTON , BS_AUTOCHECKBOX , BS_AUTORADIOBUTTON , BS_GROUPBOX EDIT Text box ES_AUTOHSCROLL , ES_MULTILINE , ES_NUMBER , ES_PASSWORD , ES_READONLY STATIC Label, picture, frame SS_LEFT , SS_RIGHT , SS_CENTER LISTBOX List of strings LBS_NOTIFY , LBS_SORT , LBS_EXTENDEDSEL COMBOBOX Drop-down list CBS_DROPDOWNLIST , CBS_DROPDOWN SCROLLBAR A separate scroll bar SBS_HORZ , SBS_VERT Talking to controls Controls are driven by messages . GetDlgItem(parent, id) finds a control's window: cpp-norun HWND list = GetDlgItem(hwnd, IDC_LIST); SendMessageW(list, LB_ADDSTRING, 0, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (L"Granite")); const int selected = static_cast<int (SendMessageW(list, LB_GETCURSEL, 0, 0)); // LB_ERR (-1) for none const bool shout = SendMessageW(GetDlgItem(hwnd, IDC_SHOUT), BM_GETCHECK, 0, 0) == BST_CHECKED; wchar_t name 256 ; GetDlgItemTextW(hwnd, IDC_NAME, name, 256); // SetDlgItemTextW to change it Each control family has its prefix: BM_ buttons, EM_ edits, LB_ list boxes, CB_ combo boxes. Reading text of unknown length: ask GetWindowTextLengthW first, then size the buffer. Notifications Controls tell their parent about events with WM_COMMAND : LOWORD(wParam) is the control's id, HIWORD(wParam) is the notification code , and lParam is the control's window: cpp-norun case WM_COMMAND: switch (LOWORD(wParam)) { case IDC_ADD: if (HIWORD(wParam) == BN_CLICKED) addName(); return 0; case IDC_NAME: if (HIWORD(wParam) == EN_CHANGE) updateAddButton(); // the text changed return 0; case IDC_LIST: if (HIWORD(wParam) == LBN_DBLCLK) openSelected(); return 0; } break; Newer controls (lesson 3.05) use WM_NOTIFY with a structure instead, because two numbers are not enough to describe their events. Fonts Controls created this way use the old bitmap "System" font, which looks wrong. Give every control the system's message font once they are created: cpp-norun NONCLIENTMETRICSW m{ sizeof(m) }; SystemParametersInfoW(SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS, sizeof(m), &m, 0); m_font = CreateFontIndirectW(&m.lfMessageFont); // delete it in WM_DESTROY EnumChildWindows(hwnd, (HWND child, LPARAM font) { SendMessageW(child, WM_SETFONT, font, TRUE); return TRUE; }, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (m_font)); With high DPI (lesson 3.04), use SystemParametersInfoForDpi so the font has the right size on each monitor. Tab between controls In an ordinary window, Tab does nothing. IsDialogMessageW adds dialog-style keyboard navigation (Tab and Shift+Tab between WS_TABSTOP controls, arrows within groups, Enter for the default button, Alt+letter for & mnemonics) to any window: cpp-norun while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { if (!IsDialogMessageW(hwnd, &msg)) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } } The Tab order is the order the controls were created in, so create them in reading order.

title: A list box model
body: Write a model of the LISTBOX control's most used messages, with their real return values: cpp constexpr int LB_ERR = -1; class ListBox { public: explicit ListBox(bool sorted); // LBS_SORT int addString(const std::string& s); // LB_ADDSTRING: the index it went to int insertString(int index, const std::string& s);// LB_INSERTSTRING: -1 appends; never sorts int deleteString(int index); // LB_DELETESTRING: the new count, or LB_ERR int getCount() const; int getCurSel() const; // LB_ERR when nothing is selected int setCurSel(int index); // -1 clears the selection and returns LB_ERR; a bad index returns LB_ERR std::string getText(int index) const; // "" for a bad index int findString(int start, const std::string& prefix) const; // LB_FINDSTRING }; - A sorted list box inserts with addString at its place in case-insensitive order (after equal strings). - Deleting the selected item clears the selection; deleting an item before it moves the selection up by one. Inserting before the selection moves it down. - findString finds the first item that starts with prefix , ignoring case, searching from the item after start to the end and then from the beginning, up to and including start ; start = -1 searches the whole list from the top. It returns LB_ERR if there is no match.

title: Commands, shortcuts and recent files
body: Every document program needs the same pieces around its menus: a table of commands with their shortcuts and state, turning key presses into commands (a run-time accelerator table), and a "recent files" list in the File menu. Write them without any windows, so the window procedure just asks them. cpp struct Key { int vk; bool ctrl{ false }, shift{ false }, alt{ false }; }; class CommandTable { public: bool add(int id, const std::string& text, const std::string& shortcut); void setEnabled(int id, bool enabled); void setChecked(int id, bool checked); int translate(const Key& k) const; std::string menuLine(int id) const; }; class RecentFiles { public: explicit RecentFiles(std::size_t max); // at most 9 void add(const std::string& path); void remove(const std::string& path); const std::vector<std::string & items() const; std::vector<std::string menuItems(std::size_t maxChars) const; static std::string shorten(const std::string& path, std::size_t maxChars); std::string save() const; void load(const std::string& text); }; CommandTable - add fails (returns false) if the id is already used, the shortcut does not parse, or another command already has the same shortcut. An empty shortcut means none. Shortcuts use practice 2.04's rules (modifiers Ctrl/Control, Shift, Alt; letters, digits, F1-F12 and the named keys), and commands start enabled and unchecked. - translate returns the id of the enabled command whose shortcut is exactly this key with exactly these modifiers, or 0. - menuLine is the text, then a tab and the shortcut in practice 2.04's canonical form if there is one; with " x " in front when checked, and " (disabled)" at the end when disabled. Unknown ids give "" . RecentFiles - add puts the path at the front; if it is already in the list (compared case-insensitively , as Windows paths are), the old entry is removed first. The list is cut to max . - remove removes a path (case-insensitively), if present. - shorten leaves paths of at most maxChars characters alone. Otherwise, with the path split on \ , it keeps the first part (such as C: ), then \...\ , then as many of the last parts as fit, preferring to keep more; if not even the file name fits that way, it returns ... followed by the last maxChars - 3 characters. - menuItems numbers the entries &1 , &2 , ... followed by the shortened path, with every & in the path doubled ( && ), since a single one would become a mnemonic. - save writes one path per line, each ending in \n ; load replaces the list with the non-empty lines of a text ( \r\n allowed), dropping later duplicates and anything beyond max .

title: 3.01  Dialog Boxes
body: Dialogs are windows built from a template, with keyboard navigation and default buttons for free. This lesson creates modal and modeless dialogs, writes the dialog procedure, moves data in and out of the controls, validates input, and returns a result. What a dialog gives you A dialog box is a window whose controls are described by a template in the resource file, created and laid out by Windows. Compared with creating controls by hand (lesson 2.05) it adds, for free: - Tab and arrow navigation, mnemonics, Enter for the default button and Esc for Cancel; - layout in dialog units , which scale with the dialog's font (so the dialog grows with the user's text size); - IDOK and IDCANCEL handling, and the focus going to the first control. The template cpp-norun IDD_RENAME DIALOGEX 0, 0, 220, 70 STYLE DS_MODALFRAME DS_SHELLFONT WS_POPUP WS_CAPTION WS_SYSMENU CAPTION "Rename" FONT 9, "Segoe UI" BEGIN LTEXT "&New name:", IDC_STATIC, 7, 9, 50, 8 EDITTEXT IDC_NAME, 60, 7, 153, 14, ES_AUTOHSCROLL AUTOCHECKBOX "&Keep the extension", IDC_KEEPEXT, 60, 26, 120, 10 DEFPUSHBUTTON "OK", IDOK, 109, 49, 50, 14 PUSHBUTTON "Cancel", IDCANCEL, 163, 49, 50, 14 END Positions and sizes are in dialog units : horizontally a quarter of the font's average character width, vertically an eighth of its height. Visual Studio's dialog editor writes this for you. The label comes just before its edit box in the template so its mnemonic (Alt+N) moves the focus to the edit box. Modal dialogs A modal dialog disables its owner and runs its own message loop until it is closed; DialogBoxParamW returns only then: cpp-norun struct RenameData { std::wstring name; bool keepExtension{ true }; }; INT_PTR CALLBACK RenameProc(HWND dlg, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { auto data = reinterpret_cast<RenameData (GetWindowLongPtrW(dlg, DWLP_USER)); switch (msg) { case WM_INITDIALOG: // data in: fill the controls data = reinterpret_cast<RenameData (lParam); SetWindowLongPtrW(dlg, DWLP_USER, lParam); SetDlgItemTextW(dlg, IDC_NAME, data- name.c_str()); CheckDlgButton(dlg, IDC_KEEPEXT, data- keepExtension ? BST_CHECKED : BST_UNCHECKED); return TRUE; // TRUE: set the focus to the first control case WM_COMMAND: switch (LOWORD(wParam)) { case IDOK: // data out: read and validate { const std::wstring name = getText(dlg, IDC_NAME); if (!validFileName(name)) { MessageBoxW(dlg, L"A name cannot contain \\ / : ? \" < ", L"Rename", MB_ICONWARNING); SetFocus(GetDlgItem(dlg, IDC_NAME)); return TRUE; // stay open } data- name = name; data- keepExtension = IsDlgButtonChecked(dlg, IDC_KEEPEXT) == BST_CHECKED; EndDialog(dlg, IDOK); return TRUE; } case IDCANCEL: EndDialog(dlg, IDCANCEL); return TRUE; // also Esc and the close button } break; } return FALSE; // not handled: the dialog manager does the default } RenameData data{ L"notes.txt" }; if (DialogBoxParamW(instance, MAKEINTRESOURCEW(IDD_RENAME), owner, RenameProc, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (&data)) == IDOK) rename(data); Note the differences from a window procedure: it returns TRUE or FALSE ("handled or not"), never calls DefWindowProcW , and ends with EndDialog , never DestroyWindow . The last parameter of DialogBoxParamW carries a pointer to the dialog's data, which arrives as lParam in WM_INITDIALOG . The data pattern A dialog is easiest to get right when it works on a plain struct : the caller fills it, WM_INITDIALOG copies it into the controls, IDOK validates and copies it back, and Cancel leaves it untouched. All the rules about valid values can then be written and tested as a normal function on the struct, as in the practice. Good validation tells the user what is wrong and puts the focus on the field, or better, disables OK while the input is invalid (check on EN_CHANGE ) and shows why next to the field. Modeless dialogs A modeless dialog (a Find window, a tool palette) stays open while the user keeps working in the main window. Create it with CreateDialogParamW , show it, and let the main message loop pass its messages through IsDialogMessageW so its keyboard navigation works: cpp-norun if (!(g_findDialog && IsDialogMessageW(g_findDialog, &msg))) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } Close a modeless dialog with DestroyWindow , not EndDialog , and set g_findDialog back to null in its WM_DESTROY . Message boxes and task dialogs For simple questions, MessageBoxW(owner, text, title, MB_YESNOCANCEL MB_ICONQUESTION) returns IDYES , IDNO or IDCANCEL . TaskDialogIndirect is its modern replacement, with a main instruction, explanatory text, command links, a check box ("Don't ask again") and a progress bar. Always pass the owner window, so the box is modal to it and appears in front of it.

title: Validating a rename dialog
body: Write the rules behind lesson 3.01's Rename dialog, as plain functions on its data: cpp std::string fileNameProblem(const std::string& name); // "" if the name is valid, else the message to show std::string applyRename(const std::string& oldName, const std::string& newName, bool keepExtension); fileNameProblem checks in this order and returns the first problem: 1. empty (after nothing is trimmed): "Enter a name." 2. contains any of \ / : ? " < or a character below 32: "A name cannot contain \ / : ? \" < " (with those characters literally) 3. ends with a space or a dot: "A name cannot end with a space or a dot." 4. is a reserved device name, ignoring case and any extension ( CON , PRN , AUX , NUL , COM1 - COM9 , LPT1 - LPT9 ; so con.txt and Lpt3 count, CONSOLE and COM0 do not): "That name is reserved by Windows." 5. longer than 255 characters: "The name is too long." applyRename : the extension is the part from the last dot, if that dot is not the first character ( .gitignore has no extension). With keepExtension , if the new name does not already end with the old extension (ignoring case), the old extension is added.

title: 3.02  Common Dialogs
body: Windows provides the Open, Save, folder, colour and font dialogs every program needs. This lesson uses the modern IFileOpenDialog and IFileSaveDialog through COM, with file type filters, default extensions and folders, and the older colour and font dialogs. COM in five minutes The modern file dialogs are COM objects. COM is Windows' system for objects shared between components: you create an object by its class id, get an interface (a table of virtual functions), call methods that return HRESULT s (lesson 1.01), and Release() the interface when done. cpp-norun include <shobjidl.h // IFileOpenDialog include <wrl/client.h // Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr: a smart pointer that calls Release using Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr; // once per thread that uses COM, at start-up; CoUninitialize at the end CoInitializeEx(nullptr, COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED COINIT_DISABLE_OLE1DDE); ComPtr is to COM what std::unique_ptr is to new : it releases the object automatically. The UI thread must use the apartment-threaded model (STA) for dialogs. Open cpp-norun std::optional<std::wstring askOpenFile(HWND owner) { ComPtr<IFileOpenDialog dialog; if (FAILED(CoCreateInstance(CLSID_FileOpenDialog, nullptr, CLSCTX_INPROC_SERVER, IID_PPV_ARGS(&dialog)))) return {}; const COMDLG_FILTERSPEC types = { { L"Text documents", L" .txt; .md" }, { L"All files", L" . " }, }; dialog- SetFileTypes(ARRAYSIZE(types), types); dialog- SetFileTypeIndex(1); // 1-based dialog- SetTitle(L"Open a note"); if (FAILED(dialog- Show(owner))) return {}; // also when the user cancels: HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED) ComPtr<IShellItem item; if (FAILED(dialog- GetResult(&item))) return {}; PWSTR path = nullptr; if (FAILED(item- GetDisplayName(SIGDN_FILESYSPATH, &path))) return {}; std::wstring result{ path }; CoTaskMemFree(path); // memory allocated by COM is freed with CoTaskMemFree return result; } IID_PPV_ARGS(&dialog) passes both the interface's id and the pointer to fill, so they cannot mismatch. Cancelling is reported as a failed HRESULT with the code ERROR_CANCELLED (1223), which is not an error to show the user. Options set with SetOptions(FOS_...) : FOS_ALLOWMULTISELECT (then use GetResults ), FOS_PICKFOLDERS (a folder picker), FOS_FILEMUSTEXIST . Save IFileSaveDialog works the same way, with a few extras: cpp-norun dialog- SetFileName(L"Untitled.txt"); // suggested name dialog- SetDefaultExtension(L"txt"); // added if the user types a name without one dialog- SetOptions(options FOS_OVERWRITEPROMPT); // "Replace existing file?" (on by default) The default extension follows the selected file type when it changes. The practice computes exactly what file name the user ends up with. The older filter string Older code uses GetOpenFileNameW with an OPENFILENAMEW structure. Its filter is a single string of pairs separated by null characters, ended by two nulls : cpp-norun const wchar_t filter = L"Text documents ( .txt)\0 .txt\0All files ( . )\0 . \0"; // the literal adds the last \0 Building that string from a list, getting the embedded nulls right, is a classic bug source; the practice builds it. Colour and font cpp-norun static COLORREF custom 16 ; // the dialog's 16 custom colours, kept between calls CHOOSECOLORW cc{ sizeof(cc) }; cc.hwndOwner = owner; cc.rgbResult = m_colour; cc.lpCustColors = custom; cc.Flags = CC_FULLOPEN CC_RGBINIT; if (ChooseColorW(&cc)) m_colour = cc.rgbResult; LOGFONTW lf = m_logFont; CHOOSEFONTW cf{ sizeof(cf) }; cf.hwndOwner = owner; cf.lpLogFont = &lf; cf.Flags = CF_SCREENFONTS CF_INITTOLOGFONTSTRUCT; if (ChooseFontW(&cf)) { m_logFont = lf; recreateFont(); } Remembering the folder Users expect the Open dialog to start in the folder they used last. The new dialogs remember it per program automatically; SetFolder sets it explicitly (from an IShellItem made with SHCreateItemFromParsingName ), and SetClientGuid keeps separate memories for different dialogs in one program ("open image" and "open project").

title: File type filters
body: Build and read the double-null filter strings of GetOpenFileNameW (lesson 3.02), and work out the name a Save dialog produces: cpp struct FileType { std::string description; std::string patterns; }; // patterns like " .txt; .md" std::string buildFilter(const std::vector<FileType & types); std::vector<FileType parseFilter(const std::string& filter); std::string defaultExtension(const FileType& type); std::string finalSaveName(const std::string& typed, const FileType& selected); - buildFilter : each type gives its description, a null character, its patterns, a null; the whole string ends with one extra null. No types gives just "\0" (one null). The returned std::string contains the nulls. - parseFilter reads such a string back; it stops at the empty description that marks the end, or at the end of the string, and ignores a description without patterns. - defaultExtension is the extension of the first pattern, without . , when it is a plain .ext (letters and digits only); . or anything else gives "" . - finalSaveName : if the typed name (the part after the last \ ) contains a dot that is not its first character, the name is used as typed; otherwise the selected type's default extension is added (if there is one). Spaces at the ends of the typed name are removed first.

title: 3.03  Layout and Resizing
body: Win32 has no layout engine - when a window is resized, you move its controls. This lesson lays controls out in WM_SIZE with anchors, sets a minimum size with WM_GETMINMAXINFO, moves many controls at once without flicker, and builds a splitter. WM_SIZE When the user resizes a window, it receives WM_SIZE with the new client size. Positioning the controls is up to you: cpp-norun case WM_SIZE: { const int w = LOWORD(lParam), h = HIWORD(lParam); const int pad = 10, buttonW = 80, buttonH = 26; MoveWindow(m_list, pad, pad, w - 2 pad, h - 3 pad - buttonH, TRUE); MoveWindow(m_ok, w - pad - 2 buttonW - pad, h - pad - buttonH, buttonW, buttonH, TRUE); MoveWindow(m_cancel, w - pad - buttonW, h - pad - buttonH, buttonW, buttonH, TRUE); return 0; } Writing that maths for every control gets messy. Most layouts are described better with anchors . Anchors Each control remembers its distances from the edges of the parent at the original size, and which edges it is anchored to: Anchored to When the window grows by dx --- --- Left only Stays where it is Right only Moves right by dx Left and right Stretches by dx Neither Stays centred in the same relative position The same on the vertical axis with top and bottom. A list that fills the window is anchored on all four sides; OK and Cancel at the bottom right are anchored right and bottom; a search box along the top is anchored left, right and top. The practice builds this layout engine. A minimum size Below some size the layout breaks: controls overlap or get negative widths. Tell Windows the minimum window size (frame included) in WM_GETMINMAXINFO : cpp-norun case WM_GETMINMAXINFO: { auto mmi = reinterpret_cast<MINMAXINFO (lParam); mmi- ptMinTrackSize.x = m_minWindowSize.cx; // computed once with AdjustWindowRectExForDpi mmi- ptMinTrackSize.y = m_minWindowSize.cy; return 0; } Moving many controls Moving twenty controls one by one repaints twenty times and flickers. Deferred window positioning moves them all in one step: cpp-norun HDWP batch = BeginDeferWindowPos(static_cast<int (m_controls.size())); for (const auto& c : m_controls) { const RECT r = c.layout(width, height); batch = DeferWindowPos(batch, c.hwnd, nullptr, r.left, r.top, r.right - r.left, r.bottom - r.top, SWP_NOZORDER SWP_NOACTIVATE); } EndDeferWindowPos(batch); Setting WS_CLIPCHILDREN on the parent stops it from painting its background over the children, the other big source of flicker on resizing. Splitters A splitter is the bar between two panes that the user drags to change their sizes. It is not a control: it is a strip of the parent's client area between the two child windows. 1. In WM_SETCURSOR , show IDC_SIZEWE when the mouse is over the strip (lesson 2.02). 2. On WM_LBUTTONDOWN over it, capture the mouse and remember the offset between the mouse and the split position. 3. On WM_MOUSEMOVE while captured, set the split position, clamped so neither pane gets smaller than its minimum, and lay out again. 4. On WM_LBUTTONUP , release the capture, and save the position in the settings (lesson 5.02). Storing the split as a fraction of the width rather than pixels keeps it sensible when the window is resized or moved to a monitor with a different DPI. Keeping the layout in one function Put all layout in one function, layout(width, height) , and call it from WM_SIZE , after the splitter moves, after a font change and after a DPI change (lesson 3.04). When the layout is computed in exactly one place, it cannot disagree with itself.

title: Anchors and a splitter
body: Write lesson 3.03's anchor layout and the splitter's clamp: cpp struct RECT { long left, top, right, bottom; }; struct Anchors { bool left, top, right, bottom; }; RECT anchorLayout(RECT design, Anchors a, int designW, int designH, int newW, int newH); int clampSplit(int pos, int total, int minLeft, int minRight, int bar); anchorLayout : design is where the control was in a client area of designW × designH . For each axis, with d the change of the client size on that axis: - both edges anchored: the far edge moves by d (the control stretches); - only the near edge (left or top): nothing changes; - only the far edge (right or bottom): both edges move by d ; - neither: the size stays, and the centre is placed at the same fraction of the new size (computed in doubles and rounded to the nearest whole pixel, halves away from zero; the near edge is that centre minus half the size, rounded down). clampSplit : the splitter bar starts at pos and is bar pixels wide inside total . The left pane is 0 .. pos and the right pane pos + bar .. total . Clamp pos so the left pane is at least minLeft and the right pane at least minRight ; if both cannot fit, the left pane wins ( pos = minLeft ).

title: 3.04  High-DPI Screens
body: Laptops and 4K monitors run at 150 % or 200 % scaling, and a program that ignores it is either tiny or blurry. This lesson declares per-monitor DPI awareness, scales sizes and fonts with the DPI, handles moving between monitors with WM_DPICHANGED, and picks the right icon sizes. What DPI scaling is Windows assumes 96 dots per inch at 100 % scaling. A 14-inch 1080p laptop usually runs at 150 % (144 DPI), a 27-inch 4K monitor at 150 % or 200 %. At 150 %, a button that should look 80 pixels wide must be 120 physical pixels wide. A program that does not declare otherwise is DPI-unaware : Windows draws it at 96 DPI and stretches the result, which makes all its text blurry. To look sharp, a program declares that it handles DPI itself, and then scales everything. Declaring awareness Declare per-monitor v2 awareness in the application manifest (lesson 6.02): cpp-norun <application xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3" <windowsSettings <dpiAwareness xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/SMI/2016/WindowsSettings" PerMonitorV2</dpiAwareness </windowsSettings </application or call SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext(DPI_AWARENESS_CONTEXT_PER_MONITOR_AWARE_V2) before creating any window. Per-monitor v2 means: each window has the DPI of the monitor it is on, and the program is told when it changes. It also makes Windows scale the non-client area, dialogs and common controls automatically. Scaling numbers Design at 96 DPI and scale every size by dpi / 96 , rounding to the nearest pixel. MulDiv does exactly that without overflow: cpp-norun const UINT dpi = GetDpiForWindow(hwnd); int scale(int value96) { return MulDiv(value96, dpi, 96); } // rounds half away from zero const int padding = scale(10); // 15 at 144 DPI const int buttonWidth = scale(80); // 120 at 144 DPI Apply it to everything measured in pixels: margins, control sizes, line widths, icon sizes, the minimum window size. Scale from the 96-DPI design value each time, not from the previous scaled value, or rounding errors build up as the window moves between monitors. System metrics have DPI-aware versions: GetSystemMetricsForDpi(SM_CXVSCROLL, dpi) , AdjustWindowRectExForDpi , SystemParametersInfoForDpi . Fonts Font sizes are in points (1/72 inch). The height in pixels is -MulDiv(points, dpi, 72) (the minus sign asks for the character height, not the cell height). Re-create fonts when the DPI changes; for the standard message font, SystemParametersInfoForDpi(SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS, ..., dpi) gives it already scaled. WM_DPICHANGED When a window moves to a monitor with a different DPI (or the user changes the scaling), it receives WM_DPICHANGED with the new DPI and a suggested rectangle : the window's new size and position so it looks the same physical size. Use that rectangle, then re-create fonts and lay out again: cpp-norun case WM_DPICHANGED: { m_dpi = HIWORD(wParam); const RECT suggested = reinterpret_cast<RECT (lParam); SetWindowPos(hwnd, nullptr, suggested- left, suggested- top, suggested- right - suggested- left, suggested- bottom - suggested- top, SWP_NOZORDER SWP_NOACTIVATE); recreateFonts(); layout(); // lesson 3.03's single layout function return 0; } Icons and images An icon at 16 × 16 looks tiny at 200 %. Ship icons in several sizes (16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 256) inside the .ico , and load the right one with LoadIconWithScaleDown or LoadImageW at scale(16) . For toolbars, prefer vector graphics (Direct2D, an icon font such as Segoe Fluent Icons) that scale to any size. When only one bitmap size is available, choose the nearest larger one and scale it down, which looks far better than scaling a small one up. Testing Test at 100 %, 150 % and 200 %, and drag the window between two monitors with different scaling. A second monitor is not required: change the scaling in Settings Display while the program runs, which sends the same WM_DPICHANGED .

title: Scaling for DPI
body: Write lesson 3.04's DPI arithmetic: cpp int mulDiv(int number, int numerator, int denominator); // like MulDiv int scaleForDpi(int value96, int dpi); int fontHeight(int points, int dpi); // LOGFONT lfHeight: negative character height int pickIconSize(const std::vector<int & available, int wanted); - mulDiv computes number × numerator / denominator with a 64-bit intermediate and rounds half away from zero ( MulDiv(3, 1, 2) is 2, MulDiv(-3, 1, 2) is -2). A denominator of 0 returns -1, as the real one does. - scaleForDpi is mulDiv(value96, dpi, 96) . - fontHeight is -mulDiv(points, dpi, 72) . - pickIconSize returns the smallest available size that is at least wanted , or the largest available size if none is that big (0 for an empty list). The list is in any order.

title: 3.05  Common Controls
body: The list view, tree view, status bar, progress bar and tab control come from the Common Controls library. This lesson enables visual styles, creates these controls, handles WM_NOTIFY, and uses a virtual list view to show a hundred thousand rows instantly. Enabling them, with visual styles The common controls ( comctl32.dll ) add the controls Explorer uses. Version 6 draws them, and the standard controls, with the modern visual style. Ask for it in the manifest, conveniently with a linker directive, and initialise the library: cpp-norun include <commctrl.h pragma comment(lib, "comctl32.lib") pragma comment(linker, "\"/manifestdependency:type='win32' name='Microsoft.Windows.Common-Controls' \ version='6.0.0.0' processorArchitecture=' ' publicKeyToken='6595b64144ccf1df' language=' '\"") INITCOMMONCONTROLSEX icc{ sizeof(icc), ICC_LISTVIEW_CLASSES ICC_TREEVIEW_CLASSES ICC_BAR_CLASSES ICC_TAB_CLASSES ICC_PROGRESS_CLASS }; InitCommonControlsEx(&icc); Without the manifest entry, buttons and check boxes look like Windows 95. The controls Class Control Typical use --- --- --- WC_LISTVIEW List view: rows with columns, or icons Files, search results WC_TREEVIEW Tree view Folders, outlines, settings categories STATUSCLASSNAME Status bar Line and column, state, progress PROGRESS_CLASS Progress bar Long operations WC_TABCONTROL Tabs Pages of settings TOOLTIPS_CLASS Tooltips Help on hover TRACKBAR_CLASS , UPDOWN_CLASS Slider, spin buttons Numbers A list view with columns cpp-norun HWND lv = CreateWindowExW(0, WC_LISTVIEW, L"", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP LVS_REPORT LVS_SHOWSELALWAYS, 0, 0, 0, 0, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_FILES), instance, nullptr); ListView_SetExtendedListViewStyle(lv, LVS_EX_FULLROWSELECT LVS_EX_DOUBLEBUFFER); LVCOLUMNW col{ LVCF_TEXT LVCF_WIDTH }; col.pszText = const_cast<wchar_t (L"Name"); col.cx = scale(240); ListView_InsertColumn(lv, 0, &col); col.pszText = const_cast<wchar_t (L"Size"); col.cx = scale(90); ListView_InsertColumn(lv, 1, &col); ListView_InsertColumn and friends are macros around SendMessageW with LVM_... messages, the same mechanism as lesson 2.05 with nicer names. WM_NOTIFY Common controls report events with WM_NOTIFY . lParam points to an NMHDR (the control's window, id and code ), which is the first member of a bigger, code-specific structure: cpp-norun case WM_NOTIFY: { const auto hdr = reinterpret_cast<NMHDR (lParam); if (hdr- idFrom == IDC_FILES) { switch (hdr- code) { case NM_DBLCLK: openSelected(); return 0; case LVN_COLUMNCLICK: sortBy(reinterpret_cast<NMLISTVIEW (lParam)- iSubItem); return 0; case LVN_GETDISPINFOW: fillDisplayInfo(reinterpret_cast<NMLVDISPINFOW (lParam)); return 0; } } break; } Virtual list views Adding 100 000 items one by one with ListView_InsertItem takes seconds and copies every string into the control. A virtual list view ( LVS_OWNERDATA ) stores nothing: you tell it how many rows there are, and it asks for the text of each row only when it needs to draw it: cpp-norun ListView_SetItemCountEx(lv, static_cast<int (m_results.size()), LVSICF_NOSCROLL); void fillDisplayInfo(NMLVDISPINFOW info) { const auto& row = m_results info- item.iItem ; if (info- item.mask & LVIF_TEXT) { const std::wstring text = info- item.iSubItem == 0 ? row.name : formatSize(row.size); wcsncpy_s(info- item.pszText, info- item.cchTextMax, text.c_str(), _TRUNCATE); } } Showing a million rows is now instant, and sorting means sorting your own vector and calling InvalidateRect . This is the list the file finder of milestone 6 uses. Formatting sizes the way Explorer does ("1.5 KB", "23.4 MB") is part of the practice. The status bar cpp-norun m_status = CreateWindowExW(0, STATUSCLASSNAME, nullptr, WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE SBARS_SIZEGRIP, 0, 0, 0, 0, hwnd, nullptr, instance, nullptr); const int parts = { scale(200), scale(320), -1 }; // right edges; -1 = to the end SendMessageW(m_status, SB_SETPARTS, 3, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (parts)); SendMessageW(m_status, SB_SETTEXTW, 0, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (L"Ln 12, Col 4")); // in WM_SIZE: SendMessageW(m_status, WM_SIZE, 0, 0); it positions itself at the bottom

title: Sizes and natural sorting
